11214518.label: Major findings and research outcome
11214518.value: The first objective focused on the relationship between information load and cognitive load. Previous studies have suggested that the effects of increasing amounts of information on decision-making efficiency and information usage follow an inverted U-shaped curve. However, by a safety dashboard monitoring task, eye-tracking metrics including fixation duration, fixation count, saccade count and dwell percentages were utilized to measure the degrees of cognitive load. The findings suggest that the relationship between information load and cognitive load may result in segmental linear relationships with different slopes, not always purely positive relationships and not inverted U-shaped curves. Specifically, in the first stage, as information load increased, cognitive load also increased, in the second stage, as information load increased, cognitive load leveled off, and in the third stage the two again showed a linear positive correlation. Secondly, the effect of cognitive load on safety performance was found. A study assessed situation awareness for typical safety elements under different degrees of cognitive load, by using electroencephalograph (EEG) characteristics and behavioral performance (response latency, accuracy) to measure situation awareness. Results discovered that increasing cognitive load imposed by the n-back task led to deteriorated behavioral performance. Specifically, the reaction time increased and accuracy decreased with increasing cognitive load. And from results of EEG metrics, lower amplitude of P300 component at the occipital lobe, and diminished frontal alpha and beta power according to time-frequency analysis related to increased cognitive load. Thirdly, the differences in cognitive load by individual factors were explored. A study provided insights into the effects of information load and field-dependent/independent cognitive style on the cognitive load of a visual site monitoring dashboard through an eye movement visual search experiment. When identifying dashboards, field-dependent individuals took longer to locate information and had a lower accuracy. Cognitive load was significantly higher in the field-dependent group than in the field-independent group as measured by fixation duration, fixation count, and saccade count. Based on a comprehensive survey of factors influencing cognitive load, a framework for a personalized information presentation system is proposed. The framework is divided into two phases; the first phase is to train and build information-cognitive load matrix, the second phase is to test the performance of prototype. The first phase aim to establish an evaluation system by subject rating, objective performance or physiological measurement to build individual cognitive load database mapped with environment, task and individual difference. The prototype includes context layer, individual propensity layer, visualized layer, to filter and present appropriate form with minimal cognitive load.

11214518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11214518.value: The next step in this study can be the refinement and deployment of the prototype system for personalized information presentation on actual construction sites. Firstly, the personal cognitive load assessment system can be refined by combining subjective, objective, and physiological measurements to establish a personal information load-cognitive load matrix database to obtain the association of environmental factors, task factors, and personal factors with individual cognitive load. Then, by designing and developing the second part of the information recommendation optimization system, the personal information load-cognitive load matrix can be used to filter and optimize the amount of information presented, the presentation format, etc., in order to provide each person with the optimal information presentation format with the minimum cognitive load. Finally, it is worthwhile to quantify the difference in safety performance improvement with or without the system or between the system and the traditional information presentation system.

11214518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11214518.value: With the advances in intelligent and digital construction, the construction task and related information will become complicated and digital-related, which impose higher cognitive burden. Whether each type of data is correctly represented and visualized in the form that the corresponding receiver can understand easily, which is worth investigation. The project aimed to present correct information in the right way to right people by personalized information presentation prototype with minimal cognitive load. Compared with other sorts of information, presenting the safety information in the right way to right people is particularly important for accidents prevention and warning. Personal preference for information representation also varies across task setting and individual difference such as task type, individual cognitive style will lead to change in needs for presentation ways. The same information would lead to different degrees of information load and cognitive burden to different employees. However, unlike other fields that preference can be collected by initiative webpage search and click intention, personal information presentation preferences of construction employees are difficult to collect and quantify. No such quantification tool or subjective evaluation can indicate individual preference and efficiency of information transformation. To fill the research gap, brainwave feedback an eye-tracking techniques were combined to quantify the cognitive load or preference for information presentation. Therefore, the project studied how information load affects cognitive load, and how does information load affect safety performance, and to propose a personalized safety information presentation framework. This project obtained the influence of different information quality on cognitive load and safety performance of security risk identification, as well as the comparison of cognitive load perception degree of people with different cognitive styles. The emphasis on the connection between cognitive load and safety performance as well as the consideration of individual cognitive characteristics are unique to this project.

11215418.label: Realisation of objectives
11215418.value: This project aimed at developing a collaborative data-driven method for improving the operations and maintenance (O&M) of wind farms. Four interrelated objectives were proposed, covering the deep learning for condition monitoring, multi-data powered wind power modeling, decision-making models for wind farm O&M, and outcome validation. All of them have been successfully achieved. Fruitful cutting-edge research outcomes have been carried out under each of the objectives including 25 journal publications, 3 PhD student graduated, and 1 patent granted. Publications, Pub.1-Pub.25, mentioned in this statement please refer to the latter publication attached in this report. Details of achievements are described one-by-one next: Objective 1. To develop a novel two-phase deep learning based CM framework 1.1 To develop a self-organized deep learning based CM modeling method 1.2 To develop a collaborative CM framework Objective 1 focuses on developing novel deep learning based method for monitoring conditions of distributed wind turbines and alarming failures or malfunctions in advance. The PI and the research team regarding research objective 1 have carried out novel results published in flagship international journals [Pub.1, Pub.6, Pub.7, Pub.9, Pub.11, Pub.15, Pub. 17, Pub.18, Pub.20]. In researches under objective 1, multiple types of data for system condition monitoring, e.g., the turbine outlook image captured by UAVs and turbine conditional data collected by SCADA systems, have been collected. Towards the turbine major components, the turbine blade and gearbox, the PI has studied novel joint and conditional convolutional autoencoder based methods for predicting and diagnosing blade and gearbox failures [Pub.7, Pub.9, Pub. 15, Pub.18]. Regarding the turbine blade surface condition inspection, the PI has developed a two-stage vision intelligence model to be implemented in UAVs [Pub.1]. Such machine vision based AI model has also been successfully applied into solar panel detection and railway facility inspection [Pub.6, Pub.17, Pub.20]. For the missing data imputation issue, a deep learning based data imputation method has been developed in [Pub.11]. In summary, the PI has successfully studied novel deep learning based method for wind turbine condition monitoring via using SCADA data and together with image data, and has extended it to similar applications in other fields. Objective 2. To develop a hierarchical framework for modeling the wind power generation by jointly learning operational data and image data 2.1 To develop a two-phase image-based condition characterization method 2.2 To develop a modeling method Objective 2 focuses on developing novel deep learning based method of multiple hierarchies for modeling and predicting the wind power generation via using the operational and image data. The first hierarchy aims to characterize the high-dimensional input including numerical data and image data to derive latent features indicating system conditions and then the second hierarchy will be the modeling for mapping latent features to wind power generation outputs. Regarding objective 2, research results have been presented in prestige power and energy field journals [Pub.4, Pub.5, Pub.8, Pub.13, Pub.16, Pub.19, Pub.21, Pub.22, Pub.24, Pub.25]. In [Pub.8, Pub.13, Pub.16, Pub.19, Pub.21, Pub.22, Pub.24, Pub.25], studies have been conducted on the novel tensor form input construction based on SCADA and image data, the novel method for learning representations of high-dimensional input in wind power modeling, and the novel deep network architecture design for the deterministic and probabilistic wind power generation estimation and forecasting tasks. Results have also been extended to study the solar power prediction, grid load prediction, and battery remaining useful life [Pub.4, Pub.5, Pub.24]. In summary, researches under objective 2 have developed the hierarchical deep learning based framework for modeling wind power generation based on operational data and image data with innovations delivered in the high-dimensional data input design, the data latent feature engineering, and the deep network based wind power modeling method. Objective 3. To develop a decision-making model for scheduling the wind farm operations and maintenance 3.1 To formulate an optimization model by integrating CM results and data-driven models 3.2 To develop a novel heuristic solution method Objective 3 aims to develop the optimal decision-making models for the wind farm O&M scheduling based on the wind turbine condition, power, and other uncertain factor predictions. Research outputs under objective 3 include Pub.2, Pub.3, Pub.10, Pub.12, Pub.14, and Pub.23. In [Pub.12], a wind farm O&M scheduling model considering the different scheduling timescale in decision-making was presented. In [Pub.14], a robust formulation of wind farm O&M scheduling model was discussed with considering the uncertainty factors in the optimal decision-making. In [Pub.23], a holistic robust optimization model for the multi-timescale wind farm operations optimization together with the energy storage system was developed. Optimization models and methods have also been applied into the combustion system and solar panel operations [Pub.2, Pub.3]. In summary, the decision-making models for scheduling wind farm O&M with considering data-driven component and uncertainties has been developed and analyzed. 4. To validate effectiveness of proposed models with computational experiments and field testing Objective 4 focuses on the effectiveness validation of developed condition monitoring, wind power prediction, and wind farm O&M scheduling models and methods. In general, they have all been separately validated in Pub.1-Pub.25 with computational numerical experiments and the collected field data. All research objectives have been successfully achieved and some extended researches have also been conducted and reported.

11215418.label: Major findings and research outcome
11215418.value: Major findings in this project can be described from following three aspects: 1) We identified a tensor-like structure for organizing the SCADA data of multiple wind turbine to enable incorporating spatial-temporal-individual-dynamics patterns in data and developed the conditional convolutional autoencoder networks for deriving indicators of monitoring wind turbine conditions; 2) We developed deep convolutional recurrent network based structure for realizing wind power estimation and prediction based on learning the spatial-temporal-individual-dynamics patterns in high-dimensional input; We particularly studied the mechanism of data organization, the mechanism of learning latent features, and the deep network structure design for modeling wind power; We have developed methods towards better adaptiveness and more effective data utilization; Moreover, methods have been developed for both deterministic and probabilistic tasks; 3) We developed decision-making model for optimal scheduling of power productions and maintenance tasks of wind farms; the model considered the different time-scale for scheduling and the principles for tackling uncertainties to realize more robust schedules. 4) We have well validated developed methods via computational experiments and using the field data to prove their claimed effectiveness and advantages. This project has results in 25 journal publications, 3 graduated Ph.D. students, and 1 granted patent.

11215418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11215418.value: The methodological and theoretical developments in this research project have strong practical implications. Therefore, one great potential is to apply for the mid- and down-stream research projects to make progresses in the knowledge transfer. The PI has taken an action and applied the Hong Kong ITC ITF Midstream Research Programmes funding for the development of AI powered wind power forecasting software, which recently got approved with a funding amount 3.6 million HKD. Meanwhile, the developed deep learning based condition monitoring, prediction, and optimization models and methods can be well extended to other renewable energy and distributed systems, e.g., solar panels and vehicle batteries. The PI has produced a few sch extension studies to prove such potential. Moreover, it is important to dive deeper into the theoretical exploration of the performance guarantee and computational efficiency guarantee of the deep learning and optimization models in renewable energy applications.

11215418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11215418.value: This project focused on developing novel data-driven methods for improving the wind farm operations and maintenance performances with collaborating deep learning algorithms, condition monitoring techniques, and optimization models. In this project, novel deep learning based condition monitoring methods were developed to enable the prediction of wind turbine blade and gearbox failures a couple of hours in advance based on SCADA data and to equip the UAVs with AI based image analytics capability in remote inspection. Novel deep convolutional recurrent network models were developed to better characterize wind power generation performance via leveraging the spatial-temporal information in SCADA data and the condition descriptions in UAV captured turbine outlook image data. The state-of-the-art performance in the wind power predictions was achieved and presented. Based on the novel methodological development on condition monitoring and wind power prediction, this project further studied more practical wind farm operations and maintenance scheduling optimization models leveraging outputs from data-driven components. Scheduling models considered different timescales of activities to be scheduled and the collaborative power production and maintenance scheduling were developed, which were pioneering in the field.

11215518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11215518.value: 发展操作简易，安全并且可控的气体储存和释放技术在气体工业中扮演着非常重要的角色，也是全球经济中的一个重要组成部分。本研究致力于开发一种新型的气体储存技术来实现温和操作条件下的高容量气体储存和容易的释放。 传统的基于多孔材料的气体储存技术主要是依靠增加压力和降低温度来提高平衡吸附量。本研究另辟蹊径，采用“胶囊封存”理念设计多孔材料以实现常温常压下的高气体储存容量。这个项目的构思是基于我们最近在“温度控制选择性气体准入吸附技术”上的突破性进展。具体说来，我们将通过构建纳米容器和控制堵孔基团来实现非高压下的高容量气体储存。 本研究将结合理论模拟和实验方法来指导构建带有堵孔基团的多孔材料以及构建核壳材料来调控胶囊封存的工作温度以最大化气体储存量。我们将会开发不同种类的多孔材料来展示我们的设计方案的可行性。这项研究将会大大丰富材料设计的工具箱，并且推动未来“量身设计”气体储存材料的发展。一系列高级实验研究手段（例如原位X光衍射等）将会被用来开展深层次的机理研究。我们将以甲烷的储存和释放为例来展示“胶囊封存”技术的实际表现。 本研究的创新将会给包括气体燃料汽车，有害气体的捕捉和去除，医用气体的提供等领域带来潜在的利益。本技术还可能被用于香港的离岸天然气储存项目从而帮助增强本地的能量供给安全。 易的释放。

11215518.label: Realisation of objectives
11215518.value: The overall goal of this project is to develop a new adsorption-based technology for gas storage under atmosphere pressure using porous materials capable of adsorption and desorption of gas molecules via a controlled gating effect. The key to such a controlled admission and release of gases operation is to install and regulate gate-keeping agents at the access to the interior pore space of the porous materials in a rational and controllable manner. Three objectives listed in 5.2 have been set and largely achieved to achieve the goal of this project. Regarding objective NO. one, we achieved it by successfully designing and preparing a series of porous adsorbents with nano-valves capable of regulating the encapsulation and dispense of gas molecules using temperature as the handle. Specifically, we prepared two types of zeolites – chabazite zeolites and LTA zeolites – featuring highly crystalline and well-defined 3D pores as “nano-containers” and installed different types of metal cations (i.e., potassium, rubidium, and cesium) at the pore aperture as “nano-valves”; we also prepared three types of metal-organic frameworks, i.e., [Cu2(BTR)2]·2 NO3·xG (BTR refers to 4,4’-bis(1,2,4-triazole)), [Cu(pytpy)]·NO3·CH3OH (pytpy refers to 2,4,6- tris(4-pyridyl)pyridine), and [Ni2(μ-pymca)3] OH, featuring highly crystalline and well-defined 3D pores or 1D channels as “nano-containers” and installed a series of anions, such as F-, Cl-, Br-, I-, CO32-, SO32-, BF4- etc., to act as “nano-valves”. Through measuring gas adsorption using different probe gas molecules at different temperatures, we proved these materials can achieve gas storage in a controlled manner using temperature as the handle. Regarding objective No. two, we achieved it by tuning the characteristics of “nano-containers” and “nano-valves” of the porous adsorbents and investigating their influence on the gas storage capacity and the operating temperatures for the admission and release of gases. For zeolites, the type, density, and the distribution of cations would affect the gas adsorption amount (because the extraframework cations serve as active binding sites for gas adsorption) and the temperature for gas admission and release (because some of the extraframework cations serve as gate-keepers and the ease of inducing the movement of the gate-keeping cations is reflected by the gas admission temperature). The distribution of cations is determined by the topology of the regular porous framework, which is ultimately determined by the type of zeolites. The density of cations needs to satisfy the required threshold to allow for sufficient cations to serve as gatekeepers. We studied the effect of the distribution of cations by comparing two types of zeolites, chabazites and LTA zeolites (as different types of zeolites featuring different pore topology allow for different patterns of cation distribution); we studied the effect of density of binding sites by preparing and examining chabazites with two different silicon to aluminum ratios (i.e., 2.5 and 1) given the threshold cation density is corresponding to silicon to aluminum ratio of 3, and LTA zeolites with three different silicon to aluminum ratios (i.e., 1, 2, 3.5, and 6) given the threshold cation density is corresponding to silicon to aluminum ratio of 7; we studied the effect of type of cations by preparing and examining both chabazites and LTA zeolites in the form of potassium, rubidium, and cesium. For metal-organic frameworks, we tuned the gas adsorption amount by varying the type and thus the pore topology of the cationic framework, namely, [Cu2(BTR)2]·2 NO3·xG (BTR refers to 4,4’-bis(1,2,4-triazole)), [Cu(pytpy)]·NO3·CH3OH (pytpy refers to 2,4,6- tris(4-pyridyl)pyridine), and [Ni2(μ-pymca)3] OH, provided that the gas uptake is mainly determined by the specific surface area of the porous metal-organic frameworks; we tuned the operating temperatures for the admission and release of gases by studying different types of gate-keeping anions, such as F-, Cl-, Br-, I-, CO32-, SO32-, BF4- etc. For each of above combination of “nano-containers” and “nano-valves”, the measurement of gas adsorption of CO2, N2, and CH4 at different temperatures allowed for determining the gas storage capacity and identifying the temperatures for the admission and release of gases. Through such a comprehensive investigation of the structure-adsorption property relationship, we established strategies for boosting the gas encapsulation capacities and tuning the operating conditions. Regarding objective NO. three, we managed to prove the gas storage performance is achievable through alternative design of experiments given we were not able to do it using high pressure gas for demonstration as originally planned. Specifically, we originally planned to demonstrate controlled gas storage and release by dosing high pressure (say 80 bar) fuel gas (H2 and CH4) or inert gas (N2) into the nano-containers for encapsulation and keeping it at atmospheric pressure and at a temperature below gas admission temperature, followed by releasing the stored gas via increasing the temperature to be above the gas release temperature. However, to obey the strict lab safety rules, we could not proceed to operate any of these the high-pressure gases as there is no separate safe room/space with appropriate measures for handling high pressure gases and low-temperature setup available. To overcome these difficulties, we measured storage of N2 and CH4 by doing it up to 1 bar and keeping it under high vacuum while following the same temperature operating protocol as that for the original plan, which showed that the gas storage and release by temperature-controlled encapsulation and decapsulation is viable. Such an alternative demonstration should be valid because both varying pressure from 80 bar to 1 bar and from 1 bar to high vacuum can prove gas molecules can be effectively encapsulated/trapped in the “nano-containers” by switching off the “nano-valves” via temperature control. Of course, the ultimate and most convincing demonstration is ideally to be conducted using high-pressure gases which will allow for the dosing of a much higher amount of gases for encapsulation and thus a remarkable gas storage performance. We will try to do such a demonstration in the future whenever it is possible, but we believe it does not compromise such a proof-of-concept demonstration.

11215518.label: Major findings and research outcome
11215518.value: The first major finding is that the concept of using negatively charged zeolite framework as “nano-containers” and positively charged extraframework metal cations as “nano-valves” works for controlled gas storage and release via encapsulation and decapsulation regulated by temperature. Moreover, this concept can also be extended to development porous adsorbents other than zeolites, metal-organic frameworks in particular where the positively charged frameworks act as “nano-containers” and negatively charged anions act as “nano-valves”, for gas storage and release. The outcomes are two types of zeolite adsorbents and three types of metal-organic frameworks adsorbents which are successfully identified to be promising gas storage materials of this type. The research findings will be included in a PhD thesis and be published as journal papers in the near future. The second major finding is that the newly established strategies that can be used to rationally tune the gas storage capacity and operating temperature for both zeolite and metal-organic frameworks adsorbents. The ability to regulate the molecular admission behavior and uptake capacity of porous adsorbents through rational design is of great importance for gas storage, separation, and sensing applications. This project revealed that the effective designing factors include the type, density, and the distribution of extraframework cations of zeolites, and the type, density, and the distribution of extraframework anions of a category of ionic metal-organic frameworks. One manuscript on design LTA zeolites by varying these designing factors for gas separation has been submitted to the flagship journal of International Adsorption Society – Adsorption – and is under review now. More research findings will be included in a PhD thesis and be published as journal papers in the near future. The third major finding is that such a new concept of gas storage by encapsulation and decapsulation regulated by temperature was proved by a demonstration of using N2 and CH4 in the pressure window of 1 bar and high vacuum. Such a proof-of-concept will lay the foundation for the further development of this new gas storage approach by us and peers in the same field. Apart from the above work, we have also explored the design of other porous support such as metal-organic frameworks (8.4, 8.5, 8.8, 8.11, 8.12, 8.13, 8.14, 8.15), carbons (8.6), layer double hydroxides (8.7, 8.10) and mesoporous alumina (8.1) and studied their adsorption and catalytic properties. Most of these materials have the potential to serve as candidate support to further design composite materials for gas storage.

11215518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11215518.value: Based on our newly established understanding of the structure-adsorption property relationship for designing porous adsorbents featuring “nano-containers” with “nano-valves” for controlled gas storage, we can further increase the gas storage capacity by installing new binding sites within “nano-containers”. For example, for zeolites, mixed cation types can be used where certain types of cations serve as gatekeepers while other cations with stronger affinity to target gases server as binding sites at non-gate sites. Another important future direction is to introduce handles other than temperature to switch on and off the “nano-valves” for controlled gas storage and release. Given the gatekeeps are charged ions in our established adsorbent systems, i.e., cations in zeolite and anions in metal-organic frameworks, we can try to use electric field as an alternative handle which could potentially allow for more swift and sensible control and increasing the operating temperature range for gas storage. We have already developed a setup for in situ measuring gas adsorption in an adjustable electric field for this potentially promising research direction.

11215518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11215518.value: The capability to store and release gas in high capacity and in an easy, safe, and controlled manner is a key technology highly sought by the gas industry – a major component of the global economy. This project developed a novel gas storage technology capable of realizing high-capacity storage and facile release at mild operating conditions. Unlike the conventional equilibrium adsorption-based gas storage in porous solids where very high pressure and/or low temperature are necessary to attain high gas storage capacity, the new approach developed from this project features “encapsulating” a large amount of gases in the nano-containers of porous crystalline materials through “regulating” pore-keeping groups at ambient pressure and temperature. The new design concept and the newly established structure-adsorption property relationship in a series of typical porous adsorbent materials will substantially enrich the materials design toolbox and present a major step forward in future generation of tailor-made gas storage solids.

11215618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11215618.value: Robotics has been utilized to restore some of the lost motor functions for patients through motor prostheses, exoskeletons and other assistive tools. Functionality of these engineering devices has been continually improving throughout the years, and now users can control the systems through electrophysiological signals or different forms of human-computer interface. However, for patients with very limited mobility due to irreversible neurological diseases (e.g. amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) or injuries, giving simple control instructions remain challenging. Thus far, the performance of upper limb prosthesis remains limited even in reach-to-grasp movement, a major component of everyday interaction between human and the environment. In this project, we propose to significantly improve the control mechanism of assistive robotic devices by fusing electrophysiological signals with visual information from video cameras using state-of-the-art artificial intelligence technologies, in particular deep learning. This fusion of technology will allow for better classification of electrophysiological signals and a clearer understanding of the physical environment, which together will create more effective control in the execution of robotic tasks. We will focus on developing practical neural interface using surface electromyography (sEMG) and electroencephalogram (EEG) as separate examples to help patients with different levels of musculoskeletal damages or neurodegenerative diseases. A mathematical model to delineate neural-muscular-movement hierarchy will be first developed from EEG, sEMG and upper limb motion data recorded from able-bodied subjects to better understand the synergies in performing reach-to-grasp tasks. A novel signal fusion technique will be developed to control robotic reach-to-grasp movements using EEG or sEMG, together with visual clues. The proposed approach will encompass different electrophysiological signals, sensor data of different modalities, and various target tasks. We will work with local practitioners to develop a practical interface for patients to manipulate virtual and physical objects with the robotic assistive system. Along the way, this project will also offer a vast amount of valuable data to address some fundamental questions in neuromuscular coordination. Investigation of the potential changes in muscle synergies and neural connectivity related to training and adaptation will provide new insights on the adaptation mechanism along the neural-muscular-movement hierarchy. We deem that the success of this work will provide a generalized framework for designing more robust and flexible control algorithms in future neural prostheses in order to achieve enhanced dexterity, beneficial for patients worldwide who are suffering from loss of motor functions. 機器人技術已經被應用於修復病人某些運動功能的喪失，包括運動假體、外骨骼以及其他輔助工具。多年來，這些工程設備的功能一直在不斷改善，現在使用者可以通過電生理信號或其他形式的人機交互來控制某些簡單系統。然而，對於由於神經系統疾病或損傷而行動不便的患者，給出簡單的指令仍然具有挑戰性。迄今為止，即使是在伸手-抓握這個人與環境互動的重要組成部分中，上肢假肢的性能依然十分有限。 在本項目中，我們計劃通過融合電生理信號和來自攝像機的視覺信息，使用最先進的人工智能技術，尤其是深度學習，來改善輔助機器設備的控制機制。我們將集中開發使用肌電(sEMG)和腦電(EEG)作為神經接口案例來幫助有不同程度肌肉骨骼損傷或神經退行性疾病的病人。我們將首先從腦電、肌電以及從身體健全的受測者記錄的上肢運動數據建立一個描述神經-肌肉-動作層次的數學模型來更好地理解進行伸手-抓握任務時的協同作用。我們將採用腦電或肌電以及視覺信息，開發一種新穎的信號融合技術來控制機器人的伸手-抓握動作。提出的方法將包含不同的電生理信號、不同模式的傳感器數據以及一系列特定的目標任務。 同時，本項目將提供大量寶貴數據來闡述一些神經肌肉協調方面的基本問題。研究與訓練和適應相關的肌肉協同作用和神經連接上的潛在變化將給沿神經-肌肉-動作層次的適應機制提供新的理解。研究團隊希望可以提供一個普遍適用的工作框架，提供更穩定靈活的控制算法，用於在未來的神經假體設計中。

11215618.label: Realisation of objectives
11215618.value: We have completed both objectives despite the challenges of campus closure and the prohibition of data collection during COVID-19. For Objective 1, we investigated into the neural and muscle activity underlying simple upper limb motions and related short-term or long-term changes. Specifically, we gained insights into the neural sources of learning-relevant motor variability across different age groups, tackled challenges of cross-subject variations and domain shifts in EEG signals, studied the role of contingent learning and neural oscillations in motor development, and examined the processing of sensory feedback in motor training. We examined how modulating muscle synergies and their variability drives motor learning in virtual bowling, which involved extra release motion, for elderlies and young adults. With multi-muscle electromyographic signals collected, we quantified trial-to-trial variability of neuromotor control modules and of their activations. In elderlies, bowling-score gain correlated with change of activation timing variability of specific synergies, but in young adults, with variability changes of synergy-activation magnitude, and of the synergies themselves. Variability modulation of specific muscle synergies and their activations contribute to early motor learning. These results highlighted that elderly and young individuals relied on different aspects of motor variability to drive learning. In our investigation of neural datasets involving imaginary simple hand movements, we used deep learning techniques to enhance the performance of EEG-based brain-computer interface applications for motor imagery tasks. The study involved integrating the Reptile meta-learning algorithm with a deep neural network for EEG motor imagery tasks and comparing its performance with other state-of-the-art models. Although the approach did not outperform simple training of deep neural networks, the research provided insights into the challenges of cross-subject variations and domain shifts in EEG signals related to motor learning and reach-to-grasp motions. We investigated neural activities related to contingent learning in infants by analyzing their motor responses. The study discovered that right temporal oscillations predicted different levels of contingent learning in infants that could elicit an audio-visual feedback. The results contribute to our understanding of the neural activity underpinning motor learning and have potential applications in clinical practice for identifying and addressing delayed motor development in infants. Furthermore, we expanded the research scope and discovered that visual and audio feedback elicit different brain activation patterns when adapting to walking. The study collected EEG and peak positive acceleration (PPA) of the heel from 23 participants walking on a treadmill with no feedback, visual feedback, or audio feedback. The feedbacks were presented after each foot strike, with sub-threshold PPA triggering positive feedback (green/low-pitched) and suprathreshold PPA triggering negative feedback (red/high-pitched). The study also investigated the influence of cognitive distraction on gait control. The results showed that PPA was significantly lower in sessions with visual or audio feedback compared to sessions without feedback, demonstrating an immediate improvement in gait pattern when feedback was provided. The study found increased alpha event-related synchronization (ERS) during the encoding of auditory feedback or the introduction of a distracting task, prominent frontal and posterior theta ERS coupled with negative feedback, and strong beta event-related desynchronization (ERD) observed only in sessions with feedbacks. These results indicate that feedback effectively enhances motor planning when acquiring a new gait. For Objective 2, we have developed new methods to study multimodal data including electrophysiological and visual data. This is particularly inspired by our work in Objective 1 which demonstrates the limits in using wrist kinematics, EEG, or EMG to classify intended upper limb motion for assistive tools. Therefore, we conducted a series of research in continual learning for assistive tools to improve performance with visual data, culminating in the construction and release of a novel lifelong learning robotic vision dataset, OpenLORIS-Object. In this work, we constructed and released a lifelong learning robotic vision dataset, OpenLORIS-Object. This dataset was collected by an RGB-D camera capturing dynamic environments in daily life scenarios with diverse factors, including illumination, occlusion, object pixel size, and clutter, of quantified difficulty levels. To the best of our knowledge, this is a unique real-world dataset for robotic vision with independent and quantifiable environmental factors, which are currently unaccounted for in other lifelong learning datasets such as CORe50 and NICO. We tested nine state-of-the-art algorithms with four evaluation metrics over the dataset in Domain Incremental Learning, Task Incremental Learning, and Class Incremental Learning scenarios. The results demonstrate that these existing algorithms are insufficient to handle lifelong learning tasks in dynamic environments. We have investigated two approaches in tackling computational issues involved with continual learning and multimodality. First, we tackled the computational power issue in training deep neural networks (DNNs). Existing DNNs exhibit low time and storage efficiency due to the high degree of redundancy. In contrast to most existing DNNs, biological and social networks with vast numbers of connections are highly efficient and exhibit scale-free properties indicative of the power law distribution, which can be originated by preferential attachment in growing networks. In this work, we investigated whether the topology of the best performing DNNs shows the power law similar to biological and social networks and how to use the power law topology to construct well-performing and compact DNNs. We first found that the connectivities of sparse DNNs can be modeled by truncated power law distribution, which is one of the variations of the power law. The comparison of different DNNs revealed that the best performing networks correlated highly with the power law distribution. We further modeled the preferential attachment in DNNs evolution and find that continual learning in networks with growth in tasks correlates with the process of preferential attachment. These identified power law dynamics in DNNs can lead to the construction of highly accurate and compact DNNs based on preferential attachment. Inspired by the discovered findings, two novel applications have been proposed, including evolving optimal DNNs in sparse network generation and continual learning tasks with efficient network growth using power law dynamics. Experimental results indicate that the proposed applications can speed up training, save storage, and learn with fewer samples than other well-established baselines. Our demonstration of preferential attachment and power law in well-performing DNNs offers insight into designing and constructing more efficient deep learning. Second, we contributed to the overarching goal of improving the efficiency and performance of DNNs in analyzing and processing complex data. Our team proposed the Community Channel-Net (CC-Net), which used a community-based graph topology for channel interaction. Each community contains channels with semantic commonalities, and inter-community connections were activated among critical channels. With this structured and dynamic topology, channels from the same community can learn channel interdependence, and critical channels from distinct communities can gain more diverse features. That is, we may enhance the learning capabilities of DNNs in processing multimodal data. In conclusion, we have advanced our understanding of how the brain and muscles orchestrate simple upper limb motions. Our studies provide new insights into the neural substrates and muscle synergies in relation to upper limb movements and how these change with training. We have developed innovative data fusion techniques, using tools from network science and deep learning, which could link electrophysiological signals with behavior. These methods can help relate neural mechanisms to muscle activity and motion, aiding neuroprosthetic design and rehabilitation. This project has achieved its aims to identify the neural and muscular bases of control of simple upper limb movements and develop new ways of learning from multimodal data.

11215618.label: Major findings and research outcome
11215618.value: We gained insights into the neural sources of learning-relevant motor variability across different age groups [8.3], tackled challenges of cross-subject variations and domain shifts in EEG signals [9.2], studied the role of contingent learning and neural oscillations in motor development [9.1], and examined the processing of sensory feedback in motor training [8.1]. Our study on modulating muscle synergies in virtual bowling for elderly and young adults revealed that different aspects of motor variability drive learning in these age groups [8.3]. Using deep learning techniques, we investigated neural datasets involving imaginary simple hand movements and improved the performance of EEG-based brain-computer interface applications for motor imagery tasks [9.2]. Our study on contingent learning in infants contributed to our understanding of neural activity underpinning motor learning and identified potential applications in clinical practice for addressing delayed motor development [9.1]. Moreover, we found that visual and audio feedback elicit different brain activation patterns when adapting walking, indicating that feedback effectively enhances motor planning when acquiring a new gait [8.1]. Moreover, we conducted research in continual learning for assistive tools to improve performance with visual data [8.2], as we observed in the limitations of performance when using EEG, EMG or wrist kinematics only [8.4, 8.5]. We constructed and released a novel lifelong learning robotic vision dataset, OpenLORIS-Object [8.6], to address dynamic environments with diverse factors. Our analysis showed that existing algorithms are insufficient for handling lifelong learning tasks in such environments. To tackle computational issues in continual learning and multimodality, we investigated the topology of the best-performing deep neural networks (DNNs) and discovered power law dynamics that can lead to highly accurate and compact DNNs based on preferential attachment [8.8]. We proposed two novel applications for evolving optimal DNNs in sparse network generation and continual learning tasks using power law dynamics. Additionally, our team proposed the Community Channel-Net (CC-Net) could enhance the learning capabilities of DNNs in processing multimodal data [8.7].

11215618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11215618.value: The potential for further development of our research is immense, especially when considering the ongoing parallel study of pianists' hand movements. Although progress has been slower than anticipated due to the COVID-19 pandemic, we have now collected all data and completed a first draft of our findings. This presents an opportunity to expand our understanding of the intricacies involved in skilled motor control and learning, as well as the neural and muscular mechanisms underlying complex hand movements. Our proposed course of action involves the thorough analysis of the collected data on pianists' hand movements to identify patterns and trends that may be specific to skilled musicians. This will allow us to compare and contrast these findings with existing research on reach-to-grasp movements in the general population. We will also investigate potential differences between novice and expert pianists, in order to gain insights into the motor learning processes that occur during the acquisition of advanced motor skills.

11215618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11215618.value: Our research project aimed to unravel the intricate relationship between the brain and muscles in controlling basic upper limb movements, as well as to understand how these movements adapt through training. We analyzed muscle activities and neural signals associated with upper limb movements, exploring how they evolve with age and differ among individuals. This knowledge holds substantial importance for various fields, including the enhancement of rehabilitation techniques, the development of advanced prosthetics, and the creation of assistive devices for individuals with disabilities. Moreover, we introduced novel methods for analyzing and processing complex data from multiple sources, including brain signals, muscle activities, activity trackers, and videos. These innovative techniques allow for a deeper understanding of the connections between the brain, muscles, and movement. Not only would this lead to improvements in assistive devices and therapeutic methods, ultimately benefiting people with motor impairments, but it would also contribute to the continual learning of computational methods.

11216318.label: Realisation of objectives
11216318.value: The project started in August 2018 and it ended in July 2021. There are five objectives of the project as follows: • Establish a new methodology for making structures earthquake-proof using seismic metamaterials. • Using theoretical and numerical simulation, explore the potential application of the seismic metamaterials for civil infrastructure. • Investigate and identify frequency bandgaps (BG) corresponding to different sizes and shape unit cells metamaterial. • Derive numerical equations for various soil types and site conditions corresponding to multiple shapes and size unit cells. • Training of research students for promoting continued expertise in this field. The first four objectives are academic related and research intended while the last objective is related to the training of research students. It is reported here that all objectives have been fully achieved. There are a total of 41 research papers published that are fully or partially supported by the funding of this papers and all of them acknowledged the project funding support. Some of the papers fully addressed the objectives of the project while the other papers may not be apparently relevant which, however, can be viewed as spin-offs research outputs that are a result of the methods or principles developed while conducting the project. With reference to the first four objectives, we investigate the propagation of surface waves through periodically arranged builtup steel section (resonator) in single and multiple layered soil medium (substrate) and to study the feasibility of surface waves attenuation by finite element technique [Objectives 1 and2]. Two types of simple and small geometric size built-up sections were taken into consideration. Due to occurrence of local resonance between resonator and surface waves propagating on the surface of semi-infinite substrate, low frequency wide bandgaps were reported [Objectives 3]. Generation of local resonance is mainly governed by (i) impedance mismatch between the resonator and substrate (ii) coupling of longitudinal resonance modes of resonator with surface waves propagating on the surface of semi-infinite substrate [Objectives 3]. To have a more general and realistic study, surface wave propagation in single and six-layered soil medium was considered and the bandgaps were compared [Objectives 4]. Furthermore, with the variation in geometrical configuration of built-up section and change in material properties (soil profile), bandgap width and location do change. In the case of a layered soil medium, a relative bandwidth greater than 1.5 for both types of resonator is achieved. This implies that the proposed built-up sections are capable of attenuating surface waves in an extremely low frequency range. The position and width of bandgaps are further validated through finite unit cell based frequency response and time transient analyses [Objectives 2 and 3]. The findings substantiate the infinite unit cell model proposed here with the conclusion of more than 50% reduction in surface wave amplitude. The feasibility study manifests that the built-up structural steel sections can be applied as resonant barriers for mitigating seismic waves to protect important civil infrastructures from earthquake hazards [Objective 1]. In a different scope of the project, the work was extended to study the resonance of forest trees with properly aligned conditions that work as naturally available locally resonant metamaterials equipped with wonderful capability of generating low frequency extremely wide bandgaps in the earthquake frequency range of interest [Objective 1]. At the geophysical scale, the propagation of Rayleigh wave in the soft sedimentary soil basin experiences strong wave attenuation when the longitudinal resonant modes of trees were coupled with vertical component of the Rayleigh wave that mimic wave hybridization phenomena [Objective 4]. A finite element-based numerical technique was adopted and a total of 10 cases were considered where spacing, height, thickness and mechanical properties of resonant trees were varied to study the Rayleigh wave propagation and attenuation mechanism [Objectives and 3]. The trapping and/or mode conversion of Rayleigh wave by resonant trees was observed as dominant phenomena for wave attenuation. A time history analysis was conducted based on an actual earthquake record to validate the performance and efficiency of the bandgaps. The effects of ground stiffness, resonant tree mechanical and geometric properties on the bandgaps were also discussed [Objective 2]. The study explores another peculiar characteristic of the forest trees that controls the propagation of seismic wave to protect a region from earthquake hazards [Objective 1]. This study may motivate the relevant organizations, authorities and global communities on the needs of forestation to reduce the earthquake catastrophe [Objective 1]. The research model and method developed was further applied to develop a study on the interaction of forest trees with the Rayleigh wave for inducing extremely wide locally resonant bandgap in the earthquake frequency range of interest [Objective 1]. To better understand this mechanism, the effect of bulky side branches connected with the main stem was investigated. We considered two types of trees configurations and the study is conducted by a computational approach based on the finite element method. The Rayleigh wave band structure was obtained by sound cone and elastic strain energy density methods [Objective 2]. The later technique is found effective in detecting the higher surface Rayleigh modes that are undetectable by the sound cone technique. At the resonator attachment point, the wave mode coupling occurs between longitudinal modes of the resonator trees and vertical component of the Rayleigh wave [Objective 3]. This coupling results in a finite phase shift for incident Rayleigh wave and the periodic arrangement of trees act constructively to generate a wide bandgap. The tree bulky side branches seemed to further enhance the coupling strength. By constructing a finite length model and performing frequency domain and time history analyses based on the actual ground earthquake records, the performance and efficiency of the bandgap are validated. Both displacement field plots, time history signals and their Fourier spectra indicate significant amount of vibration mitigation within the bandgap frequency [Objective 3]. The research output can be largely grouped into two broad classes, a primary group that targets directly the aims and objective of the project, and a further group that applies the relevant concepts and methods of analysis developed during the course of the project, ie. spin-offs research outcomes of the project. The research publications that belong to the primary group are research related to seismic and mechanical metamaterials [5,9,10,12,16,19,20,21,22,29,30,33,34,36,38,40], and acoustic metamaterials [4,11,13,14,17,27,28,32,35,39,41], while the spin-offs have been applied in research works related to thermoacoustics [1,2,6,7,26], concrete structures [3,15,18,24,25,37], fracture mechanics [8], piezoelectric energy harvester [23], and dynamics of structures [31]. The research staff and research students directly and indirectly supported and trained under this project include Dr Yida Mao (PhD 2016-2020) [6,7,26,41], Dr I.A. 11216318.label: Major findings and research outcome
11216318.value: The major findings of the project are three-fold. In the first aspect of the project, this work contributes to the literature, in the context of built-up steel sections that can also be applied for seismic surface wave mitigation at low frequency ranges to protect important civil structures from earthquake hazards. Two types of built-up steel sections were proposed and they were analyzed by infinite and finite element studies in two types of wave propagating media. To enhance the generality and practicality of this study, single and six layered soil media were considered and accuracy of model was validated by referring to reported works. The results show wide bandgaps that are located at low frequency range and it varies along with the change in soil type and material properties (in-situ soil profile). In a second aspect of the project, the work concludes an insight on the feasibility of forest trees as potentially available natural seismic metamaterials at the geophysical scale. The interaction of Rayleigh wave, with soft sedimentary soil basin considered, induces extremely wide bandgap in the earthquake frequency range of interest. It is also concluded the softer soil media helps in achieving low frequency bandgap due to the impedance matching between the ground and trees that influences the strength of local resonance mechanism and wave modes coupling. The model was validated by using the time history of Imperial Valley-1940 (ELCUp) earthquake signal. The study shows forest trees can be considered as naturally available seismic metamaterials that can protect a region from earthquake hazard. This aspect of the work may motivate the government organizations and global communities for further forestation to resist climate change and other natural disaster specifically earthquakes. In a further aspect, the project concluded the feasibility of forest trees as potentially available natural seismic metamaterials with the capability of inducing extremely wide locally resonant bandgaps to mitigate ground born vibrations and earthquake hazards. By applying actual earthquake ground data, a time history analysis was conducted to further manifest the efficiency of bandgaps. It is also concluded that forestation can be considered another effective means to combat climate change and natural disasters, including earthquakes. The results reported are valid in certain scope of assumptions. Variation in soil type and/or tree mechanical properties may affect the width and position of the bandgaps.

11216318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11216318.value: The project can be further developed in the following areas. (i) Further investigation into the effects of geometric and material properties (density, sizes, stiffness/moduli, spacing, topology, etc), on wave propagation of relevant crystals and metamaterials. This will involve the development of theory, analytical models, exact and approximate solution methodology, and numerical finite element simulation. (ii) Laboratory experiment using scale specimens of periodic superstructures and substructures for potential protection against seismic wave impact by either inducing resonance at local resonators or diverting the wave at different directions. (iii) Full-scale experiments by large scale planned plantation and/or forestation and long-term observation of ground movements using displacement and velocity sensors.

11216318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11216318.value: Earthquake is a natural catastrophic phenomenon which causes large amount of damage to human life and properties. Seismic waves are elastic inhomogeneous acoustic waves with frequency range of 0- 30 Hz. Mortality caused by this natural hazard affects the social, economic and environmental life of humans. Different conventional seismic isolation design techniques aim at vibration damping and/or isolation but these systems show many shortcomings and further research and development technologies are necessary. Metamaterials are artificially engineered materials with certain properties which are not found in nature. The anisotropic ground and soil condition makes the propagation of seismic waves more complex. A novel seismic metamaterial was proposed in this project. The metamaterial was embedded around the structure in the form of unit cell arrays to attenuate seismic waves. Embedded metamaterials attenuate the central frequencies of earthquake because of their intrinsic frequency BG property. In this project, different shapes, geometries and types of metamaterials were investigated to determine their frequency BG by theoretical, computational and experimental approaches. A finite element computational approach was applied to perform numerical simulation while the Fouquet Bloch theories was applied to verify the computational results.

11216518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11216518.value: In existing cellular systems, such as 4th generation LTE (long term evolution), a connection set-up procedure is used in the up-link to establish centralized control. This is to avoid collisions between packets sent from different user equipments (UEs) and also to allocate resources properly amongst UEs. The connection set-up procedure, however, consumes time, which reduces the resources available for transmitting data, especially in the systems with short and sporadic data communications. Random access without the connection set-up phase is an alternative, in which each UE makes its own decision to transmit its data packets. This saves the overhead but results in the possibility of packet collisions. For this reason, the throughput of the existing random access schemes (such as WiFi) are relatively low. Random access involving data packets has not been used in cellular systems where high spectral efficiency is a primary concern. Multiple packet reception (MPR) has been studied to resolve collisions when random access is used. However, the work on MPR so far has been mostly theoretical in nature and important practical difficulties remain to be addressed. These include identification of active UEs and interference cancelation among pilots and data. Also, the present MPR schemes are passive. The underlying assumption is that, due to channel fading, the arrival powers of different users are different. This provides opportunity to detect multiple packets using the successive interference cancelation principle. Such passive schemes can provide only limited throughput improvement. This project is targeted at the development of a de-centralized scheme with high throughput. We will develop an interleave-division multiple-access (IDMA) scheme without a connection set-up procedure. We will investigate efficient iterative multi-user detection techniques to resolve packet collisions. We will develop iterative techniques to perform UE activity identification, channel estimation and data detection jointly. We will also study de-centralized power and rate control, which can be seen as an active approach to maximize the probability of successful MPR. We have observed significant throughput improvement in our preliminary. Machine-type communication (MTC) is a very active research topic with profound economic implications. Potential outputs of the project include an up-link multiple-access scheme that avoids the overheads associated with connection set-up and which can provide significantly higher throughput than conventional random access schemes. Such a scheme would find important applications in meeting the demand of MTC for low overhead and high spectral efficiency. 第4代LTE的现有蜂窝系统的上行链路中使用连接建立过程来建立集中控制。用以避免不同用户设备（UE）发送信号之间的冲突，及在UE之间适当地分配资源。然而，连接建立过程消耗时间，这减少了可用于传输数据的资源。这问题在具有短和零星数据通信的系统中尤其严重。 没有连接建立阶段的随机接入是一个替代方案，在随机接入中，每个UE自己决定发送其数据分组。这节省了开销，但可能导致数据包冲突。因此，现有随机接入方案（例如WiFi）的吞吐量相对较低。因为这个原因， 随机接入尚未用于需要高频谱效率的蜂窝系统中。多包接收（MPR）可以解决随机接入时的冲突问题。然而，到目前为止，关于MPR的工作大多是理论性的，重要的实际困难仍有待解决。这些实际困难包括活动UE的识别以及导频和数据之间的干扰消除。此外，目前的MPR计划是被动的。其基本假设是，由于信道衰落，不同用户的到达能力是不同的。这提供了使用连续干扰消除原理来检测多个分组的机会。这种被动方案只能提供有限的吞吐量改进。 此项目旨在开发具有高吞吐量的分散化控制。我们将开发一种没有连接建立过程的交织多址（IDMA）方案。我们将研究有效的迭代多用户检测技术来解决数据包冲突。我们将开发迭代技术以共同执行UE活动识别，信道估计和数据检测。我们还将研究非集中功率和速率控制，这可以被视为最大化成功MPR概率的主动方法。我们在前期工作中观察到吞吐量明显提高。机器类型通信（MTC）是一个非常活跃的研究课题，具有深刻的经济意义。该项目的潜在输出是一个新的上行链路多址方案，该方案避免了与连接建立相关的开销，并且可以提供比传统随机接入方案高得多的吞吐量。这种方案将在满足MTC对低开销和高频谱效率的需求方面找到重要的应用。

11216518.label: Realisation of objectives
11216518.value: To address Task 1, we investigated the orthogonal AMP (OAMP) principle in coded linear systems. We derived a state-evolution procedure to characterize the performance of OAMP in coded systems. We showed that the new algorithm can outperform the conventional Wang and Poor algorithm under certain standard assumptions for iterative decoding. We also derived a practical implementation algorithm for OAMP. This algorithm is more robust than the existing AMP related algorithms. In particular, the new algorithm can work with local estimators without the differentiability requirement. The findings related to Task 1 are reported in Journal Publications 2 and 3. To address Task 2, we investigated massive connectivity for future wireless cellular networks, in which a large number of users are connected to a base station (BS), but only a subset of users are active at any given time. The BS needs to identify active users and estimate their channels. In the past, AMP-based solutions have been proposed for this problem. The new OAMP based technique developed in this project offers a more robust solution. The findings related to Task 2 are reported in Journal Publications 1, 4 and 6. To address Task 3, we developed a compressed coding scheme that combines compressed sensing with forward error control coding. AMP is used to decode the message. Based on the state evolution analysis of AMP, we derive the performance limits of the compressed coding scheme. The findings related to Task 3 are reported in Journal Publication 5 and Conference Publication 1.

11216518.label: Major findings and research outcome
11216518.value: We derived a semi-blind detection technique is proposed for data detection without knowing channel in an uplink multiuser a semi-blind detection method is proposed for data detection without knowing channel in an uplink multiuser system. We observed that the proposed methods achieve significant performance gain over the pilot only method. This work is reported in Journal Publications 1. We showed that OAMP can outperform the conventional Wang and Poor algorithm under certain standard assumptions for iterative decoding. The findings related to Task 1 are reported in Journal Publication 2 We devised a joint OAMP and FEC decoding scheme and derived the performance limit. We showed that compressed-coding can approach Gaussian capacity at a very low compression ratio. We showed that the capacity approaching property can still be maintained when generalized AMP is used to decode the message. This work is reported in Journal Publication 3. We also devised a joint device activity detection and channel estimation (JACE) scheme in a massive MIMO connectivity scenario in which a large number of mobile devices are connected to a base station, while only a small portion are active at any given time. We showed that the new scheme outperforms other alternatives in channels with spatial and temporal correlations. This work is reported in in Journal Publications 4. We developed a multiuser extrinsic information transfer chart area theorem for joint FEC decoding and OAMP detection systems. We proved the information theoretical optimality of the scheme. This work is reported in in Journal Publication 5 and Conference Publication 1. We devised an integral-based orthogonal AMP (IB-OAMP) technique that avoids the requirements of AMP (and also the original form of OAMP) on differentiable and separable denoisers. This work is reported in in Journal Publication 6.

11216518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11216518.value: The findings in this project provide new techniques for signal processing in complicated wireless channels. An interesting issue is to prove the convergence of OAMP. Another urgent issue is to reduce the complexity of OAMP. We are currently working on these issues.

11216518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11216518.value: We carried out an comprehensive study on OAMP and its applications in random-access communication systems. We solve the difficult issues in handling channels with spatial and temporal correlations. We devised efficient algorithms that are more robust than the existing ones. These findings provided strong evidences that OAMP is a powerful tool for signal processing in complicated wireless channels. These findings are of both theoretical and practical values.

11216618.label: Project Objectives
11216618.value: To study how to quantify the capacity of a given slice. A slice can be used to accommodate different types of traffic in terms of arrival rates and delay requirements from different users/applications, which means that the capacity of a slice should be quantified from multiple dimensions. As the first step of this project, we will develop a framework to characterize the capacity of a slice. Given the amount of resources allocated to a slice, we will derive the traffic portfolio that the slice can support under different traffic models and delay requirements. This is the foundation of the design and management of a slice. Knowing the capacity of a slice will also help determine when and how much to scale for a slice. To design a system of multiple slices with different capacities. When facing traffic from different users/applications with various arrival rates and delay requirements, a tenant can design a number of slices with appropriate capacities, so as to use resources effectively. This calls for the modeling of multiplexed traffic and the study of trade-off between resource consumption and service level, based on which we will develop algorithms to design the slices. To design methods for traffic admission. Given a system of multiple slices, and dynamic requests from various users/applications, a tenant needs to decide which users/applications can be accepted and how to direct their traffic to different slices. We will provide models and solutions for the tenant to make effective decisions.

11216618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11216618.value: In today’s telecommunication industry, a grand challenge faced by many network service providers (NSPs) is how to cost-effectively allocate resources so as to agilely accommodate a variety of applications and services with diverse quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. To address this challenge, a promising technology is network slicing, with which tenants, such as mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs), can create different network slices with desired performance guarantees on the same network infrastructure. In the past three years, network slicing has attracted significant attention from academia and industry. However, most existing studies have focused on how to dynamically partition a physical network infrastructure into many network slices, and thus assumed that each tenant knows the right amount of resources which is necessary to accommodate a certain traffic load with performance guarantees. This assumption causes a gap between tenants and NSPs, which compromises the adoption of network slicing. In this project, we aim at closing the gap and we plan to address the key issues of network slicing design and management from the perspective of a tenant that may request and operate multiple slices, each of which provides different performance guarantees (especially the delay) to end users. Particularly, we want to answer a number of key questions centered at performance guarantee: How many slices to create? How many resources to request for each slice? How to assign a service request to the right slice? When to scale? and How much to scale? The answers to such questions call for (1) deep understanding of the relationship among traffic loads, resources, and performance bounds, and (2) optimal slice creation and traffic assignment to different slices. To make the solutions to the aforementioned questions generally applicable, we propose to investigate the issues with the following three features. First, we will study and model different types of traffic, such as video streaming, device-to-device communications, Internet of Things, multimedia, interactive web access, and the aggregation of them. Second, in terms of the delay requirements, we will allow the tenants to specify the percentage of traffic whose delay must be bounded. Third, we will adopt stochastic network calculus (SNC) in performance bound analysis. We expect that, upon the completion of this project, a set of tools will be developed to help tenants make the smart slice requests at the planning stage and optimally utilize and scale slices at the operation stage. The deliverables will facilitate the adoption of network slicing. 網絡運營商所面臨的一個重要挑戰是如何靈活地為各種應用與服務分配資源，滿足這些運行在網絡裡的應用與服務的質量要求。網絡切片技術通過在一個物理網絡上為不同應用（租戶）產生不同虛擬網絡，並保證每個虛擬網絡的性能，有望解決網絡運營商所面臨的挑戰。目前網絡切片方面的研究主要是假設租戶已經知道需要多少資源的前提下，如何在物理網絡上有效地分配所需的資源，產生一個網絡切片。這個假設使得網絡切片技術很難被應用。租戶通常只知道需要容納的流量及想要的性能，而不知道為了容納這些流量及達到想要的性能所需要的資源量。本項目旨在為網絡切片的租戶解決圍繞性能保障所帶來的網絡切片管理的一系列問題，比如， 一個租戶需要產生多少個網絡切片？每個切片需要多少資源？如何將不同的服務請求分配到不同的切片上？什麼時候需要擴容？擴容多少？解決這些問題的核心是：1) 建立流量，資源，與性能之間的模型；2) 找到最優的切片生成與流量分配的方案。為了使得解決前面提到的問題的方案具有通用性，本項目將對不同的流量進行建模，包括視頻流，設備與設備的通信，物聯網，多媒體數據，交互式網站訪問以及這些流量的混合流量；對性能的保障，我們將採用通訊行業常用的性能指定， 比如，百分之多少的流量的延遲不能超過多少；我們將利用網絡演算工具提供性能上界分析。我們期待該項目能為網絡切片的租戶的決策提供幫助， 從而加速網絡切片技術在通訊網中的應用。

11216618.label: Realisation of objectives
11216618.value: All three objectives have been successfully realized. We have developed a set of models and algorithms to help ISPs manage network slices with QoS guarantee. The developed models and algorithms can answer the following questions that an ISP often faces when managing network slices, namely, how many slices to create, how many resources to request for each slice, how to assign a service request to the right slice, when to scale, and how much to scale. Specifically, Objective 1 is realized by the paper (Part C 8-1) published in IEEE Transactions on Network Science and Engineering. We first use stochastic network calculus (SNC) to study the end-to-end delay bound with given traffic demand and resources. Then, we propose a solution to find the amount of resources that should be allocated with given traffic distribution and end-to-end delay bound. We further investigate the range of traffic demands that a network slice can support and design a learning-based dynamic network slice resizing strategy, which can significantly reduce overall resizing cost with quality-of-service guarantee. Our work provides a set of useful tools for network slice tenants to (1) decide the amount of resources to request from physical network providers and (2) cost-effectively adjust the resource amounts that align with the dynamic traffic demand. Objective 2 and objective 3 are implemented by the paper (Part C 8-2) published in Network Science and Engineering. We propose strategies and develop solutions for a network service provider (NSP) to cost-effectively provision and manage a large number of network slices. Specifically, we propose a novel framework, namely, network slice bundling, in which (1) an NSP can allocate resources and create multiple network slice bundles in advance, (2) a network slice request can be quickly instantiated in the bundle that supports its service requirements, and (3) network slices in the same bundle can share the resources and achieve a multiplexing gain by leveraging the stochastic behaviors of resource usage. Within this framework, we focus on a core problem, which is how to leverage the multiplexing gain to maximize the utility by optimally assigning multiple network slices to a set of pre-defined bundles. We formulate an optimization problem and theoretically analyse the irregularity of constraints and the difficulty of the problem. We develop a novel reinforcement learning (RL) based slice assignment solution. Finally, we conduct extensive data-driven simulation experiments. The numerical results confirm that the proposed solution can efficiently solve the network slice assignment problem and achieve significantly higher utility than the best baseline algorithm. Centred at QoS guarantee, we have also investigated other aspects of QoS other than end-to-end delay. Considering fault-tolerance aspect of QoS, we have investigated how an ISP can enhance its network topology so that any failure can be detected as long as there are no more than k simultaneous non-monitor failures in the network, the work (Part C 9-2) has been presented at IWQOS 2022. Considering the coverage and connectivity aspect of QoS, we have studied network formulation for a set of UAVs to stay connected and maximize the coverage, the work (Part C 8-3) has been published in ACM Transactions on Sensor Networks. Considering QoE of end users, we have studied how a content service provider can select the initial video segment (IVS) of live streaming for end users. The work (Part C 9-1) has been published in INFOCOM 2020.

11216618.label: Major findings and research outcome
11216618.value: A comprehensive framework of network slicing management has been developed. By quantifying the relationship among workload, performance, and resource, we are able to: 1) determine how much resource is necessary in order to guarantee the QoS requirement for given traffic load; 2) answer whether a network slicing can accommodate the current traffic load, and if it is necessary to scale, how much to scale; 3) determine what is the best admission strategy to maximize the utilization of network slices for a given set of network slices supporting diverse QoS; 4) provision the right network slices to accommodate network slicing requests from diverse users. The above findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and data-driven simulations. The work has been published in top journals and conferences in the field.

11216618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11216618.value: This project mainly considers network QoS. From the end users’ perspective, they will care more on QoE. Thus, we will extend the work one step further, to map users’ QoE expectation into network QoS requirement, then apply the work generated from this GRF project to provision resources. The work from this project has attracted the attention from industry. A company (headquartered in US with a branch in Hong Kong ) has contributed 50% to an ITF project started from March 2022 to further develop the theoretical work generated from this GRF project into product. The company has donated a full set of 5G base station and MEC for us to conduct real-world experiments. Local ISPs have showed interest in the product which is currently under development.
