11500118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11500118.value: In modern developed societies, markets play a central role in the normal functioning and growth of the economy. In the present inter-connected world, understanding the specific properties with respect to pricing and market failure is of vital importance. Two such properties are: (a) asset price bubbles which emerge when individuals err collectively in pricing such that they consistently trade at prices that are further away from the fundamental value of an asset and (b) reaction to news regarding fundamental value of the asset. The last two decades of research have significantly enhanced our understanding of why bubbles occur and which features of the asset market are more likely to cause bubbles. We plan to contribute to this literature by investigating the impact of social trading on asset market outcomes. In the last few years, the market for online social network platforms has evolved rapidly that allows investors to tap into the wisdom of crowds while making investment decisions. Some examples of popular platforms are ayondo, eToro, and ZuluTrade. Millions of investors are using these networks and assets under the management of social trading platforms are reported to amount to several billion euros. Traders on such platforms are provided with the chance to interact with one another, view each other’s ranking, copy the buy-and-sell actions of others and even delegate part of their wealth to others. Although it is often argued that social trading positively influences the market by encouraging market participation, it remains unclear whether such institutions help eliminate or even reduce mis-pricing, and dampen the over/under-reaction of market to news about fundamental value of the asset. The principal goal of the proposed research is to integrate the element of social interaction into financial decision making in asset markets using the methodology of experimental economics. In the laboratory, the possibility of external shocks can be ruled out and the fundamental value of the asset is known to each trader – a condition that can seldom be satisfied in the outside world. Such a setting would allow us to control the confounding factors and focus on change in one particular variable of interest while holding other factors constant. We believe that our research would have implications for a broader research agenda on the impact of information exchange among investors in experimental asset markets. Such information exchange could include word-of-mouth communication, private information regarding fundamentals, and portfolio information sharing with peers.

11500118.label: Realisation of objectives
11500118.value: We design an asset market experiment that incorporates social trading. This social platform enables investors to observe the trading performance of their peers and delegate their trading activity to top-performing investors. Participants are randomly divided into two groups: the first group consists of socially connected investors (social traders), and the second group comprises isolated investors (non-social traders). Social traders can obtain information about the trading performance of their peers and are allowed to delegate part (or all) of their wealth to the top-two performers within their group. We vary the extent to which the delegated investors (portfolio managers) are liable for the losses incurred from the investment. In other treatments, co-existing alongside non-social investors, social traders share performance data, convey soft information through price forecast reports, and may copy top-performing traders. We have collected a reasonable amount of data and have been able to achieve the first two objectives fully. Our design features offer interaction and information exchange between investors in real-time. This allows for the possibility of sharing knowledge with others and allows investors to trade with the help of others by comparing and copying other traders' strategies. This setup mimics the basic property of social trading platforms. Given that our markets have both social and non-social traders side-by-side through exogenous control, we are able to compare their behavioral differences in terms of information acquisition, price forecast sharing, etc. We are also able to comment on the informational efficiency of asset prices in the presence of social interaction. Because of the Covid-19 pandemic, we were unable to recruit further participants to achieve our third project objective fully. We designed the experiment and prepared the basic program that extends the elements of social trading in a static environment to a dynamic information exchange environment with arrival of news/information signals. We were just able to get enough participants (slightly more than the minimum needed, given our several treatments) to achieve our first two objectives completely, and we focused on those objectives as they were more fundamental.

11500118.label: Major findings and research outcome
11500118.value: Our first set of results concerns how social trading and delegation impact the asset price dynamics and trading behavior, and what are the impacts of different types of incentive contracts in delegated portfolio management among social traders. We find that the presence of an asymmetrical incentive structure (performance fee) exacerbates price deviation from the fundamentals. The introduction of a penalty (fulcrum fee), however, reduces the extent of price deviation and enhances market efficiency. There is a positive response to delegation schemes across all incentive structures. Social traders utilize delegation opportunities provided to them. Delegators are more willing to delegate a higher proportion of their funds when the managers are compensated with performance and fulcrum fees. We also find that being part of the social group is insufficient to improve welfare. A symmetrical incentive structure improves the welfare of social traders. Delegatees make a greater profit under the Fulcrum fee setting and yield greater returns to the delegators. We further study information acquisition behavior and price efficiency in experimental asset markets in the presence of social trading. Information acquisition level is similar across social and non-social traders in markets with no insiders, while social traders acquire significantly less information than their non-social counterparts when there are insiders. This can be attributed to the informativeness of the soft information shared through price forecasts only in the latter case. Markets continue to remain informationally inefficient, except when insiders are present. The deviation of price forecast from the individual posterior is larger for social traders than for non-social ones. Top-performing traders’ activities show a positive correlation between their net buy volume and the actual urn outcome. Sharing this information on the direction of trade provides social traders with an opportunity to mimic the activities of top-performing traders and achieve higher profits when compared to non-social traders. Although the average profits of social and non-social traders are similar, social followers outperform the average non-social trader indicating a positive role of social trading. Finally, directly copying the top-performing traders does not guarantee higher profits.

11500118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11500118.value: As mentioned in section 5.3, we have not been able to achieve the third proposed objective fully due to external constraints caused by the Covid-19 pandemic, which constrained our ability to recruit enough participants during the time frame of the project. Currently, our achievements are in the static exchange of information among traders. We believe our research has tried to initiate a research agenda on social trading in Experimental Economics and Finance literature. While we have successfully integrated the element of social interaction through information sharing among peers, delegation possibilities, and copy-trading features in experimental markets, a natural next direction would be to extend our research to study the dynamics of asset prices in the presence of communication among investors. Reaction to the arrival of news is one such framework. However, there could be other possible candidates to study the effect of social communication in a dynamic asset pricing framework. Although we were not able to conduct further experiments to achieve the third objective fully, we have developed the framework and prepared the basic program that allows for arrival of news dynamically and sharing of information over time among all or a subset of traders.

11500118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11500118.value: In modern societies, markets play a central role in the normal functioning and growth of the economy. In the last few years, the market for online social network platforms has evolved rapidly that allows investors to tap into the wisdom of crowds while making investment decisions. We design an asset market experiment that incorporates the aspect of social trading, which enables investors to observe the trading performance of their peers, and delegate their trading activity to top-performing investors or may copy the strategies of top-performing traders. We integrate the element of social interaction into financial decision-making in asset markets using controlled experiments. We are able to study the informational efficiency of asset prices in the presence of social trading and carefully contrast the behavioral differences between social and non-social traders in terms of their decisions to acquire costly information, share price forecasts among themselves, and trading strategies. We believe our research would have implications for a broader research agenda on the impact of information exchange among investors. Such information exchange could include word-of-mouth communication, private information regarding fundamentals, and portfolio information sharing with peers.

rows: To theoretically and empirically investigate paying it forward in (experimental) labor markets.
To empirically investigate whether and how leaders and managers may pay forward generosity or meanness to their own subordinates.
To provide new theoretical perspectives to extend extant manager-employee exchanges models.

11500418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11500418.value: This proposal extends the research on manager-employee exchange relationships in labor markets. Exchange models in a number of different disciplines provide tremendous insights into employment relationships that are characterized by high than market wages, positive HRM inducements and investments, reciprocal obligations, and higher work efforts (e.g., Charness, 2004; Fehr & Gächter, 2000; Shaw et al, 2009; Tsui et al, 1997). However, all these exchange models exclusively focus on the direct reciprocity between managers and employees. In contrast, the current proposal extends our common understanding about direct reciprocity in employment relationships by investigating paying-it-forward behavior in experimental labor markets. First, we suggest that paying it forward can be a type of employment relationship in which managers pay forward their bosses’ generosity or meanness to their own subordinates. Paying it forward can occur in labor markets because the philosophy that managers use to financially reward their own subordinates is likely to be influenced by how the managers have learned from and interpreted their past experiences with their previous bosses. For example, managers can be either appreciative or cynical when their bosses have paid them generously or ungenerously before. As a result, they may also provide similarly generous or ungenerous compensations to their own subordinates. Following this logic, we predict that highly paid and grateful managers are more likely to offer their own employees above the market rate compensation because they are more likely to believe in positive and mutually beneficial manager-employee relationships. Second, we suggest that direct reciprocity and paying it forward can coexist in labor markets because when managers pay forward generosity or meanness to their own subordinates, their subordinates will also reciprocate accordingly. In particular, when highly paid managers pay forward generosity to their own subordinates, they are also likely to expect subordinates to reciprocate positively by working harder. In addition, subordinates’ expectations and perceived reality of their manager’s generosity will jointly determine how they reciprocate their manager’s compensation. Finally, we will investigate both the bright and dark sides of paying-it-forward behavior in employment relationships. In particular, we suggest that when highly-paid managers are burdened with involuntary obligations to pay forward generosity to their subordinates, they may engage in ethically questionable behaviors to avoid paying subordinates generously. We plan to conduct three controlled behavioral experiments using modified gift exchange games (Charness, 2004; Fehr, et al., 1993; Fehr, et al., 1998) to test our hypotheses in experimental labor markets. 該研究提案擴展了關於經理與員工在勞動力市場交換關係方面的研究。在許多不同的社會學科領域，交換關係的模型對於勞動市場的僱傭關係提供了重要的見解，其中包含關於提供高於市場的薪資為特徵的僱傭關係，積極的人力資源管理的投資，互惠義務以及員工的更多的工作付出。然而，現有的這些交換模型都專注於經理和員工之間的直接互惠。相比之下，目前的提案通過研究實驗性勞動力市場中預先支付的行為（一種間接的互惠）來擴展我們對於僱傭關係中互惠關係的理解 首先，我們提出預先支付的行為（間接的互惠）可以體現在僱傭關係中，因為管理者可能會將他們老闆的慷慨或吝嗇傳遞給自己的下屬。這種慷慨或吝嗇的傳遞之所以發生是因為管理著自身的管理哲學可能會受到老闆的深刻影響。例如，管理者可能會因為老闆以前對他們的慷慨或吝嗇的報酬，也為自己的下屬提供類似慷慨或吝嗇的酬勞。遵循這一邏輯，我們預測高薪和感恩的經理人更有可能提供給自己的員工超過市場的薪酬，因為他們可能更會相信積極和互利的經理與 員工關係。其次，我們認為直接互惠和間接性的預支行為可以在勞動力市場中共存。這是因為當經理們做出慷慨或吝嗇的預支行為之後，他們的下屬也會相應地做出回應。特別是當高薪的經理向自己的下屬付出慷慨的薪酬，他們會期望下屬通過更加努力地積極回報。此外，下属的期望和他们经理慷慨与否的现实将联合起来确定他们如何回报经理的薪酬。最后，我们也将尝试研究预支行为的积极和消极的两个方面。特别是当高薪管理人员背负着非自愿的义务，他们可能会为避免此类的义务而从事一些道德上存在问题的行为。我们计划进行三项實驗勞動力市場的试验来验测我们的假设。

11500418.label: Realisation of objectives
11500418.value: We have achieved most of the objectives that we originally planned. Specifically, our research takes a new theoretical perspective to investigate how leaders may transfer their previous organizational experience to new employees by paying forward generosity or miserliness to the employees. Paying it forward has been extensively studied in evolutionary biology, economics, social psychology, and sociology (e.g., Bartlett & DeSteno, 2006; DeSteno et al., 2010; Dufwenberg et al., 2001; Gray et al., 2014, Hamilton & Taborsky, 2005; Nowak & Sigmund, 1998; 2005; Pfeiffer et al., 2005; Roth et al., 2004; Rutte & Taborsky, 2007; Simpson et al., 2018). Except for a few studies (e.g., Baker & Levine, 2013; Baker & Buckley, 2014; Chambers & Baker, forthcoming), the phenomenon is relatively under-investigated in organizational research. In the current research, we suggest that organizational research may incorporate paying it forward into employee-organization exchange models to understand employment relationships in organizations better. All organizational exchange theories and models are based on direct reciprocity between employers and employees (e.g., Adams, 1965; Blau, 1964; Camerer, 2003; Charness, 2004; Fehr et al., 1998; Fehr & Fischbacher, 2006; Fehr, Fischbacher, & Gächter, 2002; Gouldner, 1960; Thibaut & Kelley, 1959). On the one hand, for example, a host of organizational studies have demonstrated that underinvestment in employees often results in poorly paid, poorly trained, and poorly motivated employees, who are likely to reciprocate bad compensation and benefits with malfeasant behavior (e.g., Greenberg, 1990; 1993; Hollinger & Clark, 1983; Lazear, 1979; Pritchard, 1969). On the other hand, employer-employee exchange models in different disciplines provide valuable insights into employment relationships in highly paid organizations, which are characterized by higher than market salaries, positive HRM inducements and investments, reciprocal obligations, and better work performance (e.g., Charness, 2004; Fehr & Gächter, 2000; Shaw et al., 2009; Tsui et al., 1997). Despite a plethora of research in this field, almost none of these organizational studies has considered how employee-organization exchange relationships may go beyond direct reciprocity between employers and employees. Unlike previous research, we investigate how paying it forward may be embedded in employer-organization exchange relationships. Organizations and leaders often have different management philosophies about managing and rewarding employees. Many organizations are employing low-paid employees to sustain a low-cost and low-price strategy. For example, the minimum wage earned by many workers at McDonald’s, Starbucks, and Wal-Mart in 2012 was worth 30% less than it was in 1968 in purchasing power (Thoelcke et al., 2012). In contrast, some other low-cost organizations adopt a different compensation strategy. For instance, Costco and Trade Joe’s, two low-price retailers, pay their employees substantially above the market-price salaries; Forbes named both of them America’s Best Employers in 2017. We argue that an organization’s philosophy can be shaped by its leader’s past experience because leaders’ past experience can affect their future management style and behavior (Kim & Toh, 2019). In particular, we suggest that leaders may “pay forward” their own experience to the new organization they found or joined in the future. For example, organizational founders and leaders can be either appreciative or cynical when they were paid generously or ungenerously before. As a result, they may provide similarly generous or ungenerous compensations to their own employees when they found their own organization or join a new organization. At the same time, the employment relationships between founders/leaders and their employees will also be driven by direct reciprocity because employees will directly pay back their leaders’ generosity or stinginess by reciprocating either positively or negatively. Thus, we suggest that employee-organization exchange relationships may be modeled as a mixture of both generalized and direct reciprocity. We have conducted three complementary studies to investigate the co-existence of direct and generalized reciprocity in organizations, especially how leaders may transfer their previous organizational experience to new employees by paying forward generosity or miserliness to the employees. Our results support our predictions about paying it forward in employee-organization exchange relationships, suggesting that incorporating paying it forward into employee-organization exchange models will provide new insights into the direct reciprocity between employers and employees.

11500418.label: Major findings and research outcome
11500418.value: In the first paper, we conducted three empirical studies to investigate how leaders may transfer their previous organizational experience to new employees by paying forward generosity or miserliness to the employees. Three complementary studies employed parsimonious behavioral games to precisely assess employees’ direct and generalized reciprocity. Our controlled experiments allowed us to distinguish the effects of prior wage experience, the structure of reciprocity, and the quality of reciprocity from other, potentially confounding factors in organizations, such as the resources exchanged or the substantive context of exchange. Specifically, Study 1 employed a 3 (above vs. at vs. below-market wages) × 3 (high vs. normal vs. no reciprocity) factorial design to test our hypotheses. We recruited 674 student participants from CityU. The results provided strong evidence of paying it forward in employee-organization exchanges. After controlling for direct reciprocity, highly paid leaders were more likely to pay forward generosity to their workers. Leaders’ forwarded generosity was motivated by their kindness and gratitude instead of their strategic expectations of a direct return from their own workers. In addition, strong reciprocators were more likely to pay forward generosity than other leaders. Study 2 used a wage-effort game to more clearly investigate leaders’ act of paying forward generosity. We recruited 350 U.S. and Canadian participants to replicate Study 1’s results using different behavioral measures. The results replicated Study 1’s results and supported our hypotheses, suggesting that leaders were less likely to pay forward generosity when their workers did not have the opportunity to pack them back. Finally, Study 3 also recruited 408 participants from CityU to investigate the quality of exchange in paying it forward. Study 3 generally replicated the results of the first two studies and provided consistent evidence of paying it forward. After controlling for other exchange factors, highly paid leaders were likely to pay forward generous compensation to their own workers after they themselves had received high compensation before. In addition, there was no evidence of highly paid leaders strategically paying forward generosity to simulate future returns from their own workers. Finally, strong reciprocators were mostly likely to pay forward generosity to workers who were also strong reciprocators, suggesting the importance of strong reciprocators in creating and sustaining pay-it-forward in organizations. Other than the three studies described above, we have also collected some field data. One of our papers was invited for resubmission in Organization Science. But it was rejected after the resubmission. After including new field data, we plan to supplement the experimental data with field evidence and submit the paper to another top journal soon.

11500418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11500418.value: First, we mainly investigate how leaders pay forward generosity as a result of transferring their past experience to future management. What is less known from our research is when leaders would avoid transferring past experience to the future. Thus, future research might investigate the boundary conditions of leader experience, especially when and how leaders transfer or do not transfer their past experiences to future management. Second, organizational culture may be an important missing antecedent to our research. Organizational culture may have a special bearing on the norm of generosity in organizations. Future research should investigate the role of organizational culture to enhance our understanding of this phenomenon further. Finally, our research does not investigate different forms of reciprocity. Generalized reciprocity is also called paying it forward or upstream reciprocity. Previous research has identified another form of prosocial behavior in generalized exchange systems: downstream or indirect reciprocity (e.g., Nowak & Sigmund, 2005; Simpson, et al., 2018). Unlike generalized reciprocity, indirect reciprocity is primarily driven by reputation building. Future research should investigate how reputation building constitutes another mechanism underlying leaders’ act of generalized reciprocity, especially whether leaders may strategically build different reputations for internal and external actors (e.g., employees vs. other stakeholders).

11500418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11500418.value: Drawing on cross-disciplinary insights from evolutionary biology, economics, sociology, social psychology, and management, we investigated the coexistence of paying it forward and direct reciprocity in employee-organization relationships. Three complementary studies consistently showed that leaders paid forward generous compensation to their employees after the leaders themselves had received generous compensation before. When highly paid leaders paid forward generosity to their employees, they were not necessarily motivated by the expectation of reciprocity of their own employees. In addition, strong reciprocators (leaders who reciprocated generosity with high work effort) played an important role in instigating and sustaining a pay-it-forward system because they did not only reward direct reciprocity, they also paid forward generosity, especially to other strong reciprocators. Our research contributes to the organizational research on gift exchange, reciprocity, and paying it forward by enhancing our understanding of employee-organization exchange relationships.

11500618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11500618.value: Sourcing from more than one supplier for the same component is a common practice in supply chains. This introduces more variations in the quality. Even for the same supplier, quality may vary from one batch to another. Quality for one supplier may differ from the quality for another supplier due to differences in process capabilities, production technologies and management philosophies. As customers learn about the quality of the product overtime, such variations of quality among suppliers will affect customers' perception of the product which in turn affects future demand. We will consider a single-item multi-period periodic-review model in which the firm decides not only the total quantity to produce but also the proportion to source from each supplier. In other words, the firm also has to decide the quality-mix of the product. Customers learn about the quality of the product overtime and form an expectation of the product's quality, which affect their decisions on whether to buy or not. Thus, the firm's decision on how much to source from each supplier also affects future demand through customers' expectation of the product quality. In the extensive literature on supply uncertainty, existing literatures mainly focus on quantity uncertainty. While quantity uncertainty is an important issue in procurement management, uncertainty in quality is also negligible as consumers become more concerned with quality. There is significant differences between the quantity uncertainty case and the quality uncertainty case: Demand may not be able to be satisfied in the quantity uncertainty case, but future demand is not affected. In the quality uncertainty case, current demand can be satisfied, but future demand may be affected. While the optimal sourcing strategy for the quantity uncertainty case has been widely studied, there is little known about the quality uncertainty case. The proposed project aims to fill this gap. 從同一個組件的多個供應商處採購是供應鏈中的常見做法。這引入了更多的質量變化。即使對於同一供應商，質量也可能因批次而異。由於過程能力，生產技術和管理理念的差異，一個供應商的質量可能與另一個供應商的質量不同。隨著客戶了解產品加班質量，供應商質量的這種變化將影響客戶對產品的感知，進而影響未來的需求。 我們將考慮單項多周期定期審核模型，其中公司不僅決定要生產的總量，還決定每個供應商的來源比例。換句話說，公司還必須決定產品的質量組合。客戶了解產品的加時質量，並形成對產品質量的期望，這會影響他們決定是否購買。因此，公司決定從每個供應商採購多少也通過客戶對產品質量的期望來影響未來的需求。 在關於供給不確定性的大量文獻中，現有文獻主要關注數量不確定性。雖然數量不確定性是採購管理中的一個重要問題，但隨著消費者越來越關注質量，質量的不確定性也可以忽略不計。數量不確定性案例與質量不確定性案例之間存在顯著差異：在數量不確定性案例中可能無法滿足需求，但未來需求不會受到影響。在質量不確定性的情況下，可以滿足當前的需求，但未來的需求可能會受到影響。雖然已經廣泛研究了數量不確定性案例的最優採購策略，但對質量不確定性案例知之甚少。擬議的項目旨在填補這一空白。

11500618.label: Realisation of objectives
11500618.value: Customers are always uncertain about quality, but they can find out about the quality through consumer reviews. We consider a retailer's strategic inventory and the supplier's pricing decisions when customers face quality uncertainty but can learn through reviews. Due to the problem of supplier’s restricted bargaining power, we consider that consumer reviews can provide the demand information directly for supplier. Then, we study supplier’s two-stage optimal dynamic pricing decisions in a retail channel by constructing a demand model which is affected by consumer reviews and retailer’s strategic inventory level. We find that: 1) When product quality is improved, supplier can charge a higher second-period wholesale price by the pleasant online reviews, and increase the bargaining power even with higher strategic inventory. 2) Besides the inventory holding costs, the other two important factors should be considered when making optimal decisions of strategic inventory, which includes the consumers’ review reliance and the product quality. 3) With consumer reviews, when the retailer has the ability to carry strategic inventory, the supplier should charge a higher introduction wholesale price to weaken the retailer’s purchasing power. 4) With good product quality, the supplier should set lower introduction wholesale price to strengthen the positive effect of consumer reviews. This study clarifies the role of consumer reviews on the problem of supplier’s restricted bargaining power, and enriches the relevant theories of strategic inventory, and also provides theoretical support for supplier’s optimal pricing decisions when adopting a retail channel. This piece of work was included in Jiayun Wang's PhD dissertation and published in EJOR. Under the PI's supervision, Jiayun also analyzed supplier’s behavior-based pricing discrimination in a direct channel with consumer reviews and strategic consumers’ delay purchase. The delay purchase of consumers always hurts firms’ profits and makes them unable to achieve optimal when applying behavior-based pricing discrimination. Existing research only focuses on consumers’ perception of pricing discrimination behavior , but ignores consumers’ purchase willingness. We find that: 1) Consumer reviews can strengthen positive impact of behavior-based pricing discrimination and improve supplier’s profit when consumers rely on reviews and the product quality is high. 2) When the product quality is improved, the supplier should set lower introduction price which can reduce the delay purchase of consumers and lead to pleasant consumer reviews in the later period. 3) With the influence of consumer reviews, product quality becomes an important factor for supplier’s decisions on behavior-based pricing discrimination, where the supplier will attract new consumers when the product quality is in a high level, and reward past consumers when the product quality is poor. 4) When considering consumer reviews, supplier will set a penetration pricing policy when the product quality is good, and adopt a skimming pricing strategy when the product quality is poor. This study clarifies the role of consumer reviews on the problem of unsalable products, and expands the relevant theory of firm’s behavior-based pricing discrimination, and also provides theoretical support for supplier’s optimal pricing decisions when adopting a direct channel. This piece of work is currently under preparation for submission. In view of the impact of quality uncertainty on fairness issue, we also study supplier’s channel pricing decisions in a mixed channel with consumer reviews and peer-induced fairness concerns. Firms which adopt mixed channel often meet intensified channel conflicts due to fairness concerns. The existing research only focuses on the effect of consumer value-added service level on fairness concerns, but ignores the impact of channel consumers’ perceived product quality differences. Due to the problem of supplier’s channel conflicts, we consider that consumer reviews can reduce the consumers’ perceived product quality between channels. Then, we study supplier’s two-stage optimal dual channel pricing decisions in a mixed channel by constructing a demand model affected by consumer reviews and fairness concerns. We find that: 1) When consumers rely more on reviews, the dual-channel price disparity will be shrunken in the second period, which alleviates the negative effect caused by the fairness concerns. 2) Consumer reviews can alleviate the double marginalization effect and improve the supply chain coordination when the product quality is in a high level. 3) When consumers’ review reliance is low, supplier will increase the online introduction selling price to offset the negative impact of consumers’ fairness concerns. 4) As consumer reviews can transmit the information from previous buyers, it can increase the supplier’s profit by improving consumers’ expected product quality in the later period when the quality is good. This study clarifies the role of consumer reviews on alleviating the fairness concerns and channel conflicts, and expands the relevant theory that consumer reviews can improve the supply chain coordination, and also provides theoretical support for supplier’s optimal pricing decisions when adopting a mixed channel. This piece of work is currently under preparation for submission. The idea of quality uncertainty led us to also consider the idea of availability uncertainty. As such we consider a case where customers may not be able to get the product and study whether it would be optimal for the firm to intentionally create rationing. There are three major findings. First, the scalper will join the market whenever the firm introduces scarcity, even if there are no uncertainties in the market. Second, the firm and the scalper can both benefit from customers’ conspicuous consumption. Third, the scalper’s speculative behavior may generate incentives for the firm to decrease the supply of products on purpose, which will increase the profits of both the firm and the scalper. The scalper’s existence will also increase consumers’ surplus when their level of consumption conspicuousness is rather high. This piece of work was submitted to Omega and is currently under major revision.

11501018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11501018.value: 在当今竞争激烈且动荡不安的环境中，企业必须加强运营灵活性，以便成功应对环境的快速变化。企业信息系统（EIS）被认为在实现运营灵活性方面具有重要意义;然而，只有当系统设计人员正确使用EIS时，才能实现这一价值，这一问题在文献中被称为EIS合规性。实际上，EIS合规性对于将EIS成功整合到业务实践中是必要的，这一过程有助于提高公司快速实施和稳定不断变化的业务以应对市场变化和机遇的能力。但是，合规性具有挑战性。员工可能不愿意或无法遵守，因为他们认为这样做没有个人利益，或者他们不知道如何正确使用这些系统。这一挑战在当代动态环境中更为突出，因为合规性规则和政策可随着EIS的发展而变化，以应对环境变化。因此，企业必须找到促进EIS合规的解决方案. 以前的文献主要从两个角度解释了用户EIS的合规性：基于控制. 关系选择和一般威慑理论的奖励/惩罚（制裁），政策教育，培训和意识（ETA）的程序。虽然这项研究提供了很好的见解，但所描述的正式干预措施引起了新的关注。首先，已经发现奖励和惩罚对遵守有混合效应。有理由认为，激励EIS合规的正式和直接方法也可能通过削弱他们的士气并鼓励他们变得更加自私而使员工失去动力。其次，尽管培训是一种正式的知识转移方法，有助于克服与​​正确使用EIS相关的知识障碍，但培训的定期和事后性质未能发挥用户在系统设计过程中的主观能动性，也不响应不断变化的业务需求导致的系统变化。 鉴于这些研究差距，我们总体研究目标是了解公司应该采取哪些措施来激励和实现EIS合规，而不是像文献所假设的那样通过强制性和突兀的管理干预来施加控制环境，而是通过其他方式，例如培养激发人们认可用户作为知识代理人的氛围，并促进更有利于EIS合规的机制。我们认为，组织背景视角是一种从管理文献中提取的IS新颖方法，是探索我们研究问题的适当方式。组织环境，涉及社会背景的“软元素”和绩效管理环境的“硬性要素”，是通过鼓励组织内部的高昂士气建立有效的职业道德的系统，过程和信念。众所周知，一个适当的组织环境可以促进组成单位通过加强员工士气实现公司目标的集体合作行动。 虽然组织背景视角已经在其他研究领域进行了研究，但它还没有扩展到IS领域。与其他领域的知识不同，EIS合规性是一种特定的合作行为，要求用户理解并接受EIS的业务和IT方面。因此，尚不清楚组织背景是否以及通过何种机制促进EIS合规。这促使我们致力于解决如下研究问题：组织环境在多大程度上和如何影响在动态业务环境中运营的公司的职能部门的EIS合规性？ 为了回应这个研究问题，我们通过整合社会资本理论来扩展组织背景文献，假设组织背景通过加强业务部门和IT部门之间的社会资本来促进业务部门的EIS合规性。社会资本理论强调人类互动的社会和关系价值。与通常只需要一方接受另一方安排的合作行为相反，我们将EIS合规视为业务与IT之间的价值共同创建过程，即涉及业务用户设计（即IT计划）和实施EIS（例如，操作程序，指南，规则和标准），以便了解业务实践和要求的变化。我们认为，功能和IT单位之间的社会资本是一种非正式机制，在通过交换和知识组合引导业务部门的EIS合规性方面起着关键作用。

11501018.label: Realisation of objectives
11501018.value: We have achieved the three listed objectives by completing a comprehensive literature review to propose the theoretical hypotheses and conducting a rigorous empirical design to test the proposed hypotheses. On this basis, we developed a research model and leveraged a multi-sourced data to test the research model. We wrote up a full paper and submitted it to MIS Quarterly. This study has been accepted by MIS Quarterly after three rounds of peer review. In this section, we will elaborate on how and to what extent the project objectives have been accomplished in two aspects. 1. Literature review and theoretical model proposition - We conceptually developed and extended the construct of performance management context and social context into the EIS compliance context and established the causal logic between them (objective 1). Specifically, our study draws on the organizational context perspective from the management literature, where organizational context is defined as the systems, processes, and beliefs that build an effective work ethic and positive engagement within the organization. We have summarized the literature on organizational context that includes a recognition of “hard” versus “soft” elements in the workplace. Soft elements refer to social context, defined as the extent to which an organization builds a trustworthy and supportive environment for employees that inspires them to mirror these behaviors within the organization. Hard elements refer to the performance management context (PMC), defined as the extent to which the organization sets performance goals to motivate its members to meet expectations and strive for more ambitious goals. This is a suitable perspective for our research objective because an appropriate organizational context with the soft and hard elements is found capable of promoting more collective and cooperative behaviors among employees that forward the firm’s interests. - We achieved a theoretically grounded account of how social capital between business and IT plays a role in channeling the effect of organizational context (i.e., performance management context and social context) (objective 2). The organizational context perspective is deemed as influential when an organization seeks cooperation from a collective of its employees, however, we have identified the unique characteristics of EIS context. Unlike other more general contexts where employees cooperate on the terms that the employer defines, changing EIS in response to dynamic environments requires continuous learning of technical knowledge (e.g., updated IT specifications) by EIS users and business knowledge (e.g., changing business needs) by the IT unit. In this regard, both the IT staff and EIS users, who possess the necessary domain knowledge, play an important role in influencing EIS compliance. Thus, we introduced social capital theory to address our second research objective. - We have made a literature summary to explore our objective 3 and have focused on the research context of dynamic environment to understand the performance implications of EIS compliance at the unit level. Based on our field interview of IT and business managers, they have suggested in hyper-competitive and turbulent business environments, firms must rapidly and efficiently adapt their operational processes in response to environmental changes and client needs. The set of information technology infrastructures, data management, application systems, and extended enterprise networks deployed to digitalize key business operations, must be adjusted to empower this adaption, often through improvement in existing system functionalities and/or creation of new functionalities. To attain intended benefits from EIS, it is important to ensure proper use of the system by employees in the functional units reliant on EIS, an issue termed as EIS compliance. In a changing environment, employees must still strive to use the evolving EIS in a conforming and consistent manner so that their functional unit as a whole can rapidly stabilize evolving digital operations. We have also found a practical case in customer-facing service work. The system is updated frequently to support or enable service work in order to achieve customer satisfaction in a highly competitive environment. Employees using the system should comply with the policies while playing their different roles, including answering customer inquiries, offering information about products and promotions, processing transactions, and providing post-sales support. Failure of employees to comply with EIS changes (e.g., up-dates in the digital codes to create a quick reply to customers’ queries) is detrimental to the organizational goal of delivering good customer service. 2. Research operationalization We have conducted a multiple source data collection to achieve the research objectives. Survey data were collected through a senior executive program of a well-known Chinese educational institution. From the executive connections in the program, we attained a sample pool of 300 departments from 100 firms across a variety of IT-intensive industries in the Greater China region. Data were collected from three informant sources in each firm: the manager and three employees of each functional unit, and the IT unit manager.

11501018.label: Major findings and research outcome
11501018.value: We focused on refining and improving the research study that focuses on fully addressing objectives 1, 2, and 3, based on the reviewers’ comments. By completing the three research objectives, our study has been published on the journal MIS Quarterly in 2022. The major findings are summarized in three points: First, this research establishes that business–IT social capital leads to collective EIS compliance, and that social context with trust and support positively affects business–IT social capital. It also confirms the full mediating effect of business–IT social capital between social context and collective EIS compliance. Furthermore, performance management context with discipline and stretch is found to be positively related to collective EIS compliance. These findings are consistent with our expectations and provide evidence for the base model (with the direct relationships) we advanced earlier. Third, the results confirm that performance management context amplifies the relationship between social context and business–IT social capital, such that this relationship is stronger when PMC is stronger, verifying empirically our theoretical account of the complementary effect of PMC and social context. Fourth, this confirmed moderating effect, in conjunction with the confirmed mediating relationship of business–IT social capital, provides empirical evidence to the hypothesized moderated mediation effect. This outcome lends further support to our theory on how the two important organizational contexts take effect on collective EIS compliance through business–IT capital. Finally, for the control variables, reward had a positive effect on collective EIS compliance, while the effect of punishment and training was shown to be insignificant. These findings provide three major theoretical contributions to IS literature. First, collective EIS compliance can be explained by the organizational context perspective, specifically the social and performance management context perspective that is novel to IS. Performance management context with discipline and stretch is found to be positively related to collective EIS compliance. Second, this research establishes that business–IT social capital leads to collective EIS compliance. Third, our research findings supplement the original literature on social and performance management context by extending its applicability to IS research, particularly in the area of EIS compliance.

11501018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11501018.value: This study has several limitations due to the scope of its investigation, which open important avenues for future research. First, it is necessary to conduct an empirical test regarding to the relationship between collective compliance and functional unit performance. Our current research efforts focused on the theoretical arguments and literature review that collective EIS compliance is beneficial for function units but lacks empirical research. Future development of the research could consider using empirical data to prove this point. Second, a notable portion of the firms in our sample are not large in size. While the theoretical tenet we develop to explain collective EIS compliance is logically generalizable to firms of larger size, future research could replicate the empirical test of the research model in other organizational settings that include larger firms. Third, while we develop our theoretical model with a focus on collective EIS compliance, future research could extend this research by replicating the model in the IS security compliance context. There is reason to expect that social context and performance management context can also elucidate security compliance behavior, due to their explanatory power toward understanding cooperative behavior in general (Ghoshal and Bartlett 1994).

11501018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11501018.value: This research provides guidance to managers on how to promote collective employee EIS compliance in their functional unit, particularly in a dynamically changing environment. Managers are advised to focus on developing social capital with IT for frequent social interactions, good social relationships, shared languages, and mutual trust and respect. Furthermore, this study advises managers that, since business–IT social capital is important, they could develop this social capital by building a strong supportive and trusting social context. Managers can achieve this end by reinforcing a series of management principles that support a trusting social context by (1) ensuring equity in organizational decision processes, (2) involving employees in relevant decisions and activities, and (3) staffing positions with competent people. A supportive social context is further produced by (1) allowing actors to access resources outside of their own unit, (2) encouraging autonomous initiative at lower organizational levels, and (3) coaching management staff to prioritize guidance and help over exercising authority and control (Gibson and Birkinshaw 2004).

11501718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11501718.value: Income tax represents a significant cost for most corporations and is an important input into many corporate decisions. In the United States, a tax rate ranging from 15% to 35% is imposed on the profits of US resident corporations and most corporate income is taxed at the maximum rate. The corporate income tax (CIT) is the third largest source of federal revenue, and raised $343.8 billion in fiscal 2015. The corporate income tax system has been a focus of many recent debates about tax reform that calls for a tax cut for business. Corporate income tax has a significant impact on a firm’s operating and financial decisions. As documented in a world bank report, the amount of the tax cost for businesses matters for investment and growth. A recent study shows that higher tax rates are associated with fewer formal businesses and lower private investment. A 10% increase in the effective corporate income tax rate is associated with a reduction in the ratio of investment to GDP of up to 2% and a decrease in the business entry rate of about 1% (Djankov et al. 2010). A tax increase equivalent to 1% of GDP reduces output over the next 3 years by nearly 3% (Romer and Romer 2010). Therefore, it is more accurate to use net operating profit after tax as opposed to net income when making investment and operational decisions, and it gives a better picture of a company's operational efficiencies. Corporate income tax structure is quite complex in industry. There are three tax structures in practice: progressive, proportional, and regressive tax. Different tax structures have different implications on companies’ operational decisions. However, in the operations management literature, there is only a limited study on the effect of taxation on firms' operational decisions. The proposed project attempts to fill this gap by considering inventory decisions under taxation. Starting from the newsvendor setting, we examine the structure of the optimal inventory policies under various tax functions that are prevalent in the real world, and how a firm’s inventory decision is affected by different tax structure and business environment. We then plan to generalize our analysis to dynamic settings, including dynamic inventory models with a single accounting period and multiple accounting periods. We will also consider the case with loss carry forward. 所得稅對大多數公司來說是一筆巨大的成本，是許多公司決策的重要投入。在美國2018年稅收改革以前，所得税占公司的利潤的15％至35％，大多數公司收入按最高稅率徵稅。企業所得稅是聯邦收入的第三大來源，並在2015財年籌集了3438億美元。2018年美国稅改减少企業所得稅到21%。 企業所得稅對公司的經營和財務決策有重大影響。如世界銀行報告所述，企業的稅收成本對投資和增長至關重要。最近的一項研究表明，較高的稅率與較少的正規業务和較低的私人投資相關。有效企業所得稅稅率增加10％與投資與GDP比率降低高達2％以及企業進入率降低約1％相關。相當於GDP的1％的稅收增加將使未來3年的產出減少近3％。因此，在進行投資和運營決策時，使用稅後淨營業利潤與税前淨收入相比更準確，並且可以更好地了解公司的運營效率。 企業所得稅結構相當複雜。實踐中有三種稅收結構：累進稅，比例稅和累退稅。不同的稅收結構對公司的運營決策有不同的影響。然而，在運營管理文獻中，關於稅收對公司運營決策的影響的研究卻很有限。擬議的項目試圖通過考慮稅收下的庫存決策來填補這一空白。從静态的报童模型開始，我們檢查現實世界中普遍存在的各種稅務功能下的最優庫存策略的結構，以及公司的庫存決策如何受到不同稅收結構和商業環境的影響。然後，我們計劃將我們的分析推廣到動態設置，包括具有單個會計期間和多個會計期間的動態庫存模型。我們還將考慮虧損結轉的情況。

11501718.label: Realisation of objectives
11501718.value: The objectives have been fully realized. • For objective 1, we considered a newsvendor model with a general tax function. In particular, we characterized the optimal newsvendor ordering policies for convex tax functions, including the proportional and progressive tax functions. • For objective 2, we found that various tax policies have mixed effects on inventory decisions. Convexity of the tax function introduces risk-aversion-like preference, which drives a lower order quantity compared to the case without tax consideration. The loss carryforward policy, however, may introduce a reserve incentive to drive a higher order quantity. The joint force of different policies may result in an ambiguous effect. • For objective 3, we have successfully extended the single-period (newsvendor) model to multiple period settings, including the cases of the lost-sales model and backordering model, and the cases with a single accounting period or multiple accounting periods with loss carryforward.

11501718.label: Major findings and research outcome
11501718.value: Major findings and research outcomes: As summarized above, we fully characterized the optimal policies under corporate income tax for various inventory systems, including the lost-sales and backordering systems, systems with single or multiple accounting periods, and the systems with loss carryforward. We show that state-dependent basestock policies are optimal. We also characterized the effect of taxation on optimal policies. In particular, we show that tax function convexity creates risk-aversion-like incentive to drive lower ordering quantities while loss carryforward introduces a reverse incentive. The combination of both may result in ambiguous effects, depending on the strength of the two forces. Ignoring taxation in inventory decisions may result in significant profit losses. We have published the major findings in the following article that appeared in IISE Transactions in 2023: Zhan Pang, Yixuan Xiao. 2023. Inventory control under corporate income tax and accrual accounting. IISE TRANSACTIONS. Vol. 55, No. 8, 833-845. https://doi.org/10.1080/24725854.2022.2128235

11501718.value: This project opens the door to a greater research area. There are several ongoing research topics leveraging the techniques and insights derived from the current project. For example, 1. Commodity risk management and taxation. 2. For-profit firm’s charitable inventory donation.

11501718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11501718.value: In our humble view, given the significant impact of the taxation cost that stands for 20-40% regulatory cost for firms operating in jurisdictions with taxation, arguably most of the countries in the world, including the US, our model could and should serve as a baseline model to analyze any dynamic inventory system in the real world. 11501818.label: Project Objectives
11501818.value: Develop a new framework of dynamic trading games. Apply the new framework to relevant theoretical and/or policy-related issues in economics.
rows: Develop a new framework of dynamic trading games.
Apply the new framework to relevant theoretical and/or policy-related issues in economics.

11501818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11501818.value: This project develops a new game theoretical framework for analyzing dynamic trading environments. This project primarily concerns situations in which an informed trader faces a sequence of uninformed traders who sequentially arrive and negotiate terms of trade. The key features of the framework are the following: (i) the gain from trading is the informed trader’s private information, (ii) the informed trader can freely switch from negotiating with one counterparty to another, and (iii) uninformed traders compete with each other by offering different sales mechanisms to attract the informed trader. Compared to existing frameworks in the literature, this framework affords a wider array of sales mechanisms to uninformed traders. The set of available mechanisms includes price-posting mechanisms, option contracts, and all standard bargaining protocols. This feature renders the framework applicable to various environments, including markets for retail products in which price-posting mechanisms are prevalent and financial markets in which more sophisticated mechanisms (e.g., option contracts) are commonplace. In terms of methodology, the project combines dynamic game theory and competing mechanism design approaches. The dynamic game theory approach assumes that the trading process follows a specific extensive-form game whose rule is chosen outside of the game. On the other hand, the competing mechanism design assumes that traders inside the market choose the trading process themselves. The combination of these two approaches is expected to provide a complete picture of how markets function in dynamic environments. The project applies the new framework to various theoretical and policy-related questions, such as: 1. The project examines which mechanisms are chosen by uninformed traders in different environments. This research is expected to provide insights into why different mechanisms are observed in different markets. 2. The project examines how changes in the information structure affect the equilibrium trading pattern. This research will answer the question as to how market transparency/opacity affects market outcomes. The same question has also been the focus of recent policies in, for example, insurance, credit, and financial markets. The project is expected to improve our understanding of these policies. 3. The project investigates how changes in the arrival process of uninformed traders affect the equilibrium market outcome. In particular, it aims to investigate whether or not the equilibrium outcome approaches the competitive equilibrium outcome as the friction in the arrival process vanishes. This research is expected to provide a game theoretical foundation for competitive equilibrium theory.

11501818.label: Realisation of objectives
11501818.value: Objective 1: Develop a new theoretical framework of dynamic trading games. The project has developed a new economic model for dynamic trading with three key components. Firstly, there is asymmetric information among the market participants, meaning that some have access to information that others do not. Secondly, there are frictions involved when searching for and matching with a trading counterpart. Lastly, market participants have the flexibility to choose which trading mechanism (trading protocol) to employ in determining the terms of trade. The model considers a scenario in which a single trader (a seller of a financial asset) sequentially searches for and matches with dealers to sell the asset. There is asymmetric information between the trader and dealers. The dealers do not directly observe the trader's own value of the asset, history of interaction with other dealers, or how long the trader has been searching for trading counterparts. However, the dealers can use any mechanism to solicit relevant information from the trader and ultimately determine the terms of trade. This new theoretical model is presented in the paper titled "Dynamic Trading in a Decentralized Market: A Mechanism Design Approach" (with Jin-Wook Chang). A version of the paper is available at the link provided in Part C of the report. The key feature of the model is that multiple dealers compete for a single trader, each potentially employing different mechanisms. This means that the model is formulated as a competing mechanism game (Peters, M., “Competing Mechanisms,” The Canadian Journal of Economics, Vol. 47, No. 2, 2014). Additionally, the trader can freely terminate negotiations with one dealer and switch to another. These two features pose two technical challenges for analysis. First, the revelation principle does not hold, as it does in other models of competing mechanisms. Second, because it is possible for the trader to interact with multiple dealers (either sequentially or simultaneously), it is difficult to determine each dealer's equilibrium posterior beliefs regarding the trader's private information. The research team of the project has developed a new technique, called the "internalization principle," to solve the technical issues mentioned earlier. Essentially, this principle states that it is optimal for each dealer to match any other offers available in the market. In technical terms, it is optimal for all dealers to internalize all other available mechanisms in the market into their own mechanisms. As a result, the trader never has an incentive to switch from one dealer to another in equilibrium and will trade the asset with the first encountered dealer. The internalization principle simplifies the problem of competing mechanisms to a simpler problem: each dealer's profit-maximizing problem in equilibrium is equivalent to the standard mechanism design problem with the agent's type-dependent outside option. The project's research team could analyze this problem using the existing techniques available in the literature (for example, Chang, D., "Optimal Sales Mechanism with Outside Options," Journal of Economic Theory, 2021). Overall, the project has developed a comprehensive framework that considers the complexities of real-world markets. The developed model aims to provide both theoretical and practical insights into how various dynamic markets function. The model's complexity presented substantial technical challenges, but the project has resolved these challenges by developing a novel technique. Objective 2: Apply the new framework to relevant theoretical and/or policy-related issues in economics. With the principle of internalization, the research team of the project was able to characterize the model's equilibrium. The research team then applied this characterization result to address relevant theoretical and/or policy-related issues in economics. To summarize the main findings, our first result shows when and why dealers in over-the-counter markets use multiple trading protocols (mechanisms), including a simple posting-price mechanism and an option contract. Our second result investigates the equilibrium distribution of trading mechanisms employed by different dealers. Finally, our third result analyzes the implications of competition between dealers on market efficiency and social welfare, providing theoretical guidance on how dynamic trading markets should be regulated. Overall, the project successfully fulfilled both Objectives 1 and 2. Some of the findings and outcomes are presented in a paper titled "Dynamic Trading in a Decentralized Market: A Mechanism Design Approach" (with Jin-Wook Chang), which is being prepared for submission to top-tier academic journals in economic theory and financial economics. Additional results will be included in several other drafts that are currently being prepared.

11501818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11501818.value: This project focuses on the supply side of the market, specifically examining the interaction between a single trader holding a financial asset for sale and multiple dealers competing for this trader's business. Future research may aim to extend this model by including both the demand and supply sides. Such an extension would provide a more complete picture of how dynamic markets function. Another potential direction for future research is to incorporate the idea of information design into the model developed in this project. Dealers are often more informed about alternative offers available in the market and therefore more knowledgeable about the trader's outside options. It would be interesting to investigate how this information should (or should not) be revealed to maximize each dealer's expected revenue, as well as the welfare implications that such information revelation has.

11501818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11501818.value: We investigate why buyers and sellers in decentralized markets use specific protocols to trade an asset while competing with others. Our model incorporates many realistic features, such as asymmetric information (buyers may not know how sellers value the asset), search friction (sellers have to wait to meet with a buyer at a random time), and a rich set of trading protocols (mechanisms) that each market participant can choose from to determine the terms of trades. In particular, market participants in our model can design a complex protocol that takes into account their competitors' protocols. The aim of the model is to offer both theoretical and practical insights into how various decentralized dynamic markets function in reality. The complexity of the model makes it applicable to a variety of contexts. However, this complexity also poses numerous technical challenges when analyzing the model. To address these challenges, the project developed a novel technique called the "internalization principle.” The project utilized the developed model and technique to address various economic issues. For instance, it provides insights on why and how a complex trading mechanism (such as an option contract) should be used, and what welfare implications this use of a complicated trading mechanism has. The project also applies these insights to policy-related issues in the real world.

rows: Conduct empirical tests to analyze the levels of VAT tax avoidance before and after the Business-Tax-to VAT reform for firms with different ownership interests by incorporating the changes in intergovernmental agency relationship. Identify the key factors that affects the changes in tax reporting behavior after the reform and the implications for relevant stakeholders, including governments and corporate managers.

11501918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11501918.value: Why government-controlled firms avoid taxes has long constituted an enigma for both researchers and tax professionals. Tang, Mo and Chan (2017) provide an analysis to explain this puzzle from a corporate income tax perspective. This research extends the work of Tang et al. (2017) to validate their intergovernmental tax avoidance model from a value-added tax perspective and enhances the versatility of agency theory in explaining tax avoidance. In China, a large number of listed firms are controlled either by the central or local governments. Thus, governments play dual, but conflicting, roles as controlling shareholders of firms (who want to minimize tax expenses) and tax collectors (who want to maximize tax revenues). As tax collectors, local governments who face budgetary pressures to cover welfare and other expenditures have strong incentives for discouraging firms from engaging in tax avoidance. However, as the controlling shareholder of firms, these governments are the major beneficiaries from the after-tax returns on their investments in the firms that they control. Thus, they possess a strong interest to direct their firms towards tax avoidance to maximize the resources under their control. There is thus a conflict of self-interest. Since 2012, China has launched a landmark tax reform, replacing the business tax (BT) with a value-added tax (VAT) for all industry sectors (i.e., the Business-Tax-to-VAT Reform). This reform will reduce the relevant tax burden on industries by approximately 10% (or approximately ¥500 billion) in 2016 (compared to 2015). This tax reform has significant implications for tax revenue shared by local governments and the central government. Prior to the tax reform, 100% of the business tax (BT) collected belonged to the local government, whereas the VAT collected was shared in the ratio of 3:1 between the central and the local governments. After the reform, funds collected through the VAT are to be equally shared between the central and the local governments, and there will be no BT. Due to this new requirement for sharing tax revenue, we expect that there will be an increase or a decrease in tax avoidance by government-controlled corporations, depending on the way that the tax sharing ratio changes for the respective government owners. This research project will examine the impact of this reform on intergovernmental agency conflicts and tax avoidance by government-controlled firms. Specifically, it will investigate how this tax reform affects the incentives of the relevant principals and agents in their tax-reporting decisions.

11501918.label: Realisation of objectives
11501918.value: We have successfully achieved the two revised project objectives. The research activities carried out during the project period are summarized below: 1. Investigation of the VAT mechanism and related institutional background We conducted a comprehensive review of the mechanism of the value-added tax (VAT) following the Business-Tax-to-VAT Reform. We also investigated this reform at different stages of implementation for key sectors, including construction, real estate, asset leasing, and consumer service sectors, to identify the changes in the tax burden of different companies. 2. Development of a new proxy for VAT tax avoidance The traditional effective tax rate (or its variations) used to proxy for income tax avoidance cannot be used to measure VAT avoidance because VAT is not based on income. As there is limited research on firm-level VAT avoidance, partly due to the complexity of the VAT mechanism and partly due to the lack of public disclosure of VAT paid by firms, we need to develop a new measure for VAT tax avoidance. Though we find a proxy for VAT avoidance proposed in a recent study (Zhang et al. 2021), we find that proxy is very noisy. In the Zhang et al. (2021) study, VAT avoidance is measured by the residual of a regression model based on the VAT burden and the core items related to the tax burden in financial reporting, such as sales and inventory. For the VAT burden regression model, Zhang et al. (2021) rely on the normal sales and purchases estimated by other regression models. Thus, their proxy of VAT avoidance is an indirect measure, and significant noises can be generated in different estimation stages. After consultation with practitioners, we constructed a more direct and logical measure for VAT avoidance by determining the difference between the amount of VAT actually paid and the amount that should be paid to the tax authorities. The proxy was validated by anecdotal evidence. Since VAT is an off-price tax, and there is no direct information about the current VAT payment to tax authorities in the published financial reports, we estimated a firm's VAT payment by using the information on education surcharges or urban construction and maintenance taxes to work backward to find the net VAT paid to the tax authorities. The VAT payable is calculated by the amount of output value-added tax minus the deductible input value-added tax. Therefore, the amount of net VAT payable to the tax authorities can be determined by using the book value of sales and purchases and the appropriate VAT tax rates for a given industry to estimate the output VAT and input VAT. Thus, our proxy for VAT avoidance is based on established formula relationships and not based on multiple layers of regression estimations. 3. Data Collection During the project period, the research activities were affected by Hong Kong's social unrest in 2019, and the COVID-19 pandemic started in early 2020. While we could not hire a full-time research assistant with in-depth knowledge of the Chinese tax regulations as planned initially, we subsequently hired a qualified part-time research assistant to work on the project after experiencing delays. We collected 30,568 firm-year observations of Chinese-listed companies during the period from 2010-2019. After eliminating observations in the financial sector, non-government-controlled firms, and observations with missing variables for our analyses, our final sample consists of 7,798 firm-year observations. We manually collected and processed the data to estimate the VAT tax paid to tax authorities and the VAT tax that firms should pay to the tax authorities. We spent much time resolving numerous problems related to inconsistent and missing data and some conceptual issues. Also, we further validated the proxy through consultations with tax partners of CPA firms who have served Chinese-listed clients using a number of sample firms. We consider the successful development of a VAT avoidance proxy based on clear logic and anecdotal evidence a significant research achievement because we are the first to develop such a proxy, and VAT is the largest source of tax revenue in China. 4. Identify the key factors that affect the changes in tax reporting behavior after the reform Because of the pandemic lockdowns and restrictions, we could not directly consult tax officials and tax practitioners in China to identify specific factors affecting firms’ VAT tax reporting behaviors. Instead, we conducted empirical tests based on the model in the project proposal modified by incorporating factors identified through literature review and relevant news reports. However, the preliminary results are not satisfactory. In particular, the preliminary results show that the effect of ownership (central-government owned vs. local-government-owned firms) on VAT tax avoidance is ambiguous. We spent extra efforts to identify any missing factors affecting the reporting behaviors through further literature review and discussions with CPA firm tax partners in Hong Kong and succeeded in identifying the missing variables. Thus, we achieved our Revised Objective #2. 5. We have conducted different empirical tests to examine the hypothesized effects of replacing Business tax with VAT reform and the change in tax sharing on local-government-controlled firms (LGs) and central-government-controlled firms (CGs) before and after the reform. We find that LG firms avoid more tax than CG firms in the pre-reform period, while there is no significant difference between LG and CG firms in the post-reform period. In addition, we find that LG firms avoid less tax in the post-reform period than in the pre-reform period; however, there is no significant difference for CG firms between the pre-and post-reform period. We further analyzed the effect of government ownership percentage and tax sharing ratio on LG and CG firms’ tax avoidance. The results indicate that both LG and CG firms tend to avoid more tax when the government ownership percentage is higher than the tax-sharing ratio. An implication is that a higher degree of privatization (i.e., reducing the level of government ownership) can reduce the avoidance of VAT by government-controlled firms. These results provide further evidence of the impact of intergovernmental agency conflicts on the tax avoidance of government-controlled firms in a VAT context. Together with developing a more reliable and logical proxy for VAT avoidance, we achieved our Revised Objective #1. 6. To consolidate our research findings, we have written up a working paper entitled “Why do government-controlled firms avoid taxes? Further evidence from Business-Tax – to -VAT Reform in China”. The working paper has been submitted to the Asian-Pacific Conference on International Accounting Issues to be held in 2023. Please note that the abstract of the conference paper, which is very similar to the Major Findings in Section 6.1, cannot be uploaded to the system due to technical issues. After the conference, we will incorporate the comments received for submission of the paper to a leading journal. 7. To summarize, the unprecedented lockdowns and social restrictions in the past three years do cause some delays of our research progress. In addition, literature on firm-level VAT avoidance is scant. Thus, we needed to spend extra time and effort to overcome different problems and challenges, such as identifying factors affecting VAT tax avoidance and validating the proxy for VAT avoidance. We are pleased to be able to achieve the two project objectives successfully.

11501918.label: Major findings and research outcome
11501918.value: Value-added tax is commonly levied in most countries in the World and represents the single largest tax revenue in China. Though there are numerous studies on the economic effects of VAT, studies specifically focusing on firm-level VAT avoidance are limited, partly due to the complexity of VAT computations and partly due to the lack of direct public disclosure of VAT paid and payable data. In this study, we overcome these challenges and develop a valid and logical proxy to measure VAT avoidance by firms. We then take advantage of China’s shift from Business Tax to VAT reform to examine how the change in the sharing of tax revenue from VAT between local and central governments affects the tax avoidance behavior of local-government-controlled (LG) versus central-government-controlled (CG) firms. We find that LG firms avoid more tax than CG firms in the pre-reform period, while there is no significant difference between LG and CG firms in the post-reform period. We explain the phenomenon as follows. Before the reform, LG firms had more incentives than CG firms to avoid tax because local governments only shared 25% of the VAT collected. As a result, they encouraged their controlled firms to avoid more taxes. After the reform, the VAT paid by firms is shared equally between local and central governments, and therefore we detect no significant difference in tax avoidance between LG and CG firms. In addition, focusing on the LG firms, we find that LG firms avoid less tax in the post-reform period than in the pre-reform period, while there is no difference in tax avoidance for CG firms before and after the reform. Our further analysis of the effect of government ownership and tax sharing ratio indicates that both LG and CG firms tend to avoid more tax when the government ownership percentage is higher than the tax sharing ratio. Our results provide further evidence of the impact of intergovernmental agency conflict on tax avoidance established by Tang, Mo and Chan (2017) in a new setting, i.e., avoidance of VAT. We are also the first to provide a direct and logical proxy to measure a firm’s VAT tax avoidance which can facilitate future research on VAT reporting. A working paper based on the research outcome has been submitted to Asia-Pacific Conference on International Accounting Issues, to be held in 2023, to solicit comments for further revision and subsequent journal submission.

11501918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11501918.value: Future research on supply chain and VAT avoidance: According to the VAT regulations, a firm’s VAT payable to the tax authorities equals the amount of VAT on sales minus the amount of VAT on purchases. To avoid tax, firms have strong incentives to over-report purchases to have higher input VAT or under-report sales to reduce output VAT. However, a firm’s purchases are its supplier’s sales. In other words, the same transaction affects both the input VAT of a customer and the output VAT of a supplier. Thus, a supplier’s avoidance of output VAT by underreporting sales may be constrained by its customers’ reported purchases and vice versa. Future research can examine, from a supply chain perspective, whether and how the tax avoidance of a firm’s dependent supplier or principal customer is affected after the value-added tax reform. In addition, our current findings show that government-controlled firms tend to avoid more tax when the government ownership percentage is higher than the tax-sharing ratio. It will be interesting to study the tax avoidance behavior when the government-controlled firms’ principal customers or dependent suppliers are non-government-controlled firms compared to government-controlled firms.

11501918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11501918.value: Taking China’s reform to replace Business Tax with Value-Added Tax (VAT) as the setting, this study examines how the affiliated change in the sharing of VAT revenue between local and central governments affects the tax avoidance behavior of local-government-controlled (LG) versus central-government-controlled (CG) firms. We find that LG firms avoid more tax than CG firms in the pre-reform period, while there is no significant difference between LG and CG firms in the post-reform period. In addition, we find that LG firms avoid less tax in the post-reform period than in the pre-reform period, while there is no difference in tax avoidance for CG firms before and after the reform. Our further analysis of the effect of government ownership and tax sharing ratio indicates that both LG and CG firms tend to avoid more tax when the government ownership percentage is higher than the tax sharing ratio. Our results provide further evidence of the impact of intergovernmental agency conflicts on tax avoidance for local versus central government-controlled firms. This study also provides a new proxy to measure VAT avoidance which should contribute to future research on VAT, the largest tax in China and many other countries.
