11600018.label: Major findings and research outcome
11600018.value: The main findings of this research are twofold. First, this research establishes that early modern representations and enactments of Christ’s Passion bring into being a “melodramatic imagination,” which Peter Brooks in his book The Melodramatic Imagination (1976) identified only with the emergence of the secular world of the late 18th century. This argument is established through a detailed excavation and explication of the rhetorical form and conditions of reception of early modern Compianti or Lamentation groups and passion plays. In particular, it demonstrates how, in the case of the flagellants, histrionic lamentation scenes served to encourage them to literally experience the conditions of Christ’s suffering by causing themselves physical, and hence emotional, pain. Secondly, this research establishes that modern secular melodrama grows out of medieval affective piety rather than marking a break with it. It demonstrates that while modern melodrama dramatises the secular martyrdom of ordinary men and women caught in the forces of social injustice, it does so by drawing upon the very substance, themes and history of Christian ethics. This thesis is established through a detailed analysis of the literary text and film, Under Capricorn, which shows not only a correlation between the dramatis personae of the film and Christ’s passion, as the center of the spectator’s identification, but also that melodrama re-enacts the Christian story of the fall, original sin, and redemption in secular terms. The central subsidiary finding concerns the gendered nature of affective piety and its impact on modern melodrama. We demonstrate that in affective piety the emotional paroxysms of the female witnesses to Christ’s passion, especially Mary Magdalene, are shown to lead the faithful of both genders, but especially male flagellants, to spiritual identification with Christ’s suffering. Equally, we establish that through the inspiration of Mary Magdalene, the patron saint of penitent sinners, the female protagonist of modern melodrama is conceived as “fallen woman,” who becomes the center of empathic identification for male and female spectator alike.

11600018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11600018.value: More research needs to be done to complete the inventory and study of Passion plays written between the 17th and early 20th centuries. In particular the plays written by the Jesuits need to be tracked down and their diffusion throughout Europe and South America explained. Passion plays and even films written and/or produced in the 19th and 20th centuries must be added. The history of oratorio and opera is a key tradition that remains to be studied in which the sacred form of the passion melodrama is transposed into a demotic, secular idiom. Finally, more case studies need to be developed in 19th-century literature theatre and 20th-century film to explain how Christian affective piety is transposed into modern melodrama.

11600018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11600018.value: This research contributes to re-thinking the relationship between religion and secular modernity in the West, which is of great significance in the present historical moment where the nature of the historical relationships between world civilizations are being re-conceived. Literary scholars of melodrama, like Peter Brooks, argue that melodrama is a distinctly modern and secular genre that grows out of the collapse of religious values and replaces them. For medieval art historians who study affective piety, melodrama does not exist as a genre or a category that needs to be explained. By developing a history of the rhetorical and emotional impact of art, regardless of its medium, over the long duration of western modernity, this research contributes to reorienting art history away from simply formal concerns to the rhetorical impact of art; demonstrates the centrality of affect and emotion to historical understanding; articulates the history of melodrama as an aesthetic idiom that encompasses a Christian ethics whether in sacred or secular form; and thereby transforms our understanding of the modern genre and the form of modern, western subjectivity it expresses.

11600418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11600418.value: In the past, competitive computer gaming in Hong Kong used to belong to arcades filled by cigarette smoke, deviant youths and triad members, and was shunned by aspirational middle class parents. Nevertheless, game arcades were established as an iconic feature of Hong Kong’s youth culture, to the extent that Hong Kong was recognized as one of world’s ‘arcade capitals’, alongside Tokyo. Arcades have disappeared from most regions in the world, and their number is also declining in Hong Kong. While a good amount of them continue to survive in Hong Kong, competitive gaming has largely moved to the realms of “electronic sports” (eSports). The days of Street Fighter tournaments where the Mong Kok team competed against Sheung Wan are soon over. It won’t be long before arcades and their unique counter-culture of competitive gaming are forgotten also in Hong Kong: studying them now is timely and necessary. With enormous commercial potential, perceived career possibilities, global top-down control, and rigorous training through rote repetition, eSports appears to resemble traditional sports or work as much as it does computer gaming. With Hong Kong government pushing eSports as a hybrid of IT, media and tourism industries, it is set to transform the gaming culture in Hong Kong like it has done elsewhere. This signifies a larger shift in gaming and its public perception, particularly in Hong Kong: from deviant behavior into an increasingly legitimate pursuit sanctioned by parents, teachers, and authorities, portrayed as potentially worthwhile for one’s career. This shift is not, however, without cultural, aesthetical, ethical, and financial implications: who decides what to play, and, how to play? Is this a case of a grassroots culture affording ‘authentic’ and hyper-local identities being replaced by globally uniform cookie-cutter culture? Is this a case of “play” giving way to “work”? The unique situation in Hong Kong provides an excellent and globally unique case for comparative analysis, through which to also address larger trends in the evolution of games and gaming cultures. Through a mixed-method empirical qualitative approach making use of the framework of “circuit of culture” (Du Gay et al. 1997), this project answers the following questions: What are the similarities and differences between arcade and eSports gaming cultures in Hong Kong? What are the unique features of Hong Kong’s arcade culture? Are there cultural heritage to be preserved or lessons to be learned for healthy development of eSports industry and culture in Hong Kong? 在不久的以前，一提到電子遊戲競技，人們就往往聯想起煙霧迷漫，充滿不良少年和黑道中人的「機竇」，是令一眾望子成龍的中產家長們的惡夢。雖然如此，遊戲機中心乃香港青年文化的一個標誌，香港甚至被認定為東京以外世上另一「街機之城」。不過現在遊戲機中心在全球已經式微，就算是在香港，遊戲機中心數量都正日漸減少。雖然香港仍有不少現存的遊戲機中心，街機競技已經遷移至所謂的「電子競技」(亦稱「eSports」)。旺角對上環鬥街霸的日子已告一段落。很快「機竇」和圍繞它的那種獨特反主流電競文化也將會從香港的集體回憶中消失：正因如此，研究和保育這種文化就更顯迫切。電子競技帶來龐大的商業潛能，新的就業機會，全球性上而下式操控鏈和嚴苛的機械式訓練。比起純粹電腦遊戲，電子競技看來更像傳統就業和運動。現時香港政府大力推行電子競技，將其包裝成IT，媒體及旅遊業的融合體。電子競技的到來將會和外地一樣對香港的遊戲文化帶來重大改變。電子競技的普及，顯示出公眾對遊戲的態度已經作出了轉變。尤其是在香港：「打機」由反叛行為變成一個家人，老師和長輩接受的生涯選擇，甚至被認為是出人頭地之路。可是這個改變並不是沒有在文化、美學、道德和財政上的後果：誰決定如何玩？怎樣玩？玩什麼？這一個「原汁原味」，擁有本地身份的草根文化是不是正在被千篇一律的全球式文化取代？這是不是一個犧牲「遊戲」換取「工作」的例子？ 香港的獨特情況提供一個世界上獨一無二的比較分析案例，去幫助我們回應在遊戲和遊戲文化演化上的大小趨勢。這個計劃利用「文化循環」框架 (Du Gay et al. 1997)，透過混合觀察和定性研究方法，嘗試回答以下問題：香港街機和電競文化有何相似和分別之處？香港街機文化有何獨特之處？ 香港街機文化中有沒有需要保育的文化遺產或者需要吸取的教訓，以確保香港電競工業及文化的穩健發展？

11600618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11600618.value: Recently, community art activities have been growing remarkably in Hong Kong with funded support. It is believed that community art can “bring arts closer to the people” and “converge cultural identities among local communities” (Hong Kong Arts Development Council). Substantial public resources have already been invested in community art projects. Government funding has been provided to set up and support community art spaces, examples being oi! and Shanghai Street Artspace. Urban Renewal Authority provides funding for projects integrating community arts and culture in the process of urban renewal. However, not all community art projects are popular. Members of the general public have criticized art works that try to be regional landmarks for being ugly (Ming Pao A02). People worried that community art project is a “stalking horse for gentrification” (Cheung). How to make community art acceptable to the community and bring positive change to the community? There has been very little systematic analysis of the nature and impact of Hong Kong community art (Wong 89). Without learning from past successes and failures, it is hard to conceive a long term strategy for the development of community art. To fill this gap in knowledge, this research undertakes a comparative study of four types of community art projects to evaluate how community art in Hong Kong can be used constructively for community building. These four types of projects are organized by artists, activists, social workers and government officials and serve specific communities. Media coverage and reviews of these projects will be collected and analyzed. In-depth interviews with art practitioners, active participants and audience will be conducted. Participant observation methods will be used to examine the efficacy of the projects. This research will compare the creative strategies of these different community art projects since the 1997 handover. Grant Kester’s dialogical aesthetics and Nicolas Bourriaud’s relational aesthetics will be applied to identify similarities and differences. As a “context provider” rather than “content provider” (Kester 76) art form, it is important to examine the community art within its context. This research will identify a set of best practices in community building and develop models of art making which are aligned with community needs. It will contribute to the reading of Hong Kong community art and would provide terms of reference for artists, curators, researchers, critics, funding bodies and policy-makers on the relationship between art and community. 近年香港的社區藝術活動得到不少資助，有長足的增長，香港藝術發展局相信社區藝術能「拉近社會人士與藝術之間的距離，同時加深大眾對社區的文化認同」，這類項目投入不少公共資源，例如已成立的油街實現和上海街藝術空間專為發展社區藝術，市區重建局在市區重建過程中亦為社區藝術提供資助。然而，並非所有社區藝術都受歡迎，有作為地區標誌的雕塑被受劣評（明報A02），有人擔心社區藝術項目會助長社區「士紳化」。香港的社區藝術是否真的能為社區帶來積極的影響？有關的深入研究很少。如果不了解過去的成敗，很難有效地發展社區藝術。為加深對議題的理解，本研究對四類社區藝術項目進行比較研究，以評估香港的社區藝術在營造社區方面的效能。這四類項目分別由藝術家、社運人士、社會工作者和政府官員主導組織，為特定社區服務。研究將收集這些項目的分析和評論文章，和藝術從業員，義工及觀眾進行深入訪談，並用參與觀察硏究方法去檢視活動項目的成效。這項研究將比較自1997年以來這些社區藝術項目的創作策略，亦會與Grant Kester 的對話美學和Nicolas Bourriaud 的關係美學作比較，看異同。是項研究將尋找出能有效地營造社區及符合社區需要的藝術實踐的方法與模式，並為藝術家、策展人、研究人員、評論人、資助機構和政策制定者提供有關藝術與社區之間的關係更多的參考。

11601218.value: Contribute towards disciplinary debates in public administration by examining the tensions between academic research and real-world problems. Provide systematic empirical evidence on the “social structure” of PA and how it has changed over the last twenty-years. Examine the research topics in public administration and provide a systematic analysis of their relationship to real-world problems in relation to citations and impact, methodology, geography, interdisciplinarity, and collaboration.

11601218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11601218.value: This project will tackle questions at the core of the public administration (PA) discipline by examining the tensions between academia and practice. PA is an interdisciplinary “design science” focused on solving real-world problems. However, as academia has become more professionalized, PA scholars more specialized, and research tools more sophisticated, PA scholars around the globe have argued that these changes have disconnected PA research from real-world practice. This project will systematically examine the changing landscape of PA research to ascertain whether PA scholarship has shifted over the past two decades towards more esoteric topics and an undue focus on method at the expense of tackling real-world problems. Such a project is now possible because advances in technology and methodology allow for a comprehensive evaluation of all published journal output in a given field. Topic modelling methodology identifies latent topics underlying large collections of textual data, allowing themes to emerge from a systematic analysis of a substantive corpus of material. A machine learning algorithm known as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) will be used to uncover the latent topic structure and then establish the distribution of each word and document across these topics. LDA will be applied to the corpus of approximately 13,000 PA articles published in the 16 leading PA journals between 1997 and 2018. The topics identified in this project will be contrasted with real-world problems, policies, and issues. These will be measured at both the global and local policy and administration level using the UN Sustainable Development Goals and an analysis of PA textbook topics. Variations in the relationship between theory and practice will be examined by assessing the extent to which an article is cited and published in a high impact journal, the research methods used, the geographical location of the study, and the degree of interdisciplinarity and international collaboration involved in its production. The project will contribute to the discipline of PA and its development by identifying the most influential research topics and relating these to real-world topics to provide an understanding of PA’s “social structure.” This project will be hosted by the Laboratory for Public Management and Policy, which provides the resources and facilities to undertake integration studies such as topic modelling. The project will be undertaken by scholars experienced in integration studies and the methodology and application of topic modelling. 本研究將透過檢視學術界與實踐之間的對立，來處理公共行政學科核心的問題。公共行政是一門跨學科的「設計科學」，專注於解決現實問題。然而，隨著學術界越趨專業化，公共行政界的學者亦跟隨變得更專門化，研究工具也越來越精密，全球公共行政界的學者認為這些改變促使公共行政研究與現實世界的實踐脫節。本研究將會有系統地檢測公共行政研究的改變狀況，以確定公共行政科的獎學金在過去二十年是否傾向更深奧的主題，以及過分專注於研究方法而犠性現實世界的問題。 現在，因為科技及研究方法的進步，讓我們可以對特定的領域上所有已發表的期刊進行全面評估，讓本研究變得可行。主題建模方法(Topic modelling) 能從大量文本數據中識別潛在主題，能對一分實質的文字資料進行系統性分析，產生出主題。使用名為潛在狄利克分配(LDA)的機器學習演算法來揭示潛在的主題結構，從而在這些主題之間建立每個單詞及文檔的分佈。我們將利用LDA來分析1997年至2018年期間在16份領先的公共行政期刊上發表的大約13,000篇公共行政文章。 由本研究識別出的主題將會與現實世界的問題、政策及議題推行對比。 根據聯合國可持續發展目標和公共行政教科書主題的分析，以全球和地區政策及行政層面作衡量。通過評估文章被引用及被發表於高影響力期刊的程度、所使用的研究方法、研究的地理位置、以及其製作過程所涉及的跨學科和與不同國家合作的程度，來檢測理論與實踐之間關係的變化。本研究將通過識別最有影響力的研究主題，並將其與現實主題聯繫，深入剖析公共行政的社會結構，從而為公共行政學科及其發展作出貢獻。 本研究將由公共管理及政策實驗室主辦，及提供資源和設施，以進行如主題建模等整合研究。由在整合研究，和主題建模的研究方法及應用富經驗的學者負責。

11601218.label: Realisation of objectives
11601218.value: PROJECT OBJECTIVES 1. Contribute towards disciplinary debates in public administration by examining the tensions between academic research and real-world problems. This project objective was successfully achieved. It is argued that there is academic-practitioner divide in public administration because scholarship is not relevant to practice. However, evidence is equivocal. We examined this divide in the USA in Walker et al. (2019) and internationally in Walker et al. (under review). Our more focused analysis of this divide in the USA examined scholarship in Public Administration Review and contrasted this with practitioner writing in PA Times – both journals are owned by the American Society for Public Administration. In this article we showed that just over 50% of the topics of scholars and practitioners were alike, but that the weight attached to these topics varied in each corpora, indicative of a divide. In Walker et al. (under review) we analysed the wider international literature and examined three corpora: (1) academic journals that did not include any reference to practice in the aims and scope, (2) academic journals that referred to practice in the aims and scope and (3) PAIS, a practice corpus of government documents. This study pointed towards a larger gap than Walker et al. (2019) - nearly 70% of the topics have more differences that similarities between the academic corpora and the practice corpus. Unlike much prior research on the academic-practitioner divide we were able to examine this difference over time – prior studies either examined literature over relatively short time periods or were reliant on cross-sectional primary data. Topic modelling indicated varying importance attached to topics over our twenty-year period of analysis, with few examples of congruence. Keyness analysis demonstrated strong differences between the early and late period in our dataset in all corpora. In short, our findings are suggestive that scholarship is not relevant to practice. The consequences of these findings are important for the discipline of public administration, which is characterised as a design science that connects theory with practice. 2. Provide systematic empirical evidence on the “social structure” of PA and how it has changed over the last twenty-years. This project objective will be successfully achieved, currently we are at around 80% of the way towards this goal, and it will be completed when we published a CUP Elements book. To date analysis of the “social structure’ of public administration, that is the concepts and methods used, has been often based on deductive review of topics, origins, maturity and intellectual traditions at the level of the discipline or meta-analysis or bibliometric visualisation at the topic level. Our first-time application of inductive computational social sciences techniques has identified 50 topics (topic names were agreed by an expert panel) based on the journals identified in the project proposal. The top 10 topics – health care, federal government, performance management, environmental regulation and human resource management, networks, citizen participation, transparency, science policy and local government (topic weight 31.56%) – differ from those identified in more traditional reviews that have highlighted theory (e.g. organisational theory, policy analysis) and methods. 3. Examine the research topics in public administration and provide a systematic analysis of their relationship to real-world problems in relation to citations and impact, methodology, geography, interdisciplinarity, and collaboration. This objective will be partial realised. This is because of the challenges we faced in identifying suitable practice corpora to contrast with scholarly writing – the PAIS corpus does not permit this analysis. Rather we are developing chapters in the CUP book on the practice relevance of scholarship through an analysis of the World Bank Governance Indicators, and contrasting the citation, methodology, geography and collaboration of scholar work against these indicators. 4. Extend our knowledge of bibliometric methods by introducing and demonstrating the application of topic modelling methodology to the field of PA, and show its application. This objective was successfully met. Topic modelling and corpus linguistics are still little used in the public administration discipline. For example, Hollibaugh (2019) provides an application for illustrative purposes and Kaufmann and Haans (2021) apply colocation analysis to the topic of red tape. To our knowledge, our publications in PAR (Walker et al. 2019, and under review) and our CUP remain first time application of topic modelling and corpus linguistics in the field. We thus were able to demonstrate the power and value of using these methodologies in our discipline for systematic integration studies and reviews. Walker et al. (2019) has been cited 42 times (Google Scholar), including reviews on the utilization of research in public administration and in other disciplines including energy, marketing, medicine and political science. This project paves the way for further research in public administration by demonstrating how these methodologies can be used to complement more traditional bibliometric and review process in the discipline thereby tackling major questions in the discipline. CHALLENGES ADDRESSED In the Mid-Term Report we highlighted challenges in identifying corpora that captured “real-world problems”. We identified the PAIS database that collates English-language government documents, grey literature, research reports, hearings, and internet resources on public affairs from a variety of sources. This proved to be a valuable dataset including nearly 16,000 documents published by 931 entities and was suitable for topic modelling. In the second project extension request I outlined three challenges: 1. Ongoing administrative responsibilities of the PI have continued to slow good progress on this project. Below forthcoming publications are reported. 2. Computational problems were resolved, and we were able to move forward with analysis. 3. The PAIS dataset was successfully analysed and used to inform the findings of the project and publication. Undergraduate student involvement in the project was limited because of the pandemic. RESEARCH OUTPUT Research output is not finalised; however, we anticipate the following additional publications: 1. Public Administration Review (#1 journal JCR SSCI 5-year impact ranking). A journal manuscript is under a second round of review. We are optimistic about the publication of the manuscript given the very supportive nature of two of the reviews. We expect to hear the final decision in the summer. 2. Cambridge University Press Elements in Public and Non-profit Management. A contract has been signed with CUP for the delivery of this book titled “The Topics of Public Administration: Perspectives from Computational Social Sciences and Corpus Linguistics”. Delivery date October 1, 2023. In addition to our conference presentations, the findings from this study were presented at the School of Governance, Utrecht University on March 7, 2023.

11601218.label: Major findings and research outcome
11601218.value: In this project we conducted a first-time application of computational social science and corpus linguistics techniques over a twenty-five-year period in public administration to examine (1) the relevance of academic research to practice and (2) the social structure of the discipline: (1) We developed unique databases academic and practice corpora. Academic journals drawn from the Social Science Citation Index were divided into academic and acadmic-practice related journals (based on aims and scope) and we scraped the PAIS dataset to provide a practice corpus. Using computational social science techniques, we identified topics in academic and practice corpora in (1) the USA and (2) internationally and conclude that the topics that academics and practitioners write about have more differences that similarities. Using corpus linguistics we examined this question over time – something not typically done in the extant literature – and our results again confirm the largely different agendas of academics and practitioners. The question of relevance of academic research to practice is an important topic in public administration because it is a ‘design science’ that seeks to tackle real world problems. Discussion of our findings suggests that this divide has arisen because of changes in higher education and the ‘here and now’ concerns of practice. (2) The social structure of public administration. Using the inductive method of topic modelling of an academic corpus of journal articles we identified 50 topics. The top 10 topics were: health care, federal government, performance management, environmental regulation and human resource management, networks, citizen participation, transparency, science policy and local government (topic weight 31.56%). These topics differ from more traditional deductive review approaches, which may examine theories (e.g. organizational theory, policy analysis) and methods demonstrating the value of computational technique for the review of an academic discipline. Findings have been published in Public Administration Review are expected to be published in Public Administration Review and in a Cambridge University Press book. These publications serve to demonstrate the utility of computational and linguistics techniques in public administration. Our 2019 article in Public Administration Review has received over 40 citations (Google Scholar) informing scholarship on the nature of the public administration discipline as well as in energy, marketing, medicine and political science.

11601218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11601218.value: Computational social sciences and corpus linguistics have great potential for the conduct of systematic integration studies to advance knowledge in public administration. They can be applied to a range of questions about the development of the field and questions therein. Future research will be undertaken by this team using collocation analysis to further delve into questions about the relevance of academic research to practice using the corpora from this project. For example, health care, contracting, strategic planning, and budgeting were four topics common to our academic and practice corpora. Collocation analysis can be used to delve into these corpora to understand the meaning of these topics and how they are talked about in academia and practice.

11601218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11601218.value: In this project we conducted a first-time application of computational social science and corpus linguistics techniques over a twenty-five-year period to examine: (1) The relevance of academic research to practice in public administration. Using computational social science techniques, we identified topics in academic and practice corpora in (1) the USA and (2) internationally and conclude that the topics that academics and practitioners write about have more differences that similarities. Using corpus linguistics we examined this question over time, and our results again confirm the largely different agendas of academics and practitioners. The question of relevance of academic research to practice is an important topic in public administration because it is a ‘design science’ that seeks to tackle real world problems. Discussion of our findings suggests that this divide has arisen because of changes in higher education and the ‘here and now’ concerns of practice. (2) The social structure of public administration. Using the inductive method of topic modelling of an academic corpus of journal articles we identified 50 topics. These topics differ from more traditional deductive review approaches demonstrating the value of computational technique for the review of an academic discipline.

11602618.label: Project Objectives
11602618.value: Cultural Transfer: We will investigate the practice of ceramic painting and glazing methods to identify suitable elements for a transfer to the surface glazing for 3D printing. We will achieve this through interviews with ceramic artisans and a residence of the PI at Pilchuck School of Glass 2017. We will reduce the interviews with ceramic artists. This is to reflect the change in the budget. We aim to have one studio visit to China and will attempt to have a second and third interview via skype or equivalent software permitted in China. Tools and Techniques: We aim to develop tools (software and hardware) and techniques (chemical formulas and guidelines) able to distribute, activate and preserve a series of photo-reactive chemicals on 3D printed substrates. This will be achieved through the design of prototypical small-scale Computer Aided Manufacturing (CAM) solutions and custom-made software. We will use the film/photo equipment at the School of Creative Media to document the process and results. This objective will remain unchanged, however, reflecting the budget change, we will construct only two CNC machine solutions and will need to reduce the experimenting on developing several machines for comparison. Prototypes: We will test and evaluate the fidelity of the developed chemical glazing types and tooling methods with a variety of gradually increasing geometrical complex 3D printed objects. We will demonstrate this through the design and fabrication of a series of 3D printed prototypes and document process and results. We will reduce this task, reflecting the significant change in the budget. We will work only with SLA technologies instead of a wide range of 3D printed substrates. We will though retain the idea of increased shape complexity in the prototypes. Comparative Craftsmanship: We will establish a model for the incorporation of traditional craft knowledge for 3D printing as a method for design innovation. This will be achieved through a public exhibition comparatively showcasing the 3D print and glaze prototypes and CAM systems with existing Chinese ceramics and production methods. This objective remains, yet the size of the exhibition will be adjusted, reflecting the cut in funding. Interdisciplinary Research: We will establish a method of interdisciplinary research in the field of applied arts and crafts and digital design. This will be achieved through a recorded symposium alongside the exhibition with guests from engineering, cultural heritage, material science and ceramic craft, resulting in an edited catalogue publication of the exhibition and symposium. Again, this objective remains active, yet the publication will reflect the reduced funding, by allowing other artistic research of the PI Tobias Klein to be part of the publication and with this utilize other private and grant funding sources.

11602618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11602618.value: 現今3D打印技術提供了前所未有的可能性去製造任何形狀和部件，不論是它的幾何複雜性或與傳統工業生產方式保持一致性。 儘管如此，3D打印製成的消費者等級產品在現今市場仍然佔極少數。 縱使目前3D打印技術在物件外型上的複雜性、功能、以及於部件的精確度方面表現優異，可是此技術卻不適用於雕刻複雜的圖案、花紋或著色於物件表面上。 這個將外形與表面的結合的難題要追溯至歷史上先製作陶藝器皿的形狀，然後再才在其表面雕刻以作上釉。 在中國陶瓷的悠久的歷史中，憑著強盛的求知慾及力求創新的心態，中國陶瓷工匠於燒製過程中逐漸理解、平衡有關材料間的反應、陶瓷外型、上釉等複雜知識。 自唐朝起，即使尋找一種最著名的藍色顏料，也引領著千年各種有關原料混合及上釉技術的發現。 每步有關工具、方法與技術發展，都會興起新派的藝術表達方式、風格、與設計。 本研究旨在探討此工藝的轉移方法 ── 透過綜合科學、歷史、文化及技術考慮，從而分析及深思給3D打印上釉的數位製作過程。 在發展3D打印物件的上色方法和工具的同時，會相應引起使用積層製造的工業在新設計及藝術雕刻的發展。 在此，我們將提出一套跨學科的實驗性研究方針，其結合了材料實驗、目錄冊、設計應用、以及公眾宣傳。 我們將建立一套有關適用化學試劑的指標，並研發用於3D打印表面的機械電子及軟件工具。 接著，我們將為這些工具在現有的3D打印樣本進行測試，為數位工藝建立設計初步模型。 本研究結果將與已製成的工具、材料應用、設計方式、及與傳統中國陶藝有關的初步模型同時於公共展覽中展示。 為吸引更廣泛的研究員、藝術家及設計師，我們會組織座談會，並邀請從事陶瓷藝術、材料科學、工藝、及計算機輔助製造業的嘉賓。 我們會剪輯座談會錄影去出版目錄，並會在學術刊物中發表研究發現，以進一步分享科學及科技與藝術間的混合。

11602618.label: Realisation of objectives
11602618.value: 1. OBJECTIVE: Cultural Transfer: We will investigate the practice of ceramic painting and glazing methods to identify suitable elements for a transfer to the surface glazing for 3D printing. We will achieve this through interviews with ceramic artisans and a residence of the PI at Pilchuck School of Glass 2017. REVISION: We will reduce the interviews with ceramic artists. This is to reflect the change in the budget. We aim to have one studio visit to China and will attempt to have a second and third interview via skype or equivalent software permitted in China. REALISATION: We have made no progress toward the objective of talking with China-based artisans and a visit to the ceramic capital of China - Jingdezhen, was simply not possible. Instead, we have made contact with local (Hong Kong Based) Ceramic Artists, and have developed an in-depth relationship with the University Museum and Art Gallery (UMAG) of the University of Hong Kong (HKU). This has led to the many 3D scans being made of their ceramic collection. Please see the letter about the fruitful cooperation with the UMAG that has led as well to the exhibition of the results of the research in the Xinghua Music Conservatory and later in the UMAG itself. 2. OBJECTIVE: Tools and Techniques: We aim to develop tools (software and hardware) and techniques (chemical formulas and guidelines) able to distribute, activate and preserve a series of photoreactive chemicals on 3D-printed substrates. This will be achieved through the design of prototypical small-scale Computer Aided Manufacturing (CAM) solutions and custom-made software. We will use the film/photo equipment at the School of Creative Media to document the process and results. REVISION: This objective will remain unchanged, however, reflecting the budget change, we will construct only two CNC machine solutions and will need to reduce the experimenting on developing several machines for comparison. REALISATION: The research progress is two-fold, developing CAD/CAM software on the one hand and hardware on the other. The following split reflects this and documents the progress made in both areas. We have fully achieved this through new mechanical CNC developments, chemical investigation, and software solutions. Please see the extensive documentation in part C of the report. 3. OBJECTIVE: Prototypes: We will test and evaluate the fidelity of the developed chemical glazing types and tooling methods with a variety of gradually increasing geometrical complex 3D printed objects. We will demonstrate this through the design and fabrication of a series of 3D-printed prototypes and document processes and results. REVISION: We will reduce this task, reflecting the significant change in the budget. We will work only with SLA technologies instead of a wide range of 3D-printed substrates. We will though retain the idea of increased shape complexity in the prototypes. REALISATION: We have successfully created a series of increasingly geometrically complex prototypes. The first prototypes were based not based on existing museum works but were created to test the complexity and limitations of the developed set-up. The second and third series were based on 3D scans from the UMAG collection and were working towards the adaptation of brushstroke techniques through modified software tool paths. We successfully created these high-resolution designs for publications in the area of Art, Science, and Technology as well as in the field of Museology. Please see the extensive documentation in part C of the report. 4. OBJECTIVE: Comparative Craftsmanship: We will establish a model for the incorporation of traditional craft knowledge for 3D printing as a method for design innovation. This will be achieved through a public exhibition comparatively showcasing the 3D print and glaze prototypes and CAM systems with existing Chinese ceramics and production methods. REVISION: This objective remains, yet the size of the exhibition will be adjusted, reflecting the cut in funding. REALISATION: We have held a public exhibition and workshops at the University Museum and Art Gallery. The exhibition, titled Metamorphosis or Confrontation, opened on the 20th of May 2020 and closed on the 6th of December 2020. The exhibition featured the research and was as well part of the prestigious Ars Electronica 2020 program. Additional workshops were held and artist talks promoted the research. Please see the extensive documentation in part C of the report. 5. OBJECTIVE: Interdisciplinary Research: We will establish a method of interdisciplinary research in the field of applied arts and crafts and digital design. This will be achieved through a recorded symposium alongside the exhibition with guests from engineering, cultural heritage, material science, and ceramic craft, resulting in an edited catalogue publication of the exhibition and symposium. REVISION: Again, this objective remains active, yet the publication will reflect the reduced funding, by allowing other artistic research of the PI Tobias Klein to be part of the publication and with this utilize other private and grant funding sources. REALISATION: The PI, Dr. Tobias Klein has incorporated the research in his Ph.D. dissertation. Furthermore, based on the Solo retrospective exhibition of the PI's work, we have published a book containing four views on the exhibition and on the larger issue of ceramic research, embedded in the context of the emerging discipline of Digital Craft. We have invited speakers at the prestigious Techfocus, organised by the American Institute for Conservation’s Electronic Media Group, and lastly extended the research and published it at ISEA 2022. The last journal publication is planned for 2023 and is in works with the director of the UMAG to be published in the field of Museology.

11602618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11602618.value: There are several venues for further development of the research: Technical: The research proved the viability of applying cyanotype-based gelatine coatings for UV laser activation in 3 degrees of freedom robotic set-up. Using a higher degree of freedom robotics, such as robotic arms will undoubtedly increase possible complexity. In order to do so, grants in the area of ITF would need to be developed to commercialize the findings to date. Artistic: The research has shown an impact in the area of cultural heritage. This could further be extended through reflection in other museological areas and a research proposal has been successfully submitted and awarded in the area of ceramic printing and submitted in the area of digitally enhanced glass craft. Cultural: One of the areas to improve is working with actual ceramic craft practitioners to learn and further augment the craft with digital methods, synergetically researching the potential of one of the oldest crafts, ceramics. This extends to working with the museum and the transfer of museological concepts regarding the notion of the replica in conservation. We are working on an extensive journal article to discuss the implications of this approach.

11602618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11602618.value: 3D printing offers the unprecedented possibility of manufacturing any shape regardless of its geometric complexity. However, most commercially available printing methods focus only on the shape of the object and lack surface complexity such as colouration. In contrast, Chinese ceramics have throughout millennia mastered intricately combining the shape of an object with its surface. Based on a masterful knowledge of material reactions, form, and glazing during the firing process, the search for even the single, most famous colour blue resulted in a millennium of discoveries of material combinations and glazing techniques. At each step, new tools, methods, and techniques led to new artistic expressions, styles, and designs. Through this analysis of Ceramic Craft, the research was able to develop radical new transfer methods to combine scientific, historical, cultural, and technical considerations in order to analyze and reflect the digital making process of a glaze-like process for 3D printing. It lead to the development of methods and tools to digitally paint onto the surfaces of 3D printed substrates which in turn allowed reciprocally the development of new designs and artistic articulations for creative industries using additive manufacturing.

11602718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11602718.value: With the increasing number of student-led social movements around the world, it is becoming increasingly evident that there is a pressing need to better understand the social and political participation (collectively referred to as civic participation) of our younger generations. The call to action has possibly never held more weight than it does now, especially following the recent events of “Occupy Central” in Hong Kong, a large-scale demonstration movement which, if anything, seemed to convey the growing trend of youth involvement in civic life. However, most local studies on youth civic participation define participation narrowly, often either focusing on volunteering or political participation, rather than auditing both forms of participation. Moreover, most of these studies offer a ‘snapshot’ of youth participation in society, rather than a longitudinal outlook of the casual relationships that explain civic engagement, as well as conditions relating to the changes or stability of different forms of social and political engagement over time. Hence, the current study aims to examine the developmental patterns of civic engagement among university students in Hong Kong. More specifically, using Klandermans and Oegema’s Action mobilization process model (1987), the study investigates the dynamics of civic participation, as taken in their own rights and viewed as part of an empirically-analyzed profile, over a period of time in Hong Kong. A mixed-methods longitudinal research design will be adopted, with the primary methods of data collection being self-reported e-surveys and follow-up in-depth interviews. The quantitative and qualitative components of the panel study would be collected in two waves, whereby the aim of the in-depth interviews would be to elucidate key dimensions of the causal relationships found in the results from the e-surveys. The study will use multi-stage probabilistic sampling approaches to recruit university students from all eight UGC-funded universities to join this panel study. The expected sample is 800 students, with 60-80 of them involved as a subsample in the in-depth interviews. Analyzing the quantitative data through clustering techniques and panel regression analyses, and qualitative data through thematic analysis of interviewee’s experiences and subjectivities, it is hoped that we can empirically test the process model for its validity in explaining the various patterns of civic engagement in the Hong Kong context. It is hoped that advancing this line of inquiry would enable us to achieve a deeper understanding of the changing landscapes and heterogeneous nature of civic engagement among our youth. 隨着在世界各地由學生主導的社會運動日漸上升，對年輕一代的社會和政治參與(亦被稱為公民參與)的了解變得愈來愈重要。尤其因為近年發生的｢佔領中環｣(Occupy Central)事件，更反映此研究題目的重要性更勝從前。這項大型示威活動似乎反映出一股青年投入公民生活的風氣。不過，大多數的本地研究在探討青年的公民參與時，對公民參與的定義都會有較狹窄的看法。他們多會集中於義工活動或政治參與二者其中之一，而並非將兩者皆考慮在內。再者，這些研究通常只捕捉到當下青年社會參與的片段，而非根據長遠觀察去闡明公民參與的因果關係，亦未有探討在不同時期影響着社會及政治參與形式的因素。有見及此，是次研究希望了解在香港的大學生公民參與方面的發展模式。透過運用Klandermans和Oegema (1987)的｢行動化過程模式｣ (Action mobilization process model)，是次研究會探討香港大學生在不同時期公民參與的形態，如參與者的權利及視之為實驗形式的收集。 是次研究將會使用｢混合的縱貫性研究｣(mixed-methods longitudinal research design)，以自填式網上問卷和後續的深入訪問收集第一手數據。是次追蹤研究的質性和量性部份的數據會分開兩次進行收集。質性的深入訪問收集在於進一步探究量性的網上問卷所發現的結果。是次研究會使用｢多重機率抽樣法｣ (multi-stage probabilistic sampling)去招募全部八間資助大學的學生參與研究。網上問卷的目標參與者為800人，而深入訪問的目標人數則為當中大約60至80 人。量性數據會以clustering及panel regression analyses等方法分析，而質性數據則會透過｢主題分析法｣(thematic analysis)分析受訪者的經驗與主觀看法。透過這些分析，我們希望可以以實證的方法測試｢行動化過程模式｣能否有效地解釋香港公民參與的發展模式，從而提供一個有效理解此現象的觀點。 最後，希望對此題目的進一步研究能夠讓我們更深入地了解年輕人在公民參與中不斷演化的形態及其性質的多樣性。

11602718.label: Realisation of objectives
11602718.value: Objective#1: Understanding the causal factors of social and political engagement in civic life Based on fixed effects panel regression analysis, social and political activity involvement are inter-twined with one another, according to data gathered before Anti-extradition Bill Movement (AEBM) (W1) and after AEBM (W2). Changes in involvement in community and passive activities positively associated with changes in involvement in political activities. However, the direction of causality cannot be determined. One dimension of social activities did not significantly associate with political activity involvement: Helping activities. Possibly, the driver of score changes in helping activity involvement follows a different logic or conditional circumstances than the driver of score changes in political activity involvement. Based on linear regression model, the W1 Youth Inventory of Involvement (YII) subscales did not significantly associate with W1 activism intentions. However, statistically significant associations were found in the regression model predicting W1 radicalism intentions. First, W1 political activity involvement significantly predicted W1 radicalism intentions, such that a unit increase in the predictor associated with .44 increase in the dependent variable. Second, in the opposite direction, W1 helping activity involvement negatively associated with W1 radicalism intentions, such that a unit increase predicted .25 drop in the dependent variable. After testing whether W1 political, community, passive, and helping activities significantly associated with activism and radicalism activity involvement in AEBM, non-AEBM, and both types of events (i.e. W2), it was found that only W1 passive activity involvement significantly associated with activism activity involvement in non-AEBM event. Based on the result, all other YII types of activity involvement kept constant, an increase of 1 unit of YII passive activity involvement is associated with a decrease of .22 in non-AEBM event involvement. Objective#2: Understanding the individual-level profiles of civic engagement Based on YII data, three clusters emerged as meaningfully describing the sample’s past socio-political participation. Yielded profiles differed based on the extent of involvement in all YII type activities. That is, the profile with the smallest cluster size had the highest YII scores across all subscales, while the profile with the largest cluster size had the lowest YII scores across all subscales. This supports results from panel data analysis that involvement in social and political activities are related. Objective#3: Understanding civic participation in relation to the constellation of values, cognitions, and attitudes that is personal to the university students. The panel qualitative interview data revealed heterogeneity in young people’s conception of socio-political participation between W1 and W2. By clustering the participants based on their changing participation styles in socio-political activities, we found that differences primarily existed among three groups of young people. Members of the first group (‘Shocked into action’) had no prior concrete conception of socio-political participation. During AEBM, participants in this group were mobilized due to the personal impact that memorable, unanticipated events had on them. The shift to manifest, collective activities was adventurous/explorative for this group of participants; participating largely as an independent decision instead of influences from activist networks. Members of the second group (‘Reawakened activists’) had prior concrete conceptions of socio-political participation, deeming sustained, multi-modal action as ‘necessary’ for protecting the future of the city and its inhabitants. Past experiences of participating in manifest socio-political activities contributed to this unique group characteristic. During AEBM, they were even more active in their participation, expanding in modes (e.g., on the street, online, and in terms of material consumption) as well as increasing in frequency of participation. Members of the third group (‘Participation as not a priority’) conceived of socio-political participation in pragmatic terms. The perceived collective benefits of their actions were not a contributing factor to their participation, and neither was the alignment of actions to ideals emphasized. Rather, their private, anonymous actions were the result of negotiating between their sympathy and their hierarchy of priorities. Objective#4: Understanding the circumstances surrounding their chosen mode of participation Modes of participation between W1 and W2 were shaped by past experiences (or lack thereof) of socio-political activity involvement. For instance, for the first group, as they had not participated in the past, their involvement was shaped by the perspective changes that they were experiencing as a result of being ‘shocked into action’, as well as activities they encountered by happenstance. Resultantly, their participation was largely conducted independently. For the second group, their participation was motivated by the ‘reawakening’ of feelings of comradery and thereby heavily shaped by their re-engagement with their existing mobilizing networks and/or opportunities that they were familiar with. Unlike the other two, the third group’s actions were not influenced by recruitment calls and hardly involved other people. Rather, their actions were a product of negotiating their ideals/values, anxieties associated with the personal and family-related costs of participation, and general lack of interest in self-identifying as a protester, on the one hand, with felt sympathies to the cause, on the other hand. Resultantly, their chosen modes of participation were private, anonymous, and only conducted after deep introspection. Regarding similarities, although in varying extents, all three groups expressed the need to deliberate over personal safety and their risk appetite. Relatedly, another similarity found was the role of family worries in shaping their activism. Parental disapproval did not significantly influence their participation. Rather, it indirectly affected their evaluation of how much risk they would be willing to take. Objective#5: Understanding the perceived value of their chosen mode of participation Considerable heterogeneity in the perceived value of young people’s chosen mode of participation was found. For members of the first group, engagement in socio-political activities was an adventurous endeavor. The adventurous/exploratory nature of engagement was of perceived personal value to the young people, for example, who sought some form of development/growth by participating in unfamiliar activities. The perceived social value of their chosen modes of participation was relevant to them only insofar as it related to the stimulating event, which provoked their perspective change. Members of the second group emphasized acting in accordance with the perceived social values. The value of their engagement to sustaining the momentum of the social movement via supporting the protesters. For example, some of the young people in the group engaged in donation drives and forwarded/relayed existing recruitment calls to their own social circle. For the purposes of maintaining or increasing pressure on the government, some of the young people were adamant about participating on the street in order to sustain the show of force and resistance. Unlike the first group, the perceived personal value of their engagement was not articulated nearly enough as the social value. Members of the third group uniquely engaged in socio-political activities with little to no consideration of its social value. Even when their engagement had a perceived social value, for example forwarding news feeds that are sympathetic towards the movement, it was not sustained over, particularly upon reflections on the risk their actions might carry for themselves, their families, and their imagined futures (e.g., job prospects). The perceived personal value, while articulated more frequently, was also lacking considerable weight in their decision-making process. Rather, the anticipated adverse consequences of acting in an atmosphere of increasing uncertainty and conflict and their socialized principles (e.g., through parental or religious socialization), which did not prioritize politics in the grand scheme of preferences, carried greater weight.

11602718.label: Major findings and research outcome
11602718.value: Generally speaking, social and political activity involvement are inter-twined with one another. Analyzing YII panel data, changing involvement in community and passive activities positively and significantly associated with changes in involvement in political activities. The only exception was the relationship between political activities and helping activities. Although W1 YII political action positively associated with W1 radicalism intentions, it appears that W1 YII subscales are not statistically significant predictors of actual unconventional political activity involvement, measured dimensionally as activism and radicalism activities and across types of AEBM, non-AEBM, and both types in W2. The only exception was that one type of social participation (YII passive activities) negatively associated with involvement in activities of non-AEBM event(s). Overall, the quantitative findings suggest that, while social and political participation are inter-related, past engagement in (largely) conventional socio-political activities hardly predicts involvement in real unconventional (radical) protest action. It may positively associate with intentions, but its positive relationship with real protest action is unfounded. Rather, a negative relationship was found between past involvement in passive activities and actual involvement in non-AEBM events. The panel qualitative data sheds some light on the above complexities. The heterogeneity of young people’s trajectory of socio-political participation could be clustered into three groups. Members of the first group (‘Shocked into action’) became involved in manifest, collective activities because of ‘shocking’ events they encountered during AEBM. They either had no prior experience in political activities or only engaged in latent political activities previously. Consequently, their participation during AEBM was largely independent. This differs from the second group (‘Reawakened activists’), whose members had extensive involvement in past political activities (including unconventional protests). This group was motivated to participate (independently, with family/friends, or with other activists) due to their ‘reawakened’ feelings of comradery and sense of justice. Finally, for members of ‘Participation as not a priority’, there was no evidence of gradual or sustained involvement in manifest, collective (or individual) political activities. Rather, they engaged in deep introspection, balancing their ideals/values, anxieties and costs, and level of political interest, prior to choosing their individual activities (mostly, private and anonymous). Instead of ‘recruitment calls’ or affective identification with activists, their actions were influenced by reflections of what they personally cared about. Regarding similarities, all three groups engaged in deep deliberation prior to acting, particularly over personal safety and risk appetite. Family worries was a shared factor that shaped choice sets.

11602718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11602718.value: There is great potential for further research because of the study’s research outcomes. First, further research needs to be conducted to better understand the pathway model for conventional and unconventional socio-political activity engagement. For example, which types of civic skill-acts (acquired through past involvement in civic activities) are transferable to participation in unconventional political activities? Also, what are the commonalities shared between transferable civic skill-acts, and how (if at all) does transferability vary with autobiographical, dispositional, and situational characteristics of the young person? Understanding skill-act transferability can help improve citizenship education. Second, while social and political activity engagement are found to be inter-twined, a central question to be addressed is why. What are the profiles of socio-political activities that young people in Hong Kong participate (or not) in? For example, what are their incentive structures, anticipated costs and risks, commitment demands, and institutional arrangements? As trends of civic engagement are changing, it is necessary to better understand how we can encourage youth’s active participation in societal affairs. In the coming year, the two above-mentioned directions will be pursued, yielding publications as well as the foundational basis for drafting competitive funding proposals. The findings will also be disseminated via conference presentations.

11602718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11602718.value: Our findings show that there is an inter-relationship between social and political participation among young people in Hong Kong. With some exceptions, over time, changes in involvement in social activities can predict changes in involvement in political activities (and vice-versa). While there is some linearity to this relationship, patterns of social and political participation are complicated when we consider its link with unconventional protest activities. The contextual characteristics of the AEBM had an unquestionable role to play in the complexities we unearthed. The interview data showed that individual-level factors (like risk appetite and life priorities) mattered in explaining the variations in choices made; some decided to join in protests for the first time (being ‘shocked’ into action), some who participated in protests previously were more prepared to participate again (experiencing a ‘reawakening’), and finally some chose to act privately and anonymously (placing other life priorities above politics). Regardless of their patterns of involvement before and during AEBM, all of the young interviewees demonstrated their agential capacities to engage in autonomous situational decision-making, and this decision-making notably involved active processing and deliberations of family-related factors, extra-familial factors, and personal characteristics and histories of past (non-)involvement in socio-political activities.

11604418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11604418.value: This project is proposed to conduct in-depth empirical research by means of eye tracking and computational modeling to address the following academic questions that have recently become hot spots in cognitive studies of translation process and human machine interactive translation (HMIT): How translation is carried out from the cognitive perspective? What cognitive activities are involved in the translation process? How translators' cognitive effort is distributed to cognitive activities and subtasks of translation, and which ones are more effort-demanding than the others? Exploring sound answers to these questions can not only deepen our understanding of the nature of translation but more importantly indicate (1) what computer aids are more demanded in alleviating translators’ cognitive workload and, accordingly, (2) how to design and implement HMIT for maximal utility in enhancing users' productivity and creativity. To explore these questions, we will first acquire translators’ motor event data (such as eye movements, keystrokes and mouse clicks) by eye tracking in three typical realistic scenarios: translation without vs. with a bilingual dictionary, and translation as post-editing of state-of-the-art MT output with a range of computer aids (including translation memory and examples at various granularity levels). The data will first be used for computational modeling of time intervals between keystrokes during continuous typing (vs. not typing) of target texts, in order to infer sequential patterns of motor events corresponding to Jakobsen’s (2011) notion of micro-cycle, each of which is assumed to translate a text chunk (or termed translation unit) of a source sentence, and then for unsupervised machine learning to cluster subsequences of micro-cycles into clusters corresponding to cognitive activities for specific information-processing functions. In this way, we will arrive at computational models for essential cognitive activities in pure translation and in use of a dictionary and more sophisticated computer aids to facilitate the translation. Cognitive effort distribution will be computed in a comparative way according to machine learning results in terms of gaze duration and pupil size (a known indicative index of cognitive workload intensity). Based on the distribution, we can have reliable estimation of the effectiveness of various computer aids in reducing translators' workload. The research outcomes from this novel methodology are expected to disclose many unseen cognitive details of the translation process and also point HMIT to the most promising future direction, i.e., bettering computer aids for those translation subtasks that demand more cognitive effort. 本項目提出用眼動追蹤和計算模擬對翻譯過程進行實證研究，旨在探索譯者認知精力在各翻譯子任務認知活動上的分佈。我們將首先通過眼動追蹤實驗從真實翻譯中收集譯者的動作事件數據（包括眼動、鍵擊和滑鼠點擊等），然後根據相關眼動度量指標（如注視時長和瞳孔大小等）計算認知精力的相對分佈。期望研究結果不但加深我們對翻譯本質的理解，而且為在哪些費力的翻譯子任務上發展電腦輔助工具提供線索。

11604918.label: Project Objectives
11604918.value: Examine the cross-cultural interaction and connection between Britain, Hong Kong and China from the late nineteenth to early twentieth centuries. Investigate English literary texts written and published in Hong Kong during the period and explore the ways in which they responded to, interacted with, or contested the colonial society in which they were produced. Explore the role of literature in constructing identity and a sense of place. Explore the spatial form of the narratives and consider how spatial representation became an effective means through which questions relating to race, gender and identity were raised and addressed. Examine the content and form of the narratives produced in Hong Kong and explore their relationship with print culture in Britain, especially that which relates to the metropolitan centre of London.

11604918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11604918.value: This project investigates English-language city narratives and literary journalism produced and published in Hong Kong from 1880 till 1930, with the aim of exploring how these literary texts engage with topical issues while also revealing the cross-cultural interactions, tensions and conflicts in colonial society. It will pay particular attention to texts and authors that engaged with topics, such as the bubonic plague of 1894, which were of particular relevance to key moments in the history of Hong Kong and the surrounding region. This project will shed new light on the cultural traffic and interaction between Britain, Hong Kong and China at a time when both the ‘empire’ and the ‘crown colony’ were undergoing important historical and sociopolitical transformations in response to wider global changes. Despite the recent rise of interest in literary and cultural production in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover, until now little attempt has been made to uncover English literary and journalistic connections between Hong Kong and Britain in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, despite the fact that it was a significant period in the development of a local literary culture in English. Writing in English during this period contributed to, or shaped, the multicultural outlook of the city, as well as helping to construct an image of Hong Kong that continues to have much resonance. Indeed, since the first Opium War of 1842, the city had to confront a political and social reality that was in large part a product of negotiations and conflicts between the British and Chinese empires in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It is in this context that, as this project will demonstrate, literary texts had a particular role to play in drawing attention to the quotidian underlying the ‘grand narratives’ of colonial Hong Kong, whether responding to, contesting, or re-envisioning these social and political realities and intricacies. English texts served a particularly important function in this process because they were accessible to both a local and global audience. It is through archival research and close reading of specific literary texts understood in relation to particular historic moments that the complexities of cross-cultural interaction in a colonial setting, and its wider significance in the Sino-British context, can be revealed and explored. 此研究追溯在1880-1930年期間在香港出版及關於香港的英語城市文學及報導文學, 目的是探討這些文學作品如何描繪 ˴ 建構及回應城市的生活和重要事件, 如1894年的瘟疫, 及從中反映殖民社會當不同文化的交流˴緊張關係及磨擦˳ 這項研究會提出新的視角及重新審視香港˴ 英國及中國在這段時期的文化交流及聯繫˳ 隨着1997香港的主權回歸中國,香港當代文學逐漸受到關注˳ 但直至現在,甚少關於這段時期英國和香港的文學交流和聯繫的研究, 即使本地英語文學在這段時期有顯著的發展˳ 在這段時期出版的英語文學不單止對城市文化多元化作出貢獻,這些寫作所建構的城市影像直至現在仍存在著影響力˳事實上,從1842年的鴉片戰爭開始,香港的政治和社會的現實一直受中國和英國兩帝國所牽引˳正是在這樣的環境下,文學作品能提出大敍事觀點下的殖民社會以外的視角, 及顯示描寫日常生活的意義 ˳ 正因為英語寫作能面向來自本地及國際社會的讀者, 它們在文化交流上扮演重要的角色˳ 本項目會對特定歷史時刻及作家的檔案及文學進行研究˳

11604918.label: Realisation of objectives
11604918.value: All the objectives that I have outlined in the proposal have been achieved. In this project, I have carried out extensive archival research in Britain and Hong Kong. While digital archives, especially those that can be accessed from Hong Kong, have generated important research materials , my research trips to Cambridge and London during my sabbatical leave have given me the opportunity to read unpublished writings by one of the major authors that I discussed in my project, Stella Benson, as well as accessed the archived major English-language literary periodicals and English presses, such as South China Weekly Post, Odds and Ends: An Illustrated Journal, and China Mail, which published some of the literary and journalistic writings that I considered in my project. It is through this extensive archival research that the literary and journalistic connection between Britain, Hong Kong, and China from the late nineteenth to the early twentieth centuries could be revealed and contextualised. As indicated in my project objectives, spatiality is a major focus of my inquiry. Spatiality in my project includes: the literary construction of place and space; the spatial form of narratives and the influence of race, gender and identity that shaped it; and the spatial arrangements or dynamics of the places that are covered in this book. In my monograph (the full manuscript will be due in August 2023), I have adopted a spatial lens to examine a range of literary texts, including the aforementioned unpublished or under-studied literary works though ones engage with some of the key historical moments and thematic concerns that my book explores. By doing so, I explored the role of literature in constructing identity and a sense of place. I have also examined the cross-cultural interaction and connection between Britain, Hong Kong and China from the late nineteenth to the first half of the twentieth centuries. Through archival research and close textual analysis, I have investigated English literary texts written and published in Hong Kong during the period and explored the ways in which they responded to, interacted with, or contested the colonial society in which they were produced, circulated, and read. I also examined the content and form of the narratives produced in Hong Kong and explored their relationship with print culture in Britain, especially in relation to the production of literary magazines, periodicals, and newspapers in the city.

11604918.label: Major findings and research outcome
11604918.value: This research sheds new light on the production, circulation, and consumption of literary texts produced within, and across, Hong Kong, Britain, and China. It uncovers literary works that were hitherto little known or under-studied; most importantly, by analysing a range of literary texts published not only in book form but also in literary periodicals and newspapers, it engages with different voices and perspectives in these societies. My research has showed a vibrant cultural and literary connection between these three locales, while also highlighting the parallel, yet distinct, network of literary production by English-language and Chinese-language writers. For example, my research demonstrates the intertextual relationship between the illustrated newspapers and periodicals published in the metropolitan city of London and those published in Hong Kong, paying particular attention to the narrative strategies and thematic concerns of these texts. It also unravels the various visible and invisible relationship that connects Hong Kong-based writers with those who were based in China and Britain. Through exploring various literary texts as well as the literary and journalistic networks, my research has transcended the disciplinary boundaries that frequently treated Hong Kong, British, and Chinese literary texts as separate areas of research rather than investigating their connection, especially in terms of print culture and literary form. Overall, my research contributes to areas including cross-cultural literary studies, spatiality, and the interdisciplinary study of literature and the city. During the duration of the project, I published two journal articles in English Studies, which is one of the leading academic journals in literary studies. I also presented relevant papers at three major conferences that were held during the period. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, two of these conferences were held online. A major output of this project is a monograph, 'Spatial Stories and Intersecting Geographies: Hong Kong, China, and Britain, 1890-1945', which is under contract with Liverpool University Press. The full manuscript of the monograph is due on 31 August 2023.

11604918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11604918.value: I have published two journal articles during the project duration. I’m currently working on a monograph based on the research findings, which will be published by Liverpool University Press. The full manuscript is due on 31 August 2023. While this monograph will incorporate most of the research findings, during the course of the project I have uncovered materials that I plan to use to further develop a new project on port cities and the maritime culture in the Asia-Pacific as represented, imagined, and reconfigured in the nineteenth and twentieth-century literature. This new research project aims to expand my current research while also adopting a new focus of inquiry, so that new insights can be generated through a critical engagement with studies in port cities and maritime culture, areas which have yet received a substantial attention in literary studies.

11604918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11604918.value: This research project sheds new light on the literary and journalistic connection between Hong Kong, Britain, and China, from the late nineteenth to the first half of the twentieth centuries. It uncovers different voices and perspectives through an extensive archival research of literary periodicals, newspapers, as well as published and unpublished writings by writers who have a substantial engagement with these locales. It contributes to the recent 'global' turn in literary studies by putting works that have often been seen as belonging to Hong Kong literature, Chinese literature and English literature together for analysis, thereby revealing various forms of literary production, as well as diverse visible and invisible relationships and connection (and at times tension) that have hitherto been little explored.
