11606418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11606418.value: The project investigates reconstruction in constructions typically involving A-bar-movement, whose configurations contain either a gap or a resumptive pronoun in argument position. The data are drawn primarily from Mandarin Chinese and English, and when relevant, compared with those in French. It uses the formal tools of linguistic theory and solicits new data as driven by theoretical concerns in the form of questionnaires for speakers of Mandarin Chinese. The purpose of the project is to shed some light on current theories about reconstruction. Empirically, despite Chinese being an intensively studied language, the investigation of reconstruction in the language, especially in structures with a resumptive pronoun, mostly is not very systematic, and the data it is based on are not particularly rich. Significantly, the data across different analyses appear to be inconsistent. Some data arguing for a particular view are not very well-chosen, and some apparently relevant facts are not considered. Theoretically, to the extent the analysis is correct, current work does not explain why the facts the way they are, for they do not relate the similarities and differences in reconstruction between languages to other similarities and differences. A comparative study of Chinese, English and French brings the work to a manageable level and yet provides a good overview of the similarities and differences across languages. The project investigates a range of constructions: questions, relative clauses, left-dislocation and topicalization and a spectrum of grammatical properties: island effects and various reconstruction effects including anaphor binding, variable binding, binding condition C, idiom fragments, quantifier scope and cross-over. Judgment for reconstruction effects is often quite delicate, and therefore needs to be carefully controlled for quantity and quality. We elicit grammaticality judgment of a sizeable pool of forty-five speakers on three different occasions, each of which is set apart from the others by a period of six weeks. The questionnaires consist of two sets, one for structures with a gap and one for structures with a resumptive pronoun. In addition, search in the corpus of the Peking University and Academia Sinica for naturally occurring data is also made to ensure the reliability of the data. The project has far-reaching consequences for the inventory of documented facts and for the understanding of the syntax-semantic interface. The data we consider constitute an enrichment of the data set. The discovery of grammatical principles giving rise to the observed data constitutes an understanding of the inner working of the language faculty. 詞組歸建(reconstruction)是一種語言現象，其特徵是移出的詞組要回歸到原點做解讀。如在英語的this is the picture of herself that John said Mary saw, 或是在中文的這就是張三認爲我聽到關於自己的謠言，反身代詞(reflexive pronouns)不是在表層的位置，而是在從句裏原來的位置得到解讀，理解為被從句主語所約束(binding)。這種現象可以看成把表層聽到的詞組歸建于本來的位置, 由此可以滿足約束的結構條件。理論上有不同處理的方法，如拷貝移位論(copy theory of movement)主張，詞組移位時會留下含語義的拷貝(copy)，約束的解讀是從這得到。除了關係字句，好幾個其他句型都顯示這種現象，如問句(questions)，左向位移(left-dislocation)及話題化(topicalization)。此外，某些結構還允許歸建于原位出現的普通代詞(pronouns)。這顯示詞組歸建現象的複雜性。 詞組歸建的相關的現象除了反身代詞約束之外，尚有變量受約(variable binding)，名詞定指條件(binding condition C)，熟語成分(idiom fragments)解讀，量化轄域(quantifier scope)以及跨越現象(cross-over) 。本項目主要目的是給予這些表面上看起來很不同的現象一個解析。目前的理論文獻是很豐富。可是在這領域中文的研究不多。語料沒有很系統化，其中有些忽略重点。分析上没有連上語法的其他領域。此外，語料收集沒有代表性,依靠一少數發言人。我們會使用問卷，被試人數會達四十位左右。我們收集語料的方法也有所不同。隔六周收集一次，總共三次。 這些現象的語感不易掌握。所以，發言人的語言知識不太可能從語境裏面習得，而是語言的本質。因此，理解這方面的細節，也就是理解自然語言的本質。

11606418.label: Realisation of objectives
11606418.value: 1. Empirical investigations We completed the investigation of the syntactic structures of questions, relative clauses and topicalization. We expanded the investigation of the reconstruction effects to two other constructions: VP-fronting and raising. The effects concern Binding Principles A, B and C, variable binding by a quantifier, idioms and quantifier scope. In each area, we added new data bearing on the issues at hand, some of which shed new light on the interpretation of copies left behind by movement. All the facts we consider have a bearing on the condition for possible or impossible reconstruction. 2. Theory building Our investigation strongly supports the copy theory of movement. The data we considered showed that it is the copy left behind by A-bar-movement of a phrase that is interpreted, not the displaced phrase itself. This contrasts with the current analyses in the literature in explaining not only how reconstruction effects are accounted for by interpreting the copy but also how the interpretation of the displaced phrase itself may sometimes give the same results and sometimes not. The effects show up to different degrees across the different constructions. Those concerning Binding Principles A, B, C, variable binding are observed in all constructions. We showed with additional data that they are due to the interpretation of the copy of the displaced phrase left behind in the position from which it moves. Quantifier scope behaves differently, however. Scope ambiguity is attested in topic structures, but only partially in relative clauses and not at all in VP-fronting. This is due to the independent structural differences among the three constructions. In topicalization, the topic phrase is moved as a whole to the topic position, leaving behind a copy of itself including the numeral and classifier. In relative clauses, the structures are derived from NP-raising, not DP raising, cf. Aoun and Li (2003). Thus, the numeral and the classifier in the head of the RC are necessarily higher than the quantifier in the relative clause and take scope above it. However, the lack of agreement in Chinese allows subject quantifiers to undergo quantifier raising (QR) (May 1977), but object quantifiers may not (Aoun and Li 2003). We showed on empirical grounds that subject quantifiers undergoing QR cannot move to a higher clause to scope over the numeral as Aoun and Li proposed, but adjoins to the DP containing the RC, much like inverse linking that May (1977) suggested for English. This accounts for why the quantifier takes scope above the numeral in the head of the RC. QR of this sort is nevertheless impossible for object quantifiers or a quantifier in a multi-clausal RC. The former is due to a condition on traces of QR (Aoun and Li 2003), and the latter is because QR is generally clause-bound. In these two cases, the quantifier is necessarily in the scope of the numeral that is external to the RC. In structures with VP-fronting, the subject is A-moved to the subject position but the copy it leaves behind in the VP is not interpreted, and the same holds for quantifier scope in the raising construction. An object quantifier in the fronted VP therefore cannot have wide scope over the subject, but may do so when the VP is not fronted. This is due to the fact that the object wide scope reading is obtained by undergoing QR adjoining to TP (May 1977). This is not possible for the object quantifier in a fronted VP, though, for this would require lowering (Huang 1993), an operation that is generally not available. We investigated reconstruction effects in the raising construction where anaphoric binding and scope of quantifier across negation impose apparently contradictory requirements. On the one hand, anaphoric binding requires that the copy of the A-moved subject be interpreted to meet its locality conditions. On the other hand, quantifier scope interpretation requires that the A-moved subject across negation be interpreted, not the copy it leaves behind. We thus proposed that copies left behind by movement be interpreted according to the relevance of the interpreted features to specific grammatical principles. Since morpho-syntactic features are relevant to Binding Principles but irrelevant to negation, while lexical features are relevant to negation but irrelevant to Binding Principles, morpho-syntactic features in the copies are interpreted when the locality conditions for binding are met, while lexical features of the A-moved phrase are interpreted at the landing site, without regard to locality conditions. We resolved the narrow scope reading of a quantifier with respect to modals by appealing to logical relations. Specifically, the narrow scope reading is possible just in case it is materially implied by the wide scope reading. Our approach explains why the narrow scope reading is possible even when the wide scope reading is not available. We extended our analysis to cases of PP-extraposition where a PP structurally higher than an intensional predicate may nevertheless take scope under it. Our analysis thus deepens our understanding of the interpretation of copies, i.e., formal features of a displaced phrase are not interpreted all at the same time, and thus supports the view that scope reconstruction is at least partially semantic. We investigated the aspect- and focus-related sentence-final particles (sfps) –le and –eryi ‘only’. We presented arguments based on negation, indefinite subjects, downward-entailing subjects, predicates of creation, showing that these sfps are external to TP, contrary to Erlewine (2016), and having scope over the subject. Subjects to the left of modals higher than these spfs can nevertheless take scope under them, and are susceptible to the same restrictions as those in the subject position of monoclausal structures. These can be readily accounted for by the copy theory of movement, just like the reconstruction effect observed for long-distance dou-quantification in which the quantifier dou and the phrase with which it is associated are in different clauses. We investigated gapless relative clauses (GRCs). The interesting aspect of this construction is that there is no syntactic gap in the RC, hence, there is no syntactic reconstruction to the gap position. We nevertheless argued that there is a semantic variable corresponding to a covert predicate. The advantage of this approach is that instead of considering GRCs as a totally different construction, it can capture the similarity between different types of RCs. They all have a variable of some kind. GRCs have a semantic variable corresponding to no gap, while other types of RC have a gap arising from syntactic movement that is also interpreted as a semantic variable. We presented eight different kinds of data bearing on word-order, subcategorization, the distribution of suo, coordination, iteration, long-distance extraction, N’-ellipsis and nominalization, showing that Huang’s (2016) arguments for GRCs being a complement clause to a noun do not hold. We pro-posed a RC hierarchy according to which the distributions of different types of RC are related to the extent to which the head noun is recoverable. 3. Language documentation. We collected data by online solicitations of grammaticality judgements with the help of a research assistant in the US via Amazon McTurk and a research associate who sent questionnaires to experimental subjects. Some of our data have not heretofore published before and thus enrich the databases for further research.

11606418.label: Major findings and research outcome
11606418.value: 1. Structures of RCs: we have new data supporting the view that the derivation of RCs in Chinese by NP-raising is no different from that in English. See Part C 8.1, 8.3. 2. Interpretation of copies: we present empirical evidence that the copy left behind by movement is interpreted, and the interpretation of the displaced phrase itself does not always give the correct results. In A-movement, however, it is the displaced phrase that is interpreted, not the copy left behind. This adds an empirical reason for distinguishing A- from A-bar-movement. See Part C 8.3. 3. We resolve the apparent contradictory requirements of anaphoric binding and quantifier scope across negation by differentiating morpho-syntactic features from lexical features. Formal features are not interpreted all at the same time, but according to their relevance to particular grammatical principles. See Part C 9.2. 4. We have a new account for the subject quantifier in RC having wide scope over the numeral in the head of RC, assimilating it to inverse linking in English. See Part C 8.3. 5. We propose a semantic account for the narrow quantifier scope under modals based on logical relations. Our account resolves an apparently contradictory requirements for anaphoric binding and quantifier scope across negation. See Part C 9.2. 6. We likened the failure of an object quantifier in a fronted VP to have wide scope in VP-fronting to the copy of the A-moved subject not being interpreted in general. See Part C 8.2, 8.3. 7. On the basis of four different kinds of new data, we showed that aspect- and focus-related sentence-final particles -le and eryi are external to TP and take scope above the subject. Cases where subject is structurally higher than these sfps and yet takes scope below them have the same reconstruction account by the copy theory of movement. See Part C 8.6, 9.1 8. We presented facts showing that apparently gapless RCs are a type of RC, and they have a semantic variable corresponding to a predicate, not arising from a syntactic operation. Other RCs have a syntactic gap arising from movement and are also interpreted as semantic variables. Gapless RCs show no syntactic reconstruction effect. See Part C 8.5.

11606418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11606418.value: 1. Current work including ours accounts for anaphor binding based on structural terms. However, as is well-known, reflexive binding does not require the structural relation of c-command. There are instances of logophoric binding where the reflexive is not c-commanded by its antecedent. It would be worthwhile to consider whether anaphoric binding can be brought under logophoric binding. 2. Dou-quantification is the sole instance in our investigation where the copy left behind by an A-moved phrase associated with dou 'all' is interpreted. It would be of some interest to provide a non-syntactic alternative account, e.g., in terms of logical relations, so that this is not an exception to the general case in which the A-moved phrase is interpreted, not the copy it leaves behind. 3. In our account of GRCs, there is a semantic variable that corresponds to no syntactic gap. The prediction is that there should be no syntactic reconstruction. The facts are at present unclear, as examples serving as diagnostic for reconstruction involve a phrase in the head noun that contains an anaphor, pronoun, R-expression or quantifier, but GRCs cannot contain another phrase in addition to the clausal complement.

11606418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11606418.value: The work undetaken in this project is to investigate the speaker's knowledge of language with regard to the meanings of specifically constructed examples. These concern commonly attested structures like relative clauses, topicalization, VP-fronting and raising. However, the examples used are specially constructed for our purposes, and not commonly found in the language ambience. Moreover, the semantic judgement about them is at times very subtle and often requires careful introspection. To the extent that the speaker is not explicitly instructed, but systematically having judgement about them, it can only come from his or her inherent language faculty. An account for the syntactic and semantic properties of these data is an account for the inherent properties of language.

11607518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11607518.value: This project intends to establish proper incentive measures to increase organ donations in Hong Kong. Studies have shown that compared to dialysis, significantly lower mortality, doubled life expectancy, and the better quality of life are associated with renal transplant recipients. Organ transplants can also substantially reduce health care costs. However, the shortage of organs for transplantation remains a global problem. The demand for organs (especially kidneys) in Hong Kong far outstrips the supply. Hong Kong has taken few useful incentive measures and is lacking of a shaped model for promoting organ donation. This project aims to work out a group of incentive measures that are practically effective, ethically justifiable and politically legitimate for Hong Kong to employ to enhance donation. We will study three prominent international models of organ donation to investigate what Hong Kong can learn from them. These models can be termed liberalism, compensationalism and familism and are practiced respectively in the United States, Iran, and mainland China that we have selected as three target countries for the research. This project does not attempt to affirm which model, as a whole, is overwhelmingly recommendable to Hong Kong. Rather, we will integrate the merits of each model to propose a group of incentive measures suitable for Hong Kong. This group of incentive measures will not be established unless each measure is to be confirmed as practically effective, ethically justifiable, and politically legitimate through our research. We will conduct a small pool of in-depth interviews in the three target countries to secure useful data regarding most effective and justifiable incentive measures being adopted in each model. By analyzing such data and taking Hong Kong’s culture, reality and demand into consideration, we will propose a group of incentive measures and relevant questions to conduct interviews in Hong Kong to explore its suitability. We will also analyze if legal amendment and/or legislation are needed in order to implement such incentive measures. Finally, we will conduct a quantitative survey to find out if the majority people of Hong Kong support implementing this group of incentive measures so as to test its political legitimacy. If this group of incentive measures will have met all three conditions – practical effectiveness, ethical justifiability, and political legitimacy, we will be in an academically sound position to suggest that Hong Kong must take it to optimize organ donations in the society. 本課題旨在確立能夠增加香港社會器官捐獻的適當鼓勵方式。許多研究已經表明，相對於透析治療，腎臟移植能夠顯著降低死亡率、加倍生命預期、改善生活品質。同時，器官移植還能明顯減少保健費用。然而，缺乏可供移植的器官（特別是腎臟）乃是一個全球問題。香港的器官短缺尤為嚴重，所採取的有效鼓勵方式很少，也沒有形成一個促進捐獻的模式。 本課題試圖提出一組實踐中有效、倫理上可辯護、政治上合理的鼓勵方式以供香港採用從而提升捐獻。我們將研究器官捐獻的三種國際模式，探索香港可以從中學到的東西。這些模式可稱為自由主義模式、補償主義模式以及家庭主義模式，分別在本課題所確定的三個目標國家——美國、伊朗、中國——得到實踐。本課題並不試圖整體肯定某一模式的優勢以供香港採納。相反，我們將綜合三個模式的各自優點從而提出一組適用於香港的器官捐獻鼓勵方式，並且只有當其中每個方式都能通過本課題的研究證明為實踐中有效、倫理上可辯護、政治上合理之後，這組方式才能得以確立。 我們將在三個目標國家中進行小量的深入訪談來揭示各個模式中的有效及可以辯護的鼓勵方式。通過分析這些資料並且考慮到香港的文化、現實及需求，我們將提出一組可用於香港的鼓勵方式並進行一些深入訪談來檢驗其適用性。我們也將分析是否需要修正現行的一些法律、政策以便實施這些方式。最後，我們將進行一個定量研究來發現香港大多數人是否支持這組方式從而檢驗其政治合理性。如果這組方式同時滿足了所有三個條件——實踐有效性、倫理辯護性、政治合理性——那麼我們就將處於一個良好的學術地位來建議香港採納這組方式從而促進器官捐獻。

11607518.label: Realisation of objectives
11607518.value: Thanks to the RGC's approval of extending the project to 31 August 2022, we had time to catch up all the work delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic before the ending date. We had successfully carried out all the plans to realize all five objectives. In particular, we finished 2 more interviews in Hong Kong and 2 more interviews in Beijing to finish all planned interviews (so that all planned at least 15 interviews in each site, Beijing, Chicago, Tehran, and Hong Kong, were all successfully conducted in each site) so as to fully realize Objectives 1, 2 & 3. We were also able to carry out the quantitative survey in Hong Kong and achieved valid data so that we could not only realize Objective 5, but also had time to analyze all the data and achieve Objective 4. On 29 August 2022, we send to relevant Hong Hong authorities a letter of recommendation regarding incentives for organ donation in Hong Kong with the following main content that illustrates the realization of our Objectives: Recommendations for Hong Kong 1) Comprehensively good honorary measures Culturally appropriate and effective honorary measures should be adopted. In particular, A. A memorial park of stones engraved with donors’ names may be constructed in Hong Kong. B. The government, in particular the Department of Health, may establish a website to publicize and memorize all living and deceased donors. This website should allow the organ recipients to show their gratitude virtually toward the actual organ donors and their families. 2) A Comprehensively good familist measure We recommend that a priority right to organs be provided to the deceased donors’ first-degree relatives (spouse, parents and children) and this right should last for 25 years. Our survey found that over 90% of the Hong Kong people find it fair to offer this incentive, and nearly 70% believe this incentive will be useful or very useful to promote cadaveric donation in Hong Kong. Ethically, donations driven by this incentive are mixed altruism which is still ethically valuable and justifiable. The mere fact that the donors might have a selfish motive to benefit themselves or their family members by donation under this incentive does not make the donation ethically problematic, because they also inevitably have a disinterested motive to benefit other people by donating their organs (this is so because they are aware that their families may not need organs in the future). Moreover, the claim that the fimilist incentive gives an inappropriate favour to large families does not stand well in a Confucian-influenced society like Hong Kong. A large-scale survey demonstrated that people in contemporary Hong Kong society still maintain Confucian family ethical values and endorse appropriate room to be left by public policy for family members to give preferential treatment to each other. This familist incentive is not unfair to the people with no first-degree family members because it does not reduce the chances for them to receive organs than in a situation without such incentive, given that the donors’ first-degree relatives may not have the actual need for organ transplantation despite having a priority right. Finally, regarding the worry that this incentive would increase the risk of compelling donation by the family against the deceased’s wishes, we suggest that the government in announcing this incentive should make it clear that although donation is ethically admirable, everyone has a full right to decide not to donate. Having considered all major opposing reasons, we believe that the familist incentive is ethically justifiable for Hong Kong to adopt. 3) An Honorary and Compensationalist measure We recommend that Hong Kong should offer a niche in a public columbarium to a deceased donor right away after the donation. This measure is both honorary and compensationalist, because it would not only give honor to a deceased donor by shortening the waiting time for a public niche, but also save some expenses of the family for renting a temporary private niche while waiting for a public niche. Although the government has recently built a large public columbarium and announced that with this offer, families will no longer need to wait in the queue for a niche, our investigation has found that a lot of families do not like the location of the columbarium. They will still have to wait as much time as before if they prefer to get a niche near their home or in a place they prefer. Our suggestion is that the government promise to give a deceased donor and the family first priority that they would get a niche in their favorite public columbarium as soon as it is available. Our survey shows that over 90% of the Hong Kong people support this incentive measure, and over 70% believe that it would be effective to promote cadaveric organ donation. This means this measure is politically legitimate and practically promising for Hong Kong to adopt. Ethically, some are worried that this measure is not purely honorary and might degenerate into a monetary exchange between the donor and the society. We argue that the driving force of donation under this incentive measure would primarily derive from the honor it carries rather than from its financial value, just as an athlete in pursuing a medal is primarily motivated by its honor rather than an economic value it may also have. Moreover, offering this measure is not unfair to those who are willing but eventually unable to donate due to externally uncontrollable factors. This measure is reasonably set up to award actual achievements rather than merely a good intention or effort. Finally, there are concerns that such a measure would be attractive only to low-income families to save the expenses that may incur during the waiting time for public niches and may even lead to the exploitation of individuals from low-income families by inducing them to donate in order to relieve the family’s financial burden. Our investigation shows that such concerns do not stand well due to the existence of multiple cheap alternatives, such as simple funeral homes (長生店) and certain inexpensive private niches for people to choose while waiting for a favourite public niche.

11607518.label: Major findings and research outcome
11607518.value: This research project studied relevant policies and practices in four culturally different cities (Beijing, Chicago, Tehran and Hong Kong) to seek comprehensively good incentive measures for enhancing donation rates. We investigated how three types of incentive (honorary, compensationalist, and familist) operate in the four societies, and concluded that a suitable model is to integrate all three types to set up comprehensively good incentive measures for Hong Kong to adopt. In each city we conducted in-depth interviews to obtain essential data regarding particular incentive measures. We also performed a quantitative survey in Hong Kong to discover which particular measures could gain the support of the majority population to confirm their political legitimacy in our society. The research outcome of the project includes journal article and book chapter publications, a book to be published by Springer, and recommendation letter to government authorities.

11607518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11607518.value: In addition to a few papers published and a letter of recommendation sent to relevant government authorities, a detailed academic book out of the project will be published by Springer in 2023. We will look at the responses to these publications and recommendations to decide what further research should be developed.

11607518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11607518.value: Comprehensively good incentives measures for organ donation must be practically effective, politically legitimate, and ethically justifiable. A measure is practically effective only if it can provide a strong driving force for many individuals to be willing to donate. A measure is politically legitimate if it gains the majority support of a society. And a measure is ethically justifiable if it is defensible through ethical reasons and arguments. All these conditions should be met in order for a measure to be comprehensively good for a society like Hong Kong to adopt. This research project has found that comprehensively good incentives measures for organ donation in Hong Kong should include the following: 1) a memorial park of stones engraved with donors? names be constructed; 2) a priority right to organs be provided to the deceased donors? first-degree relatives (spouse, parents and children) and this right should last for 25 years; and 3) a niche in a public columbarium (that is preferred by the deceased donor and family) be offered to a deceased donor right away after the donation.

11609318.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11609318.value: 有關十七世紀女畫家作品及其贋品的經濟活動

11609318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11609318.value: 十七世紀中國女畫家：她們在十七世紀的經濟得益與在十八世紀她們的畫作偽品 本項目將集中焦點於十七世紀江南地區（現今江蘇、安徽及浙江）的閨閣婦女與名妓，詳細分析其作品銷售的策略以及她們在畫藝市場的參與。本文有望回應以下問題： 1. 十七世紀的女畫家如何透過作品交易以換取各種可見，或不可見的利益？ 2. 在女畫家活躍的十七世紀及其過世後的十八世紀，有什麽因素影響著當中的畫作僞造與銷售？ 這研究有望為十七世紀中國女畫家的生活與作品作出新的評估。我們亦將更深入了解到作僞市場與這些作品之間的關聯。此外，有別於以往針對女性生平、繪畫技巧、家族關係等的研究，本文將從社會、政治、經濟層面呈現十七世紀中國女畫家的生活。 本研究將採用社會歷史學的角度探論女畫家與其家族及社交圈子的網絡。初步研究顯示，研讀書畫是最有效的方法，由此可理解： 1. 畫家、交易商與顧客的關係； 2. 作品的流通情況及； 3. 作品的鑒賞及其於市場上的買賣情況 雖然有學者認為部分女畫家會以畫作換取利益，但這些討論只針對金錢上的賦予或好處，唯畫作並不應只看作「委託與製造」下的產物，亦應考慮其他交易因素，如社會地位、風險、成本、喜好和限制等。此外，鑒賞亦涉及到資訊傳播的成本。因此，交易並非單靠物質的賦予便可完成，尤以名妓的畫作而言。有鑒於此，本文將運用經濟理論（如同博弈論般），檢視十七世紀中國藝術場裡顧客（或收藏家）、鑒賞家（或交易商）和畫家之間錯綜複雜的關係。

11609518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11609518.value: This project is a continuation of a current RGC funded project, "The Missing Period in Cantonese Cinema: 1949-1969) (2015-2017), a digital archive project to collect historical data on Cantonese films produced and released during the period of 1949 - 1969. Since January 2016, the PI and the research team have worked intensively on data mining, categorisation and archival research on newspaper advertisements and film reviews. A working premise of this study is that the twenty years before the dramatic comeback of Cantonese-language films in the 1970s, the films from this "missing period" exhibit important stylistic, linguistic, and generic distinctions from later works. The research team has been collaborating with the CityU Library in creating a digital archive with bilingual keyword search functions. The work done in the first phase has led to the discovery of "lost" film titles that have not been listed in the records of the Hong Kong Film Archive, so far the most comprehensive resource bank for Hong Kong films. The current project distinguishes itself by the inclusion of extracts of film advertisement and newspaper film reviews to shed light on publicity, genre branding, and popular reception of films. The first phase therefore has laid a solid foundation for further extension to the later decades to create a comprehensive digital resource bank for Hong Kong cinema and a more complete filmography of Cantonese cinema. Phase 2 of this project will focus on the 1970s and 1980s, when Hong Kong cinema made an important transition that would bring in what is now commonly known as the "golden era" of Hong Kong cinema as a distinctively "local" cinema with a global appeal. So far, primary data collection and archiving, especially film reviews, reportage, and advertisements in both English and Chinese, is lagging behind critical scholarship on Hong Kong cinema. This project will therefore be a pioneer in integrating indexical production details with media sources for a more concrete understanding of the film culture in the 1970s and 1980s. Phase 2 will incorporate English-language media sources to shed light on the international reception of Hong Kong cinema. This project lay the foundation for further research on Cantonese-language films and the translocal film culture it has helped to foster. The main deliverables are a bilingual digital archive and one research monograph. Research outcomes at different stages will also be presented at international conferences. 本研究計劃旨在建立一個完備的中英雙語粵語電影數碼資料庫，透過整理昔日各大報章、雜誌的廣告和報道，重新發現那些散失了的、香港電影資料館亦未有紀錄的粵語電影資訊 (甚至是電影) 。締造一個更全面的粵語電影數資料庫亦有利我們研究、分析粵語電影定位。 本研究計劃分為兩個階段，上階段 “The Missing Period in Cantonese Cinema Phase One: 1949-1969” (獲大學研究資助局資助2015-2017年 ) 主要集中搜集、研究1949至1969年的粵語電影風格、語言和形式上的特點和當時的電影文化，並與香港城市大學圖書館攜手合作建立一個粵語電影數碼資料庫。現階段的研究則集中探討1970、80年代(即香港電影黃金年代)的粵語電影。資料搜集範圍不只限於中文媒體，亦會包括英文媒體，以探討香港電影在世界各地引起的迴響。

11609518.label: Major findings and research outcome
11609518.value: Outcome 1: As a continuation of the “Missing Period in Cantonese Cinema (1949-1969)” project, Cantonese Cinema (1970 – 1997) presents a digital archive of film reviews, media reports, and commentaries on films and filmmakers. The most important primary source is the City Entertainment magazine (formerly known as Film Bi-weekly), which used to be the leading film magazine in Hong Kong. Founded in 1979, the magazine used to be an authoritative voice in film journalism and high quality film reviews. It was also a nurturing ground for local film critics and film audience since the 1980s. Cantonese Cinema (1970 – 1997) is a streamlined keyword searchable database that provides researchers a convenient, at-a-glance index to City Entertainment’s film reviews, interviews, and reports on filmmakers and the film industry. By entering or clicking on a film title, the user will see a complete list of entries with the article’s title, author’s name, issue number, page(s), and a short summary of the content. We hope that the Cantonese Cinema Digital Archive (1 & 2) can serve as a convenient tool for researchers on Hong Kong cinema. Outcome 2: A research monograph on left-wing film production was published by the Edinburgh University Press in May 2020. It is the first book-length study in English on Hong Kong's left-wing cinema in the Cold War era and its legacy. The PI sought to steer away from standard ethical-ideological narratives of the left-wing cinema to examine the work of cultural agents, studios, and theatre operators in the "making-of" a popular left-wing cinema in Hong Kong whose nuanced legacy goes well beyond its presumed decline toward the late 1960s.

11609518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11609518.value: This project is the second phase of the Cantonese Cinema Digital Archive project. The combined databases present a more complete searchable catalogue of Cantonese films from 1949-1997. The most original feature of the Phase 2 database is the inclusion of film reviews, media reports and commentaries on films and filmmakers with indexes to the original source. By entering or clicking on a film title, the user will see a complete list of entries with the article’s title, author’s name, issue number, page(s), and a short summary of the content. The research monograph is the first book-length study in English on the left-wing film establishment in Hong Kong in the Cold War era and its nuanced legacy that extends well beyond the left-wing studios' decline after the Cultural Revolution. This study adopts a multi-focal approach to the left-wing film network, combining textual analysis with historical and archival research to reveal the institutional and corporate practices behind the making of the popular left-wing cinema in Hong Kong.

11610118.label: Project Objectives
11610118.value: To establish an updated and comprehensive conceptualization and operationalization of academic dishonesty within Hong Kong’s higher education, To examine the prevalence of different types of academic dishonesty among university students; To identify risk factors that may encourage Hong Kong university students to engage in certain type of academic dishonesty; and To identify protective factors that discourage Hong Kong university students from engaging in certain type of academic dishonesty.

To examine the prevalence of different types of academic dishonesty among university students;
To identify risk factors that may encourage Hong Kong university students to engage in certain type of academic dishonesty; and
To identify protective factors that discourage Hong Kong university students from engaging in certain type of academic dishonesty.

11610118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11610118.value: Academic dishonesty is a rising concern in higher education. Advances in technology and a diversification of assessment tasks (i.e. not relying solely on traditional paper-and pencil tests taken in regular classroom settings) make this problem seemingly more severe nowadays, than any time before. Previous studies generally focus on these issues: (1) a lack of a well-accepted definition of what constitutes “academic dishonesty”; (2) a lack of a theoretical model that can depict relationships of factors at personal and contextual levels, as well as interactions of factors between these levels; and (3) reliance on samples drawn from Western cultures. This proposal uses a mixed-method, two-phase study to address these issues by applying a systems approach as characterized in the ecological model of human development. In the first phase, an updated and comprehensive conceptualization and operationalization of academic dishonesty will be established through literature review and data collected from a focus group study of Hong Kong university students and individual interviews with university personnel (i.e. teachers, academic, and administrative staff handling cases related to academic dishonesty). Upon completion, a self-report instrument of frequency and attitudes toward various types of academic dishonesty will be developed. In addition, factors at personal and contextual levels that can influence students’ decisions to act unethically or not in academic tasks will be identified. In phase two, the academic dishonesty scale developed [in phase one] and other scales measuring risk and protective factors of academic dishonesty will be administered to a sample of N=600 Hong Kong university students. Prevalence of various types of academic dishonesty established in phase one will be examined with these data. In addition, conceptual models identifying influencing factors of academic dishonesty at both personal and contextual levels (as well as their interactions) will be analyzed. The validated model(s) will help policy-makers and educators to formulate effective strategies and tactics on how to control (or to intervene) the emerging problem of academic dishonesty in higher education of Hong Kong, thus to prevent further widespread of the problem

11610118.label: Realisation of objectives
11610118.value: 5.3.1. How and to what extent the project objectives have been achieved Overall, all four project objectives have been fully achieved. The objectives were realised by means of a mixed-method research design, with two phases of data collection. In the first phase qualitative data were collected from students and teaching staff from the eight UGC-funded universities in Hong Kong. The second phase was built on the results of Phase One. Quantitative survey data were collected from students studying at the eight UGC-funded universities. The first phase of data collection started in May 2019 and was completed in September 2019. Fourteen student focus groups were organized, which involved 50 students. Another round of individual interviews was conducted with 18 faculty members to provide further information about the issue from the teachers’ perspective. Both student and faculty participants were recruited from diverse disciplines within the eight universities, to enhance representativeness of the sample. With permission and written consent from the participants, all focus groups and individual interviews were audio-recorded. These audio records were transcribed into text following standard procedures adopted in social science research. The transcripts were sent back to the participants for further validation. The finalised qualitative data were then analysed using thematic analysis. After several rounds of coding and recoding, the analysis of the Phase One qualitative data was completed in December 2019. Preparation for the second phase, involving a literature review and making reference to findings from Phase One data, commenced in January 2020. A draft questionnaire was developed. After several rounds of discussion among the project team members, consultation with scholars in the field, and re-examination of the extant literature, a final version was constructed. The questionnaire consisted of 123 items tapping potential risk and protective factors that might relate/contribute to various types of academically dishonest acts. Although the second phase of data collection was scheduled for late January 2020, this plan was upset due to the coronavirus outbreak and subsequent suspension of classes in the local universities. Anticipating that this might last for some time, the initial data-collection plan to use an in-person, paper-and-pencil was adapted for administration via an e-platform hosted by the project team’s university. The online survey via the e-platform Qualtrics was set up in March 2020 and pilot tests were run to assure its appropriateness. As the suspension of classes also necessitated revising the plan for issuing incentives to participants (from paper cash coupons to e-vouchers), thus causing a further two-month delay. (The process of ordering the e-vouchers was affected by the work-from-home practices of both the university and the voucher supplier). Eventually, the Phase Two data collection could only start in May 2020. During the summer semester, from May to July 2020, responses from 255 participants were recorded in the online survey system, of which 236 were complete and usable for subsequent data analysis. The online survey continued in the fall semester (September-December 2020), during which another 385 responses were recorded, of which 272 were complete and usable. Overall, 508 usable cases were collected from 640 responses. Multiple rounds of data analysis were conducted from January 2021 to June 2021 to examine the prevalence of students’ engagement in various types of academically dishonest acts and to identify the risk and protective factors. 5.3.2 Difficulties and attempts to overcome them As mentioned above, the Phase two data collection was impacted severely by the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic. Apart from the above-mentioned delays in purchasing incentive vouchers and the need to transfer the questionnaire to an online platform, the lockdown of university campuses greatly hindered promotion and recruitment of research participants. It was no longer possible for teachers to use the personal touch to invite participants to respond during face-to-face classes. To tackle the problem, several alternative recruitment methods were attempted. First, student “recruitment assistants” were employed such that a group of students were hired to distribute invitation messages, via mobile messaging and/or social media, to the fellow students with whom they had personal contact. This method was only moderately effective. One reason was that the pandemic had affected the students’ social circles. Another reason, as our recruitment assistants reported, was that some university students were hesitant to do the questionnaire because they did not want to self-disclose their own academic dishonesty. As another recruitment method, promotional flyers were posted and distributed through university campuses. Unfortunately, this method became ineffective when the campuses were closed to students. A third method used was to ask course lecturers to broadcast invitation messages via their class meetings, and also to post the messages in their course e-learning platforms. This method was quite effective, probably due to the trust being built between the teachers and their students in the teaching and learning process. This was the most successful of the three alternative data-collection strategies at the time of pandemic. 5.3.3 Achievement and Dissemination of Research Findings Despite the difficulties and some delay in the data collection, the need to adjust the participant-recruitment and data-collection methods provided valuable experience for future research activities. Specifically, collecting data online, including the logistics of promotion, recruitment, data quality assurance, and distribution of e-coupons, was not so common in local research at that point of time but it definitely will be a future trend. Our research team has shared our experience with researchers in our own university as well as with scholars in other local universities. We are glad to learn that our protocols have been adopted by some other local research teams to tackle the challenge of difficult-to-reach target participants. Based on the qualitative data collected in the first phase of the study, a paper “Promoting academic honesty among university students: What can be done by educators?” was presented on 25th October 2019 at the Hong Kong Shue Yan University Evidence-Based Practice International Conference 2019. Some key findings of the project were subsequently presented (through online presentation) in the 9th European Conference on Education (ECE2021) held at University College London (UCL), UK, from July 15–18, 2021. The presentation was titled “Why students plagiarise: Corrupted morals or failed education?” A journal paper reporting major findings from qualitative data collected in Phase One of this study has been accepted for publication and was available online from the publisher site since 16 Feb 2022: Wu, J., Chui, W. H., Yau, A. & Hue, M. T. (2022). Instilling the need for academic honesty into Hong Kong university students: how well are we doing? Asia Pacific Journal of Education, DOI: 10.1080/02188791.2022.2038083 A paper summarising some key findings of the two phases of this study has been included in published conference proceedings with the following information: Wu J., Chui W.H.,, Hue M. T.,, & Yau A. (2021) Why Students Plagiarise: Corrupted Morals or Failed Education? ISSN: 2188-1162 The European Conference on Education 2021: Official Conference Proceedings https://doi.org/10.22492/issn.2188-1162.2021.13 A manuscript titled “Student’s engagement in academic dishonesty: A mixed methods study” reporting details of the scale development, validation, and some key findingsfrom the quantitative data related to influencing factors of academic dishonesty had submitted, reviewed, and returned by the SSCI-journal “The Asia-Pacific Education Researcher”. In responding to the reviewers’ comments, the manuscript is in preparation for submission to another SSCI-journal (e.g., Studies in Higher Education published by Taylor and Francis).

11610118.label: Major findings and research outcome
11610118.value: In the first phase of this research, 50 Hong Kong university students were interviewed through 14 focus groups facilitated by a trained research assistant and teaching staff from eight UGC-funded universities were interviewed individually by both a trained research assistant and a research team member (who was also a teacher in one of the participating universities). The participants were asked questions about the prevalence of academic honesty in Hong Kong higher education and to suggest personal and contextual factors that might explain these academically dishonest acts. The collected data suggested that student academic dishonesty prevails, represented predominantly by plagiarism. Students and teachers tended to explain academic dishonesty in terms of risk factors much more than protective factors. Both groups viewed that multiple personal and contextual factors can affect students’ academically dishonest acts. (For more details, see the published journal article, Part C #8) The qualitative findings were explored in greater depth by a 26-item instrument tapping various types of students’ academically dishonest acts and another 40-item instrument tapping risk and protective factors underpinning academic dishonesty, also based on both personal and contextual domains. These measuring instruments were completed via an online survey platform (Qualtrics) to university students who were invited to join the study via messages sent by email or social-networking sites. 50.7% of the respondents (effective sample size n=508) reported having attempted one or more of the given 26 academically dishonest acts in the previous semester. Plagiarism was found to be the most prevalent. Exploratory factor analyses of the data matrix generated from the 40-item instrument tapping risk and protective factors yielded four interpretable personal and five contextual factors. Simple bivariate correlations indicated that these extracted factors did exert effects on student’s academic dishonesty. In a regression analysis with interaction between personal and contextual factors being modelled, academic dishonesty was better explained by the interactions between these factors more than a model with just individual factors. This indicated that modelling only the personal or contextual in an isolated manner might lead to a misleading finding. It suggests that students with certain characteristics situated in a certain learning environment will be more likely to engage in academic dishonesty. (For details, see Parts C #8 and #9, the paper in a conference proceedings and a manuscript in revision for subsequent submission to another SSCI journal, after returning from the SSCI journal “The Asia-Pacific Education Researcher”)

11610118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11610118.value: This mixed-method research demonstrates the importance of using an indigenous approach to study an educational issue with a strong cultural orientation and context dependency. The qualitative phase helped to identify factors leading to students’ engagement in academic dishonesty that do not operate in an isolation. This was confirmed by regression analysis of the quantitative data. As an illustration, it may be that their academic assignments are too difficult, combined with an environment that allows them to do so, this can enable the dishonesty. Multiple personal and/or contextual factors act together to drive students to choose dishonesty. Due to limited time and manpower, the present research could only focus on a limited number of personal and contextual factors in conventional higher education settings. As online teaching, learning and assessment are becoming more and more prevalent, the widespread use of online assessment creates new challenges (e.g., how to authenticate students’ identities in online examinations or to ensure that they are completing the examination away from social contacts). Further development of the research can be heading towards this direction (i.e., the impact of technological advance on the prevalence of academic dishonesty and how to control the use of technology to encourage honesty).

11610118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11610118.value: This study revealed that up to half of Hong Kong university students had engaged in at least one of 26 academically dishonest acts tapped by a survey instrument developed specifically for this research. Plagiarism was the most commonly reported dishonest act. Due to certain personal factors, some students tend to more likely to engage in certain types of academically dishonest acts while others will refrain from temptation. Likewise, certain contextual factors can lead to higher chances of activating or avoiding dishonest acts. According to this research, student’s academic dishonesty seems not to arise simply out of a single factor falling into either personal or contextual domains. It is a joint effect of factors from these two domains that can drive students to use dishonest means to complete academic tasks. This research has important implications for prevention and intervention in matters of academic dishonesty in higher education. It requires “systemic” efforts from universities and individual faculties. For instance, rather than just educating or even punishing students, the whole contexts of teaching and learning should also be modified so that the incentive to cheat is removed and students are equipped with strategies other than cheating to pursue academic achievement.

11610518.label: Project Objectives

To explore the interactions between the development of videogames and enabling applications
To document the emergence of a videogame sector on the blockchain
To provide a theoretical analysis of game solutions on the blockchain

11610518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11610518.value: The blockchain has been hyped to constitute a major disruptive technology in the near future, and will have major impact on several industries. Described as a distributed, immutable and incremental record of transactions into chained blocks, it emerged in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis as a protocol of peer-to-peer transactions aimed at counterbalancing the opaque, centralized and intermediated financial system (Nakamoto 2008). The blockchain is the technology that supports the creation and operation of cryptocurrencies - i.e. encrypted digital currencies -, such as bitcoin. However, its potentialities reach well beyond the financial sector. The obvious advantages of the blockchain are traceability, authentication of ownership and direct, truly peer-to-peer exchanges (removing transaction costs). Associated with ‘smart contracts’ which record and enforce agreements, its possibilities extend to proof-of-concept, proof-of-work, simultaneity of purchase and transfer of ownership, shorter distance between authors/creators and users/consumers, projects and investors. This project addresses the processes of emergence of videogame production using the blockchain. The videogame sector is touted to become one of the major fields of experimentation of the blockchain. Innovative technologies, cross-gaming, blurred boundaries between virtual and real world and new forms of exchanges are already being tested. This sector will probably contribute to the adoption of blockchain and cryptocurrencies by the general public via a spillover effect. However, its actual emergence hasn’t been thoroughly investigated yet. Our research is based on the proposition that blockchain technology is reconfiguring game development and that an analysis of the processes underlying such reconfiguration is timely. Our main research question – how is blockchain reconfiguring game development? - will be broken down into the following questions: what are the constitutive elements of game production on the blockchain? What are the obstacles and opportunities opened up by the blockchain for game production and how have these materialized so far? What are the connections between this emergent sector and its environment? To study this emergent subject in context, we will use a critical realist framework, which distinguishes between co-constitutive and non-constitutive relations in a situated process. Our methodology will consist in an exploratory case study of games existing on the blockchain or in an advanced development phase. It will be informed by semi-directed, open-ended interviews, and technography based on specialized sources of information and interaction on the blockchain and videogames. The current experimentations of blockchain gaming will provide valuable insights on the potentialities of blockchain technology in the field of videogame production. 區塊鏈上遊戲製作領域的興起 The emergence of a videogame production sector on the blockchain 區塊鏈已在不久的將來被大肆宣傳成為一項重大的顛覆性技術，並將對多個行業產生重大影響。作為一種分佈式、不可變以及在其鍊式區塊中記錄的漸進式交易，區塊鏈在2008年金融危機之後出現，旨在平衡不透明、集中和中介金融系統的點對點交易協議（Nakamoto 2008）。而區塊鍊是一種支持加密貨幣（即加密數字貨幣，如比特幣）的創建和運營的技術。但是，它的潛力遠遠超出了金融體系。 區塊鏈的明顯優勢是其可追溯性、所有權認證以及消除了交易成本, 是真正直接的點對點交易。它的可能性通過記錄和執行協議的“智能合約”擴展到概念驗證、工作證明、同時性的購買和所有權的轉讓，縮短了作者/創作者與用戶/消費者、項目和投資者之間的距離。 這個研究項目提出利用區塊鏈作為視頻遊戲製作的過程。電子遊戲行業被招徠成為區塊鏈的主要實驗領域之一。創新科技、誇平台遊戲、虛擬和現實世界之間模糊的邊界以及更多新式的交流已經陸續在試驗當中。這個體系可能會通過溢出效應促進公眾採用區塊鍊和加密貨幣。然而，它的出現尚未得到徹底的考察。 我們的這個研究建基於我們的觀點：區塊鏈技術正在重構遊戲開發，並且對這種重構過程進行分析是及時的。我們的主要研究問題是： 區塊鏈如何重新建構遊戲開發？而此問題將會引伸以下多個問題： 區塊鏈上游戲製作的構成要素是什麼？區塊鍊為遊戲製作帶來了哪些障礙和機遇以及到目前為止這些障礙和機遇是如何出現的？ 這個新興領域與其所屬環境之間有什麼聯繫？ 為了研究這個新興課題當中的語境，我們將使用一個批判性的現實主義框架。它會區分了在一個既定過程當中的共同構成和非構成的關係。 我們的研究方法將包括對現有在區塊鍊的遊戲或在高級開發階段的遊戲進行探索性案例研究。它將以半定向、開放式訪談和基於區塊鍊和遊戲的特定的信息來源和當中的互動來呈現。 而目前這個區塊鏈遊戲的實驗將為在區塊鏈領域的遊戲製作領域當中的潛力提供真知灼見。

11610518.label: Realisation of objectives
11610518.value: 1.To describe the constitutive elements of game development on the blockchain We achieved this objective by identifying the main blockchain games, in particular those which were listed in charts like Dappradar, then we unpacked their structure by identifying primarily the blockchain-specific components, the problems they were faced with and the solutions they were trying to offer. We then tried to follow their evolution over the duration of the project, while remaining open to newer projects which seemed to propose an interesting application of the blockchain as well: in fact, this strategy proved efficient because most of the games we identified after our initial research seemed to fall in some void after a while. This corresponded to a very speculative era in the crypto industry: the so-called ICO Craze (Initial Coin Offering), followed by a crisis that ended with the disappearance of most of the projects. While it could have been problematic to pivot and identify other projects, our initial strategy of adopting, from the beginning, a dynamic approach in case selection instead of a closed list of cases proved the most efficient. We observed how the most interesting projects aimed to offer technological solutions and create the technological layers that might be required by the whole industry. However, many projects eventually failed either because of the difficulty of the task or because they were struggling to find a market. Our conclusion was that game development often implied developing standards for the whole space as well, creating the solutions that correspond to the specific needs of the gaming industry. For instance, scalability, the cost of mini-transactions incurred within a game as well as the speed of transactions are among the major issues specific to the sector. Tackling these issues has led some of the game companies to develop their own blockchain layer. Therefore, our findings consisted in identifying those projects that were interested in offering both a playable game (what kind of game they were developing, what were the challenges they were facing, and how they were trying to develop their own standards and technological solutions) and the technological layer which would be useful for the sector or part of it. 2. To explore the interactions between the development of videogames and enabling applications This point was probably the most interesting observation we made: to compare the strategies of gaming companies who preferred to develop their own enabling solutions and the ones that preferred to trust the existing solutions. Given that both the blockchain gaming sector and the underlying layer of blockchain technology were relatively young, the solutions necessary for a smooth gaming experience were (and still are) lacking. Several solutions have been developed since the beginning of our research. However, they were mostly untested. Three to four years later, some consolidation seems to be happening however and some trends emerge, the most interesting of which being the development of solutions aimed at blockchain gaming, by gaming companies. Often times, such solutions have proven to be useful outside the gaming sector as well. For instance, the layer 2 solution (aiming to solve the problem of scalability), Immutable X, was developed for a gaming company: Gods Unchained. Similarly, some scaling solutions have started offering some form of support to blockchain gaming companies in order to attract them. 3. To document the emergence of a videogame sector on the blockchain This proved to be our first task as we strove to identify the different actors in the sector from the beginning of our research, which coincided with the emergence of the second wave of blockchain games (after the crypto games which were mostly mining games). The second wave consisted of a more diverse range of games, as more developers were interested in exploring the technology in diverse kinds of games (e.g. trading card games, racing, and so on). We kept a record of daily news on blockchain gaming from trustworthy sources (e.g. Dappradar, Playtoearn.online, Cointelegraph, Coindesk, VentureBeat to name a few). We also followed the activities of a few trailblazing games and their investors, for instance Axie Infinity and Animoca Brands, whether on Twitter, Youtube and so on, or from their newsletters. These companies were selected, since, as our research progressed, they emerged as the most viable ones. However we also observed that, during the emergence of the videogame sector, many companies also disappeared eventually. Our main conclusion was that the emergence of this sector required the parallel emergence of technological solutions aiming to make videogames viable on the blockchain. Another interesting conclusion was that the interest in having a game on the blockchain was to leverage the sector other blockchain sectors, notably Decentralized Finance (DeFi) and Decentalized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs). Therefore the blockchain gaming sector is not isolated from other blockchain sector; the specificity of some blockchain games may lie in their ability to take advantage of solutions created in other sectors. 4. To provide a theoretical analysis of game solutions on the blockchain We achieved this objective by adopting a theoretical approach rooted in Infrastructuring. This approach was particularly fruitful since it aimed to emphasize the constitution of blockchain gaming sector as an ongoing and situated process. Importantly, infrastructuring enables to account for the process of creating, maintaining and repair an infrastructure, the negotiations entailed by such process, the limiting or enabling effects of the ‘installed base”, i.e. what already exists (for instance, legal structure, electricity, internet connections and so on). Furthermore, infrastructure also makes it possible to identify the actors involved in that process, their strategies, their relations with other actors. And finally, infrastructuring also accounts for the role of technology, and other technical infrastructuring agents. This approach proved particularly relevant in the study of the emergence of blockchain gaming and enabled us to offer a novel understanding of a phenomenon like play-to-earn, one of the structuring narratives in the blockchain gaming sector. In sum, we did not encounter any particular problem during the course of this research. Surely, the research proved to be ambitious and required more processing time but the results are certainly rewarding.

Major findings Can blockchain be a mere tool? The increasing interest of the mainstream industry in the uses of blockchain as a ‘tool’ may pose other challenges to its decentralized qualities. Blockchain-evangelists and blockchain-instrumentalists will be fighting for the destiny of blockchain. While the former strives to build unique blockchain experiences, practices and interactions, the latter consider the blockchain as a tool that can complement the mainstream model without questioning the existing system. These positions are ideological, both in their premises and materializations, not so much as an opposition between capitalistic-proprietary and a collaborative-open-source mode of production - after all, some of the main advantages of blockchain for games are the true ownership of digital assets for the players-investors, and a better traceability of these assets and their secondary revenues for the developers. The tension is between a conservative order which manages to accommodate innovations, and (a search for) alternative ways of being and doing.

The PI is the director of the ACIM Laboratory for Interventions in Speculative Finance, School of Creative Media (City University of Hong Kong), which will be a platform for the development of future research on the topics of blockchain.

11610518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11610518.value: This research addresses the emergence of a blockchain gaming ecosystem between the affordances and limitations of technological solutions, intense and decentralized social interactions, and institutionalization. The blockchain gaming ecosystem has been structuring around several issues such as the degrees of decentralization; asset ownership; a new business model defined by player-led economy and the opportunity for pay-to-play; the importance of community building; platformisation and interoperability; as well as the search for common standards and the subsequent institutionalization. We use a critical realist perspective on sociomateriality and technographic method to analyse the progressive imbrication of the social, the material and the normative in the constitution of the blockchain gaming ecosystem. We conclude that, although the implementation of blockchain in the gaming sector has necessitated trade-offs with the initial ideological intents of blockchain, notably on decentralization, it has also expanded the field of its potentialities.

11610818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11610818.value: Of all of the tasks that law students must complete during their legal studies, arguably none evoke as much fear and dread as do oral advocacy performances in so-called ‘moots’. In a moot, similar to a mock trial, students are provided with a set of facts for a simulated dispute. They then work in teams and play the roles of advocates for different parties to that dispute, researching the law and formulating legal arguments that are recorded in a written memorandum. Finally, they orally present these arguments as part of a hearing before one or more judges, usually members of the legal profession. Thus, moots involve written discourse in the initial formulation of arguments and spoken discourse in the oral presentation of arguments to judges. The advocacy skills that are required for this task are extremely demanding and students must be able to think on their feet and respond to the questions of their professional judges. For students with English as a second language, like the vast majority of law students in Hong Kong, the task, which is performed in English, is a particularly challenging one. In spite of these challenges, there is little empirical research that language teachers and legal skills teachers can draw on, in order to make decisions about how best to teach the language of oral advocacy in the academic legal context. This project will address this gap by focusing on two key areas: 1) the discourse practices of oral advocacy, including the target spoken and written texts that students create and the processes that they go through to create them; 2) the learning process. The project will use a mixed-methods research design, drawing on a wide range of data sources, including: recorded team meetings and field notes, students’ written memoranda and oral advocacy performances, comments from their teachers and peers, interviews with teachers and students. The study will result in a detailed linguistic description of the key genres of oral advocacy and a taxonomy of learning processes, demonstrating the range of interactions that may foster the development of language skills and competencies. These findings will be of use to the many law students and their teachers around the world who take part in mooting competitions, or are otherwise engaged in oral advocacy tasks in the academy.

11610818.label: Realisation of objectives
11610818.value: The overall aim of this project was to examine the practice of international commercial arbitration mooting at law school. Mooting is a high-stakes law school oral advocacy activity, in which law students present arguments—first in writing and then in oral form—usually to external legal professionals. The project aimed to account for the language and multimodal practices of law students engaged in this mooting activity, as well as how the students went about learning those practices. The project objectives were achieved through the systematic analysis of a large amount of data collected as part of a longitudinal case study of a team of student mooters and their law school coaches. The data collected, processed, and analyzed included: video- and audio-recorded team meetings and practice hearings/moot presentations; contemporaneous field notes; interviews with student mooters; student drafts of legal memoranda; textual artifacts collected in the team Dropbox folder; and team social media communications. Overall, progress on the project has been relatively smooth and it has been possible to address all of the objectives fully, with publications and/or conference presentations emerging as outputs in each of the areas. Below, I summarize the progress made, taking each of the objectives in turn. Issues of genre and multimodality: ‘what’ are students learning? (Objectives 1 and 2) Objective 1: To determine the discursive, organisational, lexical and grammatical features of key oral advocacy genres, i.e. the legal memorandum and the moot presentation Objective 2: To determine how the full range of semiotic modes, including visual, kinaesthetic, written linguistic and spoken linguistic modes, play a role in the composition process of target oral advocacy genres In order to achieve these objectives, two related data sets have been processed and analyzed. The first data set relates to the collaborative writing of the legal memorandum. It consists of two main data sources: 1) drafts of the memorandum and feedback on those drafts from teachers and peers made using the track changes function of MS Word; 2) recordings and field notes of team meetings that were observed, in which the team discussed their drafts. An analysis of this data has provided insights into the genre of ‘Memorandum’ and the necessary professional discourse used in order to express that genre. This analysis has been published in RELC Journal (2020) (see Report Part C). The second set of data consists of practice hearings/moot presentations made by student members of the team. Here too, there are two data sources: 1) the videos and related field notes of the oral presentations; 2) the recordings and field notes of oral feedback from coaches and peers. Videos of moot presentations were transcribed and analyzed both quantitatively and qualitatively. The quantitative analysis provided insight into the range of language choices that students made in their presentations, in particular the extent to which they made use of ‘self-mention’ (e.g. ‘I’) or some other kind of discourse strategy to present their argument. This analysis was presented at the International Pragmatics Association conference (June, 2019) (see Report Part C). The second set of data was further analyzed using qualitative, multimodal analysis in order to determine what ‘multimodal resources’ students employed in their moot presentations. The analysis showed that students are coached to use multimodal forms of representation including: 1) gesture; 2) gaze; 3) facial expression; 4) acting; 5) dress and organization of materials; 6) non-verbal communication system between students. This analysis has been written up for publication, submitted to ‘Applied Linguistics’, and is currently under review (see Report Part C). Issues of language socialization: ‘how’ are students learning? (Objectives 3 and 4) Objective 3: To determine what opportunities for second language socialisation expert/novice interactions and novice/novice interactions afford during oral advocacy activities Objective 4: To identify developments in participants’ discipline-specific language and skills competencies over time These objectives were realized by studying the two data sets described above, namely: 1) draft memoranda with feedback recorded in MS Word track changes and orally in team meetings; 2) practice hearings/moot presentations and oral feedback on those presentations given in team meetings. The analysis showed that students could receive different kinds of feedback on their writing, targeting different levels of discourse and practice: 1) lexico-grammatical level; 2) discourse level; 3) disciplinary content level; 4) composing process level; 5) affective level. These findings are published in Hafner & Yu (2020) (see above and Report Part C). Analysis of feedback on oral performance showed that students’ performances could be understood as attempts to claim a legal professional ‘discourse identity’, which was also promoted by coaches, who suggested specific strategies. The analysis showed that feedback focused on: conventional ways of addressing colleagues, acknowledging an arbitrator’s question, making claims, and supporting claims. This analysis was presented at the Sociolinguistics Symposium (June, 2021) (see Report Part C). The analysis further showed examples of student uptake of feedback in their language practices, again based on observations of both interaction in meetings and in the MS Word feedback. Findings on longitudinal uptake were presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Association of Applied Linguistics (March, 2021) (see Report Part C). Issues of theory and practice (Objectives 5 and 6) Objective 5: To make practical recommendations for language education and legal skills education practices Objective 6: To develop enhanced theoretical models of genre analysis and second language socialization The various studies carried out have practical implications for language education and legal skills education practices. In order to make practical recommendations in this area, it is necessary to reach out to the legal education community, in order to share findings with the members of that community and discuss implications. This has been achieved with a presentation on the linguistic and discursive elements of oral advocacy performance, given at the Asian Law Schools Association (ALSA) Symposium (April, 2021) (see Report Part C). Based on the various empirical studies carried out in relation to the case study research, it has been possible to generate (preliminary) theoretical models that enhance understanding of genre and language socialization. With respect to genre, the studies suggest that genres are realized through a wide range of different kinds of resources, not all of which are adequately accounted for in current models. Most obviously missing from contemporary accounts of genre is the multimodal dimension and this dimension is particularly relevant to the realization of a spoken genre like the practice hearing/moot presentation. Another important and under researched dimension is the process dimension. Theoretical insights related to genre are written up in Hafner & Yu (2020) and Hafner & Sun (under review) (see above and see Report Part C). With respect to language socialization, a model of language socializing inputs emerges from the data. There are three key parts to this: kinds of socializing interactions (textual mentoring, modelling, scaffolding, coaching, and negotiating); kinds of socializing agents (peers, teachers); longitudinal developments. These theoretical insights on the nature of language socialization were presented to the research community in two conference presentations, the first at the Annual Meeting of the American Association of Applied Linguistics (March, 2021, see above and Report Part C) and the second at the Sociolinguistics Symposium (June, 2021, see above and Report Part C).
