11610818.label: Major findings and research outcome
11610818.value: This research investigated oral advocacy practices at law school, in particular the questions of ‘what’ language practices students are learning and ‘how’ they went about learning those practices. The research continued an existing project of research, building on a genre analysis of the moot presentation. Hafner (2018) provided the foundations for the research and showed that the ‘international commercial arbitration moot’ could be understood as a genre, involving three main stages: introductions, procedural arguments, substantive arguments. The study demonstrated the central importance of ‘questions and answers’ in practice hearings in mooting presentations as well as illustrating strategies that students and moot ‘arbitrators’ use in order to negotiate control of the interaction. This addresses the question of what language practices students are learning. Hafner & Yu (2020) ("Language Socialization in Digitally Mediated Collaborative Writing: Evidence from Disciplinary Peer and Teacher Feedback”, Part C) focused on the collaborative processes involved in drafting the written arguments in the form of a ‘Memorandum for Claimant/Respondent’. The study showed how both teachers and peers contribute to the learning/socialization processes of students as they provide feedback on different levels of language practice: 1) lexico-grammatical level; 2) discourse level; 3) Disciplinary content level; 4) Composing process level; 5) Affective level. The paper addresses both what kind of language is expected as well as how it is developed. Hafner & Sun (under review) ("Multimodal expression of an expert professional discourse identity: The case of oral advocacy at law school”, Part C) focused on multimodal conduct in the practice hearings. It showed that students receive feedback on their oral presentations that goes beyond their use of language to include their multimodal performance, including: 1) keeping gesture to a minimum; 2) strategic use of gaze; 3) composing yourself and your facial expression; 4) mooting as acting; 5) physical appearance and organization of materials; 6) non-verbal communication system between counsel. The paper addresses what kind of multimodal conduct is expected as well as how it is developed. Of the conference papers given (see Part C), one (“Powerful and powerless language…”) addressed particular use of language, two addressed the discursive construction of an expert identity (“Mooting interactions: what is going on…”; “Discourse identities in oral argument in law…”), and one addressed the learning processes of students in the oral advocacy mooting activity (“Academic subject specialists as language teachers…”). Again, these provide insights into both ‘what’ is being learned and ‘how’.

11610818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11610818.value: This research can be further developed in two main ways. The first is to further engage with the ethnographic data collected in the oral advocacy research site in order to provide additional accounts of genre and learning. At this stage, a number of interesting avenues remain open to further investigation. In particular, these include: 1) the use of ‘small stories’ among team members in order to index affiliation to a range of different disciplinary cultures at different levels (e.g. the team, the university, the profession); 2) the use of humour and ordeal by coaches and members of the team in order to facilitate language socialization and learning processes; 3) students’ learning trajectories understood through multiple case studies of individual students. I propose to pick up these themes in a book length treatment of this research. The second way to further develop the research is by extending the research into other areas of specialized discourse, building on the themes of genre, language socialization, multimodal interaction and multimodal composing that are prevalent in this research. I propose to begin by examining multimodal genres in the specialized domain of academic science and will seek funding in order to conduct new studies.

11610818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11610818.value: For professionals of all kinds to be effective, it is essential that they be able to communicate well. This is especially true of lawyers, whose job always involves working with words in one way or another. This project focuses on the way that lawyers learn the communication skills of their discipline. It does this by focusing on two important questions: first a ‘what’ and then a ‘how’. These questions are: 1) what does successful communication in the specialized disciplinary context of law look like? And 2) how is disciplinary communication in academic and professional legal settings learned? To answer these questions we conducted a case study of a team of law students and their law teacher coaches, as they went about preparing for an international oral advocacy ‘mooting’ competition. Mooting is a high-stakes law school oral advocacy activity, in which law students present arguments—first in writing and then in oral form—usually to external legal professionals. By observing the way that this team first drafted their arguments and then practiced orally presenting them, we were able to understand: 1) the way that language is used in relevant legal texts and interactions; and 2) how law students learn that language.

11611118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11611118.value: Gender mainstreaming is a policy making framework and global strategy that aims to achieve gender equality. The strategy has been endorsed and adopted by international organizations and governments that participated in the 4th Beijing Women’s Conference in 1995. The Hong Kong SAR government has a responsibility to make sure that the gender perspective is integrated at all levels of policy formation and implementation to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of governance. The concept of gender mainstreaming has been widely adopted in many countries, however, since the 1990s, translating this concept in different social and cultural contexts has become a policy priority for the international agenda. This study will explore how the international concept of gender mainstreaming has been translated into local policy formation and practice, and will take the “active ageing” policy in Hong Kong as a case study. “Active ageing” is a policy strategy that aims at facilitating the rights of older people, enabling them to remain healthy, stay in employment longer, and participate in community life. However, ageing is not a gender-neutral issue. As well as differences in life expectancy between males and females, women and men also have different ageing trajectories that affect them differently. Studies into “active ageing” are not new, however, the gender perspective is largely missing from both Western and local studies. A broad-brush approach to policy making, disregarding gender differences, could result in widening the gap between women and men. How far has the ageing policy in Hong Kong addressed the gendered nature of ageing and the diverse life course of the different sexes? Do the existing policy and measures reflect the special needs of women and men, allowing older people who have different experiences and resources in their life course to live well? These questions remain unanswered. The proposed study aims to undertake a gender audit of the existing active ageing policy in Hong Kong and to identify possibilities for gender mainstreaming the policy to address the special needs of older women and men in employment, family, and community. The proposed study will have a long-term impact on developing a proactive and gender-sensitive active ageing policy that addresses the diverse needs of older women and men in Hong Kong and on developing policy alternatives for the local context.

11611518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11611518.value: 六七暴動與冷戰：美國、台灣與港英政府的互動 關於六七暴動的文獻，近年稍有增加。但觀乎現存的硏究，一般祗聚焦於左派的抗爭策略、中共的角色和港英的回應，卻普遍忽略了冷戰這個大環境因素的影響。二戰之後，位處內地邊沿的香港，無法置身於共產主義與資本主義的意識型態鬥爭之外。英國的重要盟友美國一直以香港作為重要情報搜集中心，充份利用這個殖民地去監視大陸政權。而在它的默許下，國民黨亦在香港十分活躍。這兩股勢力，對倫敦以至港英政府回應左派挑戰的考慮時，應起重要作用。 這個硏究，將集中硏究四個方面，去考証美台在六七暴動的角色： （一）英方撤退考慮； （二）暴動期間的軍事調動； （三）暴動後恢復公眾信心計劃；及 （四）暴動期間國民黨在港的部署及行動。 這個分析，可以提供新的視角去理解殖民管治：殖民地政治從來不是純粹由內部因素決定，而國際形勢變化，對它的決策也有關鍵作用。

11611818.label: Project Objectives
11611818.value: To combine comparable data on a series of health measures and demographic characteristics from representative panel surveys in Hong Kong and mainland China with similar research designs, namely, the Hong Kong Panel Study of Social Dynamics (HKPSSD) and China Family Panel Studies (CFPS, Guangdong self-representative subsample). To collect data on measures of cognitive performance in Hong Kong that are comparable to the corresponding and repeatedly collected data in CFPS using a special module to be attached to the coming wave of HKPSSD. To investigate the long-term effects of famine exposure on objective measures of adult health, including height, weight, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and hospitalization. To investigate the long-term effects of famine exposure on cognitive performance, including vocabulary, mathematics, memory, and number series tests. To adopt a migrant–stayer approach to compare emigrants who moved to Hong Kong from Guangdong province before 1959 and who thus avoided the Chinese Famine (the control group, using the HKPSSD data) and Guangdong residents who remained in Guangdong and experienced the famine (the treatment group, using CFPS data). Hong Kong natives will also be included as an additional comparison group. To conduct the migrant–stayer comparisons separately for two pre-famine birth cohorts: the 1923–1940 and 1941–1958 birth cohorts. Considering that emigrants may be different from stayers because of migration selectivity, a post-famine 1963–1980 birth cohort will also be included (neither emigrants nor stayers in this cohort experienced the famine), and a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis will be further conducted to partial out the influence of migration selectivity and obtain unbiased estimates of the famine effect. Specifically, the DID analysis refers to estimating the difference between emigrants and stayers in the pre-famine cohorts minus the difference in the post-famine cohort.

11611818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11611818.value: The 1959–1961 Chinese Famine was one of the worst human catastrophes in history. The famine caused about 30 million deaths, led to a sharp increase in miscarriages and stillbirths during the famine years, and had long-term negative impacts on survivors’ various outcomes such as height, weight, hypertension, mental health, educational attainment, and labor supply. Although a myriad of studies have focused on the long-term consequences of the famine, those studies are subject to a common weakness: the absence of a genuine comparison group that was not exposed to the famine because the famine afflicted all of China and no regions within the then border of the People's Republic of China were completely shielded. This project will tackle the above problem by using a novel migrant–stayer comparison to identify the causal effect of the famine on adult health and cognitive performance. Specifically, this study will use cross-border emigrants who moved out of mainland China to Hong Kong before the famine started as a comparison group; and this study will compare these “unexposed” emigrants to their “exposed” counterparts who stayed in the mainland and experienced the famine using comparable data from the Hong Kong Panel Study of Social Dynamics (HKPSSD) and the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS). HKPSSD and CFPS are representative panel surveys with similar research designs. HKPSSD includes over 3,000 immigrants who came from mainland China. These immigrants will be used to match their origin counterparts in CFPS (Guangdong sample) for the migrant–stayer comparison. Both surveys include comparable data on height, weight, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and demographic and socioeconomic characteristics. CFPS repeatedly collected data on various measures on cognitive performance. This project will propose that a special module be attached to the coming wave of HKPSSD to collect comparable cognition data. The empirical findings from this project will provide a solid basis for the accurate assessment of the long-term consequences of early-life exposure to malnutrition. The project will generate large volumes of data and produce a series of studies that adopt a migrant–stayer comparison to enrich the literature on famine impact. 中國1959年至1961年間的大饑荒是歷史上最嚴重的人為災難之一。這個饑荒造成三千萬人死亡，導致受災期間流產和死胎數量的急劇上升，並且對倖存者的身高、體重、血壓、心理健康、教育程度以及勞動市場參與等諸多方面有著長期的不良影響。 目前已有大量研究聚焦于饑荒的長期影響，但有一個共同的不足：缺乏一個理想的比較群體——這個群體必須是沒有受到饑荒影響的。由於大饑荒波及當時整個中國，所以境內區域沒有任何群體是符合這個條件的。 本項目利用一個新穎的“移民-留守者”比較設計解決這個難題，研究饑荒對於成人的健康和認知能力的影響。具體而言，這個研究將利用香港社會動態追蹤調查（Hong Kong Panel Study of Social Dynamics ，HKPSSD）和 中國家庭追蹤調查（China Family Panel Studies ，CFPS）的數據，以在大饑荒前從中國大陸移民到香港的跨境移民作為比較群體，將這些“未受災”移民與那些留在大陸的“受災”群體做比較。 HKPSSD和 CFPS是有著相似研究設計的代表性追蹤調查。HKPSSD裡面有超過3000個來自中國大陸的移民樣本。本研究以這些移民去匹配CFPS中當時留在大陸的群體（廣東樣本）， 從而構成一個“移民-留守者”的對比。兩個調查都包含類似的身高、體重、糖尿病、高血壓、心臟疾病、以及人口社會經濟特征等變量。此外，CFPS已多次收集關於認知能力的數據。這個項目會在HKPSSD新一輪的調查中加入特定模塊，以收集認知能力數據。 本項目可以更加精準地評估早期營養不良對成人健康的長期影響。這個項目將會產生大量數據以供更加深入的相關課題研究。其新穎的“移民-留守者”對比設計，也將激發更多類似的比較研究，從而豐富有關饑荒影響的文獻。

11611818.label: Realisation of objectives
11611818.value: The project objectives have been successfully achieved. The following key accomplishments were made: 1. We adopted the migrant-stayer approach to simultaneously compare 1) cross-border immigrants, 2) stayers in mainland China, and 3) natives in Hong Kong, using two comparable datasets: the China Family Panel Study and the Hong Kong Panel Studies of Social Dynamics. 2. We collected data on measures of cognitive performance in the latest wave of HKPSSD and obtained the cognitive measures of the 2016 CFPS, and examined the famine effect on cognitive performance by applying the migrant-stayers approach. 3. We used the migrant-stayer approach to study cognitive performance, including the vocabulary test, immediate word recall, and delayed word recall. 4. We also examined the intergenerational effect of famine on survivors themselves and their children's health conditions by using the hospitalization outcome. 5. By adopting the migrant-stayers approach, we included emigrants from Guangdong to Hong Kong, who were exempted from the Chinese famine, as the control group. We defined people who remained in Guangdong and experienced the famine as the exposed group. 6. We classified three birth cohorts using the migrant-stayer approach: the 1923-1940 cohort, the 1941-1958 cohort, and the 1963-68 cohort. To address the potential concern of migration selectivity, we included the 1963-1968 cohort as a post-famine cohort with none of the three subgroups being exposed to the famine. We conducted a difference-in-differences analysis by comparing the difference between the stayers and emigrants in the 1923-1940 and 1941-1958 cohorts, respectively (difference 1), to the difference between the stayers and emigrants in the 1963-1968 cohort (difference 2), to obtain an estimate of the famine effect. 7. We extended our project to study the intergenerational mobility of Chinese immigrants on occupational attainment, applying the China Family Panel Study and Hong Kong Panel Study of Social Dynamics using the migrant-stayer approach. Overall, the project has successfully achieved its objectives by utilizing the migrant-stayer approach to study the effects of the Chinese famine on cognitive performance and intergenerational health outcomes and mobility.

11611818.label: Major findings and research outcome
11611818.value: 1. People who experienced the famine in early childhood (aged 1-3) had lower score on a vocabulary test and those who were exposed to the famine in utero did not differ from those born after the famine. Please refer to the reported paper by Zhang and Ho in Part C. 2. To deal with the problem of the lack of a comparable control group, the PI and PI’s collaborator compared the people who stayed in Guangdong with the people who crossed the border to Hong Kong before the famine. Results showed that Guangdong stayers who experienced the famine when they were aged 1-18 had worse performance in immediate word recall. Please refer to the reported paper by Zhang and Ho in Part C. 3. The early-life malnutrition experience not only has a long-term effect on survivors themselves but also has an intergenerational transmission to their children. Please refer to the reported paper by Zhang and Zhang in Part C. 4. Mothers exposed to famine in utero are more likely to have lower socioeconomic outcomes, and this poor condition is transmitted to their children in terms of annual income and monthly salary. But children’s health conditions not transmit through the maternal line. Please refer to the reported paper by Zhang and Zhang in Part C. 5. The adverse effects of famine for fathers themselves are insignificant and this intergenerational effects of famine on children’s economic outcomes are not transmitted through the paternal line. Whereas children’s health conditions only transmit through fathers who exposed to famine during childhood. Please refer to the reported paper by Zhang and Zhang in Part C. 6. The PI (and her collaborators) also examined the intergenerational mobility of Chinese immigrants’ occupational attainment in comparison to individuals who stayed in Guangdong stayers and Hong Kong natives by using the origin-destination approach. Findings show that children of Chinese immigrants achieve higher levels of occupational mobility compared with Guangdong stayers and Hong Kong natives. (Please refer to Part C) 7. Within immigrant groups, no matter how mobile parents’ occupational status is, all descendants achieve similar levels of occupational attainment in the labor market. Children of highly-skilled immigrants track their parents’ occupational status before migration (Please refer to Part C).

11611818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11611818.value: The adopted migrant-stayer approach in this project has demonstrated its effectiveness in exploring relevant research topics in migration studies, utilizing comparable data from the China Family Panel Study and the Hong Kong Panel Studies of Social Dynamics. This approach is likely to stimulate future research with similar research designs. For example, it can be used to examine intergenerational mobility on immigrants, stayers, and natives' educational attainment. The project's success in utilizing the migrant-stayer approach provides a valuable methodological contribution to the field of migration studies. This approach has the potential to be applied to other relevant research questions, utilizing comparable data from various countries or regions to explore the intergenerational effects of migration on various outcomes such as education, health, and socioeconomic status. Overall, the migrant-stayer approach used in this project is a promising research design that can be further utilized to address relevant research topics in migration studies and stimulate future research in this field.

11611818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11611818.value: In this project, we utilized a novel migrant-stayer approach to identify the causal effects of the Chinese famine on individuals' cognitive performance, utilizing comparable survey data from the China Family Panel Study and the Hong Kong Panel Studies of Social Dynamics. Our findings suggest that exposure to malnutrition during childhood has long-term effects on cognitive performance. The migrant-stayer approach used in this project is distinguished from the vast majority of famine-based studies that analyze data on survivors with comparisons between cohorts or regions exposed to different levels of famine. This approach provides better estimations of famine effects by comparing individuals who migrated across borders with those who stayed in their original region. This project extends the scope of the current fetal origins literature by providing empirical evidence that experiencing famine during early childhood has a long-term impact on cognitive performance. Our findings provide valuable insights into the intergenerational effects of famine and the importance of early-life nutrition on cognitive development. Overall, the migrant-stayer approach used in this project has proven to be a robust research design for exploring the long-term effects of early-life malnutrition on cognitive performance. Our findings have the potential to inform policies and interventions aimed at improving nutrition and cognitive development in early childhood.

11611918.label: Project Objectives
11611918.value: To investigate whether men and women in the police and social work are encouraged to perform specific types of emotional labor that correspond to conventional gender stereotypes (special treatment), or to embrace the same requirements of emotional labor regardless of sex (equal treatment). To compare how gender minorities in the police and social work react to the demands of emotional labor, by investigating their expected, felt, and displayed emotions at work. To build a holistic theoretical framework to understand attitudinal and behavioral consequences of gendered emotional labor, by integrating theories of emotional labor and gender-emotion stereotypes. To provide a general conclusion about gendered emotional labor in the police and social work, by integrating qualitative and quantitative methods, and comparing Chinese and American samples. This project will gather quantitative and qualitative evidence to build the breadth and depth of knowledge on this particular subject. Findings from Chinese and American samples will also be compared to assess their generalizability across cultural boundaries.

11611918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11611918.value: The proposed research project will investigate and compare gendered emotional labor and its consequences for men and women in the police (disproportionately male) and social work (disproportionately female). Emotional labor refers to work that requires the expression of appropriate emotions during service encounters. Conventional gender roles determine the types of emotional labor performed by each sex, i.e. men as disciplinarians and women as caretakers. Yet, as men and women progressively move into occupations traditionally dominated by the opposite sex, will stereotypical patterns of emotional labor still exist and exact a toll on gender minorities due to their marginalized status in the workplace? Will minority males and females confront different consequences of gendered emotional labor? Will that effect hinge on one’s gender role orientation? Answers to these questions will advance managerial knowledge yet they remain unavailable in extant research. This project will draw on two lines of research to answer the research questions: (1) the theory of emotional labor, which will lay the theoretical groundwork for understanding gendered emotional labor and its consequences, and (2) evidence from a range of gender-emotion studies that will add contextual elements to the theoretical framework. Moreover, as culture is relevant to gender norms, research will be conducted in both Chinese and American contexts to assess the generalizability of the research findings across boundaries. It is proposed that gender minorities perceive and perform emotional labor differently compared with their colleagues in the majority. Moreover, this difference will be greater for both those working in the male-dominated police force, and those in patriarchal Chinese society. Additionally, workers who deviate from prevailing norms of emotional labor will impair work morale and reduce effort to meet organizational expectations, but this effect will be mitigated by gender role orientation. This project will use the explanatory sequential mixed-methods design to investigate these propositions and explain research results, as this design will allow the researchers to build the broadest and deepest knowledge on this particular subject. The research team will be led by two public administration scholars with expertise in emotional labor. The PI has previously conducted extensive research on this subject using Chinese and American samples, while the Co-I is considered the pioneering researcher of emotional labor in the public administration community. They will form an ideal team to undertake this study. This project will produce research papers that disseminate findings and offer guidance for more effective management of emotional labor in gender-skewed workplaces.

11611918.label: Realisation of objectives
11611918.value: Following recent advances in emotional labor studies in public administration, this project was proposed to present an investigation of emotional labor with three comparative aspects: dual genders, occupations, and cultures. It aimed to investigate gendered emotional labor and its consequences for men and women in two gender-skewed public service professions, the police (disproportionately male) and social work (disproportionately female), and in two distinctive contexts, Chinese (relatively patriarchal) and American (relatively equalitarian) cultures. However, undertaking this project in turbulent times has proven more difficult than expected. Initially, several police and social work agencies were willing to participate in or support this project, including Taipei City Police Department, Dallas Police Department, the Department of Social Welfare of Taipei City, and the Kempe Center (the Colorado Child Welfare Training System). Yet, fatal police shootings in Dallas provoked mass demonstrations against police brutality in September 2018—right around the time this project was about to commence. The deteriorated relationship with the community led Dallas Police Department to take a cynical approach and therefore withdrew their support for this project. Thus, the research team decided to distribute the survey via the Utah Fraternal Order of Police. However, the target population became smaller than initially planned, and this association did not allow us to interview its members. The survey via the Colorado Child Welfare Training System did not generate a sufficient sample either. As a result, we yielded only 56 responses from American social workers and 253 from American police officers. Even though we collected survey responses from a larger group of social workers (n = 326) and police officers (n = 465) in Taiwan, the COVID-19 pandemic made our qualitative research challenging. We interviewed 26 social workers and 11 police officers in Taipei when we concluded this project. All in all, the research team believes the following project objectives have been fully achieved: • To investigate whether men and women in the police and social work are encouraged to perform specific types of emotional labor that correspond to conventional gender stereotypes (special treatment), or to embrace the same requirements of emotional labor regardless of sex (equal treatment). Reason: The research team successfully collected survey responses from 263 male and 202 female police officers and 72 male and 182 female social workers in Taiwan. As all respondents were asked to indicate their emotional job demands, the collected survey data, coupled with qualitative interviews conducted in Taiwan, allowed the research team to divulge if there exists gendered emotional labor between men and women in the police and social work. • To compare how gender minorities in the police and social work react to the demands of emotional labor, by investigating their expected, felt, and displayed emotions at work. Reason: Emotional labor is often perceived as an organizational meme embedded in a broader social context. In the survey, there were also questions enquiring how respondents react to such a social/professional norm. With the data collected, the research team is positioned to reveal the coping strategies used by gender minorities in the police and social work. • To build a holistic theoretical framework to understand attitudinal and behavioral consequences of gendered emotional labor, by integrating theories of emotional labor and gender-emotion stereotypes. Reason: The research team has tested the relationship between various emotional labor requirements and emotional exhaustion between men and women in police and social work. Intriguing findings have been yielded and will be disseminated at the KAPA International Conference 2022 this June. The following objectives were achieved partially due to all the challenges encountered: • To provide a general conclusion about gendered emotional labor in the police and social work, by integrating qualitative and quantitative methods, and comparing Chinese and American samples. This project will gather quantitative and qualitative evidence to build the breadth and depth of knowledge on this particular subject. Findings from Chinese and American samples will also be compared to assess their generalizability across cultural boundaries. Reason: Due to deficiencies in the U.S. data, we were only able to partially achieve this project objective using the data collected in Taiwan.

11611918.label: Major findings and research outcome
11611918.value: This project was the PI’s first GRF. Due to a lack of experience, he forgot to include research outputs that should have been reported in the midterm report, i.e., two bibliometric review papers on emotional labor studies in public administration. Those two articles, one published in the Journal of Public and Nonprofit Affairs (English) and the other in Public Administration and Policy Review (Chinese), are directly related to this project because they lay the foundation for further research works. As for the two papers that will soon be presented at the KAPA International Conference 2022 and submitted to journals, the research team has found a divergence between social workers and police officers and between male and female workers in how they respond to emotional labor demands. Findings from the police sample uphold that “service with a smile” does not affect public service professionals. Yet, we discover that the excessive demand for politeness leads to burnout among social workers. Moreover, the strategy of faking one’s emotions aggravates the adverse effect on those workers. However, when they opt to align their feeling with the required emotion, this job demand would do less harm. In the second paper, we have also found that masculine display rules in police positively predict female police officers’ emotional exhaustion, while gender identity will moderate such a relationship. The practical implications of these findings are discussed in these papers.

11611918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11611918.value: As indicated in the two bibliometric review papers, future research should probe into the intersection of emotional labor, citizen-state interaction, and social norms. The PI has directed his doctoral students to develop thesis research to investigate how public service professionals exert emotional labor to manage the citizen's and their own emotions in times of service failure and how such emotive work contributes to citizen satisfaction. The gender effect is one of the key variables.

11611918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11611918.value: The research of emotional labor has been deeply rooted in women’s studies. Although further analysis of gender differences could significantly broaden the research spectrum, a simultaneous comparison between genders and occupations has rarely been conducted in the extant literature. To fill this void, this project examines (1) gender differences in emotional labor in both male- and female-dominated workplaces, and (2) the attitudinal and behavioral consequences of such differences. This project thus generates a research momentum that will benefit emotional labor and gender studies in public administration. From a practical perspective, this project contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of gendered emotional labor and its effects, particularly in male- and female-dominated public service workplaces. Generally, public service jobs entail face-to-face or voice-to-voice interactions with citizens, in which successful work performance rests on a worker’s ability to respond to a variety of citizens with the correct vocal, facial, and/or bodily displays. Dyadic interactions decisively influence citizens’ perceptions of the quality of services received. While better management of emotional labor has been considered one of the recipes for continual service improvement, this project provides insights into how to achieve this goal. For example, its recommendations to remedy the consequences of gendered emotional labor will be used for human resource management purposes (e.g., job design and training), and will help thousands of police and social work personnel sustain their professional selves with dedication and perseverance.

11612318.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11612318.value: 冲突性媒介事件、象征性政治和威权语境下的协商：转型中国“社会戏剧”中的情、法、理

11612318.label: Project Objectives
11612318.value: The project will further our understanding of the intimate but troubled relationship between the nascent “rational public sphere” and “emotional public sphere” in China, or the under-studied topic on the links between events and issues in general. It tries to further both cultural theories in the “media events” tradition (Dayan and Katz 1992, 2017) and political theories on “authoritarian deliberation” (He and Warren 2011) The project hopes to examine the framing practices of the Chinese media in covering “moral outrage” stories and “resistance” stories. It will analyze how the deliberative frame of “social problem” engages the cultural/ritual frame of “social drama”, and the corresponding discursive processes at play, including “articulation” (narrative construction), “punctuation” (problem definition) and “attribution” (diagnostic and prognostic reasoning). In terms of explanation, the project tries to shed light on the structural level influences on the journalists’ discursive choices in conflict reporting, including opportunities and constraints at the political (state control over the means of symbolic production and dissemination), economic (market incentives) and organizational levels (production routines); as well as cultural level influences from personal to professional ideology (how elite and popular strands of party journalism as well as professional and tabloid strands of marketized journalism influence discursive choices). In terms of interpretation, the project will further our understanding on the craft of Chinese journalists as both reason-givers and storytellers. It tries to understand how journalists “make their stories work” when narrating moral tales of innocence and guilt to solicit righteous indignation (“moral outrage stories”) or sympathy (“resistance stories”) from audience, while at the same time trying to meet the requirements of objectivity-driven professionalism. In trying to bridge the three fundamental modes of communication, “ritual, strategy and deliberation”, the proposal highlights the importance of the “liminal” phase inherent in a media event and explores how this phase shares a similar structure with deliberation. It sheds light on why contentious media events are particularly vital for societies lacking regime-level democratic institutions for deliberation, such as China, and reflects on the genre’s social and political implications. I hope to produce conference papers, journal articles and a full-length monograph.

11612318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11612318.value: China’s recent social and economic transformation is accompanied by a loss of ideological hegemony and increased social stratification. Occasionally, these conflicts burst into mediated “social dramas”, constituting either “moral outrage” highlighting miscarriage of justice or “resistance stories” in which the underprivileged revenge against the powerful. These stories offer rich symbolic texts in studying contentious politics in China and media’s interaction with other institutions. This proposal constructs a typology of cases according to “the nature of offense” (including “moral outrage” and “resistance story”) and “effect on society” (ranging from “consensus” to “perpetuated conflict”). While “excused resistance” and “corrected moral outrage” achieve reconciliation, “punished resistance” and “divided moral outrage” perpetuate conflicts. By examining the events’ discursive processes, this project highlights a crucial but under-studied dimension of “media events”, i.e., the embodiment of a liminal phase that brings the “normative” (morally compelling) to bear on the “indicative” (politically efficacious) and holds potential for social renewal. Ideally, reflexivity can be achieved through deliberation. However, there is also the danger of populist moral gloaming. At an explanation level, the project seeks to identify the circumstances under which an event achieves “ritualization”, i.e., moving from contest to consensus, through studying how structural forces (e.g. political, economic and organizational factors) inform discursive choices and their relative success. At an interpretation level, through studying the craft of journalists as both reason-givers and storytellers in defining a society’s supreme virtue – justice – this project tries to unpack the meaning of these events as moral tales in contemporary China, revealing not only “large, universal truths of life, death, goodness and evil”, but also “parochial truths involving class, privilege, ambition, and resentment” (Tucker 1994: 61). To sum up, this project proposes a synthesized model for studying media events as ritual, strategy and deliberation, by trying to disentangle the different layers of “truth” embedded in mediation. These include individual-level truth attainable through the strategies of professionalism, social-level truth on the nature of underlying social problems through deliberation, as well as cultural-level truth or the meaning of the resonant moral tales. The negotiation of different levels of “truth” and the final form they take constitutes the “deliberative” or “populist” nature of events, with outcomes ranging from a narrowing of the gap between the “normative” and the “indicative” which produces social reconciliation, to an expansion of the gap that produces perpetuated schism, to rare instances of transformation resulting in deeper changes to institutions. 中国的市场化转型伴随以意识形态霸权的逐渐缺失以及日益严重的社会问题和社会分层。这些社会问题常常间歇性的以“社会戏剧”的形式呈现出来。它们或表现为由权力失范造成的“道德义愤”，或表现为弱势个体面对不公奋起反抗而导致的“复仇故事”。这两类故事为研究当今中国的抗争性政治以及媒体与社会的互动提供了丰富的范本。 基于“事件冲突的性质” (“道德义愤”亦或“复仇故事”)以及“事件对社会产生的效果”(“促进和解”亦或“加剧分化”) 这两个标准，本研究为争议性媒介事件的研究提供了一种类型学的思考。具体而言，“被宽恕的复仇故事”和“被纠正的道德义愤”两类事件往往有助于社会和解，而“被惩戒的复仇故事”以及“有争议的道德义愤”这两类事件则往往起到加剧冲突的作用。 在问题的“解释”层面，本课题试图探究不同的结构性因素（包括政治的、经济的以及组织层面的因素）如何影响不同主体的话语策略，以及这种话语竞争如何影响冲突的化解。换言之，在“解释”层面，本课题探究一个事件得以“仪式化”（从争议进入和解）的条件。而在现象的“解读”层面，本课题通过分析报道争议性事件的记者的双重身份（同时作为说理者和叙事者）以及他们的话术，来探究此类事件对于变迁中的中国社会的文化意义，即：这些事件如何描摹当代中国的道德边界。这里既有对于“绝对价值”，如关于“生、死、正义和邪恶”的定义，也有关于“相对价值”，如关于“阶级、地位、野心和怨恨”的探讨。由此，本课题将“阈限区间”这一此前被忽略的概念带入媒介事件研究。 “阈限区间”通过展现 (价值取向的) 应然标准和 (工具取向的) 现实之间的冲突从而激发社会变革力量。在理想状态下，变革的力量由阈限区间内带有自反性的协商催生。然而，在非理想的状态下，变革的呼声亦可带有民粹主义倾向。 总之，这个研究旨在探索一种从“仪式”、“策略”和“协商”的不同视角来研究媒介事件的新的理论模式，并通过这种模式在具体个案中的应用揭示争议性媒介事件中不同层次的“真实”：这既包括在个案层面通过新闻专业主义的实践可以达及的“个案真实”，也包括在中观层面通过对社会问题的协商可达及的“社会真实”，以及在文化层面由事件和经典道德故事脚本之间的勾连所揭示的“文化真实”。本课题通过对于数个典型案例的研究，揭示争议性媒介事件中不同层次的“真实”之间如何互动，如何形塑事件最终呈现的形式，以及在何种条件下冲突的发展符合以下一种路径：阈限区间缩小从而达成社会和解、阈限区间被放大从而导致冲突加剧、阈限区间被超越从而诞生新的社会建制。

11612318.label: Realisation of objectives
11612318.value: I have addressed all the objectives in my research output, notably through my China Quarterly article (2021) and Communication Monographs article (2023). 1. How the China Quarterly article realizes the project’s objectives: The linkage between the “rational” and “emotional” public spheres is evident in the article title – “between emotion, politics and law”. Of the two event genres, this article takes up the “resistance story” for scrutiny. Through studying a revenge murder triggered by a land dispute in China and its subsequent trial, the article explores the “narrative transformation” in the unfolding of the case and proposes an event-based model for authoritarian deliberation. It argues that an obscure murder rose to prominence because it came to be narrated as a different kind of story. Initially viewed as “a normal killing” (an event), the case morphed into a “contest” (a meta-narrative that contains issue frames) between a law-and-order frame emphasizing individual guilt, and a righteous-revenge frame symbolizing wider social conflicts. In the absence of an institutionalized issue forum in China, authoritarian deliberation is often pegged onto social dramas on the “judicial periphery”, thanks to a liminal phase inviting reflexivity. Such crisis-driven contentious politics exposes elite dissent that is otherwise veiled by an interest-driven alliance. In this study, the media engaged other social institutions in contentious performances that affirmed hidden social fault-lines but also encouraged deliberation. [Objectives 1, 2, 3 & 4]. 2. How the Communication Monographs article realizes the project’s objectives: This article (in collaboration with leading crisis communication scholar Prof. Yi-hui Christine Huang) studies the “moral outrage” genre in the form of crises involving organizational misconduct but also embodying deeper social problems. It introduces insights that enhance the project’s outcome: 1) The analytical lens is broadened from discursive practices of journalists/opinion leaders alone to engaging the interaction between journalists, crisis managers, the public and the state. In creatively engaging investigative journalism and crisis communication theories, we compare and critique the craft of journalists and crisis managers, each a variation on the phenomenological themes of “verification, justification and representation” [furthering objectives 2 & 3]. 2) Its interactional approach brings together micro- and macro-level factors [furthering objectives 3] by zeroing on the framing contest among key institutional actors that moves from a strategic model of locating “individual attribution” to a deliberative model that interrogates the “collective guilt” of social actors in contributing to the social problems underlying a crisis, which may herald regulatory changes [furthering objectives 1, 2 & 4]. 3) It argues the deliberative turn (which invokes a “scapegoat” embodying “collective guilt”) takes place when neither a journalistic narrative portraying the accused as a “villain” nor an organizational account foregrounding a “victim” self-perception manages to contain attribution at individual levels. By developing key crisis communication concepts such as “individual attribution” and rediscovering the multiple meanings of a “scapegoat”, the article innovates existing theories. [furthering objectives 2 & 4]. The following excerpt captures this essence: “Throughout this paper, we underline the importance of storytelling in crisis communication. But narrators do have choices, which are then driven by their own interest. We thus conceptualize crisis storytelling as a framing contest between crisis managers, investigative journalists, enterprising netizens, and the state over the definition and attribution of the crisis event. The contest commences with an encounter of two interpretive communities with divergent craft – crisis managers who are strategic communicators with a logic of rationalization and journalists who are storytellers adept at using irony and the logic of fundamental attribution. While both crafts initially treat attribution as an individual matter, their encounter produces a…deliberative logic that dwells on the collective ills of social actors and the legitimacy of underlying norms, during which the accused acquires the limbo character of the scapegoat.” (Liang and Huang, 2023, pp. 25-26) 4) It uses comparative case studies method based on theoretical sampling and presents a more elegant research design and more sophisticated arguments. [furthering objectives 3] 5) The article transcends western crisis theories that assume the stability of underlying norms with a focus on individual attribution. By analysing three cases that Chinese crisis managers initially identified as “commission”, “control” and “agreement” situations but ended up as crises involving “absent standards”, “bad standards” and “overrated standards”, the article highlights the deliberative potential of crisis communication embodied in the “standards situation”, and theorizes crisis-induced regulatory changes which is a recurring phenomenon in China [furthering objectives 1, 2, 3 & 4]. The following excerpt captures the essence: “In Bradford and Garratt’s model, A (commission), B (control), and D (agreement) all point to a static normative regime in which attribution can be assigned at individual levels. But C (standards situation) points to competing norms and suggests the possibility of normative change. We highlight the importance of “standards situation” for crisis communication in general, and Chinese crisis communication in particular. For a country without regime-level democratic empowerments, the rare window of deliberation induced by a crisis provides an opportunity for changing the normative status quo on issues that are usually papered over to advance public interest…The liminal phase opened up by a crisis not only augurs disorder (danger), but also impregnates change of order (opportunity).” (Liang and Huang, 2023, p.26) 6) I suggest that the field of crisis communication with its strategic outlook may benefit from a “ritual” dimension from cultural studies that underscores the narrative and rhetorical features of crisis discourse, and a “deliberative” dimension from political communication that interrogates the open-endedness of all values and standards. In addition to “furthering cultural…and political theories” (stated in the original proposal), I produced the unintended but significant result of localizing western crisis/strategic communication theories. [furthering objectives 1, 2, 3 & 4] 3. A note on how the project advances key conceptual binaries of moral outrage vs. resistance stories: I further develop the western-originated “social drama” concept, whose outcome have been confined to either a restoration of order or perpetuated schism, to anticipate the likelihood of a transformation of order, i.e., to focus on the liberating potential of “moral outrage” stories in China. I argue that while Chinese political culture values a higher ground of morality and shies away from an explicit validation of strategy, which impedes the development of “procedural rationality” underlining western traditions, this morality-based legitimacy becomes crucial during a crisis whose highly-charged political theatre compels power elites to be accountable to substantive sufferings of people. Such crisis-driven politics may even result in swift reforms to fine-tune the technicality of governance should public grievances become palpable, therefore making “moral outrage” events more germane to regulatory changes. Allowing crisis-induced legislative change on the judicial periphery pre-empts regime-level democratization while channelling grassroots grievances. This departs from the prevailing western conception of “moral outrage stories”, which focuses on the genre’s conservative social function. By comparison, I argue that the anger embodied in the “resistance story” carries less legitimacy. While revenge acts driven by social inequality symbolize calls for substantive justice and have deep roots in the Chinese moral universe (e.g. the knight-errantry tradition), therefore commanding authorities’ attention and encouraging deliberation, these stories augur less well for normative changes because the authorities are vigilant against an “avenger” who transforms him/herself from a victim to an agent. Differentiating the implications of “revenge stories” and “moral outrage stories” for the stability and change of contemporary social order in China is a major theoretical contribution of the project.

11612318.label: Major findings and research outcome
11612318.value: Major Findings: Through studying quintessential “resistance/revenge” and “moral outrage" stories in the nascent Chinese public sphere, my research explores the “narrative transformation” in the unfolding of these events and proposes an event-based model for authoritarian deliberation. I.e., in the absence of an institutionalized issue forum in China, authoritarian deliberation is pegged onto social dramas on the “judicial/regulatory periphery,” thanks to a liminal phase inviting reflexivity that follows the initial “breach”. Such crisis-driven contentious politics exposes elite dissent otherwise veiled by an interest-driven alliance. In these cases, media engaged other institutions in contentious performances that affirmed hidden social fault-lines but also encouraged deliberation. In particular, my research sheds interesting light on the uniquely liberating potential of “moral outrage stories” in China in harbingering normative/regulatory changes, which sets it apart from prevailing western conception of “moral outrage stories” that largely focuses on the genre’s conservative social function in maintaining dominant order through individualized attribution. In this project, by zeroing on framing contests among institutional actors during moral outrage-driven crises in China, I observe that when neither a journalistic narrative portraying the accused as a “villain” nor an organizational account foregrounding a “victim/scapegoat” self-perception manages to contain attribution at individual levels, the society enters a deliberative mode that interrogates social actors’ collective guilt complicit in a crisis, hence heralding regulatory changes. Differentiating the implications of “revenge/resistance stories” and “moral outrage stories” for the stability and change of contemporary social order in China is a highlight of the project. Research Outcomes: I have produced three journal articles spanning prestigious journals in the fields of communication studies, area studies and film studies, including two single-authored and one first-authored articles). In addition, I have also published one related book review and given numerous conference presentations. The highlights are below: Liang, Limin & Yi-Hui Christine Huang (2023): Victim, villain, or scapegoat? Mediating organizational crises embedded in social problems and the transformation of order, Communication Monographs [SSCI Communication Q2] Liang, Limin. (2022). Consuming the Pastoral Desire: Li Ziqi, Food Vlogging and the Structure of Feeling in the Era of Microcelebrity. Global Storytelling: Journal of Digital and Moving Images, 1(2), 7-39 [Lead Article] Liang, Limin. (2021). Between Emotion, Politics and Law: Narrative Transformation and Authoritarian Deliberation in a Land Dispute-triggered Social Drama in China. The China Quarterly, 245, 94-121. 11612318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11612318.value: I will carry out further research on the interstice of journalism studies, crisis communication and political communication, which link the three fundamental communicative forms of ritual, strategy and deliberation. Already, this effort has culminated in my latest publication co-authored with Prof. Yi-hui Christine Huang, a leading crisis communication scholar, that localizes western crisis communication theories within a Chinese context. By dissecting the craft of two interpretive communities (i.e. crisis managers and journalists) through three carefully chosen "moral outrage" cases, each revolving around the phenomenological concepts of "verification, justification and representation", we built a bridge connecting the fields of journalism studies and crisis communication. We also proposed a few original concepts for future development, including "the deliberative potential of Chinese crisis communication" which is a departure from the field's current strategic orientation, the turn from studying "individual attribution" that underlines current strategic communication theories to studying "collective attribution" of social actors complicit in a crisis, as well as the rediscovered cultural significance of the archetype of "scapegoat" for both crisis communication and journalism studies. This article, along with other research output under this project, point to a new avenue for interdisciplinary research connecting cultural studies of journalism, crisis communication and political communication.

11612318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11612318.value: Through studying paradigmatic “resistance stories” and “moral outrage stories” in the nascent Chinese public sphere, my research proposes an event-based model for authoritarian deliberation. I.e., in the absence of an institutionalized issue forum in China, authoritarian deliberation is often pegged onto social dramas on the “judicial periphery,” thanks to a reflexive phase that brings the “ought” to bear on the “is”. Crisis-driven contentious politics exposes elite discord that is otherwise veiled by an interest-driven alliance. In these case studies, the media engaged other social institutions in contentious performances that affirmed hidden social fault-lines but also encouraged deliberation. In particular, my research explores the liberating potential of “moral outrage stories” in China in harbingering normative changes, which departs from western conception of “moral outrage” that largely focuses on the genre’s conservative function. By zeroing on framing contests among institutional actors during moral outrage-driven crises in China, I observe that when neither a journalistic narrative portraying the accused as a “villain” nor an organizational account foregrounding a “victim/scapegoat” self-perception manages to contain attribution at individual levels, the society enters a deliberative mode that interrogates social actors’ collective guilt complicit in a crisis (which contributes to underlying social problems), hence heralding regulatory changes.

11612418.label: Project Objectives
11612418.value: To elucidate the cross-cultural generalizability of partisan selective exposure. To unpack the differential cross-cultural impact of partisan selective exposure on attitudinal and affective polarization. To make methodological advancements such as the use of cultural priming and the IAT in the study of political communication. 11612418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11612418.value: Partisan selective exposure—the tendency of individuals to seek political information that confirms their existing beliefs over such information that does not—has been well documented in the Western political communication literature. However, its cross-cultural validity has been tested rarely. Drawing on a recent development in cultural psychology, which indicates that Westerners polarize whereas Easterners moderate their attitudes and affect when exposed to conflicting information, this study tests the hypothesis that Easterners will demonstrate weaker partisan selective exposure compared with Westerners. Cross-cultural experiments and surveys will be fielded in Japan (East), the U.S. (West), and Hong Kong, where East meets West. Specifically, the bicultural nature of the Hong Kong citizenry and psychological cultural priming provide a unique setting in which cultures are randomly assigned, allowing for unprecedentedly strong causal inference on cultural influence. Findings from experiments using an online news website as well as online surveys in the three regions will elucidate the cultural contingency of partisan selective exposure and its impact on attitudinal and affective polarization, which will provide insightful policy implication on how to alleviate political polarization in different cultures. 黨派選擇性關注——個人尋求與自己現有觀點一致的政治信息的傾向——在西方政治傳播文獻中已有很多記載。但是，它的跨文化有效性卻很少得到測試。文化心理學的最新發展表明，在接觸到相互矛盾的信息時，西方人的態度會兩極化，而東方人的態度和情感則會變得更緩和。借鑒這一最新觀點，本研究檢驗了東方人與西方人相比會表現出較弱的黨派選擇性關注的假設。跨文化實驗和調查將在日本（東方），美國（西方）和東方與西方相碰撞的香港進行。具體而言，香港公民的雙重文化性和心理文化啟蒙提供了一種獨特的環境，在這種環境中，文化被隨機分配，從而允許我們對文化影響進行前所未有的因果推斷。使用在線新聞網站進行的實驗以及三個地區的在線調查結果將闡明黨派選擇性關注的文化偶然性及其對態度和情感兩極分化的影響，這將為如何緩解不同文化中的政治兩極分化提供有見地的政策啟示。

11613018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11613018.value: In recent decades, restorative justice (RJ) has provided an alternative means for dealing with criminal matters and has emerged as one of the mainstream sentencing options in criminological practice worldwide. Among scholars, lawyers, and government officials in Taiwan and mainland China, there is growing interest in RJ such as mediation, criminal reconciliation, alternative measures to prosecution, and community correction programmes. RJ is currently regarded as an important element in criminal justice (CJ) systems for handling crimes in both Taiwan and mainland China. In mainland China, amendments to the Criminal Procedure Law (CPL) that were enforced in 2012 appear to have consolidated existing RJ practices and facilitated the future development of RJ. In Taiwan, the Ministry of Justice (MOJ) has adopted RJ as its priority policy of criminal justice reform. In 2010, the Government launched a pioneering programme entitled the ‘Restorative Justice Initiative’ (RJI), which was conducted at the District Prosecutor’s Office. Unlike Taiwan and mainland China, no statutory restorative measures have yet been incorporated into the mainstream criminal justice system in Hong Kong. Some non-governmental organisations (NGOs) endeavour to develop innovative strategies to prevent misbehaving adolescents from delinquency. Despite these efforts, however, a statutory RJ option is not formally included in the CJ system in Hong Kong. As part of the 2015-17 General Research Fund (GRF) study on RJ in the Greater China Region, the PI investigated the laws, mechanisms and conditions that allow RJ to be used for treating delinquents in Taiwan and mainland China. Drawing upon existing research data from both jurisdictions, the present study will explore how RJ could be employed in Hong Kong. The study will be conducted in two phases. Phase one will focus on constructing a framework for implementing RJ in Hong Kong, built upon analysis of laws and policies currently adopted in Taiwan and mainland China. Phase two will include the collection of primary qualitative data through in-depth interviews, which will be used to develop effective service models of RJ in Hong Kong. The respondents will be drawn from five different groups of key informants including government officials and/or committee members involved in law reform, police, lawyers/prosecutors, judges, and social workers to examine their opinions concerning the future development of RJ. The research findings will make a significant contribution to the advancement of RJ theory and practices in Chinese communities. Furthermore, the publications will be a valuable addition to the growing RJ literature. 復和司法(restorative justice) 是近二十年來急促發展概念之一，涵蓋了司法、罪案預防，罪犯更生及社區調解等範疇，滙聚了世界各地的學者、法律人士及政策制定者之關注。目前，復和司法的重點在於協助犯事者透過修復式措施向受害人或有關人士表達悔意並作出補償，在澳洲、新西蘭、北美、歐洲和亞洲等地相繼流行。自中華人民共和國刑事訴訟法(2012修正)通過後，復和司法在中國內地進一步發展起來。新的修正刑事訴訟法鼓勵非監禁化及非刑事化手法，以暫緩起訴或社區管制代替監禁，協助青少年罪犯從司法制度轉向出來，以達到預防犯罪及減少重犯等目標。隨著越來越多的司法人士意識到復和司法對少年罪犯的潛在好處，更多法官判予青少年違法者緩刑並附加條件要求加害人對受害人或社區作出賠償。在台灣，法務部於2010 年頒行了「推動修復式司法試行方案」實施計畫，由八個地檢署試辦在各個刑事司法階段內採用復和司法以促進犯罪者與受害人的對話。法務部推動之修復式司法試行方案主要採用「受害人與加害人調解」模式，以協助雙方透過會議尋求真相、伸張正義、道歉、撫慰、與復原。經過兩年時間試行，法務部於2012 年將方案進一步擴展致全台灣試行。 香港在英國殖民地統治的多年內，所訂立的法律基本上是依照英國普通法為標準。自1997年回歸後，儘管香港政府並沒有採用嚴厲的處遇及安置措施對待青少年罪犯，青少年司法模式似乎落後於大部份先進的國家或司法管轄區。由最初香港跟隨英國普通法之規定，將最低刑事責任年齡定於7歲及其後修改為10歲，以及各種罪犯更新事務的發展等事實來看，香港對少年罪犯之處理哲學其實反映著一種保護主義，以穩定社會秩序及協助少年自新為主。政府透過有關的司法及懲治機構提供了不少罪犯處遇及安置措施，而這些措施分別由警方、法院、社會福利署、懲教署及非政府機構負責管理。然而，復和司法到目前還沒有被納入刑事司法制度內，有關當局也沒有採用任何以復和司法來處理少年犯罪行為。相反地，復和司法在中國內地及台灣的應用愈來愈廣泛，我們審視香港青少年的司法措施的同時，此研究探索復和司法如何進一步在香港少年司法制度內以轉向或懲治之措施加以應用及討論復和司法如何處理偏差青少年行為。

11613018.label: Realisation of objectives
11613018.value: 1. The research has thoroughly studied laws and mechanisms that could allow restorative justice (RJ) be used for delinquents in Taiwan, mainland China and Hong Kong. In Chinese societies, the concept of ‘mediation’ is more popular than the concept of ‘restorative justice’. Given the long history of mediation in Chinese communities, RJ has a broader meaning in China than in Western countries. It may include any form of alternative dispute resolution, alternatives to prosecution or sentencing, and community reintegration programmes. In the mainland, practices related to RJ have been pioneered at various levels of the criminal justice system including at the pre-court, during-court, and post-court levels in recent years. For details of findings, please refer to journal paper generated from this project published by Wong and Kwan (2020). In Taiwan, RJ came to prominence in the late 1990s. The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) published a White Paper on Prosecution Reform in response to growing problems in the justice sectors in 1999. Since then, the MOJ has adopted RJ as its priority policy of criminal justice reform. Under existing criminal procedures in Taiwan, prosecutors are encouraged to adopt VOM to resolve disputes between conflicting parties before the case formally goes to trial in court. The RJ operational manual and handbooks were subsequently developed in Taiwan and these materials have provided good reference for Hong Kong. Please refer to a publication published by Wong and Lui (2018). 2. Based on the experiences collected from the mainland and Taiwan, Hong Kong has been struggling with how to incorporate RJ into the current justice system. To formulate RJ practice models, the research team conducted a comprehensive literature review of RJ development in Hong Kong. As attention on the use of RJ to handle juvenile offenders increased in many parts of the world, the decision of whether to implement the practice in Hong Kong eventually became a concern for the Hong Kong Government in 2002. A research team was formed that year to investigate whether the minimum age of criminal responsibility should be revised and alternative measures for treating juvenile offenders. In submitting the report to the Government, the team proposed a number of pre-court restorative options including the use of family group conferences for developing restorative plans to respond to juvenile offending (Lo, Wong, & Maxwell, 2003). Despite these endeavours, the Hong Kong Government rejected the experts’ recommendations. Until today, a statutory RJ option has not been formally incorporated into the mainstream justice system. Over the past 20 years, however, RJ proponents have worked hard to do restorative practices outside the mainstream criminal justice system, including apply RJ to resolve school bullying and restore relationships between conflicting parties in the community. A few NGOs in Hong Kong launched post-cautioning VOM for juveniles, victims, their family members, or supporters 15 years ago. The current research team worked closely with these NGOs and further developed different kinds of innovative RJ services for delinquents under the constraints of current legal system. A RJ practice approach was preliminary figured out and put on trial (see Wong & Tu, 2018). 3. The research team has examined applicability of the RJ practice models for delinquents, with the help of in-depth interviews with 30 professionals during the research period. We conducted interviews with 10 police (including Police Constables, Sergeant, Senior Inspector, Chief Inspector and Superintendent), 4 policy makers (including government officials and legislative counselors), 4 teachers (including school principals and front-line teachers), 6 social workers (including supervisor, team leader and front line staff), and 4 mediators, and 2 lawyers. Based on the data collected from the interviews, practice models of RJ are fine tuned. A more detailed set of operational procedures and skill sets related to restorative practices are consolidated. 4. To evaluate whether the proposed practice models match with RJ standards, three RJ conferences for those young people who were involved in the ‘2019 Social Unrest’ were run in the period between September 2020 and April 2021. The Hong Kong Extradition Law Amendment Bill (proposed in March 2019) had caused much anxiety among the public, thereby leading to numerous massive public rallies, starting June 2019. A few thousands of young people were arrested and subsequently charged for public rallies or rioting etc. A substantial number of young people were eventually sentenced into youth prison or other punitive measures. Nonetheless, some young people who were involved in some less serious acts were given a chance to receive alternative treatment such as the Police Superintendent’s Discretion Scheme (PSDS). Under the PSDS, the youth arrestees would be given rehabilitation opportunities. Currently, it is under the auspices of the PSDS that provision of RJ services are delivered. To ensure the quality of RJ services, the PI acted as the chief mediator for the conferences, with the help of police officers at the Regional Crime Prevention Division of NT South of Hong Kong Police and social workers from the Hong Kong Federation Youth Groups. The three RJ conferences, considered as the first of its kind in Hong Kong, were smoothly and successfully conducted, with participation of the offenders, victims, police, social workers, supporters of the offenders, supporters of victims, and relevant stakeholders. The process of the conferences were video-taped and detailed analyses on the RJ standards adopted were undertaken.

11613018.label: Major findings and research outcome
11613018.value: The current research has investigated the feasibility of different RJ models in the Greater China region. We compare and contrast practices models among these jurisdictions including Hong Kong, Taiwan and the mainland China. Hong Kong is a Chinese community, which has inherited cultures from both the East and West. Our research findings suggest that Western RJ concepts, to a large degree, are compatible with the legal, criminal justice and culture in Hong Kong. With the experimental RJ projects conducted for assisting youth delinquents to resolve their conflicts with the authorities, the RJ models so developed could establish new standards that are best suited to the situations facing Chinese communities. The practice model so developed and the successful implementation of conferences conducted, had increased positive views and trust on the use of RJ amongst the general public in Hong Kong. Judging from the responses of the co-workers and conference participants, the RJ model and high standards of facilitator’s skills were confirmed to have induced positive impacts on repairing the harm done between offenders and victims. Sincere dialogues were noted between different pairs of antagonistic parties such as police vs youth, parent vs child, social worker vs police, youth vs shopkeeper etc. At the end of conference, genuine apologies were voiced out from the offenders and words of forgiveness were also heard from the victims or from the family members. There were touching moments which clearly signified a reconciliation and restoration of human relationships. The RJ conferences were video-taped with written consents from all parties involved. The video episodes not just documented the process but the strategies and skills adopted for making a RJ conference success. Such a set of RJ practice data, the first of its kind, has definitely filled the knowledge gap of mediation practices in Hong Kong. This set of knowledge transfer initiatives will add value to both academic and practical fields of social work and criminology. Our research findings have generated academic papers and a set of operational procedures related to RJ theory and restorative practices in Hong Kong.

11613018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11613018.value: The current project has usefully informed academia and conflict management professionals by providing theoretical insights into the actual operation of RJ in Hong Kong. It has also made contribution to the development of indigenous models for practicing RJ in Chinese communities. The study has added value to Chinese RJ theory-building and provided insights for future research on applicability of RJ in Chinese communities. We believe, with more publications be published and local seminars be held, Chinese practice wisdom of restorative practices would be further developed. Such practice wisdom will inspire relevant governmental officials to consider adopting RJ into the current justice system in Hong Kong.

11613018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11613018.value: Restorative justice (RJ) offers a different perspective to responding to crime. Instead of viewing the state as the primary victim, RJ views crime as being directed against individual people. RJ has evolved as a community-based response to conflicts in many countries. It is a process that enables the victim, the offender and all related stakeholders to develop a solution to a crime, and is an alternative means of asking offenders to take responsibility and repair the harm caused. Based on a comprehensive review of laws and mechanisms of RJ, the research developed indigenous RJ models that are compatible with the legal system and culture in Hong Kong. With the help of the data collected from interviews of professionals and policy makers, the practice models of RJ are fine tuned. To evaluate whether the proposed practice models match with RJ standards, three RJ conferences were run and evaluated. The processes of the conferences were video-taped with written consents from all parties involved. The video episodes not just documented the process but the strategies and skills adopted for making a conference success. There are also academic publications generated from the current project.

11613618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11613618.value: This proposal will undertake cutting edge research to resolve the fundamental challenge of creating a narrative driven cognitive and interpretive framework for audiences to engage with digital cultural atlases in museological contexts. The investigation amalgamates the Atlas of Maritime Buddhism – a unique cultural heritage database that documents historical evidence of the maritime journeys of Buddhism from India via the seaports of South East Asia [35]. The research aims to develop a pioneering deep mapping architecture for interactively exploring the narrative patterns, processes and phenomena in the Atlas, which will be implanted in an experimental cultural heritage data browser – an immersive 360-degree 3D visualization environment. This research responds to salient issues regarding public access and interaction with cultural heritage archives. Firstly, while narrative lies at the heart of museum interpretation, it is significantly underdeveloped in information visualisation [20]. Secondly, mapping has become a powerful cultural phenomenon in the public domain (e.g. Google Maps [9] and Open Street Map [25]. If museums are to take advantage of the burgeoning investments in cultural mapping datasets, visualisation tools are needed that allow users to create narrative sense where the data is both spatially and temporally contextualised [4, 28]. The Atlas was selected for this study because of its data-rich sources and potential for the development of a narrative-driven deep mapping architecture. Developed and maintained under the Electronic Cultural Atlas Initiative (ECAI) administered by University of California, Berkeley (UCB) [1], it is of great academic importance because of its pan-Asian maritime focus on Buddhism entrepreneurship in the expansion of trade from 2nd century BC to the 12th century AD. Researchers around the world have contributed to the Atlas, providing geospatial coordinates, gazetteers and visual documentation of hundreds of archaeological sites and artifacts as well as religious and geopolitical empires and zones of influence, inscriptions and transcriptions of Sanskrit texts, historic maps, accounts by Buddhist monks and ambassadors, records of trade, hydrographic data, monsoon records, and shipwreck datasets [3]. Given this tremendous heterogeneity the Atlas requires a new form of visual, cartographic and time-space cognitive strategy that is currently outside traditional forms of interpretation [29]. Unlocking the narratives from the Atlas for museum audiences poses the crucial theoretical and experimental challenges that will be undertaken in this project. 在博物館環境下如何為觀眾創建一個以敘事驅動觀眾的認知和理解的框架并有互動性的數碼文化地圖集。調研合併了海上佛教地圖集 —— 一個獨特的文化遺產數據庫與歷史證據，其記錄了佛教從印度的東南亞海港出發的海上旅程。該研究旨在開發一種開創性的有互動性的深度製圖（mapping）架構探索海上佛教地圖集之敘事模式、過程和現象，此架構將被植入一個具實驗性的文化遺產數據瀏覽器中——一個沉浸式的360度三維立體可視化環境。該研究回應了關於公眾如何獲取文化遺產檔案和如何與其互動的顯著問題。 首先，雖然敘事的核心依賴於來自博物館的闡釋，但其在信息可視化方面卻顯然發展不足。其次，製圖（mapping）已經在公眾視野中成為了有影響力的文化現象（例如：谷歌地圖 和開放街圖）。如果博物館要利用好對文化地圖數據集不斷擴大的投資，其可視化工具便要讓用戶可建立敘事意義，而這種敘事使數據對觀眾而言無論在空間上與時間感知上都是情境化的。 此研究選擇了地圖集Atlas是因其數據豐富的資源以及為其開發以敘事驅動的深度繪圖架構的潛力。其在加州大學伯克利分校（UCB）管理的電子文化地圖集計（ECAI）下開發和維護有重要的學術意義，因其泛亞洲海事重點關注佛教企業在公元前二世紀至公元十二世紀之間貿易擴大中的作用。世界各地的研究人員一直為地圖集 Atlas作貢獻，提供了地理坐標、地名錄和數以百計的視覺記錄包括考古遺跡、文物、宗教、地緣政治帝國和影響區、梵文文本的銘文和抄本、歷史地圖、佛教僧侶與使者之據聞、 貿易記錄，水文數據，季風記錄和沈船數據集。鑑於這種巨大的異質性，地圖集Atlas需要一種新的視覺形式，目前用製圖（mapping）和增強觀眾在博物館中對時間、空間感知的策略形式并不在傳統的博物館解釋形式之中。為博物館的觀眾解鎖地圖集Atlas的新敘事將成為該項目關鍵的理論，亦是一個具有實驗性的挑戰。

11614218.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11614218.value: 信息透明化及其对棕地地价的影响

11614218.label: Project Objectives
11614218.value: The overall aim of this research is to address two primary questions: is there a learning curve for real estate developers who bid on former industrial sites, and are there any differences across cities in terms of policy initiatives, learning curve of developers, and price response to contamination? More specifically, over time, the goal of this research is to measure and compare the impact of increasing awareness of brownfields on the real estate market in Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou. I seek answers to the following questions: (1) What are the policy initiatives and regulations adopted by the three cities related to brownfields? (2) Over the past thirteen years, during which cities gradually promulgated brownfield redevelopment regulations, are there any changes in the land transaction prices of brownfields? If we find that the changes in prices are statistically significant after controlling for other factors, indications are that there is a learning curve among real estate developers dealing with industrial sites. (3) Under the land auction system, are brownfield sites sold at a discounted rate than other sites? and (4) Given the heterogeneity of brownfield regulations across cities, how do these variations affect land values?
