12100918.label: Major findings and research outcome
12100918.value: In the current project, we found that: (1) (DSS)6 facilitated the in vivo osteoblast-specific distribution of the conjugated chalcone derivative in BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of age-related osteoporotic rats. (2) (DSS)6-chalcone derivative, rather than other formulations, significantly inhibited Smurf1 activity and improved p-Smad1 expression, Runx2 activation and osteocalcin mRNA expression at the dose of 6 μmol/kg in BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of age-related osteoporotic rats. Further, (DSS)6-chalcone derivative maintained the therapeutic effects for a desirable period in BMP-2n/Smurf1esubgroup of age-related osteoporotic rats. (3) (DSS)6-chalcone derivative, rather than other chalcone derivative formulations, significantly promoted bone formation and enhanced bone mass in BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of age-related osteoporotic rats, which was similar to those of PTH. (4) The liver function indicators, kidney function indicator and hematology parameters stayed within the normal range in BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of age-related osteoporotic rats after a single/multiple injection(s) of (DSS)6-chalcone derivative.

12100918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12100918.value: All the results indicated that inhibition of osteoblastic Smurf1 could be a precision medicine-based bone anabolic strategy for BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of age-related osteoporotic individuals. The chalcone derivative targeting Smurf1 demonstrated great potential to enhance local bone formation during spinal fusion in BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup. (DSS)6-chalcone derivative conjugate could be an alternative systemic bone anabolic agent for BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup. The current results would advance the precision medicine-based bone anabolic strategy, i.e., osteoblastic inhibition of Smurf1 activity by the (DSS)6-chalcone derivative conjugate, for the BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of osteoporotic individuals. In the future: scientists in translational research might cite and employ the conjugate for their further translational study in metabolic skeletal disorders associated with impaired bone formation.

12100918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12100918.value: Clinically, recombinant human BMP-2 (rhBMP-2) exhibited large inter-individual variations in local bone formation. In the current project, the scientists revealed that individuals (human and rats) with age-related osteoporosis could be classified into different subgroups based on distinct makers (BMP-2 and Smurf1). One major subgroup with a normal BMP-2 level and elevated Smurf1 activity (BMP-2n/Smurf1e) showed poor response to rhBMP-2. Then, an inhibitor (chalcone derivative) for Smurf1 was identified and conjugated with an osteoblast (a cell type in bone)-specific targeting tool (DSS6) as a potential candidate drug, i.e., DSS6-chalcone derivative. It was demonstrated that DSS6-chalcone derivative could target osteoblasts and promote systemic bone formation in BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of age-related osteoporosis animal models. The study would advance the precision medicine-based bone anabolic strategy for the BMP-2n/Smurf1e subgroup of age-related osteoporosis.

12101018.label: Realisation of objectives
12101018.value: Objective 1. To construct and optimize a CRISPR/Cas9 system targeting human VEGFA gene (hCRISPR/Cas9). All achieved. We selected 6 guide RNAs targeting human VEGFA in GeCKOv2 library A and B (Table 1) and identified sgRNA 5 showed the best inhibition efficiency. Therefore, sgRNA 5 was used for further research. Primary OS cells were used for the following ex vivo studies. The uptake of the above prepared formulations in primary OS cells were examined by flow cytometry. Consistently with the assay using aptamers alone, after 2 h incubation, Cy5-labeled LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 and Cy5-labeled LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 Ctrl showed more substantial uptake in OS cells than Cy5-Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9. 72 hours after incubation, the fluorescence of EGFP-Cas9 was assessed by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy. LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 and LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 Ctrl treated cells both exhibited more intensive EGFP fluorescence compared to Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9. The Cas9 expressions in cells treated with two LC09 formulated groups were also detected to be much higher than those in Rd formulated group by western blot. After 96 h of treatment, the indel frequency of VEGFA gene by Surveyor assay were also determined. A reasonable indel was detected in LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 treated cells, while little indels were observed in Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 and LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 Ctrl treated cells. VEGFA in the cell lysate and supernatant of cells from each group were also examined by western blot. Dramatically decreased VEGFA expression in both cell lysate and supernatant were detected in LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 treated cells compared to the other two control groups. In addition, LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 treated cells exhibited slower proliferation and migration properties than the other two groups. Objective 2. To examine the LC09-mediated changes in the distribution of hCRISPR/Cas9 in OS and non-tumor tissue in an orthotopic PDX mouse model. All achieved. To investigate the LC09-mediated OS selective distribution of the CRISPR system, Cy5-labeled LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 and Cy5-labeled Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 were intravenously administered to tumor bearing PDX mice with a single dose. The mice were sacrificed 3 h and 6 h after administration. The OS tumor and major organs were collected for biophotonic imaging analysis. Appearance of Cy5 signal in the OS tumor were observed in Cy5-labeled LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 dosed mice 3 h after injection and the accumulation of the fluorescence became stronger at 6 h time point. In contrast, Cy5-labeled Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 had very little accumulation in OS tumor at both time points. A substantial amount of Cy5 signal in liver and kidney were observed for both groups at 3 h, however the remaining fluorescence in these two organs dramatically decreased in both groups at 6 h. The accumulation of both formulations in other organs were neglectable. The organs and tumors were then homogenized and the fluorescence intensities of Cy5 were quantified using a fluorescence microplate reader. The percentage of injected dose for two formulations in difference tissues were calculated. Consistently with biophotonic imaging results, major distribution of both formulated systems was detected in liver and kidney at 3 h and cleared out at 6 h. There was an increased proportion of Cy5-labeled LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 accumulating in OS tumor from 3 h to 6 h, while Cy5-labeled Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 showed little distribution besides liver and kidney throughout the assay. To inspect the LC09-mediated distribution of hCRISPR/Cas9 at cellular level, confocal microscopy imaging of the OS tissue sections and flow cytometry of the digested OS cell suspensions were also conducted. More intensive Cy5 fluorescence was detected in Cy5-labeled LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 dosed mice compared to the Rd counterpart in both assays. Objective 3. To detect the LC09-mediated changes in VEGFA editing of hCRISPR/Cas9 in an orthotopic PDX mouse model. All achieved. LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 and LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 Ctrl groups showed significantly higher EGFP-Cas9 expressions compared to Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9. The EGFP-Cas9 levels of two LC09 modified groups increased steadily after administration and achieved the peak at approximately day 7, and then slowly dropped down to the initial levels after 2 weeks. The OS tissues collected from each group at day 7 were digested into single cell suspensions and analyzed by flow cytometry. Higher percentages of EGFP-Cas9 positive cells were observed in LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 and LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 Ctrl groups than Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9. Consistently with the ELISA result, the average mean fluorescence intensities (MFI) of EGFP of two LC09 groups were also stronger than the Rd control group. The Cas9 levels of each group detected by western blot at day 7 also showed the same pattern. Indel frequency in the above tissues were determined by Surveyor assay. Expectedly, OS tissues in LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 exhibited the highest indel frequency compared to non-specific aptamer control group (Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9) and non-specific CRISPR/Cas9 control group (LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 Ctrl). VEGFA expressions in OS tissues of each group along time after administration were also detected by ELISA. Only LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 group showed observable decrease in VEGFA level. In consistency with the EGFP-Cas9 expression levels, VEGFA of LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 group reached the lowest bottom at around day 7, and slowly rose back to the origin level after another week. The expression difference of each group at day 7 were also confirmed by western blot. Objective 4. To evaluate the LC09-mediated changes in anti-tumor and anti-metastasis activity of hCRISPR/Cas9 in an orthotopic PDX mouse model. All achieved. The PDX mice administrated with LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 showed hindered tumor growth compared to those treated with Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 or LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9. The LC09-mediated changes in tumor proliferation and metastasis were also examined by immunohistochemistry analysis of a series of markers in the OS tissue sections, decreased expression levels of Ki67, ezrin, MMP9 and survivin were observed for LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 treated mice in comparison with the control groups. In addition, the LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 treatment also prolonged the survival of PDX mice revealed in Kaplan-Meier plot. Objective 5. To assess anti-angiogenesis, anti-bone disruption activity and safety of LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 in an orthotopic PDX mouse model. All achieved. The Matrigel plug assay showed that compared to the rich vessel formation in the plug collected from Rd-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 and LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 Ctrl treated mice, LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 treated mice showed alleviative angiogenesis with much clearer plugs. MicroCT examination of bone destruction by osteosarcoma tumor in each group were also conducted, and LC09-PPC-hCRISPR/Cas9 treated mice showed the least bone destruction pattern. No significant toxicity was observed for the delivery system in terms of hemotoxicity and tissue H&E analysis for major organs.

12101018.label: Major findings and research outcome
12101018.value: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 was jointly awarded to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer A. Doudna for their 2012 work on CRISPR-Cas9. CRISPR/Cas9, as one of the most popular gene editing technologies, has been widely used in scientific community, especially in the field of cancer therapy. However, due to the lack of highly specific and efficient in vivo targeted delivery systems, the further translation of CRISPR/Cas9 is hindered. Aptamers are short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotide segments, which bind to their targets, such as proteins with high affinity and specificity by unique three-dimensional (3D) structure. Aptamer has shown great potential in diagnosis of disease, new biomarker discovery, bio-imaging and targeted in vivo drug delivery. Therefore, the modification of aptamer on CRISPR/Cas9 might could achieve targeted delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 to increase its efficiency. In our previous work, we have designed and synthesized an aptamer-functionalized lipopolymer delivery system for CRISPR/Cas9, which achieved excellent therapeutic genome editing and efficient inhibition of VEGFA in an orthotopic osteosarcoma mouse model. To investigate the translational value of this targeted delivery system, we further construct a similar aptamer-functionalized lipopolymer delivery system for CRISPR/Cas9 which targeting human VEGFA and examined the therapeutic activity of this conjugate in a patient-derived xenograft model of osteosarcoma. As expected, we discovered that this targeted delivery system could facilitate the selective accumulation of a human VEGFA gene-targeting CRISPR/Cas9 in OS tissues in PDX mouse model, leading to subsequent disruption of VEGFA and resulting in inhibited tumor growth and prolonged the survival time. This work provides a novel aptamer-functionalized osteosarcoma cell-targeting delivery system of CRISPR/Cas9 to achieve genome editing for silencing tumor-promoting genes toward clinical translation.

12101018.value: Aptamer-based delivery system could be further developed and optimized for clinical usage of delivery of genetic editing materials including CRISPR/Cas9 systems or mRNA vaccines. Better sequences, chemical modifications for higher specificity, stability and longer half lives.

12101718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12101718.value: Upon pancreatic injury or inflammatory events, extracellular matrices (ECMs), such as type-I collagen and fibronectin, are massively produced by activated pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) for tissue repair and/or regeneration. In chronic pancreatitis, the aberrant PSC activation promotes pathologic ECM stiffness of pancreatic parenchyma, and results in fibrogenesis, permanent tissue destruction and systemic complications. According to recent statistics, over 50% of chronic pancreatitis patients develop diabetes as the disease progresses. Substantial decrease of beta-cell area was observed in these patients, so as overt hyperglycemia and abated insulin secretion. Such endocrine deficiency secondary to pancreatitis is now classified as pancreatogenic diabetes or type 3c diabetes mellitus (T3cDM), a subtype that has been consistently underestimated. In line with the clinical reports, our preliminary trials demonstrated that chronic pancreatitis mice exhibited impaired glucose tolerance in addition to PSC activation and pathological fibrosis. Their mass of endocrine beta cells and transcript levels of beta-cell genes, namely insulin, Pdx-1, MafA and FoxM1, were conjointly diminished. As 80% of T3cDM cases are ascribed to chronic pancreatitis, we postulate that the molecular signals and matrices from activated PSCs in the fibrotic inflammatory milieu are detrimental to beta-cell biology. Over the past decades, trans-resveratrol has been scrutinized for numerous health-promoting benefits; however, it has a poor systemic bioavailability. In this regard, we synthesized 3,5,4′-trihydroxybibenzyl (THB) via resveratrol structural modification. Upon eliminating the central aliphatic double bond, the structural flexibility and solubility of THB are largely enhanced. As THB exists as a resveratrol metabolite without further breakdown in the human bowel, it possesses a precious bioavailability. Our preliminary results showed that THB suppressed PSC phenotype in vitro and ameliorated fibrotic conditions in chronic pancreatitis mice in a manner superior to trans-resveratrol. Despite modest structural difference, the mitigation of THB, but not trans-resveratrol, on PSC phenotype and pancreatic fibrosis involved a down-regulation of membrane type 1-matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP), an interstitial peptidase that cleaves ECMs and transduces signals instigating perpetual PSC activation via autocrine loops. In co-culturing assays, THB reduced beta-cell apoptosis while preserving beta-cell functions against PSCs or inflammatory cytokines. Therefore, we hypothesize that THB preserves beta-cell mass and functions in pancreatogenic diabetes via attenuating PSC phenotype and MT1-MMP-mediated fibrogenesis. In this proposal, we aim to explore the deactivation of PSCs by THB and RNAi of MT1-MMP in cellular experiments; and elucidate the involvement of MT1-MMP in pancreatogenic diabetes utilizing a transgenic mouse model complemented with chronic pancreatitis.

12101718.label: Realisation of objectives
12101718.value: The cited references refer to the following attached files in PART C (page numbers refer to the pages in Page Thumbnails of the pdf file of the full completion report): 1. PharmRes: publication No1 (p14-100); 2. MidtRep: The mid-term progress report. 3. ExtRep: The extension report. A.1. Objective 1: To evaluate the in vitro effect of THB (i.e. DR2) on PSCs, pancreatic endocrine cells and co-cultures A.1.1. Cytotoxic effects of THB (DR2) on PSCs and different pancreatic cell lines We evaluated the cytotoxicic effects of THB (i.e. DR2) on different pancreatic cell lines and the assay result indicated the lower cytotoxicities of DR2 than resveratrol (RES) to the pancreatic cell lines. (please see PharmRes: section 3.11. and Fig. 1 of the paper) A.1.2. Suppressive effects of THB (DR2) on extracellular matrix productions in PSCs and its modulation on PI3K/AKT/mTOR cell signaling pathway and p38 MAPK protein We determined the suppressive effects of DR2 on activation of PSCs via the modulation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR cell signaling pathway. Our experiments revealed that DR2 inhibited the activation of rat pancreatic stellate cells on downregulation of the ECM markers α-SMA and FN1 proteins, and the EMT marker, N-cadherin via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR cell signaling pathway and p38/MAPK cascades as DR2 could significantly suppress the phosphorylation of PI3K, AKT and mTOR proteins in TGF-β-pretreated LTC-14 cells and notably inhibit the TGF-β induced phosphorylation of p38α/β proteins. (please see PharmRes: section 3.1.4 and Fig. 4 of the paper) A.1.3. Anti-apoptotic effects of THB (DR2) on pancreatic β cells We further determined that DR2 could contain protective effects against cyclosporine A (CsA) induced apoptosis in pancreatic β cells. We observed that the addition of CsA induced early and late apoptosis events could be suppressed by DR2 at 2.5 µM in the flow cytometry analysis, which was confirmed by the qPCR experiments in which the elevated Caspase3 transcript levels in CsA-pretreated NIT-1 cells could be ameliorated after the treatment of DR2. (please see PharmRes: section 3.1.5 and Fig. 5 of the paper) A.1.4. THB (DR2) on the detrimental effects of PSCs on pancreatic β cells in co-culture assays In electron microscopy (EM), the microstructure and secretory granules in the primary pancreatic β cells were found notably deteriorated when co-cultured with PSCs. When NIT-1 β cells were co-cultured with PSCs grown in hanging inserts, apoptosis (TUNEL) was enhanced whilst endocrine regulators, explicitly INS2, were markedly decreased when compared to the monoculture of β cells by immunostaining. When cells were treated with DR2, the detrimental effects of PSCs on NIT-1 β cells was efficiently abolished. (please see MidtRep: “Detrimental effects of PSCs on pancreatic β cells in co-culture assays” and the figures in Objective 1 of the mid-term progress report) A.2. Objective 2: To assess the biological effect of THB on MT1-MMP expression and beta-cell preservation in chronic pancreatitis A.2.1. Suppressive effect of THB (DR2) on MT1-MMP expression in chronic pancreatitis We examined the expression levels of MT1-MMP during the activation of PSCs by using TGF-β induced pancreatic fibrosis model. The fluorescence signal of MT1-MMP was increased in the cells treated with TGF-β, and such elevation could be inhibited by DR2 at 12.5 and 50 µM. Besides, we also treated the PSCs with recombinant MT1-MMP protein to induce upregulation of Mt1-mmp and fibrotic marker Acta2 transcript levels, which could be significantly downregulated by DR2 in a dose dependent manner. (please see ExtRep: sections 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 and Figures 4 and 5 of the project extension report) A.2.2. Effects of THB (DR2) on reducing the fibrotic progression in chronic pancreatitis (CP) DR2 treatment could also reduce the severity of chronic pancreaitis in a mouse model study. In the in vivo experiment, the relative pancreatic weights of mice with cerulein (CER) injection and DR2 treatment were found to be significantly higher than those of the mice receiving CER injections only, revealing that DR2 could help reserve the mass of pancreas from CER damage. Apart from this, the effects of DR2 on ameliorating the pancreatic fibrosis (PF) and CP were shown upon histopathological examination and real time-qPCR analysis. From the staining of tissue sections, the pancreas from CER group revealed significant signs of CP such as acinar cell atrophy, while remarkedly relieved signs of CP were observed in the CER group treated with DR2. And we also observed that DR2 could reduce the upregulated gene transcripts in mice, providing further evidence that DR2 could reduce the severity of PF progression. (please see PharmRes: sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 and Fig. 8C, 8D, 8F-8H of the paper) A.2.3. Effect of THB (DR2) on beta-cell preservation in chronic pancreatitis We examined the effect of DR2 on beta-cell preservation by using glucose tolerance test and immunofluorescent staining and observed that CER mice with DR2 treatment showed faster clearance of blood glucose comparing to the mice with CER injection only, indicating that the mice with DR2 treatment had a better glucose tolerance. From the immunofluorescent images, the reductions in sizes and loss of original round shapes were found less prominent in the DR2 group, revealing that DR2 could help protect islets and maintain the normal beta cell conditions. (please see PharmRes: section 3.3.3 and Fig. 8B and 8E of the paper) A.3. Objective 3: To validate the involvement of MT1-MMP in perpetuating PSC activation in pancreatogenic diabetes A.3.1. Transcriptional silencing of Mt1-mmp in PSCs Silencing of Mt1-mmp in PSCs was achieved by the application of siRNA oligos against Mt1-mmp. When compared to the control siRNAs, decreased levels of fibro-filaments, including α-SMA and VIM, and fibrillar matrices (e.g. FN1 and COL I-1α) were observed. Expression levels of other fibrotic regulators, such as AKT and MMP2, were also down-regulated upon the knockdown of Mt1-mmp. please see MidtRep: “Transcriptional silencing of Mt1-mmp in PSCs” and the figures in Objective 3 of the mid-term progress report) A.3.2. MT1-MMP+/- mice have slightly lower degree of chronic pancreatitis but better islets conditions in the cerulein induced chronic pancreatitis mouse model Glucose tolerance test was used to measure the clearance of an intraperitoneally (i.p.) injected glucose load from the body to detect disturbances in glucose metabolism of the chronic pancreatitis / pancreatogenic diabetes mice. We observed that MT1-MMP+/- mice showed faster glucose clearance compared to the wild-type mice. (please see ExtRep: section 6.3.6.1 Figure 6 of the project extension report) Tissue damage was observed in term of abnormal pancreatic architecture, increased leukocyte infiltration and increased collagen deposition in the mice with the cerulein injection after the 6-week experiment with the use of Masson trichrome staining, Sirius red staining and IHC staining of α-SMA. Such elevation of fibrotic marker, α-SMA, collagen deposition and leukocyte infiltration were found to be lower in the group of MT1-MMP+/- mice with CER injection than that of the wild type mice. Reduced in islets size were observed in both the wild-type and MT1-MMP+/- mice after 6-week cerulein injections and such reduction in size were more significant in the wild-type mice with cerulein injections, revealing that islets of wild-type mice are more vulnerable to the cerulein challenge. All these results indicated that MT1-MMP involved in perpetuating PSC activation in chronic pancreatitis and pancreatogenic diabetes. (please see ExtRep: sections 6.3.6.2 and 6.3.6.3 and Figures 7-9 of the project extension report)

12101718.value: The cited sections in PART C refer to the page numbers in Page Thumbnails of the pdf file of the full completion report). 1) In the present study, we have demonstrated THB (DR2) could serve as a potential therapeutic agent against chronic pancreatitis (CP) as DR2 was shown to reduce the severity of CER-induced murine CP by ameliorating the activation of pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) and macrophage infiltration by the means of tissue sections and real time-qPCR analysis. (#8. publication No1, p59-63: 3.3. in PharmRes paper) 2) With the transcriptomic and phospho-proteomic analysis and related experiments in PSCs, we revealed that DR2 downregulated the fibrotic mediators and EMT proteins of PSCs through PI3K/AKT signaling pathway and modulate the p38 MAPK proteins involved in MAPK/p38 signaling pathway to achieve its anti-fibrotic effect in PSCs. (#8. publication No1, p41-50: 3.1 in PharmRes paper) 3) We synthesized the biotinylated DR2 to perform pulldown assays to identify the binding proteins of DR2 in PSCs followed by the validations using DARTS and MST experiments. The pulldown assays revealed that acetyl-CoA carboxylase subunit alpha (ACCA) was the potential direct binding protein of DR2. (#8. publication No1, p51-58: 3.2. in PharmRes paper) 4) The identified protein bindning target, ACCA (also known as ACC1), is the key lipogenic enzyme. It has been a popular target of interest for obesity, diabetes and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) therapies and the administration of an ACC inhibitor to the high fat diet treated rats has been suggested to improve insulin sensitivity. In our CP mouse model, we observed that mice with high-dose DR2 treatment had a better glucose tolerance. The sizes of the islets were found to be reduced, and the original round shape loss due to CP was rescued by the DR2 treatment. These findings provide clear evidence that DR2 could also serve as a potential therapeutic agent for treatment of pancreatogenic diabetes. 12101718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12101718.value: As our result suggested that THB (DR2) is an effective ACCA inhibitor and did not impair the glucose tolerance and DR2 treatment to choronic pancreatitis (CP) mice showed faster blood glucose clearance, DR2 could be an effective on the modulation of insulin secretions and insulin sensitivity in beta cells/islets. Further study is thus desired to explore the potential of DR2 not only on the treatment of pancreatic fibrosis but also on the treatment of diabetes. Since we have shown that MT1-MMP is involved in perpetuating PSC activation, we may establish a pancreatogenic diabetes animal model to explore the effect of DR2 on MT1-MMP during the progression of pancreatogenic diabetes. Additionally, further DR2 analogues could be synthesized with enhanced therapeutic effects in treatment of CP and pancreatogenic diabetes. As we have showed the promising effect of DR2 on treatment of CP, the chronic toxicity of DR2 should be further investigated to ensure the safety of DR2 in a long term use. The follow up preclinical studies to include the pharmacokinetic and safety profile analysis in a GLP facility would warrant DR2 as a safety drug candidate to enter the subsequent human clinical trials to treat patients with CP and related diabetes.

12101718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12101718.value: We have shown that the naturally occurred DR2 compound could be a potential drug for the treatment of chronic pancreatitis, the syndrome involving inflammation, fibrosis, and loss of acinar and islet cells of the pancreas, and its related diabetes. Currently, there is no therapeutic agent for the treatment of pancreatic fibrosis and chronic pancreatitis. The significance of the present study is that we determined DR2 as a natural agent that could be used to treat the disease with a prevalence of approximately 50/100,000 persons. In our celluar and animal studies, DR2 was demonstrated with promising effects in reducing the fibrosis level. The compound was found to reduce pancreatic fibrosis by inhibiting the protein levels of PI3K, AKT and p38α/β in the cellular experiments. In the chronic pancreaitits mouse model, DR2 could reduce the tissue damage and protect the islets, the groups of cells that secrete insulin and responsible for regulating blood glucose level. Moreover, we also found that DR2 could directly bind ACCA, a protein linked to obesity and diabetes, which provided the molecular evidence for developing DR2 as a potential therapeutic drug of obesity and diabetes. These results indicated that DR2 could treat chronic pancreatitis and its related diabetes.

12102018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12102018.value: Recent studies indicate that subtropical coral communities can serve as refuges of global environmental change, but the relative susceptibility of subtropical species to environmental stressors and the underlying mechanisms of stress responses are largely unknown. Here we propose to study the effects of high temperature and low salinity on subtropical corals in the northern South China Sea. These two environmental stressors have been known to cause bleaching in these subtropical corals in recent years. We propose to construct an exposure system for determining coral bleaching thresholds, select nine species of common corals of different growth forms and expose them to a combination of thermal and salinity treatments in the laboratory to determine their bleaching thresholds. For the two most sensitive and two most resistant species, a laboratory experiment will be conducted to compare their physiological and transcriptomic responses to temperature and salinity stresses, followed by gene co-expression network analysis and positive selection analysis to identify underlying mechanisms of stress responses. Overall, our study will determine the potential coral “winners and losers” of global environmental change in the northern South China Sea for the first time, uncover molecular mechanisms of coral bleaching considering coral as a holobiont of coral host and its symbionts, and develop a set of diagnostic biomarkers of coral thermal/salinity stress. 12102018.label: Realisation of objectives
12102018.value: The four objectives have been fully realized as detailed below: 5.3.1. To construct an exposure system for studying coral bleaching We constructed one 12-tank exposure system for processing experiments. Instead of three replicate exposure tank systems, we made an adjustment of constructing two 3-stocking tank systems which were larger than exposure tanks for acclimating corals collected from the field. The six stock tanks were of two separate water flow systems which provided more space for culturing coral colonies collected from the field and allowing acclimation before fragmentation. 1) Constructed 12 exposure tanks for temperature and salinity treatments. 2) Constructed two 3-large stocking tank systems for acclimating coral colonies. 3) Constructed a heater and chiller system to control a stable water temperature for each set of exposure tanks. 4) Constructed stocking seawater buckets for artificial seawater and adjusting salinity. 5.3.2. To determine the bleaching thresholds We conducted bleaching experiments on thermal and hyposalinity stress firstly and observed that different coral species had very different responses in terms of the way they bleached and other physiological responses such as tissue sloughing. Base on a preliminary experiment using Platygyra carnosa, we slightly adjusted our experimental design to test temperature and salinity effects separately to simplify the design – otherwise it was difficult to maintain good water quality and coral health. For salinity gradient, since our preliminary test showed that corals did not respond to slight salinity changes, we adjusted the gradient from 33psu, 30 psu, 27 psu, and 24 psu to 33psu, 29 psu, 25 psu, and 21 psu. For temperature treatment, we only compare the control (room temperature) and high temperature treatment (32oC) since at lower temperatures it took very long time (> 1.5 month) for Platygyra carnosa to show bleaching signs. We have accomplished thermal and salinity experiments using the following nine coral species: Acropora pruinosa, Acropora digitifera, and Acropora solitaryensis (branching growth form), Montipora peltiformis, Echinophyllia aspera, and Pavona decussata (plate-like growth form), and Platygyra carnosa, Dipsastaea rotumana, and Porites lutea (massive growth form). We have also identified the symbiotic algae strains of the nine coral species based on PCR analysis of ITS gene. Based on these experiments, we have found that all tested species are very resistant to high temperature and low salinity stresses, except Acropora and Montipora that are more sensitive to these stresses. 5.3.3. We have compared the physiological responses of thermal treatments among the nine hard coral species. For each species, we have measured the photosynthetic efficiency, chlorophyll a concentration, zooxanthellae density, and coral colour in the different temperature and salinity treatments during the course of each experiment. We found that these physiological parameters reflected the health statuses of the corals well. We have compared the molecular responses to thermal and salinity stresses among four hard coral species, including two tough (Platygyra carnosa and Pavona decussata) and two sensitive (Montipora peltiformis and Acropora pruinosa) species. All samples have been collected and their RNA extracted and sequenced. Please see the file RealizationOfObjectives.docx for a summary of the data and analyses. 5.3.4. To discover warning biomarkers for coral bleaching For each species, we have discovered a set of 18 to 21 potential markers of stresses. Please see the file RealizationOfObjectives.docx for a summary of the data and analyses.

12102018.label: Major findings and research outcome
12102018.value: We have constructed a new exposure system and used the system to test temperature and salinity thresholds of nine species of corals. The system can be applied to test responses of other marine organisms such as molluscs and crustaceans to global environmental changes as well. We have constructed and published a transcriptome database for 14 species of corals. The database is open to everyone with access to the Internet, and is useful for studies of molecular responses to stressors in corals, as well as comparative studies of coral immunity. We have conducted physiological studies of nine species of corals, and transcriptomic studies for two sensitive and to resistant coral species. We have discovered a set of early warning biomarkers for coral bleaching from each of these species. Overall, our results indicate that most of the tested corals are resistant to high temperature and low salinity, with the exception that Acropora and Montipora are less resistant. Comparing the differential responses of resistant and sensitive species to thermal and salinity stresses have led to the identification of molecular pathways that may affect their survival in the changing climate. Identifying the potential "winners and losers" has implications for management of coral ecosystems. During coral collection and laboratory culture, we have also discovered a new species of coral and two new species of coral-eating nudibranchs. While encountering coral bleaching in the field, we collected and analysed the transcriptome of bleached and healthy tissues of three coral species in order to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying their bleaching and recovery.

12102018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12102018.value: Based on our results, we will propose other related studies of the responses of local corals to global and regional stressors. For instance, we have only analysed nine species in this study, with the exposure system available, we intend to study the responses of more local coral species to temperature and salinity stressors. We also intend conduct a more detailed study of the compositional changes of zooxanthellae during natural bleaching and recovery. Overall, the results of this study will allow us to propose further studies the resilience of local corals, and extend coral studies to other regions of the Greater Bay area.

12102518.label: Realisation of objectives
12102518.value: Objective 1. To validate the nucleolin aptamer-mediated distribution of NucA-PTX in an orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer-fully achieved. To examine the tumor-targeting property of the NucA conjugated PTX-Rh, the tissue distribution of PTX-Rh was evaluated in our established orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer by biophotonic imaging. It was shown that the Rh fluorescence intensities in ovarian tumor tissues collected from the NucA-PTX-Rh treated mice were significantly higher than those from the CRO-PTX-Rh treated mice at 2 h and 4 h after intravenous injection of NucA-PTX-Rh and CRO-PTX-Rh, respectively. Moreover, the Rh fluorescence intensities in livers and kidneys from the NucA-PTX-Rh treated mice were remarkably lower when compared to those from the CRO-PTX-Rh treated mice at 4h after injection. Interestingly, the fluorescence signal was hardly detected in hearts, spleens and lungs in both groups. Objective 2. To study the pharmacokinetics parameters of NucA-PTX in circulation upon time in an orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer-fully achieved. The pharmacokinetics parameters of NucA-PTX in circulation upon time were evaluated in our establishd orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer. The serum half-life of NucA-PTX-Rh was evaluated to be approximately 2.78 h. The percentage of injected dose of NucA-PTX-Rh and CRO-PTX-Rh in tumor and other major viscera was also analyzed to quantitatively examine the effect of NucA on the excretion of the conjugated PTX-Rh. In consistency, the excretion of NucA-PTX-Rh in tumor was significantly slower than that CRO-PTX-Rh, while the clearance of NucA-PTX-Rh in liver and kidney was considerably faster. Objective 3. To evaluate the nucleolin aptamer-mediated change in antitumor activity of NucA-PTX in an orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer-fully achieved. The in vivo anti-tumor effect of NucA-PTX was evaluated in our establishd orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer. Compared with PBS-treated group (control group) and CRO-treated group (aptamer control group), the others groups exhibited significantly lower tumor volumes, wherein the NucA-PTX treated group showed a better inhibitory effect against tumor growth that PTX-treated group or nucleolin aptamer-treated group. Especially, the average tumor volume of the NucA-PTX treated group was significantly smaller than that treated with PTX and other groups (P < 0.05) on day 28. Then, Ki-67 antigen staining, a commonly used cell proliferation marker, together with H&E staining, were performed to further investigate the tumor suppression efficiency of NucA-PTX. For Ki-67 staining, we found numerous instances of Ki-67-positive cells in tumor tissue from PBS-treated and aptamer-treated xenografted mice, indicating active cell proliferation. In contrast, the NucA-PTX treated group showed a lower Ki-67-positive cells than PTX treated groups and the other control groups, suggesting a higher inhibition effect on tumor growth. For H&E staining, the nuclei were stained with hematoxylin in blue and the cytoplasm was stained by eosin in pink. The PBS-treated and both aptamer-treated groups showed rhombic or polygonal cells with large spherical or spindle-shaped nuclei, which indicating the normal cells without apoptosis and necrosis. Objective 4. To examine the nucleolin aptamer-mediated change in toxicity of NucA-PTX in an orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer-fully achieved. Considering the toxicities of paclitaxel (e.g. hematological toxicity and neurotoxicity) reported in clinical application, we further evaluate the toxicity of NucA-PTX in our establishd orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer. Firstly, we measured the body weight of the treated mice every 4 days during the treatments. PTX-treated group showed obvious weight loss throughout the experiment, indicating the potential of systematic toxicity. In contrast, no remarkably body weight loss was observed in PBS-, CRO-, NucA- and NucA-PTX-treated groups, revealing a slightly low potential of systemic toxicity. Next, we investigated the myelosuppression of NucA-PTX through white blood cell (WBC) count test. No obvious change of WBC count was observed in xenografted mice after treatment with PBS and CRO, whereas PTX and CRO-PTX induced a significant decrease in the value of WBC count. The value of WBC count in the NucA-PTX-treated mice was also decreased compared with the value before administration but to a much lesser extent than that in PTX-treated group. Furthermore, we evaluated the potential neurotoxicity of NucA-PTX using an electromyography apparatus. PTX and CRO-PTX induced a marked and significant reduction in caudal and digital nerve conduction velocities (NCVs) when compared to the PBS- and CRO-treated groups, hinting the potential neurotoxicity of PTX. NucA-PTX also induced caudal and digital NCVs reduction compared to PBS control group, but the value of NCVs was higher than that in CRO-PTX-treated group. Finally, The PTX-related toxicities to major organs were evaluated by histology analysis with H&E staining and serum biochemical assay, respectively. As expected, serious damages were observed in the H&E-stained sections of heart, liver, spleen and lung, respectively, in PDX mice with PTX- and CRO-PTX-treatment. For heart damage, myofibrillar loss and atrophy of myocardial cells were found. For liver damage, hepatic cords loss, mild steatosis and dilatayion of blood sinus were observed. For lung injury, broken lung fibers were found. For spleen damage, the atrophy of the white pulp was detected. However, the above damages to these tissues was greatly reduced or absent in NucA-PTX treated group when compared to those in PTX and CRO-PTX treated groups. Consistently, the histological scores of liver, kidney, lung, heart and spleen were all significantly lower in the NucA-PTX-treated mice as compared to the mice treated with PTX or CRO-PTX. Interestingly, there is no visible damage in kidneys from all the groups. Moreover, serum biochemical assays showed that the levels of liver function enzymes, i.e. aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and cardiac function enzymes, i.e. creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and creatine kinase myocardial bound (CK-MB) were all significantly lower in the NucA-PTX-treated mice as compared to the mice treated with PTX or CRO-PTX.

12102518.label: Major findings and research outcome
12102518.value: For tumor-targeted drug delivery, antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) is a promising strategy. Nevertheless, the risks of immunogenicity and the raising incidents of resistance for antibodies remain clinical challenges. In addition, difficulties in synthesis and chemical modification, and rigorous storage requirement are also the major concerns. Nucleic acid aptamers are small single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotide segments, which bind to their targets such as proteins on tumor cell surface with high affinity and specificity by unique three-dimensional structure. In contrast to antibodies, aptamers have limited immunogenicity and are unlikely for body to develop resistance. Besides, rapid tissue penetration and excellent stability and homogeneity of aptamers are also desired advantages. Therefore, aptamer-drug conjugate (ApDC) could be an improved version of ADC for targeted cancer therapy with higher efficiency and safety. Paclitaxel (PTX) is one of the most commonly used first-line drug for treating a variety of cancers in clinical chemotherapy. However, its poor water solubility and adverse side effects restrict its clinical applications. In this study, we designed and synthesized a nucleolin aptamer-paclitaxel conjugate (NucA-PTX) – an ApDC with both excellent water-solubility and tumor-selectivity. The bioactive C-2’ hydroxyl group on PTX was connected to a tumor-targeting nucleolin aptamer (NucA) via a cathepsin B-labile dipeptide linker, which remained stable in circulation for PTX deactivation, and broke then release PTX once the conjugate entered tumor cells. The NucA modification facilitated the selective accumulation of the conjugated PTX in tumor tissue, and subsequently resulting in notably improved antitumor activity and reduced toxicity in an orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer. This work not only establishes an innovative technology platform for ApDC design and synthesis, more importantly, it opens up a whole fresh field for the development of personalized aptamer-paclitaxel conjugates as alternatives of ADCs toward precision medicine. By altering aptamers that target different cancer cells (e.g. Her2 positive breast cancer cells, triple negative breast cancer cells, non-small cell lung cancer cells, osteosarcoma cells etc.), the personalized paclitaxel derivatives could be developed for the clinical treatment of patients with the according cancer types.

12102518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12102518.value: Paclitaxel (PTX) is among the most commonly used first-line drugs for cancer chemotherapy. However, its poor water solubility and indiscriminate distribution in normal tissues remain clinical challenges. Here we designed and synthesized a highly water-soluble nucleolin aptamer-paclitaxel conjugate (NucA-PTX) that could selectively deliver PTX to the tumor site. By connecting a tumor-targeting nucleolin aptamer (NucA) to the active hydroxyl group at 2’ position of PTX via a cathepsin B sensitive dipeptide bond, NucA-PTX could remain stable and inactive in the circulation. The tumor-recognition component NucA facilitated the uptake of the conjugated PTX specifically in tumor cells. Once inside cells, the dipeptide bond linker of NucA-PTX was cleaved by cathepsin B and then the conjugated PTX was released for action. The NucA modification facilitated the uptake of the conjugated PTX in ovarian cancer cells mainly by macropinocytosis in a nucleolin expression-dependent manner, and lead to higher cytotoxicity of the conjugated PTX to ovarian cancer cells compared to normal cells. The in vivo data collected from a orthotopic PDX mouse model of ovarian cancer demonstrated that the NucA modification facilitated the selective accumulation of the conjugated PTX in ovarian tumor tissue, and subsequently resulting in notably improved antitumor activity and reduced toxicity.

Brief Introduction of the Anti-HIV Aryl Naphthalide Lignans (ANLs) In our search for active lead compounds from tropical plants, we identified several potent anti-HIV ANL glycosides as lead molecules from Justicia plants. The present project was designed to synthesize the ANL analogues to improve their anti-HIV potency, and to elucidate their antiviral mechanism of actions. As a result, a total of 101 new ANL molecules have been produced, and many of them showed potent anti-HIV activities. A.2. Synthesis of ANL Analogues (to fulfill Objective 1: b.1.2 to b.1.4) Our synthetic approach to improve the antiviral potency of ANLs was directed to our major focus on the synthesis of different functional groups at C-7, accompanied with modification of the lactone and phenyl groups. [For the synthetic design, please see CS: Figure 1] A.2.1. Synthesis of ANL analogues through derivatization of phenyl ring A and the lactone ring Through a total synthesis approach (please see JOC: Scheme 1), 10 ANL derivatives (4a-4c, 5a, 5b, 6a, 6b, 7-9) including diphyllin (5a) were obtained (please see CS: the compound numbers are the same as those in Figure 2 of the paper) A.2.2. Synthesis of ANL analogues through derivatization of phenyl ring B The similar total synthetic approach in A.2.1 was applied to synthesize the ANL analogues, which produced 14 new ANL derivatives (10a-10d, 11a-11d, 12-15, 14a, 15a). (please see CS: the compound numbers are the same as those in Figure 3 of the paper) A.2.3. Synthesis of ANL analogues through derivatization of C-7 Reactions such as esterification, alkylation, carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen coupling have been applied in this study. 37 ANL derivatives (16a, 16b, 17, 18a, 18b, 19a, 19b, 20, 21a-21h, 23a-23o, 24-28) were synthesized. (please see CS: the compound numbers are the same as those in Figures 4 and 5 of the paper) A.2.4. Synthesis of ANL glycoside analogues. 40 ANL glycosides (29a-29g and 30a-30g) and derivatives (31-36) were obtained in this study. (please see CS: the compound numbers are the same as those in Figures 6 and 7 of the paper) A.3. Anti-HIV Evaluation of Synthesized ANL Compounds Using “One-Stone-Two-Birds” Assay (to fulfill Objective 3: b.3.2) One-Stone-Two-Birds” pseudotyped protocol was established for evaluation of the anti-HIV activities of the 101 synthetic ANL compounds, and the structure-activity relationship (SAR) information was concluded. (please see JOC: p5581); AJOC: p8; CJNM: p950; IJMS: 4.5.3, 4.5.4 and 4.6; ChemS: Supp Inf 2.3) The anti-HIV activities of all the ANL derivatives with rings A and B and the lactone ring being modified (4–15) were significantly reduced comparing with diphyllin (5a). This result revealed that the maintenance of an intact diphyllin core structure appeared to be important in retaining their antiviral activities of ANL compounds. (please see CS: Tables 1 and 2) The synthetic C-7 ANLs include those substituted with a 7-O-alkyl, a 7-C-subsituent, a 7-N-subtituent or a 7-O-ester. Among them, higher number of potent antiviral ANLs were found for the 7-O-esterificated ANL analogues than those ANLs with a 7-C or a 7-N or a 7-O-esterficated substituent. Compounds 16b, 19b, 21a, 21b, 23a, 25 and 27 are the most active ones with IC50 values in the range of 1.6-207 nM and selective indices (SIs) over 100. (please see CS: Figure 9 and Table 3) Among the synthetic ANL glycosides and derivatives (29a-29g, 30a-30g, 31-36), 29a, 30d, 31b and 35c were found to be the most active ones with IC50 values ranging from 0.026-58 nM and SIs over 100. (please see CS: Table 4) A.4. Antiviral Effects against HIV-1 Infectious Strains (to fulfill Objective 3: b.3.2) Compounds 21a and 25 were selected to be evaluated against a broad spectrum of HIV-1 clinical and resistant strains. The two compounds could inhibit viral growth to all the tested six strains with IC50 values ranging from 3.44–38.84 nM, which are not only more potent than the naturally occurred patentiflorin A (30b), but also more potent than the two clinically used drugs (AZT and NVP). These results clearly demonstrated that 21a and 25 could be good lead molecules for further development as anti-HIV agents. (please see CS: Figure 10 and Table 5) A.5. Antiviral effects of ANLs against simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) (this is an added extra study) To further confirm the anti-HIV activities of the ANLs and to select the ANLs for subsequent in vivo antiviral efficacy assessment in simian model, an in vitro antiviral assay protocol using SIVmac293 clone was established. Among our synthetic ANL derivatives, 23 ANLs were chosen for further anti-SIV evaluation study. We observed that the measured antiviral activity potency of the ANLs by using SIVmac239 is generally in line with the assay results obtained from the “One-Stone-Two-Birds” assay. (please see CS: Figure 11 and Table 6) A.6. Elucidation of the Potential Anti-HIV Mechanism of Action of ANL Compounds (to fulfill Objective 2: b.2.2 and b.2.4) Diphyllin is used as a representative ANL compound to explore the antiviral mechanism action of ANLs. A.6.1. To determine the viral target stage of ANLs through time-of-addition assay By applying this approach, the mode of action of an antiviral compound can be identified by comparing its efficiency dynamic over the time to that of reference drugs. Compared to the two reference compounds, the viral infection rate increased rapidly after 1 h or longer postponed by diphyllin treatment for H5N1/HIV or VSV/HIV infection, indicating that diphyllin possibly inhibited virus replication at the entry stage. [please see KCF PhD thesis: section 2.4 of pages 38-39) A.6.2. To elucidate biological potency of ANL compounds by computing analysis Three-dimensional quantitative structure-activity relationship (3D-QSAR) model is constructed to illustrate the correlation between structures and biological activities of a series of compounds mathematically. The pharmacophore information from the constructed model could give insights into the design of new compounds with desired bioactivity. Twenty-five synthetic ANL were selected to establish predictive 3D-QSAR models using comparative molecular field analysis (CoMFA) and comparative similarity indices analysis (CoMSIA). According to the information given in the 3D-QSAR analysis, 13 new molecules were designed and synthesized. (please see KCF PhD thesis: Chapter 3 of pages 49-78) A.6.3. identify the antiviral target(s) through affinity-based pull-down assay Both comparative and competitive approaches of activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) were successfully applied to determine the protein target(s) of diphyllin. Based on the result of 3D-QSAR analysis of A.6.2, we designed the total synthesis of diazirine-based probe (P1) for the competitive ABPP approach and benzophenone-based probes (P2 & P3) for the comparative ABPP approach. Among the identified 2,343 proteins, TFAM is the only shared protein hit twice in the dual strategic ABPP assays. TFAM as the antiviral target of diphyllin was confirmed by drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS) assay and the siRNA-mediated TFAM-knockdown assay. (please see KCF PhD thesis: Chapter 4 of pages 79-111)

12103618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12103618.value: Our present study has led to synthesis of 101 ANL compounds including some anti-HIV lead molecules, which have shown potent inhibitory effects against a broad spectrum of HIV and SIV strains with low toxicity. Eleven new ANL analogues were found to show antiviral activities with IC50 values ranging from 0.026-207 nM and SIs over 100, and two of them were found to possess potent inhibitory effects against a broad spectrum of HIV-1 clinical and resistant strains. The high anti-HIV potency of ANLs deems them as lead molecules for further drug development as antiviral agents. Demonstration of the antiviral activities of ANLs in an in vitro anti-SIV assay paves a way for their anti-HIV efficacy evaluation in simian in vivo models. In addition, the obtained structure-activity relationship and molecular target information of ANLs can provide more focused structure modification direction to fine-tune the structures toward the druggability (e.g. toxicology and pharmacokinetic effects) of ANL analogues in preclinical studies. Further, since our mechanism action study determined that ANLs are targeting on the host cells, ANL compounds could be explored for their potential against other emerging and re-emerging viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, Ebola virus and influenza virus in preparation of next viral outbreaks.

12103618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12103618.value: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) was established as the viral agent that causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) in humans 41 years ago. Over 74 million people have been infected with HIV, and about 36 million of them have died. There are currently no cure drugs or vaccines to treatment or prevent HIV infection. The discovery and development of new anti-HIV drugs are very much needed. In the present study, we have identified potent anti-HIV ANL (aryl naphthalide lignans) compounds by total synthesis and structure modification. Structure-activity relationship analysis of the synthesized 101 ANL compounds identified higher number of potent antiviral ANLs in the class of 7-O-esterificated substituted analogues than the other types of ANLs. Two new ANLs were then selected to be evaluated against a broad spectrum of HIV-1 clinical and resistant strains, and they showed more potent inhibitory effects against the viral strains than the clinically used drugs AZT and NVP. The antiviral mechanism study determined that ANLs inhibited virus replication at the entry stage, and the affinity-based pull-down assay identified TFAM (mitochondrial transcription factor A) protein as the potential antiviral target of ANLs. Our study has thus established ANL compounds as lead molecules deeming for further antiviral drug development.

12200118.label: Major findings and research outcome
12200118.value: The manipulation of molecular chirality in the absence of chiral molecule-based inductor is challenging and of fundamental interest toward elucidating the mysterious origin of homochirality. In this project, we show an unprecedented manipulation of molecular chirality via controlling the handedness of helical metal nanostructures (referred to as chiral nanoparticles or CNPs) that are produced by glancing angle deposition (GLAD, Small 16 (2020) 2001473). The left/right helical handedness, sculptured by macroscopic shear forces applied by rotating a supporting substrate in a counterclockwise/clockwise direction along with the translation of obliquely deposited metal atoms, gives rise to a specific enantiopreference in the photo-induced cyclodimerization of 2-anthracenecarboxylic acid (AC), i.e., counterclockwise rotation → left-handed (LH) → (+)-cyclodimers; clockwise rotation → right-handed (RH) → (-)-cyclodimers. The enantiopreference has been found to be mediated with silver and copper CNPs, and the enantioselectivity tends to increase with a decrease of helical pitch from ~225 nm to ~8 nm (Nature Chem. 12 (2020) 551-559). We have found the main contribution to the observed enantiopreference is the stereoselective adsorption of the enantiomorphous anti-head-to-head AC dimer precursors with the si-si/re-re facial stacking on the LH/RH CNPs, respectively (Adv. Mater. (2021) 2005506). Density functional theory calculations, in good agreement with the experimental results, show that the enantioselectivity originates from the meta-stable wavelike chiral lattices at the helical surfaces (InfoMat 2 (2020) 1216-1224), which enable the differential adsorption of AC pairs in the si-si and re-re facial stackings due to selective spatial matching. However, the wavelike chiral lattices exist in a small portion at the helical surfaces, and the rest are achiral lattices that will not lead to the enantiospecific adsorption of the AC dimer precursors. As a result, the obtained enantiopreference was evaluated to have a mean enantiomeric excess (ee) value < 6%. Furthermore, the photo-induced enantiopreference may be positively influenced by chiroptical enhancement of optical chirality of near-field scattering at the helical surfaces (i.e., the chiroplasmonic effect). However, currently we used non-polarized light (NPL) to trigger the photo-induced cyclodimerization of AC. We carried out finite element method to calculate the chiroplasmonic effect and found that NPL could not produce circularly polarized light (CPL) with single circular polarization (either LH- or RH-CPL), resulting in significantly deteriorating the enhancement of optical chirality of near-field scattering at the NH surfaces.

12200118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12200118.value: It is necessary to further maximize the enantiopreference. On one hand, the chiral lattices should be increase in their portion at the helical surfaces. We operated galvanic replacement reactions (GRR) of Ag CNPs with a helical pitch < 10 nm to generate binary CNPs (Ag:Au, Ag:Pt and Ag:Pd) exhibiting mesoporous morphology that will definitely increase the surface density of the atomically chiral lattices (Nano Lett. 19 (2019) 7427). Furthermore, we devised layer-by-layer GLAD (i.e., LbL-GLAD) to produce binary CNPs (Ag:M, and the solute M: Cu, Al, Au and Fe), and the combination of GRR and LbL-GLAD to produce ternary CNPs (Adv. Sci. 7 (2020) 2001321). The chiral alloying of M generally resulted in an amplification of optical activity of the host Ag CNPs, indicating an increase of the atomically chiral lattices in the CNPs (Small 16 (2020) 1906048). Alloy CNPs, using these three methods, will be used to enhance the photo-induced enantioselectivity. On the other hand, finite element simulation showed that the irradiation of LH/RH CPL will generate CPL with a given circular polarization and amplify optical chirality in the CNP vicinity. CPL will be applied to enhance the photo-induced enantioselectivity.

12200118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12200118.value: The generation of molecular chirality in the absence of any molecular chiral inductor is challenging and of fundamental interest for developing a better understanding of homochirality. In this project, we show the manipulation of molecular chirality through control of the handedness of helical metal nanostructures (referred to as nanohelices) that are produced by glancing angle deposition onto a substrate that rotates in either a clockwise or counterclockwise direction. A prochiral molecule, 2-anthracenecarboxylic acid, is stereoselectively adsorbed on the metal nanohelices as enantiomorphous anti-head-to-head dimers. The dimers show either Si–Si or Re–Re facial stacking depending on the handedness of the nanohelices, which results in a specific enantiopreference during their photoinduced cyclodimerization: a left-handed nanohelix leads to the formation of (+)-cyclodimers, whereas a right-handed one gives (–)-cyclodimers. Density functional theory calculations, in good agreement with the experimental results, point to the enantioselectivity mainly arising from the selective spatial matching of either Si–Si or Re–Re facial stacking at the helical surface; it may also be influenced by chiroplasmonic effects.

12200418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12200418.value: Training complex deep learning models is very time-consuming. High performance GPU clusters have been deployed widely to accelerate training jobs. Many excellent research projects have been carried out recently to improve the scalability of GPU clusters for a single training job. However, there are two important issues that have not yet been well addressed, one related to performance and another one related to operational cost. First, a GPU cluster is often shared by multiple users who can execute their training jobs concurrently but compete for hardware and network resources. Our preliminary research shows that if those resources are not allocated well, the total time of multiple training jobs can become 2.83 times slower due to I/O and network competition, despite the fact that the same number of GPUs are used. Second, GPUs consume significantly more power than CPUs and generate high electricity costs that dominate the overall operational cost of the cluster. Hence, it becomes critical to reduce the overall energy consumption without affecting the performance. Although many energy conservation techniques, such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) and resource allocation and task scheduling (RATS), have been proposed previously, the impact of DVFS on GPU performance and power is not fully understood due to the complicated GPU memory hierarchy. Developing accurate GPU performance and power models is also critical to solving the RATS problem. To address these challenges, we propose to carry out the following research tasks. First, we will build up an open data set of the performance and power consumption of abundant GPU kernels with DVFS for contemporary GPUs. Second, based on the data set, we will continue to develop efficient yet accurate GPU performance and power models for deep learning training jobs. Third, based on the performance and power models, we will tackle the RATS problem by designing energy-efficient algorithms. Finally, we will implement an open-source prototype of a job management and scheduling system for GPU clusters and evaluate the performance of our proposals using real-world experiments. We believe our new GPU performance and power models will be of interest to the general GPU computing community, and that our RATS algorithms and open-source system will make a significant contribution to the deep learning community. 訓練複雜的深度學習模型非常耗時，因此高性能的GPU集群被廣泛用於加速模型的訓練。最近許多優秀的研究聚焦在如何提高GPU集群的可擴展性來完成一個大規模的訓練工作。但是，有兩個重要的問題還沒有完美的解決，一個與性能相關，另一個與運行成本相關。首先，一個GPU集群通常由多個用戶共享，他們在同時訓練多個深度學習模型的時候會競爭硬件和網絡資源。我們的初步研究表明，如果資源分配沒有優化，這些I / O和網絡競爭會導致2.83倍的任務完成時間。其次，GPU比CPU消耗更多的功率，從而產生昂貴的電力成本。因此，在不影響用戶體驗的同時盡可能的降低系統總能量消耗變得至關重要。目前常用的節能技術包括動態電壓頻率調節（DVFS）和資源分配和任務調度（RATS）。然後，由於GPU複雜的內存層級結構， DVFS對GPU性能和功率的影響還沒有被完全理解。開發準確的GPU性能和功耗模型對解決RATS問題也非常關鍵。 為了應對這些挑戰，我們建議開展以下的研究工作。 第一，我們將建立一個關於GPU DVFS性能和功率的開放數據集。 其次，基於該數據集我們將針對深度學習訓練任務開發一套高效而準確的GPU性能和功率模型。 第三，基於性能和功率模型，我們將通過設計節能算法來解決RATS問題。最後，我們將實現一套GPU集群的作業管理和調度系統的原型，並通過實際試驗來評估我們的方案。

12200418.label: Realisation of objectives
12200418.value: In this project, we have fully realized the four project objectives. Objective 1: to build up an open data set of GPU performance and power with DVFS; To facilitate the data-driven research on the performance and power models of GPU applications, we have built a comprehensive data set, based on which we published two research papers [1] [2]. In [1], we designed a cross-benchmarking suite, which simulates kernels with a wide range of instruction distributions. In [2], we empirically investigated the impact of GPU Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) on the energy consumption and performance of deep learning. Our findings suggest that GPU DVFS has great potential to help develop energy-efficient training/inference schemes. Objective 2: to develop performance and power models for the training jobs of deep learning models; We have taken both analytical and data-driven approaches to building prediction models. In [1], we took the data-driven approach and developed a machine-learning model for predicting the execution time of GPU kernels. In [3], we developed a fine-grained analytical model to estimate the execution time of GPU kernels with both core and memory frequency scaling. In [4], we empirically benchmarked the performance and power of the training of different deep learning models and illustrated the impact of DVFS on deep learning performance and power consumption. Objective 3: to design online algorithms for resource allocation and task scheduling problems on GPU clusters; We first tackle the communication challenges in distributed training of deep learning tasks on GPU clusters. A typical distributed deep learning training job includes iterative computational tasks and communication tasks. In [5-6], we proposed an efficient and optimal scheduling algorithm to pipeline the computations and communications during the backpropagation stage, aiming to reduce the overall iteration time. In [7-8], we proposed an efficient data sparsification scheme gTop-k for distributed machine learning and analyzed the convergence properties of the proposed gTop-K algorithm. In [9], we extended the gradient sparsification scheme and further developed an optimal merged gradient sparsification algorithm with SGD (OMGS-SGD) for distributed training of deep learning. In [10], we noticed that simultaneous All-Reduce communications can effectively improve the communication efficiency of small tensors and therefore exploited both tensor fusion and simultaneous communications to improve the training performance. In [11], we proposed energy-efficient task scheduling algorithms on GPU clusters for both the offline and online modes with the following features: (i) it exploits GPU DVFS to conserve energy consumption without violating task deadlines; (ii) it effectively packs a set of tasks on a number of servers to reduce static energy consumption; (iii) it intelligently adjusts the DVFS setting for better energy savings. In [12], we conducted a comprehensive study on the inference performance and energy efficiency of Transformer models on GPU clusters. We proposed an online batch inference scheduling scheme for Transformer on GPU servers which can improve the throughput and energy efficiency by up to 61.56% and 69.79% on our testbed. Objective 4: to implement an open-source job management and scheduling system, and to evaluate the performance of the proposed solutions using real-world experiments. We have implemented many open-source systems throughout this project, including [1], [3], [4], [5-6], [7], [9], [10], [11]. All results presented in our papers have been evaluated through real-world experiments. References: [1] Q. Wang, C. Liu, and X.-W. 12200418.label: Major findings and research outcome
12200418.value: In this project, we aim to design energy-efficient resource allocation and task scheduling solutions for a GPU cluster that runs a set of deep learning training jobs. We have carried out a sequence of research tasks and generated fruitful research outcomes, including 5 journal articles (IEEE TPDS x 3, IEEE Network, and IEEE TGCN) and 9 conference papers (IEEE INFOCOM x 3, ICDCS, IJCAI, ACM e-Energy, etc). We have also won a Best Paper Award from IEEE INFOCOM 2021. More details about these publications have been reported in Sec 5.3. Our major findings are summarized as follows: 1. Although there is a trade-off between GPU performance and GPU power consumption, we can leverage GPU DVFS as an effective tool to reduce the overall energy consumption while satisfying the performance requirement. We have empirically shown the great impact of GPU DVFS on the performance of deep learning training jobs. We have also developed offline and online energy-efficient scheduling algorithms to schedule a set of jobs with deadline constraints. 2. Performance models and power models are of critical importance for the proper setting of DVFS parameters in resource allocation and task scheduling. We have shown two different approaches for such models: data-driven approach and analytical approach. The quality of data-driven approach usually relies on the quality of the data set. We have developed a cross-benchmarking suite that can generate high-quality data sets on the given GPU platform. 3. A distributed deep learning training job includes iterative computation and communication tasks. It is of critical importance to reduce the communication overhead to improve the system scalability. We have explored two directions for reducing the communication overhead: gradient sparsification and pipelining. Pipelining is a lossless method that doesn't hurt the training convergence, whilst gradient sparsification is lossy and we need to carefully fine-tune the hyperparameters to reduce the impact of convergence performance.

12200418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12200418.value: Although this project has fully achieved its original objectives, we found more interesting related problems that are worthy of further investigation. First, our current research assumes that a GPU will be fully occupied by a single training job at one moment. However, the newly developed GPU techniques enable the sharing of a single GPU by several jobs, with the potential of better GPU utilization. Many recent scheduling works have been done to support GPU sharing, but without considering the impact on energy consumption. Second, the current training systems such as PyTorch and Tensorflow rely on checkpointing techniques to handle training failures (either hardware failure or software failure). For large AI models, the overhead of checkpointing is very high. But reducing the frequency of checkpointing will increase the loss of computing resources upon a failure event. Since checkpointing is I/O extensive (such as network bandwidth and disk throughput), how to schedule the computing, communication, and disk I/O will be an interesting topic.

12200418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12200418.value: AI models have been widely used in many application domains. Generating (or training) a useful AI model requires a lot of computations, which are usually done on powerful AI processors such as GPUs. Unfortunately, there is a tradeoff between the speed of GPU and its power consumption. It becomes critical to reduce the overall energy consumption when building AI models, without affecting the speed too much. In this project, we took the following steps to design energy-efficient solutions for building AI models. First, we build up models to predict the performance and power consumption of GPU computing tasks, based on which we can develop efficient yet accurate performance and power models for AI training jobs. Second, we designed efficient scheduling algorithms for distributed AI training jobs by reducing the communication overhead. Third, we designed energy-efficient resource allocation and task scheduling algorithms for multiple AI training jobs on a shared GPU cluster. The effectiveness of our proposals have been evaluated via simulations and real-world experiments. We have also open-sourced our systems to benefit the whole research community.
