12606118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12606118.value: The mental health of university students has always been a concern in the higher education system. University students are vulnerable to mental health problems as they face a variety of challenges in university life. However, university counseling services are often inadequate to meet their mental health needs, especially in Hong Kong. In recent years, the advent of internet-based psychosocial intervention has rapidly ensued, and hailed as a possible solution as it is highly cost-effective yet has promising efficacy, with internet-based cognitive behavioral intervention (iCBI) as the most prevalent means. Nevertheless, this kind of internet-based intervention is underdeveloped in Hong Kong. Moreover, prevention is better than treatment. Given the high costs of treating mental illness for individuals and society as a whole, it is important to develop early intervention programs to prevent at-risk populations from developing various mental health problems (Cukrowicz, Smith, Hohmeister & Joiner, 2009). This project therefore aims to develop and evaluate a culturally appropriate iCBI program to reduce the psychological distress and improve the mental health of Chinese university students in Hong Kong. Participants will be openly recruited from the 8 public universities in Hong Kong and those with mild to moderate levels of psychological distress as assessed by an online pre-program questionnaire will be invited to take part in this project. A waiting-list control group design will be adopted to conduct a randomized controlled trial. Two hundred and eighty Chinese students will participate, with 140 in the immediate treatment group (i.e. the iCBI program) and the remaining 140 in a waiting-list control group. The iCBI program will include 8 online modules of CBI and 1 final review session with a telephone follow-up by a qualified cognitive behavioral therapist. The program will feature an interactive design with multi-media contents, and includes mood checks, informational briefings, case demonstrations, interactive exercises, and online homework and feedback. An outcome measurement package will be administered at pre-test, post-test and 3-month follow-up for both the experimental and control groups. Repeated measures MANCOVA will be conducted to test the effectiveness of the program at both the cognitive and affective levels. The findings of this project will provide empirical evidence of the effectiveness of iCBI for Chinese university students. Most importantly, in the long run, the program will be a valuable supplementary resource for Hong Kong university counselors to better address the needs of their student clients. 大學生的精神健康一直都是高等教育系統的一個重要關注。大學生由於要面對大學生活的種種挑戰， 容易出現各種精神問題。然而，大學的心理咨詢服務往往不足以應付學生的精神健康需要，特別是在香港。由於其高效能和低成本，今年網絡心理干預的興起為此提供了一個可能的解決方法，尤其以網絡認知行為干預最為流行。但是，這種網絡干預在香港卻鮮有發展。而且，干預勝過治療。考慮到治療精神疾病對個人和社會帶來的高昂費用，開發早期預防項目以防止高危人群產生各種精神疾病顯得尤為重要。 本項目致力於為香港大學生開發一個適合本地文化的網絡認知行為干預項目以減低他們的心理壓力並提升其精神健康水平。參加者將從香港的八間公立大學公開招募，他們將填寫一份網上評估問卷，有輕度至中度壓力的學生將被邀請參加本項目。研究設計將採用等待控制組的隨機對照試驗設計。280个香港大学生将参加本研究，其中140個為實驗組（即接受即時的網絡認知行為干預），另外140人為等待控制組。該網絡認知行為干預項目將包括8節網上課程和一節由認可認知行為治療師提供的電話隨訪。該項目的特色是配合多媒體的互動設計，包括情緒檢測，資訊簡介，個案示範，互動練習和網上家課和反饋。實驗組和控制組都將填寫一份前測、後測和三個月後的跟蹤問卷。數據將用重復測量MANCOVA來分析本項目在認知和情緒層面的干預效果。本研究結果將為網絡認知行為干預運用於華裔大學生的效果提供實證依據。更重要的是，從長遠來說，本項目將為香港的大學心理咨詢師提供一個重要的補充資源，以更好地應付大學生日益增長的精神健康需要。

12606118.label: Realisation of objectives
12606118.value: Objective 1 has been 100% achieved. An internet-based cognitive behavioral intervention (iCBI) program, which is called “REST Online”, was culturally appropriately developed for Chinese university students in Hong Kong. The REST Online Program was delivered in a blended mode in 10 weeks, which includes 8 online modules and 2 counseling sessions provided by a qualified therapist. The program can be accessed at the website (https://restonline.hkbu.edu.hk/) and a smartphone application can be downloaded on Google Play or Apple Store. The functions of the program include: (1) 8 online modules, which focus on a variety of cognitive behavioral skills to cope with university stress. The skillsets include cognitive skills such as self-talk, building evidence for and against, advantage and disadvantage analyses, pie chart and cognitive continuum, and behavioral skills such as behavioral experiments and behavioral activation. The skillsets are briefed and debriefed with animation videos and demonstrated by self-produced case videos of Hong Kong university students. Each module contains a mood check at the beginning and an exercise assignment at the end to practice the CBT skills to manage their own issues; (2) Online forums, where students can share their experiences and feelings under the guidance of a therapist. (3) Internal messaging, which students can communicate with their therapist by one-on-one text messages; (4) Online questionnaire, which the students can submit online at pre-test, post-test and 3-month follow-up in the system; (5) Booking counseling sessions, which students can book with the therapist for face-to-face or online counseling (Zoom, WhatsApp video call or telephone call due to COVID-19 pandemic), to discuss the application of the CBT skills for managing personal issues; (6) Client portfolio, which students can access to check their progress; and (6) Reminders on the implementation of different tasks at different times, such as online modules, counseling sessions and assessments. An introductory video shows participants how to use this online program after logging in. A user acceptance test (UAT) was carried out before the program was launched. All of the program contents are in Cantonese. All of the collected electronic data were encrypted. Objective 2, 3 & 4 have been 100% achieved by a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to test the program effectiveness. A total of 897 Hong Kong university students applied for the REST Online Program by open recruitment. A research assistant with a Master’s degree in Counseling completed 256 intake interviews to screen the participants, among whom 205 were randomly assigned to three conditions: (1) Web-based iCBI program (n = 71); (2) App-based iCBI program (n = 70); (3) waiting-list control (WLC) group (n = 64). A total of 189 students started the service and 16 didn’t login the REST Online system. The REST Online service was delivered by a certified cognitive behavior therapist with more than 10 years of counseling experiences. A total of 186, 131 and 80 data were collected at pre-, post- and 3-month follow-up test, and 55 additional data were collected as the second pre-test data for the WLC group before they started the REST Online service.

12606118.label: Major findings and research outcome
12606118.value: Results showed that compared with waiting-list control (WLC) group, students in both the web-based and App-based iCBI group showed significant reduction in psychological distress, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and significant increase in positive automatic thoughts and positive emotions. The positive effects maintained at 3-month follow-up. Based on the cutoff point of 1/2 on the GHQ-12 score (Goldberg et al., 1997), participant with a GHQ-12 score of 2 or above was identified as cases at risk of developing mental health problems. All of the participants were classified as at-risk cases at the screening test so that they were eligible to participate in the study. At the posttest, 71%, 68% and 20% of the participants in the web-based iCBI group, app-based iCBI group and the WLC group, respectively, were classified as non-at-risk cases. As for the user experience, 41% and 22% of the participants were satisfied and strongly satisfied with the REST Online service at post-test, respectively. These results demonstrated the “REST Online” Program as an effective iCBI program with high user satisfaction for improving the mental health of Chinese university students in Hong Kong.

12606118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12606118.value: The REST Online Program was developed for Hong Kong university students to help them cope with academic stress and improve mental health. As Hong Kong secondary school students, especially DSE students, are also facing a high level of academic stress which may have negative impact on their mental health, this program can be revised to an iCBI program for secondary school students by replacing the case demonstration videos with the ones that fits the needs of local secondary school students. They can learn a variety of CBI skills to cope with their academic stress with the assistance of IT technology and therapist support. Another direction for potential development is to revise the REST Online Program to an e-learning course in mental health education in secondary school and collaborate with local secondary schools to integrate it into the school curriculum. Professional training will be provided to school teachers to deliver this course in local secondary school to enhance students’ mental health.

12606118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12606118.value: This study developed a culturally and linguistically appropriate iCBI program called “REST Online” for Chinese university students in Hong Kong in a randomized controlled trial (RCT). The 10-week “REST Online” program includes 8 online modules and 2 counseling sessions. Therapist support was provided by a CBT therapist. A total of 897 Chinese university students applied for this program by open recruitment and 205 participants with mild to moderate levels of psychological distress was randomized to three groups: (1) web-based and (2) app-based REST Online groups, and (3) waiting-list control (WLC) group. A total of 189 participants successfully joined the program. A battery of standardized online questionnaires was administered to the students at pre-, post- and 3-month follow-up test. Compared with WLC group, students in both the web-based and App-based iCBI group showed significant reduction in psychological distress, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and significant increase in positive automatic thoughts and positive emotions. The positive effects maintained at 3-month follow-up. This study provided some empirical evidence for the effectiveness of iCBI program in the Hong Kong context for Chinese university students. The “REST Online” program can be provided to local university counselors as an alternative option for service delivery at post-COVID-19 era.

12606618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12606618.value: The proposed research-based contemporary art project will be built on the PI’s previous projects on landscape art. It will look into the use and reinterpretation of the landscape aesthetic in contemporary Chinese art and the correlation between the Chinese landscape aesthetic and contemporary society. The genre of landscape painting, a representative form of Chinese art, has resurfaced and gained currency in contemporary Chinese art, particularly in the discourse of ink art. Focusing on the use of landscape elements including actual scenes and landscape aesthetic in Hong Kong art, the proposed project will 1) investigate visual and textual representations of Hong Kong’s scenic landscape, 2) offer a new perspective on Hong Kong scenic sites and landscape art, and 3) explore the the relationship between landscape, identity and the contemporary re-imagination of place and space. The project will be organised into three phases. The first phase will involve archival and library research to collect information for an historical analysis of Hong Kong’s scenic landscape and to construct an image database. In the second phase, the project will explore the cultural tradition of landscape art based on findings from phase one, culminating in a cross-disciplinary symposium for curators, academics and artists to stimulate debate and discussion about the cultural tradition of landscape art. The third phase will transform the ideas and research gathered in the previous phases into works of art, using an exhibition as a site for further exploration of the topic of the Hong Kong landscape. Artists specialising in various media will be invited to experiment with the possibilities of landscape art through art-making, and an exhibition catalogue with visual images of the artwork and the findings of the research will be published. The project will offer a holistic perspective to fill the gap in existing scholarship and advance our understanding of the relationships between man and nature, and landscape and cultural identity. The four key deliverables – the digital database, symposium, thematic exhibition and travel guidebook – will offer a new perspective on Hong Kong landscape and landscape art, and open up a new dialogue on the relationship between landscape and the contemporary re-imagination of place and space. 是項有關探索當代藝術的研究計劃，是承繼了PI以往的山水項目，目的在於了解當代山水如何為人所使用和重繹，並梳理出山水與當代社會之間的關係。誠言，山水自古已是中國藝術的文化表徵，且在近年的中國藝壇上大放異采，尤其在水墨的論述中更為突出。是項計劃，委實是以香港風景和中國美學為中心，用以1）研究實景山水的圖像及文獻；2）建構一個嶄新的角度來審視香港的實景寫生和中國的山水藝術；以及3 ）探究山水藝術、文化身分和時空重構（re-imagination）三者之間的關係。 是項計劃將分為三個時期。第一期擬從各研究檔案室和圖書館資料庫中搜集香港實景山水的歷史資料，並建立一個圖像資料庫。第二期則從前期的資料和跨學科的研討中，探索山水畫中的傳統問題。第三階段則將前兩期的研究結果轉化成一系列的藝術作品，並舉辦展覽，以作進一步研究香港山水之用。是項計劃將會邀請不同專長的藝術家，以藝術創作的形式來探索當代山水畫的可能性，及製作一本展覽文字圖錄來呈現展品的面貌和研究的成果，所以將會帶來一個較全面的角度來修補現時的學術上的空白，以及加強人們了解人與造化、山水藝術與文化身分之間的關係。研究結果最終呈現四種不同的形式：電子資料庫、研討會、主題展覽和旅遊指引，賦予香港山水和山水藝術多一個不同的視野，並且在山水藝術與時空重構（re-imagination）中建立一個全新的對話方式。

12606618.label: Realisation of objectives
12606618.value: Objective 1: Four archives titled 1) “Local Landscape: Photos and Postcards”, 2) “Travel Biweekly: Wah Kiu Yat Po” (Vol. 1-411), 3) “Textual Database of Hong Kong Landscapes I: Hong Kong Island and Outlying Islands” and 4) “Textual Database of Hong Kong Landscapes II: New Territories and Kowloon” as well as two database websites related to Hong Kong landscape and artworks (https://imagesofhongkong.omeka.net/items and https://imagininghk.omeka.net/collections/browse) were produced. Objective 2 and 3: For the artistic practices, Ho Yuen Leung re-examined the relationship between man and nature, and re-investigated the farming culture of the old New Territories, Yuen Long in particular, by a series of abstract forms of the “sprouts”-like sculptures. In three pieces of video works in an installation setting, Lam Tung Pang questioned the role of a “visitor/stranger” in his hometown to re-explore the familiarity and unfamiliarity of this city along the northern coastline of Hong Kong Island. Joey Leung transformed what she received from the scenery of The Peak by her subjective visual, audio, scent and tactile senses into her imaginative 2-D images, while Wong Chun Hei took a time journey to go back to Hong Kong of the early and the mid of last century by restoring the nostalgic looks of the peninsula and the mountain range of Kowloon. Fiona Wong’s ceramic works brought the viewers back to the history of the catchwater drains in Pokfulan and let us pay homage to the artistry and the craftsmanship of the stone-chiselling by the stone artisans. In a series of installation works, the PI reinvestigated the understanding of 55 outlying Hong Kong islets and islands to record their appearances, history, legends, geology and culture by the Chinese aesthetics of brush and ink. Objective 4: An exhibition “Here & There: Re-imagining Hong Kong Landscapes” featuring the artworks in wide range of media and art forms was organised as the primary deliverable of the research. In association with the exhibition, a catalogue serving as a travel-guide book of six Hong Kong scenic spots was published by the Hong Kong Arts Centre. Along with it, a website (https://www.hereandthere.hk) was produced. In these two research deliverables, a long curatorial statement and six creative responses authored by the curator Dr Vivian Ting, an academic writing by Prof Pedith Chan as well as six artist statements by the artists were included. For stimulating discussion of landscape art among artists, curators and academic researchers, two artist talks and a public seminar called “Revisiting the Early Hong Kong Travel Activities from Travel Guidebooks” by Dr Yuen Chi and two sketching tours were arranged.

12606618.label: Major findings and research outcome
12606618.value: This project aimed to find six visual artists to investigate the use and reinterpretation of the landscape aesthetic in contemporary Chinese art and the correlation between Chinese landscape aesthetic and contemporary society. The genre of landscape painting, a representative form of Chinese art, has resurfaced and gained currency in contemporary Chinese art, particularly in contemporary Chinese art, particularly in the discourse of ink art. Focusing on the use of landscape elements including actual scenes and landscape aesthetic in Hong Kong art, the project achieved 1) the visual and textual representations of Hong Kong’s landscape, 2) a new perspective on the Hong Kong scenic sites and landscape art, and 3) the transformation of the research into an inquiry on the relationship between landscape, identity and the contemporary re-imagination of place and space. The project had two research outputs. The first output was to build up a research archive in textual and visual forms to carry the information of an historical analysis of Hong Kong’s scenic landscape and construct an image database. In the second output, it consisted of an exhibition, a catalogue, three seminars/talks, two tours and a website. Titled as “Here & There: Re-imagining Hong Kong Landscapes” and held at Hong Kong Arts Centre between 8 and 30 October 2022, the art exhibition displayed the research of the first output by the artistic practices of six artists (Ho Yuen Leung, Lam Tung Pang, Wong Chun Hei, Fiona Wong and the PI). They all specialised in a specific media (sculpture, moving images, 2-D artworks, painting, ceramics and ink art) and were invited to experiment with the possibilities of landscape art (Yuen Long, North coast of Hong Kong Island, The peak, Kowloon mountain range, Pokfulan and the outlying islands) through art making and offered a holistic perspective to fill the gap in existing scholarship and advance our understanding of the relationship between man and nature, and landscape and cultural identity. In association with the art exhibition, a catalogue along with a long curatorial statement and an academic writing was produced. In addition, two artist talks and a public seminar called “Revisiting the Early Hong Kong Travel Activities from Travel Guidebooks” by Dr Yuen Chi and two sketching tours were arranged. At the end of the project, a website (https://www.hereandthere.hk) serving as a digital version of the project record, the exhibition and the catalogue was produced.

12606618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12606618.value: This project showed an example how to investigate the use and reinterpretation of the local landscape aesthetic in contemporary Chinese art and the correlation between landscape aesthetic and contemporary society. For the further development, other proposals can extend the research to other places other than Hong Kong, such as Taiwan, the Mainland China, Japan/ Korean or even Europe and the US are highly potential and viable.

The vital part is to build up a research archive and share it with the artists for their artistic investigation imagination. The artistic inputs in the artworks by the six artists successfully showcase the under-researched values of the six scenic spots of Hong Kong, widening the understanding of Hong Kong history and culture.

12607018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12607018.value: The Ci poetry has undergone great revival and appeared in various features in the Qing dynasty. Owing to its short distance from the modern years, a lot of manuscripts of Qing Ci poetry have been well conserved There are more than 100 volumes of manuscripts by different authors which were seldom researched by the researchers before. This project will be developed in the following ways: firstly, it will make comparison and contrast of the manuscripts and the printed copies, finding the changes in the writers’ creating ideas; secondly, it will analyze the original texts and rethink the fixed literary conclusions; thirdly, it will find out the features of the group activities of the ci writers through the comments and prefaces on the manuscripts; fourthly, it will discuss the theoretical topics according to the records on the manuscripts; finally, it will re-evaluate the values of the individual writers including the women ci writers’ writing activities. The significance of the research is that it will explore the moving features of the texts, discussing its given ways of production and conservation, in order to provide new angles for ci research. To reach this goal, this project will adopt the methodology of philology, literature history and culture history. 清代是詞發展的復興時期，出現了很多新的現象。由於距離現在比較近，清代保留下來大量詞的稿本，這是以前的任何一個朝代所沒有的。清詞稿本的數量在100種以上，是一批以往很少利用的珍貴資料。本課題擬從以下幾個方面進行硏究：通過和刊刻本的對照，考察二者的異同，思考作家的創作思想的發展變化；通過對原始文本的分析，對以往文學史硏究的一些結論進行重新討論；通過稿本上面的批點或序跋，探討詞學群體活動的特徵；通過稿本上的某些記錄，探討清代詞學理論的相關問題。同時，也對一些創作個體的價値進行重新評估，對女詞人的作品的生成狀況等，提供新的認識。本課題的意義體現在，挖掘文本的流動性特徵，探討其特定的生成方式和存在方式，從而為詞的硏究提供新的角度。為了達到這個目標，本課題擬採取文獻學、文學史和文化史相結合的方法。 清代是詞發展的復興時期，出現了很多新的現象。由於距離現在比較近，清代保留下來大量詞的稿本，這是以前的任何一個朝代所沒有的。清詞稿本的數量在100種以上，是一批以往很少利用的珍貴資料。本課題擬從以下幾個方面進行硏究：通過和刊刻本的對照，考察二者的異同，思考作家的創作思想的發展變化；通過對原始文本的分析，對以往文學史硏究的一些結論進行重新討論；通過稿本上面的批點或序跋，探討詞學群體活動的特徵；通過稿本上的某些記錄，探討清代詞學理論的相關問題。同時，也對一些創作個體的價値進行重新評估，對女詞人的作品的生成狀況等，提供新的認識。本課題的意義體現在，挖掘文本的流動性特徵，探討其特定的生成方式和存在方式，從而為詞的硏究提供新的角度。為了達到這個目標，本課題擬採取文獻學、文學史和文化史相結合的方法。

12607018.label: Realisation of objectives
12607018.value: 稿本是文學發展過程中的重要文獻。清代的詞學號稱中興，許多方面都有新的成績。在清代，出現了稿本、抄本和刻本並存的現象，這是以前任何一個時代所沒有的。本課題考察了清代的不少稿本，把稿本當作一個重要的入口，認為清詞創作從稿本到刻本，有一個過程，正式定稿之後的文本，也能夠顯示出各個方面的資訊 。因此，在執行此一研究計劃時，並不拘囿於字面意義上的稿本，而是將包括刻本在內的清詞文本的各個方面都考慮進去，從文本的關聯中探討清詞的內容發展、風格特徵、美學特色等。另外，清代的詞和詩有著緊密的關係，探討清詞，難免會涉及到清詩，因此，執行研究計劃時，若發現有價值、有意義的問題，也會將詩和詞結合起來，加以思考。具體而言，本課題對張惠言《茗柯詞》稿本進行了研究，指出其原初形態和刊刻成集之後的不同面貌；對王國維所搜集的《鷗夢詞》稿本進行了研究，指出了王國維在詞學上所下的功夫，並進一步對王國維著名的《人間詞話》進行了思考。由於明清之際的詞稿本是現在所能看到的最早的詞稿本，因此在關注這一問題時，發展出對來鎔書寫江東遺事的相關作品的討論，指出其在詞史研究方面的價值和意義。由於姜夔的詞作在明代得到極大的忽視，清初朱彝尊等人開始大量搜集整理，因此發展出從姜夔這個特定的典型入手，從現場感的角度，考察在清詞發展過程中對白石詞風的接受。清代的女性詩詞作品有不少未正式刊刻者，在整理的過程中，發展出對清代女性詩詞中的寄外書寫的研究，並揭示了其在文學史發展中的意義。本課題增強了對清詞發展的認識和理解，體現了清詞研究的新進展。

12607318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12607318.value: This project aims to fills a gap in both communication scholarship and professional development by using the “best practices” approach to investigate corporate social responsibility communication in Asia. Unlike previous studies, the unit of analysis is not the individual practitioner but taking the organizational settings (meso-factors) and socio-political environment (macro-factors) into consideration from 10 best exemplars in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Australia. This study also attempts to address the existing gap in knowledge about how Asian companies interpret “best practices” in CSR and stakeholder engagement which have predominantly relied on international regulatory standards and Western/overseas textbook examples. Drawing upon the Circuit of Culture framework and Communication Constitutes Organization theory, this study aims to explore the interplay between macro- and meso-factors to uncover the true communication dynamics connected with the sensemaking and co-creation of best practices in Asia among CEOs, CSR directors, communication practitioners, employees, NGO partners, and local community stakeholders. A key challenge in developing a best-practices approach is to identify a sufficiently large sample of cases from which generalized rules and principles can be synthesized. Therefore, a three-pronged approach is proposed to reveal the power, conflicts, and tensions as well as the challenges and strategies for CSR communication and engagement. First, document analysis will be conducted to systematically review the best practices in CSR communication from past five years of academic papers and professional reports. Second, a Delphi study will be conducted among CSR experts and scholars to articulate a set of principles for best practices based on the guided theories. Third, 10 case studies of existing best practices organizations in Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia will be conducted through ethnomethodological approach to observe, record, and transcribe available organizational resources from agency and non-human actors. This is so as to identify the key factors and communication dynamics in order to construct a relevant model for best practices in CSR and stakeholder engagement is Asia, which can be transferred into an open-source website to educate communication students and CSR practitioners in Asia with vivid case examples along with luncheon workshops partnered with professional associations.

12607318.label: Realisation of objectives
12607318.value: For Objective 1, a systematic review of academic articles and professional reports published in the past five years was conducted. In addition, a thorough analysis of studying the Communicative Constitution of Organization (CCO) approach in CSR communication allowed us to identify the key research gaps on the macro- and meso-factors (i.e., Objective 5) to study the best practices of CSR communication and stakeholder engagement in Asia. For Objective 2, five Hong Kong companies were first selected to examine the CSR discourses in how the organizations 1) make sense of their presence as society-committed actors in the process of meaning construction in relation to the socio-cultural operating environments and 2) how the organizations demonstrated their aspirational talk and relational vs. episodic communication engagement practices in their latest sustainability reports. The selected companies represent various industries including banking, airlines, real estate development, utilities and trading and have subsidiaries and business in Greater China and/or the Asian region. Using the cultural discourse analysis (CuDA), the socio-cultural meanings derived from the five discursive hubs (i.e., identity, action, relation, emotion and dwelling) were identified to explain the constitutional approach of CSR communication. Findings were presented to the International Communication Association annual conference in 2020 and published in Public Relations Review (SSCI-indexed) in 2021. To fully realize Objectives 2-4-5, we further examined the sustainability reports of a prominent multinational agribusiness group based in Singapore over a 10-year period by adopting the propositions from the Circuit of Culture (COC) and the CCO to analyze how an MNC headquartered in Asia makes sense of the multiple elements that feature the interrelationships of actions and aspirations, and uncovers how it presents and deals with the manifestation of talk-action tensions in its CSR discourses. The five moments of COC (i.e., regulation, production, representations, identity and consumption) were identified along with analyzing the tension mechanisms in terms of CSR communication by tracking the key CSR topics such as sustainability palm oil certification, traceability of palm oil, burning methods, use of herbicides and pesticides. In addition, five Singapore based companies were selected to replicate the analysis by studying their latest sustainability reports in order to test out the proposed relevant model (Objective 6), develop the education materials (Objective 7) and reach the conclusions about the best practices in CSR communication and stakeholder engagement in Asia (Objective 4). The selected companies represent various industries such as banking, properties, energy and telecommunication. Findings were presented to the ICA annual conference in 2022 and the manuscript based on a case study has been submitted to Public Relations Review (2nd R&R) in 2022. We faced a series of critical challenges in conducting our study to realize Objective 3. The social unrest in Hong Kong in 2019 has put many business organizations in Hong Kong on media spotlight and the aftermath of the political movement has intensified politicization, polarization and media fragmentation. Many organizations have reservations on granting access for academic scholars to their companies to collect data especially toward internal communication and tensions dynamics in CSR communication. We also had difficulty in arranging face-to-face participatory observations amid the widespread and unpredictable lockdowns and restrictions during the COVID situations. Nevertheless, PI managed to participate in a project consultation of a large Hong Kong organization by joining four Zoom sessions (1.5 hours each) with top executives, communication managers, employees, NGO partners and community users (40 participants in total) with an aim to co-create a multi-purpose community project in a local district as a back-up plan for doing ethnomethodology to observe, record and transcribe meetings. ESG (Environment, Social and Governance) has become a recent hot topic because HKEX issued “ESG Reporting Guide” and made the disclosure obligation mandatory. PI was able to participate in five forums and expertise discussion meetings with communication practitioners, ESG consultants and executive members of industry associations. Many topics and ideas exchanged and shared in the meeting discussions are relevant to the project such as effective means to conduct stakeholder engagement, striking the balance between talk and action, addressing impacts and remedies in global vs. local ESG efforts as well as ESG disclosure reporting issues in sustainability contexts and concerted communication efforts in CSR storytelling. PI also joined an internationally recognized professional certification program with 10 practitioner participants from different industries and sectors to learn the latest international reporting standards. The 20-hour program provided fluid and vivid local and regional examples from the teaching materials and sharing from the participants of how their organizations make sense of their CSR discourses while fulfilling the ESG disclosure requirements and engaging with stakeholders throughout the materiality decision making and report planning process. Originally, we planned to include a few companies from Thailand (to replace Australia) but with the COVID travel restrictions during our study period for Objective 3, we decided to focus on companies from Hong Kong and Singapore (in a total of 12) that operate business in Greater China and Asia (e.g., Australia, Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, Indonesia and India) which can still give us a full picture of best practices of CSR communication and stakeholder engagement. The selected companies are CSR award recipients, embrace CSR culture, adopt international reporting standards and are active in social media platforms in communicating their CSR works. The rich amount of systematic literature review, case studies and active participation in joining the design and preparation process of stakeholder engagement and ESG reporting from Hong Kong and Singapore based companies that put CSR communication in their top priority has allowed us to capture the important macro- and meso-factors to reach conclusions about the best practices in articulating aspirational talks, managing tensions and sensemaking in CSR actions (i.e., Objective 4). Based on the findings, we have also developed a model (i.e., Objective 6) to bridge the gap by integrating the propositions of COC (i.e., macro factors) and CCO (i.e., meso factors) to enrich our understanding of the highly interrelated, steadily evolving and conflictual dynamics that manifest in CSR discourse. The integration of COC and CCO also provides theoretical means to bridge the structural analysis of CSR communication with situated logics and processes and deepen our knowledge of the associated, transactional and tensional character of matters of talk and action in the CSR discourses of the studied companies in transnational and multicultural environments (i.e., Objective 5). Currently, to fulfill the ESG reporting standards set by HKEX and SGX, much of the emphasis is limited to materiality topics and ESG disclosure standards. Results of this project contribute a significant amount of real-case examples on how to apply the reporting principles (e.g., accuracy, balance, clarity, comparability, reliability and sustainability context) in ESG reporting and CSR communication. A website (www.coms.hkbu.edu.hk/esgcomm) has been developing to document the relevant details such as ESG communication basic overview, key reporting principles, the Circuit of Culture moments and managing tension dynamics, with 10 selected company cases. The initial education materials have been incorporated in teaching final-year public relations students and PI plans to use the website to teach Advanced PR Writing and CSR communication & Stakeholder Engagement in AY2022-2023 (i.e., Objective 7). Also, PI has been invited to share the preliminary findings to a local academic conference on Sustaining Hong Kong’s Leadership in International Business Communication organized by Hang Seng University.

12607318.label: Major findings and research outcome
12607318.value: In our CuDA analysis of the Hong Kong companies, two themes have been identified to examine how engagement and aspirational talk for social license to operate (SLO) are constructed: 1) Establishing “we-ness” in community engagement and 2) Advancing leadership in sustainability practices. Also, the cultural meanings are manifested when these organizations constructed their commitment to society in their CSR communication such as 1) relating to local languages, cultures and places, 2) seeking credibility through external validation and 3) connecting global challenges to local practices. (For specific discursive hub examples, see our published journal article.). Our study illustrates that best practices companies seemed to accept the aspirational challenge and confident in meeting promises to gain long-term SLO outcomes by listening and responding to stakeholder concerns and negotiating themes, actions and practices, and with contextualized references through a step-by-step relational community engagement approach in addressing sustainability issues (actions) in the negotiated process. In our study of Singapore based companies, the five moments of the Circuit of Culture are manifested in aspirational talk through the dynamic CSR communication process: 1) Meeting international certification requirements vs. contextual situations (regulation), 2) Aspirations documents in reports vs. topic-specific CSR actions (production), 3) Numerical and textual representations of commitment to CSR action (representation), 4) Balancing corporate identity as a responsible actor vs. co-constructed CSR values in response to stakeholder concerns (identity) and 5) Developing measures to keep standard and adjust their CSR programs (consumption). In addition, five tension-coping mechanisms illuminated in the interplays of COC moments include: 1) The “good precedes the bad” mechanism to address the unmet plans, 2) The “it doesn’t depend on us” mechanism, 3) The “anticipation of the (potentially) negative” mechanism, 4) The “we embrace then we are” mechanism and 5) The “territory drives the difference” mechanism. (For CSR discourse examples, see our ICA conference paper in 2022.) Our study concludes that embracing CSR discourse as fluid and situational means recognizing its tensional nature – an intersection of multiple broad and situational elements that by supporting diverging interests, goals and concerns, come to clash and orient how organizations negotiate their aspirations and actions in CSR. We propose a COC-CCO integration model in theorizing CSR discourses – the five moments and the interactions remain but undergirding the five moments are four CCO associated concepts: Articulating aspirational talk, managing tensions, sensemaking in CSR actions and at the core, the constant process of negotiation and co-constructing of meaning.

12607318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12607318.value: Due to the unexpected circumstances, this project primarily adopted an organizational perspective and analyzed how the interests and concerns of various stakeholders were incorporated and negotiated in CSR discourses. Future studies can broaden this research scope by including more diversity of views, criticism and tensions from different stakeholders to fully capture every organizational and social process using other research methods such as in-depth interviews and ethnography. Specific materiality/CSR topics can be selected to further understand the best practices approaches within the industries. For example, PI has recently supervised an undergraduate thesis looking at how Hong Kong companies communicate the latest CSR issue on Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DE&I) toward the LGBTQ community by replicating the CuDA analysis and analyzing different levels of legitimacy. Results of the study are accepted for presentation to a regional conference (ANZCA) in November 2022 and submitted to Media International Australia (SSCI-indexed). After a couple of trial runs, the education website will become the first and most comprehensive platform on CSR communication and stakeholder engagement in Asia. More cases will be studied and added periodically from different industries, sectors (business/NGO/public/SME) and Asian countries. Concerted CSR communication efforts in cross-sector collaboration can also be further investigated.

12607318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12607318.value: With the rise of ESG reporting and sustainability development, organizations are putting more effort in CSR communication to meet the regulatory standards and expectations from different stakeholder groups. Using guided frameworks including the Circuit of Culture, the Communication Constitutes Organization theory and CuDA, this project aims to explore the interplay between macro- and meso-factors to uncover how Asian companies manage the power, conflicts and communication dynamics through articulating talk and actions, sensemaking their CSR actions, managing tensions and negotiating and co-constructing of social-cultural meaning. To conclude the best practices approach, this study conducted a mix of systematic review, cultural discourse analysis of selected companies based in Hong Kong and Singapore that have business in Greater China and the Asian region and participatory observations with industry practitioners, CEOs, employees, NGO partners and the local community to identify the fluid and vivid examples and observe how organizations make sense of the CSR discourse in such communication dynamic process. An integration model is proposed and an education website is developed to guide practitioners how to take social-cultural meanings manifested in CSR talk and actions into consideration when engaging and addressing concerns from stakeholders while fulfilling the reporting standards in preparing the sustainability reports.

12607418.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12607418.value: 外語與二語教育的自主性：深圳和香港在職教師的個案研究

12607418.label: Project Objectives
12607418.value: To document in-service English teachers’ perceptions of opportunities (possibilities) for and constraints on their teaching and their personal and professional development in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. To understand how in-service English teachers respond to the perceived opportunities and constraints in the two settings. To compare and contrast the trajectories of teacher identity construction and teacher autonomy development in Shenzhen and Hong Kong.
rows: To document in-service English teachers’ perceptions of opportunities (possibilities) for and constraints on their teaching and their personal and professional development in Shenzhen and Hong Kong.
To understand how in-service English teachers respond to the perceived opportunities and constraints in the two settings.
To compare and contrast the trajectories of teacher identity construction and teacher autonomy development in Shenzhen and Hong Kong.

12607418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12607418.value: Over the past few decades, autonomy has been considered as an educational goal in the field of foreign and second language education. Research demonstrates that teacher autonomy depends substantially on the achievement and exercise of teacher agency to construct teacher identity (Huang, 2010; Huang & Benson, 2013). Despite the wealth of literature on teacher identity, agency and autonomy among pre-service, novice, and in-service teachers, there has been scant research on synthesizing the three notions in exploring how particularly in-service teachers maintain their work momentum after they survive their initial years of teaching; how their agency and identity work is afforded or constrained by the socio-institutional contexts in which they are engaged; how they create spaces to exercise personal agency in their day-to-day teaching; and how they construct a professional teacher identity to take greater control over their teaching. In addition, teacher identity construction is enacted individually, mediated by the immediate contextual factors, shaped by their socio-economic backgrounds and influenced by social discourses on teachers and teaching profession in particular settings (Gu & Benson, 2015). This suggests that teachers’ views about themselves are not fixed or constant, but subjective, vulnerable, dynamic and fluid, that is, shifting due to contextual factors. Therefore, it is essential to go beyond the existing framework for language teacher development and knowledge in cognitive and rational terms to understand teacher identity (Song, 2016). Shenzhen and Hong Kong, separated by a river, are similar in their geographical locations and rapid economic growth, and yet different in their socio-political systems. It is against this background that this comparative study, interpretative qualitative in nature, is proposed. The study adopts a longitudinal multiple case-study approach to investigate the teaching lives of a small number of English teachers in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, focusing on how these teachers perceive affordances (opportunities, possibilities) and constraints in their teaching and how they respond to the perceived affordances and constraints. Data sources include interviews, teaching journals, school visits, and school documents. Through a close examination and comparison of two groups of in-service teachers in two different socio-political and educational contexts, the proposed research will extend our understanding of the complexities of teacher development, as well as the interconnected relationships between teacher agency, teacher identity, and teacher autonomy in such contexts. Such a comparative study will also provide valuable insights into in-service language teacher education practices for teacher educators, institutional administrators, and policy makers. 在過去的幾十年，學習者（和教師）自主性已成為外語與二語教育的一個目標。研究表明教師自主性在很大程度上依靠教師獲得並發揮教師能動性以構建教師身份 (Huang, 2010; Huang & Benson, 2013)。儘管關於職前教師、新手教師以及在職教師的教師身份、教師能動、教師自主的研究已經很充分，但是很少有研究整合這三個概念以探討特別是在職教師在成功跨越最初幾年的教學後如何保持工作動力；探討他們所處的社會機構環境如何促進或制約他們的能動性的發揮和身份的構建；探討他們如何創造空間從而在日常教學中發揮個人能動性；探討他們如何構建一個專業教師身份從而對他們的教學進行更有力的控制。此外，教師身份構建是在個人層面上發生的，受身邊環境因素所仲介，受教師社會經濟背景所左右，也受特別情景下關于教師以及教師職業的社會話語所影響 (Gu & Benson, 2015)。這說明教師的自我觀念不是固定的或持久的，而是主觀的、脆弱的、動態的和流動的，也即是根據環境因素而改變的。因此，我們有必要超越語言教師發展的現行框架和認知的、理性的知識體系去理解教師身份認同 (Song, 2016)。

12607418.label: Realisation of objectives
12607418.value: All the project objectives have been achieved successfully. The current GRF project (Identity, agency and autonomy in foreign and second language education: Case studies of in-service teachers in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. 1 January 2019 – 30 June 2021. RGC Ref No. 12607418) was closely connected to the PI’s previous GRF project (Autonomy in the transition from learner to teacher: A longitudinal multiple-case study. 1 January 2015 – 31 December 2017. RGC Ref No. 12403214). The current project was built upon the previous project and can be considered as an extension of the previous project in the following aspects: (1) The previous project investigated issues of autonomy in the TRANSITION FROM LEARNER TO TEACHER, with student teachers and teachers in their initial years of school teaching in Shenzhen and Hong Kong as major research participants; (2) The current project investigated similar issues of identity, agency and autonomy, with MORE EXPERIENCED TEACHERS (teachers with at least three-year teaching experience) as major research participants, in both settings of Shenzhen and Hong Kong; (3) More than half of the key participants of the previous project (data collection starting from school year 2014/2015) joined the current project when they had become more experienced school teachers (in 2018/2019). The three research questions of the current project correspond with the three objectives in the current project. However, since the overarching research question (objective) for the two projects was “How do English teachers in Hong Kong and Shenzhen schools take control of their teaching and personal-professional development?” (to investigate how these English teachers take control of their teaching and personal-professional development), part of the data collected in the previous project can be used to document the long-term development of the key participants with whom the PI had maintained close interaction for a 7-year period from the academic school year 2014/15 to 2020/21 (and beyond). Given the really longitudinal nature of the project, the PI conducted many rounds of semi-structured or relatively unstructured interviews with school teachers in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, in his research fieldwork in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. In each in-depth interview, questions regarding how these school teachers perceived affordances (opportunities, possibilities) and constraints and how they actually responded to these perceived affordances and constraints in their English teaching and their personal-professional development, were repeatedly asked at different time points, to elicit sufficient information to first fully address the first two research questions/objectives. Research participants in both settings were all articulate in sharing their personal understandings of affordances and constraints and meanwhile their respective strategies to act on the perceived affordances and constraints (e.g., making full use of existing resources and opportunities; critically interpreting the curriculum and teaching materials provided and teaching methods advocated; acknowledging personal shortcomings as novice teachers and taking initiative to seek help from senior colleagues and to look for various opportunities for improving teaching inside and outside the school setting). In all these interviews, the PI also invited the research participants in Shenzhen and Hong Kong to compare their professional environments (conditions for teaching and resources/supports for personal-professional development) and their actual teaching and personal-professional development experiences, in the two similar and yet different social-educational settings of Shenzhen and Hong Kong, for the purpose of collecting ample data to fully address the third research question/objective. In addition to in-depth interviews (major data source), the PI had also conducted school visits, had informal conversations with the research participants during school visits, and maintained regular email/WeChat/WhatsApp/telephone conversations with the participants, in both settings, for around 7-8 years. Some participants especially school teachers in Shenzhen also shared with the PI their teaching diaries (reflections), annual reports, lesson plans, school documents, photos of school/class activities, and student homework. All these multiple forms of data proved useful in answering the research questions of the current project. In summary, the PI’s research design and research fieldwork proved highly fruitful and all the three objectives are fully achieved.

12607418.label: Major findings and research outcome
12607418.value: The research participants, English as foreign/second language (EFL/ESL) teachers in primary and secondary schools in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, are generally prepared (ready) for autonomous teaching. An invitational, supportive and collaborative school environment plays a decisive role in affording opportunities for novice teachers to exercise their agency to take control over their teaching and personal-professional development (e.g., by creating spaces for autonomous teaching) and to construct a positive professional identity in school settings. The teacher participants exercised different degrees of proactive, reactive, and passive agency in their professional work. The four properties of human agency, i.e., intentionality, forethought, self-reactiveness, and self-reflectiveness, influence their proactive, reactive, and passive agency when they responded to personal, behavioral, and environmental determinants. The extent to which agency was exercised by the teachers depended on their positionings within their institutional contexts. This project also examined teacher attrition and teacher (sustainable) development, in relation to teacher agency and teacher identity. Findings revealed that school and social contexts intertwined with personal experiences, culminating in the participants’ leaving or staying in the teaching profession. This research consolidates our understanding of teacher identity as being complex, dynamic, discontinuous, and multi-faceted and teacher agency as being influenced by accumulated teacher experiences, previous patterns of thoughts and actions, evolving situation, and future vision. Novice teachers need much more personal and professional support than the school can usually provide. In most school settings, interpersonal relationships can work as a buffer, to alleviate the tension between the institution and individual teachers. Therefore, an open culture and effective communication among colleagues are of primary importance for maintaining the sustainability of professional development for early career teachers. Comparing EFL/ESL school teachers in the two settings, it is found that Shenzhen and Hong Kong teachers were all able to capitalise on existing opportunities/resources and overcome some of the constraints imposed by the social institutional structure. Agency-identity work mediates teachers’ perceptions of affordances and constraints and their corresponding actions. Shenzhen teachers exercised more proactive agency while Hong Kong teachers enacted more reactive agency. Hong Kong teachers were better educated and should be more capable for innovation but the context did not seem to encourage teacher agency for innovation. Shenzhen teachers were less professionally competent/ready before their first-year teaching but were more engaged and proactive in experimenting new methods. Shenzhen schools encouraged innovation, invested more resources and were more generous in reducing novice teachers’ workload.

12607418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12607418.value: The interrelationships among the concepts of teacher agency, identity and autonomy remain highly complex. More research of ethnographic designs is needed to further investigate these issues among school teachers of English as foreign/second language and other subjects in Hong Kong, mainland China and beyond. Given the COVID-19 pandemic and the lockdown of schools, the PI was able to carry out only part of the planned research fieldwork (school visits and observations). Future research should invest more in ethnographic research fieldwork if the situation allows. On the other hand, given the fact that site entry to school settings is usually more challenging than entry to other settings (e.g., universities), future research may need to explore other fruitful data collection methods without sacrificing the quality of the data collected for ethnographic designs. Most studies on teacher identity, agency and autonomy in the past were investigations under naturalistic settings. While these studies were really helpful in understanding the complex issues of identity, agency and autonomy, intervention studies, for example, action research projects can be carried out to examine the (in)effectiveness of supporting teachers in developing a positive professional identity, enhancing teacher agency and fostering teacher autonomy in their day-to-day teaching.

12607418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12607418.value: Research demonstrates that teacher autonomy depends substantially on the achievement of teacher agency to construct teacher identity. Despite the ample literature on teacher identity, agency and autonomy in language education, there has been scant research on synthesizing these notions in exploring how teachers maintain their work momentum after they survive their initial years of teaching; how their agency and identity work is afforded or constrained by the socio-institutional contexts; how they create spaces to exercise agency in their day-to-day teaching; and how they construct a professional identity to take greater control over their teaching. Shenzhen and Hong Kong are similar in their geographical locations and rapid economic growth, and yet different in their socio-political systems. This study adopts a longitudinal multiple case-study approach to investigate the teaching lives of a small number of English teachers in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, focusing on how these teachers perceive affordances and constraints in their teaching and how they respond to the perceived affordances and constraints. The research extends our understanding of the complexities of teacher development, and the interconnected relationships between teacher agency, identity, and autonomy in such contexts. It also provides valuable insights for teacher educators, institutional administrators and policy makers.

to explore the factors for evaluating the link between youth’s transnational civic participation and their social idealism at a time purportedly marked by precariousness.

12607618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12607618.value: This research examines whether there has been a revival of “youth idealism” in the age of neoliberalism, through examining youth groups’ transnational civic participation in “volunteer traveling” (hereafter, VT) in Asia. Today, many sociologists, economists, and cultural analysts have called young people the “precariats” who are caught in socioeconomic processes that saw them pushed and pulled in and out of employment, causing considerable anxieties. Have all young people become despondent, lethargic, or indifferent to social affairs? Studies indicate that youth voluntarism has not necessarily diminished. Their interest in volunteer work may be indicating a renewed idealism for social change, precisely at a time of their own personal and collective insecurities. The notion of the “precariat” carrying complicated sentiments is taken as a conceptual hypothesis for investigating the personal, emotional, ideological, and structural shifts in youth idealism. Voltra, a Hong Kong-based VT organization established in 2009, represents a uniquely significant case for in-depth analysis. It is a rare VT organization of its kind in HK; there is no other comparable organization like it operating out of HK. Up till 2016, Voltra has provided, coordinated, or linked up over 4,000 international workcamps and voluntary service projects in over 55 countries each year. Since its inception, more than 4,000 “Voltrateers” from HK have participated in workcamps mainly in Japan, Mongolia, India, Nepal, Cambodia, Taiwan, Thailand, and also in Europe, Latin America, and Africa. Our core research objectives are: (a) to critically examine Voltra (its history, ethos and philosophy, institutional development (local and transnational), impact assessment, etc.) as a strong representative case to see whether a renewed transnational youth idealism has emerged in recent years; (b) to document and analyze qualitatively the firsthand experiences, motivations, aspirations, and challenges arising from VT among youth participants; and (c) to produce a data set of qualitative cultural indicators for measuring and evaluating the link between youth’s transnational civic participation and their social idealism at a time purportedly marked by precariousness. Methods include a thorough historical and institutional review of Voltra, in-depth interviews with 100 Voltrateers, firsthand fieldwork immersion in a Voltra-coordinated workcamp in Asia, and a cultural indicator survey. The research results will provide important insights for mapping, for the first time, the development of “cosmopolitan civic citizenship” among HK youth during “hard times”, thus bearing implications for resource allocation for the development of international civic participation as a positive youth movement for Hong Kong. 這項研究通過考察青年團體在亞洲義工旅遊中的跨國公民參與，探討「青年理想主義」是否在新自由主義時代復甦？今天有不少社會、 經濟和文化的分析家都把年輕人稱為陷入社會經濟過程的「不安定者」，不穩定的職場經驗令他們產生相當大的焦慮。那麼面對社會議題時，年青人是否都會變得沮喪和冷漠呢? 有研究指出年青人的義工服務一直沒有減少。 他們參與的意願，可能在重建一種渴望社會改革的理想主義，尤其是身處於對個人及集體都沒有把握的社會環境。帶著複雜情感的「不安定者」概念，常被視為驗証青年理想主義的個人、情感、意識形態及結構變化的概念假說。本研究會對「義遊」作深入的個案分析。「義遊」創自2009年的國際義工﹙或稱義工旅遊﹚組織，它特殊的宗旨和運作在香港是絕無僅有的。 直至2016年，「義遊」籌辦、協辦及連繫的國際工作營和義工計劃多達4千個，遍及55個國家。超過4千名香港年青人參加過的工作營遍及亞洲各地，還有歐州、拉丁美洲和非洲。我們的核心研究目標是︰1﹚批判地檢視「義遊」的歷史、精神、制度發展(本地及國際)、影響等作為一個代表性案例，驗證近年是否出現了新的跨國青年理想主義；2﹚定性紀錄和分析「義遊」參加者的經驗、動機、志願和挑戰等第一手資料；3﹚探索一些影響青年跨國公民參與以其社會理想主義之間的關係之因素。研究方法包括對「義遊」進行深入的歷史和制度性回顧，對40名參加者進行深入訪談，對在「義遊」在亞洲的工作營中進行第一手的田野考察，以及使用文化指標作問卷調查。研究結果將首次為香港青年在「困難時期」所發展的「世界公民身份」提供重要的見解，從而對香港國際公民參與發展作為積極的青年運動捉供理論和知識資源。

12607618.label: Realisation of objectives
12607618.value: In this project, the PI studied a unique class of “voluntourists” with the urge to rethink the ambiguities and contradictions of mobility marked by idealism and “good intentions.” For objective 1, we successfully conducted a detailed “institutional capacity analysis” of VolTra as a representative case for studying youth’s aspirations for social change. As stated in the proposal, we intended to become friends to VolTra in order to gain their trust. The PI was successful in building a trusting relationship with various members of the organization’s executive committee, in particular with Mr. Bird Tang, Executive Director and Ms. Karin Wan, Chair of the Board of Director. Through them, the PI was given access to the organization’s archive, including early documents on VolTra’s founding history, principles and strategies of development, the philosophy of the “workcamp learning model” through international volunteerism, marketing efforts, and so on. In addition, the PI also had lengthy interviews of Mr. Tang and Ms. Wan for in-depth insights. In sum, to accomplish objective 1, our work included: a. Reviewed VolTra’s past Annual Reports b. Interviewed VolTra’s Executive Director and Chair of the Board of Director c. Interviewed two founding members of VolTra, four VolTrateers who became VolTra’s staff, and six VolTrateers who pursued extended projects after their workcamp experience d. Reviewed VolTra’s application database, and the volunteers’ post-trip reflection and evaluation e. At the pilot stage, reviewed social media, news coverage, as well as through our first-hand observation at the Glocal-Hero training camp, and an International Conference of Global Volunteering and the NDVA’s 13th General Assembly, both held in Hong Kong. In Hong Kong, VolTra is a unique non-governmental organization of its kind in Hong Kong; there are no other youth organizations like it. Combining volunteer work with traveling, it is an organization whose very name combines the involvement of volunteer labor, especially community services, and the experience of traveling. The good amount of valuable archival and interview materials has allowed us to capture the important developments in VolTra’s history. Important themes and tendencies were identified and discussed to form a baseline understanding of the capacity of VolTra to be a leading organization with which to understand youth’s aspirations for social change. This kind of “cultural inventory,” we believe, is very important for not only opening a window for us to understand an institutionally-grounded and empirically-driven approach to youth volunteerism, but also to theorize the many contextual, historical, ideological, and personal factors that drive youth idealism. We are in discussion with VolTra to present our institutional capacity analysis at their next Annual Meeting to be held in summer 2022. By continuing to work with VolTra, the PI hopes to develop a long term project with public impact to support youth volunteer work. For objective 2, the PI was able to obtain from VolTra two databases on their participants’ questionnaires filled out when they joined the workcamps. Signed agreements on privacy protection were made. These databases were extremely important for us to understand the informants’ background views, motivations, and thoughts, and to assist us in identifying appropriate interview subjects. However, the social unrest in the second half of 2019 has caused a delay. In the end, we successfully interviewed 26 VolTrateers. Our informants included 7 males and 19 females, aged 20 to 39, whose participation in VolTra’s workcamps and other activities spanned from 2015 to 2019. Their workcamp locations included Spain, France, Russia, Thailand, Costa Rica, Korea, Taiwan, etc. As with the batch of 30 VolTrateers whom we interviewed for the small pilot project before we commenced this project, many of our informants joined VolTra’s workcamps multiple times; some up to three times. Our findings show that repeated engagement is one of the hallmarks of voltrateering, dispelling a certain scepticism about voluntourists’ alleged casual or non-committal attitude toward doing VT work. Their ideas, opinions, and narratives were interpreted for major themes, recurring emphases, emotional and subjective reflections, even contradictions. Comparison and cross-checking among informants’ narratives were also performed. Further, a special characteristic of this group of informants is that a majority of them had to confront the decision of going abroad for workcamps while the social unrest was unfolding in HK in the second half of 2019. We say “confront” because these informants expressed discomfort, even “guilt,” for leaving HK at that unsettling time. We began to speculate whether their discomfort was in any way linked to their underlying values and beliefs (including political beliefs) that formed a part of their identity in search for social change. In other words, was there any overlap between the VolTrateers’ consciousness for change (through volunteering) and “conscience” for change (through being worried and troubled about the development and consequence of the youth-led movement in 2019)? Seeing this, we selected 12 of our informants for a second round of interviews for more in-depth interviews to specifically explore that question, in order to attempt to probe further on the whole question of youth idealism and the challenges therein. For objective 3, our concern was to attempt to theorize the transformation, if any, of youth’s identity and idealism as they are shaped by the changing social, cultural, and political environment in which they find themselves. If objective 1 has to do with the specific institutional infrastructure, and objective 2 is concerned with the informants’ subjectivity and sense of agency, then objective 3 zooms out to consider the wider constellation of forces/factors that shape both VolTra’s institutional development and the VolTrateers’ sense of mission. This last objective is an important aspect of this project for providing researchers with a theoretical compass for navigating the complex “structure of feelings” that idealistic organizations and youth make in order for them to construct a sense of authenticity in search for social change. As mentioned above, besides the set of factors that normally explain our informants’ participation in the work of VolTra, the period of our investigation (2019-2021) dovetails with a significant moment of social upheaval. Further interview work had led us to add an additional layer of reflection on the changing social and political context that significantly enriches our findings. In short, the task set out for objective 3 has been accomplished with the additional “twist” of events, yielding fascinating insights, we thought, about youth idealism and the complicated challenges related to it. The investigation of the longer-term implications of youth idealism, as well as the future significance of organizations like VolTra, can and should continue after the completion of this project.

12607618.label: Major findings and research outcome
12607618.value: The two major findings in this project include (a) a detailed institutional ethnography of VolTra and (b) a theoretical discussion on youth identity and idealism in challenging times. For (a), we read VolTra’s reports, deciphered the participants’ reflections, and talked to key personnel, to construct what we called the “mobility paradigm” of the organization. Through its work on providing international workcamps and voluntary service projects across many countries in the world, VolTra has established an “infrastructure of mobility” during the disenchanting times of economic downturn and rising social inequality. Our institutional ethnography discovered that VolTra was conscious of the fact that the practice of combining travel with voluntary service was part of the historical legacy of “working for world peace,” in which youthful energy and idealism was “extracted” to serve for world peace. Yet ideologically, by adopting the language of humanitarian development, voluntourism reinforced the dominant narrative of the middle-class benevolence. But co-existing with this, we found, is the organization’s rigorous reflection on the unique kind of social and cultural capital that the volunteers brought to the encounter with strangers in the workcamp setting, as a part of their “whole person” development. (See outputs: Erni, 2019a, 2019b, 2021a). For (b), we were able to develop a unique framework to explain the “clashing aspirations” of youth seeking social change at a time of social upheaval. We ended up focusing on theorizing the question of “moderate youth” as an under-explored identity category that crosses between volunteering and activist participation. We argue that in studies of youth social activism, little is understood about the less sensational forms of participation among more moderate youth, or their strategic repertoires of action in conception and in practice. Drawing on the special interview of 12 VolTrateers who went to workcamps during HK’s social unrest, we were able to delineate the underlying political conditions that generated a particular form of moralist activism centering on the discourse of “conscience awakening.” More specifically, we traced and compared the rise of a “social consciousness” for change among youth who engage in international volunteerism with the rise of a “political conscience” for ethical redemption among youth who participated in civil disobedience. (See outputs: Erni, 2020, 2021b, 2022; Erni & So, in preparation).

12607618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12607618.value: According to our analytical model, the similarities and differences of youth motivation and identity-formation that underline “social consciousness for change” and “political conscience for redemption,” should be further studied. These aspects should be incorporated into a long-term study of the characteristics and sociocultural significance of the “moderate youth” in HK, in conjunction with a continued analysis of various youth NGOs supporting youth’s aspirations. Specifically, the analysis of capacity-building of youth NGOs could be conducted periodically (say every 5 years), while the insights around mobility, “moderate identity,” and the search for social change, should be re-tested and further refined through further empirical studies. In addition, there are potentials for a policy study of HK’s moderate youth on how to support them to explore the world with other change-makers in the global community.

12607618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12607618.value: This project fills the gap in the scholarship on youth global cultural participation as developed in sociology, international studies, and cultural studies. It asks: why do so many young people engage in volunteering work, despite feeling disappointed about the possibility of a “good life,” and despite feelings of unease when witnessing the rising social inequalities in their own society and abroad? How does the notion of being a “change-maker” reveal about their “guarded idealism” going forward? We conducted an institutional ethnography of a representative NGO, VolTra, and interviewed many “VolTrateers” who participated in international workcamps. We also conducted a special set of interviews of those who went abroad during the time of social unrest in 2019 in Hong Kong, in order to examine their overlapping or contradicting aspirations for change during a challenging time. Our findings point to (a) a “mobility paradigm” of organizations like VolTra, which espouses an ideology of “neoliberalism” but also an aspiration toward cosmopolitanism that rewrites our understanding of “whole person development” for youth, and (b) a theoretical discussion on identity and idealism among “moderate youth” in changing times, a complicated sense of duty and authenticity that revolves around the questions of “consciousness” and “conscience.”

12608618.label: Project Objectives
12608618.value: To examine the extent to which the social changes experienced in China have affected its cultural and education policies (including music education), with respect to the values of creativity in the twenty-first century; To explore and study the perceptions of students on music participation in their preferred music activities, preferred music cultures, and creativity education in school education and music education; To investigate and examine the perceptions of music teachers on teaching creativity in school music education; To examine and discuss the perceptions of other subject teachers and school leaders on implementing or promoting creativity education and creativity music education; and To disseminate the data of this project to policymakers and the academic community to encourage greater communication between those involved in music education and the public.
