12608618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12608618.value: With particular reference to school music education in China, this study will examine the under-researched relationships between social transformation, cultural diversity, creativity, and education reforms. Education, knowledge, information, and creativity are progressively becoming driving forces behind our new social, cultural, and educational structures. In response to social change, this study will examine the development of school music education in China, focusing on culture-based creativity. The concept of culture-based creativity in education goes beyond artistic achievements in thinking imaginatively or metaphorically, challenging the conventional, and calling on symbolic and affective elements to communicate. Based on an examination of the nature of creativity and its diverse cultures in music education and forms, this study will explore the challenges of fostering creativity in school music education in general. The essential elements of music education include perception and creativity, stimulation, the enjoyment and adventure of seeing and hearing and of trying things out, the integration of musical creativity in diverse cultures, and achieving new effects in school education. These initiatives and changes have also seen ever-increasing dynamism in the artistic creation of cultural reforms in school music education. To analyse the impact of relevant social change on creativity in music education, this study will employ multiple research and data-collection methods, including the analysis of official documents and official approved music textbooks; other relevant literature; a student questionnaire; in-depth and semi-structured interviews with students, teachers, and school leaders; and non-participant observation of music lessons in primary and secondary schools. The empirical research will be based on observed and measured phenomena, and this will enable pragmatic recommendations for creative cultural and music education to meet the music education challenges of the twenty-first century in China. This empirical approach will focus on the investigation of how teacher training and knowledge is related to informed pedagogical decisions, and how specialist knowledge can guide teachers’ subsequent teaching actions in classroom music teaching. In this context, besides exploring the views of school students regarding their learning of creativity through music education, this study will also look at how music teachers, other subject teachers, and school leaders who are involved in creative arts education or creativity education think and behave in their approaches to school music education to promote creativity in students. 本文的研究重點在於探討社會改革、文化多樣性、創意，及教育改革之間的關係。教育、知識、資訊科技及創意已逐漸成為現今社會背後的驅動力。本研究將會探究中國的學校音樂教育中的發展趨勢，並集中分析建基於文化的創意，以回應急速的社會變遷。文化創意提倡富有想像力及隱喻的創造力，鼓勵突破傳統，也強調以符號及情感的元素進行溝通。本研究亦會探討創意的本質及其多樣性，及在學校中推行創意音樂教育的困難。此外，音樂教育的基本元素包括：創意音樂聆聽、音樂導賞、音樂視聽和對創作勇於嘗試、音樂創意在不同文化中的融合、及為學校教育帶來新影響。在學校音樂教育的改革中，上述元素備受重視，並且漸趨強化學生在藝術創作的動力。為了分析社會變遷對創意音樂教育的影響，本研究將採用多種研究方法去收集數據，包括分析官方文件及受官方批核的音樂教科書，查閱相關文獻，收集學生問卷，與學生、教師和學校領導人進行半開放式的深入訪談，及觀察中小學音樂課堂的授課。本研究會建基於觀察和數據分析，為創意文化和音樂教育提供務實及可行的建議，以應對二十一世紀中國音樂教育面臨的挑戰。同時，本研究也會調查師資培訓及專業知識如何影響教與學的決策，以及檢視專科知識如何幫助教師在音樂課堂中優化他們的教學。在這個脈絡中，本研究除了探討學生對創意音樂教育的意見，也會分析學校中不同持份者如音樂教師、其他學科教師，及學校領導者等對創意藝術教育的看法，並探究他們如何在思考及施行上提高學生的創意。

12608618.label: Realisation of objectives
12608618.value: Though creativity is deeply rooted in all cultures, its conceptions and definitions vary across cultures. Given the complexity of conceptualising creativity across cultures and contexts, the dichotomy of the East and the West is one of the most influential approaches to characterising differences in defining and assessing creativity. Challenges often exist in school music education because of conflicts between the needs and interests of individuals and the values, needs, and ideology of the state. In Chinese society, collectivism has long been a tradition based on Confucianism, in which a social personality is less valued. In contemporary China, a fundamental attribute of socialist ideology is the promotion of the good of the collective over individualism. The Chinese education system has long been blamed for its lack of creativity education in school learning and teaching. With particular reference to school music education in China, this project examined the underresearched relationships between social transformation, creativity, music, and education reforms. The essential elements of music education include perception and creativity, sources and stimulation, the integration of musical creativity in diverse cultures and music participation, and the achievement of new effects in school education. These initiatives and changes have also seen ever-increasing dynamism in the artistic creation of cultural reforms in school music education. The key features of the project are that it explains (1) music and non-music learning as a reflection of the relative sociopolitical ideologies of China and (2) how the music curriculum is structured in accordance with political ideologies from the perspective of students and teachers’ perceptions of creativity and music education. The dynamics and dilemmas of introducing creativity, imagination, self-expression, quality education, and whole-person education into school music education in the new global age in China were examined by analysing official documents, selected current music textbooks adopted by schools, other relevant literatures, a student survey questionnaire, and in-depth and/or semi-structured interviews with students, teachers, and school leaders in different Chinese localities between the beginning of 2019 and the beginning of 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study focused on three Chinese cities, including Changsha (the capital of China’s Central Hunan Province and a hub for China’s creative industries), Shijiazhuang (the capital and largest city of North China’s Hebei Province and a city of growing culture industries), and the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) of China (an important centre for creative industries). In this context, besides exploring the views of school students regarding their learning of creativity through music education, this study also looked at how music teachers and other subject teachers who are involved in creative arts education and creativity education think and behave in their approaches to school music education to promote creativity in students. This project attempted to provide a balance between theoretical/methodological and empirical chapters. The writer believes that the case studies of the three Chinese cities will appeal to an international audience. A theoretical contribution to cultural diversity and creativity in education is the first long-term impact. This book examines, in a general and exploratory way, the issue of music cultures and creativity education in a specific framework of theory and world knowledge (i.e., beyond China-focused studies). This project drew upon and applied a framework that took into account the environmental and social contexts of creativity in music teaching and learning to improve music education by including creativity education in the music curriculum. Taken together, theoretical articulation and refinement of creativity, music cultures, and school music education is underdeveloped, lagging behind practical explorations of international knowledge. Beyond the contribution to the improvement of international knowledge and understanding of creativity in school music education, this study assessed the importance of creativity from a music education point of view and from the perspective of diverse music cultures. Based on the survey findings from the primary and secondary school students’ responses in this study, in exploring the role and function of creativity and innovation in the educational domain and the factors which are likely to enable or inhibit creative learning and innovative teaching, the second potential scholarship is the contribution to the understanding of education theory and policy on creativity and music education. While there is a growing trend towards incorporating creativity education into maker education, this area is underresearched; dialogue on this issue will help map music education policies and practices in contemporary and future music education. The third contribution is the understanding of teachers’ teaching and students’ learning of creativity in Chinese cultural (Confucian) and socialist contexts (in which authority and obedience, along the lines of creativity and innovation, are the focus). There were some limitations in this study, the foremost of which was the representativeness of the students and teachers, as well as the sample of school leaders in China as a whole. This challenge was compounded by the distribution limitations of the survey questionnaires during the critical periods of Hong Kong’s social movement and the COVID-19 pandemic. After several attempts to invite Shanghai schools and teachers, their participation in this study was not accepted and approved. In Beijing, only six schoolteachers and school leaders from four schools agreed to take part in the interviews, but the students were not permitted to participate in the survey questionnaire. Thus, this project included participants from Hong Kong schools between late 2019 and early 2021.

12608618.label: Major findings and research outcome
12608618.value: The principal research question of this project was threefold: (1) to discover the values of students’ creativity in school education and the role of music teachers; (2) to assess creativity in taught music genres in classroom music education; and (3) to examine the importance of creativity through music activities in formal and informal education. The data were obtained from 1,958 students (915 girls, 973 boys, and 70 unknown gender) from Changsha, 2,015 students (971 boys, 1,043 girls, and one unknown gender) from Shijiazhuang, and 3,519 students (1,783 boys, 1,709 girls, and 27 unknown gender) from Hong Kong. Among the well-founded responses in the survey questionnaires, most of the students were between the ages of 11 and 15. Seventy-one students from a sample of five secondary and two primary schools in Changsha and 129 students from four primary and six secondary schools in Hong Kong participated in the interviews, along with eight Changsha teachers from seven schools, 27 Shijiazhuang teachers from 10 schools, six Beijing teachers from four schools, and 27 Hong Kong teachers from 13 schools. Some major findings of this project were presented at three international conferences (please refer to Part C). Data were also published in three international refereed journals and three refereed chapters between 2019 and 2022 (please refer to Part C). Two referred book chapters have been accepted for publication (please refer to Part C). In April 2022, a book proposal and one sample chapter were submitted to Routledge for publication (please refer to Part C).

12608618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12608618.value: Though this small school-based study is not representative of Beijing, Changsha, Shijiazhuang, and Hong Kong (and even other Chinese cities), it is a preliminary step in the examination of students’ and teachers’ perceptions of creativity and music education and the extent to which creativity is significant in music activities and learning music types in a culturally diverse community. Though the influences and values of creativity in education and music education were similar among the primary and secondary school students, differences in their conceptions of creativity in music education were also noted in respect to preferred music activities and music genres. Subject teachers and music teachers brought up the priority they have given to creativity and music education to promote the creative development of students and to encourage an ethos in which cultural diversity and diverse music participation are valued and supported. Perhaps new technologies for music learning, creativity development, teacher education, and teachers’ preferences will supply some answers to the further development of research on creativity in classroom music education and education reforms regarding creativity, not only in Chinese communities but also in other Asian countries, Europe, and the United States.

12608618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12608618.value: The dynamics and dilemmas of introducing creativity, imagination, self-expression, quality education, and whole-person education into school music education in the new global age in China was examined by analysing official documents, selected current music textbooks adopted by schools, other relevant literatures, a student survey questionnaire, and in-depth and/or semi-structured interviews with students, teachers, and school leaders in three Chinese cities between the beginning of 2019 and the beginning of 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Besides exploring the views of school students regarding their learning of creativity through music education, this project also looked at how music teachers, other subject teachers and school leaders involved in creative arts education and creativity education think and behave in their approaches to school music education to promote creativity in students to meet the music education challenges of the twenty-first century in China. The findings of this study showed that there are fundamental issues in evaluating creativity in school music education in response to the role of the school subjects and the music teachers, as well as the incorporation of creativity into music genres and music activities to be delivered in the school curriculum.

12609918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12609918.value: This research project is aimed at analyzing the priorities and major features of China’s military and security cooperation with Africa. This project is also aimed at comparing China’s growing role in Africa’s security to the action of some of the continent’s more traditional military and security partners, as the United States, France and the European Union (EU), assessing the areas of cooperation as well as competition between China and these countries and, in so doing, better comprehending China’s geo-strategic objectives and interests in Africa. The PI’s hypothesis is that China’s security goals are diverse and expanding, including both hard and soft security objectives, but all aim at consolidating China’s diplomatic and geo-strategic influence as well as great power status in Africa, and beyond. China wants now to be seen as a major stakeholder of Africa’s security and probably also to weaken African countries’ dependence upon their traditional security partners and providers. This research will first analyze and compare a few cases of hard and soft security (as medical and humanitarian) cooperation between China and African countries. To conduct this research, the PI has selected seven African countries which have been chosen because of their close security partnership with China as well as their differences: Algeria, Comoros, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, Mauritania, Sao Tome and Principe and Sierra Leone. Secondly, this research will analyze China’s growing involvement in United Nations Peacekeeping Operations (PKOs) in Africa, studying the case of South Sudan. This project's third objective is to study China’s military and security cooperation with the African Union (AU) and to evaluate China’s role in the AU’s effort to establish an African Peace and Security Architecture as well as its contribution since 2015 to the establishment of an African rapid reaction force. Its fourth objective is to analyze China’s plan to offer a better security to its companies and nationals based in Africa, in assessing in particular the role played in this plan by China’s newly-built dual-use naval base in Djibouti. The major questions that this research project wishes to address are to what extent Beijing’s growing role in Africa’s security is contributing to changing the geo-strategic map of the continent; to what extent it offers new security options to African countries as well as the AU or Africa’s sub-regional organizations; and to what extent it compels Africa’s more traditional security partners to take into account China’s stake and security interests on the continent.

12609918.label: Realisation of objectives
12609918.value: The project’s objectives have all been achieved. This research project was aimed at analyzing the priorities and major features of China’s military and security cooperation with Africa. This project has also attempted to compare China’s growing role in Africa’s security with the action of some of the continent’s more traditional military and security partners, as the United States, France and the European Union (EU), to assess the areas of cooperation as well as competition between China and these countries, and in so doing to better comprehend China’s geo-strategic interests and objectives in Africa. This research has been based both on data collected in Hong Kong as well as fieldwork conducted in Africa. It initially included four major objectives. A fifth objective was added when Prof. Alistair Cole joined the GRF and later became its PI. This research’s first objective was to analyze and compare a few cases of hard and soft security (as medical and humanitarian) cooperation between China and African countries. As soft security is concerned the case of the Ebola crisis in West Africa was selected, leading the PI to conduct in 2019 fieldwork in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia where China’s People’s Liberation Army was involved in 2014-16. Chinese medical missions were also studied later in Mauritania, Sao Tome and Principe, and Comoros. Secondly, this research analyzed China’s growing involvement in UN Peacekeeping Operations (PKOs) in Africa. The case of South Sudan where the PLA had deployed more than 1,000 peacekeepers, among them some 700 combat troops, was selected. The PI visited the Chinese contingent in August 2021. The third objective of this research was to study more closely China’s military and security cooperation with African countries. Interviews on this cooperation were conducted in Guinea in 2019, Seychelles in 2020, Guinea Bissau and South Sudan in 2021, Mauritania, Central African Republic, Zambia, Comoros and Algeria in 2022. The fourth objective was to analyze China’s security role in Africa and in the Indian Ocean, since it has established a naval base in Djibouti. Fieldwork in Seychelles, Comoros and Mauritius was conducted for that purpose. From the first four objectives, a rich dataset of publications has appeared (13 publications, two under review and seven conferences), with more output being considered by specialised ( African and Asian Studies) and general (Geopolitics) reviews. We would signal in particular the article by JP Cabestan in Journal of Contemporary China, one of the key reviews in the field. The final objective of this research was to add a European and French dimension to China’s role in Africa and look in particular at the cases of the French territories of the Indian Ocean (Mayotte and Réunion) and their relationship both with the French’s central authorities and also their neighbours (Comoros, Mauritius) as well as China. Despite the pandemic, the PI and the CI have been able to meet all the initial and new objectives of this research. The major conclusion of this research is that China’s security goals are diverse and expanding, including both soft and hard security objectives. All these objectives aim at consolidating China’s diplomatic and geo-strategic influence as well as great power status in Africa, and beyond. It is clear that China wants now to be seen as a major stakeholder of Africa’s security and probably also to weaken African countries’ dependence upon their traditional security partners and providers. The other conclusion is that Africa and African countries have become subjects of competition among big powers in a kind of zero-sum game. However, China’s and Africa’s other partners’ security objectives do not always clash in Africa. In South Sudan, Sierra Leone or Liberia, they tend to converge: In terms of security stabilization or soft security, outside powers’ respective goals and interests are more complementary than contradictory. Yet, Beijing’s growing role in Africa’s security has contributed to changing the geo-strategic map of the continent and offering new security options to African countries. It has also compelled Africa’s traditional security partners to take more into account both China’s security interests on the continent and African countries own agency in the new and more competitive economic, political and security environment in which the world is now living.

12609918.label: Major findings and research outcome
12609918.value: There are two major and four significant findings. The first major finding is that China’s security goals are diverse and expanding, including both soft and hard security objectives. All these objectives aim at consolidating China’s diplomatic and geo-strategic influence as well as great power status in Africa, and beyond. The second main conclusion is that Africa and African countries have become subjects of increasing competition among big powers in a kind of zero-sum game. Beijing’s growing role in Africa’s security has contributed to changing the geo-strategic map of the continent and offering new security options to African countries. Four significant findings are as follows: 1n relation to the Ebola crisis, China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) was for the first time involved in managing a health epidemic overseas. It deployed medical teams both in Sierra Leone and Liberia and coordinated actions with other actors, as the US or the United Kingdom. In relation to China’s growing involvement in UN Peacekeeping Operations (PKOs) in Africa, the Chinese PLA deployed for the first time combat forces in Mali and South Sudan While cooperating with other PKO contingents, these forces have remained by and large more risk adverse, the sign of a more general learning process. In relation to China’s military and security cooperation with African countries. China has become an important weapon provider in Africa, although behind Russia, the US or France. It has also developed military cooperation with a growing number of African countries, training every year in China dozens of African military officers and building military facilities, including sensitive communications systems, for African militaries. Concerning China’s security role in Africa and in the Indian Ocean, China’s naval base in Djibouti, opened in 2017, has allowed the PLA, particularly its Navy, to play a more visible role both in Africa’s security and the Indian Ocean. This new base has fed a growing strategic competition between China and the US as well as China and India. In terms of research outcomes, this project is unprecedented in its empirical reach. Fieldwork was led by Jean-Pierre Cabestan in Guinea and Sierra Leone (2019), Ivory Coast, and Liberia (2019), Equatorial Guinea and Sao Tome and Principe (2019): Seychelles (2020), Cape Verde and Guinea Bissau (2021), South Sudan and Somaliland (2021), Mauritania (2022), Central African Republic and Zambia (2022) and Algeria (2022). Cabestan was accompanied by Alistair Cole in Comoros, Mayotte, Reunion, and Mauritius (2022).

12609918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12609918.value: Africa is made of 54 nation-states and each of them has a specific security relationship with China. In order to better grasp this complex set of relations and cooperation, more fieldwork would be needed, particularly in North Africa (Morocco, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt) and in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Tchad) and central Africa (Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo). Only one country, Algeria, was included in the previous sample. Other North African nations have also developed a substantial security and military cooperation with China that is worth exploring. In the Sahel and the Central African Republic (CAR), comparing China’s and Russia’s security role would be very useful, as Russia’s Wagner groups are playing a growing security role in Mali and the CAR. This would help better comprehend the degree of security cooperation both powers have agreed upon as well as the actual division of labour that has taken shape on the ground. Finally, better understanding the security implications of all the sensitive infrastructures built by Chinese companies for African governments and military would constitute another important further development for this research.

12609918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12609918.value: This research project analyses the priorities and major features of China’s military and security cooperation with Africa. Based on extensive fieldwork in 17 African countries (and two French overseas regions), the project concludes that China is determined to consolidate its diplomatic and geo-strategic influence as well as great power status in Africa, and beyond. Africa and African countries have become subjects of competition among big powers. China’s security objectives do not always clash in Africa with those of other players. In South Sudan, Sierra Leone or Liberia, they converge in favour of security stabilization Nonetheless, Beijing’s growing role in Africa’s security has contributed to changing the geo-strategic map of the continent and offering new security options to African countries. It has also compelled Africa’s traditional (United States, France, United Kingdom, European Union) and new (Japan, Russia, Turkey) security partners to take more into account both China’s security interests on the continent and African countries own agency in the new and more competitive world in which we are now living. Going forward, the challenge for China is to keep pushing its security interests and influence while refraining from directly infringing upon both African countries’ and other external stakeholders’ interests and priorities.

12613818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12613818.value: This project scrutinizes the media enterprises established during the 1950s and 1960s by Chang Kuo-sin (1916–2006), with the support of the Asia Foundation (a US-funded private nonprofit organization), to counteract communist cultural influences in Cold War Asia. Taking Hong Kong as a strategic battlefield, Chang founded Asia Press to publish the works of émigré Chinese writers in Hong Kong and Taiwan in order to build up a creative anticommunist Chinese literature. He launched Asia Pictures to produce commercial movies through inter-Asian networks that would propagate Chinese traditions and values. This project investigates Asia Foundation’s secretive aid to Chang’s media enterprises. At the same time, it probes the impacts and legacies of his Asia enterprises in fostering creativity and cultural consumption in the literary, cinematic, and popular realms. The study conceives the significance of Chinese cosmopolitanism to go beyond a conventional political understanding of Cold War culture as manipulated by the big state players. It examines how the vernacular and the popular were experienced in everyday life through inter-media productions of popular novels, dramas, translations, music, and motion pictures. It also considers the crucial role of colonial Hong Kong as an important source of Chinese-language cultural production in Cold War Asia. By examining how localized agents and communities wrestled with Cold War politics and harnessed creativity in response to turmoil and conflict, this project investigates the promises and predicaments of Chinese cosmopolitanism. First, it delineates the legacy of Asia Pictures in Chinese-language film history and its competition with leftwing Chinese filmmaking in Hong Kong. Second, to probe the impact of US-funded projects and appraise how the cultural Cold War has shaped multicultural Chinese mentalities, it explores the technology, consumption, readership, and material production of popular fictions, magazines, and translations. Furthermore, it looks into the migratory detours and creative experiences of Chinese intellectuals and writers to understand how their exilic or diasporic movements contributed to the intercultural vision of modern Chinese cosmopolites. To address these questions necessitates a combination of archival study, historical contextualization, and inter-media/textual examination. To this end, the PI will conduct interregional and trans-Pacific research in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, and US. The research outcome will be a number of international conference presentations, refereed journal articles, and a book manuscript. 12613818.label: Realisation of objectives
12613818.value: 1. Delineate the impacts of Asia Pictures in Chinese-language film history In 2019, I (PI) undertook overseas research trips at the U.S. National Archive II of the National Archives (NARA) at College Park, Maryland. I managed to locate US diplomatic materials (such as USIS and the State Department) on Hong Kong affairs and broadly on Cold War Asia. I discovered relevant Chinese-language cultural programs and publications in Hong Kong and Asia done under the collaboration of US agencies and their Chinese counterparts in Asia. I also visited C. V. Starr East Asian Library at U.C. Berkeley. There I recovered the collection of Great Wall Pictorial collection, a crucial left-wing film publication in the 1950s and 60s. Since Asia Pictures under Chang Kuo-sin’s directorship put leftist Great Wall Studio as the main competitor in the cultural Cold War, the research on the leftist film magazine has proved to be fruitful in understanding the cultural strategies of Asia Pictures. I also made a visit to the Hoover Institution of Stanford University, and specifically consult files of the Asia Foundation, particularly regarding Asia Publishing Company and Asia Pictures, as well as the correspondence between Chang Kuo-sin and his American agents. The research has allowed the PI to look into and study how US connections and collaborations has contributed to shaper the cultural Cold War in Hong Kong and Southeast Asia. 2. Study popular fictions, magazines, and translations as Cold War cultural legacies I previously had research in the National Archive in Singapore and National University of Singapore (NUS), and had collected some extant issues of The Story Paper, which began publication in 1955. I also collected some key issues of Asia Pictorial in the NUS library. In the NUS university library, I located a few popular Chinese-language magazines published in the 1950s and 60s that were read as popular literature in Southeast Asian and Hong Kong. These publications included a few issues of Ying deng (Spotlight), a small-scale entertainment magazine, carried abundant popular fictions and news about Chinese film circles. These popular journals and magazines have allowed the PI to understand and develop the Southeast Asian and Cold War cultural connections in relation to Hong Kong as the key cultural production center. In Hong Kong, throughout the project period, I have hired research assistants to look at the Union Institute's (under US support) publications and news materials in the Hong Kong Baptist University library. The RAs also helped me conduct research on my conference papers and journal articles in relation to the cultural legacies of the Cold War, and continuously look into other university libraries and the Hong Kong Public Records Office to locate historical materials, old newspapers, journals and movie magazines in relation to the topic of cultural Cold War in Asia and Hong Kong. 3. Examine the migrations and experiences of authors and artists as Chinese cosmopolites The PI has managed to work out a couple of academic publications and previously conference papers drawing on the research materials to examine the diasporic experiences of authors and artists during the cultural Cold War. For instance, The Story Paper drew diasporic Chinese authors to write for middle-brow fiction newspapers. My published chapter on Liu Yichang, who has been known as a modernist writer of experimental fiction in Hong Kong literature, is a discovery and close study of Liu’s “The Singapore Story” which was produced in a US-financed popular fictional magazine under the shadows of anticommunist propaganda, modernism, and consumerism.  Published chapter: “Soft-boiled Anti-Communist Romance at the Crossroads of Hong Kong, China, and Southeast Asia.” In Chineseness and the Cold War Contested Cultures and Diaspora in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, edited by Jeremy E. Taylor and Lanjun Xu, 94–109. New York: Routledge, 2021. Other major finds include the production and marketing strategies and cultural politics of Asia Pictures, through which Chang Kuo-sin employed many cultural elites, exiles and film workers from China (mainly Shanghai) to work for the film company and produce softcore anti-communist pictures. The research outcome has been published in:  Journal article: “Chang Kuo-sin’s Asia Pictures and Its Cold War Cultural Legacy” [張國興的「亞洲電影」與冷戰中的文化傳承], Twenty-First Century Bimonthly, no. 193 (Oct 2022): 142–59.  Conference paper: “Right Screen in Hong Kong: Chang Kuo-sin’s Asia Pictures and Contested Overseas Chinese Identity in Cold War Asia,” Panel: “Intra-Asian networks of propaganda and intelligence Cold War Sinosphere (1930-1970),” Annual Conference of Association of Asian Scholars, Denver (USA), March 21–24, 2019. There are issues that have not been fully addressed. The PI proposed to get a chance to talk to Chang Kuo-sin’s family members, who have maintained contact with the Baptist University in the past years. During the pandemic the family members had not got a chance to come to Hong Kong. Also because of the longtime travel restrictions and inconvenience, the PI could not go to the Taiwan Film Institute and Academia Sinica in Taiwan, as it was proposed to look up collections of Chinese-language film materials and literature in relation to my project of Asian Cold War studies. In reflection, however, the Taiwan Cold War connections are worth another independent project to study. The PI would consider such a possibility to undertake another research in the future.

12613818.label: Major findings and research outcome
12613818.value: The years of archival research have proved to be very productive leading to a number of published research articles and prior conference papers. The research in the US National Archive and Singapore libraries has uncovered The Story Paper and the production and dissemination conditions between Hong Kong and Southeast Asia as supported by USIS. The outcome is my published chapter, “Soft-boiled Anti-Communist Romance at the Crossroads of Hong Kong, China, and Southeast Asia,” in Chineseness and the Cold War Contested Cultures and Diaspora in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong (Routledge, 2021). Further discovery was made in the Hoover Library in Stanford in the files of Asia Foundation, in which I could trace the development and promotion of Asia Pictures. My Chinese journal article, “Chang Kuo-sin’s Asia Pictures and Its Cold War Cultural Legacy,” is an initial investigation of it, published in Twenty-First Century Bimonthly (2022). Local research in Hong Kong’s historical archives and libraries plus online database research has recovered historical materials about the cinematic production and reception against the odds of censorship in Cold War Hong Kong. Two other publications are achieved in this vein: they are “Screening without China: Transregional Cinematic Smuggling between Cold War Taiwan and Colonial Hong Kong,” Journal of the European Association for Chinese Studies (2020); “The Man without a Country: British Imperial Nostalgia in Ferry to Hong Kong (1959),” in Global Storytelling: Journal of Digital and Moving Images (2023).

12613818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12613818.value: With the research materials collected and ongoing research writing that have been benefited from the project, I am going to propose a book manuscript to a European or US university press to delineates the impacts of Chinese cultural politics, British colonial film policies, U.S. interventionist culture on Chinese-language cinemas circulating in Hong Kong and inter-Asian regions. It will examine how the Cold War factors have shaped the minds and hearts of Asian Chinese audiences, the reception, resistance, and the cultural and historical meanings of Hong Kong cinema and Chinese-language films in the Cold War period.

12613818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12613818.value: This project started from investigating the business and cultural operations of Asia Pictures, a short-lived film company active during the 1950s and 1960s, producing only nine Chinese-language pictures with good quality in their time. Secondly, the PI sought to look into the Cold War factors in mid-century Hong Kong, which became an important center of film and cultural productions of all sorts in Southeast Asia and inter-Asian regions. In terms of methodology, the project is archive-driven. The PI undertook research work in the US, UK, Singapore, and Hong Kong. The groundwork research has helped to delineate the impacts of Chinese cultural politics, British colonial film policies, and U.S. interventionist culture on Chinese-language cinemas circulating in Hong Kong and inter-Asian regions. Third, the project will help us to appreciate the cultural legacy of Asia Pictures on the development of Chinese-language cinema in Hong Kong, rather than taking a narrowly political or ideological understanding of the movie enterprise. It is because Hong Kong has been a commercial and cultural hub, and moviemaking has to cater to the tastes of the mass Chinese audience. Creativity and popularity always matter in Hong Kong cinema against the odds of politics and other limitations.

13501018.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13501018.value: 反壟斷政策，持續創新和研發

13501018.label: Project Objectives
13501018.value: To provide a dynamic model of innovation that allows us to improve our understanding of how antitrust policy can alter R&D incentives across different research paths. To characterize the equilibrium of the model, conduct comparative statics on relevant parameters and fine-tune our understanding of what makes optimal antitrust policy. 13501018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13501018.value: Traditional antitrust analysis has tended to focus on practices that restrict pricing or contractual relationships and has paid relatively little attention to the potential effects of antitrust policy on innovation incentives. Understanding the effects of antitrust policy on incentives to innovate is, however, crucial to determine the welfare of high-innovation industries because innovation is central to competition and innovative products can greatly benefit the consumers served by such industries. Moreover, the effects of antitrust policy on innovation incentives can be complex. For example, antitrust policy that is more protective of entrants will tend to encourage innovation by raising a successful entrant's initial profits but may also retard innovation by lowering the future profits to be made by the entrant once it becomes an incumbent. This project will aim to study the effects of antitrust policy on innovative industries. To this end, I will develop an infinite-horizon model in which innovations occur continuously and a potential entrant can choose between conventional and novel (new) research paths. Preliminary analysis suggests that a more protective antitrust policy has opposite effects on the entrant's R&D rate of innovation depending on the chosen research path. Moreover, in a stationary Markov perfect equilibrium in which the entrant's choice on R&D path is endogenized, a more protective antitrust policy increases (decreases) the expected R&D rate in the industry when the initial antitrust protection is low (high). This project will contribute to the literature by providing a new and important piece of economic analysis on the effect of antitrust policies on innovation incentive, an increasingly relevant topic in the economics of innovation that has thus far received little attention. The proposed research project will also aim to derive some testable results on the relationship between the protectiveness of antitrust policy and the rate of innovation, to shed lights on the recent debate on the effects of antitrust policy on innovation and to produce some practical guidelines for the design of optimal antitrust policy. 傳統反壟斷分析主要關註價格或者合同，較少分析對創新的影響。然而，對高科技產業，創新是競爭的核心，影響著產業發展和福利。此課題就反壟斷政策對創新的影響進行新的經濟分析，提出可供實證研究的理論和可行的公共政策。

13501018.label: Realisation of objectives
13501018.value: To achieve objective 1, we have developed a dynamic model of continual innovation that follows closely Segal and Whinston (2007) but incorporates the choice of research directions. Specifically, our stylized model consists of two potential innovating firms. In each period, one of the innovating firms is the incumbent, who, through innovation at an earlier period can produce a product of a certain quality; whereas the other is the potential entrant who, if successful in discovering a higher-quality product through R&D, will enter the industry, replace the current incumbent, and becomes the new incumbent next period. To achieve certain innovation outcomes, the potential entrant can choose one from two different research directions. One research direction, which we call conventional direction, is along the research direction taken by the previous innovator, the current incumbent. In this direction, if the innovation is successful, the entrant shares profits with the incumbent (e.g. through exclusive dealing contracts) depending on the strength of antitrust policy. Regarding objective 2, we have solved the model and characterized the stationary Markov Perfect Equilibrium (MPE). Moreover, we have also examined how the key parameter, the strength of antitrust policy, affects the innovation incentive of the incumbent and the potential entrant. Since the innovation incentives of both the incumbent and the potential entrant contribute to the overall technology progress, the optimal antitrust policy should balance the interests of the two parties. To achieve objective 3, we have identified the condition under which greater antitrust protection promotes the dynamism of R&D competition and thus of innovation. We find that, as the strength of antitrust policy increases, the expected R&D rate increases if the initial policy strength is strong while R&D rate decreases if the initial policy strength is weak. These findings suggest that strengthening antitrust policy may not necessarily promote innovation.

13501018.label: Major findings and research outcome
13501018.value: This project has studied the effects of antitrust policy on innovative industries. The effects of antitrust policy on innovation incentives can be complex. For example, antitrust policy that is more protective of entrants will tend to encourage innovation by raising a successful entrant's initial profits but may also retard innovation by lowering the future profits to be made by the entrant once it becomes an incumbent. To disentangle these effects, I developed an infinite-horizon model in which innovations occur continuously and a potential entrant can choose between conventional and novel (new) research paths. A more protective antitrust policy has opposite effects on the entrant's R&D rate of innovation depending on the chosen research path. I have obtained the following findings. First, stronger antitrust protection for an incumbent has opposite effects on the entrant's R&D rate of innovation depending on the chosen research direction. In particular, as protection for the incumbent increases, the R&D rate decreases if the entrant chooses the conventional research direction. This is consistent with the result obtained by Segal and Whiston (2007). However, in contrast to the static model where the R&D rate is independent of protection under the conventional direction, stronger protection increases the R&D rate under the new research direction. This is because, under the new research direction, the entrant will become the future incumbent, the value of which increases with protection. Thus, in contrast to Segal and Whinton, in my model front-loading can also increase the R&D rate. Second, in the stationary Markov Perfect Equilibrium, as protection increases, the expected R&D rate decreases (increases) for low (high) protection. When the protection is relatively low, the entrant has a high probability of choosing the conventional research direction. Hence, the profit-division effect is more prominent and deters the expected R&D rate. When the protection is relatively high, the entrant likely opts for the new research direction. As a result, stronger protection for the incumbent increases the expected R&D rate. The research project has generated two research papers. The first paper (Lin and Zhang, 2022) was published in the Journal of Economics. The progress of the second paper has been largely delayed due to COVID-19. In particular, the process of hiring a full-time research staff had been delayed. I plan to submit the working paper to a top economics journal for publication and present the research findings at some international conferences and workshops in the near future.

13501018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13501018.value: Recently, much attention has been paid to acquisitions by large incumbent firms. One antitrust concern is that an incumbent firm may engage in the so-called killer acquisition by purchasing start-ups with the sole purpose of eliminating potential competition without intending to develop the new product. As a further development of the current research project, I, together with other scholars, will study the effect of antitrust policy on innovation incentives by allowing the possibility that the incumbent firm may acquire a potential entrant ( Cao, Lin and Zhang, work-in-progress). This study will shed light on how to evaluate the welfare consequence of merger acquisitions concerning startups.

13501018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13501018.value: Antitrust policy has been playing an increasingly important role in the digital economy. Many high-profile companies such as Microsoft, Apple, Alibaba and Tencent have been or are currently subjected to antitrust investigations. Traditional antitrust analysis has tended to focus on practices that restrict pricing or contractual relationships and has paid relatively little attention to the potential effects of antitrust policy on innovation incentives. Understanding the effects of antitrust policy on incentives to innovate is, however, crucial to determine the welfare of high-innovation industries because innovation is central to competition and innovative products can greatly benefit the consumers served by such industries. This project has contributed to the literature by providing a new and important piece of economic analysis on the effect of antitrust policies on innovation incentives. The research project has developed a dynamic model of innovation, derived some testable results on the relationship between the protectiveness of antitrust policy and the rate of innovation, shed light on the recent debate on the effects of antitrust policy on innovation, and produced some practical guidelines for the design of optimal antitrust policy

13600618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600618.value: 近年來，對非民主國家立法機關和立法者行為的研究越來越受到學術界的關注。 雖然在非民主政權下提供了對立法機關政治的重要見解，但現有的作品缺乏時間維度。 也就是說，當立法機構經歷了民主化等深刻的政治變革時，他們還沒有分析立法者的行為。我之前的一部作品（Tam 2017）通過分析民主轉型對婦女在香港立法機關中的實質代表性的影響來審視這個問題。然而，譚（2017）只關注民主化對香港立法機關的性別影響，並沒有涉及其他同樣重要的方面，例如立法監督可能發生的變化以及政府對此的反應。 為填補這一重要空白，我的研究項目研究立法機關在過去三十年經歷逐步民主化的立法機關和立法行為。 鑑於所有立法者均由殖民地總督任命，香港在1960年至1985年期間有一個不民主的立法機關。 隨著立法會在一九八五年推行功能組別選舉，香港的立法機關開始經歷民主化。 具體而言，我的研究項目通過分析1960 - 2017年期間香港立法會議員提出的議會質詢問題，回答以下問題。 一個不民主和/或半民選的立法機關能否有效地監督政府？ 一個不民主的政府如何回應立法機關的監督？ 在什麼條件下，一個不民主的政府會對立法監督採取行動呢？ 民主化會給立法者的行為帶來什麼樣的變化？ 當立法機構經歷逐步民主化時，香港的情況可能會對立法行為產生新的見解。 比較立法研究的學者們強調，議會問題可以為了解個別立法者的行為和偏好提供有用的視角。 正如馬丁（2011a，2011b）所論述的那樣，對議會問題內容的研究使我們能夠確定提問者（在會議質詢期間提出問題的立法者）的政策利益，議程，代表取向和選區焦點。 我的研究數據主要來自香港立法會的官方網站，並輔以香港報章。 香港立法會的官方網站載有關於立法會運作的詳細資料。 會議記錄逐字記錄在香港立法會議事錄中，可追溯至1858年的立法會議。

13600618.label: Realisation of objectives
13600618.value: With the assistance provided by the research assistants, the PI finished the construction of a database on parliamentary questions asked by the Hong Kong legislators from 1950 to 2020. We also finished coding these parliamentary questions. The coding results allow the PI to achieve the first, second and fourth objectives of this project. By analysing the changes in the number of parliamentary questions, the background of the questioners, and the content of parliamentary questions during the period of this study, the PI examines legislators' behavior during the gradual democratization of the legislature. The following issues are addressed. First, did increasing electoral competition motivate legislators to ask more parliamentary questions? Second, which types of legislators were more active in asking parliamentary questions? Third, what were the changes in the content of parliamentary questions during the gradual democratization? Specifically, what are the focuses of the parliamentary questions and did the new topics emerge over time? Fourth, had the legislature effectively scrutinized the executive branch? In other words, had legislators actively asked questions so as to scrutinize the government? Did they ask expository and critical questions? Or did they ask Dorothy Dixer questions (i.e., questions that support the government and allow the government to showcase their achievement? The PI and his research assistants also studied the government responses to the parliamentary questions. The responses are classified into a) full responses, b) intermediate responses, and c) non-responses. Full responses implied the government reacted responsively to legislative oversight and non-responses showed that the government sought to ignore legislative oversight. We also investigated the factors that affected the degree of government responsiveness to parliamentary questions (legislative oversight). This part allows the PI to achieve the third objectives of this project. The PI attained the first and final objectives of this project by examining whether and how democratization in Hong Kong has effected women’s and worker political representation. Specifically, as gradual democratization brought more women and working-class legislators to the legislature, have these two groups of legislators more likely to promote women’s and workers’ rights in the legislature? This research question also seeks to answer whether social identities will affect elite behavior.

13600618.label: Major findings and research outcome
13600618.value: The major findings of this project are as follows. First, the number of parliamentary questions had increased significantly, as gradual democratization was implemented. Second, the legislature had exercised its oversight over the executive branch. Most legislators had asked parliamentary questions. Most questions were either expository questions or critical questions. Third, pro-democracy legislators were significantly more likely to ask critical questions than pro-establishment legislators. Fourth, all the Dorothy Dixer questions were asked by pro-establishment legislators, although this type of questions only accounted for a very small proportion of the total number of parliamentary questions. Fifth, the number of locally-oriented questions increased significantly following the introduction of elections in 1985. Sixth, there is much room for improving the government’s response to legislative oversight. This is because the government tended to provide non-responses to critical parliamentary questions. Finally, women’s legislators and working-class legislators were more likely to represent the interests of women and the working class by asking questions related to these two groups. The finding shows that social identities significantly affect elite (legislator) behavior. The research outcomes of this project are as follows. A manuscript “Does the Age of Legislators Matter to their Representational Behavior? Evidence from Hong Kong” is under revise & resubmit by Japanese Journal of Political Science. I am writing the other two papers. The first is “Horizontal Accountability under a Hybrid Regime: Could Hong Kong’s Semi-democratic Legislature Exercise Effective Scrutiny over the Executive Branch?”. The second is “Democratic Transition and Political Representation of the Working Class: Evidence from Hong Kong.”

13600618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13600618.value: I plan to write a book based on the finding of this research project. The book examines and explains the Hong Kong legislature and the behavior of its legislators through content analysis of the questions posed by legislators during query sessions in LegCo. The period of the study is from 1950 to 2020. Specifically, the book studies how gradual, incomplete democratization and the sovereignty transition affect the legislative behavior in Hong Kong.

13600618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13600618.value: This research project aims to examine how legislators and the government responded to the gradual democratization and the sovereignty transition in Hong Kong. The period of this study is between 1950 and 2020. Specifically, the project investigates whether an undemocratic and/or a semi-democratic legislature can effectively scrutinize the executive branch and how the executive branch responds to the increasing legislative oversight.

13601118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13601118.value: This project investigates the formation of the field of applied linguistics in the mid-twentieth-century United States and the circulation of linguistic knowledge in relation to American power after 1945. The Second World War and ensuing Cold War produced pressing new questions for American policymakers and social scientists. How could Americans learn languages vital to the nation’s foreign-policy goals as quickly and cost-efficiently as possible? In what languages and by what means could Washington convey technical and military expertise to its Cold War allies? What methods would help new and developing states to educate their citizens, given that many contained linguistically heterogeneous populations? The project examines a period of intense methodological experimentation, institution building, and thickening networks of contact between Washington and other actors interested in language education. Its outcomes included a constellation of new research and teaching centers, from Michigan to Manila; heightened linguistic cooperation and competition with European allies; and new forms of “expertise” that informed maneuvers ranging from 1940s military operations in the Pacific to early post-Maoist educational exchanges between American and Chinese universities. Historical scholarship on the United States in the world, though vibrant, has heretofore largely elided questions of language. This project expands this body of scholarship by bridging it with the history of the social science of foreign-language acquisition, a field which informed the United States’ relationships with its wartime allies in the 1940s and with both the decolonizing world and the European powers in the following decades. Previous studies of Cold War foreign aid have analyzed the decline of the development paradigm and U.S. power since the 1970s, a framework which also informs this study: By then, Washington and American foundations had cut funding for postcolonial educational expansion and associated language-teaching projects. But preliminary research suggests that the history of applied linguistics may also provide a window onto two areas in which American institutions have continued to exert international influence in spite of the United States’ relative decline: higher education and educational technology. The project’s chief output will be the first scholarly monograph to examine how the social science of foreign-language acquisition shaped and was shaped by U.S. foreign policy from the Second World War onwards. The project will be of interest not only to historians of the United States but also to historians of twentieth-century Asian-American connections; scholars interested in the history of linguistics; and historians of decolonization and postcolonial state-building. 本研究項目聚焦於二十世紀中期的美國，旨在探討應用語言學獨立成科的過程，以及語言知識的普及與1945年後美國勢力的關係。第二次世界大戰後，冷戰隨之而來，美國的決策者和社會科學家遇到前所未見的問題，極待解決。要達成外交目標，語言能力至關重要，美國人如何用合乎成本效益的方法，在最短時間內掌握及傳授相關知識？政府應該以哪些語言、哪種途徑，向冷戰的盟友傳達技術和軍事實學？新建立的國家尚在發展，人民之間存在不少語言差異，當局又應如何協助當地政府制定教育政策？因此種種，美國政府於二十世紀中期不斷研發方案，創建院校，並加強與民間的連繫，積極接觸從事語言教育的學者及基金會。當局最終在密芝根州以至馬尼拉等地成立研究及教學中心；同時，「策」與「術」的新發展亦影響其對外互動，當中除了包括1940年代太平洋戰區的軍事行動外，還有遠至後毛澤東時代初美中大學之間的學術交流。 現時不乏編纂美國歷史的學者，但他們大多省略了語言方面的討論。因此，本研究把有關學問擴展至近代社會科學歷史的層面，以探究史學和語言學的連繫為主，其次從現代化、政治學和相關角度展開討論。前人對於冷戰援助及外交政策的論述，都曾以發展模式和國家實力為框架，分析美國自1970年代起相對衰落的狀態；這亦跟是次研究有一定關係：當時，華府及國內基金會已大幅削減對後殖民教育和相關語言學習計劃的支持。然而，儘管國家相對衰落，美國院校至今仍在兩大範疇發揮國際影響力：大學教研及教育技術。按初步研究所得，應用語言學的發展歷程或能提供全新視角，協助我們了解上述情況。 本研究加入社會科學的角度，探討外語習得與二戰後美國外交政策的關係，是首份分析兩者如何互相影響的學術專論，不但可供研究美國歷史的學者參考，亦適合二十世紀亞美研究的歷史學家，以及對應用語言學的歷史、非殖民化和後殖民國家建構有興趣的學者。

13601218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13601218.value: Our project aims to develop an expressivist theory of meaning. Expressivism is the view that at least some portion of apparently descriptive language should be understood not as in fact describing the way the world is, but rather expressing the speaker’s state of mind, or expressing certain commitments to interact with the world in certain ways. Expressivism has historically been offered primarily as a theory of moral language or normative language. The sentence ‘Lying is wrong’ should not be understood, then, as describing some property which lying possesses. Rather the sentence is used to express the speaker’s disapproval of lying, to express the speaker will refrain from lying and is encouraging others to refrain as well. The theory promises to explain the close connection we expect to find between a person’s moral judgments and her motivation. It also promises to explain the difficulty we seem to face in locating moral properties in the world revealed by science, but in a way that makes that difficulty non-threatening to moral practice: moral language has a fundamentally different job than describing the world, and so the failure to find moral properties in our systematic descriptions of the world does not reveal our moral claims to be in any way defective. There are a number of challenges facing expressivism, the most central of which is the need for an account of the meaning of logically complex sentences. If the simple sentence ‘Lying is wrong’ expresses disapproval for lying, what is expressed by more logically complex sentences such as ‘Lying is not wrong’ or ‘If lying is wrong then stealing is wrong’? Our plan is to offer a solution to this problem which treats logical terms (such as ‘not’, ‘or’, ‘and’, ‘if…then’) as attitude-modifiers. That is, the meaning of these terms is explained by the way they systematically modify the type of attitude expressed by the sentences in which they occur. Our solution will commit us to expressivism, not just about evaluative language, but about modal language (using terms such as ‘possibly’ and ‘necessarily’) as well. We will argue that modals serve to express commitment to principles of reasoning, both theoretical and practical.

13601218.label: Realisation of objectives
13601218.value: Objective 1 has been fully achieved. The paper "Handling Rejection" (currently under review) provides our solution to the Frege-Geach problem. We are able to tell a story about how certain normative claims logically follow from other claims, without presupposing that there are normative properties. Objective 2 has been 80% achieved, more or less. We have an integrated theory of deontic and epistemic modals, also offered in our paper "Handling Rejection." Modal claims are claims about various kinds of possibilities. Deontic modals are terms such as "must" and "may," typically used to express obligations and permissions. An example of a deontic modal statement would be "You must not murder." Epistemic modals are terms such as "must" or "might," typically used to expressed uncertainty. An example of an epistemic modal sentence would be "You might be sick." Our aim was to give an integrated expressivist account of these terms. We achieve this, understanding these claims as being ways of expressing commitment to certain kinds of metalinguistic principles within the object language. Epistemic modals are ways of expressing commitments regarding whether to accept certain assertions. For example, "You might be sick" expresses a commitment not to accept the assertion "You are not sick" in the current conversational context. Deontic modals express commitments regarding imperatives (e.g., commands). "You must not murder" expresses a commitment to treat the command "do not murder" as already in effect in the conversational context. This allows us to account for the inferential properties of the relevant modal terms without talking about possibilities, possible worlds, or other kinds of modal facts. We still do not have a fully integrated account of alethic modals, however. Examples of alethic modal claims are "It is impossible to travel faster than the speed of light" or "2+2 must equal 4." There are several reasons this was not fully completed. First, I was unable to meet with my Co-Investigator, Jack Woods, located in the United Kingdom. The GRF included funds for Dr Woods to fly to Hong Kong for purposes of collaborating on the project. Initially we planned that he would visit in November 2019. Because of the civil disturbances in Hong Kong at that point, we decided to cancel the trip and for Dr Woods to visit in the spring semester of 2020. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, this turned out to be effectively impossible. While Dr Woods and I were able to complete the main paper together, we found collaborating entirely online difficult. Second, in the course of working on objectives 1 and 2, I realized that the research we had done provided obvious ways to address other problems with expressivism, issues that were being discussed in top venues. Waiting to complete a theory of alethic modals, for which I will probably need Dr Woods's collaboration, when I could, much more quickly offer solutions to other issues that are currently of high interest seemed unwise. So I wrote a paper on the nature of explanation for expressivists ("If You're Quasi-Explaining, You're Quasi-Losing"), puzzling attitude attributions ("Deflating the Many Attitudes Problem") and the problem of creeping minimalism ("Quasirealism as Semantic Dispensability"). All three of these papers were accepted for publication in top-ranked venues. These papers incorporate aspects of objective 2 and also what I initially proposed as objective 3. They address, for example, terms such as "because" and attitudinal verbs such as "desires" or "hopes." These belong to the same broader logical "family" as modal terms--they are all intentional terms, terms that express a way of being related to a content. Additionally, the three papers together should be seen as making substantial progress toward what was originally objective 3 of the proposal. All three are concerned with ways of showing how practical and theoretical reasoning can have enough in common that both deserve to be treated as forms of reasoning, while remaining distinctive enough that expressivism remains an interesting thesis. "If You're Quasi-Explaining, You're Quasi-Losing" shows how we can make sense of explanations such as, "Kicking dogs is wrong because it hurts them" without assuming that there is a property of being wrong, by looking to the practical role these explanations play. "Deflating the Many Attitudes Problem," explains how it can make sense to hope that an action isn't wrong, even if there are no moral properties, because of the way that are moral judgments will be constrained by reasoning. "Quasirealism as Semantic Dispensability" tries to solve the problem of creeping minimalism by showing how expressivists are committed to a distinctive theory about the nature of normative reasoning as a kind of practical rather than theoretical reasoning. In short, the nature of the project changed somewhat in the course of working on it, both because of realizations about how it tied in with other related questions, and because external circumstances changed my ability to work with my Co-Investigator on issues regarding alethic modality. These changes led to a number of strong publications. In the proposal for the project, I aimed to have three papers completed and either accepted or under review. In the end, I exceeded this goal. As of the writing of this report, I have three papers accepted, all in prestigious venues, and a fourth paper completed and under review. A fifth paper is in progress. This is despite the fact that the GRF grant provided less teaching relief than requested, also inhibiting progress on the objectives.

13601218.label: Major findings and research outcome
13601218.value: Major research findings: 1. Gentzen's sequent calculus provides a useful tool for the expressivist in solving the Frege-Geach problem, given that the formalism of the calculus can be easily interpreted as making claims about how various commitments are incompatible with each other. 2. Epistemic and deontic modal terms can be understood as devices for expressing metalinguistic commitments within the object language, allowing for a unified expressivist account of two main pieces of modality. 3. Expressivists should appeal to "pragmatic" theories of explanation, in order to make sense of explanatory claims such as "kicking dogs is wrong because it hurts them," while minimizing theoretical and metaphysical commitments. 4. The many attitudes problem for expressivism is not really a problem. 5. Quasirealist forms of expressivism are best understood as claiming that we could in principle translate sentences of the form "X is wrong" into non-assertoric sentences which do not mention the property of being wrong, without losing anything of interest.

13601218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13601218.value: I would like to develop an account of alethic modals. I would also like to develop an account of evaluative terms, such as "good" and "bad," and of other normative notions, such as a reason. Additionally, I have a partially completed draft paper regarding how expressivists should make sense of sentences such as "nothing matters" or "life has no meaning." My further action plan is to continue reading relevant literature on these topics and to keep writing papers.

13601218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13601218.value: Expressivism is in the first place a theory about normative language, and indirectly a theory about normative reasoning. It holds that sentences such as "murder is wrong" do not actually describe the world is like. These sentences, despite having the surface form of descriptions, should be understood as something closer to commands ("Don't murder!") or exclamations ("Hooray for truth-telling!"). This suggests that moral thinking is not really a matter of discovering anything about the world. The central problems for expressivists is explaining how it is that normative sentences can have logical complexity (e.g., "If murder is wrong, then encouraging murder is wrong"; "Murder is not wrong") or other forms of complexity (e.g., "Murder is wrong *because* it fails to respect the humanity of the victim") if normative terms such as "wrong" do not denote properties. Similarly, how can moral thinking amount to moral *reasoning* if there is nothing out in the world for it to reason about? These papers solve several of these kinds problems for expressivism. This leads to a picture on which much of our reasoning should be thought of as negotiating with others on what sorts of commitments to jointly accept.

13602818.label: Project Objectives
13602818.value: We aim to further investigate the relationship between the causal model semantics and the Stalnaker-Lewis possible-world semantics for counterfactuals, and develop an extension of the framework of structural equation models to facilitate multi-level causal modeling. We will explore a new and general approach to studying the relationship between causal models and counterfactual structures, by using the language and machinery of category theory. In particular, we will construct categories for each, and aim to establish mathematical results that reflect or reveal a close relationship between the two categories (via the technical device of adjunction) and investigate the philosophical implications of the results. In terms of deliverables, we aim to produce at least 4 papers for publications in leading journals or premier conference proceedings of the relevant fields, including logic, philosophy of science, artificial intelligence, and possibly mathematics.
