14500118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14500118.value: Forecasting is one of the fundamental tasks of quantitative economic studies. When multiple forecasters are available, we can combine them to form a better strategy. With the advent of big data, the proliferation of many forecasters challenges the conventional wisdom of optimal combination. To handle the high-dimensional setting in which the number of forecasters may potentially excess the sample size, we propose a new method inspired by machine learning techniques. The idea of relaxing constraints is applicable not only to forecast combination but also to related problems such as model averaging, portfolio optimization and covariate balancing. This project seeks to understand the theoretical properties of the new estimation procedure and its performance in empirical applications in the real world. 經濟學定量研究的一個最基本任務是預測。當對同一個目標有多個預測值的時候，我們可以把它們組合在一起形成一個更好的預測策略。傳統的所謂最優預測組合在大數據時代面對大量預測值的時候並不適用。我們提出基於機器學習的新方法來處理預測值多於樣本量的高維情形。放鬆約束的基本思想不僅適用於估計預測組合權重，還可以應用於模型加權和資產組合優化等相關問題。我們希望通過本項目的研究來理解新估計步驟的理論性質以及評價它在實際問題中的經驗表現。

14500118.label: Realisation of objectives
14500118.value: We thank RGC for its generous support. We are happy to report that all objectives are accomplished. We respond to the 4 objectives one by one. 1. Understand the asymptotic behavior of the relaxed estimator in high-dimensional setting. This objective is specific to the L2-relaxation estimator. Given that we propose a new estimator, we must establish the theoretical properties in an innovative analytical framework. To echo the call for (approximate) equal weights in the literature of forecast combination, we analyze the behavior of the estimator given a data generating process where the covariance matrix of the forecast errors is driven mainly by latent group structures. Latent group structures are ubiquitous in economic and financial applications, and they can be formally deduced from factor models. We allow the number of cross-sectional units to be larger than the sample size in the high-dimensional setting. We assume that the observed sample covariance matrix can be decomposed into an oracle block equicorrelation matrix and an idiosyncratic component. We creatively work on its dual problem, which happens to be an L1-penalized optimization that resembles Lasso to some extent. This formulation allows us to show that the estimated combination weights converge in probability to the equal-weight oracle weights, and the predictor error asymptotic converges to the smallest possible bound of the prediction error. These desirable properties ensure the asymptotic validity of L2-relaxation. 2. Perform forecasting in real-world empirical applications with big data. In the four papers produced by this project, we have applied machine learning methods to several real-world big data problems to understand the best practice when we intend to use either combined unbiased estimators, for example those coming out of expert opinions and simple statistical models, or ensembles of economically relevant predictors. In particular, these papers cover the prediction of - Box office - Inflation in EU - Fama-French 100 portfolios - S&P 500 excess returns - Inflation in USA - Housing prices in Beijing These exercises deepened our understanding of machine learning methods in reality, and we acquired valuable experience in the selection of tuning parameters, which is a step beyond the coverage of theory. The applications helped us gain domain knowledge about the contexts and how to tweak, tailor, reshape existing methods, and how to create new estimators when necessary. 3. Complete two or three research papers for submission to top economic journal. In Section C we uploaded four published papers. Two papers have been printed, and the other two papers have been published online. The two theoretical papers appear in Review of Economics and Statistics and Journal of Econometrics. The former is a top general-interest economic journal and the latter is the top field journal. In addition, given the heavy computational component of this project, the third paper that appears on Computational Economics also finds its proper outlet. 4. Provide documented code for the machine learning algorithms. The algorithm of L2-relaxation has been documented and shared on Github at https://zhentaoshi.github.io/L2Relax/. We have submitted the replication files and data to the website designated by Review of Economics and Statistics as required by its publication policy. The link will be available when the paper is included in an issue with complete bibliographic information. Journal of Econometrics does not host data. We have shared the code and replication data at https://github.com/zhan-gao/Alasso_Predictive_Regression. Moreover, Zhan Gao and I have developed a framework for predictive regressions with machine learning methods (https://github.com/zhan-gao/LasForecast). This R package automates the sample splitting step and can be used by other machine learning algorithms that researchers are interested in. As an open-source project, multiple students of mine have contributed to this repository. For the machine learning exercise with Beijing housing data, we provide code and data at https://github.com/ishwang1/Beijing-Housing-prediction. We have also developed a Shiny app (https://metricshilab.github.io/apps) as a modern, interactive way to visualize the data, which goes beyond the practice of standard academic publication. We hope these efforts will help with the impact of this project.

14500118.label: Major findings and research outcome
14500118.value: By carrying out this project, we produce multiple outputs that extend our knowledge. In terms of publications, the leading paper is "L2-Relaxation: With Applications to Forecast Combination and Portfolio Analysis" (with Liangjun Su, and Tian Xie, accepted at the Review of Economics and Statistics). To combine many expert opinions, we propose a brand-new machine learning method called L2-relaxation and then establish its asymptotic theory. We find that if the historical forecast errors exhibit latent group structures, L2-relaxation achieves desirable consistency and efficiency in parameter estimation and out-of-sample forecast. In other words, L2-relaxation asymptotically is as good as if we knew an oracle about the true group identity. Another salient difference from the burgeoning literature on grouping in the panel data is that L2-relaxation does not explicitly identify the group membership. The second paper "On LASSO for Predictive Regression" (with Ji Hyung Lee, Zhan Gao, 2022, Journal of Econometrics) studies the popular machine learning method LASSO when it is used to linearly combine many time series predictors. It covers LASSO and adaptive Lasso (adaLasso). When nonstationary regressors are present with potential cointegrations. we find that adaLasso's variable selection consistency, which is a well-known property under standard cross-sectional or weakly dependent time series settings, collapses. Fortunately, it is simple to fix this problem: we just need to run another post-selection adaLasso, which we call in this paper "twin adaptive Lasso", to restore variable selection consistent in the predictive regressions. These two papers are presented at three high-profile international conferences, as well as about 12 seminars invited by leading universities in the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Hong Kong, and Mainland China. These academic events helped disseminate the findings and gather feedback. In addition to journal publications, we have provided open-source repositories at Github to share the code of the algorithms, and the source data and replication files for the real-data applications. Two of my postgraduate students, Yishu Wang and Ka Yan Cheng assisted in data collection, data processing and algorithms implementation, and they became coauthors. Another coauthor Zhan Gao was my formal M.Phil. student at CUHK, and we continued to work together after his graduation.

14500118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14500118.value: The code and data produced in the research are now published online as open-source materials. We are committed to continuing the maintenance of the code, data, and documents. More importantly, in October this year (2022), I submitted a new RGC proposal titled "Generalizing L2-Relaxation" to continue the research. Theoretical analyses of statistical high-dimensional models are dominated by sparse estimation methods, which pick a few important explanatory variables from many potential candidates. In economic and financial applications, the sparse approximation is unsatisfactory due to the complex nature of the issue under investigation and thus it is critical to developing theory to support dense estimation methods. This completed project demonstrates excellent empirical performance of L2-relaxation and these results are supported by formal statistical theory. I intend to generalize the method under more flexible assumptions and settings. If successful, these extensions will make the L2-relaxation approach a complete, ready-to-use, and hopefully influential class of estimators for high-dimensional learning. Its conceivable applicability will be far beyond the field of econometrics and it has the potential to rise as one of the off-the-shelf methods for statistical learning.

14500118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14500118.value: Prediction is one of the fundamental tasks of econometrics. This project investigates the best way to conduct forecast combination to predict an economic variable of interest. It makes advancements in both the theoretical and empirical frontiers. Most importantly, we propose an innovative machine learning algorithm called L2-relaxation. We show that L2-relaxation works very well, better than the off-the-shelf machine learning methods in extensive artificial data simulations and three real-data empirical applications in microeconomics, macroeconomics and finance. To understand what drives the excellent performance, we provide formal statistical results to explain the mechanisms. We make several theoretical breakthroughs to prove that L2-relaxation achieves the best possible prediction outcome under reasonable assumptions. Besides L2-relaxation, this project explores other machine learning methods and evaluates their forecast performance in housing prices, inflation rate, stock returns, and portfolio selection. These findings showcase the usefulness and the potential of machine learning in economics.

14500818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14500818.value: China’s bond market has grown rapidly in recent years. Its total market value now ranks third in the world. It has also become increasingly open. For example, the recently launched bond connect program between mainland China and Hong Kong enables overseas investors to invest in China. Meanwhile, more domestic firms are allowed to issue bonds offshore. Nevertheless, academic studies on this topic remain surprisingly limited. In this project, we will aim to fill this research gap by empirically analyzing China’s corporate bond market, which has experienced the most dramatic growth in recent years. We will investigate two main issues. First, we will investigate whether issuing corporate bonds requires government approval results in resource misallocations. Specifically, we will seek to answer the following questions. 1) Is the selection based on firm performance or non-market-oriented government objectives such as protecting state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and employment? 2) If so, how does the degree of favoritism for SOEs and employment vary with political and economic conditions over time and across different regions? 3) How do firm characteristics affect bond yields conditional on issuance? The answers to these questions should shed light on the efficiency of China’s corporate bond market and China’s high corporate leverages and zombie SOE financing problems. Second, we will investigate offshore issuance. We will seek to answer the following questions. 1) Are the selection criteria for issuing bonds onshore and offshore significantly different, such that more efficient firms go abroad to issue bonds? 2) What are the motivations for firms to issue bonds in foreign markets/currencies? Do they use the bond proceeds to support investment, to simply pay for their debts, or to conduct carry trades? 3) How do domestic and global liquidity conditions affect firms’ offshore issuance decisions? The answers to these questions have important implications for China’s partial financial liberalization strategy and the transmission of global liquidity shocks to China. To carry out our project, we will merge data from the Dealogic and Orbis databases. The former contains the most comprehensive bond issuance information, while the latter covers other firm information. In a merged subsample, we find preliminary evidence supporting our key speculations. First, regulatory authorities use both domestic and offshore issuance to support SOEs and employment. Second, different firms use their proceeds differently. SOEs pay their debts, but private firms use foreign currency proceeds to conduct carry trades, especially during the post global financial crisis period. 研究摘要 中國的公司債券市場近年來經歷了快速的發展，目前總市值已居全球第三。同時該市場也在變得日益開放。例如最近内地和香港的債券通項目令得海外投資者可以投資國内債券，同時内地的公司也可以在離岸市場發債。 然而該領域的現有學術研究卻相當有限。本項目旨在對中國快速發展的公司債券市場進行實證分析，著重研究兩個方面的問題。首先，我們將研究中國的公司債券發行審批制度是否會導致資源的錯配。在這方面我們將分析以下具體問題：1）債券發行審批決策是基於公司業績還是出於保護國企和就業等其他非市場因素？2）如果是基於非市場因素，那麽這些非市場因素的影響又如何隨政治和經濟條件而異？3）獲得發行資格后， 企業的經營表現和其他特徵如何影響其發債成本？厘清這些問題對於理解中國的公司債券市場和當前的高杠桿和僵尸企業的問題具有重要意義。 其次，我們還計劃研究中國公司債券的離岸市場發行。這方面的研究包括以下具體問題：1）離岸市場發行的審批標準是否不同于在岸市場從而令得高效率的企業有更高機會在離岸市場發行？2）企業在離岸市場發行的目的是什麽？是爲了投資，償債還是套利？3）國内外的金融環境又如何影響企業的離岸發行決策？分析這些問題有助於我們更好理解中國的漸進是金融開放策略和國際流動性對中國影響。 為開展該項研究計劃，我們將對Dealogic和Orbis數據庫進行匹配和合并。前者包含和中國公司債券發行的信息而後者則覆蓋了中國企業的其他信息。在一個已經完成匹配的子樣本中，我們發現了一些初步的證據支持我們的研究假設。首先，我們發現中國審批機構在在岸和離岸發行審批中都偏袒國企和有大量雇員的企業。其次，不同的企業將發債所得用於不同目的。國企和有大量雇員的企業通常用來償還其他債務而私營企業更傾向於用離岸發行來套利，特別是在全球金融危機以後。

14500818.label: Realisation of objectives
14500818.value: The project results in a working paper. The empirical findings in the paper achieve the two objectives of the project. For the first objective, our overall findings suggest that the selection is not completely based on firm performance. Specifically, we find strong and robust evidence of an employment protection motive and favoritism towards state ownership in government approval of bond issuance. Firms with a larger employment size or state ownership have a significantly higher likelihood of bond issuance. Moreover, the employment effect on bond issuance also varies with political and economic conditions over time and across different regions. Consistent with the employment protection motive, we find that the effect of employment on bond issuance is more pronounced when local labor market condition deteriorates, economic growth slows down, in industries with a higher concentration of low-skilled workers, or in prefectures where local government officials have a stronger career incentive to maintain social stability. While employment does not affect bond yields, we find that larger employers have significantly higher chance of issuing high-yield bonds. We also investigate the potential implications for the efficiency of financial resource allocation associated with the employment favoritism in bond issuance. We first document that firms with a larger employment size are associated with a significantly lower total factor productivity (TFP). Our analysis on firm's pre-issuance performance further demonstrates that underperforming firms can have a higher chance of bond issuance as long as their employment sizes are sufficiently large. Moreover, our assessment of firms' post-issuance performance based on the matched sample also indicates that the beneficial effects of bond issuance on firm's investment, sales, and productivity are significantly attenuated for large employers and that larger employers are more likely to hoard cash following bond issuance. We take these results as being indicative of potential inefficiency in bond credit allocation arising from the employment favoritism in bond issuance For the second objective, we find that no significant difference in the selection criteria for issuing bonds offshore. The employment protection motive exists for bonds issued in both onshore and offshore markets. There is no evidence of significant difference in selection criteria for foreign currency bond issuance either. In addition, we also find no evidence of carry trade activities for firms issuing in offshore markets. Finally, while not reported in the latest version of the working paper as a key finding, we do show in an early version of the paper that employment effect on both onshore and offshore bond issuance is significantly amplified by domestic economic downturns and domestic bank credit tightening.

Moreover, the employment protection effect on bond issuance also varies with political and economic conditions over time and across different regions. It is more pronounced when local labor market condition deteriorates, economic growth slows down, in industries with a higher concentration of low-skilled workers, or in prefectures where local government officials have a stronger career incentive to maintain social stability. Further assessment of firms' post-issuance performance based on the matched sample also indicates that the beneficial effects of bond issuance on firm's investment, sales, and productivity are significantly attenuated for large employers and that larger employers are more likely to hoard cash following bond issuance. Finally, there is no significant difference in the selection criteria for issuing bonds offshore or in foreign currency. The employment protection effect and the favoritism towards state ownership also exist for these bonds. The project results in a working paper appeared in the social science research network (SSRN): https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4275468.

14500818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14500818.value: On March 1, 2020, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) issued the "Notice on Matters Concerning Implementation of Registration-based System for Public Issuance of Corporate Bonds" which kicked off the official implementation of the registration-based system for the public issuance of corporate bonds. There is a potentail for further development of the researching in which one can analyze the new registration-based system and compare it the direct government-approval-based system as data become available.

14500818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14500818.value: A prominent feature of China's corporate bond market before 2020 is that bond issuance is subject to direct government approval. This project thus investigates whether government selection criteria of corporate bond issuance in China results in resource misallocations. The overall findings of the investigation suggest that it is the case. In particular, the investigation finds evidence for an employment protection motive and favoritism towards state ownership in government approval of bond issuance. Underperforming firms can have a higher chance of bond issuance as long as their employment sizes are sufficiently large. This is also true for bonds issued offshore or in foreign currencies. These findings are new to the academic literature. They also help us understand the potential drawbacks of the government-approval-based system implemented in China before 2020 and thus have important policy implications. They provide justifications for the recent switch to the registration-based system for the public issuance of corporate bonds in China starting from March 2020.

This allows us to understand whether marketization matters for the stability of these fiscal rules. 14501618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14501618.value: Macroeconomists have worried about the stability of balanced-budget tax rules (BBR) since the seminal work of Schmitt-Grohé and Uribe (1997), which they showed that economic activities are subject to endogenous fluctuations in the absence of exogenous shocks to the economy under balanced-budget income taxes. Although it has been suggested that consumption taxation can be exempted from these indeterminate outcomes, the model assumptions are under very restrictive and the conclusion is not robust. Motivated by the time-use data sets across countries that the home sector is a significant part of the macroeconomy, this project contributes to the literature by understanding how the interactions between the market and home sectors affect the equilibrium outcomes of the BBR. The interaction that we emphasize is the marketization of the home sector. Specifically, we observe that some home consumption goods are produced by the market sector, whereas some of the market goods are products of home production. Under these different types of marketization, we are interested in finding out the stability nature of the BBR. The extension to non-linear BBR with tax-rate variability is also investigated. According to the time-use data sets, work time is classified into SNA (System of National Accounts) and non-SNA productive activities, with the SNA activities divided into establishment-based and home-based. Usually, we identify the home-based SNA activities as home-produced market goods and the non-SNA productive activities as home-produced home goods. With these data, we plan to develop a quantitative model to carry out calibrations based on the time-use data to assess the equilibrium dynamics of the BBR of a country. By performing counterfactuals of the calibrated model, we hope to obtain some useful policy implications of the BBR. For instance, this allows us to evaluate the stability outcomes of a tax reform program for a developing country that goes through the marketization process. 自Schmitt-Grohé和Uribe（1997）的開創性論文以來，宏觀經濟學家一直擔心平衡預算稅收規則（BBR）的穩定性，尤其是平衡預算所得稅, 其存在促使經濟活動在沒有外部經濟衝擊的情況下仍然可以產生內生波動。雖然有人建議消費稅可以免除這些不確定的結果，但要求的模型假設是非常嚴格, 因此結論並不穩健。 基於不同國家時間使用數據，我們知道家庭部門是宏觀經濟的重要組成部分，此項目通過了解市場與家庭部門之間的相互作用如何影響BBR的均衡結果，為文獻做出了貢獻。我們強調的互動是家庭部門的市場化。具體而言，我們觀察到一些家庭消費品是由市場生產的，而一些市場商品則是家庭產品。在這些不同類型的市場化下，我們有興趣找出BBR的穩定性，並進一步研究具有稅率變化的非線性BBR的擴展。 根據時間使用數據集，工作時間分為SNA（國民賬戶體系）和非SNA生產活動，SNA活動可再分為以企業為基礎和以家庭為基礎。我們通常將以家庭為基礎的SNA活動確定為家庭生産的市場商品，將非SNA生產活動確定為家庭生産的家庭商品。根據這些數據，我們計劃開發一個量化模型，根據時間使用數據進行分析，以評估一個國家BBR的均衡動態。通過執行校準模型的反事實，我們希望獲得BBR的一些有用的政策含義。例如，這使我們能夠評估經歷市場化進程的發展中國家稅制改革計劃的穩定性結果。

14501618.label: Realisation of objectives
14501618.value: As stated in the mid-term progress report, the first two objectives were completed for the period ending 31-8-2019. By then, we have already started the research work on the third and the fifth objective. During the remainder of the grant period, we have completed all remaining three objectives. We first address the quantitative work related to the fifth objective, which is a direct extension of the first two objectives done in the mid-term progress report. In the quantitative analysis, we apply our model to a group of 19 OECD countries and quantitatively study the effects of marketization on stability. The degree of marketization for each country is backed out from each country's market labor share data. The average degree is 0.543, ranging from 0.2 to 0.671 on a unit-interval scale. Seven of the 19 countries, including the Western Offshore and only two Asian economies, fall outside the indeterminacy region, accounting for more than one third of the sample.3 Our counterfactual shows that once the marketization of home production stops, there are only four countries left in the stable region, accounting for a drop of 16 percentage points (from 37% to 21%) in instability in the sample. Thus, marketization does contribute significantly to macroeconomic stability in the presence of balanced budget wage taxation. Our analysis on the first, second and fifth objectives focused on proportional tax rules, while the third and the fourth objectives focused on the discussion of non-linear balanced budget taxation. 14501618.label: Major findings and research outcome
14501618.value: We have combined the analytical findings of our working paper (submitted in the mid-term progress report) together with our new quantitative findings into a new version and have submitted to the Journal of Money, Credit, and Banking. The version is attached as Item 1 in Part C in the current report. For the research of nonlinear taxation rules, we have followed the common practice of the existing literature to study the effects based on two approaches. One approach takes the relation between the tax rate and the tax base as given (e.g., Nourry et al, JET 2013), whereas another approach allows the representative agent to include the effect of the tax rate on the tax base in the optimization (e.g., Guo and Lansing, JET 1998). After a thorough comparison of the equilibrium outcomes of the two approaches, we conclude that seemingly contradictory findings of the literature are mainly due to the approach that are adopted in the analyses. Given the importance of the topic, we have decided to write up a separate research paper for the comparison of the two approaches under a general canonical model. Nevertheless, we have added the relevant results of the nonlinear taxation on marketization in a new section of the revised version of the existing working paper (research output no. 1 of item 8 in Part C). During the visits of Prof Ping Wang (Washington University in St. Louis) and Prof. Jianpo Xue (Xiamen University), our discussions on the current project had inspired us with new extended ideas. Given the expertise of Prof. Wang on regional science, he suggested that we explored the insights from dynamic taxation to apply to human capital accumulation and regional migration. This led to the research publication in the Economic Theory which is reported as Item 3 in Part C. With his research experience on indeterminacy, Prof. Xue proposed to me to extend the indeterminacy analysis of the current project to the credit market. This led to the research publication in the Economics Letters which is reported as Item 4 in Part C.

14501618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14501618.value: For research output no. 1 of item 8 in Part C, we will revise the paper once we hear back from the journal and make decision on its progress. For the research on nonlinear taxation rules, we are in the process of fine tuning the stability findings. We plan to organize them into a working paper and present it to the profession for feedback. Once we have collected useful comments and suggestions, we will revise the version and prepare for its submission to refereed journals.

14501618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14501618.value: Given the recurrent debate on the US government budget deficit, the importance of balanced-budget taxation is non-disputable. However, economists have been cautious about the practice of balanced-budget taxation rules because these rules have been shown to be destabilising. This research project shows that the destabilising effect of balanced-budget taxation depends on the size of the home sector (i.e., the degree of marketization) and the substitutability between home and market products. We apply our model to a group of 19 OECD countries and show that marketization has a significant effect on economic stability. If the marketization of home production stops, there is a drop of 16 percentage points (from 37% to 21%) in instability in our sample.

14502118.value: 戰爭、市場准入與經濟發展：中國經濟地理分佈的連續與變遷，600-1900

14502118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502118.value: Market access has been argued to be a key determinant of economic prosperity in different parts of the world. Populous or rich regions are more likely to be connected to transport networks and thus to have a higher level of market access. This mutually reinforcing interaction between market access and economic activities can generate multiple equilibria, and poor regions may be caught in a “bad” equilibrium, or poverty trap. If multiple equilibria are possible, a large, temporary shock could potentially lead to a shift between equilibria and hence have a permanent impact on economic activity. However, empirical studies on the impact of temporary shocks in the long run have delivered mixed findings. While some studies show that temporary factors can have long-lasting effects and change the spatial allocation of economic activities, others find rapid recovery, implying a strong persistence in economic development. In this study, we attempt to reconcile these findings by documenting that both cases can happen and providing an explanation for the underlying channels. In particular, we argue that endogenous infrastructure construction is an important factor for explaining why we observe persistence and changes under different scenarios. Empirically, we will focus on the Mongol conquest of the northern part of China during 1211-34, which led to 35-40 million deaths, a 75-80 percent decline in population. By constructing a grid- and prefecture-level panel dataset for the years 580-1820 and using the death tolls to measure shock intensity, we first aim to identify the conquest’s effect on economic activities in the long run. Our preliminary analysis suggests interesting heterogeneity: we observe more persistence in certain parts of China but more changes in the rest. Based on our reading of history, this heterogeneity can be partially explained by the variation in the reconstruction of the Grand Canal after the war shock. Our main hypothesis is that we observe more persistence (and changes) in regions where the Grand Canal was reconstructed (and not reconstructed). In our theoretical framework, the reconstruction of the Grand Canal is an endogenous decision affected by market access that is altered by the war. Our study will contribute to understanding the role of market access in economic development. We also hope to speak to the studies on the persistence and changes in economic activities in the long run. The historical context of China gives us an opportunity to uncover why scholars have observed both patterns (in different countries). 市場准入（或市場可達性）被認為是地區經濟繁榮的關鍵決定因素。然而，與人口稀少或者貧窮地區相比，人口眾多或富裕地區更有可能被交通網絡覆蓋, 從而具有更高的市場准入水準。由於市場准入和經濟活動之間相互加強的交互作用，經濟可能存在多重平衡。 如果存在多重均衡, 那麼暫時性的負面衝擊可能會導致一個地區經從“好”（高水準）的均衡滑向“壞”（低水準）的均衡，從而暫時性的衝擊會對經濟活動產生永久性影響。但是，實證研究卻提供了兩種截然不同的證據。有些研究表明，暫時性衝擊會產生長期影響，永久性地改變經濟活動的地理分佈（變遷）；另外一些研究卻發現，經濟會從衝擊中快速復蘇（連續）。在本研究中, 我們試圖調和這些貌似矛盾的發現。我們認為，內生化的市場網路可以有助於我們理解為什麼在相似的暫時性的衝擊下，會產生變遷與連續兩種不同的模式。 具體而言，由於蒙古入侵（1211-34），中國北方地區人口下降了大約3500-4000萬（大約75-80%）。我們計畫通過建立580-1820 年的面板資料，用死亡率來衡量衝擊的程度，分析其對經濟活動的長期影響。初步分析表明，一些地區經濟可以快速恢復（連續），而另外一些地區產生持久性的衰退（變遷）。我們認為京杭大運河及其相關水利運輸網路可以有助於我們理解這一異質性。與現有研究不同,我們認為京杭 運河的重建是由被戰爭改變的市場（人口）規模所影響的內生決策。在有些受到人口衝擊的地區，由於市場規模下降，從而沒有被新的運河覆蓋，所以經濟無法復蘇，從而產生持續性衰退。 我們希望，這一研究將有助於瞭解市場准入或市場可達性在經濟發展中的作用。我們亦希望利用中國歷史資料，在一個統一的框架中，分析為什麼會產生連續與變遷兩種不同的經濟演化模式。

14502118.label: Realisation of objectives
14502118.value: All objectives have been realized. 1. To document that the consequences of a large war shock on economic development can be heterogeneous: we observe a persistent decline and fast recovery in different regions. (1) The PI has construct a prefecture-level panel dataset covering the 980–2000 period, which includes the number of population at the prefecture level in 980, 1078, 1102, 1393, 1580, 1776, 1820, 1851, 1910, and 2000. I take the log term of the number of populations per squared kilometer to measure the economic development during different historical periods. Moreover, urbanization is used as one alternative measure of economic development. (2) The results show that the large war shock, which caused regime changes, can have a huge effect on economic performance. But, the effect is very heterogeneous. The prefectures which gain higher political status, i.e. provincial capital, have a better economic performance after the regime change, while those which lose political status, i.e. provincial capital, was negatively affected by the regime change. Overall, changes in the status of the provincial capital, which is riven by war and regime changes, led to the rise and decline of different prefectures as measured by population and urbanization. 2. To show that endogenous infrastructure is important for explaining the heterogeneous pattern. (1) To trace how transportation networks evolved over time, the PI digitized roads and waterway maps corresponding to three historical periods (represented by specific years)—the Song (1078), Ming (1587), and Qing (1820) dynasties—and a railroad map from the People’s Republic (1990). To account for the relative importance of different links in the transportation network, the PI applied a centrality measure to be the proxy of a region’s position in a transportation network. (2) The results show that regime changes and the change in political status shaped economic development not only through public employment but also through the development of important infrastructure, such as transportation networks. 3. To evaluate the counterfactual if the infrastructure were not changed due to war. (1) The background is that China is a centralized regime, and hence regime change can lead to the relocation of provincial capital, and re-organize the transportation networks. The PI’s political economy counterfactual of interest is a decentralized scenario affected by only provincial autonomy. Therefore, the PI conducted a simple analysis by comparing provincial market access in the current political system with that in a scenario in which provincial capitals are set in the provincial centroids after the war and regime change. (2) The results show that that if the provincial capital is located 100 kilometers from the provincial centroid, the provincial aggregate market access declines by 8.6%. In our data, the average deviation is 125 kilometers, suggesting that on average, provincial aggregate market access could be 10.8% higher.

14502118.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502118.value: The project studies the impact of war and regime change on economic development, and examine how political hierarchy shapes regional development in China, using variation driven by regime changes during the 1000-2000 period. Using a prefecture-level panel dataset covering the 980–2000 period, which includes the population density and urbanization at the prefecture level in 980, 1078, 1102, 1393, 1580, 1776, 1820, 1851, 1910, and 2000, I find that that the large war shock, which caused regime changes, can have a huge effect on economic performance. However, the effect is very heterogeneous. The prefectures with increase in political status, i.e. provincial capital, have a better economic performance after the regime change, while those with decrease in political status, i.e. provincial capital, was negatively affected by the regime change. Changes in the status of the provincial capital, which is riven by war and regime changes, led to the rise and decline of different prefectures as measured by population and urbanization (Objective 1). I then examine the channel. The results show that political hierarchy shaped economic development not only through public employment but also through the development of important infrastructure, such as transportation networks (Objective 2). In addition, the PI conducted a counterfactual analysis to illustrate the economic cost of setting up provincial capitals following the political logic. In a politically decentralized counterfactual scenario where provincial capitals were set at the provincial centroid, which is not affected by the war and regime change, provincial aggregate market access could be 10.8% higher (Objective 3).

14502118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502118.value: In this study, the PI also discusses the underlying reasons for relocating provincial capitals. Although the choice of a provincial capital certainly involves many factors, the process is subject to general and testable political logic. Specifically, a provincial capital plays two roles: it acts as an administrative center responsible for fiscal, judicial and welfare governance within a province, and as a node through which to transfer resources and information from a province to the central government. Thus, when determining the location of a provincial capital, the central government faces a trade-off between granting provincial autonomy and maintaining central control. This trade-off can be proxied empirically by the weighted sum of the distances to the other prefectures within a province and the distance to the national capital (what we call the “hierarchical distance”). This measure, namely the hierarchical distance, could be applied to other countries. Then, it is worthy of examining the location of provincial capitals using a cross-country dataset. Moreover, we also can derive auxiliary testable hypotheses. For instance, in one authoritarian regime, the effect of hierarchical distance on capital location is much similar with that in China, while in one democratic regime, the hierarchical distance does not matter.

14502118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502118.value: This project studies how political hierarchy shapes regional development in China, using variations driven by war and regime changes during the 1000–2000 period. I find that changes in the status of the provincial capital led to the rise and decline of different prefectures as measured by population and urbanization. Unsurprisingly, I find that gaining political importance led to improved development. In light of the large body of literature on the persistence of economic activities, however, it is less clear whether losing political importance leads to significant declines of provincial capital cities. In this context, I find that such a loss of status is very important: once status was lost, a provincial capital returned to a level of development similar to that of its non-capital peers within 75 years. Three economic forces may drive this link between politics and development: the direct effects of public employment, the spillover effects of public employment (through private employment and agglomeration), and improvements in market access (mediated by investments in infrastructure). The results show that political hierarchy shaped economic development not only through public employment but also through the development of important infrastructure, such as transportation networks.

14502318.label: Project Objectives
14502318.value: Propose a new approach to estimate market beta and idiosyncratic volatility using ETF holdings and returns. Investigate beta anomaly, idiosyncratic volatility puzzle, and announcement day effect using ETF-implied proxies. Explore the factors that weaken and strengthen the effect of ETF involvement on stock prices and identify a causal relationship using regression discontinuity design. Study the relative importance of mismeasurement and other frictions that lead to the beta anomaly and idiosyncratic volatility puzzle. Provide guidance to understand return predictability in both cross-section and time-series, and develop new trading strategies.

Study the relative importance of mismeasurement and other frictions that lead to the beta anomaly and idiosyncratic volatility puzzle.
Provide guidance to understand return predictability in both cross-section and time-series, and develop new trading strategies.

14502318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502318.value: A large number of previous studies have documented two puzzles in the cross-section of stock returns ─ beta anomaly and idiosyncratic volatility puzzle, and have suggested possible reasons mainly related to market frictions and investor irrationality. Our proposed study breaks new ground by estimating market beta and idiosyncratic volatility using holdings and returns of Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs). We intend to investigate whether and how ETF-implied measures of market beta and idiosyncratic volatility help to reconcile the asset pricing puzzles. We hypothesize that if the cross-sectional return predictability is due to mismeasurement in beta and idiosyncratic volatility, it should not persist in the (theoretically more precise) ETF-implied estimates. Preliminary results in this proposal demonstrate a positive beta-return relationship in the universe of ETFs while a negative beta-return relationship in stock portfolios. Secondly, we will examine whether the market risk is priced and whether the risk-return tradeoff varies with news announcements, as the positive risk-return relationship on announcement days could be a result of higher risk premium due to uncertainty prior to the announcement or less mismeasurement due to more information. Our ETF-implied proxies could help pin down the relative importance of these two channels. Thirdly, we will employ the annual Russell index reconstitution as a quasi-natural experiment to establish a causal effect of ETF participation and trading on stock pricing. We hypothesize that the mismeasurement will decrease when stocks experience an exogenous increase in ETF ownership, as our proposed approach will benefit if underlying ETFs are representative and efficiently priced. Finally, we will reconcile our findings with previously-discussed alternative channels. This study will shed new light on the beta anomaly and idiosyncratic volatility puzzle as well as related trading strategies in practice. Its findings will improve our understanding of the effect of ETFs on stock prices and will reveal an alternative channel for the spill-over effect between individual stocks and ETFs. It will therefore have important implications for practitioners and individual investors. Our ETF-implied measures could help better identify mispriced stocks and develop more profitable trading strategies. Individual investors will be able to allocate capital more efficiently and only reward skilled managers. Our approach can be generalized to other scenarios when inference needs to be made from other asset classes in order to price a security. The study will be of particular significance for Hong Kong, given its status as a leading global financial center with a developing asset management business.

14502318.label: Realisation of objectives
14502318.value: We comprehensively examining whether investors can harvest extra profits generated by various machine learning signals that are detailed in the following paragraph. To do so, we first impose several economic restrictions. In the cross-section, we limit the universe of stocks to those that are relatively cheap to trade by excluding microcaps or distressed firms. In the time series, we examine whether investment profitability is more pronounced during high limits-to-arbitrage market states, such as high volatility and low liquidity. We then assess the turnover and the corresponding transaction costs associated with implementing machine learning-based investments and finally explore the economic foundations of trading strategies advocated by seemingly opaque machine learning methods. We consider a comprehensive set of linear and nonlinear models, study both spread and tangency portfolios, and account for both the stochastic discount factor (SDF) and beta pricing formulations. We first implement a neural network with three hidden layers (NN3) as in Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2020) (GKX) and then follow Chen, Pelger, and Zhu (2020) (CPZ) to incorporate a no-arbitrage condition into multiple connected neural networks. We then analyze two conditional beta pricing models in the machine learning universe, namely, instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) per Kelly, Pruitt, and Su (2019) (KPS) and the conditional autoencoder (CA) extension by Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2021). The empirical experiments are based on a large sample of U.S. stocks from 1987 to 2017. The analysis proceeds as follows. To set the stage, we replicate the results reported in the original papers. The value-weighted long-short portfolio return across all stocks is 1.56% (2.18%, 0.95%, 1.16%) per month based on the GKX (CPZ, IPCA, CA) signal, and the corresponding Fama-French 6-factor-adjusted (FF6-adjusted) return is 0.92% (1.87%, 0.62%, 0.75%). Such large and significant figures reflect the impressive success of machine learning techniques in generating outstanding performance relative to traditional methods such as nonregulated regressions and portfolio sorts based on individual anomalies. Imposing economic restrictions reveals that the predictability of deep learning methods (i.e., GKX, CPZ, and CA) weakens considerably. Relative to the full sample evidence across all stocks, the value-weighted FF6-adjusted return based on the GKX (CPZ, CA) signal is 66% (71%, 48%) lower after excluding microcaps, 53% (77%, 75%) lower after excluding firms that do not have credit rating coverage, and 78% (69%, 94%) lower after excluding financially distressed firms that face further deteriorating credit conditions. None of the deep learning methods generates significant value-weighted FF6-adjusted returns at the 5% level after excluding distressed firms. For perspective, we apply the same economic restrictions to traditional methods and find a similar proportional magnitude of performance deterioration. While IPCA underperforms deep learning models for the full sample, its performance only deteriorates modestly for subsamples that consist of cheap-to-trade stocks. The evidence is thus consistent with the concept that accounting for nonlinearities is especially useful for difficult-to-value and difficult-to-arbitrage stocks. We then show that all four machine learning signals generate portfolio turnover that is considerably higher than most individual anomalies. The monthly turnover in the long-short portfolio is at least 87% (163%, 113%, 148%) for the GKX (CPZ, IPCA, CA) method. Altogether, in the presence of reasonable trading costs, the machine learning-based investments that we analyze would struggle to achieve a statistically and economically meaningful risk-adjusted payoff. The above-described findings are further confirmed in an investment universe consisting of equity portfolios rather than individual stocks. In particular, we employ the Kozak, Nagel, and Santosh (2020) (KNS) approach to estimate the SDF. We find that the performance of the SDF-implied portfolio also deteriorates in subsamples with economic restrictions. Moreover, conditional on a predetermined level of market volatility, the SDF is estimated based on rather extreme portfolio positions. For instance, the SDF implies a -234% (-91%) short position in an individual anomaly portfolio at the 5th (25th) percentile and a 190% (96%) long position at the 95th (75th) percentile. Thus, the pricing kernel might be inadmissible from a real-time investment perspective. Restricting the investment universe to relatively cheap-to-trade stocks considerably mitigates equity positions. We next examine whether and how machine learning-based performance varies with market conditions. Consistent with the economic notion of limits to arbitrage, we demonstrate that the investment strategy based on GKX and CPZ signals (across all stocks) is considerably more profitable during periods of high investor sentiment, high market volatility, and low market liquidity. For instance, the monthly value-weighted FF6-adjusted return based on the GKX signal is statistically insignificant at 0.22% at times of low VIX and increases dramatically to 1.66% at times of high VIX, while the full sample average is 0.92%. In contrast, IPCA and CA models display relatively modest time series variation in trading profits and could even outperform in low limits-to-arbitrage market states. We also examine the most recent years and find that unlike traditional anomaly-based trading strategies, all four machine learning signals continue to predict cross-sectional stock returns in the post-2001 period across all stocks. This finding supports the concept that machine learning techniques combine multiple weak sources of information into a meaningful composite signal. Consistent with our main results, anomalous return patterns in recent years are also confined to difficult-to-arbitrage stocks. Finally, we propose two experiments to gauge the economic foundations. We first examine whether stocks with similar machine learning signals share common characteristics that are known to predict returns. The evidence shows that all four machine learning methods successfully identify mispriced stocks consistent with most anomaly-based trading strategies. Stocks in the long positions of machine learning-based investments are typically small, value, illiquid, and old stocks with a low price, low beta, high 11-month return (medium-term winners), low asset growth, low equity issuance, low credit rating coverage, and low analyst coverage. Therefore, despite their opaque nature, machine learning signals successfully identify mispriced stocks consistent with well-established empirical facts, without preselection of truly useful characteristics and models. Our findings highlight the merits of employing machine learning methods to avoid the data snooping problem in the anomaly literature and suggest that black-box-like machine learning models are reasonably interpretable, which is essential for a robust and credible assessment of out-of-sample predictability. Second, we control for the industry benchmark in machine learning signals and decompose the unconditional payoff into two components: intra-industry and inter-industry payoffs. Taking the GKX signal as an example, we construct three trading strategies based on NN3-predicted returns for all investable stocks (beyond the extreme long and short portfolios), including (1) an unconditional strategy that takes long (short) positions on market winners (market losers); (2) an intra-industry strategy that takes long (short) positions on industry winners (industry losers); and (3) an inter-industry strategy that takes long (short) positions on winner industries (loser industries). We show that the intra-industry strategy outperforms the unconditional strategy and the inter-industry strategy, suggesting that GKX signal is more informative for stock selection than for industry rotation. Our findings are robust to similar return decompositions based on IPCA and CA signals. Consistent with the finding that machine learning signals identify mispricing in difficult-to-arbitrage stocks, adjusting for industry averages further controls for similar firm fundamentals within the same industry and thus better predicts subsequent corrections due to market frictions.

14502318.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502318.value: We provide large-scale evidence on the economic significance of machine learning methods. The machine learning (especially deep learning) techniques that we analyze face many of the challenges regarding cross-sectional return predictability. In particular, anomalous return patterns characterize difficult-to-value and difficult-to-arbitrage stocks. Relative to the full sample evidence across all stocks, the risk-adjusted return is 48% to 71% lower after excluding microcaps, 53% to 77% lower after excluding firms that do not have credit rating coverage, and 69% to 94% lower after excluding financially distressed firms that face further deteriorating credit conditions. None of the deep learning methods generates significant value-weighted risk-adjusted returns at the 5% level after excluding distressed firms. In addition, to the extent that deep learning signals predict cross-sectional stock returns for the full sample, the trading strategy is more profitable during periods of high market volatility and low market liquidity. For instance, the monthly value-weighted FF6-adjusted return based on the GKX signal is statistically insignificant at 0.22% at times of low VIX and increases dramatically to 1.66% at times of high VIX, while the full sample average is 0.92%. Machine learning signals also involve remarkably high turnover and often require taking extreme long-short positions in the tangency portfolio implied by the pricing kernel. Altogether, in the presence of reasonable trading costs, the machine learning-based investments that we analyze would struggle to achieve a statistically and economically meaningful risk-adjusted payoff. Beyond economic restrictions, machine learning-based trading strategies nonetheless display less downside risk, yield considerable profit in long positions, and remain viable in the post-2001 period and the crisis period. For instance, for major episodes of market downturns, the GKX (CPZ, IPCA, CA) method generates, on average, a monthly value-weighted return of 3.56% (0.68%, 1.49%, -0.53%) after excluding microcaps. For perspective, the contemporaneous market excess return is -6.91%. Finally, black-box-like machine learning methods still generate economically interpretable trading strategies and are more meaningful for stock selection than for industry rotation. Stocks in the long positions of machine learning-based investments are typically small, value, illiquid, and old stocks with a low price, low beta, high 11-month return (medium-term winners), low asset growth, low equity issuance, low credit rating coverage, and low analyst coverage. Therefore, despite their opaque nature, machine learning signals successfully identify mispriced stocks consistent with well-established empirical facts, without preselection of truly useful characteristics and models.

14502318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502318.value: Our analysis initiates a protocol for future work to demonstrate the feasibility of trading profits, such as (1) constructing value-weighted portfolios after excluding difficult-to-arbitrage stocks, (2) considering portfolio turnover and the corresponding transaction costs, (3) ensuring that the proposed tangency portfolio mitigates extreme long-short positions, (4) excluding high limits-to-arbitrage market states, (5) emphasizing performance over recent years, and (6) focusing on long positions. Our paper also suggests an important avenue for future research. In particular, the optimization routines that mix various anomalies could inherently display a high turnover of stocks in extreme long-short portfolios and thus generate high trading costs. Similarly, pricing kernel estimates could rely on rather extreme long and short positions that are inadmissible in real time. Thus, it would be useful to extend machine learning methods to endogenously account for trading costs and further impose plausible portfolio constraints. Machine learning methods can also be used to evaluate practical transaction costs of strategic trading through relaxing the assumed functional forms of dependence between the trading costs and the invested capital and introducing a nonlinear time series model of trading costs of a patient trader.

14502318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502318.value: The machine learning (especially deep learning) techniques that we analyze face many of the challenges regarding cross-sectional return predictability. In particular, anomalous return patterns characterize difficult-to-value and difficult-to-arbitrage stocks. In addition, the trading strategy is more profitable during periods of high market volatility and low market liquidity. Machine learning signals also involve remarkably high turnover and often require taking extreme long-short positions. Beyond economic restrictions, machine learning-based trading strategies nonetheless display less downside risk, yield considerable profit in long positions, and remain viable in the post-2001 period and the crisis period. Finally, black-box-like machine learning methods still generate economically interpretable trading strategies and are more meaningful for stock selection than for industry rotation. Our analysis initiates a protocol for future work to demonstrate the feasibility of trading profits. Some recent studies have already responded to our findings and considered these economic hurdles when advocating new machine learning tools. These studies indicate the potential promise of understanding the cross-section of equity returns through the lens of deep learning and artificial intelligence.

14502618.label: Project Objectives
14502618.value: We study the commitment effect and signalling effect of the public filing and adjudication of ISDS disputes as well as BIT signature and ratification on FDI. We study the differential effects of direct and indirect expropriation claims in respondent states with differential quality of institutions on FDI. We investigate the heterogeneity in the responsiveness of FDI to BITs and ISDS filings across sectors/industries which exhibit varying degrees of vulnerability to the risk of both direct and indirect expropriation in countries with differential institutional quality. We explore how BITs and ISDS claims affect the jurisdictional arbitrage behaviour reflected in MNEs’ new acquisition investment and adjustment of business expansion plan among existing subsidiaries. We examine how BITs and ISDS filings and arbitrations affect various M&A characteristics and the corporate behaviour of existing MNEs.

14502618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14502618.value: Since the 1990s, the number of bilateral investment treaties (BITs) has grown tremendously, which are enacted for the purpose of reciprocal promotion and protection of investment between signatory governments. One important aspect of BITs is the investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) mechanism, which allows investors to bring claims of treaty violations to arbitration tribunals outside of the host state. BITs and ISDS are found to have promoted foreign direct investment (FDI) flows because they promote a more enabling, stable and transparent regulatory and legal framework (see, e.g., Egger and Pfaffermayr, 2004; Neumayer and Spess, 2005). However, some studies challenge this positive effect (e.g., Aisbett, 2007; Yackee, 2016). Moreover, there is criticism of ISDS for its infringement of host state sovereignty. For instance, multinational enterprises (MNEs) are increasingly using ISDS to challenge the legal and regulatory systems and policy-making sovereignty of the BIT contracting states, posing a growing risk to the ability of the host states to govern in the public interests (Johnson, et al. 2015). This project intends to contribute to the literature on the economic impacts of BITs and ISDS on FDI flows by using new data sources and new empirical methods and by exploring some new dimensions of the issue. We examine the effects of BITs and ISDS disputes on FDI by employing the fixed effects model and the difference-in-differences (DID) event-study approach. We investigate the heterogeneity in the effects of BITs and direct and indirect expropriation claims on FDI in sectors with varying degrees of susceptibility toward expropriations across countries exhibiting variations in institutional quality. In view of the prevalence of jurisdictional or legal system arbitrage behavior of MNEs (see, e.g., Dine, 2012; Levine, et al., 2015; Banerjee and Noe, 2016), we explore one type of jurisdictional arbitrage in gaining access to BITs and ISDS, i.e., an MNE can invest in a host country without BIT with its home country via second-country subsidiaries and indirectly access BITs when its subsidiaries are located in countries with relevant BITs. We examine how the effects of BIT or ISDS status changes affect this behavior in terms of MNEs’ new overseas acquisitions and existing MNEs’ business expansion plans. The project also contributes to the literature by analyzing the effects of BITs and ISDS disputes on cross-border merger and acquisition (M&A) location choice, entry modes, and various other M&A characteristics. The business operations of existing MNEs in the host states are also examined. 自20世代90年代以來，雙邊投資條約（BITs）的數量大幅增加，其目的是促使簽署國政府相互促進和保護跨國投資。雙邊投資協定的一個重要方面是投資者 - 國家爭端解決（ISDS）機制，它允許投資者將條約違規的主張提交給東道國以外的仲裁庭。 已有研究發現BIT和ISDS促進了外國直接投資（FDI）流動，因為它們幫助營造了一個更有利，更穩定和更透明的監管和法律框架（參見，例如，埃格和Pfaffermayr，2004;諾伊邁爾和Spess，2005）然而，一些研究對這種積極影響提出了挑戰（例如，Aisbett，2007年。 Yackee，2016）。此外，還有人批評ISDS侵犯了東道國主權。例如，跨國企業（跨國公司）越來越多地使用ISDS來挑戰BIT締約國的法律和監管制度以及決策主權，這對東道國為公共利益進行治理的能力構成了越來越大的風險（約翰遜，等人，2015）。 本項目旨在通過使用新的數據來源和新的經驗分析方法以及探索該問題的一些新方面，為關於雙邊投資條約和ISDS對外國直接投資流動的經濟影響的文獻作出貢獻。我們通過採用固定效應模型和雙重差分（DID）事件研究方法來研究雙邊投資條約和ISDS爭端仲裁機制對FDI的影響。我們將考察雙邊投資條約的影響以及直接和間接徵收對外國直接投資的影響的異質性，考察制度質量存在差異的不同國家間和對於國家的徵收具有不同程度的易感性的產業部門之間的影響的差異性。 鑑於跨國公司的司法或法律制度套利行為普遍存在（參見，例如，就餐，2012;萊文等，2015年;納吉和野老，2016），我們探討了一種管轄套利方式，以獲取雙邊投資條約和ISDS的有利條件，即跨國公司可以通過在第三方與東道國有BIT的國家運作的子公司，在與本國沒有BIT的東道國投資，從而享有其子公司所在國具有的相關雙邊投資條約的便利來間接獲得雙邊投資條約的保護。我們將研究BIT或ISDS狀態變化對跨國公司新的海外收購和現有跨國公司業務擴張計劃的影響。 本項目還通過分析雙邊投資條約和ISDS爭議對跨境併購（M＆A）地點選擇，進入模式和各種其他併購特徵的影響，希冀為文獻做出貢獻。本項目還考察了東道國現有跨國公司的業務運營情況。

14502618.label: Realisation of objectives
14502618.value: We are grateful to RGC for this GRF. Over these several years, we have been keeping working on the project despite the disruption and difficulties caused by the social movement and the Covid-19 pandemic to arranging research assistants, obtaining feedback from some originally scheduled conferences, etc. After several presentations in 2019 and 2020, we have obtained some valuable feedbacks. At the same time, several new competing studies on BITs and cross-border M&As have appeared. We therefore placed primary emphasis on the analysis of the Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) scheme and touch upon the role of BITs. In June of 2021, we submitted two research reports in our progress report. Since then, we have considerably modified our empirical strategy and developed a refined research framework. We address three major aspects of ISDS claims: the initiation of ISDS claims, the types of ISDS claims, i.e., direct expropriation or indirect expropriation, and the verdict of ISDS claims, i.e., investor-win, state-win, settlement, and no outcome. We explore their impact on cross-border M&As and cross-border bank loan flows. In the paper entitled “ISDS Disputes, Adjudications and Cross-Border M&As”, we conduct both country-level and deal-level analysis of how ISDS disputes and adjudications affect M&As from claimant home countries to respondent states. In the aggregate-level analysis, we find that ISDS claims reduce the likelihood, frequency, and dollar volume of cross-border merger deals. This negative effect is concentrated in direct expropriation claims. We find that investor-win claims reduce subsequent cross-border merger deal flows. We interpret it as that the investor-win claims substantiate the host government expropriation of foreign investors, which discourages the entry of foreign capital. Meanwhile, we find that state-win or investor-lose claims increase subsequent cross-border M&A deals to the respondent state. We interpret it as that the state-win claims acquit the suspected misconduct of the respondent state in expropriating foreign investors, and restore, to a certain degree, international investors’ confidence in the respondent state, which encourages cross-border merger deal flows to the responding country. The effects of ISDS claims are typically stronger for better-institution or Northern responding states. We interpret it as these claims are contrary to the stereotype image of those strong-institution host states and thus contain more informational surprises to the international business community, which arouses more vehement reactions from foreign acquirers. We further conduct deal-level analysis of how deal features are shaped by ISDS claims, their types and their adjudications. ISDS claims prompt foreign acquirers to adopt risk-avoiding strategies, which affect various deal features. For example, foreign acquirers are less likely to adopt majority-ownership-share acquisitions to reduce their exposure to the risk of property losses. Foreign acquirers tend to prefer cash payment as it contains more certainty of value. Foreign acquirers tend to conduct nationality arbitrage by making acquisitions through a subsidiary operating in a third-party country. This paper is currently under revision with Journal of Corporate Finance. In the paper entitled “ISDS Arbitration and Cross-Border Bank Loans”, we expand the scope of our analysis to cross-border bank loans. We first point out that the ISDS scheme covers not only foreign direct investment but also cross-border bank loans. ISDS claims help the international banking community assess government expropriation risk in host countries. Furthermore, the adjudication of ISDS claims affects the perception of the international banking sector about the availability of international legal recourse against sovereign expropriation and the credibility of international judicial protection. We conduct both aggregate-level and deal-level analysis to examine how the occurrences, types and adjudication of ISDS arbitration claims affect cross-border loan flows from the claimant home country to the respondent state. We find that the occurrences of ISDS claims produce negative effects on the likelihood and value of cross-border loan flows at the country level. The negative effects are mostly concentrated in direct expropriation claims. Nevertheless, the higher overall institutional strength of respondent states could mitigate these negative effects. We then turn to the impact of ISDS claim adjudication. Investor-win arbitration decisions stimulate bank loan inflows. This could be the judicial credibility effect, that is, given the complaints about the credibility and reliability of the ISDS scheme, investor-win arbitration cases may boost investors’ confidence in the availability of credible legal recourse against host government expropriation for foreign lenders. Meanwhile, investor-lose arbitration outcomes repress loan inflows. This could be the judicial partiality effect. Under the party-appointed arbitration panel system, foreign investors often complain about the lack of independence of arbitrators and the lack of consistence and coherence of arbitration verdicts. Investor-lose arbitration decisions may deepen such suspicion. At the deal level, the occurrences of ISDS claims in the recent three years increase interest rate spread, reduce loan size, and increase the adoption of collaterals and covenants. These effects are more striking for direct expropriation claims. These effects are found to be attenuated in strong-institution respondent states. Moreover, investor-win (state-win) arbitration decisions lower (increase) interest rate spread, raise (reduce) loan size, and decrease (increase) the demand for collateral, which lends support to the judicial credibility (judicial partiality) effect. In addition, the judicial credibility effect is more salient in respondent states with stronger overall institution, while the judicial partiality effect is mitigated in strong-institution responding states. In the paper entitled “Breach of Commitment and Contagion: How ISDS Dispute Shocks Shape Cross-Border M&As”, we explore the intra-national (between the focal home country and focal host state) and/or intra-industry effects of ISDS claims on cross-border merger deals as well as the cross-national and cross-industry spillover effects. We treat the impact of ISDS disputes between the focal home country investors and the focal host state on merger deal flows from the claimant home country to the respondent state as the breach of commitment effect. Meanwhile, we examine several cross-national and/or cross-industry contagion or spillover of ISDS shocks. One is the cross-home-country spillover effect, i.e., when investors from non-focal home countries lodge ISDS disputes against the focal host country, the merger deal flow from the focal home country to the focal host state may be affected. The other is the cross-host-country spillover effect, that is, when the focal home country firms operating in non-focal host states get involved in ISDS disputes, it could influence the merger deal flow from the focal home country to the focal target country. In addition, we consider the within-host-country-within-industry spillover effect and the within-host-country-cross-home-country-cross-industry spillover effect. We compare the breach of commitment effect and various spillover effects on various aspects of merger deals such as deal size, acquisitions of targets in high-tech industries or sensitive sectors, and acquisition costs. Overall, the breach-of-commitment effect is more significant than various spillover effects. The cross-home-country spillover effect is often the most statistically significant one among spillover effects. Both effects are more striking in the subsample of weak-institution host states. There are some signs of a positive cross-host-country effect, which suggests a “flight to safe haven” effect. The breach-of-commitment effect is concentrated in direct expropriation claims. The spillover effects of direct expropriation claims and indirect expropriation claims are most striking in the cross-home-country-within-industry spillover effect. For the adjudication of ISDS claims, the breach-of-commitment effect of investor-win claims is mostly statistically significantly negative, showing the substantiation effect of investor-win cases. There is limited evidence in support of the acquittal effect of state-win cases.

14502618.label: Major findings and research outcome
14502618.value: This project primarily investigates how disputes between foreign claimant-investors and sovereign host states lodged to international arbitral tribunal through the investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) scheme affects international investment activities. First, we examine the occurrences, types and adjudications of ISDS disputes affect M&As from claimant home countries to respondent states. It is found that ISDS claims reduce the likelihood, frequency, and dollar volume at the aggregate level. They also prompt foreign acquirers to adopt risk-avoiding strategies, which affect various deal features such as less likely deal completion and majority-ownership-share acquisitions, smaller deal size and bid premium, cash payment, and nationality arbitrage. We detect strong substantiation effects of investor-win cases and some acquittal effects of state-win cases. The effects of ISDS claims are typically concentrated in direct expropriation claims, and are stronger for better-institution or Northern responding states. Second, we explore how the occurrences, types and adjudication of ISDS arbitration affect cross-border loan flows from the claimant home country to the respondent state. The occurrences of ISDS claims produce negative effects on the likelihood and value of loans at the country level. The negative effects are mostly concentrated in direct expropriation claims. The higher overall institutional strength of respondent states can mitigate these negative effects. Investor-win arbitration decisions stimulate bank loan flows to respondent states, supporting the judicial credibility effect, while investor-lose arbitration outcomes repress loan inflows, showing the judicial partiality effect. At the deal level, the occurrences of ISDS claims increase interest rate spread, reduce loan size, and increase the adoption of collaterals and covenants. Investor-win arbitration decisions improve loan terms, which shows the existence of judicial credibility effect. Third, we examine the impact of the initiation, types and adjudication of ISDS cases on cross-border merger flows by comparing the breach-of-commitment effect aroused by the ISDS claims lodged by the focal home country investors against the focal host state with several cross-national and cross-industrial spillover effects. The breach-of-commitment effect of ISDS claims is more striking than spillover effects in repressing deals. The ISDS claims filed by the non-focal-home-country investors against the focal host state produce the strongest negative spillover effect (the cross-home-country spillover effect) such as curtailing deal size and the likelihood of acquiring high-tech or sensitive sector targets. The impacts of ISDS claims are more striking for direct expropriation claims and in weak-institution host states. The investor-win arbitration outcomes produce significant repressive effects on merger deal features (the substantiation effect).

14502618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14502618.value: The impartiality of the ISDS arbitration tribunal and its decision-making has been increasingly under criticism in recent years. The appointment mechanism of arbitrators, the potential conflicts of interests of their different roles in the arbitration procedure, and the apparent biases of their decisions have aroused reflections from various parties concerned such as the international investment community and sovereign governments. At the same time, there has been an ever-rising demand of various host states for upholding their sovereign power in strengthening business regulations in the public interests. The BITs and the ISDS mechanism have imposed serious constraints on sovereign states to fulfill this objective. Sovereign states have called for a reform of BITs and the ISDS mechanism to give them more freedom, immunity and exemptions in regulating foreign investors. Conducting economic studies along these lines may capture and shed light on the new developments in this important area and deepen our understanding of BITs and ISDS scheme.

14502618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14502618.value: Foreign investor protection is widely regarded as instrumental to attracting foreign investment. Numerous bilateral investment treaties (BITs) and multilateral treaties are intended to provide legal protection for foreign investors in host countries. One major strength of such treaties lies in the Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) scheme through which foreign investors can lodge a complaint about host state misconduct to an international arbitral tribunal, which provides a potential international legal recourse against host government expropriation. This project assesses whether and how the occurrences, the types and the decisions of ISDS claims affect cross-border direct investment in the form of merger and acquisition deals and cross-border loan deals. We find that ISDS claims exert significant deterrent effects on cross-border merger and loan deals from claimant home countries to respondent states. ISDS claims also produce contagion or negative spillover effects across industries and across home or host countries. This suggests an amplified impact of ISDS claims on the flow of foreign direct investment to respondent states. It is advisable for host states to comply with various investment treaties in order to keep a stable foreign investment inflow.
