14606918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14606918.value: 荀子乃先秦儒家代表人物，學識淵博，哲學思想影響深邃。後世學者了解荀子學說，唯賴《荀子》一書。然而，《荀子》三十二篇之作者、撰寫年代與地域，歷來未有公論。《荀子》各篇之間內容多有重合，亦廣與先秦兩漢文獻互見。然而學者探究此論題時，未有全盤考慮。本計劃擬結合傳世文獻與出土文獻，全盤排列《荀子》內在與外在之相近文辭、段落、義理等內容，考論《荀子》篇章重合現象，並借助電腦推算篇章年代。傳世先秦兩漢文獻與《荀子》文獻重合情況實遠超固有之認識，有必要詳加鉤稽。至於出土文獻而有相關者，如郭店楚簡、包山楚簡、上海博物館藏戰國楚竹書、睡虎地秦簡、定縣漢簡以及最新發表之清華大學藏戰國楚竹書等，本計劃亦會加以利用及考察。 本研究計劃目的有四：（一）分析《荀子》篇章內在與外在之重合關係；（二）重新考訂《荀子》之成篇及成書狀況；（三）釐清何者為荀子之核心思想？何者為荀門後學發揮師說之辭？（四）重新思考古籍之成書過程。 Xunzi was a key figure of pre-Qin Confucianism, whose scholarship and philosophical thoughts have had an immense influence over generations of the Chinese people. Researchers on his ideas have to rely on his eponymous title, Xunzi; however, the authorship and the year(s) and place(s) of composition of its thirty-two chapters have remained subjects of intense debates. A significant number of parallel passages can be found both among its chapters and with other Han and pre-Han texts. Yet no comprehensive analysis has been carried out on this topic. The present study will target this niche and compile a full listing of all occurrences of similar wordings, passages, and ideas within Xunzi as well as with other transmitted and excavated Han and pre-Han texts, with a view to a thorough investigation of the intratextuality and intertextuality of Xunzi. Based on such data, a computer program will be developed to estimate the year of composition of a text. The phenomenon of parallel passages between Xunzi and other transmitted Han and pre-Han texts far exceeds our existing understanding and calls for an in-depth examination. Relevant excavated texts—such as the Chu bamboo scripts from Guodian and Baoshan, the Shanghai Museum manuscripts, the Shuihudi bamboo manuscripts, the Dingxian Han scripts, and the recently available Chu bamboo scripts from the Warring States period collected by Tsinghua University—will also be covered in the present study. The main objectives of the present study are: 1. To analyse the intertextuality and intratextuality of Xunzi; 2. To reassess the date of and the circumstances surrounding the formation of Xunzi as a book and the composition of its individual chapters; 3. To distinguish Xunzi’s core ideas from those developed by his followers; and 4. To revisit the composition and formation process of ancient Chinese texts.

14606918.label: Realisation of objectives
14606918.value: 荀子哲學思想影響深邃，後世學者了解其學說，唯賴《荀子》一書。歷年來，《荀子》三十二篇之作者、撰寫年代與地域，未有公論。《荀子》各篇之間內容多有重合，亦廣與先秦兩漢文獻互見，過去學者在探究此論題時並未考慮及此。本計劃結合傳世文獻與出土文獻，全盤排列《荀子》內在與外在之相近文辭、段落、義理等內容，考論其篇章重合現象，並借助電腦推算篇章年代。同時，本計劃詳加鉤稽傳世先秦兩漢文獻與《荀子》文獻重合情況，以補固有認識之不足。本計劃透過全面整理《荀子》篇章重合之內容，期望達到四個目的，包括：（一）分析《荀子》篇章內在與外在之重合關係；（二）重新考訂《荀子》之成篇及成書狀況；（三）釐清何者為荀子之核心思想？何者為荀門後學發揮師說之辭？（四）重新思考古籍之成書過程。 由本計劃主持主理之大型傳世及出土文獻網上資料庫「漢達文庫」，其中「先秦兩漢傳世文獻資料庫」所載《荀子》文本，為本計劃所用之底本。在本計劃初期，電腦小組運用電腦程式將《荀子》全文以單音節至四音節詞彙、短語、句子及段落一律標上「通用唯一識別碼」(Universally Unique Identifier)，使文本中各種元素轉換成可被電腦配對之格式，通過全書詞彙排列出3,089組資料（30,590條詞例），經研究人員逐一篩選及對比，由計劃主持分析及核實，整理出《荀子》內部重合資料共193組。 本計劃除排列《荀子》內部重合資料外，研究人員亦全面配對《荀子》與其他先秦兩漢文獻如《孟子》、《莊子》、《韓詩外傳》、《史記》、《禮記》、《大戴禮記》、《漢書》等之重合資料，深入考察《荀子》與先秦兩漢文獻重合的內容，以作出最完備之分析。 本計劃之研究成果，已悉數輸入「《荀子》內部重合文辭資料庫」，並設置於「漢達文庫」之內，供學術界免費使用。瀏覽重合文辭資料步驟如下： (1) 前往「漢達文庫—先秦兩漢傳世文獻資料庫」《荀子》全文連結： https://web.chant.org/text/book/ce149db0-40b4-11e9-8a63-4d68518ef8be； (2) 所有「漢達文庫」的用戶（包括付費和非付費用戶）均可以瀏覽及使用有關資料［評審專用戶口登入資料：名稱：RGCreviewer；密碼：RGCreviewer］； (3) 選取需要之篇章，點擊視窗右方之「重合」功能鍵，以開啟顯示重合資料功能； (4) 凡有重合文辭資料的文字均以淺綠色標示，點擊文字後，視窗下方即顯示重合內容。 此外，本計劃設計了「篇章年代辨識系統」（Chinese Texts Composition-date Identification System, CTCIS），並開發電腦程式平臺，從數碼人文角度，嘗試利用大數據協助識別古籍篇章的年代。研究人員蒐集整理各種可作為斷代依據之材料，全部輸入電腦系統內進行分析。辨識系統以詞彙為單位，根據資料庫的數據鑑別使用者上傳篇章內詞彙的性質及年代，計算不同年代詞彙所佔百分比，以推算上傳篇章的可能年代。辨識系統可啟動人物斷代功能，根據篇章涉及人物的生存年代，進一步推算其可能撰作年代上限。辨識系統已設置於「漢達文庫」之內，供學術界免費使用。使用辨識系統方法如下： (1) 前往「漢達文庫篇章年代辨識系統」連結：https://web.chant.org/tools/AgeCalc； (2) 上傳需要進行篇章年代辨識之文字； (3) 結果顯示數據包括：有效詞、可能性、可能年代； (4) 點擊「啟動人物斷代功能」以分析篇章所涉及的人物資料； (5) 系統列出所有人物資料，並自動篩選出最有參考價值的人物。 在進行研究工作期間，本計劃的主持及研究人員根據整理及分析的成果，迄今完成七篇學術論文。該七篇論文，除了關注《荀子》文本的義理訓解（李洛旻〈《荀子》「接人則用抴」解詁及其禮學意涵〉）和內部重合文辭現象（何志華〈《荀子》篇章內部重合文辭考論〉、〈重合與分歧：《荀子》篇章內部文辭對讀〉），也詳盡考察《荀子》與其他先秦兩漢古籍的重合文辭（何志華“Use of Alternative Characters in the Annotations of Ancient Texts”、〈《荀子》與經籍相合文辭考證〉）。當中“Use of Alternative Characters in the Annotations of Ancient Texts”既有《荀子》與其他文獻的比對，同時列舉楊倞據他書重見異文說解《荀子》文意的例子，足證以重合文辭考釋文獻之價值。以上研究全面整理《荀子》內在和外在的重合資料，仔細分析重合文辭的複雜情況。相關成果均發表於知名學術期刊，包括《中國語言學報》（Journal of Chinese Linguistics）、《中國文化研究所學報》和《諸子學刊》（預計2022年出版），也曾在學術會議上宣讀，並收入會議論文集內。此外，通過梳理《荀子》內部重合文辭之關係，也有助解決過去學界對《荀子》篇章關係及成篇年代的爭議，其研究成果已撰成兩篇英文論文（何志華“An Analysis of Parallel Passages in Xunzi”、“Rethink the Authorship of the ‘Xing E’ Chapter: Through Investigating the Parallel Passages among Different Chapters in the Xunzi”），並已於2021年初投稿到國際知名學術期刊《文史哲》（Journal of Chinese Humanities），現正由專家評審進行審核。 除以論文形式發表研究成果外，本計劃在篩選《荀子》各篇之間重合的詞、短語及句子，並歸納成193組內部重合文辭資料後，計劃主持已將有關結果編輯成《〈荀子〉內部重合文辭資料彙編》。全書以《荀子》三十二篇編排，重合文辭資料詳列於對應段落之下，同時摘錄過去學者對重合部份內容的注解。該書為《漢達古籍研究叢書》第五十一種，已交香港中文大學出版社印刷，預計將於2021年12月出版。

14607218.label: Project Objectives
14607218.value: Understand how the quality of territorial governance affects the distribution on Foreign Direct Investment projects in China. Provide a better understanding of the drivers behind China's highly unequal distribution of economic outcomes, even within provinces and regions that are often labeled as "developed" or "wealthy" but exhibit a very high degree of intra-provincial or intra-municipal economic disparities. Develop highly dis-aggregated and gridded measures of the quality of local governance through a unified geographical information system of China at the square-kilometer level. Develop a geo-referenced dataset of FDI in China at the project level in order to track precisely the nature and the distribution of investment in time and space. By mapping project-level FDI data to the detailed GIS grid of territorial governance, we seek to test relative importance of the quality of governance at each level of government in steering investments into specific Chinese localities.

14607218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14607218.value: This project seeks to elucidate how the quality of local governance influences the decision by foreign firms to locate investment projects on the Chinese mainland. We contend that existing research focused large and highly aggregated units (such as provincial governments and municipalities) overlooks the importance of county, township and local actors who play a critical role in the production of good (and sometimes bad) governance where firms consider locating Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) projects. By taking a highly disaggregated and multi-level approach to the study of how governance affects the behavior of economic agents, we will advance the political-economic research on governance and development. Empirically, we plan to combine two strands of highly-disaggregated data. First, we make use of an extensive dataset of over 275,000 FDI projects implemented since 1978 that covers the entire era of reform and opening in China. We will geo-reference these data in order to precisely map the size, scope and distribution of FDI over space and time. Second, we will use a detailed geospatial grid of China defined at the square-kilometer level order to map good and bad governance, using multilevel data collected and geo-referenced so as to measure how each level of territorial administration attracts (and possible discourage) the location of FDI into specific localities. This project also relates to public policy in Hong Kong, insofar as the location of foreign investment projects and their relationship to the quality of local governance is of great importance to Hong Kong based firms seeking to invest in Mainland China, especially under CEPA. Furthermore, a great deal of the empirical data to be used in this proposed project concerns Hong Kong firms that have invested on the Mainland since 1978. 該項目解釋了地方治理的質量如何影響外國公司在中國大陸尋找投資項目的決策。我們認為現有的研究主要集中在大型高度集中的單位（如省政府和市政當局）忽視了縣的重要性，鄉鎮和地方行為者在制定良好（有時是壞的）治理方面發揮關鍵作用，公司考慮將其放在外國直接投資項目中。通過採用高度分解和多層次的方法進行研究關於治理如何影響經濟主體的行為，我們將推進關於治理和發展的政治經濟研究。 根據經驗，我們計劃將兩組高度分解的數據結合起來。首先，我們利用自1978年年以來實施的超過275,000個外商直接投資項目的大量數據集，涵蓋了中國改革開放的整個時代。我們將對這些進行地理參考數據，以便精確地繪製外國直接投資在空間和時間上的規模，範圍和分佈。其次，我們將使用在平方公里定義的詳細的中國地理空間網格利用收集的多層次數據和地理參考來繪製治理良好和不良的水平順序，以衡量各級領土管理如何吸引（並可能阻止）外國直接投資到特定地區的位置。 該項目還涉及香港的公共政策，因為外國投資項目的位置及其與地方治理質量的關係對尋求在中國大陸投資的香港公司來說非常重要，特別是在CEPA下。此外，擬議項目中使用的大量實證數據涉及自1978年年以來在內地投資的香港公司。 根據經驗，我們計劃將兩組高度分解的數據結合起來。首先，我們利用自1978年年以來實施的超過275,000個外商直接投資項目的大量數據集，涵蓋了中國改革開放的整個時代。我們將對這些進行地理參考數據，以便精確地繪製外國直接投資在空間和時間上的規模，範圍和分佈。其次，我們將使用在平方公里定義的詳細的中國地理空間網格利用收集的多層次數據和地理參考來繪製治理良好和不良的水平順序，以衡量各級領土管理如何吸引（並可能阻止）外國直接投資到特定地區的位置。 該項目還涉及香港的公共政策，因為外國投資項目的位置及其與地方治理質量的關係對尋求在中國大陸投資的香港公司來說非常重要，特別是在CEPA下。此外，擬議項目中使用的大量實證數據涉及自1978年年以來在內地投資的香港公司。

14607218.label: Realisation of objectives
14607218.value: The partial completion of the objective is due to unforeseen changes to data availability during this project. The COVID period corresponded with rapid changes to the foreign direct investment climate and a deep decline in new FDI registrations nationwide. It appears that as a result, the foreign investment registration database platform on which we had relied initially was suddenly and radically restructured in ways that precluded continuing the data collection process that we had envisaged. We thus had to turn to other possible sources, mostly local statistical yearbooks, but had to patiently wait for the physical volumes corresponding to recent years data to gradually make their way to the CUHK and other University libraries in Hong Kong, We also relied on the CNKI statistical yearbook database. Those effort help use obtained data aggregated at the municipal level, which is a helpful though not entirely satisfactory substitute to the firm-level information that had been available on the old Ministry of Commerce registration platform. Finally, and much to our dismay, CNKI withdrew access to its statistical yearbook database for all users in HK, including University libraries, which has further hampered our efforts to continue updating data from statistical yearbooks. As a result, our initial goals were only partly reached. The percentages reflect the best we can do at this time given current [and unfortunately degraded] levels of data availability, as we stressed in our interim reports. We continue to seek ways to complete this process, through physical books [even though they arrive slowly] as well as any alternative online access that remains available, but this will take time. We remain committed to completing this process and to continue publishing based on this work beyond the date by which this project must formally end.

14607218.label: Major findings and research outcome
14607218.value: This project has uncovered the relationship between the penetration of foreign direct investment at the local level and the quality of governance particularly with respect to the management of land and the conversion from rural to urban land, an issue which has been a source of considerable tension in rural China since the beginning of economic reforms in 1978. The key finding is that provinces that are generally favorable to foreign capital (measured by the amount of FDI per capita per year in a given province) are conducive to a local governance environment in which local officials are eager to convert more agricultural land to urban land as they accommodate and actually utilize international Investments. At the same time, FDI is not only a source of economic growth in the abstract, but also amplifies the urbanization process in China. Since FDI is associated with net shrinkage of agricultural and natural land, we were thus able to to measure explicitly the extent to which Foreign Direct Investment contributes to environmental degradation and impairs sustainable development. We find however that such negative externalities are not equally distributed in space, but are particularly prevalent in Central and Western regions, where Foreign Direct Investment remains relatively rare. By contrast, further conversion to urban land in coastal provinces-- namely, those that have been receiving substantial amounts of FDI since the very beginning of the reform process-- has been tapering off. This task was accomplished successfully thanks to the creation of geographical datasets to capture the variability of land use over time based on satellite imagery (MODIS and Sentinel2),the collection of characteristics of the localities at the level of the county, municipality, and province, as well as variable that captures the institutional and political covariates that co-determine the outcomes of interests. Our findings can already be accessed on the social science research Network. The underlying data will be made available once the relevant submissions for review are accepted for publication. As explained in our intermediary reports, we faced unexpected considerable difficulties in the data collection process due to the changes in disclosures regarding FDI registration through the website of the Ministry of Commerce whilst data collection was under way. In addition, as we turned to alternative sources to remedy the situation, our efforts were hampered once again by the interruption of access to statistical yearbooks formerly provided for universities in Hong Kong via CNKI.

14607218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14607218.value: Our current research output and conference presentations reflect these limitations. We are determined to continue working on this project in order to improve on the quality of FDI data at the county level rather than relying on provincial aggregates for our empirical analysis. We are most grateful for the support received and will continue to improve our data collection effort as we prepare in further publications that will of course acknowledge RCG support for this phase of our research on local governance.

14607218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14607218.value: Foreign Direct Investment is associated with shrinking agricultural and natural land and affect the quality of local governance. In this project, we measured explicitly the extent to which Foreign Direct Investment contributes to environmental degradation and impairs sustainable development. We find however that such negative effect are concentrated in Central and Western regions, where Foreign Direct Investment remains relatively rare, and that remaining rural land is relatively better preserved in coastal regions that have a longer and deeper experience with FDI.

14607518.label: Project Objectives
14607518.value: To explore the village industries around the town of Mashi in Hunan at which site the Ping-Liu-Li Uprising broke out. To explore the social organization that backed up the transportation networks between Lukou (that served Mashi and nearby towns) and Xiangtan (the major city in the vicinity). To take into account developments in Anyuan to understand not only the participation of Anyuan workers in the uprising but also its role in shaping the reactions of the provincial authorities which caused the uprising to spread. To reconstruct the history of the Ping-Liu-Li Uprising to examine how local society was drawn into rapid economic and social changes in the early twentieth century.

14607518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14607518.value: The Ping-Liu-Li Uprising has been included in the history of the 1911 Revolution as a demonstration of massive support for secret society involvement in the revolution. As evidence, it is often said that supporters had been drawn from three counties (Pingxiang, Liuyang and Liling) in two provinces (Jiangxi and Hunan), under the leadership of the Gelao hui. No-one has demonstrated what structure the Gelao hui embodied or how it could have mustered the numbers reported in contemporary records. On the contrary, doubts have been cast on those records and it is obvious the revolutionary party, the Tongmeng hui, had a vested interest in claiming mass support. This project explores the possibility that the claim of popular support can be read in a different way. Mashi village, at which the uprising occurred, was so located that it spread across Pingxiang and Liuyang, and lay on the main route that went from Liling to Pingxiang. Mashi’s village temple, no less, lay in Pingxiang, and the theatrical stage across the road at which operas were performed lay in Liuyang. The interspersing of land (known in Qing documents as “flower planting” chahua) was common in villages on county boundaries. Any village crowd at Mashi’s temple festival would have included people from three counties and two provinces. This project will also explore how popular memory might have misrepresented the presence of the Gelao hui. The Gelao hui is often said to be made up of lodges (tang). In the case of Ping-Liu-Li, popular memory recalls the “inner” and “outer” eight halls (nei ba tang and wai ba tang). In this project, I shall explore if that terminology might have been related to transport organizations between the town of Lukou and Xiangtan city which were known as “head offices” (zong). Mashi was located among villages that were engaged in the fire-cracker industry, and the fire-crackers had to be exported down the Lujiang river at Lukou to Xiangtan. Rather than a secret society, popular memory might well have recalled the well-known and vital transport networks of the area, which were not at all secret.

14607518.label: Realisation of objectives
14607518.value: Realisation of objectives: As always, research has not turned out exactly as expected. Of the four objectives stated in the original application, objectives 1 and 2 were quite easily completed, while 3 and 4 took much work to elucidate. Objective 1 I first learnt about the fire-crackers industry at Mashi from my visit in 2015. Covid restrictions since project funding was granted prevented further visits, but I was fortunate in locating a Republican period study of the firecrackers industry in Hunan that provided details on the Mashi surroundings. I cite Zhang Renjia, Hunan zhi bianpao (np: Hunansheng jingji diaochasuo, 1935) in my English article now submitted to Twentieth-century China. Objective 2 The principal collection of documents on the Ping-Liu-Li Uprising (Pingxiang shi zhengxie, Liuyang xian zhengxie and Liling shi zhengxie, eds. Ping, Liu, Li qiyi ziliao huibian, Changsha: Hunan renmin chubanshe, 1986) refers to the leaders of the uprising as “matouguan” (river station officials). From contemporary government and later oral reports, Rao Huaimin pieced together an impression of the territorial influence of those people. (Rao Huaimin, Tongmeng hui yu Ping-Liu-Li qiyi. Changsha: Yuelu shushe, 1994, pp. 44-52) I have been able to add to that by relating (1) their said connections to the Gelaohui to the Qing dynasty government’s reaction to the Charles Mason gun-running case of 1891, and (2) the locations of the various river stations to the transportation networks linking the Jiangxi-Hunan border and Xiangtan. I present the results of (1) in chapter 6 of my book Mimi shehui de mimi, and (2) primarily in the English article. Obective 3 I had suspected that the involvement of Anyuan workers in the Ping-Liu-Li uprising was exaggerated but, upon examination, it became clear why Anyuan remained so important in highlighting its significance. That became clear from the Sheng Xuanhuai papers held in the Shanghai Library. I am glad I had visited the library and read some of those records before Covid struck, and when held back in Hong Kong by the long lockdown, I went through the published records of the Hanyeping Company in detail. Meanwhile, Shanghai Library had also published some portions of the Sheng Xuanhuai archive which I could make use of. The Qing dynasty government as well as the newspapers reacted to the events of the Ping-Liu-Li uprising with preconceptions dominated by the belief that an extensive secret society known as the Gelaohui was in existence. I deconstructed that view in Mimi shehui de mimi, in effect, by exploring how the idea of the “secret society” evolved over the entire nineteenth century. Deconstructing that view was necessary to allow me to appreciate how local the uprising really was. Objective 4 Indeed, local society was drawn into rapid economic and social changes in the early twentieth century, but not in ways I had anticipated. Economic changes were only beginning with the expanding fire-crackers market, the Anyuan mine and the Pingxiang-Zhuzhou railroad. The immediate impact of modern technology was felt, not on the social background, but on the mechanics of the uprising and the mobilization of government troops. I summarized those changes in the last paragraph of my English-language essay as “guns, the telegraph, the railway and newspapers”. Allow me to cite from that conclusion: “Gang bosses needed guns not only to counter government intervention, although that was serious when the government was itself arming its troops with guns, but they needed guns also to defend their turfs against competitors, that is to say, other gangs. No evidence may be found in the Ping-Liu-Li documentation that the gangs saw the railway as a threat to their very existence. That would have lain in the future when the railway made the river ports controlled by the gangs redundant. Nevertheless, the impact of the railway was obvious in the fast movement of troops. It was more obvious still in highlighting the importance of Pingxiang to the national interest. The speed at which news travelled by telegraph linked the troops in the field with the senior officials back at the provincial capitals. The newspapers were only a few days away by the same means of communication. News was sourced close to the scene of action, but that was not to say it was necessarily accurate. It did not come from independent reporting but reflected impressions formed by people within the news-gathering network.” In gist, those were the external influences that acted upon the uprising. In my English-language essay, I examined in detail the events of the uprising in order to come to that conclusion. Covid lockdown meant I could not use the budget portions earmarked for research on the mainland. I think I achieved all the objectives I had promised. Had it not been for the Covid restrictions, I would have revisited Mashi and learnt more about local society. I regret that and hope to make up for it in future.

14607518.label: Major findings and research outcome
14607518.value: Major findings and research outcome: 1. In my research outcome Mimi shehui de mimi: Qingdai de Tiandi hui yu Gelao hui （Beijing: Beijing Normal University Publishing Group, 2022), I reconstructed the history of the Gelao hui in the light of the Tiandi hui. I argued that the Qing government, the popular press, as well as the revolutionaries transposed a framework of the "secret societies" based on the Tiandi hui to incidents that in the second half of the nineteenth century came to be ascribed to the Gelao hui. The Ping-Liu-Li uprising was a major event that contributed to the emergence of this view. 2. In my second research outcome, my article "The Ping-Liu-Li Uprising of 1906 up close: its local context and its national significance", I argue that the novelty of the Ping-Liu-Li uprising arose from new technology, consisting of "guns, the telegraph, the railway and the newspapers". Guns changed the nature of territorial domination and provided a motive for local gangs to connect to the revolutionaries. The telegraph put provincial officials in direct contact with troops on the ground and enabled the national newspapers located on the China coast rapid access to information, even if not always accurate. The railway proved to be an effective way to move troops quickly. Modern industry, in the form of the Anyuan coal mine, gave the incident national prominence, but it was the technological changes that signaled the incident had opened the gate to a new stage of popular uprisings.

14607518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14607518.value: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action: Technological changes making an impact on popular uprisings deserves a great deal more attention. However, to put that in context, they led to new developments in city life and the relationship between city dwellers, their countryside compatriots and government. I think that leads on to my new project, the historical anthropology of the city in China.

14607518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14607518.value: The Layman's Summary: The Ping-Liu-Li Uprising has been included in the history of the 1911 Revolution as a demonstration of massive support for secret society involvement in the revolution. As evidence, it is often said that supporters had been drawn from three counties (Pingxiang, Liuyang and Liling) in two provinces (Jiangxi and Hunan), under the leadership of the Gelao hui. This project explores another reading of the incident. Mashi village, at which the uprising occurred, was so located that it spread across Pingxiang and Liuyang, and lay on the main route that went from Liling to Pingxiang. Any village crowd at Mashi’s temple festival would have included people from three counties and two provinces. The omnipresence of the Gelao hui had resulted from the application of the “secret society” model to little connected local gangs guarding their turfs. Yet, the uprising introduced novelties. Guns, the telegraph, the railway, the newspapers, made their impact, not on the social background, but on the uprising itself and on the manner in which government and popular opinion reacted. Ping-Liu-Li deserves attention as representing the beginning of a new stage of popular uprisings, and, as such, it feeds into the history of the 1911 Revolution.

14607918.label: Project Objectives
14607918.value: To assess the force of a major philosophical and ethical concern (appealing to considerations of identity and authenticity) relating to the use of neuro-interventions to cure mental disorder and enhance normal mental function; To argue that there is no such thing as a single “correct” account of authenticity (even within the specific context of the ethical debate on neurotechnology), but rather several legitimate uses of that concept, some of greater relevance in some contexts than others, and to offer a taxonomy of those uses that goes beyond the traditional contrasts suggested in the existing literature (e.g. “self-creation” vs. “self-discovery”, “gratitude” vs. “creativity”); To criticize the currently dominant understanding of “narrative” identity, and to defend a new account that incorporates some objective constraints while acknowledging the unavoidably subjective dimension of the notion; By bringing contemporary research in psychology to bear on this debate, to show that the popular notion of a “true self”, while not philosophically or scientifically exact, is nonetheless not entirely flawed, contrary to what a number of bioethicists have argued; To distinguish objections from identity and authenticity from related but distinct concerns with which they are sometimes confused, such as the risk of changing oneself in compliance with suspect social norms, and to evaluate those distinct concerns; To argue that the impact of neuro-interventions on human identity and authenticity is complex, but can sometimes be positive (besides its other benefits), and does not warrant a wholesale condemnation (let alone prohibition) of those interventions, whether for treatment or enhancement; and in the process, to reply to some of the criticisms that have been levelled at my previous work; To seek input, via informal discussions, from academics with relevant expertise in Hong Kong about the concerns raised by neuro-interventions in contexts beyond that of philosophical debate, and use that input to inform my own analysis.

14607918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14607918.value: From time immemorial, human beings have striven to shape their mental features in ways they considered desirable, through education, meditation and many other methods. The past few decades, however, have seen the rise of a new breed of interventions (“neuro-interventions”) made possible by advances in neurotechnology, that are giving us unprecedented control over our psychological characteristics. These include pharmaceuticals and other biomedical (e.g. brain stimulation) devices, which are primarily used to treat mental disorders, but also open up the prospect of improving “normal” traits, including mood, personality, or cognition. This development has given rise to a rich debate in biomedical ethics, with one key concern relating to the impact of such interventions on the “identity” or “authenticity” of those who use them. For instance, is the person who undergoes Deep Brain Stimulation the “same” person as before, if the intervention produces a striking change in personality? This project proposes to contribute to that debate, in the form a book to be submitted for publication to a prestigious academic press. The PI will present a philosophical analysis of the concepts of human identity and authenticity, engaging with the existing literature, and will propose new ways of understanding those concepts. In particular, the book will argue for a pluralistic and contextual understanding of authenticity, according to which there is more than one legitimate use of that concept, leading to greater complexity than has been recognized in the distinctions commonly made in the literature. The book will also seek to enlighten the concept of “narrative” identity at the core of the debate and challenge the currently dominant paradigm, by incorporating insights from contemporary research in psychology that have been surprisingly neglected in that context. To ensure the social relevance of the project, the PI will also be seeking input, via informal exchanges, from academics with relevant expertise in Hong Kong about the ethical issues raised by neuro-interventions, and will use that input to inform his discussion. Ultimately, the book will argue that the impact of neuro-interventions on human identity and authenticity is complex, but can sometimes be positive (besides its other benefits), and does not warrant a wholesale condemnation (let alone prohibition) of those interventions, whether for treatment or enhancement. Combining rigorous philosophical analysis with the lastest scientific evidence, it will help move the debate forward, responding in the process to some of the criticisms that have been levelled at the PI’s past work.

14608118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14608118.value: AIM To understand how China’s key energy partners along the Belt and Road (New Silk Road) institutionally protect Chinese energy investments, and formulate proposals on the external normative influence that China can exercise to improve energy investment protection in these strategic destinations. PROJECT BACKGROUND China's “Belt and Road Initiative” aims to increase regional integration based on infrastructure investments. In the energy sector, integration with the Eurasian market is an essential part of China’s ambitious foreign energy policy. By linking the Russian and Central Asian resource bases with its domestic infrastructure, China expects to improve national energy security. However, foreign investments face significant regulatory risks relating to the strategic importance and political sensitivity of energy. The regulation of foreign energy relations is the subject of growing interest in the academic literature, but the Chinese and Eurasian perspectives remain largely unexplored. There is no doubt that Chinese investments reshaped the Eurasian energy landscape, but little is known about China's influence on domestic energy regulation in neighbouring countries, in particular in the key Russian and Central Asian energy investment destinations. PROJECT DESCRIPTION Focusing on strategic markets for China’s energy security, this project critically analyzes the protection of energy investments under the domestic law of China’s partner countries. On this basis, the project examines the regulatory influence that China can exercise over the design of these markets to improve the protection of energy investments. Three theoretical strands underpin this project. First, building on the literature on the regulation of “network-related industries”, this research examines investors’ rights under Russian, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz law. Second, based on the literature on “constitutional economics” in the former Soviet Union, it assesses how domestic courts balance private and public interests in the resolution of investment disputes involving the government. Third, building on the “legal approximation” literature, it analyses how existing regulatory harmonization in the Eurasian region (Eurasian Economic Union) limits the possibility for China to further shape the Eurasian energy market. SIGNIFICANCE OF PROJECT With depleting domestic energy reserves, foreign investments are an essential component of China’s energy security policy. This project contributes to the Belt and Road energy objectives by making recommendations on how China can cooperate with its strategic energy partners to mitigate investment risks. This analysis is relevant to Hong Kong’s role as Belt and Road investment and arbitration hub. More fundamentally, this analysis contributes to understanding the legal implications of China’s increasing influence on the regional and world energy markets. 中國對歐亞能源市場的塑造：保護中國在“一帶一路”沿線的對外投資 項目目的 瞭解中國在“一帶一路”（新絲綢之路）沿線上的主要能源合作夥伴如何從制度上保護中國的能源投資，並就中國可以在這些戰畧目的地發揮的外部規範性影響製定建議，以改善這些戰畧目的地的能源監管。 項目背景 中國政府在2015年提出了“一帶一路”倡議，目標是在基礎設施投資的基礎上加强區域一體化建設。在能源領域，融入歐亞市場是中國雄心勃勃的對外能源政策的重要組成部分。中國希望通過將俄羅斯和中亞的資源基地與其國內基礎設施連接起來以改善國家能源安全。然而，外國投資面臨著與能源戰畧重要性和政治敏感性有關的重大法律和政治風險。對外能源關係的監管是學術界越來越感興趣的話題，但中國和歐亞的觀點在很大程度上仍未得到探討。此外，投資法文獻主要側重於國際保護，對國內法律和法院的關注較少。 項目介紹 本項目圍繞中國能源安全的戰畧市場，對中國合作夥伴國內法下的能源投資保護問題進行了批判性的分析。在此基礎上，該項目考察了中國可以對這些市場的設計施加的監管影響，以改善其對能源投資的保護。此項目有三個理論基礎。首先，本研究以有關“能源網絡輸送和筦道相關企業”監管的文獻為基礎，調查了俄羅斯、哈薩克共和國、烏茲別克和吉爾吉斯斯坦法律下投資者的權利。其次，在前蘇聯“憲法經濟學”文獻的基礎上，該項目評估了國內法院在解决涉及政府投資糾紛時如何平衡私人利益與公共利益。第三，在“法律近似”文獻的基礎上，該項目分析了歐亞地區現行的統一監管如何限制中國進一步塑造歐亞能源市場的可能性。 項目意義 隨著國內能源儲備的不斷减少，外商投資是中國能源安全政策的重要組成部分。該項目為“一帶一路”能源目標做出了貢獻，在中國如何與戰畧能源合作夥伴合作以及降低投資風險方面提出了建議。這一分析與“一帶一路”倡議下的將香港作為投資和仲裁中心的角色有關。更重要的是，此分析有助於理解中國對區域和世界能源市場日益增長的影響力的法律影響。

14608118.label: Realisation of objectives
14608118.value: All the research objectives of the project have been achieved, and have resulted in publications in some of the leading journals in the field of energy law and geopolitics. OBJECTIVE 1: Gain in-depth understanding of domestic energy, investment and natural monopoly laws, and their application by domestic courts, in countries of strategic importance for China’s energy security (Russia, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan). Produce scholarly output on the “Domestic Protection of Energy Infrastructure Investments in the Former Soviet Union”. The project engaged in a detailed analysis of energy market regulation, energy tariff reforms, and what these mean for energy investors’ rights in strategic jurisdictions along the Belt and Road Initiative, with a focus on Central Asia and in particular Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan. The analysis looked at national regulation, and its application by domestic courts, with a focus on the balancing of investors' right to cost-recovery energy tariffs and consumers' tight to affordable prices. The outcome of the research, entitled “Energy Justice Along the ‘New Silk Road’: Balancing Investors’ and Consumers’ Rights in Central Asia”, appeared with Oxford University Press, in the book Energy Justice and Energy Law, that is part of the prestigious series edited by the Academic Advisory Group on Energy, Environment, Natural Resources and Infrastructure Law to the International Bar Association. Taking into account the focus of the project on energy law and geopolitics along the Belt and Road, research was done on the important decision of the European Court of Justice in the OPAL case concerning access to gas pipeline interconnections in the context of geopolitical tensions. The case is highly relevant to understand the interactions of energy, investment and natural monopoly laws, and geopolitics, in a region that is also of great relevance for Chinese energy investments along the Belt and Road. The outcome of the research was published in the Common Market Law Review, the leading European law journal, and was cited by the Advocate General to the European Court of Justice. OBJECTIVE 2: Influence the debate on China’s increasing foreign power by analyzing the scope for Chinese regulatory influence in shaping market rules in the strategic Eurasian energy market. Produce scholarly output on "China's Shaping of the Eurasian Energy Market: Exporting the 'Chinese Energy Model' Abroad?" The project researched China’s regulatory influence on the shaping of the Eurasian energy market by looking at (1) the role of investments by China’s State-owned Enterprises (SOEs); (2) regulatory competition between the EU, Russia and China on the shaping of energy market rules in the former Soviet space; (3) the existence of a Chinese energy market “model”. First, the project focused on the influence China exercises through foreign investments by its SOEs. Analysis was done on the extent to which foreign investments are used as instrument of geopolitical influence, by researching the regulatory channels through which the government can shape investment decisions. The outcome of the research is an article on "For Profit or Strategic Influence? Chinese Outbound Investments and the International Economic Regime", published in the Journal of World Energy Law & Business, the leading energy law journal, published by Oxford University Press. Second, research was done on the regulatory competition that China faces in the post-Soviet energy sector. The analysis looked at China’s external regulatory approach to the shaping of energy markets in the region and compared this to the strategies adopted by the EU and Russia. The focus was on gas market regulation, with a focus on gas pricing and network access regimes. The research, entitled “Shaping the Eurasian Gas Market: the Geopolitics of Energy Market Regulation”, was published in Geopolitics, a leading International Relations journal. Third, the project engaged in an in-depth study of the Chinese gas market model, in order to understand what market approach China can export to its neighbors. The analysis focuses on gas price and tariff regulation and gas pipeline regulation in China and the outcome is a publication on “China’s textbook approach to regulatory reform of the natural gas market”, published in Utilities Policy, one of the leading journals in the field of energy policy. OBJECTIVE 3: Contribute to the study of China’s external energy relations by providing an in-depth analysis of existing harmonization of energy, investment and natural monopoly rules under the Eurasian Economic Union. Produce scholarly output on “Regional Energy Market Integration in Eurasia: the Belt and Road and the Eurasian Economic Union”. The project engaged in in-depth analysis of the existing harmonization of energy, investment and natural monopoly rules under the Eurasian Economic Union. The outcome of this research was published in the Russian law review Oil and Gas Law journal (to make the analysis available to the legal community working on Eurasian gas market regulation in Russia and Central Asia). The research was also used for the publication on “Shaping the Eurasian Gas Market: the Geopolitics of Energy Market Regulation” (with Geopolitics). The conclusions of the research have also been presented at different conferences and webinars. OBJECTIVE 4: Influence the debate on investment arbitration by highlighting the merits and limits of bringing investment disputes before national courts. The project's analysis of domestic energy and natural monopoly laws, and their application by national courts, has helped understand the importance of national tribunals in the shaping of energy law, including on matters of high geopolitical sensitivity. By helping to understand how domestic courts apply tariff regulations, and enforce network access regimes, the project contributed to the debate on the regulation of energy investments under national law, and the interactions of national and international judicial protection. The citation of one research output from this project by the Advocate General to the European Court of Justice in the famous OPAL case (concerning a Russian gas pipeline investment in the EU) demonstrates that the project already has impacted the debate on national energy law, judicial protection and geopolitics. OBJECTIVE 5: Present conclusions at international energy and investment law conferences, as well as to the Hong Kong legal community (e.g., HK law firms) and government (Belt and Road Commission) to disseminate findings on Eurasian energy law and domestic protection. A webinar (due to Covid restrictions) was organised in July 2021 to present the outcome of the research conducted during the project. The event, entitled “Gas Market Reform Along the Belt and Road”, was attended by the legal industry (including practicing lawyers in China, Central Asia and the EU), energy law and policy scholars (based in Hong Kong and abroad), energy analysts at leading consulting and analysis companies, the energy industry (oil and gas companies), international organisations (such the Energy Charter Secretariat that is active in the Central Asian energy market) and non-governmental organisations (such as the Konrad Adenauer Foundation Energy Security and Climate Change program, based in Hong Kong). In addition, the PI shared the conclusions of the research with representatives of multilateral development banks working on gas market reforms in Central Asia and with local government bodies (energy ministry). The project helped to make recommendations on ongoing gas market reforms in the region. The research was also presented at international conferences, including “The European Union in Central Asia: An Uninvited Guest in China’s and Russia’s Backyard?” (conference at the University of Groningen); and “International Law and Distribution” (the joint conference organised by the University of Edinburgh and Glasgow).

14608118.label: Major findings and research outcome
14608118.value: The research project contributed to the understanding of energy market regulation as a geopolitical instrument, and the influence that China exercises on the shaping of the Eurasian energy market. It also helped understand the relevance of national energy and investment law for Chinese investments in energy projects along the Belt and Road. The project first analysed how national governments and regulators in key energy jurisdictions along the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) regulate energy tariffs, and balance investors and consumers' rights in this process. To facilitate the financial viability of energy investments, governments are engaging in tariff reforms, and courts have in certain cases played an important role in enforcing investors' rights. This sheds light on the role of national law and the judiciary, in protecting investors' rights along the BRI. The project then engaged in a legal analysis of the use of foreign investments for geopolitical purposes, by examining the Chinese regulation of outbound investments based on international principles of governance of state-owned enterprises. Most of the regulatory steps previously in place to direct outbound investments have been eliminated or simplified, giving companies greater control over their own investments. Third, the project examined China's gas market regulation model, to understand what approach to gas regulation China could export to the BRI. The analysis demonstrated that reforms in 2019–2021 integrated key aspects of the liberalisation textbook model in China’s gas regulations. In many ways, China thus follows the approach already promoted by the EU in the field of energy market regulation in the region. Fourth, the analysis looked at regulatory competition in China's strategic rear, looking at how the EU, Russia and China seek to shape the Eurasian energy market. Paradoxically, the EU, Russia and China recognize common principles of gas market regulation at the domestic level, but geopolitical considerations prevent the implementation of these principles at the regional level, hindering the creation of a competitive Eurasian gas market. Fifth, the project analysed existing regulatory approximation in strategic energy jurisdictions along the Belt and Road, with a focus on the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) gas market. By allowing foreign (e.g. Chinese) investments to derogate from the EAEU gas regime based on bilateral agreements, the EAEU accommodates China’s increasing importance as investor in the Eurasian energy infrastructure. On the same basis, the EAEU gas regime does also not pre-empt a possible Chinese initiative of regulatory integration in the energy sector, with one or more EAEU members.

14608118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14608118.value: The Ukraine war has a significant geopolitical impact on the region, and it is necessary to examine how this will affect the regulation of energy markets. In particular, China - that will replace the EU as main importer of Russian gas - is now in a stronger position to influence Russia's natural gas market structure, e.g. by demanding reform to the monopoly of pipeline exports. In addition, the Chinese gas market remains in development, and continued analysis of regulatory changes is needed to understand how this can impact on China's possible role as an exporter of rules in the region. Similarly, the national gas markets in Central Asia, and other BRI countries, are being reformed, and it would be important to keep researching the changes that are introduced to the national regulatory arrangements in the gas sector of these strategic partners for China's energy security.

14608118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14608118.value: China's Shaping of the Eurasian Energy Market contributed to the understanding of regulation as an instrument of foreign policy and geopolitics. Energy, and in particular natural gas, is a key component of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). For Chinese infrastructure investments in the energy sector of BRI countries, national regulation is important as it influences the financial viability of these investments. At the same time, foreign investments, and their home state governments, can influence the regulation of national energy markets. States can seek to influence energy market rules abroad in order to exercise strategic influence, or protect the interests of their foreign investors. The European Union and Russia have actively sought to shape the energy market rules in key energy investment destinations along the BRI, but there is still scope for Chinese influence, in particular in the states that participate in the Eurasian Economic Union. As the Eurasian Economic Union gas market is being developed, China has a role to play in helping to shape the regional gas market architecture.

14609018.label: Project Objectives
14609018.value: To build up a database of all porcelain associated with princely households and a historical archive of each principality. 14609018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14609018.value: The proposed project is an investigation of the porcelain production and consumption of princely households during the Ming dynasty, especially in the periods of interregnum (mid-15th century) and late Ming (16th century to early 17th century), by examining porcelain wares associated with Ming princes in totality and comparing them with the latest archaeological findings from the imperial and private kiln sites in Jingdezhen and pieces in local and overseas collections. Fanwang藩王, as imperial princes enfeoffed with designated land throughout the empire’s provinces, have been considered key players in the development of art and culture in the Ming dynasty (1368-1644). Among their material remains, porcelain was one of the types that are the most abundant and clearly display their interaction with the imperial court and the ordinary people. In the past decades, large quantities of porcelain shards and wares associated with the fanwang (or princes) and their households are found through excavation of palace sites and princely tombs and identification of wares in museum collections. These porcelain shards and wares have, thus far, not been put together and systematically studied. The aims of the project are threefold: First, it aims at establishing an overall picture of the porcelain consumption of princely households by conducting a comparative study of porcelain excavated from princely palaces and tombs in provinces throughout the Ming dynasty. Second, it will explore the princes’ involvement in the imperial porcelain production in the interregnum period by examining the latest excavated materials from sites of the imperial factory at Jingdezhen and comparing them with the database of Ming princes’ porcelain built up by the proposed project. Third, the project will investigate the role of Ming princes in facilitating the exchange of design and consumption practice of and taste for porcelain between the imperial court and the ordinary people, by studying the development of polychrome enamelled porcelain (some with gold foils) in late Ming times. The porcelain concerned was confined to the court in the 15th century, but became popular among princely households shortly after that, and began to be produced in considerable quantities by private kilns from the mid-16th century onwards. How princes who had access to such confined wares contributed to their mass production for domestic and export markets will serve as a way of assessing the status of Ming princes in the social and cultural realms of Ming society. 本研究計劃旨在透過全面檢視現存跟明代藩王有關的瓷器，並將之與景德鎮官、民窯考古出土的瓷片和海內外傳世品作對比，以揭示明代藩王及其王府對瓷器生產和消費的參與和影響，尤其針對空白期（十五世紀中期）和晚明（十六世紀至十七世紀初期）兩個時期進行探討。 明代分佈於全國的藩王，一直被視為明代文化和藝術發展的重要推動者。在他們遺存的眾多文物中，瓷器不僅量大且最能清晰展示他們當時跟皇室和民間的互動情況。過去幾十年，全國各地明藩王王府遺址和相關墓葬出土了大量瓷器和瓷片，且收藏在各大博物館的藩王府用瓷亦漸漸得到辨識，惜這些藩王相關的瓷器一直沒有得到全面的整理和分析。本研究計劃的目的有三： 首先，通過將不同時期各地藩王王府和墓葬等考古遺址出土的瓷器進行比較，從而建立明代藩王及其王府在整個明代的瓷器使用情況。其二，透過將上述藩王相關遺址出土的瓷器跟景德鎮御窯遺址新近出土的空白期瓷片作對比，藉以探討十五世紀中期藩王對官窯瓷器生產的參與。其三，考察晚明彩瓷的發展，從而思考藩王在推動瓷器紋飾設計、消費品味和習慣等方面扮演的角色。十五世紀初，裝飾有多種彩料的瓷器只限於皇室使用，但其後它們在藩王中的使用日漸普遍，並於十六世紀中以後在民窯大量生產。本計劃將研究各地藩王最初如何取用這些官窯瓷器，及其使用跟後來彩瓷大量生產予國內外市場的關係，藉以了解藩王在明代社會的物質和文化生活中扮演的角色。

14609018.label: Realisation of objectives
14609018.value: 1. Objective 1 1.1 An image archive with approximately 1000 pieces of excavated and extant porcelain and shards related to Ming princely households and a literary archive with about 120 books and essays about Ming princes and their porcelain have been built with data collected through fieldwork, searching ancient books and modern publications. 1.2 Based on the aforementioned archives, a comprehensive table has been created and uploaded to our departmental website. This table lists all the Ming princes in different prefectures of Ming China, providing information about their excavated tombs, a summary of the findings, and sources of references. Due to copyright restrictions, the images of the ceramics and shards cannot be provided. However, readers can easily locate images and written works related to all the ceramic pieces through online research databases such as CNKI and Wanfang. The table is open to the public and can be accessed via the “Research Project (Ref CUHK 14609018) section of the following website: https://www.arts.cuhk.edu.hk/~fadept/academic-staff/wan-chui-ki-maggie/ Object 1 has been achieved. 2. Objective 2 2.1 During most of the project period, from 2019 to 2022, the closure of borders in many countries and exceptionally long quarantine periods due to the Covid-19 pandemic made it impossible to carry out the originally planned field trips to Mainland China and other countries. Project members were only able to conduct field trips to Jiangxi and Sichuan provinces in 2019. Nonetheless, these two sites proved to be of utmost importance as they are the only places where princely palaces with rich ceramic finds have been archaeologically excavated, and where many princely tombs and kiln sites for producing ceramics for Ming princes have been discovered. 2.2 Based on data collected from field trips and other research materials, Project RA, Gao Xianping, published an article in the academic journal Nanfang wenwu, attributing some of the ceramics excavated from the Princely Palace in Chengdu to private kilns in the "Zhenqu" (鎮區) area of Jingdezhen, Jiangxi (Part C, 8(3)). The article contributes to clarifying an important source of ceramics for Ming princes during the early to middle Ming period. 2.3 The PI published a monograph entitled "Power and Symbol: Porcelains with Five-Clawed Dragon Designs for Ming Princes in the Mid-15th Century" in the National Palace Museum Research Quarterly (Part C, 8 (2)). Taking the dragon motif as a point of departure, the monograph reviews previous research on Ming princes' porcelain and discusses how Ming princely households attempted different means to acquire porcelain to meet their needs. It argues that Ming princes commissioned or purchased dragon porcelain from specific private kilns in Jingdezhen, likely with the tacit approval of the emperor. The porcelain pieces feature standard imperial dragon motifs but avoid the ascending dragon that symbolizes the reigning emperor, expressing the unique social status of the Ming princes. Through this intensive study of dragon porcelains, the monograph clarifies porcelains of different origins used by Ming princely households. 2.4 The PI delivered three lectures on the dragon porcelain of Ming princes at the Graduate Institute of Art History, National Taiwan University (Part C, 11(2)), Academia Sinica, Taipei (Part C, 11 (3)), and the China Project Workshop of The Institute of Fine Arts, New York University (Part C, 11 (4)). The lectures were very well received, with much feedback from scholars and the general audience. The PI was invited to condense the monograph and have it reproduced in the art magazine Orientations (美成在久) in January 2024, (Part C, 11 (5)) so that the new knowledge about the Ming princes and their porcelain can reach a wider audience of general readers. 2.5 An in-person one-day conference was organized on October 20, 2023, on the campus of the Chinese University of Hong Kong, with the participation of 11 scholars from different parts of China (Part C, 11(1)). The conference had a total of 300 in-person and online attendees. During the conference, the project team, including the PI, Co-I, and RA, presented their new discoveries, and additional materials provided by other scholars helped ensure that the understanding of the different sources of porcelain used by Ming princes is up-to-date and comprehensive. 2.6 Since an exhibition was held in 2021 and a substantial catalogue of 650 pages featuring numerous porcelain related to Ming princes was published by Zhongguo taoci bowuguan (中國陶瓷博物館) in 2023, the PI sees no point in producing a general survey on ceramics for princely households in different provinces, as this would duplicate the efforts of others. By focusing on the dragon porcelain of the Ming princes, the PI's monograph offers a new perspective for understanding how Ming princes in different provinces were involved in various types of ceramic production. Objective 2 has been achieved. Objective 3 3.1 As mentioned in the progress report, the project team found that there was minimal involvement of Ming princes in the production of imperial porcelain. To understand how the Ming princes interacted with the Ming court, the PI conducted an intensive case study on the Shu Principality in Chengdu, Sichuan, and produced a paper discussing the relationship between the porcelain discovered in the princely palace and the imperial porcelain and court of that time. The paper was selected to be presented at the refereed academic conference "2023 International Conference on Ming-Qing Studies, Academia Sinica" in Taipei (Part C, 8 (5); (11(3)). Following the conference, the paper will be submitted for publication. 3.2 Through our research and intensive case study, it has been confirmed that the Ming Princes had minimal involvement in the production of imperial porcelain. Objective 3 has been achieved. Objective 4 4.1 The Co-I focused on investigating the exchange of design, consumption practices, and taste for porcelain between the imperial court and the general population. She produced two articles. The first article is a background study that examines the changes in types and characteristics of ceramics produced by the general population for export markets from the early 16th century to the 17th century (Part C, 8(1)). It was published in the journal Haiyang shi yanjiu. 4.2 The second article focuses on the discovery of "kraak ware" (traditionally considered as a type of export ceramics) in sites related to Ming princes' tombs and the central court (Part C, 8 (4). The Co-I argues that the Ming princes were also interested in this new type of porcelain, aware of its prevalence beyond Ming China, and actively purchased or commissioned kraak wares for their own use. This article effectively demonstrates how Ming princes participated in shaping the taste for porcelain during the late Ming period and facilitated the spread of porcelain design between the central court and the general population. This work is particularly important as it opens up a new dimension for understanding the involvement of Ming princes in the spread of porcelain design and consumption during the 16th and 17th centuries. The article was initially presented at the refereed conference titled "2021 International Conference on Ming-Qing Studies, Academia Sinica" in Taipei (Part C, 9 (3)). It was then revised and accepted for publication in Gugong bowuyuan yuankan. 8(4)). Objective 4 has been achieved.

14609018.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609018.value: 1. The project has revealed the changes in the various sources of porcelain used by Ming princely households. In the early Ming period, they utilized porcelain from diverse sources, including gifts from the imperial court and wares produced by private kilns in the "Zhenqu" (鎮區) area of Jingdezhen, Jiangxi province (Part C, 8(3)). 2. During the early to middle Ming dynasty, Ming princes also began commissioning or purchasing porcelain adorned with the five-clawed dragon motif from specific private kilns in Jingdezhen, likely with the tacit approval of the emperor. The dragon porcelain of the Ming princes depicted images of dragons that were either no longer in use or newly created, avoiding the ascending dragon motif that symbolized the reigning emperor. This was so done to express the unique social status of the Ming princes, who were subordinate to the Emperor but held a higher position than ordinary people. Therefore, by the early to mid-15th century, some Ming princes were already involved in commissioning porcelain with their own designs (Part C, 8(2)). 3. In the case of the Shu Principality, the Ming princely household commissioned dragon porcelain to be made not only in specific private kiln sites in Jingdezhen but also in local kilns in Sichuan. They also obtained imperial porcelain through channels other than imperial endowment, intentionally grinding and removing the reign marks on the imperial wares. It is proposed that the commissioning of dragon porcelain was common between the late Xuande and the third year of the Zhengtong reign (1433-1438) and became less prevalent afterward. It only became a common practice among Ming princes after the 16th century (Part C, 8(5)). 4. It has been found that Ming princes had minimal involvement in the production of imperial porcelain during the interregnum period. 5. In the 16th century, global trade and changes in foreign markets brought about shifts in fashion for porcelain (Part C, 8(1)). Ming princes were aware of the dynamic world beyond Ming China, and some favored "kraak ware," which was previously only considered porcelain for export. Based on the kraak wares found in Ming princes' tombs, the imperial palace, and other archaeological sites, it is believed that Ming princes were involved in the exchange of porcelain taste between the court and the general population by commissioning kraak wares with special dragon designs (Part C, 8(4)).

14609018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609018.value: The research project has revealed that Ming princes played a significant role in the development of ceramic design and production during the Ming dynasty. They received porcelain gifts from the imperial court, purchased porcelain from private kilns, commissioned wares with unique designs, and acquired imperial wares through illicit means from various sources. The involvement of Ming princes in Ming society was much more extensive than previously suggested in the literature. The study of porcelain has proven to be an excellent avenue for investigating the evolving dynamics in the relationship between the imperial court, Ming princes, ordinary people, and the wider world. It allows for a better understanding of the exchange of art, ideas, and practices among individuals from different social strata and regions. The PI and Co-I plan to focus on the different depictions of dragons found on porcelain made for the court, Ming princes, tributary states, and other states beyond the Ming Empire. This will further explore the interactions between these social groups during the Ming dynasty. A GRF proposal has been submitted to seek funding for this new project.

14609018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609018.value: This project focuses on the study of porcelain production and consumption within princely households during the Ming dynasty. It utilizes recent archaeological excavations of Ming princely palace sites, tombs, and kiln sites in Jingdezhen to examine the involvement of Ming princes in porcelain production and their role in facilitating the exchange of porcelain design and consumption practices between the court and the general population. The research has demonstrated that Ming princes were not merely passive recipients of porcelain gifts from the court, but actively engaged in purchasing porcelain from private kilns, commissioning wares with unique designs, and acquiring imperial wares through various channels for their personal use. Throughout the early to late Ming period, Ming princes were conscious of their imperial status and contemporary fashion trends when commissioning porcelain from private kilns. In the mid-15th century, they began commissioning porcelain with distinctive five-clawed dragon designs to differentiate themselves from the Emperor and ordinary people. In the 16th century, some Ming princes followed the global trade trends and commissioned kraak wares adorned with dragon motifs to emphasize their own status. While their involvement in imperial porcelain production was limited, they made significant contribution to the development of porcelain for the general population.

14609818.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14609818.value: 「發展障礙症」的日本研究：通往共融的途徑及社會價值的轉變

14609818.label: Project Objectives
14609818.value: The study aims to understand the rise of “developmental disabilities” (hattatsu shôgai) as an accepted biomedical category in Japan. This will be achieved through historical research tracing the emergence of the term in the media, government documents, and medical publications. The study seeks to discover areas of innovation in schools and community support groups. It explores educators and activists' responses to the expansion of biomedical frameworks. It investigates school policies and teaching arrangements for children deemed to have developmental disabilities, and how children are identified as having these disabilities (as support groups and schools do not necessarily categorize children according to official diagnoses). The study aims to understand how young adults from the first generation of children diagnosed in large numbers with developmental disabilities and their family members, particularly mothers, interpret the disabled identity and labeling process. It will uncover how disability appears in narratives of young adults’ educational, work, and personal experiences. The study also aims to understand how parents narrate the experiences of their child’s “problem behavior”, diagnosis, and subsequent educational, work, and personal endeavors. The study seeks to reveal the social consequences of the medicalization of developmental disabilities. How has the emergence of developmental disabilities changed the way that Japanese talk about diversity and standardization? To what extent does the diagnosis liberate individuals from self-blame and result in provision of appropriate resources? To what extent does the labeling result in stigmatization and marginalization? How are changing understandings of developmental disabilities involved in transforming educational policies, diagnostic practices and treatment, court rulings and laws regarding criminal liability?

14609818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14609818.value: This project investigates the rise of “developmental disabilities” (hattatsu shôgai) as a category of impairment in Japan and explores its meanings for affected individuals, their parents, educators and medical professionals. In Japan, developmental disability refers to congenital disabilities that do not include intellectual disability; the three disabilities most often included are Learning Disability (LD), Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) (Teruyama 2014: 3). The term has arisen to describe clinically distinct disabilities because it covers individuals who are otherwise not recognized as disabled by the Japanese welfare system (Teruyama 2014: 3). Developmental disabilities emerged in public discourse in the past twenty years, starting in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and have become household words in the past decade. In the 2000s, The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) has implemented reforms requiring schools, starting with elementary and junior high schools, to provide appropriate educational services to children with developmental disabilities. In other words, for the first time, a generation of children with various disabilities are labeled as having “developmental disabilities” and are receiving relevant services and treatment. This new biomedical category has triggered widespread therapeutic, biomedical, and educational intervention into the lives of affected children and their families, and is inspiring reforms in the education system emphasizing the need to accommodate diverse learning styles and results. In the wider society, discussion of the suffering of those with developmental disabilities is closely tied to criticism of the Japanese social environment that provides little space for those unable to adjust to standardized social norms, leading to bullying and social withdrawal such as “shut-ins” (hikikomori). Building on recent anthropological studies of medicalization, this study investigates how parents, educators, experts, and affected individuals negotiate new understandings of “developmental disability” and explores the political subjectivities that this process creates. The study does not assume that medicalization liberates individuals from suffering (as often celebrated in the media) nor does it assume that it imposes a top-down homogenization of treatment and experience (as asserted in some social science literature). Rather, drawing on recent anthropological studies (such as Rapp and Ginsburg 2011a, 2011b, Kitanaka 2015) it considers biomedical intervention in the name of “developmental disability” as a political and generative process that creates new understandings and vocabularies to articulate ability, disability, and inclusion. 本項目研究「發展障礙綜合症（発達障害，下稱發展障礙）」作為其中一種障礙症在日本的興起，探討其對病患自身、雙親，特別是母親、教育工作者及專業醫務人員的意義。在日本，發展障礙指不包括智能障礙的先天性障礙症，經常包括以下三項：學習障礙（Learning Disability，LD），自閉症（Autism Spectrum Disorder，ASD）及過度活躍症（Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder，ADHD）（照山，2014：3）。此用詞之所以開始被用作形容臨床上不同的障礙症，是由於此字涵蓋了在其他層面上未被日本福利制度承認為殘疾之人士（照山，2014：3）。從1990年代末及2000年初起，發展障礙在過去二十年出現於公眾討論中，並在以往十年成為家喻戶曉的用字。於2000年代期間，日本文部科學省（The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology，簡稱MEXT）曾進行改革，由小學及初中起，要求學校提供適合的教育服務予患有發展障礙的兒童。換句話說，此為身患障礙症的一代兒童首次被歸類為患上「發展障礙」，並接受著相關服務與治療。新生物醫學領域的出現，引發起治療、醫學及教育上對病患兒童及其家屬生活的廣泛介入，並驅動著教育制度改革，強調包容多元學習模式與成果的需要。在廣泛社會中，有關發展障礙患者所面對的困難，其討論與對日本社會環境的批評關係密切，包括認為日本提供甚少空間給予無法適應標準社會規範的人士，而導致欺凌問題及隱蔽青年（引き籠もり）產生。建基於近期人類學對醫療化（medicalization）的研究，本論文調查父母、教育工作者、專業人士與病患個人如何協商對「發展障礙」的新認知，探討此過程產生的政治主體性。本研究並非假設醫療化令病患從困難中解脫（如媒體所經常渲染），或認為醫療化強行實施了由上而下的治療與經驗的單一化（如某些社會科學文獻所主張）；相反，透過參考近期的人類學研究（例如Rapp and Ginsburg，2011a，2011b；Kitanaka，2015）本項目視以「發展障礙」為名的生物醫學介入，為一種對表達能力、障礙症與共融產生新認知與字彙的政治與生成過程。

14609918.label: Project Objectives
14609918.value: To investigate the influence a guilty plea and the timing of guilty pleas may have on court sentences; To investigate the influence other variables besides guilty pleas may have on court sentences; and To ascertain whether judges in Hong Kong depart from the recommended sentences provided by the sliding scale of sentence discounts for guilty pleas.
rows: To investigate the influence a guilty plea and the timing of guilty pleas may have on court sentences;
To investigate the influence other variables besides guilty pleas may have on court sentences; and
To ascertain whether judges in Hong Kong depart from the recommended sentences provided by the sliding scale of sentence discounts for guilty pleas.

14609918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14609918.value: The plea and the sentence are two of the most important, if not the two most important, aspects of the criminal justice process. The aim of the study is to investigate the impact of the timing of guilty pleas on court sentencing under Hong Kong’s new sentencing framework for guilty pleas. This study builds on the PI’s previous work on late guilty pleas. Previously in Hong Kong, a one-third general sentence discount was given by the court regardless of when the plea was entered until the start of trial. This fundamentally changed with the new sentencing guidelines – the sliding scale of sentence discounts – introduced in September 2016. Now the court must consider the stage at which the guilty plea was entered. Nonetheless, the law still provides judges with flexibility to depart from the guidelines. Previous studies in other jurisdictions have found that sentence reductions are dependent on other variables such as the defendant’s demographic characteristics and criminal record. Therefore, it would be incorrect to simply presume that all criminal cases correspond exactly to the sentence discounts recommended by the sliding scale guidelines and more in-depth research on this is vitally needed. The purpose of the study is to determine the potential effects the stage of guilty plea has on the criminal sentences in Hong Kong and whether the impact of sentence reductions differs for different offences and defendants. The study also seeks to ascertain whether judges depart from the recommended reductions, and if so, under what situations would they do so. A quantitative methodology will be adopted. Using the “Reasons for Sentence” in court cases provided by the Hong Kong Judiciary, a series of variables affecting sentencing will be codified, including the stage when the guilty plea was entered or if the defendant was convicted after trial. The empirical data will then be subjected to statistical analyses. Despite the significance of sentencing and the attention that it often draws from the media and the public, there is a dearth of research on sentencing in Hong Kong especially from an empirical perspective. This study will help to identify what impact the timing of guilty pleas has on sentence outcomes under the new sentencing regime along with other variables that may influence sentencing in Hong Kong. This study will show how the new sliding scale of sentence discounts works in practice and provide useful findings for researchers and practitioners. 認罪及判決是刑事司法程序中最重要的兩個方面。這項研究的目的是調查香港在新的判刑框架下，認罪的時間對法庭判決的影響。這項研究建基於首席調查員早前關於遲延認罪的工作上。 以往在香港，無論在審判開始之前何時認罪，法院都給予三分之一的一般刑期折扣。2016年9月引入的新的量刑指南從根本上改變了這情況 – 即刑期折扣遞減比率。 現在法院必須考量表示認罪的階段。儘管如此，法律仍然為法官提供了可不同與準則的靈活性。之前在其他司法管轄區的研究發現，減刑取決於其他變量因素，例如被告的背景特徵和犯罪記錄。因此，簡單地假定所有刑事案件的判決須跟從刑期折扣遞減指引是不正確。故此，須對此進行更深入的研究。 本研究的目的是考量認罪階段對香港刑事判決的潛在影響，以及減刑幅度會否因罪行及被告的不同而有所不同。本研究還試圖研究法官是否偏離建議的減刑幅度，如果是，他們將在何種情況下這樣做。本研究會採用定量方法。當採用香港司法機構提供“判刑理由“時， 將會數據化一系列影響判刑的可變因素，包括認罪的階段或被告是否在審訊後被定罪，然後對數據進行統計分析。儘管判刑的重要性經常引起媒體和公眾的關注，但在香港判刑方面的研究卻相當缺乏，特別是從實證的角度的研究。本研究將有助於了解香港在新的判刑制度下，認罪請求的時間對判決結果的影響，以及可能影響判刑的其他變量因素。本研究將說明新的刑期折扣遞減比率如何在實踐中發揮作用，並為研究人員和從業人員提供有用的結論。

14609918.label: Realisation of objectives
14609918.value: The project objectives, as outlined above, have all been realized. Let me begin by providing some background to the project and its general purpose. Since 2016, the Hong Kong courts, have introduced what is referred to a “sliding scale of sentence discounts” based on the defendant’s timing of guilty pleas. Previously in Hong Kong, defendants who plead guilty to the crimes that they are charged with, would customarily receive a one-third sentence discount compared to what they would otherwise have received if they had opted to go to trial but ultimately lost i.e., being convicted post-trial. The one-third sentence discount would typically be available up until the day of trial. After the Court of Appeal ruling in HKSAR v. Ngo Van Nam; HKSAR v. Abdou Maikido Abdoulkarim [2016] 5 HKLRD 1; [2016] HKCA 397, however, new sentencing guidelines were issued so that the amount of sentence discount awarded by the courts would correspond with the stage of when the guilty plea by the defendant was made. The full one-third sentence discount would be awarded if the defendant pleaded guilty at the first available opportunity. The sentence discount would be reduced to 20-25% if a trial date has been fixed but the defendant pleaded guilty before the day of trial. The sentence discount is to be 25% if the defendant pleaded guilty on the first day of trial. The sentence discount is further reduced to less than 20% of the defendant pleaded guilty after the trial has commenced. In other words, the sentence discount now operates on a sliding scale based on the timing of guilty pleas. The Court of Appeal has held that sentencing judges have overriding discretion in deviating from the sentencing guidelines. The general purpose of the current project was to empirically investigate how the sliding scale of sentence discounts for guilty pleas work in practice by closely examining sentencing decisions in Hong Kong’s District Court. To achieve this overarching purpose, the project objectives was broken down into three parts: to investigate how guilty pleas and its timing influence sentence outcomes; how other factors besides guilty pleas influence sentence outcomes; and to ascertain whether judges in Hong Kong depart from the recommended sentences provided by the sliding scale of sentence discounts for guilty pleas. The major findings and research outcomes of the three objectives are elaborated in section 6.1 below. As originally indicated in the original proposal submitted, to achieve the project objectives, a dataset would need to be created. An original dataset was created through coding over 1000 ‘Reasons for Sentence’ by the Hong Kong District Court from the beginning of 2018 to the end of 2019. These reasons are written and are made publicly available by the Hong Kong Judiciary. My research team and I meticulously coded the Reasons for Sentence to a dataset for quantitative analyses. Descriptive statistics were first used to give an overview of the sample, including how many cases corresponded to the different stages of when defendants pleaded guilty or not pleaded guilty. In short, descriptive analyses allowed us to determine the prevalence of early and late guilty pleas. It would also allow for an enumeration of the percentage of cases that do and do not abide by the guilty plea guidelines (objective 3). Statistical models were performed to determine the potential effects of the timing of guilty pleas on sentence (objective 1) and the potential effects of other variables besides guilty pleas on sentence (objective 2). Different models that used the actual guilty plea discount awarded by the judge instead of the sentence as the outcome variable helped us to determine to what extent the new sentencing guidelines for guilty pleas were adhered to (objective 3). All the efforts of this 36 months project accumulated to a research monograph entitled “The Timing of Guilty Pleas: Lessons from Common Law Jurisdictions” that at the time of this completion report has been accepted and is in production by Cambridge University Press (CUP). Two additional peer-reviewed articles were published based on the project, which are both more methodology-focused compared with the monograph.
