14609918.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609918.value: Objective 1: Descriptive statistics revealed that there were no major differences in terms of being sentenced to immediate imprisonment for defendants who pleaded early, late or not at all. Differences were found for sentence length, where defendants who pleaded not guilty received prison terms in the highest range. The most interesting result from multivariate models was that the guilty plea stage did not influence whether the defendant was sentenced to immediate imprisonment. Similarly, no significant difference was found between early and late guilty pleas in terms of sentence length. However, defendants who pleaded not guilty and were convicted after trial were found to receive significant higher sentence lengths. This underscores a plea-trial difference in Hong Kong (See Cheng, Timing of Guilty Pleas). Objective 2: Other variables besides guilty pleas were found to be significantly associated with sentence as well. An important variable was age, where the youngest adult defendants in Hong Kong were less likely to receive an immediate imprisonment sentence. Drug offenses in particular would likely lead to a longer imprisonment term. Likewise for defendants with a prior criminal record (See Cheng, Timing of Guilty Pleas). Focusing on just drug trafficking, age was also found to be negatively associated with plea-adjusted sentence length (Cheng, Ri, & Pushkarna, 2020). Objective 3: Judges, despite having discretion to depart from the sentencing guidelines, were found to closely adhere to the sliding scale of sentence discounts (See Cheng, Timing of Guilty Pleas). Where there are departures, female defendants were found to receive higher guilty plea discounts than their male counterparts (See Ri & Cheng, 2022).

14609918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609918.value: The findings of the project revealed that there is much to be studied about sentencing in Hong Kong. In response, I have applied for and was successful in receiving another GRF grant to empirically investigate the influence of sentencing factors on sentences, this time not just in the District Court but High Court as well. The methodology will be similar, however, next project will focus on aggravating and mitigating factors as well as potential influences of different actors, such as judges, prosecutors, and defence lawyers on sentence outcomes.

14609918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609918.value: The aim of the study is to investigate the impact of the timing of guilty pleas on court sentencing under Hong Kong?s new sentencing framework for guilty pleas. Guilty pleas play a significant role in the day-to-day criminal process, but little attention has been paid to the study of guilty pleas in Hong Kong. This project helps to identify what impact the timing of guilty pleas has on sentence outcomes under the new sentencing regime along with other variables that may influence sentencing in Hong Kong. Overall, the findings of this project show how the new sliding scale of sentence discounts works in practice in Hong Kong?s courts.

14610418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14610418.value: While there have been earlier studies on the role of metaphor in music analysis and cognition, the extant research has focused exclusively on writings about music. This project investigates the conceptual and rhetorical uses of metaphor in the context of performance, and is the major component of an on-going research collaboration between three scholars with expertise in music theory and linguistics and two professional string quartets based in Hong Kong and Japan. We approach metaphorical usage in the discourse of string quartet rehearsal from four inter-related perspectives. First, using George Lakoff and Mark Johnson’s theoretical framework of conceptual metaphor (1980) as a starting point, we view metaphorical language as indicative of metaphorical conceptualization, a process by which a target domain (here music) is understood in terms of the entities, properties and relations of a source domain drawn from everyday human perceptions and actions. Thus, analysis of the metaphors used by professional practicing musicians can be a means to access how they understand abstract musical concepts in terms of concrete, embodied experiences. Second, we examine agential ascriptions implied by the players’ metaphorical usage, and argue that the act of performance not only realises potentially agential elements within the musical work, but also create levels of agency beyond the score. Third, we study the metaphors as rhetorical devices and aim to discover how they serve specific discursive needs. Finally, we consider the interactions between verbal and non-verbal modes of communication in rehearsal, and hypothesize that speech and gesture serve as complementary modes of expressing conceptual metaphors about musical events and processes. In developing a new critical paradigm for how performers create (rather than merely reveal) musical structure by way of metaphorical mediation, we also propose redefinition of the meaning of structure in performance and prompt the assessment and refinement of current analytical and pedagogical methods in music theory. The project integrates ethnographic-documentary and critical-analytical approaches in unprecedented ways. At the same time that it draws upon perspectives from music theory, ethnomusicology and linguistics, it is also firmly grounded in empirical fieldwork. The project’s unique audiovisual rehearsal data collection can serve as a valuable resource for future research in Performance Studies, and its analytical outcome may suggest directions for the development of new theories of musical structure. Its interdisciplinary methodology, in turn, has the potential to inform scholarship not only in Performance Studies and music-related fields, but also other disciplines of inquiry. 當代音樂分析學與音樂認知學的隱喻研究全皆聚焦於音樂文獻，未有涉獵音樂演奏者的經驗。 本計劃為香港與日本學者的協同研究，通過實地考察，記錄兩個分別以香港和東京為基地的專業弦樂四重奏排練時樂手間的對話，進而從四個相互關聯的角度，審視當中隱喻運用所呈現的概念思考及溝通模式。 （一）本研究計劃承接雷可夫和強生 （Lakoff and Johnson）的「概念隱喻理論」(conceptual metaphor theory, 1980)，視話語中的隱喻為跨領域認知的呈現。此二元理論模式是由「來源域」(source domain; 基於人類日常行為及感知的具體概念) 和「目標域」(target domain, 抽象概念) 兩個概念領域構成，並以來源域所涵蓋的事物特性、經驗秩序及邏輯關係理解目標域 。因此，藉著以概念系統為主導的隱喻分析， 便可發掘專業樂手們如何把與音樂相關的抽象概念，通過隱喻意涵之映 (mapping)，落實於其具體的生活經驗之中。 （二）檢視樂手的隱喻中如何暗示不同性質和程度的「能動主體」(agencies)，從而論證演奏不但可呈現音樂作品內潛在的能動性，亦能創造樂譜以外的能動層面。 （三）分析隱喻在不同語境中的溝通功能； （四）探討言語溝通與非言語交流之間的互動， 並假設與音樂形態相關的概念隱喻，往往同時依賴話語和肢體語言這兩個相輔相成的表達模式。 除了建立一嶄新的批判範式，研究演奏者如何以隱喻為中介，創造（而不單只是揭示）音樂結構，此研究亦更新「結構」在音樂演奏中的定義，冀能有助評估及改進當下音樂學界沿用的各種分析法及教學法。 本計劃開風氣之先，融合「民族誌」 及「批判分析」的研究取向。以「實證採風」形式蒐集的質性資料， 當可為日後有關音樂表演的研究提供寶貴的參照；同時，集音樂學、民族音樂學及語言學理論觀點於一爐的跨領域研究模式，許亦能對不同專業的學者，有所啟發。

14610418.label: Realisation of objectives
14610418.value: Objective 1 As noted in the midterm progress report, we seriously underestimated the amount of time required for these tasks, which were completed behind schedule. We overcame this problem by adjusting our research plan, pushing ahead with the qualitative components of the project before the complete data corpus is available for quantitative analysis. Objectives 2 and 3 Research activities related to these two objectives were undertaken in tandem. Because metaphorical meaning construction is heavily dependent on context, an inductive approach was adopted to develop a master list of codes incrementally as the conversational transcripts were analysed. The tagging and classification of metaphorical usage in both data sets began with 9 categories of prototypical cross-domain conceptual mappings in the Western art music tradition (e.g., motion, discourse, spatialization). The provisional taxonomy was then refined in iterative steps of (1) preliminary coding, (2) identifying gaps and problems, (3) adjusting the labels and definitions based on consensus discussions and (4) recoding data entries in accordance with the revised labels if needed. During this process, conceptual overlap between categories was resolved, some categories were split while others were amalgamated, and new categories were added. Mixed and compound metaphors were double-coded. Moreover, nearly all categories were subdivided, yielding a two-tiered taxonomy comprising 14 categories and 87 subcategories. The finer level of classification enables metaphor types to be more precisely defined and identifies relationships of dependence between them to facilitate the investigation of concept hierarchies. The following example illustrates: Subcategories of ‘Motion’ Category (1) Journey: moving player The players as moving along a ‘journey’ across a musical landscape, with musical events as points or regions within that landscape. (2) Journey: moving music Musical events are conceptualized as agents moving across a musical landscape while the player remains stationary. (3) Journey: unclear agency Motion across a musical landscape is indicated but agential ascription is unclear. (4) Player as moving force The players act on the musical event to move it from one state-location to another along a path of metaphorical motion. (5) Music as moving force Musical forces act on the players to move them from one state-location to another along a path of metaphorical motion. (6) Direction The focus is on the direction of motion rather than state-locations. (7) Manner of motion The focus is on how motion is achieved rather than state-locations. Inductive analysis for our large data corpus proved time consuming and labour intensive. Although these objectives were fully realised, they were completed behind schedule, resulting in a delay in publication plans. Objective 4 Through contextual analysis of conversational excerpts, we discovered that metaphors may assume the following communicative functions in rehearsal: (1) Elucidation: The speaker evokes metaphor to present a viewpoint. The metaphor may be used in lieu of or in tandem with literal statements to clarify, illustrate, summarize, or amplify the speaker’s meaning. (2) Persuasion: The speaker uses metaphor as a means of convincing listeners to support his/her viewpoint. (3) Verbalizing musical ineffability: The speaker uses multiple metaphors to grasp at and articulate nuances of sound that cannot be expressed with literal or technical language. (4) Circumspection: the players often exchanged different metaphors when negotiating interpretative options. Metaphors facilitates the sharing of speculative opinions by relieving speakers from the need to make categorical statements before their ideas are fully formed. Disagreement may also be expressed by the offer of an alternative metaphor rather than a direct challenge, thereby avoiding confrontation and possible interpersonal conflict. (5) Social bonding: the use of a surprising and often humorous analogical reference promotes collegiality through a shared joke, and levels out possible intellectual or task-oriented differences. Objective 5 Through detailed analysis of rehearsal segments, we discovered that the performers manifested their agencies both physically and metaphorically during rehearsal, and that these intersect with perceived intra-opus agencies in fluid and dynamic ways. We explored the theoretical implications of our findings and proposed an original paradigm, in the form of a circular network of dialogues, to model the interactions between metaphorical conceptualization and agential ascription in ensemble coordination and communication: (1) interactions between metaphorical intra-opus musical elements; (2) discussions and exchanges between real-world performers; and (3) a continuous metaphorical dialogue between the musical work and the performers. Objective 6 Our analysis began with dividing the rehearsal activities into three broad categories: (1) Play through: continuous playing of music; (2) Musical conversations: discussions about the music being performed, complemented by co-speech musicking and physical gestures; and (3) Non-musical interactions: activities that are unrelated to music performance, such as social chit chat. We then focused on musical conversations and classified the co-speech gestures found therein by function: Typology of Co-speech Gestures A. Physical gestures (1) Emphatic: Gesticulation enhancing rhetorical impact, e.g., waving hands in the air to express enthusiasm. (2) Iconic: Visualization of musical elements or verbal meaning, e.g., tracing the ‘shape’ of a musical phrase with the arm; pinching thumb and forefinger together to accompany the word ‘small’. (3) Emblematic: Conventionalized hand movements whose meaning is widely established and shared, e.g., thumbs up to indicate ‘like’. (4) Indexical: Pointing to an object, person, or location, e.g., using the bow to indicate a place in the score. B. Musicking gestures: performers use playing or singing rather than words to express what they mean (1) Playing: Demonstration using instruments. (2) Singing: Demonstration using singing. (3) Bodily musicking: Demonstration using parts of the body, e.g., tapping out a rhythm. (4) Linguistic musicking: Phonetic, non-lexical uses of language to imitate sound gestures. Comparing the gesture coding against the metaphor coding, we observed that iconic and emblematic gestures were often used to visualize metaphors (e.g., a flexed-biceps gesture with the personification metaphor ‘like Hercules’; arms reaching outward in a circular motion to indicate a ‘plump’ sound). They synchronized with speech to embody a single underlying meaning. Emphatic and indexical gestures accompanied both metaphorical and non-metaphorical utterances. They may add rhetorical emphasis to metaphors but do not provide imagery for them. Some, but not all, examples of musicking gestures were related to metaphorical usage. The iconic and emblematic gestures have interesting semiotic and agential implications. Given that the notion of musical gestures is inherently metaphorical and premised on the conceptual mapping of sonic phenomena to imagined human gestures, when these mental representations are embodied and enacted by real-life human beings, the ‘gesture’ metaphor is turned back onto itself, and the agency of the musical work becomes merged with that of the performer. We also found that the players frequently used the phonetic features of language as a means of musicking. Both subject groups used non-lexical vocal syllables to mimic the rhythms, articulations, accentuations, and phrasing of sound gestures. Some strategies were language-specific: Romer added made-up lyrics to melodies, using Cantonese speech tones to illustrate melodic inflections; Excelsior used gitaigo (擬態語), Japanese ideophones that depict non-auditory states, conditions and actions, in discussions of interpretation and execution. Surprisingly, sound-imitating onomatopoeic words were rarely used by either group. We propose the term ‘linguistic musicking’ for these non-lexical uses of language. Objective 7 The two data sets were coded using the taxonomies for metaphor, agent, and gesture types (described above), as well as for representative keywords and recurrent themes. The multi-coded data is stored and presented in the form of a searchable database, with each entry linked to the video file, transcription, and score passage of the relevant rehearsal segment. We extracted the segments involving discussion of musical structure and examined how their conceptual understanding is expressed through the mediation of metaphor.

14610418.label: Major findings and research outcome
14610418.value: Research outputs: 2 peer-reviewed publications (#s 1: published; #2: in press); 1 conference paper (#4). A book-length study is under preparation (see #3 for book proposal). Major findings: 1. This project created a large database of metaphors used in the rehearsal discourse of two professional string quartets and developed a taxonomy for their classification. See #3 for charts and diagrams illustrating the quantitative analysis of data. 2. Qualitative analysis of the links between metaphor categories and topics of discussion led to the following generalizations for the most frequently occurring categories: a. ‘Motion’ metaphors were typically used in the context of ensemble coordination to describe the ‘real-time’ unfolding of musical events. Musical structure was conceptualized as teleological and emergent. b. ‘Spatial’ metaphors typically appeared in discussions of form, such as descriptions of melodies in terms of ‘shape’, texture in terms of ‘density’, and large-scale organization in terms of ‘frameworks’. Musical structure was conceptualized as synchronic. c. ‘Sensory’ metaphors compared musical phenomena to bodily states and the non-sonic modalities of sight, touch, and taste. They typically functioned as expressive shorthands for nuances of tone quality (see #4). d. ‘Personification’ and ‘affective’ metaphors were typically used to describe stylistic character through associations with mood, atmosphere, emotions, and imaginary personas. 3. Most rehearsal discussions focused on structural elements that were immediately perceptible from moment to moment, such as phrasing, stylistic character, tempo, and tone quality. Metaphors were evoked on an ad hoc basis and abandoned once they serve their rhetorical purpose. 4. Metaphors often served as a means of exploring interpretative ideas before they are fully formed. Aside from representing structural understanding, they also enacted the process of discovering such understanding. 5. Metaphorical utterances were characterised by agential ambiguity and ascriptive fluidity. Both subject groups constantly and seamlessly shifted between assigning agency to the music and themselves. The composer was never named as an agent; instead, intra-opus agency was often attributed to an unspecified agent ‘it’ and implicitly cast as autonomous. These findings suggest the subsumption of work agency under the agency of the performer and challenge the semiotic hierarchy that score-based, composer-centric ideologies often assume (see #1). 6. Speaking, musicking, and physical gestures may serve as synchronous and co-expressive means of communication in metaphorical utterances. 7. Practical applications of the research outcome include the use of drama as metaphor and method in public music theory (see #2).

14610418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610418.value: Potential for further development: 1. Since this project focused on the impact of metaphorical usage on musical structure, follow-up research will engage non-structural aspects of performance, especially the players’ use of sensory and embodied metaphors to discuss aspects of tone quality and execution. 2. Our new paradigm for the interactions between metaphorical conceptualization and agential ascription in ensemble music-making has strong methodological implications for music theory and can inform the development of a performer-oriented analytical approach for chamber music. 3. The research outcome on the co-expressiveness between auditory imagery and physical movement and the metaphorical uses of gestures in rehearsal discussions may provide the groundwork for a broader study of the communicative functions of non-playing gestures in performance. 4. The notion of ‘linguistic musicking’ prompts further investigation of how speech sounds are used to represent musical gestures within the rehearsal context, the semiotic functions of non-lexical vocable syllables, tonal inflections, and ideophones, and the role of affect and voice in speech-music interactions. 5. Further practical applications in public music theory may be explored. Proposed Course of action: Completion of the book manuscript and presentation of new research outcome as peer-reviewed publications and international conference papers. The PI will be responsible for all follow-up research.

14610418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14610418.value: This project investigates the role of metaphor in shaping and representing musical understanding in the context of music rehearsal. Our research is empirically grounded in audio-visual recordings of 15 rehearsals by two professional string quartets over two nine-month periods. We created a large, 1393-item database of metaphorical usage and inductively developed a two-tiered taxonomy for their classification. Discourse analysis of conversational segments discovers close links between metaphorical usage and moment-to-moment perception, and identifies ‘motion’, ‘spatial’, ‘sensory’, ‘personification’ and ‘affective’ metaphors as the most frequently occurring categories. Agential analysis reveals considerable interaction and overlap between intra-opus and performers’ agencies and prompts our proposition of a circular-network paradigm to model their metaphorical dialogue. Gestural analysis based on an original typology demonstrate that speaking, musicking, and physical movement are synchronous and co-expressive means of metaphorical representation. We propose that, by enabling the experiential impact of musical sound to be mentally conceptualized, verbally discussed and physically embodied, metaphors enact processes of interpretative discovery and exploration and serve as a means for performers to create musical structure together. This performer-oriented perspective of musical structure interrogates the score-based, composer-centred ideologies behind current music-analytical models and suggests new methodological directions for music theory and performance studies.

14610918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14610918.value: China is commonly seen as an importer of legal thought rather than as its exporter. Scholarship on Chinese law examines the relationship between Chinese law and global legal thought almost exclusively in terms of the reception of foreign legal thought into China. This oversight masks an important recent trend in the globalization of legal thought. Each year, the Chinese government trains hundreds of lawyers from developing countries in aspects of Chinese law and sends missions to developing countries to provide assistance on law reform. While there exists some scholarship on the global relevance of specific Chinese legal institutions and development policies, no sustained attempts have been made to assess the global relevance of Chinese legal thought. To address this oversight, this project constructs a Chinese mode of legal thought through a comparative legal theoretical inquiry, and examines Chinese efforts to disseminate information about it in developing countries. A mode of legal thought refers to the legal vocabulary, institutional arrangements and the style of legal reasoning in a given legal system. It is, hence, a more foundational category of legal theoretical analysis than the study of particular legal rules, legal institutions, political ideology, and the rule of law. The present project constructs a mode of contemporary Chinese legal thought through: (i) a survey of theoretical and comparative Chinese legal scholarship; (ii) analysis of a selection of people’s courts’ decisions and; (iii) study of policy statements on adjudicative techniques and other elements of Chinese legal thought. The project also examines how Chinese law is actually portrayed to foreign lawyers in Chinese legal development cooperation. This project establishes a theoretical framework for examining the global policy relevance of Chinese legal thought. Chinese legal scholars and development organizations have identified the informal use of power and the informal “local knowledge” about such uses of power as distinct elements of the Chinese legal system. In contrast to advocates of liberal legal thought in the West and in developing countries, Chinese legal scholarship and policy documents embrace this form of knowledge as a valuable governance tool in its own right. Such anti-formal pragmatism stands in stark contrast to even the most pragmatic forms of legal thought promoted in Western legal development assistance and in Western legal scholarship. Finally, the very fact that legal knowledge now flows from China to other developing countries calls for a profound perspective change to our understanding of the globalization of law.

14610918.label: Realisation of objectives
14610918.value: 1. The first research objective yields a (relatively) new method for studying the globalization of Chinese and other forms of law and legal knowledge: rhetorical theory. This method is discussed in an article entitled “Chinese Legal Thought on the Global and the Domestic Stage: A Rhetorical Study” (15,000 words), which is forthcoming with the Asian Journal of Comparative Law in 2023. As this article argues, the study of the global relevance of Chinese legal thought calls for a close examination of various genres of Chinese ideological and legal speech. This is because different statements in Chinese ideological and legal speech aim to achieve different things. Whereas statements about the global relevance of Chinese legal thought are extremely ambitious in some genres of Chinese ideological speech, other genres of speech in China neither seek to establish clear distinctions between Chinese and foreign legal thought nor argue that Chinese legal thought constitutes a paradigm-changing improvement to global law. The forthcoming article explains these differences through the perspectives of rhetorical theory. The globalization of Chinese legal thought also calls for the study of communication and persuasion between authors and their audiences, which is another topic in rhetorical theory. In contrast to Western colonial powers, China is not willing to (or capable to) forcibly spread its legal thought in foreign countries. While some specific Chinese legal institutions may be influential abroad (such as the concept of internet sovereignty), Chinese legal thought needs to be perceived as persuasive in order to have a global footprint. This methodological point is discussed in an article entitled “Production and Global Dissemination of Chinese Legal Ideology: Implications for the Study of Illiberalism” (21,000 words), which is forthcoming with The Cardozo Journal of International and Comparative Law in 2023. 2. The PI and RA conducted a survey of contemporary Chinese legal scholarship on the idiosyncratic nature of Chinese legal thought as well as on a close reading of selected Chinese judicial decisions, which illustrate adjudicative techniques deployed by judges. To this end, the PI and the RA (who started his 12-months appointment on 10 July 2019) examined textual sources for the analysis and identified the most relevant sources for achieving the project objectives. After studying Chinese scholarship and policy texts, the PI and RA moved on to examine Chinese adjudicative techniques. The PI and RA chose to conduct this study by examining a selection of the Guiding Cases issued by the Chinese Supreme People’s Court (SPC). Guiding Cases are selected by the SPC to address particularly important issues in Chinese legislation and, consequently, they can be expected to display officially sanctioned Chinese adjudicative techniques. Fifty Guiding Cases were selected for analysis at this stage, starting from the most recently issued decisions. The findings from the above survey are discussed in the above-mentioned article entitled “Chinese Legal Thought on the Global and the Domestic Stage: A Rhetorical Study” and in an article tentatively entitled “A Global Turn in Chinese Legal Ideology?”, which is forthcoming with World Comparative Law. The former article describes how the idiosyncratic nature of Chinese legal thought is discussed in different genres of Chinese law. The so-called ceremonial genre of Chinese law – e.g., many ideologically oriented texts and political speeches – has insisted on the unique advantages of Chinese legal thought, without deliberating about these advantages. Some texts in the so-called deliberative genre of Chinese legal thought – which typically comprises legal scholarship – characterizing Chinese legal thought through its commitment to substantive justice and pragmatism. In these texts, the Chinese approach also fits contextual social realities better than the Western approach, serves the people’s needs better than the Western approach, and facilitates pragmatist and informal solutions better than the Western approach. The latter article focuses on the Xi Jinping era, pointing out that Chinese ideological ambitions have increased significantly in the ceremonial genre of speech compared to texts in the previous Hu Jintao era. 3. The third research objective concerned Chinese efforts to disseminate information about Chinese law in developing countries. This research objective was severly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, which made it impossible to use much of the budget reserved for conducting interviews. Fortunately the PI was able to conduct a research trip to Nairobi, Kenya, from 3-17 November 2019, just before international travel became impossible and many Chinese legal development programs came to a halt. Nairobi was chosen as a destination because of Kenya’s close ties with China and because Kenyan (private sector) lawyers are relatively open to being interviewed on this topic. The PI conducted 13 interviews in Kenya, meeting Kenyan lawyers, academics and members of the international community. The interviews were semi-structured, generally addressing information about Kenya’s legal cooperation with China, the portrayal of Chinese law in legal development cooperation, Kenyan perceptions on Chinese law, and perceptions on the Chinese legal development model generally. Kenya was meant to be only a starting point for these interview studies, which are crucial for studying a relatively sensitive topic, such as Chinese legal development cooperation. Unfortunately, it was not possible to conduct more research trips due to the COVID-19 situation even with the maximum number of project extensions. The pandemic worsened suddenly in early 2022 due to the emergence of the omicron variant, which again closed international borders. Instead of conducting more field research, the PI completed a literary review on jurisprudence in China’s development partners, focusing on post-colonial legal theoretical scholarship in Kenya, Tanzania and Ethiopia. These findings are presented in the above-mentioned article entitled “Production and Global Dissemination of Chinese Legal Ideology: Implications for the Study of Illiberalism.” This article describes the image of Chinese law in Chinese government whitepapers and in the deliberative genre of Chinese law (mostly legal scholarship), which can provide potential arguments for Chinese legal development cooperation. 4. The above-mentioned article, “Production and Global Dissemination of Chinese Legal Ideology: Implications for the Study of Illiberalism,” examines the contrast between Chinese and Western legal thought, expanding this analysis to the production of legal ideology and persuasion. In order to gain more relevance for the article’s findings, the article also expands its scope from China to illiberal regimes (without classifying China as “an illiberal regime,” however). In addition to describing the above-mentioned statements about the unique advantages of Chinese legal thought (see part 5.3.3 above), this article explains how the production of ideological statements about Chinese law is influenced by China’s circumstances, which may differ from the “Western” circumstances and influence Chinese development experts’ ability to engage in persuasion in front of foreign audiences. 5. The above-mentioned article “Production and Global Dissemination of Chinese Legal Ideology: Implications for the Study of Illiberalism” discusses the potential policy-relevance of Chinese legal thought in developing countries, focusing on East Africa. Due to the tentative nature of Chinese legal development cooperation in this region – which was mostly halted during the COVID pandemic – this discussion relies on existing arguments in Chinese and East African legal discourses, assessing how East African audiences may respond to arguments about the relevance of Chinese law and legal ideology in East Africa. The theoretical framework for discussing this relevance is derived from rhetorical theory. The article describes how specific argumentative moves about the relevance of Chinese law (see above Part 5.3.3) relate to the rhetorical landscape in East Africa.

14610918.label: Major findings and research outcome
14610918.value: This project has studied the as globalization of Chinese legal thought through the interaction between the domestic and global stages of Chinese ideological advocacy, using the tools of rhetorical theory. It has found that arguments about the nature and global significance of Chinese law are made for different purposes and for different audiences. The most ambitious statements about the global significance of Chinese legal thought are produced within a “ceremonial” genre of speech. Domestic Chinese ceremonial speech is meaningful in the Chinese context, but it translates poorly to globally influential ideological speech. Foreign audiences will find more persuasive arguments about the significance of Chinese legal thought in Chinese deliberative speech, such as parts of Chinese legal scholarship. While arguments made in the deliberative genre are more persuasive than ceremonial speech, specific argumentative moves within this genre are not always helpful for the international advocacy of Chinese legal thought. Moreover, arguments in the deliberative genre are not consistently reflected in Chinese judicial decisions. This analysis highlights the role of language and persuasion in the globalization of law. This project also highlights the differences between the production of ideology in different regimes, including China, “the West” and various illiberal regimes. First, the domestic priorities of illiberal ideological speech may not support ideological advocacy efforts in foreign contexts. Second, characteristically illiberal argumentative strategies may be less effective in front of foreign audiences than they are domestically. Third, illiberal ideological sensitivities may impair, or make unavailable, certain advocacy strategies, which could be effective in front of foreign audiences. As regards the advocacy of Chinese legal ideology, these challenges should be partly understood as consequences of domestic Chinese politics. While globally ambitious speech in CCP ideology and pro-establishment legal scholarship reflects China’s international aspirations, it does not aim to persuade foreign audiences about the advantages of Chinese legal thought. Despite such challenges, this project has concluded that Chinese ideological speech has been effective in foreign contexts. Among other things, Chinese ideological advocacy has made it easier for foreign politicians and legal scholars to criticize Western promotion of the rule of law and human rights. This project illustrates the possibilities and challenges of Chinese ideological advocacy efforts by situating various arguments about the advantages of Chinese legal thought within the East African context.

14610918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14610918.value: As China is starting to open up to the world, Chinese legal development cooperation programs are likely to resume. When this happens, field research will again become possible and fruitful both in China and in China’s development partners. The methodological tools and theoretical frameworks established in this project will help researchers to assess the global relevance of Chinese legal thought in specific contexts.

14610918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14610918.value: China is commonly seen as an importer of legal thought rather than as its exporter. This oversight masks an important recent trend in the globalization of law. Today Chinese legal scholars and development experts believe that Chinese law is globally influential. China was active in disseminating information about its law to foreign lawyers before the COVID-19 pandemic. This research project has studied the globalization of Chinese law both as a matter of domestic Chinese politics and as a question of the foreign reception of Chinese law. The articles produced in this research project explain how Chinese legal scholars and experts see the unique features and advantages of Chinese law. For instance, some Chinese legal scholars argue that Chinese law is more just than “bookish” western law. Some Chinese legal scholars and government experts also argue that Chinese law presents profoundly new innovations for the world. The articles produced in this research project consider how such arguments about the unique nature of Chinese law and its advantages may be received in foreign regions and in East Africa, in particular.

14611618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14611618.value: New video remote sensing satellites capture continuous multispectral images at multiple angles. They can stare at the same site continuously and produce videos which are indeed hundreds of images at a very short period of time. Different from conventional remote sensing, they offer a brand new data which can be used to monitor moving objects like vehicles. New research challenges appear as the added angular effect may provide new information in addition to spectral reflectance. So far, it has been difficult to model accurately the relationship between spectral reflectance and viewing angles which vary among different land covers. With the new video data, this becomes possible and will significantly improve remote sensing research and applications. This proposal will formulate a general research framework for this continuous multi-angle remote sensing data. We will first analyze characteristics of the new data and devise new techniques to reduce noise within these images. Feature extraction will help unravel the hidden dimensions embedded in this data. New dimension with the added angular effect is anticipated. Image classification will be implemented to verify whether this new angular dimension can improve classification accuracy. Since most existing remote sensing software cannot process this brand new data, a software system will be constructed to process and analyze this new video satellite data efficiently. This project will advance the research frontier of multi-angle remote sensing with novel approach to de-noising, parsimonious and effective feature extraction, and accurate classification. It will extend the scope of real-life applications to a variety of problems with complex structures whose analysis is beyond the capability of single-angle remote sensing.

14611618.label: Realisation of objectives
14611618.value: 1. General Framework A general research framework was set up initially at pixel and object levels to ascertain the variation of spectral, spatial and viewing angles within the CMARS images. Noise distribution, de-nosing and feature selection were also explored. At pixel level, the additional dimension of viewing angles resembles hyperspectral images for which over hundred spectral bands wee available. Spectral values of CMARS data exhibited great variation along the changing viewing angles with fluctuations with an obvious trend. Apparently, it was difficult to discern some objects at pixel level based on one single viewing angle. Yet, we could observe from the fitted curves that spectral values intermittently varied within different angle ranges under different bands. Using a single angle for classification became risky and unreliable. The trends along the varying viewing angles exhibited by different land covers was explored for their discrimination. New classifier at later stage was designed for this. Working at object levels was also attempted in initial experiments. Different land covers also exhibited different trend. However, as work at pixel level constituted more rigorous testing. The project focused more on works at pixel level. 2. Denoising and 3. Feature Selection CMARS images were taken as fourth-order tensor. Principal component analysis was adopted as the de-nosing model which retains structural information of the angle dimension. It helped denoise and retain essential structural information in a few major principal components which also fulfilled the purpose of feature selection. The first major PC was found to be loaded heavily as an average brightness image. Minor PCs depicted changes of objects due to both actual moving objects such as vehicles and ships. They also captured salient height features. Loadings in these minor PCS showed a consistent pattern which highlighted the changing viewing angle and height information which were critical for development in the classification module. 4. Classification Paper 1 is published in Remote Sensing (Impact Factor: 4.509). In this paper, we tested the CMARS data with different combination of CMARS data (one angle, double angle, multiple angle) together with the machine learning support vector machine and random forest algorithms. To achieve a higher accuracy, deep convolutional neural network (CNN) was developed. In this CNN, CMARS data was deeply explored in order to make full use of changing reflectance curve of land covers, spatial information in one frame, and height feature, thus, three separate branches were introduced first in our CNN. For each branch, three different low level features are inputted to convolutional layers to extract corresponding high level semantic features. Then a layer normalization was applied before the ReLu activation function to alleviate the small sample set problem and avoided gradient vanishing phenomenon as well. After applying the ReLu activation function on the three normalized feature cubes, they were concatenated together as input of a convolutional layer to extract joint feature, followed by a pooling layer. The final layer was a fully connected layer with a softmax function, which could map the feature into the sample label space whose dimensions were equal to the number of classes. Overall accuracy could be raised for 9% with the test data in New Delhi, India. We found multi‐angle did add value to classification result than single angle data. Images of adjacent angles had a higher level of commonness and lower level of complementarity. More angles did improve classification accuracy but the effect tapered off gradually. Paper 2 is developed and will be submitted to IEEE Transaction for Geoscience and Remote Sensing (Impact Factor 8.125) for publication. To make the best use of CMARS data, a novel convolution neural network classifier was developed with 3 key modules. First, A 4D convolution layer was introduced to extract joint spectral spatial angular features. Second, based on the de-noised principal components, a height attention module was developed to obtain salient height features of land covers in accordance with their angular dimension. Third, an effective fusion module was further devised to interact height features with spectral-spatial-angular features. The classifier was tested using New Delhi and Hong Kong data acquired by Jilin-1 satellite. To compare the effectiveness of this novel CNN classifier, 5 state-of-the-art deep learning based methods, namely ResNet, HybridSN 3D-2D, SSRN, 3DOC-SSAN and A2S2K -ResNet were also experimented and verified on their accuracy. An ablation study was done with different combination of the 3 developed modules. Four different fusion methods were tested against the proposed method. All the result showed highest accuracy attained using the proposed method with Kappa of 96.69 and 98.37 for the New Delhi and Hong Kong data respectively. In terms of computation cost, the proposed method took the second lowest computational cost and the least training time as compared with the 5 other DL methods. 5 & 6 Software System ad Real life applications Aligning closely with 3 and 4, the software system based on 4D convolution together with height attention module and fusion module was developed. This system was tested to classify relevant land use and land cover using the Jilin-1 satellite CMARS data in New Delphi and Hong Kong.

14611618.value: CMARS data or satellite video, opens new research potential for more effective information extraction of remote sensing data. For further research, we plan to work on • incorporation of 4D normalization into the network design to improve the stability of the model. • Optimization of angle information will be a further development. In addition to applications for capturing moving objects such as ships, cars and trains, the viewing angle and height information are important data for geographical studies. This project explores how the changing viewing angles affect the remote sensing spectral. We have effectively reduced the noise inherent in the data and extract essential height features. A new 4D convolution neural network with height attention and fusion modules is developed. This new method is tested effective to produce very accurate land cover information.

14611718.label: Realisation of objectives
14611718.value: Objective 1: In previous research, two-level regression (TLR) has been used as an alternative to the traditional regression method which assumes a deterministic effect from a moderator to the association between an independent variable and a dependent variable, leading to a natural consequence of heteroscedasticity. We made use of the unique pattern of heteroscedasticity in each moderation model, and applied TLR to address the problem of analytically equivalent moderation models. Specifically, we proposed a two-step procedure. In Step 1, two sets of TLR analysis are conducted in which the roles of independent variable and moderator are reversed across the two sets. As such, the reduced equations of the two sets of TLR would be different, yielding different model fit to the data. In Step 2, using BIC, we compare the model fit to the data between the two reduced equations. With this comparison, statistical evidence is available for determining whether a particular variable should be better positioned as an independent variable or a moderator in a moderation model. Hence, with the aforementioned two-step procedure, objective 1 was achieved. Objective 2: In single-level coefficient-as-outcome method (SiLCO), we conceptualized a moderation effect with a two-level structure in which a moderator W is treated as a Level-2 variable while the independent variable X and dependent variable Y are treated as Level-1 variables. The effect of W on the association between X and Y can then be tested to conclude a moderation effect (i.e., a cross-level moderation). As the way to form a two-level structure depends on the choice of the Level-2 variable, we can alternatively construct a competing model by choosing the independent variable X as the Level-2 variable and form another two-level structure. To conduct moderation analysis under SiLCO, we proposed a two-step procedure. In Step 1, two two-level models are constructed by treating (1) W as the Level-2 variable within which X and Y (Level-1 variables) are nested, and (2) X as the Level-2 variable within which W and Y (Level-1 variables) are nested. In Step 2, given the two specified models in Step 1, two sets of hierarchical linear modeling analysis can be performed and goodness of fit measures such as AIC can be used to compare the results and to decide whether W or X should be better positioned as a moderator in a moderation model. As a result, with the aforementioned two-step procedure, objective 2 was achieved. Objective 3: In direction dependence analysis in moderation (DMod), the skewness of the residual in a regression model can help determine which direction of prediction (X→Y vs. Y→X) approximates better the actual data generation process. Therefore, we made use of this property and extended the directional dependence analysis to the test of a moderation model. Specifically, to conduct DMod, we proposed a two-step procedure. In Step 1, two regression models are tested on the three variables of X, W, and Y that constitute a moderation model. The first regression model tests the prediction of X on Y, while second regression model tests the prediction of W on Y. In Step 2, the skewness of the two residuals in the regression models are compared using a bootstrapping confidence interval. If W is better positioned as a moderator which contains a normal error term at the Level-2 equation under the two-level moderation structure, the skewness of the residual in the second regression model will be smaller than that in the first regression model. With this two-step procedure, objective 3 was achieved. Objective 4: A series of simulation studies has been conducted to compare the performance of the three methods under different model conditions including Level-2 sample size, Level-1 sample size, size of the moderation effect, and size of the intraclass correlation. Based on the results of the simulation study, the practical guidelines for the applied researchers can be summarized as follow: 1. When the data dependency level in each Level-2 unit is not trivial (e.g., ICC > 0.10), SiLCO is a legitimate method in differentiating analytically equivalent moderation models. 2. When the data dependency level in each Level-2 unit is trivial (e.g., ICC < 0.05), both SiLCO and TLR are the legitimate methods in differentiating analytically equivalent moderation models. 3. Given a medium size of moderation effect (i.e., the explained variance in outcome equals 13%), SiLCO and TLR require a minimum sample size of 200 to achieve sufficient empirical power (i.e., empirical power exceeds 90%) in differentiating analytically equivalent moderation models. 4. DMod generally failed to work well in a reasonable range of sample size (e.g., N < 2,500). Hence, objective 4 is achieved. Objectives 5 - 6: To cross-validate the simulation results, we applied the proposed methods to analyze real data sets in two empirical studies. Since TLR and SiLCO had yielded acceptable performance in our simulation study, these two methods were used to cross-validate the simulation results. 1. Test of competing moderation models with different temporal sequence The first empirical study (N = 192) measured three variables in two different time points (a 3-month interval) to examine the person-environment interaction on psychological well-being. The three variables are social cynicism belief measured at time 1 (environmental factor), dispositional envy measured at time 2 (personal factor) and life satisfaction measured at time 2 (psychological well-being). Given that the three variables were measured in two time points, two competing moderation models can be specified. Model 1 hypothesized a moderation effect of social cynicism belief at time 1 on the prediction between dispositional envy and life satisfaction at time 2, while model 2 hypothesized a moderation effect of dispositional envy at time 2 on the prediction between social cynicism belief at time 1 and life satisfaction at time 2. In essence, Model 1 should be conceptually more reasonable than Model 2, which hypothesized that a variable at a later time point could influence the effect of a variable at an earlier time point. Empirical results were consistent with our expectation in which both TLR and SiLCO showed a better model fit in Model 1 than that in Model 2. Hence, objective 5 was achieved. 2. Test of moderated mediation and mediated moderation models The second data analysis relied on a real data set in a published study (Ng, Cheung, & Lau, 2019). This empirical study recruited 586 adolescents and young adults, and measured three variables of self-esteem, dispositional envy and subjective happiness at a single time point. This study hypothesized a mediated moderation process in which the moderation effect of group membership (adolescents vs. young adults) on the prediction between dispositional envy and subjective happiness was mediated by one’s level of self-esteem. In fact, given the same set of variables, there exists an alternative model representing a moderated mediation process in which the mediation effect from group membership to subjective happiness through self-esteem could be moderated by one’s level of dispositional envy. By applying TLR and SiLCO, it was observed that the model with self-esteem as a moderator fitted the data better than the model with dispositional envy as a moderator, supporting the hypothesis of a mediated moderation process. Therefore, objective 6 was achieved.

14611718.label: Major findings and research outcome
14611718.value: Research outcome: In this project, we proposed three methods (TLR, SiLCO, DMod) for differentiating analytically equivalent moderation models. Empirical results indicated that TLR and SiLCO performed satisfactorily under a variety of model conditions. Practical guidelines, in terms of sample size determination and data dependency, for a successful differentiation between two analytically equivalent moderation models were given. We also demonstrated how the methods can be extended to compare complicated models (e.g., moderation mediation) that include a moderation process as a component. Major findings: Through a series of simulation studies, we (1) tested the performance and efficiency of the methods in estimating the moderation effect and (2) examined the empirical power to differentiate two competing moderation models. First, simulation results indicated that both TLR and SiLCO performed satisfactorily in estimating the moderation effect with relative percentage bias less than 5% across all sample size combinations and data dependency levels. When data dependency is trivial, both TLR and SiLCO yielded unbiased standard error estimates of moderation effect with relative percentage bias less than 10%. However, when data dependency is not trivial (e.g., ICC > 0.10), SiLCO maintained to achieve the unbiased standard error estimates while TLR started to show a substantial underestimation in standard error. More importantly, the bias in standard error increases as the increase of Level-1 sample size. Overall, these findings highlighted that the conceptualizations of hierarchical structure underlying TLR and SiLCO may be different. Second, both SiLCO and TLR generally yielded acceptable empirical power in differentiating between two competing moderation models when data dependency is trivial. To achieve at least 90% of empirical power, a minimum sample size of 200 (e.g., N_j = 20 and N_i = 10) is required for both SiLCO and TLR. Consistent with the results of the estimated standard error, when the data dependency is not trivial, SiLCO showed acceptable empirical power with a sample size of at least 200 and TLR showed a decrease of empirical power along with the increase of Level-1 sample size. Third, across all data dependency levels, DMod did not achieve sufficient empirical power (i.e., less than 80%) in differentiating between two competing moderation models under all combinations of sample size being investigated. As a whole, these findings indicated that both SiLCO and TLR are the legitimate methods in differentiating analytically equivalent moderation models whereas DMod fails to perform well in a reasonable range of sample size and is subjected to further modification.

14611718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14611718.value: Further development of the research can be focused on two areas. The first area focuses on extending the currently-proposed methods to accommodate latent variables. Conceptually, psychological constructs are not directly observable and should be modeled as latent variables. Although this project showed that TLR and SiLCO may work well in a manifest moderation model, they may not be directly extendable to a latent moderation model. Future studies may further develop a latent variable version for these methods. The second area focuses on extending the currently-proposed methods to differentiate more complicated analytically equivalent models. By analyzing real data sets, this project showed that the proposed methods have the potential to differentiate between moderated mediation model and mediated moderation model. Nonetheless, this potential has not been further validated using simulation studies that systematically examine the performance under different model conditions. Besides, other than the pair of moderated mediation and mediated moderation models, there are plenty other competing models sharing a common analytically-equivalent moderation component (e.g., a direct moderation model vs. a second-stage moderated mediation model). Therefore, future studies may design a more comprehensive simulation study to examine the performance of these methods in differentiating more complicated analytically equivalent models.

14611718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14611718.value: This project proposed different methods in differentiating analytically equivalent moderation models. Moderation occurs when the effect of an independent variable on a dependent variable varies as a function of a moderator variable. One can typically test a simple moderation model with a statistical model that includes the independent variable, the moderator variable and the product of independent and moderator variables as the predictors of the dependent variable. However, it is obvious that this statistical model does not clearly define which variable should be considered as the independent variable or moderator. Therefore, given the same statistical model, researchers can always come up with two entirely different interpretations that depict two different moderation process, leading to conceptual confusion in different psychological phenomenon. The significance and value of this project lie on its development of methods to address this problem, attempting to differentiate analytically equivalent moderation models. The proposed methods can help applied researchers evaluate the model fit of two competing moderation models, thereby providing a statistical justification of which variable should be better positioned as a moderator or an independent variable in a moderation model.

14612118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612118.value: Escalation of commitment refers to a decision bias wherein decision makers non-rationally escalation their commitment toward failing course of action. Because key decision makers exhibit this bias in organizations will yield extremely bad consequences to the organizations, this bias probably is the most studied managerial decision bias by organizational researchers (Brockner, 1992; Kwong & Wong, 2014; Staw, 1976, 1981; Wong & Kwong, 2007a, in press). This bias is very paradoxical because it is exactly opposite to the consensus of human behaviors under the law-of-effect (Thorndike, 1989), which posits that people behavioral tendency decreases after the behavior receives negative feedback. This paradox is called learning-escalation paradox. In our early work funded by General Research Fund (#16503614), we successfully resolve this paradox by extending the unit of law-of-effect from a decision level to a decision-strategy level (see Wong & Kwong, in press for details). The successful resolution of the learning-escalation paradox points to adaptive learning to be a new approach in understanding escalation of commitment. Our previous work (Wong & Kwong, in press) in the earlier GRF project serve as a “proof-of-concept” showing that the adaptive learning approach can be compatible with escalation of commitment. However, our previous works has not yet been a formal approach of escalation of commitment because it does not specify exactly how different major characteristics of escalation of commitment is explicated under adaptive learning. The current proposed research aims to formally propose and test adaptive learning as a new approach in understanding escalation of commitment. The adaptive learning approach is a breakthrough to the escalation literature because it offers new insights into a number of issues that the current research and theories of escalation of commitment literature could not address. Building upon the proven basic principle of resolving the learning-escalation paradox from our earlier works, in this proposed research, we attempt to significantly expand the scope of coverage of the adaptive learning from simply a proof-of-concept to a formal theory of escalation. To do so, we will follow the dominant research method in adaptive learning, testing the core ideas of this proposal using computer simulations followed by empirical behavioral data (Busemeyer, et al., 1992; Pleskac & Busemeyer, 2010; Teodorescu & Usher, 2013). The major goal is to illustrate and test how adaptive learning can be operating under situations that realistically represent escalation situations. 承諾的升級是指一種決策偏見，其中決策者非理性地升級他們對失敗行動的承諾。 由於關鍵決策者在組織中表現出這種偏見會給組織帶來極其糟糕的後果，這種偏見可能是組織研究人員研究最多的管理決策偏見（Brockner，1992; Kwong＆Wong，2014; Staw，1976,1981; Wong＆ Kwong，2007a，in press）。這種偏見是非常矛盾的，因為它與效力法下的人類行為的共識正好相反（Thorndike，1989），它假定在行為得到負面反饋後人們的行為傾向減少。 這個悖論被稱為學習-承諾的升級悖論。 在我們由GRF研究基金（＃16503614）資助的早期工作中，我們通過將效果法律單位從決策層面擴展到決策層面來成功解決這一悖論（詳見Wong＆Kwong，in press）。 學習-承諾的升級悖論的成功解決表明，適應性學習是理解承諾升級的新方法。 我們之前在GRF項目中的工作（Wong和Kwong, in press）充當了“概念驗證”，表明自適應學習方法可以與承諾的升級兼容。 然而，我們以前的工作尚未成為承諾升級的正式方法，因為它沒有具體說明在適應性學習中如何闡明承諾升級的不同主要特徵。 目前提出的研究旨在正式提出並測試自適應學習作為理解承諾升級的新方法。自適應學習方法是承諾升級文獻的一個突破，因為它對當前研究承諾升級理論當中許多無法解決的問題提供了新見解。根據我們早期解決學習升級悖論的基礎上，在本項研究計劃中，我們試圖將自適應學習的覆蓋範圍從簡單的概念驗證擴展到形式化的升級理論。為此，我們將遵循自適應學習中的主導研究方法，使用計算機模擬測試該提議的核心思想，再加上經驗行為數據助證（Busemeyer，et al。，1992; Pleskac＆Busemeyer，2010; Teodorescu＆Usher，2013 ）。本項研究計劃主要目標是說明和測試自適應學習如何真實地反映承諾升級的運行。

14612118.label: Realisation of objectives
14612118.value: A unique strength of the adaptive learning approach is that it can shed light on the development of escalation of commitment. While the extant literature has paid little attention to the origin and development of the escalation bias, the adaptive learning approach of decision-making readily reveals how this decision bias may gradually emerge as a result of the law-of-effect. For example, in all our previous simulations (Wong & Kwong, 2018), the escalation and law-of-effect strategies are always set to share equal probability of being chosen at the outset. Despite this neutral starting point, escalation strategy quickly becomes the dominant choice over the law-of-effect strategy because it is associated with a higher average expected degree of reinforcement at the beginning of learning. Our previous works implied that escalation bias emerges because of the higher expected degree of reinforcement associated with escalation (vs. law-of-effect) strategy. In the current research, we aim to expand the score of coverage of the adaptive learning from simply a proof-of-concept to a formal theory of escalation. To do so, we applied the theory to predict and explain phenomena that could not be readily explained by existing theories and to offer new insights into antecedents that are implied from the theory. In the first project, we addressed the developmental trajectory of the escalation tendency. That is, why escalation bias exhibits an inverted U-shape pattern over life span. Specifically, compared with young adults, children tend to exhibit less escalation bias (Arkes & Atyon, 1999), and so do the elderly (Strough et al., 2008). We proposed that the rise and then decline in escalation tendency could be resulted from the corresponding changes in an individual’s higher-order cognitive ability. The central theme for explaining escalation of commitment through adaptive learning is that learning happens not at individual decision level but rather at a decision-strategy level. Within a strategy, each single decision is represented as one component or unit carefully coordinated according to prescribed higher order rules (i.e., the strategy). As such, the execution of a strategy requires higher-order cognitive ability (a.k.a. meta-cognitive ability) in abstract thinking, which includes planning, coordinating, and monitoring of individual decisions (Wong & Kwong, 2018). That means, escalation tendency should be weaker when the meta-cognitive ability is not as high as that of young adults, such as when it is not yet fully developed in children (Alexander, Martha, & Schwanenflugel, 1995; Kuhn, 2000) or when it is deteriorated in elderly adults (Palmer, David, & Fleming, 2014). Under the current framework, meta-cognitive ability could be captured by the number of decisions or decision components that a person can coordinate in a systematic manner. We refer to this number as the quota size or “complexity” of a decision strategy. When this quota is small, the strategy is less complex, and individuals need to only plan and monitor relatively small amount of information, thus requiring little meta-cognitive ability. When the quota increases, higher meta-cognitive ability is required. In sum, the inverted U-shape relationship between age and meta-cognitive ability has been documented in developmental psychology (Alexander et al., 1995; Kuhn, 2000; Palmer et al., 2014). To explain the developmental trajectory of the escalation tendency across life span, we proposed that the linkage between escalation tendency and meta-cognitive ability can be captured by the variation of decision quota size or strategy complexity. To do so, we addressed two specific limitations in previous works (Wong and Kwong, 2018). First, previous simulations on learners with larger versus smaller quota only captured between-learner comparisons, which does not directly examine the within-learner developmental pattern. A pattern observed in between-individual comparisons may not hold or be even reversed when studied under within-individual comparison contexts (e.g., Vancouver et al., 2001, 2002). Thus, a developmental pattern must be observed from longitudinal data from the same learner (i.e., within-learner simulation). Second, a learner’s quota size is always held constant in previous simulations. To test changes over time, the learner’s quota size should vary across age following an inverted U-shape. Under the proposed setup, we successfully found that the relative probability of choosing the escalation strategy indeed follows an inverted-U shape using longitudinal within-individual learning models. In the second project, we offered a novel way to explain the individual differences in escalation tendency. Conventionally, the escalation literature has documented stable individual differences in escalation bias by using dispositional correlates. The dispositional perspective assumes that individual differences in escalation are determined by personality traits or chronic dispositional factors that are inherent in the person. In this project, we offer the adaptive learning perspective as an alternative, modeling the development of the individual differences of escalation bias without the presumption of dispositions. To explain individual differences of escalation, the framework should be able to capture four essential dimensions of understanding individual differences, namely (a) the origin of individual differences, (b) the emergence of individual differences, (c) the stability of individual differences, and (d) the change of individual differences. Our simulation results gave clear support that major characteristics pertaining to the individual differences of escalation can be successfully developed through multi-level adaptive learning, without the need to presume dispositional differences among people. In the third project, we tested the robustness of the adaptive learning approach by empirically testing unique antecedents implied in the simulation results. One implication of the adaptive learning approach is that if a learner’s focus is at the decision-level, their decisions or choices would be more likely guided by law-of-effect; whereas a focus at the strategy-level would likely lead to decision patterns that mimic escalation of commitment. If learning is possible at decision and strategy levels, it leads to a fundamental question—what guides decision makers to shift their focus of learning between levels? In the third project, we addressed this question by identifying factors that may influence the shift, which should in turn affect escalation tendency. We found that when decision makers represent information at a higher level-of-construal or are more engaged with growth mindset, they will exhibit higher escalation of commitment. It is worth noting that the above three projects adopted two very different methodologies. The first two projects used computer simulations whereas the third project relied on empirical testing with behavioral data. Because of the social unrest happened in 2019, then the pandemic since 2020, it has been very difficult if not impossible to recruit participants into the lab to take part in our experiments. We tried running the studies online with our students during this period. However, sign-up rates were really low. We also conducted the studies online using crowdsourcing platforms such as MTurk. However, the data quality was not as good. In sum, the progress of the third project has been severely affected. We still obtained empirical evidence with correlational data. However, because of limited supply for quality participants, the statistical power for our lab data was compromised. On the contrary, the first two projects have relied on computer simulations, and their progresses were relatively unaffected. The projects have led to conference presentations which are listed in part C, and two working papers with one already under journal review and another one to be submitted for journal review soon.

14612118.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612118.value: In the first research project, our simulations show that when we operationalize age difference changing mental capacity as indicated by quota size, the degree of escalation biases increases from young children to young adults, and then decreases from young adults to elderly. The results are generally consistent with the inverted U-shape between in the age-escalation relationship. The project has led to presentations (virtual) in two major international conferences, one best paper proceeding, and one working paper under reviewed for journal publication. In the second project, we used the adaptive learning framework to model individual differences in the escalation tendency. We showed that individual differences could be developed from an origin where all individual are “neutral” (not biased) and gradually emerge as learning proceeds. According to our model, individual differences emerge because each learner’s decision develops unique experience through probabilistic learning. As the learning process unfolds, each individual has a unique course of decision experience in terms of their decisions and the decision outcomes. Once emerged, the individual difference becomes stable because each learner naturally preserves its accumulated experience in the learning process. This project has led to one working paper, which we submitted for conference presentation in the summer of 2023. In the third project, we examined potential antecedents of escalation implied by our simulation works. According to our multi-level adaptive learning model, we expect decision makers to exhibit a stronger escalation tendency when they are more likely to shift their learning focus to a higher level strategy learning. In line with this core ideas, we found that escalation tendency is stronger when people construe information at a higher and more abstract level rather than a lower and more concrete level for a psychologically distant event. Similarly, decision-makers with a stronger growth mindset tend to escalate their commitment to a troubled project. Existing research has suggested that they may have a more positive response to negative project feedbacks (Burnette et al., 2013), where their perseverance may imply a learning focus in a broader horizon. Consistently with that idea, we found that decision-makers holding growth mindset are more motivated to escalate their commitment to a project despite the negative feedback. That is because only by continuing, they could achieve high level strategy learning. We worked with an M Phil student on this project and the findings were summarized in his thesis.

14612118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612118.value: Future research can examine the usefulness of the adaptive learning approach in explaining other characteristics of escalation such as sunk costs, responsibility, and goal completion. For instance, so far all the simulations demonstrated in the current research use the simple frequency-rule (i.e., counting number of success or failure) in demonstrating how people may increase their commitment to failing course of action. In these works, failure or success is represented as all-or-none. However, this assumption is not realistic because with very few exceptions (Zikmund-Fisher, 2004), most studies represent failure associated with partial resources loss in the previous decisions, such as time, efforts, or money, which are often referred to as sunk-costs (Arkes & Blumer, 1985; Sleesman et al., 2012). To allow adaptive learning to be a useful theory of escalation of commitment, this approach has to be applicable to a more realistic situations in which failure is represented as sunk-costs. Thus, another challenge is to examine how the basic principle of the law-of-effect dealing with simple all-or-none feedback can be modified to be a more complicated and also more realistic way dealing with failure understood as sunk costs.

14612118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612118.value: Escalation of commitment refers to a decision bias wherein decision makers escalate their commitment toward failing course of action. Because key decision makers exhibit this bias in organizations will yield extremely bad consequences to the organizations, this bias has been well documented in the literature. The escalation bias is very paradoxical because it is exactly opposite to the consensus of human behaviors under the law-of-effect (Thorndike, 1989), which posits that people’s commitment to an action should decrease after the action receives negative feedback. This paradox is called learning-escalation paradox. The current research resolved the paradox by adopting a multi-level adaptive learning framework, wherein people learn to escalate because of its reinforcement value. The adaptive learning approach is a breakthrough because it offers new insights into a number of issues that the current research and theories of escalation of commitment literature could not address. We illustrated and tested how adaptive learning can be operating under situations that realistically represent escalation situations. For instance, our results showed that inverted U-shape relationship between age and escalation can be successfully modelled by assuming that age changes mental capacity. The implications of the current findings to escalation at individual- and organization-level are discussed.

14612318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612318.value: Background: Although humans posses an innate ability to recognize the emotions of others, this ability varies considerably between individuals leaving some behind. Here we seek to establish entrainment – that is the temporal synchronization of internal with external rhythms – as a means for improving emotion recognition. Moreover, we aim to explore a direct effect involving the entrainment of the processes underpinning emotion recognition and an indirect effect involving a change in social emotions. Project description: A first project phase comprises a series of behavioral studies examining the conditions that elicit and facilitate entrainment to an auditory rhythm and that enable entrainment effects on emotion recognition. To this end, we will contrast different auditory rhythm conditions, different tasks and different expression modalities. Additionally, we will employ psychological tools to measure entrainment, social emotions, and emotion recognition as well as their interrelations. In a second phase, an optimal entrainment design will be employed in conjunction with neuronal and autonomic measures. Specifically, the scalp recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) as well as intracranial recordings will be used to examine the effect of entrainment on oscillatory phase and power and on evoked responses to stimuli that are rhythmically expected as compared to unexpected. Average heart-rate and heart-rate variability will be obtained as measures of emotional arousal and positive affect, respectively. Together, entrainment effects on brain and heart-rate will be linked to markers of emotion recognition. Emerging biological relations are expected to complement the behavioral findings of phase one and provide mechanistic insights. The latter will be furthered by a final study combining electrophysiology with a psychopharmacological manipulation targeting the brain's opioid system – a candidate for regulating social feelings of connectedness and self-other merging. Using a double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over design we will examine whether naltrexone, an opiate antagonist, blocks entrainment and/or entrainment effects on social emotions and emotion recognition. Outcomes and significance: Together, ensuing evidence will offer new insights into entrainment, establish its influence on emotion recognition, and characterize this influence as a direct entrainment phenomenon and/or indirect consequence of emotional change. Moreover, the combined behavioral, electrophysiological, and pharmacological approach as well as the integration of correlational with causal evidence will enable holistic insights and the formulation of a social processing model that informs existing psychological and brain theories and identifies avenues for the enhancement of social perception in healthy and clinical populations. 背景: 雖然人類天生擁有識別情緒的能力 ，但人與人之間可以有很大的差異。而有些人在這方面的能力亦比一般人差。在這裡，我們試圖建立內外偶聯 — 即內部與外部節奏的時序同步化 — 作為改善情感認別的方法。此外，我們意圖探索內外偶聯產生的直接及間接影響：直接影響涉及到內外偶聯的過程如何加強了情感認別，而間接影響涉及到社會情緒的改變。 項目簡介: 研究項目中，第一階段包括一系列的行為研究，調查可引發和促進與聽覺節奏產生內外偶聯的狀況，並使內外偶聯能夠對情感認別產生影響作用。為此，我們將對比不同聽覺節奏的狀況，不同的作業和不同的表達模式。此外，我們將採用心理學的分析工具來量度內外偶聯，社會情緒和情感認別之間的相互關係。在第二階段，一個最合適的內外偶聯實驗設計將與神經元和自律神經測量結合使用。具體來說，於頭皮記錄的腦電圖（EEG）和顱內記錄將用於檢測內外偶聯對振盪相位和功率的影響，以及用於對比預期性節律刺激和意外性節律刺激的誘發反應，如何受到內外偶聯的影響。平均心率和心率變異性將分別作為情感喚起和積極情感的度量。結合起來，內外偶聯對大腦和心率的影響將與情感認別的標誌相關聯。所呈現的生理關係是被期望可補足第一階段的行為發現以及提供機制見解。後者將繼續進一步的研究，而該最終研究將會把電生理學與針對大腦鴉片類藥物系統的心理藥物操縱結合起來 — 大腦鴉片類藥物系統是一個調節社會關聯感及自我−他者融合的候選者。使用雙盲，安慰劑對照，交叉設計，我們將檢測納曲酮，一種鴉片拮抗劑，會否阻礙內外偶聯和/或內外偶聯對社會情緒和情感認別的影響。 結果和意義：結合起來，隨後的證據將對內外偶聯提供嶄新的見解，確立其對情感認別的影響，並描述這種影響為直接內外偶聯現象和/或情緒改變的間接後果。此外，綜合了行為，電生理學和藥理學的方法，以及相關性與因果證據的整合，將可以集成全面的見解，並形成社會歷程模式。此模式能為現有的心理學和大腦學理論提供更多資訊，並為健康和臨床族群辨出能增強社會認知的途徑。
