14612718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612718.value: Both normative social beliefs and psychological research associate aging with increased vulnerability to fraud; that is, older adults are believed to be generally more gullible than younger adults. An age-related decline in cognitive abilities may make older adults less capable of detecting and dealing with fraud. However, real-life stories of fraud suggest that older adults who are otherwise cognitively competent are particularly likely to believe in fraudulent narratives that appeal to their emotions, e.g., their care for family members. Therefore, the role of emotion in fraud should not be ignored. In the last decade, our laboratory and others around the world have identified several emotional processes that vary with age. Compared with younger adults, older adults display a greater preference for positive over negative emotions (positivity bias, such as preference for happiness over sadness), and for low-arousal over high arousal emotions (low-arousal bias, such as preference for calmness over excitement). These age-related changes in emotion have been shown to impact on perception, attention, and decision-making. For example, the positivity bias among older adults drives them to pay more attention to positive stimuli and value social partners who are more emotionally meaningful to them (Fung, 2013). The low-arousal bias among older adults makes them prefer activities that can elicit low arousal emotions (e.g., calmness: choosing to practice Tai Chi) rather than high arousal emotions (e.g., excitement: choosing to practice aerobics) (Jiang, Fung, Sims, Tsai, & Zhang, 2016). Given this evidence demonstrating the critical role of emotion in older adults’ information processing and decision-making, the proposed project aims at shedding light on the ways in which these age-related changes in emotion impact older adults’ fraud vulnerability. To achieve this objective, three studies will be conducted. In Study 1, behavioral experimental and eye-tracking techniques will be used to examine older adults’ positivity bias (i.e., preference for positive vs. negative emotions) as a mechanism of an age-related increase in fraud vulnerability. In Study 2, psychological and physiological measures will be used to examine older adults’ preference for low-arousal (vs. high-arousal) emotions as a mechanism of an age-related increase in fraud vulnerability. In Study 3, interventions will be developed to reduce aforementioned emotional biases among older adults. We will examine the effectiveness of such interventions in mitigating older adults’ fraud vulnerability. 隨著智能設備及社交媒體的普及，以及人口老齡化的加劇，越來越多的老年人成為各種詐騙的首選目標和受害者。美國2010年的一項調查顯示，大約有730萬65歲及以上的老年人遭受過商業詐騙。根據中國銀聯2016年發布的移動支付安全調查報告，超過四成網絡詐騙受害者是50歲以上的中老年人。有人認為，由於認知能力的衰退 ，老年人更容易上當受騙。老齡化心理學研究也發現，與年輕人相比，老年人更容易地信任虛假信息，更難識破騙局，從而更容易成為商業騙局的受害者。認知能力衰退固然是引致老年人容易上當受騙的重要成因，但是情緒作為時刻影響著人們行為決策的重要因素，其作用也不能被忽視。與年輕人相比，老年人更加偏好正向的、低激發的情緒，過往研究表明這樣的情緒偏好 (emotional bias) 會影響老年人的知覺、注意力和決策。 通過行為、眼動、生理和腦成像技術，探究老年人易受騙性背後的情緒與認知機制，具有重要的科學理論意義。在實驗一中，我們將用行為實驗和眼動技術探究年人的正向偏好(positivity bias)在信息處理中的作用；在實驗二中，我們將用心理和生理測量驗證低激發偏好(preference for low-arousal emotions)在老年人易受騙性中的機制；在實驗三中，本研究將采取幹預手段降低上述情緒偏好對老年人的影響。 同時，本研究還能為老年人易受騙性的幹預提供依據和方向，幫助老年人規避受騙風險，具有社會實踐價值。

14612718.label: Realisation of objectives
14612718.value: Objective 1 is about whether, compared with younger adults, older adults’ greater focus on positivity may affect how they evaluate advertisements and products, contributing to higher fraud vulnerability. To achieve Objective 1, we conducted Study 1 in which 118 younger (aged 18-39 yrs, mean age =19.91, SD=3.71) and 144 older (aged 60 yrs or above, mean age = 68.22, SD=5.46) adults read advertisements of 32 products when their eye movement (fixation duration) was tracked. The advertisements varied in credibility of the content, trustworthiness of the face of the salesperson, and framing (gain- vs. loss-framed) of the product description. A loss-framed product description is one that describes what the consumer would lose if not buying the product whereas a gain-framed product description describes what the consumer would gain if buying the product. The advertisements were about products in four different life domains: charity, entertainment, finance, health. How face trustworthiness, credibility and framing influenced age-related visual attention toward different elements of the advertisements (central vs. peripheral cues) and purchase intention of the products in each domain were examined. Objective 2 is about whether, compared with younger adults, older adults learn less (have lower physiological arousal) from feedback about frauds, contributing to higher fraud vulnerability. To achieve Objective 2, we conducted Study 2 that investigated the role of emotion in young and older adults’ fraud vulnerability using physiological techniques. A total of 93 younger adults (aged 18–37 years, mean age = 22.3, SD = 4.64) and 90 older adults (aged 55–80 years, mean age = 67.7, SD = 5.11) were recruited from communities in Hong Kong to participate in the study. The experiment consisted of three 3 phases: a free learning phase (P1), a feedback learning phase (P2), and a testing phase (P3). During phase P1, all participants freely viewed 20 advertisements (10 credible and 10 deceitful) one by one without any feedback. During phase P2, participants viewed the same set of advertisements from phase P1, each being presented for 10 seconds. After each advertisement, participants in the credibility-feedback group received feedback about the credibility of the advertisement, whereas participants in the random-feedback group received random feedback that had nothing to do with the credibility of the advertisements. During phase P3, all participants viewed 30 advertisements, including 10 old advertisements from P1 and P2 and 20 new advertisements. We expected those who received credibility feedback in P2 would be more likely to learn – that is, having stronger physiological reactions and less purchase intention – toward deceitful ads (relative to credible ads) in P3 than in P1, compared with those who received random feedback. Against this backdrop, we tested whether older adults would exhibit this kind of learning less readily than did younger adults. If so, this may be another mechanism through which older adults are more vulnerable to frauds. Because both studies required face-in-face contact in individual testing sessions, data collection of both studies were severely delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and the strict social distance measures in Hong Kong. Despite our best efforts, we only managed to finish running Study 1 and half of Study 2 by the completion date of the project (Dec 2021). This has already been after a 6-month extension granted at the institutional level. As the funding was largely used up at that point (due to fixed costs like salary that we had to pay regardless of the number of participants run), we decided not to ask for further extension of the project. Instead, we used our own funding to complete the data collection of Study 2 from Jan 2022 to Nov 2022. By now (Dec 2022), we have already completed all data collection and data analysis. We thus report 100% completion of both objectives in this report. However, since there was not much time between our completion of the projects and the submission of this report, we only managed to publish a conceptual review, and submit two empirical manuscripts for publication. The conceptual review was published in Journal of Gerontology: Psychological Sciences. One of the empirical manuscripts was originally submitted to a special issue of Journal of Gerontology: Psychological Sciences. When it was rejected, we revised and submitted it to the Gerontologist. The second empirical manuscript was submitted to Computers in Human Behavior. We have also written up a third manuscript that we list as “in preparation” in this report. In addition, we have three conference presentations and three graduate students trained. We hope the panel could evaluate our research reports in view of the challenges we faced.

14612718.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612718.value: Objective 1: 1. In contrast to hypothesis, older adults paid more visual attention to central cues of all advertisements across all life domains than did younger adults. How these age differences in cognitive processing have implications on how society views older adults and how older adults view themselves are reviewed in a conceptual review (Research Output #1). 2. Both age groups showed attentional preferences toward central information in advertisements that was more credible and away from information that was more deceitful. Yet, older adults only showed the above attention preferences when the face of the salesperson was less trustworthy. When the face was more trustworthy, older adults paid equal attention to credible and deceitful central information. This may be one mechanism that makes older adults more vulnerable to frauds (Output #3 & Conference presentation #3). 3. Moreover, in the financial domain, both age groups showed higher attentional preferences for loss-framed than gain-framed central cues; and higher attentional preferences for loss-framed (but not gain-framed) central cues were associated with stronger purchase intentions (Research Output #4). 4. In addition, a graduate student used part of the data to examine age differences in clickbait preference of health information. Clickbait refers to articles, photographs, etc. on the Internet that are intended to attract attention and encourage people to click on links to particular websites. Our findings revealed that older adults held a more positive attitude to clickbait messages compared with younger adults. Over 30 days when both age groups showed forgetting of the information described in messages, older adults, but not younger adults, showed less memory decline of the information from clickbait messages (conference presentation #2; Research Output #2). Objective 2: 1. Compared to younger adults, older adults generally had weaker electrodermal activity responses to all advertisements, suggesting that older adults were less physiologically sensitive and had weaker emotional reactions to the advertisements overall. Whether participants were alone or not moderated these age differences (conference presentation #1). 2. Participants reported weaker purchase intentions toward deceitful advertisements at phases P1 and P3. This difference was more evident for those in the credibility-feedback group than those in the random-feedback group, and more evident among younger adults than older adults. These findings suggested that participants could learn about whether an advertisement was credible through their previous experiences, but that older adults were less capable of using this information to distinguish deceitful ads from credible ones, compared with younger adults. These findings will be written up for publication soon.

14612718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612718.value: Findings from Study 1 suggest that although older adults do not pay more attention to peripheral cues, specific peripheral cues such as face trustworthiness and gain- vs. loss-framing, make older adults less likely to discriminate between credible from deceitful advertisements. We plan to extend this line of research to age differences in information sharing to examine whether similar mechanisms also explain why older adults in general are more likely to spread misinformation than are younger adults. We have already submitted a proposal to the General Research Fund for such a project. In addition, exactly why older adults showed less physiological reasons toward messages than did younger adults in Study 2 also needs further investigation. We now explain these age differences in terms of older adults’ lower ability to learn from prior feedback about frauds. But it might also be the case that older adults are less interested in the messages and are thus less motivated to encode, either physiologically or cognitively, any information about them. We plan to conduct future studies to test these competing explanations.

14612718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612718.value: Prior literature attributed age differences in fraud vulnerability to older adults’ greater attention to peripheral cues of messages, compared to younger adults. We found, using eye tracking techniques, that older adults did not pay more attention to peripheral cues than did younger adults. However, some peripheral cues, including face trustworthiness of the salesperson, whether an advertisement emphasized what could be gained from buying the project or what would be lost if not buying the product, and whether there was a clickbait (e.g., attention-grasping terms such as “You won’t believe it”) in the message, influenced the ability of older adults to visually discriminate between credible and deceitful messages, but not that of younger adults. Moreover, when provided with feedback on the credibility of formerly encountered messages, older adults showed less physiological reactions and a lower purchase intention when they encountered deceitful messages again, less so than did younger adults. Demographic characteristics other than age, personality, and visual and cognitive abilities did not explain these age differences. Findings pinpoint specific mechanisms that may make older adults more vulnerable to frauds, compared with younger adults.

14612818.label: Project Objectives
14612818.value: Identify important quan-related concepts in the media culture in China that are relevant to gender/sexuality such as nüquan (women’s rights), xingquan (sex rights), and the quanli (rights and interests) and quanyi (rights and benefits) for women and LGBT people. Analyze how feminist and queer activists and organizations use media to engage, develop or challenge quan-related concepts so as to contribute to the emergent interdisciplinary field that explores the intersection between human rights and media. Develop theoretical insights on the concept of quan as mediation of feminist and queer rights that problematizes the Eurocentric, normativized, and teleological conceptions of rights, while not falling into the trap of Chinese cultural exceptionalism. Expand the existing bilingual (Chinese and English) website on feminist and queer media activism generated from PI’s ECS project by adding the new data collected about gender/sexuality advocacy and quan discourse. This website can facilitate teaching and learning about feminist and queer media culture in China. It can also provide relevant information to activists. Present the findings in international conferences and publish articles in international peer-reviewed journals or prepare a book manuscript.

14612818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612818.value: 近年來，「權」這個字以及相關概念如「女權」、性小眾「權利」和「權益」等在中國女權及酷兒運動中有一定能見度 。 面對政治和法律改革的困難，這些運動多以媒體相關形式來推動，比如舉辦女性及酷兒影展或媒體活動，為女性和性小眾發聲，爭取各樣「權」。當「權」為不同女權人士、酷兒運動者和組織在不同語境所採用時，它的實質定義是甚麼？女權及酷兒運動人士如何使用媒體來提出、推動或挑戰「權」以及其他性/別權益相關的概念？更重要的是，中國這些與「權」相關的媒體運動為現今學術界對權的討論帶來甚麼啟示？ 本研究將深討中國女權及酷兒媒體文化如何傳遞、生成和爭辯各種權益相關概念的過程，由此與西方人權的批判理論研究，以及女權及酷兒運動的社會學研究進行對話。透過與相關組織的人員和義工進行半結構式訪談，分析所選媒體文本和運動對「權」的相關討論，並參與觀察研究當前影展和媒體活動，本研究將探討中國女權及酷兒運動中「權」的實踐如何對西方中心、規範化和目的論的人權概念提出質疑，又免於陷入中國文化例外主義的論述。

14612818.label: Realisation of objectives
14612818.value: The understanding of rights-related feminist and queer concepts and practices in China has been mainly presented in one journal articles as well as a book manuscript under contract with New York University Press. The objectives are mainly realized through the following four aspects: a journal article, a book manuscript of scholarly monograph, conference presentations, and a bilingual website. First, PI published “Networking Asia Pacific: Queer Film Festivals and the Spatiotemporal Politics of Inter-referencing” (2016) in the SSCI-indexed journal Inter-Asia Cultural Studies, a leading journal in cultural studies. Addressing Objectives 1, 2, and 3, PI investigates how the queer film festival alliance serves as the sites for articulating queer rights, which sometimes cast a progressivist temporal narrative based on geographical hierarchies. Specifically, by tracing the discourses of rights in film festival organizing, including China Women’s Film Festival and queer film festivals in China, PI proposes to think about film festival networks not only as citation, collaboration, and competition among its members, but also in terms of the spatiotemporal politics of inter-referencing. Second, addressing Objectives 1, 2 and mainly 3, PI has completed a book manuscript titled Digitized Entanglements: Feminist and Queer Media and Rights in China. This book project offers a timely analysis of the convergence of digital media, feminist, queer culture and rights consciousness in China. Specifically, it examines the formation of what I call “rights feminism,” or the appropriation of rights framework in contemporary feminist articulations, as well as queer activism and rights advocacy. The rights framework refers to a rich repertoire of international human rights concepts, domestic political norms and rhetoric related to rights, legal activism and rights-defense practices. As political and legal reforms remain elusive, a significant portion of activist practices that advocate different kinds of rights for women and sexual minorities turn to media-related forms. (Please see 6.1 for details). Third, PI also presented and disseminated the findings in two international conferences (responding to Objective 5), including the biannual Inter-Asia Cultural Studies Conference in the Philippines in 2019, as well as the International Communication Association (ICA) Conference in Washington D.C. the same year (please see Part C for details). Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, PI was not able to attend conferences in 2020. Hence, PI put more effort in constructing the website to be mentioned below. Fourth, addressing Objectives 1, 2 and mainly 4, a bilingual (Chinese and English) website for archiving rights-related feminist and queer concepts and practices is now available at https://feministqueerchina.wixsite.com/rights. This website lists the feminist and queer concepts, discourses, and practices related to rights under the three categories: the legal contexts of rights, the popular discourse of rights, and rights-related organizations and practices. The “Legal Contexts of Rights” section outlines the background of the legal aspects of women’s rights. This section summarizes important laws and legal events that have contributed to the understanding of human rights and women’s rights since the 1990s in China, including: 1) the World Conference on Women in 1995, specifically the use of “rights” in the Beijing Platform for Action, and the impact of the Conference on subsequent feminist activities and organizations; 2) Law on the Protection of Women’s Rights and Interests, specifically the legislative history and background, the main contents, and the identification of the use of the terms quanyi and quanli in the Law. A brief introduction and relevant links to each sub-entry are provided. For the detailed legal text and conference declaration, links to the full text are also included. In the “Popular Discourse of Rights” section, an introduction of popular words that emerge around rights-related concept of feminism in media reports, the Internet and everyday life is included. This section demonstrates the diverse understanding of the concept of rights in the popular discourse, reflecting the complexity of feminist thoughts as they have developed in China in recent years. This section is divided into five parts: 1) an overview of the misogynistic sentiment prevalent on the internet and in everyday life, which lays out the background for the popularity and development of the following terms; 2) the definition and expression of tianyuan nüquan田園女權 (which literally means “garden feminism”), the context of its generation, the divergent deployment of the term, and the evaluation of this popular term; 3) the definition and expression of nüquan女拳 (which literally means “fist feminism”), and the evaluation of the notion; 4) the representative figures and views of feminism associated with Weibo, the contexts for their popularity, their limitations, and other feminist accounts on Weibo; as well as 5) other concepts related to rights, including those privileged women’s rights over the others, and their expressions and positions. In the “Rights-related Organizations and Practices” section, feminist and queer organizations and their understanding and use of the concept of quan, or rights, are introduced. Topics touched on include: 1) the meaning and cross-referencing of the concepts of quanli, quanyi, human rights, among others in feminist discourses, and the representative Women’s Voice e-journal is cited as an example; 2) feminist and queer organizations and how they incorporate the rights discourses into their mission statements and their activities; 3) how feminist and queer individuals and communities actively use the legal framework and rights-related concepts to advocate gender and sexual equality. Specific legal dispute cases will be introduced in this part. This section also illustrate concrete examples that supplement the “Legal Contexts of Rights” section. Additionally, a bibliography of references and further academic reading pertaining to both rights-related feminism and queer concepts and practices is included in the section of “Selected Bibliography”. The “Other Links” section has listed out complimentary materials for understanding how the notion of rights intersects with gender/sexuality in contemporary China. Through the aforementioned output, the objectives of the project have been fully achieved.

14612818.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612818.value: The major findings in this GRF project have been crystallized in the aforementioned journal article and book manuscript. PI explores the entangled relationship between digital technology and contemporary feminist, queer and rights articulations in China. PI highlights the techno-historical embeddedness of feminism, queerness and rights, which are usually analyzed as discourses or intellectual thoughts. This research explores four notions of quan in relation to gender and sexuality—namely, nüquan (women’s rights or rights feminism), renquan (human rights), quanyi (rights and benefits), and weiquan (rights defense). In particular, this research looks at the rise of contemporary “rights feminism,” the identity of rights feminists as new subjects of rights, and their relationship with the lesbian social movement. This research also examines how activists use the international human rights framework, domestic legal norms and rights-defense practices to mobilize their actions. (For details, see chapter 2 in 8.2 in Part C). In particular, by examining rights feminism and LGBT rights advocacy in China, the major findings of this research offer a new conceptualization of rights that is more-than-human. The concept of rights is usually understood as grounded in individual autonomy and privacy, in which human is by default the bearer of rights. PI uses “more-than-human”, rather than “non-human” or “posthuman”, to describe the entanglement between technology and discourse in the process. In this sense, the bearer of rights is more than the human, and it includes non-human specificities such as media-related formations. Media technologies are not simply facilitators, or channels to disseminate the ideas of rights. Rather, the idea of rights is formed in relation to techno-social specificities. (For details, see chapter 1 in 8.2 in Part C.) Furthermore, this research looks at feminist and queer media culture in China as processes that articulate, generate, and contest rights-related concepts and practices to create a dialogue between critical human rights studies that caution against Eurocentric, normativized, and teleological conceptions of rights and the studies of rights-based feminist and queer social movements that stress the usefulness and importance of the rights discourse. PI investigates how the queer film festival alliance serves as the space for the articulation of queer rights, which sometimes casts a progressivist temporal narrative based on a hierarchical arrangement of geographical places. (For details, see 8.1 in Part C.)

14612818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612818.value: My conceptualization of rights feminist and queer rights articulation as an assemblage of concepts, images and technology points to the notion of more-than-human rights, which is responding to a larger field of posthuman legal practice and studies. As suggested by Braidotti (2020), a posthuman approach in legal studies subverts the majoritarian model of human rights, modelled on the vision of the subject as a white neo-liberal male. Furthermore, a theoretical argument based on technology as various assemblages and articulation that are constitutive of gender, sexuality class, and other differences may be developed in this posthuman approach. The posthuman approach speaks to our current moment of the Anthropocene, in which human activities are making unprecedented impact on the planet. Based on these reasons, PI plans to explore this posthuman turn in further studies and apply for new research projects developed from this direction.

14612818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612818.value: The project investigates rights-related feminist and queer concepts as well as practices in China. This project will also raise public awareness and contribute to public knowledge of issues of rights, gender and sexuality in China. The results and data generated from this study will be useful for scholars from different fields, such as sexuality and gender studies, human rights studies, China studies, and so on. The findings, especially those published on the bilingual website on rights-related feminist and queer concepts and practices in China, can also be beneficial for activists and NGO practitioners in China as well as those in other national and cultural contexts. Furthermore, the research findings will be useful for teaching undergraduate and postgraduate courses of gender/sexuality studies, media studies, human rights studies, and China studies. The findings from this study and the website can demonstrate the creativity of activist practices in China and the complexity of Chinese society, and provide new learning materials for understanding contemporary China as a dynamic society.

14613518.label: Project Objectives
14613518.value: To investigate teachers’ perceptions towards multicultural education, their sense of cultural awareness and the problems they encounter in teaching ethnic minority students; To identify influential factors to develop culturally responsive teachers; To evaluate the relevance of teacher education programmes in the area of teaching ethnic minority students; To recommend possible ways to nurture teachers as ‘cultural brokers’ by (re)designing multicultural teacher education probably with an emphasis on social justice.
rows: To investigate teachers’ perceptions towards multicultural education, their sense of cultural awareness and the problems they encounter in teaching ethnic minority students;
To identify influential factors to develop culturally responsive teachers;
To evaluate the relevance of teacher education programmes in the area of teaching ethnic minority students;
To recommend possible ways to nurture teachers as ‘cultural brokers’ by (re)designing multicultural teacher education probably with an emphasis on social justice.

14613518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14613518.value: Ethnic minority students have long been perceived as a disadvantaged group in schools. In Hong Kong, research on school performance of ethnic minority students has had a key focus on language learning and cultural adaptation but not much has been done regarding the role of teachers. Teachers’ cultural awareness, professional needs and training highly affect their interaction with and teaching of ethnic minority students. Studies focusing on teachers’ competency to develop a culturally responsive learning environment for ethnic minority students are also rare. To bridge this research gap, this study will be guided by the research question “How can teachers be equipped to be culturally responsive teachers?” It will examine teachers’ views on cultural diversity, views that will affect their multicultural daily practice. Their professional needs and whether their needs have been addressed by existing teacher education programmes will be fully explored to seek a basis to develop culturally responsive classrooms. Suggestions on ways to improve the existing teacher training to equip teachers as culturally responsive will also be discussed. This study will apply a mixed method approach with three stages of the data collection process. Data collected from individual interviews with 20 school teachers and the analysis of school document (Stage 1) will identify teachers’ sense of cultural diversity, their daily practice of teaching ethnic minority students, their professional needs, teacher training and ways to encounter challenges. In Stage 2, documentary analysis of teacher education courses aiming at equipping teachers with competency to teach ethnic minority students will take place. Results of these two stages will serve as the foundation for the design of a questionnaire (Stage 3). It is planned that 300 questionnaires to 60 schools will be delivered in order to collect wider views from teachers who teach ethnic minority students. Findings of this study will contribute to the global discussions on influential factors and ways to develop culturally responsive teachers by examining their views, daily practice, professional needs and the teacher training they received. It is expected that the current research gap regarding this particular aspect will be reduced by this study. Furthermore, identifying ways to help schools and teachers develop socially just classrooms will not only contribute to the re-examination of the existing teacher education programmes by placing more emphasis on social justice but also may help initiate the reallocation of education resources to support the educational initiative to provide equal learning opportunity for students.

14613518.label: Realisation of objectives
14613518.value: This study applied a mixed method approach to explore local teachers’ perceptions on their sense of multiculturalism, and their professional needs when they encounter challenges brought by students with diverse cultural background. Their views on ways to enhance their roles to perform as multicultural teachers has also been discussed. All of these shed light on the discussion of the revisited of the teacher education programme for helping teachers to develop a culturally responsive practice in schools. The data collection process included three stages. Firstly, qualitative data were generated from interviews with 33 teachers with varied experience to teach ethnic minority students from both primary and secondary schools. Secondly, the existing teacher education programmes offered by the tertiary education institutions, the government and NGOs, aiming at nurturing teachers with multicultural competency were collected. Thirdly, a questionnaire based on findings of the interviews plus several related surveys was designed. 197 valid questionnaires from 31 secondary schools and 30 primary schools were collected. Exploratory Factor analysis was applied to analyze the collected data. Viewing the results of this study, the four stated objectives are all fully achieved. Details are explained as belows: Objective 1: Fully achieved Findings of Research question 1 “What are teachers’ views on multicultural education for ethnic minority students?” provide relevant information to respond Objective 1 of this study. Two data set can address this objective. Firstly, multicultural awareness of teachers who teach ethnic minority students was statistically analyzed and divided into three major groups: "N1 Getting along with people of different cultural backgrounds," "N2 How I communicate and connect with people of different cultural backgrounds," and "N3 Bias against people of different cultural backgrounds. Except for the third factor, the other two factors (N1, N2) are higher than 3.45. Hence, "N1 Getting along with people from different cultural backgrounds" and "N2 How I communicate and connect with people from different cultural backgrounds" are "more necessary" and "very necessary" in terms of respondents' professional needs. Viewing this, teachers’ perceptions on multiculturalism is deemed the basis of how they deliver multicultural education to their ethnic minority students. Teachers’ perceptions on implementing multicultural education can also be viewed from the challenges faced by them. After the analysis, these challenges can be broadly classified into three major categories: "A1 Teach and understand ethnic minority students" (3.52), "A2 Teaching and administrative support for inclusive learning for ethnic minority" (3.61), and "A3 Ethnic minority students’ Chinese language teaching"(3.94). Therefore, it shows that the majority of the respondents were most concerned about teaching Chinese to ethnic minority students and how the students can use Chinese language as a medium of learning. The above two set of data have been highly associated with teachers’ views on their willingness to implement multicultural education in their daily practice. Objective 1 of this study, therefore, has been fully achieved. Objective 2: Fully achieved Findings of Research question 2 “What are the professional needs of teachers who work closely with ethnic minority students?” provided answers for Objective 2 of this study. Data address the intellectual and structural needs for teachers to develop their cultural competency. Intellectual needs mainly refer to learning needs of teachers including the knowledge, skills and attitudes they expected to acquire. Among five learning needs of teachers studied, skills issues are ranked higher than other needs, such as knowledge and attitudes. Skills needs seem to involve three parts, all of which were rated as a higher score as 4, including “N2 Needs in having skills to teach ethnic minority students effectively” and “N5 Needs in having skills to help ethnic minority students to overcome learning disadvantages” have the same score as 4.06. “N3 Needs in having skills to guide and educate ethnic minority students” is slightly lower with the scoring as 4.01. Relatively, knowledge which is named as “N1 Needs in having knowledge about teaching ethnic minority students” covered nine questions, the largest number of this section, but its scoring only at 3.95. Learning having appropriate attitude seems to have the lowest means score among all five learning needs with scoring at 3.90 on “N4 Needs in having inclusive attitude to ethnic minority students”. From the data shown, interestingly, respondents seem to generally feel that learning how to teach ethnic minority students (Skill needs N2, 3 and 5) was rather important than what to teach (knowledge needs N1), and why have to teach (attitude needs N4). For the structural needs, teachers would like to have supports from their schools and the government. Data showed that teachers' needs for support can be categorized into two major groups: "R1 Substantive training" and "R2 Teachers' autonomy in teaching". Almost all of the questions had a mean value higher than 4. Among the 16 items, only "Reducing overall teaching time" scored lower than 4, with a score of 3.85. Combined findings from both structural needs and learning needs, Objective 2 has been addressed. Objective 3: Fully achieved Findings of Research Question 3 “What teacher education programmes have they received, if any, to equip them to have cultural competency and cultural awareness in teaching?” provided answers for Objective 3 of this study. This study showed that only 27.5% of respondents had received relevant teacher training to equip their teaching competency for ethnic minority students. They grouped their learning content into three types: “PP1 Learn to guide ethnic minority students to have cultural inclusiveness”, “PP2 Enhance ability to teach ethnic minority students effectively” and “PP3 Have Better understanding of ethnic minority students”. However, the means sore of each group of factors showed that such training programmes seem to put a more learning content in the skill aspect rather than knowledge of cultural diversity. Equipping teachers with the view of cultural diversity as a way to help students to develop their sense of inclusiveness has not yet been placed at a higher priority of the existing training programmes. Objective 4: Fully achieved Findings of Research Question 3 also provided answers for Objective 4 of this study. Teachers were asked their expected training to equip them with cultural awareness. After the analysis, their responses were grouped as two: “ET1 Expect to have better understanding of ethnic minority students and have ability to guide them to be cultural inclusive” (4.03) and “ET2. Expect to have ability to teach ethnic minority students effectively” (4.16). Clearly, teachers studied seem to put their key focus on how to teach rather than develop their cultural understanding of ethnic minority students. Viewing this, a proposed teacher education framework with a three level study scheme for frontline teachers has been suggested based on Van Manen view’s (1977) on reflection. Practical reflection helps teachers have a clear alignment of what and how they have to teach (Level 2) with the consideration of their knowledge of different cultures (Level 1). Critical reflection may shape teachers’ understanding of Level 1 if a whole school approach to the diversity issue is applied. If so, teachers may move away from their monocultural mindset and transform their role as ‘cultural broker’ with an ‘emic view’. Level 3 courses can act as independent or action research which serves as a platform for participants to put what they have learnt about multiculturalism in Level 1 and 2 into their school practice.

14613518.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613518.value: Major findings of this research are presented as follows: 1. Language competency of multicultural teachers Teachers studied generally face the greatest challenges is to use Chinese to teach. Ability to address both native and learning languages in order to create an effective communication environment could be one type of efficiency competency that a multicultural teacher should have. 2. Focus of teacher learning programmes Interestingly, respondents seemed to view that attitude aspect (why to teach) is less important than teaching skills (how to teach) and knowledge to teach (what to teach). Therefore, the design of the teacher education programme should put a strong emphasis on nurturing teachers with openness to diversity, self-awareness and self-reflectiveness and commitment to provide a socially just learning environment for students. 3. Being human relations multicultural teachers Teachers studied ideally would like to take up their role as ‘human relations” multicultural teachers but the existing classroom language arrangement may force them being “assimilationist”. A revisited of the language policy in schools may help teachers to bridge such a gap. 4. Reflection in teacher education programme Teachers studied have not yet reached a level of social action approach of diversity. Therefore, a proposed teacher education framework with a three level study scheme may help to respond this challenge. Outcomes of this research project take three forms. Firstly, one manuscript entitled as “What type of knowledge can equip teachers to be culturally responsive?” was submitted to Teaching and Teacher Education (Q1 SSCI) for review. Another manuscript entitled as “What do I need to learn when I teach ethnic minority students in moncultural school settings? A study in Hong Kong” was submitted to International Journal of Educational Research (Q2 SSCI) for review . Another manuscript entitled as “Cultural awareness of teachers in Hong Kong: A perspective of professional capital” is in the pipeline. It is planned to be submit to Journal of Education for Teaching, a Q1 SSCI journal, in July 2023. Secondly, three conference presentations funded by the GRF grant were delivered. Another conference presentation with the acknowledgement of GRF grant will be conducted in July 2023. Thirdly, one technical report based on the findings of this research was sent to each participating school and each interviewee respectively. Suggestions on ways to improve the quality of teaching ethnic minority students have been made.

14613518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613518.value: Two possible future research directions can be further considered: Firstly, research on the design of appropriate assessment framework that can facilitate ethnic minority students’ learning could be a way forward. The Education Bureau in Hong Kong continues to use the same standards to teach ethnic minority students whose cultural traditions are different from the local culture and values. This not only makes it more difficult for teachers to teach ethnic minority students, but also makes it more difficult for ethnic minority students to pursue higher education. Research on the differentiation, rather than one size fit all approach, of assessment framework can match the learning needs of ethnic minority students will definitely motivate ethnic minority students to learn. Secondly, home school collaboration has been an influential factor to promote good quality of learning experience for ethnic minority students. However, this is an area that has not yet been fully discussed. In Hong Kong, moncultural school practice make home school collaboration with ethnic minority parents being unlikely to achieve. Viewing this, research on how to encourage ethnic minority parents to engage in local schools is important.

14613518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613518.value: Research on teaching ethnic minority students has put its key focus on students’ learning difficulties. Little attention has been paid to the professional needs of teachers when they have to face challenges brought by diverse student background. To address this research gap, this study focusses on “what teachers learn and how they develop themselves to be culturally responsive” by identifying their professional needs, examining challenges they encountered when they interacting with ethnic minority students, their expected teacher education programmes that can nurture them with a sense of cultural awareness and teaching competency. Data gathered in this study help us to understand teachers’ sense of multiculturalism, challenges they have to face, their learning needs and expected supports from their schools and the government. Findings of this study may contribute to the design of teacher education programmes for nurturing teachers in Hong Kong with multicultural competency by pinpointing key areas where the skillsets and knowledge bases of teachers studied need to be supplemented for maximum effectiveness. More importantly, this study sheds further light on the global discussion on improving teaching quality for ethnic minority students by addressing teachers’ professional needs.

14615718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14615718.value: The primary aim of this project is to formulate a proposal for the evaluation and revitalisation of modern architecture in Hong Kong. Although Hong Kong has had a mechanism for evaluating and protecting historic monuments since 1976, the evaluation and revitalisation of modern architecture is a rather new challenge with the redevelopment of Wan Chai Market in the early 1990s being one of the earliest instances. Modern architecture here refers to buildings designed following the principles of the Modern Movement which originated in Europe at the turn of the 20th century. In Hong Kong, there has been controversy over the conservation and revitalisation of buildings of modern architecture, many of which were constructed during the 1950s. Style has been adopted as one of the key criteria for the assessment of architectural value. However, based upon our long term research on the design achievements of Hong Kong modern architecture, we believe that the design value of modern architecture is not about its style, but about its unity of form, space, structure, function and context. It requires different evaluation criteria and revitalisation strategies compared to those for Western classic architecture and Chinese traditional architecture. We consider that, after these years of experience, Hong Kong has reached the point where a re-examination and reflection of existing guidelines and strategies are necessary in order to establish better practices in the future for the protection of modern architecture. The proposed study is a critical reflection on the conservation and revitalisation of modern architecture in Hong Kong through a comparative approach from a global perspective. The study will be carried out in three phases: Firstly to gain a comprehensive understanding on the evaluation guidelines and good practices of revitalisation of modern architecture in a global perspective. Secondly to continue our review of Hong Kong’s evaluation guidelines and studies on revitalisation projects in Hong Kong. Thirdly, to conduct a critical reflection between Hong Kong experiences and global experiences and formulate a proposal for evaluation and revitalisation of modern architecture in Hong Kong. The project addresses the shortcomings of the existing evaluation guidelines and revitalisation strategies which do not adequately cover crucial aspects of modern architecture. The research will certainly have a long term impact by providing a specific set of criteria for the assessment of modern architecture and a pool of revitalisation strategies applicable to Hong Kong condition. 該研究的主要目的是提出一個評估和保育香港現代建築的建議。雖然香港自1976年以來一直有評估和保護歷史古蹟的機制，但現代建築的評估和活化是一項相當新的挑戰，灣仔街市在二十世紀九十年代初期的重建是其中最早的一例。這裡的現代建築是指遵循現代運動原則設計的建築，起源於20世紀之交的歐洲。在香港，人們對現代建築的保護和活化存在爭議，因為其中許多都是在20世紀50年代以後建造的。風格已被採納為評估建築價值的關鍵標準之一。然而，基於我們對香港現代建築設計成就的長期研究，我們認為現代建築的設計價值不是關於它的風格，而是關於它的形式，空間，結構，功能和背景的統一。與西方經典建築和中國傳統建築相比，它需要不同的評估標準和活化策略。我們認為，經過這些年的經驗，香港迫切需要重新審視和反思現有指引和策略，以便在未來建立更好的保護現代建築的做法。擬議的研究是通過全球視角下的比較研究，對香港現代建築的保育和活化進行批判性反思。該研究將分三個階段進行：首先，從全球視角全面瞭解活化現代建築的評估指南和良好做法。其次，檢討香港的評估指引及活化計劃的案例。最後，對香港的經驗和全球經驗進行批判性反思，並提出評估和活化香港現代建築的建議。該研究解決了現有評估指南和活化策略的缺點，這些缺點未充分涵蓋現代建築的關鍵方面。這項研究為現代建築評估提供一套特定的標準以及適用於香港情況的一系列活化策略，肯定會對香港的現代建築保育和活化有一個長遠的影響。

14615718.label: Realisation of objectives
14615718.value: Although Hong Kong has had a mechanism for evaluating and protecting historic monuments since 1976, the evaluation and revitalisation of modern architecture is a rather new challenge since late 1990s. Modern architecture here refers to buildings designed following the principles of the Modern Movement. In Hong Kong, there has been controversy over the conservation and revitalisation of modern architecture through several important instances such as Wan Chai Market, Star Ferry at Central, Hollywood Road Married Police Quarter, the Central Market and the Central Government Offices. After these years of experience, Hong Kong has reached the point where a re-examination and reflection of social mechanism and conservation strategies are necessary in order to establish better practices in the future for the protection of modern architecture. This is the first research on this topic and will certainly have a long term impact by providing a set of criteria for the assessment of modern architecture and proper conservation strategies applicable to Hong Kong condition. The PI has done extensive researches on Hong Kong’s modern architecture with previous two GRFs with a focus on the design achievement. In this project, we shift the focus from building to the process of conservation and revitalisation with following questions: why the conservation of modern architecture has encountered so much difficulties compared with classic Western architecture and Chinese class buildings, what is wrong in the revitalization of PMQ and the Central Market, what are lessons learned from three projects, how to see Hong Kong’s modern architecture conservation and revitalization within a global context, and how can we improve Hong Kong’s system better for modern architecture conservation. The task can break down into 7 objectives (as stated above). During the research process we realised that these objectives can be further consolidated into two specific interests. One looks into the social mechanism of conservation and the other looks into the practice of revitalisation. We planed to tackle each topic from two directions, first a detailed analysis of a local case then followed with a comparative study with international reference. 1, The social mechanism and the case of the Government Hill The Government Hill could be considered one of the most successful conservation projects in Hong Kong so far. By examining the development of the CGO affair, focusing on the interactions between the stakeholders involved, this study argues that the NGOs and the participation of normal citizens played a crucial role in the successful campaign for conserving the CGO as an integrity. We unfolded the research in the following steps: First a historic review of the CGO project from a point of view of social event based on collected literature from social media and interviews. Second a critical analysis of the dynamic interaction between three major parties: government, profession and NGO in four critical phases: the dilemma of conservation and redevelopment, the redefinition of land use, regrading the West Wing, and revitalization strategy. And third, the conclusion on the role of the non-architect-lead NGOs. 2, The social mechanism within global context Following the first case study about CGO conservation project, we conducted a comparative study between CGO in Hong Kong and the Robin Hood Gardens (RHG) in London which is regarded as one of the landmark project of modern architecture in England and Europe. The former is a successful case but the latter is regarded as a failure case because it was eventually demolished after a long time campaign. In Hong Kong’s case, NGOs and normal citizens played an important role but in London’s case, it was professional body urged for conservation however not general public. This study further highlights our previous discovery that the active role of NGOs and citizens’ participation in Hong Kong’s case shows the uniqueness of Hong Kong modern architecture conservation. The research team also noticed two recent cases in Shenzhen and Guangzhou that the professional bodies made a strong request for conservation but have failed due to the lack of support from general public, similar to the case in London. 3, How does the lack of understanding about the essential value of modern architecture effects the conservation and revitalization in the case of Central Market The Central Market is another important case of modern architecture conservation in Hong Kong. But its revitalization has encountered many difficulties. The accepted proposal for revitalization does not respect the quality of space and structure, therefore we consider it as a failure case. Why a right process leads in a wrong or unsatisfactory result? We unfolded the research in the following steps: First the comparative analysis of the original design and renovation proposal to reveal the major difference in its quality of space-structure. Second the examination of the whole process from grading to design to find out in which stage the thing went wrong. Third a discussion leads to a conclusion that it is the lack of understanding of the essential value of modern architecture which is the main cause of the failure. 4, A critical examination of heritage conservation policies and mechanisms in Hong Kong within a global context Following the previous study, we further examined heritage conservation policies and mechanisms in Hong Kong. The main purpose is to find out whether the essential value of modern architecture, its main characteristics of space and structure, has been well reflected in its documents and processes. In parallel, we also check relevant documents from international organizations such as Docomomo International, ICOMOS and the Getty Conservation Institute. Through analysis, we discover that there are actually no specific items on modern architecture evaluation in Hong Kong’s relevant documents. This is mainly because modern architecture conservation in Hong Kong is a rather new problem. As a conclusion, we urge government to review the current documents and add a specific section on the evaluation of modern architecture so that the characteristics of modern architecture could be well reflected in the documents. Originally we plan to write 4 articles with above 4 studies. We choose 《时代建筑》“Time+Architecture” as the venue for publication. The main reason is that the journal has published Gu Daqing’s other 6 articles relating to the study of Hong Kong modern architecture from previous GRFs in 2015 and 2016. Among 6 articles, one is a general survey on Hong Kong modern architecture and 5 case studies focusing purely on the design quality of selected buildings and sites. The newly added articles on social mechanism and conservation practice complete the whole research. However, in preparing for publication, we realised that the planed article 1 and 2 have a large part of the content overlapped. It seems inappropriate to conduct a detailed analysis on CGO in the first article then to repeat the major part of it in the second article to be able to have a comparative study with another case. Most importantly, we cannot reach the conclusion that CGO project as an exemplary of good practice of conservation without comparing it with other local and international cases. The same thing also happened with the planned article 3 and 4. In the end, we decided to focus on two articles in this sequence of studies published on “Time+Architecture”.

14615718.label: Major findings and research outcome
14615718.value: Two journal articles have been accepted by academic journal 时代建筑 (Time+Architecture). One is published in 2021 July and the other will be in the following issue on September. Article I: A Study on the Social Mechanism of Modernism Architectural Conservation in Hong Kong: The Case of Former Central Government Offices This article takes the case of the former Central Government Offices compound in Hong Kong as an example to discuss the conservation of modernist architecture from the perspective of social mechanisms. By restoring the incident, analyzing the role played by social stakeholders such as government departments, the public, non-governmental organizations, professional organizations, we then put forward a point of view that conserving modernist architecture does not entirely depend on the design value of the building itself. It depends on how a mature society learns to deal with such problems and forms a consensus in the interaction of different stakeholders. It is clear that CGO project can be a good reference for future practice both in Hong Kong and elsewhere. Article II: Space-Structure as the Primary Consideration for the Conservation and Revitalization of Modernist Architecture: Lessons Learnt from the Hong Kong Central Market Project The Central Market, built in 1939, is one of the most important pieces of modern architecture in Hong Kong and is currently undergoing conservation and revitalization. Through a comparative analysis of the revitalization design and the original building, as well as a review of various aspects of the revitalization project process, this paper points out that the original spatial quality of the Central Market has been disrupted, reveals that stakeholders involved in the project are not sufficiently aware of one of the fundamental values of modern architecture - the spatial-structure, and suggests that it is one of the reasons why the Central Market has not been adequately conserved. It then advocates that space-structure needs to be primary consideration for the conservation and revitalization of modernist architecture.

Dr. Han Man has recently accepted an invitation from AIA HK to participate in an event “Bauhaus in HK” in the Central Market. (Refer to 80% of objective 6 & 7) 3, To consider the possibility of a book publication There is a potential to compile those previous published articles (6 on design quality and 2 on conservation) into a book publication. The PI will explore publication funds from Hong Kong Arts Development Council. 4, To apply the research methodology to the mainland China The conservation and revitalisation of modern architecture is an emerging issue in the mainland China too. Dr. Wu Jiawei, one of the key team member, is now working at Nanjing University. It is natural that she will continue this research with a shift of focus from Hong Kong to the mainland China.

14615718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14615718.value: Although Hong Kong has had a mechanism for evaluating and protecting historic monuments since 1976, the evaluation and revitalisation of modern architecture is a rather new challenge since late 1990s. Modern architecture here refers to buildings designed following the principles of the Modern Movement. In Hong Kong, there has been controversy over the conservation and revitalisation of modern architecture through several important instances such as Wan Chai Market, Star Ferry at Central, Hollywood Road Married Police Quarter, the Central Market and the Central Government Offices. After these years of experience, Hong Kong has reached the point where a re-examination and reflection of social mechanism and conservation strategies are necessary in order to establish better practices in the future for the protection of modern architecture. This is the first research on this topic and will certainly have a long term impact by providing a set of criteria for the assessment of modern architecture and proper conservation strategies applicable to Hong Kong condition.

14615818.value: This research plan aims to establish a digital database of Daoist literati and gentry in Guangdong. This database will provide access to biographical information concerning these literati and gentry. This database will establish an independent page to illustrate the Daoist trajectory of each individual in the literati and gentry group, showing all noteworthy Daoist-related events each personality of individual in the literati and gentry group had taken part in since their joining Daoism, which may include gatherings at spirit-writing altars, letters in which they discussed Daoism with their Daoist friends, and calligraphies and inscriptions made for Daoist temples. 14615818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14615818.value: This project investigates the important connection between Daoism and late Qing/Republican literati and gentry in Guangdong in terms of their Daoist beliefs in relation to their respective biographical trajectories, thoughts and works in the formation of Daoist networks, as well as their important role in the development of Daoism. This project focuses on the literati and gentry in Guangdong who, during the late Qing/Republican periods, either adhered to Daoism or were influenced by Daoist culture. The time scope for this project starts from Daoguang 道光 1（1821) until Republican 民國 38（1949), covering a period of more than a hundred years during which Chinese society changed rapidly. This research plan represents a new milestone in the investigation of Guangdong Daoism, its breakthrough character being connected to the fact that not only does this research focus on Daoist documents, lineages and rituals, but it also investigates a group of the late Qing/Republican literati and gentry in Guangdong who played an important role in the transmission of Daoist culture. The approach advocated in this research plan is that, from the mid-Ming onwards, the important role of transmitting Daoist scriptures would not be played merely by officially recognized Daoist temples and priests, but, to a greater degree, was also performed by literati and gentry, who had inherited and promoted this important transition. The most innovative aspect of this research plan is the creation of a database which concerns the organization of the Daoist trajectory of each personality of the literati and gentry group, which will be showed according to a spatial-temporal line. Unlike previous approaches, which are exclusively devoted to documental analysis, this new spatial-temporal approach will not only be able to show clearly the transformations in the Daoist trajectory of a given historical figure according to source materials of different periods, but will also be able to show the specific geographical position of the various Daoist temples, spirit-writing altars, and Daoist scenic spots visited by these historical figures. By means of this spatial-temporal platform, therefore, the user will be able to search and read documents related to a given historical figure and Daoism, as well as appreciate related works of art, such as calligraphies, paintings, and inscriptions, and also to access a map-page that shows the footprints of a given historical figure in relation to Daoism, and the information on the Daoist background of the places visited by the historical figure.

14615818.label: Realisation of objectives
14615818.value: 1. The Establishment of the Digital Database of “Daoist Literati and Gentry in Guangdong during the Late Qing and the Republican Periods” (晚清至民國廣東信道文人士紳數位資料庫) The PI has established an open-access database, the “Digital Database of Daoist Literati and Gentry in Guangdong during the Late Qing and the Republican Periods” (http://icsddm3t.ddns.net:81/). It consists of five major sections and functions, namely, the “Search,” “Basic Information of Literati and Gentry,” “Social Networks of Literati and Gentry,” “Daoist Impacts of Literati and Gentry,” and “Daoist Places/temples (related to the literati and gentry group).” The database not only showcases and digitalizes the detailed information of the focused personalities but also visualizes their trajectories, social networks, and Daoist influences with supplementary documents and photos attached for research and public use. This Digital Database has a back end for administration, data entry, maintenance, and categorization. This platform, with high feasibility, is ready to serve as a long-term resource portal and welcomes further expansion and updates on personalities, texts, maps, images, and videos. The PI aims to openly introduce this Digital Database to researchers and the public in September 2023. 2. The Collection of 100 Detailed Biographical Profiles of Daoist Literati and Gentry as the Fundamentals of the Digital Database The PI collected anthologies, genealogies, letters, newspapers and journals, paintings and calligraphies, and other published works of a hundred Daoist literati and gentry, gazetteers, academic papers, books, news reports, chronicles, and databases. Along with digitization and enhancement of the readability (by adding punctuations and dividing texts into paragraphs) of the related texts and documents, a profile for each studied personality with detailed biographical information and all supplementary documents are attached. The Database includes personalities’ information, such as names, birth and death years, origin, education, examinations grade, official title(s), publication(s), biography, and the figure’s networks. The unique feature of this Digital Database is the connection between the Daoist personalities and their Daoist faith and network. The database lists their Daoist style names, Daoist identities, associated Daoist groups, published Daoist texts, Daoist stele inscriptions, plaques, couplets, affiliated monasteries, and fellows they cultivated and studied the Daoist tradition together. To illustrate the Daoist network, a “spider chart” is specially created for each personality to show the multiple levels of correlation between the Daoist identities and their Daoist background and activities. These 100 listed Daoist literati and gentry include twenty-four jinshi (metropolitan graduate), nine juren (provincial graduate), fifteen zhusheng (licentiate), and three xiucai scholars. They taught and studied in twenty-two institutions. Thirty-eight have Daoist-style names (daohao); fourteen served as an abbot in Daoist monasteries. These 100 personalities were closely connected to twenty-eight Daoist sanctuaries and altars. These archival profiles serve as a solid foundation for further research projects. They are also the primary sources of the digital database and related publications. 3. The Visualization of Daoist Literati and Gentry’s Trajectories and Social Networks as the Unique Features of the Digital Database The unique features of the Digital Database are the visualization of the Daoist literati and gentry’s trajectories and social networks. On the main page of the platform is a general view of the 100 literati and gentry’s network presented in a network chart. In each profile, alongside the biographical information section, the “Trajectory” section uses a line chart to display the figure's significant events and Daoist trajectory. In the “Social Network” section, a network graph exhibits the figure’s community by connecting his/her teacher(s), students, relatives, fellows, friends, and Daoist fellows with edges. Each node, with the person’s portrait attached and his/her name labeled, links to the person’s profile; each bite visibly states the relationship between the two nodes. On the left of this section is a table of further details, such as key events and textual pieces of evidence, of these networks. The “Daoist Impacts of Literati and Gentry” on the main page uses word clouds to evaluate the connection of all listed literati and gentry to Daoism. The font size of the names suggests how close an individual was connected to Daoism. This graphical depiction vividly highlights those figures in the group. Furthermore, the “Daoist Places” section has all the geographical information and related data embedded in a map. Five types of Daoist sites are mapped: monasteries, temples, halls/altars/oratories, sacred mountains/places, and related Daoist institutions. With the advantage of using geographical information system (GIS), the map is engaging and interactive, allowing users to travel around Guangdong through the paths of distinguished Daoist personalities. 4. Publications: Two Academic Articles and Two Books The PI published two academic articles, one authored book, and one edited book, presenting rewarding first-hand results on the literati and gentry through field trips and textual research. The first academic article is 鄭觀應與陳攖寧仙道追求的現代意義——以五四新文化運動前後為考察脈絡 (collected in Miaw-fen Lu and Paul R. Katz eds., The May Fourth Movement and Chinese Religion Adjustment and Evolution, 2020). The second is a journal article, "Spirit-Writing and Salvation – the Development of the Ming-Qing Daoist Spirit-Writing Cults of Lüzu and Related Literati Altars," published in Daoism: Religion, History, and Society. For the latter publication, I apologize for the absence of reference to this project. It is only due to the publication schedule being very tight then. The PI authored the book, The Source of the Dao in Lingnan: The Gazetteer of the Three Principles Temple at Guangzhou 道貫嶺南——廣州三元宮志 (The Chinese University of Hong Kong Press, 2019). In the book, the PI inserted a chapter, “Daoist Literati,” giving the accounts of Daoist literati and gentry related to the Three Principles Temple in Guangzhou. The PI’s edited book is the three-volume Companion to the Essentials of the Daoist Canon 道藏輯要•提要 (The Chinese University of Hong Kong Press, 2021). The PI is motivated and highly influenced by this research project to pay closer attention to the literati related to the Qing period's Essentials of the Daoist Canon. Part of the research presented in the author’s “Introduction” (pp.59-151) is supported by this research project. 5. Fieldtrips The PI went on field trips to former residences and ancestral halls of the selected Daoist literati and gentry, as well as Daoist monasteries and historical sites in Guangdong province, with fruitful and productive outcomes. He visited the Sun Yat-sen Library of Guangdong Province to collect the texts on/by the focused personalities, as well as the Guangzhou Archives for the historical records of the Guangzhou Daoist monasteries in the Republican era. Six productive trips are made during the research period. He visited the former residence of Zheng Guanying in the Yongmo village of Sanxiang in Zhongshan, the former residence of Deng Rongjing and Deng Erya in Dongguan, and the Chen Ancestral Hall of Chen Botao in Fengchong village of Zhongtang in Dongguan, the former residence and the ancestral hall of Lai Jixi in the Ziran village of Hutangpu in Zengcheng, the former residence of Kong Zhaodu in Kongjia village of Nanzhuang in Chancheng district of Foshan, the Kong Ancestral Hall in Nanzhuang, the Great Ancestral Hall of the Wen Family in Longshan of Shunde, and the Qinghui Yuan of the Long family in Daliang in Shunde. Besides, Daoist monasteries that the team has done fieldwork are the Chunyang Guan and Three Principles Temple (Sanyuan gong) of Guangzhou, the Yuanmiao Guan in Huizhou, as well as the Chongxu Guan, Sulao Guan, Huanglong Guan, and Jiutian Guan.

14615818.value: 1. The PI successfully established the Digital Database of Daoist Literati and Gentry in Guangdong during the Late Qing and the Republican Periods (http://icsddm3t.ddns.net:81/). The database presents the biographical studies of the selected figures. It displays the large-scale complexed networks of the Daoist literati and gentry group in Guangdong. This confirms the focused group’s key and active role in promoting and developing Daoism during the late Qing and the Republican times. 2. The team collected and collated one hundred literati and gentry profiles, as well as scanned, exported, and categorized hard copies of materials with punctuation added. The team further examined the biographical information of these personalities, their Daoist trajectories, significant events, and their social networks with various groups, including their Daoist fellows. 3. Six field trips are held to the Guangdong province (including Guangzhou, Zhongshan, Huizhou, Foshan, Dongguan). In addition, the team also gathered first-hand historical records and documents from the Sun Yat-sen Library of Guangdong Province and the Guangzhou Archives. 4. The PI published two academic articles on a significant figure, Zheng Guanying 鄭觀應 and his poems, letters, Daoist scriptures, and other works, aiming to examine the Daoist thought, practices, and pursuits that have long been neglected. The PI also worked as the chief editor of two books, namely the gazetteer of the Three Principles Temple (Sanyuan gong 三元宫) in Guangzhou with a chapter written on the accounts of Daoist literati and gentry related to the Temple, as well as the Companion to the Essentials of the Daoist Canon, which includes a section on Daoist literati and spirt-writing altars of Patriarch Lü in the Qing dynasty. 5. The PI expands the scope of research to the construction and evolution of the Lingnan culture by investigating the lives and experiences of a much larger group of Guangdong literati and gentry in the late Qing and Republican eras. 14615818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14615818.value: This research project is a milestone of Daoist culture studies in Guangdong. It investigates Daoist thought, Daoist publications, and activities of the Guangdong literati and gentry during the late Qing and Republican eras, especially with a focus on Daoism in everyday lives, culture, and inner alchemical cultivation of a hundred studied personalities that have long been overlooked. The open-access Digital Database of Daoist Literati and Gentry in Guangdong during the Late Qing and the Republican Periods (http://icsddm3t.ddns.net:81/) is established to present and showcase the outcomes of this project through the visualization of social networks, biographies, and trajectories of the focused literati and gentry group. This project aims to promote the study of Daoism among literati, as well as fill the research gap in the study of Guangdong literati and gentry, as well as their Daoist thoughts, beliefs, and pursuits. It also breaks through the confines of the decline in the practice of Daoism in the late Qing and Republican era stereotypes.

14616018.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14616018.value: 經書評點與晚明士人的知識世界

14616018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14616018.value: The Confucian classics exerted long-lasting and pivotal influence on literary writing and knowledge acquisition in pre-modern China. The representation as well as interpretation of Confucian canon, however, was flexible throughout history. After the Wanli period of the Ming dynasty, there appeared an exuberant amount of new editions of Confucian Classics featuring pingdian (評點punctuation and critique) commentary of the original texts. Over 60 titles of pingdian editions of Shijing詩經, Shangshu尚書, Liji禮記, Zhouli周禮, Zuozhuan左傳 etc. were published during the late Ming, not to mention the legion of reproductions or recompilations throughout the seventeen-to-eighteenth century. While Chinese intellectual history often neglects such works, Chinese literary history dismisses them as an illustration of “the preference for the examination essay” without conducting any in-depth research. In fact, the pingdian commentaries play an important role in the re-canonization of the pre-Qin classics. The present project takes Sun Kuang孫鑛 (1543-1613), the most renowned commentators in the late Ming, as the core case, and then treats other literati such as Chen Shen陳深, Zhong Xing鍾惺, and Tu Long屠隆. It aims to reconstruct the system of pingdian criticism through detailed analysis of the technique terms with which the commentators single out the formal features of classical texts. I hope to argue that, while citing ancient texts to exemplify their aesthetic preferences of “antiquarian wonder”, these literati have introduced a new way to read the classics. In addition to textual and literary studies, this project will explore the socio-historical background that nurtured the flourishing of pingdian. Many publishers produced pingdian books with black and vermilion print so as to differentiate the main text from the commentaries. How were the literary commentaries promoted by new printing techniques? In what circumstances were the classical texts repackaged and republished? Was the hierarchy of knowledge undermined when the method of pingdian insinuated itself into the highly varied contexts of novels, dramas, Eight-Legged essays, histories and canons? This research will investigate the interaction between elite culture and mass publication; and discuss how intellectuals, stimulated by literary interest, opened up their vision to a broader epistemological landscape with the help of the publishing industry. This research project aims to integrate the methodologies of literary criticism, social networks analysis and material culture. With such interdisciplinary approach, it will not only deepen our understanding of traditional Chinese literary criticism, but also provide new perspectives for the study of reading culture and intellectual history in late imperial China.

14616418.label: Project Objectives
14616418.value: Determine the extent to which parafoveal preview benefits at the neural and behavioral levels in reading Chinese characters are driven by magnocellular projections. Based on previous EEG studies on preview benefits, we expect that magnocellular, but not parvocellular same-character previews in the parafovea lead to shorter fixations and reduced activation in the late N1/N250 ERP component. Determine the extent to which behavioral and neural effects of masked repetition priming of Chinese characters in the fovea are driven by magnocellular projections. Based on masked repetition priming studies with EEG, we expect that magnocellular, but not parvocellular same-character primes lead to shorter response times and to a reduced late N1/N250 ERP component. Determine the neural network and connectivity pattern that give rise to magnocellular facilitation in reading. Based on previous studies in reading and visual object processing, we expect that magnocellular, but not parvocellular information leads to early frontal/parietal activation, and to early connectivity from frontal/parietal to occipitotemporal regions.
