14621018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14621018.value: The importance of ritual in the social and religious life of the Chinese people cannot be overstated. It is generally believed that the Chinese accept a priority on ritual over belief in religion. It has been noted by scholars that Buddhist studies generally focus on Buddhist philosophy rather than ritual practice. In this study, we propose to study rituals performed by the Buddhist household (huoju火居) ritual specialists in rural China. More specifically we will focus on the study of two central rituals in the local life of rural China, namely the ‘white’ ritual of funeral and the ‘red’ ritual of communal sacrifice (Jiao 醮). Insofar as religion is defined as the structuring value and practices of a given society, our study will demonstrate that the funeral and communal sacrifice ritual practices had preserved views of the social world and basic value of the common people. As the local ritual is documented in ritual manuscripts of the ritual specialists, the ‘white’ ritual of funeral and the ‘red’ ritual of communal sacrifice will provide us with precious materials to study local society and their religion. One important difference between this study and our previous studies on local ritual traditions is that while we build on our studies before, in this study we concentrate on local Buddhist ritual traditions we discovered recently. These include the Ācārya Buddhism (locally known as the Achali jiao 阿吒力教) in Dali of Yunnan, the Yingjiao (應教) Buddhism in central Hunan, the Xianghua (literally incense & flower 香花) Buddhism in southern Zhejiang and southern Fujian. A characteristic that run through these ritual traditions is that they are surviving folk Buddhist local ritual traditions found in rural China. They are not recognized by the official Buddhist Association of China as ‘orthodox’ Buddhist traditions and hence we use the term ‘popular Buddhism’ to refer to them. We believe that a study of these ritual traditions will contribute to our understanding of the role of Buddhism in the formation of local society and its ritual tradition. 中國民間佛教儀式的歷史人類學研究 儀式在中國民眾的社會和宗教生活中的重要性是不容置疑的！一般相信中國人在宗教上，把重點放於儀式多於信條。可是，學者發現過往的佛學研究卻比較著重哲學多於儀式。是次研究我們決定以鄉村的「火居」儀式專家及其所做的儀式為題。更確切地說，我們要研究中國地方農村生活中兩種核心儀式：紅事的醮儀和白事的喪禮。若宗教代表一個社會的結構價值和實踐，我們的研究會證實醮儀與喪禮保存了平民百姓的社會觀和核心價值。地方儀式被記錄於儀式專家的科儀本中。紅事的醮儀和白事的喪禮會提供許多珍貴的材料讓我們研究地方社會及其宗教。是次研究與過往我們對地方儀式研究不一樣的地方是：一方面我們仍建基於我們過往的研究，另一方面我們將集中於新近發現的地方佛教儀式傳統——包括雲南大理的「阿吒力」教和湘中、特別是新化的「應教」。上述儀式傳統的共通點是它們都是中國農村地方民間佛教儀式傳統的倖存者。中國佛教協會不會承認它們為「正信」佛教。因此我們以「民間佛教」來稱呼它們。我們相信我們的研究會幫助我們更了解佛教對地方社會及其儀式傳統的形成所扮演的角色。

14621018.label: Realisation of objectives
14621018.value: The focus of our project is to study local popular Buddhist ritual traditions. As soon as we went into the field, we realize immediately that we could not study any local ritual tradition without a good knowledge of its neighbors. This never came as a surprise to us. Research in the past 50 years had well demonstrated that there were constant historical interactions between Buddhism and Daoism, and them with diverse local religious traditions (Teiser and Verellen 2011). There were constant crossovers, interchanges, hybridizations, blending, borrowings and sometimes polemics between the three. Any local ritual tradition would, therefore, be hopelessly complex and multi-layered rather than monolithic. Our study of the local Azhali Buddhism in Yunnan has shown that Daoism has provided a ritual framework for their ritual performance. The Azhali tradition, which is known to us as an esoteric form of Buddhism of the Bai people in Yunnan and as the national religion of the Dali Kingdom (937–1094, 1096–1253) formed by the Bai before they were destroyed by the Mongol empire, appears to have undergone a ‘Daoization’ process. We submit that this happened in the Qing. To cut a long story short, after the Dali Kingdom was destroyed by the Mongolian Yuan, the Azhali Buddhism became a popular tradition of Yunnan. Azhali monks were later involved in the resistant movement against the Ming and were suppressed by the court until the Qing. It was during the Qing that the Azhali tradition started to perform Buddhist ritual in a Daoist framework for survival. In mid-Hunan, we have a different situation with the Yingjiao Buddhism. Mid-Hunan was known as the Meishan area which was beyond the control of imperial China until the Song. Chinese Buddhist monks of the Song played an important role in helping the court to take control of the Meishan area. This indicates that Buddhism was well established in the Meishan area before the Song and had won the trust of the indigenous people so that Buddhism could act as a middleman between the court and the indigenous people of Meishan. Our fieldwork study in mid-Hunan has shown that some time in the Qing, the Yingjiao Buddhism had integrated many elements from the Daoist tradition. The pandemic, however, had prevented us to do enough fieldwork to further substantiate our claim by studying the parallel Daoist ritual tradition in mid-Hunan for a comparison. In Zhenan (southern Zhejian) and southern Fujian, the pandemic had, again, prevented us to do enough fieldwork to understand the ritual tradition there. The Co-I had managed to do research on southern Fujian and published an article to compare the ritual tradition in southern Fujian and with those in Taiwan. The PI and Co-I had collected 8 precious ritual manuscripts from Zhenan that dated back to the Qing. They belong to the Yao ethnic group in the area. There had been an important awakening among scholars of Chinese religions that Daoism and Chinese Buddhism as a historical phenomenon is greatly obscured by the abundance of our source materials (Eric Zürcher, 1982). The authors and compilers of both the Buddhist and Daoist canon were overwhelmingly members of the literate elite who took an exclusive view toward religious affiliation. For the majority of Chinese, religion was primarily a matter of worshiping at local temples and a matter of hiring ritual specialists to perform rituals. (Teiser and Verellen 2011). Therefore, to complete our picture of what Buddhism (or Daoism) really was, we must look beyond the Chinese Buddhist and Daoist canon (Zürcher 1982). It was with such an inspiration that we engaged in a collection of local ritual manuscripts as an alternative source in understanding Chinese religion. An analysis of the 8 Qing period ritual manuscripts that we collected in Zhenan has shown that they are primarily Daoist texts. They, however, contain layers of new Daoist schools in the Song-Yuan period and a local Buddhist tradition known as Shijiao. We also found that the ritual tradition of the Shijao had integrated a lot of Daoist elements in their rituals. We were, unfortunately, not able to collect more evidence from the field to support our claim because of the pandemic. It is regrettable that our GRF project's fieldwork plan came to a halt because of the pandemic. We, however, were still able to formulate a hypothesis that some time in Qing, there was a ritual revolution in China. It started in the ‘frontier areas’ like southwestern Yunnan, mid-Hunan and the Hexi corridor in Dunhuang in which Daoism dominated the scene. We would need more fieldwork data cases to support our hypothesis. Richard Wang has shown convincingly that the Ming emperor had sent his princes to different frontier areas a great number of whom were devoted Daoists (Richard Wang, 2012). They were responsible for introducing Daoism to the frontier areas in the Ming. During the mid-Ming, the court decided to give up Dunhuang by closing the border to Dunhuang to concentrate its strength to suppress the rebellion in Yunnan. This was the background for Daoists in Dunhuang to take over the Dunhuang Buddhist caves. Since then, rituals in the area had undergone a Daoist transformation (i.e. Daoization). After the Cultural Revolution, we could not find any existing popular Buddhist ritual tradition in the Dunhuang area. If they were still there, they would have embedded in a strong Daoist framework. After the end of our GRF project, we began to collect evidence from the Hexi corridor and published a book on Daoism in Dunhuang (Tam and Duan 2022). We believe that the Dunhuang case will provide us with further evidence to support our GRF hypothesis. To conclude, while our project was adversely affected by the pandemic, we were still able to formulate a hypothesis: there was a ritual revolution some time in Qing when Daoism has transformed the ritual performance in China especially the Buddhist ritual. This hypothesis will be proved or disproved by further studies. The PI has taken up a privately funded project to study Daoism in Dunhuang. He also has successfully applied for a Direct grant to continue studying the ritual traditions in mid-Hunan. During the pandemic, the ritual study carried out by the PI and Co-I have attracted a private funding for a commissioned study on the rituals of the famous Wong Tai Sin Temple in Hong Kong. A book has been published on the topic (Tam and Lin 2023). 14621018.label: Major findings and research outcome
14621018.value: Our project aims at studying the rituals of popular Buddhism through intensive fieldwork in Yunnan, Hunan, Minnan and Zhenan. Because of the social unrest and the pandemic, fieldwork was not possible after December 2019. The PI had conducted 32 days of fieldwork and had applied for 2 extensions for the project until August of 2022. Eventually the border of mainland was re-opened in February of 2023 but was too late for the fieldwork of this project. Despite limited time for fieldwork, the PI had collected 8 ritual manuscripts dated to Qianlong (1735-1796) from the Wencheng county in Zhenan. Without a chance to do fieldwork on the rituals, the Co-I, as a Daoist specialist, helped to analyze the manuscripts and concluded that the manuscripts, which came from a minority group called ‘She’, preserve a Song-Yuan Daoist ritual tradition of Tiantai Lingbao and Tianxin schools mixed with the Lüshan and the Maoshan Daoist ritual schools, and a local popular Buddhist tradition called Shijiao (see the book chapter by LIN 2020). The PI, as a Buddhist specialist, concentrated his research on Yunnan and mid-Hunan. In Yunnan, he studied the Buddhist ritual tradition called Azhali that belongs to a minority called the ‘Bai people’. The tradition could be traced back to the Dali kingdom (937-1253). The Azhali was supposed to belong to the esoteric Buddhist tradition, but our fieldwork has shown that it had undergone a Daoization process (transformed by Daoism) at around the Qing period (see the journal article by TAM in 2023). Mr. Duanpeng from Yunnan who was hired by the project as a part-time RA was able to produce one book chapter and one journal article on the Azhali tradition (journal article by Duan 2019, book chapter by Duan 2020). The PI also studied the local Buddhist ritual tradition in mid-Hunan known as the Yingjiao. Daoist elements could also be identified in the Yingjiao tradition. The PI has published one journal article on the Yingjiao (journal article by TAM 2022). As the Yingjiao tradition claimed to trace themselves back to the monk Pu’an (1115-1169) in Jiangxi, the PI has conducted research on Pu’an and have published two journal articles on him (Journal article by TAM in 2020 and 2022). In Minnan, the Co-I has published one Book Chapter to compare the ritual traditions in Minnan with those in Taiwan (LIN Book chapter 2019).

14621018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14621018.value: Our fieldwork had shown that a holistic and comparative approach is needed in studying local ritual traditions. We know that there were a lot of crossovers between Buddhism and Daoism but there seems to be a point in history when Daoism has provided a ritual framework for ritual performance in China. This is not a new thesis but when and why it happened is still unknown. We need to do a comparative study in each location between the existing local Buddhist and Daoist ritual tradition. We also need more cases to support our hypothesis that during some time in Qing, there was a major ritual revolution in which Daoism played an important role in transforming all ritual traditions, especially, the Buddhist ritual tradition in China. In this connection, we have expanded our research, under a private funding, to the Hexi corridor in Dunhuang where we have evidence to show Daoists in the Qing performed rituals in the famous Dunhuang Buddhist caves. With the support of a smaller Direct grant, we will return to mid-Hunan in the new academic year to study the local Daoist ritual tradition for a comparison. Local Daoism in Yunnan will be the next subject for research.

14621018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14621018.value: We know well that there are crossovers between Buddhism and Daoism but it appears that some time in Qing, there was a ritual revolution when Daoism has transformed Chinese rituals and provided a ritual framework for all ritual performance in China. We need more cases to support this hypothesis. In this project, we have found that the Azhali tradition of the Bai people in Yunnan, which was once a national religion of the Dali kingdlom (937-1094, 1096-1254) and supposed to be an esoteric form of Buddhism, has now put on a Daoist cloak. A similar phenomenon is found with the Buddhist Yingjiao tradition in mid-Hunan which could be traced back to the early Song (960-1279) when mid-Hunan was taken over by the Song emperor. Obviously, we need more cases to support our tentative hypothesis, cases like in the Hexi corridor in Dunhuang where we found Daoists in the Qing performed rituals in the famous Dunhuang Buddhist caves. Scholars have already suggested that the Ming Princes, who were sent by the founder of the Ming emperor to frontier areas, played a role in spreading Daoism to the frontier areas. A holistic and comparative approach is needed to further substantiate our hypothesis.

14621718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14621718.value: Trade and commodity exchange played an important role in the Han state (221 BCE - CE 220), as is clearly evidenced archaeologically in both the capital region and periphery. However, the nature of the market system in most intermediate regions within the Han Empire is still poorly understood. In order to investigate the market in frontier regions and interregional interaction, this project focuses on the Jingnan (荊南) region (southern Jingzhou province 荊州) as a case study to shed new light on this long-overlooked issue. Jingnan is a geographical unit bounded by the Yangtze River to the north and lies mostly within present-day Hunan. Being an important intermediate region, Jingnan includes major communication routes connecting the imperial core to the Lingnan region where major maritime ports were found. Although metal artifacts, whose supply was closely controlled by the Han state, are often found in tombs in imperial peripheries, their distribution mechanism has not been explored before. For this reason, the PI launches a project to focus on metal objects and their underlying distribution system in Jingnan in order to enhance our understanding of the Han Empire’s control over the transportation network. This project will integrate its results with the “distribution models” previously proposed by the PI in order to address the issue of regional markets. The project will employ three major methodologies: I. Digital database and GIS analysis; II. Non-destructive chemical analysis and 3D-scanner recording; III. Cross-regional comparison and statistical analysis. Through these multi-disciplinary methods, the PI will attempt to determine if discoveries of metal objects can be correlated with distance from production centres, distance from centres of different ranks, and the ethnic affiliation of tomb owners. The PI will conduct a fieldwork employing a portable XRF (X-ray fluorescence) to study the chemical composition of bronze objects (especially mirrors) and to record typical types of metal objects from Hunan. Ultimately, the PI hopes to determine if the objects tested were potentially derived from a common source and if the distribution patterns in the Jingnan assemblage are indicative of a well-integrated market network. The results of the project aims to: 1) understand the mechanism through which Han-style materials was circulated in the Jingnan region; 2) evaluate the development of the market system in the southern imperial periphery; and 3) illustrate the interregional market system and provide a new perspective to explain the extent to which the Han Empire integrated trade on various geographical scales. 在漢代(221 BCE- CE 220)貿易與商品交易扮演著重要角色，不論是在中心京畿還是漢帝國的周邊也有確切的考古學證據。但是，在連接中心與周邊的中間地帶，市場系統的性質卻一直並不清楚。為推動在漢代周邊與中間地帶古代市場情況的研究，本項目以荊州南部為案例，釐清長久以來一直未被重視的題目。 在地理單元上，荊南的北部以長江為界，主體就是現今湖南省。作為重要的中間地帶，荊南覆蓋了連接漢帝國都城與嶺南的主要路徑，而嶺南則是漢代主要港口所在。雖然漢代受帝國控制的金屬製品常常在邊緣區的墓葬中有所發現，但其背後的分布和流通機制卻有待更多討論。為此，本項目主持者提出要在荊南開展有關金屬製品和其流通情況的研究，以望能進一步提升我們對漢帝國如何控制古代的交通網絡的認識。 這個項目是為了應用本項目主持者在之前研究中提出過的古代商品“分布模式”模型，以解決古代地區性市場的問題。本項目主要由三部分組成：I. 數據庫與GIS分析；II. 無損成份分析及三維建模 (並配合少量的有損成份分析，以確定無損分析的可靠性)；III. 跨區域的對比及定量分析。結合這幾種方法，本項目主持者探討到底金屬製品的分布與生產中心關系，與不同等級聚落之間的關系，以及在分布上是否與所在墓葬墓主身份有關。 本項目主持者將開展田野工作，用手持XRF分析銅器的成份，並記錄湖南發現金屬製品的特點。最終，本項目主持者希望能提供更多線索，確定金屬製品是否有可能是同源，以及其分布顯示出較高度整合的市場網絡。 項目最終結果希望:1) 理解在荊南地區漢式器物的流通機制；2)評估在帝國南方的邊境市場的發展情況；3)說明跨地區的市場情況，並以此說明漢帝國如何整個在不同地理單元上的貿易運輸。

14621718.label: Realisation of objectives
14621718.value: With the help of the "Research Experience for Undergraduate Students" scheme, the PI has built up of a database including 1266 tombs in the Hunan region (including both the Warring States and the Han periods) (Objectives 1&3). Besides the basic information of tombs, this dataset included the typological information of 356 pieces of mirrors from these burials. In order to identify the typological characteristics, the dataset generated by this project also incorporated the typological information of more than 1400 pieces of bronzes presenting the major types of weapons and vessels yielded from the entire Hunan region. Part of this dataset (the typological information) will be released in the in prep. monograph co-authored with one of the collaborators in this project (output 10). To further characterize the types of mirrors in the region, which represent the most commonly seen type of bronze goods in Han tombs, this project collected the information of more than 2000 pieces of Han mirrors in the Nanyang, Luoyang, and Guanzhong regions (Objectives 1&2), which resulted in a under-review paper coauthored with the PI’s supervised Mphil student (output 7) to explore the regional differences of bronze mirrors through statistical analysis and the presence/absence of various types of bronze mirrors in different centers on the routs from Chang’an to Chenzhou, or the north-south traffic route during the Han time, facilitated by GIS (Objective 4). To provide a deep-portrait of bronze materials in southern Jingzhou with regard to the production and distribution system, this project funded a fieldwork collaborating with the Chenzhou museum to conduct an on-site analysis of bronze artifacts for non-destructive chemical compositions together with the collection of samples for metallurgical analysis (destructive analysis) (Objective 3). The GRF grant also supported 10 students from CUHK to join the fieldwork. More than 300 Han bronzes were analyzed using portable XRF. In addition, this project has employed 3d scanning to record more than 70 Han bronzes and 60 relatively well preserved iron implements stored in the museum. Most importantly, the museum allowed the PI to sample around 120 pieces of bronze objects to generate the chemical compositions and metallographic identification that can tremendously supplement the non-destructive analysis. The fieldwork and analyses of bronzes directly led to the two publications based on the nondestructive compositional analysis, SEM-EDS, and metallographic examination (output 6&8; also see conference output 2). To fully make the research outcome more available to the public, the PI is preparing a monography co-authored with a researcher in Chenzhou to publicize photos, drawing (generated by the 3d-scanning), results of non-destructive analysis, and metallographic analysis (output 10), which will be the first kind of research monography exploring the regional characteristics of Han bronzes. The PI is also discussing with the university library to upload some of the 3d bronze models to the digital humanities platform for later teaching purposes after the publication of output 10. The support of this GRF grant also generated fruitful results that tremendously enhanced our understanding about the iron industry in the Jingzhou region. This project supported a fieldwork for the PI to visit a site in Sangzhi, Hunan, to study iron objects from a Han ironworks (Objectives 2&3). The collaboration with the Hunan provincial institute of archaeology led to the generation of a paper reporting the excavation discoveries and results of metallurgical analysis of 30 iron remains from the excavation (output 1), which is the first study of iron production system in present-day Hunan. Building upon this foundation, the PI has initiated a cooperative project with the municipal museum in Chenzhou and provincial institute to collect iron implements from Han tombs in Chenzhou. Because Chenzhou is located in the Guiyang commandery where the only ironworks in the southern region mentioned in Han texts is located, the result can help understand the supply and transportation system in a bigger context (Objective 4&5). A total of 91 iron objects were sampled and studied in terms of the microstructure and chemical composition, and the result has been submitted to Journal of Archaeological Science: Report for review (output 5; also see conference presentation no.3). This project also supported the construction of a dataset including a total of 115 artifacts from the Guanzhong region (Objective 1&2). Together with research output1, the PI conducted a regional comparison to understand the differences of manufacturing techniques between Hunan and Guanzhong (output 5). Various factors, such as the distances to manufacturing centers, costs associated with manufacturing, and challenges in the transportation were also articulated to explain the differences observed through the statistical analysis (i.e., the lack of fined iron in the Hunan region) (Objective 4). In addition, the PI has worked with Zhuzhou museum in Hunan (the third collaborative institute in this project) and analyzed 12 artifacts from Han tomb. Since the collaborative institute required to publish the analytical results after the publication of the preliminary excavation report of those Han tombs, I have included the analytical report (in the area of others) to this realisation report. Needless to say, the outbreak of COVID during the last three years has greatly affected the research progress. For instance, the lockdown delayed not only the analytical works in the PI's lab at CUHK but also the photo-taking, measurement, verification of information, etc. on the PI's collaborators' side in Hunan. Therefore, the monograph (output10) is still under preparation. However, based on the new analytical results and insight generated by the project, the PI has managed to deliver the research outcomes via various venues. For instance, the journal articles (output 5&7) are the new attempts through statistical analysis to discussion the exchange network of bronze and iron implements (Objective 5). Also, the study of the iron industry in the south generates a significant body of information that bridges the gap in our understanding. The dominance of cast iron-based products in major nodes on the traffic routes in present-day Hunan indicates that the production and transportation of iron at various scales played a significant role in generating the "connectivity" between various parts of the Western Han empire. This new insight prompted the PI to conceptualize the issue and to finish the writing-up of the book monograph "Connectivity, Imperialism, and the Han Iron Industry" published by Routledge (output 4). This book allows the PI to introduce the rise of the iron industry and related state-controlled transportation system during the Warring States and Western Han periods (ca. 400 BCE–9 CE) in ancient China to a wide spectrum of audiences (Objective 5). Based on the new empirical data, output 4 also casts new light on the workings of the economic system and “economic rationality” in imperial China. Furthermore, the new understanding about the metal supply system (Objective 4&5) laid the foundation for the conceptualization and writing of two book chapters about craft production system in another book-length manuscript co-authored with Dr. Alice Yao to introduce Han archaeology (output 2&3, which have gone through second peer-review). This project also supports part of the analysis and writing of a paper analyzing bronze remains from Yunnan, China. Although it is not directly related to Hunan, this paper allows the PI to collect published datasets of bronze chemical compositions in the entire southwest China, which facilitates the characterization of bronzes in Hunan discussed in output 6,8,9.

14621718.label: Major findings and research outcome
14621718.value: [1] The first study that casts light on the local production of iron on southern frontiers and articulates the regional characteristics of the iron-making techniques in the region. The metallurgical dataset of iron implements from the southern Jingzhou region (output 1&5) is the largest one related to Han iron implements that has been so far published. The research outcome for the first time revealed that most implements even on the interior southern frontiers were made using solid-state decarburization of cast iron together with malleable iron and fined iron. The outputs highlight the importance of transportation and provide hints for further exploring the regional differences of manufacturing techniques that have been overlooked in the previous study (output 2-4). [2] The research outcomes provide the first (and only) case study illuminating the typological characteristics of bronzeware and their manufacturing techniques from a regional perspective (output 6-8, 10). Even though a good portion of bronzewares from the study region may have been introduced from other bronze foundries, the results highlight the potential of a local production in southern Jingzhou. In addition, one important contribution of this project is that it is the first search demonstrating the potential existence of an individual bronze mirror industry in Jingzhou during the Western Han period. [3] The outputs (1,5,6,7,8) provide new evidence demonstrating the importance of cross-regional transportation of metal goods and enhancing the understanding of the economic system of the Han state. Through combining the studies of bronze and iron implements, the new results can contribute to the further investigation of regional characteristics of the iron/bronze manufacturing techniques and exchange networks (also see output 4 & 9). The transportation system of metal goods illustrated by the distribution pattern and metallurgical analysis, alongside the existence of small-scale local industries evidenced by the project (output 1, 5, 7), cast light on the mechanism leading to the widespread of the Han material culture and strategies maneuvered by the state that could strengthen the connection of its various parts (output 2-4). Resonating with existed discussion about ancient economies in China, this project provides an important set of material culture demonstrating that the state control was deeply involved in, instead of isolated from, the market-exchange network of commodities. The role of various factors that could have contributed to such a situation are also discussed in the research outputs (5&7), which can enhance the understanding of the craft production system.

14621718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14621718.value: 1) Regional characteristics of iron manufacturing techniques. Since the outcomes of this project demonstrate the differences in terms of the manufacturing techniques represented by iron implements from different regions, the PI proposes that future studies should continue to fill the knowledge gap and to provide more case studies showing how various cast iron-based steel-making techniques were practiced in different geographic and environmental settings and how iron-making industries in different regions were integrated into the state economic system. 2) The project also demonstrates that regional differences of typology together with the analysis of chemical composition and manufacturing technique can bridge the gap in the study of the bronze production system. Besides incorporating new techniques studying the provenience of raw materials (e.g., lead isotopic analysis), the PI proposes that future projects can focus on other potential bronze production regions, or intersectional nodes on traffic routs, and can combine multiple approaches (i.e., typology, chemical compositions, metallographic examination) in the methodology in order to productively unentangle the complexity of bronze production during the Han period.

14621718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14621718.value: This projects provide new evidence for understanding how iron and bronze implements were suppled in the southern extreme of the Han empire. The new results generated by the fieldworks and various outputs can collectively serve as an important piece of puzzle for reconstructing the Han iron and bronze industries, and for illuminating how the market exchange system extended from the core of the Han state to its various parts. In particular, the PI highlights that the production and distribution system reconstructed by the research outputs illustrates the economic idea in ancient China mentioned in traditional texts, one that emphasized on the active role of the state in the redistribution of goods to make sure even distribution of resources and maintenance of social stability. More importantly, this project provides an important set of material culture demonstrating how such an economic mechanism was operated in daily lives in southern Jingzhou during the Han time.

14621818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14621818.value: Research findings in the past decades have pointed out that sign language learning is beneficial to deaf/hard-of-hearing (D/HH) children in various developmental aspects. What about typically developing hearing children? Can they benefit from sign language learning as well? If the answer is yes, in what developmental aspects? In the field of bilingual studies, there is growing evidence that learning a second spoken language leads to cognitive and linguistic benefits for hearing learners (e.g., Bilingual Advantage Hypothesis by Bialystok, 1999), and such benefits are more pronounced if the learning starts earlier in life. Since sign languages are natural languages, in principle, learning a sign language should also be beneficial to hearing learners. However, not much research has been done to explore this issue. Given that sign languages adopt the visual-gestural mode of communication, there is a possibility that learning a sign language may lead to benefits related to the visual-spatial and motor aspects. This proposed project aims at addressing these questions by investigating the developmental impact of sign language learning on two types of children longitudinally over a three-year period: a group of ~25 D/HH children (age 4 to 10) who are educated in a sign-bilingual co-enrollment setting involving Cantonese and Hong Kong Sign Language (HKSL) as the medium of instruction, and a group of ~80 hearing children (age 0 to10) who are regularly exposed to HKSL input in the baby crèche, kindergarten or primary school they are attending. The two major research questions to be addressed are: (a) For the sign-bilingual D/HH children, does sign language learning lead to better spoken language and cognitive skills when compared to other mainstreamed D/HH children without sign language exposure? (b) For the hearing children who are learning HKSL as a second language, do they have better fine-motor skills, better Cantonese development, better metalinguistic awareness as well as better cognitive skills than non-signing hearing children? Research findings of this project have both theoretical and applied values. First, this project will contribute to the on-going debate on the linguistic and cognitive benefits of childhood bilingualism by offering valuable data from a cross-modal bilingual setting, which is globally uncommon. Second, the data generated from this project will shed light on the nature and extent of benefits of sign language learning among hearing people, which can become an effective means of promoting social inclusion of deaf people in the hearing society if positive evidence can be found. 過往數十年的研究顯示，手語學習有利聾/聽障兒童不同方面的發展，那麼學習手語對發展正常的健聽兒童同樣會有幫助嗎？如果有，會是在哪一個發展的層面？在雙語研究中，越來越多的證據顯示學習第二語言會為健聽人帶來認知和語言方面的好處，而且開始學習的歲數越早，這些好處會越明顯。手語跟口語一樣同屬人類的自然語言，按道理，學習手語對健聽人也應該有益處。但目前這方面的研究為數不多。由於手語採用視覺和身體動作作為溝通的渠道，學習手語可能有助視覺空間和肌動技能的發展。本研究旨在回答以上的問題，將會在三年間以追蹤研究方法觀察手語學習對兩組兒童的影響：第一組是約25 (4至10 歲)名就讀於手語雙語共融計劃的聾/聽障兒童，這個融合教育計劃採用廣東話和香港手語作為教學語言，第二組為約140名(零至10歲)健聽兒童，他們分別在育嬰院、幼稚園和小學長期接觸香港手語。本研究主要討論兩個問題：一）相對沒有學習手語的聾/聽障兒童，有學習手語的聾/聽障兒童的口語和認知能力發展會更好嗎？ 二）相對沒有學習手語的健聽兒童，有學習手語作為第二語言的健聽學童會有較佳的肌動能力、廣東話能力、後設語言覺識和認知能力嗎？本研究同時具有理論和應用的價值。首先，研究人員對兒童雙語發展帶來的語言和認知的益處仍有不少爭論，本計劃能提供跨語言渠道的有用數據。第二，本計劃探討健聽人學手語所帶來的益處，如果我們得出正面的結論，健聽人學手語將會成為聾人融入健聽人社會的有效方法之一。

14621818.label: Realisation of objectives
14621818.value: This project investigated the impact of sign language learning on the linguistic, cognitive and fine motor development of hearing and deaf/hard of hearing children (D/HH) (from age 0 to P2). When the proposal was submitted in 2017, the Centre for Sign Linguistics and Deaf Studies was supporting sign language learning of young hearing children at several baby crèches under the Hong Kong Society for the Protection of Children. It helped run the sign bilingual co-enrolment programmes for D/HH children in a mainstream kindergarten and a primary school. In these contexts, sign language learning for the D/HH and hearing children was immersive. The baby crèches were visited by the deaf instructors regularly for storytelling times and other activities, and the hearing teachers included signs in their daily interactions with children. At each grade level in the co-enrolment kindergarten and primary school, there was a co-enrolment class in which 4-6 D/HH children studied with other hearing kids, and the lessons were co-taught by a hearing speaking teacher and a deaf signing teacher. At these whole-day programmes, the hearing children had plenty opportunities to interact with the deaf teachers and schoolmates inside and outside the classrooms. Our research goal was to find out whether immersive sign language learning would be beneficial to hearing and D/HH children. Unfortunately, the pandemics from 2020-2022 led to frequent suspensions of face-to-face teaching, depriving the hearing children of receiving sign language input naturally in the school environment. Our data collection was postponed for multiple times, and we only managed to collect one round of data, instead of having multiple data points. When the schools resumed face-to-face teaching, the Education Bureau only allowed half-day classes. Due to health concerns, our partner schools did not allow us to collect data at their school and we needed to arrange for the parents to bring their children elsewhere for data collection. Many parents were unwilling to do so because of the ongoing COVID. Hence, none of the objectives was achieved, and there was no way for us to remedy the situation. What we did instead was to develop sign language assessment tools not originally stated in the proposal. Our research activities are summarized below. 2019 Before the commencement of this project, two computerized vocabulary tests (Cantonese and HKSL), were developed for children under age 3. The Cantonese data were collected from ~250 hearing unimodal Cantonese-speaking children (i.e., they only knew spoken language) and ~40 hearing bimodal Cantonese speaking children who were learning HKSL (i.e., they could speak and sign) in baby crèches. In 2019, ~100 more unimodal children and ~60 more bimodal children were tested. The bimodal children also took the HKSL test as well. Among these children, ~210 participated in retesting after a six-month period, resulting over 600 data points. Overall speaking, a stronger correlation between age and Cantonese scores was found among the bimodal children, suggesting potential benefits of sign language learning in their spoken language development. Nonetheless, some children achieved full scores as early as 21 months of age, meaning that the test was too easy for them. The findings were presented in a local linguistic forum in December 2019. • Sze, Felix, Kloris Lau & David Lam. 2019. Computerized tests for vocabulary knowledge in Cantonese and Hong Kong Sign Language for children under the age of three. Paper presented at the LSHK Annual Research Forum, 7 December 2019, The Education University of Hong Kong. In view of the early ceiling effect of the Cantonese test and the feedbacks we obtained from the presentation over the reliability of a two-choice format, we decided to revise the tests by increasing the difficulty level and adopt a four-choice format. We also began to develop the following assessment tools: (a) The Hong Kong Sign Language Sentence Repetition Test. This test involves 40 HKSL sentences with increasing length and difficulty and a shortened version was created for children. A journal paper was published. (b) Adaptation of three British Sign Language (BSL) Tests into HKSL. We started to adapt the BSL Receptive Skills Test (BSL-RST), Vocabulary test (BSL-VT), and Production Test (BSL-PT) into HKSL. A progress report was presented in a local forum in December 2019. • Sze, Felix, Jafi Lee & Monica Wei Xiao. 2019. Adaptation and development of sign language assessment tools for hearing and deaf children in Hong Kong. Paper presented at the LSHK Annual Research Forum, 7 December 2019, The Education University of Hong Kong. The materials and instructions of the executive function tests, metalinguistic awareness tests and several cognitive skills tests were prepared (link: http://www.cslds.org/GRF_14621818_Sze_CUHK/). In-house training was organized for the research assistants. 2020 – 2022 All schools were closed starting from January 2020 due to COVID. K3, P1 and P2 classes resumed face-to-face teaching briefly between 15 June and 13 July in 2020. K1-K2 classes were suspended until September 2020. In late September, face-to-face lessons resumed for kindergartens and primary schools. However, all schools were closed in November 2020 again, followed by a territory-wide adoption of online learning. According to our school partners, although the online lessons were co-hosted by hearing and deaf teachers, it was unsure if the hearing children paid attention to the deaf teacher, who was only one of the many participant screens in Zoom. Moreover, the hearing children had no opportunity to interact with the deaf children and teachers outside the classrooms. The lesson time was reduced, as EDB advised against long online lessons. In light of these, we decided to wait until face-to-face teaching resumed. In late February 2021, face-to-face teaching resumed by phases, with a reduction in teaching hours and restrictions on the number of students present in school. It was not until late May 2021 that schools had face-to-face lessons again. However, the duration of sign language exposure was too short before summer. In September 2021, all schools resumed half-day classes. We planned to collect data in January 2022, after several months of sign language exposure. Unfortunately, all schools were closed again in mid-January 2022. In late April 2022, most schools resumed half-day face-to-face teaching. The half-day policy continued until December 2022 when our project officially ended. The partner baby crèches were closed for multiple times between 2020 and 2022. In 2021 and 2022, our team managed to collect one round of data. A summary of the data collected can be found at http://www.cslds.org/GRF_14621818_Sze_CUHK/. Unfortunately, as the data were limited, we were not able to publish any papers on the findings. Between 2020 and 2022, we continued to refine the language assessment. (i) The Computerized Receptive Vocabulary Test in Cantonese and Hong Kong Sign Language for Young Children (ii) The Hong Kong Sign Language Receptive Skills Test (iii) The Hong Kong Sign Language Vocabulary Test (iv) The Hong Kong Sign Language Production Test All tests were digitized online. The descriptions and video demonstrations of these tools can be accessed at http://www.cslds.org/GRF_14621818_Sze_CUHK/. Another presentation was made in a local linguistic forum recently: • Sze, Felix, Philip Thierfelder, Wei Xiao Monica, David Lam, Jafi Lee and Pollyan Chan. 2023. The adaptation of three British sign language assessment tools into Hong Kong Sign Language. Paper presented at the LSHK Annual Research Forum, 2 December 2023, City University of Hong Kong.

14621818.label: Major findings and research outcome
14621818.value: Due to the pandemics of COVID-19 during 2020 and 2022, most of the planned data collection could not be carried out. We managed to collect one round of data from the target children in 2021 and 2022. As the data were limited, we could not provide any proof to argue for or against the hypothesis that sign language learning is beneficial to both hearing and deaf/hard of hearing children in various developmental aspects. Hence, none of the original project objectives can be achieved. However, several language assessment tools were developed while we waited for the COVID-19 to subside. These tests included the Hong Kong Sign Language Sentence Repetition Test (HKSL_SRT), a shortened version of it, the Computerized Receptive Vocabulary Test in Cantonese and Hong Kong Sign Language for Young Children, The Hong Kong Sign Language Receptive Skills Test, The Hong Kong Sign Language Vocabulary Test, and the Hong Kong Sign Language Production Test. All of these tests were digitized to facilitate administration and data scoring. These tests will be useful for experimental and clinical purposes in the long run.

14621818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14621818.value: Although we only collected one round of data and no conclusive findings can be presented in this report, our preliminary observations show that sign language learning can potentially benefit hearing children. For example, more than half of the hearing babies/toddlers at the baby crèches outperformed their non-signing peers in the standardized norms in the fine motor developments. In some of the executive function tasks, the hearing signing children also did better than the non-signing kids. If future resources are available, we will re-do this study again, given that the findings will have a strong potential for building a more inclusive society in Hong Kong for deaf people. In this project. we developed several sign language assessment tools while waiting for the pandemic to subside. However, due to COVID and the limited population size of deaf signing children, most of these tests were not yet standardized. If future resources are available, further data will be collected (e.g., longitudinal data from the same group of deaf children) for testing the reliability and validity of the tests.

14621818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14621818.value: This GRF project aimed at investigating the potential impact of sign language learning on hearing and deaf/hard of hearing children who were exposed to HKSL inputs naturally in their school/daycare centre. These potential areas for benefits include spoken language development, fine motor development, and cognitive skills. However, due to COVID, most of the planned data collection and experiments could not be carried out. As only one round of data could be collected, we were unable to draw any reliable conclusion from our data. Despite this, we channeled our resources to develop several sign language assessment tools that were not originally stated in the proposal. These tests will be useful for clinical and experimental purposes in the future.

14622018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14622018.value: Development coordination disorder (DCD) is rarely recognized by educators and healthcare professionals until children begin to struggle at school. Children with DCD have deficits in motor and cognitive functions, which result in restricted participation in daily activities, poor academic performance and psychosocial outcomes such as anxiety and depression, limited social support and low self-concept. Early intervention is important because problems associated with DCD will carry over into adulthood. Conventional or therapeutic approaches to motor intervention on DCD are less promising, mainly because traditional rehabilitation practices impose economic and psychological burdens on both children with DCD and their families. In view of the positive associations of physical activity (PA) with improved cognitive function and psychosocial health in children, ecological PA intervention in the school setting has gained much attention. Our research team has conducted school-based PA interventions in children with DCD, and found significant positive effects on (1) motor performance, self-perceived competence and enjoyment; and (2) inhibitory control, a critical cognitive function that involves an ability to react and adapt to environmental changes in different contexts such as learning and social interaction. Further research is still needed to determine the sustainability of the intervention effects and determine whether improved motor and cognitive functions can translate into increases in psychosocial health as secondary outcomes in the longer term. Grounded in the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health for Children and Youth (ICF-CY) framework, this study is the first cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) to examine the effects of a school-based PA intervention on motor and cognitive functions (inhibitory control) and psychosocial outcomes (anxiety and depression, social support, self-concept) of children with DCD. It is also the first study to use salivary cortisol as biomarker of stress in Hong Kong children with DCD. Based on power calculation, 240 children with DCD in twelve Hong Kong primary schools will be cluster randomized allocated into either a 12-week PA intervention or a control condition. Measurements of motor performance, inhibitory control, and psychosocial outcomes (self-report, proxy-report, biomarker) will be conducted at (i) baseline, (ii) post-intervention (immediately after 12-week intervention), (iii) 3-month after post-intervention, and (iv) 12-month after post-intervention. This cluster RCT brings experts in PA interventions together, and its findings will assist educators and healthcare policy makers to develop early treatment strategies for DCD and to introduce school-based health promotion practices for children with DCD.

14622018.label: Realisation of objectives
14622018.value: Grounded in the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health for Children and Youth (ICF-CY) framework, the purpose of this project was to examine the effects of a school-based PA intervention on motor and cognitive functions (inhibitory control), and psychosocial outcomes (depression, anxiety, stress, perceived social support, self-concept) of children with DCD using a cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT). As proposed in the protocol, a total of 240 participants from 12 schools would be included with the consideration of potential attrition. Because of the influence of the COVID-19 pandemic, the research team had faced unpredictable and great challenges. Eventually, a total of 241 children aged 6-10 years were successfully recruited from 11 local primary schools. Among 241 children, 126 of them were diagnosed as having DCD or at risk. Among the 11 participating schools, 6 schools were allocated to the intervention condition, and the other 5 schools were allocated to the control condition. A 12-week PA intervention was delivered in the intervention schools during school time, and children were required to perform activities at a moderate intensity level (50-60% of the maximum heart rate), which was objectively measured with a Polar heart rate monitor. To achieve Objective 1, a series of assessments at baseline (prior to intervention), immediately after intervention (immediate effect), 3-month post-intervention (short-term effect), and 12-month post-intervention (longer-term effect) were performed. Motor performance was assessed using the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2nd edition (MABC-2) and relevant checklists. Cognitive function of children was assessed by the endogenous model of the Posner paradigm to determine the children’s inhibitory control ability. The psychosocial outcomes (anxiety, depression, social support, self-concept) of the children were assessed by self-reported questionnaires. In addition to self-reported measures, salivary cortisol was collected as an objective biomarker to assess stress level of children. Additionally, cardiorespiratory fitness was measured with the Pacer test, a multistage progressive 20m shuttle run test in the Brockport Physical Fitness Test Kit. Sedentary behavior and PA at different levels (i.e., light PA, moderate-to-vigorous PA [MVPA]) were objectively assessed for consecutive seven days using Actigraph accelerometers. To achieve Objective 2, information on gender and DCD status of children was either collected or determined. DCD status was assessed by the MABC-2 test and relevant checklists (e.g., Developmental Coordination Disorder Questionnaire-Chinese version completed by parents). Children with a MABC-2 total score in the 5th percentile or below were identified as DCD, and those within the 6th-15th percentile were identified as DCD. The impacts of gender and DCD status on children’s health outcomes and intervention effects were further explored. Therefore, the two objectives have been achieved.

14622018.label: Major findings and research outcome
14622018.value: This project was the first attempt to determine the effects of a school-based physical activity (PA) intervention on motor performance, cognitive function, and psychosocial outcomes in school-aged children with DCD using an RCT design. The findings of this project advanced our understanding of the effectiveness of early PA intervention on the improvement of physical and mental health in children with DCD. Importantly, it helped aid the development of early treatment strategies for DCD and inclusive health promotion practices in a school setting for children with DCD in Hong Kong. Key findings of this project are presented as follows. As predicted, gender and DCD status were significant factors that influenced the expected outcomes. Compared to children with typical development (TD), children with DCD showed significant poorer motor performance, inhibitory control ability, self-concept (particularly in physical coordination and body fat), and had a higher level of anxiety. Children with DCD were also found to spend more time being sedentary in day time and had poorer cardiorespiratory fitness than their TD peers. Additionally, boys with DCD were more likely to have poorer self-concept on physical coordination and tended to experience a higher level of stress than girls with DCD, even though boys with DCD were more physically active than girls with DCD (i.e., spent shorter time being sedentary and more time in MVPA per day). However, such gender disparity was not evident in children with TD. After receiving a 12-week PA intervention during school time, children with DCD significantly reduced their stress level (based on the biomarker of salivary cortisol) and improved cardiorespiratory fitness immediate and 12-month after the intervention. The findings indicate that a school-based intervention appears to be a promising way to improve physical fitness and mental health of children with DCD and its effectiveness can be even sustained for one year. Besides, children with DCD who received the intervention also significantly increased their time spent in MVPA immediate after the intervention. However, no significant improvements were observed in other outcomes (i.e., motor performance, inhibitory control, self-concept, and social support) for children with DCD in the intervention group when compared to children with DCD in the control group. Interestingly, children with TD who received the intervention showed significant improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness (immediate, 3-month, and 12-month after the intervention), PA participation (i.e., spent shorter time being sedentary and more time in MVPA per day at 3-month after the intervention when compared to the baseline level), and mental health (i.e., reported lower levels of both depression and anxiety level immediate and 3-month after the intervention than baseline). Taken together, PA intervention developed in this project is beneficial for both children with and without DCD in terms of improving physical and psychological health.

14622018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14622018.value: DCD is a common neurodevelopmental disorder among school-aged children worldwide including in Hong Kong, which is rarely recognized in its early stage. Development of ecological and cost-effective intervention strategies to alleviate primary deficits of DCD and its related secondary health consequences is very important. Based on the key findings of this project, it is worth considering some gaps and directions for future development of the research in the field. First, children with DCD demonstrated significant deficits in various physical and psychosocial health outcomes as well as cognitive functions, which were moderated by gender. With the consideration of such complex situation in this group of children and limited empirical evidence up to now, more future research from a multi-disciplinary perspective is needed for a better understanding on the association of DCD deficits with healthy development in children. Second, school-based PA intervention appears to be a feasible and effective way to improve overall physical and psychological health of children with DCD. However, more future research is warranted to optimize the design of PA intervention programs tailored for children with DCD for the sake of further improvements in their psychosocial health (e.g., cognitive function, self-concept, and social support).

14622018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14622018.value: Children with Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a group of children who have impairments in learning and executing motor skills that significantly impact their daily activities and result in poor physical and psychosocial health consequences. Early intervention is important because problems associated with DCD will carry over into adulthood. Grounded in the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health for Children and Youth (ICF-CY) framework, this project was the first to examine whether a 12-week physical activity intervention at school is effective (both short- and long- term) in improving physical and psychosocial health for children with DCD using a cluster randomized controlled trial. The effectiveness of intervention was determined using multi-dimensional outcomes including motor performance, cognitive (inhibitory control) and psychosocial (depression, anxiety, stress, perceived social support, self-concept) functions, physical activity (sedentary time, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity), and fitness (cardiorespiratory fitness). Our findings showed that a 12-week school-based physical activity intervention appears to be effective in improving overall physical and psychological health in children with DCD. We believe the findings gained are of significance to assist educators and healthcare policy makers in developing early treatment strategies for DCD and to introduce school-based health promotion practices for children with DCD in Hong Kong.

14622818.label: Project Objectives

rows: To understand the role of visual perceptual skills in skilled reading and education;

14622818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14622818.value: In educational settings, learners often need to efficiently perceive and extract information from visual inputs, be they words, faces, musical notation or figures. While the visual perceptual challenge is common to many domains of learning, we know little about its role in education since this research area is relatively understudied. This proposal focuses on the role of visual perceptual ability in a type of real-world skilled reading – music sight-reading. Sight-reading refers to the ability to play a piece of music when one reads the score for the first time. It is one of the most important skills to acquire in music education, with a wide range of skill levels in the population. These make it an ideal window to understand how visual perception affects skilled reading and education in general. The proposed project will examine the role of visual discrimination of musical notation patterns in predicting and enhancing music sight-reading abilities. Study One will use an individual-difference approach to build a new theoretical model on the basic cognitive abilities underlying sight-reading, including the ability in reading musical notation that was missing in previous studies. Study Two will use an experimental approach to test whether improved visual perceptual ability in the laboratory can transfer to enhanced sight-reading, a real-world complex skill that involves coordinated information processing in multiple modalities. This research will have important theoretical impacts: First, it will build a new cognitive theory of music sight-reading that takes into account the role of visual perceptual ability, a missing component in the current model. Second, it will establish the causal relationship between visual perceptual abilities and sight-reading. Third, the findings will serve as a proof of concept of the role of visual perceptual learning in education in general. It is well expected that theoretical insights generated from this proposal will be applicable to other domains of skilled reading requiring visual perceptual extraction of visual codes, such as Chinese and English reading. Pedagogically, the findings will provide an empirically tested solution to promote perceptual learning of musical notation, which addresses a long-standing problem in sight-reading pedagogy. The computerized training will be highly promising since it can be accessible to students once it is adapted to mobile platforms, adopts the self-teaching approach in learning, and can cater for individual differences in their skill levels and pace of learning. This will be an important contribution to evidence-based teaching of sight-reading. 在教育的場境中，不論是文字、人臉、音符和圖案，學生都需要有效率地處理和提取視覺訊息。雖然視覺感知能力對許多學習領域均構成挑戰，可是視覺感知在教育的角色卻缺乏研究，所以我們對這方面所知甚少。 本研究計劃旨在了解視覺感知能力在日常閱讀中所扮演的角色，並以音樂視奏所涉及的閱讀能力作為研究重點。視奏是指彈奏第一次閱讀的樂譜，乃音樂教育裡其中一項最需要掌握的能力，惟不同的人在視奏能力上存在具大差異。因此，透過音樂視奏這個窗口，我們能夠窺探視覺感知如何影響高階閱讀以及一般的教育。 本研究將探究視覺分辨音符在預測及提升音樂視奏能力的角色。研究的第一部份將利用個人差異的研究方法建構一個理論模型，以解釋音樂視奏背後的相關基本認知能力，包括研究文獻鮮有觸及的音符閱讀能力。第二部份則測試透過實驗提升的視覺感知能力能否轉移至涉及多感官訊息整合的視奏能力。 本計劃有著以下幾項重要意義：第一，它會建構一個解釋音樂視奏能力的認知理論，並把過往所忽略的視覺感知能力加入其中；第二，它會確立視覺感知能力和音樂視奏的因果關係；第三，研究結果能夠證明視覺感知訓練對於一般的教育的角色。研究所得可應用到其他同樣需要從符碼中提取視覺訊息的閱讀領域，包括中英文閱讀。 在教學層面上，研究所得能夠提供一套經過實證測試的音符閱讀學習方法，有助音樂視奏教學。研究計劃所發展出來的一套電腦訓練採用自我導向的學習模式，並能照顧個人學習差異和進度，將來可發展成方便的應用程式。是以本研究能為以實證為本的音樂視奏教學作出重要貢獻。

14622818.label: Realisation of objectives
14622818.value: Both objectives are completely achieved. For the 1st objective, our findings showed that the long-overlooked association between visual shape processing ability and sight-reading is important and has substantial predictor power over one's sight-reading ability. This led to a better understanding of music sight-reading. For the 2nd objective, we built a cognitive model that explains music sight-reading ability with an individual difference approach and based on basic cognitive abilities, including visual fluency for notes, general visual fluency, motor dexterity, visual-auditory association for notes, visual-motor association for numbers, working memory capacity, and executive function. Correlation and regression analyses showed that sight-reading performance can be largely explained by three abilities related to vision, including visual fluency for notes, visual-auditory association for notes, and visual-motor association for numbers.

The importance of visual shape processing ability may also apply to other domains of skilled reading requiring visual perceptual extraction of visual codes, such as word reading.

14622818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14622818.value: The ability to recognise and read musical notation can explain how well one can do music sight-reading. After considering one's finger dexterity, visual-motor association for numbers, working memory and executive function, we find that music sight-reading ability can be predicted by one's fluency for recognising musical notation and ability in matching the musical notation with sound. This calls for a major revision of the current cognitive model of music sight-reading to consider visual and visual association abilities. This also suggests that music educators should pay attention to these abilities in teaching more in teaching music sight-reading.

14623118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14623118.value: Research shows that Chinese students tend to have higher achievement than their Western counterparts, but also experience more psychological distress, with parents’ high expectations for children and exertion of control implicated as contributing factors. Most parenting and family intervention programs to date, however, were developed in the West and target behavioral and emotional problems among children. Given that children’s development and family dynamics are embedded in the larger societal and cultural contexts, and cultural differences in learning-related parenting have been documented, existing programs may not be effective in preventing and reducing parents’ exertion of undue academic pressure on children and other forms of controlling parenting in Hong Kong, thereby unlikely to mitigate students’ psychological distress. The proposed research entails a culturally sensitive parenting intervention program to promote positive parenting especially in, but not limited to, the academic realm in Hong Kong. The program aim is fourfold: (1) enriching parenting knowledge, (2) facilitating parents’ setting of realistic goals and expectations for children across developmental domains, (3) empowering parents for effective parenting by fostering parent-child communications and promoting parental self-care and parenting efficacy, and (4) promoting self-reflection in parents. Central to the program is a 15-week mobile application-based intervention with a series of mini-modules for parents. Moreover, this mobile application-based intervention may be supplemented by parent meetings held by trained school personnel. Participants will be about 480 parent-child dyads from 60 schools. Schools will be randomly assigned to one of three conditions in Time 1: the App-meeting condition with both the use of the mobile application and parent meetings; the App-only condition with just the mobile application and no parent meetings; the Wait-list condition with no intervention at Time 1 (to be given the mobile application in Time 2). In the App-meeting condition, about 40 school personnel will be involved as trained facilitators of parent meetings. Focus group interviews will be conducted with 64 parents in the App-meeting and App-only conditions. Short-term and long-term effectiveness of the mobile application-based intervention with and without school-based parent meetings will be evaluated based on quantitative and qualitative data obtained from parents and children before and after the intervention as well as from parents during the intervention through diary surveys. Specifically, program effectiveness will be assessed in terms of improving parents’ outcomes (parenting knowledge, other cognitions such as goals and expectations for children, parenting practices, and psychological functioning), children’s outcomes (psychological functioning), and the parent-child relationship. 有研究發現華人學生比西方學生成就更高，但承受更大的心理困擾，父母在育兒方面的高期望與高壓的管教模式被視為問題成因。然而迄今為止，大部分協助父母育兒及促進家庭和諧生活的介入計劃皆在西方制定，而且專門針對兒童的行為及情緒問題。兒童的發展及家庭成員的互動狀況與社會及文化環境不可分割，文獻亦已廣為論述在父母對子女學習的教養模式上之文化差異。有鑑於此，現有的介入計劃恐未能有效防止或減少本地家長對學童過度施予學業壓力以及其他控制性管教行為，故此不太可能減輕學生所承受的心理困擾。 本研究擬在香港建構一個注重本地文化因素的育兒介入計劃以鼓勵正面育兒，尤其是在（但不僅限於）學業層面的管教。計劃的主要目標有四：一、豐富父母的育兒知識；二、引導父母對子女各方面的成長和發展訂立合理的目標和期望；三、透過促進親子溝通、提高父母的自我照顧意識及親職效能感，提高父母有效養育子女的能力；四、鼓勵父母自我反省。計劃的核心內容為一項為期十五周、以手機應用程式為平台的介入計劃，其中包含一系列為家長而設的迷你課程。此外，由受過專業訓練的教職人員主持的家長小組亦可能會支援該計劃。 本研究參加者為約480對、來自60間學校的親子組合。有關學校將會被隨機分配成三組，各組實驗條件不同。第一階段：第一組參加者將同時參加應用程式介入計劃和家長小組；第二組參加者只參加應用程式介入計劃，不會參加家長小組；第三組參加者處於等候名單控制組，暫不獲安排任何形式的介入（但他們將在第二階段參與應用程式介入計劃）。在第一組，大約有40位教職員將會協助計劃，作為受過訓練的家長小組主持人。另外，第一和第二組中64位家長會參與焦點組群訪談。手機應用程式介入計劃的短期及長期成效（輔以校本家長小組與否），將根據是次研究所收集的量化及質化數據去評估，數據來源包括父母和孩子參與介入計劃的前後對照，以及介入計劃進行期間父母撰寫的日誌。具體來說，計劃成效將會從家長(育兒知識、其他如父母對子女的目標和期望等相關認知、教養行為、心理狀況)、子女(心理狀況)、親子關係三個向度作出評估。

14623518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14623518.value: The objective of this project is to understand the how elite Chinese universities divide undergraduate slots among provinces. Under the current system, within province admissions are determined by a entrance exam. But because tests scores are not comparable across provinces, universities assign separate admission quotas to different provinces. A generally held belief is that elite universities in Beijing and Shanghai discriminate against out-of-province students. The first part of the project is to develop a theoretical model of college admissions that captures the key features of the Chinese system. Our assumptions are as follows: 1.Universities care about student quality in addition to the number of local students. 2.Students in different provinces may have different preferences over universities. 3.The distributions of student ability are different across provinces. We will characterize the equilibrium of the model and carry out comparative statics analysis. We will show that the over-representation of local students in universities in Shanghai and Beijing does not necessarily imply bias. The same outcome would also occur if Shanghai and Beijing students have higher average quality and prefer Shanghai and Beijing. The second part of the project is to estimate the key parameters of the model empirically. We have collected the cutoff scores and admissions quotas of the top 112 Chinese universities, and the distribution of the test score of the college entrance exam in 27 provinces from 2013-2016. Our theoretical model implies that in equilibrium each university should set admission quotas to equalize the quality of the marginal students in all non-home provinces. This implies that we can regress the normalized cutoff scores of each university in each non-base province on the cutoff score of the university in a base province to recover student quality in each province (compared to the base province), as well as the local bias of each university. Student behavior will be modeled as a logit demand system. Following Akyol and Krishna (2017) we can identify in each province the average utility a student obtains from each university. We will conduct counterfactual experiments to understand the effects of different admission policies. 本研究試圖理解中國的精英大學如何在各省之間分配本科生招生名額。在現行招生制度下，每個省內部的招生由高考分數來確定。但是由於不同省之間的高考分數並不可比，大學在錄取時會給每個省分配壹個招生指標。人們通常認為北京和上海的大學會歧視省外的學生。 本研究的第壹部分建立了壹個理論模型來解釋中國的高考錄取。我們有以下的假設： 1.大學不僅考慮本地學生的錄取數量，也會考慮學生的整體質量。 2.不同省份的學生對學校的偏好可能不同。 3.不同省份的學生的能力分布可能不同。 根據模型求解出的均衡以及比較靜態分析，我們發現：北京和上海大學錄取的本地學生占比過高，不壹定意味著這些大學對本地和非本地的學生區分對待。這可能是因為上海和北京的學生的平均能力更高，或者他們更傾向於待在本地讀書。 本研究項目的第二部分利用數據估計了上述模型的重要變量。我們搜集了2013年至2016年間，中國最好的112所大學的在各省的錄取分數線和錄取名額；以及27個省高考分數的分布。理論模型表明：在均衡的條件下，大學應該讓每個省在最低錄取分數線上的學生的質量都壹樣。這意味著我們可以將標準化後每個學校在非本省的錄取分數線，對每個學校在本省的錄取分數線回歸，來推測出每個省的學生質量（相對於本省），以及學校偏袒本地學生的程度。我們假設學生的行為符合 logit需求系統。根據Akyol and Krishna (2017)， 我們可以確定各省的學生進入各大學所能夠獲得的平均效用。我們將進行反事實實驗來理解不同錄取政策的影響。

14623518.label: Realisation of objectives
14623518.value: Objective 1. We modeled the admissions process as a quota-setting game. The basic assumptions of the models are: 1. All universities prefer high test-score applicants. But controlling for test scores, universities may have different preferences over applicants from different provinces. The preference may reflect either the interests of the universities or those of the central or provincial governments. 2. Applicants have preferences over universities. In each province, applicants apply to a university after learning the admissions quotas. 3. Universities choose quotas non-cooperatively, each trying to maximize its own utility. The central or provincial governments may influence the objective functions of the universities, but they do not set quotas directly. These assumptions are consistent with the information we obtained through a literature review of the Chinese admissions system and interviews with admissions officials at two universities in our sample. Throughout the history of the People's Republic, university places have been divided among provinces through a quota system. Since the mid-1980s, the central government has delegated more decision power to universities. In recent years, the central government has tightened control to shift more places to poorer provinces. Nevertheless, both admissions officials we interviewed told us that, despite tighter control, universities retained some leeway to fine-tune their admissions plans. We proved the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium. In equilibrium, applicants apply to their favorite universities among the ones that will accept them, and universities set quotas optimally given the behavior of the applicants and other universities. Objective 2. The first-order condition of the universities’ optimization problem implies that in equilibrium, each university should allocate its places so that its valuation of the marginal student (i.e., the applicant with the lowest test score among the admitted) is the same in every province. The condition implies that a university will assign more places to a province either if it has a stronger preference for the province or if the province’s applicants have a stronger preference for the university. Our model suggests that the proper way to discern a university's preferences is through its cutoff scores. Universities release their cutoff scores (i.e., the lowest test score among admitted students) every year. In equilibrium, each university is indifferent between marginal students of different provinces. If a university's cutoff score is lower in province A than in province B, then, controlling for test scores, the university must prefer province A's applicants to province B's. Objective 3. We collected a unique data set of cutoffs and quotas. Our study focuses on 107 of the 119 universities that belong to the prestigious Project-211 program. The sample includes all top universities in China. Our analysis relies on three data sets: cutoff scores from 2013 to 2016, admission quotas from 2013 to 2015, and test-score distributions from 2013 to 2016. Stream-specific cutoff scores in each province were collected from the universities' websites. When they are not available, we use figures from two. Enrollment data were downloaded from gaokao.chsi.com.cn, a website affiliated with the Ministry of Education. We also downloaded admission plans, when available, from universities' websites. Test-score distributions for each stream in 27 provinces and provincial-level cities were obtained through various sources, including provincial education examination authority websites and college guides. The distribution of test scores varies both across provinces and over time. To facilitate cross-province comparison, we used the test-score distribution to rescale the test scores. The transformed test scores follow the standard normal distribution in every province and year. One surprising finding is that universities in our sample have very similar cutoff-score gaps. If one university has a lower cutoff score in province i than in province j, then other universities are likely to have the same. For each pair of provinces, i and k, we regressed each university’s cutoff score in province i against its cutoff score in province k. The average slope is about 0.9, and the average R-squared value is over 0.7. The results indicate that universities in our sample value different provinces similarly. To compute the average provincial values, we chose a province as the base and normalized its value to zero. We then measured the average value of a non-base province by the average cutoff-score gap between the base and the province among universities located in a third province. A province has a higher average value if universities have lower cutoff scores in the province than in the base province. For robustness, we also measured university preferences using the cutoff scores of the least and most popular majors in a subsample of 38 universities that published major-specific cutoff scores. In both cases, the results are almost identical to the original estimates. We used a difference-in-differences approach to test whether a university is biased in favor of home applicants. We first computed the difference between the home province’s cutoff score of a university and its non-home provinces’ cutoff scores. We then computed the difference between the average value of the home province and the average value of other provinces. The difference between the two differences measured a university’s home bias. Finally, we measured the preferences of the applicants over universities by estimating a logit-demand system following the procedure in Akyol and Krishna (2017). Objective 4. We regressed the average provincial value against provincial admissions rates. As expected, provinces with higher values have higher admissions rates. On average, a one-standard-deviation increase in a province’s average value raises its admissions rate by 2.43 percent. The variation in average values explains about 73 percent of the variation in admissions rates. We fitted our estimates into our theoretical model to obtain counter-factual estimates. Eliminating home bias has little effect on either the provincial distribution of places or the fraction of places allocated to the universities’ home provinces. Further eliminating students' preference for attending universities close to home reduces the fraction of places allocated to home-province students but exacerbates the unequal distribution of places. As more students from Beijing and Shanghai are willing to attend universities outside of their home provinces, the fraction of places allocated to Beijing and Shanghai increases further. The result suggests that the unequal distribution of elite university places is mainly due to a systematic preference favoring Beijing, Shanghai, and other richer provinces. Our methodology does not allow us to say for sure whether the preferences reflect the objectives of the universities or the central government. However, anecdotal evidence suggests that the interests of the universities partly drive them. One possibility is that universities believe students from richer provinces are better trained on average. Provincial pre-college education spending is highly correlated with provincial per-capita GDP, and parents in richer provinces are likely to spend more on their children's education. We regressed the average values on various provincial characteristics. Provincial GDP per capita and educational spending are both positively associated with provincial value. Educational spending, however, seems to be the more important of the two: it alone explains nearly 80 percent of the variation in provincial values. Controlling for education spending, per-capita GDP is statistically insignificant.
