15220618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15220618.value: More than 1000 new buildings over 200m tall have been built since the year 2000, representing 80% of the total. Proliferation of such challenging architecture in densely populated urban environments has led engineers to question the fitness of the prevalent prescriptive approaches in ensuring the safety of occupants in the event of fire. The current practice of assuming post-flashover compartment fires as the sole paradigm for fire safety in buildings has been challenged as inadequate for much of modern infrastructure with wide cavernous spaces, such as atria and large open plan offices. Alternative scenarios such as localised and travelling fires have been proposed to address some of these concerns. The fundamental premise of this proposal is that a rational framework for engineered fire safety can only be based on a range of idealised fire scenarios. However considerable research needs to be done before a set of scenarios can be agreed upon for use in engineering practice. This will require full scale experiments, but given the cost and complexity of such testing only a limited number will materialise. The only option therefore is to augment full-scale experiments with computational simulation. There are commercial tools capable of modelling all relevant phenomena individually, but there is no single package capable of modelling the full sequence of a fire scenario, heat transfer to the structure and the thermomechanical response of the structure. We will develop this capability by integrating free, efficient and open source computational tools: FireFOAM (based on OpenFOAM); FDS from NIST; and OpenSees software framework from PEER, University of California, Berkeley. We will develop a wrapper software and middleware interfaces between FireFOAM and OpenSees (and FDS and OpenSees) to enable complete simulation of a realistic fire and resulting heat transfer to structural components and the consequent structural response. The integrated simulation tool OpenFIRE thus created will be validated against the fire and thermo-mechanical response data from Cardington and Dalmarnock tests. This will be followed by demonstration case studies for a range of building and bridge fire scenarios. Finally the OpenFIRE will be used to simulate the progressive collapses of: the September 11, 2001, WTC Twin Towers; and the Plasco Building, Tehran in January 2017. 從2000年起，全球已經建造了1000多座超過200米的超高層建築，占目前所有超高層建築的80%。這些快速增長的超高層建築促使工程師們重新反思住戶在建築火災中的安全問題。現有防火規範通常假設，閃燃後的火災僅限於建築分區。這樣的假設已不足以應對現代建築中出現的大空間，如中庭和大型開放式辦公室。所以需要考慮包括局部火和漫遊火等在內的其他火災形式。本項研究的出發點在於：只有基於大量理想化火災形式的研究才能提出一個有效的消防工程準則。但是，提出新的工程標準需要對不同火災案例進行大量的研究。這通常需要進行大尺度的實驗，但是考慮到這些測試的高成本和複雜性，只可能進行少量的實驗。 除此之外，只能通過電腦類比來補充缺失的全尺寸實驗。目前，市面上的商用軟體可以單獨類比火災中出現的各種現象，但是沒有單獨的軟體可以全面地類比包括傳熱、結構以及熱機械回應。在本項研究中，我們將開發一個免費而高效的計算平臺，並結合多種軟體，包括基於OpenFOAM開發的 FireFOAM、美國國家標準局開發的FDS，以及美國加州大學柏克萊分校基於PEER開發的OpenSees。同時，我們將研發一個中介軟體來處理FireFOAM和OpenSees，以及FDS和OpenSees之間的耦合，從而完整地模擬真實的火災，火災對建築的傳熱和建築結構的回應。通過綜合計算平臺OpenFIRE來模擬的火災和熱機械回應的資料，將與Cardington和Dalmarnock火災實驗來比對，並通過一系列的建築和橋樑火災的案例來驗證。最終，OpenFIRE計算平臺將用於模擬超高層建築的倒塌過程，包括2001年“9-11”事件中倒塌的世貿中心雙子塔和2017年在德黑蘭倒塌Plasco大樓。

15220618.label: Realisation of objectives
15220618.value: REALISATION OF OBJECTIVE 1 A generic framework named OpenFIRE for sequential coupling of CFD-FEM has been developed. OpenFIRE models the complete sequence of a fire scenario, heat transfer to the structure and the thermomechanical response of the structure, through a sequential coupling of open source Computational Fluid Dynamics tool (FDS) with open source Finite Element software tool (OpenSEES). To couple the FDS and OpenSEES, a generic middleware named; Fire and Structural Data Mapping (FSDM) was developed, which can transfer the time-varying boundary conditions from FDS output to the OpenSEES model for heat transfer analysis. FSDM is developed by utilising an open-source programming language (Python). The script file from the structural model is used by the middleware to generate the point devices in FDS (thermocouples, heat flux, Adiabatic Surface Temperature (AST) devices, gas temperature devices, etc.). While generating the thermocouples or devices, it generates script files for conducting heat transfer and thermo-mechanical analysis. Another module of the middleware transfers the FDS output in the OpenSees format to conduct heat transfer analysis. The output of the heat transfer can be used as a boundary condition for the thermo-mechanical analysis using the part of the script generated by the middleware. As OpenFIRE integrates free, efficient and open-source computational tools: FDS and OpenSEES by employing the open-source programming language (Python), it maintains the open-source and licence-free nature of the framework. REALISATION OF OBJECTIVE 2 OpenFIRE framework has been applied to fire scenarios such as localized fire and flashover fire in a fire compartment to study the structural response to fire. The case of collapse of the Plasco building due to an accidental fire in January 2017 is used to demonstrate the application of the OpenFIRE for forensic study and represent different regimes of fire behaviour. The forensic investigation of the structural failure of the Plasco Building is done by first organising observed data (images, interviews, reports, and other resources) into a coherent timeline and presenting the actual fire spread obtained from the visual evidence. The estimated fire progression history within the building is calibrated with the CFD model. A CFD model is generated to represent the fire spread on the 13th floor of the Plasco Building. The temperature contour plots show the travelling behaviour of the fire on the 13th floor. To capture thermal gradients in all structural components such as slabs, trusses and columns on each floor, many ‘AST (Adiabatic Surface Temperature) measuring devices’ are installed in the CFD simulations. Using the middleware (FSDM) the thermal output is transferred to OpenSees to perform heat transfer and thermomechanical analysis. The temperature history of the structural components is established after the heat transfer analysis in OpenSees for the 13th floor fire at two locations: (a) temperature history near the north-west corner (where the fire first broke out), and (b) temperature history near the south-east corner of the building (where the fire was present just before the final collapse). Once heat transfer analysis is finished, the temperature output from OpenSees is applied as the loading condition for structural analysis. The middleware maps the respective temperature history from the heat transfer analysis to each element of the structural model (beam-column elements are used for truss and columns, and shell elements are used for slabs). Results show the sagging of the floor area which is exposed to fire. Preliminary results show that due to high temperatures in trusses around the column at the south-east of the floor, the column is pulled in by the sagging trusses, which may cause the failure of this column and trigger the collapse of the entire building (as observed in visual evidence). Work is continuing to further understand the local and global collapse of the Plasco Building during the fire. REALISATION OF OBJECTIVE 3 OpenFIRE framework is validated and demonstrated using the well documented experimental and numerical results. To validate the framework, the thermal response of the SHS steel column to a pool fire is predicted using an FDS model. In the experiment, a SHS column (STKR400) of 0.1 m x 0.1 m and 1.6 m tall with thickness of 3.2 mm was exposed to a pool fire. A model was developed for the CFD analysis with the same perimeter and thermocouples as used in experimental study. First, CFD-HT (heat transfer) is validated with the experimental data. The results show a reasonably good agreement between the experimental and predicted steel temperatures. To validate the HT-TM (thermo-mechanical), a thermal stress analysis has been conducted by importing the temperature history from the heat transfer analysis using a component of the FSDM. An excellent comparison of time-vertical deflection behaviour from FE simulation with the test results has been obtained for the entire duration of fire. The results from OpenSEES are much closer to the experimental data than the previous numerical results by commercial packages. Validation work is continuing on larger tests and being published in relevant journals.

15220618.label: Major findings and research outcome
15220618.value: 1. The OpenFIRE package (one of the outputs of this project) is the first and only open-source and licence-free package for CFD-FEM coupling. This kind of fully open-source framework can be freely and independently updated and improved by other researchers. 2. OpenFIRE can be used by both researchers and practising engineers. GUIs have also been created for the whole process, making it easier to use the middleware for users who have no programming experience. 3. OpenFIRE can facilitate large numbers of simulations of large structural models under realistic fire scenarios and simulating the progressive collapse of tall buildings so it is an ideal tool for performance based engineering. 4. OpenFIRE is being further developed to be able to use third party tools for 3D visualization of heat transfer and thermomechanical results. 5. OpenFIRE has also been used for analysing the bridge failures in fire.

15220618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15220618.value: The PI has been awarded a RGC Theme based project for developing the theoretical basis for smart firefighting (SureFire: Smart Urban Resilience and Firefighting). SureFire system will use AI tools trained by large database of CFD models to provide an accurate forecast of the fire evolution within a building. A large library of critical events has been compiled from literature and from hours of interviews with retired fire fighters. There are various critical events that affect the firefighting process and put the life of firefighters in danger such as failure of structural components, failure of windows and so on. OpenFIRE is able to simulate such failures. Very large number of CFD and FEM simulations need to be carried out for each target building to generate its corresponding big data repository. The repository will contain an exhaustive range of critical events. OpenFIRE will be used to synthesize data to train an AI for predicting failures (or critical events). This will be combined with the fire evolution prediction to create an artificial intelligence forecast system to respond to building fires in real time. The data obtained from the sensors can be read at the server over the cloud or be processed on site (edge processing). The data from IoT devices will be used to identify the situation and forecast or predict the events presented in the Critical Event Library

15220618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15220618.value: One of the key features of the OpenFIRE package is that it is a freely available open-source tool. This makes this tool an ideal package for researchers and practicing engineers for simulating structural failures in fire and for use in performance based engineering of complex structures against the fire hazard. In the past three to four years research was conducted to demonstrate the capability of the OpenFIRE tool in the field of forensic investigation, bridge failure analysis and performance based engineering. The PI team is continuing the use of the OpenFIRE tool in smart firefighting for predicting critical failure events during a major fire emergency.

15220818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15220818.value: The rapid development of electronic devices and electric vehicles has laid an ever-increasing demand and more stringent requirements on electric energy storage devices. Low capacities of the current commercially available cathode materials are becoming the bottleneck for the large-scale applications of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in electric vehicles due to limited driving range. There is an urgent need to call for high-performance cathode materials for LIBs. Nickel-rich layered oxides (NLOs) are regarded as an attractive candidate for high-capacity and high energy density cathodes. However, they are suffered from capacity lose on cycling due to structure instability and side-reactions with electrolyte. Conventional coating techniques which only address one aspect of the encountered problem cannot provide a satisfactory solution. In this project, we propose a novel multifunctional surface coating technique to tackle the challenges faced by NLO cathodes. Three functionalities can be simultaneously realized by the proposed coating technique: (1) the coating layer being electrochemically stable and structurally compactible with NLO, (2) the coating being able to remove the surface lithium residues, and (3) the coating layer being ionically conducting. Various kinds of in-situ techniques, such as X-ray diffraction (XRD), electrochemical strain microscopy, transmission electron microscopy and electron energy loss spectroscopy, will be employed to study the mechanism of charge storage and performance degradation. The evolution of microstructure and phase, and the crystallographic heterogeneities in electrochemical activity and kinetics, will be fully studied as a function of scan rate and voltage during the charge/discharge process. Accompanied by other ex-situ characterizations, a detailed mechanism of the protective role played the coating layer will be proposed. The results obtained will guide us in the control of morphology, design of nanostructure, and optimization of composition for the further enhancement of the electrochemical performance of cathodes. Finally, the multifunctional coating technique will be applied to other Li- and Mn-rich layered oxide cathode materials as well. 電子器件和電動汽車的飛速發展給電能儲存器件帶來了更多的需求和更嚴格的要求。目前，商用鋰離子電池正極材料的較低比容量已經成為限制電動汽車續航裏程的瓶頸，發展高性能正極材料迫在眉睫。富鎳層狀材料被認為是極具吸引力的高容量和高能量密度的鋰離子電池正極材料。然而，富鎳材料在電化學循環過程中結構不穩定並易與電解液發生付反應從而導致容量的不可逆損失，傳統的顆粒包覆技術只解決部分的問題。在本項目中，我們提出利用多功能包覆材料來解決富鎳層狀材料所遇到的困境。我們的包覆技術可以同時實現包覆材料的三大功能：（1）具有電化學穩定性並在結構上與富鎳層狀材料兼容；（2）能去除電極材料表面的殘余鋰化合物；（3）具有離子導電性。我們將采用多種原位表征技術如：X-射線衍射、電化學應力顯微鏡、透射電子顯微鏡和電子能量損失譜來研究富鎳層狀材料的儲鋰和容量衰減機制，並對電化學循環過程中材料的微觀結構演變、具有晶體各向異性的電化學活性和動力學特性進行深入的研究。同時再結合其他多種非原位表征技術，我們可以解析出包覆材料對正極顆粒的保護機制。研究結果將對材料的形貌控制、微觀結構設計和組分優化起指導作用並有利於正極材料的電化學性能的提高。另外，這種多功能包覆技術也可以推廣應用於其他富鋰和富錳層狀正極材料。

15220818.label: Realisation of objectives
15220818.value: All objectives are 100% achieved. Objective 1: To synthesize NLO cathode material with the novel multifunctional coating layer. Ni-poor and Ni-rich precursors [Ni0.2Co0.4Mn0.4](OH)2 and [Ni0.6Co0.2Mn0.2](OH)2 were preliminarily prepared via co-precipitation reactions. Single crystal spinel oxide Li[Ni0.4Co0.8Mn0.8]O4 was firstly synthesized as a transition phase for the preparation of single crystal Ni-rich oxides. Namely, the precursors mixed with stoichiometric Li2CO3 (Li/TM=0.5) were calcined at 1000°C for 4h. After that, the spinel oxide and stoichiometric Ni(OH)2 (Li0.5TMO2/Ni(OH)2=1:1) were added into deionized water, in which a small amount of polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP) as binder were also added. The mixture was further stirred and dried at 100 °C to form the spinel/Ni(OH)2 composite. Finally, the composite mixed with stoichiometric Li2CO3 (Li/TM=0.5) was calcined at 850 °C for 20h under pure oxygen atmosphere to prepare single crystal Ni-rich oxide Li[Ni0.6Co0.2Mn0.2]O2. The polycrystalline Ni-rich oxide Li[Ni0.6Co0.2Mn0.2]O2 was also prepared from secondary particles of precursors at 850 °C for 20h under pure oxygen atmosphere. If we increased the molar ratio of spinel oxide and Ni(OH)2 (Li0.5TMO2/Ni(OH)2=1:3) and decreased the calcined temperature (800°C), single crystal Ni-rich Li[Ni0.8Co0.1Mn0.1]O2 was also prepared. Due to lithium volatilization during solid-state reactions, 5% excess lithium source was added during all of calcination processes. The prepared Ni-rich layered oxides were further dry-mixed with boric acid in different molar ratios. After calcination, a thin layer of ionically conducting LiBO2 was coated on the Ni-rich cathode particles. Objective 2: To use a combination of in-situ and ex-situ techniques to study the local structure/phase evolution, electrochemical activity and kinetics of the electrode material during a charge/discharge process. The morphology analysis and phase measurement of spinel and layered oxides were investigated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Rietveld refinement of XRD was performed by Fullprof software package. In-situ electrochemical XRD was employed to reveal the crystal structure evolution during charge at 0.1 C. The data were collected from 10° to 80° at a scan rate of 10° per minute. The fine structure and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) of single crystal was analyzed by high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM). The chemical compositions of Ni-rich oxides and elements dissolved into electrolyte after cycling were measured by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). The valence states of elements on the grain surface were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The specific surface area of single crystal particles was measured by N2 adsorption/desorption isotherm. For differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurement, the cathode materials were initially charged to 4.4 V (Li/Li+) at 0.1C in half cells, after which the delithiated cells were disassembled in an Ar-filled glovebox. Meanwhile, these materials were scraped off from Al foil and enclosed into a high-pressure crucible. Last, the DSC analysis was performed by a NETZSCH 204F1 instrument at a rate of 10 °C min−1 from 100 to 300 °C. Various kinds of electrochemical characterization techniques, such as, cyclic voltammogram (CV), Galvanostatic charge discharge (GCD), cyclic test, rate performance test and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were used to fully characterize the electrochemical performances of the cathode materials. EIS was used to study the charge transfer process at the electrode-electrolyte interface. An equivalent circuit was used to analyze the experimental EIS data. Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) was conducted to determine the ion diffusion coefficient. The coin cells were charged and discharged at 0.1 C for the first cycle. After that, the coin cells were given a constant current flux (0.2 C) for 10 min, followed by 60-min rest to achieve steady state. Then, the procedure was repeated until the voltage was increased to 4.5 V. Online electrochemical mass spectrometry (OEMS) was carried out by a self-modified electrochemical cell under a voltage range from 2.7 to 4.7 V at 0.1 C rate. The loading of active materials is about 10 mg cm-2. Aluminum mesh was used as the current collector to facilitate the flow and detection of gases (CO2 and O2). The Ni K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) were measured at TLS-17C of Taiwan Light Source in National Synchrotron Radiation Research Center. The energy resolution (ΔE/E) for the incident X-ray photons was approximated to be 1.4×10-4 eV by using a Si (111) double-crystal monochromator. The measurements were carried out in the fluorescence mode. The software Artemis and Athena were used to analyze the XANES and EXAFS spectra, respectively. Objective 3: To propose a detailed charge storage mechanism of the electrode material based on the combined results obtained from in-situ and ex-situ measurements. We performed theoretical calculations in the framework of density functional theory (DFT) implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP). The generalized gradient approximation (GGA)+U with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) flavour was chosen as the exchange-correlation functional, in which, the Hubbard U parameters for the d-orbitals of Ni, Co and Mn were set to 6.2, 3.32 and 3.9 eV, respectively. For geometry optimization, the plane-wave cut-off energy of 450 eV was employed. A 5×1×1 supercell was built for the layered structure of the cathode materials, and a 2×1×1 supercell was built for spinel structure. The Brillouin-zone was sampled using 3×13×3 Monkhorst-Pack grid for he layered structure and system and 2×3×3 for the spinel system. The convergence criterion for energy was set to be 10-5 eV and that for the force was set as 0.01 eV Å-1. Spin polarization was considered in the calculations. Then the detailed charge storage mechanism was proposed based on the results from experimental measurements and theoretical calculations. Objective 4: To further optimize the electrochemical performance of the electrode material through proper control of morphology, design of nanostructure, and optimization of composition. Based on the results obtained above, we further fabricate Co-free Ni-rich cathode to lower the material cost, large single crystal particles to reduce the side reactions with electrolyte, and two-step coating technology to deal with ions with different diffusivities.

15220818.label: Major findings and research outcome
15220818.value: We found that cycling at a low voltage after initial activation at a high voltage would greatly improve the reversibility of cationic/anionic redox reactions in the layered cathode materials. STEM and EELS confirm that the structural transitions from the layered to the rock-salt phase along with the valence decrease of Mn ions are consequently mitigated. As a result, the electrochemical properties of the cathodes, especially the capacity/voltage stability, are remarkably improved. The assembled MCMB|LLO full cells deliver a high energy density exceeding 300 Wh/kg and enhanced cycling lifespan. This work provides a simple and effective strategy to stabilize the cationic/anionic redox chemistries of LLOs. The use of the low upper cut-off voltage can not only reduce the voltage fade but also eliminate the need to use a high-voltage electrolyte, which will promote the practical application of LLOs in high energy-density LIBs (J.Mater.Chem.A, 2020). It is usually difficult to fabricate Ni-rich single crystal particles due to the differences in thermodynamic stability of lithium ternary metal oxides. We found that by using a Li-containing spinel oxide as the transition phase, the kinetics of crystal growth can be greatly improved and large single crystal particles can be obtained. DFT calculations demonstrate that the spinel phase has much lower formation energy and improved thermal stability even at 1300 K compared with those of the layered phase, suggesting faster growth kinetics and suppressing segregation of the NiO rock-salt phase during high temperature solid state reactions. In contrast to polycrystalline Ni-rich oxides, the single crystal electrode shows an improved cycling lifespan and thermal stability. This proposed strategy offers a general approach to the preparation of single crystal Ni-rich cathodes for advanced LIBs (J.Mater.Chem.A, 2022). We designed and fabricated P2-type layered oxides with radially oriented {010} exposed primary nanoplates, which improves the ion diffusion during redox reactions through the exposed electrochemically active {010} planes. We also found that trivalent cobalt substitution enables the high-exposed {010} planes, promotes the Na+/vacancy disordering, and suppresses the P2–O2 phase transition. The remarkably boosted redox kinetics gives rise to the outstanding high-rate capability of this hierarchical P2-tpye cathode, with a large capacity of 112 mAh/g maintained even at 20 C. Furthermore, the hierarchical P2-type oxide|hard carbon full cells show high energy density and power density (Small Struct., 2022).

15220818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15220818.value: Ni-rich cobalt-free layered cathode material (LiNixMn1-xO2) is promising due to its low cost, excellent structural stability, and thermal stability. However, cation mixing, highly reactive Ni4+, and stress-induced intragranular micro-cracking restrict its further application. In the future, we will use a combination of bulk doping and surface coating to stabilize the material’s electrochemical performance at high charge/discharge voltage for practical applications.

15220818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15220818.value: The rapid development of electric vehicles has laid an ever-increasing demand and more stringent requirements on electric energy storage devices. Low capacities of the current commercially available cathode materials are becoming the bottleneck for the large-scale applications of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in electric vehicles due to limited driving range. There is an urgent need to call for high-performance cathode materials for LIBs. Nickel-rich layered oxides (NLOs) are regarded as an attractive candidate for high-capacity and high energy density cathodes. However, they are suffered from capacity lose on cycling due to structure instability and side-reactions with electrolyte. Conventional coating techniques which only address one aspect of the encountered problem cannot provide a satisfactory solution. In this project, we propose a novel multifunctional surface coating technique to tackle the challenges faced by NLO cathodes, where the coating layer is itself electrochemically stable, able to remove surface lithium residues, and ionically conducting. The results obtained will guide us in the control of morphology, design of nanostructure, and optimization of composition for the further enhancement of the electrochemical performance of cathodes. Finally, the multifunctional coating technique will be applied to other Li- and Mn-rich layered oxide cathode materials as well.

15221018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15221018.value: This project is to study stimulated Raman dispersion spectroscopy (SRDS) in gas-filled hollow-core fibres (HCFs) and to create highly sensitive all-fibre sensors to detect hydrogen and other gases. Optical fibre sensors based on laser absorption spectroscopy (LAS) and its derivatives have been studied for detecting absorptive gases such as methane, acetylene and ammonia, and demonstrated limit-of-detection (LOD) from ppm (parts-per-million) to ppb (parts-per-billion) levels, depending on the type of gas and the specific technique used. However, they are not applicable to gases that have no absorption in the low-loss transmission window of optical fibres, which is in the near-infrared (IR) for silica fibres. Raman spectroscopy can detect Raman-active gases that do not necessarily have absorption in the near-IR. The use of HCFs enhances Raman signals (spontaneous and stimulated) significantly over the free-space systems, enabling hydrogen (and other) gas sensors with LOD down to hundreds of ppm for ~1 second lock-in time constant (integration time) at ambient conditions. These sensors however used pump lasers around 532 or 1064 nm and free-space optics to couple light into HCFs. We recently demonstrated all-fiber hydrogen gas sensors based on stimulated Raman gain spectroscopy (SRGS) with HCFs. These sensors operated in the near-IR telecom-wavelength-band (1530 to 1625 nm), where cost-effective fiber-optic components are available. The all-fibre systems avoid complex optical alignment, have the capability for remote detection, and are flexible for practical applications. However, the LOD was ~140 ppm for 1 second integration time, limited by the intensity fluctuation received at the photodetector. Here, we propose to study all-fibre gas sensors based on the measurement of dispersion (i.e., detecting phase change with wavelength via optical interferometry) in the vicinity of a stimulated Raman transition, which is termed as SRDS. The dispersion measurement has high immunity to photo-detected intensity fluctuation as well as a linear relationship with gas concentration over a large dynamic range. Our preliminary analysis shows that, with 10-meter-long sensing HCF and pump power of ~310 mW in the hollow-core, SRDS-based hydrogen sensors could achieve 1 ppm LOD with 1s integration time. To our knowledge, SRDS-based gas sensors (free-space or fibre-based) have not been reported previously. We plan to investigate theoretically and experimentally the stimulated Raman dispersion-induced phase modulation in gas-filled HCFs, design appropriate fibre-optic phase detection systems, analyze performance-limiting factors, and optimize system parameters to achieve record-breaking LOD of ~1 ppm with dynamic range up to 100% hydrogen. 本项目研究在充气空芯光纤 (HCF) 中的受激拉曼色散谱技术, 并基于该技术创建高灵敏度的全光纤氢气传感器。 基于激光吸收光谱及其衍生物的光纤传感器已有较多研究,并成功用于甲烷、乙炔和氨等气体的检测, 实现了 ppm 到 ppb 的检量下限 (LOD) 。但这些技术并不适用于在光纤传输窗口内没有吸收的气体。 拉曼光谱技术可用于探测在近红外波段没有吸收的拉曼活性气体。使用 HCF可以大大增强自发和受激拉曼信号，实现比自由空间系统更好的性能。目前报道了LOD 下至百 ppm的氢气传感器。然而这些传感器使用532或1064微米的大功率泵浦激光器，并用空间光学系统将泵浦光耦合到HCF中。 我们最近演示了基于受激拉曼增益谱 (SRGS) 的HCF全光纤氢气传感器。这些传感器工作在近红外光纤通讯波段 (1530 到 1625 nm), 器件较便宜。全光纤系统避免了复杂的光学对准, 具有远程检测的能力, 对实际应用具有灵活性。然而, 受光强波动等噪声的影响，LOD仅为140 ppm 。 这里我们研究基于受激拉曼色散测量的全光纤气体传感器 (通过光学干涉仪检测相位变化) 称为 SRDS。色散测量对光强度波动具有较高的抗扰性, 并在大动态范围内与气体浓度呈线性关系。初步分析表明, 以10米长的传感 HCF 和310毫瓦的泵浦功率，SRDS 型氢气传感器可以实现 1 ppm 的LOD。据我们所知, 基于SRDS 的气体传感器 (自由空间或基于光纤) 以前都没有报告过。 我们将从理论和实验上对充气 HCF 中受激拉曼色散及其诱导的相位调制进行研究, 设计合适的光纤相位检测系统, 分析性能限制因素, 优化系统参数，突破 1 ppm的 LOD 和实现100% 氢气的测量范围。

15221018.label: Realisation of objectives
15221018.value: Objective 1: Stimulated Raman Dispersion Spectroscopies (SRDS) of gas-filled hollow-core fibers (HCFs) as well as gas-immersed optical nanofibers are studied theoretically and numerically. Relationship between the phase modulation of the probe (Stokes) beam and the pump power level, Raman gain and dispersion that are proportional to gas (e.g., hydrogen) concentration, gain linewidth, Raman frequency shift and interaction length are established. The effect of fiber mode field area and fractional mode power in the gas medium on the stimulated Raman dispersion phase modulation are studied. The magnitudes of Raman dispersion signal for photonic bandgap (PBG) HCFs, anti-resonant (AR) HCFs with different core sizes as well as optical nanofibers are modelled and compared. Both sinusoidally modulated continuous wave (CW) pump modulation and pulsed pump modulation are considered. The mode interference noise in PBG-HCFs, AR-HCFs and nanofibers that are directly drawn from standard telecommunication fibers are compared. Both homodyne and heterodyne interferometers are studied for the detection of Raman dispersion and their performances are compared in terms of sensitivity, dynamic range and system complexity. Objective 2: Hydrogen detection based SRDS using both HCFs and optical nanofibers are experimentally studied. For HCF-based sensors, a sinusoidally wavelength-modulated CW pump around 1530 nm is used to generate Raman dispersion, and an all-fiber homodyne Mach-Zehnder interferometer powered by a probe (Stokes) laser source with wavelength fixed at 1620 nm is used to detect the Raman dispersion. A balanced detector is used to minimize the effect of Raman gain on the dispersion measurement. The noise performance of the hydrogen sensor is experimentally evaluated. The sensing system achieves limit of detection (LOD) in terms of noise equivalent concentration (NEC) of 25 ppm hydrogen in nitrogen with 1 s lock-in time constant, 98 mW pump power and seven meters of PBG HCF, corresponding to a normalized LOD of 17.4 ppm/(m·W). The dynamic range is over four orders of magnitude. For the nanofiber-based sensors, an electro-optic intensity modulator is used to generate two sidebands (with carrier suppressed) to facilitate heterodyne detection with a single fiber common-path interferometer. The Raman dispersion signal can be separated from the Raman gain signal by using a proper reference phase of the lock-in amplifier. With a 32-mm-long, 700-nm-diamater nanofiber, hydrogen detection with LOD of 1400 ppm is demonstrated with 60 s integration time. Objective 3: HCF-based all-fibre SRDS hydrogen sensors with a pulsed pump is experimentally studied. However, the LOD is not as good as that of the sinusoidally modulated CW, due to limited peak power of the pulsed pump source available in our laboratory. However, we find that the stimulated Raman scattering-induced dispersion in a hydrogen-filled HCF can be used to tune the group delay of signal pulses. Experiments with an 80-m-long HCF filled with 2.5 bar hydrogen achieved continuous tuning of pulse delay up to 1.42 ns by varying the Raman amplification from 0 to 10 dB.

15221018.label: Major findings and research outcome
15221018.value: 1. We demonstrated controllable laser-induced dispersion based on stimulated Raman scattering in gas-filled HCFs, which provides an all-optical means for dynamically controlling light propagation. Flexible dispersion tuning can be achieved by varying pump power and wavelength as well as gas concentration and pressure in the hollow-core. As an example of application, we demonstrated the use of such laser-induced dispersion for high-sensitivity hydrogen detection and achieved a normalized LOD of 17.4 ppm/(m·W) with dynamic range over four orders of magnitude. To our knowledge, this is the first optical gas sensor based on stimulated Raman dispersion measurement. (H. Bao et al, JLT, Vol.37, No.9, 2019) . 2. We demonstrated for the first time the tuning of group delay with stimulated Raman scattering-induced dispersion in a hydrogen-filled HCF. A pump laser induces a sharp refractive index change near the S0(0) Raman transition of hydrogen molecules, enabling the control of the group velocity of signal pulses around the Stokes wavelength. Experiments with an 80-m-long HCF filled with 2.5 bar hydrogen achieved continuous tuning of pulse delay up to 1.42 ns by varying the Raman amplification from 0 to 10 dB. The tunable pulse delay is realized by changing the pump power and gas pressure. This provides a new technique for controlling the pulse propagation in optical fibers with high flexibility. (H. Bao et al, COL Vol.18, No.6, 060601, 2020). 3. We demonstrated a novel heterodyne approach for stimulated Raman dispersion gas spectroscopy with phase-sensitive harmonic measurement. It is accomplished by optically manipulating the Raman transition through pump modulation and harmonically extracting the associated change on the beatnote generated by the sidebands of the Stokes (probe) beam. This approach enables the use of a single fiber common-path interferometer to detect the very weak Raman disperison, avoiding the use of a two-path interferometer that is not stable and complex to construct. Preliminary experiment with a 32-mm-long, 700-nm-diameter nanofiber demonstrates 1400 ppm NEC with 60s integration time and dynamic range of three orders of magnitude for hydrogen detection. (H. Liao et al, under preparation, to be submitted for publication soon). 4. We observed experimentally the pump absorption-induced birefringence in a gas-immersed optical nanofiber via photothermal effect. With a 12-mm-long nanofiber, phase retardance of more than 9 rad is achieved. It can be used a platform for all-optical polarization manipulation, gas-surface interaction and molecular gas spectroscopy. (Y. Qi et. al,. accepted in 2023) .

15221018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15221018.value: The stimulated Raman scattering-induced dispersion could be used to detect a range Raman-active gases. The recent development of HCFs enables gas cells with very broadband operating wavelength range, which provides more flexibility for the selection of the pump and the probe (Stokes) wavelengths and hence the detection of a larger variety of gas species. We may apply research grants to conduct further investigation on this.

15221018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15221018.value: Previous work has demonstrated all-fiber gas sensors based on stimulated Raman gain spectroscopy with hollow-core fibers (HCFs). The use of HCF enhances Raman scattering significantly over the free-space systems, due to smaller mode-field-area and longer interaction distance. Here, we study all-fiber gas sensors based on the measurement of stimulated Raman dispersion via detecting the phase change in the vicinity of a Raman transition by use of optical fiber interferometry. With a 7-m-long HCF, a pump laser at 1530 nm and a probe (Stokes) laser at 1620 nm, we have demonstrated hydrogen detection with a noise-equivalent-concentration of 25 ppm with 1 s lock-in time constant and dynamic range of over 4 orders of magnitude. We also demonstration the tuning of group delay of signal pulses by use of stimulated Raman dispersion. We have also demonstrated stimulated Raman dispersion spectroscopy with heterodyne interferometry with harmonic detection by use of a 32-mm-long, 700-nm-diameter nanofiber as the sensing element. Preliminary experiment demonstrated detection of hydrogen with a noise-equivalent-concentration of 1400 ppm with 60 s integration time and dynamic range of 3 orders of magnitude.

15221518.label: Project Objectives
15221518.value: To develop a specialty optical maskless lithography technology for direct plasmonic printing We will develop a specialty optical maskless exposure technology to control the growth of silver/gold nanostructures on a substrate to create plasmonic devices. A dual-wavelength (i.e. 365-nm UV and 450 or 550-nm visible) optical engine will be built to initiate photoreduction and maneuver plasmon excitation on the surfaces of silver/gold nanostructures toward specific shape and size. High-numerical-aperture microlens array will be integrated to enhance the spatial resolution of the projection optics of the optical engine to the range of 200 ~ 800 nm. Special optical exposure modes will be developed to generate an array of dynamic light patterns to control the photoreduction of silver/gold nanostructures in a parallel manner. Pattern stitching technology will be developed to enable the fabrication of large-scale arrays of silver/gold nanostructures. Such a technology will exert dynamic photoreduction (using UV light) and plasmon resonances (using visible laser) to directly print plasmonic nanostructures and thus is called as direct plasmonic printing. To reveal the kinetics of light-controlled growth of silver and gold nanostructures upon a substrate With the specialty lithography platform, we will systematically investigate the light-controlled growth of silver/gold nanostructures (e.g. nanospheres, nanorods and nanorings) on a semiconductor-nanocrystal-coated substrate. We will use UV patterns to irradiate the semiconductor nanocrystal layer, e.g. nano-TiO2 photocatalyst layer, so as to generate electrons for reducing silver/gold ions to elemental metal. Dynamic light patterns will be exerted to examine the correlationship between the time-dependent distribution of the UV-generated electrons and the obtained metal nanostructures. Simulations of the generation, redistribution and consumption of photo-generated electrons will be performed by using the information obtained from the experiments so as to reveal the kinetics and underlying physics of the bottom-up nanostructure growth process. The effects of light-excited plasmon resonance on the shapes of metal nanostructures will be evaluated by using visible lasers with different wavelengths. Moreover, the influence of the semiconductor nanocrystal layer on the nucleation and growing process of metal nanostructures will also be investigated. The morphology and orientation of the semiconductor nanocrystals, e.g. TiO2, ZnS or CdSe, will be engineered to provide “seeds” for defining the initial placement of nanostructures. To develop new plasmonic metasurface structures for plasmon-enhanced infrared spectroscopic biosensing We will employ the patternable silver/gold nanostructures as plasmonic meta-atoms to create metasurface structures and then exploit metasurface-enhanced infrared spectroscopy (mSEIRS) for biomolecule detection. Those plasmonic meta-atoms will be devised to form 2D arrays whose in-phase dipolar coupling is collectively excited to achieve ultra-high near-field intensity so as to enhance the vibrational absorption signatures of biomolecules. The period of 2D arrays of meta-atoms and their orientations will be optimized to excite different kinds of optical responses. The influence of the dielectric substrate on coupling and hybridization of plasmonic modes will be examined. Experiments will be conducted to characterize the degree of enhancement of vibration/absorption signatures of biomolecules by plasmonic metasurface structures. The ultimate goal of this project is to create a new pathway to cost-effectively fabricate silver/gold plasmonic metasurface structures (up to a few square centimeters) and thereby develop directly printable plasmon-enhanced infrared spectroscopic biosensors whose degree of enhancement of vibration/absorption signatures of biomolecules can reach state-of-the-art level (i.e. 10^4 ~ 10^5).

15221518.label: Realisation of objectives
15221518.value: This project proposed to study the light-controlled growth of metal nanostructures and develop direct printing technology for plasmonic structures in biosensing applications. In the past several years, many remarkable research results in line with the project objectives have been achieved: 1. To develop a specialty optical maskless lithography technology for direct plasmonic printing We have successfully developed a specialty optical maskless lithography technology, called digital ultraviolet (UV) lithography, to study the light-controlled growth of metal nanostructures for direct printing of plasmonic silver/gold structures. With a digital-micromirror device (DMD) and a UV light source (at 365 nm), a fully own-developed optical maskless exposure system has been built. A visible laser with a wavelength of 532 nm has been integrated to provide extra light manipulation ability of the system. An objective lens with the numerical aperture of 0.4 has been used to enhance the optical resolution of the optical exposure system. After upgradation, the optical resolution of the system is about 294 nm, which has achieved the target resolution, i.e., in the range of 200 ~ 800 nm. Algorithms have been developed to enable the generation of dynamic light patterns for optical exposure processes. The pixels of DMD chip (with 1920×1080 pixels in total) are grouped into clusters, and each cluster can be applied to control a light pattern designed for a specific metal atom or metallic nanostructure. Empowered by a ultrahigh-precision motorized stage (Aerotech ANT130XY), a seamless pattern stitching algorithm has been developed to enable the exposure of large-area patterns. Such a fully own-developed digital UV lithography system provides a foundation for a systematic study of the light-controlled growth of silver or gold nanostructures for plasmonic applications. 2. To reveal the kinetics of light-controlled growth of silver and gold nanostructures upon a substrate. With the own-built digital UV lithography platform, we have systematically investigated the kinetics and optimized the processes of light-controlled growth of silver and gold nanostructures. A technology, named precision photoreduction, has been developed to directly print plasmonic micropatterns of silver/gold nanostructures for biosensing applications. Lots of experiments have been carried out to investigate the processes of light-controlled growth of gold nanostructure. A gold salt solution was prepared by mixing 0.1 mol/L gold(III) chloride hydrate solution, 0.4 mol/L thiourea solution, 0.2 mol/L potassium sodium tartrate tetrahydrate solution, deionized (DI) water, and 0.2 mol/L citric acid trisodium salt dihydrate solution at a volume ratio of 1:1:1:1:4. Quartz substrates with the TiO2 nanolayer were cleaned by rinsing with IPA and blown dry with a nitrogen gun. The own-developed digital UV lithography system was used to expose the substrate upon the gold salt solution. The pattern design generated using computer was loaded to the DMD in a given time sequence to dynamically generate light patterns. After exposure, the quartz substrate was rinsed sequentially using DI water and IPA and finally dried with nitrogen gas. Remarkably, such a direct printing technology enables the fabrication of ultraminiature optical fiber-tip plasmonic biosensors. We experimentally demonstrated that the micropatterns of size-controlled AuNPs can be additively printed on the end face of a standard optical fiber at visible light range. These AuNPs appear distinct localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) whose peak wavelength is an ideal for label-free biodetection. Such an optical fiber-tip plasmonic biosensor can not only detect antibody, but also test SARS-CoV-2 mimetic DNA sequence at the concentration level of 0.8 pM. Experimental studies on the light controlled growth of silver nanostructures have also been systematically conducted. Here, silver salt and its reduction agent are used to replace auric salt and its reduction agent. Using a substrate with the same photocatalyst (i.e., TiO2) nanolayer, we have demonstrated that micropatterns of size-controlled silver nanoparticles can be rapidly printed. 3. To develop new plasmonic metasurface structures for plasmon-enhanced infrared spectroscopic biosensing. Based on our developed precision photoreduction technology, we have designed and fabricated a plasmonic metasurface substrate of gold oblong micro-flake array for plasmoncally-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (PEIRAS) biodetection. As the printing resolution of precision photoreduction technology is about 1 μm, the plasmonic atoms were designed to be gold oblong micro-flake whose width is about 1 μm while its length is about 2.0 ~ 3.0 μm. Such a gold micro-flake has a LSPR at the wavenumber of 1400 ~ 1650 cm^-1. When these god oblong micro-flakes are further arranged into periodic array with the period of 3.9 ~ 4.9 μm, the light diffracted by gold micro-flakes will couple with the LSPR associated with individual oblong elements, which is referred as surface lattice resonance (SLR), to produce strong light-field enhancements and narrow the spectral peak of plasmonic resonance. A precision photoreduction and replacement reaction combined technology has been developed to directly print such plasmonic gold micro-flake arrays. The substrate was prepared by spin-coating of a TiO2 /isopropyl alcohol (IPA) solution upon a quartz plate. It was then baked on a hot plate at 110 ℃ for 10 min. The substrate was put upside-down upon a self-made glass holder with a silver salt solution, in which silver nitrate is diluted in ethylene glycol at the weight ratio of 2:100. Then, the own-developed digital UV lithography system is used to expose the substrate with designed patterns. After exposure process, the formed silver micropatterns were immersed into a 30 mM chloroauric acid and 40 mM hydroxylamine mixed solution for 10 min, and then silver micropatterns were replaced by gold micropatterns. A thermal treatment was finally applied to improve the surface smoothness of gold micropatterns as well as their crystallinity. The limit of such a plasmonic substrate for PEIRAS detection of a protein bovine serum albumin (BSA) has been tested by using a series BSA solutions at different concentration levels. The result showed that the detection limit of such a PEIRAS technology is about 10 nM (or 0.66 µg·mL^-1). A better result has been achieved, compared with previously reported results using gold nanoparticles-based infrared absorption spectroscopy. The enhancement factor (EF) of such plasmonic substrates were estimated by comparing with the absorption spectral fingerprints measured by using a flat gold mirror. The measured absorption signal for amide-I is 0.1%, which is significantly lower than the absorption signal measured by using the plasmonic SLR substrate, which is 9%. If further consider the area of illumination spot, the area for measuring the IR absorption signal is around 5.76×104 µm^2 in the testing using the flat gold mirror, while the estimated area of all ends of gold micro-flakes for PEIRAS measurement is about 1.11×102 µm^2. Therefore, the calculated EF of such a gold micro-flake array-based PEIRAS is about 46400. 4. The ultimate goal of this project is to create a new pathway to cost-effectively fabricate silver/gold plasmonic metasurface structures and thereby develop directly printable plasmon-enhanced infrared spectroscopic biosensors. We have successfully developed a precision photoreduction technology that can directly print either large-area plasmonic substrates up to a few square centimeters or ultrasmall patterns to develop different kinds of plasmonic biosensors. After further combining precision photoreduction and replacement reaction technologies, we have successfully demonstrated a plasmonic metasurface substrate of gold oblong micro-flake array, whose local enhancement factor is about 46400 reaching the target level i.e., 10^4 ~ 10^5, for plasmonically-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopic biodetection.

15221518.label: Major findings and research outcome
15221518.value: This project proposed to develop a specialty optical maskless lithography technology and study the light-controlled growth of metal nanostructures for direct printing of plasmonic structures in biosensing applications. Major findings and research outcomes of the project include: i. A specialty optical maskless lithography technology, called digital ultraviolet (UV) lithography, has been independently developed. Such a fully own-developed digital UV lithography system provides a technological foundation for a systematic study of the light-controlled growth of silver or gold nanostructures in plasmonic applications. ii. After a systematical study on the light controlled growth of metallic nanostructures, a direct printing technology, named precision photoreduction, has been developed to rapid print plasmonic micropatterns of size-controlled silver/gold nanoparticles in an additive manufacturing manner. It may maximally save the fabrication cost of plasmonic micro/nanostructures based on noble metals and therefore greatly boost the widespread use of plasmonic substrates in various applications. (See the papers published in Advanced Optical Materials, 2020 and SPIE Plasmonics: Design, Materials, Fabrication, Characterization, and Applications XX, 2022) iii. Based on the own-developed precision photoreduction technology, we have developed an ultraminiature optical fiber-tip plasmonic biosensor for label-free biodetection. We demonstrated that the micropatterns of size-controlled AuNPs can be additively printed on the end face of a standard optical fiber at visible light range. These AuNPs appear distinct localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) whose peak wavelength is an ideal for label-free biodetection. Such an optical fiber-tip plasmonic biosensor can not only detect antibody, but also test SARS-CoV-2 mimetic DNA sequence at the concentration level of 0.8 pM. (See the paper published in Biosensors and Bioelectronics, 2022). iv. We have designed and fabricated a plasmonic metasurface substrate, i.e. plasmonic gold oblong micro-flake array, for plasmoncally-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (PEIRAS) biodetection. A precision photoreduction and replacement reaction combined technology has been developed to directly print such plasmonic gold micro-flake arrays. The limit of such a plasmonic substrate for PEIRAS detection of a protein bovine serum albumin (BSA) is about 10 nM (or 0.66 µg·mL-1). The local enhancement factor of such plasmonic substrates was estimated to be about 46400. (See the paper submitted to ACS Sensors 2023). In short, we have developed a new technological pathway to cost-effectively fabricate silver/gold plasmonic structures in this project, which may play an important role in the development of various plasmonic structures and sensors, such as plasmonically-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopic biosensors.

15221518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15221518.value: We will continue to study the light-controlled growth of metallic nanostructures and improve the precision photoreduction technology developed in this project to pursue more printable metallic materials, higher printing resolution, and better printed geometry. Currently, we can mainly directly print size-controlled silver or gold nanoparticles by using precision photoreduction technology or micrometer-scale gold patterns by using precision photoreduction and replacement reaction combined technology. We will further optimize both digital UV lithography system and the processes of precision photoreduction technology to enable the direct printing of sub-micrometer metallic patterns. Moreover, we will exploit different applications of such directly printed plasmonic micro/nanostructures in different areas, such as plasmonic metamaterials, plasmonically-enhanced Raman spectroscopy and second harmonic spectroscopy.

15221518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15221518.value: This project aims to develop a specialty optical maskless lithography technology and study the light-controlled growth of metal nanostructures for direct printing of plasmonic structures in biosensing applications. In the project, we have successfully developed a specialty optical maskless lithography technology, called digital ultraviolet (UV) lithography, and utilized the own-built system to carry out a systematic study on the light-controlled growth of metal nanostructures for plasmonic applications. Particularly, a direct printing technology, named precision photoreduction, has been developed to rapidly print plasmonic micropatterns of size-controlled silver or gold nanoparticles in an additive manufacturing manner. Such an innovative fabrication technology can enable the creation of many new plasmonic devices and sensors. In the project, ultraminiature optical fiber-tip plasmonic biosensors have been fabricated by direct printing of size-controlled gold nanoparticles on the end face of a standard optical fiber. Plasmonic metasurface substrates of gold oblong micro-flake array have been fabricated for plasmonically-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopic biodetection. By innovation of such direct printing technologies, plasmonics may be able to unleash its full potential on manipulation of light at nanoscale and becomes an enabling technology in a wide range of fields and applications.

15221618.label: Project Objectives
15221618.value: To design knowledge-driven deep models by optimization unrolling -- We aim to provide a novel optimization perspective to understand basic network units and operators. Furthermore, we will provide a new unrolling framework to build deep models with rich domain-knowledge of the tasks. Some theoretical properties (e.g., convergence and rate) of the proposed unrolling framework are also expected. To train and analyze knowledge-driven deep model by dynamical system and control theory -- We will develop a dynamical system perspective to reformulate popular deep networks such as ResNet, and then provide new analyses using tools and theories from dynamic system and control areas. We would like to build a novel PID control framework for network optimization, under which new network training algorithms with better efficiency will be developed. To solve real-world complex visual enhancement tasks -- We investigate the proposed knowledge-driven deep models under the scenarios of challenging visual enhancement tasks, including non-uniform blind image deblurring and task-aware image layer pursuit. We will design hybrid networks to incorporate domain knowledge and available data into network propagation, enhancing the adaptation ability and robustness of deep models for real-world dynamic scenes.

15221618.label: Realisation of objectives
15221618.value: Objective 1: To design knowledge-driven deep models by optimization unrolling. Most of the previous deep neural networks (DNN) based image restoration methods adopts the simple bicubic degradation model, which cannot be generalized to low quality images with arbitrary blur kernels. In this project, we propose a principled formulation and framework by extending bicubic degradation based deep models with the help of plug-and-play framework to handle images with arbitrary blur kernels. Specifically, we design a new degradation model so as to take advantage of existing blind deblurring methods for blur kernel estimation. To optimize the new degradation induced energy function, we derive a plug-and-play algorithm via variable splitting technique, which allows us to plug any super-resolver prior rather than the denoiser prior as a modular part. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on synthetic and real LR images demonstrate that the proposed deep plug-and-play framework is flexible and effective to deal with blurry images. Please refer to [C4] for details. We also propose a variational inference method for blind image denoising, which integrates both noise estimation and image denoising into a Bayesian framework. Specifically, an approximate posterior, parameterized by deep neural networks, is presented by taking the intrinsic clean image and noise variances as latent variables conditioned on the input noisy image. On one hand, as other data-driven deep learning methods, our variational denoising network (VDN) can perform denoising efficiently due to its explicit form of posterior expression. On the other hand, VDN inherits the advantages of traditional model-driven approaches by unrolling the iterative optimization processing via DNN training. VDN has good interpretability and can be flexibly utilized to estimate and remove complicated non-i.i.d. noise collected in real scenarios. Comprehensive experiments are performed to substantiate the superiority of our method in blind image denoising. Please refer to [C2] for details. Objective 2: To train and analyze knowledge-driven deep model by dynamical system and control theory. While DNNs have been successfully used in many low-level vision problems, recent studies on the mathematical foundation of DNN has revealed that the forward propagation of DNN corresponds to a dynamic system, which can be described by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) and solved by the optimal control method. However, most of these methods employ integer-order differential equation, which has local connectivity in time space and cannot describe the long-term memory of the system. Inspired by the fact that the fractional-order differential equation has long-term memory, we develop an advanced image denoising network, namely FOCNet, by solving a fractional optimal control (FOC) problem. Specifically, the network structure is designed based on the discretization of a fractional-order differential equation, which enjoys long-term memory in both forward and backward passes. Besides, multi-scale feature interactions are introduced into the FOCNet to strengthen the control of the dynamic system. Extensive experiments demonstrate the leading performance of the proposed FOCNet on image denoising. Please refer to [C3] for details. Objective 3: To solve real-world complex visual enhancement tasks. A few works have been done in this project to solve real-world visual enhancement tasks, including denoising and super-resolution. First, we built one of the earliest real-world image super-resolution benchmark. Most of the existing learning-based single image superresolution (SISR) methods are trained and evaluated on simulated datasets, where the low-resolution (LR) images are generated by applying a simple and uniform degradation (i.e., bicubic downsampling) to their high-resolution (HR) counterparts. However, the degradations in real-world LR images are far more complicated. As a consequence, the SISR models trained on simulated data become less effective when applied to practical scenarios. We hence build a real-world super-resolution (RealSR) dataset where paired LR-HR images on the same scene are captured by adjusting the focal length of a digital camera. An image registration algorithm is developed to progressively align the image pairs at different resolutions. Considering that the degradation kernels are naturally non-uniform in our dataset, we present a Laplacian pyramid based kernel prediction network (LP-KPN), which efficiently learns per-pixel kernels to recover the HR image. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that SISR models trained on our RealSR dataset deliver better visual quality with sharper edges and finer textures on real-world scenes than those trained on simulated datasets. Please refer to [C1] for details. Second, we proposed a blind denoising method for real-world photographs. While deep CNNs have achieved impressive success in image denoising with additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), their performance remains limited on real-world noisy photographs. The main reason is that their learned models are easy to overfit on the simplified AWGN model which deviates severely from the complicated real-world noise model. In order to improve the generalization ability of deep CNN denoisers, we suggest training a convolutional blind denoising network (CBDNet) with more realistic noise model and real-world noisy-clean image pairs. On one hand, both signal-dependent noise and in-camera signal processing pipeline is considered to synthesize realistic noisy images. On the other hand, real-world noisy photographs and their nearly noise-free counterparts are also included to train our CBDNet. To further provide an interactive strategy to rectify denoising result conveniently, a noise estimation subnetwork with asymmetric learning to suppress under-estimation of noise level is embedded into CBDNet. Extensive experimental results on three datasets of real-world noisy photographs clearly demonstrate the superior performance of CBDNet over state-of-the-arts in terms of quantitative metrics and visual quality. Please refer to [C5] for details. Third, we proposed a Dark and Bright Channel Priors embedded Network (DBCPeNet) to plug the channel priors into a CNN for effective dynamic scene deblurring. Recent years have witnessed the significant progress on CNNs in dynamic scene deblurring. While most of the CNN models are generally learned by the reconstruction loss defined on training data, incorporating suitable image priors as well as regularization terms into the network architecture could boost the deblurring performance. We propose DBCPeNet to plug the channel priors into CNN for effective dynamic scene deblurring. A novel trainable dark and bright channel priors embedded layer (DBCPeL) is developed to aggregate both channel priors and blurry image representations, and a sparse regularization is introduced to regularize the DBCPeNet model learning. Furthermore, we present an effective multi-scale network architecture, namely image full scale exploitation (IFSE), which works in both coarse-to-fine and fine-to-coarse manners for better exploiting information flow across scales. Experimental results on the GoPro and K¨ohler datasets show that our proposed DBCPeNet performs favorably against state-of-the-art deep image deblurring methods in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality. Please refer to [J1] for details. In addition to the above works, we also developed a degradation model learning approach for real-world SISR (Please refer to [C6] for details), an online rain/snow removal method for surveillance videos (Please refer to [J3] for details), and a deep confidence-based method for large-scale dense multi-view stereo (Please refer to [J2] for details).

15221618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15221618.value: First, all the methods developed in this projected are based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Recently, Transformer based architectures have shown significant improvement over CNNs in different tasks. Therefore, one direct further development is to extend the models and methods in this project from CNN based ones to Transformer based ones. Second, while our proposed knowledge driven deep models can improve much the generalization performance of deep models, the domain gap between training data and test data remains large. Therefore, domain adaptation techniques can be used to further enhance the generalization capability of our methods. Third, one interesting question is can we extend the proposed methods to unsupervised learning settings? We will make further investigations in the future. Last but not the least, though we developed a real-world image super-resolution dataset in this project, it can only cover a small subspace of the whole image degradation space. How to synthesize more realistic training image pairs is a very important problem. The recently developed diffusion models can be potential solution.

15221618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15221618.value: Image restoration and enhancement in real-world scenarios is a very challenging problem because of the complex and unknown degradations of real-world images. The deep models trained on simulated data are difficult to be generalized to real-world data, while the paired training data in real scenes are difficult to collect. To address these problems, in this project we conducted the following in-depth investigations. First, we proposed to integrate human knowledge as prior models into the deep neural network (DNN) learning, and developed unrolling optimization algorithms to train these knowledge-embedded models. Second, inspired by the dynamic system control theory, we model the DNN as a dynamic control system, and develop an advanced image denoising network by solving a fractional optimal control problem. Lastly, we developed a few effectiveness methods to solve real-world visual enhancement tasks, including one of the earliest real-world image super-resolution benchmark, a blind denoising method for real-world photographs, and a dark and bright channel priors embedded network for effective dynamic scene deblurring, etc. Some of the research outputs of this project have been widely cited in the community, facilitating the methodology development and the practical application of image restoration and enhancement research.

rows: To improve the usability of Boltzmann entropy for remote sensing images;
To develop information-theoretic approaches for various analysis of remote sensing images, based on Boltzmann entropy.

15221918.label: Realisation of objectives
15221918.value: Realization of the first objective: The first objective is to improve the usability of Boltzmann entropy for remote sensing images. Two aspects have been improved, i.e. improvement in thermodynamic performance and generalization for other usage. This objective is fully completed and was fully reported in the mid-term report. To improve the thermodynamic performance, the first step was validation, i.e. to validate whether the Boltzmann entropy computed by using our previous method was thermodynamically consistent (i.e., consistent with statistical thermodynamics). A kinetic-theory-based approach was proposed and then applied to Boltzmann entropies (both relative and absolute) computed by our previous method. Results reveal that the absolute Boltzmann entropy is only partly consistent. Hypothesis-driven experiments were designed and carried out to determine the cause. It has been found that the cause was the upscaling method (i.e. resampling) for generating multi-scale representation of images. The second step was to develop a new method for computing thermodynamically consistent entropy on the basis of an alternative upscaling technique. We made use of aggregation technique. Experimental results showed that the entropy computed using this new method successfully passed the validation. A paper entitled “Aggregation-based method for computing absolute Boltzmann entropy of landscape gradient with full thermodynamic consistency” has been published in a SCI journal[1]. This method were developed for landscape gradients, i.e. for raster-based numerical data (e.g. image data). However, when images are classified into landcover map (mosaic), the data is transformed from numerical to categorical. Therefore, in this project, an attempt has been made to generalize the method for the computation of the entropy of categorical data. A paper entitled “Computation of the Boltzmann entropy of a landscape: A review and a generalization” has been published in a SCI journal[2]. Realization of the second objective: The second objective is to develop information-theoretic approaches for various analysis of remote sensing images, based on Boltzmann entropy. Four kinds of new approaches have been tackled, i.e., for compression, encryption, fusion, mapping (classification and cartography) and GIScience. The objective is fully realized. Compression: Shannon Source Coding Theorem has been the basis for predicting lossless image compression ratio. Extensive experimental tests have been carried to reveal that compression ratio by modern compression techniques which consider spatial configuration of images has exceeded the upper limit set by Shannon’s Source Coding Theorem. We then hypothesize that a mathematical model can be developed for predicting compression ratio by such modern methods if we make use of an appropriate metric for configurational information of images. Extensive evaluation showed that Boltzmann entropy is the most appropriate choice. Finally, mathematical models describing compression ratio and Boltzmann entropy of digital images have been developed. So far, two short papers have been presented at international conferences and one paper published in a SCI journal[3]. Encryption: Encryption is another important application of information theory. In this project, a method for the encryption of imagery with the assistance of Boltzmann entropy was developed. In this method, Boltzmann entropy was used to capture both compositional and configurational information for optimizing encryption from the perspective of the Second Law of Thermodynamics. Subsequently, an encryption algorithm based on the integration of the chaos system and linear prediction is designed, where the one with the maximum absolute configurational entropy difference compared to the original image (or DEM) is selected. The experiments have been carried out and, results and security analysis show that the proposed algorithm is very effective. The work was presented at an international conference and the extended version was later published in SCI journal[4]. Mapping (classification and cartography): Mapping is a process to make maps from remote sensing images. This process can be regarded as an information flow or information transfer. Researchers made efforts to apply Shannon information theory to this process to establish a new theory. However, due to the fact that Shannon entropy is not capable of capturing configuration information, such efforts were not very successful. In this project, we build a theoretical framework based on Boltzmann entropy —— Information Theory of Cartography. It has been published in Journal of Geodesy and Geoinformation[5]. The second investigation is (i) to verify whether the energy flow from remote sensing images to land cover maps is consistent with the law of energy conversation, and (ii) to build a model for such energy flow based on Boltzmann entropy. An article had been submitted to Landscape Ecology for a special issue in early 2022[7], but we faced a problem (see explanation below). GIScience: We realized that current GIScience (geographical information science) deals with only spatial data handling and argued that information-theoretical approaches should be developed based on information theory and Boltzmann entropy should play a key role in such development. A paper has been published as book chapter[6]. Fusion: We proposed a no-reference method for assessing image fusion quality, with Boltzmann entropy. To be specific, we developed a linear model disentangling the relationship among two coarse images of high temporal resolution, a fine image of low temporal resolution, and the fused image. With this model, the energy (information) conversion efficiency was proposed to quantify the performance of different spatial-temporal image fusion models. The result is being converted into an article [8] and should be submitted to a journal soon. Problem faced and solution: An article had been submitted to Landscape Ecology for a special issue in early 2022, but we were told by the editor on 5 December 2022 that, due to the problems associated with the new manuscript-handling software (SNAPP), “dozens of manuscripts fall between the cracks without notice” and our manuscript is among them. The editor encourages us to resubmit it for regular issues and we have just done so. Papers published in Journals and reported in mid-term report [1] GAO Peichao and LI Zhilin, 2019. 15221918.label: Major findings and research outcome
15221918.value: In the section Realization of Objectives, we reported our investigations into various aspects of Boltzmann entropy. Research outcomes of this project is also outlined, and a list of papers is also provided. From this project, we have the following major findings: 1. Boltzmann entropy computed by aggregation-based method is fully thermodynamically consistent; 2. Boltzmann entropy is the most appropriate measure for describing the configurational information of remote sensing images; 3. It is possible to build a Boltzmann-entropy-based model for prediction of lossless compression ratio of remote sensing images by up-to-date compression methods; 4. Boltzmann entropy is a reliable measure for selection of optimal parameter for generating chaotic sequence derived from the chaos theory in encryption; 5. Energy flow from remote sensing images to landcover maps is consistent with the first law of thermodynamics (i.e., the law of energy conservation); 6. Spatiotemporal remote sensing image fusion complies with the first law of thermodynamics. To report these findings, we have published 5 papers in peer-reviewed journals (3 in JCR Q1 journals), 1 book chapter, 2 presentations in international conference, and 2 papers submitted or prepared to SCI journals.

15221918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15221918.value: Many techniques have been developed for processing remote sensing images. However, the mechanism behind such processing is rare understood. On the other hand, as thermodynamics of images is captured by sensors, the application of Boltzmann entropy to remote sensing image processing will contribute a lot to the explanation of image classification and/or fusion. This project found that Boltzmann entropy overcomes the shortcomings of Shannon entropy which is able to captures only statistical but not configurational information). Therefore, Boltzmann entropy will play a key role in the development of information-theoretic approaches for GIScience. Boltzmann entropy will play a key role in the study of ecological process because such a process is believed to be governed by the second law of thermodynamics. Boltzmann entropy is expected to serve as a thermodynamically relevant tool (that captures both statistical and structural information) for classifying landscape zones with multi-source remote sensing data, soil and climate data. Actually, the Co-I and his team are communicating with one famous landscape ecologist, Dr. Samuel Cushman at USFS. Furthermore, the PI’s team members are investigating the phenological responses to climate change over different tree species, trying to quantify the spatial-temporal pattern of those responses with Boltzmann entropy.

15221918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15221918.value: Shannon’s Information Theory has found wide applications but not very successful in mapping science (cartography and remote sensing). The main reason is that Shannon entropy (i.e. measure of information) is a statistical measure and not capable of characterizing spatial configuration contained in maps and images. This opens a door for development of Boltzmann-entropy-based information-theoretic approaches for remote sensing image analysis. Therefore, the project aims (1) to improve the usability of Boltzmann entropy for remote sensing images; and (2) to develop information-theoretic approaches for various analysis of remote sensing images, based on Boltzmann entropy. To achieve the first objective, a kinetic-theory-based approach has been designed and employed to test the thermodynamic consistency of the Boltzmann-entropy. Results show that the absolute Boltzmann entropy is only partially consistent and thus a new computation method is developed. Also the computational method is generalized for the computation of landcover map data (i.e. categorical data) from image data. To achieve the second objective, Boltzmann-based new approaches/models have been developed for a number of processing such as compression, encryption, fusion, mapping (classification and cartography) and GIScience. This study shows that Boltzmann-entropy-based information-theoretic approaches have great potential in remote sensing image analysis and GIScience in general.
