15500018.label: Project Title(Chinese)
15500018.value: 面試官的真實性表現：概念化及考察其對招聘結果的影響

15500018.label: Co - Investigator(s)
15500018.value: Prof Cable, Daniel M Dr Wilhelmy, Annika

15500018.label: Project Objectives
15500018.value: To propose a new construct of interviewer authentic behavior and suggest its conceptual criteria. To develop and validate a scale for measuring interviewer authentic behavior that can be used for the proposed project and future studies. To examine the effect of interviewer authentic behavior on recruitment outcomes and to identify a psychological mechanism that explains the proposed relationship between interviewer authentic behavior and recruitment outcomes.
rows: To propose a new construct of interviewer authentic behavior and suggest its conceptual criteria.
To develop and validate a scale for measuring interviewer authentic behavior that can be used for the proposed project and future studies.

To examine the effect of interviewer authentic behavior on recruitment outcomes and to identify a psychological mechanism that explains the proposed relationship between interviewer authentic behavior and recruitment outcomes.

15500018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15500018.value: Extensive studies on job interviews emphasize selling oneself as the goal of both applicants and interviewers. To sell their organizations as good workplaces (Marr & Cable, 2014), interviewers often create positive images of themselves, for example by emphasizing their competence and professionalism to applicants (Turban, Forret, & Hendrickson, 1998; Wilhelmy, Kleinmann, König, Melchers, & Truxillo, 2016). To sell themselves as the best candidates (Barrick, Shaffer, & DeGrassi, 2009), applicants often promote their image in the eyes of interviewers by emphasizing their strengths and concealing their weaknesses (Levashina & Campion, 2007; Stevens & Kristof, 1995). Thus, research seems to suggest that polished self-promotion is a common and effective interview strategy. However, in a recent study, my colleagues and I propose a new approach to employment interviews by demonstrating the value of authentic strategies (Moore, Lee, Kim, & Cable, in press). By focusing on applicants’ authentic behaviors, we find that some candidates present themselves accurately and honestly during interviews. Moreover, we find that high-quality candidates are more likely to receive job offers if they engage in such strategies. These results suggest that authentic self-presentation is an unidentified route to job market success, amplifying the chances that applicants can convert positive evaluations into job offers. The proposed project will build on this work and examine authentic interview strategies from the other side of the interviews by focusing on interviewers’ behaviors. While research has highlighted the important role of interviewers in attracting applicants (e.g., Turban et al., 1998; Wilhelmy et al., 2016), the literature on interviewer behaviors is dominated by the perspective of self-promotion (Wilhelmy, Kleinmann, Melchers, & Götz, 2017). Departing from this, the proposed project presents interviewer authenticity as a rarely examined but effective recruitment behavior that can lead to applicants’ job acceptance and purchase of organizational products. Toward this aim, we will first conceptualize and develop a measurement scale of interviewer authentic behavior (IAB). Second, we will examine how IAB exerts its positive influence on applicant job acceptance and product purchase through addressing the relational uncertainty inherent in applicants’ experience of the recruitment processes. Finally, we will investigate whether the effect of IAB on recruitment outcomes is stronger for applicants having less work experience and minority demographic status, both of which are associated with higher relational uncertainty. In doing so, we aim to contribute to the growing body of literature on the value of authenticity in organizational entry process. 很多有關工作面試的研究都強調自我推銷同是應徵者和面試官的目標。為了推銷機構為一個良好的工作場所 (Marr & Cable, 2014)，面試官時常為自己營造正面的形象，例如，面試官會向應徵者強調自己的能力和專業水準 (Turban, Forret, & Hendrickson, 1998; Wilhelmy, Kleinmann, König, Melchers, & Truxillo, 2016)。為了推銷自己為最佳人選 (Barrick, Shaffer, & DeGrassi, 2009)，應徵者亦時常透過強調自己的強項和掩飾弱點來提升自己在面試官眼中的形象 (Levashina & Campion, 2007; Stevens & Kristof, 1995)。因此，研究似乎認為嫻熟的自我推銷是一項有效的面試策略。 然而，在最近的一項研究中，我和合作者透過展示真實性策略的價值，提倡一個全新的就業面試方法 (Moore, Lee, Kim, & Cable, 2017)。透過側重於應徵者的真實性表現，我們發現一些應徵者能於面試中凖確而誠懇地表達自己。此外，我們亦發現高質量的應徵者能靠著應用這些策略而更有可能得到就業機會。這些研究結果顯示真實性的自我表現是一條未被以往研究認定的路徑，應徵者能憑藉這策略把別人對他們的正面評價轉化成就業機會。 擬議的項目將建基於這些文獻之上，通過側重於面試官的行為，從面試過程的另一角度探討與真實性有關的面試策略。縱然過往的研究早已強調過面試官扮演著吸引應徵者的重要角色 (如Turban et al., 1998; Wilhelmy et al., 2016)，有關面試官行為的文獻大多採用自我形象提升的理論角度 (Wilhelmy, Kleinmann, Melchers, & Götz, 2017)。本研究背離這個角度為出發點，提出面試官之真實性表現為一個甚少被探討但行之有效的招聘策略。透過減低應徵者的關係不確定性（即應徵者能預測他們在開始工作後與組織建立關係的程度; Walker, Bauer, Cole, Bernerth, Field, & Short, 2013, 第3128頁），面試官之真實性表現不但能令應徵者更大可能接受工作機會，並且能促使他們有可能購買該公司的產品，而成為招聘公司的未來顧客。以這些目標作前題，我們將首先為真實性表現進行概念化並製定量表。接著，我們會針對應徵者在招聘過程中對關係不確定性的體驗，考察面試官之真實性表現如何對應徵者接受工作機會和購買公司產品構成正面的影響。最後，我們將探討面試官之真實性表現對招聘結果的影響會否因應徵者的面試經驗較少或屬少數人口類別而變得更強，我們的推測建基於以往的研究發現，較少的面試經驗和作為少數的人口類別均與較高的關係不確定性有關。為此，我們希望能為正在不斷增長和有關真實性對組織進入時之價值的文獻作貢獻。

15500618.label: Project Title(Chinese)
15500618.value: 遊客情緒體驗之縱向追蹤研究: 潛在情緒生成和調節過程

15500618.label: Co - Investigator(s)
15500618.value: Dr Chen, Nan Prof Fesenmaier, Daniel R.

15500618.label: Project Objectives
15500618.value: Examine tourist emotional experiences across pre-, during-, and post-travel stages. Investigate how and why tourists develop various emotions during a leisure trip. Develop a comprehensive model on tourist emotional experiences by including potential intrinsic and extrinsic factors that influence the underlying psychological process which generates and regulates emotions.
rows: Examine tourist emotional experiences across pre-, during-, and post-travel stages.
Investigate how and why tourists develop various emotions during a leisure trip.

Develop a comprehensive model on tourist emotional experiences by including potential intrinsic and extrinsic factors that influence the underlying psychological process which generates and regulates emotions.

15500618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15500618.value: Understanding the nature and structure of tourists’ emotional experiences (EE) is an important and challenging topic in tourism research. This issue is worthy of in-depth and innovative investigation because tourists’ experiences are lived through a variety of positive and negative emotions, but little is known about why and how tourists develop and experience such a subjective emotional journey. Responding to the call for shifting the research focus away from the authentic-fake binary classification, and concentrating on the emotional and bodily dimensions, the embodiment research paradigm is employed to guide this study. Further, the development of new technologies in emotion-identification and continuous tracking makes the examination of tourists’ real-time emotions in natural settings possible. This longitudinal study will examine tourist EE throughout a leisure trip by exploring the underlying emotion generative and regulatory processes, in the context of Mainland Chinese tourists’ outbound trip, due to the importance of this market to international destinations. This research is guided by a framework of pre-trip expectation of EE, during-trip emotional generation and regulation, and post-trip evaluation of EE. A multidisciplinary, mixed-method approach will incorporate concepts and methods applied in the fields of psychology, geography, consumer behaviour, and tourism. A comprehensive Tourist EE Model is proposed to examine relationships among emotion determinants, formation process, regulations, and outcomes both in real-time and over time. To explore the invisible emotion generative and regulatory processes, and empirically test the full model, a rigorous five-phase plan is developed. Besides a comprehensive literature review (Phase 1), the nature of pre-trip expectation will be identified via a short survey and interviews with a panel of tourists (Phase 2). Tourists’ during-the-trip EE will be examined through three techniques (Phase 3): (1) a wristband tracking individual emotional arousal throughout the trip based on psychophysiological indicators; (2) participant observation capturing tourists’ expressive emotional responses, such as facial, vocal, and bodily expressions; and (3) brief interviews on every other evening during the trip to interpret and supplement the above emotional indicators. Post-trip interviews will collect panel members’ recalled EE and emotion regulation process (Phase 4). A survey (Phase 5) with a large consumer sample will empirically test the model proposed. This project will result in theoretical and methodological breakthroughs in understanding the nature and structure of tourist EE, and in general emotion research. Findings of the study promise new tools for designing and managing tourist EE for various stakeholders including tour operators and destination managers. 瞭解遊客情感體驗的實質和構成是旅遊研究中一個重要且具有挑戰性的課題。 這個課題值得研究者採用創新性方法進行更加深入的調查,因為遊客的經歷是通過各種積極和消極的情感實現的,然而我們對於遊客在旅遊過程中為什麼、以及如何產生並體驗如此主觀的、多樣複雜的情感還知之甚少。 由於在情緒識別和持續跟蹤領域中新技術的不斷進步,研究者在實驗室以外的自然環境中跟蹤調查遊客的即時情緒狀態和變化已經不再是個夢想。 因此,這項縱向追蹤研究將跟蹤調查中國大陸遊客在海外旅行過程中的情緒體驗、並探索潛在的情感生成和調節的過程。 選取中國大陸出境遊客是因為近些年這個市場的井噴式發展、及其對全球旅遊目的地不言而喻的重要性。 該研究擬以「旅行前所期望的情緒體驗—行程中情緒的生成和調節—旅行後對情緒體驗的評價」 為框架,採用多學科、混合式研究法(即定性,定量和可穿戴技術的綜合使用),融合心理學、地理學、消費者行為和旅遊等多領域中的概念和方法, 以期建立起一個綜合性的遊客情緒體驗模型——該模型可以揭示情緒的決定因素、生成和調節過程,以及情緒調節的結果等一系列概念及其之間的複雜關係。 為了探索無形的情感生成和調節過程、並通過實證檢驗整個模型,研究者提出了一個嚴謹的五階段計畫。 第一階段需要進行全面的文獻搜集和回顧,以深入瞭解不同學科領域對情緒研究的已有成果。 第二階段將通過對參與調查研究的遊客發放簡短問卷以及進行深度訪談來瞭解他們在旅行前所期望的情緒體驗。 遊客在行程中的情緒體驗將通過三種方法(第三階段)來進行跟蹤調查:(1)通過可以測試個體情緒指標(皮膚電活動資料)的手環在整個行程中收集客觀的心理生理指數、繪製每位遊客的情緒波動圖;(2) 研究者通過參與觀察法細心捕捉所觀察遊客表達出來的情緒反應,包括面部表情、聲音和身體表達;(3)在旅途中每隔一晚對每位遊客進行一次簡短的訪談,以解釋和補充上述情緒指標、找出引發其情緒波動的原因。 旅行結束後的第四階段,研究者將主要通過深度訪談來收集所有參與調查的遊客所能回憶起來的情緒體驗以及情緒調節過程。 最後一個階段,研究者將通過問卷收集一個大樣本來檢測所提出的模型。 該專案將不僅對深入理解遊客情緒體驗的本質和構成做出理論和方法論上的雙重突破,也可能對心理學等傳統學寇里的情緒研究做出新的貢獻。 該研究的結果還將為包括旅遊經營者和旅遊目的地管理者在內的各利益相關方提供設計、管理遊客情緒體驗的新工具。

15500618.label: Realisation of objectives
15500618.value: All research objectives have been achieved. A comprehensive review of literature was conducted in psychology, geography, consumer behaviour, and tourism to finetune the comprehensive conceptual framework developed during the proposal stage. The framework was be used to guide the study, following the pre-trip – during-trip – post-trip longitudinal approach. The mixed research design under the embodiment emotion paradigm combines the strengths of both qualitative and quantitative approaches. Qualitative methods include participant observation and individual in-depth interviews. Quantitative methods consist of real-time emotion tracking by a wristband sensor and a structured questionnaire to empirically test the proposed model. Leisure tourists were recruited that allowed us to collect data on pre-trip emotional status and anticipated emotions, then tracking their real-time emotions during the whole trip, and finally investigating their emotional memory after returning home. Examination of tourists’ emotional responses throughout a leisure trip provided both tourism academia and practitioners with new insights into optimizing tourists’ full-range experiences from physical, mental, and cognitive perspectives. Field Data Collection A group of 8 Chinese outbound tourists, who had purchased a 6-day all-inclusive package tour to New Zealand in December 2019 was recruited. All recruited research subjects were asked to complete a survey on personality, current emotional states, trip party and planned itinerary, trip expectations in terms of perceived values and benefits, knowledge and emotions related to trip destinations, and demographics. Basic statistical analyses were performed in SPSS. Interviews using introspective (i.e., think aloud) protocols were conducted with each participant to identify specific expected emotional experience, which served as a benchmark for longitudinal comparison purpose. All interview transcripts were analysed using NVivo which facilitated data management, coding, and theme synthesis. As tourist emotions is to be measured from subjective experience, expressive behaviours, and peripheral physiological responses, three different but complementary methods were used to capture the complete picture of tourist emotional experience and emotion regulation. Using the standard experience sampling method, during-trip emotions (both positive and negative) were tracked using psychophysiological techniques and participant observation. All tourists recruited were asked to wear a wristband sensor throughout the 6-day trip to collect electrodermal activity (EDA) data. Two research team members participated tour as observers and capture tourists’ emotional expressions, including facial, vocal, and behavioural, in various emotion-eliciting settings. At the end of each day, researchers examined the real-time EDA data via software to identify emotional patterns of each participant. A brief interview was conducted with each participant every other day on alternate basis to confirm the emotional patterns provided by EDA data, and dig into the reasons and psychological processes underlying major emotional fluctuations. Analyses were conducted to assess the impact of various emotional experience patterns on tourists’ overall evaluation of their travel experience. As such, the interviews helped identify emotion regulation strategies, determinants of strategy choices, and consequences. Post-trip in-depth interviews were conducted with each participant within two weeks after their return to examine the recalled emotional experience and emotion regulation during the trip. The post-trip interviews used both prompted and unprompted cues to identify tourists’ perceptions of their emotions, which are suggested to be collected as soon as the trip is finished to diminish the impact of recall bias. Importantly, these retrospective data triangulated and provided different explanations for the findings of during-trip investigations. A second group of tourists was recruited and ready to depart to New Zealand during the Chinese New Year holidays in February 2020. However, the outbreak of COVID-19 forced the research team to cancel the plan. As the pandemic situation eased in Mainland China in late 2021, domestic travel became possible although outbound leisure travel was still not allowed. A group of 8 tourists was recruited to participate in this study. A 6-day trip to Yunan, a relatively distanced and unfamiliar region to participants, was the study context. All other data collection activities were the same as the trip to New Zealand, as explained above. Due to the unstable condition of COVID-19 and evidence of data saturation based on analysis results from the two trips, a conceptual model, showing tourist emotional experiences across pre-, during-, and post-travel stages as well as illustrating how and why tourists develop various emotions during a leisure trip, was finalized. Thus, objectives one and two were accomplished. Online Questionnaire Survey A questionnaire, including measurements of all study constructs (e.g., influencing factors of emotion regulation, emotion regulation strategies, and emotional experience before and during trip), was designed based on findings of the field study and relevant literature. The instrument was pilot tested in March 2022 with a convenience sample of Mainland Chinese who had package tour experience (n = 300) in the past one year to check the suitability of wording, accuracy of translation, clarity of instruction, and other design issues. Some initial testing, such as exploratory factor analysis and reliability test, was also conducted to refine the scales. Then, an online survey was conducted with Mainland Chinese who had participated in a package tour(s) in the past one year. Quota sampling was used to obtain a nationally representative sample of Mainland Chinese for gender, age and region. Due to the length of the questionnaire, data were collected in two waves. The first wave was completed by 1,055 respondents and the second wave was completed by 406 of those who completed the wave one survey. Exploratory factor analysis was conducted using data from those who only completed the wave one survey. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to finetune the measurement of emotion regulation and emotional experience. The proposed relationships among tourists’ pre-trip emotional expectations, emotional experience and emotion regulation during the trip, and post-trip emotional memory were examined using structural equation modelling. Thus, research objective three was accomplished.

15500618.label: Major findings and research outcome
15500618.value: The field data collection and online survey assembled a wealth of qualitative and quantitative data. In-depth analyses have yielded many interesting findings beyond our expectations which will help us compose more research articles than originally planned. As a result, it took longer than envisioned for the team to strategize publication plans. The paper, “Emotion Regulation Research in Hospitality and Tourism,” published in the International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management (A+ journal), developed a comprehensive conceptual model of emotion regulation in hospitality and tourism service encounters and proposed various innovative methodologies to investigate the various stages of emotion regulation, from both interpersonal and intrapersonal perspectives. Results from short surveys, interviews, and participant observation obtained throughout the pre-trip, during-trip, and post-trip journey are discussed in a paper under review by Annals of Tourism Research (A+ journal). Based on tourists’ emotional experience and emotional regulation strategies employed, a framework outlining the psychological mechanism underlying tourism emotion generation and regulation was developed. Emotional reactions and transmissions from the host viewpoint was investigated using a real-time multi-modal method. Facial expressions of hosts and tourists were videorecorded and analyzed by the FaceReader software for facial emotion recognition at milliseconds. Artificial intelligence-based sentiment analytics were also used to capture tourists’ moment-to-moment emotions in vocal and semantic expressions. Results theoretically consolidated the dual-process mechanism underpinning automatic emotional contagion and empirically verified an Emotional Contagion Model from tourists to hosts. The paper, “Multi-Modal-based Emotional Contagion from Tourists to Hosts: The Dual-Process Mechanism,” was published in the Journal of Travel Research (A+ journal), extended the knowledge boundary of host-tourist interaction to micro-level interpersonal emotional connection. One additional journal manuscript will be prepared based on quantitative data collected from a large-scale survey to report the development and refinement of an emotion regulation strategy scale and examination of the influence of emotion regulation strategies on travel experiences and emotional memory.

15500618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15500618.value: The conceptual model of emotion regulation in hospitality and tourism service encounters should be empirically validated in a series of future studies, as the model is quite comprehensive and involves multiple stakeholders, time points and scenarios. Moreover, the research team is interested in expanding the current project to include local residents’ emotional experience and regulation when interacting with tourists, as tourist-host interactions are essential to tourism success. Additionally, besides primary data collected from tourists and residents, publicly available data from social media, forums, and news media could be mined to reveal sentiments and emotions of different parties and identify their emotion contagion and emotion regulation strategies. With the assistance of artificial intelligence, scope of data and investigation can be greatly expanded. It is also anticipated that several subsequent publications will be prepared in the next two years as the project collected a wealth of data yet to be fully explored within the project period. The research team will prepare a follow-up study proposal for funding from GRF, and possibly from the RGC Research Impact Fund.

15500618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15500618.value: Understanding the nature and structure of tourists’ emotional experiences is an important and challenging topic in tourism research because tourists’ experiences are lived through a variety of positive and negative emotions. However, little is known about why and how tourists develop and experience such a subjective emotional journey. This study examined tourist emotional experiences throughout a leisure trip by exploring the underlying emotion generative and regulatory processes, in the context of Mainland Chinese tourists’ packaged tours, due to the importance of this market to domestic and international destinations. This research is guided by a framework of pre-trip expectation of emotional experiences, during-trip emotional generation and regulation, and post-trip evaluation of emotional experiences. A comprehensive model is proposed to examine relationships among emotion determinants, formation process, regulations, and outcomes. To explore the invisible emotion generative and regulatory processes, and empirically test the full model, a rigorous research plan was implemented. This project offered theoretical and methodological breakthroughs in understanding the nature and structure of tourist emotional experiences, and in general emotion research. Findings of the study provided new tools for designing and managing tourist emotional experiences for various stakeholders including tour operators and destination managers.

15501218.label: Project Objectives
15501218.value: To describe the constructive choice process when tourists make decisions about different activities in a destination, including sightseeing, dining, and shopping. This study will develop thick descriptions of decision tasks, information environments, information selectivity, decision strategies, and decision time spans; To identify the information processing and patterns of decision strategy in each type of tourist decision task; To develop concepts and propositions theorizing tourists’ activity decision making during a trip combining state-of-the-art theories and evidence gathered from the proposed study.
rows: To describe the constructive choice process when tourists make decisions about different activities in a destination, including sightseeing, dining, and shopping. This study will develop thick descriptions of decision tasks, information environments, information selectivity, decision strategies, and decision time spans;
To identify the information processing and patterns of decision strategy in each type of tourist decision task;
To develop concepts and propositions theorizing tourists’ activity decision making during a trip combining state-of-the-art theories and evidence gathered from the proposed study.

15501218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501218.value: Nowadays, more and more tourists make decisions on activities after arriving in the destination. This trend is largely unavoidable for two reasons. First, although tourists plan their trip in order to reduce uncertainties, avoid risks, and have an enjoyable experience, no plan is perfect. Many tourists must change their plans or make new ones as their trip unfolds because they obtain new information or face various physical or emotional constraints that prompt their behavior to diverge from their intention. Second, tourists intentionally leave some parts of their itinerary to decide during a trip due to uncertainty and a need for flexibility and/or a surprise factor. As tourists make more of decisions during the trip, decision problems expand to encompass other trip components, including core and secondary decisions related to accommodation and attractions, respectively. These changes are shaped by a variety of factors, such as opportunities resulting from improved economic situations, travelers becoming more experienced, better educated, and more independent, as well as the ubiquitous support of mobile Internet afforded by the use of smartphones and tablets during traveling. Over the past decades, knowledge about tourists’ in-destination decision-making has remained underexplored. Beyond some development in examining unplanned behavior among tourists on the move, a few studies have contributed to understanding this decision making process. The theoretical development of tourists’ in-destination decision making is important for advancing the body of knowledge on the general travel decision making. It provides guidelines for designing recommendation systems and applications and for informing the selection of marketing contexts (e.g., timing and location) for tourism and hospitality businesses. The proposed study aims to conceptualize tourists’ in-destination decision making. Specifically, it will focus on the process of decision making, including elements such as goals, decision timing, information and attention selectivity, decision strategies (e.g., choice heuristics), and the factors influencing them, such as decision task characteristics, choice environment, and the decision maker’s experience, training, skill, and knowledge. Based on the theories of constructive consumer choice and heuristic decision making, the proposed study is designed to achieve the aforementioned goal by tracking tourists’ decision making process while on the move. Focusing on Korean, Japanese, and Chinese tourists will provide practical implications for the travel and tourism stakeholders in Hong Kong.

15501218.label: Realisation of objectives
15501218.value: This study proposed three objectives: • To describe the constructive choice process when tourists make decisions about different activities in a destination, including sightseeing, dining, and shopping. This study will develop thick descriptions of decision tasks, information environments, information selectivity, decision strategies, and decision time spans; • To identify the information processing and patterns of decision strategy in each type of tourist decision task; • To develop concepts and propositions theorizing tourists’ activity decision-making during a trip combining state-of-the-art theories and evidence gathered from the proposed study. In order to achieve the research objectives, we designed the study as stated in the proposal. Specifically, following a critical realist tradition, we employed a research design to provide a contextual understanding of travelers’ choices during trips. Process-tracking design. A process-tracking study was designed to capture the details of participants’ in-destination decision-making, including the context (why), the decision item (what), and the ways the decision was made (how). As experienced by Moore et al. (2012), participants cannot recall specific decisions unless they are interviewed about events that occurred on the previous day or immediately before the interview. Thus, the following protocol and tools were used for data collection: 1. Participants were asked to complete a pre-trip schedule plan one day before departure, to understand their planned and unplanned schedule for each day, and to allow the capture of changes and decisions during the trip. Participants were asked to complete the form with the activities and locations at different time slots. Time ranges were given as a reference for the participants, as they were not required to report their plans every hour. 2. During the trip, participants were required to keep in contact with the researchers through instant messaging platforms such as WeChat or Whatsapp. The researchers sent messages to participants roughly every four hours, to chat about their experiences and particularly with a focus on decisions made. In the evening or the morning of the next day, the researchers conducted a phone interview with the participants to review the chat records and clarify their decisions. The interview and instant messaging followed the questions below: • If the time slot had been filled according to the pre-trip plan, the researchers asked if the plan was executed, and, if not, why; what else they had done, and how these decisions were made. • If the time slot was left empty, the researcher asked what the participant did and how the decision was made. • Finally, the researchers asked about the plan for the rest of the trip, examined any changes to the original plans, and probed in detail if any in-destination decisions were made. 3. Around 30% of participants agreed to wear eye-tracking glasses to capture their eye movement for half-day of their day trips. Table 1 Pre-trip schedule plan Participants were recruited from a variety of channels, including personal social circles, online travel communities, and alumni communities. A total of 57 cases were completed, including 21 from mainland China, 32 from Korea, 2 from the USA, 1 from Japan, and 1 from the UK. Data Analysis. Data analysis included two parts. The first analyzed the number of in-destination decisions by each participant and the number of decisions on different items including activities, attractions, day tours, transportation, meals, and purchases. The second analyzed content to determine how decisions were made. The unit of data analysis is a group decision-making process during trips. Thus, first, we identified each decision-making process involving travel companions and/or social contacts online from the interview transcripts. Then, three rounds of content analysis were conducted to identify the different uses of smartphones for group decision-making, group decision-making patterns, and the sociomateriality of smartphones in travel. In the first round of content analysis, we coded for the decision item (i.e. what to decide), the smartphone functions/apps used, and the purpose of using a smartphone. In the second round of content analysis, we focus on group decision-making patterns (i.e., the interactions and communications). In the third analysis, to code scenarios, we applied the different sociomaterialities of smartphones that emerged and were conceptualized from the first two rounds of content analysis. The codes were developed by one researcher, and the other researcher applied those codes to the transcripts. The codes were reviewed and revised until the two researchers’ separate codings are consistent at a 90% level (the inter-coder reliability was calculated by using https://idostatistics.com/cohen-kappa-free-calculator/). Achievement of research objectives: In total, the participants reported 845 decision-making scenarios, including 376 pre-trip decisions and 469 in-destination decisions, 123 of which were facilitated by smartphones. The decisions are categorized by decision items, including activities, attractions, day tours, transportation, meals, and shopping items. Before the trips, tourists mainly planned for attractions to visit, with 55% of pre-trip decisions involving attractions. During their trips, the participants’ decisions are further classified into three categories based on the purposes of decision-making: modifications, cancellations, and newly emergent decisions when tourists initiated an information search and made a choice to fill unplanned time slots. The participants reported a large number of newly emergent decisions during the trip (342 decisions in total). The participants also occasionally changed their original plans (68 decisions) and canceled originally planned items (59 decisions). Overall, during trips, most of the decisions were about meals (38.7%) and attractions (29.1%). This study developed three manuscripts to illustrate decision tasks, information environments, information selectivity, decision strategies, and decision time spans. The main conclusions are: • The active smartphone users tend to leave their travel itineraries open and postpone many decisions on destination activities until during their trip. Moreover, active smartphone users re-evaluated many pre-planned items such as attractions, restaurants, and visiting schedules based on on-location circumstances. • The in-destination decision-making process reflected the shadow of smartphone usage in their daily life, which developed a structure-within-knowledgeability in their mind and equipped them with known rules and resources for in-destination decisions. • Smartphone use during the trip influences tourists’ cognitive representations of the physical environment and increases the interactions with their physical and social contexts. The smartphone also actively changes the context. • Rather than just providing access to information as discussed in previous research (Kang, Jodice & Norman, 2020), this study found smartphones to be active mediators of decision-making contexts by expanding and changing perceptions, drawing attention to specific context elements, triggering decision processes, facilitating decision-making, and guiding decision implementation. • This study shows that tourist decisions are embedded socially in their communication with travel companions on the trip as well as with family and friends (remotely through social apps) and with online travel communities. • Tourists collectively activated the materialities (i.e., functions) of smartphones in different decision-making scenarios. Interestingly, we observed that technology agency is now dominating tourists’ decision-making. In all three group decision-making patterns, the information acquired from smartphones was the foundation for group discussion and negotiation and had absolute authority among any travel parties.

15501218.label: Major findings and research outcome
15501218.value: This study develops three papers to report major findings: 1. “On-site decision-making in smartphone-mediated contexts”. (Published) The smartphone has become an indispensable travel companion for contemporary tourists. However, how smartphone use during the trip changes the travel context and related travel decision-making is still unclear. By tracing the in-situ decision-making processes in a real-world setting, this empirical study develops a deep understanding of the role of smartphones in shaping the physical and social contexts within which on-site decisions are made. The findings suggest that smartphones create a complex phygital-social context that triggers and supports the development of new travel plans, re-examination of pre-trip plans, and cancellation of pre-trip plans. Interactions with the smartphone-mediated context facilitate efficient decision-making and enable experience optimization. This study provides implications for decision-making theory in tourism and offers practical implications for destination marketing and management. 2. “Shaping In-Destination Group Decision-Making: The Sociomateriality of Smartphones” (under second review) In-destination travel decisions are unavoidable due to uncertainties after arrival and the nature of leisure travel. Smartphone use encourages more instant information search and communication, and, thus, promotes in-destination decision-making and plan changes. This study adopts sociomateriality as a theoretical tool to offer the sociotechnical view in examining the interactions of travelers and their smartphones in in-destination group decision-making. This study identifies three patterns of communication in group decision-making during trips and four features of the sociomateriality of smartphones: knowledgeability, thriftiness, referenceability, and negotiability. This study responds to recent calls to extend the theoretical repertoire of information technology and tourism research and the need for more empirical studies on tourists’ in-destination behaviors in the age of the mobile Internet. 3. “Context-driven processes in Tourists’ Decision-making in Motion” (Finalizing for submission) Analysis of data revealed that during decision-making in motion, interactions between participants and the destination environment can be decomposed along two independent dimensions: goal ambiguity vs. specificity and active vs. reactive predisposition. These dimensions yield four modes of tourist-environment interaction: Mode 1 (goal ambiguity-active predisposition), Mode 2 (goal ambiguity-passive predisposition), Mode 3 (goal specificity-active predisposition), Mode 4 (goal specificity-passive predisposition). These modes evoked different cognitive processes that lead to decisions emerging in various scenarios concerning different categories of decision tasks. Four general categories of scenarios were identified that are conducive to inspiring or triggering tourists’ decision-making in motion: sightseeing, dining, shopping, and transportation decision scenarios.

15501218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15501218.value: This study investigates the interactive adjustment process of travel planning and decision-making in real-world settings. This study contributes to knowledge development by considering the complex destination environment, the actuation and revision of pre-trip plans, and the spontaneous nature of some travel behaviors (e.g., unplanned behaviors) as a direct result of smartphone interaction. Smartphones not only change the contexts but also afford new interaction possibilities and new opportunities for optimizing trip experiences. As a result, the interdisciplinary research is planned for the development of mobile applications that seek to optimize on-site decision-making by emphasizing specific context dimensions that seem to have an impact in urban travel contexts. The PI is working with researchers in computer science to design a mobile app that supports on-site decision-making. Moreover, the PI is planning to extend the scope of the study from qualitative case studies to a quantitative study with a larger sample size. The GIS techniques will be employed to track travelers’ movement in a destination in order to develop prediction models regarding tourists’ itinerary development after arrival.

15501218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15501218.value: Nowadays, more and more tourists make decisions on their destination activities after their arrival of the destination. Over the past three decades plus, knowledge about tourists’ destination activity decision making during trips has remained underexplored. Thus, besides advancing the body of knowledge on travel decision making, this study provides guidelines for designing recommendation system applications based on information technology and informing the selection of marketing contexts (e.g., timing and location) for tourism and hospitality businesses. This study investigates the interactive adjustment process of travel planning and decision-making in real-world settings. This study responds to recent calls to extend the theoretical repertoire of information technology and tourism research and the need for more empirical studies on tourists’ in-destination behaviors in the age of the mobile Internet. The research findings inform the design of context-aware mobile applications by highlighting that both physical and social contexts need to be considered when making recommendations. This study identified that tourists rely on the smartphone apps that they use in their daily life to facilitate in-destination decision-making. Tourism businesses or destinations looking to focus on contextual and location-based marketing should consider collaboration with the platforms/apps that people use daily at their point of origin.

15502618.label: Project Objectives

15502618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15502618.value: Over the past decade, social media has transformed the way information about firms is produced, disseminated, and processed. Recent disclosure literature on social media largely focuses on corporate use of social media. Existing studies find that firms can reduce information asymmetry by disseminating news via social media and the text content on Twitter can help predict stock market or firm performance. Because social media allows users to disseminate information to a wider audience much more quickly than traditional disclosure channels, executives have increasingly accessed social media for business purposes. Anecdotal evidence suggests that executives’ postings on social media could have significant capital market consequences. For example, Netflix’s CEO Reed Hastings used his Facebook page on July 3, 2012, to announce a streaming milestone reached by Netflix without an accompanying press release or Form 8-K filing. The posting immediately caused 6.2% stock surge on the same day. This triggered the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to investigate the appropriateness of releasing company-related information on social media. Consequently, viewing social media as “public enough” information source, the SEC issued guidance in April 2013 permitting firms to use social media to communicate with shareholders in compliance with Regulation Fair Disclosure. The proposed research begins with evaluating executives’ tweeting activities on their personal Twitter accounts, especially if executives tweet more after the SEC guidance. We then ask two research questions. First, what are the determinants of executives’ tweeting activities? We ask if executives will tweet more when there are more individual investors because an important goal for Twitter is to improve person-to-person communications with a focused point. We also investigate if executives tweet more when there are fewer conference calls because Twitter complements other disclosure channels in broadcasting information. The second research question investigates the capital market consequences of executive tweets. Motivated by the classic media theory (McLuhan 1964) which suggests the way by which a message is relayed, the medium, influences how the message is perceived, we posit that investors will respond to the tweets even if similar information were presented. As executives are likely to cherry pick the corporate events by disclosing good news while depressing bad news, we ask if tweets containing such information can help predict firm performance. Moreover, if executive tweets are credible, they should reduce information asymmetry. The results will provide useful insights on the role executive disclosure on Twitter plays in the capital market. 在过去的十年里，社交媒体已经改变了企业信息的产生、传播和处理的方式。最近披露的社交媒体文献主要集中在企业对社交媒体使用上。现有研究发现，企业可以通过社交媒体传播新闻来减少信息不对称，Twitter上的文本内容可以帮助预测整个股市或企业绩效 由于社交媒体允许用户比传统披露渠道更快地向更广泛的受众传播信息，因此高管们越来越多地出于商业目的访问社交媒体。轶事证据表明，高管在社交媒体上发的帖子可能会对资本市场产生重大影响。例如，Netflix的CEO Reed Hastings在2012年7月3日用他的Facebook页面宣布了Netflix在没有附带的新闻稿或8-K表格的情况下达到的流媒体里程碑。这个消息公布的当天立即导致当天的股票飙升6.2%。这促使美国证券交易委员会 (SEC)调查在社交媒体上发布公司相关信息的适当性。因此，SEC将社交媒体视为 “足够公开”的信息源，在2013年4月发布了指导方针，允许公司根据公平披露条例使用社交媒体与股东沟通 这个研究提案从评估高管们在个人Twitter账户上的Twitter活动开始，尤其是从看高管们是否在SEC的指导下更多地在Twitter账户上发推文。紧接着我们提出了两个研究问题。首先，高管的推特活动的决定因素是什么？我们询问，当有更多的个人投资者时，高管们是否会多发推特，因为Twitter的一个重要目标是改善与关注个人层面的人际交流。我们还会调查当电话会议较少时，高管们是否会多发Twitter，因为Twitter弥补了传播信息的其他渠道。 第二个研究问题研究了高管推特的资本市场后果。受经典媒体理论(McLuhan 1964) 的启发，该理论提出了信息传递的方式，即媒体，影响信息如何被感知，我们假设即使出现类似的信息，投资者也会对推文作出回应。由于高管们可能会通过披露好消息同时压抑坏消息来挑选公司事件，所以我们问到，包含这些信息的推文是否有助于预测公司业绩。此外，如果高管推文是可信的，他们应该减少信息不对称。研究结果将为资本市场中Twitter的高管披露提供有益的启示。

15502618.label: Realisation of objectives
15502618.value: The paper has successfully achieved the objectives of examining executive tweeting activities, their associated determinants and the role that executive disclosure on social media plays in capital market. Specifically, in the paper titled “Executive Tweets”, we examine the tweeting behavior of S&P 1500 firms’ executives (CEOs and CFOs) on Twitter and its consequences. We find that following the release of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s 2013 report on social media usage by corporations and executives, executives from firms with high litigation risk are less likely to join Twitter. We also document that executives tweet financial information related to their firms and time these tweets to firms’ major financial and non-financial events, and that investors respond to executive tweets in addition to firm tweets. Using an innovative construct measuring the content similarity between executive tweets and firm tweets, we find evidence consistent with the view that investors trust similar information from executive Twitter accounts more than information from firm Twitter accounts. More importantly, we not only show that the market responds to executive tweets, we show – using an innovative similarity measure – that the market appears to respond due to trust of the executives, responding more to executive tweets that are more similar to firm tweets in content. We interpret this as evidence consistent with the view that investors trust similar information from executive Twitter accounts more than information from firm Twitter accounts. Our study has policy implications for whether investors trust and respond to executive tweets and whether executives’ tweets on their individual account should be regulated. From the methodology point of view, the similarity measure we adopt is innovative in capturing the level of similarity between content of disclosure and can be applied to other similar settings. Specifically, when testing Hypothesis 4 “The market responds more strongly to executive tweets with content similar to firm tweets,” we introduce a fine-grained measure of content or meaning of text to the accounting literature, called Universal Sentence Encoder (USE). The USE algorithm leverages neural networks to process text on the order of sentences or short paragraphs, factoring in word order. As such, this model breaks away from the typically bag-of-words based approaches used in accounting, such as dictionaries or LDA, allowing it to ascribe a more precise meaning to a sentence. See also related discussion on future development in subsection 6.2 of this report. The above mentioned paper has received an invitation to revise and resubmit at the top-tier accounting journal The Accounting Review. We fully acknowledge the funding support from RGC. We are now preparing for resubmission for the second-round review. This paper is one of the series of papers I’ve been working on social media. Together with my other related paper titled “Discretionary Disclosure on Twitter,” which (though not RGC-funded) is being revised for the 3rd round resubmission at the Contemporary Accounting Research, our research findings overall contribute to our understanding of executive disclosure versus firm disclosure on social media, and whether investors value information about the same firm on one channel more than those on another channel. On a separate note on the budget expenditure, the reason I spent less than originally proposed is related to a significant amount of funding reserved for hiring RA. But due to the social movements ongoing in HK at the time she had to postpone her trip a few times for security reasons. Although I had a back-up plan to try to hire another RA from local, but things became difficult during the pandemic, so we ended up not being able to use any RA afterwards. Of course, when many countries and regions were locked down due to Covid-19, I could no longer travel, therefore some costs reserved for conference presentation in 2019 and 2020 were “saved”, so are the cost of traveling to working with co-authors in foreign countries. For instance, the paper was accepted for European Accounting Association Annual Congress in 2020, but the conference was forced to cancel due to pandemic and now is postponed to 2022.

15502618.label: Major findings and research outcome
15502618.value: The paper titled “EXECUTIVE TWEETS” examines the tweeting behavior of executives. We find that the primary effect of the 2013 Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) report on executives was to decrease the likelihood of joining Twitter by executives at high litigation risk firms. We then examine whether executives tweet around important financial and business disclosures. We show that executives post financial-related tweets around important financial events including earnings announcements, earnings conference calls, and 10-K and 10-Q filings. We also document that executives post both financial and non-financial business-related information on Twitter around more general information events for their firms, such as 8-K filings, press releases, and news articles. We then find that the market reacts to financial tweets by executives and that this reaction is much stronger than the market’s reaction to financial tweets by firms. This reaction is mostly concentrated in the trading day following the tweets. Lastly, we examine the mechanism underlying the market reaction using an innovative measure based on the similarity of content between executives’ and firms’ tweets. We find that the market reacts more to executives’ financial tweets that contain content similar to firms’ prior tweets, showing that the mechanism is the increased reliability of the information coming from the executives. The paper has been presented at seminars and conferences at Iowa State University, Singapore Management University, University of Central Florida, University of Washington, and the Humboldt University Internal Research Training Group (IRTG) 1792 Summer Camp held in Germany in 2019. The paper was also accepted by international conferences such as 2020 Annual Congress of the European Accounting Association, though the conference was forced to cancel later on due to Covid-19. The paper has received an invitation to revise and resubmit at the top-tier accounting journal The Accounting Review. We fully acknowledge the funding support from RGC. As of the time of this report, we are preparing for resubmission for the second-round review soon. This paper is one of the series of papers I’ve been working on disclosure on social media. Together with my other related paper titled “Discretionary Disclosure on Twitter,” which (though not RGC-funded) is being revised for the 3rd round resubmission at the Contemporary Accounting Research, our research findings overall contribute to our understanding of executive disclosure versus firm disclosure on social media, and whether investors value information about the same firm on one channel more than those on another channel.

15502618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15502618.value: 1. Our paper fits into a broader view that Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning can be applied to support critical thinking in the business world. The similarity measure that we adopt in this study is both innovative and effective in capturing the level of similarity in the content of disclosure by different market participants or via different platforms. Appendix C of the paper explains the technical details of Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) method. This method can be extended and applied to other settings that demand for comparing the content similarity. Although we were unable to hire RA for this type of training due to pandemic and other reasons explained in the preceding section of this report, we hope that future resources can be provided to train graduate students to use this technique and benefit future research. 2. As discussed earlier, both the RGC-funded paper “Executive Tweets” and my other paper “Discretionary Disclosure on Twitter” received R&R at top-tier accounting journals, the reviewers find the topics relevant and timely and have potential contributions to the literature. Going forward, I plan to extend the study to other content comparisons between firms and managers on a different disclosure platform.

15502618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15502618.value: The paper examines the tweeting behavior of executives. We find that following the release of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s 2013 report on social media usage by corporations and executives, executives from firms with high litigation risk are less likely to join Twitter. We also document that executives tweet financial information related to their firms and time these tweets to firms’ major financial and non-financial events, and that investors respond to executive tweets in addition to firm tweets. Interestingly, we show that the market reacts more to executives’ financial tweets that contain content similar to firms’ prior tweets, showing that the mechanism is the increased reliability of the information coming from the executives. These findings provide an answer to the intriguing question of whether executive tweets provide information incremental to those in firm tweets and whether investors respond to executive tweets. They also have policy implications for whether managers’ disclosure about firm information on their individual social media accounts should be regulated.

15503218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15503218.value: Product design is an important factor influencing consumers’ willingness to purchase the products. Novel product designs not only fascinate global consumers, but also bring huge potential profits and reputations for brands producing these products. How to communicate brand values and product worthiness through product design thus has become an important research direction for marketing researchers. The current research focuses on one essential element of product design: the visual glossiness of the product surface. Specifically, in this research, we plan to investigate when and how the level of visual glossiness of a product’s appearance influence consumers’ inference about this product, and the downstream consequences of these consumer inferences. Based on past literature on visual perception and psychological newness, in the current research we hypothesize that consumers will perceive a product with glossy appearance as psychologically newer than a similar product with matte appearance. This inference regarding the psychological newness of the product will in turn influence product evaluation, purchase intention, and consumers’ willingness to pay for the product. We further predict that perceived risk, the feeling of nostalgia, the concern about product durability, and the functional attribution of glossiness will moderate the proposed effect. 產品設計是影響消費者購買產品意願的重要因素。新穎的產品外觀設計不但吸引消費者，還可給品牌和廠商帶來巨大利益和名氣。如何才能利用產品外觀設計正確表述品牌價值和產品特性呢？本研究致力于研究產品外觀設計的一個重要元素：產品外觀光澤度。在本研究中，我們計劃研究何時和如何不同級別的產品外觀光澤度影響消費者對於該產品的印象。基於過去視覺感知和產品創新度的研究文獻，在本研究中我們假設消費者會認為外觀有較高光澤度的產品具有更高的產品創新度，繼而對該產品產生更強的產品評價和購買欲望。我們進一步預測風險感知，懷舊情感，以及對於產品耐用性的考慮將有可能會調節這個效果。

15503218.label: Realisation of objectives
15503218.value: The objectives of this project have been largely completed. Through a series of studies, we demonstrate that consumers generally have more favorable attitudes toward products with a glossy, as opposed to a matte, surface. This effect is driven by the heightened perceived newness of glossy products and is thereby more salient among consumers with a higher dispositional newness-seeking inclination. In addition, the effect of product glossiness on product attitudes diminishes when the product has a nostalgic positioning. The current research contributes to the product design and visual marketing literature by demonstrating the important role played by a largely overlooked visual aspect in product evaluation: product glossiness. This work also contributes to the growing literature on psychological newness by showing that psychological newness can be achieved by modifying the visual appearance of the product—a comparatively minor and inexpensive move for companies. This research reveals how consumers may alter their reactions to visual marketing elements based on the product positioning. From a managerial perspective, this research suggests tactics that companies can use strategically to utilize visual glossiness in their product design. A paper based on this project is currently under review at the Journal of Marketing (JM). In addition, two related papers partially supported by the grant have been published on top-tier academic journals.

15503218.label: Major findings and research outcome
15503218.value: Three major outcomes are yielded from this project with a general focus of the antecedents and consequences of consumers’ visual product preferences. In the focal paper, we look at how consumers’ attitude toward products with a glossy, as opposed to a matte, surface. We found that consumers generally have more favorable attitudes toward glossy (vs. matte) products. This effect is driven by the heightened perceived newness of glossy products and is thereby more salient among consumers with a higher dispositional newness-seeking inclination. In addition, the effect of product glossiness on product attitudes diminishes when the product has a nostalgic positioning. A paper based on this project has been submitted to the Journal of Consumer Research (JCR), and received a revision invitation. But unfortunately, it was rejected by JCR at the second-round review. After that, we have revised the paper, and now this paper is under review at the Journal of Marketing (JM). We also extended our research interest from glossiness to consumers’ visual product preferences in general. Two papers related to this broader focus were published on top-tier marketing journals. In one paper, we examined the effect of social exclusion on consumers’ preferences for visual density. Based on seven experimental studies, we revealed that consumers who perceive themselves as socially excluded evaluate products with dense visual patterns more positively than their non-excluded peers. This effect occurs because social exclusion triggers a feeling of psychological emptiness and dense patterns can provide a sense of being “filled,” which helps to alleviate this feeling of emptiness. This effect is attenuated when consumers physically fill something or experience a feeling of “temporal density” (i.e., imagining a busy schedule with many tasks packed into a short time). This paper was published on the Journal of Consumer Research (JCR) in 2019. In the other paper, we investigated how secrecy (i.e., a state in which people have an active intention to conceal information from others) affects consumers’ visual preferences. Six studies revealed that making consumers’ secrets salient increases their tendency to conform in their consumption and prefer conforming visual product designs, and showed that this effect is driven by the desire to avoid social attention. This effect is moderated by consumers’ perceived self-control capacity. This paper is forthcoming on the Journal of Consumer Research (JCR).

15503218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15503218.value: As may be evident from the above section, this project is productive and there is great potential for further development of this research. My first priority is to push the glossiness paper through the review process and hopefully publish it in the following year. I also plan to further extend findings of some of these published papers and develop new research projects accordingly.

15503218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15503218.value: Despite the importance of the attribute visual glossiness in product design, there is a dearth of research on product glossiness in the marketing realm. In an attempt to fill this gap, the current research examines how and why the visual glossiness of a product influences consumers’ product attitude. Through a series of studies, we demonstrate that consumers generally have more favorable attitudes toward products with a glossy, as opposed to a matte, surface. This work contributes to the product design and visual marketing literature by demonstrating the important role played by a largely overlooked visual aspect in product evaluation: product glossiness. Our findings suggest that a general preference for glossiness among consumers arises because of the heightened psychological newness of glossy products, and we examine when and how this general liking of glossy products can be diminished or reversed. Our work further contributes to the growing literature on psychological newness by showing that newness perception can be shaped by modifying the visual appearance of the product—a comparatively minor and inexpensive move for companies. From a managerial perspective, this research suggests tactics that companies can use strategically to utilize visual glossiness in their product design.

15503418.label: Project Objectives
15503418.value: To analyze which stocks investors trade at slow exchange (IEX). To analyze under what circumstances investors move from fast to slow exchange. To analyze how volatility plays in choosing which exchange to trade at.
rows: To analyze which stocks investors trade at slow exchange (IEX).

15503418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15503418.value: This study plans to investigate the effect of speed bumps that delay orders on market quality. For example, the IEX’s symmetric speed bump -- the speed bump on IEX is non-discriminatory and applies to all orders and market data -- slows down the orders by 350 microseconds so that opportunistic traders could not benefit from the stale quotes on the IEX and also to protect investors using IEX’s router to be not beaten to other exchanges by observing their orders. The speed bump is likely to encourage traders to submit limit orders to IEX. It is also likely to attract market orders as users of IEX’s order router obtain some protection. First, we wish to extend the model of fast and slow traders in the context of fragmented markets with different speed. Using the baseline model of van Kervel (2015), we intend to solve for the partial equilibrium model that can theoretically explain how traders will choose which market to place their orders. With the guidance from theory, we can explore which empirical regularities to focus on and what they imply. Next, we plan to compare the order submission across different venues by investor speed. When multiple venues are available, fast traders will be able to pick off some slower traders that trade on exchanges without speed bumps. In an informational event, slower traders will prefer to submit orders at IEX and/or would not trade at exchanges without speed bumps so we expect the order flow to vary across exchanges. Finally, if an investor were informed prior to information disclosure, she can trade in both fast and slow markets. In the case where there is only a fast market, fast traders may act quicker than the informed trader and remove liquidity or pick off stale quotes faster. This will cause the total profit of the informed trader to decrease. Thus, informed traders may benefit by using the speed bump feature of the slow market. We expect that the informed trading to happen more in the slow market. By studying the changes in market participation across different venues, we may analyze the effect of fast and slow exchanges. This project can provide policy implications to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange and relevant regulators in order to protect investors from fast traders picking off stale quotes, to improve market efficiency and liquidity, as well as to mitigate the arms race. 本文旨在研究減速帶（speed bump）措施的效果。減速帶措施，即對市場上的訂單增加物理延遲設置。例如，美國投資者交易所（The Investors Exchange，簡稱IEX）的對稱減速帶，這個減速帶對所有的訂單和市場數據一視同仁，統一將訂單時間延遲350微秒。如此一來，高頻交易者就不能從舊的報價中受益。同時，這一做法也保護了使用IEX路由器的投資者們，他們訂單不會因為被高頻交易者觀察到而受到衝擊。減速帶措施可能會促進交易者向IEX提交限價訂單。IEX 訂單路由器可以使市價訂單受到保護，所以這一措施也可能為IEX 訂單路由器吸引更多的用戶。首先，我們希望在不同市場速度的背景下，拓展高頻和低頻交易者的模型。基於van Kervel (2015)的模型，我們旨在求解局部均衡模型，使其可以在理論上解釋交易者會如何選擇不同的市場來提交他們的訂單。通過理論的指引，我們可以探索出應重點研究的經驗規律，並發現它們的意義。其次，我們計劃去比較不同地區間投資者提交訂單的速度。當有眾多地區可供交易者提交訂單時，高頻交易者們會挑選沒有設置減速帶的交易所作為交易場所，並以其中的低頻交易者作為其交易對象。在一個信息事件中，低頻交易者會更傾向於在IEX提交訂單，又或者不在沒有減速帶的交易所進行交易。因此，我們預期不同交易所的訂單流量會有所不同。最後，如果一個投資者在信息披露之前就獲知消息，並且他可以選擇高頻或低頻市場進行交易。在只有高頻市場的情況下，高頻交易者可能比內幕交易者更快地採取行動並消除流動性，又或者更快地發現舊的報價。這將導致內幕交易者的總利潤減少。因此，內幕交易者可以通過使用有減速帶特性的低頻市場來獲益。我們預期低頻市場中會有更多的內幕交易。通過研究不同地區市場參與者的變化，我們可以分析高頻和低頻交易所的影響。這個課題可以為香港交易所和相關監管機構提供政策指引，以此保護投資者利益，提高市場效率和流動性，同時減弱“技術軍備競賽”的影響。

15504118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15504118.value: In this study, we examine whether disclosure of the use of conflict minerals pressures firms to improve its corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance. Conflict minerals are minerals sourced from conflict zones where there is violence and humanitarian crises The four most commonly mined conflict minerals are cassiterite (for tin), wolframite (for tungsten), coltan (for tantalum), and gold ore. These minerals, which typically pass through various intermediaries before their final use, are essential in the manufacture of various devices including consumer electronics. We posit that when a firm disclosure indicates the use of conflict minerals in its products, greater CSR performance will mitigate the reputational damage related to the use of conflict minerals. To examine this issue, we rely on a recent attempt in the United States (U.S.) to mandate the disclosures about the use of conflict minerals. In the U.S., because of lobbying by human rights groups, the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act (fully known as the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection) Act included a provision, Section 1502, that required firms to make disclosures related to their use of conflict minerals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and surrounding areas. The Securities and Exchange Commission then adopted conflict minerals disclosure requirements in 2012, effective from 2014 onwards. Legal challengers resulted in the court ruling that certain provisions violated the First Amendment because they required a regulated entity to report to the Commission and to state on its website about the use of conflict minerals in its products. Accordingly, the SEC issued updated guidance stating that while firms still have to abide by most of the disclosure requirements (e.g., the disclosure of processes that the company uses to detect the use of conflict minerals), they no longer have to state specifically whether any of their products use conflict minerals. In this study, we aim to address these CSR-related questions about disclosure/non-disclosure: i) How do the various stakeholders including firm managers and shareholders react to the disclosures about the use of conflict minerals? ii) How do the disclosures affect the firm’s future CSR performance in general, as well as specifically in the use of conflict minerals? To conclude, understanding the social implications of conflict minerals disclosure is an important objective and the outcome can guide policymaking. The use of disclosure to compel better corporate behavior and the litigation to reduce the extent of the mandate suggest that disclosure has “real effects” that are important to various stakeholders.

15504118.label: Realisation of objectives
15504118.value: A complete working paper titled "Does Supply Chain Visibility Enhance Trade Credit? Evidence through Operational Improvements" has been written. This working paper achieves the revised objectives as stated in section 5.2. 15504118.label: Major findings and research outcome
15504118.value: Scholars and practitioners believe that supply chain visibility (SCV) is critical to effective supply chain management, enabling firms to lower operational costs and enhance efficiency. In this research, we investigate the impact of SCV on firms’ trade credit, a widely neglected yet critical supply chain resource that reduces costs and fuels business growth. Relying on disclosures specified by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act for supply chain–related conflict minerals, we investigate how a firm’s SCV might lead to higher trade credit received from its suppliers. We adopt a large sample of US firms during 2014–2016, and show that firms with higher SCV actually gain more trade credit from their suppliers. Specifically, customers with higher SCV receive 5.84% more trade credit, which is equivalent to an average of US$39 million. Our evidence indicates that SCV enhances trade credit through improving cost management and operational efficiency, leading to higher creditworthiness of the firms. We also demonstrate that SCV has a more significant effect on trade credit for customers with higher financial constraints and product market uncertainty, indicating that weak and vulnerable firms benefit more from SCV. We further find that SCV leads to less downstream trade credit, indicating that suppliers with higher SCV rely less on trade credit as a mean to attract or capture customers. Overall, our research shows that SCV enhances supply chain finance, which can further be a driver of shareholder value.

15504818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15504818.value: “金融時報”最近的一篇文章指出，一些公司能夠實現以“不可思議的準確性”擊敗其獎金合同中的績效目標的表現儘管他們的運營結果不穩定，但他們自己承認，很難預測。例如，正如英國“金融時報”文章上圖所示，Netflix擊中了它績效目標在2015-2016學年的七個八季度中正好落後於其中2006年收入目標為​​82.7億美元（減少1,200萬美元，或0.14％）。這很有意思現象，因為Netflix以其不穩定的性能而聞名;就在最近，該公司的新的季度訂戶比先前的估計高出約63％（5.2百萬對320萬人），首席財務官大衛威爾斯承認“我們的業務有點難以預測“。文章指出，這種現象引發了一些問題投資者和稅務專家對績效目標是否屬於既成事實。受這些軼事觀察的啟發，我們在此提出以下研究問題項目。首先，總體而言，企業實現績效目標的可能性有多大？對於賠償支出可以抵稅，美國稅法要求的結果（實現與績效目標相比的績效）需要基本不確定;就這樣回答這個問題對稅收法規和執法產生影響。第二，怎麼樣對於公司來說，通常是以較小的利潤來實現其績效目標（如同的情況一樣）Netflix），以及公司治理，薪酬設計和經濟方面的作用 解釋這種現象的因素？第三，績效目標是既成事實嗎？使用大量已實現的性能和性能目標，該項目將會提供這些問題的答案。除了對高管的研究做出貢獻薪酬合同和公司治理，我們的研究將有趣的稅收當局和金融市場監管機構。

15504818.label: Realisation of objectives
15504818.value: Despite the social unrest in Hong Kong and the COVID crisis, which has spanned over the full duration of this GRF project, we have managed to complete the intended analyses for this project. The objective of this research project has been full realized. We have conducted the corresponding analyses, and these analyses have been incorporated into the paper titled “Rounding of Internal Performance Targets: Determinants and Implications”, co-authored by Ying Gan (Erasmus University Rotterdam, Netherlands), Xiaoxu Ling (Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, China, who is a recent PhD graduate at Hong Kong Polytechnic University), Ivy Zhang (University of California, Riverside, U.S.A.), and Yong Zhang (Hong Kong Polytechnic University). In this paper, we use a large sample to examine the pattern of rounding (placing a zero or five at the penny digit) for earnings-per-share (EPS) performance targets that are used in CEO bonus plans. We find that over 42% of the EPS targets end with a zero or five at the penny location, more than double the unconditional expected percentage of 20%. Analyses indicate that EPS targets are more likely to be rounded when the penny digit is less important, when there is more information uncertainty, and when the compensation committee is more co-opted. As a consequence of the information uncertainty, we expect firms with rounded performance targets to be more likely to issue rounded management forecasts, to issue management forecasts closer to earnings announcements, and the issued forecasts to exhibit lower accuracy, have a wider range, and convey less information. Results are consistent with these predictions. We also find that the CEO receives higher compensation when EPS targets are rounded after controlling for financial performance and other firm characteristics. Relatedly, we also find that rounded EPS targets are easier targets ex ante in that they are less likely to exceed contemporaneous consensus analyst forecasts than non-rounded targets, thus likely to play a role in facilitating higher compensation payout to the CEO. We contribute to the growing literature on performance targets in two ways. First, we report the first evidence of heaping in CEO performance targets. Our findings indicate that decision makers (the board, potentially with input from top executives) are subject to psychological heuristics in determining internal performance targets, which serve the essential function of internally coordinating firm-wide activities and providing team incentives. Second, we provide new evidence suggesting that CEOs can influence the compensation process for self-serving purposes. Our findings that co-opted compensation committees are more likely to round EPS targets and that rounded EPS targets are easier to achieve are consistent with CEOs influencing the compensation committee to obtain higher compensation. Furthermore, our findings have implications beyond CEO compensation. The performance target is an important part of the corporate capital budgeting process and, as a central component of bonus plans, serves the essential function of internally coordinating firm-wide activities and providing team incentives (e.g., Indjejikian, Matějka, Merchant, and Van der Stede, 2014; Guay, Kepler, and Tsui, 2019; Bloomfield, 2021; Bloomfield, Gipper, Kepler, and Tsui, 2021; Bushman, 2021). Thus, the process of determining performance targets can have important implications regarding the real operations of firms that are beyond executive compensation. We have obtained comments on our research from productive scholars such as Joanna Wu and Ke Na. We are also in the process of scheduling workshops (at Erasmus University Rotterdam, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, University of California, Riverside, and Hong Kong Polytechnic University), as well as submitting the paper to international conferences in order to present this paper and obtain helpful comments and suggestions. After obtaining comments and suggestions, we will make corresponding revisions and will submit the paper to an A* journal, most likely The Accounting Review.

15504918.label: Project Objectives
15504918.value: Develop a model that is sufficiently general to describe families of arrival processes and passenger demands that are decreasing in the generalized price of traveling (sum of price and waiting time costs) and exhibit concave or convex curvatures. Derive a clear understanding of how the curvature of passenger demand functions affects pricing, headway and information strategies from the viewpoint of profit-maximizing and welfare-maximizing carriers, where welfare is described by the sum of carrier profit and consumer surplus.
