15600418.label: Major findings and research outcome
15600418.value: In this single-blind, randomised parallel-group controlled trial, we recruited male and female adults with schizophrenia (18–60 years) in outpatient settings. Participants were randomly assigned into a 12-week computerised brain training (CogniFit), an entertainment gaming (SIMS 4) in addition to usual treatment (TAU), or a TAU only. The comparison between cognitive-training games and commercial non-therapeutic games permits us to dissect the critical elements in gaming that could be responsible for the hypothesized beneficial effects of gaming on the negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. We elected to use openly available games, which are more easily accessible outside research settings as opposed to games used in laboratory settings to facilitate ease and wide application. Gaming was conducted with computer laptops, and participants played game in small-groups. This study was unique amongst existing published studies as it was targeting a high dose gaming amounting to 60 hours in 12 consecutive weeks. Verbal working memory was the primary outcome. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03133143) and is complete. From May 2019 to November 2020, 131 patients were randomly allocated to CogniFit (n=45), SIMS 4 (n=43) or TAU (n=43) group. Results demonstrated no intervention effects of CogniFit on the verbal working memory. The verbal memory test was significantly reduced in the CogniFit group relative to the TAU group from 3 to 6 months (p=0.045). Eight adverse events were reported. We showed that the gaming regimes were feasible in this clinical population in Hong Kong. The potential concern that cognitive gaming might be less attractive was dispelled. Indeed, subjects allocated to cognitive gaming engaged in more hours of gaming, showed a lower drop-out rate, and reported less adverse effects in comparison to subjects in the entertainment gaming group. In addition, both cognitive gaming and entertainment gaming showed some positive effects on individual cognitive or clinical outcomes, such as visuospatial working memory and motivation and pleasure in negative symptoms. Gaming intervention, however, had no effect on verbal memory in people with schizophrenia at 3 or 6 months although it was beneficial for single cognitive and negative symptom metrics. In conclusion, due to inconclusive and nonmature results, there is a need for continuing investment in exploring effective interventions to support patients with schizophrenia. The research yielded two accepted publications in peered reviewed journals, two additional manuscripts are currently under reviewed, and contributed to five presentations in scientific conferences. The data also contributed to one PhD student.

15600418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15600418.value: The study evaluated the effectiveness of gaming to improve psychiatric symptoms and cognitive function in adults of both genders with schizophrenia in the community. Participants were given either computerised brain training (CogniFit), entertainment gaming (SIMS 4), or no gaming in addition to their usual treatment. The study provided new knowledge on how functioning, symptoms and treatment motivation could be modified through gaming. Although the clinical benefits derived from gaming demonstrated here may be limited, a larger sample size would be expected to yield a strong statistical effect. Our study had demonstrated the feasibility of gaming interventions as a potential treatment to improve motivation, pleasure, and social engagement, especially for those who have problems in engaging with other behavioural treatments. Despite half of our participants had never played computer games before, the intervention was completed with positive engagement. Given that the majority of existing behavioural therapies or trainings are unable to engage people with serious mental illnesses, the gaming interventions evaluated here have reinforced the global interests and recent promises of gaming in mental health care, including the need for continuing innovation in their safe application in rehabilitation for people suffering from schizophrenia and other psychiatric conditions.

15601118.label: Project Title(Chinese)
15601118.value: 非洲農業的中國推動力：邁向新綠色革命？

15601118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15601118.value: Chinese engagement in African agriculture has mainly been examined in terms of farming, especially in relation to global controversies about land acquisition. Yet, scholars have found that Chinese “land grabs” in Africa are largely illusory. Meanwhile, Chinese agribusiness has developed new strategic interests in upstream and downstream activities within the value chain, such as mechanization, inputs, and processing. Chinese agribusiness’ expansion in Africa intersects with the United Nations’ 2017-2021 plan for eradicating hunger and creating food sustainability in Africa. It also coincides with the New Green Revolution (NGR) promoted by African and international development institutions. Development specialists commonly assume that an NGR is needed to create greater food security and agricultural development in Africa and call for greater integration of small producers with the market through upstream and downstream activities. The NGR approach has been criticized however as a technocratic solution to Africa’s agricultural problems, which have both technical and socio-political dimensions. Given claimed successes in China’s own Green Revolution, the Chinese and African governments expect China to play a signal role in realizing these goals. Indeed, President Xi Jinping has designated agricultural modernization as a key aspect of China/Africa engagement. In this project, we will examine processes of Chinese engagement in African agricultural development and its intersection with promotion of an NGR in Africa. We will assess whether Chinese upstream/downstream activities help address the social development goal of enhancing African food security. We will draw conclusions about whether Chinese agribusiness in Africa has “Chinese characteristics.” Hong Kong-based entities are becoming involved in finance and marketing aspects of African agricultural development. Such activities will also be highlighted. Scattered news reports of Chinese agribusiness expansion exist and we have collected many. We have also touched on Chinese agribusiness in our past field research in African countries. The most useful data on Chinese agribusiness in Africa can only be secured however through field research and focused surveys. We propose to do that in four African states and have already established the contacts needed to carry out the work. The result will be a monograph-length study and several articles. These works will analyze problems and prospects of a greater Chinese agribusiness presence in the continent. They will offer policy suggestions about ways to overcome obstacles to sustainable agricultural development and food security. Our research on this up-and-coming aspect of the Chinese presence in Africa will also contribute to the global discourse of China/Africa links. 關於中國在非洲農業中的作用，既有的研究和關注主要在農業種植方面，尤其聚焦中國有否參與了國際上飽受爭議的“圈地運動”。不過，學者們的研究已經證實，關於中國在非洲的“圈地”指責往往是虛幻的。其實，中國企業的興趣開始更多地放在產業鏈的上下游，比如提供機械化服務、農資、農產品加工等。中國農業企業在非洲的拓展與聯合國消除非洲飢餓、創造食物可持續性的2017-2021計劃相交叉，也與非洲和國際機構倡導的“新綠色革命”相契合。 發展專家們通常假設，非洲需要一個新綠色革命才能保障非洲的糧食安全和農業發展，他們倡導把農業小生產者整合到產業的上下游產業鏈中。然而，新綠色革命的倡導也遭到一些學者的批評，因為這是一個技術主導的方案，而非洲農業的問題不僅是技術層面的，也具有社會和政治的層面。 因為中國被視為綠色革命的成功典範，中國和諸多非洲國家的政府都期待中國在非洲農業發展這一目標上發揮標桿性的作用。中國國家主席習近平已經把農業現代化作為中非合作的關鍵領域。 在本項研究中，我們將調研中國對非洲農業發展的影響、以及這一影響如何與非洲“新綠色革命”的倡導相互作用。我們將評估中國公司在產業鏈上下游的活動是否有助於增強非洲的糧食安全這一社會發展的目標。我們也將評估中國涉農企業在非洲是否具有“中國特色”。香港的公司和機構也涉足到非洲農業發展的金融和營銷方面。我們也會關注這些活動。 關於中國涉農企業在非洲的拓展，已經有一些新聞報道，我們也有很多這些報道的收集。在過去的非洲田野調研中，我們已經接觸了一些涉足非洲農業的中國企業，但是只有專注的田野調研和問卷調查才能產出能夠回答上述問題所需要實證數據。我們打算在四個非洲國家進行相關調研，也已經在這些國家建立了調研所需要的的初步聯繫。我們希望調研的成果是一部學術專著和相關的文章，其中我們將對中國涉農企業在非洲的問題和前景進行分析，也會針對可持續農業發展和糧食安全提出政策建議。我們關於中國企業對非洲農業產業上下游影響的分析也會有助於人們更豐富地把握中國-非洲的關聯。

15601718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15601718.value: Semantic access (i.e., retrieval of meanings) and semantic integration (i.e., formation of complex meanings) are traditionally regarded as intact in normal aging. Recent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have begun to challenge this notion. For example, compared with young subjects, older subjects tend to rely more on the prefrontal cortex in many semantic tasks, including speech comprehension. Resting-state fMRI studies have also revealed robust age-related changes in functional connectivity (FC), most notably an inverted U-shaped trajectory for long-range connections within the frontotemporal and frontoparietal networks (FTN/FPN), which subserve high-order language and executive functions. Intriguingly, the peak of this developmental trajectory appears to coincide with the onset of behavioral decline in semantic ability. However, how these large-scale changes in the brain’s “functional connectome” relate to semantic processing has yet to be elucidated. This project aims to extend our knowledge regarding the age-related neural reorganization that underlies the changes in semantic ability across the adult lifespan, by clarifying the behavioral and neural consequences of the changing resting-state functional connectivities (RSFCs) in the left FTN. We aim to examine two main hypotheses: (1) the continued growth in semantic ability in middle age is accompanied by increases in RSFCs in the left FTN; (2) the decline in semantic ability during senescence is associated with weakened RSFCs in the same network. Because fMRI is only sensitive to slow-varying (< 0.1 Hz) blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signals, but language processing depends on neurocomputations that operate at much faster timescales, electroencephalography (EEG) will be jointly employed in order to develop a more comprehensive understanding on the developmental trajectory of semantic processing during adulthood. Four cohorts of cognitively normal Cantonese speakers aged 20–34, 35–49, 50–64, and 65–79, matched for handedness and gender, will be recruited. These subjects will attend resting-state experiments and perform two tasks (semantic priming and sentence comprehension), with which the possible link between functional connectivities/activations of key semantic loci and both behavioral indices of semantic ability and EEG neuromarkers will be established. Collectively, our findings will provide an extensive account of how semantic processing changes, both neuroanatomically and spectrotemporally, across the adult lifespan. The data from the 240+ subjects will be used to launch an open-access EEG/fMRI database to advance neurophysiological research on cognitive aging and semantic processing. Our results will find application in clinical assessment and monitoring for neurological disorders in which semantic processes are strongly affected, including semantic dementia and aphasia. 傳統上認為語義擷取（即擷取詞語的意思） 和語義整合（即整合複雜的意思） 在正常老化中是不會衰退的。然而，近期的功能性磁共振成像 (fMRI) 研究開始挑戰這一觀點。 與年輕人相比，年齡較大的人在理解語言時會傾向使用更多前額皮質 (prefrontal cortex)。靜息態 fMRI 研究亦發現了功能連結 (functional connectivity) 會呈現與年齡相關的強烈變化。其中，用來處理高階語言和決定執行功能的額顳網絡 (frontotemporal network, FTN) 和額頂網絡 (frontoparietal network, FPN) 的遠程連結與年齡呈現倒 U 形趨勢。有趣的是，遠程連結的發展峰值似乎與語義能力開始下降的時間一致。 不過，這些大腦功能連結圖譜中的大規模變化是否與語義處理能力的轉變相關尚未得到闡明。 此項目旨在研究左額顳網絡靜息態功能連結 (resting state functional connectivity, RSFC) 的改變及其對行為和神經活動的影響，以理解語義能力在成人生命週期內的變化及擴展對年齡相關神經重組的知識。此項目有兩個重要假說。一方面，我們推想語義能力在中年時期持續增長的同時，左額顳網絡的 RSFC 會隨之而增長。另一方面，我們也推想語義能力在衰老過程中的下降與左額顳網絡中 RSFC 弱化是有相關性的。 由於 fMRI 僅對緩慢變化的 (<0.1 Hz) 血氧濃度相依對比 (BOLD) 信號敏感，但語言處理卻依賴更快速的神經計算，所以本項目將聯合使用腦電圖 (EEG)，以全面了解成年期語義處理的發展軌跡。 本項目將招募四組認知能力正常、並以廣東話為母語的受試者。受試者年齡分別為 20-34 歲，35-49 歲，50-64 歲和 65-79 歲，組別之間慣用手和性別將會相互匹配。 通過靜息態實驗及兩項與語義有關的任務（語義促發和句子理解），本項目將針對某些處理語義有關的腦區，以釐清其功能連結及激活與語義能力及腦電指標間的聯繫。 總括而言，研究將全面地探索語義處理在成人生命週期中的變化，尤其是在腦神經定位及時頻域分析方面提供新知識。來自240多名受試者的數據將用於建立一個開放式EEG / fMRI數據庫，以推進認知衰老和語義處理的神經生理學研究。預料研究結果可應用於一些神經疾病的臨床評估和監測，尤其是那些語義處理會受到嚴重影響的病症，如語意型腦退化症 (semantic dementia) 和失語症 (aphasia)。

15601718.label: Realisation of objectives
15601718.value: To achieve the four (revised) project objectives, over 200 native speakers of Cantonese were tested on a range of semantic tasks (semantic fluency, semantic judgment, semantic priming, and sentence comprehension) in two rounds of data collection. The first round included a smaller-scale behavioral and EEG study comprising only younger and older adults, focusing on establishing the paradigms and obtaining initial evaluation of the hypotheses. These results were published in 4 journal publications (Fong et al., 2020; Fong et al., 2021; Hui et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2021). The second round focused on formally testing the hypotheses through a sample comprising 100+ adults uniformly sampled across the age range of 18-81. The level of education was matched in four age-groups: 18-34; 35-49; 50-64; and 65-81. For Objective 1 (To investigate the behavioral and neurophysiological (fMRI and EEG) implications of the age-related changes in resting-state functional connectivities within the left frontotemporal language network), a comprehensive cognitive and semantic task battery was compiled and was administered to the participants in both rounds of data collection. During the first round of data collection, cognitive associations of semantic performances were established, including the associations of semantic fluency with lexical retrieval speed in younger adults (Fong et al., 2020), inhibition function with an L2 synonym test (Hui et al., 2020), and the age-related decline in controlled retrieval in older adults (Fong et al., 2021). Resting-state EEG measures were also correlated with cognitive task performances (Ma, Fong, Lee, & Wang, 2022). In the second round of data collection, a Cantonese psycholinguistic database was compiled, and the database was central to the design two tasks (semantic priming and sentence comprehension), since it allows for the control of various psycholinguistic factors that modulate the behavioral performance. For semantic priming, EEG and fMRI versions were administered, while for sentence comprehension, only the fMRI experiment was conducted. For the MRI dataset, structural analysis has been conducted with FreeSurfer (Fong et al., 2023), while functional activation and connectivity analysis have been conducted with SPM and CONN toolboxes. However, because the data collection was delayed due to COVID-19, the overall dataset is still under active analysis by the project team. The project team will continue to publish the results towards completely achieving this objective. For Objective 2 (To test whether semantic access and semantic integration are maximally efficient during middle age but not during early adulthood), two auditory tasks were designed—semantic priming and sentence comprehension. Behaviorally, we found no evidence that semantic access is maximally efficient during middle age. Instead, a hyper-priming effect was found, i.e., the semantic priming effect (SPE) was the largest for older adults. This increase in priming effect was not associated with the decline in inhibition function; nor could it be attributed to decreasing processing speed. Instead, we found evidence that the SPE was associated with semantic knowledge (as measured using a verbal fluency task). This finding suggests that older adults may have improved automatic semantic access due either to their growth in semantic knowledge or accumulated exposures to the semantic relations. In contrast, controlled retrieval appeared to peak during early adulthood. For Objective 3 (To test whether abstract and concrete words have dissociable developmental trajectories due to normal aging), behaviorally, an interaction between Concreteness and Age was found by ANOVA, i.e., we found that the concreteness effect based on RT was positively related with age. A corresponding effect was observed with ERP data. These findings support the hypothesis that abstract and concrete words have dissociable developmental trajectories. Regarding Objective 4 (To launch an open-access, web-based EEG/fMRI database that includes both task-related and resting-state data for the study of cognitive aging), we originally aimed to release it through a webpage administered by PolyU. However, in view of data security, it was decided that the data would be uploaded to two platforms—ADRES managed by the Research Institute for Smart Ageing, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, as well as OpenNeuro, a widely used platform in the public domain for sharing neuroimaging data. Using these web services will enhance the impact of the present project. In total, fifteen conference papers / abstracts were presented in international conferences (including International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing 2020, Cognitive Neuroscience Society 2019/2020, International Symposium on Chinese Spoken Language Processing, The 34th Pacific Asia Conference on Language, Information and Computation, The 34th International Congress of Psychology, and The 13th International Symposium on Bilingualism) and a local conference (PolyU Academy for Interdisciplinary Research Conference 2023). In addition, the PI and Dr. Manson Fong (a key member in this project) have also presented some of the findings in the present project in RGC Public Lecture. In terms of education impact, four different undergraduate student assistants have been trained, and two final-year undergraduate projects arose directly from the present project.

15601718.label: Major findings and research outcome
15601718.value: The first round of data collection focused on how cognitive differences contribute to individual differences in semantic abilities. In younger adults, semantic fluency was influenced by lexical retrieval speed, but inhibitory control functions appeared to play little role (Fong et al., 2020). For older adults, the decline in inhibitory control function was posited to contribute to their declining cognitive performance. To test this hypothesis within the domain of lexico-semantic retrieval, event-related potential (ERP) was adopted to measure several inhibition-related functions. Mixed-effects modelling on semantic fluency revealed that the number of concepts retrieved in a controlled manner, but not in an automatic manner, was negatively associated with age (Fong et al., 2021). This interaction was partially accounted for by the stimulus-locked P2 and response-locked correct positivity (Pc), lending support to the hypothesis. Other relevant results were as follows. The Stroop test performance was predicted by an English synonym test, demonstrating the link between inhibition and language (Hui et al., 2020). The loss of complexity in ageing hypothesis (LOCH), which postulates that ageing is accompanied by the loss of complexity, was supported by EEG data (Ma et al., 2021). In the second round of data collection, cognitively normal participants aged 18–81 were recruited. Older adults were found to exhibit hyper-priming, i.e., the auditory semantic priming effect (SPE) was positively associated with age. This is consistent with the hypothesis that the automatic semantic processing of older adults improves with age. Also, the concreteness effect was found to increase with age (Fong et al., under preparation). Across the adult lifespan, an inverted U-shaped pattern in the complexity trajectory was found (Ma, Fong, & Wang, 2023; Ma, Fong, & Wang, under preparation). A Cantonese psycholinguistic database for over 7000 words was constructed and will be released soon (Fong, Ng, & Wang, under preparation). In total, six journal articles were published based on the data collected in the present project, along with 15 conference abstracts/presentations. Three manuscripts are being prepared. Because of the pandemic and that an MRI machine was available for use only midway through, data collection in the second round was much delayed; the research findings will be disseminated via journal publications. A postdoctoral fellow trained in this project, Dr. Manson Fong, was promoted to Research Assistant Professor. Four PhD students were directly trained in the present project, including Dr. Matthew Ma, who was awarded the RGC postdoctoral fellowship.

15601718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15601718.value: The present research will be extended along two tracks. First, having collected detailed semantic data for a representative cohort of 100+ adults aged 18-81, the team is in a primed position to study the differential semantic impairments in pathological populations (e.g., mild cognitive impairment, dementia). The project team will seek collaboration with medical colleagues to document the semantic, cognitive, and neuroimaging profile for different sub-types of dementia (e.g., Alzheimer’s disease and semantic dementia). The results will contribute towards the early detection, diagnosis, and prognosis of dementia. Second, the brain’s cognitive reserve has been linked with bilingualism or bilingual experience. The present research can be extended in a bilingual setting (e.g., Cantonese–English) to obtain measures of bilingual semantic performance, for providing converging evidence on how bilingualism may benefit brain health and contributes towards the protection against dementia.

15601718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15601718.value: Normal ageing is typically accompanied by a growth in semantic knowledge and relatively intact semantic functions (automatic access and controlled retrieval). The present project aims to find out when semantic functions become maximally efficient, and the underlying age-related neural changes. Over 100 participants aged 18-81 were recruited to the study, with each participant completing some semantic tasks while their brain activities are measured using electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Surprisingly, we found that in the presence of a categorically or associatively related prime word, older adults are more efficient than their younger counterparts in extracting semantic relations of a target word. This phenomenon is known as hyper-priming, and it reflects the more efficient automatic access of semantic knowledge by older adults. In contrast, controlled retrieval exhibited a small but significant decline. We also found that the age-related facilitation in semantic access was more robust for concrete than for abstract words. Overall, the present study provides an initial norm for understanding the semantic development across the adult lifespan. The results will be applied to studying the semantic impairment in various forms of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease and semantic dementia.

15601818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15601818.value: The globalization of agriculture and food systems has brought unprecedented opportunities to rural communities around the world, but the rise of corporate capital in agri-food politics and the predominance of free trade agendas have also challenged sustainable rural development. In China, market transition and integration into the global economy have contributed to growth and transformational changes in the countryside, especially during the early phase of reform through rural industrialization. From the mid-1990s onwards, however, rural China has experienced economic stagnation and increasingly manifest social problems such as the loss of manpower to rural-urban migration and the growth of “left-behind” populations. The industrialization and commercialization of agriculture has further challenged small producers on the ground in terms of sustaining agricultural production and livelihoods. This project seeks to research alternative pathways to agrarian change by investigating the development of community-based collective and cooperative economies in rural China. Community-oriented economic practices have been promoted by reformers as a viable alternative to corporate agriculture, and the past decade has seen the flourishing of local experimentations with cooperation and collectivism in rural China. While these grassroots initiatives have begun to receive scholarly attention, more in-depth research is needed to systematically examine the diverse institutional forms and implementation outcomes of emerging economic organizations. Adopting a comparative multiple-case study methodology, this project will examine three types of community-based economies that respectively emphasize the state coordination, market coordination, and social coordination of economic activities. Based on the comparative analysis of their historical context, political economy, and socio-cultural impact, this project seeks to provide a structured survey of the landscape of community-based agrarian economies in post-socialist China. As a country that has experienced decades of agricultural collectivization under state socialism, followed by market reform and agrarian globalization, China provides a unique and significant case for exploring alternative trajectories of agrarian change. This project will yield important insights for understanding Chinese farmers’ response to agrarian globalization, advance theorization of rural China’s post-socialist transition, and enrich the study of community economy development in the rural global South. Its findings should be of practical relevance to policymakers and practitioners both locally and internationally for advancing sustainable agriculture and rural development.

15601818.label: Realisation of objectives
15601818.value: This project aims to critically survey and appraise ongoing experimentations in collective and cooperative economies in rural China through a comparative multiple-case study methodology. As a country that has experienced decades of collectivization under state socialism, followed by market reform and agrarian globalization, China provides a unique and theoretically significant case for exploring alternative trajectories of agrarian transition. Based on fieldwork in Guangdong province, this project sets out to explore collective and cooperative economic organizations and investigate the opportunities and challenges faced by rural communities and small producers on the ground. Despite the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic, the research team has successfully achieved the following objectives during the project period: 1) Objectives 1 and 2 concern surveying the different types of collective and cooperative economies that have emerged in post-socialist rural China and comparing them in terms of the organization of political and economic power and socio-cultural characteristics. To achieve these aims, three rounds of fieldwork were carried out in Guangdong province between 2019 and 2022. The first research trip took place before the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in January 2020, the second upon the relaxation of lockdown measures from March to May 2022, and the third from October to December 2022. The project extension granted by the RGC enabled the research team to successfully complete fieldwork despite the two-year interruption caused by the pandemic. Overall, our fieldwork covered key research sites across Guangdong province, in rural towns and villages under the jurisdiction of cities including Guangzhou, Zhongshan, Zhuhai, Huizhou, and Jiangmen. Interviews were carried out with local officials, village leaders, rural residents, representatives of entities such as family farms and professional cooperatives, business owners, employees, as well as local and migrant farm workers. Through in-depth interviews and on-site observations, we were able to examine the structures and processes of power in collective and cooperative organizations and evaluate their impact on local communities. It is found that while community-led initiatives created space for participation and autonomous organization by local residents and social organizations, these bottom-up experiments remained constrained by insufficieny of funding and lack of certification and distribution channels. In comparison, collective economies that are state- or capital-led enjoyed financial viability, but the extent of grassroots participation varied and economic gains were often unevenly distributed. 2) Objective 3 concerns deepening understanding of the opportunities and challenges faced by rural communities and small producers in contemporary China in the context of agrarian globalization. Our updated field research in Guangdong province provided a window into some of the key challenges confronting farming communities in China today, and in our work we derived comparative insights by engaging with scholars working in other regions of China. Research findings were disseminated through journal publication and conference presentation. For journal publication, papers were published in the China Quarterly in 2023 and the International Journal of Social Welfare in 2020. The PI also guest-edited a special issue in the SSCI-indexed journal China Perspectives in June 2021 on “Negotiating Agrarian Futures in China”. The special issue was edited in collaboration with Dr René Trappel (University of Freiburg) and consisted of papers published by scholars based in Germany, France, Hong Kong and Mainland China. Drawing on case studies in Gansu, Guangxi, Guangdong and Yunnan, the papers share a common interest in exploring the dynamics of agrarian change in contemporary China. Examining the role of and interaction between capital, collectives, and communities in rural China against the background of socialist legacies and capitalist transformation, the special issue shed light on the politics and power relations underlying food and agricultural production in China today. For conference presentation, abstracts were accepted for presentation at four international conferences, including the International Convention of Asia Scholars (2021), AAS-in-Asia, Association for Asian Studies virtual conference (2020), World Congress of Rural Sociology (2020), and Biennial Conference of the Asian Studies Association of Australia (2020). The latter two conferences were cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. For AAS-in-Asia (2020), the PI successfully organized and chaired a panel entitled "Whither Rural Collectives: Village Communities and Economies under Rapid Urbanization in China". The panel brought together academics based in Hong Kong and Mainland China to explore how rural collectives may be reinforced, weakened, or transformed as they confront de-agrarianization and urbanization in post-socialist China. The PI also disseminated this project’s findings on rural cooperation and the collective economy in a paper presentation in the organized panel. 3) Objective 4 concerns promoting sustainable models of rural development through engagement with local practitioners and organization of workshop for knowledge exchange and network building. In terms of engagement with local practitioners, the team has participated in extensive knowledge sharing and exchange during field study. Through meetings with village leaders, members of collectives/cooperatives and social workers stationed in the villages, we were able to gain insight into the opportunities and challenges faced by local villagers, rural producers, and the cooperatives, while also sharing our observations and suggestions. We will continue to foster the ties and connections established. In terms of the organization of a workshop for knowledge exchange and network building, our original plan was to host an in-person workshop at the Hong Kong Polytechnic University in summer 2020, inviting rural China scholars based in institutions in Hong Kong, mainland China, Australia, France, and Denmark as well as practitioners and social workers based in Hong Kong and mainland China who are engaged in the practice of rural social work and community economy to share their insights and to facilitate direct exchange between academics and practitioners. As a result of the pandemic and travel restrictions, we organized two online events instead. The first, an international workshop on based on the special issue on agrarian futures in China, took place in October 2021. The event was jointly organized by the Department of Applied Social Sciences and China and Global Development Network of Hong Kong Polytechnic University, as well as the French Centre for Research on Contemporary China. There were 124 registered attendees and 66 participants on the day. The second event took place in November 2022 on collective economy and rural development in China. There were 195 registered attendees and 139 participants on the day. Aside from the above online events, our team members also gave invited talks on collective and cooperative economy during the project period that drew on this project’s findings. They included a talk for the School of Philosophy and Sociology, Lanzhou University (July 2020); a talk at the Forum of the People’s Food Sovereignty Network (August 2020); and a training workshop for social work frontline practitioners (March 2022). Joined by scholars, students, as well as practitioners, it is hoped that these events will not only facilitate knowledge exchange within academia but effect impact beyond academia as well.

15601818.label: Major findings and research outcome
15601818.value: This project has three major findings: 1. First, by investigating community-based experiments in rural collectives and cooperatives in contemporary China, this project examined the efficacy of bottom-up initiatives in responding to the agrarian and environmental issues confronting the Chinese countryside. Through empirical case studies, we demonstrated how local experiments in rural cooperation, sustainable farming practices and collective purchase have reconfigured relations of production and rural-urban dynamics in selected communities. Findings can be found in our paper published in the International Journal of Social Welfare (2020). 2. Second, the changing role of nonprofits and social work organizations in organizing community initiatives in rural areas was examined. Based on the longitudinal case study of villages in Guangdong province, our research revealed how and why the role of social organizations and state-NGO dynamics changed over the years. At the beginning, operating in an emerging field of practice, the organizations involved in community initiatives demonstrated agency and autonomy in setting agendas and designing programmes that are aligned with their organizational goals, such as forming producer cooperatives and promoting ecological farming. Over time, we found a trend towards state incorporation where the government imposed increasing demands on NGOs while subjecting them to more regularized and quantitative forms of appraisal. We argued that this might limit the room for bottom-up initiative, as discussed in our paper published in the China Quarterly (2023). 3. Last but not least, our project analyzed the broader context within which these community-based initiatives took place, namely the government’s drive to modernize the agricultural sector through state- and capital-led transformations. Our fieldwork in family farms, professional cooperatives, and agricultural parks demonstrated the growing prominence of organized capital in agricultural production, whether through processes of accumulation from above or from below. A special issue in China Perspectives (2021) was organized to discuss emerging agrarian futures in contemporary China and state-capital-community dynamics.

15601818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15601818.value: Given the Chinese government’s continued prioritization of “rural revitalization” as a national development strategy, there is strong potential and significant value in furthering the research agendas of this project. In particular, two areas for further development have been identified. First, the government’s recent call for capital to go to the countryside has engendered new dynamics of agricultural modernization and land development in peri-urban and rural areas. To investigate new technologies of governing rural space, resources, and population, the PI has submitted a funding application to the RGC on agricultural modernization and frontiers of urban-rural development in China. Second, research for this project has highlighted to our team the nuanced social dynamics of agrarian transition. The impact of development on rural society is highly differentiated by factors such as class and gender. To further this line of inquiry, the PI has applied for and successfully obtained research funding to examine gender dynamics and the micropolitics of rural development in China and beyond. It is expected that these projects will yield new insights into the variegated impact of agrarian change on local communities.

15601818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15601818.value: The globalization of agricultural production and food systems has brought fundamental changes to national agrarian economies around the world. While connecting rural communities to global circuits of production and distribution, the rise of corporate capital in agri-food politics has increasingly come under challenge for subsuming local development needs and environmental sustainability to market-oriented agendas. Based on fieldwork in Guangdong province, this project explores alternative pathways to agrarian change by researching the development of community-based collective and cooperative economies in rural China. By investigating the opportunities and challenges faced by rural communities and small producers on the ground, this project provides timely research for understanding the state of rural development in China and for theorizing local responses to agrarian globalization. It is argued that bottom-up experimentations in collectives and cooperatives offer important theoretical insights for the comparative study of pathways of agrarian transition worldwide. Through engaging in knowledge exchange with local practitioners and policymakers, this project creates policy impact in terms of social innovation and supporting grassroots experiments in community economies.

15602018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15602018.value: Blood is critical to medical treatment. Identifying strategies to promote and facilitate voluntary blood donation is thus important to maintain a stable blood supply. In Hong Kong, 97% of the blood-donation-suitable population are non-donors, and 22% of the existing voluntary blood donors had left the donor pool from 2015 to 2016. The consistently low proportion of voluntary blood donors is expected to create difficulty in meeting the increasing blood demand due to a rapid aging population in Hong Kong. As the demand for blood is estimated to increase by 2.1% every year, there is a critical need to understand the barriers to participating in voluntary blood donation and the barriers to continuing with voluntary blood donation of the Hong Kong people in different age-groups. Most of the past studies of voluntary blood donation are conducted in non-Chinese communities, with a paucity of qualitative research specific to Asian and Chinese-based populations. Altruism and Theory of Planned Behavior have been proposed in literature as a means of understanding voluntary donation of blood. However, recent literature and the preliminary data of our exploratory study shows that these two theories have remarkable limitation in explaining blood donation behavior. There is a lack of literature about how people in different age-groups perceive the meanings of blood donation, and about the barriers to having blood donation among Chinese population in different generations. Therefore, using Hong Kong as the field-site, the proposed project will employ a qualitative approach adopting 130 semi-structured interviews with: (1) 40 non-donors, (2) 40 drop-out donors, (3) 40 current donors, and (4) 10 health care providers of the Hong Kong Red Cross Blood Transfusion Service, investigating the meanings of blood donation and the barriers to participating in blood donation among the Hong Kong people in different age-groups. To fill the theoretical gap of altruism and Theory of Planned Behavior in blood donation literature, Critical Medical Anthropology will be adopted as the theoretical framework to provide a holistic investigation of blood donation at four social-levels – from individual, micro-social, intermediate-social, and macro-social levels. The proposed study will also add new elements to the Critical Medical Anthropology framework about how the relationship and/or tension between different ethnic groups can have an impact on people’s willingness to become voluntary blood donors, based on our exploratory data. This proposed study will therefore refine the four-level investigation model, which has been rarely covered in the blood donation literature.

15602018.label: Realisation of objectives
15602018.value: All the four objectives as originally stated in the proposal have been fully achieved. The focus of this study is to investigate the incentives of and barriers to participating in blood donation among the current donors, non-donors, and drop-out donors. As our study notes, the incentives and barriers of these three groups of informants are closely interlocked with their perceptions and perceived values and meanings of blood donation. In view of the comments from the review panel on our proposal, this study, however, added a quantitative research phase prior to the implementation of qualitative research phase, making this study to move from a pure qualitative study to a mixed method study involving two research phases. The additional quantitative phase has given a more comprehensive understanding in the incentives and barriers of having blood donation. The quantitative phase involves a questionnaire-based cross-sectional survey, aiming at investigating determine the knowledge level of young adults towards blood donation, and to understand their donor identity and the meanings of blood donation to them. The survey study sampled 542 young adults who were coming from a university in Hong Kong, of which 274 were reported to be non-blood donors and 268 were blood donors. Blood donor respondents generally have a better knowledge towards blood donation than non-blood donor respondents. Being a female, aged 22 years or above, studying at year 4 or 5, studying health-related programmes, being registered as an organ donor, had prior experience of receiving blood or prior experience of being refused for blood donation were significantly associated with being a blood donor. Having prior experience of receiving blood was the strongest predictor for being a blood donor, followed by being registered as an organ donor. The quantitative research phase informed the development of the qualitative research phase. The qualitative research phase, however, did not merely focus on the young adults as the quantitative phase did, but it focused on a wider age-range of informants from 18 to 65 years old as this age range are eligible for blood donation in Hong Kong. The qualitative research phase interviewed 120 informants in total, with 40 informants in the current donor, drop-out donors, and non-donors respectively. As the study was conducted in the years of COVID-19 pandemic, therefore, the research team made use of this opportunity to further investigate how the COVID-19 pandemic could affect the incentives of and barriers to having blood donation among these three groups of informants, and whether the pandemic has changed the perceived meanings and values of blood donation among the informants that could affect their donation incentives and/or barriers. This study has theoretical contribution, showing that altruism and Theory of Planned Behavior—which are the two most popular theories used in the past studies about blood donation—are inadequate in understanding the blood donation incentives and barriers. Rather, the social and institutional factors had a remarkable role in explaining the informants’ motivations and deterrents in having blood donation.

15602018.label: Major findings and research outcome
15602018.value: The quantitative research phase involves a questionnaire-based cross-sectional survey, aiming at investigating determine the knowledge level of young adults towards blood donation, and to understand their donor identity and the meanings of blood donation to them. The survey study sampled 542 young adults who were coming from a university in Hong Kong, of which 274 were reported to be non-blood donors and 268 were blood donors. Blood donor respondents generally have a better knowledge towards blood donation than non-blood donor respondents. Being a female (OR=1.99, p<0.001), aged 22 years or above (OR=234, p<0.001), studying at year 4 or 5 (OR=2.12, p=0.003), studying health-related programmes (OR=1.96, p<0.001), being registered as an organ donor (OR=6.59, p<0.001), had prior experience of receiving blood (OR=7.60, p<0.001) or prior experience of being refused for blood donation (OR=5.14, p<0.001) were significantly associated with being a blood donor. Having prior experience of receiving blood was the strongest predictor for being a blood donor, followed by being registered as an organ donor. The qualitative research phase focused on a wider age-range of informants from 18 to 65 years old as this age range are eligible for blood donation in Hong Kong. The qualitative research phase interviewed 120 informants in total, with 40 informants in the current donor, drop-out donors, and non-donors respectively. As the study was conducted in the years of COVID-19 pandemic, therefore, the research team made use of this opportunity to further investigate how the COVID-19 pandemic could affect the incentives of and barriers to having blood donation among these three groups of informants, and whether the pandemic has changed the perceived meanings and values of blood donation among the informants that could affect their donation incentives and/or barriers. This study shows that altruism and Theory of Planned Behavior are inadequate in understanding the blood donation incentives and barriers. Rather, the social and institutional factors had a remarkable role in explaining the informants’ motivations and deterrents in having blood donation, in particular at times of the COVID-19 pandemic. Instead of focusing on the individual level factors of attitude, subjective norms, behavioural intention, perceived behavioural control and perceived power noted by the theory of planned behavior, our study suggests further that macro sociocultural forces and government's infection control appeals as institutional factors interacted with individual perceptual factors to cause the participants' reluctance of blood donation in the COVID‐19 pandemic.

15602018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15602018.value: This study examines the motivations of and barriers to having blood donation before and during the COVID-19 pandemic from the participants’ perspectives. As one of the co-investigators was a department operations manager of the Hong Kong Red Cross Blood Transfusion Service (BTS) during the study period, the findings could allow knowledge transfer in the practical settings. Our study yields a lot of valuable in-depth qualitative data from the informants’ perspectives and experiences in the interviews. In many cases, the informants encountered many obstacles, difficulties, and unpleasant experiences in the donation procedures, no matter for those who had dropped out from or still retained in blood donation. This assists the BTS in designing a more responsive strategies in attracting new and drop-out donors, and facilitating the retainment of the current blood donors in this pandemic time. This study has limitations though. The high percentage of the informants in both the quantitative and qualitative research phases possessed (or will possess) at least a university degree. This makes this study to include mostly the ideas of those with a tertiary education level. Future research should consider interviewing those with a lower education level.

15602018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15602018.value: In 2016, 97% of the blood-donation-suitable population are non-donors. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of blood donation has dropped even more significantly. This study, therefore, was conducted between January 2019 and December 2021 to investigate the barriers to donating blood before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. This study adopts a mixed method research approach, with a cross-sectional survey conducted on 274 non-donors and 268 donors as the first research phase, following with a qualitative research phase with semi-structured individual interviews conducted on 40 non-donors, drop-out donors, and current donors respectively to obtain the informants’ in-depth experiences regarding blood donation. This study expands the existing literature on the study of blood donation behavior in which the theory of planned behavior has been the dominant approach of literature. Instead of focusing on the individual level factors of attitude, subjective norms, behavioral intention, perceived behavioral control, and perceived power noted by the theory, our study suggests further that macro sociocultural forces (before and during the COVID-19 pandemic) and government’s infection control appeals (during the COVID-19 pandemic) as institutional factors interacted with individual perceptual factors to cause the participants’ reluctance of blood donation before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

15602318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15602318.value: This project develops new methods for the study of Chinese poetry and drama using research in the fields of linguistics and cognitive musicology to analyze and interpret a database of traditional Chinese vocal music. In addition to suggesting novel interpretations of classic works, such a methodology can answer important questions in the fields of Chinese poetics and drama criticism, such as the nature of the interaction of language and music in the art of Kunqu singing. In preparation for the project, I am digitizing the Qianlong-era Jiugong dacheng nanbei ci gongpu 九宮大成南北詞宮譜 (“Great Perfection of the Nine Modes Musical Manual,” hereafter JGDC), the largest extant collection of traditional vocal melodies. With help from research assistants funded by my school, I am using a combination of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and manual input to record the raw data, which consists of Chinese characters paired with melodic and rhythmic notations. The goal of the proposed GRF project is to develop and test digital tools for analyzing the raw musical and linguistic data, and to write peer-reviewed articles analyzing the implications of those findings. The parameters I intend to analyze include similarities between different melodies of the same and different titles, the relationships between linguistic tone and melodic ornaments, between syntax and musical rhythm, and between traditional mode-key prescriptions and melodic motifs and registers. In addition to providing a convenient way for myself and others to analyze and interpret the authorial choices of premodern lyricists and singers like Tang Xianzu 湯顯祖 and Hong Sheng 洪昇, each of these tools will help answer important questions about the nature of Kunqu singing and its place in world music history. After developing and testing the tools, I will produce three peer-reviewed articles. The first will be a quantitative analysis of the question of so-called “core melodies” (zhuqiang 主腔) in Kunqu singing. The second will be an analysis of the principles of music-language relationships underlying the process of melody-lyric pairing (duoqu 度曲) in Kunqu. The third article will combine statistical data with hands-on experience of the living performance art of Shua hai’er 耍孩兒 in Datong, Shanxi with the goal of revealing new aspects of Kunqu’s complex, diverse history. 這項研究計劃運用語言學、音樂學、認知科學等學科的角度去分析一份中國傳統樂譜《九宮大成南北詞宮譜》。本計劃的目的是通過數字人文的方式創造一些新的分析工具，最後將完整的數據庫以及工具公開發佈。數字人文的方法能解決傳統戲曲中的語言、音樂方面的問題。 為了完成文獻的數字化，本人已開始發展光符識別程序（OCR），在開始研究計劃之前希望能完成數字化計劃的一部分，直接開始發展分析工具的工作。本計劃的主要目的是：分析《九宮大成》文獻中的同名曲牌之間的異同、語法與音樂節奏以及聲調與音樂旋律之間的關係、以及“宮調”與“管色”等音樂因素對其他方面的影響。計劃在兩年之內出版兩篇有關語言與音樂關係的同行評審文章。 此計劃完成以後，不但能為學者提供一些方便易用的數字化分析工具，也能幫我們理解崑曲在世界詩歌、音樂傳統當中的獨特位置。

15602318.label: Realisation of objectives
15602318.value: The three main objectives of the project were as follows: 1. Develop digital tools for analysis of music-language relationships in Kunqu melodies 2. Receive publication acceptance for one article and one monograph on findings 3. Publish bilingual database and tools online, hosted at PolyU, for free, public use Of these three, goals one and three are satisfactorily complete in their entirety. Goal two is only partially complete in that, while I have completed the manuscript and submitted it to Oxford University Press for peer review in March of 2021, I have not yet received a definitive answer from them as to whether they will publish it, presumably because the peer review process is ongoing. I submitted a proposal and sample chapter in September of 2020, in response to which Oxford agreed to consider the full manuscript for inclusion in their “Global Asias” series. Therefore, I believe there is a strong possibility they will publish it, but it is not yet certain. If Oxford UP decides not to publish this monograph, titled The Voice Extended: Music, Mind, and Language in Chinese Poetry and Performance, I am confident it will be possible to find another appropriate venue for the work, such as University of Hawai‘i. Goal two is also incomplete in that I have not published a separate article dedicated to these findings, though I did give a number of presentations on them, such as at the European Foundation for Chinese Music Research (CHIME) annual meeting (title: “Singing Writing and Singing Speech: The Influence of Literary and Vernacular Diction on Late Imperial Chinese Music”), and they formed important support for arguments in published writings, such as my Poetics Today (2020) article titled “Staging Sincerity in Renaissance Italy and Early Modern China; or, Why Real Lovers Quarrel.” Goal one is complete in that, with help from a research assistant and freelance programmer, we were able to successfully digitize the entire Qianlong-era collection, comprising over 6,000 detailed vocal notations of lyrics. Moreover, we created all the analytical tools I hoped to include, such as for analysing the interactions of rhythm, prosody, tone, and motifs, as well as some new ones I thought of during the process. I hope this tool may be useful to other Kunqu researchers in the future, in addition to having provided me valuable quantitate data for the monograph. With help from the library staff, this database has been published through the Pao Yue-Kong Library University Learning Hub Digital Collections: https://dc.lib.polyu.edu.hk/ninemodes/intro.html

15602318.label: Major findings and research outcome
15602318.value: In addition to digitizing and enabling analysis of one of the most important early resources for Kun opera, the major research outcome of the project was to produce a monograph detailing the history of evolution of aspects of rhythm, melody, and tone in Chinese poetry and vocal performance history. The book covers rhythm and its interaction with poetic grammar, melody and its interaction with linguistic tone, pronunciation standards and the evolution of vernacular language, and higher-order organization of longer works, including use of repeating motifs. The data from the collection enabled arguments about the nature of Chinese prosody and musical composition that would have been difficult to support otherwise, such as a tendency to accent initial, and elongate final, syllables of binomes. Such information has relevance for the study of both performance practice and poetic composition, because it can explain features like, for example, the need to achieve tonal contrast in certain positions within a poem and not others. It also helped answer difficult questions about the nature of Kunqu melodies and their composition, such as to what extend they exist independently of the lyrics for which they are arranged. Analysis of overlapping motifs from a large number of pieces enabled arguments about their palimpsest-like nature (mixture of fixed and formulaic segments). Cognitive perspectives further enabled fruitful interpretation of such results by way of such concepts as “predictive coding” and “map and territory.”

15602318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15602318.value: The information and tools included in the database should be helpful to researchers interested in Kunqu, Chinese music, Chinese poetry, and related areas. As the database is large and the tools varied, they should make possible a wide range of future studies on musical characteristics of Chinese poems and plays, as well as potential transregional comparisons. Although I do not personally have plans to do so at this time, this same platform could easily expand to include data from other Kunqu sources, such as the Nashu ying qupu 納書楹曲譜 (Book Storage Hall Aria Manual). For my second major book project, I plan to write on the historical relationships of sacred chant, like those that form a part of Daoist and Buddhist ritual, and vernacular performance arts, like Yiyang opera. I may also create a similar database of chant notations for analysis of their features, which could prove a useful point of comparison for the current database and potentially prove connections between, for example, the melodic techniques of Kunqu and early religious chant.

15602318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15602318.value: This project digitized one of the largest, oldest collections of traditional Chinese vocal melody notations. These notations are for an elite style called Kunqu as performed in the Qing Dynasty, but likely draw upon many other, older arts, like the “all-keys-and-modes” (zhu gongdiao 諸宮調) of the Jin Dynasty and the variety drama (zaju 雜劇) and art songs (sanqu 散曲) of the Yuan and Ming Dynasties. Moreover, the style of the lyrics is a form of poetry with indebtedness to the Chinese canon stretching back three thousand years or more. In addition to making the full collection searchable within a wide variety of parameters, the database enables detailed comparisons of a great number of musical and poetic features, such as poetic grammar, linguistic tone, melody, rhythm, rhyme, and more. This enabled me to support arguments about poetic and performance evolution with quantitative data in my monograph, The Voice Extended: Music, Mind, and Language in Chinese Poetry and Performance. These arguments included explanations for many features of Chinese poetry and vocal music not previously well understood or agreed upon, including the nature of tonal prosody and traditional Chinese opera composition.

15602518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15602518.value: When women engage in sexual activity has evolutionary implications. The proposed study examines women’s mate preferences and sexual behaviors throughout the ovulatory cycle as functions of life history (LH) strategies for acquiring good genes, good provisioning, and good parenting. In contrast to the female sexuality of most mammals, which is confined to the brief window of estrus, women’s ovulation is concealed, and women are sexually receptive throughout the ovulatory cycle. Known as extended sexuality, why women remain sexually active despite being nonfertile for most of the ovulatory cycle is an evolutionary puzzle. Added to this puzzle are recent findings that during the nonfertile phase, women are sexually attracted to certain types of men who can be characterized as good providers and good fathers. Another puzzle regarding the human female sexuality is known as the ovulatory shift hypothesis. Research has indicated that despite extended sexuality throughout the cycle, women’s sexual interest peaks during ovulation, suggesting that women have not completely lost estrus. During the fertile phase, women prefer certain male mate attributes such as masculinity, symmetry, and overall physical attractiveness that indicate good genes. The conception of fast–slow LH strategies, which focuses on energetic trade-offs among various LH traits including that between present-oriented mating and future-oriented parenting, provides a theoretical framework to integrate these two hypotheses about human female sexuality; the ovulatory shift hypothesis focuses on immediate mating outcomes, whereas the extended sexuality hypothesis emphasizes future parental and spousal investment. I will investigate the associations between fast–slow LH strategies and relevant mating behaviors prescribed by the ovulatory shift and extended sexuality hypotheses in two studies. Study 1 consists of surveys and reported cycles from 300 Chinese women, and Study 2 includes laboratory experiments and diaries of ovulatory changes of 130 women identified from Study 1 to be of fast vs. slow LH. Women identified as fast LH strategists are expected to prefer good-genes over good-provider and good-father mate values both generally and especially during the ovulation window, whereas women pursuing slow LH strategies are expected to prefer good-provider and good-father over good-genes mate attributes both generally and especially on nonfertile days. These and other results will expand the existing LH literature, contribute to a more comprehensive theory about human female sexuality, and as a practical implication, facilitate the understanding of the increase in the number of unmarried women beyond marriageable age. 在一個月經周期中，女性何時與男性發生性行，是有進化意義的。本研究旨在考察女性在月經周期中的性行爲與擇偶偏好，以及個體的生命史策略如何影響女性喜好擁有“好基因”、“好資源”、和“好爸爸”特質的男性。 大多數雌性哺乳動物在排卵期都有明顯的身體變化和發情跡象。與雌性動物不同，人類女性的排卵期是隱蔽的。女性在一個月經周期的任何時候，包括非排卵期，都可以接受性行爲，這稱之爲延長的性欲。非排卵期的性欲無助于繁衍後代，但它在人類女性中爲何存在，是個謎題。令這個謎題更加複雜的是，女性在非排卵期似乎喜歡擁有好資源和好爸爸特質的男性。另外，根據排卵期性欲變高假設，儘管女性在整個月經周期中都有性欲，她們在排卵期左右性欲會變高，這説明人類女性的發情跡象并未完全消失。在排卵期，女性喜歡好基因男性，也就是那些長得陽剛、對稱、外形有吸引力的男性。 生命史策略指的是個體如何在不同的生命史特質中權衡如何分配能量和精力，分爲快策略和慢策略。例如，快策略者把精力投放在當下，著重不斷求偶，而慢策略者主力爲將來做準備，著重教養後代。用生命史策略這個理論框架，我們可以整合延長的性欲和排卵期性欲變高這兩個假設，因爲延長的性欲涉及未來撫養後代以及如何讓配偶投資在後代身上，而排卵期性欲變高涉及當下的求偶。 本研究調查女性的生命史策略以及她們在月經周期中的性行爲和心理。在研究一中，我們將招募300名女性完成問卷調查，從中選出快策略和慢策略的女性參與研究二。在研究二中，研究對象需要報告在一個月經周期中每日的性狀態，以及分別在排卵期和非排卵期完成一次電腦任務。我們假設快策略女性的排卵期性欲變高現象更明顯，她們在排卵期更喜歡好基因男性；而慢策略女性的延長性欲現象更明顯，她們在非排卵期更喜歡好資源和好爸爸型的男性。研究結果將會增加我們對生命史策略的認識，讓我們對女性的性行爲和偏好有一個更全面的瞭解，有助於理解當今社會高齡未婚女性增多的現象。

15602518.label: Realisation of objectives
15602518.value: I conducted and completed the two studies originally proposed under this project. In Study 1, 753 female participants completed questionnaires regarding their life history strategies and intimate relationship experiences. The participants also reported their sexual desire on the survey date, real-time mate preference, and the first day of their current ovulatory cycle. The participants subsequently reported the first day of their next cycle. By knowing the first day of the current and the next ovulatory cycle, respectively, I was able to calculate each participant’s cycle duration. By recording the survey date and using the backward-counting method (Gangestad et al., 2004), I could determine each participant’s cycle status (i.e., in the follicular, ovulation or luteal phase). Fast and slow life-history participants were identified from the results of Study 1. In Study 2, 130 participants (65 fast and slow life-history ones, respectively) from Study 1 were recruited to participate in Study 2 that required daily reporting for about one month. From the first day to the last day of one ovulatory cycle, each participant completed a daily questionnaire regarding her sexual desire and attraction to mate attributes categorized as good genes, good providers, and good fathers. In addition, the level of luteinizing hormone of each participant were observed and the surge of the luteinizing hormone was adopted to determine ovulation. Participants completed a computer task when they ovulated (high-fertility period) and another task 9–10 days after the ovulation (low-fertility period). In relation to objective 1, I have employed the life-history approach to integrate the literature about the ovulatory shift hypothesis and the literature on extended sexuality and developed a differential peaking hypothesis for explaining the cyclical change of female sexual desire. The ovulatory shift hypothesis posits that heightened sexual desire in terms of physiological, cognitive, and behavioral responses is theoretically expected and empirically observed in women during ovulation (Gangestad et al., 2005). This phenomenon occurs because increased sexual behavior during the fertile window, which resembles estrus of female primates, enhances reproductive success. Compared with women in the low-fertility phase, those in the fertile window are more likely to experience sexual desire and accept sexual invitation (Haselton & Gangestad, 2006). By contrast, the extended sexuality hypothesis asserts that women exhibit enhanced sexual behaviors not only on fertile days but also on nonfertile days because sex during the nonfertile period enables women to obtain nongenetic benefits such as spousal and paternal investment from men (Grebe et al., 2013; Rodrı́guez-Gironés & Enquist, 2001). In integrating these two bodies of literature, I use life history to bridge them and develop a differential peaking hypothesis to explicate the cyclical change of female sexual desire as functions of fast and slow life history. The ovulatory shift hypothesis aligns with the reproductive strategy of fast life-history women, who emphasize instant mating while fertile and who prefer good-gene mate attributes both to secure offspring fitness enhancement right from the time of insemination. The extended sexuality hypothesis characterizes the reproductive strategy of slow life-history women, who achieve reproductive success mostly through cooperating with their long-term partners by engaging in non-fertile copulation to elicit continuous paternal care, protection, and resource investment from their partner. From data collected in Study 1 and 2, I can draw a curve of sexual desire throughout an ovulatory cycle, for fast and slow life-history women, respectively, and examine different peaks in the curve and different patterns of the curve between fast and slow women. In relation to objective 2, I have collected data of women’s life history and their mate preferences for good genes, good providers, and good fathers in both Study 1, a one-off survey, and Study 2, a diary study throughout an ovulatory cycle. I investigate women’s mate preference throughout their cycle as a function of life history. Women’s mate preferences involve three “Gs”: attributes of good genes, good providers, and good fathers (Lu et al., 2015). Good-gene mate attributes that include symmetrical facial structure and other symmetrical features, physical and facial attractiveness and muscularity represent good genetic stock to ensure the best possible outcome of a women’s obligatory parental investment (Trivers, 1972). Good-provider attributes that includes intrasexual weapon-like characteristics such as large body size and upper-body strength, social dominance and formidability, and competitive personalities and behaviors contribute to indirect paternal investment in the form of resources and provisioning. Good-father attributes that represent direct paternal investment in the form of a helper at the nest are indicated by underlying characteristics such as desiring a home, being domestic, and loving children. The time frame for realizing the benefits of the three “Gs” preferences in women’s reproductive success corresponds to the LH strategic continuum ranging from mating-oriented fast strategies to parenting-oriented slow strategies (Ellis et al., 2009). Feelings of attraction may be malleable according to different periods of the ovulatory cycle. Because fast life-history women achieve reproductive success mainly through immediate insemination to secure good genetic stock, whereas slow life-history women do so by nurturing competitive offspring who can receive paternal care and resource investment, I hypothesize that fast women are more attracted to good-gene attributes during the midcycle or the fertile window, whereas slow women are more attracted to good fathers and good providers in the nonfertile phase. The data collected from both Study 1 and 2 are used to test the hypothesis. Difficulties I encountered in this project mostly lie in recruitment of participants, particularly for Study 2, the diary study in which the participants are required to submit daily reports throughout the ovulatory cycle and observe their surge of the luteinizing hormone that indicates ovulation by applying self-test toolkits. Besides, because of the pandemic, some participants who have agreed to participate in Study 2 discontinued or postponed their participation after Study 1. I barely collected the required data within the project period and had little time left for data analysis and writing. Consequently, I was able to complete and submit one manuscript for publication and I am working on a second paper.

15602518.label: Major findings and research outcome
15602518.value: The major findings of this project include sexual desire throughout the ovulatory cycle in fast and slow life-history women, respectively, and their mate preference for good genes, good fathers, and good providers in the fertile or nonfertile phase of the cycle. In terms of sexual desire, I examined how the pattern of the cyclical change of female sexual desire was associated with women’s life history. Each participating woman reported her level of sexual desire on the survey day and the first day of their current and subsequent cycle, respectively (Study 1), or recorded her sexual desire throughout an entire cycle by submitting daily reports (Study 2). Both studies revealed that the participants with a fast life history experienced a high level of sexual desire midcycle, whereas those with a slow life history experienced a high level of sexual desire both midcycle and around menstruation. These findings partially support both the ovulatory shift hypothesis and the extended sexuality hypothesis, and I used the life history approach to bridge literature of those two hypotheses and developed a differential peaking hypothesis in explicating these findings. Specifically, in support of the ovulatory hypothesis, the mating-oriented fast life-history women experience a single peak of sexual desire of high magnitude midcycle when their conception probability is high, whereas supporting the extended sexuality hypothesis, the slow life-history women, who follow the parenting-oriented reproductive strategy, experience sexual desire that drives their sexual behaviors in the nonfertile phase more closely related to the function of parenting rather than mating (Lu, in press). In terms of female mate preference, I compared between the fast and the slow life-history women in preliminary data analyses. Results revealed a fast–slow difference in the preference for good-father attributes and such a difference was larger in the nonfertile phase than the fertile phase. The results also showed a fast–slow difference in the preference for good-gene attributes, but only in the fertile but not the nonfertile phase. There was no fast–slow difference in the preference for good-provider attributes in either the fertile or nonfertile phase. These findings suggest that depending on the timing of fertility in the ovulatory cycle, fast and slow life-history women, who adopt different reproductive strategies, are attracted different mate attributes that facilitate achievement of their reproductive goals.

15602518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15602518.value: Many mixed findings in studies examining the cyclical change of female sexuality can be explained by adopting the life history approach. This study provides an example on how the life history approach can resolve the apparent contradiction between the ovulatory shift hypothesis and the extended sexuality hypothesis on female sexual desire. By adopting a similar rationale and research method, future studies can examine the mixed findings on the frequency of female sexual behaviors throughout the ovulatory cycle and the preference for facial, body, and vocal masculinity midcycle. It is expected that the inconsistent findings are caused by the unseparation of fast and slow life-history individuals. If we separately look into these two types of individuals who have distinct reproductive goals and strategies, clearer and more consistent findings should be observed. In addition, because life history that defines reproductive strategies along the fast–slow spectrum refers to not only women but also men and not only mating but also parenting, future studies can investigate how mate preferences differ between fast and slow life-history men in short-term (with mating goal only) and in long-term (with both mating and parenting goals) mating contexts.

15602518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15602518.value: When women engage in sexual activity has evolutionary implications. This study investigated the cyclical change of women’s sexual desire and mate preference for good-gene, good-father, and good-provider male attributes as a function of life history. Fast and slow life history strategies are each associated with different mating characteristics and preferences. A fast strategy is associated with a mate preference for good genes and the related mating behavior aimed at securing instantaneous endowment of high-quality genes, whereas a slow strategy prioritizes parenting over mating to achieve reproductive success by nurturing competitive offspring with high parental efforts that include paternal care and investment. Findings of this study revealed that fast life-history women preferred good genes and experienced peak sexual desire midcycle, whereas slow life-history women preferred good fathers and experienced two peaks of sexual desire midcycle and around their menses. This study is among the first ones that adopt life history approach to investigate the cyclically changing pattern of women’s sexual desire and mate preference, and the findings help expand the existing life history literature and contribute to a more comprehensive theory about human female sexuality.

15602818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15602818.value: Background: Postnatal depression is a common public health problem which has long-term sequelae on the family and the infant’s psychosocial development. Interpersonal psychotherapy has demonstrated its value as one of the most effective interventions for postnatal depression. Enhancement of family sense of coherence may be helpful for women who are at risk for postnatal depression. However, few studies in the context of Chinese parenthood have evaluated the effect of interpersonal psychotherapy on postnatal depression and the underlying mechanisms. Aims: This study seeks (1) to examine the effect of a couple-based intervention using an interpersonal psychotherapy approach in preventing postnatal depression and promoting family sense of coherence and marital relationship among first-time Chinese mothers and fathers; and (2) to explore the possible mediation effects of family sense of coherence on depression reduction in interpersonal therapy. Methods: This will be a randomised controlled trial. A convenience sample of 472 couples will be recruited at antenatal clinics and randomly assigned to either experimental or control group. The experimental group will receive the intervention in addition to the standard perinatal care, while the control group will only receive the standard perinatal care. The intervention consists of three weekly 2-hour antenatal sessions using an interpersonal psychotherapy approach that focused on enhancement of family sense of coherence and two telephone follow-ups within the first four weeks after delivery. The primary outcome measure of postnatal depression will be assessed by the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Secondary outcome measures of family sense of coherence and the marital relationship, will be assessed by the Family Sense of Coherence Scale and Dyadic Adjustment, respectively, at baseline, immediately post-intervention, 6 weeks and 6 months postpartum. Data analysis: Linear mixed models will be used to test for significant differences between the groups on outcome variables. The classical 3-step algorithm will be used to test if family sense of coherence has a mediating effect between the intervention and postnatal depression. Significance: This study will contribute to both the theoretical development and the clinical applications of interpersonal psychotherapy and family sense of coherence for the prevention of postnatal depression in the context of Chinese parenthood. The results may help to improve perinatal services and reduce healthcare costs for the treatment of postnatal depression in the light of fiscal limitations in the contemporary healthcare system.

15602818.label: Realisation of objectives
15602818.value: Objective 1 and 2 have been completed. A total of 455 childbearing couples were recruited at three regional public hospitals and were randomly allocated to the couple-based interpersonal psychotherapy (n = 224) and the usual care (n = 231). All of the participants completed the questionnaires at baseline, 414 (91.0%) at 6 weeks postpartum and 398 (87.5%) at 6 months postpartum. In the intervention group, 178 (79.5%) women and 169 (75.4%) men completed all three antenatal sessions, and 182 (81.3%) women and 178 (79.5%) men received both telephone follow-up sessions.
