15602818.label: Major findings and research outcome
15602818.value: The results showed that both mothers and fathers in the intervention demonstrated significant and sustained improvement in depressive symptoms at 6 weeks (mean difference in mothers = 1.91, p < .001; mean difference in fathers = 1.14, p = .005) and 6 months postpartum (mean difference in mothers = 0.89, p = .039; mean difference in fathers = 1.29, p = .003), compared to those in usual care. There were no significant between group differences in family sense of coherence and marital relationship. Family sense of coherence had a direct effect on postnatal depression at six weeks and six months postpartum (p < .001), and a mediating effect between couple-based IPT and postnatal depression at six weeks postpartum (p < .001) (Please refer to the first publication in Part C).

15602818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15602818.value: The finding that not only the mothers, but also their partners reported significant improvement in postnatal depression after receiving the couple-based interpersonal psychotherapy highlights the potential benefits of the treatment for both partners. The involvement of the partner during the therapy seems promising, as it may enhance treatment response and collaborative coping when the couple are faced with the demands of new parenthood. Given the restricted access to perinatal services during the COVID-19 pandemic, mobile apps and Internet-based booster programmes, which allow for flexible scheduling, self-pacing and self-control, are growing and have the potential to further improve long-term outcomes for perinatal health.

15602818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15602818.value: The present findings add to the growing evidence that couple-based interpersonal psychotherapy is associated with a significant reduction in postnatal depressive symptoms among Chinese mothers and fathers. Couple-based therapy is providing a growing conceptual and empirical foundation for prevention efforts in postnatal depression, given the growing evidence of its prevalence among both parents and the close relationship between maternal and paternal depression. The successful delivery of this trial shows the possibility of engaging both partners and promoting their collaborative coping to prevent postnatal depression in the Chinese society.

15603318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15603318.value: 精神健康專家通常認為，使用隱喻性語言能夠有效幫助理解和改變客戶的情緒與態度，而用字面意義的語言便較難實現(Stott, Mansell, Salkovskis, Lavender, & Cartwright-Hatton, 2010)。例如，“我好像激流中的一片羽毛”這句說話能夠讓客戶和咨詢師使用“被推動拍打”的實體感受來具體地探討情感經歷。過往研究對於隱喻在短期咨詢與長期心理治療中的價值已有豐富探討；唯客戶對隱喻使用持何種態度與反應這一基本問題未受到研究關注。鑒於咨詢被廣泛視為一種合作性活動，在咨詢技巧客觀發揮作用的情況下，客戶對於咨詢技巧的態度仍會影響到咨詢的結果(Greenberg, Constantino, & Bruce, 2006)，故該問題亟待關注。本研究以大學生學習困難為考察語境，採用多角度考察咨詢對象對於咨詢中隱喻使用的態度與反應。本研究包含三個應用不同方法的獨立部分：第一部分採用調查問卷與半結構式訪談來考察對於隱喻是否能在咨詢中起到所標榜作用的有意識的看法；第二部分比較被試者對隱喻性與非隱喻性刺激的反應與皮膚電導水平，從而研究隱喻處理與無意識的情感反應之間的關係；第三部分使用話語研究的方法描述咨詢對話中的隱喻使用及其反應規律，分析包括從共建隱喻到未能對隱喻有所反應的一系列不同反應類型與其他互動變量的聯繫。本研究的參與者是華僑大學心理健康教育中心所服務的學生，兩位合作研究者在該中心擔任高級輔導員。研究成果將加深對咨詢中技巧性運用隱喻受到客戶何種反應的理解，并探討語言學家、心理學家、隱喻學家所關心的理論性問題。本研究綜合了三個採用不同的研究方法的、各具研究價值的獨立議題，其體現的多元化對於隱喻研究這一跨學科性領域有積極的意義。

15603318.label: Realisation of objectives
15603318.value: The four objectives from the original application were reduced to three in response to comments from the panel and reviewers. The three revised project objectives have been fully achieved as detailed below. Objective 1: To study conscious attitudes and beliefs about the utility of metaphors in counseling A large-scale survey study was conducted on university students who i) responded to a 15-item questionnaire comparing their preferences for metaphorical and literal stimuli vignettes, and ii) took part in a semi-structured interview probing the reasons for their preferences. The questionnaire data were statistically modeled (e.g. CFA, EFA, and within-subject comparisons) and the interviews were transcribed for thematic and discourse analyses. The results were presented at two major international conferences (RaAM 2019, 15th International Cognitive Linguistics Conference) and published as a journal article listed below. Tay, D. (2020). Surveying views of metaphor vs. Literal language in psychotherapy: A factor analysis. Metaphor and the Social World, 10(2), 273–291. Objective 2: To analyze response patterns to metaphor use in spontaneous counseling talk Mixed-methods discourse analysis was conducted on transcripts of spontaneous counseling talk involving seven dyads conducted at Co-I’s university counseling centers. Results of the qualitative analysis informed the proposal of a typology of counselor/client responses to each other’s metaphors. The quantitative analysis further examined distributional patterns between counselors and clients with respect to these taxonomic categories. The results challenged existing theoretical views of client-centeredness, and clinical implications were highlighted accordingly. These were presented at an invited talk jointly organized by the University of Birmingham and Eötvös Loránd University, and published as a journal article listed below. Tay, D. (2021). Metaphor Response Categories and Distribution Between Therapists and Clients: A Case Study in the Chinese Context. Journal of Constructivist Psychology, 34(4), 378–394. In addition to the above studies, psycholinguistic studies of electrodermal activity were also carried out to explore relative affective engagements levels under i) metaphorical versus literal communication styles in face-to-face counseling, and ii) when describing pictures with and without metaphors in picture-based counseling. The results lend further support to the above studies by demonstrating significant differences in participants’ unconscious psycho-physiological responses to the use of metaphors vs. literal language in counseling. Clinical implications were highlighted accordingly. These were presented at invited talks at several international conferences (12th International Forum on Cognitive Linguistics, 5th International Conference of Semiosis Research Center) and published as journal articles/book chapters as listed below. Tay, D. (2020). Affective Engagement in Metaphorical versus Literal Communication Styles in Counseling. Discourse Processes, 57(4), 360–375. Tay, D., Huang, J., & Zeng, H. (2020). Prompting Strategies and Outcomes in Picture-Based Counseling. In B. Watson & J. Krieger (Eds.), Expanding Horizons in Health Communication (pp. 29–46). Springer. Tay, D., Huang, J., & Zeng, H. (2019). Affective and discursive outcomes of symbolic interpretations in picture-based counseling: A skin conductance and discourse analytic study. Metaphor & Symbol, 34(2), 96–110. Objective 3: To articulate the implications of the above for counseling practice Implications for counseling practice derived from each study were articulated in the respective talks and publications above. The collective implications derived by triangulating these studies will also be disseminated in the form of a contracted monograph with Cambridge University Press, titled 'Navigating the realities of metaphor and psychotherapy research'. It has been submitted in Nov 2021 and is expected to be published in 2022-2023. The project did not encounter any major problems despite the COVID-19 pandemic.

15603318.label: Major findings and research outcome
15603318.value: The major published findings from the project are summarized as follows. 1. Metaphorical language is perceived as better than literal language in fulfilling major therapeutic functions including i) building collaborative relationships, ii) expressing emotions and experiences, iii) explaining difficult concepts, iv) introducing new frames of reference, v) working through client resistance. However, clients as laypersons do not perceive these functions as distinctly as therapists and researchers, seeing them instead in a more holistic way. Potential drawbacks of metaphor use were also reported by clients. (Output 3, 5) 2. Therapists and clients respond to each other’s spontaneous metaphors to different extents in terms of a hierarchy: repeating, rejecting, exploring, and extending. However, the distribution of these response categories varies. Therapists are more likely to explore, but also reject client-initiated metaphors, clients are more likely to repeat therapist-initiated metaphors, and both are equally likely to extend metaphors. The category of ‘rejected metaphors’ deserves more attention as it violates the ideal of ‘collaborative co-construction’ in counseling. (Output 3, 5) 3. A metaphorical style of communication is more affectively engaging than a literal style of communication in counseling, as reflected by significantly greater increase in skin conductance levels over time. Potential linguistic correlates of this increase include various paraphrases of source domains, metaphor signals, and markers of uncertainty around metaphors. Similar results were found in the related context of picture-based counseling where clients who were asked to elaborate pictures metaphorically were found to be more engaged. (Output 1, 2, 4) The above findings collectively suggest that metaphor use in various counseling contexts, as evidenced by both conscious and unconscious feedback, elicit significantly different responses than their literal alternatives. The overarching hypothesis posed in the research project is thus supported. Implications and practical recommendations for therapists were also advanced on this basis. Importantly, the findings also suggest that metaphor use needs to be more critically interrogated because of its reported drawbacks, and the tendency for useful metaphors to be overlooked or even rejected by therapists or clients. A combined discussion of these findings is under preparation in a contracted monograph by Cambridge University Press, submitted in Nov 2021 and expected to be published in 2022-2023.

15603318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15603318.value: The research can be further developed in several ways. Firstly, as mentioned, more attention is needed on potential drawbacks despite the reported preferences for and higher engagement levels associated with metaphors. This is particularly important as a critical response to the truism of ‘collaborative co-construction’ in many parts of the metaphor and psychotherapy literature. Secondly, there is scope for investigating whether the findings above, from a Chinese-speaking context, would be replicated in other linguistic contexts such as English. The proposed methods for investigation are suitable for such replication work. Relatedly, the tendency for metaphors to be responded to, or ‘dropped’ in various ways in spontaneous counseling talk, requires more extensive modeling across larger (cross-linguistic) datasets. Underexplored methods like survival regression would be highly relevant and insightful in this regard, and this is the topic of PI’s latest GRF application.

15603318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15603318.value: Metaphors are believed to be useful in counseling because they help clients express complicated emotions and feelings in terms of something else similar, but easier to understand. However, there is little research evidence on how clients actually feel about, and respond to metaphors in different counseling situations. This project investigated i) large-scale survey ratings of whether clients prefer metaphorical or literal language, ii) a large database of counseling talk for different response patterns to metaphors, and iii) skin conductance measurements of clients as a measure of how emotionally engaged they are when metaphors or literal language is used in counseling. Our results show that clients generally found metaphors to be more effective than literal language in performing counseling functions, and are more emotionally engaged when they are used. However, we also found drawbacks with using metaphors, and scenarios where useful metaphors are not properly managed or followed up. These findings can help therapists and other mental health professionals to adopt metaphor as a useful counseling strategy, while also recognizing potential problems with using them.

15603818.label: Realisation of objectives
15603818.value: This research project employed a mixed methods design following the two-phase QUAN→qual paradigm. Phase I was conducted as a joint quantitative study with Wave 5 of the HKPSSD in 2020–2021. In addition, quantitative data were collected from 213 pairs of older parents (aged over 50 years) and their adult children. In phase II, individual semi-structured interviews with 60 older parent-adult child pairs were conducted. Objective 1 Objective 1 was examined by the newly adapted and validated Chinese version of the Preparation for Future Care Needs (PFCN) scale. The PI conducted and published a study on translating, adapting, and validating two short forms of a multidimensional scale that measures the preparation for future care needs (PFCN) among Chinese older adults in Hong Kong. The scale measured five subdomains of care preparation among ageing adults in Hong Kong, including awareness (mean score was 12.056, range 4-20), avoidance (mean score was 8.704, range 3-15), gathering information, decision making (mean score was 9.684, range 3-15), and concrete planning (mean score was 8.639, range 4-20). Influenced by the cultural value of family care and by the limited formal care options available in Hong Kong, the information-gathering step was skipped by Chinese older adults. The items intended to measure the information-gathering domain loaded onto the other three domains. This factor pattern reflected Chinese older adults' passive information-gathering behaviors and their reliance on family members in care planning. Notably, compared with their Western counterparts, Chinese older adults appeared less likely to engage in care preparation activities (mean item score: 3.09 vs 2.79) and demonstrated lower levels of planning in all subdomains. Chinese older adults in Hong Kong tended to regard future care as a negative topic and avoided thinking about it. These scales provide researchers and service practitioners with a valuable tool to identify individuals at risk of inadequate planning and inform the development of interventions to enhance care preparation in targeted domains. The manuscript entitled "Adaptation and Validation of the Preparation for Future Care Needs Scale for Chinese Older Adults in Hong Kong" was published by the Gerontologist in 2022. Based on the qualitative data collected from older parents and adult children, the PI also examined the experiences and processes of future care planning focusing on the changes and challenges faced by both local residents and mainland Chinese immigrants, amid the pandemic and the 2019–2020 social unrest. The findings indicated that people had increased awareness of care preparation and financial planning. They preferred home-based care and considered residential care homes as a suboptimal choice. In addition, there was a noticeable increase in distant family arrangements which in turn prompted individuals to reassess their plans for future care arrangements, emphasising the linked lives in Chinese family settings. The manuscript entitled "Care Planning in Ageing Families during the COVID-19 Pandemic and Social Unrest in Hong Kong" is currently under the second round of review for publication in Applied Research in Quality of Life. Objective 2 Through latent profile analysis of quantitative data, three care planning profiles: child-active intergenerational planners, dyadic thinkers, and filial-uninvolved intergenerational avoiders were identified. The child-active intergenerational planners consisting of approximately 21.6% (n = 46) of the older parents-adult children pairs, represented participants who exhibited the highest level of preparation in all care planning domains. The adult children often take the lead or playing a collaborative role. The adult children reported better intergenerational relationships and family functioning than those in the other groups. The dyadic thinkers comprising 68.5% (n=146) of the pairs, demonstrated a moderate level of preparation. The participants in this profile exhibited a high awareness of future care needs but were unlikely to engage in definite planning activities. The filial-uninvolved intergenerational avoiders, which comprised approximately 9.9% (n=21) of the pairs, exhibited the highest levels of avoidance and reluctance toward care planning. Additionally, this study indicated that all three care planning profiles exhibited a child-centred approach. The role of the adult children has a greater influence on the level and process of care preparation than the individual efforts of their older parents. Moreover, this study also identified intergenerational discrepancies in care preparation processes and expectations. 35.7% of the older parents expected to live with their spouse, and 18.8% expected to live and be cared by their adult children. In addition, 36.6% of adult children expected their parents to live with them, and 20.2% of adult children expected their parents to live independently and rely on community services. The percentage of adult children who expected to provide filial care was nearly two times higher than that indicated by older parents. These results indicate a discrepancy between older parents’ preferences and their actual choices. Although they mostly prefer to be cared for by their children, they often sacrifice their expectations to alleviate the burden on their children. Objective 3 and 4 The third and fourth objectives were achieved by examining how economic capital and family and community social capital affect care preparedness independently and jointly. The results revealed that older parents and their adult children exhibited moderate levels of attitudinal avoidance and behavioural engagement in care preparation. In addition, this study investigated the effect of economic capital and family and community social capital. Economic capital was related to intergenerational care planning. Adult children with higher household incomes were less likely to avoid thinking about their parents' future care. Further, adult children’s levels of behavioural engagement in care preparation for their parents were negatively associated with their parents’ household income. Concerning family social capital, ageing parents with siblings and adult children with higher quality of intergenerational relationships perceived by either side engaged more in care preparation. Overall, the results show that family social capital could interact with household income and community social capital and affect parents’ care preparedness. The manuscript entitled“The Roles of Economic and Social Capital in Intergenerational Care Preparation for Older Chinese Adults: An Actor-partner Interdependence Model” is currently under peer review for publication in the Journal of Applied Gerontology. Objective 5 In the data collection period of HKPSSD Wave 5, the dyadic sample of older parents and adult children was recruited by asking older people to invite their adult children or children-in-law or by asking adult children to invite a parent or a parent-in-law to participate in the study. This recruitment method also helps to achieve objective five. Based on the data from qualitative interviews with 15 older parent-adult child pairs and 4 adult children, the processes and experiences of intergenerationally tied relocation, care circulation and intergenerational care preparation were examined. This study contributed to the realization of the first, second, third and fourth objectives by using a subsample with unique experience of intergenerationally tied relocation in which older parents from mainland China, referred to as the tied movers, join their already migrated children in Hong Kong to provide domestic and childcare support. The findings highlight that tied relocation links the lives of individuals within a larger family system and reflects changing role in care circulation over their life course. The manuscript entitled“Intergenerationally Tied Relocation and Care Circulation: Motivations, Struggles, and Future Arrangements” is currently under peer review for publication in the Journal of Applied Gerontology.

15603818.label: Major findings and research outcome
15603818.value: As the first systematic investigation examined future care planning among Hong Kong ageing families in the changing familial and sociocultural contexts, the findings of this research project have added crucial methodological, conceptual and theoretical contributions. This research project offered an innovative approach for researching future care planning using a longitudinal ‘QUAN→qual’ mixed methods research design. This approach enhances triangulation and explanation and deepens understanding of the subject under investigation. This research project translated, adapted, and validated 2 short forms of the multidimensional, theory-guided scale measuring preparation for future care needs (PFCN) among Chinese older adults in Hong Kong. The PFCN scale is a standardized tool that enables researchers and service practitioners to accurately understand and assess older adults’ processes and efforts in care planning, facilitate the identification of individuals at risk from inadequate planning, and inform the development of interventions to enhance care preparation in target domains. This research provides an approach to investigate care preparation in the family context and intergenerational relationships. The study findings contribute to our understanding of dyadic proactive coping styles in relation to the future care needs of older parents with reference to the life stage and situation of the dyad members, and highlight the impact of Chinese cultural and family contexts on care planning. These findings also extend the applicability of proactive coping theory, family systems theory, and the norms of reciprocity and familism to care planning research within specific intergenerational and ethnocultural contexts, providing a solid foundation for the development of individual- and family-level care planning interventions. The project also identified the insight into associations between economic capital, family social capital, and intergenerational care planning. Family social capital could interact with household income and community social capital and affect parents’ care preparedness. Intergenerational care planning may be considered a strategic response to both adult children's and parents’ economic situations. These findings can inform the development of care planning services sensitive to socioeconomic differentials, facilitate the integration of individual and intergenerational services, and broaden family services to encompass care planning interventions in response to diverse care preparation needs. The project extended HKPSSD’s survey scope from coresiding household members to non-coresiding adult children and children-in-law, which would inform the future use of multiple, cost-effective data collection methods.

15603818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15603818.value: This research project elucidated the extent, processes, and content of intergenerational care planning among Hong Kong ageing families, as well as how older adults’ and adult children’s economic capital and family social capital independently and jointly influence intergenerational care planning. Further research can examine older adults’ care planning in a broader family system beyond older parent-adult child dayd, considering the role of siblings or other relatives, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of eldercare and care preparation in the family context. Second, the HKSAR government announced to broaden service of District Elderly Community Centres and Neighbourhood Elderly Centres to cover later life planning in 2023. In response, the PI submitted a new GRF project this year to develop and employ a theory-guided intervention that integrates Motivational Interviewing with Photovoice, empowering older adults to actively engage in the intervention and facilitate more productive attitudinal and behavioural changes in care preparation. The proposed project is expected to provide a theory-guided, validated service model to enhance future care preparation for older adults. Overall, the findings of this project may assist policymakers and service providers in alleviating unpreparedness for future care and intergenerational discrepancies concerning care arrangements

15604018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15604018.value: Background: The state of being closed-minded refers to a mind firmly unreceptive to new ideas or arguments. It may affect information processing and social interactions, such as the tendency to rely on first impressions. It is both a trait that varies across individuals, and a tendency that is shaped by a person’s social environment. Recent studies suggest the potential to reducing closed-mindedness by using well-crafted learning designs. Nevertheless, many educational studies focus more on academic outcomes than psychosocial outcomes, and many of them are theoretical discussions rather than experimental studies. Against this background, this study adopts an experimental design to fill this research gap. Objective: This study aims to examine participants’ tendency of being closed-minded in different web-based project learning designs in civic education, namely: argumentative writing (AW), propaganda production (PP), and scoping review (SR). We hypothesize that AW will induce the highest level, PP will induce medium level, and SR will induce the lowest level. Intervention: Participants in different groups (AW group, PP group, SR group) will complete their respective projects based on the same project theme (e.g., a controversial social issue). Participants in each group will be further sub-divided into 5 small teams. Each small team will have its own Facebook page and an editable Google Document. Over a 3-month-period, the RA will systematically share the same set of materials (news and web resources) to respective Facebook pages of different teams on a daily basis. Finally, each small team will complete a summary report using their Google doc page, according to the format required by their respective groups. The best reports in respective groups will receive awards. Method: The intervention will be researched using a randomised controlled trial (RCT). Participants will include N=90 Chinese, aged 18-24, born in HK, and completed their Liberal Studies examination. They will be recruited by teachers, and/or social workers. Participants will be randomly assigned to the AW group, PP group or SR group, each with 30 participants. There will be three waves of assessment, namely: pre-intervention, post-intervention, and 2 months after completion of intervention. Core outcome measures include: the need for cognitive closure, critical thinking dispositions, and positions toward the issue being addressed by the project. Implication: These findings may help inform pedagogies, intervention strategies, and public policies in relation to local youth civic engagement. 背景：思想封閉狀態是指一種堅定不接受新思想或論點的思想。它會影響信息處理和社交互動，例如傾向依賴第一印象。它既是個人特質，也是個人與社會環境互動的結果。研究顯示，學習設計可降低封閉性。然而，不少教育研究傾向關注學術成果而非心理社會結果，而且流於理論討論而非實踐研究。在這背景下，本研究採用實驗設計來填補這空白。 目標：本研究旨在探討參與者在參與不同的公民教育網上研習活動後的思想封閉狀態。探討的活動形式包括：議事立論式寫作（AW），撰文宣廣指定立場（PP）及撰寫範疇概覽（SR）。研究假設AW將誘導最高水平，PP將誘導中等水平，並且SR將誘導最低水平。 活動內容：不同群體（AW小組，PP小組，SR小組）的參與者將根據相同的主題（例如，有爭議的社會問題）完成專題研習。每組參與者將進一步細分為5個小組。每個小團隊都有自己的網上平台（例如Facebook、Google文檔）。在3個月的時間內，研究人員將每天系統地將相同的材料（新聞和網絡資源）分享到不同團隊的頁面。最後，每小團隊將根據指定格式完成報告。各組別的最佳報告將獲獎勵。 研究方法：使用隨機對照試驗（RCT）研究設計。參與者將包括 90名中國人，年齡在18-24歲，在香港出生，完成通識教育考試。他們透過教師或社工招募。參與者將被隨機分配到AW組，PP組或SR組，每組30名參與者。設三階段評估，活動前，活動後和活動後2個月。評估包括：思想封閉狀態傾向、批判性思維傾向、對議題的立場等等。 意義：研究結果對公民教育、社會服務、公共政策等均有所啟示。

15604018.label: Realisation of objectives
15604018.value: 1. To examine participants’ tendency of being closed-minded in different web-based project learning designs in civic education, namely: argumentative writing, propaganda production, and scoping reviews. As note in the mid-term report, because of the massive destruction of PolyU campus in 2019 that affected the university of the PI, and the pandemic in 2019 and 2020 that affected all schools, research progress was hindered, and regular school-based activities were suspended during most of the time of the project period (Jan 2019 to Dec 2020). Under these circumstances, research protocol was modified to fit the changing situations. Instead of coworking with teachers in their regular project-based teaching activities, the project devised an O2O (online-to-offline) workshop model to engage students and collect data. First, students needed to enrol online and read a thematic page on the project website before the workshop (in our experiment, the topic was “what is meant by Hongkonger”). Second, a guest would meet students face-to-face in the workshop, furthering the topic presented on the project website and answering questions from students. Finally, students would be divided into different groups, working on different assignments to respond to contents delivered in the workshop. Two major assignment formats were experimented: i) story-retelling activities, and; ii) analytical writing activities. Such an O2O workshop became the background context that the project used to examine psychological outcomes from different assignment designs. The results provided preliminary evidence indicating that different types of civic education assignments will lead to different psychological outcomes – this is an aspect the local exam-based education system has largely ignored. Results from a series of pretest-posttest studies indicated that analytical writing activities did not induce significant changes in psychological outcomes; nonetheless, story-retelling activities consistently decreased participants’ closed-mindedness, increased participants’ critical openness, cognitive empathy, and curiosity toward seeking new information (Chan, 2019; Chan et al., 2021). The pilot RCT (Chan et al., 2021) further showed that story-retelling activities were more efficient than analytical writings in achieving these outcomes. In the story-retelling group, each participant had opportunities to express their views and interact with others’ views. The retelling and title creation required students to consider expectations from different audiences. They knew that they needed to present their respective ideas to a panel consisting of the protagonist, the workshop host, as well as other invited panellists. In such a context, what is meant by “good” was not clearly stated as a rubric, and it was such vagueness that invited students to consider what they should present. Such retelling activities are considered to create a safe space for participants to play with different voices, because they are explicitly encouraged to brainstorm different ideas. When students genuinely understand that the same story can be told differently, they are likely to be aware of the significance and impact of different perspectives. This deconstruction and reconstruction process embedded in story retelling supports a pedagogy that is highly relevant to critical openness. This observation also echoes with results from my earlier studies supported by RGC’s ECS (see project 25605317. Paradoxically, participants in the analytical writing group tended to use more sophisticated phrasing and repeat some “model answers”. A possible limitation of the analytical writing approach is that once students recognise what such teachers want in assessments, they will tend to play the game by rehearsing the politically correct positions without genuine personal reflection. Moreover, when students easily believe that they can objectively oversee all information and make a judgment, they may easily fall into an echo chamber that increases the likelihood of reconfirming what they already believe or understand. This could explain why students in the analytical writing group demonstrated a decrease in critical openness and cognitive empathy (see Section 63.1 of this completion report). When learners may have insufficient prior knowledge to provide internal guidance, they tend to follow their limited (or even biased) preunderstanding in their objective analysis. Psychological studies have long discovered the phenomenon of confirmation bias (myside bias), which refers to a cognitive bias that leads a person to misinterpret new information as supporting previously held hypotheses. Confirmation bias is more easily activated in situations where people must assess correlations and make judgments, and Need for Cognitive Closure will also be increased by fatigue and tight deadlines. In other words, when learners work alone on a tight schedule, they may tend to adopt information supporting their current convictions. 2. To inform pedagogies, intervention strategies, and public policies in relation to youth civic engagement. It is worth to note that while the story-retelling group was more efficient than the analytical writing group in achieving intended outcomes, the analytical writing group triggered significantly more pageviews than the story-retelling group did, particularly on the website section about different definitions of Hongkongers (Chan et al., 2021). This observation implies that students’ access to diverse viewpoints (in texts) cannot ensure students have an open attitude. These results imply that textual content does not directly help induce psychological outcomes. The results of this study also remind us to be aware of the possible constraints of independent inquiry and analytical writing. Educators tend to assign students a significant amount of essay writing and web-based inquiry to develop their ability to consider different perspectives and think critically. Such an emphasis is widespread among different types of social studies programmes, for instance, Liberal Studies (renamed as / replaced by “Citizenship and Social Development” since 2021, in which the “independent inquiry study” component was deleted). In principle, instructors’ reflective questioning and rigorous argumentation enhances students’ openness and helps offset personal biases. This can be found in research degrees such as MPhil or PhD studies, where supervisors coach students over time and students eventually produce well-crafted dissertations. However, when analytical writing is frequently and extensively implemented across a number of subjects in a full, tight training program, a different outcome may arise. For example, in mainstream education with larger class sizes, instructors often do not have the time or space to coach each student step-by-step. Many students are, therefore, unguided. Moreover, a high school/ college student often works on multiple project tasks required by different subjects at the same time. Project assignment deadlines, the perceived need for concise conclusions, grading, and fatigue can all increase a student’s need for cognitive closure, and students’ biases may easily become unchecked. This scenario could last for years, possible extending over the whole period of a student’s educational endeavours. In sum, to enhance learning outcomes such as openness to diversity and/or cognitive empathy, narrative means may be more suitable than some other means (such as augmentative/analytical essay). Of course, storytelling may have its limitations, for example, it may not be useful in developing data presentation skills. A thorough comparison between storytelling and analytical writing is beyond the scope of this study. What we can take away from this study is that this particular form of story-retelling activity can nurture a learning outcome that is core to education in Hong Kong nowadays, and that it does not require complex technology tools or expensive academic staff. Nonetheless, the true potential of narrative means can be actualised only if policymakers and stakeholders can have the openness to recognise that playful means may achieve significant educational ends. More discussion, debate, and research are indeed necessary.

15604018.label: Major findings and research outcome
15604018.value: This study examined students’ tendency of closed-mindedness in different assignment designs in an O2O workshop context. Results from a series of pretest-posttest studies indicated that story-retelling activities consistently decreased participants’ closed-mindedness, and increased participants’ critical openness, cognitive empathy, and curiosity toward seeking new information (Chan, 2019). To summarize: * Closed-mindedness (NFC scores) decreased significantly after the intervention (-0.24, p = .03, d = -.33). * Critical Openness (CTO scores) increased significantly after the intervention (+0.30, p = .01, d = .41). * The scores on perspective-taking (PTM scores) ability increased significantly after the intervention (+0.47, p < .001, d = .58). * The level of curiosity (CSI scores) toward seeking new information increased significantly after the intervention (+0.33, p = .04, d = .31). Result from the RCT (two groups, comparing story-retelling activities and analytical writing activities) further showed that story-retelling activities were more efficient than analytical writings in reducing closed-mindedness, and increasing critical openness, cognitive empathy, and curiosity toward seeking new information (Chan et al., 2021). * The ANOVA test indicated that all participants (regardless of the group they were assigned to) indicated a statistically significant decrease in NFC scores (F = 16.571, p < .001). * The ANOVA test showed that the workshop had a statistically significant effect of group-by-time on CTO (F = 5.986, p = .018), PTM, (F = 4.145, p = .048) and CSI (F = 4.319, p = .043) scores, meaning that these outcomes changed differently over time between the two groups. *Paired t-tests showed that both groups had a statistically significant decrease in the NFC scores. However, the story-retelling group, t (23) = -3.45, p = .002, d = -.69, power = .432 showed a greater decrease in the NFC score with a greater effect size and power than the comparison group, t (24) = -2.09, p = .05, d = -.42, power = .151. * Paired t-tests further showed that the story-retelling group showed a significant increase in the CTO score with a 0.55 effect size and .296 power. However, the comparison group showed a decrease in the CTO score with a -.12 effect size and .065 power. * The Two Groups Used the Web-based Materials Differently. The comparison group triggered more pageviews than the storytelling group on the webpage section introducing different views defining Hongkongers, t (47) = -2.86, p = .01, d = -.41, power = .815.

15604018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15604018.value: This research study has showed that different civic education project learning designs will induce different levels of closed-mindedness, it is reasonable to extend the research to examine what types of learning activities can best fit particular educational aims. Fostering students’ empathetic capability is a new policy focus of the Education Bureau of the Hong Kong government since 2020. It is worth to note that closed-mindedness (need for cognitive closure, a key psychological construct examined in this study) is a moderating construct that is closely related to cognitive empathy. Some studies particularly show that individuals who have high need for cognitive closure are more likely to utilize stereotypical information in judgment formation and more likely to have strong prejudice, and therefore high need for cognitive closure will hinder individuals’ cognitive empathy. As such, it means that narrative-based assignments may be more useful than analytical/argumentative assignments in reducing closed-mindedness and enhancing cognitive empathy. Therefore, it is worthwhile to further examine what types of narrative-based learning designs can effectively deliver such learning outcomes. The story-retelling activities used in the research is just one of the many methods among the pool of narrative-based methods, more research and theorization can be directed toward this area.

15604018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15604018.value: This research project started with a prediction that different types of civic education assignments will lead to different psychological outcomes – this is an aspect the local exam-based education system has largely ignored. The project particularly compared i) story-retelling activities and ii) analytical writing activities. Based on the findings from a series of O2O (online to offline) workshops for students in Hong Kong, the results provided initial evidence that narrative means make unique contributions. Our findings showed that story-retelling activities were more efficient than analytical writings in reducing closed-mindedness, increasing critical openness, cognitive empathy, and curiosity toward seeking new information. These results open a discussion about whether we have been using appropriate means to achieve our intended educational aims. If fostering students’ cognitive empathy and critical openness is a policy focus of the Education Bureau of the Hong Kong government, it is worthwhile to further develop narrative-based pedagogy rather than one-sidedly emphasizing analytical writing and exam-oriented curriculum designs.

15604118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15604118.value: According to the World Health Organization Global Burden of Disease Study, for youth aged 10 to 24 years old, schizophrenia ranked as the third among all causes of disability. Schizophrenia shows a marked increase in prevalence after aged 15 and many manifests in early 20s. The term early psychosis is used for young people before and after their first identified psychotic episode. The support of family members during the treatment and recovery of early psychosis is critical. Schizophrenia results in serious functional impairment, including a delimited social networks, termination or suspension of schooling. Caregivers encounter much psychological distress, particularly in handling the violent behaviours, suicidal ideation, failures in treatment, and other illness behaviours of such students. One-third of such caregivers have experienced emotional difficulties, such as depression. Family psychoeducation intervention has been recommended as a major component in the treatment of early psychosis. International and local studies have reported positive outcomes using family psychoeducation interventions, but many limitations have also been identified. Many previous studies implemented an intensive programme design, with an emphasis on improvements in illness outcome of patients only. A recent review concluded that benefits of such programmes to caregivers were limited. There have been calls for a time-limited but more cost-effective programme for caregivers of a youth with early psychosis to mitigate the looming realities of eventual serious mental illness and family suffering. A brief Mindfulness-Based Family Psychoeducation programme is developed to reduce the caregiver’s stress and to promote young people’s recovery. Results from the pilot study suggested that such programme could reduce caregiver stress, and promote positive caregiving experience. A more rigorous study is proposed using a mixed methods design. A randomized controlled trial will be conducted to compare a mindfulness-based family psychoeducation intervention, with an ordinary family psychoeducation intervention. 300 caregivers of a youth who have experienced early psychosis will be recruited, with the assistance of five NGO collaborators. Programme effectiveness will be assessed by comparing outcomes measuring caregiver’s perceived stress, positive well-being, and the young people’s mental health symptoms. As part of the programme activity, Photovoice approach is selected to explore the complex family experiences and the benefits of mindfulness from the caregiver’s personal perspectives. Caregivers can offer their voices about their burdens, and how mindfulness can benefit to the families through their involvement in a photo taking activity during the psychoeducation programme. 根據世界衛生組織全球疾病負擔研究，在10至24歲的青少年組別中，精神分裂症在所有殘疾原因中排名第三。精神分裂症的患病率在15歲後出現顯著的增加，在20多歲時會出現許多症狀。「思覺失調」用於第一次發現重性精神病發作前後的年輕人。 家庭成員在治療思覺失調和康復期間的支持至關重要。精神分裂症導致嚴重的功能障礙，包括分隔的社交網絡，以及終止或暫停學校教育。照顧者會遇到很多心理困擾，特別是在處理這些學生的暴力行為、自殺念頭、治療失敗以及其他病患行為。三分之一的這類照顧者經歷過情緒困擾，例如抑鬱症。家庭心理教育介入被推薦為治療思覺失調的主要組成部分。 國際和各地研究初步顯示使用家庭心理教育介入的正面結果，但也發現了許多局限。許多先前的研究都實施密集式的課程設計，只強調改善患者的疾病結果。最近的一份回顧總結此類方案對照顧者的益處有限。有人呼籲為患思覺失調的青少年之照顧者提供一個短時間而更具成本效益的課程，以改善嚴重精神疾病迫在眉睫的現實和家庭的痛苦。這項研究是基於一個短期的靜觀為本家庭心理教育課程, 旨在減輕照顧者的壓力，以及促進年輕人的康復。先導研究的結果表明此類課程可以減輕照顧者的壓力，並促進正面的照顧體驗。 一個更嚴謹的研究將提議使用混合方法的設計進行。以隨機對照試驗方法比較靜觀為本家庭心理教育與普通的家庭心理教育。在五個非政府組織及青山醫院的協助下，將招募300名經歷過思覺失調的青年之照顧者。計劃的效果將透過比較照顧者所感知的壓力、正面幸福感和年輕人的精神健康症狀的測量結果以作評估。作為課程活動的一部分，影像發聲 (Photovoice) 的質性研究方法選擇用來從照顧者的個人觀點探索複雜的家庭經歷。照顧者可以透過參與在心理教育課程期間的攝影活動，表達他們對自己負擔所感覺的心聲，以及靜觀如何使家庭受益。

15604118.label: Realisation of objectives
15604118.value: 5.3 Realisation of objectives (3 pages) Objectives 1: To investigate the effectiveness of a mindfulness-based family psychoeducation (MBFPE) programme in reducing stress and promoting positive well-being of Chinese caregivers of students with early psychosis in Hong Kong. Within-group effects of MBFPE Among the caregivers in the MBFPE group, there were small-to-large effect sizes over time, as shown in the within-group data analysis. After controlling the covariance in caregiver burden, we found improvements in anxiety (d = 0.201), and positive caring experience (d = 0.286), and both indicated small effect sizes. Improvements Reductions in physical distress (d = 0.659), and depression (d = 0.565) had medium effect sizes, and those of effect on family (d = .804) showed a significant large size improvement. The caregivers reported changes in all outcomes in the expected directions, except caregiver burden and non-attachment, which showed very mild deterioration after MBFPE. Between-group effects We used 2 × 2 ANOVA to investigate the time × group interaction effects of the MBFPE and ordinary family psychoeducation programs. No statistically significant interactions were found in the data related to the caregivers. After controlling the covariance in caregiver burden, MBFPE showed a non-significant superior effect in physical distress (d = 0.278). Since the MBFPE and control group programme completed in October 2022, the data collection of 9-month follow-up has not been completed due to the delay of project implementation. PI will continue the data collection using own time and resources and all follow-up data collection. Objective 2: To investigate the effectiveness of a MBFPE in improving the psychiatric symptoms and recovery of Hong Kong students with early psychosis. We used 2 × 2 ANOVA to investigate the time × group interaction effects of the outcome of students by comparing students with caregivers completing MBFPE and those completing ordinary psychoeducation program. Students from MBFPE group showed significantly larger improvement in recovery than those from ordinary family psychoeducation programs (F=8.268, p=.012, d=1.484). No statistically significant interactions were found in the rating by professionals (F=.407, p=.533, d=.327). The recruitment of caregivers encountered much difficulty due to CCOVID-19 and suspension of collaborator’s face-to-face services. Besides, only 30% of the students (young people in recovery) agreed to participate in our study, and the student sample in our study has 18 people. Although our data analyses showed small to large effect sizes in some of the variables, our findings has limitations due to small sample size. Objective 3: To explore the mediation effects of interpersonal mindfulness, family expressed emotions and over-attachment in the recovery of students with early psychosis, by comparing changes in selected outcome measures of treatment group and control group participants before, and after the MBFPE There was no time × group interaction effects on the change in interpersonal mindfulness and non-attachment at post-intervention. Therefore, we did not conduct analysis on their mediation effect on study outcomes. Based on student’s rating of caregiver expressed emotions (EE), we found a trend of decrease in EE in MBFPE group, and a trend of increase in EE in ordinary psychoeducation group. After controlling caregiver burden as covariates, there is a significant interaction effect in over-involvement, one of the subscales of EE (F = 4.846, p = .044, d = 1.136) reflecting a large effect size of MBFPE over ordinary psychoeducation. A similar trend was found in the EE total score and hostility another subscale of EE but analysis did not reach the level of statistical significance. Due to the small size of student sample (N=19), we did not conduct the quantitative mediating analyses. However, based on the photovoice, a qualitative research method, we have identified six different themes among the voices capturing the experience of the caregiving and recovery process. It showed caregivers experienced improved emotion regulation and reduced EE. The six themes of caregiver identified in photovoice are: Voice 1: I Pay Attention to the Present Moment: Although they faced challenges, mindfulness practice allowed them to focus on and stay open to the present moment and acknowledging the positive experiences of caregiving. Voice 2: I Care about My Family: The caregivers saw their care for the persons in recovery as one of the core elements of their recovery. Voice 3: I Trust My Children: Caregivers support their children in becoming independent and willing to try doing things on their own. Voice 4: I Appreciate the Connection with and Support from Nature and the Universe: After practicing mindfulness, the caregivers became more aware of the support they received from friends, nature, and their beliefs. Voice 5: I Observe My Worries and Guilt and Learn Not to Be Reactive: Although caregivers were uncertain about what they could do and what would be helpful, they learned to observe them and are aware of the possible negative consequences of being reactive. Voice 6: I Find Space in Offering Care and Exercising Self‐Care: The caregivers observed conflicts between their children and within the family but tried to hold their strong emotions within themselves. Reasons for underachievement and attempts to overcome problems 1. Impact of COVID-19 on recruitment and program implementation Although our research team had spent around 20 days stationing at outpatient units of the collaborators, less than expected young adults and caregivers responded to our invitations in-between and after the waves of COVID-19. Many of them explicitly expressed their reservations about participating in a face-to-face caregiver program. The young adults were even less responsive to our invitations than the caregivers, although we offered incentives for participation. The sample size is smaller than estimation in proposal. 2. Additional time spent and resources in recruitment and ethics clearing with collaborators One of our collaborators Baptist Oi Kwan Social Service used to be the largest number of family psychoeducation programme in Hong Kong have suspended all face-to-face program in our project periods. They were not able to recruit adequate caregivers in 2022. Two other NGO collaborators failed to identify another suitable caregivers in the whole project period. PI also made use of Facebook page and advertisement to recruit caregivers to enrolment for our study program directly. Unfortunately, the effect was very limited. PI found one new collaborator Kowloon Hospital EASY team in mid-2021. Unfortunately, the ethics clearing takes more than eight months as the review process was further delayed by COVID-19. PI managed to complete all MBFPE programs for the new collaborator by October 2022, that is one year after the original plan. 3. P-I’s prolonged leave and use of temporary waiver during project period Due to personal and family reasons, PI was on leave for one year after successful application of temporary wavier from RGC. Due to the reasons discussed above, PI originally planned to apply for project extension at the end of 2021. Unfortunately, PI was not recommended for such application after seeking for the advice of Research and Innovation Office of PolyU. PI continued to work closely with collaborators during and after his leave. Data collection will be continued, and PI will complete the follow-up data collection using own time and resources and the final time point data collection is expected to complete in mid-2023.

15604118.label: Major findings and research outcome
15604118.value: A brief psychoeducation may not be adequate to reduce the burden and improve the mental health outcome of caregivers of individuals who have resent onset of psychosis. Compared with caregivers who experienced chronic caregiving stress, the caregivers in our study may have felt overwhelmed by the drastic changes in the mental condition of their family members after the onset of psychosis and the subsequent adjustments made by the entire family. However, preliminary results show that integrating mindfulness into a conventional family psychoeducation program may reduce the expressed emotions of caregivers, especially over-involvement. Further studies should explore how mindfulness-based psychoeducation programs can reduce the impact of psychosis on family with sustainable effects by reducing their burden and expressed emotions with a rigorous study and adequate sample size.

15604118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15604118.value: Further studies may consider adjusting the inclusion criteria to include caregivers whose family member’s onset of psychosis occurred over 3 years. It is likely that families may benefit more from a brief psychoeducation program when their family members with psychosis are in a relatively stable condition. For caregivers of students with recent onset of psychosis, a study on the outcome of a benchmark mindfulness-based program that lasts for 20 hours can be considered. With the adequate sample size, interested researchers should consider inclusion of expressed emotions as mediator and explore its benefits in improving caregiver burden and student recovery outcomes. Additional recruitment strategies such as accessing clinical records of the collaborators should be developed as recruiting young people in recovery is challenging.

15604118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15604118.value: In this study, we investigated the effects of mindfulness-based family psychoeducation on the outcomes of both caregivers and the young adults with early psychosis who had onset in recent three years. Sixty-five caregivers of young adults with psychosis were randomly assigned to mindfulness-based family psychoeducation programme or an ordinary family psychoeducation programme. Among them, 18 young adults in recovery also participated for evaluation of outcomes. No significant effect was found in any of the caregiver outcomes. However, the young adults with psychosis reported higher levels of recovery after their caregivers completed a mindfulness program than those completed an ordinary psychoeducation programme. They also reported significant lower levels of over-involvement of their caregivers. A brief psychoeducation may not be adequate to reduce the burden and improve the mental health of caregivers of individuals who have resent onset of psychosis. However, integrating mindfulness into a conventional family psychoeducation program may reduce the expressed emotions of caregivers, especially over-involvement, that may be critical for relapse prevention of psychosis. Further studies should explore how brief psychoeducation programs can reduce the impact of psychosis on family with sustainable effects in reducing their burden and expressed emotions with a rigorous study and adequate sample size.

15604418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15604418.value: Disaster management includes four phases: preparedness, mitigation, response and recovery. Social workers have long been providing support for survivors in the last two of these phases after disasters. However, little is known about social workers’ involvement in mitigation and preparedness before disasters. Current social work research in disaster management is underdeveloped, and other professionals are unclear about social workers’ role in it. This impedes practice, teaching, research and policymaking for effective work in this important practice area. The overarching purpose of this 36-month project is empirically to develop a core competency framework for social workers in the field of disaster management in China. Specifically, this framework will serve to describe a specific set of values, knowledge and skills that are integral to social work practice at different phases of the disaster management cycle and essential for efficacious practice. We will use a mixed-method research design that includes the use of in-depth interviews in Phase One (P1) with six different Chinese stakeholder groups to examine a taxonomy of unique values, knowledge, and skills that anchor competent social work practice in all phases of the disaster management cycle. This core competency framework for social work practice in China will be developed after completing P1. A Delphi method will be used in Phase Two (P2) to discuss and corroborate the competency framework developed in P1, thereby achieving consensus about it by prioritising and ranking the competencies identified. P2 will involve three panels of 10 to 18 Chinese experts who are academics, practitioners and government officials, including some who were involved in P1, should they agree. This study is designed to develop a scaffolding framework for guiding current social work practice in the disaster management field of China. It aims to inform educational curricula, facilitate research, and provide an integrated knowledge base to formulate policy. Furthermore, the framework may potentially be used by social work accreditation bodies, educators, researchers, regulators and policymakers in China. This could be achieved via the established connections of the PI and second Co-I with the Chinese government (e.g., National Disaster Reduction Center of China), academic institutes (e.g., the China Association of Social Work Education), which have already indicated their support for this study. This could also be a useful resource for international work in this area given the PI’s on-going collaboration with international institutes (e.g., International Association of Schools of Social Work, United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction).

15604418.label: Major findings and research outcome
15604418.value: Although social workers are often deeply involved in disaster management, their distinct roles and tasks in its various phases have not been adequately recognised. This may impede social work training and practice in disaster contexts and particularly in China, which regularly experiences disasters. In this study, we investigated the unique roles and tasks of Chinese social workers in disaster management. We began with an integrative review of 183 international empirical studies and practice reflections, comprising a systematic search, selection, review, and content analysis, guided by ecological systems theory. This rudimentary framework consists of 73 competencies, including 33 micro-level competencies, 18 mesolevel ones and 22 macro-level ones, covering knowledge, values and skills in four disaster management phases. Compared to other competence frameworks, this framework further elucidated and classified the salient knowledge, values, and skills in disaster management training and practice for social work. Our rudimentary competence framework for social work in disaster management based on the integrative review, includes 73 competencies in three domains (i.e., knowledge, values, and skills) for the four respective phases of disaster management (i.e., mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery). Based on the framework, we conducted a series of in-depth interviews with stakeholders including front line social workers, academics, government officials, other professionals and survivors, and a content analysis. A purposeful sampling method was used to locate potential interviewees by targeting stakeholders who (i) had sufficient first-hand experience of working with social workers in Chinese disaster management and (ii) were familiar with the specific cultural, social, political and economic contexts. We recruited thirty-two interviewees including: thirteen front line social workers, five social work academics, three local government officials, six other professionals (two doctors, a nurse, a geologist and a psychologist) and five earthquake survivors. Their average experience working with social workers in Chinese disaster management was about seven years. Three key social worker roles and tasks in the field of disaster management were identified: Key Role 1: Social workers as conduits for different disciplines, sectors and stakeholders Key Role 2: Social workers as strategic mediators between the government and residents Key Role 3: Social workers as psychosocial support providers at different levels Following the interviews, three-round Delphi study involving 25 Delphi panelists was conducted. A final framework based on the integrative review, in-depth interviews and the three-round Delphi study was developed. Using the generic social work competence framework and the disaster management cycle, all competencies were classified according to knowledge, values and skills under all phases, in addition to mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery. A further thematic analysis found four interconnected themes related to disaster resilience building and social justice at various phases of disaster management.

15604418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15604418.value: This ground-breaking competence framework could serve as an important reference for Chinese social work practice and training in disaster management, which could enable Chinese social workers to articulate their professional roles and tasks in disaster contexts. Moreover, this framework is expected to enhance transdisciplinary collaboration among social workers and various stakeholders in disaster management, and could be useful for developing social work core competencies beyond China.

15604418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15604418.value: Social workers have important role in disaster management. However, little is known about the specific skill sets and attitudes that help them achieve this role. We examined the ?core competence? of social workers who engaged in disaster management. First we conducted a thorough review of the academic papers and reports in this area. Then we interviewed experienced and knowledgeable people in the area. Based on what we found, we consulted professionals to arrive at a consensus and propose a model suitable for perfecting social workers? work in disaster management.

15604618.label: Realisation of objectives
15604618.value: Using random sampling from all secondary schools in Hong Kong, we successfully recruited 20 schools to participate in the project. The number of participating schools was greater than in the proposal (N = 9), due to more schools showing interest and providing their consent to join the project. Therefore, after obtaining consent forms from schools, parents, and students, a total of 1,896 Secondary One students (age = 13.19 ± 0.52 years; 911 girls and 985 boys) completed the Wave 1 questionnaire survey between February and June, 2019. All 20 participating schools had agreed to join the Wave 2 data collection, originally scheduled to be conducted from February to June of 2020. However, the unexpected outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 caused the suspension of face-to-face teaching and the lockdown of almost all schools in Hong Kong in the second semester of the 2019/20 academic year. Under these circumstances, and despite the effort of the research team in communicating with the schools, only 12 schools agreed to continue participating in our Wave 2 survey and the data collection dates were postponed to June to September 2020. During the limited time when the schools reopened, 1,169 Secondary Two students (age = 15.19 ± 0.53 years; 602 girls and 546 boys) completed our Wave 2 survey in classroom settings. The number of schools participating in both waves of data collection (N = 12) remained larger than the original number of participating schools in our proposal (N = 9). A final matched dataset is consisted of 878 cases who completed both waves of survey. The first objective was fully achieved. We analyzed both waves of data to examine the cross-sectional relationships between positive youth development (PYD) attributes and adolescent social networking addiction (SNA). Based on the matched dataset we further examined the predictive effects of 15 PYD attributes on the adolescents' SNA across two waves of longitudinal study using the static score model of change. First, Wave 1 cross-sectional data suggested that students’ belief in the future (β = -.11, p < .01) and in spirituality (β = -.11, p < .01) were negatively associated with SNA, while social competence (β = .08, p < .05) and positive identity (β = .10, p < .05) were positively related to SNA. Second, Wave 2 cross-sectional data showed that students' behavioral competence (β = -.20, p < .001) and belief in the future (β = -.17, p < .001) were negatively associated with SNA, while positive identity (β = .14, p < .05) was positively related to SNA. Third, when we used Wave 1 PYD attributes and changes in PYD attributes across the two waves to predict SNA in Wave 2 after controlling for participants' age and gender, the results suggested: 1) Behavioral competence (β = -.20, p = .01)) and belief in the future (β = -.14, p = .05) in Wave 1 were negatively related to SNA in Wave 2. 2) Self-efficacy (β = .17, p < .05) in Wave 1 was positively related to SNA in Wave 2. 3) Changes in belief in the future (β = -.16, p = .01) across the two waves were negatively associated with SNA in Wave 2. 4) Changes in clear and positive identity (β = .22, p < .01) across the two waves were positively associated with SNA in Wave 2. These findings suggest that adolescents' behavioral competence and their belief in the future play an important protective role in preventing them from excessively using SNSs and services, even during the pandemic. However, a high level of self-efficacy and enhanced positive identity appeared to predict more SNA behavior among Hong Kong adolescents. The second objective was to investigate the impact of general and Internet-specific parenting behavior on adolescent SNA in terms of three specific research questions (RQ). For RQ1, regression analysis based on Wave 1 data was first conducted. The results suggested that paternal responsiveness (β = -.09, p < .05) and maternal demandingness (β = -.10, p < .01) were negatively associated with students’ SNA. Wave 2 cross-sectional data showed that paternal responsiveness (β = -.10, p < .05) and maternal responsiveness (β = -.09, p < .05) were negatively associated with students' SNA, while the relationship between maternal demandingness and SNA became non-significant. Based on the two-wave cross-lagging models, we further tested the predictive effects of general parenting behavior on adolescents' SNA across time. The results suggest that after controlling for the effects of age and gender as well as the auto-regressive effects, there are significant mutual effects between paternal responsiveness and adolescents' SNA, and between maternal responsiveness and adolescents' SNA. Specifically, both paternal responsiveness (β = -.13, p < .001) and maternal responsiveness in Wave 1 (β = .07, p < .05) significantly predicted adolescents’ SNA in Wave 2. On the other hand, adolescents’ SNA in Wave 1 also significantly predicted paternal responsiveness (β = -.05, p < .05) and maternal responsiveness (β = -.05, p < .05). RQ2 focuses on the relationships between parental Internet-specific parenting behavior (i.e., restrictive mediation, active mediation, and the co-use of the Internet) and adolescents' SNA. Regression analysis based on Wave 1 cross-sectional data was first conducted to evaluate the association between Internet-specific parenting behavior and adolescents’ SNA. The results suggested that only parental own use of the Internet and social media (β = .21, p < .001) was positively associated with adolescents’ SNA, while parental restrictive mediation and active mediation had no significant relationship with adolescents' SNA. Wave 2 cross-sectional data showed that parental restrictive mediation (β = .07, p < .05) and parental own use of the Internet and social media (β = .16, p < .01) were positively associated with students’ SNA, while the relationship between parental active mediation and SNA were non-significant. Based on the two-wave cross-lagging model, we further tested the relationships between Internet-specific parenting behavior and adolescents’ SNA over time. After controlling for the effects of age and gender, as well as the auto-regressive effects of variables, only parental own Internet and social media use behavior in Wave 1 significantly predicted adolescents’ SNA at Wave 2 (β = .07, p < .05); other regression coefficients were non-significant. RQ3 addresses the moderating effects of general parenting behavior on the relationship between Internet-specific parenting behavior and adolescents' SNA. Similar to the previous process, we analyzed Wave 1 and Wave 2 data and the two-wave data using Wave 2 SNA as the outcome variable, general parenting behavior in Wave 1 as the moderator, and Internet-specific parenting behavior in Wave 1 as the predictor. The results of structural equation modeling consistently showed that general parenting behavior (paternal and maternal responsiveness and demandingness) did not moderate any of the relationships between Internet-specific parenting behavior and adolescents’ SNA. As our second wave of data collection occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, other personal (such as mental health status) and contextual factors (such as online learning requirements and peer influence) may play a more important role in mitigating adolescents’ overuse of social networking sites and services than does Internet-specific parenting behavior. Despite the fact that the present findings do not provide empirical support to our original hypothesis, the third research question of Objective 2 has been well addressed.

15604618.label: Major findings and research outcome
15604618.value: The present project revealed that behavioral competence, belief in the future, emotional competence, and spirituality are important positive youth development attributes that are conducive to the prevention and reduction of social networking addiction (SNA). In particular, longitudinal data analysis suggests the important protective role of positive development in behavioral competence (the ability to make effective behavioral choices and perform socially acceptable behavior) and belief in the future (having valued and attainable goals and positive expectancies for the future) in reducing Hong Kong adolescents’ SNA behavior over time, even in the face of life adversities such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, we found that positive identity and self-efficacy positively predicted SNA behavior longitudinally, which seems to suggest that high self-esteem, exploration, and commitment to self-definition during early adolescence may result in more SNA behavior. Secondly, both our cross-sectional and longitudinal data analysis showed that paternal and maternal responsiveness were negatively associated with adolescents’ social networking addictive behavior, while on the other hand, neither paternal nor maternal demandingness exerted significant effects on adolescents’ SNA. Cross-lagged modeling further suggests a mutual effect between parental responsiveness and adolescents’ SNA: both paternal responsiveness (β = -.13, p < .001) and maternal responsiveness in Wave 1 (β = .07, p < .05) significantly predicted adolescents’ SNA in Wave 2, and adolescents’ SNA in Wave 1 also significantly predicted paternal responsiveness (β = -.05, p < .05) and maternal responsiveness (β = -.05, p < .05). In terms of Internet-specific parenting behavior, cross-sectional data in both waves indicate a positive relationship between parental own use of social media and the Internet and adolescents’ SNA, while in Wave 2, parental restrictive mediation was also positively related to adolescents’ SNA. Cross-lagged modeling further revealed that only parental own Internet and social media use behavior significantly predicted adolescents’ SNA (β = .07, p < .05). Parental active mediation and restrictive mediation failed to predict changes in adolescents’ SNA. Lastly, structural equation modeling based on the two waves of data showed that although paternal and maternal responsiveness consistently predicted a reduction of SNA, general parenting behavior did not moderate the relationship between parental restrictive or active mediation and adolescents’ SNA. It is speculated that other personal and contextual factors (such as mental health status, online learning, peer influence) may play a more important role in affecting adolescents’ SNA than parental Internet-specific behavior during the pandemic.

15604618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15604618.value: First, based on the present findings, we aim to develop an e-learning program that incorporates components of behavioral competence training specifically focusing on social media and Internet use and reflective activities that guide youths to develop a sense of meaning in life and a positive belief in the future. This program can either be used as a stand-alone program to prevent SNA or can be integrated into other existing PYD programs to prevent youth problems in general. The finding that paternal responsiveness consistently predicted less SNA behavior highlights the importance of fathers' emotional support and responsiveness in youth development. We will further disseminate the findings in journal publications, conferences, and reports to advocate for more strategies to support and empower fathers to actively participate in their children's education. Several lines of in-depth investigation into the mechanism underlying the unexpected findings will also be conducted. We will propose a qualitative study that focuses on families of adolescents who use SNSs regularly but in a controllable manner, to examine what parental behavior contributes to adolescents’ healthy use of SNSs. We will also examine how a clear and positive identity is associated with SNA and other problem behavior during adolescence through qualitative methods.

15604618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15604618.value: Based on a two-year longitudinal study using a stratified sample of Hong Kong secondary school students, we investigated the effects of a range of important positive youth development (PYD) attributes on adolescent social networking addiction (SNA) and examined the roles of both general parenting behavior and Internet-specific parental practice, (i.e., parental mediation) in adolescent SNA. The findings provide important empirical evidence on the protective effects of adolescents’ behavioral competence, belief in the future, and paternal and maternal responsiveness in preventing SNA, which helps us to understand SNA from a non-pathological perspective. The identification of these PYD attributes and positive parenting behavior as protective factors of SNA also shed light on the development of innovative prevention programs based on a PYD approach and evidence-informed parental training. Our findings lay the foundations for several important lines of future research. First, when parental mediation is ineffective in preventing adolescent SNA, we must identify what specific parenting practices can help. Second, the role of parental demandingness on youths’ SNA should be re-examined especially in the context of the contemporary information society. Third, the second wave of data we collected will help us explore other personal and contextual factors that affect adolescents’ SNA during the pandemic.
