15610218.label: Major findings and research outcome
15610218.value: The study found that community facility resources are not equitably distributed between neighborhoods with high socio-economic status and low socio-economic status. This study also identified three barriers of capabilities of older people to use community facilities. First, older people’s right to community facilities is violated during the urban renewal process in urban old districts. Second, the transit-oriented development mode results in inequitable provision of community facility resources between neighborhoods located close to or distant from metro stations. Third, older people living in neighborhoods distant from metro stations may have a lower level of mobility to gain access to alternative community facilities. (Research output 1) This study illustrated that older people’s usage and frequency of visiting community facilities mainly depended on the purpose of the visits and the activities the facilities provided. Planning and design quality variables played a less important role in older people’s frequency of visiting community facilities. Facility size, diversity, and proximity to other amenities were three important factors that impacted older people’s subjective experience with using most types of community facilities. (Research output 2) Regarding mobility, perceived public transport and satisfaction with public transport would affect older people’s use of community facilities. Satisfaction levels with public transport were also found to affect older people’s satisfaction with using community facilities. In addition, satisfaction levels with using community facilities and walking environments would affect older people’s neighborhood satisfaction. Besides, insufficient provision of community facilities may be related to longer moving distances, moving time, and larger daily activity space, especially for commercial, cultural, and religious facilities. It is also found that sufficient provision of community service facilities could help to increase older people’s out-of-home activity level. (Research output 4) In terms of the built environment of the community, land use diversity has a negative effect on satisfaction with community facilities. Regarding socio-demographics, proportion of elderly in a neighbourhood, the socio-economic status of the neighbourhood and the age of the older people affect older people’s satisfaction with community facilities, physical well-being, psychological well-being and overall satisfaction with the neighbourhood differently. Overall, a strong social network could increase older people’s neighborhood satisfaction, psychological well-being, and capability well-being. (Research output 3) In sum, the study illustrated that increasing older people satisfaction level with community facilities is much more important than the mere provision of community facilities or encouraging usage in enhancing older people’s neighborhood satisfaction and well-being.

15610218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15610218.value: As the study indicates walking environment is a key issue to older people’s usage of community facilities and well-being,future studies could examine how and to what extent the walkability of the community could support older people’s use of community facilities. The advanced technology, such as street view image analysis using machine learning could be used to capture objective pedestrian environment characteristics. The 3D pedestrian network could be used to understand older people’s actual walking behaviors. Regarding the methodology, possible refinement could be made in future study. First, the accuracy of GPS data in the context of compact urban environments and recall bias of self-reports of the usage pattern of community facilities collected from a questionnaire survey could be minimsed by using both the GPS method and a travel diary. Second, mobile phone data could be used to overcome the relatively small sample size of GPS data. Third, older people’s health status measured by the SF-12 questionnaire relies on subjective evaluation of their general health status which may not be directly related to older people’s mobility (motility). Future studies could use the objective evaluation method to assess mobility-related health status.

15610218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15610218.value: This research develops a novel framework for understanding community facility planning and older people’s well-being by adopting and extending the Capability Approach theory originated from the welfare economics discipline. The evaluation framework can help planners better distribute community facility resources. A mixed methods research design, including both qualitative research methods (focus group meeting and expert interview) and quantitative research methods (spatial analysis, GPS experiment, and questionnaire survey), is employed in this research. The provision of community facility resources indirectly affects older people’s well-being by affecting their usage of and satisfaction with community facilities. Mobility is identified as older people’s capability to use community facilities and promote their well-being, especially in walking environments and out-of-home activity levels. The perceived built environment is identified as the significant factor that helps older people convert community facility resources to well-being. Theoretically, it provides a novel framework to understand the planning and design of different types of community facilities and their effect on neighborhood satisfaction and well-being. It also provides essential principles for community facility planning and design to help urban planners enhance aging-in-place in the neighborhood and improve older people’s well-being.

16100318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16100318.value: Plant cells are able to perceive diverse force stimuli from strong winds, heavy rain, herbivore and pathogen attack, and crowding by neighboring plants in ways that enable their acclimation to local environments. Touch is a unique form of force signal because such physical perturbation is associated with environmental forces. In response to touch, plants undergo touch-induced developmental and morphological changes, called thigmomorphogenesis, that confer enhanced resistance to herbivores and wind. Furthermore, root growth is also guided by touch and normally moves away from physical barriers via thigmotropism. In thigmonasty, a touch-induced organ movement is important for tendril curling and/or leaf movements. Although the expression of more than 2.5% of genes of Arabidopsis, a model plant species, are rapidly up-regulated in response to mechanical stimulation, the mechano-sensors and force-signaling components responsible for mechanotransduction are largely unknown. To address such interesting and complex phenomena, we previously performed a high-throughput SILIA (stable isotope labeling in Arabidopsis)-based quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis to profile the protein phosphorylation changes that result from 40 seconds of force stimulation in Arabidopsis. A total of 24 mechano-responsive phosphopeptides were identified, and many were putative kinases, phosphatases, cytoskeleton proteins and transporters. The consequent multidisciplinary molecular biological investigations have confirmed that protein phosphorylation is an essential component in mechano-responses in Arabidopsis (Figure 1). In this proposed project, quantitative phosphoproteomics, molecular genetics, cell biology and bioinformatics will be adopted in combination to identity mechano-responsive membrane phosphoproteins, to study phosphor-relay-mediated force signaling in the Arabidopsis mechano-response and to identify force signaling components, probably novel force receptors. To that end, we propose (1) to identify mechanostimulation rapidly (20 seconds) regulated membrane phosphoproteins using quantitative phosphoproteins; (2) to perform molecular, cellular and genetic studies of mechano-responsive membrane phosphoproteins and to identify their interacting proteins that mediate force signaling in the Arabidopsis mechano-response; (3) to identify TREPH1-, TREPH3- or MKK2-interacting proteins using quantitative interactomics; and (4) to investigate the relationship between the putative sodium-pump activities of TREPH3 and the Arabidopsis mechano-response. The study of the functions of these phosphorylated mechano-responsive phosphoproteins in mechanotransduction will provide information on the molecular mechanisms and post-translational modification (PTM) network that underlie mechanotransduction in thigmotropism, thigmonasty and thigmomorphogenesis. The outcome of this study will contribute to the development of a model of molecular systems biology and possibly application of the findings to improve crop productivity for food, bioremediation and bioenergy.

16100418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16100418.value: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a major form of dementia characterized by progressive memory loss and cognitive impairment. The three pathological hallmarks of AD are amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptide deposition, neurofibrillary tangles, and neuroinflammation. The impairment of Aβ clearance due to the disturbance or loss of microglial homeostasis, including reduced Aβ phagocytosis, results in Aβ accumulation in the brain. In turn, Aβ accumulation activates microglia and other cell types, resulting in chronic neuroinflammation in AD. Emerging studies have revealed that modulating microglial polarization and activation alleviates the pathogenesis of AD. For example, injection of interleukin-33 in AD transgenic APP/PS1 mice switches the phenotype of microglia from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory, suggesting that restoring microglial homeostasis may retard AD pathogenesis. While the transcriptional program controls microglial dysregulation, the detailed mechanisms underlying the transition of microglial phenotypes in AD are unclear. In the study proposed herein, we will characterize the transition of microglial phenotypes in AD as well as investigate the epigenetic and transcriptional control of microglial dysregulation in AD progression. First, we will examine the transcriptional signatures of different microglial subpopulations in AD and determine the association between the subpopulation changes and AD progression. Next, we will examine the stimuli that trigger the microglial dysregulation in APP/PS1 mouse brains and determine how their regulation is associated with the changes of homeostatic and dysregulated microglia subpopulations. We will also study the epigenetic and transcriptomic control of microglial dysregulation in APP/PS1 mice by profiling the chromatin accessibility, transcription factor-binding, and transcriptome in the brain at different ages. Finally, we will examine the associations of the epigenetic and transcriptomic changes with AD pathology using a systems approach by analyzing dysregulated pathways in microglia in APP/PS1 mice. The findings of the proposed study will contribute to our understanding of the initial microglial dysregulation in AD and elucidate how the epigenetic and transcriptomic changes in microglia result in AD pathology. Furthermore, the findings can provide insights for the development of novel AD therapies that restore homeostatic microglial function.

16100418.label: Realisation of objectives
16100418.value: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) suggested that microglia play a critical role in AD pathology. Microglia play major roles in maintaining brain homeostasis. Perturbation of homeostasis due to the accumulation of misfolded proteins such as beta-amyloid (Aβ, one of the pathological hallmarks of AD) triggers the microglial activation, which adopt a phagocytic phenotype in order to restrain cytotoxicity and limit damage to surrounding cells. Prolonged Aβ exposure leads to the microglial dysfunction, characterized by failed Aβ clearance and increase in inflammatory cytokine secretion, causing severe damage to neural cells. On the other hand, many factors have been identified with the ability to restore the homeostatic function of microglia. However, it remains unclear how microglia change their functional phenotypes under AD pathogenesis. Understanding the molecular basis that underlies the phenotypic transition of microglia in AD is critical for studying AD pathogenesis. Previously, we demonstrated that enhancing interleukin (IL)-33 signaling ameliorate amyloid pathology in various AD transgenic mouse models (Fu et al., 2016). Here, we examine how this signaling influences the regulatory mechanisms underlying the functional changes of microglia in AD pathogenesis. IL-33 injection enhances the co-localization of microglia with Aβ plaques and promotes Aβ clearance. Here, we further demonstrated that IL-33 regulates the dynamic interaction of microglia with Aβ plaques. We performed time-lapse in vivo two-photon imaging of microglia and Aβ deposition in APP/PS1;Cx3cr1eYFP mice (10–12 months old), in which the morphological changes of microglia can be traced via expression of the green fluorescent protein. The chemotactic response of a subpopulation of microglia to Aβ plaques was significantly enhanced in IL-33-administered AD mice when compared with AD mice. This microglial subpopulation migrated closer to the nearby Aβ plaques after IL-33 injection. Collectively, IL-33 enhances the Aβ chemotactic responses of a microglial subpopulation, resulting in their recruitment to Aβ plaques. Recent studies revealed a microglial subpopulation, known as disease-associated microglia (DAM), in AD transgenic mouse model to be associated with Aβ-plaque and acquires a distinct transcriptome profile characterized by the expression of DAM markers (e.g., Cst7). Consistently, our RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis showed that IL-33 injection also increased the number of DAMs that were associated with Aβ plaques. The functional changes in microglial subpopulations are driven by the changes of their transcriptome profiles. Since IL-33 induces a microglial subpopulation with enhanced chemotactic and phagocytic activity, we examined the regulation of the microglial transcriptome in APP/PS1 mice upon IL-33 injection. We conducted single-cell transcriptome sequencing analysis of the microglial cells (i.e., CD11b+) in the forebrain of APP/PS1 mice. Consistent with other findings, unsupervised clustering of CD11b+ cells using the t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding algorithm identified two unique microglial clusters based on transcriptome signatures: DAMs and homeostatic microglia. IL-33 increased the expression of genes that are associated with antigen presentation (e.g., Cd74, H2-Ab1 and H2-Eb1) and actin filament organization, while reducing those associated with lipid metabolism in microglia in APP/PS1 mice. Moreover, IL-33-induced transcriptional changes in the microglia of APP/PS1 mice were negatively correlated with the changes in microglial gene expression as induced by Aβ deposition, suggesting that IL-33 was able to restore some of these transcriptomic changes. The restoration was not due to a decrease in the DAM proportion in APP/PS1 mice after IL-33 injection. To understand the transcriptome reprogramming in microglial subpopulations induced by IL-33, we examined the expression changes of the IL-33-induced DEGs at the single-cell level. IL-33 restored the expression of homeostatic signature genes in all microglia. Thus, IL-33 restored the expression of homeostatic signature genes while maintaining the expression of DAM signature genes in the DAM subpopulation. Interestingly, IL-33 specifically induced the expression of major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-II genes (i.e., Cd74, H2-Ab1, and H2-Eb1) in a DAM subpopulation that co-expressed the homeostatic signature genes, which we termed IL-33RMs. This subpopulation is a transcriptionally distinct microglial subpopulation when compared to the other MHC-II+ microglia previously reported. Multiplex FISH analysis confirmed IL-33 injection significantly increased the proportion of H2-Ab1+ Cst7+ Cx3cr1+ microglia (i.e., IL-33RMs) in APP/PS1 mice. Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis showed that only few microglia express MHC-II in APP/PS1 mice, while IL-33 significantly increased the proportion of MHC-II+ microglia. As MHC-II is a microglial activation marker, our data show that IL-33RMs represent a subpopulation of activated DAMs that co-expresses homeostatic signature genes. We further compared the transcriptome profile of IL-33RMs with that of the MHC-II− DAMs or homeostatic microglia in the APP/PS1 mice following IL-33 injection. The enriched genes in IL-33RMs were found to be associated with angiogenesis, antigen presentation (e.g., H2-Aa and H2-Eb1), and endocytosis, highlighting their role in phagocytic response. These highlighted pathways support the notion that IL-33RMs adopt phenotypes characterized by enhanced chemotaxis and phagocytosis. This is concordant with the function of MHC-II in antigen presentation, during which degraded proteins are presented on the cell surface after phagocytosis. We then investigated how IL-33RMs interact with Aβ plaques. IHC analysis revealed that most of the IL-33-induced MHC-II+ microglia were associated with Aβ plaques. Meanwhile, the proportion of Aβ plaque-associated MHC-II− microglia remained relatively unchanged in the IL-33-injected APP/PS1 mice. Moreover, IL-33 increased the proportion of MHC-II+ microglial cells with Aβ phagocytic activity, as well as enhancing the Aβ phagocytic capacity than that in MHC-II− microglia. In addition, these Aβ plaque-associated MHC-II+ microglial subpopulations exhibited higher lysosomal content than the MHC-II− microglia. Thus, we demonstrate that IL-33RMs possess higher Aβ phagocytic capacity than that of other microglial subpopulations. Collectively, these findings demonstrated that IL-33-induced transcriptional regulation of microglial functional transition contributes to the alleviation of AD pathology. As the transcriptome profile of microglia is critical in determining microglial functions, we examined the differences in transcriptome and molecular pathways for microglia in the prefrontal cortex of AD patients (n = 12) versus normal control (NC; n = 9) subjects using single-nuclei RNA-sequencing analysis. Unbiased uniform manifold approximation and projection clustering determined 6 major cell types including astrocytes, endothelial cells, excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, microglia and oligodendrocytes. Among these cell types, microglia as identified by their signature marker, C3+, occupied ~5% of whole cell population. The proportions of microglia were similar between the AD and NC brain samples. We have also identified some novel human microglial markers, including Lrmda and Dock8As. As changes in molecular phenotypes provide insights into the functional changes in individual cell types, we functionally annotated the DEGs associated with AD in microglia by performing pathway analysis. We identified 340 DEGs in microglia between the AD and NC brain samples, and found that the DEGs in microglia were mainly associated with immune response. Further subcluster analysis of the microglial data identified 13 subpopulations; only 3 of them contributed to the transcriptomic changes in microglia in AD. Compared to the NC samples, the AD samples exhibited a smaller proportion for one of the three subpopulations, which expresses genes encode complement component 1q and cytokine response. Given that aberrant complement signaling mediates synaptic pruning via phagocytosis, our results suggest that the loss of this particular microglial subpopulation can contribute to the imbalanced complement signaling and synaptic pruning observed in AD. As a conclusion, our results provide more understanding on the molecular mechanisms and functional changes in microglia during AD pathogenesis.

16100418.label: Major findings and research outcome
16100418.value: This study aimed to understand the functional changes of microglia and examine the associated underlying molecular regulatory mechanisms that contribute to AD pathogenesis. Our major findings and research outcomes are as follows: IL-33 signaling mediates a disease-associated microglia (DAM) subpopulation with enhanced chemotactic and phagocytic activities: enhancing IL-33 signaling in the brain ameliorates amyloid-associated pathology via modulated chemotactic and phagocytic activities of a microglial subpopulation, which we termed IL33-RMs (Lau et al., 2021a). In vivo imaging revealed that IL-33 directs the IL33-RM subpopulation toward amyloid plaques with greater mobility. IHC together with flow cytometry analyses also revealed that IL-33 induces IL33-RMs that are closely associated with amyloid plaques, while enhancing their phagocytic capacity and activity. Our finding further demonstrates that reprogramming of the transcriptomic profiles of DAM induces the differentiation of a DAM subpopulation with enhanced phagocytic activity. We examined the microglial transcriptomic changes in WT and APP/PS1 mice at the single-cell level after IL-33 treatment. We found that IL-33 signals drive a DAM subpopulation (the IL-33RMs) that expresses a distinct transcriptome signature highlighted by increased expression of major histocompatibility complex class II genes and restored expression of homeostatic signature genes (Lau et al., 2021a). These transcriptomic changes direct the IL-33RMs towards a chemotactic response state, exhibiting increased migration towards Aβ plaques and enhanced Aβ clearance activity. Meanwhile, we also examined the molecular changes in microglia in AD patients. We undertook snRNA-seq analysis on the postmortem prefrontal cortices of AD patients and normal controls, and observed the presence of major deregulated molecular pathways in the microglia of the AD patients. After identifying the DEGs using this approach, we found that such dysregulated pathways are involved in immune activation and synaptic pruning activity (Lau et al 2021c). Moreover, a change in the proportion of microglial subpopulations is shown between AD patients and NC individuals, suggesting dysregulated microglial differentiation.

16100418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16100418.value: In this study, we showed that administering IL-33 in the APP/PS1 AD transgenic mouse model enhances microglial chemotactic response and Aβ clearance capacity. Our current transcriptomic analysis at the single-cell level suggests that the transition from DAM subpopulation to IL-33-RMs represents a microglial state transition, from partially restoring the homeostatic state to the chemotactic state and finally the phagocytic state. These microglia migrate towards and uptake the Aβ plaques. To better understand the regulatory mechanisms underlying how IL-33 mediates these molecular and functional state transitions in microglia, we are in the process of dissecting the temporal transcriptional regulatory network underlying the microglial state transition upon IL-33 administration. Moreover, we have performed ATAC-Seq (assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing) to identify the transcriptional regulation of the microglial state transitions induced by IL-33 and the involvement of transcription factors (TFs) in the process. The involvement of several candidate TF families, including AP-1, PU.1, C/EBP, and NF-κB, have been suggested. Mass spectrometry and immunohistochemical analyses of transgenic mouse models are in progress to illustrate which TF candidates are critical for such state transition of microglia. Further analysis will be performed to determine how the candidate TFs are regulated in microglia in AD pathogenesis and whether they are critical for mediating microglial state transitions. This will be achieved through manipulating expression of the candidate TFs in AD transgenic mouse models.

16100418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16100418.value: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia. However, there is no effective treatment for AD, due to an incomplete understanding of molecular basis underlying the cell type-specific responses during AD pathogenesis. One of the pathological hallmarks of AD is the deposition of amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides. Impairment of the microglial clearance of Aβ is one of the major causes for the detrimental effects on neuronal communication hence neuronal health. In the current study, our group demonstrated that a cytokine, interleukin-33 (IL-33), ameliorates Aβ pathology through enhancing microglial Aβ clearance capacity in an AD transgenic mouse model, APP/PS1. The underlying molecular mechanisms were delineated through the temporal and spatial analysis of the microglial gene expression profiles at the single-cell level — IL-33 stimulates the differentiation of a subpopulation of microglia to adopt different molecular states, characterized by a chemotactic state followed by a phagocytic state. Thus, IL-33 treatment stimulates microglia to migrate towards and carry out the phagocytic uptake of Aβ plaques, resulting in a decrease in Aβ deposition and related pathology. In sum, this study provides new understanding of the modulation of microglial functional states through the reprogramming of gene expression profiles, providing insights into therapeutic development for AD.

16100718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16100718.value: Ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare recessively inherited disorder resulting from mutations in the ATM gene. The loss of ATM function results in a debilitating multi-system disease. Among all possible symptoms, the most taunting clinical feature is progressive ataxia resulting from the Purkinje cell degeneration in early childhood. Currently, there is no therapy to cure the progression of cerebellar degeneration, nor does the field understands the ties between ATM loss and the underlying cause of pronounced vulnerability observed in the Purkinje cells. Anatomically, Purkinje cells are one of the largest neurons. Upon receiving about 200,000 synaptic connections from the neighboring granule neurons, Purkinje cells fire synchronously forming one of the most powerful connections in the nervous system. This renders them with an exceptionally high oxygen and metabolic demand in order to sustain such intense synaptic activities; but it also implies that they are particularly vulnerable to oxidative stress and metabolic insufficiency. By analyzing a public disease database and our own human A-T cerebella expression array dataset, we revealed that cerebellar atrophy but not other common symptoms of A-T are highly associated with metabolic defects resulting from dysfunctional mitochondria, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). This leads to ATM-deficient neurons with impaired capacities to enhance ATP production in response to increased energy demands upon sustained neuronal activities. Mechanistically, systems analyses using the array dataset indicated that loss of activity of nuclear respiratory factor-1 (NRF1) is the most likely link underlying the global changes in gene expression observed in A-T. NRF1 is a classic trans-activator of nuclear-encoded respiratory genes. Our preliminary data suggested that NRF1 is a novel target of ATM, and its phosphorylation by ATM enhanced its homo-dimerization and nuclear localisation. In addition, ATM can be activated by mitochondrial oxidative stress, which can be induced during ATP insufficiency. Taken together, these data suggested ATM may well facilitate the mito-nuclear communication in response to changes in cellular energy demand. Our first goal is to conduct detailed analyses on changes in the OXPHOS system, TCA cycle landscape and the overall mitochondrial physiology in ATM-deficient neurons. Secondly, we will perform biochemical analyses to elucidate how ATM modulates NRF1 transcriptional activities. Finally, a follow-up metabolomic study on the role of glutamine supplementation in preventing degeneration of ATM-deficient neurons will also be performed. Our long-term goal is to propose dietary interventions as a potential strategy to prevent or act against progressive ataxia in A-T. 共濟失調毛細血管擴張症候群 （A-T） 是一種由ATM基因突變引發的罕見隱性遺傳疾病。症狀一般會累及神經、血管、皮膚、免疫細胞等系統；當中以小腦區浦金氏神經細胞病變所引起的小腦運動失調為最主要的問題。此症狀可能早在患者童年時已出現，繼而其步態及軀幹上的運動失調會加劇惡化而至喪失活動能力。現時並沒有可以控制或根治有關小腦區退化的方案，而醫學界亦無法解釋在腦部所有細胞都遺傳了ATM基因突變時，只有小腦區浦金氏神經細胞出現明顯退化。從解剖學上分析，浦金氏細胞是腦部中體積最大的神經細胞。在神經訊息傳遞層面上，浦金氏細胞會在接收約200,000個由相鄰顆粒神經元發送出的突觸連接後，在同一時間與多個浦金氏細胞釋放出強大訊號。為了維持這種密集式的訊息傳遞模式，浦金氏細胞對能量、氧氣及代謝的需求均十分高；但這亦意味它們對代謝機能不全及過氧壓力特別敏感。我們的研究團隊通過分析公共疾病數據庫以及人類A-T小腦轉錄組數據，發現在各種症狀中，只有與小腦退化相關症狀與TCA循環和氧化磷酸化（OXPHOS）這兩大線粒體代謝功能不全有莫大的關聯。綜合以上缺陷，我們發現A-T神經元無法有效補充及支持訊息傳遞活動時對能量的需求，繼而陷入能量長期處於不足狀態而凋亡。在分子機理層面上，我們以人類A-T小腦轉錄組的數據進行系統性分析，發現核呼吸因子-1 （NRF1）為A-T小腦轉錄組變化中最強的聯繫。核呼吸因子-1是調控核編碼中與線粒體相關功能的重要轉錄子。我們的數據表明核呼吸因子-1可被ATM磷酸化，繼而促進其同二聚化及核定位反應。同時，我們在正常的細胞中發現，ATM會在細胞能量水平不足時所產生的自由基而激活。總括而言，ATM的活性及下游反應是作為細胞核與線粒體間調節能量代謝功能的重要通訊橋樑。在這建議書中，我們的研究目標為：在A-T神經元中，對TCA循環和氧化磷酸化，及線粒體的功能進行全面的分析。其次，我們將以分子生物及生物化學技術闡明ATM如何調節核呼吸因子-1 （NRF1）的轉錄活性。最後，我們會延續谷氨酰胺（Glutamine）在A-T小鼠中有效延遲浦金氏神經細胞病變的相關的代謝組學研究。長遠來說，我們希望從營養學的角度提出一個能有效控制及緩和A-T小腦運動失調及退化的方案。

16100718.label: Realisation of objectives
16100718.value: Objective 1— To perform detailed analysis on changes in the OXPHOS system, TCA cycle landscape, metabolomics profile and overall physiology of mitochondria in neurons of ATM knockout mice (A) Published data—We have successfully published the part of data related to changes in OXPHOS system, TCA cycle landscape and overall physiology of mitochondria in neurons of ATM knockout mice in the Journal of Cell Biology (Research Output: Item 1). There, we reported that (1) reduced expression and function of metabolic enzymes in the TCA cycle and OXPHOS system is associated with the lack of ATM, this situation is reflected as (2) an impaired mitochondrial respiratory response to enhanced energy demand, particularly at times after sustained firing of neurons. In cells lacking ATM, cells replenish ATP poorly and chronic ATP insufficiency endangers cell survival. Since ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is the autosomal genetic disease associated with ATM gene loss-in-function mutations, all cells inside the body are expected to face such metabolic challenges. In attempt to explain how the cerebellar Purkinje cells—the type of neurons that are mostly affected in the genetic disease, leading to ataxic phenotype in ALL the A-T patients, we have adopted a computational modelling approach, which illustrated that among all major types of neurons in the brain, Purkinje cells are the one with the highest energy demand—at nearly 3.5-fold higher than the next kind of neuron at the rank. These together explained how the cerebellar Purkinje cells became the most vulnerable in the brain when all other brain cells are facing the same kind of metabolic challenges in the absence of ATM. All these data are published in Research Output: Item 1. The experimental platforms established from this objective also contributed to other projects and be acknowledged in Research Output: Item 2-4. (B) Manuscript to-be submitted—For the metabolic profiling part, the task is completed and the associated data will be included in a submitted manuscript by early Jan 2023 (Research Out: Item 5). There, by the global metabolite profiling, ATM-deficient neurons not only revealed a global reduction in glycolytic metabolites, but unexpectedly also multiple lipid-derivatives such as triglycerides, phosphorylcholine, ethanolamine and sphingolipids. Such lack of anabolic capacities indeed could be explained by the compromised insulin response among these cells. We were able to show that Purkinje cells are the only type of neurons in the cerebellum expressing insulin receptors (i.e. INSRβ) and insulin receptor substrates (i.e. IRS-1). Moreover, ATM is insulin-sensitive and could be activated via the physiological H2O2 triggered by the early insulin receptor-NADPH oxidase signalling. Once activated, ATM as a serine-threonine kinase, phosphorylates an array of targets. By SILAC, we identified novel ATM phosphorylation targets under the influence of insulin, most notably the PKM2 and HIF1A—the acute and chronic regulators of aerobic glycolysis (i.e. Warburg effect). PKM2, upon phosphorylation by ATM, showed higher tendencies to enter the nucleus and loss its function as pyruvate kinase, allowing a transient switching from the catabolic-ATP generating towards anabolic-biomass biosynthesis mode. In the absence of ATM, such metabolic switching flexibility is lost. This not only renders the cells at constant catalytic mode, but also incapable to remove and utilize the circulating fuel metabolites from diet, leading a mixed lipodystrophic, insulin resistance, non-alcoholic fatty liver conditions that could be frequently observed in A-T patients. For the ATM phosphorylation effect on HIF1A, the latter becomes more stabilized as a heterodimer with HIF1B and facilitates nuclear entry. However, since physiological insulin signals after meal lasts only for 4-6 hours, versus meaningful events of gene expression to protein translation, in general, takes much longer timespan, the effect of HIF1A on metabolic reprogramming is not as spontaneous and obvious as that of PKM2. However, the changes become significant upon chronic exposure of insulin, i.e. pre-diabetic stage hyperinsulinemia, leading to chronic activation of HIF1A and in that sense, PKM2 can further enhance HIF1A-mediated transcription via serving as co-activator. Multiple downstream targets of HIF1A are involved in glycolysis, adipogenesis and fatty acid metabolism. This facilitates glucose-driven de novo lipid biogenesis, leading to increased fat deposition, lipid accumulation in insulin-sensitive cells that frequently seen in pre-diabetes. Objective 2— To investigate how ATM modulated NRF1 transcriptional activity All the data related to tasks proposed in this objective are published (Research Output: Item 1). We confirmed that NRF1 is a phosphorylation target of ATM when the latter is activated by ATP deficiency-associated oxidative stress (For the sub-objective—Mode of ATM activation in mediating NRF1 phosphorylation). The key site of phosphorylation is located at the T259 residue located within the bromodomain of the protein, which is also the dimerization domain. Phosphorylation of T259 introduces negative charges, this facilitates interaction with the phenyl ring of R255 residue on the opposite monomer (For the sub-objective—Protein biochemistry analysis). This results in homodimerization, nuclear localization and activation of NRF1. NRF1 facilitates the transcription of an array of nuclear genome-encoded mitochondrial genes essential for mitochondrial biogenesis in response to increased energy demands (For the sub-objective—NRF1 functional analysis). Objective 3—To evaluate the metabolomics roles of glutamine supplementation in fulfilling the alternative modes of metabolism adopted by ATM-deficient neurons All the data related to tasks proposed in this objective will be submitted in the upcoming manuscript (Research Output: Item 5). Linking to the unpublished findings from Objective 1 (see above), we performed fuel dependence analysis which confirmed that ATM-deficient neurons switched from glucose-dependence to glutamine-dependence as insulin-induced signalling and the associated glycolytic metabolic network is malfunctioning. Further isotopologue tracing experiments validated such findings. In the absence of insulin stimulus, normal cells utilize glucose as the major carbon source in supporting the TCA cycle and ATP generation. In the contrary, ATM-deficient neurons revealed lower glycolytic capacities—a possible outcome of chronic HIF1A inactivation; rather oxidative glutamine metabolism (i.e. glutaminolysis) is activated and serving as a surrogate. Upon receiving insulin stimulus at times after meal, ATM-activation and hence nuclear localization of PKM2 (see above for details) diverts the fate of glucose carbons to the anabolic biosynthesis of nucleotides via the pentose phosphate shunt, amino acids (e.g. serine, glycine) and lipid-derivatives. However, ATM-deficiency fails to induce such responses, in other words oxidative glutamine metabolism is turned on at all times, which explains their glutamine-dependence and metabolic inflexibility that our had reported in earlier studies (Chan et al., Mol. Neurodegener 2016, 11:60). In the manuscript (Research Output: Item 5), we have performed an more comprehensive dietary intervention study which we concluded that on the top of glutamine supplementation, alpha-ketoglutarate is however more effective (while potentially less neurotoxic due to ammonia release) in alleviating insulin resistance, cerebellar degeneration (ataxia) and extending the lifespan of ATM-deficient mice. A patent filing is underway on the application of dietary alpha-ketoglutarate to the management of A-T.

16100718.label: Major findings and research outcome
16100718.value: We have defined a new role of ATM in sensing the high cellular ATP demands of cerebellar Purkinje cells by oxidative stresses and responding by activating the NRF1-dependent transcription of nuclear-encoded respiration proteins necessary for ATP production in the mitochondria (Research Output: Item 1). In the prepared manuscript (Research Output: Item 5), we have defined the detailed mechanism on how insulin activates ATM, and uncovered how the ATM-PKM2/HIF1A axis serves as a critical metabolic switch that controls the catabolic and anabolic dynamics of insulin-sensitive cells. Not only this explains the metabolic stresses, stunted growth and compromised thrivingness among A-T (ATM-deficient) patients; the model also explains how sustained activation of ATM-PKM2/HIF1A axis explains the overproduction of biomasses observed during pre-diabetic conditions (i.e. hyperinsulinemia/chronic insulin stimulus) among ordinary individuals. For A-T, we have strong evidence that alpha-ketoglutarate is a better surrogate supplement than glutamine for sustaining the metabolic need with less concerns on ammonium toxicity. The protocols and analytical platforms established by this funding, including the “live cell energy phenotype testing”; “TCA cycle and OXPHOS qPCR arrays”; “metabolomics profiling mass-spectrometry”; metabolite isotopologue mass-spectrometry profiling” were also adopted by other projects in the laboratory (Research Output: Item 2-4). Information related to this grant are acknowledged in those publications.

16100718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16100718.value: This earlier finding associated with this project (Research Output: Item 1) has led to an award of the NSFC-EYSC grant, which aimed at investigating the metabolic rewiring status of other hereditary cerebellar disease. The data in the prepared manuscript (Research Output: Item 5), will potentially lead to an application of another research grant (i.e. Action for A-T research project grant or another RGC-GRF grant) for further investigation on how the ATM-PKM2/HIF1A axis affects metabolic enzymes needed to support glutamine metabolism. A patent filing is underway to propose dietary supplement of CaAKG (calcium alpha-ketoglutarate), a divalent form of alpha-ketoglutarate acid for symptoms management in A-T. An invited review article on the topic “Potential crosstalk between metabolism and DNA repair in ataxia telangiectasia and hereditary ataxia diseases” will be submitted to the Journal of Neurochemistry (IF: 5.546) by the end of March 2023.

16100718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16100718.value: This work connects ATM’s oxidative stress response functions to sensing of metabolic ATP energetics distinctively important in high energy-demanding cerebellar Purkinje neuron, which could explain the most distinct A-T patient feature, cerebellar ataxia. The connections between insulin, ATM and the Warburg effect explains how insulin flips the catabolic versus anabolic status acutely and transiently in cells responding to the stimulus. A lost in such flexibility, either due to ATM-deficiency (i.e. A-T) or sustained ATM activation (i.e. hyperinsulinemia), respectively results in lipodystrophy and adiposity status in the corresponding conditions.

16101118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16101118.value: Adult humans have two types of fat, or adipose tissue: White adipose tissue (WAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT). The fat that accumulates in obesity is WAT, and is mainly a way for the body to store excess energy. BAT, however, packs a high density of cellular machinery that can metabolize lipids into heat energy in a process known as thermogenesis. In other words, WAT stores fat while BAT burns fat. Previously, it was thought that BAT was only present in significant amounts in human infants and rodents, but recent studies show that there are also important BAT depots in adult humans; higher amounts of BAT and thermogenic activity has been linked to leaner body mass and better insulin responses. Despite the surging interest in brown fat and its beneficial effects, the developmental origins of brown fat are poorly understood. Recent research suggests that brown fat and skeletal muscle arise from the same progenitor cell lineage during embryonic development; in fact, experiments have shown it is possible to convert brown fat into muscle and vice versa by manipulating expression of the factor PRDM16. However, the timing of when this happens in embryonic development, as well as the mechanism of how PRDM16 is regulated and its other binding partners, are only partially understood. When do progenitor cells decide to become brown fat, what happens to the progenitor cell identity when it makes this fate commitment, and what are the biological molecules that control this process? These are fundamentally interesting biological questions to be addressed. Furthermore, obesity is now one of the biggest public health problems worldwide, with over 2 billion overweight/obese adults (source: WHO). In Hong Kong, almost 40% of our work force (aged 18-64) are overweight or obese; worse, Hong Kong’s young adults are increasingly overweight as well (source: Hong Kong CHP). Obesity is associated with a multitude of chronic diseases and co-morbidities, including hypertension and coronary-heart disease, type 2 diabetes, disease of the liver and gall bladder, and various cancers. If we can better understand the formation of brown fat, it may help us to address obesity and obesity-associated diseases. In our proposed research, we will use state-of-the-art single-cell genomics technologies to interrogate embryonic tissues over various time-points, to identify additional factors important in the regulation of skeletal muscle/brown fat lineage commitment and progenitor cell differentiation, thereby uncovering ways to harness brown fat to combat the obesity epidemic. 成年人有兩種類型的脂肪組織：白色脂肪組織（WAT）和褐色脂肪組織（BAT）。在身體肥胖時積累的脂肪是WAT細胞，它們存在的主要目的是為身體儲存多餘的能量。不同於WAT ， BAT細胞內雖然也儲有脂肪滴，但BAT還含有大量的線粒體，是進行新陳代謝的細胞器，因此BAT的功能是將脂肪儲備代謝成熱能。換句話說，WAT儲存脂肪，而BAT燃燒脂肪。以前，人們認為BAT只在人類嬰兒和囓齒動物中大量存在，但最近的研究表明，成年人中也存在重要的BAT儲蓄；且更高的BAT和其相關的產熱活性與更瘦的體重和更優的胰島素反應有關。儘管人們對褐色脂肪及其益處的興趣日益濃厚，卻依然對褐色脂肪的發育過程與機制知之甚少。近期研究表明，在胚胎發育過程中，褐色脂肪和骨骼肌來自於同一細胞譜系。實驗表明，通過操縱名為PRDM16的因子的表達，可以將褐色脂肪轉化為肌肉，反之亦然。關於這支細胞譜系，這些發現是非常好的開始，但是還存有許多未解之謎。比如，這支脂肪與肌肉細胞譜系的的定型與分化發生在胚胎髮育過程中的哪個時間點？這個分化定型的過程當中，細胞本身會發生哪些變化？PRDM16自身是否或如何受到調控？除了PRDM16是否還有其它調控因子或機制？這些都是還需回答的、有趣的基礎生物學問題。此外，全球已有超過20億的超重/肥胖成人（來源：世界衛生組織），而肥胖也已成為全球最大的健康問題之一。在香港，我們近40％的勞動力（18-64歲）體重超重或患有肥胖症；更令人憂慮的是，香港的年輕人也越來越多患有肥胖症（來源：香港衛生防護中心）。肥胖症帶來多種慢性疾病和併發症，包括高血壓和冠心病，第二型糖尿病，肝臟和膽囊疾病，以及各種癌症。通過更好地了解褐色脂肪的形成，我們或會發現解決肥胖與其相關疾病的新契機。在該研究中，我們將在胚胎發育過程中不同的時間點，使用最先進的單細胞轉錄組學技術去剖析與研究胚胎組織中的細胞。並且，通過對單細胞轉錄組的大數據分析，來揭示骨骼肌/褐色脂肪細胞譜系的定型與分化過程中的重要機制與其調控因子。

16101118.label: Realisation of objectives
16101118.value: 1. Identify the time point during development when Pax7+ progenitors commit to skeletal muscle-specific or brown fat-specific fates by using single cell RNA-seq to profile the gene expression of individual cells descended from the Pax7+ lineage at various time points. We used single-cell RNA-seq to profile the labeled progeny of the Pax7+ progenitors in mouse embryo at E12.5, E14.5, and E16.5. By integrating all the cell types at each of these stages, we identified trends that showed emergence of early committed cell-types in each lineage at different time points. The myogenic lineage was the first to emerge, as we could detect labeled cells expressing Myf5 as early as E12.5. At this time point, there are no cells expressing brown fat markers of any kind, indicating that the time point of the myogenic commitment from Pax7 progenitors is earlier than the brown fat commitment. A group of cells that are Thy1-/Pdgfra+ begin to appear at E14.5. These progenitor-like cells not only express fibroblast-like marker Pdgfra but also express both adipogenic and dermal lineage genes Ebf2 and Crabp1/Twist2. We hypothesized that these could be late progenitor cells that are excluded from the myogenic lineage and are restricted to either adipogenic or dermal lineages, but have yet to commit to one or the other. At E14.5 there is another group of cells that express dermal lineage markers Crabp1/Twist2 more strongly than the late progenitors, indicating more progressed differentiation towared the dermal lineage. However, at E14.5, there are still no brown-fat marker-expressing cells. In the myogenic lineage at E14.5 we found plenty of more differentiated skeletal muscle cells that express MyoD, which again fits our earlier observation that the commitment of myogenic lineage is earlier and occurs more quickly during development. Adding in the data from E16.5, we find that the Adipoq and Ucp1 expressing brown fat cells only appear at E16.5. In addition, many dermal fibroblasts are also seen to emerge at E16.5, marked by the expression of Crabp1 and Twist2, along with Pdgfra. These Twist2-positive dermal fibroblast cells that emerge at E16.5 show a transcriptomic continuum extending from the Thy1-/Pdgfra+ cells found at E14.5, as they progressively gain Thy1 expression to become double positive Thy1+/Pdgfra+, suggesting that they could be of the same lineage. In summary, we have identified using single-cell RNA-seq that myogenic commitment occurs as early as E12.5, and dermal lineage commitment happens next, around E14.5 by first generating late progenitor cells that express both adipogenic and dermal markers, and then committing to dermal lineage indicated in cells with higher Twist2 expression. Both the late progenitors and the more committed dermal cells can be observed at E14.5. The adipogenic cells commit to their fate the latest, with Ucp1/Adipoq expressing cells only appearing at E16.5, along with more dermal fibroblasts expressing high Twist2. All the goals in this objective were completed. 2. Survey of heterogeneity of Pax7+ cells at one early embryonic time-point to preliminarily assess degree of gene expression heterogeneity of Pax7+ progenitors. We have also profiled Pax7-expressing cells at E10.5, and within the Pax7+ cells, we did not find any additional sub-clustering of cells that could be separated by the usual statistical methods for significance in cluster distance/similarity. This suggests that the Pax7-expressing progenitors at E10.5 are relatively homogeneous, and most of the gene expression differences among these cells appears stochastic without having clusters of subpopulations, at least with no indication of learning toward any particular lineage at that stage in time. However, given the limited budget, we were only able to assess one biological replicate and one earlier time point. It is possible that heterogeneity would be visible with a large number of Pax7+ cells profiled, or at a slightly later time point such as E11.5. This could be left to later studies. All the goals in this objective were completed. 3. Elucidate regulatory signalling molecules or transcription factors that regulate the brown fat/muscle fate commitment process by single-cell transcriptomic profiling. Using our data obtained for objective 1, we also examined the molecular factors that differentially characterize each lineage at the different time points in the single-cell data, aided by the use of trajectory analysis. All the goals in this objective were completed. First, we identified the late progenitor population expressing Thy1/Pdgfra, and using these two surface markers, we could isolate these late progenitors at E14.5 for further perturbation studies in-vitro. We hypothesized that if these are progenitors with bipotency, we could induce them to commit to either adipogenic lineage or dermal fibroblast lineage in-vitro using external cues. Indeed, when these Thy1-/Pdgfra+ progenitors from E14.5 were cultured in adipogenic medium, they eventually gave rise to oil droplet containing cells that could be stained by Oil-Red O. Cells that express both Thy1+/Pdgfra+, which arise later and begin to express dermal lineage markers, were not as capable of giving rise to oil droplet-containing cells when cultured in adipogenic medium. This indicates that double positive cells are already more committed to the dermal lineage, and hard to direct into adipogenic lineage. Conversely, the late progenitor cells Thy1-/Pdgfra+ cultured with TGFbeta added to the media began to express more Twist2 and Crabp1, and did not stain with Oil-Red O. This provides evidence that we were able to using our single-cell RNA-seq data to identify surface markers for an important intermediate population with bipotency. We then also looked at genes that are differentially expressed in the Adipoq-expressing cells compared to the late progenitors, to see if we could find factors that drive this lineage commitment. One marker we found was Rgcc. When we performed silencing of this gene on late progenitors sorted from E14.5, we observed lower expression of Adipoq, Pparg2, and Prdm16 in the shRgcc treated cells, indicating inhibition of the adipogenic lineage commitment. Furthermore, when cultured in adipogenic medium, the Rgcc-silenced cells were much less effective at generating oil droplet containing cells as compared to control. This indicates that Rgcc indeed plays a role in adipogenic fate commitment, and silencing this gene results in a less effective commitment to the adipogenic lineage from the late progenitors. We similarly looked at Wnt5, which was found as a factor upregulated in committed dermal fibroblasts at E16.5. Upon Wnt5a treatment, adipogenesis from late progenitors was again impeded, shown as marked reduction in Pparg2 expression in cells derived from late progenitors cultured in Wnt5a containing media. Budget expenditures deviation: Note that some of the salary was rebudgeted to general expenses, mainly consumables. Due to receiving some university matching for this project, we were able to spend less on the personnels, and re-direct some of the budget to the consumables. This is necessary as the proposed single-cell RNA-seq work is quite expensive, and some of our new findings led to additional validation experiments that were unplanned in the original proposal.

16101118.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101118.value: As a summary of what we have done toward our objectives, we have completed a single-cell transcriptomic analysis on Pax7 lineages from the developing dermomyotome. Transcriptomic profiling of Pax7 lineages allowed us to identify cell fate commitment time points for the myogenic, dermal, and adipogenic lineages. We discovered surface markers for robustly isolating distinct cell populations from embryos, thus enabling in vitro culture and functional characterization of these populations. Our analyses also generated candidate genes that could be involved in determining or reprogramming cell fate. We further demonstrated that Rgcc and Wnt5a are important for lineage development during embryogenesis. We also propose eFAP cells, a previously uncharacterized embryonic bipotent progenitor population marked by Pdgfra+/Thy1− expression emerging predominantly at E14.5 that resembles adult FAPs in their lineage potentials. Overall, this work, which is now published in Cell Discovery, has furthered our understanding of lineage diversification in Pax7+ progenitor cells during embryonic development and provided new avenues for future in-depth mechanistic studies of cell fate choice during development.

16101118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101118.value: As mentioned in the work done for objective 2, given the limited budget of this project, we were only able to assess one biological replicate and one earlier time point for the heterogeneity of Pax7 progenitors themselves. It is possible that within-progenitor heterogeneity would be visible with a larger number of Pax7+ cells profiled, or at a slightly later time point such as E11.5. This could be of interst in later studies. Secondly, there are still some drawbacks to the single-cell transcriptomics approach used in this study for the adipogenic lineage. Due to the way that cells are isolated for profiling, oil-containing adipocytes, especially more mature/differentiated ones, could be lost due to the difference in cell buoyancy. Future studies that focus more on the dermal/adipogenic lineage decision could consider using single nuclei profiling instead, which could sacrifice some of the transcript diversit per cell, but be able to capture a larger diversity of adipogenic cell types. Integration of single nuclei data with our existing data could generate a more comprehensive and detailed adipogenic lineage map and molecular decision tree.

16101118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101118.value: During embryo development, a type of stem cell called the Pax7 stem cell can eventually produce muscle, skin, and fat cells in the body. But previously, it was not clear when these stem cells decide to become each tissue type. In addition, we also want to determine which genes are responsible for this important decision. In our study, we used advance technology to observe the activity of individual cells at different time points, using mouse as a model. By profiling the activity of each cell, we connected the chain of gene expression change events that trace the events converting the Pax7 stem cell into the other three cell types. We found that the muscle cell types are generated first, at 12.5 days, followed by skin cell types at 14.5 days, and finally brown fat cell types at 16.5 days. We also found some genes that are involved in these fate decisions, and showed that regulating these genes in the stem cells can alter the likelihood of each fate decision. This gives us clues as to how cellular function and identity are programmed during normal development, laying the foundation for better understading of disease states when these fate decisions go wrong.

16101318.label: Project Objectives
16101318.value: To demonstrate, through laboratory experiments, whether marine heterotrophic protists, which are the main grazers of the marine primary producers, the photosynthetic plankton, have a higher activation energy (Ea) than their photosynthetic prey. A higher Ea means a stronger response to temperature rise. To reveal how mixotrophic protists growing in auto-, mixo-, and heterotrophic nutritional conditions respond to increasing temperature, and whether mixotrophs have advantages over both autotrophs and heterotrophs in a warming ocean.

16101318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16101318.value: As an essential component of marine ecosystems, phytoplankton and heterotrophic protists play a vital role in the marine food web and global biogeochemical cycling. The temperature sensitivity of plankton, in terms of activation energy described in the Arrhenius equation, is critical to predict how marine productivity and carbon export will respond to warming. The metabolic theory of ecology (MTE) was proposed and widely accepted in the last decade to quantify the effect of temperature and body size on individual basal metabolic rates via a combination of the laws of thermodynamics and the allometric scaling of body size. On the grounds that all organisms share the same fundamental metabolic reactions, the MTE can therefore be extrapolated to the population, community, and ecosystem properties. In the framework of the MTE, the Bolzmann-Arrhenius (BA) model scales the response of metabolism-linked traits to temperature within a “physiological temperature range” (PTR), and predicts that the temperature sensitivity of metabolism-linked traits in terms of activation energy (Ea) should be around 0.65 eV. However, some studies have suggested a lower temperature sensitivity for autotrophic processes (~0.32 eV) due to an enhanced photorespiration effect at high temperatures. Although this difference is supported by several meta-analyses, the underlying mechanism is still unclear as a result of the lack of a physiological basis. Therefore, we propose to conduct a series of laboratory incubation experiments using representative autotrophic, heterotrophic, and mixotrophic marine protistan plankton to evaluate whether different Eas exist between auto- and heterotrophic processes. We will also examine whether mixotrophic organisms have advantages over both autotrophs and heterotrophs in a warming ocean. Such information is of critical importance to understand the metabolic balance of oceanic ecosystems in responding to rising seawater temperature and the capacity of the ocean to absorb anthropogenic CO2 in the coming century.

16101318.label: Realisation of objectives
16101318.value: To address the first objective, we have conducted both laboratory and field experiments and used statistical models to comprehensively demonstrate the temperature sensitivity of microzooplankton and phytoplankton and the difference between them. We have achieved this objective and our project have greatly advanced our understanding on the temperature sensitivity of marine heterotrophic protists (i.e., microzooplankton) and their photosynthetic prey (i.e., phytoplankton). (1) The temperature sensitivity of microzooplankton rates We have conducted laboratory experiments to measure the growth rate, ingestion rate, and respiration rate of four marine protists (two heterotrophic nano-flagellates Cafeteria sp. and Paraphysomonas longispina, one ciliate Pseudocohnilembus persalinus, and one heterotrophic dinoflagellate Oxyrrhis marina) under 6 temperatures and calculated their activation energy (Ea, eV). We found that the Ea of the growth rate of four protists was 0.68 ± 0.08 eV, while the Ea of ingestion rate and respiration rate were 1.31 ± 0.13 eV and 1.20 ± 0.12 eV, respectively. The ingestion and respiration are the direct processes of energy gain and energy loss, respectively, which are more sensitive to temperature changes, whereas the growth rate reflecting the results of energy balance and the fitness of these protists has a relatively low temperature sensitivity which is consistent with classical value (i.e., ~0.65 eV) based on MTE (Qian et al. 2023, Sci. Total Environ.). In addition to estimate the temperature sensitivity of individual protists, we also investigated the temperature sensitivity of microzooplankton community. We compiled a dataset including the 224 microzooplankton grazing rates that measured by dilution experiments across the marginal seas of China and constructed a model based on MTE and functional responses of grazing to quantify the effects of temperature and prey concentrations on microzooplankton grazing rate. We estimated an activation energy of 0.51 eV of microzooplankton, which is also close to the classical value based on MTE (Liu et al. 2020, Limnol. Oceanogr.). (2) The difference in temperature sensitivity between microzooplankton and phytoplankton As mentioned above, the average activation energies of microzooplankton rates are close to 0.65eV and higher. However, the average activation energies of phytoplankton growth rate are lower, and it could be affected by nutrient availability and would be reduced by long-term adaptation (i.e., hotter is partial better). We conducted temperature-modulated dilution experiments to measured phytoplankton growth and microzooplankton grazing rates simultaneously under 5 temperatures at two subtropical coastal sites. The results showed that the activation energy of phytoplankton growth rate was significantly lower than that of microzooplankton grazing rate (Liu et al. 2019, Limnol. Oceanogr. ). Based on this evidence, we concluded that marine microzooplankton have higher temperature sensitivity than their photosynthetic prey. For objective 2, our studies via a series of laboratory work revealed the advantages of mixotrophs over autotrophs and heterotrophs in a warming ocean, which provide insights into mixotrophs nutritional strategy and functional role under the global warming scenario. (1) Mixotrophs growing in mixotrophic mode have advantages over autotrophic mode. We investigated the thermal responses of growth rate and functional traits of a mixotrophic dinoflagellate (Lepidodinium sp.) and found that this facultative mixotroph with an obligate phototrophic lifestyle showed higher thermal sensitivity (Ea, eV) grown in mixotrophic mode (with sufficient prey, 0.69−0.89 eV) than in autotrophic mode (without prey, 0.30−0.37 eV). Warming stimulated a higher growth rate of Lepidodinium sp. grown in mixotrophic conditions than in autotrophic conditions, indicating that mixotrophic dinoflagellates may benefit substantially from mixotrophy when temperature increases, and prey is sufficient (Liu et al. 2021; Mar. Ecol. Prog. Ser.). In addition to the difference in thermal sensitivity of growth rates in mixotrophic and heterotrophic modes, our study also found the difference in optimal temperature between autotrophic process (i.e., photosynthesis) and heterotrophic process (i.e., ingestion) in a green mixotroph, Picochlorum sp. GLMF1. Our study has proved this green alga as an obligate mixotroph implying that both photoautotrophy and phago-heterotrophy are essential for their survival (Pang et al. 2022; J. Phycol). We then examined the growth performance, photosynthesis traits, and phagotrophic activities of this green mixotroph over a wide range of temperature-irradiance combinations. Our results showed that the ingestion rates showed higher thermal tolerance than the photosynthesis rates. The increased phagotrophy with rising temperature compensated the photosynthesis that was constrained by high temperature, which helped Picochlorum sp. to achieve higher growth rates and to be more competitive in the warming ocean (Pang et al. 2023; Mar. Ecol. Prog. Ser. Accepted). (2) Mixotrophs shift towards more heterotrophy with rising temperatures Our finding on the higher thermal sensitivity of mixotrophic dinoflagellate (Lepidodinium sp.) in mixotrophic mode is consistent with the results of predominantly heterotrophic mixotrophs, providing experimental evidence for the hypothesis that mixotrophs shift towards more heterotrophy with rising temperatures (Liu et al. 2021; Mar. Ecol. Prog. Ser.). On the other hand, we have compared the carbon acquisition from autotrophic (inorganic carbon uptake via photosynthesis) and phago-heterotrophic process (organic carbon uptake via ingestion) in the green mixotroph (Picochlorum sp. GLMF1) and found that proportion of organic carbon uptake to total carbon acquisition increased with rising temperature, suggesting that the green mixotroph will become more phago-heterotrophic in the warming ocean (Pang et al. 2023; Mar. Ecol. Prog. Ser. Accepted). The subsequent changes in their functional role from primary producers to consumers with rising temperature may affect food web dynamics and carbon and nutrient cycling. (3) Transcriptomic study The dinoflagellate Lepidodinium sp. growing in auto- and mixo- conditions have significant morphological and physiological differences. We compared the gene expression between auto- and mixo- Lepidodinium cultures under 23℃ and 28℃. Based on differential expression analysis, we found the providing of prey mainly induced up-regulated genes, while warming leads to a relatively equivalent number of up- and down-regulated genes. We first focused explicitly on differentially expressed genes (DEGs) involved in the two strongly interconnected and high-profile processes, i.e., photosynthesis and respiration. Our results showed that the providing of prey did not impact photosynthesis genes significantly, but led to the up-regulation of many DEGs involved in oxidative phosphorylation, which consumes oxygen and produces adenosine triphosphate (ATP). However, the increasing temperature leads to the up-regulation of DEGs involved in both photosynthesis and oxidative phosphorylation. We further conducted KEGG enrichment analysis to identify key biological pathways stimulated by active feeding. Our results showed that DEGs were significantly enriched in 37 pathways which could be clustered into three main categories of phagocytosis: focal adhesion, regulation of actin cytoskeleton, and oxidative phosphorylation. Since phagocytosis is evolutionarily conserved and functionally relevant in other species, the expression profile of this process can be a promising marker for exploring the feeding behavior in mixotrophs in marine ecosystems. By applying this marker in Tara Ocean metatranscriptome dataset, we tested the well-known hypothesis “mixotrophic organisms become more heterotrophic with rising temperature”. Our results showed that the expression of phagocytosis genes was positively correlated to rising temperatures only when the ambient chlorophyll a concentration is higher than 0.3 mg.m-3, which suggest this trend can only be found in regions where both inorganic nutrients and micro prey organisms are sufficient. Based on NASA's Aqua satellite's 18-year chlorophyll observations, the regions that fulfill the condition cover an average of 20.58% of the sea surface (Chen et al. submitted to New Phytologist). Explanation for the over-spending on "general expense": high cost for transcriptome sequencing and listing one equipment (parts) as consumable.

16101318.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101318.value: • Verified that marine heterotrophic protists have higher temperature sensitivity than their autotrophic prey through both laboratory and field experiments (Liu et al. 2019; 2020a; 2020b; 2021; Qian et al. 2023), and found that microzooplankton grazing rate has higher optimal temperature than phytoplankton growth rate in subtropical coastal waters (Liu et al. 2019). • Constructed a semi-mechanical model to quantify the effect of temperature and prey concentration on microzooplankton grazing rate across China Seas and verified that the temperature sensitivity of microzooplankton in natural waters was 0.51 eV which was close the classical value predicted in MTE (Liu et al. 2020a). • Discovered that a mixotrophic dinoflagellate (Lepidodinium sp.) grown in mixotrophic mode were more sensitive to warming than grown in autotrophic mode; and warming stimulated a higher growth rate of Lepidodinium sp. grown in mixotrophic mode, suggesting a competitive edge of mixotrophs in future warmer ocean (Liu et al. 2021). • Identified a green alga (Picochlorum sp. GLMF1.) as a mixotrophic alga and found that both photo-autotrophy and phago-heterotrophy are essential for their survival and growth (Pang et al. 2022). We also examined the physiological rates of this green alga under different temperatures and found that its ingestion rate has a higher thermal tolerance than its photosynthesis rates and aids it to achieve higher growth rates, which suggests that mixotrophs would be more competitive in the warming ocean (Pang et al. 2023, accepted). • Discovered that the mixotrophic dinoflagellate (Lepidodinium sp.) and green alage (Picochlorum sp. GLMF1.) shift towards more heterotrophy with rising temperatures (Liu et al. 2021; Pang et al. 2023, accepted). To further investigate the underlying mechanisms, we conducted transcriptomic study on the Lepidodinium sp. and we found that genes involved in phagocytosis were significantly stimulated in well-fed compared to starved cultures. We further used the expression profile of phagocytosis genes in Lepidodinium sp. to target their feeding behavior in the global sunlit ocean. Our results showed that Lepidodinium sp. become more heterotrophic with rising temperatures only when the ambient chlorophyll concentration is higher than 0.3 mg.m-3. We suggest that the expression profile of phagocytosis genes could be a molecular marker to target the shifting of trophic modes in mixotrophic dinoflagellates (Chen et al. submitted to New Phytologist). A total of 17 papers acknowledged this grant, among them 9 are listed and uploaded in Part C as they are closely related to the objectives of proposed study.

16101318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101318.value: There is a great potential for further development of research on this topic. I am considering furthering this study in two directions. First, to test the hypothesis using different types of mixotrophs. There are several types of mixotrophic plankton, ranging from mostly autotroph to mostly heterotroph. Their physiological and ecological characteristics, as well as the molecular biology and evolutionary history are quite different. Second, to study the long-term adaptation at physiological and molecular level. Most of the laboratory experiments testing the effect of warming on biological processes is by short-term manipulation, which may not reflect the real scenario of climate change, which is a slow process. I plan to keep some of the mixotrophic plankton in temperature 2-3 degree above the current summer water temperature for several years, and then study their thermal sensitivity, physiological traits and epigenomic and transcriptomic changes.

16101318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101318.value: Micro-algae are the most important primary producers (convert CO2 to organic carbon via photosynthesis). Some of these single cell organisms can also obtain their carbon and nutrients through feeding on bacteria or other small cells, we call them mixotroph or mixoplankton. One hypothesis is that these organisms have advantages over pure autotrophs in the warming waters because they can obtain organic carbon and nutrients as supplement in nutrient poor waters (and warming will strengthen the stratification of the upper ocean and further reduce the nutrient supply to the sunlit layer of the ocean). In this study, we conducted laboratory and field experiment to test this hypothesis at physiological and molecular level. We find that the heterotrophic activity, such as ingestion and respiration rates, of the mixoplankton increased faster than the autotrophic activity, such as photosynthesis, when temperature increases. At the same time, genes regulating phagocytosis (feeding) were upregulated. Our results support the hypothesis that mixotrophs may become more heterotrophic with rising temperatures, but only in waters that can supply sufficient amount of prey for them to feed on.

16101418.label: Project Objectives
16101418.value: To characterize the inhibitory effect of GCP6 on γTuRCs We will examine the following aspects of the GCP6-mediated inhibition of γTuRCs in microtubule nucleation assays. First, we will assess the specificity of the inhibitory effect of GCP6 and confirm that this effect is unique to GCP6 among the γTuRC-specific GCPs. Second, we will determine the potency of the GCP6-mediated inhibition of interphase and mitotic γTuRCs and relate the measured potencies to the cytoplasmic concentration of GCP6. Third, we will examine the functional relationship between GCP6 and the γTuRC stimulator CDK5RAP2 in the regulation of γTuRCs. Similarly, we will test whether the γTuRC receptor Nedd1 has any effect on the GCP6-mediated inhibition. Results from the above assays will help understand the action of GCP6. To identify the mechanism by which GCP6 inhibits γTuRCs We will devise experiments to address the following issues of γTuRC inhibition by GCP6. First, we will assess the structural integrity and determine the stoichiometry of γTuRCs that are inhibited or saturated by GCP6. The structural integrity will be evaluated by centrifugation of γTuRCs over a sucrose gradient. γTuRCs separated by sucrose gradient centrifugation or isolated by affinity capture will be used for stoichiometry analyses. Second, we will perform a GTP-loading assay and analyze whether GCP6 blocks GTP loading onto γ-tubulins within γTuRCs to inhibit the complexes. Third, we will conduct mutational an analysis of the GCP6 middle region, a region that is lacking in other GCPs, to explore the role of this region in the GCP6-mediated inhibition of γTuRCs. Collectively, these analyses will provide mechanistic insights into the GCP6’s action. To reveal the role of GCP6-mediated γTuRC inhibition in microtubule organization during the cell cycle We will analyze the function of GCP6-mediated γTuRC inhibition by using the following methods: (1) to rescue GCP6 knockdown with the γTuRC-inhibition-defective GCP6 mutant that is generated in the mutational analysis, and (2) to rapidly eliminate cellular GCP6 by small-molecule-induced protein degradation (e.g., protein tagging with the fluorescent destabilizing domain or the auxin-inducible degron). The loss of GCP6 or its function may have an impact on the followings: (1) the assembly, subcellular distribution, and activity of γTuRCs, (2) the microtubule-organizing function of microtubule-organizing centers, such as centrosomes, the Golgi complex, and mitotic spindles, (3) the organization of interphase microtubules and mitotic spindles, and (4) cell cycle progression. All these aspects will be examined. We will also construct GCP4 and GCP5 for induced degradation and compare the degradation effects with those of GCP6 degradation. Results from these experiments will not only reveal the function of GCP6 but also provide information on the differential roles of the γTuRC-specific GCPs.
