16304418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16304418.value: Cosmic inflation is the leading paradigm of the early universe, during which the universe expanded exponentially. It is generally believed that the structures of our universe originate from the quantum vacuum fluctuations of inflation. The quantum fluctuations of matter (especially the inflaton, which drives inflation) stretched out of the Hubble horizon, and became classical fluctuations. Those classical fluctuations became the seeds of the structures of our universe. However, we still lack observational evidence of the quantum origin of the inflationary fluctuations. In some modified versions of inflation, thermal fluctuations may have played a role in the origin of structure. Also, it is valuable to test the principles of quantum mechanics at an energy scale as high as inflation, because this energy scale has never been reached in lab experiments. Some quantum features of the inflationary fluctuations have been well observed. For example, the inflationary fluctuations are random and nearly Gaussian. Some other features are proposed but have not yet been observed, for example, the quantum phase of massive fields in cosmological correlation functions. But thermal fluctuations of waves also share those features. We propose to systematically test the quantum nature of the inflationary fluctuations, especially their wave-particle duality, and quantum entanglement, which cannot be mimicked by thermal fluctuations. We point out that massive fields during inflation play a key role in testing the quantum nature of the inflationary fluctuations, because their excited massive particles remain in quantum single-particle states. This is unlike the case of the inflaton, whose fluctuations quickly become classical once they are no longer in their vacuum states. The wave feature of inflationary fluctuations is relatively manifest, as the fluctuations are observed in the form of density fields. However, the particle nature has not been tested. This is why thermal fluctuations may still be a possible origin of structures. We propose to study the Compton-scattering-like limit of cosmological correlation functions, to test the particle feature of inflationary fluctuations. We also propose to study the exponential tail of the quantum wave function of massive particles, which also show that the inflationary fluctuations have their particle nature. We propose to study the quantum entanglement of inflationary fluctuations through a Bell-like experiment with three entangled particles. The prototype of the proposal is known as the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) experiment. We propose to develop a cosmological version of the GHZ experiment and study its predictions in the cosmological correlation functions. 目前，暴漲宇宙學是解釋早期宇宙的最佳理論。暴漲過程中，宇宙指數膨脹。 我們普遍相信，當今宇宙中的結構來自於早期宇宙中的量子漲落。物質的量子漲落（特別是驅動暴漲的“暴漲子”的漲落）被空間膨脹拉到視界之外，並成爲經典擾動。這些經典擾動成爲了我們宇宙中結構形成的種子。 然而，我們目前仍然缺乏實驗證據，以確認暴漲期間的擾動確實是量子的。在一些暴漲模型中，擾動的起源是熱漲落。此外，我們也應該在暴漲能標下檢驗量子力學。這是因爲我們目前的實驗室裏還不能達到暴漲能標。 暴漲擾動的一些量子性質已經被實驗觀測很好地驗證。例如，暴漲的擾動是隨機的，是接近高斯分佈的。另一些量子性質目前還沒有被觀測到。例如，宇宙學關聯函數中的量子相位。然而，波動性的熱擾動也具有這樣的性質。我們建議對暴漲擾動的量子性質進行系統的檢驗。特別是波粒二象性和量子糾纏。這兩個特點不能被熱擾動所模擬。 我們指出，爲了檢驗暴漲擾動的量子性質，需要藉助重場。這是因爲重場所激發出的粒子在暴漲期間保持單粒子狀態。這與暴漲子不同。在暴漲期間，暴漲子的擾動一旦脫離真空狀態，就很快變為經典擾動。 暴漲擾動的波動性是相對顯然的，因為我們通過密度場來觀測這些擾動。然而，暴漲擾動的例子性尚未被檢驗。這是熱擾動仍然可以解釋結構形成的原因。我們建議用宇宙學關聯函數類似康普頓散射的極限來檢驗原初擾動的粒子性。我們也建議研究重場被指數壓低的效應。這顯示著暴漲擾動的粒子特性。 我們建議利用類似貝爾不等式的實驗來研究暴漲場漲落的量子糾纏。我們建議的原型是Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger（GHZ）實驗。我們建議研究一個宇宙學版本的GHZ實驗，並且研究它對宇宙關聯函數的影響。

16304418.label: Realisation of objectives
16304418.value: We have carried on the study of studying Compton-like scattering in cosmology. We noted a relation between the angle of correlation function and the position of the resonant peak. The relation can help for identifying the cosmological collider signal in future experiments. We discuss the non-Gaussianity of superheavy dark matter in "Cosmological signatures of superheavy dark matter". This paper is also published in JHEP. The first of the above two projects show the Campton scattering nature of cosmological perturbations. And the second of the above work use the quantum wave-particle dual nature of cosmological perturbations to generate cosmological non-Gaussianities for dark matter. These two projects complete the Objective 1. We have studied the quantum creation of a toy universe, published on Class. Quantum Grav. This work shows that the quantum fluctuations of the universe can originate from an Euclidean phase of evolution instead of real-time evolution. Further, we studied the difference between inflationary quantum fluctuations with the quantum fluctuations of bouncing cosmology in "Non-standard primordial clocks from induced mass in alternative to inflation scenarios". The quantum correlation function generated and imprinted on primordial fluctuations show the difference of different cosmological scenarios, which has a quantum origin. The work is published on JCAP. The above two publications completes the Objective 2. We have applied super-adiabatic approximation to study the production of super-heavy dark matter. The dark matter production is due to the exponential tail of the quantum wave function. The research is published as "Gravitational Production of Superheavy Dark Matter and Associated Cosmological Signatures" on Journal of High Energy Physics (JHEP). As reported in the mid-term report, this completes the Objective 3.

16304418.label: Major findings and research outcome
16304418.value: We find that superheavy dark matter can be produced during inflation, by gravitational production mechanism, which is, mathematically, identical to a quantum harmonic oscillator with a time dependent mass. The quantum mechanically created dark matter fluctuation can have implications on cosmological curvature perturbations, which may be observable in future precision experiments. This is reported in Part C in Publication [1] and [7]. In [4], we illustrate another idea to probe quantum particles in the cosmos by studying a cosmological Higgs collider. And in [3] we show that gravitational waves may be generated by massive vectors. We studied a toy model of quantum creation of universe. In a deformed instanton, the universe may be quantum-mechanically created, as Hartle and Hawking conjectured. But in our work, we show that after the instaton is deformed, we can generate primordial fluctuations, which are scale invariant and consistent with current observations. Thus, this toy model of the universe can be considered as an alternative to inflation. This is reported in Publication [2]. In [6], we also reported the difference between inflation and alternative to inflation models using non-standard primordial clocks.

16304418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16304418.value: During our research, we noted that the decoherence feature of cosmological perturbations is non-trivial and this leads to a paper (currently it's a preprint 2207.04435 and submitted to journal). Making use of the experience and technique developed in this project, we are also collaborating with University of Oxford to further explore the quantum superposition of mass and it's gravitational effect.

16304418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16304418.value: We studied the quantum nature of the early universe in this project. Namely, we studied the quantum natures of the Higgs, dark matter, massive vectors and the quantum creation of the universe itself. The project led to 7 publications and one PhD thesis (other two PhD thesis are also related to this project, but the defense happened after the completion of this project).

16304518.label: Project Objectives
16304518.value: To synthesize high-quality patterned graphene, with the desired architecture, using a carbon gettering strategy applied to chemical vapor deposition on Cu foil. We will focus on the development of the capability to pattern graphene growth in situ and thereby actively control crystal formation. The pattern design can be modified depending on the desired device configuration. To study the growth of patterned graphene/h-BN lateral heterostructures by in situ CVD method on Cu foil and to obtain a fundamental understanding of the mechanism whereby edges of existing crystallites function as substrates for the lateral growth of the other material that enables the formation of laterally heterostructured films. We will develop the capacity to engineer graphene/h-BN heterostructures with controlled shapes, sizes and interface structures and with desirable properties. To elucidate the structure–property relationships by comparing the atomic-scale structural information, such as interface intermixing, local strain and disorder, with the electronic and optical characteristics of the fabricated heterostructure devices. We will use the results obtained from spectroscopy to correlate with the atomic-scale structural information and compare it with theoretical predictions.

16304518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16304518.value: This proposed project explores a new synthetic approach to design, fabricate and characterize arrays of lateral heterostructures made of sheets of two-dimensional (2D) materials, in which they are patterned to allow the direct integration into commercial electronic devices. Heterostructures of 2D materials have enhanced electrical and optical properties far beyond those of the individual constituent materials and can be used as the enabling element in energy harvesting, modern telecommunication technologies and energy-efficient displays. More specifically, we will leverage our recently developed carbon gettering approach to obtain an in situ patterned growth of high-quality, exclusively single-layer graphene (SLG) on copper foil during a chemical vapor deposition (CVD) process. The strategy for obtaining lateral patterning is to employ a "carbon-gettering" metals mask of designed pattern of atomic resolution, such as Ni, on catalytical Cu surface, which exclude the graphene growth in the masked area and form desired pattern. Graphene properties can then be finely tuned by tailoring the pattern by selecting the geometry and lattice of the pattern structures. Subsequently, we will integrate the patterned graphene with its semiconducting counterpart, hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), through seamless stitching, all of which is achieved through in situ CVD. This project will facilitate the novel design and synthesis of new materials with unprecedented properties and functionalities beyond the limits of materials that currently exist in nature. More importantly, the use of the new concept of a carbon gettering mask will allow us to eliminate all of the post-growth lithographic patterning steps, which are both expensive and a source of cross-contamination. Successful completion of the project will substantially advance state-of-the-art nanofabrication by enabling the integration of nanostructures in practical devices by the direct growth and placement of patterned heterostructures. This will establish the scientific foundation for CVD methods enabling the production of devices based on 2D materials. Moreover, the program will strongly emphasize the training of postgraduate and undergraduate students from Hong Kong, thus preparing them for academic or industrial careers. 本項目旨在探索了一種新的合成方法，即原位模式化方法，來設計，製造和表徵由二維（2D）材料製成的橫向異質結構，實現直接集成到商業電子設備中二維。材料的異質節結構具有增強的電學和光學性能，遠遠超出其中單個組成材料的性能，並且可以用作能量收集，現代電信技術和節能顯示器中的元件。更具體地說，我們將利用我們最近開發的碳吸方法，在化學氣相沉積（CVD）過程中在銅箔上獲得高質量，全單層石墨烯（SLG）的原位模式化生長。本項目使用的橫向模式化的策略是在催化銅箔表面上採用設計的原子級分辨率圖案（例如鎳）的“吸碳”金屬掩模，使的掩模區域中的石墨烯無法生長，形成所設計圖案。通過選擇圖案結構的幾何形狀和晶格來設計圖案，實現精細調整石墨烯的性質。隨後，我們將通過將整合圖案化的石墨烯與其半導體的h-BN集成，所有這些都通過原位化學氣相層積法實現。該項目將促進新材料的新穎設計和合成，具有超出當前自然存在的材料，賦予其前所未有的特性和功能。更重要的是，使用碳吸掩模的新概念將使我們能夠避免所有後生長光刻模式化步驟，這些步驟既昂貴又是交叉污染的主要來源。 該項目的成功完成將實現採用直接生長模式化異質節結構，整合納米結構在實際裝置中，從而大大推進最先進的納米製造。這將為新型的化學氣相沉積法奠定科學基礎，最終製成基於二維材料的設備。此外，該計劃將強調培訓來自香港的研究生和本科生，從而為他們的學術或工業職業做好準備。

16304518.label: Realisation of objectives
16304518.value: In this project, we have made a significant step towards the proposed objectives. Our achievements and accomplishments were summarized as the following. First, the high-quality patterned graphene with desired architecture was successfully achieved via chemical vapor deposition (CVD) using a backside carbon-gettering mechanism. We have thoroughly investigated from computational and experimental aspect for the parameters that are important during this process, such as the growth rate, grain boundary (please refer to article #4, #5 and #6 in Part C.8). By optimizing the CVD system, including the flow rate of carbon precursor, annealing duration, growth time, etc., the high-quality patterned graphene with desired monolayer structure, squared shape, reduced grain boundary, and high uniformity was obtained. Here, based on the gettering method, we achieved single-crystal graphene growth by seamless stitching of the graphene domains. Based on such results, we obtained highly crystalline graphene in desired periodic pattern, and it enables significant progress towards the subsequence graphene/h-BN lateral heterostructures growth. We have also investigated the substrate effect and the quality of the as-grown patterned graphene using optical microscopy, SEM, TEM, AFM, Raman spectroscopy, and secondary ion mass spectroscopy (SIMS). We have investigated the growth of patterned graphene/h-BN lateral heterostructures by in situ CVD method on Cu foil and to acquire fundamental understanding of the mechanism. (please refer to article #4 and #7 in Part C.8). We have obtained laterally heterostructured using the edges of existing crystallites as substrates We achieved the patterned graphene growth with desired shape, size, and orientation. In addition to patterned graphene growth, we have investigated the hBN-CVD growth under different “surface parameters”, such as surface roughness, surface oxygen concentration, etc. Three kinds of copper conditions were used to study their influence on hBN growth, including 1) the standard method for Cu was treated with acetic acid only, 2) molten Cu at growth temperature above 1085℃, and 3) recrystallized Cu from molten state (1085℃) to solidified state (1045℃). We observed significant difference in the morphology for hBN grown on molten Cu, contrasting to standard Cu and recrystallized Cu. Meanwhile, we also illustrated the structure of hBN flakes growth on molten Cu shows a high correlation to the precursor flux and heating temperature of ammonia borane (AB) source (see paper #4 in Part C of this report). By regulating the sublimation temperature of the AB source, we observed the structure evolution of hBN flakes from triangle to truncated triangle. The reason for additional B-terminated edges in hBN was explained by kinetic Wulff construction. Moreover, to figure out if there was structural difference, we initially investigated their structures by Raman spectroscopy, in which all the main peaks are located near 1370 cm-1 (corresponding to the E2g vibrational mode), indicating that the as-grown h-BN crystals are all in monolayer and high quality. However, even though the h-BN peaks are not shifted, the intensity of the peaks vary among these two samples, with sharper and stronger peak obtained from the sample grown on molten Cu. The growth of patterned graphene/hBN lateral heterostructure was studied by fundamentally exploring of the hBN growth mechanism. We also demonstrated the structure evolution of hBN grown on molten copper via APCVD and illustrated that the precursor flux plays a crucial role in shape-dependent mechanisms. The increasing precursor flux resulted to the shape evolution of the hBN deposition-controlled growth, from equilibrium growth (triangle shape) to kinetically controlled growth (truncated triangle shape), and finally reached deposition-controlled growth (circular shape). The kinetic of edge growth, including N-terminated and B-terminated, is highly corresponding to the energy barriers of hBN formation and is predicted by utilizing the kinetic Wulff construction theory. The result dominated the strong anisotropy and the high sensitivity to B and N chemical ratio during hBN edge growth, e.g., triangle-shaped flakes with N-terminated edges will be more preferred in B-rich conditions. We have also studied the graphene/hBN lateral heterostructure fabrication based on the patterned design mentioned above by utilizing the in-situ CVD method. Toward this, we illustrated the edges of existing crystallites functions as the nucleation sites for the hBN lateral growth. The subsequences atomically stitching of the patterned graphene and hBN flakes were achieved by precise control during CVD growth. The project objective of fabricating the graphene/hBN lateral heterostructure with controlled shapes, sizes, interface structures, and desirable properties, was achieved. We have also elucidated the structure–property relationships by comparing the atomic-scale structural information with the electronic and optical characteristics of the fabricated heterostructure devices. (Please refer to article #4 and #7 in Part C.8). For the patterned graphene/h-BN atomic sheet-based FET devices fabrication, the graphene/hBN lateral heterostructure was first transferred to SiO2/Si or flexible PDMS substrates. The seamless stitching interface was also observed in the as-grown graphene/hBN heterostructure, which strongly supports the subsequent high-quality FET devices fabrication. With the incorporation of hBN into the graphene-based FET device, the enhanced electronic properties were shown due to the inertness characteristic of hBN. Our graphene/hBN FET device demonstrated higher electron mobilities and ON-OFF ratio than the monolayer pure graphene-based FET, which achieved the project objective of exploring the structure-property relationships of the graphene/hBN-based FET device. Our results proved that our strategy is reliable for fabricating the lateral heterostructure for device uses, because of the high-quality and strong mechanical integrity of the interface between graphene and hBN. The interface between the two materials was characterized by STEM, showing the seamlessly stitched interface without observed vacancy, dislocation, etc. We also applied the density functional theory (DFT) calculation for the fundamental understanding of the seamless stitching mechanism. The seamless stitching between two interfaces enables the high quality of the fabricated heterostructure-based devices. The heterostructure based device fabrication is extended from graphene/hBN-based FET devices to other 2D materials to obtain a comprehensive understanding on the electronic properties of 2D semiconductor devices. We designed a MoS2/WS2/MoS2 lateral superlattices-based electronic device. Non-linear I-V curves were shown from the devices due to the intrinsic barrier at the interface between the heterostructure, different from the electronic properties (linear) of pure MoS2. The interface between the two materials showed the seamlessly stitched interface without observed vacancy, dislocation, etc., indicating the high quality of the fabricated MoS2/WS2/MoS2 heterostructure-based devices. We have also extended our research to include broadly other two-dimensional materials and investigated their structure–property relationships by comparing the atomic-scale structural information, with the electronic and optical characteristics of the fabricated heterostructure devices. For example, we demonstrate that by by in situ formation of an artificial NaF-rich protective layer on Na metal, we were able to enable a low-cost and effective strategy to reduce the dendrite growth (see paper #3 in Part C of this report).. Furthermore, we have also shown that using functionalized graphene oxides, the binding to toxins can be significantly improved. (see paper #2 in Part C of this report). In addition, we have developed a method for fabrication of a nitrogen-doped carbon-coating as a lithophilic diffusion barrier layer, to suppress Li dendrite formation during Li deposition. (See paper #1 in Part C of this report). In short, the proposed objectives are completely achieved with impact to the academic communication and society.

We will focus on the development of the capability to pattern graphene growth in situ and thereby actively control crystal formation. The pattern design can be modified depending on the desired device configuration.

To elucidate the structure–property relationships by comparing the atomic-scale structural information, such as interface intermixing, local strain and disorder, with the electronic and optical characteristics of the fabricated heterostructure devices. 16304518.label: Major findings and research outcome
16304518.value: Since the project starting date, we have been working with our team members to develop a patterned deposition of graphene thin film by chemical vapor deposition using the backside carbon gettering mechanism that was established early by us. Meanwhile, the high controllability in array, shaping, sizing, etc., allow us to actively achieve the precise control of graphene formation, and the subsequence heterostructure fabrication. The development of CVD growth for large area heterojunction is realized. The corresponding result is published in top journal in material field (Liu et al, 2D materials, 2021 or article #4 in part C) The fabrication of graphene/hBN lateral heterostructure with designated patterning and controlled interface structure, size, orientation, shapes, etc., was also achieved. Thus, we have explored the growth of patterned heterostructures and improved our understanding of the edge-epitaxial growth mechanism. In addition, we also studied the electronic and optical performance of the graphene/hBN heterostructure in FET devices, with the analysis of the correlated structure-property relationships. From the fundamental aspect, we have utilized a variety of experimental methods to synthesize our desired structure of heterostructure, which improved our practical hands-on skills to fabricate two-dimensional materials via CVD, which is not only limited to graphene and hBN, but also MoS2, MoTe2, etc.

16304518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16304518.value: After the achievement of this project, we will also transfer the graphene/hBN heterostructure into the flexible substrate (PDMS) for fabricating other devices, such as optoelectronic device applications. By studying the device application, this project can provide a significant step towards fabricating new generation two-dimensional materials based flexible and transparent devices. In addition, we will design some other 2D materials-based heterostructures with the desired pattern. For example, by utilizing the extraordinary electronic and optical properties of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), we can design a suitable pattern for TMD-based heterostructures and study their structure-property relationships. Besides, through more in-depth research in integrating device applications broader to other graphene and 2D materials, we can create new possibilities for new material combinations, heterogeneous structure engineering, and unique device fabrication.

16304518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16304518.value: The graphene/hBN heterostructure-based fabricated devices exhibit improved performance, such as reduced carrier inhomogeneity, enhanced high-bias performance, etc., contrasting to the conventional oxide dielectric-based devices. In addition, the better dielectric properties of hBN compared with SiO2, provides a significant advantage for FET devices application with improved heat dissipation and enhanced thermal conductivity. The research of this project provides a experimental basis for developing high-performance devices, thus promoting the development of the contemporary semiconductor industry. The preparation of heterojunction materials and the study of their physical and optoelectronic properties are crucial to the theoretical study of two-dimensional material engineering. The research on the preparation strategies, physical properties, and industrial applications of heterojunctions is an important development of the semiconductor industry in the future, enhancing our country's scientific quality and national competitiveness.

16304618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16304618.value: Berkeleyacetal C (BAC) is a representative member of a growing family of meroterpenoid natural products that includes the berkeleyacetals A-C, purpurogenolides, miniolutelides, and chrysogenolides. Since 2007, when BAC was first isolated by Stierle and co-workers from an acidified culture of the fungus Penicilium sp. obtained from metal-sulfate-rich water from Berkeley Pit Lake, USA, three other research groups have found this secondary metabolite in other Penicilium fungus sources. Remarkably, these four groups have consistently found that among the known members of this family, BAC displayed the most potent anti-inflammatory activity (IC50 = 0.8 μM; positive control indomethacin IC50 = 34.5 μM) without significant cytotoxicity up to 80 μM, which suggests that BAC is a very promising lead compound for the development of anti-inflammatory drugs. However, the scarce availability of this secondary metabolite from natural sources precludes such drug development. This proposed project will aim to develop the first chemical synthesis of BAC and provide a library of BAC analogues for establishing the structure-activity relationship. However, the daunting structural complexity of BAC presents an unprecedented synthetic challenge and there has been no synthetic study since its isolation in 2007. In this proposal, we describe an efficient strategy involving two cycloadditions ([4+2] and [5+2]) for the construction of the 6-7-6-5-6 pentacyclic framework and put forward a three-stage research plan. In Stage I, efforts will be focused on model studies of the intramolecular Diels-Alder reaction ([4+2]) of pyranulose derivatives with dienes to provide general guidelines on substitution of diene substrates, functional group tolerance, and diastereoselectivity (endo/exo). In Stage II, we will explore the inter- and intramolecular [5+2] cycloadditions of 3-oxidopyrylium ylides with alkenes/alkynes by investigating the effects of substitution on 3-oxidopyrulium ylides and dipolarophiles as well as detachable linker strategy. Preliminary results from the first and second stages of research, verifying the viability of two cycloadditions, will be critical to the success of our strategy. Finally, based on the findings of model studies of the two key cycloadditions a detailed route to synthesizing BAC will be developed. The sequence of ring formation could be different and we propose an alternative route to BAC, in which an A ring and epoxide are created after the two key cycloadditions. In addition, we will explore the possible approaches to accessing the other members of this family (berkeleyacetals, purpurogenolides, and chrysogenolides) by installation of a methyl ester group at C11 and manipulation of functional groups on A/B rings. Berkeleyacetal C（BAC）是一類家族成員數目不斷增長的萜類天然產物的代表，其中包括Berkeleyacetals A-C，purpurogenolides, miniolutelides, and chrysogenolides。自2007年以來，BAC首次由Stierle和同事從美國伯克利皮特湖的富含金屬硫酸鹽的水中獲得的真菌Penicilium sp.樣品的酸化培養物中分離出來，其他三個研究小組在其他青黴菌來源中發現了這種次生代謝產物。值得注意的是，這四個研究組一致發現，在這個家族的已知成員中，BAC顯示出最有效的抗炎活性（IC50 =0.8μM; 陽性對照吲哚美辛IC50 =34.5μM），沒有顯著的細胞毒性，高達80μM，這表明 BAC是一種非常有前途的抗炎藥物開發先導化合物。然而，這種次級代謝物的天然來源非常稀缺，是開發這種藥物的主要障礙。 本項目旨在開發BAC的第一個化學合成，並提供BAC類似物庫，以建立結構 - 活性關係。但是，BAC令人生畏的結構複雜性給化學合成帶來了前所未有的挑戰，自2007年被分離以來，沒有任何有關化學合成研究報導。在這個提案中，我們設計了一個有效的合成策略，涉及兩個環加成（[4 + 2]和[5 + 2]），用於構建6-7-6-5-6五環框架，並提出了一個三階段研究計劃。在第一階段的研究中，我們將集中研究模型分子含二烯吡喃酮的分子內Diels-Alder反應（[4 + 2]），以獲得此反應的有關信息包括二烯底物取代基影響，官能團耐受性和非對映選擇性（endo/exo）。在第二階段，我們將通過研究取代對3-氧化吡啶葉立德和親偶極物的影響以及可拆卸的連接策略，探討3-氧化吡喃基葉立德與烯烴/炔烴的分子間和分子內[5 + 2]環加成反應。 第一和第二階段研究的初步結果，驗證兩個環加成的可行性，對我們的策略成功至關重要。最後，基於兩個關鍵環加成的模型研究結果，將開發合成BAC的詳細途徑。環形成的順序可以變化，並且我們提出了到BAC的替代途徑，其中在兩個關鍵環加成之後產生A環和環氧化物。此外，我們將研究通過在C11（Diels-Alder反應）中安裝甲酯基團和改變A /B上的官能團方法來獲得該家族其他成員（berkeleyacetals, purpurogenolides, miniolutelides, and chrysogenolides）。

16304618.label: Realisation of objectives
16304618.value: With this funding support, we have achieved the overall goal of this project. Specifically, we have developed an efficient intramolecular Diels-Alder [4+2] cycloaddition to construct the tetracyclic core (BCDE ring systems) (Objective 1), which had been confirmed by X-ray diffraction analysis. To further explore the utility of this new method, we employed intermolecular [5+2] cycloaddition of oxidopyrylium ylide generated from Achmatowicz rearrangement product for the synthesis of diene substrate for Diels-Alder cycloaddition (Objective 2), which was successfully implemented to provide the key ring system for berkeleyacetal C. This work was published in a top peer-reviewed international journal in organic chemistry (Organic Letters). In an effort to achieve the first total synthesis of berkeleyacetal C (Objective 3), we advanced smoothly to the late stage of synthesis (17 steps) but encountered significant synthetic challenge because the stereochemistry outcome of Diels-Alder cycloaddition was unexpectedly wrong and the correction of this stereochemistry problem was very time-consuming and labor-intensive. We had to start over again with new design of substrates to overcome the unfavorable steric bias. However, the limited GRF funding (~0.5M HKD for three years) does not allow us to continue the exploration for this synthetic challenge. As for Objective 4, the project has trained one PhD student (Miguel Adrian Mraquez-Cadena, PhD in 2021) and provided research opportunity for more than 5 undergraduates who involved in this project by preparing some starting materials and intermediates.

16304618.value: The major findings and research outcome of this project include (1) development of an efficient synthetic strategy for the construction of the structurally complex natural products (berkeleyacetals), featuring Achmatowicz rearrangement and two cycloadditions ([4+2] and [5+2]) to forge the tetracyclic core (Org.Lett. 2021, 23, 9277-9231), (2) the expanded application of Achmatowicz rearrangement in total synthesis of complex natural products and accomplishment of total synthesis of marine natural products siladenoserinols A and H (Org. Lett. 2019, 21, 9704-9708), (3) discovery of the antibacterial activity of siladenoserinols, (4) development of a new reaction (C-aryl glycosylation) that allow for expedite synthesis of highly medicine-valued heterocycles (tetrahydropyrans) via Achmatowicz rearrangement (J. Org. Chem. 2020, 85, 6663-6674).

16304618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16304618.value: The chemical synthesis of berkelyacetals remains unattained for its extremely complex structure and highly condensed oxygen functionality. With our establishment of the synthetic strategy, it is possible to achieve the first chemical synthesis by (1) re-arranging the reaction sequence and (2) reducing the steric hindrance of the seven-membered ring before the Diels-Alder reaction (i.e., breaking the ether bridge). Additionally, the synthetic work of berkeleyacetals has great potential to generate a library of small molecules and lead to discovery of a lead compound with high medicinal value (anti-inflammatory, anti-tumor and antibiotics). Therefore, it is suggested to use our synthetic strategy for synthesis of a library of tetracyclic compounds and evaluate their potential biological activity.

16304618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16304618.value: This project is focused on development of the first chemical synthesis of a natural product called berkeleyacetal C, which are structurally complex but exhibit interesting anti-inflammation activity. Our synthetic studies led to the development of an efficient synthetic strategy that allows for construction of the core structure of berkeleyacetal C. While the chemical synthesis of berkeleyacetal C could not be accomplished, our work lay led to several new discoveries including [5+2] cycloaddition of oxidopyrylium ion derived from Achmatowicz rearrangement products, palladium-catalyzed C-aryl glycosylation, and antibacterial activity of two related natural products siladenoserinols A and H. These findings might be of significance in organic synthesis and drug discovery.

16304718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16304718.value: The preparation of high quality specimens of atomically-thin graphene was a breakthrough that opened the door to the discovery of its exceptional electronic, vibrational, mechanical, chemical and optical properties. Efforts to enhance graphene’s functionality were undertaken to support the development of practical graphene-based devices. These efforts have resulted in the development of various ways of manipulating its properties, for example, by substitutional doping or other chemical modification. Additionally, significant strain-induced effects have also been observed that raise the prospect of tuning graphene’s properties through strain engineering. In order to expand our toolbox for controlling graphene, it is desirable to explore the interplay between various functionalizing modifications and the elastic properties of graphene that underpin its manipulation by strain engineering. In the proposed research, we will study how modifications that alter the bonding character within graphene affect its elastic properties. We will explore the influences of reversible adsorptive hydrogenation, nitrogen substitutional doping, and the introduction of vacancy point defects. This will be done by examining how the quasi-periodically rippled morphology of suspended graphene under small lateral tension changes in response to in-situ graphene modifications. Non-contact measurements of ripple morphology will be carried out using low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM). This will be accomplished by evaluating the LEEM phase contrast produced by graphene ripples using the Fourier optics modeling approach, to determine quantitatively the characteristic ripple period and amplitude. Changes in ripple morphology that are induced by modifications of graphene will be related to relative changes in elastic properties using classical elasticity theory of membranes. Performance of in-situ measurement and graphene modification will be carried out in a meticulously clean ultra-high vacuum environment. This will facilitate well-controlled modifications that exclude unwanted extrinsic effects due to contamination. Supplementary in-situ characterization using electron diffraction and spectroscopy will help to correlate changes in graphene’s defect structure, strain and chemical state with morphological changes. The behavior of exfoliated graphene and CVD-grown graphene will be compared to determine if intrinsic effects exhibited by pristine graphene survive for less perfect scalable graphene. This work will test the hypothesis that the elastic properties of graphene can be manipulated by altering electronic bonds within the layer through various modifications. Establishing these effects will add a new dimension to control of graphene’s electronic, optical, vibrational properties via strain engineering. Our investigations may also contribute to the current intense debate about the role of crumpling in the elastic properties of graphene.

16304718.label: Realisation of objectives
16304718.value: The project objectives were addressed by performing in-situ, non-contact measurements of suspended graphene samples using low energy electron microscopy (LEEM) and by carrying out advanced development of LEEM image formation theory related to the measurement approach: 1. Sample fabrication The fabrication of suspended graphene samples used in this research was described in detail in the mid-term report. In summary, - fabrication procedures were developed in collaboration with Dr. Stefano Roddaro at the Institute of Nanoscience in Pisa, Italy during the first reporting period. This work overcame several challenges to producing samples with adequate yield and quality. The first batch of samples was available close to the end of the first reporting period. - The samples were made by transferring graphene flakes (~150 m diameter) grown by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) a metal growth substrate to an insulating SiN substate. Flakes were suspended over trenches (100 m length x 7 m width) that had been etched in the SiN substrate with their edges on opposite sides of the trenches overlaid on metallic contacts. - The original research plan described in the proposal was to transition from remote sample fabrication by Dr. Roddaro in Italy to in-house sample fabrication at HKUST. However, as reported in the mid-term report, this plan had to be revised because the funding awarded to the project was not sufficient to support research staff to develop in-house fabrication capabilities. We relied upon our external collaborator for fabrication of all subsequent samples and focused our resources on measurements that could only be done using the instrumentation in our laboratory. In accordance with the plan for subsequent work outlined in the mid-term report, the samples were integrated into devices suitable for study using LEEM. An external electrical circuit was connected to the metallic contacts on the sample by wire bonding. The closed electrical circuit was later used to pass current through graphene for cleaning by resistive heating and potentiometry measurements described below. A shortcoming of the first set of samples was identified during our initial experiments. It was found that the suspended sections of the graphene flakes could be easily damaged during cleaning by resistive heating. Rapid vaporization of suspended graphene was initiated at its freestanding edges, presumably because it was hotter there due to low conductive heat dissipation. Several approaches were used to address this problem: - We monitored the voltage-current characteristics of the on-sample circuit to detect initial signs of anomalous heating behavior that may signal the onset of damage. - We modified the layout of graphene in subsequent sample batches. Graphene was mounted with all edges in contact with the SiN substrate to enhance heat dissipation and avoid unstable freestanding graphene edges. This was challenging. - We explored the use of an ancillary cleaning method: graphene was exposed to atomic hydrogen or atomic oxygen with the aim of promoting cleaning at lower temperature under safe heating conditions. These approaches extended the sample lifetime but did not completely protect them. 2. Experimental measurements The objectives of the experiments were to study how the elastic properties of suspended single-layer graphene prepared by CVD-growth and/or exfoliation are affected by modifications, particularly hydrogenation but possibly also others. This demanded the use of atomically-clean graphene, hence the efforts to clean graphene described above, and that in-situ measurements be made in a clean ultra-high vacuum environment. The experiments performed in a LEEM met this requirement. Our work on CVD-grown graphene concentrated exclusively on hydrogenation due to limited funding resources. Our principle approach to achieving the objectives was to observe how the sinusoidally-rippled morphology of suspended graphene induced by tensile strain was affected by hydrogenation. The method we used for characterizing the rippled morphology of graphene in a LEEM is discussed further below. However, ripples could not be observed in our investigations. This was not due to a shortcoming of the characterization method that we employed since the sensitivity of LEEM to the rippled morphology had been demonstrated in our earlier published work. Rather, the problem must have been the inability to prepare suspended graphene samples with sufficient strain to produce ripples, despite several preparation attempts. The second experimental approach we took was to perform in-situ, non-contact potentiometry measurements using the low energy potentiometry (LEEP) imaging method in a LEEM instrument [P4,C2]. In LEEP, the local surface potential can be determined because of the measurable effect it has on the reflectivity of low energy electrons. We performed operando LEEP measurements to determine the potential variation across the sample when current was applied via the sample heating circuitry. The local sheet resistance was determined from the current dependence of the potential gradients in the suspended graphene and the graphene on SiN substrate regions. The spatially resolved measurements in the suspended graphene provided a tantalizing clue about strain that is presented below. After establishing the baseline behavior of clean graphene, the effects of hydrogenation on the sheet resistance were then explored. This was done by performing measurements after exposing graphene to an atomic hydrogen flux generated by a thermal cracker. One control experiment correlated the reversibility of sheet resistance variations with the reversible adsorption and thermal desorption of hydrogen. Another control experiment was performed to test the effect of exposing the sample to molecular hydrogen on its sheet resistance. The negative result of this control experiment is consistent with expectations that graphene does not react with molecular hydrogen. The surface potential variation in the graphene on metal contact during current flow was also measured. This measurement provided insight about charge injection into graphene. Characteristic non-linear potential profiles were observed that were evaluated using models developed earlier to describe current injection in traditional semiconductor devices. 3. Foundations of sample characterization An important part of the planned experimental investigations was to characterize the rippled morphology of strained suspended graphene by an in-situ, non-contact method in a LEEM. The principle of this approach was demonstrated in earlier published work. That work showed that details of sample morphology, including graphene ripples, can be determined by comparing a series of LEEM images obtained at different focus, i.e., a LEEM image focal series, to Fourier optics (FO) image simulations. A key project objective underpinning the use of this approach was to ensure its quantitative accuracy. This goal was achieved by work on three topics: - We developed the two-dimensional FO imaging theory [P1,C1]. This was done by extending the scalar form of the existing one-dimensional FO theory to vector form. The extended FO theory was demonstrated explicitly for the sinusoidally rippled morphology of strained free-standing graphene (Fig. 3 in [C1]). - We developed a method to characterize the divergence of the electron source in a LEEM instrument [P2]. The source divergence was determined experimentally by evaluating the image focal series of a well-known test object using FO image simulations. An atomic step on a metal surface was chosen as the test object. - We updated the theoretical treatment of partial electron temporal coherence to improve our understanding of how it affects image formation in microscopes that employ FE electron sources [P3,C2]. This was done by formulating a temporal coherence envelope function for a FE energy distribution that is used in FO image simulations. P#/C# refer to publications/conference presentations in Part C.

16304718.label: Major findings and research outcome
16304718.value: Operando LEEP measurements of suspended graphene structures demonstrated the targeted effect of hydrogenation and other phenomena [P4,C3]: (1) A comparative study of suspended graphene and graphene in contact with a supporting SiN substrate in a series configuration revealed that the sheet resistance of suspended and supported graphene differed by a factor of 2. The relatively lower sheet resistance of supported graphene was attributed to the graphene-SiN interfacial interaction and/or differences of tensile strain in suspended and supported graphene. (2) The sheet resistance of suspended graphene was anomalously enhanced by an additional factor of 2.5 at its edges, in contrast to the spatially uniform sheet resistance of supported graphene. This intriguing observation suggests that bending strain in graphene affects its transport properties. (3) The hydrogenation of suspended graphene produced a reversible 15%-25% reduction of its sheet resistance depending upon atomic hydrogen dosage. This is consistent with the reversible formation of hydrogen-terminated graphane. (4) Evidence of “current crowding” in current injection due to the resistivity mismatch at the metal electrode-graphene junction was observed. The contact resistance was determined from the characteristic non-linear potential gradient that this caused at the junction. Advances in the understanding of image formation in electron microscopy were also made that underpinned the research: (1) The two-dimensional (2D) Fourier optics (FO) imaging theory was developed [P1,C1]. 2D FO is essential for performing an accurate quantitative evaluation of ripples in suspended graphene or other sample features that may not be appropriately described by the preceding 1D theory. (2) A method for characterizing the electron source divergence in low energy electron microscopy was developed [P2]. The divergence is an important instrumental parameter because it affects how sample features appear, particularly graphene ripples, under defocus conditions. We determined the divergence to be a substantial factor of 2 smaller than had been assumed in the past. This advance ensures the quantitative accuracy of sample morphology characterization by the evaluation of image focal series using FO simulations. (3) An envelope function that describes the effect of partial electron coherence in FO was developed for electrons emitted by a field emission (FE) source [P3,C2]. This envelope function produces a substantial focus offset in FO image simulations. Quantitative evaluations of sample morphological features, such as graphene ripples, by FO simulations of image focal series must take this novel effect into account to ensure their accuracy. P#/C# refer to publications/conference presentations in Part C.

16304718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16304718.value: Further attempts at mastery of sample fabrication may finally produce strained suspended graphene samples with rippled morphology suitable for in-situ, non-contact measurements of elastic properties using LEEM. This may be pursued by building upon the know-how developed during the project by extending our external collaboration with Dr. Roddaro. The alternative approach to the problem using LEEP that we successfully adopted in this project is an excellent foundation for expanding research on the imaging of electronic transport phenomena in 2D nanoelectronic devices. We envision that the experimental approach can be adapted for in operando measurements of charge carrier mobility during the application source-drain and back-gate voltages in FET devices. Pending the preliminary demonstration of the measurement principle for devices, we intend to seek funding to pursue this new line of research. Additional work may be carried out to characterize the source divergence and temporal coherence envelope function for a full range of electron source operation conditions. This work will address the variation of these source characteristics that may occur when operation conditions are adjusted to control the electron emission current in real experiments.

16304718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16304718.value: The properties of an atomically-thin graphene layer in hybrid suspended/supported structures were investigated using the low energy electron potentiometry method. This non-contact, imaging method revealed intrinsic spatial variations of the sheet resistance that could not be detected without disturbance by potentiometry methods requiring contact to the sensitive graphene sample. The observations are attributed to the effects of bending strain in suspended graphene, tensile strain differences between suspended and supported graphene, and its interaction with the supporting substrate. Hydrogenation reduced(increased) the sheet resistance of suspended(supported) graphene. Furthermore, important characteristics of current flow into graphene were ascertained from observations of “current crowding” at the graphene-metal electrode contact. These results may play a role in enhancing the functionality of practical graphene-based two-dimensional nanoelectronic devices currently under development. Advances in the understanding of image formation in low energy electron microscopy (LEEM) were also made. The two-dimensional Fourier optics imaging theory was developed. A method for characterizing the electron source divergence was developed and implemented in LEEM for the first time. The effects of field emission sources used in state-of-the-art instruments on image formation were also elucidated. These advances will ensure the quantitative accuracy of a non-contact method to characterize sample morphology with LEEM.

16304918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16304918.value: Ultracold atoms, pristine and highly tunable systems, allow one to synthesize and explore topological phases analogous to topological electronic materials in which a topology plays an important role along with strong correlation and symmetry in the system. Owing to their full control of atomic Hamiltonian, a variety of topological phenomena have been observed in cold atoms including the long sought-after model such as the Haldane model. With the exception of very recent studies, however, most of the experimental work done on topological states realized in ultracold atoms has been conducted in a weakly interacting regime. The experimental investigation of interacting topological states has been rare in cold atoms. Interestingly, strongly interacting atomic systems can exhibit exotic topological phases with correlated pairing mechanisms, many of which have not been observed even in condensed-matter systems. In the proposed study, we will study such rich interacting topological phases with erbium fermions using their unique electronic and optical properties. To realize non-trivial band topology, spin-orbit coupling will be implemented in optical lattices using a narrow optical transition of erbium atoms, giving rise to long-lived spin-orbit-coupled gases. Second, the band spectrum and the stability of spin-orbit-coupled fermions can be spectroscopically probed near multiple known Feshbach resonances. In addition, the strong magnetic dipole-dipole interactions of erbium fermions may generate unprecedented correlation effects. In the proposed project, we will expand our capability to explore topological physics with interacting cold atoms. We propose (1) the development of an apparatus for cooling erbium atoms, (2) the realization of spin-orbit-coupled Fermi gases of erbium atoms using a narrow optical transition, and (3) the investigation of topological properties of spin-orbit-coupled fermions with tunable interactions. The successful completion of the proposed project will advance our understanding of interacting topological phases. 超冷原子是一種純淨和高度可調控的系統，允許人們合成和探索類似於拓撲電子材料中的拓撲相，其中拓撲和强關聯性以及對稱性一起發揮著重要的作用。由於冷原子系統的原子哈密頓量可被充分調控，所以在冷原子中已經觀察到各種拓撲現象，包括人们長期尋找的模型，如霍爾丹（Haldane）模型。然而，除了最近的研究之外，大多數在超冷原子中實現拓撲態的實驗工作都限局於弱相互作用的情况。强相互作用拓撲態的實驗研究在冷原子中非常罕見。 有趣的是，强相互作用原子系統可以表現出具有關聯配對機制的奇异拓撲相，其中許多甚至在凝態系統中也沒有被觀察到。在所提出的研究中，我們將會利用鉺費米子獨特的電學和光學性質來研究這些豐富的相互作用拓撲相。為了實現非平庸的拓撲能帶，我們將利用鉺原子的窄線光學躍遷在光學晶格中實現自旋-軌道耦合，從而產生長壽命的自旋-軌道耦合氣體。其次，自旋-軌道耦合費米子的能譜和穩定性可以在多個已知的費什巴赫共振附近進行光譜探測。此外，鉺費米子的强磁偶極-偶極相互作用可能產生新奇的關聯效應。 在擬議的項目中，我們將會擴展我們利用相互作用冷原子探索拓撲物理的能力，我們提出（1）搭建冷卻鉺原子的實驗裝置，（2）利用窄線光學躍遷實現自旋-軌道耦合的鉺原子費米氣體，和（3）利用可調控的相互作用研究自旋-軌道耦合費米子的拓撲性質。該項目的成功將促進我們對相互作用拓撲相的理解。

16304918.label: Realisation of objectives
16304918.value: During the project, we aimed to construct a new quantum gas apparatus in which a cold erbium gas can be produced and to experimentally reveal the effect of dipole-dipole interaction especially when external lights interact with atoms. The erbium atomic system is expected to provide an exceptional opportunity to explore dipolar physics with spin-orbit coupling, atom-lights interactions or topological phases. In the proposed project, several PhD students were trained by participating in the experimental project. Three of them graduated, and some other junior students have continued to study in the program. In the first phase of the project, we first realized a magneto-optical trap of erbium atoms but the limited number of atoms in the trap prohibited us from realizing a degenerate gas of atoms. To overcome this issue, we devised an alternative scheme for slowing down atoms by implementing the second stage slower. This new scheme allowed us to enhance the number of atoms by an order of magnitude, leading to a Bose-Einstein condensate of erbium of >40,000 atoms. In parallel, we developed a stabilization scheme for homebuilt laser systems, which significantly improved the performance of the experiment. In the second phase, we expanded our experimental capability, including implementing radio-frequency pulses, Feshbach resonances, and tunable trap geometry. In particular, we developed a control scheme for tuning the strength of the dipolar effect with respect to the s-wave scattering. On the one hand, we for the first time revealed the effect of dipolar interactions on the atom-light interaction. For example, we investigated a matter-wave superradiance process from a dipolar Bose-Einstein condensate, and discover a new way to control such phenomenon via dipolar interactions. Our finding suggests that an isotropic dispersion relation plays a critical role when atoms are outcoupled to the lights, which hints at the spin-momentum locking in the presence of dipolar interactions. Over the past years, we had extended our understanding of spin-orbit coupling in neutral atoms. In this project, we generalized the spin-orbit coupling to non-Hermitian regime when the dissipation plays the role. This non-Hermitian spin-orbit coupling was successfully realized and observed in a bulk atomic gas, and is being examined even in lattices.

16304918.label: Major findings and research outcome
16304918.value: [1] Realization of an Erbium Bose-Einstein condensate We realized Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of Er atoms with tunable s-wave and dipolar interactions in a newly developed apparatus. In the project, we developed an efficient method for trapping slow Er atoms in a narrow linewidth magneto-optical trap. After evaporative cooling in a crossed optical dipole trap, we achieved a spin-polarized condensate of 40,000 atoms at the temperature of T~50nK. The efficient preparation of ultracold erbium bosons offers new possibilities for studying many-body physics with dipolar interactions. [Ref] Bojeong Seo, Ziting Chen, Mingchen Huang, Mithilesh K Parit, Yifei He, Peng Chen and Gyu-Boong Jo Apparatus for producing a 168Er Bose-Einstein condensate, Journal of Korean Physical Society, In press (2022) [2] Spin-orbit coupling in the non-Hermitian regime Despite the considerable progress in non-Hermitian physics, the spin-orbit coupling mechanism and its related topological phases have been widely studied only in Hermitian systems , and much less is known experimentally about scenarios in which dissipation plays a major role in spin-orbit-coupled quantum systems. A good understanding of such non-Hermitian spin-orbit coupling is of particular importance for classifying non-Hermitian topological phases, a classification that remains elusive in condensed matter physics. To date, no non-Hermitian SOC has been experimentally realized in quantum systems. we have realized tunable dissipative spin-orbit-coupled bands for ultracold atoms, fully characterized the parity-time symmetry-breaking transition (i.e., its exceptional point), and observed the topological features of non-Hermitian spin-orbit-coupled bands. This work set the stage for exploring topological phases in the non-Hermitian regime and open up a new direction in bandgap engineering using non-Hermitian spin-orbit coupling in many-body physics. The second-stage slowing beams together with active stabilization of the laser system allowed us to achieve a Bose-Einstein condensate of erbium. A 102 013319 (2020); Ziting Chen et al., Active control of a diode laser with injection locking using a laser line filter, Review of Scientific Instruments 92 123005 (2021)

16304918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16304918.value: The achievement of the GRF project opened a new opportunity of exploring dipolar physics in various systems. For example, our system lays out the foundation for investigating spin-orbit-coupled quantum systems beyond natural conditions, such as with dissipation or dipolar interactions. We envision that unprecedented quantum states can be discovered in such systems. One of the open questions is how spin-orbit coupling interplays with dissipation, dipolar interactions, and s-wave interactions in the many-body dynamics. As an immediate follow-up experiment, we plan to investigate the ground state in the dipolar quantum gas with spin-orbit coupling.

16304918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16304918.value: In the proposed project, we aimed to explore synthetic spin-orbit coupling, a key physical mechanism underlying topological phenomena, with ultracold atoms. Despite extensive studies, however, much less is known about the role interactions or dissipation play in spin-orbit-coupled systems. The result of the project laid out the foundation for investigating such systems. Several novel topological lattice platforms were developed by using a tailored spin-orbit coupling configuration, and the dissipative spin-orbit coupling was experimentally realized. The finding reported in the project will lead to a better understanding of topological matter and its key mechanism behind, and highlights our capability of quantum simulation with ultracold atoms.

16305018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16305018.value: Inverse problems are problems where the cause for an observed or desired effect is to be determined. We obtain a large part of our information about the world by probing it with waves -- electromagnetic, acoustic, elastic, quantum and other types -- and measuring the response. A large class of inverse problems involves determining the properties of the object being probed from those responses. Inverse problems arise in all fields of science and engineering. The proposed research considers fundamental questions in the mathematical theory of inverse problems which are motivated by applications in medical imaging, geophysics and cosmology among others. Developing mathematical techniques to address these difficult questions will undoubtedly have real world applications in the future that will benefit mankind. The proposal plans to probe the interior of the earth, determine the structure of space-time from observations made now and probe the human body with electrical currents. The mathematics of X-ray tomography has, for instance, contributed to the development of CAT scans and other medical imaging techniques which help save lives every day. The proposer will address the mathematical theory of several fundamental inverse problems arising in many areas of science and technology including medical imaging, geophysics, astrophysics and nondestructive testing to name a few. We propose three major topics of research. The first one is travel time tomography in anisotropic media. In mathematical terms this involves the determination of a Riemannian metric (anisotropic sound speed) in the interior of a domain from the lengths of geodesics joining points on the boundary (travel times) and from other kinematic information. We will also consider travel time tomography in anisotropic elastic media. The second topic is inverse problems for non-linear hyperbolic equations, including Einstein's equations that arise in cosmology and many other areas of science and technology. We propose to solve inverse problems that have not been solved for the corresponding linear equations. The third topic is electrical impedance tomography (EIT), also called Calderón's problem. In this inverse method one attempts to determine the conductivity of a medium by making voltage and current measurements at the boundary. This problem also arises in geophysics and medical imaging. 逆問題是關於如何將觀測和測量的結果轉換為物體或系統的信息的廣義框架。我們通過電磁波，聲波，彈性波，量子波等並量度其反應來獲取關於世界的大部分信息。大部分逆問題嘗試從這些反應中確定被探測對象的屬性，並廣泛出現在所有科學和工程領域。這次研究探討逆問題的數學理論中的基本問題，這些問題出現於醫學成像，地球物理學和宇宙學等領域。探討數學技術來解決這些難題無疑將為人類帶來莫大裨益，可用於探測地球內部觀測時空結構，利用電流探測人體等範疇。例如研究X射線斷層掃描的數學有助於CAT掃描和其他醫學成像技術的發展，這些技術都有助於挽救生命。我們將討論在許多科學和技術領域出現的幾個基本逆問題的數學理論，包括醫學成像，地球物理學，天體物理學和非破壞性測試等等。我們提出了三個主要的研究課題。第一個是各向異性介質中的走時層析成像。在數學術語中，這涉及從邊界上的測地線連接點（行進時間）和其他運動學信息確定域內部的黎曼度量（各向異性聲速）。我們還將考慮各向異性彈性介質中的走時層析成像。第二個主題是非線性雙曲方程的逆問題，包括在宇宙學和許多其他科學和技術領域出現的愛因斯坦方程。我們建議解決相應線性方程尚未解決的逆問題。第三個主題是電阻抗斷層成像（EIT），也稱為Calderón問題。在該反向方法中，人們試圖通過在邊界處進行電壓和電流測量來確定介質的電導率。這問題也出現在地球物理學和醫學成像中。

16305018.label: Major findings and research outcome
16305018.value: We have considered an inverse boundary value problem for a semilinear wave equation on a time-dependent Lorentzian manifold with time-like boundary. The time-dependent coefficients of the nonlinear terms can be recovered in the interior from the knowledge of the Neumann-to-Dirichlet map. Either distorted plane waves or Gaussian beams can be used to derive uniqueness. For an inverse boundary value problem for a nonlinear elastic wave equation, we have showed that all the parameters appearing in the equation can be uniquely determined from boundary measurements under certain geometric assumptions. The proof is based on second order linearization and Gaussian beams. We also studied the mixed ray transform of tensor fields on a three-dimensional compact simple Riemannian manifold with boundary. We proved the injectivity of the transform, up to natural obstructions, and establish stability estimates for the normal operator on generic three-dimensional simple manifold in the case of 1 +1 and 2+2 tensors fields. We introduced a model featuring a Lévy process in a bounded domain with semi-transparent boundary, by considering the fractional Laplacian operator with lower order non-local perturbations. In ultrasound imaging problem governed by a nonlinear wave equation of Westervelt type with variable wave speed, we showed that the coefficient of nonlinearity can be recovered uniquely from knowledge of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map.

16305018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16305018.value: The PI will continue the exploration on inverse problems for nonlinear equations. Expected results include inverse boundary value problem, nonlinear elastic wave equation, mixed ray transform, lower order non-local perturbations, and solutions to the nonlinear ultrasound imaging problem.

16305018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16305018.value: Inverse Problems (IP) are problems where causes for a desired or an observed effect are to be determined. They lie at the heart of scientific inquiry and technological development. The enormous increase in computing power and the development of powerful algorithms has made it possible to apply the techniques of IP to real-world problems of growing complexity. Applications include a number of medical as well as other imaging techniques, location of oil and mineral deposits in the earth's substructure, creation of astrophysical images from telescope data, finding cracks and interfaces within materials, shape optimization, model identification in growth processes and modelling in the life sciences. This research project combines techniques from mathematical analysis, differential geometry, numerical analysis, machine learning, image processing, scientific computing, and computer science.

16305418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16305418.value: Accurate identification of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) primary and secondary sources and quantification of their contributions shapes the scientific basis underlying pollution control policies. Traditional measurement-based source apportionment often relies on daily or sub-daily time series of molecular markers and elemental tracers, coupled with receptor modeling using positive matrix factorization (PMF). However, the off-line nature of filter-based measurements severely limits its utility in addressing episodic pollution events and in developing timely response. The bottleneck for a rapid source analysis is a lack of highly time-resolved data of various source-specific tracers. In this project, this data constrain will be resolved by augmenting existing air quality research supersites with an online X-Ray fluorescence spectrometer for elements and an in-situ thermal desorption aerosol gas chromatography-mass spectrometry analyzer for organic molecular source markers. We will first conduct field campaigns to collect collocated hourly measurements of individual PM2.5 components in months of high pollution borne from photochemical activity or poor dispersion conditions. The online data availability and high-time resolution nature open up an opportunity for rapid source apportionment that is not possible with daily/sub-daily measurements. The second phase of the project will focus on developing rapid source apportionment capability using the array of online molecular and elemental tracer data. In principle, a rapid source diagnosis of an episodic event could be obtained by incorporating the episode measurements into a dataset that has previously been analyzed for source contributions using PMF and subsequently re-running PMF with the expanded dataset. We will characterize stability performance of source apportionment results to achieve the aim of establishing a robust procedure for rapid source apportionment under different pollution conditions. The results from this project will provide policy makers with valuable information to enable a faster response to pollution events and to formulate more timely PM emission control strategies. 准确定量识别一次及二次污染源对细颗粒物（PM2.5）的贡献是有效防治PM2.5的重要科学前提。传统的受体模型源解析大多基于滤膜采样及离线实验室分析所获得的分子和元素示踪物数据，再结合受体模型正矩阵因子分解法（PMF）对污染源进行分析。然而，样品采集和化学分析所需要的时间从本质上限制了传统受体模型法在短时间高污染事件中研究诊断污染源的能力。要实现快速源解析，当前的瓶颈在于缺少各种源示踪物的高时间分辨率观测数据。本项目拟通过在现有的空气质量研究超级站里增加一台在线X射线荧光光谱仪和一台原位热脱附气溶胶气相色谱质谱分析器对元素和有机分子源示踪物进行在线测量，从而突破上述数据限制。 第一阶段，我们将选取重污染高发的月份进行野外观测、采样和分析，获取包括PM2.5主要化学成分（水溶性离子、元素碳和有机碳、金属和半金属元素）、无机和有机示踪物在内的高时间分辨率观测数据。第二阶段，我们将利用所采集到的数据，研究建立基于无机和有机示踪物的PM2.5快速源解析程序。主要思路是先将一部分高时间分辨率观测数据输入PMF模型中进行源解析并对重污染时段进行综合分析，以建立污染源经验数据库；接着引入新的重污染时段数据，与原有数据合并后输入PMF进行源解析，以得到对新加入高污染事件的诊断分析。随着观测数据的不断增加，不同污染情境下获得的源解析结果可以进行交叉验证，并用于测试程序的稳定性及降低不确定性，提高分析结果的准确度。 本项目的研究成果可以使大量的在线观测数据得到更好的整合分析从而及时反映大气颗粒物的来源及其贡献，以期为应对重污染过程的环境政策决定提供技术支持，更科学合理地防治颗粒物污染。

16305418.label: Realisation of objectives
16305418.value: Objective 1: To characterize and optimize the field operation of an online instrument for PM2.5 organic molecular markers (i.e. TAG-GC/MS) in a polluted environment The online instrument (i.e. the TAG-GC/MS system) we acquired was among the first two commercial sets made by Aerodyne Research Inc. Some components have not been field-tested and therefore their suitability was unknown at the state of this project. We carried out a series of experiments to field-test the online instrument for PM2.5 organic molecular markers, initially at the HKUST Air Quality Research Supersite on the campus of our university, and subsequently in an urban location in Shanghai on the site of Shanghai Academy of Environmental Science (SAES). Through the field tests, we have resolved/verified the following issues: (1) A HEPA filter originally designed to remove particles in the sampling stream so that only gas-phase organics would be collected downstream and analysed. We found this type of filter is not suitable for use with monitoring trace-level individual organic compounds in ambient samples, as they released some target organic analytes. To avoid any problems with the HEPA filters, we have decided not to use a HEPA filter in the sampling path. Subsequent sampling was conducted with a carbon-adsorbent based denuder in line to remove gaseous organic carbon upstream so that only particles would proceed to the CTD device for collection and subsequent GCMS quantification. (2) The carbon-adsorbent based denuder was tested to be effective in removing gaseous organics such as light alkane species. Residue heavy organics in the sampling path could be reduced by flushing the sampling line with clean carrier gas and checked with repeating the field blank samples. (3) The presence of the derivatization agent does not cause negative impact on the quantification of nonpolar organic analytes. Instead, slight to significant enhancement in responses of nonpolar organics was observed in the presence of the derivatization agent. This test ensures that the TAG-GC/MS system can analyze both nonpolar and polar organics in one analysis run. (4) Two sections, focus trap (FT) and the section connecting to GC column, when insulated by flame retardant glass fibre, helps with maintaining stable elevated temperature along the flow path, thus improves repeatability of signals. (5) The backflash time of the FT component is an important parameter and a 10-12 min backflash time is likely a good comprise setting for the list of target organic compounds. (6) Water condensation issue in the sampling inlet was solved by adding a heating tape and a silicone drier immediately after the cyclone or adding a Nafier dryer. (7) In the first set-up of the instrument, Teflon-coated plastic tubing and silicone tubing were used in many places in the sampling path for convenience. Our tests indicated that the silicone tubing should not be used to avoid introduction of the extra plastic-related compounds and siloxanes in the GC chromatograms. Objective 2: To obtain through field campaigns collocated measurements of PM2.5 major components, organic markers and elemental tracers in a polluted environment in months of high pollution borne from photochemical activity or poor dispersion conditions. We successfully operated the TAG-GC/MS system in two campaigns in collaboration with collaboration partner SAES. The first one lasted three weeks from 9 November to 3 December 2018 at the SAES urban site in Shanghai. The second one lasted ca. six weeks from Dec. 29, 2019 to Feb. 9, 2020. The second campaign spanned two unique time sections, namely before lockdown (Dec. 28, 2019 to Jan. 23, 2020) and during lockdown (Jan. 24 to Feb. 9, 2020), allowing us to examine the impact of reductions in transportation-related emissions on air quality. The detailed results from these two field campaigns have been documented in five peer-reviewed publications (Wang QQ et al, 2020; He et al., 2020; Li et al 2020; Wang and Yu, 2021; Wang S et al 2022). Objective 3: To develop a rapid source apportionment method based on the combined online data sets of molecular markers and elemental tracers. The rapid source apportionment method is based on receptor modelling of the combined data sets of organic molecular markers and elemental tracers. Two commonly used receptor models, chemical mass balance (CMB) and positive matrix factorization (PMF) are explored in this project. One piece of method development work in source apportionment that has been carried out is to understand how atmospheric degradation of organic tracers would impact source apportionment in CMB, using hopanes as an example group of organic tracers (Wong et al., 2019). We used data collected by our group in past projects to probe this issue. We found that a static representation of vehicular source profiles in CMB modeling would create flawed source estimation from vehicles and demonstrated the necessity of considering gas-particle partitioning of organic aerosol and hopane oxidation degradation in receptor models. We used the Source Finder Professional (SoFi Pro) to explore rapid source apportionment of PM2.5 with a set of online chemical speciation data collected in Shanghai during the second field campaign (i.e., 29/12/2019-9/2/2020). PMF runs with campaign-wide data as input (PMFref) were initially performed to obtain the reference profiles for the primary source factors. Short-term PMF analysis with a window length set as the initial 18 d (29/12/2019-15/1/2020) was conducted and the primary source profiles were constrained using the a-value approach embedded in SoFi software. Rolling PMF was then conducted with the fixed window length of 18 d and a step of 1 d using the remaining dataset. With the a-value constrains of the primary sources, the short-term rolling PMF can reproduce the individual primary sources well (slope 0.9-1.0), except for firework emission factor which showed clear lower estimation from the rolling PMF compared with the PMFref (slope 0.8). The results suggested the unique advantage of short-term PMF analysis to accurately apportion the sporadic sources. The total secondary sources were also modeled well (slope 1.0), but larger bias was observed for individual secondary sources. Source profile variation results suggested higher variability for the secondary sources, with average relative differences ranging 42-237%, while the primary source profiles showed much smaller variabilities (relative differences of 8-26%). The results from this study suggested that short-term PMF analysis with the a-value constrain in SoFi can be adopted to apportion the primary sources, while future improvement is needed to better predict the individual secondary sources.
