16502518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16502518.value: The objective of this study is to examine adoption by contestants of feedback in innovation tournaments. Firms initiate such tournaments to solicit solutions from the crowd for specific problems. An important element in innovation tournaments is the feedback that the contestants receive for the ideas that they generate. This feedback could help them refine their ideas and come up with better solutions for the tournament sponsors. In this study, we plan to examine and compare adoption by contestants of high-quality and low-quality feedback from tournament sponsors and tournament competitors. Doing so allows us to extend current research, which has not directly compared feedback from sponsors and competitors, and often implicitly assumes that the feedback given by the sponsors or competitors is of reasonably good quality. Our findings can contribute to a better feedback process and mechanism for innovation tournaments to benefit the various stakeholders and achieve better outcomes. 本研究的目的是检查参赛者对创新竞赛反馈建议的采用情况。企业发起此类竞赛，以征求群众针对具体问题寻找解决方案。创新竞赛里的一个重点是参赛者使用对他们的点子的反馈建议。 这些建议可以帮助参赛者改进他们的点子，并为比赛赞助商提供更好的解决方案。在这项研究中，我们计划检查和比较参赛者对比赛赞助商和其他比赛参赛者所给的高质量和低质量反馈建议的采用情况。这样做可以让我们扩展当前的研究，因为目前的研究没有直接比较赞助商和竞争对手的反馈建议，并且经常假设赞助商或竞争对手给出的建议具有相当好的质量。我们的研究结果可以为创新竞赛提供更好的反馈建议过程和机制，使各利益相关方受益并取得更好的成果。

16502518.label: Realisation of objectives
16502518.value: Through one field survey and two online experiments, I fully meet the project objectives of examining and comparing solvers’ use of feedback in crowdsourcing contests. In the field survey involving design contest participants, I demonstrate a source effect that causes solvers to exhibit a stronger intention to use seeker feedback than peer feedback. In an online experiment using a product naming contest, I show that the source effect affects solvers’ use of feedback of different practicality. A key insight is that, although solvers ideally should use practical feedback more than less practical feedback, they do not always do so in practice. A consequence of this is that the solvers may end up not generating high-quality ideas to address the seekers’ problems. In another online experiment, I propose a feedback rating mechanism to attenuate the source effect; the study of this mechanism was not in the initial proposal but an extension that I made in the project during the course of this research. I show that this mechanism can lead solvers to generate ideas in a manner that is more seeker-optimal.

16502518.label: Major findings and research outcome
16502518.value: This research examines the source effect in solvers’ use of feedback during crowdsourcing contests. In the first study, I discuss how solvers’ intention to use a feedback depends on whether the feedback is given by seekers or peers. The results from a field survey show that solvers have a stronger intention to use seeker feedback than peer feedback, even if the feedback is identical. In the second study, I further compare solvers’ use of feedback from different sources and of different practicality. One interesting result in the experiment is that solvers used less practical seeker feedback 1) almost as much as they used practical seeker feedback and 2) significantly more than they used peer feedback of any level of practicality. I also show that using less practical feedback could hurt idea quality. Hence, solvers may use feedback in a manner that does not help seekers obtain high-quality ideas that address their focal problems. In Study C, I test an intervention that requires solvers to evaluate the feedback for their initial idea, before they generate subsequent ideas. The results from an experiment show that the use of less practical seeker feedback decreased when solvers had to rate it. The mechanism also increased the use of practical peer feedback for certain solvers. Thus, the mechanism can cause the crowd to more deeply consider how ideas can improve during contests. In terms of the research outcome, I have presented this project at the International Conference on Information Systems, INFORMS Annual Meeting, Chinese University of Hong Kong, and University of Auckland. I have submitted to Organization Science, where one reviewer commented: "Let me congratulate the authors on an interesting paper. I think this area has a great deal of value for the field and the topic of feedback is a fruitful area. The use of controlled experiments is very well conceived (and also well argued for, as field experiments would be particularly problematic as the authors rightly argue). In short, there is a lot to like about the paper. " Another reviewer said: "I enjoyed reading this paper. I found the research question intriguing and has the potential to contribute to extant literature as well as practice. Additionally, the paper is well-structured and written. The authors provided details of their experiments, and analyses are adequate." I am currently addressing the review team's comments and revising the paper for resubmission.

16502518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16502518.value: As this project focuses on developmental feedback, an extension is to look at how the ideation process in is affected when such feedback and numerical ratings, which is another common form of in-process feedback in crowdsourcing contests, are given at the same time. Also, as solvers are likely to receive multiple feedback over the duration of the contests, future research can examine solvers’ behavior when they receive multiple feedback from a particular source or from different sources. In addition, subsequent works can examine contests in which the criteria to judge idea quality are clearer; the findings would either demonstrate the prominence of and/or ways to mitigate the source effect, and thus have important implications for crowdsourcing contests. In addition, new studies can incorporate the traits of solvers (e.g., their expertise or the extent that they take pride in delivering high-quality ideas) in the theorizing, as such factors could moderate the impacts of feedback source and practicality that I propose in this study.

16502518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16502518.value: Crowdsourcing contests allow idea-seeking firms (seekers) to address their problems by engaging agents (solvers) in the crowd to generate ideas. Feedback is an important aspect in crowdsourcing contests, and solvers often receive feedback from seekers but sometimes also from other competing solvers (i.e., peers). In an ideal situation, solvers should use practical feedback more than less practical feedback, so that they can generate high-quality ideas in the contests to help address seekers’ problems. However, in this research, I show that solvers use of feedback is affect the feedback source and, consequently, they at times overuse less practical feedback but underuse practical feedback. Such behaviors can have adverse impacts on the quality of the ideas that solvers generate. To address this problem, I test a mechanism to attenuate the source effect. The findings in this research can help us better understand and address certain issues in crowdsourcing contests. It also provides recommendations for seekers and platforms to improve the likelihood of obtaining high-quality ideas in crowdsourcing contests.

16502918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16502918.value: Focusing on the text in a large sample of analyst reports, we attempt to make the first investigation into the effect of analyst conflicts of interest on their reports and how the regulatory reform around 2002 (e.g., NASD Rule 2711, NYSE Rule 472 and the Global Settlement, which was intended to curb analyst conflicts of interest) impact analyst biases in their reports. Previous literature on analyst conflicts of interest focuses exclusively on analyst quantitative research output, including analyst recommendations and earnings forecasts. In contrast, investors consider the text in analyst reports far more important than analyst stock recommendations and earnings forecasts (see the Institutional Investor annual surveys of What Investors Really Want 1998-2015). We argue that, failing to consider the text of these reports, the extant literature has not developed a comprehensive understanding of the research quality of conflicted analysts or the impact of the regulation reform on the quality of their research. As Mehran and Stulz (2007) argue in their review, we still do not have conclusive evidence of whether affiliated analysts provide better research as a consequence of the conflicts, or whether regulation reform may enhance or reduce the quality of their research. In particular, it is still unknown whether conflicted analyst textual reports are just as biased as their recommendations, or whether they could be more informative because conflicted analysts are more familiar with the companies and industries covered. We believe that, by investigating analyst report texts, our proposed research project will fill an important void in the literature on analyst conflicts of interest. 我們專注於大量的金融分析師報告中的文本，試圖做出第一個調查分析師利益衝突對其報告中文字的影響，以及2002年左右的監管改革（例如，NASD規則2711，紐約證券交易所規則472和Global Settlement，都旨在遏制分析師的利益衝突）如何影響分析師的報告里的偏見。以前關於分析師利益衝突的文獻集中在分析師量化的研究產品，包括分析師的買賣建議和和盈利預測。相比之下，投資者認為分析師報告中的文字遠比分析師的買賣推薦和盈利預測更重要（見“投資者真正想要的”，《機構投資者》的年度調查1998-2015）。我們認為，沒有考慮這些報告的文字，現存的文獻并沒有全面了解利益衝突對分析師的研究質量或者監管改革對其研究質量的影響。正如Mehran和Stulz（2007）在他們的評論中辯稱，我們仍然沒有確鑿的證據證明，是否有嚴重利益衝突的關聯分析師可以提供更好的研究，以及，針對解決利益衝突問題的監管改革是否提高或降低了分析師的研究質量。特別是，我們仍然不知道有利益沖突的分析師寫的文字報告是否與他們的量化研究產品一樣有偏見， 或者他們的文字報告是否提供更多信息，因為這些分析師更熟悉所涵蓋的公司和行業。我們相信，通過調查分析師報告中的文字，我們提出的研究項目將填補一個重要的關於分析師利益衝突的文獻中的空缺。

16502918.label: Realisation of objectives
16502918.value: The project objectives are not achieved. The reason is mainly because the predicted results are not there. First, when we investigate whether in the pre- Reform period, affiliated analysts were more optimistic in the textual discussion of their research reports than unaffiliated analysts. We find that 24.8% of the affiliated analysts are optimistic, compared to 22.3% of the unaffiliated analysts. However, this slight difference between them is not statistically significant. We tried various different subsamples, aiming to enhance the differences, however, all attempts failed. The two samples are similar in their level of optimism. Second, we proposed but did not find evidence that affiliated analysts provide more positive statements than unaffiliated analysts. We also cannot find any evidence that suggests affiliated analysts are more reluctant to issue negative statements. Thrid, when we examined analysts by recommendation types. The predicted resulst did not exist in the much bigger sample of Buy. It is barely there in the Sell sample, however, the Sell is very small sample (fewer than 5% of the overall sample). The result is actually the opposite to our prediction for the Hold sample. Hence, we are quite convinced the main prediction does not exist. Because this is our main prediction, and our next prediction is only meaningful if affiliated analysts are more optimistic than unaffiliated analysts, the null results render the rest of the research design irrelevant. Nevertheless, we still made the attempt to answer the next question of whether the affiliated analyst optimism in report texts decreased after the Reforms in 2002. Overall, we found that 16.9% vs 20.5% for affiliated vs unaffiliated analysts have decreased optimism after the Reforms in samples of buy and sell recommendations. Evidence on hold recommendations is inconclusive. We do not think we can provide a coherent story based on these results, especially given that our main prediction was not supported by the empirical results. Given the null results and inconclusive results in the first two parts of the proposal, we did not believe it made sense to proceed. However, we continued with the proposal even though it is not meaningful to do so. In the attempt to answer whether in the pre-Reform period, affiliated analysts' report texts were more informative than those of unaffiliated analysts, we find, again, insignificant results between the two groups. We also made the attempt to answer the question of whether the affiliated analyst report texts become less informative post-regulation, we, once again, found insignificant changes. That is, we found that after regulation there is less information over all IBs; however, there is no evidence there is any difference between that of affiliated and unaffiliated analysts. In this long process of many failed attempts, we tried to diverge and examine other issues. The null results above prompt us to doubt whether our measure of tone is a good measure of information content. We found that both informativeness and conflict of interest affect the market reaction. We found weak evidence that the change in bias affects positive statements differently from its effect on negative statements. We found that tone affects textual informativeness regardless of the recommendation level, and that optimistic bias is weakly different depending on the recommendation level. Overall, the tone seems to work as a measure of information content, as suggested in the prior literature. Therefore, we conclude that the null results are not caused by the measurement of tone but by the possibility that our story does not exist. For all the tests, we also tried splitting samples with upgrades and downgrades, as opposed to recommendation levels. However, we did not find any significant results for our main story. Overall, the under-achievement is driven by the conjecture not being valid, but not the poor measurement of empirical proxies.

16503218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16503218.value: In research and development projects, decision makers rely on project reviews to learn about the potential of the project and decide whether to continue investing or abandon the project. There is strong evidence that decision makers tend to delay terminating the project, even after receiving consistently negative feedback. Existing studies on project termination delay have focused on individual decision makers. However, in reality project continue/abandon decisions are often made by groups of decision makers. In this project, we intend to study how groups make continue/abandon decisions, and the conditions under which they improve the quality of project decisions compared with individual decision makers. On one hand, there is evidence that groups are better at processing information and making strategic decisions. On the other hand, some existing research suggests that groups could lead to greater inertia and sunk cost bias, hence exacerbating project termination delay in firms. We consider a multi-period project. At each period, the decision maker receives some feedback (e.g., technical or market survey reports) about the potential of the project, and decides whether to continue or abandon the project. The decision could be made by either (1) an individual decision maker, or (2) a group of decision makers. We intend to investigate: 1) how groups and individuals differ in their project continue/abandon decisions.. 2) conditions under which groups make fewer continuation errors (i.e., are less likely to delay project termination) than individual decision makers. 3) the effect of project feedback on continue/abandon decisions for groups versus individuals. 4) the process through which groups arrive at a continue/abandon decision. 在新产品研发项目中，管理者通常用设立关卡的方式（比如门径管理系统）对项目进行阶段性评估，并决定是要继续投资还是放弃该项目。大量证据表明，管理者在这些决策点经常会做出非理性的决策，比如即使一直得到负面反馈却还是不愿放弃项目。这些不必要的延续投资极大地降低了企业的投资效率和研发回报。目前学界对这个问题的研究主要停留在单个决策者的层面。然而在现实生活中，这些投资决策通常由多人组成的管理团队共同做出。一个重要的问题是：团队和个人在做项目投资决策中有何不同，以及企业是否应该用团队来管理研发项目？ 在此研究项目中，我们计划通过实验来研究团队如何做研发项目管理中的投资决策，并将其与个人决策者做比较。我们希望发现在何种情况下团队会比个人做出更优的项目投资决策。我们拟研究如下问题：（1） 团队和个人决策者做的项目投资决策是否有显著不同？（2）在何种情况下团队会比个人决策者做出更优的决策？（3）项目评估中所产生的信息对团队和个人决策有何不同影响？（4）在决策过程中，团队通常用何种方式达成一致？

16503918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16503918.value: Dynamic pricing and revenue management have been central topics in the operations field for decades. Dynamic pricing is invoked as an effective strategy in the travel industry for exploiting the variability of customers' willingness to pay, and it has been well integrated with the capacity/yield management problem. While similar ideas of market segmentation and temporal price discrimination can be carried over from the travel industry to other industries, there are new aspects when applying these concepts to food, groceries, home appliances and office equipment, among others. Unlike selling airline seats for a specific itinerary or hotel rooms for a particular date, retail outlets and supermarkets typically face inventory replenishment problems and need to balance their holding and ordering costs. Replenishment opportunities inevitably create a linkage across time, and thus for a seller of a going-concern the typical finite-horizon planning framework assumed in the revenue management literature no longer applies. Furthermore, since cost considerations are crucial for inventory management in the retail industry, the problem differs from those studied in the economics and marketing literature, which usually focuses exclusively on the revenue side. We propose to explore interaction between the seller and customers with uncertain demands. Replenishment requires a fixed setup cost without any lead time, and the seller has to incur variable and holding costs alike. Deviating from the classical joint pricing and inventory management setup, a customer is willing to wait if by doing so a better deal is available. But waiting is costly and therefore undesirable, all other things being equal. The seller's objective is to maximize his long-term average cash flow. We study such a cat-and-mouse game between sophisticated sellers and strategic customers. If successful, this research is expected to characterize joint revenue-management (pricing) strategies as well as inventory management (replenishment) policies. We shall examine the optimality of the following cyclic strategy. The seller offers price discount at the time he replenishes the inventory, and accordingly some customers are induced to wait for such price discount. This is in spirit similar to the "post-promotion dip" phenomenon in that spikes in quantities sold occur immediately after price promotions. Our theoretical model prediction corresponds to the phenomenon that some items are displayed with only moderate availability and face extremely low demand because customers are waiting for upcoming deals. Cyclic pricing promotions are important features of supermarkets and retail outlets, which frequently offer discounts in a predetermined fashion. 動態定價在航空以及旅館業已經被證明可以有效地解決存量配置與策略性消費者的問題，然而在零售業面臨著另一個更大的挑戰: 如何將這些定價模式整合日常的庫存管理與補貨策略。本研究使用賽局分析來了解機制設計，以及這個動態定價與補貨管理的重要因子。模型設計上我們引進了補貨的固定成本，以及策略性消費者的等待成本與購買時機的考量。我們預期將證明有規律的定價與補貨模式是零售業應使用的最佳策略，並且價格折扣跟補貨的時機應該要完全同步。本研究也對於網路經濟以及可持續能源系統設計提出方針建議。

16503918.label: Major findings and research outcome
16503918.value: For this project, we initially focused on one research paper “Synchronizing pricing and replenishment to serve forward-looking customers with lost sales.” We incorporate strategic customer waiting behavior in the classical economic order quantity (EOQ) setting. The seller determines not only the timing and quantities of the inventory replenishment, but also the selling prices over time. While similar ideas of market segmentation and intertemporal price discrimination can be carried over from the travel industries to other industries, inventory replenishment considerations common to retail outlets and supermarkets introduce additional features to the optimal pricing scheme. Specifically, our study provides concrete managerial recommendations that are against the conventional wisdom on ``everyday low price'' (EDLP) versus ``high-low pricing'' (Hi-Lo). We show that in the presence of inventory costs and strategic customers, Hi-Lo instead of EDLP is optimal when customers have homogeneous valuations. This result suggests that because of strategic customer behavior, the seller obtains a new source of flexibility---the ability to induce customers to wait---which always leads to a strictly positive increase of the seller's profit. Moreover, the optimal inventory policy may feature a dry period with zero inventory, but this period does not necessarily result in a loss of sales as customers strategically wait for the upcoming promotion. Furthermore, we derive the solution approach for the optimal policy under heterogeneous customer valuation setting. Under the optimal policy, the replenishments and price promotions are synchronized, and the seller adopts high selling prices when the inventory level is low and plans a discontinuous price discount at the replenishment point when inventory is the highest. As mentioned in our midterm report, we have undergone a tough submission process for Activity 1. During the period we started to revisit our proposal plan and thought about how we can take the key ingredients of the proposal for other papers. In the objectives we identified a few key factors: revenue management, strategic customers, pricing optimality, inventory replenishment, and sustainability. These objectives are therefore implemented in a number of papers. - Objective 1 is related to the paper with Pi-Ying Yen and Qiao-Chu He, the paper with Ningyuan Chen, the paper with Qiaozhen Guo and Wei Huang, and the paper with Allen Wu and Chen Jin. - Objective 2 is related to the paper with Xi Li and Yanzhi Li, and the paper with Jiguang Chen. - Objective 3 is related to the paper with Pi-Ying Yen and Qiao-Chu He, the paper with Qiaozhen Guo and Wei Huang, and the paper with Allen Wu and Chen Jin. - Objective 3 is related to the paper with Pi-Ying Yen and Qiao-Chu He, and the paper with Jiguang Chen. In all these papers, GRF support has been acknowledged. Please see the corresponding papers for our findings.

16503918.value: We hope that our analysis invites further investigation of this practical problem. One possible extension is to consider the impact of customer stockpiling. In our context, customers make repeated purchases; thus, in some cases, they may consider purchasing way ahead of the time they actually need the products. This would create a two-sided inventory holding problems between the seller and customers.

16504618.label: Project Objectives
16504618.value: Propose a production-based general equilibrium with a novel learning mechanism and a cross-section of firms differing in capital age. The model can quantitatively account for the capital age premium. Empirically measure firms’ capital age, document the capital age premium and investigate the robustness of the evidence. The capital age premium refers to the evidence that old capital firms earn a significantly higher average return than young capital firms. Calibrate the parameters, study model implications through plotting impulse response functions, and demonstrate the quantitative performance of the model through model simulation. In particular, I will ask the model to deliver: (a) high equity premium and low and smooth risk-free rate at the aggregate level; and more importantly, (b) a reasonable firm heterogeneity in capital age and a quantitatively sizable capital premium, while I also check whether the model can match the joint dynamics of consumption, investment, and output. 16504618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16504618.value: Following the definition in my prior work Ai, Croce and Li (2013), I calculate the capital age of a firm as the weighted average age of its capital vintages. As a preliminary empirical investigation to motivate this proposal, I further sort U.S. firms contained in the Compustat dataset by firms' capital age and find firms with a larger capital age (i.e. old capital firms) earn average returns 8.41% higher than those with a smaller capital age (i.e. young capital firms). I call this evidence the capital age premium. It is consistent with the finding in Lin, Palazzo and Yang (2017). In this project, I propose a production-based general equilibrium model which features capital vintages and a learning mechanism to quantitatively account for the above capital age premium. The key element is that firms are uncertain about their exposures to aggregate productivity shocks, and have to learn about them over time. Young capital firms have less information about their exposures, while old capital firms have observed additional signals over time and have been constantly learning their exposures and therefore have improved the precision of their information about the exposures. That is to say, old capital firms have more information about their exposures than young capital firms. More information allows the old capital firms to take better advantage of aggregate technological progress, and therefore they feature a higher exposure to aggregate shocks than young capital firms. A higher exposure means old capital firms are more risky and justifiably earn higher average returns, consistent with the emprical evidence on capital age premium. I find some promising preliminary empirical evidence that supports the key learning mechanism. In particular, the cash flow growth (represented by the growth rate of operating income) of old capital firms has a significantly higher exposure to the aggregate productivity shocks than that of young capital firms. I plan to build the above learning mechanism into a full-brown general equilibrium model with production. The model generates a rich heterogeneity and transition dynamics in the cross-section of capital age, meanwhile it still maintains the aggregation property and tractability. I will use firm-level data to calibrate the key parameters related to the learning mechanism, and conduct a comprehensive quantitative analysis of the model. I will also further investigate additional testable implications implied from the model. This project provides new insights to practioners that learning is an important determinant of cross-sectional expected returns. 本文研究在金融市場中參數學習對橫截面股票收益率的影響。我們提出了一個基於生產函數的一般均衡模型來研究資本年齡，現金流的久期和股票橫截面的預期收益率之間的聯繫。我們模型的主要機制是關於企業對經濟總生產率衝擊的風險彈性的緩慢學習。我們假設擁有舊資本的公司比擁有年輕資本的公司有更多關於其風險彈性的信息。我們的框架對以下經驗事實提供了統一的解釋：舊資本公司（1）具有較高的資本配置效率; （2）更容易受到總生產率衝擊的影響，從而獲得更高的預期回報，我們將其稱為資本年齡溢價; （3）與年輕資本公司相比，現金流的久期更短。

16504618.label: Realisation of objectives
16504618.value: This project has turned into a working paper “Learning and the Capital Age Premium” (joint with Chi-Yang Tsou and Chenjie Xu). This paper is currently under second round revise and resubmit at the top macro finance field journal – Journal of Monetary Economics. We have achieved all the project objectives, including model building, empirical measurement, quantitative study, and the empirical facts that directly support the model mechanism. We would like to explain the full realizations of these objectives in details as below. Parameter uncertainty is ubiquitous in economics and finance. In this paper, we study the role of parameter learning in a general equilibrium asset pricing model on cross-sections of stock returns. In a large class of models that links production and investment to the cross-sections of expected returns, we typically assume that market participants can directly observe firm-specific productivity and can distinguish its systematic component from the idiosyncratic component. We refer to this assumption as the full information paradigm. While this paradigm offers a natural starting place and an important analytic benchmark, we consider an alternative but more realistic specification in this paper: that in which individual firms' managers have imperfect information about their productivity; Specifically, we explore cases in which firms with newly installed capital (i.e., young capital vintages) have limited information about their exposure to aggregate productivity shocks, but receive noisy signals from which they learn over time. We show that this single deviation from the full information case coherently explains a wide set of empirical facts with respect to the links between capital age, resource allocation efficiency, the timing of cash flows and, most importantly, expected returns in the cross-section of stocks. Our model also offers a joint framework to understand the cash flow duration and the duration premium in the cross-section, and its relation to the term structure of aggregate dividends. Information about the separation between the systematic and idiosyncratic components of firm-level productivity is likely to be limited. Indeed, for newly installed capital, there is not enough historical data that firm managers may use to estimate its firm-specific exposure to aggregate productivity. Thus, the full information assumption may overestimate the amount of information that agents have. In this paper, we propose an alternative imperfect information structure: that individual firms' managers have imperfect information about their capital's productivity and, in turn, face a signal extraction problem. In particular, we assume young capital vintage firms have less precise signals about their firm-specific exposure with respect to aggregate productivity growth than those of old vintage firms. In this paper, we propose a novel general equilibrium production-based model. In the model, capital vintages differ with respect to information precision about their capital-specific productivities, which firm managers must learn about over time. In our setting, the endogenous responses of firms' investment and payouts to news about future productivity can coherently explain the relationship among firm-level capital age, the cross-section of stock returns, and cash-flow duration. First and most importantly, the model generates a positive capital age and expected return relation in the cross section. Second, it also simultaneously produces a negative link between capital age and the duration of cash flow. In contrast, in the full information case, both the expected returns and cash flow duration are completely flat with capital age. The intuition for these key model implications is as follows. As compared with young capital firms, old firms have more precise information about their exposure to aggregate productivity shocks, and are therefore more capable of taking advantage of aggregate technological progress. High information precision acts like a risk exposure amplification mechanism, and makes old capital firms more sensitive to aggregate productivity shocks, which implies a high average return. In other words, heterogeneity in information translates into heterogeneity in risk exposure across different capital vintages. For similar reasons, young capital firms have lower resource reallocation efficiency, are less able to take advantage of aggregate technology growth, and pay lower payouts compared to old capital firms. Therefore, young capital firms possesses longer cash flow duration, as their future cash flows obtain more weight. Old capital firms, in contrast, have shorter cash flow duration. These model implications are strongly supported by empirical evidence. In order to investigate the empirical link between capital age, the duration of cash flows, and expected returns in the cross-section, we first construct the capital age measure, in particular, we measure a firm's capital age of U.S. publicly listed companies as a weighted average of the age of each capital vintage. We then implement the standard procedure and sort firms into quintile portfolios based on these firms' capital ages within Fama-French 30 industries. The average equity excess return for firms with old capital age (Quintile O) is 5.79% higher on an annualized basis than that of young capital firms (Quintile Y). We call the return spread of a long-short old-minus-young (OMY) strategy the ``capital age premium." The positive capital age-expected return relation is consistent with the first model implication in that old capital firms' more precise information translates into higher risk exposure, and in turn, leads to a higher average return when compared to that of young capital firms. Next, we document a negative correlation between capital age and cash flow, consistent with the model's second implication that explores the relation between the timing of cash flow and capital age. Guided by our theory, we also provide extensive empirical evidence that directly supports the key learning mechanism. First, we document that the productivity of new vintages of capital is less sensitive to aggregate productivity shocks than that of older vintages, consistent with our model implication. Second, we find that young capital firms have a lower learning rate about their exposure compared to that of old capital firms, consistent with the assumption about heterogenous information across capital vintages. Finally, we also empirically document that normalized payouts for young capital firms have a lower exposure to both long-run and short-run aggregate productivity shocks than do those of old capital firms, which strongly supports our model. We also examine if the positive capital age-return relation can be attributed to several possible explanations, including value premium, market power, life cycles, and embodied technology shocks documented in the literature. We show that the capital age premium cannot be explained by these explanations. In our quantitative analysis, we show that our model, when calibrated to match both conventional macroeconomic quantity dynamics and asset pricing moments, generates a significant capital age premium and a negative capital age and cash flow duration relation. As the data confirm, firms with an older capital age have a higher average return and a shorter cash flow duration. Quantitatively, our model reproduces the joint empirical relationships between capital age, expected returns, and cash flow duration in the data quite well.

16504618.label: Major findings and research outcome
16504618.value: The main contribution of our paper is to emphasize the role of experience in acquiring capital-specific information and study the implications of parameter learning on the cross-section of stock returns. Theoretically, we first illustrate our intuition through a static model with parameter learning, and then extend our setup into a tractable dynamic general equilibrium model which can quantitatively account for the cross-section of firms with heterogeneity in their capital age and expect returns. Our model prediction is as follows. As the unique sorting variable, capital age simultaneously drives capital misallocation, returns spread, and cash flow duration. Moreover, such variable facilitates our understanding of the duration premium in the cross-section and its connection with the term structure of aggregate cash flow. Empirically, we first provide extensive empirical evidence that directly supports the key learning mechanism. We also examine empirical evidence that differentiates our explanation from other alternative economic channels, including value premium, market power, life cycles, and embodied technology shocks documented in the literature. We show that the capital age premium cannot be explained by these explanations. This paper is under the revise and resubmit at the top international journal of macroeconomics -- Journal of Monetary Economics. And it is presented at several leading academic conferences as listed in Part C.

16504618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16504618.value: Upon the revision comments coming up in the review process at the Journal of Monetary Economics, we have explored the following further developments and hence strengthened the paper. 1. We explicitly introduce costly learning into our static model to micro-found a positive relation between capital age and information precision. 2. We further extend our endogenous learning model to incorporate firms with different market power. 3. We emphasize an additional theoretical contribution of our model to provide a joint framework to understand the cash flow duration, the cross-sectional duration premium, and their relation with respect to the equity term structure. 4. Empirically, first, we present and reorganize the direct evidence that supports our learning mechanism. Second, we provide an extensive and systematic empirical study of evidence differentiating our explanation from existing literature. More importantly, we study how our results align with findings in the previous literature on the cross-section of returns.

16504618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16504618.value: In this paper, we study the role of parameter learning on the cross-section of stock returns through the lens of a general equilibrium asset pricing model. There is a large class of models that link production and investment to the cross-section of expected returns, which assumes market participants directly observe firm-specific productivity and can also distinguish their systematic components from their idiosyncratic components. In this paper, we propose an alternative but more realistic imperfect information structure: that of individual firms having imperfect information about their productivity and facing a signal extraction problem. In particular, we assume that young capital vintage experiences less precise signals about their exposure when compared with old capital vintage. We demonstrate that this parameter learning channel is highly useful for studying the joint link between capital age, reallocation efficiency, the timing of cash flows, and, most importantly, expected returns in the cross-section. In contrast, a standard asset pricing model with full information generates flat relations between capital age and these aforementioned important economic variables. Our findings suggest that imperfect information and parameter learning can significantly impact asset prices.

16504818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16504818.value: It is documented in the literature that idiosyncratic volatility in the stock returns has been on the rise in various countries and in more developed countries such idiosyncratic volatility is higher. There are several different theories to explain such a phenomenon. The most prominent one claims that idiosyncratic volatility is higher because more firm-specific information is impounded in stock prices, a phenomenon pointing to a more efficient market. But authors of other theories and empirical findings disagree. One view of the phenomenon is that firms become more competitive and riskier as the economy changes from traditional industries to more high-tech based industries. This project will adopt a news database to test these theories. This line of research is important because the magnitude of idiosyncratic volatility affects the effectiveness of investment diversification and how information affects asset pricing is important in designing security market regulation and accounting disclosure policies. 公司新闻与资产回报波幅 文献中记载，股票收益率的特质波幅在各个国家一直在上升， 较发达国家中这种特质波幅更高。 有几种不同的理论可以解释 这种现象。最突出的理论声称特质波幅高是因为股票价格中存 在更多特定于公司的信息。这一现象意味着更有效的市场。但 其他理论和实证研究的作者并不同意。这种现象的另一种观点 是，随着经济从传统产业向更高科技产业转变，企业变得更具 竞争性和高风险。该项目将采用新闻数据库来测试这些理论。 这一研究领域很有意义，因为特质波幅的程度会影响投资分散 化的有效性，而信息影响资产定价。 这些对于设计证券市场 监管和会计披露政策会非常重要。

16504818.label: Realisation of objectives
16504818.value: Roll (1988) examines NYSE/AMEX firms during 1982-1987. By comparing news days and no-news days of the same set of firms and finding no significant difference in idiosyncratic volatility between the two types of days, he concludes that idiosyncratic volatility is not explainable by corporate news. Using information about news coverage provided by RavenPack, I document that news coverage contributes to idiosyncratic volatility for firm-years that have sufficient news coverage. This is achieved by separating firm-years into two groups: one with at least 25 news days per year (the news sample) and the other less than that (the no-news sample). The firms in the no-news sample tend to be smaller, less traded, more value than growth oriented, with lower earnings and higher earnings volatility. These features determine that firms in this group have greater idiosyncratic volatility than the firms in the news sample. 41% of the firm-years falls into this group. As such, without separating the two groups, the relationship between idiosyncratic volatility and news coverage will be obscured. Within the news sample, the news score at the daily frequency explains about 4\% of the total return variations in either the extended market model or the extended Fama-French five-factor model. The news intensity at the firm-year level significantly explains both the log of absolute idiosyncratic volatility and the log of relative idiosyncratic volatility, once equity size is controlled for. Beside equity size, trading volume also affects the explanatory power of the news intensity as they are positively correlated. Other variables used in the literature to explain idiosyncratic volatility in earlier samples continue to be useful in the current sample of 2000-2019. These include earnings related variables, which are more useful for the absolute idiosyncratic volatility, and growth option variables, which are more useful for the relative idiosyncratic volatility. In the extant literature, cross-sectional differences in idiosyncratic volatility are explained by firm characteristics, such as firm size, growth options, etc. The relationship of idiosyncratic volatility with these firm characteristics can have both rational asset pricing interpretations and behavioral interpretations. The contribution of the finding in this paper to the literature is that it is the first to lend support to the notion that higher idiosyncratic volatility can be partially due to more firm-specific information being impounded in the stock prices, a notion consistent with rational asset pricing. While many cross-country studies seem to align with the more general point that legal protection for investors and transparency of the market environment lead to lower market model $R^2$s, hence higher relative idiosyncratic volatility, direct evidence between information and idiosyncratic volatility within a country has never been documented. Therefore, the finding in this paper marks a breakthrough in this direction.

16504818.label: Major findings and research outcome
16504818.value: I focus on firms with sufficient news coverage days at a minimum of 25 news days per year, roughly 10% of the trading days per year, to generate the main results. The firm-year sample with this news coverage threshold constraint, dubbed as the news sample, represents 59% of all possible firm-years. For the news sample, I construct news scores at daily frequency, taking into consideration of good-news orientation (i.e., good or bad news for investors), news relevance, and news freshness. For this sample of firms, a market model extended to include the industry return at daily frequency has a median R-square of 25%. The news score can explain 4% of the remaining 75% of the idiosyncratic variance in total variance. When the other four of the Fama-French factors (Fama and French (2015)) are added to the extended market model, the median R-square increases modestly to 30% and the news score can again explain 4% of the remaining 70% of the idiosyncratic variance in total variance. I also construct firm-year observations of idiosyncratic return volatility and a measure of news intensity for firm-years satisfying the news sample. The news intensity is found to be positively related to idiosyncratic volatility either at absolute level of relative to systematic volatility, after firm size is controlled for. The relationship is robust to the inclusion of other firm-specific variables known to explain idiosyncratic volatility. I also look into the sample firms that do not meet the news coverage threshold criteria (the no-news sample) and are therefore left out for the main analyses. The firms in the no-news sample tend to be smaller, less traded, more value than growth oriented, and have lower average earnings, but larger volatility of earnings. These features make the idiosyncratic volatility in the no-news sample greater than that of the news sample on average. Pooling the news sample and the no-news sample together obscures the relationship between news coverage and idiosyncratic volatility.

16504818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16504818.value: I used a simple model/structure to provide evidence that media coverage explains part of the idiosyncratic volatility. This can be viewed as the minimum amount in the idiosyncratic volatility that can be traced to media reports. There are two directions in which the results can be further improved. One is to consider non-linear relationships between media coverage and idiosyncratic volatility. The other is to consider heterogeneity in the relationships between media coverage and idiosyncratic volatility. I am exploring these two directions and contemplating of adding new results to the paper in the review process.

16504818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16504818.value: Stock return volatility is important subject to both individual investors and financial market regulators. It can be decomposed into a systematic component and an idiosyncratic component. The former can be traced to the change in expectation of business cycles. The latter is more firm-specific. It has been observed that idiosyncratic volatility is a larger component of the total volatility than the systematic component on average and there is a trend that the idiosyncratic component is getting even larger. There are two views among academics about the main sources of the idiosyncratic volatility in stock returns. In one extreme, idiosyncratic volatility is caused by investors' sentiment. Excessive trades cause the price fluctuate too much to be justified. In the other extreme, idiosyncratic volatility is reflection of information about company's future prospects being compounded into stock prices, a rational asset pricing view. One of the challenge to the rational asset pricing view is that researchers have never established the link between stock price volatility with media coverage of the company. Using a relative new database on media coverage, this project finds evidence that idiosyncratic volatility can be partially explained by media coverage, providing support to the rational asset pricing argument.

16505018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16505018.value: One of the fundamental questions in economics, marketing and management is how to design incentive contracts or market mechanisms to motivate innovation. Over the past decade, contests have emerged as an important market mechanism for firms to procure innovation or creative solutions externally, from growing freelancing and crowdsourcing marketplaces. We propose to study how firms should design contests to motivate freelancers or external innovators. In particular, we investigate the important role of information structure plays in incentivizing innovation in contests. On one hand, firms seeking innovation can provide interim feedback to freelancers, who can then decide whether to improve on existing solutions or explore in a different, untested direction. On the other hand, whether freelancers can observe the output of competitors can influence their decision to participate and the effort they expend in a contest. Free riding may become an issue when outputs are publicly observable. Freelancers may free ride on the good ideas of rivals to enhance their probability of winning. Consequently, free riding could potentially discourage participation and innovation effort. However, allowing free riding could generate a snowballing effect so that one improves on another's idea, enhancing the quality of outputs. In this research, we plan to examine empirically the effects on freelancer incentive to be innovative of interim feedback and output observability, and their interaction. 经济学、营销学、以及管理学里的一个重要课题是如何设计激励机制去鼓励创新。在过去十几年里，自由工作者平台或众包平台的发展让创新竞赛逐渐发展成为一种重要的机制让机构外部提供创新或创意产品。在这个背景下，本课题主要研究如何利用信息结构的设计来有效地激励外部创作人员。一方面，企业可以提供反馈信息给创作人员，让他们决定是否应该探索新的方向还是改进原有作品。另一方面，创作人员可以观察竞争者的作品并决定去模仿还是探索新方向。这时候会出现搭便车的问题：公开的作品可能会被模仿，降低创作人员参与的积极性。尽管如此，公开作品可以带来头脑风暴的好处：集合群体的力量可以更有效地产生创新的方案。本课题通过实证和理论来研究信息反馈和作品公开对激励的影响以及它们的交互作用。

16505018.label: Realisation of objectives
16505018.value: Background Let us first introduce the background and implementation of the research before discussing the realization of objectives. In this research, we aim to examine the influence of information on individuals’ creativity in a contest. An individual’s creativity has significant implications for contest design as firms widely use contests to solicit ideas and generate innovation. Firms can benefit from the “wisdom of crowds” in innovation contests when different contestants bring in various solutions. We consider two types of information in a contest: feedback and observability. The first type of information refers to an environment in which a contest-holder can provide feedback to contestants on their submissions. This feedback typically takes the form of a numerical rating indicating the contest-holder’s satisfaction with a submission. The second type of information refers to whether a contestant is allowed to observe what other competitors have submitted. Our main goal is to understand whether and how these two types of information influence an individual’s creativity in a contest. To that end, we focus on the setting of logo design contests which is an ideal context for testing theory. Like contestants in other innovation contests, designers in a logo design contest face substantial uncertainty as to how the logos they submitted will be perceived in terms of quality. Designers are often unable to evaluate how much contest holders will like their designs, regardless of their efforts, and expanding more effort does not necessarily guarantee a submission to be judged to be a high-quality design. In addition, a logo represents the identity of a firm, and thus it can be one of the most important assets. Firms spend a tremendous amount of time and resources evaluating logo candidates and choosing the most optimal design. We collect our data from 99Designs because it is one of the main platforms that hold logo design contests and implements the two types of information we study in this research. In a logo design contest, a firm solicits a custom logo from participating designers in exchange for a fixed prize for the design the firm judges to be the best. To start a contest, the firm posts a contest brief that describes its business nature and requirements for the logo, announces the prize of the contest, and determines the observability of the contest. If the contest is sealed, a designer may only observe her own submitted designs and not those designs submitted by her competitors. In contrast, if the contest is open, a designer is permitted to observe all designs in the contest. A designer is allowed to submit as many designs as she wants at any time before the deadline. When the firm receives a design, it can provide real-time, 1- to 5-star ratings-based feedback on the design. At the end of the contest, the firm chooses one design as the best and awards its designer the prize. Implementation Our contest data include the logo images submitted by contestants, which provide us a unique opportunity to develop an alternative approach to measuring an individual’s creativity. We postulate that each logo image can be decomposed into a set of artistic features and their representations can describe the design style of the logo. We adopt several machine-learning models to extract these features such as brand typeface, brand name representation, and logo color from each logo image. Designers are permitted to submit multiple logos in a contest. By comparing different images submitted by one contestant, we learn the extent of changes she has made to the design. Specifically, a design is regarded as creative if the logo contains new feature styles and we say its designer chooses exploration when designing the logo. Otherwise, we say the designer chooses exploitation if no feature styles are introduced in a new design. In our data, we observe contests with various information structures including all possible combinations of feedback and observability. Designers observe ratings for all submissions in both sealed and open contests, but competing submissions are only observable in open contests. This feature in the data allows us to examine the impact of each information type and its interaction effect. We check whether the probability of an exploration-based approach being taken by a designer varies with the observability and ratings in a contest. By estimating a logit regression using a choice of exploration as the dependent variable, we achieve the first two objectives. We include ratings, observability, and their interaction as our independent variables in the regression model. We group design ratings into three categories: unrated, low rating, and high rating. An important challenge is the endogeneity issue because contest-holders’ choice of providing feedback and observability may be correlated. We solve the endogeneity issue of observability by comparing the requirements of sealed and open contests and no significant differences are found. We conduct a follow-up survey with some contest-holders and designers to investigate their motivations to hold and participate in contests. Again, no significant differences are found. The survey also illustrates that designers cannot anticipant what ratings they receive for their submissions, addressing the endogeneity of feedback. By using the feature in our data that some designers submit new designs before receiving ratings for their prior submissions, we further demonstrate that unobserved ratings do not influence a designer’s choice of exploration and address the endogeneity issue. Other robustness checks are done to make sure that our findings are not confounded by factors such as prize amount, contest duration, and performance of competing submissions. Realizations of objectives We have achieved the first objective. We explore the impact of information disclosure and consider two types of information: feedback on submission and observability of competing submissions. We empirically find that observing competing submissions increases an individual’s motivation to explore novel designs. We can identify the impact because some contests allow contestants to observe competing submissions while the remaining contests do not. We have further performed a few analyses to show the robustness of our findings and discuss the possible endogeneity issue. We have also achieved the second objective using some features in our data. In addition, to determine whether competing submissions are observable, contest-holders may or may not provide feedback to submissions. Therefore, we have some contestants in a contest who receive feedback while others receive no feedback. We not only find the main effect of the two types of information on an individual’s creativity but also find an interaction effect. A few robustness checks have been done to make sure that our findings are robust. We have not completely achieved the third objective as we decided not to directly model the equilibrium of designers' submission and contest-holders' selection. Instead, we have estimated separately their behaviors in our regression models. This allows us to identify the mechanisms that drive designers' and contest-holders' behaviors. Based on experts' feedback we collected, it is more insightful to compare contests with various information structures in a field experiment. We planned to conduct the field experiment, but it has been significantly delayed because we were unable to find a suitable contest platform to collaborate due to the pandemic and travel restrictions in both mainland China and Hong Kong. However, we expect these restrictions will be lifted soon. We can then carry out the field experiments and conduct further analysis.

16505018.label: Major findings and research outcome
16505018.value: First, we find that ratings, especially high ratings decrease a designer’s motivation to explore. We find that a designer becomes less likely to explore new styles after receiving a high rating than when she receives no rating. The designer tends to submit a design that is very similar to her prior submissions when she has received a 4-star or above. On the other hand, when she receives a low rating or no rating, she is more likely to choose exploration and adopt a new style in her new design. We name this the “demotivating effect” of providing feedback. This occurs because rating is informative of a firm’s preferences and a designer can infer what design styles are favored by firms based on the ratings she receives. This information effectively reduces designers’ incentive to explore. When receiving a high rating, a designer infers that the design style in her submission is favored by the firm, and exploring other styles could be suboptimal. The designer may receive a lower rating for a new submission if she chooses exploration rather than exploitation, which may decrease the probability of winning. Second, we find a significant difference between sealed and open contests. Designers participating in open contests who receive ratings are more motivated to explore new design styles than those participating in sealed contests. However, if designers receive no rating, their incentives to explore new styles are similar, no matter what types of contests they are participating in. When designers observe competing submissions, they may be inspired by others’ designs and therefore be motivated to apply the design styles used by others. That is, a designer may learn from competing submissions. We find that design styles with a higher rating are more likely to inspire designers to use the same style than those with a low rating. Interestingly, we also find that a designer is not necessarily inspired by the design style with the highest rating. Even though some competitors achieve a 3-star rating or above, a designer is most likely to find inspiration from design styles receiving no rating. This result suggests that designers have substantial heterogeneity in choosing which design style to follow and it also illustrates that inspiration is different from the free-riding behavior of copy-cats. Copy-cats should always adopt the design style with the highest rating to increase their chances of winning.

16505018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16505018.value: In the next step, we could conduct more analyses to explore the underlying mechanism, especially for the inspiration effect of observing competing submissions. The finding is interesting and opposite to people?s belief that observing competing submissions would lead to free-riding and design styles in submissions would converge eventually. Our data provide us a unique opportunity to understand why inspiration rather than free-riding occurs because we have the logo images submitted. By comparing the submissions in a contest, we can easily monitor the evolution of design style and identify the prior design that a new design is built on. We find substantial heterogeneity in designers? choice of which design style to follow. It would be interesting to explore the factors that influence the decision. Second, we could run a field experiment to test a richer set of information structures in innovation contests. A field experiment could help us achieve the third objective proposed and we can compare contests with various information designs in terms of the quality of the winning design, the number of participants, the number of submissions, and the number of design styles. Previous literature focuses only one or two of them but not all. Running a field experiment also allows us to investigate the impact of feedback and observability in other dimensions. For example, we may test the impact of the amount of feedback provided (e.g., provide feedback to all submissions vs 50% of the submissions).

16505018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16505018.value: Innovation plays a critical role in the success of a firm. It can be either developed in-house or outsourced to a third party. In-house development is more efficient but procuring innovation from external sources, such as contests, allows firms to reach a larger pool of expertise. Contests allow firms to benefit from the ?wisdom of crowds? because many contestants work on the same challenge at the same time, increasing the chance of obtaining innovative solutions. However, the success of the ?wisdom of crowds? rests on contestants? creativity and motivation to explore various approaches to find the optimal solution. In the research, we investigate how the design of information environments can shape contestants? creativity. We use the context of logo-design contests and focus on two types of information: feedback on submissions and observability of competing submissions. We find that contestants are more likely to explore novel designs when they can observe competing submissions and receive non-positive ratings. Contest organizers can use the information structure to influence creativity and it is less costly compared to simply increasing the prize amount. More generally, our research findings can help firms or contest holders design the appropriate information environment to nurture creativity or innovation.

16505418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16505418.value: There has been rapid growth in on-demand ride-hailing platforms that serve as an intermediary to match individual service providers with consumer demand. Ride-hailing platforms are essentially intermediary firms that connect self-scheduling and earnings-sensitive drivers who decide whether and when to work, with price-sensitive customers, who submit ride requests randomly. The growth of some of the well-known players in this market has been phenomenal: it took Uber just six months to reach 2 billion rides and the company operates in 60 counties. China’s Didi Chuxing processes more than 20 million rides on an average day. Within the on-demand ride-hailing market, several major players have introduced a car-pooling service. This car-pooling service option enables drivers to pick up multiple passengers heading in the same direction and each passenger shares the ride with others, typically in return for a discounted price. However, this discounted price often comes at the expense of a lower-quality service because of the lack of privacy and longer trip duration to pick up or drop off other passengers. Although it is generally believed that car-pooling can provide environmental benefits, rigorous research on its operational, economical and social implications is scarce. In the proposed project, we aim to investigate the operational issues faced by the ride-sharing platforms in the presence of car-pooling services. We propose to build a two-sided market model to identify the most important economic forces of the (two-sided) pricing strategies in the presence of car-pooling services, and to predict the equilibrium behaviors of the platform, the drivers and the riders. Furthermore, we aim to study the economic and social implications car-pooling services will have. We also propose to characterize the relationship between car-pooling and surge pricing and the optimal car-pooling service quality decision, both of which have the potential to guide platforms to implement car-pooling services. 近年来，我们见证了共享移动出行平台的快速增长。共享移动出行平台作为中介，促使个体驾驶服务提供商与消费者的出行需求相匹配—— 该平台将对收入敏感并自主决定是否以及何时工作的驾驶员与对价格敏感并随机提交乘车请求的客户进行对接。 共享移动出行平台这个市场上一些知名企业的增长是惊人的：优步完成其第二个十亿次出行只用了六个月，现在在超过60个国家运营。滴滴出行现在平均每天处理超过2000万次出行。 在共享移动出行平台的市场中，几家主要参与者都推出了拼车服务。 这种拼车服务选项使司机能够接载多名前往同一方向的乘客，从而每位乘客需要与其他乘客共享出行。 该平台通常对拼车服务提供折扣，然而这种折扣价格通常以牺牲服务质量为代价——拼车服务通常会涉及隐私问题，以及由于额外接送多位乘客上下车从而导致的迂回和较长的行程时间。 虽然人们普遍认为拼车服务对环境有益，但对其运营，经济和社会影响的严谨研究却很少。 在此项目中，我们的目标是研究共享移动出行平台在提供拼车服务时所面临的运营问题。 我们将建立一个双边市场模型，以确定在拼车服务存在的情况下对（双边）定价策略最重要的经济因素，并预测均衡结果中平台，驾驶员和乘客的行为选择。 此外，我们将研究拼车服务所带来的对经济和社会的影响。 我们还将刻画拼车和动态定价之间的关系以及有关最佳拼车服务质量的决策，这两者都有可能对平台提供拼车服务的决策产生影响。

16505418.label: Realisation of objectives
16505418.value: The objectives of this GRF research project (16505418) have been fully achieved. We next summarize the research activities and outcomes related to the project objectives stated in the initial proposal. First, we have developed an analytical model to investigate the operational issues faced by the ridesharing platforms in the presence of car-pooling services. In particular, we have built a two-sided market model to analyze the price and wage optimization problem of ride-hailing platforms in the presence of carpool services, which helps predict the equilibrium behaviors of the platform, the drivers and the riders, and identify the most important economic forces of the pricing strategies in the presence of car-pooling services. We show that the platform should provide the carpool service option when the value deterioration of the carpool service is not too high compared with the normal service, and/or when the pooling efficiency is not too low. Our analysis reveals that, as expected, the optimal price for the carpool services is lower than that of the normal services, which is consistent with the business practice. More interestingly, the presence of carpool services also prompts the platform to charge a lower price for its normal service when both service modes are offered, compared with the benchmark system where only the normal service is available. One may intuit that, by offering an additional service mode, the platform should be in a better position to discriminate between customers with different valuations and can charge a higher price for the (high-quality) normal service. However, our results suggest that the opposite is true. Besides the price discrimination effect, the introduction of the carpool service also has the demand cannibalization effect and the cost reduction effect. On one hand, the carpool service cannibalizes the demand for the normal service, which prompts the platform to charge a lower price for the normal service as well. On the other hand, there also exists a cost reduction effect that arises from the drivers’ self-scheduling behavior. The overall effect of cannibalization and cost reduction together outweighs the price discrimination effect when the platform finds it attractive to introduce the carpool option, resulting in a lower price for the normal service. As a consequence, offering the carpool service enables riders to enjoy more affordable rides without compromising on service quality. Second, we have examined welfare implications of the carpool services on different stakeholders. We find that offering carpool services benefits the riders by improving riders’ surplus in general. This is intuitive given that riders are provided with an additional service option when the platform offers carpool services. However, we show that the provision of carpool services acts as a double-edged sword for the drivers as it may improve or hurt the driver surplus. On one hand, the presence of carpool services expands market coverage and hence brings in more riders to be matched with drivers and may increase the drivers’ earnings. On the other hand, carpool services also enlarge the capacity per driver by pooling multiple passengers into a single ride, which decreases the total need and earning potentials for the drivers. We show that when the drivers’ reservation wage is uniformly distributed, the latter outweighs the former and overall the drivers are worse off. Finally, from the perspective of the entire society, our numerical analysis suggests that the introduction of the carpool services increases the total social welfare in general. Third, we have investigated the strategic relationship between surge pricing and the provision of carpool services. We have characterized the interplay between carpool services and surge pricing as two levers to match supply with demand. We find that the strategic relationship between these two operational strategies exhibits an interesting pattern that depends on the demand-supply ratio of the platform. In particular, carpool services and surge pricing are strategic substitutes if the total number of registered drivers is neither too large nor too small compared with the total demand rate. When there exists extreme imbalance between the total supply and demand, these two operations levers complement each other instead. In other words, our results suggest that the carpool service and surge pricing are strategic complements when the demand-supply imbalance is severe, and they become strategic substitutes with balanced demand and supply. Finally, we have also investigated the impact of various model primitives on the benefit of providing carpool services. We show that the platform could earn a higher profit either when the rider arrival rate or the driver capacity is higher. Moreover, we find that as the pooling efficiency increases, the platform would achieve a more expanded market coverage and enjoy a higher profit. Here, the pooling efficiency is defined as the ratio between the number of riders per shared ride (m) and the average trip length of a carpool ride (Tp), where a higher value of pooling efficiency suggests that the platform is able to pool more riders together in a single trip (i.e., m is large) without increasing the total trip duration too much (i.e., Tp is not too long). Intuitively, a more efficient carpool system that routes drivers to match with riders prompts the platform to increase the usage of carpool services, which in turn also expands the total market coverage.

This project has led to two publications: Wang and Zhang (2022) published in Naval Research Logistics; and Zeng et al. (2022) accepted by Management Science.

16505418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16505418.value: There are several potential avenues to further develop this research, and the PI plans to explore along the following directions. First, we have assumed that the customer?s valuation type is uniformly distributed between zero and one. It would be interesting to see whether the results and insights are robust under more general distributions. Second, we have focused on the equilibrium behavior of the system and did not consider the spatial heterogeneity of riders and drivers for a ride-hailing platform. An interesting future direction is to incorporate the spatial dimension into the joint price and wage optimization problem under demand and supply uncertainty with carpool services. Finally, we have considered a monopolistic platform and ignored competition among platforms. It is not uncommon in practice that there may exist multiple platforms competing for both riders and drivers in the market. Another potential future research direction is to study platform competition in the presence of carpool services, and characterize the optimal price and wage strategies in a competitive setting.

16505418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16505418.value: There has been rapid growth in on-demand ride-hailing platforms that serve as an intermediary to match individual service providers (drivers) with consumer demand (riders). Several major players of this market have introduced carpool services that allow passengers heading toward the same direction to share a ride at a discounted fare. In this project, we develop an analytical framework to examine the operational, economical, and social implications of carpool services on ride-hailing platforms. We characterize the optimal price and wage strategy of the platform, and find that it is optimal for the platform to offer the carpool service if its value deterioration relative to the normal service is not too high, and/or when the pooling efficiency is not too low. When the platform finds it optimal to offer the carpool service option, the platform achieves a larger market coverage and the riders are able to enjoy more affordable rides without compromising on service quality. Our analysis reveals that the provision of carpool services benefits the platform and the riders in general, but may hurt the drivers.

16506018.label: Project Objectives

16506018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16506018.value: The recent study of Bakshi, Gao and Panayotov (2017) has proposed a measure of dissimilarity between stochastic discount factors (SDFs) in different economies, which is forward looking and can be extracted from currency option prices. The measure quantifies the difference between SDF's across international borders, and is in the spirit of Hansen and Jagannathan (1991), but in a two-economy context, and conceptually related to the notion of market integration. The current proposal aims to investigate in-depth empirically SDF dissimilarity, with explicit focus on the dynamic properties of the new measure, as it exhibits distinct patterns of evolution over time, with significant variation and also apparent strong co-movement across different pairs of economies. Important open questions which involve dynamic aspects of the dissimilarity measure remain unanswered: How does SDF dissimilarity vary over time and with economic conditions? Do economies get closer together or farther apart during periods with adverse economic shocks? Is there a common component in the evolution of the measures describing different country pairs, and if so, what global trends does it capture? Does the dissimilarity between specific country pairs exhibit distinct dynamic features, different from those of other pairs? Does the dissimilarity between some pairs influence that of others (lead-lag relation), and if so, what may be the underlying economic mechanism? The current proposal envisions to address some of these questions, which can deepen our understanding of financial interrelations among economies in general, and of the nature of SDF dissimilarity in particular. It will further examine the relation between the new dissimilarity measure and other, conceptually related notions that have been previously explored, and thus help clarify the position of the new measure in the international finance literature. In particular, we will explore possible relations with two strands of literature: the one studying market integration and the related one devoted to financial spillovers and contagion, possibly global, and/or financial cycles, also possibly their global version. 最近Bakshi，Gao和Panayotov（2017）的研究提出了衡量不同经济体中随机贴现因子（SDF）之间差异的指标，该指标具有前瞻性，可以从货币期权价格中提取。该衡量标准量化了SDF跨越国际边界的差异，并且符合Hansen和Jagannathan（1991）的精神，但是在双重经济背景下，并且在概念上与市场一体化的概念相关。目前的提案旨在深入研究深入研究SDF的差异性，并明确关注新措施的动态特性，因为它表现出不同的进化模式，具有显着的变化，并且在不同的经济对中也表现出明显的强烈共同运动。 涉及相异性度量的动态方面的重要开放性问题仍然没有答案：SDF的不同性如何随着时间和经济条件而变化？在遭受不利经济冲击的时期，经济体是否会更紧密地联系在一起或更远？在描述不同国家/地区对的措施的演变中是否存在共同的组成部分，如果是，那么它捕获的全球趋势是什么？特定国家/地区对之间的差异是否表现出与其他对不同的动态特征？某些货币对之间的差异是否会影响其他货币对（超前 - 滞后关系），如果是，那么潜在的经济机制可能是什么？ 目前的提案设想解决其中一些问题，这些问题可以加深我们对一般经济体之间金融相互关系的理解，特别是SDF相异性的性质。它将进一步研究新的不相似性度量与之前已经探索过的其他概念相关概念之间的关系，从而有助于阐明新度量在国际金融文献中的地位。特别是，我们将探讨与两个文献的可能关系：一个研究市场一体化的问题，另一个关注金融溢出和传染，可能是全球和/或金融周期，也可能是它们的全球版本。

16506018.label: Realisation of objectives
16506018.value: Extant finance theory predicts that the stochastic discount factors (SDF's) of pairs of economies can be directly mapped into the exchange rates between the currencies of these economy pairs. Accordingly, the original premise of this project was that one can exploit the dynamic patterns of different exchange rates to infer conclusions about patterns in the joint evolution through time of various economies, synthesized through their SDF's. Originally, we intended to extract from exchange rates (as traded in the currency option market) direct measures of SDF dissimilarity across different economies. We intended to use in our investigation the time series of such measures, constructed for many pairs of economies. In the first stage of the project, however, we found out that, since these measures are derived from option prices, they are (i) very tightly related to measures of volatility for different exchange rates, (ii) very highly correlated across different economy pairs, and (iii) not too different from other standard volatility-based risk measures, as for example the VIX index. We note that (i) implies that these measures do not have much more information about SDF's than simple volatilities, (ii) implies that the common component of the measures explains almost entirely their time variation, and (iii) implies that the currency market perspective does not add too much relative to other standard risk measures. Collectively, these findings indicate that our original measure is not particularly suitable to address our main question about the joint dynamics of different SDF's and the respective economies. Therefore, at the second stage of the project we moved away from option-based direct measures of SDF dissimilarity and resorted to existing and more explicit models of SDF's, again based on exchange rates. This turned out to be a fruitful direction of our research. In particular, we were able to relate one such model (the LRV model of Lustig, Roussanov and Verdelhan (JFE'2014)) to a very salient change in time-series pattern of various currency returns. Importantly, we were able to link this change to several major currency puzzles. Previous studies have found that these puzzles have been reversed in the recent years, but have treated these findings separately. The main advantage of our approach to the changes in the relations between various SDF's is that it allows to build a common framework for understanding these changes. Furthermore, this approach allows us to address each of the original three objectives of the paper, because the model explicitly yields SDF's and allows to estimate them for the economies in our sample. The original idea underlying the project was to use SDF's to understand the economic mechanisms that drive the joint evolution of economies over time. With the focus shifted to the LRV model, the changes in currency markets and currency puzzles, we were able to specify this idea to one particular salient aspect of this joint evolution. We identified, within the model, two component of the SDF's which were responsible for these changes - one related to a global risk factor, and the second to a local risk factor specific to the central economy - i.e., the US. Our further empirical investigation allowed to pinpoint this local risk, and thus link the currency puzzles with the oil price. The economic mechanism that we thus uncovered involves the differential response of economies to the oil price, but also a stronger impact of the oil price on U.S. inflation and weaker link between the real interest rates in the U.S. and other advanced economies in the recent 15 years.
