17100418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17100418.value: 肝癌是全球最常見的惡性腫瘤之一，因其具有確診時間晚，高復發率及高轉移率等特徵而導致其預後較差。小窩蛋白-1是小窩的主要結構蛋白，在人類癌症中具有重要的作用。在多種癌症早期，小窩蛋白-1的表達和功能不盡一致。然而其被確信在癌轉移組織中高度表達且導致癌症轉移。近期研究顯示小窩蛋白-1在癌細胞代謝中發揮作用。為了適應癌細胞快速生長及侵襲特性，癌細胞自身代謝紊亂而產生了更多的代謝產物。因此我們研究了小窩蛋白-1介導的肝癌代謝能量重新整合及癌化特徵。敲除小窩蛋白-1減少了肝癌細胞甘油三酯和脂類堆積提示了小窩蛋白-1調節肝癌細胞脂肪酸代謝的全新功能。使用脂肪酸β-氧化的抑制劑Etomoxir恢復了小窩蛋白-1敲除細胞中降低的細胞甘油三酯含量及部分恢復了細胞增殖和活動力。以上結果提示抑制脂肪酸β-氧化可以部分解釋小窩蛋白-1的致癌能力。中鏈脂酰基輔酶A脫氫酶（ACADM）催化β-氧化的第一步脫氫。我們的結果顯示小窩蛋白-1和ACADM在多條肝癌細胞系和肝癌組織中的表達成負相關。我們也揭示了ACADM通過調節低密度蛋白受體相關蛋白6（LRP6）/ β-actin/過氧化物酶體增殖物活化受體α（PPARα）信號通路來調節小窩蛋白-1。敲除ACADM增強了肝癌細胞的脂肪酸富集，錨定非依賴生長，細胞活動力和侵襲性。ACADM在肝癌中表達降低且其的低表達與侵襲性病理特徵顯著相關。以上的前期數據令我們猜想高表達小窩蛋白-1通過降低ACADM的表達來抑制β-氧化，從而導致肝癌細胞生長能力及惡性程度增強。為了驗證上述猜想我們將1）功能性的驗證小窩蛋白-1通過調節ACADM來抑制β-氧化，2）釐清小窩蛋白-1/ACADM通路在調節β-氧化背後的分子基礎，3）評價ACADM在肝癌臨床中的作用。我們的研究發現將揭示小窩蛋白-1作為肝癌重要的轉移促進因子，改變了脂肪酸代謝及功能上抑制了肝癌的進展。此項目的成功實施將拓展我們對肝癌代謝依賴的認識以及提示調節代謝方式對於肝癌臨床治療的重要性。

17100418.label: Realisation of objectives
17100418.value: 1. To functionally characterize Cav1-mediated suppression of β-oxidation via ACADM (The study of this objective was fully completed) To investigate the prospective role of Cav1 in β-oxidation, Cav1 was suppressed in metastatic MHCC97L cells. Knockdown of Cav1 significantly reduced the cellular triglycerides, phospholipids and lipid accumulation levels compared to control cells. The oxygen consumption rate increased in Cav1 knockdown cells, indicating the increase in β-oxidation compared to control cells. Cav1 knockdown significantly diminished the growth, motility and tumorigenesis of HCC cells. However, such diminishment in HCC properties was partly restored in Cav1 knockdown cells treated with Etomoxir (ETO), an inhibitor of β-oxidation. In Cav1 knockdown cells, level of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (ACADM), an enzyme that catalyzes the first step of β-oxidation, was found to be upregulated. To validate whether Cav1 mediates β-oxidation via ACADM in HCC, ACADM was suppressed in Cav1 knockdown cells to recapitulate the functional effect of Cav1 overexpression. The resulting effects were that the levels of triglycerides, phospholipids, intracellular lipid contents as well as fatty acid oxidation were elevated in double knockdown cells of Cav1 and ACADM. The enhancement of HCC anchorage independent growth, cell growth and motility were also observed in the double knockdown cells compared to the Cav1 knockdown cells. The same effect was observed in animal models, with tumors derived from double knockdown cells developed faster than tumors derived from Cav1 knockdown cells. Furthermore, knockdown of ACADM in non-metastatic HCC cells recapitulated the Cav1 knockdown effect in promoting HCC aggressiveness and retarding β-oxidation. These data demonstrated that Cav1 downregulated β-oxidation via ACADM. 2. To delineate the molecular basis of Cav1/ACADM pathway in the regulation of β-oxidation (The study of this objective was fully completed) In the proposal, it was originally hypothesized that Cav1 downregulates ACADM via low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 6 (LRP6)/β-catenin/ peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) axis in HCC based on the preliminary data. However, we did not observe a good correlation between ACADM and PPARα expressions. SREBP-1 has previously been reported to interact with Cav1 in other diseases, this warrants further investigation into their interplay in HCC. It was observed that knockdown of Cav1 prevented the nuclear accumulation of SREBP-1 and resulted in an enhanced ACADM expression in MHCC97L cells, with treatment of filipin, a Cav1 inhibitor, inducing the same effect in MHCC97L cells. Cav1 was shown to interact with full-length SREBP-1 in MHCC97L cells, supporting the potential role of Cav1 to mediate the maturation and nuclear accumulation of SREBP-1. SREBP-1 is a transcription factor which prompted us to question if SREBP-1 regulates transcription of ACADM. In silico analysis identified putative sterol regulatory element (SRE) binding site in promotor of ACADM. In MHCC97L cells, high ACADM promoter activity was observed for the SRE-mutant versus the wildtype ACADM promoter. SRE is the binding site of SREBP-1; RT-qPCR using primers flanking SRE amplifying ACADM promoter revealed an increased copy number of ACADM promoter fragments pulled down by anti-SREBP-1 antibody in MHCC97L cells. These findings suggested that SREBP-1 is a negative regulator of ACADM. These results implicate that Cav1 facilitates nuclear accumulation of SREBP-1 leading to the negative transcriptional regulation of ACADM. To demonstrate the functional interaction between Cav1 and SREBP-1, SREBP-1 was overexpressed in MHCC97L Cav1 knockdown cells; the enhancement of β-oxidation in Cav1 knockdown cells was suppressed by SREBP-1 restoration. The abilities of cells to grow, migrate and invade were also recused. 3. To evaluate the clinical significance of ACADM in human HCC (The study of this objective was fully completed) To evaluate the clinical significance of ACADM in HCC, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database of liver cancer, mRNA of 50 paired cases of HCC and the corresponding non-tumorous tissues obtained from patients of Queen Mary Hospital and tissue microarray comprises 51 paired tumorous and non-tumorous tissues of patients at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, China were used to analyze the expression of ACADM. ACADM expression data from TCGA database revealed a significant decrease in ACADM expression in tumorous samples. Consistently, ACADM underexpression was observed in 64% (32/50) of patients of Queen Mary Hospital and significantly correlated with bigger tumor size, presence of venous invasion, advanced HCC tumor stage and poor cell differentiation. Receiver operating characteristic curves indicate the significant discrimination of ACADM expression between non-tumorous and early stage. Immunohistochemical staining of ACADM protein expression in paired HCC tissues was scored as strong (45/51) and moderate (6/51) positive in 100% of non-tumorous liver tissues, when compared to strong and moderate positive in 52.9% (27/51) of tumorous tissues. Weak positive and negative were observed in 47.1% (24/51) of tumorous tissues. Among 51 cases, ACADM was downregulated in 86.3% (44/51) of HCC tumors when compared to the adjacent non-tumorous liver tissues. Together, these findings indicate that the reduced ACADM level in tumorous tissues could be a valuable biomarker of HCC. To investigate whether Cav1 correlates with ACADM in HCC, their mRNA and protein expression levels were analyzed. In the HCC cell line panel, ACADM and Cav1 expressions were found to be negatively correlated. In HCC cells with Cav1 knockdown, ACADM level was enhanced. The transcriptional expressions of ACADM and Cav1 in HCC samples of Queen Mary Hospital and liver cancer database of TCGA were found to be negatively correlated with significance. In addition to the proposed work, physiological relevance of SREBP-1/ACADM pathway was analyzed for the expressions of SREBP-1 and ACADM in clinical samples. The SREBP-1 expression was inversely correlated with ACADM expression with significance; in cases with SREBP-1 overexpression, reduced levels of ACADM were detected in tumorous tissues. In tissue microarray comprising of 46 HCC specimens, strong and moderate positive staining of SREBP-1 were detected in 41.3% (19/46) of tumorous tissues while only weak positive and negative were detected in non-tumorous tissues. The nuclear immunoreactivity of SREBP-1 was significantly higher in tumorous tissues as indicated by the higher H-score. The overall SREBP-1 expression was higher in tumorous tissues when compared to non-tumorous tissues, and SREBP-1 overexpression was found in 56.5% (26/46) of the cases. These data established the association between ACADM underexpression and SREBP-1 upregulation in human HCC.

17100418.label: Major findings and research outcome
17100418.value: Lipid accumulation exacerbates tumor development, as it provides power to fuel the proliferative growth of cancer cells. The role of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (ACADM), an enzyme that catalyzes the first step of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, remains elusive in tumor biology. Therefore, investigating its mode of dysregulation can shed light on the metabolic reliance in cancer development. Among the fatty acid oxidation (FAO) regulators, acyl co-enzyme A dehydrogenase, medium chain (ACADM), which is an enzyme that catalyzes the first step of FAO is investigated. Suppression of ACADM promotes HCC cell motility with elevated triglyceride, phospholipid and cellular lipid droplet levels, indicating the tumor suppressive ability of ACADM in HCC. The oncogenic effect of ACADM knockdown in promoting tumor formation is further validated using subcutaneous xenograft and hydrodynamic injection mouse models. This study identifies Sterol Regulatory Element Binding Transcription Factor 1 (SREBP-1) to be a negative transcriptional regulator of ACADM. The nuclear translocation of SREBP-1 is enhanced by caveolin-1 (Cav1). Functionally, knockdown of Cav1 in metastatic HCC cells reduces cellular triglyceride, phospholipid and lipid accumulation in cells, and inhibits HCC cell growth, motility and tumorigenesis. Treatment of Cav1 knockdown cells with Etomoxir, a drug that inhibits fatty acid oxidation, elevates fatty acid content and restores the attenuated aggressiveness of HCC cells. In Cav1 knockdown cells, SREBP-1c was retained in the cytoplasm. Lastly, in an animal model injected with metastatic HCC cells in which Cav1 and SREBP-1 are highly expressed while ACADM expression is low, administration with sorafenib and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) that inhibits maturation of SREBP-1 protein significantly reduced tumor formation. Tumors treated with EPA alone or in combination with sorafenib resulted in the decrease in SREPB-1 and increase in ACADM expressions. In clinical HCC tissues, ACADM is significantly reduced and correlated to bigger tumor size, presence of venous invasion, advanced HCC tumor stage and poor cell differentiation. The physiological relevance of ACADM and SREBP-1 is reflected by their significant inverse correlation in tissue microarray comprises 46 paired tumorous and non-tumorous tissues. Nuclear SREBP-1 expression is higher in tumorous tissues when compared to non-tumorous tissues. In conclusion, this study reveals that the deregulation of fatty acid oxidation mediated by the Cav1/SREBP-1/ACADM axis results in HCC progression and provides insight into the limitation of fatty acid availability to cancer cells as a therapeutic strategy for HCC. This study is published in Cancer Research 2021, 81(13):3679-3692 by Ma et al.

17100418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17100418.value: EPA is a major component of ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids which can enhance fatty acid oxidation and reduce de novo lipogenesis by modulating transcription factors to inhibit SREBP-1 nuclear translocation. The study here showed that the combinational treatment of EPA and sorafenib markedly suppressed the growth of HCC xenografts when compared to treatments with either drug alone. This phenomenon can be attributed to the broad-spectrum protein kinase inhibitor activity of EPA observed in prostate and breast cancers, which further enhanced the multikinase inhibitor and anti-tumor properties of sorafenib. Thus, our data indicates the immense potential of the co-administration of EPA and sorafenib in slowing down HCC progression to provide a better prognosis for patients. Tumor metabolism plays such a key role in cancer development, the findings in this study contributes to a better understanding of the mechanistic pathways that shape the dysregulation of fatty acid metabolism in HCC, which will be beneficial to the advancement of targeted therapies for cancer patients.

17100418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17100418.value: Lipid accumulation promotes tumor development, as it provides power to support the proliferative growth of cancer cells. The role of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (ACADM), an enzyme that catalyzes the breakdown of fatty acids is important to maintain the low level of lipid in cells. However, the role of ACADM in cancer cells remains elusive in tumor biology. In this study, we found that ACADM was frequently reduced in liver cancer and correlated to aggressive parameters of cancer patients. ACADM underexpression resulted in an enhanced aggressive properties of cancer cells and an elevated cellular level of triglyceride, phospholipid and lipid droplet. This study also revealed how ACADM was downregulated in liver cancer cells. It was revealed that high level of caveolin-1 (Cav1) enhanced the nuclear accumulation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein-1 (SREBP-1) leading to the suppression of ACADM. In tissues of liver cancer patients, the expression of SREBP-1 and ACADM was negatively correlated. Lastly, this study showed that the administration of a SREBP-1 inhibitor in combination with sorafenib significantly reduced HCC tumor growth in mouse model. In conclusion, this study reveals a new pathway of deregulated lipid metabolism that leads to liver cancer and implicates the limitation of fatty acid availability to cancer cells as a strategy for cancer treatment.

17100718.label: Project Objectives
17100718.value: To examine the spatiotemporal assembly of PLSs by ECM micropatterns for the formation of aneural AChR clusters. In order to understand how ECM proteins regulate PLS assembly, we will employ the multiphoton biofabrication technique to dissect the role of ECM geometry and stiffness in the spatiotemporal regulation of PLS assembly for the formation of aneural AChR clusters in live cells. To investigate the local degradation of ECM proteins for the remodeling of aneural AChR clusters via PLS-directed surface insertion of MT1-MMP. In order to understand the functions of PLSs in skeletal muscles, we will test an exciting hypothesis that PLS directs the surface targeting of MT1-MMP via microtubule-capturing mechanisms, thus it functions to control the stability and remodeling of aneural AChR clusters by locally modulating ECM environment. To study the regulation of synaptic AChR clustering and remodeling by MT1-MMP surface insertion in vitro and in vivo. As the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of AChR re-distribution in response to synaptic induction remain poorly understood, we will determine if PLS-directed MT1-MMP surface insertion regulates the clustering and remodeling of synaptic AChR clusters at the nascent postsynaptic sites, and the dispersal of aneural AChR clusters in nerve-muscle co-cultures and in MT1-MMP-deficient animals.

17100718.label: Realisation of objectives
17100718.value: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ), a peripheral nerve-muscle synapse, serves as an excellent model for investigating the cellular and molecular mechanisms of synapse formation and remodelling. At the NMJ, acetylcholine receptor (AChR) molecules are highly clustered at the synaptic region. Even in the absence of motor neurons, AChR clustering can still be found at the end plates of muscle fibres in vivo. Such aneural AChR cluster structures can be induced in Xenopus primary muscles or immortalized C2C12 myotubes cultured on extracellular matrix (ECM) protein laminin-containing substrates. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the assembly and morphological remodelling of ECM-induced aneural AChR clusters are largely unclear. In this GRF grant project, we have studied the molecular regulation of aneural AChR cluster formation and its contribution to the assembly of the postsynaptic apparatus at developing NMJs. Through a combination of molecular manipulations and cellular imaging techniques, we revealed that podosome-like structures (PLSs) induced by ubiquitous ECM proteins regulate the formation and remodelling of AChR clusters via focal ECM degradation. PLSs are highly dynamic actin-rich organelles found in transformed fibroblasts and many other motile or invasive cells. Our results suggested that PLSs direct the vesicular trafficking and surface insertion of membrane-type 1 matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP) via microtubule-based mechanisms to focally mediate ECM degradation during NMJ formation. Microtubules are important cytoskeletal structures for the intracellular transport of proteins. EB1, a key regulator of the plus-end-tracking protein complex, functions to modulate microtubule dynamics and interaction with other intracellular organelles. Direct interactions between EB1 and other microtubule plus-end-tracking proteins, e.g., CLIP-associating proteins (CLASPs), are implicated in the ‘recruitment mechanism’, by which EB1 functions to search-and-capture post-Golgi vesicles and to spatially capture microtubules at the cell cortex. We found that antisense morpholino (MO)-mediated knockdown of endogenous Xenopus CLASP, the homolog of mammalian CLASP1, in cultured muscle cells significantly reduced the local capture of microtubules at AChR clusters. Given that MT1-MMP surface insertion at aneural AChR clusters was significantly inhibited in CLASP-MO muscle cells, we hypothesize that EB1-mediated microtubule capturing mechanisms can be regulated by PLSs at both cortex (adhesion molecule-based) and core (actin-based) domains in a CLASP-dependent and -independent manner, respectively. MT1-MMP is the best characterized and most prevalent isoform of the large MMP family, including membrane-type or soluble MMPs. MT1-MMP deficiency causes myogenic impediments and central nucleation of myofibers, which are typically found in muscular dystrophy. In addition, MT1-MMP knockout mice develop multiple abnormalities and die between 50–90 postnatal days, suggesting that the possibility of functional redundancy by other MMP isoforms is low. In this study, we used mutant mice lacking MT1-MMP in all cells and observed that the density of aneural AChR clusters was significantly higher than that in wild-type mice at E13.5, consistent with the in vitro findings on the involvement of MT1-MMP in the recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural to synaptic AChR clusters. However, at E18.5, the density of aneural AChR clusters between MT1-MMP knockout and wild-type mice was comparable. While MT1-MMP knockdown caused a significant inhibition in synaptic AChR clustering at the nerve-muscle contacts, it is intriguing to note that diffuse AChRs were constantly recruited to aneural AChR clusters that were stabilized by MT1-MMP knockdown. Therefore, we hypothesize that MT1-MMP facilitates the disassembly of extracellular (e.g., ECM proteins) and/or intracellular (e.g., cytoskeletal proteins) molecular scaffolds that are tightly associated with aneural AChR clusters, such that AChR molecules from dispersing aneural clusters can be recruited to synaptic clusters in response to nerve induction. While aneural AChR clusters in MT1-MMP knockout mice were not recruited to synaptic AChR clusters, they were subjected to regular metabolic turnover/degradation, leading to the disappearance of aneural AChR clusters at E18.5. Collectively, our present study further supported that postsynaptic MT1-MMP plays a dual-functional role in regulating the formation and dispersal of synaptic and aneural AChR clusters, respectively, via focal ECM degradation. In addition, we have made another important observation related to this project that temperature stress could also regulate the structure and function of vertebrate NMJs. Specifically, we use Xenopus primary cultures as a vertebrate model system for investigating the involvement of the heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) family of stress proteins, particularly glucose-regulated protein 94 (Grp94), in NMJ development. Cold temperature treatment or Grp94 inhibition attenuates the formation of aneural AChR clusters but increases their stability after they are formed in cultured muscles. Grp94 inhibition specifically affects the stability of aneural AChR clusters and their associated intracellular scaffolding protein rapsyn instead of causing a global change in cell metabolism and protein expression in Xenopus muscle cultures. Upon synaptogenic stimulation, Grp94 modulates the phosphorylation and dynamic turnover of actin depolymerizing factor (ADF)/cofilin at aneural AChR clusters, leading to the recruitment of AChR molecules from aneural clusters to the assembly of nerve- or agrin-induced postsynaptic specializations. Collectively, this study suggests that temperature-dependent alterations in Grp94 expression and activity inhibit the assembly of postsynaptic specializations by modulating ADF/cofilin phosphorylation and activity at aneural AChR clusters, which prevents AChR molecules from being recruited to postsynaptic sites via actin-dependent vesicular trafficking at developing vertebrate NMJs.

17100718.label: Major findings and research outcome
17100718.value: The major findings of this project have been published in two original research articles: 1. Chan ZC, Kwan HR, Wong YS, Jiang Z, Zhou Z, Tam KW, Chan YS, Chan CB, and Lee CW (2020) Site-directed MT1-MMP trafficking and surface insertion regulate AChR clustering and remodelling at developing NMJs. eLife. Mar 24; 9: e54379. doi: 10.7554/eLife.54379. Major findings: - The assembly of podosomes induced by several key ECM proteins focally regulates matrix degradation at perforations of AChR clusters in primary myotomal muscle cultures. - Intracellular trafficking and surface insertion of MT1-MMP are targeted to AChR clusters at sites of podosomes through EB1-/CLASP-mediated microtubule-capturing mechanisms. - MT1-MMP activity precisely regulates focal degradation of ubiquitous ECM proteins, which clears up the nascent synaptic site for AChR cluster formation and topological remodelling. - Upon synaptic induction, postsynaptic MT1-MMP differentially regulates the formation of nerve-induced AChR clusters and the dispersal of aneural AChR clusters. 2. Chan ZC, Deng L, and Lee CW (2020) Grp94 regulates the recruitment of aneural AChR clusters for the assembly of postsynaptic specializations by modulating ADF/cofilin activity and turnover. eNeuro. Sep 8; 7(5): ENEURO.0025-20.2020. doi: 10.1523/ENEURO.0025-20.2020. Major findings: - The HSP90 family of stress proteins regulates the formation and stability of aneural AChR clusters in cultured muscle cells. - The HSP90 family member Grp94 (glucose-regulated protein 94) is required for AChR redistribution from aneural to agrin-induced AChR clusters through local modulation of ADF/cofilin turnover and site-directed vesicular trafficking. - Postsynaptic Grp94 is essential for nerve-induced AChR clustering and synaptic transmission at developing NMJs.

17100718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17100718.value: To build upon the conclusions of our recently published work demonstrating the involvement of MT1-MMP in focal ECM remodelling to facilitate the topological maturation of the postsynaptic apparatus (Chan et al., eLife 2020), it would be of interest to further understand how the dynamic remodelling of ECM proteins regulates the development of structural architecture at NMJs. For example, one follow-up study further demonstrated that membrane infoldings, mirroring the junctional folds of NMJs, are developed in cultured muscle cells in the absence of motor neurons. While MMP-mediated ECM degradation is detected at PLS-enriched perforations of aneural AChR clusters, our new study further observed that membrane infoldings were spatially associated with the perforation sites of aneural AChR clusters with extensive focal degradation of fluorescent gelatin (Kwan et al., Science Advances 2023), suggesting that dynamic ECM remodelling may modulate substrate stiffness to promote membrane infolding formation. In addition, the broad-spectrum MMP inhibitor BB-94 completely significantly reduced the volume of membrane infoldings and the colocalization volume between AChR clusters and membrane infoldings. Together, these data demonstrated the requirement of MMP-mediated ECM remodelling for the formation and/or maintenance of membrane infoldings at aneural AChR clusters. Since abnormalities of the junctional fold architecture are the most common phenotypes associated with several neuromuscular disorders in humans, the results of our study provide a better understanding of the molecular regulation of membrane infolding formation and maintenance at the postsynaptic apparatus, which could potentially be translated to understand how junctional fold abnormalities impair synaptic functions in various neuromuscular diseases.

17100718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17100718.value: At the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), the spatial localization of acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the postsynaptic apparatus allows nerve cells to effectively communicate with the muscle cell. Alongside these AChR clusters are dynamic actin-enriched structures, which are responsible for releasing enzymes that digest the surrounding matrix and are commonly found in migrating cells. This GRF project used advanced microscopy techniques to show how these actin-enriched structures can help acetylcholine receptors cluster together at the site of communication between the nerve and muscle cells. The experiments showed that these structures direct a molecule called MT1-MMP to the muscle surface. This molecule then clears the surrounding matrix so that signals sent from the nerve can be effectively deposited at the narrow space between these two cells. When the muscle cells receive this initiating signal, acetylcholine receptors are recruited from the spontaneously formed clusters to the communication site, allowing the muscle to contract. When MT1-MMP was experimentally eliminated in mice, this disrupted the recruitment of acetylcholine receptors to the NMJ. Overall, these experiments help researchers understand how clearing the matrix between nerve and muscle cells contributes to the deposition of factors that build the communication site at developing NMJs.

17101118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17101118.value: Adipose tissue can go through extensive expansion or reduction upon change of our diet. Various types of adipose tissues distribute throughout our body, and can be categorized by their functions into three types: white, brown and beige adipose tissues. White adipose tissue (WAT) is the storage for extra energy whereas brown adipose tissue (BAT) is the heat generator. Beige adipose tissue is a type of WAT that is transformed into a BAT-like state, a process called browning, upon cold exposure. During browning, the number of mitochondria and the expression of uncoupling protein-1 (UCP1), the heat generating protein, are increased. This process is particularly important for human as there is a loss of BAT when entering adulthood. Moreover, other than cold exposure, food intake also increases energy expenditure by stimulating heat generation. UCP1 is the key protein controlling both cold- and diet-induced thermogenesis, thus maintaining the homeostasis of energy balance and body weight. Finding ways to regulate UCP1 has drawn much of the clinical attention for combating obesity and the related metabolic disorders. Several mechanisms have been proposed but limited to the transcriptional regulation, and it has been frequently reported that the expression of UCP1 mRNA poorly projects the protein abundance. Hence, the bench-to-bed translation has limited progress. Toll-like receptor (TLR) is one of the innate immunity receptor families. In general, engagement of these receptors with their corresponding ligands triggers inflammatory responses that are beneficial in acute infections but detrimental in chronic metabolic diseases. However, unlike other TLRs, TLR5 protects against overeating and obesity, and suppresses cytokines released from adipose tissues. Here, we found that TLR5 participated in regulating UCP1 protein. Absence of TLR5 not only attenuated UCP1 expression but also impaired thermogenesis upon cold challenge leading to hypothermic death. The selective suppression of UCP protein by TLR5 without affecting other thermogenic proteins and Ucp1 mRNA makes TLR5 as a suitable pharmacological target in regulating thermogenesis. In this proposal, we will further elucidate the molecular mechanism of how TLR5 regulates UCP1 protein and thermogenesis. Understanding the interplay between TLR5 and UCP1 will shed light on the novel role of TLR in metabolism. With the knowledge of ligand-receptor dynamic, our next aim will be to identify small molecules to target TLR5 in the thermogenic adipocytes to combat obesity and the related metabolic disorders.

17102218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17102218.value: New therapeutic strategies are needed for treating cancers. There is increasing acceptance that a more effective approach to cancer treatment is to use a combination of therapeutic agents, instead of a single agent. Combination therapy allows the simultaneous targeting of multiple cellular targets to eliminate cancer cells, as well as the suppression of compensatory pathways to limit cancer survival. Applying combinations of existing drugs represent an attractive strategy to explore the unanticipated and hard-to-predict drug interactions that exhibit synergistic anti-cancer effects. However, the identification of new therapeutic combinations has been challenging because of the limited technologies available and their prohibitively high cost to run and scale up. To breakthrough this bottleneck, we have developed a new technology platform, termed CombiGEM-CRISPR (Combinatorial Genetics En Masse-Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats), and applied it to enable high-throughput functional characterization of genetic combinations in human cancer cells (Wong et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2015; Wong, Choi, Cui et al., PNAS, 2016). Being able to systematically and rapidly discover effective cancer therapeutics would be an important step forward in accelerating the development of cancer treatments. We have recently extended our effort to apply CombiGEM-CRISPR to search for druggable gene combinations that exerted anti-cancer effects in ovarian cancer cells. Here, we shall move beyond our prior and recent work in this proposal to characterize the newly identified therapeutic combinations that inhibit ovarian cancer cell growth, with the aim to tackle the need for new and effective treatments for human ovarian cancer. 癌症治療需要新策略。 越來越多的人認為，更有效的癌症治療方法是使用聯合，而非單一藥物。 聯合治療允許同時靶向多個細胞靶標以消除癌細胞，并抑制代償通路以限制腫瘤存活。 一種具有吸引力的治療手段是組合現有的藥物，以探索意料外及難預測的藥物相互作用表現出的協同抗癌療效。 然而，鑑於有限的技術以及大規模實驗的過高成本，新治療組合的鑑定一直具有挑戰性。 為突破這一瓶頸，我們開發了一種新的技術平台， CombiGEM-CRISPR（Combinatorial Genetics En Masse-Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats），並應用其實現了在人癌細胞中高通量基因組合功能的研究（Wong et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2015; Wong, Choi, Cui et al., PNAS, 2016）。 能夠系統並快速地發現有效的抗癌藥物組合將是加速癌症治療發展的重要一步。 最近我們通過CombiGEM-CRISPR竭力找尋了在卵巢癌細胞中發揮抗癌作用的可藥物基因組合。 在這裡，我們將超越在此提案中先前和最近的工作，研究新發現的抑制卵巢癌細胞生長的聯合療法，以滿足探索卵巢癌新型并且有效治療方案的需求。

17102218.label: Realisation of objectives
17102218.value: We have successfully achieved all the objectives in this project. As described in our progress report, we set out to select a therapeutic combination for ovarian cancer to be focused on based on its translational potential and novelty (Aim 2). To evaluate the translation potential of the therapeutic candidates, we applied drug combinations targeting PARP1 and DNMT1, as well as CDK2 and FKBP1A, at multiple doses and measure their effects on cell proliferation using two HGSOC cells (OVSAHO and KURAMOCHI). Olaparib (OLA), azacitdine (AZA), seliciclib (SEL), and sirolimus (SIR) were used as the drugs to target PARP1, DNMT1, CDK2, and FKBP1A, respectively. These drug molecules have been reported to have potent effects on their targets. While our results showed that the drug combination targeting PARP1 and DNMT1 resulted in a synergistic growth inhibitory effect in both OVSAHO and KURAMOCHI, similar observations were then published by another research group (Pulliam et a., Clin Cancer Res, 2018), which showed that co-administration of PARP1 inhibitor and DNMT1 inhibitor synergistically suppressed tumour growth of ovarian cancer cells including OVCAR4, PEO1, and PEO4. Our results also demonstrated that the drug combination targeting CDK2 and FKBP1A resulted in strong growth inhibitory effect in both OVSAHO and KURAMOCHI, but only in an additive manner and no synergistic mechanism could be studied. We therefore switched to study another combination DNMT1 + POLA1 + EGFR, which we identified to suppress the growth of ovarian cancer OVCAR8-ADR and OVSAHO cells. AZA, fludarabine (FLU), and erlotinib (ERL) were used to target DNMT1, POLA1, and EGFR, respectively. The three-drug treatment of AZA, FLU, and ERL showed significantly stronger growth-inhibitory effects than the single- and double- drug treatments. We further extended our validation work in vivo. In collaboration with Dr. Lydia Cheung at School of Biomedical Sciences, HKU, we subcutaneously implanted OVCAR8-ADR cells to form tumors in BALB/cAnN-nu mice followed by drug treatment. We confirmed a significant decrease in tumor weight in mice treated with the AZA + FLU + ERL formulation, whereas no behavior abnormalities and changes in body weight were observed, indicating minimal side effects induced by the drug interactions. We further characterized the mechanism by which the AZA + FLU + ERL combination inhibits ovarian cancer cell proliferation (Aim 1). We performed RNA-seq experiments and found that the drug combination resulted in a different set of perturbed genes, when comparing cells treated with the three-drug regimen with all of the respective two-drug combinations. More specifically, 3,834 genes were identified with an FDR < 0.05 as differentially expressed in OVCAR8-ADR cells treated with the three-drug regimen (AZA + FLU + ERL) when compared to the untreated control. We mapped pathways for the differentially expressed genes, which were at least 20% up- or down- regulated in OVCAR8-ADR cells treated with the three-drug regimen (AZA + FLU + ERL) when compared to the untreated control and also had a fold change of > 10%, > 5%, or < 5% in cells treated with the three-drug regimen over all of those treated with the corresponding two-drug regimens. Genes involved in cell cycle regulation were shown to be differentially perturbed. With cell-cycle experiments and analyses, we further demonstrated that fewer G2 phase-arrested cells stained positive for pH3 after AZA + FLU + ERL treatment, suggesting reduced mitotic entry. With the goal to tackle the need for new and effective combination treatments for cancers, we also extended our Aim 1 to characterize the mechanism by which our another newly identified therapeutic combinations (ifenoprodil (IFEN) + sorafenib (SOR) inhibits liver (HCC) cancer cell growth. We adopted a similar approach described above and used RNA-seq to analyse differentially expressed genes and their enriched pathways in drug(s)-treated HCC cancer cells MHCC97L as compared with nontreated cells. Mapping of the differentially expressed genes to Gene Ontology groups revealed that genes involved in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response are significantly upregulated, whereas many cell-cycle– and DNA replication–related genes are downregulated, in cells treated with IFEN + SOR combination. Upon ER stress, cells activate the unfolded protein response (UPR). We performed Western blot analysis and confirmed that IFEN + SOR treatment activates UPR effectors, including phosphorylated IRE1-alpha, ATF6, and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP), in MHCC97L cells (Fig. 3D and E). We also confirmed that IFEN + SOR combination treatment greatly increased the expression of p21Cip1, a regulator of cell-cycle progression at G1–S phase, which was accompanied by the downregulation of CDK2 and other cell-cycle– and DNA replication–related proteins including PCNA and TTK, as well as the activation of the apoptosis signaling pathway. Similar results were also detected in another HCC cell line HepG2 treated with IFEN + SOR. Cell-cycle analysis was then performed, and G1-phase arrest was detected in MHCC97L cells treated with IFEN + SOR, but not with either IFEN or SOR alone. To analyze whether IFEN + SOR treatment causes G1-phase arrest through UPR signaling, we created cells that are deficient in UPR sensing. Because UPR is an integrated ER stress–response pathway that is coordinated by three sensor proteins (i.e., IRE1-alpha, PERK, and ATF6), we thus generated cells that are depleted of all the three sensors. We found that G1-phase arrest and p21Cip1 expression induced by IFEN + SOR treatment was rescued in these cells, indicating that the drug combination-induced G1-phase arrest critically depends on UPR. Collectively, our data suggest that IFEN and SOR synergized to induce UPR, thereby suppressing the growth of HCC cells.

17102318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17102318.value: Peptide amphiphiles self-assemble into biomimetic nanofibers which show exceptional promise for regenerative medicine applications. A key challenge for peptide amphiphile application is the development of better approaches for the display of bioactive signals on the peptide amphiphile surface. The typical approach thus far has been to use peptides or other protein/antibody based ligands but such approaches can be limited by their specificities, availabilities and affinities. Nucleic acid aptamers can have advantages in such molecular recognition applications, particularly including tailored specificity, direct simpler chemical synthesis and the ability to target otherwise intractable surfaces on protein targets. However, no investigation of the potential for nucleic acid aptamers as innovative bioactive targeting signals on peptide amphiphile architectures has yet been performed. Here, we bring together a multidisciplinary international team incorporating world-leading expertise in both nucleic acid aptamers and in peptide amphiphiles to develop an innovative aptamer-peptide amphiphile scaffold for osteogenesis. Our preliminary collaborative data has already optimized the experimental strategy for the chimeric nanostructure synthesis. We have observed that the nanofiber architecture can work in synergy with the molecular recognition properties of the aptamer, particularly when the aptamer is mounted on a DNA tetrahedron ‘pedestal’. We now propose to evolve new classes of DNA aptamer which specifically target three bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), important extracellular cytokines which stimulate the production of bone and are key targets for many regenerative medicine applications. We will target BMP-2, BMP-4 and BMP-6 which we consider the most promising targets for regenerative medicine applications. We will investigate and compare aptamers against these targets decorated on the surface of a peptide amphiphile. In Stage I, we will select DNA aptamers against BMP-2, BMP-4 and BMP-6 then characterize, optimize and stabilize for therapeutic application. In Stage II, we will integrate these aptamers with peptide amphiphile and characterize their properties in binding the respective BMP target relative to the aptamer alone. In Stage III, we will compare the aptamers alone on the peptide amphiphile relative to the aptamers displayed on a DNA tetrahedron ‘pedestal’. Finally, in Stage IV, we will investigate the potential for our innovative nucleic acid aptamer peptide amphiphile scaffold to promote osteogenesis in a rat model with a specific study investigating spinal arthrodesis. Taken together, this study will provide new aptamers against three BMP targets, will open a new angle for peptide amphiphile application in regenerative medicine, and will lay a foundation for subsequent clinical studies. 肽兩親物自組裝成的仿生納米纖維，於再生醫學的應用上表現優異。肽兩親物應用的關鍵挑戰，是開發用於在肽兩親物表面上展示生物活性信號的更好方法。迄今為止的典型方法是使用肽或其他基於蛋白質或抗體的配體，但這些方法可受其獨特性、可用性和親和力的限制。核酸適體在這樣的分子識別應用中具有優勢，特別是可制定的獨特性，直接而簡單的化學合成和針對蛋白質目標上棘手表面的能力。然而，至今仍未有人對核酸適體在肽兩親物結構上展示生物活性靶向信號的可能性進行研究。在此，我們匯集了一個多學科的國際團隊，結合了世界領先的核酸適體和肽兩親物專業知識，開發出一種創新、用於成骨的適體肽兩親性支架。我們的初步協作數據已經優化了合成嵌合納米結構的實驗策略。我們已經觀察到，特別是將適體處於DNA四面體“基座”上的時候，納米纖維結構可以與適體的分子識別產生協同效應。我們現在提出開發新類型的DNA適體，特別針對三種骨塑型蛋白（BMP）—用於刺激骨生成的重要細胞外細胞因子，亦是許多再生醫學應用的關鍵目標。我們將針對BMP-2、BMP-4和BMP-6，我們認為這些是在再生醫學應用中最有希望的目標。我們將研究並比較在肽兩親物表面上針對這些標靶的適體。在第一階段，我們將篩選針對BMP-2，BMP-4和BMP-6的DNA適體，然後為治療應用方面進行表徵分析、優化和穩定化。在第二階段，我們會將這些適體與肽兩親物整合，並為其相對於單獨的適體與BMP結合的性質進行表徵分析。在第三階段，我們將比較肽兩親物上的適體與在DNA四面體“基座”上的適體。最後，在第四階段，我們將研究我們的創新核酸適體肽兩親物支架，在老鼠模型中促進成骨的潛力，並專門研究脊柱關節固定。總括而言，本研究將提供針對三種BMP標靶的新適體，為肽兩親物在再生醫學上的應用開闢全新的視角，並為隨後的臨床研究奠定基礎。

17102318.label: Realisation of objectives
17102318.value: We report realisation of all project objectives in general with further details as reported below and in the associated journal manuscripts, two PhD theses, and nine conference presentations. Recombinant human BMP-2 (rhBMP-2) is recognized as one of the most effective osteoinductive factors, with significant promise for tissue engineering applications. RhBMP-2 delivered on an absorbable collagen sponge is a US FDA-approved bone graft substitute widely used for bone repair in patients under challenging conditions such as spinal arthrodesis and open tibial fractures. However, natural collagen sponges capture rhBMP-2 only through unstable physical absorption, leading to requirements of a high dose of rhBMP-2 for clinical therapy thereby increasing costs and complications including ectopic ossification, exaggerated inflammation, and soft tissue hematomas.The development of a scaffold with high BMP-2 capture capability and enhanced osteoinductive activity would have significant value. Some newly reported BMP-2 scaffolds have been assembled with artificial extracellular matrix (ECM) biomaterials including peptide amphiphile nanofibers and 3D electrospun fibers.11-14 Such scaffolds capture BMP-2 via BMP-2-binding motifs such as heparin and affinity peptides to prolong drug retention, to mimic native ECM, and to facilitate osteoinductive function. For practical applications, undesirable toxicities from synthetic materials and non-specific molecular interactions remain an issue of concern.15 Novel scaffolds assembled with safe materials that enable specific capture of BMP-2 would have significant clinical value. In this funded project, we have successfully selected an rhBMP-2-specific DNA aptamer, functionalization of the aptamer in an ECM-like scaffold, and have investigated its application in a cellular context. A DNA aptamer BA1 was evolved and shown to have high affinity and specificity to rhBMP-2. A molecular docking model demonstrated that BA1 was bound to rhBMP-2 at its heparin-binding domain, as verified by experimental competitive binding assays. The BA1 aptamer was used to functionalize a type I collagen scaffold and fraction ratios were optimized to mimic the natural ECM. Studies in the myoblast cell model C2C12 showed that the aptamer-enhanced scaffold could specifically augment the osteoinductive function of rhBMP-2 in vitro. This aptamer-functionalized scaffold may have value to enhance rhBMP-2 mediated bone regeneration. For the specific objectives we report for the first stage "Select DNA aptamers against BMP-2, BMP-4 and BMP-6 then characterize, optimize and stabilize for therapeutic application" 100% is achieved. For the second stage "Integrate selected aptamers with peptide amphiphile and characterize their properties in binding the respective BMP target relative to the aptamer alone." 80% is achieved. For the third stage "Characterize and compare aptamers alone on the peptide amphiphile relative to the aptamers displayed on a DNA tetrahedron ‘pedestal’" 80% has been achieved. Please refer to Wang Lin's PhD thesis for more achievements regarding DNA nanostructures in conjunction with this study. For the final stage, 50% has been achieved, and some work towards the next stage of clinical application is ongoing. There are some limitations in the study. The BA1 aptamer was selected against rhBMP-2 with histidine tags. Histidine is positively charged and may contribute to the binding affinity of the negatively charged DNA aptamer. However, the specificity assays which we performed with other histidine-tagged targets (His-peptide, His-pfLDH) gives confidence that the binding is indeed to rhBMP-2 and not to the histidine tag. It will also be of interest to more deeply investigate the structures of the tDNA-interlinked collagen fibers. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging and X-ray diffraction can be used to further determine and normalize the morphologies and sizes of DNA-collagen fibers to enable better comparisons with other studies in the literature. Nevertheless, our study provides a new BMP-2 aptamer and also demonstrates its translational potential for enhancing BMP-2-induced osteogenesis.

17102318.label: Major findings and research outcome
17102318.value: This study demonstrated the evolution of a DNA aptamer, BA1, exhibiting high affinity and specificity to the growth factor applied for bone regeneration, rhBMP-2. Through rigorous counter selections, BA1 markedly discriminated rhBMP-2 and its analog rhBMP-3, to achieve selective drug capture as functional motifs on scaffolds. In addition, molecular docking analysis was performed to better understand the molecular interactions of the BA1-BMP-2 complex. The putative interaction model revealed that BA1 may adopt hairpin-like conformations and bind to rhBMP-2 mainly at the heparin-binding domain, which was consistent with experimental binding competition assays with heparin and polyphosphate. BA1 was then applied to assemble fibrous scaffolds with type I collagen, which could promote the osteogenesis ability of rhBMP-2 as observed in assays measuring ALP, mineralization, cell adhesion, and wound healing. The BA1 aptamer as well as the scaffold of BA1 integrated with collagen may be useful for BMP-2 mediated bone regeneration applications.

17102318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17102318.value: For proceeding to in vivo studies, the aptamer-collagen fibers should be encapsulated in 3D matrix biomaterials such as agarose to enable controllable drug release. Besides, the fibrous scaffold requires further refinement to improve nuclease resistance and osteoinductive potency. DNA aptamers and collagen are highly biodegradable in vivo, and the combination of two materials was observed to stabilize fibers in the cellular milieu. To achieve long-lasting efficacy in vivo, fibers could be further stabilized by modifying aptamers with 2’-F, 2’-OMe, or phosphorothioate bonds, and constructing composite hydrogels with more resilient biomaterials such as agarose. In addition, to improve the potency for bone regeneration, some strategies that could be adopted include 1) an optimization of fiber formulation to generate unified fibers with efficient functional morphologies, 2) the incorporation of additional growth factors like VEGF into fibers to enable synergistic regenerative effects and 3) the integration of cell-binding moieties to recruit bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) or osteoblast lineage (MC3T3-E1 cells, etc) to achieve cell-free in-situ bone regeneration.

17102318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17102318.value: Better approaches are needed for bone regeneration and bone repair in general medical practice. One therapy which has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration is recombinant bone morphogenetic protein 2 (rhBMP-2) which has had a major positive impact for bone grafting. rhBMP-2 is delivered on an absorbable collagen sponge as a bone graft substitute widely used for bone repair in patients under challenging conditions such as spinal arthrodesis and open tibial fractures. However, natural collagen sponges capture rhBMP-2 only through unstable physical absorption, leading to requirements of a high dose of rhBMP-2 for clinical therapy thereby increasing costs and complications including ectopic ossification, exaggerated inflammation, and soft tissue hematomas. The development of a scaffold with high BMP-2 capture capability and enhanced osteoinductive activity would have significant value. In this project we have discovered a new class of therapeutic called a DNA aptamer which binds to rhBMP-2 specifically. We have discovered the aptamer, functionalized it, and investigated its application in cell culture work. We also performed molecular docking models computationally to investigate its mechanism of action. We integrated with a collagen scaffold and showed that the aptamer could increase the function of the BMP-2 therapy in a cell culture model. This aptamer could have value in bone regeneration applications in future.

17103218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17103218.value: 中國南方包括香港地區是鼻咽癌高發地區之一。鼻咽癌發病年齡比許多常見癌癥提前了20多年。大約20-30%的患者有癌症復發和轉移，因此鼻咽癌成為了影響香港經濟發展的一大健康問題。家族遺傳性鼻咽癌占該病患者的百分之十，對於家庭一級血親中患有鼻咽癌的個體，其患鼻咽癌的危險性大大增高，可見遺傳在鼻咽癌發生過程中起到重要作用。但是，目前還沒有關於鼻咽癌遺傳機理的深入研究。我們的研究小組長期以來致力於研究鼻咽癌遺傳易感性以及染色體3p21.3區域的抑癌作用。我們以往的抑癌基因功能性研究和兩篇利用全基因組測序和靶向測序技術研究鼻咽癌遺傳易感基因MST1R和鼻咽癌腫瘤遺傳變異圖譜的PNAS科研文章為我們即將開展的研究提供了有力的研究基礎。 近年，我們在多個鼻咽癌患者的血液裏發現MST1R基因的遺傳變異，特別是在發病年齡小於20歲的患者當中，MST1R基因遺傳變異同對照組相比頻率顯著增高。我們進壹步發現MST1R相關蛋白質結合網酪中多個基因都在鼻咽癌患者中存在遺傳變異，在我們研究的患者當中其變異頻率高達35%。 MST1R基因位於3號染色體3p21.3區域。該基因在鼻咽癌患者中的體細胞改變包括拷貝數量變化和啟動子甲基化。此外，全基因組測序顯示在3p21.3區域存在多個鼻咽癌遺傳易感候選基因。我們和其他科研小組的研究都表明3p21.3區域具有非常重要的抑癌作用並且3號染色體短臂丟失是鼻咽癌發病早期分子變化之一。因此，我們假設多個鼻咽癌易感基因存在於該區域，雜合遺傳性變異和體細胞拷貝丟失或者表觀遺傳學變化導致這些重要抑癌基因的失活，因此導致個體對鼻咽癌的易感性；此外，遺傳變異導致MST1R蛋白質結合網酪的失調在鼻咽癌發病過程中起到重要作用，並能提供病人臨床預後信息。 為了檢驗我們的假設，我們提出利用靶向測序的方法檢查1000名鼻咽癌患者包括220名家族遺傳性病例和780名散發病例以及1000名年齡和性別匹配的香港健康對照者。在該研究中，我們會全面檢查5Mb區域其中包括3p21.3連續區域（包含MST1R，其配體MST1及其調節基因HYAL2）和MST1R蛋白質結合網酪的基因。我們會檢測在編碼區和調節區的遺傳變異，及其同臨床預後的相關性。此外，我們還會檢查遺傳變異攜帶者的腫瘤組織。 我們預期可以驗證更多的鼻咽癌候選易感基因。這些研究成果將幫助我們闡述鼻咽癌的發病機理，為有家族性鼻咽癌歷史的個體提供有效的遺傳檢測方法。我們希望這些遺傳變異可以提供病人的臨床預後信息，用於病人分層管理，從而提高鼻咽癌的治愈率和病人愈後的生活質量。

17103218.value: 1. Validate the association of germline variants in the coding regions of candidate genes with NPC We proposed to evaluate the germline variants in the targeted regions including 5Mb region (4.5Mb from chromosome 3p21.3 and 0.5Mb for MST1R interaction network from the other chromosomes) from 1000 independent NPC cases including 220 familial and 780 sporadic cases, as well as 1000 age and gender-matched non-cancer controls provided by Hong Kong Red Cross. In the completed project, we finally evaluated the germline pathogenic variants at MST1R, MST1R interaction network genes, 3p21.3 genes and selected DNA repair genes including MutS homologs (MSH2 and MSH6), MutL homologs (MLH1, MLH3, PMS1 and PMS2), DNA repair genes (ATM, BRCA2, FANCA, and POLE) in the blood samples from a total of 1152 NPC cases including 207 FH+ cases and 945 sporadic cases by targeted sequencing and compared to 1205 non-cancer controls of matched ancestry. The ratio of males to females and age are comparable between the case and control groups (1.73 vs. 1.78, Chi-square test P = 0.66; 49±11 y vs. 49±9 y, Student’s T test P = 0.88). So, we achieved 100% completion of this proposed objective. 2. Identify the germline variants in the important regulatory regions and systematically evaluate the association of these variants with NPC Besides the variants in the coding region, the targeted capture kit also covers some of the regulatory regions within exons or UTRs. We analyzed germline variants in regulatory regions with promoter or enhancer activity. We identified rare germline variants (minor allele frequency (MAF)) from FH+ and sporadic cases in promoter or enhancer regions defined by the chromatin state predicted by the Hidden Markov Model (HMM) from ENCODE/Broad22 using the ChIP-seq data from UCSC genome browser (https://genome.ucsc.edu). We also performed the CUT&RUN-Seq for H3K4me3 and H3K27ac in normal nasopharyngeal epithelial cell line NP69 and EBV+ NPC cell line C666 to evaluate the germline variants in the promoter and super-enhancer regions. So, we achieved 100% completion of this proposed objective. 3. Evaluate the clinical significance of the germline variants in association with clinical parameters and outcomes The association between the genes with frequent germline variants and clinical parameters and outcomes was evaluated in the sporadic patients with complete follow-up data. A total of 807 sporadic patients had clinical data including 402 new cases and 405 follow-up cases. For validation of the association between the germline variants of selected genes and clinical outcomes, we assumed that the relevant germline rare variants occurred in 10% of the cases, and 417 cases were required for detecting an HR at 2.6 with the analysis power to be 90%. So only the genes with germline pathogenic variants were included for the survival analysis. We achieved 100% completion of this proposed objective. 4. Investigate the somatic alterations of the targeted regions in NPC tumors We investigated a total of 216 NPC tumors for the somatic mutations of selected genes and evaluated whether the germline variants of selected genes are associated with somatic mutational signatures and clinical outcomes. We also evaluated if there were somatic alterations in the tumor biopsies as the second hit in the genes with pathogenic germline variants, as proposed. So, we achieved 100% completion of this proposed objective.

17103218.label: Major findings and research outcome
17103218.value: 1. BRCA2 germline variants are associated with homologous repair deficient (HRD) mutational signature and clinical outcomes We identified 27 BRCA2 germline rare variants in 57 cases, accounting for 14.1% of the total cases in the study cohort. The germline rare variants had no association with age and stage, while the female cases were more likely to carry these germline rare variants than the male cases (20.4% vs. 11.9%; P = 0.043). The univariate analysis showed that the BRCA2 germline rare variants were significantly correlated with both overall survival and progression-free survival. This prognostic value remained after adjustment for age, gender, and overall stage. In the NPC biopsies, we confirmed that BRCA2 germline pathogenic variants were enriched in the patients who carried COSMIC signature 3 relevant to HRD. This study has been published in Clinical Cancer Research in 2020 (Dai et al. Clin Cancer Res, 2020; 26(24):6494-6504) and the findings were presented at Gordon Research Conference for NPC in 2022. 2. Gene-level validation of MST1R as NPC genetic susceptibility gene In total, we detected the MST1R variants at the gene level in 17 (4.97%) FH+ cases, 32 (2.56%) sporadic cases, and 45 (1.96%) controls, which confirmed the association of MST1R pathogenetic variants and risk of FH+ NPC at the gene-level analysis (Chi-square test P = 0.001). More importantly, the sporadic cases carrying MST1R variants were more likely to have advanced NPC (Stage VI vs. others: 42.1% vs. 25%, P < 0.001), and thus, subject to have shorter progression-free survival (PFS). 3. Identification of mismatch repair (MMR) genes as putative NPC genetic predisposition genes Among all the MMR genes, the gene-level burden tests indicate that the germline pathogenic variants at MLH1 were correlated with the risk of NPC in the FH+ cases (OR=3.6, SKAT test P = 0.0002, VT test P = 0.0068 and CMC test P = 0.0019). We identified MLH1 pathogenetic variants from 9 (4.3%) FH+ cases, 15 (1.6%) sporadic cases and 15 (1.2%) controls. In total, the MMR germline variants account for 12% of FH+ cases, 5.9% of sporadic cases, and 5.1% of controls. Multiple mechanisms for inactivating MMR including somatic mutation and suppression of gene expression through histone modifications were identified in NPC tumor biopsies, NPC cell lines, and patient-derived xenografts. The relevant manuscript is in preparation for submission. 4. Epigenomic molecular subtypes in NPC In addition, we also investigated the DNA methylation changes in the matched NPC tumor samples (N=15) and identified the epigenomic molecular subtypes for NPC, named as global hypermethylated NPC and global hypomethylated NPC. This result has been published on eBioMedicine in 2022 (Chow LKY et al. eBioMedicine, 2022; 86:104357) and the findings were presented at Gordon Research Conference for NPC in 2022.

17103218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17103218.value: 1. Elucidation of the impact of genomic and epigenomic subtypes on clinical outcome in NPC We have proposed to further study the impact of genomic subtypes on clinical outcomes. This study entitled “Understanding NPC Molecular Subtypes Associated with Clinical Outcomes and Their Impact on Tumor Microenvironment” is currently funded by Health and Medical Research Fund (HMRF). Meanwhile, we submitted the GRF application (17108623) for the project entitled “Elucidation of Cross-Species Chromatin Interactions by 3D Genome in Metastasis in Epstein-Barr Virus-associated Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma”. 2. Functional validation of the role of MST1R in NPC pathogenesis In the current study, CRISPR-CAS9 knock-out MST1R in the NPC cell line did not influence cancer cell growth, suggesting that the functional impact of MST1R for NPC risk is independent of its function of tyrosine kinase. Interestingly, MST1R KD downregulated the expression of AP-1 transcription factor early growth receptor 1 (EGR1). EGR1 is an early response transcriptional factor that can be rapidly induced by environmental stimuli. Downregulation of this gene by MST1R KD suggests loss of MST1R impairs host response to the virus infection and environmental factors. We plan to further validate this preliminary finding and investigate the functional role of MST1R and EGR1 in NPC pathogenesis.

17103218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17103218.value: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) has remarkable ethnic and geographical distribution. Dramatically elevated incidence of NPC is observed in the Cantonese population of Southern China including Hong Kong. Familial clustering of NPC is often observed in Chinese population, suggesting there is a strong inherited genetic predisposition in NPC. In this project, we evaluated the germline pathogenic variants at MST1R, its interaction network genes and selected DNA repair genes in the blood samples from a total of 1152 NPC cases including 207 FH+ cases and 945 sporadic cases by targeted sequencing and compared to 1205 non-cancer controls of matched ancestry, age and gender. We confirmed the association of MST1R pathogenetic variants and risk of FH+ NPC and newly identified the mismatch repair (MMR) genes as the putative NPC genetic predisposition genes with multiple inactivating mechanisms in tumors. In addition, we found that BRCA2 germline pathogenic variants were enriched in the patients who carried the mutational signature relevant to homologous recombination defect (HRD) and were associated with poor clinical outcomes in NPC. The study provides further evidence for NPC genetic susceptibility and supports genetic screening for the early detection of familial NPC and prognostication of NPC cases in clinical management.

17103318.value: Dissect the biochemical activities of actinopain peptidases from three distinct evolutionary lineages. Screen their peptide substrate specificities, and determine their abilities to cleave proteins/peptides of biological relevance. Map their autolytic processing patterns into catalytically-active/inactive mature forms. Use protein X-ray crystallography and modelling-based approaches to elucidate structure-activity relationships within actinopain- and bacterial calpain-family proteases. Create selected point-mutated actinopain proteins to test/validate structural and mechanistic predictions. Utilize activity-based chemical probes that target calpain-family cysteine proteases to label actinopain peptidases in Actinomyces cells, to characterize protein expression patterns during cultivation under different biologically-relevant conditions. Compare and contrast results with data obtained from analogous transcriptional analyses. 17103318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17103318.value: Background Actinomyces bacteria are part of the ‘normal’ human microbiota; commonly found in the mouth and pharynx. Whilst they are generally associated with health, they cause serious clinical infections (actinomycosis), and are implicated in caries (tooth decay). Our bioinformatic analyses have revealed that most of the clinically-relevant Actinomyces species encode a cysteine protease belonging to the calpain family, which is only sporadically found in other types of bacteria. We call these proteases ‘actinopains’, to reflect their origins. We have performed a preliminary investigation into the biochemical activities of five actinopain proteases from four different species of oral Actinomyces. Our initial results have revealed that the actinopains have a highly-distinctive set of activities, and can cleave proteins/peptides that play key biological roles. Aims and objectives Here, we will build on our exciting initial results to elucidate the properties and activities of actinopain proteases, to identify their potential roles in bacterial cell growth, proliferation and infection. We will: 1) Dissect the protein/peptide cleaving activities of representative actinopain proteases: to elucidate their respective involvement in key biological processes related to bacterial growth within clinical niches. 2) Employ protein X-ray crystallography and modelling-based approaches to elucidate structure-activity relationships within representative actinopain proteases: to gain a mechanistic understanding of how and why specific proteins/peptides are cleaved. 3) Use activity-based small molecule probes to selectively label actinopain proteases in Actinomyces cell cultures, to characterize their expression patterns under clinically-relevant conditions 4) Inactivate (‘knock-out’) actinopain genes in selected Actinomyces strains, to analyze how actinopain expression affects their cellular growth and physiological properties; especially regarding their cell-binding activities, biofilm-forming abilities, and ability to cause infection. Novelty, significance and impact Actinomyces bacteria are major components of the human oral microbiome, and play pivotal roles in maintaining human oral health. However, we have an extremely limited molecular understanding of precisely how their unique cellular properties and biological activities promote health, or may function to cause serious clinical infections. Here, we will determine the biological functions of the actinopains: a previously-unexplored group of proteases that are uniquely prevalent within Actinomyces species. Our initial findings suggest that the actinopains possess activities that may have a profound effect on the abilities of Actinomyces bacteria to proliferate within human clinical niches; eliciting effects that may be indirectly, or directly harmful to our oral or systemic health. By studying molecular processes in ‘Janus-faced’ oral bacteria, we can gain valuable insight into finely-balanced homeostatic-relationships between host and resident microbiota. 背景 放線菌是“正常”人類微生物群落的一部分，常見於口腔和咽部。 雖然它們通常不致病，但有时會引起嚴重的臨床感染（放線菌病），还能导致齲齒（蛀牙）。我們的生物信息學分析顯示，大多數臨床相關的放線菌編碼一种鈣蛋白酶家族的半胱氨酸蛋白酶，而這類蛋白酶在其它類型的細菌中鮮有發現。我們將這些蛋白酶稱為“actinopains”，以反映它們的起源。 我們對來自4種不同口腔放線菌的5種放線菌蛋白酶的生化活性進行了初步研究，发现actinopains具有一系列非常獨特的活性，可以分解具有重要生物學作用的蛋白質/多肽。 研究目的 基於令人興奮的初步結果，我们将表征actinopain蛋白酶的特性和活性，以確定它們在細菌細胞生長、增殖和感染中的潛在作用。我們将开展以下研究： 1）深入研究代表性actinopain蛋白酶的蛋白質/肽分解活性：闡明它們在與臨床生境相關的關鍵生物學過程中的相应功能。 2）運用蛋白質X射線晶體學和結構模擬的手段來闡明代表性actinopain蛋白酶的結構—活性關係，以解釋特定蛋白質/肽被剪切的內在機理性。 3）使用基於活性的小分子探針選擇性標記培養的放線菌中的actinopain蛋白酶，以表徵其在臨床相關條件下的表達模式。 4）在選定的放線菌菌株中敲除相應actinopain基因，以分析actinopain的表達對其細胞生長和生理特性的影響，特別是對它們的細胞黏附活性、生物膜形成能力和誘發感染的能力的影響。 創新，意義和影響 放線菌是人類口腔微生物組的主要成員，在維持人類口腔健康方面發揮著關鍵作用。 然而，我們對其獨特的細胞特性和生物活性是如何促進健康或可能導致嚴重的臨床感染的分子學理解非常有限。actinopains是一類未曾研究的、獨特廣泛存在于放線菌中的蛋白酶，通過本課題，我們將測定actinopains的生物學功能。我們的初步研究結果表明，actinopains的活性可能對放線菌在人類臨床生境內增殖的能力產生重要影響，actinopains可能間接或直接損害我們的口腔或全身的健康。通過研究兩面性（既正常又致病）的口腔細菌的分子過程，我們將獲得有關宿主輿自身菌群之間精細調控的動態平衡的寶貴知識。

17103318.label: Realisation of objectives
17103318.value: Objectives 1 and 2 were fully realized for several different sets of actinopain protein homologues, within several different Actinomyces and Schaalia species. N.B. Many species previously classified as ‘Actinomyces’ are now formally classified as ‘Schaalia’. These objectives were generally tackled in a co-ordinated manner. We carefully selected a representative, diverse selection of actinopain homologues for study. The thiol protease from Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg-Tpr) was studied in parallel, to enable results to be compared, contrasted, and extended to calpain homologues from other bacterial phyla: especially the Bacteroidetes, which are of notable clinical interest. We successfully characterized the biochemical activities of the sole actinopain from Actinomyces israelii (AiCP). This included the site-directed mutational analysis of catalytic residues and structural modelling (AlphaFold), to identify putative factors underlying the hydrolytic mechanism and substrate selectivity. We revealed a notable structural similarity between AiCP and human Calpain-9 and Pg-Tpr. We analyzed actinopain transcription levels in biofilm and planktonic cells. We also performed a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of bacterial calpain peptidases, identifying ca. 150 actinopain homologues. Our results reveal a complex phylogenetic (evolutionary) pattern, with notable differences between species. This work formed the first manuscript (see draft attached, also summarized below). We characterized 3 actinopain homologues from Actinomyces gerencseriae (AgCP1-3), but noted no catalytic activity for AgCP2 We performed analogous sets of biochemical analyses; mapping of autolytic self-digestion patterns; protein mechanistic analysis via site-directed mutagenesis; protein structural modelling; transcriptional analysis. This manuscript is being prepared (see below). In an analogous manner, we performed a comprehensive characterization of one actinopain homologue from Actinomyces viscosus (AvCP3). This manuscript is being prepared (see below). Intriguingly we cannot yet identify the reason why some recombinant actinopains lack detectable catalytic activities or self-digestion activities after their heterologous expression in Escherichia coli. For example, we found that the respective actinopains from Schaalia odontolytica (Actinomyces odontolyticus; AoCP), Schaalia meyeri (Actinomyces meyeri; AmCP), Schaalia georgiae (Actinomyces georgiae; AgeoCP) expressed well and had good stability, but lacked identifiable in vitro peptidolytic activities. Objective 3 required the availability of the DGC-04 chemical affinity probe (or similar ‘cysteine-reactive’ chemical labelling agent) for proteomic experiments. Due to the sole supplier of this chemical ceasing business just before the grant commenced, it could not be obtained. Commercial synthesis was prohibitively expensive. I tried in vain to convince several chemists at Hong Kong universities to collaborate to synthesize similar chemical probes. However, I have recently started a collaboration with a scientist in HKU Medicine to use non-specific cysteine-reactive chemical affinity probes to screen several Actinomyces strains to try to ‘fish-out’ cysteine peptidases. Results from these experiments will be included in future manuscripts. As it is impossible to express soluble actinopain protein with extra amino acids added to the C-terminus, we have used N-terminally-tagged versions of non-self-cleaving actinopain mutants in proteomic affinity pull-down experiments. (N.B. If we use catalytically active homologues, they cleave-off the N-terminal affinity tag!). We have obtained intriguing but mixed results so far. We hypothesize that this may be due to the affinity of the N-terminal putative 'helix-turn-helix' domain to the cell membrane, possibly due to association with components of the cell-secretion machinery. Efforts are ongoing. As an alternative strategy, we have performed transcriptional analyses of actinopain gene expression under various growth and nutritional conditions have been performed using quantitative reverse-transcriptase PCR versus rpoB, tuf or gyrA reference genes. This has been done in A. israelii, A. gerencseriae, A. odontolyticus and A. viscosus. Results have indicated that all calpain genes were transcribed to various extents, under different conditions. However, phenotypic analyses of cell lysates (extracts) and intact cells have failed to definitively identify actinopain activities – except A. gerencseriae, which is currently under further detailed investigation, as it contains additional peptidases (see below). We have investigated actinopain transcription levels in mixed-species biofilms, which respectively incorporate different Actinomyces species. These efforts are currently being extended (relevant to objective 4). Objective 4 was considered to be a bit ambitious, as there are no genetic manipulation systems currently available for the main Actinomyces species of interest, especially A. gerencseriae and A. israelii. There is a system available for Actinomyces oris (Wu et al. Mol Microbiol 2014, 94(6):1227-1241), but unfortunately, none of the commercially available genome-sequenced A. oris strains encode calpain homologues! We used a variety of transformation approaches and gene targeting ‘cassettes’ to try to perform allelic exchange conditions in A. genrecseriae and A. israelii. We have been unsuccessful so far, but are persevering. This has precluded us from studying the phenotypes of actinopain gene deletion mutants (Objective 4). However, mixed species biofilms are being investigated, as well as biofilms grown under ‘infectious’, or ‘clinically-relevant’ conditions. Hence objective 4 has been attempted, but has not yet been fully realized. 3 manuscripts are in the final stages preparation (with myself as sole or co-corresponding author), which are attached to this grant report. I will submit another 2 or 3 papers within next 3-9 months (as corresponding author). Manuscript 1. Key content: comprehensive biochemical characterization of actinopain homologue from A. israelii ATCC 12012 (AiCP); AlphaFold protein structural modelling; mechanistic analysis via protein site-directed mutagenesis; identification of initial autocatalytic AiCP self-cleavage between Ala-166 and Gly-167 to remove an N-terminal putative ‘helix-turn-helix’ domain. Includes actinopain transcriptional analysis (biofilm vs. planktonic), detailed phylogenetic analysis of actinopain homologues (non-classical bacterial calpains) across bacteria, with focus on Actinomyces; genome sequencing of A. israelii ATCC 10048 reference strain, which encodes an actinopain homologue with subtly different amino acid sequence and predicted geometry within active site. Manuscript includes inhibition analysis of peptidase activities. This encompasses objectives 1 and 2 (with relevance to objectives 3 and 4). Manuscript 2. Key content: Several X-ray crystal structures of the P. gingivalis Tpr (PgTpr) protein were solved, including ‘active’ (calcium ion-complexed) and ‘inactive’ (non-calcium ion complexed) states. One structure of an ‘initial’ form captured a section of the polypeptide backbone within the active site revealing the structural mechanism for the initial autolytic processing event (cleavage between Gly-62 and Met-63). This manuscript also includes a comprehensive mutational analysis of Pg-Tpr, relating to both substrate selectivity and autolysis. This encompasses objectives 1 and 2. Manuscript 3. Biochemical, biophysical and transcriptional characterization of the three sialidase (neuraminidase) protein homologues from S. odontolytica (AoSia1-Sia3; draft attached) Manuscript 4. A. gerencseriae calpain homologues (AgCP1-AgCP4). This includes major analysis of AgCP3 protein, the most potent actinopain characterized so far. The general content of this manuscript is analogous to that of the A. israelii paper, but with greater depth. This encompasses objectives 1 and 2 (with relevance to objectives 3 and 4). Manuscript 5. Actinomyces viscosus calpain homologues (AvCP1-AvCP3) - with focus on AvCP3, which has very interesting catalytic and autolytic activities, notably different to those of other calpains. This encompasses objectives 1 and 2 (with relevance to objectives 3 and 4). Manuscript 6. This manuscript will include biochemical and transcriptional analysis of apparently non-catalytic actinopains from S. odontolytica (AoCP); Schaalia meyeri (Actinomyces meyeri; AmCP), Schaalia georgiae (Actinomyces georgiae; AgeoCP). It will also include other families of peptidases including A. gerencseriae DAP2 aminopeptidase (AgDAP2; WP_026407215) and C1 peptidase (AgC1Pep; WP_026408322), which are suspected virulence factors. AgDAP2 is a homologue of the puromycin hydrolase from Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MtPMH; CNE19725), and C1 peptidase is a homologue of Streptopain (SpeB) from Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphopain from Staphylococcus aureus.

17103318.label: Major findings and research outcome
17103318.value: This GRF project has been challenging but reasonably successful, and has generated a substantial body of interesting and scientifically-notable results. However, COVID-19 had a major impact on the progress of this project during the past 3 years (elaborated above). Thus, we are probably >1 year behind schedule. Research efforts are ongoing and manuscripts are being written and finalized for publication over the next 3-12 months. Updates will be given, and submitted manuscripts will be uploaded to pre-print servers to speed-up public accessibility to the research output from this grant. Major Findings The C2-peptidase, calpain-family ‘actinopains’ (from Actinomyces) and Porphyromonas gingivalis Thiol protease (Pg-Tpr) proteins were technically-challenging to purify and study due to their complex autocatalytic self-digesting activities. The Actinomyces israelii (AiCP) and Actinomyces gerencseriae (AgCP3) proteins, were identified as prototypical ‘actinopain’ peptidases. They share analogous calcium-activated self-digestion patterns, similar substrate preferences, and similar predicted protein structures. They are differentially transcribed during planktonic and biofilm growth. Their biological functions currently remain obscure: but investigations are actively ongoing. The biophysical properties and biochemical activities of Porphyromonas gingivalis Thiol protease (PgTPr) are notably different to those of actinopains. We solved X-ray crystal structures of ‘activated’ and ‘non-activated’ forms of PgTpr, including one containing the peptide backbone in a pre-cleavage state. Actinopains and Pg-Tpr preferentially cleave peptides after arginine residues: trypsin-like activities akin to oligopeptidase-B homologues. We comprehensively surveyed the taxonomic distributions and phylogeny of calpain homologues across bacteria, revealing a complex array of (inferred) evolutionary relationships. We established putative structure-function-activity relationships between divergent actinopain and ‘Tpr-like’ clades (phylogenetic lineages) of bacterial calpains. Research Outcomes Three manuscripts are in the final stages preparation (with myself as sole or co-corresponding author), which are attached to this grant report. Another 2 or 3 papers will be submitted during 2023 (with myself as corresponding author). All are directly funded by this GRF grant. 2 PhD students have successfully graduated, whose projects were focused on actinopains (Dr. Haijing WANG and Dr. Intad SRIPRASERT). Their PhD thesis abstracts are attached to this report. A third PhD student, Ms. Jing HE, and a research assistant, Ms. Amelia WANG, are continuing work on this project. The research collaboration with Prof. Mark Bartlam is ongoing, and we are working closely together to publish the manuscript funded from this grant. A new research collaboration with Prof. Graham Stafford (University of Sheffield, UK) was been formed, which has resulted in one manuscript (draft attached).

17103318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17103318.value: Efforts to develop effective genetic manipulation techniques for A. gerencseriae and A. israelii are ongoing. These would be used to create actinopain gene ‘knock-outs’ via allelic exchange with an antibiotic resistance cassette. We aim to genome sequence several other reference strains of A. gerencseriae and A. israelii, as these species appear to be the most interesting from a genetic, phenotypic and clinical perspective. This would enable us to further explore the biological roles of actinopains and other peptidases (e.g. C1 peptidase, DAP2). Improved genomic data will facilitate future RNA-seq experiments on clinical isolates as well as metagenomic mining for evidence of the transcription of actinopains and other peptidases (and sialidases) across Actinomyces. We also aim to explore the biochemical activities of bacterial calpains in other Bacteroidetes species of clinical importance. This will be invaluable in reconciling the activities of ‘actinopain’ versus ‘Tpr-like’ calpain lineages. Our X-ray structures, structure models and existing experimental data strongly suggest there will be notable differences in biochemical activities and biological functions. We also aim to solve the X-ray crystal structures of bacterial calpain peptidases from diverse phylogenetic lineages. This will give us a more holistic understanding of structure-function-activity relationships within this important family of cysteine peptidases.

17103318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17103318.value: Species of Actinomyces bacteria are abundant in the oral cavity, and are key components of healthy dental plaque (oral biofilms). However, Actinomyces israelli, Actinomyces gerencseriae and several other species may cause serious opportunistic infections in humans, including the disease actinomycosis. Here, we studied the activities of a family of peptidases (enzymes that degrade peptides/protein chains) that we call ‘Actinopains’, which are encoded in many species of Actinomyces bacteria. We reveal that Actinopains become activated in the presence of calcium ions, and digest themselves to form several different catalytically-active, mature forms. We identified the target peptide sequences that are degraded by Actinopain peptidases from several different species. We used computational modelling (using Google AlphaFold) to predict the ‘common’ structural features shared by Actinopains. We used mutagenesis to identify the catalytic roles of amino acids in several different Actinopain peptidases. We solved the crystal structure of a closely-related peptidase (Tpr) from Porphyromonas gingivalis, an oral bacterium that causes periodontitis (destructive gum disease). We identified notable similarities between the (predicted) structures and catalytic functions of Tpr and Actinopains. Whilst the precise biological functions of Actinopain peptidases remain obscure, we have made significant progress in understanding their biological distributions, biochemical activities and catalytic mechanisms.
