17115618.label: Major findings and research outcome
17115618.value: There are 3 important findings in our study, to support the use of small-for-size grafts in adult LDLT. Firstly, the risk of SFSS in our cohort was low 21.3% and none developed hospital mortality. Secondly, portal flow modulation was only used selectively and only 10.7% patients required pre-emptive or rescue portal flow modulation. We have also proposed for simplifying portal flow modulation with SAL or SAE used in our study for portal hyperperfusion only, obviating the need for splenectomy. The overall complication rate in our recipients remained low and the risk of HAT, which is known to be associated with small-for-size graft was only 5.3%. Finally the 5-year patient and graft survival rates were >80% irrespective of right or left lobe used, irrespective of graft size. All these provided strong indication to adopt a GRWR of 0.6% as minimum requirement for adult LDLT.

17115618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17115618.value: The promising outcomes from our study would lay important groundwork for international collaboration. In order for the practice to be generalized, we plan to initiate international multicenter study to prove that the concept of lowering GRWR in adult LDLT is safe. As a council member of International Living Donor Liver Transplant Group (iLDLT Group), I have proposed for prospective multicenter collaboration. Our simplified approach for portal flow modulation i.e with SAL and SAE only, should be advocated. My MRes student Ms Simone Chan has showed there was no longterm effect after portal flow modulation and the graft, irrespective of graft size and portal flow modulation is as durable as standard graft. She has also demonstrated that with postoperative portal flow monitoring using percutaneous doppler, it took about 1 week for portal hemodynamic to equilibrate and normalized. These findings need to be validated in a large cohort, therefore we have extended the study and continue a prospective portal flow monitoring in all LDLT recipients in our center. Also, some Japanese centers advocate splenectomy as portal flow modulation, we also plan for a retrospective comparative study to show the efficacy and safety of each approach.

17115618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17115618.value: In adult living donor liver transplant, one controversy is how big a piece of donor liver is considered adequate. If we can procure a small piece of liver from donor, more people will be eligible to donate and it will also make donor surgery safer. In this study, we proposed for a smaller liver graft weight requirement for adult transplant, and we have showed that it is safe in the short and longterm. The risk of small-for-size syndrome, meaning the new liver is too small to support the metabolic demand of patients. The risk was only 20% and all these patients recovered and survived. In order to alleviate and reduce the chance of small-for-size syndrome, surgeons can manipulate the portal flow using various measures. There was no consensus in literature but we have showed that the need to manipulate the portal flow was low (only 10%) and simple measure like ligating or blocking the splenic artery is adequate. High risk procedure like removing of the patient's spleen is not necessary. The long term liver graft and patient survival at 5-year were more than 80% showing that our proposed criteria is safe and effective.

17115818.label: Realisation of objectives
17115818.value: Based on original plans, we have achieved all research objectives completely. Under objective 1: To determine the role of Δ42PD-1 in human DCs on regulating HIV-1 infection and transmission (year 1-1.5), we have carefully investigated the following: Objective 1: To determine the role of Δ42PD-1 in human DCs on regulating HIV-1 infection and transmission (year 1-1.5) 1) ∆42PD-1 expression on monocyte-derived DCs (MDDCs) of healthy and HIV-1-infected individuals. Since we previously reported that there was a significant reduction of ∆42PD-1 expression on CD14+ monocytes in HIV-1 patients when compared with healthy donors, we here measured ∆42PD-1 expression on MDDCs in HIV patients who either received or not received cART as compared with healthy donors. We found that ∆42PD-1 was significantly down-regulated on the surface of HIV patient-derived MDDCs. Moreover, cART did not recover the reduced frequency significantly and may require further investigation on duration of cART. These results are consistent to our previous findings and set up the solid basis for further studies. 2) Influence of ∆42PD-1 on infection of MDDCs by measuring HIV-1 p24 and viral load as well as host restriction factors. Considering the key role of R5-tropic HIV-1 in sexual transmission, we sought to measuring the effect of ∆42PD-1 on HIV infection. We found firstly that the HIV-1 receptor CD4, co-receptors CXCR4 and CCR5, and capture molecule DC-SIGN were mostly expressed on ∆42PD-1 positive cells, indicating the possibility that ∆42PD-1-expressing MDDCs might be susceptible to HIV-1 infection. We therefore sorted out the ∆42PD-1 negative and positive MDDCs from healthy donor and further infected with HIV-JRFL, respectively. Interestingly, higher HIV-1 p24 was detected in ∆42PD-1 positive MDDCs. This is a new finding and has not been previously reported. We will further investigate mechanism underlying this interesting finding. 3) Transmission of HIV-1 from virus-pulsed ∆42PD-1+ and ∆42PD-1- MDDCs to CD4 T cells. Since the activation of the DC-SIGN/LARG/LSP1 complex will promote the formation of the transmission synapse between DCs and CD4 T cells, we determine the effect of ∆42PD-1 on HIV-1 transfer in trans into CD4 T cells. We have confirmed that HIV-1 can be transmission from infected MDDCs to CD4 T cells. Furthermore, the ability of transmission was partially blocked by the high dose treatment of the ∆42PD-1 blocking antibody (CH101). This result indicated that ∆42PD-1 might have involved in the event of HIV-1 transfer from MDDCs to CD4 T cells, which requires further investigation. Objective 2: To determine the role of Δ42PD-1 in regulating DC maturation and HIV-1 antigen presentation (year 1.5-3) 1) Influence of ∆42PD-1 on LPS-mediated DC maturation through TLR4 signaling. We sought to measure ∆42PD-1 expression during monocyte differentiation. Purified monocytes were cultured in the presence of GM-CSF and IL-4 for DC induction. After the induction for 6 days, monocytes increased in size and developed dendritic-like shape. Moreover, as DC markers, the expression of CD1a and DC-SIGN were significantly increased, while CD14 was decreased to a extremely low level. These data indicated that the generation of immature monocyte-derived dendritic cells (iMoDCs) was successful. Interestingly, after the cells differentiated into iMoDCs, Δ42PD-1 expression was increased on the cell surface, arising the hypothesis that Δ42PD-1 may contribute to maintenance of MDDC in immature state. It is well known that the capacity of DCs to regulate immune responses is mostly dependent on DC maturation. To determine the correlation between Δ42PD-1 and MoDC maturation, we matured firstly iMoDCs by LPS using a standard protocol. After 24 h stimulation, Δ42PD-1 negative MoDCs showed a fully mature phenotype (~90% of CD83+ CD86+) while semi-mature phenotype (~50% of CD83+ CD86+) was observed in Δ42PD-1 positive MoDCs. In contrast to immature MoDCs, Δ42PD-1 was significantly decreased in mature MoDCs. Therefore, a strong negative correlation was found between Δ42PD-1 expression and MoDC maturation. MoDC maturation can be trigger by a variety of factors, including TLR agonists and proinflammatory cytokines (28). Similar to the LPS stimulation, the agonists of TLR2, TLR5 and TNF-α decreased Δ42PD-1 expression. These data suggested that Δ42PD-1 may perform negative effect on DC maturation to affect immune system. The expression of costimulatory molecules on DC is essentially for T cell activation. To determine the role of Δ42PD-1 in regulating costimulatory molecule expression, we first sorted out the Δ42PD-1 negative and positive MoDCs by FACS and further stimulated with different dose of LPS. Consistently, Δ42PD-1 negative MoDCs had significant higher maturation level (% of CD83+ CD86+) than Δ42PD-1 positive MoDCs. Moreover, Δ42PD-1 negative MoDCs were fully mature (>90% of CD83+ CD86+) after LPS stimulation at a low dose manner (1 ng/mL). Numbers of costimulatory molecules expressed on DCs are required for T cell activation and proliferation (29). Compared to Δ42PD-1 positive MoDCs, Δ42PD-1 negative MoDCs were possessed higher expression of costimulatory molecules after LPS stimulation, including CD40, CD80 and CD86. Therefore, Δ42PD-1 suppresses MoDC maturation as well as the costimulatory molecules expression. We subsequently investigated the effect of Δ42PD-1 on cytokine production, which provides the third signal to affect T cell activation. FACS-sorted negative and positive Δ42PD-1 iMoDCs were treated with LPS for 3 h. LPS-mediated increase of cytokine (IL-6, IL-12, TNF-a) mRNA in Δ42PD-1 negative MoDCs were significantly higher than that in Δ42PD-1 positive MoDCs. Meantime, the IL-10 mRNA was highly expressed in Δ42PD-1 positive MoDCs. Consistently, FACS analysis showed that IL-12 were mostly expressed in the Δ42PD-1 negative MoDCs, while IL-10 were only expressed in Δ42PD-1 positive MoDCs. Further analysis showed that the IL-12/IL-10 ratio were significantly higher in Δ42PD-1 negative MoDCs than in Δ42PD-1 positive MoDCs after LPS stimulation. As a high IL-12/IL-10 ratio has been associated with the capacity of dendritic cells to stimulate T cell response and IFN-γ production, suggesting that Δ42PD-1 leads MoDC toward a tolerance state. 2) Influence of ∆42PD-1 on intracellular processing of viral particles and DC maturation for antigen presentation. After exogenous antigen uptake by DCs, the antigen is localized to early endosomes (Rab5+), then diverted to the Rab 14+ compartment through MHC class I cross-presentation for CD8 T cell activation or late endosomal (Rab9+ or Lamp1+) routing to the lysomal compartment that is apparently required for adequate processing and MHC class II presentation and subsequent CD4 T cell activation. Here, we first found that the blocking antibody, CH34 mAb could enhance LPS-mediated MDDCs maturation as well as promote MDDC-mediated allogeneic T cell proliferation. Furthermore, to determine whether CH34 mAb’s effect also applies to antigen-specific T-cell stimulation, we used the human CMV (HCMV) pp65 matrix peptide pool (HCMVpp65) as a model antigen. We first tested the effect of CH34 mAb on MHC expression of MoDCs in the presence of HCMVpp65. However, CH34 mAb only had little effect on both MHC-I and MHC-II expression. Subsequently, HCMVpp65-pulsed MoDCs were cocultured with autologous PBLs from HCMV sero-positive donors. After a longer duration of coculture (5 days), CH34 mAb significantly enhanced the proliferation (HLA-DR+CFSE low) of HCMVpp65-specific CD8 T cells. These results supported a possible role of Δ42PD-1 for antigen presentation.

17115818.label: Major findings and research outcome
17115818.value: Major findings include 1) ∆42PD-1 is highly expressed in immature MDDCs, but it is downregulated in HIV-infected individuals; 2) ∆42PD-1 positive MDDCs express higher HIV receptors (CD4) and co-receptors (CXCR4 and CCR5), leading that ∆42PD-1 positive MDDCs susceptible for HIV infection; 3) DC-mediated HIV-1 transmission to CD4 T cells is one of the early events in mucosal transmission. The ability of transmission was partially blocked by the high dose treatment of the ∆42PD-1 blocking antibody (CH101), indicating that ∆42PD-1 might have involved in the event of HIV-1 transfer from MDDCs to CD4 T cells. 4) ∆42PD-1 was negatively correlated with MoDC maturation after different TLRs ligations. ∆42PD-1 negative MDDC displayed a higher level of costimulatory molecules (CD40/CD80/CD86) with or without stimulation compared with ∆42PD-1 positive MoDC. 5) Mechanistically, Δ42PD-1 positive MDDC could produce large amounts of interleukin 10 (IL-10) to suppress maturation-associated signal pathway through recruitment of SHP-1. IL-10 neutralization antibody can reverse the ∆42PD-1-medaited inhibition of MoDC maturation. 6) Pre-treatment of CH34 (an anti-∆42PD-1 antibody) can enhance MDDC maturation and subsequently improve the T-cell-stimulatory capacity of MMDC in the allogeneic MLR assay and CMV-specific T cell stimulation.

17115818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17115818.value: Monocyte-derived dendritic cells (MDDCs) widely used as source of DCs in most clinical studies for cell-based immunotherapy. In this study, we demonstrated that anti-Δ42PD-1 can partially block DC-mediated HIV transmission to CD4 T cells. It is necessary to further evaluate the effect of anti-Δ42PD-1 on HIV infection in vivo. In addition, we found that Δ42PD-1 suppresses immunostimulatory function of MDDC through inducing IL-10 production. Of note, blockage with CH34 mAb of MoDCs showed enhanced costimulatory capacities resulting in augmented antigen specific T cell proliferation. For human relevance, it is necessary to explore whether the humanized CH34 mAb can also improve MDDCs-mediated T cell function.

17115818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17115818.value: Activation of the DC-SIGN/LARG/LSP1 complex promotes the formation of the transmission synapse between dendritic cells (DCs) and CD4 T cells during HIV infection. In this study, we firstly discover that Δ42PD-1 positive DCs are susceptible for HIV infection and anti-Δ42PD-1 antibody can block DC-mediated HIV transmission to CD4 T cells, indicating the potential use of anti-Δ42PD-1 antibody for HIV immunotherapy. In addition, immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) is designed to target inhibitory pathways in T cells to raise antitumor and antiviral immune response. However, despite these promising long-term responses, most patients fail to respond to ICB. Therefore, recently growing attention has been paid to use of myeloid cell-specific immune checkpoints as targets for anticancer and antiviral therapies. Due to the low frequency of circulating DCs in human peripheral blood, the MoDCs differentiated from large number of monocytes is thus widely used as source of DCs in most clinical studies for cell-based immunotherapy. However, the major issue affecting DC-based immunotherapy is low maturation of antigen-pulsed MDDCs. In this regard, we firstly discover that Δ42PD-1 plays a negative regulatory role in MDDC maturation through inducing IL-10 production. Of note, the Δ42PD-1 blockage antibody, CH34 can block Δ42PD-1 in DCs to promote T cell function, highlighting the potential of CH34 mAb for DC-based immunotherapy for HIV and cancer.

17116018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17116018.value: Toll樣受體（TLR）是偵測入侵微生物的病原體相關分子模式的關鍵先天免疫傳感器。現已發現人類擁有10個已知的TLR家族成員，而TLR10仍然是孤兒受體──關於該受體的研究有限。最近的研究指出TLR10的多態性可能與多種疾病的發病機理有重要的關係。我們最近的數據揭示了TLR10作為一個全新的核苷酸受體及其嶄新的作用，其中雙鏈核糖核酸(dsRNA)是其信號傳導的配體。有趣的是，我們觀察到當TLR10受到不同配體刺激時可能引發不同的TLR10信號傳導機理。首先，我們發現當TLR10基因被敲落時，細胞在流感病毒感染後的干扰素(IFN)基因表達會被抑制，相反地，通過陽離子脂質體轉染的dsRNA則刺激細胞表達IFN基因。另一方面，當直接添加脂多糖(LPS)到培養基中以刺激細胞表面上的TLR10時，我們觀察到與病毒感染相似的炎性細胞因子的表達反應。這些數據意味著與病毒感染和LPS刺激相比，來自dsRNA的刺激觸發了不同的TLR10信號傳導。我們進一步揭示了dsRNA而非流感病毒能引發藉由MyD88傳遞的TLR10信號傳導。此外，我們也發現dsRNA刺激和病毒感染引發相反的TLR10介導的干擾素調節因子(IRF)信號傳導。總括來說，我們的初步數據顯示，面對不同的刺激，獨特的TLR10信號通路會被觸發。但是，詳細的機理仍有待探究。於本研究中，我們計劃探討TLR10在不同細胞擾動中作用的詳細機理。基於我們的初步數據顯示受刺激於dsRNA或流感病毒感染，不同的TLR10信令會被觸發，這會作為研究的第一步去剖析因應這兩種不同刺激所分別引發的不同TLR10傳導機理。具體而言，我們計劃1)使用接近依賴性生物素識別方法以剖析不同的信號轉導通路，及2)使用人類TLR10基因敲入小鼠，以剖析當面對不同的擾動時，TLR10的功能。隨著越來越多的證據表明TLR10跟不同的疾病發病機理有關，理解於不同刺激下觸發的不同TLR10信號轉導通路，將有助提供重要信息，訂定針對特定信號傳導分子的策略，以開發相關疾病的治療藥物。

17116018.label: Realisation of objectives
17116018.value: To dissect the distinct signalling pathways in response to different stimulations, proximity-dependent biotin identification (BioID) and mass spectrometry were conducted. Overall, 956 TLR10-associated candidate proteins were identified, with 105 (10.98%) as mitochondrial proteins, while in the control samples, 64 (7.13%) of the 897 were mitochondrial. Only 87 candidate proteins were confidently identified in the two independent experiments, including 12 from the influenza infection group. Amongst these, LPCAT2 and TRAP1 were found interacting with TLR10 TIR domain, while TRAP1 and mitochondrial marker TOMM20 co-localized with TLR10. To investigate the role of the well-known TLR adaptor protein MyD88 in TLR10 signalling, TLR10-overexpressing cell lines with or without MyD88 knockout were generated. Results suggested that MyD88 was required for TLR10 mediated type-I interferon (IFN) response both in influenza infection and dsRNA stimulation. Upon poly(I:C) stimulation, MyD88 co-localized with TLR10, and recruitment of MyD88 to TLR10 was confirmed by immunoprecipitation. Activation (phosphorylation) of IFN Regulator Factor 7 (IRF7) but not IRF3 was involved in regulating IFN production in response to poly(I:C) treatment, which was more prominent in the TLR10 overexpressing THP-1 cells, as demonstrated using anti-phospho-IRF7 or -IRF3 in Western blot. In addition to the synthetic poly(I:C), dsRNA that occurred during influenza infection was confirmed to be a natural ligand for TLR10, by co-localization, pulldown and UV-crosslinking immunoprecipitation. THP-1 cells expressing a TwinStrep-tagged TLR10 (TLR10-TS) was used in biolayer interferometry to demonstrate that ectodomain (ECD) of TLR10 could bind biotinylated dsRNA at an acidic pH 5.5, which was reversible at the physiological pH 7.4. TLR10-ECD could also be pulled-down by biotinylated vRNA in a dose-dependent fashion. Evidence of post-translational proteolytic cleavage of TLR10 was found during its interactions with the dsRNA, as multiple specific bands of different molecular weights were seen in the TLR10-TS pulldown. To understand the effect of TLR10 expression during influenza infection, it was noted that at an high MOI, expression of type-I and -III IFNs were positively correlated with TLR10 expression level, but viral replication kinetics were not altered by TLR10 expression. An inverse relationship between the expression level of IFNs and TLR10 were observed at low MOI which enables multiple rounds of viral replication and infection which better mimics the physiological situation. In line with the increased expression of IFN in TLR10 depleted cells, cells with lower TLR10 expression level showed a lower replication kinetics. Also, at low MOI, expression of the IFN-signalling-negative-regulator USP18 positively correlated with TLR10 expression and may therefore interfere the IFN positive feedback loop. Apart from IFNs, induction of the anti-viral gene Mx1 during IAV infection was also suppressed in cells overexpressing TLR10. Apoptosis or programmed cell death is thought to be a major mode of death in influenza infection. At low MOI, overexpression of TLR10 led to an upregulation of caspase-10 but not caspase-3, 8 and 9, while at high MOI, knockdown of TLR10 led to a significant reduction in caspase-3, -8 and -9 activities. A more prominent lytic phenotypic cell death was observed in TLR10 depleted cells infected with influenza virus, suggesting that TLR10 may also modulate differential cell death. To investigate the role of TLR10 in differential perturbations using human TLR10 (hTLR10) knock-in (KI) mice, a male hemizygous C57BL/6-Tg(TLR10)5-1Tapp/J mouse was imported from The Jackson Laboratory, USA, then crossed with non-carriers using in vitro fertilization. Genotyping was conducted to identify the carriers. Non-carriers were used as wildtype (WT) controls. To determine the inoculation dose of influenza virus in vivo, the MID50 and MLD50 of an H1N1 influenza virus strain (A/California/07/2009) were determined in the WT C57BL/6J mice, as 10^1 and 10^2.89 TCID50 respectively, when loss of body weight of >25% was regarded as a fatal illness and humane endpoint. When intranasally inoculated with 10^3 TCID50 of virus, 4 of the 5 (80%) WT mice died at 8-9 days post-inoculation (dpi) due to excessive body weight loss and humane euthanasia, while in the KI mice, all five (100%) died at 7-8 dpi, showing an increased fatality rate and body weight loss, as well as deaths at an earlier time point than the control group. Moreover, antibody responses were not detected in the KI or WT mice upon their death, but for the only survivor from the WT group, the H1N1-specific antibody titer was 1:80 at 14 dpi, as determined by a standard hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay. When intranasally inoculated with 10^5 TCID50 of virus, 4 out of the 5 (80%) WT mice died at 5-7 dpi, while all the five KI mice (100%) died at 4-7 dpi, again with undetectable antibody levels upon their death. The only survivor from the WT group shown an HI titer of 1:320 against the virus. In the KI group of mice, an increase in the IL6 level and lung pathology was observed, with a slightly higher viral titer in the respiratory tissues at 5 dpi (but not statistically significant from those of the WT group, as examined at 3, 5, 7 dpi). A lower inoculation dose of the virus may help to distinguish the pathology and immunological changes in WT or KI mice, as virus may be allowed to replicate at a lower kinetics and the animals may survive to have antibody production. For the dsRNA inoculation group, we used 100ug/50ul of poly(I:C) for intranasal inoculation. Interstitial pneumonitis with inflammatory infiltrate and thickening of alveolar septa and bronchial epithelium was observed at 3 and 5dpi. IL6, CXCL10 and IFN mRNA levels were increased in the WT mice, but in the hTLR10 KI mice, only IL6 was seen to increase. As dsRNA can also trigger responses of the other TLR members, interactions between TLR10 and the other TLR signalling need further investigations. Indeed, co-localization of poly(I:C) with TLR3 and TLR10 was found in endosomes, and competition of these two TLR for dsRNA binding and reduction of IFN expression have been confirmed in THP-1 cells. Additionally, we used the hTLR10 transgenic mouse p388 cell line to find that hTLR10 was functionally expressed as shown in Western blot, and triggered mouse cytokine and IFN production upon influenza infection. It also recruited MyD88 in response to poly(I:C) stimulation but not influenza infection, as detected by Western blot. These were consistent to observations in the human THP-1 cells and in mice, demonstrating the functions of TLR10 cross species.

17116018.label: Major findings and research outcome
17116018.value: Major findings of this project: (1) We found that double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) occurred during influenza A virus (IAV) infection, which served as a natural ligand for TLR10, and it could bind to the ectodomain of TLR10. (2) IAV infection increased TLR10 expression and cytokine induction, including proinflammatory cytokines and interferons (IFN). This TLR10 mediated inflammatory cytokine response was similar upon H1N1 influenza infection and bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation, but was opposite upon dsRNA stimulation. This phenomenon was more prominent in the TLR10 overexpressed or knock-down THP-1 cells. (3) MyD88 was a key adaptor protein in TLR10 signalling. It was required for TLR10 mediated type I IFN response in IAV infection. Upon Poly(I:C) stimulation, MyD88 was recruited, followed by suppression of IFN Regulator Factor 7 (IRF7)-dependent type I IFN production in the human THP-1 cells. (4) LPCAT2, TRAP1 and the mitochondrial marker TOMM20 could be recruited to TLR10 proximity upon IAV infection. Many other mitochondrial proteins may also be involved in the TLR10 signalling or interactions. (5) Overexpression of TLR10 suppressed the anti-viral gene Mx1 and altered the type I and III IFN expression during IAV infection, likely involving regulation by the ubiquitin‐specific protease 18 (USP18). (6) Knockdown of TLR10 led to a significant reduction in caspase-3, -8 and -9 activities, showing a more prominent lytic phenotypic cell death post IAV infection. (7) TLR10 could compete with TLR3 for dsRNA binding, reducing TLR3 expression and signalling, which may suppress IFN expression. (8) In the human TLR10 transgenic mice or mouse cell line, IFN expression increased upon IAV infection, while dsRNA stimulated TLR10 to interact with MyD88, reducing the IFN expression. Therefore, TLR10 mediated opposite IFN response upon IAV infection and dsRNA stimulation. We have published one article acknowledging this research project and attended several international conferences (see Part C). Another two major manuscripts were under preparations. PI has received several highly prestigious and competitive awards related to the control and prevention of influenza and other emerging infectious diseases. Four PhD students were trained with three of them graduated. Details were given in Part C. Importantly, through the conduct of this project, we have set up the collaborations with the Guangdong Laboratory Animals Monitoring Institute, Zhuhai BesTest Bio-Tech Co., Ltd. and Shantou University, where we can maintain the gene knock-in mice as an important animal model for TLR10 research.

17116018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17116018.value: We have established different cell lines with overexpression (OE), gene knockdown (KD) or gene knockout (KO) of TLR10. We also maintain a transgenic mouse colony (C57BL/6-Tg(TLR10)5-1Tapp/J) with human TLR10 gene knock-in to the C57BL/6J mice. These are all valuable resources for the research of TLR10. Our unpublished data suggested that TLR10 may have a role in regulating pro-inflammatory cytokines/ interferons in SARS-CoV-2 infection. We will try to further understand the functional relevance of TLR10 in COVID-19 pathogenesis, by using the research models set up in this study. We have also identified a list of proteins that may potentially have some interactions with TLR10. Functional studies of these candidate proteins in the TLR10 signalling pathway will help to more systematically elucidate the role of TLR10 in the microbial infections. Our present work used an H1N1 influenza virus strain for the study of TLR10. Findings may not be directly extrapolated to other subtypes or strains. Viruses from different lineages or species can be used for future study, which may help to reveal the universal signalling and function of TLR10.

17116018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17116018.value: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are crucial innate immune sensors of pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) of invading microbes. Among the ten TLR members identified in human, TLR10 remains the only orphan receptor with limited information about its ligand(s), signalling and function. It was found that Influenza A virus (IAV) infection could increase TLR10 expression and cytokine induction, including proinflammatory cytokines and interferons (IFN). This was similar upon H1N1 IAV infection and lipopolysaccharide (LPS, a bacterial endotoxin) stimulation, but opposite upon double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) stimulation. However, the mechanisms were not known. In this research project, we have identified dsRNA as a natural ligand for TLR10, and MyD88 as a key adaptor protein in TLR10 signalling. LPCAT2, TRAP1 and the mitochondrial marker TOMM20 appeared to have direct interaction with TLR10 during IAV infection, while anti-viral gene Mx1, IFN Regulator Factor 7 (IRF7), ubiquitin-specific protease 18 (USP18) were involved in the IFN expression. Regulation by caspase-3, -8 and -9 activities also occurred post IAV infection. As increasing evidences have demonstrated the involvement of TLR10 in different disease pathogenesis, understanding the distinct TLR10 signalling and function may provide important information for targeting specific molecules in therapeutic drug development for related diseases.

17116618.label: Major findings and research outcome
17116618.value: Treatment of BCL6-dependent DLBCL cell lines in vitro with As2O3 led to growth inhibition and apoptosis in patterns similar to those of the specific BCL6 siRNA and selective BCL6 inhibitor FX1. These effects were replicated in vivo, with As2O3 treatment significantly inhibiting growth of and inducing apoptosis in murine xenografts. As2O3 treatment did not affect BCL6 gene expression, but led to BCL6 protein ubiquitination and its proteasomal degradation; which was independent of reactive oxygen species generation. Lentiviral over-expression of BCL6 rescued DLBCL lines from As2O3 treatment, confirming BCL6 as the main target of As2O3. As2O3-induced BCL6 down-regulation de-repressed downstream genes including TP53, CHK1 and ATR, which were involved in DNA damage response; suggesting that As2O3 might enhance action of drugs that induced DNA damage. Accordingly, As2O3 was shown to synergize with the DNA damaging drug cisplatin in suppressing the growth of and inducing apoptosis in BCL6-dependent DLBCL cells through reactivation of the DNA damage response. These findings suggested that As2O3 has inhibitory activity against BCL6-dependent DLBCLs specifically, and therapeutic use of As2O3 in the treatment for this group of DLBCLs should be further explored.

17116618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17116618.value: The exact mechanism underlying the arsenic trioxide-induced inhibition of binding between HSP90 to BCL6 remains undefined. An pathological algorithm for identification of DLBCL that is BCL6 dependent remains to be determined.

17116618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17116618.value: Arsenic trioxide degrades BCL6 protein in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma resulting in suppression of growth of BCL6-dependent lymphoma cells in vitro and in vivo in mouse models. Arsenic trioxide may serve as a potential therapeutic agent for the treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the most common type of aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma in the world.

17117018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117018.value: 用於評估臨床上顯著的前列腺癌 - 磁共振指紋圖譜 Magnetic Resonance Fingerprinting (MRF) 由於不同的掃描儀和患者的可變性，MRI值無法準確量化。採用一種新的MRI fingerprinting，我們可以解決這個問題。我們想要研究這種新技術在男性中發現 “有臨床意義的前列腺癌” 的臨床應用和可譯性。 該研究的目標如下： （1）比較有臨床意義的前列腺癌的分類準確性，並評估MRI fingerprinting與傳統PI-RADS v2相比的附加效果。 （2）評估不同觀察者在使用MRI fingerprinting時與其他觀察者之間的量化變異性。 （3）成功開發和實施應用於擴散加權序列的MRI fingerprinting。

17117018.label: Realisation of objectives
17117018.value: This project proposes to develop a novel MRI fingerprinting technique for prostate cancer detection. The objectives and their achievements are outlined below. General Statement:- We had difficulty recruiting subjects for the study during the COVID-19 pandemic. The recruitment was significantly delayed, but extending the project, we managed to recruit all the subjects finally by March 2022. We have since been performing the evaluation and this is currently complete, with the final results to be written in the manuscript for submission. Objective 1: This is 100% complete. We completed the analysis by comparing the added value of MRF to PI-RADS v.2. MRF was able to discriminate clinically significant cancer from non-clinically significant cancer/normal prostate. This was already demonstrated in some prior studies. PI-RADS categorisation is an international grading system that visually grade the likelihood of significant prostate cancers and is used in clinical practice widely internationally for reporting prostate MRI findings. It does not require special MRI sequence or measurements, and is based on subjective visual assessment by the radiologist. Unfortunately, by analysing different PI-RADS categorisation and using different thresholds for MRF, we did not demonstrate added value of MRF to the existing PI-RADS categorisation. This was demonstrated across the PI-RADS 3, 4, and 5 categorisation. We can speculate why this is, but ultimately the results do not reach statistically significant at this time. We believe the sample size calculation is reasonable, and do not believe the study is underpowered. It is possible that the MRF technique could be optimised further to boost the signal to noise ration, for example, in the diffusion sequence, (but technically this is challenging). Objective 2. We have completed around 50% of this task. It has been difficult to recruit readers for this study, owing to the 'negative' results as demonstrated from objective 1. The preliminary analysis demonstrated that there is no significant inter-reader variability between the 2 readers that have completed the study so far. We are continuing this objective to completion. Objective 3. From a technical standpoint, we have successfully implemented the MRF sequence in diffusion weighted sequence.

17117818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117818.value: 肺動脈高壓症是具破壞性且經常危及生命的結締組織疾病併發症。REVEAL登記研究指出，在3,515名肺動脈高壓患者，有超過50%的患者同時患有結締組織疾病，而當中系統性硬皮症是最常見的結締組織疾病。雖然藥物治療發展迅速，但大部份肺動脈高壓患者早期都是沒有症狀，因此診斷時間多為患病的較後期。現今國際臨床指南建議每年利用心臟超聲波、肺功能測試與及生物標記血液檢查作肺動篩查的方法。有研究數據指出，利用心臟超聲波與及生物標記血液檢查是一種敏感度高並且非創傷性的方案去診斷肺動脈高壓症。在高危的結締組織疾病患者中，及早診斷肺動脈高壓症是改善臨床預後的最重要一環。 與西方人不同，在亞太地區，系統性紅斑狼瘡症，相對於硬皮症，是一種較常見的結締組織疾病。而現有的臨床研究數據當中，肺動脈高壓症在紅斑狼瘡患者的發病率亦有很大差異。因此，此研究是希望 1) 找出肺動脈高壓症在華人的系統性紅斑狼瘡患者中的發病率，並希望 2) 找出預測肺動脈高壓症的臨床因素，從而去 3) 建立一個預測肺動脈高壓症之模型。 此研究結果能獲得非常重要的臨床數據，可以有助優化或改變現行肺動脈高壓症於系統性紅斑狼瘡患者的臨床治療，及早治療並可以改變這些患者之預後。

17117918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117918.value: During progression of disease/cancer, gene expression is mainly governed by a set of transcription factors (TFs) through binding to DNA sequences or TF binding sites (TFBSs) on promoters. A central to transcriptional regulation is to dissect interactions between TFs and TFBSs, and the factors affecting this process. Mutations on promoters will disrupt the TF-TFBS interactions, which cause many diseases/cancer. Human genome sequencing projects like The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and GWAS have identified tens of thousands of genomic variants (GVs) associated with human diseases. The majority of these detected GVs are located at non-coding regions; some of them are believed to harbor regulatory elements that affect target gene expression. We have reported that NF-κB, TP53 and TP63 are key TFs in regulating target genes mediating cancer progression of HNSCC. Other researchers have published data supporting our finding. However, how these or other TFs cooperatively and mechanistically works together to modulate progressive transformation of tumors remains elusive. Moreover, dissecting the interactions between TF regulation and non-coding GVs is not only important for understanding of mechanisms of cancer pathogenesis but also for discovery of molecular markers or therapeutic treatments. We have developed algorithms to identify target genes of TFs forming logics that control dynamic gene expression. Based on TCGA or other cancer genomic data, we further annotated GVs to regulatory regions that also contain binding sites of these TFs in HNSCC. It is reasoned that cancer development carries out collaborative action between TF binding and GVs, and based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that correlated analysis of their interactions will help us identify TF target genes in cancer. The study will develop a novel bioinformatics framework for two aims. First, we will build on recent published method at Nature Communications and then devise a model Logic-Stage to decode cooperative gene regulation of TF logics during dynamic processes cross different stages. Second, we will incorporate TF logics with regulatory GVs to identify target genes which are distinct to HNSCC metastasis. The framework will be more robust than the existing methods. Validation of the predicted results will be used to define the molecular determinants of cancer progression that can also be used to provide clues for the causes of other cancers. The completion of this project will help to understand the nature of TF regulation in driving metastatic transformation of tumor cells in HNSCC. 在疾病或癌症的發生發展過程中，基因的表達主要受一系列轉錄因子調控，這些轉錄因子能夠通過結合到啟動子DNA序列即轉錄因子結合位點發揮作用。研究基因的轉錄調節關鍵是揭示轉錄因子和轉錄因子結合位點之間的如何相互作用及其影響因素。啟動子的突變會干擾轉錄因子和轉錄因子結合位點間的相互作用，導致疾病的發生（如癌症）。人類基因組測序計畫，如癌症基因組圖譜(The Cancer Genome Atlas, TCGA)和全基因組關聯研究(Genome-Wide Association Studies, GWAS)，已經鑒定出成千上萬種與人類疾病相關的基因組變異（GVs），這些檢測到的GVs大多位於非編碼區，其中一些被認為含有影響靶基因表達的調節元件。 我們和其他研究人員已經報導了NF-κB、AP1、STAT3、TP53和TP63等轉錄因子能夠在頭頸腫瘤（HNSCC）中調控基因表達、引導癌症轉移有關的途徑或過程。但是，這些轉錄因子或其他調節因子如何協作調節腫瘤轉移仍然讓人捉摸不定。此外，解析轉錄因子調控和非編碼GVs間的相互作用不僅有助於瞭解癌症發病機制，還有助於發現相關分子標誌物或治療方法。我們已經開發出了能夠鑒定轉錄因子靶基因的演算法，形成了控制動態基因表達的邏輯。基於TCCA或其它癌症基因組數據，我們還進一步對HNSCC中含有這些轉錄因子結合位元點的調控區域內的GVs進行了注釋。據信癌症發展過程會改變轉錄因子調控和GVs間的協同作用，根據我們的初步資料，我們推測對它們相互作用的相關分析將幫助我們鑒定出癌症中轉錄因子的靶基因。 本研究將為這兩個目標開發一種新的生物資訊學框架。首先，我們基於我們發表在自然通訊2017的演算法設計一個模型Logic-Stage，解析在癌症不同階段動態過程的轉錄因子logics的協同調節作用。其次，我們將轉錄因子logics與調節區域內的GVs相結合來鑒定與HNSCC轉移亞組不同的靶基因。該框架將比現有方法更準確，並可廣泛用於其他癌症基因組研究。驗證的結果將用於定義腫瘤發展的分子決定因素，其也可用於其他癌症病因的探索。該項目的完成將有助於瞭解HNSCC中轉錄因子調控在腫瘤細胞轉移轉化中的本質。

17118518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17118518.value: Unfortunately children with learning disabilities (LD) have poorer health than typically developing children. Findings from community-wide epidemiological studies that we have conducted in Hong Kong have observed poorer oral cleanliness, poorer gingival health and more dental caries among children with LD compared to typically developing children. Moreover, parents of children with LD report many barriers to oral health for their children. They typically only seek care when there is a ‘dental emergency’ and this often requires treatment to be carried out under general anesthesia. Thus, for many children with LD in Hong Kong, their experience of dental care is not only traumatic but potentially life threatening. Fortunately, oral health problems are preventable. A Cochrane systematic review provides the scientific evidence to recommend ‘daily tooth brushing with a fluoride toothpaste’ as the mainstay of oral health promotion (OHP) activities to protect oral health and prevent oral diseases. Other preventive approaches (backed by Cochrane systematic reviews) have also been advocated; but these approaches are more challenging to implement among children with LD, owing to their more invasive nature. Thus, reliance on ‘daily tooth brushing with a fluoride toothpaste’ remains the cornerstone of OHP activities for children with LD. Despite the apparent simple nature of the practice of ‘daily tooth brushing with a fluoride toothpaste’; teaching and implementing this practice among children with LD is complex and challenging. We have been working in this field in collaboration with Special Child Care Centres (SCCC) in Hong Kong for almost a decade involving educationalist and psychologists to develop oral health literacy tools and social-stories to support the implementation of ‘daily tooth brushing with a fluoride tooth paste’ in OHP activities (two previously funded GRF grants). ‘Social Stories’ are learning tools that have been used since the 1990’s to teach children with LD life skills for self-care through social cues. We developed a Cantonese social-story for teaching tooth-brushing among children with autism, and found it to be a valid and reliable tool that enhances learning and improves oral cleanliness. To date no clinical trial has evaluated the effectiveness of social-stories-based OHP in preventing dental caries. We now plan to determine the effectiveness of a social-stories-based OHP intervention compared to the existing (conventional) OHP intervention used in protecting oral health and preventing oral disease among children with LD. The findings have potential to inform OHP practices for children with LD in SCCC in Hong Kong and beyond.

17118518.label: Major findings and research outcome
17118518.value: There was no significant difference in caries experience among children in both groups after 24 months. However, children in the test group showed better oral hygiene status and better toothbrushing performance, and they were more likely to visit a dentist (OR = 2.00, 95% CI:1.15,3.49) than their peers in the control group. Caries progression was more likely to be observed among children who had low social skills or whose parents were not working full-time. Children from high-income families showed better oral hygiene status than their peers (Estimate = -0.11, 95%CI: -0.20,-0.01).

17119518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17119518.value: Introduction: In the economic evaluation of healthcare services for paediatric populations, cost per quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained is commonly the main outcome measure, and correspondingly, the health utility score is one of the main components needed to calculate QALYs. Currently, there are no health utility scores that have been elicited for a paediatric-specific health state classification system. The EQ-5D Youth (EQ-5D-Y) is a generic instrument developed by the EuroQol Group for the measurement and valuation of health among children and adolescents. Like the EQ-5D for adults, EQ-5D-Y describes health in five dimensions: mobility, looking after myself, doing usual activities, having pain or discomfort, and feeling worried, sad or unhappy. However, there is currently no available EQ-5D-Y value set in any language or country. This study will develop EQ-5D-Y value sets and evaluate different valuation methods. Objectives: 1) To estimate weights or value sets for translating EQ-5D-Y data into health utility scores, 2) to compare health utility scores produced using different elicitation techniques, 3) to assess the perspective effects on the value set, and 4) to establish population norms based on derived value sets. Design: A valuation survey of EQ-5D-Y health states using discrete choice, composite time trade-off and standard gamble methods, and a population norm survey. Setting: A random sample of adult residents will be recruited by telephone and interviewed face-to-face to complete valuation tasks. A sample of the gerenal child population will be recruited for the population norm survey. Participants: Representative samples of Chinese adults and children aged 8-15 from the general population in Hong Kong. Outcome measures: Value sets will be estimated by regression analysis of respondents' preferences for and trade-offs between the different dimensions of EQ-5D-Y health state classification system. Results: In this study, value sets will be derived from societal health state values elicied using three preference elicitation techniques. Those value sets will enable the generation of health utility scores and population norms using existing or future EQ-5D-Y datasets for the calculation of QALYs in economic evaluations of paediatric healthcare interventions.

17119518.label: Major findings and research outcome
17119518.value: The project developed EQ-5D-Y (original three-level) value set for Hong Kong. The observed/censoring-adjusted mean of C-TTO values ranged from -0.173/-0.227 for 33333 to 0.939/0.939 for 11112. The estimated coefficients for all parameters in the three hybrid models (including C-TTO data with (1) all DCE responses, (2) DCE responses from an adult perspective, or (3) DCE responses from a child perspective) were statistically significant. Using the coefficients of level 3 problems, the most important dimensions were “having pain or discomfort” (Overall: -0.229, 95%CI -0.243 to -0.215; Adult perspective: -0.223, 95%CI -0.241 to -0.204; Child perspective: -0.234, 95%CI -0.252 to -0.217). While the least important dimensions were “looking after myself” (Overall: -0.146, 95%CI -0.156 to -0.136: Adult perspective: -0.155, 95%CI -0.169 to -0.141: Child perspective: -0.139, 95%CI -0.153 to -0.126). The proportions of respondents with best-reported health state (11111) in both perspective samples were similar. 52.8% of child perspective group and 49.0% of adult perspective group reported the best health state. Implied rankings from the hybrid regression for both groups were similar: the five most important attributes were on the ‘level 3’ levels and the five least important attributes were on the ‘level 2’ levels. Among the five most important attributes were PD3, UA3 and AD3, followed by MO3 then SC3. Among the least five least important attributes, PD2, UA2, and AD2 were more important, while MO2 and SC2 were the two least important attributes. There is no remarkable difference in preferences for EQ-5D-Y health states between the adult and hypothetical 10-year-old child perspectives. The most important dimension was ‘Having pain or discomfort’ dimension, consistent with the EQ-5D-Y value set in main China, Belgium, Hungary, Japan, Netherlands, Slovenia, Spain, and Germany. Those findings were reported in the paper titled ‘Methodological comparisons of preferences towards EQ-5D-Y health states between adult own and child perspectives in Hong Kong’. A representative sample of 7,487 children and adolescents (female: 55.2%; Age 6-8: 25.7% Age 9-11: 33.2% Age 12-17: 41.1; mean age 11.6, SD 3.2) from 12 primary and 7 secondary schools in Hong Kong completed the EQ-5D-Y questionnaire all independently without the aid from teachers between May and July 2018. EQ-5D-Y utility decreased with increasing age (p<0.001): age groups 6-8 (mean±SD 0.945±0.086), 9-11 (0.942±0.073), and 12-17 (0.933±0.071). Male (0.941±0.079) had higher utility scores than female (0.938±0.073, p=0.038). EQ-5D-Y health utility scores differ across age and gender groups of school-attending children and adolescent in Hong Kong.

17119518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17119518.value: EQ-5D-Y value set for Hong Kong was derived from societal health state values elicited using preference elicitation techniques, time-trade off and discrete choice experiments. The value set enabled the generation of health utility scores and Hong Kong population norms using existing or future EQ-5D-Y datasets for the calculation of QALYs in economic evaluations of pediatric healthcare interventions. Future research is needed to ascertain the reasons for the variations in EQ-5D-Y health utility scores on top of age- and gender-specific variations. Future comparisons of EQ-5D-Y value set (such as mainland China, Belgium, Hungary, Japan, Netherlands, Slovenia, Spain, and Germany) as well as population norms across different countries and populations are warranted. The extended five-level version of EQ-5D-Y (EQ-5D-Y-5L) is under cognitive and psychometric experiment, while further development of the EQ-5D-Y-5L is ongoing.

17119518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17119518.value: This study presented evidence on the EQ-5D-Y value set in Hong Kong to generate health utility scores using existing and future pediatric EQ-5D-Y datasets. Health utility population norms for Hong Kong pediatric population is available, enabling normative comparisons in certain diseases, and estimating age-gender adjusted health utility scores. Such information provides insights to health issues at the local population level, and informs policy making, and thus helps on formulating the Hong Kong Government’s policies in public health, pediatrics and social policy.

17119618.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17119618.value: EB 病毒非編碼RNA（lnc-BART）在鼻咽癌細胞的功能

17119618.label: Project Objectives
17119618.value: To analyze the effect of lnc-BART RNAs on methylation of host and viral genes in NPC cells. EBV infection is known to lead to global methylation of host genes in associated tumors, but details of the mechanism are unclear. Our pilot study found that some genes which are regulated by methylation in other cancers are also affected by lnc-BART RNAs in EBV infected NPC cells. To study the epigenetic effects, including histone methylation/demethylation, caused by lnc-BART RNAs through induction of KDM1B expression in NPC cells. Genomic imprinting and promoter histone demethylation are important epigenetic processes for regulation of gene expression. We postulate that lnc-BARTs are involved in this process; this hypothesis is supported by our preliminary observation that KDM1B, which is required for genomic imprinting and promoter histone demethylation, is induced by BART lncRNA in EBV infected epithelial cells. To characterize the role of Aiolos expression in NPC cells. Our pilot study found that lnc-BARTs significantly upregulate IKZF3 (Aiolos) in NPC cells. Expression of Aiolos is normally restricted to lymphoid cells, being silenced in epithelial cells through regulation of DNA methylation. Aberrant expression of Aiolos in lung cancer cells is associated with metastasis. It is likely that induction of Aiolos expression by lnc-BART is associated with EBV oncogenesis in NPC. To characterize the molecular basis of lnc-BART RNA regulation of host gene expression in EBV infected epithelial cells. Our pilot study showed that lnc-BART RNAs form nuclear speckles and co-localize with CBP/p300 in the nucleus. This study will analyze in detail the mechanism of lnc-BART RNA action in EBV infected NPC cells.

17119818.label: Realisation of objectives
17119818.value: In this project, we have completed our research objectives and demonstrated that renal tubular β-catenin signaling plays a protective role in acute kidney injury (AKI), and we have even gone further to perform the investigations on one more animal model (the septic LPS model) in addition to the planned IRI model, and generated an additional transgenic mouse, the tubule-specific β-catenin knock out mouse, in addition to the planned tubule-specific β-catenin over-expressing mouse. For these objectives, first, we found that mice with overexpression of tubular β-catenin (TubCat mice) were protected from kidney injury in renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI)-induced AKI model. TubCat mice exhibited less tubular cell death, inflammation and improved kidney function upon AKI (completion of Aim 1). Upregulation of TLR4 signaling was found to contribute in the pathogenesis of IRI-induced AKI. However, we found no significant difference in TLR4 expression between TubCat and control kidney after AKI, indicating that TLR4 expression was not modulated by β-catenin signaling. In view of the contradictory results in alleviating renal inflammation by β-catenin overexpression from our original hypothesis, we instead put forward the study of tubular β-catenin signaling on mitochondrial dysfunction in AKI. Interestingly, we showed that stabilization of tubular β-catenin restored mitochondrial homeostasis in AKI via activation of FOXO3/PGC-1α signaling pathways (completion of Aim 2). To confirm our novel findings of protective tubular β-catenin upon AKI, we further extended our study to another lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced septic AKI model using TubCat mice as well as a tubule-specific β-catenin knockout (TubCatKO) mice. As expected, TubCat mice were protected against AKI in LPS-induced AKI whereas depletion of tubular β-catenin aggravated kidney injury, renal inflammation, tubular cell death and further deteriorated renal function in both aseptic and septic AKI models. The above findings were published in Cell Death Dis. 2022; 13(12):1061 doi: 10.1038/s41419-022-05395-3

17119818.label: Major findings and research outcome
17119818.value: 1. Tubular β-catenin protects against AKI To address the role of β-catenin in tubular cell death upon AKI, tubular β-catenin was stabilized in transgenic TubCat mice (Ksp-CreERT2, Catnblox(ex3)/WT) by tamoxifen injection and their littermates without the Ksp-CreERT2 allele were used as control. Upon renal IRI, TubCat mice exhibited amelioration of tubular damage (morphological abnormality and kidney injury marker of NGAL) with reduced apoptosis (AKT/p53 signaling and TUNEL positive cells) and necroptosis (pMLKL and p-RIP3) in kidney cortical tissues compared to that of control. Tubular β-catenin stabilization in TubCat mice alleviated renal inflammation (inflammatory cytokines CXCL2, IL-1β, MCP-1, IL-6) and improved renal function (serum BUN and creatinine levels) in IRI-induced AKI. All these findings on the protective role of tubular β-catenin were further confirmed in LPS-induced AKI model and demonstrated using TubCatKO mice. (All these findings were published in Cell Death Dis. 2022; 13(12):1061 doi: 10.1038/s41419-022-05395-3) 2. Stabilization of β-catenin restores tubular mitochondrial homeostasis in AKI Mitochondrial dysfunction in renal tubules contributes to the development and progression of AKI. In IRI-induced AKI, TubCat mice showed increased mitochondrial number and less swollen mitochondria in IRI kidneys (Transmission Electron Microscopy) compared to control mice. Mitochondrial mass (TIM23, integral protein of inner mitochondrial membrane) and function (ATP production and mtDNA copy number) were also rescued in TubCat IRI kidneys. The regulatory role of β-catenin in mitochondrial biogenesis was evident with the upregulation of PGC-1α found in β-catenin-positively stained tubules and the increased in NRF1 expression in TubCat mice. In addition, tubular stabilization of β-catenin promoted mitochondrial fusion (MFN2, OPA1) and reduced fission (DRP1) expression. Similar results of mitochondrial homeostasis were found in TubCat mice in LPS-induced AKI model. Taken together, our findings suggest a mitochondrial protective function of β-catenin in renal tubules upon AKI. (All these findings were published in Cell Death Dis. 2022; 13(12):1061 doi: 10.1038/s41419-022-05395-3) 3. β-catenin interacts with FOXO3 and affects the transcriptional activity of PGC-1α in renal tubular epithelial cells The role of β-catenin in mitochondrial biogenesis and its underlying mechanism were elucidated in human renal tubular epithelial cells (HK-2). Consistent with in vivo results, HK-2 cells overexpressing β-catenin mutant (stabilized form) rescued the reduction of mitochondrial mass (MitoTracker staining) and PGC-1α upon LPS treatment. Interestingly, we found an increase in the transcription factor FOXO3 expression in HK-2 cells with stabilized β-catenin. Upon LPS stimulation, β-catenin was found to translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus where it formed a complex with FOXO3 (as shown by co-immunoprecipitation) and enhanced the FOXO3-dependent PGC-1α transcription in HK-2 cells (as shown by chromatin immunoprecipitation). (All these findings were published in Cell Death Dis. 2022; 13(12):1061 doi: 10.1038/s41419-022-05395-3) 4. Tubular β-catenin signaling is involved in inflammatory responses in renal tubular epithelial cells Based on our in vivo findings that stabilized tubular β-catenin alleviated inflammation in AKI, we further investigated the acute inflammatory responses upon modulation of β-catenin activation in LPS-stimulated HK-2 cells. However, our results showed that stabilizing β-catenin with a Wnt agonist, SKL2001 amplified the LPS-induced proinflammatory responses (TNF-α, CXCL-2 and IL-6) in HK-2 cells whereas knockdown of β-catenin dampened the LPS-induced inflammation. Additionally, phosphorylation levels of p38 MAPK and ERK were ameliorated in LPS-induced HK-2 cells with β-catenin silencing. The contradiction between in vitro and in vivo findings may be due to the dynamic change of β-catenin signaling in AKI model as it was revealed in our previous study of TubCat mice in the murine protein overload model.

17119818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17119818.value: Based on the findings from this study, we demonstrate a protective role of tubular β-catenin in AKI, specifically restoring mitochondrial biogenesis in renal tubules upon injury. The link between β-catenin and mitochondrial homeostasis further our interest in investigating the novel role of β-catenin in regulating autophagy and mitophagy in AKI. Preliminary data showed enhanced expression of autophagy components (Atg7 and Maplc3b) and mitophagy markers (Pink1 and Bnip3) in HK-2 cells overexpressing β-catenin as well as in kidney tissues of LPS-treated TubCat mice. Together, our study will open new insights into the mitochondria-targeted therapy for kidney injury.

17119818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17119818.value: Kidney tubular β-catenin signaling plays a pivotal role in acute kidney injury (AKI) but the underlying mechanisms remain exclusive. In this study, we generated an inducible mouse strain with tubule-specific β-catenin overexpression (TubCat) to show that tubular β-catenin stabilization significantly reduced renal inflammation, attenuated apoptosis and necroptosis via AKT activation and p53 suppression, particularly enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis by promoting FOXO3-dependent PGC-1α transcription and restored mitochondrial homeostasis through regulating mitochondrial fusion/fission. Collectively, our findings suggest a protective role of tubular β-catenin against AKI, specifically providing new insights and foundation for further development of mitochondria-targeted therapy for AKI.

17120718.label: Realisation of objectives
17120718.value: Two objectives of the study have been fully achieved, including 1) to develop a novel microneedle array loaded with aPD-1-CDDP-NPs, and to evaluate its anticancer effect in vitro, and 2)To investigate its synergistic immuno-chemotherapeutic effects and to elucidate the underlying cellular mechanism in vivo. The details are listed as follows. 1. Synthesis of pH-responsive tumour-targeted lipid-NPs coated with aPD-1 and CDDP The aPD-1-CDDP-NPs were synthesized through reverse-phase microemulsion. A well-prepared CDDP precursor was utilized to increase the solubility and further facilitate the encapsulation of CDDP. DOPA formed a bilayer to enable linking with other lipids, such as DOTAP, DSPE-PEG-AA and cholesterol. These lipids had the advantages of tumor targeting and selectivity. Additionally, aPD-1 was loaded onto the outer layer of the NPs because of hydrophobic and electrostatic non-specific interactions. The encapsulation efficiency of aPD-1 was 50%. No significant antibody release was detected within one month of storage at 4 °C. NPs exhibited spherical morphology with a diameter of approximately 57.6 nm, which was consistent with the result of dynamic light scattering (DLS). A higher proportion of aPD-1 dissociated from the NPs in acidic environment within 24 h, whereas Pt in the inner layer of the NPs could promise sustained release for 72 h. The aPD-1-CDDP-NPs facilitated the synergistic delivery of chemotherapeutic agents and immunotherapeutic agents. 2. Antitumor Activity of aPD1-CDDP-NPs In Vitro Lower IC50 values and higher cellular uptake were found for NPs, which could induce more apoptosis by reducing the number of cells in the G2 phase. All the data suggested that NPs could significantly enhance the antitumor efficiency, although adding aPD-1 did not internalize the medical effects. 3. Characterization of Dissolving MNs To target the immune region on the skin through transdermal delivery, drugs were further encapsulated into dissolving MNs. Dissolving MNs were fabricated following a molding method. PVP was selected as a structural material, because it offered the advantages of biocompatibility, strong mechanical property and highly water solubility. MN consisted of 9 × 9 needles with 800 µm in height and a base diameter of approximately 400 µm. Liss Rhod PE lipids were applied to label the NPs. The obtained MNs could be completely dissolved in water within 5 minutes and they could be dissolved into mouse skin in 20 minutes. After the MN-array was pressed on the mouse skin with appropriate strength for 20 minutes, obvious pinholes could be observed, and tips could be dissolved in the process. Moreover, the skin region with the pinholes could recover in less than one day without causing any skin ulceration. In addition, the bioactivity of the loaded aPD-1 and NPs did not degrade after one month of storage at 4 °C. Taken together, the results indicate that this type of PVP-structured MN may mediate drug delivery with a uniform distribution and high solubility in the skin, as well as mechanical strong. 4. PD-L1 expression in vitro and in vivo The SCC VII cell line is a murine squamous cell carcinoma cell line that spontaneously arises in the abdominal wall of a C3H mouse. We determined whether PD-L1 protein and mRNA were expressed in the SCC VII cell lines through western blot and qPCR respectively. RAW 264.7 exhibited higher PD-L1 expression after LPS stimulation; however, no expression was observed in SCC VII cells. Whether PD-L1 is expressed in an immunocompetent murine tumor homograft model was further detected using IHC. It has been demonstrated high PD-L1 expression in tumor tissues. 5. Antitumor Efficiency In Vivo We further investigated tumor inhibition on an immunocompetent murine tumor homograft model. SCC VII cell lines were subcutaneously inoculated into the right flank of C3H/HeJ mice to obtain superficial tumors. Mice treated with PBS showed natural tumor growth, whereas those treated with CDDP exhibited a limited treatment efficacy compared to the control group. Although 85% of tumors positively expressed PD-L1, aPD-1 systemic treatments caused a negligible inhibitory effect. However, aPD-1 delivered by MN patches revealed significant anticancer effects. Our results demonstrated that aPD-1 delivered by MN could achieve potent antitumor effects in the animal model unresponsive to aPD-1 systemic therapy. This represented a promising treatment strategy for immunotherapy-unresponsive cancers. Moreover, the aPD-1-CDDP-NPs MNs group displayed the most notable tumor regression effect compared with any other groups. These results proved that MN provided a highly promising tool for the transdermal co-delivery of chemotherapeutic and immunotherapeutic drugs. Cell proliferation was further confirmed through IHC in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue sections. Mice treated with CDDP achieved delayed tumor growth, with 25% of the cells continuing to proliferate, however, mice treated with aPD-1 still exhibited sufficient cell proliferation of approximately 70%. Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) like CD4+ cells and CD8+ infiltrated the tumor tissue and started to proliferate after aPD-1 treatment. We concluded that CDDP could inhibit cell proliferation, and aPD-1 could enhance T-cell infiltration. aPD-1 delivered through MN patches could amplify the results. TILs attacked the tumor tissues and killed the tumor cells afterwards. Additionally, tumor cell apoptosis was assessed through in situ TUNEL assay. The cell apoptotic indexes in the aPD-1 MN and aPD-1-CDDP-NPs MNs groups were significantly higher than those in the CDDP and aPD-1 groups. These data further substantiated our hypothesis that MN could provoke T-cell activity and then induce cell apoptosis though T-cells. 6. T-cell Responses and Immune Profile To evaluate T-cell responses and the immune profile, tumor tissues and blood were harvested after mice sacrifice. aPD-1, being an ICB, could be a positive regulator of TILs. The infiltration of CD4+ T-cells and CD8+ T-cells into tumor cells was assessed through flow cytometry. Mice in aPD-1 or aPD-1 + CDDP groups demonstrated 4-fold T-cells infiltration compared with that in the control group. In addition, significantly increased activated CD8+ T-cells and CD4+ T-cells were detected in both the aPD-1-CDDP-NPs and aPD-1 MN groups, indicating that tumor cells were remarkably infiltrated by T-cells after nano-encapsulation or transdermal delivery of the medication. More importantly, MN mediated aPD-1-CDDP-NPs exhibited the highest T-cell infiltration compared with the other groups. These results were consistent with the IHC-detected Ki-67. The increase of effect T-cells was correlated with the tumor regression efficiency, indicating that activated T-cells were attacking the tumor cells. To reveal the cellular mechanism in vivo, the production of IFN-γ and TNF-α was determined using ELISA kit in mice serum. No significant difference was detected in TNF-α levels; however, IFN-γ demonstrated a positive correlation with CD8+ T-cells. Notably, the MN-mediated delivery system could contribute more to IFN-γ expression; among the groups aPD-1-CDDP-NPs MNs group showed the highest IFN-γ expression. Taken together, increased T-cell responses activated by MNs might explain why MN loaded aPD-1 or aPD-1-CDDP-NPs demonstrated potent anticancer effects in the animal model unresponsive to aPD-1 systemic therapy. The aPD-1-CDDP-NPs delivered by MN patches could robust more T-cells and then infiltrate into the tumor site as well as release chemotherapeutic drugs into the tumor site, leading to synergistic anticancer efficiency.

17120718.label: Major findings and research outcome
17120718.value: Four papers were published in international journals with high impact factors, including ACS Appl Mater Interfaces (IF: 9.229), Nanoscale (IF: 7.790), J Dent Res (IF: 6.116), Ann Surg Oncol (IF: 5.344), and Oral Oncology (IF: 5.337). One USA patent was awarded. We investigated for the first time the efficiency and safety of a lipid-coated cisplatin nanoparticles (LCC-NPs) incorporated microneedle to enhance transdermal drug delivery for cancer therapy. Cisplatin was encapsulated by tumor-targeting pH-responsive lipid nanoparticles with a high loading rate of 80%, and the encapsulation per se substantially improved the drug solubility and yet increased its antitumor efficiency in vitro. The LCC-NPs were embedded in dissolving microneedles and released from the MNs after insertion into the skin, thereby enabling the nanoparticles to pass the stratum corneum for local delivery safely. The in vivo study with a xenograft tumor animal model demonstrated that microneedle arrays loaded with cisplatin nanoparticles significantly augmented cytotoxicity and apoptosis in cancer cells with an apoptotic index of 58.6%, resulting in significantly reduced volume and weight of tumors. Moreover, serum platinum, pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, and nephrotoxicity were not detected in vivo, highlighting that this microneedle technique is bio-safe. The novel cisplatin-nanoparticle microneedle system may offer promising opportunities to enhance antitumor effects and reduce systemic toxicity and side effects. Programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) located on T-cells combined with programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) critically accounts for tumor immune evasion. Anti-PD-1 (aPD-1) blocks the binding and activates T-cells to attack the tumor cells. However, improving the response rate and overcoming drug resistance are the major challenges in cancer immunotherapy. Skin is a highly active immune organ containing a large population of resident antigen-presenting cells. Microneedle arrays can pierce the immune-cell-rich epidermis, leading to a robust T-cell response in the microenvironment of tumor cells. In this study, microneedles were successfully fabricated with loading of pH-responsive tumor-targeted lipid-nanoparticles, allowing a local delivery of aPD-1 and CDDP precisely to cancer tissues. The SCC VII cell line was injected into the right flank of C3H/HeJ mice. Tumor-bearing mice were treated with aPD-1 drugs or NPs either intraperitoneally or through microneedle delivery. aPD-1-CDDP-NPs delivered through microneedles indicated a remarkable tumor regression effect and effectively boosted the immune response. Synergistic anticancer mechanisms were therefore activated through robust microneedle-induced T-cell response, blockage of PD-1 in T-cells by aPD-1, and increasing direct cytotoxicity of CDDP in tumor cells. This exhibited promise in the treatment of immunotherapy-unresponsive cancers. Taken together, microneedle-mediated local delivery of nano-encapsulated chemotherapeutic and immunotherapeutic agents provides a novel treatment strategy and provides insights into cancer therapy.

17120718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17120718.value: First, we will try to verify the conclusions in an alternative animal model, 4NQO-treated C57BL/6 mice. 4NQO is a water-soluble quinoline derivative that can induce DNA adduct formation and has an effect similar to tobacco. Mice will receive 4NQO in drinking water continuously for 16 weeks. Most of the tumors will occur in oral tongue. We will use MNs to provide transmucosal delivery of aPD-1-CDDP-NPs. The advantage of this animal model is the ability to specifically mimic the oral cavity carcinoma. Second, since this kind of MN has been authorized by US patent, we would like to extend the application of the MN for the treatment of superficial carcinomas that are unresponsive to aPD-1 systemic therapy. We would like to evaluate the therapeutic effect in large animals. The ultimate goal is to use MN-mediated aPD-1-CDDP-NPs in cancer patients.

17120718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17120718.value: Head and neck cancer is one of the most common cancers in the world with a survival rate of around 50%. The severe side effects of chemotherapy and low response rate of immunotherapy limit the clinical application. Nanoparticles are used for drug delivery to enhance drug efficiency due to the control release and target delivery ability. Lipid-coated NPs have advantages of biocompatibility and high loading efficiency. Cisplatin is encapsulated in a lipid core in order to achieve tumor targeting ability and to enhance therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, aPD-1 can be adsorbed onto this type of NP. A combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy can be thus achieved. Then the nanoparticles are embedded into microneedles for transdermal delivery. MNs ensure the precise delivery of drugs to the target tissue, being minimally invasive and painless. By combining the merits of MNs and NPs, a novel transdermal delivery system has been formulated to enhance anticancer effects and reduce side effects. The MN can provoke robust and durable T-cells activity, thus enhancing the efficacy of aPD-1 and increasing direct cytotoxicity of CDDP in tumor cells. In summary, MN-mediated aPD-1-CDDP-NPs renders a powerful tool for cancer therapy.

17122918.label: Realisation of objectives
17122918.value: In this project, we have well synthesized and characterized the carbon dots (CDs)-doped mesoporous silica nanoparticles (CD@MSNs). The constructed CD@MSNs with different surface modifications exhibit an excitation-dependent fluorescent emission. Unexpectedly, the CD@MSNs constructed from calcination show poor dispersity and significant aggregation in aqueous solution, and therefore these CD@MSNs have not been used in the biological experiments. Instead, as an alternative and refined approach, we have successfully synthesized three novel types of biomaterials for the subsequent experiments related to Objectives 1-3, including i) CD-Gu+-AmB, ii) CPDs-coated red-fluorescent MSNs and iii) CAU-17 and ZIF-65. The major research achievements and findings are summarized as follows: 1. Synthesis and characterization of CD@MSNs: The CD@MSNs were obtained by calcining the APTES-modified MSNs, via a programmed heating procedure. An intensive blue fluorescence of CD@MSNs can be identified under UV excitation. However, the calcinated nanoparticles exhibited poor dispersity in aqueous solution and aggregated significantly. Thus, the amine and boronic acid surface-modification were further conducted on the CD@MSNs for refining purposes. The as-prepared nanoparticles showed an excitation-dependent emission pattern, with reference to the non-fluorescent MSNs. As concerned above, CD@MSNs were not used in the biological experiments. Instead, three novel nano/micro-systems including i) CD-Gu+-AmB, ii) CPDs-coated red-fluorescent MSNs and iii) CAU-17 & ZIF-65 were well constructed by our multidisciplinary team for the subsequent experiments. 2. Constructing red-emissive guanylated polyene-functionalized carbon dots (CD) against invasive oral pathogens like C. albicans in the reconstituted human oral epithelia (RHOE): A novel CD-based theranostic nanoplatform (CD-Gu+-AmB) was specifically designed for tracking the penetration of antimicrobials like antifungal agents and effectively perturbing the invasion of C. albicans in oral epithelial tissues. The red-emissive water-soluble CDs with positively-charged guanidine groups (Gu+) and AmB favorably accumulated inside C. albicans cells, and exhibited potent antifungal effects in both planktonic and biofilm forms. There was no detectable toxicity to the host cells tested. Moreover, this study has provided the first evidence on the penetration and exfoliation profiles of CDs in a 3-D organotypic model of human oral epithelial tissues, highlighting that the as-synthesized CDs are able to rapidly penetrate oral epithelia, distribute extra- and intra-cellularly yet gradually exfoliate during the period of tissue culture up to 8 days. Notably, the constructed theranostic nanoplatform could accumulate in the oral tissues and effectively protect the tissues from invasion of C. albicans, by forming a “shielding” layer throughout the entire tissues (Li et al, ACS Appl Mater Interfaces 2019). 3. Intracellular delivery of baicalein by CPDs-coated MSNs for effectively modulating immuno-inflammatory responses in host cells: A novel facile approach was developed to construct a glutathione-responsive polymer coated silica-based nanosystem for precisely intracellular delivery of an herbal extract (baicalein) as an established inflammation modulatory agent. Notably, the polymer coating was performed via a one-step in-situ polymerization on the nanoparticle surfaces within 30 mins, which significantly simplified the coating process and the subsequent characterization. Additionally, the coated polymer as the analogue of cell-penetrating peptides could greatly enhance the cellular internalization of the nanosystems and consequently contribute to improving delivery efficiency of the therapeutic agents. Moreover, both the constructed nanosystem and the encapsulated baicalein could downregulate the immuno-inflammatory responses in gingival epithelial cells, via modulating the NF-κB signaling pathway. Interestingly, the nanosystem per se could upregulate the expression of A20, and properly passivate the cellular responses to IL-1β stimulation, thereby generating the modulatory effect synergistically with baicalein (Li et al, J Colloid Interf Sci 2022). 4. Developing a new facile approach to synthesizing bismuth metal-organic frameworks (Bi-MOFs) against the biofilms of oral pathogens: Two novel approaches were established for the first time to construct bismuth particles at room temperature within 30 min. One of the particles was characterized as porous Bi-MOFs with a crystalline structure of CAU-17. This approach can greatly simplify the synthesis of bismuth particles, via our unique ‘two-step’ crystallization process of CAU-17. Importantly, its size could be precisely controlled from micro- to nano-meter scales, thereby maximizing the application flexibility in further translational studies. The as-synthesized bismuth particles demonstrated potent antimicrobial and antibiofilm effects on three periodontal pathogens - Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans (Aa), P. gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) (Huang et al, Mater Today Bio 2022, in revision). 5. New discoveries on microbial persisters and their interactions with host cells: Persisters as a tiny subset of microorganisms are extremely tolerant to the lethal treatments of various antimicrobials, and thereby crucially account for common infections and the resultant inflammatory diseases (Wang & Jin, Crit Rev Microbiol 2022). Novel strategic approaches need to be developed for tackling the persisters of major pathogens like Pg as the keystone periodontal pathogen, and favorably modulating the dysregulated host responses. Our extended studies indicate that Pg persisters can maintain their capability to invade into human gingival epithelial cells, and markedly perturb the innate host defense (Wang et al, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2020), via upregulating the FOXO signaling pathway (Wang et al, Int J Mol Sci 2022). Indeed, these novel research findings lay down the foundation for further persister studies, and facilitate the development of new approaches like chemical MOFs (as shown below) for tackling microbial persisters. 6. Synthesizing the novel zinc MOFs for tackling microbial persisters: In our experiments, Zinc ion with both anti-bacterial and anti-inflammatory effects was applied with 2-nitroimidazole to synthesize ZIF-65 with an average diameter of 400 nm. Importantly, the as-synthesized ZIF-65 demonstrated potent antibacterial effects on the gram-negative periodontal pathogens (Aa, Pg and Fn). Notably, ZIF-65 at 100 μg/mL completely eradicated Pg persisters after 24-h treatment. This interesting finding suggests that ZIF-65 could be further developed to tackle Pg persisters for effective control of periodontitis and Pg-related inflammatory comorbidities. 7. Reflection of the project and future perspectives: During our experiments, we have noted that it is highly challenging to secure a microbe-host interaction model in vitro. For establishing this essential model, the 2-D host cells and/or 3-D tissues need to be cultured together with the microbes aerobically. Indeed, Pg is an anaerobic bacterium with a short invasion window (< 120 min), and it is hard to maintain a reliable and dynamic crosstalk of microbes with host cells for testing our constructed nanomedicines mentioned above. Thus, the potential tissue protection effects of CD-Gu+-AmB have been well evaluated in Candida-invaded oral epithelial tissue model. In spite of certain impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and time restriction, two MOFs (CAU-17 with antibacterial effects and ZIF-65 with antibacterial/potential anti-inflammatory effects) have been synthesized from metal ions (Bi3+ and Zn2+) and appropriately characterized. Their antibacterial effects on Pg have been thoroughly investigated, while the potential immuno-inflammatory modulatory effects in the crosstalk of Pg with host cells should be further investigated in vitro and in vivo.
