17602618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17602618.value: This research project aims to expand our understanding of Hong Kong history from 1949 to 1997 through the lens of travel and tourism, particularly tourism promotion. From the establishment of the PRC in October 1949 to the reversion to Chinese sovereignty in July 1997, a range of state and non-state actors tried to promote colonial Hong Kong as a unique place. The establishment of the Hong Kong Tourist Association (HKTA) in 1957 marked the beginning of concerted efforts to promote the city as a regional and global tourist destination. This promotion occurred within the contexts of the Cold War, the decolonization of Asia and the disintegration of the British Empire, as well as the rise of China and its reopening to the wider world. My project will look at how these authorities were able to convince the Hong Kong public that tourism needed to be promoted more aggressively. It will examine how the local tourist industry responded to the changes of the 1950s, 1960s, and the long 1970s, including the reopening of China which attracted more tourists to Hong Kong but also enabled others to sidestep Hong Kong and travel directly to the mainland. The project will also illustrate how the thirteen-year-long countdown, from the signing of the Sino-British Declaration in December 1984 to the return to China in July 1997, provided both challenges and opportunities for the Hong Kong tourist industry to retailor itself to meet the changing geopolitical scene. Moreover, I will ask how tourism affected and shaped local identity over this period, including how through tourism Hong Kong people came to think about their city, themselves, and their future. The findings from this research project will be disseminated through a scholarly monograph aimed at both academic and general audiences, through two or three articles in high-impact journals, and through a companion website. In a larger transnational and theoretical context, my project will add a local, geographical, and historical dimension to the growing and exciting field of travel and tourism by making comparisons with cities with similar historical backdrops such as Singapore. It will also ask how tourism may help us better understand Hong Kong during this period in ways that other approaches to history may not, and how the history of tourism can help Hong Kong's current government and tourist authorities understand how better to brand the region as a major tourist destination. 這項研究計劃旨在由旅行與旅遊業(特別是旅遊業推廣) 的角度出發，擴闊我們對1949年至97年間香港歷史的認識。從1949年10月中華人民共和國成立、到1997年7月中國對香港恢復行使主權期間，一系列政府和非政府個體嘗試以「獨一無二」為賣點推廣殖民地香港。1957年香港旅遊發展局（HKTA）的成立，標誌著各方在冷戰、亞洲非殖民化、大英帝國解體、中國的崛起及改革開放的背景下，協力推動香港成為地方與全球旅遊目的地的開始。 本研究將探討當局如何促使香港公眾了解積極推廣旅遊業的需要。它將探究20世紀50年代至70年代本地旅遊業如何面對包括中國開放下增加的到港內地遊客、與及香港喪失作為前往大陸中轉站的功能所帶來的改變。它也會說明由1984年12月中英聯合聲明簽署、到1997年7月香港回歸間十三年的倒數階段和不斷變化的地緣政治局面，如何為香港旅遊業及零售業帶來挑戰和機遇。此外，我們會探索這段時期間旅遊業如何影響及塑造本地特色或文化身份，包括香港人如何通過旅遊業來思考他們的城市，自身、和他們的未來。 我們將於一本以學者及普通讀者為對象的學術專著、兩或三篇刊載於高影響力期刊的文章以及一個配套網站發放本研究的結果。在跨國歷史(transnational history)和理論的背景下，透過與具有類似歷史背景的城市（如新加坡）進行比較，本研究會為新興的旅行與旅遊業研究添上充滿本地元素、地理學與歷史的一頁。本研究還會尋問旅遊業能如何以異於其他史學分支的方式，幫助我們更了解現今香港。還有旅遊業歷史能如何幫助當今香港政府和旅遊部門，更有效地將香港打造成主要旅遊目的地品牌。

17602618.label: Realisation of objectives
17602618.value: Writing a book about Hong Kong tourism from 1945 to 1997 became more challenging than I had expected or imagined. Travel restrictions during the Covid-19 pandemic prevented me from visiting several important overseas archives. Moreover, I was busy during much of 2020 and 2021 helping to build our new MA programme in Hong Kong History (launched in September 2022) and finishing two other books. The first was China Hands and Old Cantons: Britons and the Middle Kingdom (published in October 2021), from my previous GRF project. I completed this book in addition to the original monograph specified in my proposal, Canton Days: British Life and Death in China (published in February 2020). Because the second book I wrote over 2020 and 2021, The Hong Kong-China Nexus: A Brief History (published in March 2022), addressed Hong Kong’s acute political and social crises following the 2019 social unrest and the enactment of the National Security Law in June 2020, I felt obliged to complete it as soon as possible. During this period, I also published Chinese translations of my first book, Edge of Empires: Chinese Elites and British Colonials in Hong Kong, and my second book, A Concise History of Hong Kong, both of which involved editing and proofreading, and, in the case of the concise history, updating to include the changes since the last Chinese edition was published in 2013. After submitting my request for an extension in March 2022, I devised a more manageable and realistic plan for this project. As with my previous GRF project, I have divided it into two complementary projects: one on the founding of the Hong Kong Tourist Association in 1957, and another on tourist promotion from 1957 to 1997 (and perhaps beyond). I have almost finished writing the first book and aim to submit it for review in the spring or summer of 2024. Tentatively titled The Metropolis of the East: The Making of Hong Kong Tourism, this book looks at how Hong Kong became a major tourist destination after World War II and as the Cold War unfolded. Early Cold War Hong Kong is known best for its troubles, Yet it was also during this period that Hong Kong became a unique tourist destination, where travelers could both enjoy a taste of Chinese culture and peer through the “Bamboo Curtain” at the Communist giant lying just across the Shenzhen River. Then, thanks to the wars in Korea and Indochina, when thousands of American military personnel visited each year for “R & R” (rest and recreation), Hong Kong became an international tourism space. The Hong Kong Tourist Association, established in 1957, promoted Hong Kong as a place unlike any other in the world: Chinese but not China, and a harmonious mixture, not only of East and West but also of traditional and modern – a bustling metropolis, coexisting with the rural New Territories. All of which makes it even more surprising that so little was done in Hong Kong to promote tourism until the 1950s – almost fifty years after the South China Morning Post, the colony’s main English-language newspaper, had urged in early 1908. A committee formed in early 1920, in the wake of World War I, produced a list of recommendations for making Hong Kong more attractive to visitors from overseas and from China, but little happened. In 1934, during the Great Depression, a commission appointed by Governor William Peel offered suggestions for making the colony a holiday resort. After more than a year of bureaucratic torpor and urging from members of the colony’s Legislative Council, the Hong Kong Travel Association was finally established in July 1935. But its work ended with the Japanese invasion in December 1941. Soon after the Japanese surrendered in August 1945 and the British reoccupied Hong Kong, the local press began calling for tourism to be revived. A report in 1948 by Britain’s leading town planner, Patrick Abercrombie, included a detailed list of suggestions regarding tourism but had little effect. As late as the early 1950s, out of the thirty Commonwealth members, Hong Kong was one of the few without an official or at least officially sponsored tourist body. No one from Hong Kong served on the Commonwealth Liaison Committee’s Working Group on Tourism. Writing about tourism usually means examining how places are publicized or sold. My book tells a different story. Starting with the British reoccupation in late August 1945, it traces how government officials, businessmen, and members of the public decided that Hong Kong ought to be promoted as a tourist destination. It shows how in the mid-1950s the Hong Kong government finally, and reluctantly, agreed that tourism needed to be pushed more actively and with official support – a bold move in a colony known for its tightfistedness. At one level, the book is about the resolution in 1957 to form the Hong Kong Tourist Association, a decision that was made at a glacial pace and only after years of stalling. But it is also about how tourism became such an important part of Hong Kong’s economy that the government had little choice but to support it. Tourism played an active role in Hong Kong’s recovery from World War II. By the mid-1950s, it had become one of Hong Kong’s most important industries, second only to textiles. However, this impressive growth happened with little official coordination or support. Especially compared with countries such as Britain and Japan (to which my book devotes an entire chapter for comparison), there was little official interest in boosting tourism, even in a colony characterized by its lack of government intervention in the economy. Both before and after World War II, the local English- language press encouraged tourism – if not always directly then at least by providing a space for discussing its value, by drawing attention to tourism elsewhere, and by announcing the arrivals of passenger ships and airplanes. Yet there was little concerted action from the local business community. As my book shows, until the establishment of the Hong Kong Tourist Association, the rise of tourism owed less to local efforts and more to several interrelated changes beyond Hong Kong’s initiative or control – including the revival of passenger shipping and the global expansion of civil aviation, the growth of American overseas travel, the reopening of Japan to tourism under the Allied occupation, and the Korean War. Although a bold move in a colony known for its tightfistedness, the resolution to form a tourist association was made at a glacial pace and after years of stalling and bureaucratic inertia. Government officials and business leaders came to agree that Hong Kong ought to be promoted as a tourist destination, but only after the closing of the border with mainland China and the outbreak of the Korean War had already made Hong Kong alluring to tourists who went there for a sense of adventure and danger.

17602618.label: Major findings and research outcome
17602618.value: This project shows how tourism played an active role in Hong Kong’s recovery from World War II and into the early Cold War. By the mid-1950s, tourism had become one of Hong Kong’s most important industries, second only to textiles. However, this impressive growth happened with little official coordination or support. Especially compared with countries such as Britain and Japan, which used tourism actively to aid postwar recovery, in Hong Kong there was little official interest in boosting tourism. Some of the loudest voices for promoting tourism during this period came not from business interests but from the local English-language press, which encouraged tourism both directly through editorials and by providing a space for discussing its value, by drawing attention to tourism elsewhere, and by announcing the arrivals of passenger ships and airplanes. Unlike in Britain and Japan, until the establishment of the Hong Kong Tourist Association, the rise of tourism owed less to local efforts and more to several interrelated global and regional developments beyond Hong Kong’s initiative or control. The establishment of the Hong Kong Tourist Association in 1957 helps us understand Hong Kong’s changing geopolitical position and the colony’s state-society relations, in particular the historical reluctance of the government to intervene in the economy. Today, as government officials and tourism authorities struggle to promote Hong Kong as a tourist destination, there is much to be learned from the history of Hong Kong tourism in the late 1940s and 1950s. Apart from completing this book, my plans over the next few months related to this project include delivering one paper, titled “‘A Spice of Imaginary Danger’: Hong Kong and Cold War Tourism,” at the annual conference of the Association for Asian Studies, to be held in March 2024 in Seattle, Washington, and one workshop for schoolteachers on tourism and Hong Kong history, to be held by the Hong Kong Education Bureau in April 2024. After submitting the first book manuscript for review in the spring or summer, I will begin writing the second project based on the many materials my research assistants and I have collected during the course of this project.

17602618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17602618.value: As mentioned in section 5.3, I have divided this project into two complementary projects: one on the founding of the Hong Kong Tourist Association in 1957, and another on tourist promotion from 1957 to 1997. In the second project, I hope to explore some of the questions I proposed in my original proposal but have not yet been able to do so. These include: How did tourism authorities promote Hong Kong during crises such as the 1967 riots? How did the Hong Kong tourist industry respond to the changes of the long 1970s, including the global oil crisis and the reopening of the PRC, which both attracted more tourists to Hong Kong but also enabled others to sidestep Hong Kong and travel directly to the mainland? How did the thirteen-year-long countdown, from the signing of the Sino-British Declaration in December 1984 to the return to China in July 1997, provide both challenges and opportunities for the Hong Kong tourist industry to retailor itself to meet the changing geopolitical scene? How were visual images, including posters and films, used to sell Hong Kong across the globe, and how did these images change over time?

17602818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17602818.value: Most large-scale educational assessments are summative in nature largely because they are developed and analyzed using unidimensional item response theory (IRT) models. These assessments are useful for auditing, but not necessarily for promoting learning. Attempts such as subscoring and item mapping can make summative assessments more diagnostically informative. However, the intrinsic unidimensional nature of these assessments limits the extent to which they can provide information relevant to classroom practices. As an alternative to traditional IRT models, cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) can be used to develop and analyze assessments that have greater formative value. CDMs are psychometric models developed primarily for identifying the presence or absence of finer-grained skills involved in solving problems on a test. The mastery profiles for individual students derived from CDMs can be used by teachers to adapt their classroom instruction. Targeted instruction implemented at the individual student level can further improve student learning outcomes. Until more diagnostic assessments can be developed, CDMs can be used with extant large-scale assessments, such as the ACT tests in the US. Once mastery profiles have been generated, students can be directed to available learning resources (e.g., the OpenEd platform) to address their needs. The same approach can be adopted to large-scale assessments being used in Hong Kong (e.g., Territory-wide Student Assessment). CDMs are also suitable for the Student Adaptive Learning System the Hong Kong Education Bureau is planning to develop. To date, most of the CDM developments pertain to dichotomous skills (i.e., whether or not students have mastered the skills being measured). However, for some applications, classifying students into more categories (e.g., no mastery, basic mastery, and advanced mastery) would be more instructionally relevant. Such classifications require polytomous skills. A CDM model that can accommodate polytomous skills, the polytmous general deterministic input, noisy “and” gate (pG-DINA), will be the focus of this proposal. Although the pG-DINA has been shown to be empirically viable, its wider application has been hampered by two important limitations, namely, a rigid assumption and a lack of associated methodologies. This project will address these limitations by proposing more general versions of the pG-DINA and developing pG-DINA-based methodologies for validating the assumed item and attribute level association. The proposed models and methods will be carefully investigated using both simulated data and real data from Hong Kong students. The new developments are expected to help establish the practicability of the CDMs as a psychometric framework for developing and analyzing formative assessments. 大多數大規模教育評測基於單維的項目反應理論（item response theory, IRT）模型進行開發和分析，因此在本質上都是總結性的。雖然這些評測對學業評價是有用的，但不一定有助於促進學習。報告維度分數（subscoring）和題目映射（item mapping）之類的嘗試可以使得總結性評估提供更多診斷性信息。然而，這些評估本質上是單維的，導致他們難以提供足夠的與課堂實踐相關的信息。 作為傳統IRT模型的一個替代方案，認知診斷模型（cognitive diagnosis models, CDMs）可用於開發和分析可用於形成性評價的測驗。CDMs是一種旨在識別考生是否掌握了解答考試問題所需的精細技能的心理測量模型（psychometric models）。教師可以使用從CDMs中獲得的學生個人掌握情況檔案以調整他們的課堂教學。在學生個人層面施行針對性教學可以進一步提升學生的學習成果。 在開發出更多的診斷性測驗之前，CDMs可以與現有的大規模測評一起使用，例如美國的ACT測試。一旦生成了學生的掌握情況檔案，就可以提供給他們可利用的學習資源（例如，OpenEd平台）以滿足他們的需求。相同的方法也可應用於香港的大規模評估（例如，全港性系統評估）。另外，CDMs也適用於香港教育局計劃發展的學生自適應學習系統（Student Adaptive Learning System）。 迄今為止，大多數CDMs的發展都是基於與二級評分(dichotomous)技能的（即，學生是否掌握了被測驗的技能）。然而，對於某些應用而言，將學生分為更多的類別（例如，沒有掌握，基本程度掌握和高級程度掌握）會更具教學意義。 這種分類則需要多級評分(polytomous)技能。 有一種CDM模型可以適用於多級評分技能，即pG-DINA（polytomous general deterministic input, noisy “and” gate, pG-DINA），這將是本提案的重點。雖然pG-DINA已被證明在經驗上是可行的，但其更廣泛的應用受到兩方面的限制：嚴苛的假設和缺乏相關的方法論。 透過擴展pG-DINA模型以及開發基於pG-DINA的用於驗證假定的題目和屬性層次關聯的方法可以解除這些限制。我們將會使用仿真數據和來自香港學生的真實數據，仔細研究提議的模型和方法。預計提議的模型和方法將有助於提高CDMs作為用於開發和分析形成性評估的心理測量框架的實用性。

17602818.label: Realisation of objectives
17602818.value: Upon the completion of the project, the four objectives have been successfully achieved. Objective 1: To develop CDM procedure for empirical validating item and attribute level associations that domain or subject-matter experts have specified a priori Our team has successfully developed an empirical Q-matrix validation method for the polytomous G-DINA model. The new method can be used not only to identify potential misspecified Q-entries but also suggest more appropriate attribute-level specifications. The theoretical properties of the proposed method have been established by mathematically proving several lemmas and one theorem. The manuscript has published in a prestigious journal, Psychometrika, which is the official journal of the Psychometric Society. Objective 2: To develop more general versions of the pG-DINA model to afford it greater flexibility to adequately fit more varied assessment data; Our team has developed a more general polytomous-attribute cognitive diagnosis model (CDM) by relaxing the stringent specific attribute level mastery assumption, and allowing for the different attribute levels to contribute differentially to the success probabilities. The new model subsumes several simpler CDMs as special cases. Moreover, it provides a more accurate diagnosis of students’ true mastery levels. We are in the process of completing a new manuscript, which will be soon submitted for publication to a top academic journal. Objective 3: To develop computer programs that can implement the proposed models and methods We have built a customized EM algorithm code, which can implement the proposed methods and models efficiently. Moreover, the code can generate mesa plots, which allow for quantitative and graphical information to be combined, resulting in a more effective implementation of the proposed method. The code was developed within the R environment and can be used free of charge by interested practitioners. The code will be integrated into the GDINA package, a popular R package for cognitive diagnosis modeling that the PI and his former student developed and are currently maintaining. Objective 4: Prior to their actual use, to establish the theoretical properties and practical viability of the proposed models and methods using simulation studies and analyses of locally collected data Our team has conducted extensive simulation studies to evaluate the new initiatives under various conditions. For example, we evaluated the performances of the new empirical Q-matrix validation method under different percentages of misspecified Q-entries, attribute structures, item quality and CDMs, and found the new method is viable. We also examined the parameter recovery of the new polytomous-attribute CDM and the consequences of improperly using constrained CDMs under several conditions. We have applied the new initiatives to locally collected data to illustrate their practical viability and implications. The real data consisted of responses of 1,408 Hong Kong students to a 31-item proportional reasoning (PR) test. We applied the developed Q-matrix validation method to the dataset and compared the results with the specifications defined by the domain or subject-matter experts. It was found the Q-matrix recommendations based on the proposed method were in general consistent with those based on expert opinions for the PR test. Thus, the method is deemed viable.

17602818.label: Major findings and research outcome
17602818.value: The outcome from this project is substantial and have significant theoretical and practical impact. The major findings include: 1. An empirical Q-matrix validation method for the polytomous G-DINA model: The new method is innovative because it can be used not only to identify potential misspecified Q-entries, but to also suggest more appropriate attribute-level specifications. The method is implemented in combination with the mesa plot, which can present the results graphically, making the method more practically useful. 2. A general and flexible CDM model for polytomous attributes: Theoretically, the new model subsumes the existing models and many simplified CDM models as special cases. Practically, the new model can be used to analyze real data to produce more accurate and finer-grained results of students’ mastery of skills. 3. Customized computer codes that implement the new method and model: These codes are available for free to the public. Researchers and practitioners can directly apply the new initiate developed in this project to their real test data. The findings have been widely disseminated – an article has been published in a high-ranking journal, presentations given in international conference meetings, and keynote/invited talks delivered in different countries/areas. Another article is close to being completed. The detailed information can be found in Part C of this report. The project team will continue to prepare additional manuscripts for publication and generate more outcome.

17602818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17602818.value: Although we have made significant progress in developing new model and algorithms for polytomous-attribute CDMs, more studies are in need. Three potential future topics are listed below: (1) This project proposed and implemented an exhaustive search algorithm, which can be computationally demanding in the context of the polytomous attributes. Future studies can consider the viability of the more e?cient sequential search algorithms; (2) The current algorithm is non-iterative, which is suboptimal because the misspecification of the Q-matrix may not be detected in a one-pass validation procedure. Future studies can also explore iterative Q-matrix validation procedures to improve the chances of ?nding the correct Q-vectors; and (3) Future research can create user-friendly and stand-alone computer programs that can implement the exhaustive and iterative algorithms to facilitate the use of the new models and algorithms.

17602818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17602818.value: Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) are psychometric models developed in recent decades for identifying the presence or absence of finer-grained skills, which can be used by teachers to adapt their classroom instruction, or students to direct their own learning. To date, most of the CDM are developed for dichotomous skills (i.e., whether or not students have mastered the skills). However, for many applications, classifying students into more categories (e.g., no mastery, basic mastery, and advanced mastery) would be more instructionally relevant. Such classifications require polytomous skills. This project focuses on methods and models that can accommodate polytomous skills. We develop a new method for validating the Q-matrix such that the misspecified Q-entries can be identified and more appropriate specifications can be suggested. Additionally, we propose a more general CDM for polytomous skills. We investigated the proposed method and model carefully using simulated data and real data from Hong Kong students. Both the method and the model can help better identify the presence or absence of students? skills, which can serve as feedback to different stakeholders. In the long term, this project can help establish the CDMs as a psychometric framework for developing and analyzing various types of formative assessments.

17602918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17602918.value: This proposed study aims at investigating the status of education equity in Hong Kong utilizing data of the most recent cycle of TIMSS – TIMSS 2015, through further analyses of the relations between the background questionnaire data and students’ mathematics achievement. Education equity has been an issue of concern in many countries, and beyond attaining a high level of achievements, it is important for Hong Kong to aspire to the goal of ensuring education equity. Based on the findings, educational policies and classroom practices will be suggested to help improve education equity in Hong Kong. International studies of mathematics achievements such as TIMSS and PISA have been considered important for decision making by policymakers to improve their educational systems. However, the TIMSS international reports only provide rough relations between different variables and student achievements. Thus, secondary analyses are needed to address additional research questions such as education equity, and to provide in-depth insights into the impact of different factors on students’ learning of mathematics, which in turn will suggest measures for the improvement of curriculum and school programmes. Secondary analyses of the TIMSS 2015 data in this proposed study will be performed at the individual student level, and various statistical techniques will be employed to establish specific relationships between the background variables and student achievement. The PI of this proposed study was involved in the secondary analyses of the TIMSS 1995 data (Leung et. al., 1999), the results of which had significantly impacted the curriculum reform in 2000. A team led by the PI also performed secondary analyses on the TIMSS 2011 data (F. Leung, Wong, & C. Leung, 2014). The experience gained from the TIMSS 2011 study and the strengthened expertise of the current team provide a solid platform for performing secondary analyses of the TIMSS 2015 data using more sophisticated methods of analyses. This project will provide timely and important interpretations on the mathematics performance of Hong Kong students in TIMSS 2015 in relation to education equity in Hong Kong. The findings will also contribute to better understanding of the issue of education equity in a highly successful education system, and the framework and methodology adopted in this study will serve as useful reference for secondary analysis of large-scale international assessment data. The results may also lead to further studies to identify additional conceptual discussions that are not only beneficial to Hong Kong, but also to other regions. 這項研究旨在通過進一步分析最新的國際數學與科學趨勢研究 (TIMSS) – TIMSS 2015背景問卷數據與學生數學成績之間的關係，調查香港教育公平的現況。 教育公平一直是許多國家關心的議題，香港除了取得高水平的成就外，也必須致力確保能達到教育公平的目標。本研究將根據調查結果，就教育政策和課堂實踐作出建議，以改善香港的教育公平。 TIMSS和學生能力國際評估計劃（PISA）等數學成就國際研究，一向被政策制定者認為對改善其教育制度的決策具有重大意義。儘管如此，TIMSS國際報告僅提供不同變數與學生成績之間的粗略關係。 因此，有需要進行二次分析，以探討教育公平等其他研究問題，並深入檢視不同因素對學生學習數學的影響，從而提出改善課程和學校活動的措施。這項TIMSS 2015數據二次分析將在個別學生層面進行，並會採用各種統計方法來確定背景變數與學生成績之間的特定關係。 這項研究的負責人曾經參與過TIMSS 1995數據的二次分析（Leung et. al., 1999），其結果對2000年的課程改革產生了重大影響。由該名負責人領導的團隊，也為TIMSS 2011數據進行了二次分析 (F. Leung, Wong, & C. Leung, 2014)。憑藉TIMSS 2011研究所獲得的經驗以及當前團隊豐富的專業知識，TIMSS 2015數據二次分析可在一個堅實的平台上，採用更複雜的方法進行分析。 本項目可爲TIMSS 2015香港學生數學表現與香港教育公平的關係提供既及時又重要的詮釋。 同時，調查結果亦將有助深入理解在一個超卓教育制度下的教育公平問題。研究所採用的框架和方法也可作為大規模國際評估數據二次分析的有用參考。研究結果也可引伸至進一步研究，誘發其他概念性討論，這些討論不僅令香港受惠，亦有利於其他地區。

17602918.label: Realisation of objectives
17602918.value: This project utilized the data from TIMSS 2015 and 2011 to study the objectives raised in the proposal. As the recent two cycles of TIMSS that Hong Kong students participated in, they can reflect the equity issues in Hong Kong’s education system concerned in the proposal. A systematic analysis of these two datasets were conducted in this project, which helped to reveal the current status and developmental trajectory of students’ achievement in Hong Kong and the underlying factors contributing to education equity. The project findings were based on a series of secondary analysis of these two datasets beyond the original results published by TIMSS. The analysis is quantitative in nature, using the software packages SPSS, R, Mplus and HLM. All secondary analysis conducted in this project followed the conceptual framework formulated in the proposal, which was based on issues of education equity in mathematics teaching and learning in Hong Kong. Under this framework, the project identified several equity factors at the student, school and family levels based on the questionnaire data collected in TIMSS. These factors were investigated by in-depth analyses of their relationships with students’ mathematics achievement. The analysis was also integrated with the specificities in Hong Kong to better represent the equity issues in mathematics teaching and learning relevant to Hong Kong students. This project used the Hong Kong part of the TIMSS dataset collected in 2015 and 2011, including: 1) a total of 3,600 grade 4 students from 132 schools and 3,232 grade 8 students from 133 schools in TIMSS 2015; 2) a total of 3,957 grade 4 students from 136 schools and 3,250 grade 8 students from 117 schools in TIMSS 2011. The variables under study were derived from the TIMSS 2015 and 2011 data respectively. The outcome variable was Hong Kong students’ mathematics achievement, the scores of which were obtained through the methodology of multiple imputation. All five plausible values were taken into consideration in the analyses. Following the TIMSS mathematics framework, the scores representing students’ mathematics achievement covered three cognitive domains (knowing, applying, and reasoning) and various content domains (numbers, geometric shapes and measures, and data display for grade 4; and numbers, algebra, geometry, and data and chance for grade 8). The explanatory variables involved in this project were organized into two levels. At the student/family level, the explanatory variables included student gender, self-efficacy, family socioeconomic status (SES), home resources for learning, language(s) spoken in the home, parental educational expectations and academic socialization, as well as early home experiences and preschool experiences in learning mathematics. Among them, the family SES of students was directly or indirectly examined through items on parents’ education and occupations; and the home resources for learning were examined through number of books and number of study supports in the home – own room and internet connection. At the school/classroom level, the explanatory variables involved school resources, school climate and safety, school type, teacher background and characteristics, formal education and training, teacher perception of mathematics teaching/learning, teacher preparation and collaboration, classroom characteristics, and instructional strategies. These variables at different levels were merged into separate data files and were linked through mapping the student ID and teacher ID variables from student-teacher linkage file. After identifying the variables of interest based on the conceptual framework of this study, hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) at both student and school level were performed to address the objectives of the proposal related to education equity in Hong Kong. Before conducting HLM analysis, a preprocessing procedure for missing data was conducted: we first excluded all invalid data with missingness in all variables and then performed Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) multiple imputation method to impute missing values for the variables at both the student and school levels. The preprocessing of missing data was followed by a series of test on the normality, multicollinearity, and outliers of the data: we first tested the normal distribution of the residuals of the outcome variable mathematics achievement by QQ normality plots; then we examined the multicollinearity among the explanatory variables via the correlation matrix, variance inflation factor and tolerance indicators; and lastly, we detected outliers and extreme cases for continuous variables. The HLM analysis were specified at the student level and the school level, as only one intact class was sampled per school in the Hong Kong TIMSS data. The objectives proposed in this project were addressed as follows. First, in regard to the effects of education equity factors on students’ mathematics achievement, two-level (student level and school level) analysis was conducted using the Hong Kong grade 4 and grade 8 datasets from TIMSS 2015 and 2011 separately to identify the explanatory variables and compare the four model fitting results to understand the effects at the two age groups in two time points. Specifically, the indices for the abovementioned student and school level variables were input as explanatory variables, while a set of five plausible values of students’ achievement were the outcome variables. The total variances in student and school levels were obtained by conducting a variance analysis using the null model for each grade and for each cycle. Second, the final models depicting the effects of all relevant sources (at both student and school level) of influence on students’ mathematics achievement at two grades were further compared. The comparisons demonstrated different effects on students’ mathematics achievement results caused by each set of equity factors. Third, similar comparisons were performed to investigate effects of all relevant sources of influence on students’ mathematics achievement at two time points – TIMSS 2015 and 2011 to capture the development trajectory over times. The major findings are listed in section 6, based on which recommendations were generated for educational researchers, educators, and policy makers with an aim to improve education equity.

17602918.label: Major findings and research outcome
17602918.value: This project was dedicated to obtaining a better understanding of education equity in Hong Kong. According to the assessment results from many large-scale international comparative studies such as the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) and Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), Hong Kong’ education system has been a highly successful one: mathematics performance of students in Hong Kong has been staying at an outstanding level for many cycles. It is, therefore, a timely project to examine the issues related to education equity in Hong Kong education system. To this end, this project mainly investigated the relationships between equity factors (from student, school and family levels) and students’ mathematics achievement based on a comprehensive secondary analysis of large-scale datasets from Hong Kong TIMSS 2015 and 2011. The major findings and research outcome include: 1. Boys of grade 4 and grade 8 performed better in mathematics achievement than girls in both TIMSS 2011 and 2015. The gender gap was larger in grade 8 than in grade 4 and the gap slightly decreased from TIMSS 2011 to 2015. Together, these findings suggest that gender inequity in mathematics learning was still likely to exist in the education system in Hong Kong, especially for students at the secondary-school-age level. The findings point to the need of further work by researchers, educators, and policy makers toward addressing gender inequity in mathematics learning in Hong Kong. 2. Both family SES and school SES (averaged student SES in each school) contributed to Hong Kong students’ mathematics achievement as revealed by Hong Kong TIMSS 2011 and 2015 data. Students from high SES families performed better in mathematics achievement than students from low SES families; controlling for family SES, students attending high SES schools outperformed their counterparts attending low SES schools. These findings call for more attention to low SES students who attend low SES schools, as they are likely to be in a “double jeopardy” situation in mathematics learning. In addition, school SES contributed more to mathematics achievement at grade 8 than at grade 4. 3. School resources for mathematics instruction (RESM) played a more important role in mathematics achievement in TIMSS 2015 than in 2011. RESM did not show a significant effect on mathematics achievement for both grades in 2011. In contrast, grade 4 students from schools with more RESM performed better in 2015, though the RESM effect was not significant for grade 8 students in 2015. The effect of school RESM on mathematics achievement implies that the distribution of educational resources among schools could be a potential factor affecting education equity.

17602918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17602918.value: As education equity has been an issue of concern in many countries in recent years, it is time to turn to the goal of building up an education system that minimizes the inequity problem. In this regard, the findings gleaned from this project call for more research and understanding on the role of various factors contributing to education equality in the learning of mathematics as well as other subjects, thereby informing educational policies and practices and benefiting a wide range of schools and students. Moreover, this project paves a promising way for tracking the developing trajectory of students’ educational achievements and their associations with education equity issue in Hong Kong. Further cycles of research on education equity issues in Hong Kong are expected to reveal more characteristics of the trajectory and contribute to educational development in terms of the improvement of teaching and learning and the allocation of educational resources. In addition, the seminars and workshops based on the project are expected to benefit educational researchers dealing with methodological complexities in the secondary analysis of large-scale datasets for addressing educational issues. The valuable lessons from this project is planned to be integrated into a series of courses and then be distributed online, which will make further contribution to the understanding and research of education equity.

17602918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17602918.value: This project investigated the relationships between equity factors (from student, school and family levels) and students’ mathematics achievement based on a comprehensive secondary analysis of large-scale datasets from Hong Kong TIMSS 2015 and 2011. There are several notable findings on education equity in Hong Kong. First, we found that gender inequity still exists for Hong Kong students. Boys outperformed girls at both secondary and primary school age levels. Second, students from higher socioeconomic status (SES) families performed better; moreover, students attending schools that had higher average student SES tended to score higher. Third, students from schools with more resources for mathematics instruction tended to perform better. Together, these findings helped identify the factors that could potentially affect education equity in Hong Kong. To achieve better equity in Hong Kong, researchers, educators and policy makers could pay more attention to gender gap, SES effects at both family and school levels, and the distribution of educational resources between and within schools.

17603318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17603318.value: What are the consequences of older adults being unable to walk safely in the modern challenging environment? Can we design an effective intervention to enhance the chance that older adults at risk of falling can walk safely even in a complicated environment requiring multi-task walking capability? Walking is the most common fall-related daily activity by older adults. Unfortunately, older adult falls were proved to affect walking capability and lead to high fear of falling. In response to movement difficulties and/or fear of falling during walking, older adults were found to redirect their attention internally to the mechanisms of their movements by means of conscious motor processing, in an attempt to ensure the effectiveness of their movements when encountering movement difficulties or under stress. However, previous research showed that conscious motor processing requires the explicit processing of movement-related declarative knowledge using working memory. Conscious motor processing was found to cause movement disruption by constraining or interfering with automatic motor control mechanisms. In addition, focusing internally during conscious motor processing was also discovered to interfere with allocation of attention for navigation of the environment and/or multitasking in older adults during walking that overloads resources of working memory. It can subsequently cause movement failure and increase risk of falling of the older adults, especially in a complicated environment requiring multi-task walking capability. Although conscious motor processing in older adults during walking was shown to be problematic, no research has examined a potential intervention to ameliorate the propensity for conscious motor processing in older adults during walking. It is therefore believed that there is significant clinical value in developing an effective training method to ameliorate the predisposition for conscious motor processing by older adults during gait re-education by physiotherapists. The objective of the proposed randomized controlled trial is to examine the effect of single-task, dual-task and analogy training during gait rehabilitation on conscious motor processing propensity, balance and multi-task walking ability of older adults at risk of falling in Hong Kong. Pilot studies were completed successfully to develop the rehabilitation training protocols and the training feasibility, safety and preliminary effectiveness have been ascertained. The proposed study will make significant contribution to the application of novel and effective evidence-based rehabilitation methods to ameliorate propensity for conscious motor processing by older adults. Consequently, it can help improve older adults’ multi-task walking capability and decrease their risk of falling in the modern challenging and complicated environment.

17603318.label: Realisation of objectives
17603318.value: The single objective of this research was to examine the effect of single-task, dual-task and analogy training during gait rehabilitation on conscious motor processing propensity, balance, walking ability and fear of falling by older adults at risk of falling in Hong Kong. Drawing from well-established evidence that conscious motor processing can cause movement disruption by interfering with automatic control of walking, this research involved a randomised controlled trial where older adults at risk of falling were randomly allocated to participate in one of three kinds of walking training. The training protocols were developed by expert physiotherapists and pilot-tested prior to this project. Outcomes were measured using validated instruments, including those that were developed and tested by the project team (i.e., Chinese Movement-Specific Reinvestment Scale, MSRS-C). The project commenced in September 2018, with Dr. WONG Wai Lung Thomson as the Principal Investigator (PI) at the University of Hong Kong (HKU). Research activities went in full swing, where participant recruitment and data collection made timely progress and the study protocol was published (Wong, 2019). Due to staff changes, a change request was submitted for Dr. CAPIO Catherine Mamaid at the Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) to take up the project as PI in November 2019. A six-month extension was also requested to make up for the time taken by administrative procedures that transferred the project from HKU to EdUHK. The project team, however, encountered prolonged challenges due to the social unrest of 2019 and the pandemic that began in early 2020. A further six-month extension was requested, which ultimately allowed the project objective as stated in section 5.1 to be achieved despite some limitations. We outline the challenges and our responses in the succeeding sections. As of the last quarter of 2019, the project had recruited over 40% of the target sample size, and approximately 37% had completed their training sessions and first post-training assessment. The number of community elderly centres that expressed their interest in participating in the project was more than sufficient, and we were on track to meeting our targets. However, the social unrest escalated in the latter part of 2019, which led to all our activities at the elderly centres being put on hold. We were able to administer the second post-training assessment (i.e., retention) of the participants who had completed their training sessions, but we were unable to commence with any new participants. We planned to resume our research activities after the lunar new year of 2020. However, as the COVID-19 pandemic began around the lunar new year, all our planned activities were effectively cancelled. Because older adults are more vulnerable to COVID-19 due to underlying conditions and have a high risk of mortality, the Social Welfare Department (SWD) did not allow research activities to proceed in elderly centres until the public health situation stabilised. Essentially, we were unable to proceed with any data collection until the pandemic was deemed under control, and the SWD gave clearance for elderly centres to engage with research activities. While we were not able to implement data collection, we resumed recruitment of elderly centres in the third quarter of 2020 (i.e., prior to the 4th wave of the pandemic in Hong Kong). We engaged with 14 elderly centres across the territory, of which two were scheduled to commence participation in the second or third quarter of 2021 on the assumption that (a) vaccination of older adults would proceed smoothly after the lunar new year of 2021, and (b) the pandemic would be under control before mid-year and the SWD would allow research activities to proceed. It was in the fourth quarter of 2021 when we were finally able to resume data collection after nine elderly centres re-engaged with the research team from the second to the third quarters of the year. We were able to screen 179 potential participants and recruited an additional 39 eligible participants, reaching approximately 75% of our original target sample size. A further 13 participants were eligible and could have taken us to approximately 87% of our target sample size. However, the elderly centres can only schedule the activities after the first quarter of 2022, which was beyond the extended period of the project. We considered requesting a further extension of the project. However, no further data gathering was ultimately possible as the fifth wave of the pandemic began in Hong Kong. Over the entire duration of the project, the project team persistently engaged with elderly centres to reach the target sample size and complete all trainings and assessments. We were largely successful with securing the cooperation of more than enough elderly centres, and we were on track to complete our targets successfully. However, the circumstances faced by our research were unprecedented and outside of our control. Despite our persistent efforts, we were largely dependent on the social and public health situation and the policies adopted by the SWD. In the end, we were able to collect data from N = 79 participants, which was sufficient for us to analyse and answer our research objective. We also continued with efforts to disseminate our findings despite the ongoing pandemic. We presented (a) related data in the World Physiotherapy Congress (i.e., official congress of the World Confederation of Physical Therapy) in 2021 and (b) our preliminary findings in the World Physiotherapy – Asia Western Pacific Regional Congress in 2022. The findings that answer our research objective have been published in the International Journal for Environmental Research and Public Health (JCR IF: 4.614). The publication is open access, thereby allowing greater dissemination potential. We acknowledge that there are limitations in our study findings that are largely associated with the reduced sample size and inability to analyse retention tests. We outlined the recommendations and ways forwards in the publication (Mak, Capio, & Wong, 2023) and in sections 6.1 and 6.2 in this report.

17603318.label: Major findings and research outcome
17603318.value: The risk of falling among older adults is a serious concern because falls can lead to serious physical injuries, such as hip fractures, hospitalisation, and death. It can also lead to wellbeing issues such as heightened fear of falling and reduced quality of life. The majority of falls among older adults occur during walking. When encountering movement difficulties, older individuals – especially those with a high risk of falling – tend to shift towards consciously monitoring and controlling their movements. Previous research has shown that conscious motor processing could lead to compromised walking performance in older adults. Therefore, strategies that can reduce the propensity for conscious motor processing could potentially improve outcomes for older adults who are at risk of falls. This research aimed to examine the effects of training protocols (i.e., single-task, dual-task, and analogy training) on conscious motor processing propensity and fall-related outcomes (i.e., balance, walking ability, fear of falling) among older adults at risk of falling (Wong, 2019). Our theoretical foundation was that implicit motor learning strategies (i.e., dual-task, analogy) could reduce the propensity for conscious motor processing. It was hypothesised that at-risk older adults who complete dual-task or analogy training will display a greater reduction in conscious motor processing propensity and greater improvements in fall-related outcomes than those who complete single-task training. Fall-related outcomes include functional gait/balance, balance ability, functional mobility, single-task and dual-task walking abilities, and fear of falling. Our findings only partially support our hypotheses (Mak, Capio, & Wong, 2023). There were no significant changes in conscious motor processing propensity and fear of falling following all types of training. There were significant but comparable improvements in functional gait/balance, balance ability, and functional mobility following training across the three groups. Only analogy training improved single-task and dual-task walking abilities after training. These findings address the objective of this research. There appear to be (a) no effects of the three types of training on conscious motor processing propensity and fear of falling, (b) comparable improvements in balance and function following training, and (c) an advantageous effect of analogy training on the single-task and dual-task walking abilities of older adults who are at risk of falling. These findings have potential implications for the design of psychomotor interventions for fall prevention in older adults. Implementing analogy learning could be a beneficial strategy to facilitate improved walking abilities in geriatric rehabilitation settings.

17603318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17603318.value: Only analogy training led to significant improvements in single-task and dual-task walking abilities. We suggest that expert-designed analogy instructions be considered when training walking abilities of at-risk older adults. This is especially important because dual-task demands commonly occur in daily walking, where concurrent tasks require attention (e.g., walking while talking or navigating obstacles). When dual-task walking ability is compromised, fall risks are heightened. Thus, enhancing this ability could be critical to preventing falls among at-risk older adults. While there appears to be no effect of training on conscious motor processing, it is possible that our measurement instrument (i.e., MSRS-C) was insufficiently sensitive to detect real-time changes. Recent research found that MSRS-C scores of community-dwelling older adults are not associated with neurophysiological measures of brain activity (i.e., electroencephalography [EEG]) when walking. Future studies could measure real-time conscious motor processing through neurophysiological methods (e.g., EEG, functional near-infrared spectrum imaging) to confirm/refute the notion that training could affect conscious motor processing. Due to COVID-19, we could not meet our target sample size and did not have sufficient retention data to analyse. When the public health situation stabilises, further work is recommended to examine the long-term effects of training on walking abilities.

17603318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17603318.value: Walking is the most common daily activity where older adults are at risk of falling. Older adults who experience movement difficulties and/or fear of falling during walking tend to redirect their attention to how they move, and consciously monitor their movements. However, previous research has shown that such conscious monitoring can cause movement disruption, which can subsequently cause movement failure and increase the risk of falling. Because it is unknown whether training can ameliorate older adults’ propensity for conscious monitoring of movement during walking, this research examined the effects of three expert-designed walking training protocols. We compared the effects of single-task, dual-task and analogy training for walking on the (a) propensity for conscious monitoring of movement, (b) mobility/balance, (c) multi-task walking ability, and (d) fear of falling among at-risk older adults. We found that all training protocols improved mobility/balance following training, but there were no effects on the propensity for conscious monitoring of movement and fear of falling. Only analogy training led to significant improvements in walking ability in single-task and dual-task conditions. The evidence suggests that training walking using analogy instructions is potentially useful to help older adults walk safely in multi-tasking conditions, such as when navigating environmental obstacles.

17603518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17603518.value: Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) programmes, in which students learn content subjects through their second/foreign language (L2), have become widespread worldwide. Many researchers have attempted to evaluate the effectiveness of CLIL programmes, yet very few have scrutinised the validity of assessments in CLIL. It has been argued that bilingual students perform cognitively demanding tasks in their first language (L1), and have established stronger links between various concepts and their L1 than their L2. This issue raises the question of whether it is valid to assess CLIL students’ content knowledge through their less proficient language. The proposed experimental study will address this important yet under-explored question by examining the cognitive processes of teachers and students when they mark and complete CLIL assessments. It will be conducted in Hong Kong for its relatively long history of CLIL implementation and examination-oriented culture. The study will explore the cognitive processes of teachers and students through the eye-tracking method and stimulated recalls. Biology will be used as the subject context in designing the tasks, and 20 teachers and 80 students will be randomly selected from a stratified sample of schools. The teacher participants will mark three sample scripts, written in good English (L2), weak English and Chinese (L1), but expressing similar content. The student participants, comprising English native speakers, those with high- and low-English proficiency and those using Chinese to learn the subject, will read and complete a set of biology questions in either English or Chinese. The eye movements of the teacher and student participants will be recorded as they perform these tasks so as to capture their real-time thinking processes. Various eye movement measures (e.g. fixations and regressions) will be compared across the three scripts and four groups of students to reveal the potential role of language in mediating the participants’ cognitive processes. The participants will also attend stimulated recall interviews, which prompt their verbal reports of thinking processes to complement the eye-movement data. By adopting an innovative combination of methods to address an under-researched question in CLIL assessments, this study will contribute to the understanding of the possible role of language proficiency in assessing students’ content knowledge in CLIL. It will also demonstrate the different cognitive processes and strategies experienced by students with different levels of language proficiency. Considering the backwash effect of assessments, the findings of this study will have significant implications for effective teaching and learning in CLIL. 在學科内容與語言融合教學（CLIL）課程中，學生通過他們的第二語言（L2）學習非語文學科。對於這種已在全世界廣泛流行的課程，許多研究試圖評估其效能和影響，但鮮有研究審視其評估的效度。有研究曾發現當處理認知要求很高的任務時，雙語學生傾向使用他們的第一語言（L1），而他們記憶中的各種概念和他們第一語言之間的聯繫，往往比第二語言更強。這些發現令人懷疑在CLIL課程中，通過學生的第二語言來評估其學科知識是否有效。為解答這條重要的問題，本實驗研究將探討教師和學生在批改和作答CLIL評估試題時的認知過程。 本研究將在有較長實施CLIL歷史和應試文化的香港進行，研究人員將通過眼動追蹤方法 (eye-tracking) 和刺激回憶法(stimulated recalls)來探索教師和學生的認知過程。研究中的評估試題為生物科試題，參與者為從分層學校樣本中隨機選取的20名教師和80名學生。教師參與者將批改三個由研究人員撰寫的作答樣本，該三個樣本表達相似的內容，但分別以較精準的英語、較差的英語和中文書寫。學生參與者則分為四組，包括以英語為母語的學生、具有高英語水平和低英語水平的學生，以及使用中文為學習語言的學生，他們將閱讀並完成一些生物科的試題。教師和學生參與者在批改和作答試題過程中的眼球活動將會被記錄下來，以便捕捉他們的實時思考過程。而教師參與者在批改三個作答樣本，以及四組學生參與者在作答試題時的各種眼球活動數據（例如注視和回顧）將會被分析和比較，以揭示語言在參與者認知過程中的潛在作用。參與者還將參加以刺激回憶法進行的訪談，分享他們在實驗中的思考過程，以補充眼球活動的數據。 本研究通過採用創新的研究方法來解答CLIL評估的問題，研究結果將有助理解語言能力在評估CLIL學生的學科知識方面的角色，並展示具有不同語言水平的學生在評估過程中所經歷的不同認知過程和採取之策略。由於評估往往為學習與教學帶來「倒流效應」，本研究的結果亦會對CLIL的教學效能提供重要的啟示。

17603518.label: Realisation of objectives
17603518.value: The research project is contextualised in Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) programmes, where students learn non-linguistic content knowledge through their additional language (L2). Considering the under-researched area of assessment of students’ content knowledge in their L2, this project seeks to examine whether and how “language” i.e., students’ less proficient L2 would mediate their cognitive processes and performance, as well as teachers’ marking. Research methodology Approach 1: Eye-tracking experiments and stimulated recall interviews To explore the real-time cognitive processes of teachers and students when marking and tackling assessment questions in their L2, the eye-tracking technology was employed. 81 university students were recruited to complete 6 carefully selected multiple choice questions and one 3-part data-based structured questions for the subject of Biology. After the eye-tracking experiment, participants were invited to attend stimulated recall interviews to tap into their cognitive processes and strategies. At the same time, 10 teacher participants were recruited to mark three carefully designed answer scripts addressing one 3-part data-based structured question in Biology. The designed answer scripts included one written in Chinese (L1), one in proficient English and one in less proficient English. Again, the teachers’ eye-tracking experiment was followed by a stimulated recall interview. The number of teacher participants was lower than expected, mainly because it was extremely difficult to ask the teachers to perform the experiment in the eye-tracking laboratory in the University, especially during the repeated periods of school suspension and online teaching (when the study was conducted between 2019 and 2021). Approach 2: Analysis of academic performance and written scripts During the period of school suspension where data collection with teachers and students could not be conducted, the research team analysed the academic performance and written scripts of students taking the Biology public examination in their L2, with the data solicited from the Hong Kong Examinations and Assessment Authority. First, the performance of 480 students (half taking the test in their L1 and half in their L2 English) on the questions with different cognitive and linguistic demands was compared so as to examine the mediating effect of language of testing on students’ performance in assessments. Second, 204 essay scripts written by a stratified sample of students in L2 in the Biology examination were analysed with multidimensional analysis, so as to examine the potential relationship between their academic performance and their academic literacy. The findings of this approach could complement and elaborate the findings of the eye-tracking experiments in approach 1. Findings With regard to research objective 1, although the sample size of teacher participants was relatively small, some interesting findings were observed. Comparing their eye movement measures when marking the three sample scripts, teachers had the least and shortest fixations (the duration that eyes remain still) and regressions (the backward movement of eyes) when marking answers scripts in L1 Chinese. These imply that teachers may undergo more cognitive processes when marking answer scripts in their L2. They also needed to re-read and spend more time to understand scripts written in less proficient English. Stimulated recall interviews revealed that teachers tended to locate subject specific words and academic vocabulary specified in the marking rubrics. All teacher participants mentioned that language mistakes such as grammatical inaccuracy would not affect their marking, unless those mistakes impeded meaning expression. Interestingly, when comparing the scores that the teachers gave to the scripts, the mean score for the script written in proficient L2 was the highest, followed by that written in L1 and then in less proficient L2. However, the three scripts were designed in a way that they covered all the necessary “points” in the marking rubrics, and hence they should get the full score. The eye-tracking data, together with the average scores given to the three scripts, seem to suggest that content subject teachers did take L2 proficiency into consideration when marking students’ assessments, although subconsciously. With regard to research objective 2, the data collected from the eye-tracking experiments with student participants were analysed with mixed ANOVAs. We were interested in the effect of students’ L2 proficiency on their eye movement patterns, which in turn reflected their cognitive processes. For multiple-choice questions, the more L2 proficient participants in general had fewer and shorter fixations, fewer regressions and shorter regression duration. For the structured question, the patterns were less consistent, with the more proficient participants having shorter fixation duration, but more fixations, more regressions and longer regression duration than the less proficient group. There was an intriguing interaction effect between L2 proficiency and linguistic demands on regression duration, with more proficient participants manifesting longer regression duration when attempting productive questions (i.e., structured questions) than receptive questions (i.e., multiple choice questions), while less proficient participants showing an opposite trend. Such interaction effects may be explained in different dimensions. When attempting receptive questions (i.e., multiple-choice questions in this study), students needed to read the questions and four options so as to choose the correct option. Comparatively speaking, there was more “language “to read, which may prompt the less proficient participants to go back to previous parts of the question and read again. When it comes to the productive questions (i.e., the structured question in this study), there was less language to read. The regressions that took place may not be highly related to comprehending the question itself, but more concerned about looking for clues in the scenario and constructing their responses. In this way, the more proficient group may spend more time than the less proficient group. Despite the differences in eye movement patterns between proficient and less proficient students, they reported similar strategies when attempting assessments in their L2 during the stimulated recall interviews. The most common strategies for both groups included locating keywords in the questions, eliminating incorrect options for multiple choice questions, skipping redundant contextual information in the structured question, and focusing on the mark allocation to decide the length of the answers. These examination-oriented strategies could be regarded as students’ attempts to reduce the cognitive load of processing redundant L2, thereby lowering the language demand. The analysis of students’ academic performance in the public examination shows that students taking the Biology examination in their L2 were adversely affected by an amalgam of cognitive and productive linguistic demands. That is, their performance was significantly suppressed when they attempted cognitively demanding questions that required them to express their answers in sentences or short texts. These statistical findings could be further corroborated by the textual analysis of students’ written essays. Our multidimensional analysis shows that the essays produced by students with better overall subject grade (i.e., academic achievement) were more similar to academic texts, consisted of denser and more abstract information and used more academic vocabulary, nominalisation, conjunctions, and passive voice. These findings demonstrate a potential relationship between students’ mastery of academic literacy and their academic achievement in L2. Taking all these results together, this project demonstrates the mediating effect of students’ L2 proficiency level on their cognitive processes when attempting assessments of content knowledge in their L2 and hence their “products” such as the written essays and eventually their academic performance. At the same time, students’ L2 proficiency appears to affect teachers’ marking processes and scores they give. These together address research objective 3.

17603518.label: Major findings and research outcome
17603518.value: This study aims to examine the role of language (or language proficiency) in assessment of students’ content subject knowledge in Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) programmes, where they learn content knowledge through their less proficient additional language (L2). A total of 10 science teacher educators and teachers, and 81 university students in Hong Kong were recruited to participate in this study. They all participated in carefully designed eye-tracking experiments and follow-up stimulated recall interviews to capture their cognitive processes and strategies when grading or attempting Biology assessments in their L2. To complement the laboratory-based experiments, students’ performance in Biology public examination was examined to reveal the potential impact of language, and their written essays were analysed with multidimensional analysis in terms of their genres and language features. The results show that while teachers reported paying attention mainly to the content of students’ responses, their eye movement patterns and scores given to the designed scripts revealed the impact of language, with less difficulty in reading and higher scores given to scripts written in more proficient L2. Students having higher and lower L2 proficiency reported similar strategies when comprehending assessment questions, but the former group generally had less difficulty understanding the questions. They instead spent more time formulating their answers which may be more elaborate than the less proficient group. The performance and scripts of stratified sample of students in the public examination also revealed that students studying through their L2 were adversely affected in their academic performance. There seems to be a correlation between their mastery of L2 academic literacy and their academic performance. To conclude, this research study demonstrates the mediating role of language (or language proficiency) in assessing students’ content knowledge or academic achievement in CLIL programmes. In particular, students with lower L2 proficiency may have more difficulty understanding the assessment questions, formulating elaborate responses to the questions, especially those requiring higher-order cognitive skills, and expressing their ideas with appropriate academic language. The same mediating effect was also observed during teachers’ marking process. All these have important implications for valid design of assessment questions and teacher education in CLIL programmes. The major findings of this study have been presented at two international conferences and published in two international journal articles. Another manuscript is currently under review by an international journal. Part of the major findings will also be incorporated into a sole-authored book (see Part C for details).

17603518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17603518.value: When analysing students’ cognitive processes and written scripts, one interesting finding is their examination-oriented strategies, particularly how to make good use of key words and non-linguistic clues in the questions, such as the pictures and graphs. These indeed align with the proposition that meaning is not construed with the language mode only, but in combination with other modes or semiotic resources. Hence, one potential area for further research is to examine the role of multimodal resources when assessing students’ content knowledge, particularly how non-linguistic modes may relieve the potential language barriers in L2. The PI has already put in a proposal for this research idea. Regarding CLIL teachers, the results of this study revealed some discrepancies between what they believed (e.g., prioritising content in assessment) and what they actually did when marking assessments (e.g., favouring scripts written in more fluent and accurate L2). This may reflect teachers’ lack of knowledge about how to assess students in CLIL, which is also known as their assessment literacy. This notion is believed to be a key component of teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge and hence an important area to further explore. The PI is currently doing a project conceptualising and capturing CLIL teachers’ assessment literacy.

17603518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17603518.value: In Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) programmes, students learn content subjects through an additional language (L2), and their content knowledge is often assessed in their less proficient L2. This study aims to examine the potential role played by students’ L2 proficiency level when teachers grade students’ assessments and when students tackle assessments in their L2. 10 Science teachers and 81 university students participated in eye-tracking experiments and stimulated recall interviews, and the scores and scripts of a stratified sample of students taking the public examination in L2 were also examined. The results showed that teachers did not explicitly mark students’ language performance, but students’ L2 proficiency did mediate the scores they gave. Students generally adopted some examination-oriented strategies to comprehend the assessment questions quickly, but students with different L2 proficiency levels had different cognitive processes when comprehending questions and formulating their written responses. Students’ examination results were adversely affected when they were required to answer in sentences or short texts, probably because they had to express their ideas in appropriate academic language. These findings demonstrate the mediating role of language when assessing students’ content knowledge in CLIL programmes, thereby yielding important implications for assessment design and teacher education.

17603918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17603918.value: My project will explore the clash between antitrust legislation, a body of law originally designed to address market failures in Western democracies, and China, an economic superpower under authoritarian control. Set against the backdrop of China’s increasing integration with the globalized market, the project will analyze the significant challenges that Chinese antitrust regulation poses to foreign multinational companies doing business in China. It will chronicle those challenges and unravel their complex network of causes. By showing that the conflicts we observe on the surface are in fact deeply rooted in institutional factors, my research will offer a cautionary tale of the challenges that globalization poses to law and the economic order. Thus far, most academic attention to Chinese antitrust law has focused on formal rules, procedures, and precedents. Few studies have examined the informal rules and extralegal factors that may also play an important role in driving law enforcement outcomes. My project will be the first to examine how key institutional factors, such as bureaucratic politics, reputation, and the media, can influence antitrust enforcement outcomes in China. It will analyze the incentive structure of Chinese administrative agencies, the constraints that they face when operating within the country’s vast bureaucratic system, the tactics that they use to establish their legal authority, and the reputation sanction on firms subjected to antitrust investigations, as well as the role the media plays in law enforcement. Although my project will focus on antitrust law, its findings will have implications beyond the law. The idiosyncrasies in Chinese antitrust enforcement will serve as a reminder of how distinct China is from the rest of the world, and how important it is for the financial, legal, and political communities to fully recognize that distinction and prepare for the complex challenges involved. My project’s anticipated output is a monograph systematically examining the institutional issues in the enforcement of Chinese antitrust law and two peer-reviewed articles. 我的项目将探讨反垄断立法，一部最初旨在解决西方民主国家市场失灵的法律与中国这个专治控制下的经济超级大国之间的冲突。在中国与全球化市场日益融合的背景下，该项目将分析中国反垄断监管对在中国开展业务的外国跨国公司所面临的重大挑战。它将记录这些挑战并解开其复杂的原因网络。通过表明我们在表面上观察到的冲突实际上深深扎根于制度因素，我的研究将提供一个关于全球化对法律和经济秩序构成的挑战的警示故事。到目前为止，大多数学术界对中国反垄断法的关注都集中在正式的规则，程序和先例上。很少有研究检查过非正式规则和法外因素，这些因素也可能在推动执法结果方面发挥重要作用。我的项目将是第一个研究官僚政治，声誉和媒体等关键制度因素如何影响中国反垄断执法结果的项目。它将分析中国行政机构的激励结构，他们在国家庞大的官僚体制中运作时所面临的制约因素，他们用来建立法律权威的策略，以及对遭受反垄断调查的公司的声誉制裁，以及媒体在执法中的作用。虽然我的项目将侧重于反垄断法，但其研究结果将超出法律范围。中国反垄断执法的特质将提醒人们中国与世界其他地区的区别，以及金融，法律和政治界充分认识到这种区别并为所涉及的复杂挑战做好准备的重要性。我的项目预期成果是一本专着，系统地研究了中国反垄断法执行中的制度问题和两篇文章。

17603918.label: Realisation of objectives
17603918.value: My project has fulfilled exploring the main objectives as per my original application. First, through extensive interviews with government officials working at different antitrust agencies, I was able to present a complex network of Chinese administrative agencies involved in the enforcement of Chinese antitrust law. I found that antitrust enforcement is a pluralistic process involving many different government departments. As such, the bureaucratic missions, cultures and structure of an antitrust authority can affect its enforcement priority and agenda. I also identify a consensus-building process among enforcers during merger enforcement. Looking ahead, I explained how the power fragmentation in the Chinese bureaucracy will continue to challenge Chinese antitrust enforcement in the years to come. Second, by searching for relevant news articles using Wisenews database, I found that Chinese antitrust agencies are adept at applying media strategies and found that they regulate firms through strategic shaming sanctions. My interviews with various case handlers, as well as the reading of the relevant news articles and the final decisions of the cases show that Chinese authorities are aware of the potential negative market consequences once a firm is subject to an antitrust investigation, and could strategically leak news to the state media depending on the firms’ level of cooperation. This entices firms to cooperate with the government and deters them from challenging the government authority. Third, with the help from my research assistants, I analyzed the market reactions to the antitrust authority’s strategic announcement of an antitrust investigation and the penalty decision which followed. I found that for many firms (whether domestic or foreign) under investigation, the stock market would react very negatively if the agencies made a high-profile announcement of its investigation. In an extreme example, a firm lost over one-third of its market capitalization within one week after such an announcement. This creates very strong chilling effects for companies ever thinking about challenging the agency, which helps explain the paucity of appeals against the government’s decision. Fourth, by reading and coding thousands of relevant news article I found on Wisenews, I found that media bias can be driven by both supply and demand factors. On the one hand, the government can act as a whistle blower and leak information to the media to shame firms under investigation. On the other hand, Chinese readers are also biased as they are more interested in reading news relating to price reduction rather than about the legal merits of a case. This explains why media reports focus heavily on whether companies had volunteered to offer price reduction and whether such promises from companies have been carried out in practice, rather than whether an agency had a solid basis in bringing those cases. Lastly, my research findings show that it is important to appoint an agency that is familiar with law enforcement and due process requirements to enforce antitrust law. As media exposure can have such a big impact on a firm’s market value, it is important that the agency applies a consistent approach in deciding when and how to make an announcement of its investigation. More transparency should be introduced to curb administrative discretion.
