17607018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17607018.value: Music - often played in the background as an accompaniment to everyday activities - is known to be powerful in modulating emotion, changing behaviors, and affecting task performance and engagement. It is socially acceptable, inexpensive, ubiquitous and popular among students from primary school to university, and thus has unique potential for benefiting these students's learning. The effects of music on learning, particularly learning performance and engagement, have been studied in education, psychology, and neuroscience, but largely inconsistent findings call for new evidence at both behavioral and physiological levels. With rapid developments in digital music, music computing and retrieval technologies, large quantities and varieties of musical pieces can now be computationally analyzed and automatically recommended to individual listeners based on their tastes and needs. With the ultimate goal of optimizing music listening for learning, this project combines the powers of experimental and computational approaches to investigate: 1) how background music affects learning performance and engagement at both behavioral and physiological levels, and 2) to what extent the effects of background music can be predicted from acoustic features of music and learners' individual traits. Our interdisciplinary team will fulfill the objectives of this project by analyzing both behavioral and physiological data collected through two user experiments involving two types of learning tasks performed with computationally selected, ecologically valid, and personalized music in the background. The two task types are verbal memory as a fundamental learning mechanism, and reading comprehension as an essential activity in everyday learning. In each experiment, physiological signals, such as high-density electroencephalogram (EEG), heart rate, and skin conductance, will be collected from a background-balanced sample of 50 university students, together with learning performance and self-reported engagement levels. Besides statistical tests on the effects of different constructs (e.g., types of music) involved, advanced computational methods will be applied to analyze EEG signals from functionally distinct brain regions, extract salient physiological features, and construct machine learning models to analyze the relationships between learning performance, engagement, physiological signals, music acoustic features and individual traits (e.g., personality, music preferences). This project is innovative in 1) investigating the effects of background music on learning at both behavioral and physiological levels; 2) exploring music and learning with ecologically valid music and learning tasks; and 3) using advanced computational and signal processing methods. The project will contribute to theories on music and learning, interdisciplinary research methodology, and practical strategies for optimizing learning with music. 音樂時常以背景音樂的形式伴隨日常活動，並能有效地 調節情緒、改變行為及影響各種任務的表現和投入度 。音樂的社會接受程度好、價格低廉、普及度廣，以及受不同年紀的學生所歡迎，因此擁有利於學生學習的獨有潛力。教育、心理學及神經科學等領域曾研究音樂對學習的影響，尤其是在學習表現及投入度兩方面，但往往得出不一致的研究結果，因而需要行為及生理層面的新證據。隨著數碼音樂、音樂計算及檢索技術的急速發展，大量各式各樣的音樂作品可透過電腦技術分析，並根據聽眾的偏好及需求進行自動推薦。是次研究旨在為學習優化對音樂的聆聽 ，結合實驗及計算的方法來探討：一) 背景音樂在行為及生理層面如何影響學習表現及投入度 ，二) 音樂的聲學特徵及學習者的特點在多大程度下能預測背景音樂的影響。 為實現研究目標, 是次研究將會進行兩輪用戶實驗，分別涉及兩種學習任務: 作為基本學習機制的言語記憶及作為日常學習中必要活動的閱讀理解。而所測試的背景音樂將由計算方法個人化訂製並確保符合真實場景。實驗將收集大學生參與者的生理訊號，包括心率和皮膚電導，學習表現及投入度。除了用統計檢驗查看不同因素（如：音樂的種類）的影響，是次研究亦會應用先進的計算方法來提取顯著的生理特徵並建構機器學習模型，從而分析學習表現、投入度、生理訊號、音樂的聲學特徵和學習者的個人特點（如個性及音樂偏好）之間的關係。 是次研究的創新性在於 1) 以行為及生理層面來探索背景音樂對學習的影響、2) 以符合真實場景的音樂及學習任務探討音樂和學習、3) 運用先進的計算及訊號處理方法。是次研究成果將有效推動有關音樂和學習的理論、跨學科的研究方法、以及透過音樂優化學習的實用策略等方面的發展。

17607018.label: Realisation of objectives
17607018.value: Objective 1. To investigate how background music affects learning performance and engagement at both behavioral and physiological levels To fulfill this objective, we conducted two user experiments on reading with background music (BGM). Both were carefully controlled experiments in laboratory with between-group and within-group designs respectively. The first experiment (experiment #1) involved 100 participants, with half of them reading with background music (the experimental group) while the other half without music (the control group). During the experiment, participants’ reading logs, self-reported metacognition and emotion status were recorded, so were physiological signals of the participants during the whole experiment and the eye movement data when they read the given text passages. We compared measures on reading comprehension performance, metacognition and emotion changes between the two groups. Results showed no salient differences on passage comprehension accuracy or metacognition between the two groups. Comparisons on fine-grained eye movement measures revealed that BGM imposed heavier cognitive load during reading on post-lexical processes (e.g., combining linguistic information with contextual cues) but not on lexical processes (e.g., recognizing a word). Results of statistical analyses and interviews also revealed significant differences between the two groups in learners’ self-reported emotions and automatically measured physiological responses when the experimental group was exposed to classical, easy-listening, rebellious and rhythmic music. It was also found that fine-grained music characteristics (e.g., instrumentation, tempo) could predict learners’ emotions, pupillary, and physiological responses during reading comprehension. The expected contributions include: 1) providing empirical evidence for understanding the affective dimensions of learning with BGM, 2) applying multimodal learning analytics methods for examining the impacts of background music on learning, and 3) yielding practical implications for researchers, educators and students to improve learning through the use of background music. The second laboratory experiment (experiment #2) involved 33 graduate students in reading text passages under five controlled background audio conditions, including four types of music and one environmental sound. A series of cognitive, metacognitive, affective variables and physiological signals were collected and analyzed. Through a series of linear mixed models for data analysis, we found that, while music characteristics did not directly predict reading comprehension performance, BGM with different tempi and modes could lead to significantly different self-reported emotion measures, facial expressions, and physiological responses. On the other hand, music-induced emotions measured by self-reported valence, body temperature, and heart rate were significantly associated with reading comprehension performance. Therefore, through multiple modalities of emotion measures, this study establishes that background music characteristics have indirect effects on reading comprehension performance through the mediation of music-induced emotions. Findings of these experiments contribute to refining the current understanding of the effects of BGM on reading through providing evidence at both behavioral and physiological levels. They also have practical implications on music selection and music/learning system design for improving learning. Objective 2. To explore to what extent the effects of background music on learning can be predicted from the acoustic features of music and learners' individual traits To fulfill this objective, we further analyzed the data collected from the aforementioned user experiments. We extracted a range of acoustic features of music, including rhythm, pitch, timbre and genre. Statistical analyses and predictive modeling were conducted with these acoustic features and learners’ individual traits including cognitive capacities (e.g., working memory capacity, multitasking ability), music preferences, and usage of background music in learning occasions. In experiment #1, we analyzed the relationships between participants’ cognitive load and their personal traits. It was revealed that students with higher English proficiency or more frequent background music usage in daily self-learning/reading experienced less cognitive load when reading with background music, whereas students with a higher working memory capacity (WMC) invested more mental effort than those with lower WMC during learning with BGM. Moreover, we also built robust predictive models to predict learners’ cognitive load based on learner characteristics (e.g., WMC, English proficiency), eye movements, electrodermal activities, and heart rates in the context of reading with background music. Besides the aforementioned user experiments in the laboratory, we also conducted another two field studies where participants used BGM during self-learning in their own learning environment. To enable conducting remote experiments and data collection, we developed a mobile music discovery application, Moody, that could support learners searching for music by emotion and genre, playing and skipping music tracks, saving preferred tracks, and recording learners’ music interactions with the application as well as self-reported learning performances and engagement. The third experiment (experiment #3) was a field experiment with 30 participants who studied at their own paces and places for one week. During the experiment, participants were asked to perform learning sessions with music in the background and collect music tracks they deemed suitable for learning using Moody. A set of participant related, context-related, and music-related data were collected via a pre-experiment questionnaire, surveys popped up in the music app, and the logging system of the music app. Our findings demonstrated the power of music in fostering positive learning experience (e.g., perceived engagement) and revealed how some background music characteristics may be linked to perceived engagement in certain (but not all) conditions. Specifically, when studying with background music, tasks of a high mental or temporal demand may increase learners’ arousal level and task involvement. Learners’ attention might be mainly on the task itself and thus the effect of music would be less prominent. Under a low task load, on the other hand, learners might pay more attention to background music and were more likely to be influenced by the characteristics of music. For example, dynamic music helped keep learners from experiencing boredom, whereas bright music enhanced students’ task engagement. The fourth experiment (experiment #4) was also a field experiment and was conducted during the pandemic. Due to social distancing measures, we mailed experiment devices to 55 participants and monitored their music listening behaviors for two months. A new function of Moody was added to fetch mainstream music from Spotify, a music streaming platform popular among learners worldwide, to further improve the ecological validity of this study. Statistical tests and machine learning methods were adopted respectively for uncovering the associations between music listening and learning and for constructing a music recommendation model. Findings revealed positive associations between listening to music and learning engagement. In addition, learners’ music preference was found to be positively related to learning performance and engagement. Furthermore, machine learning modeling demonstrated promising results for developing a personalized music recommender for studying in naturalistic settings. These results contribute to research on not only learning with background music but also learning-oriented music recommendation. Unlike laboratory-based experiments that dominate existing studies on music and learning, the naturalistic experimental approach enables examining the effects of BGM in everyday, authentic learning settings. This higher level of ecological validity can only be achieved by the availability of a self-developed mobile app (e.g., Moody in this project) that enables both music listening behavior tracking and experience sampling. This project also leveraged audio processing techniques developed in the field of music information retrieval to extract fine-grained music features. The empirical evidence from these experiments verify and further refine theoretical research on BGM, and provide implications for generating personalized and context-sensitive background music selections and recommendation in music-enhanced learning environments.

17607018.label: Major findings and research outcome
17607018.value: Through rigorous literature reviews on physiological measures for affective learning (Ba & Hu, 2023), both lab-based (Que et al., 2023) and naturalistic (Li & Hu, 2023) user experiments, along with development of novel music systems (e.g., Liu et al., 2023), this project has improved theoretical understanding and yielded empirical evidence for the effects of background music (BGM) on learning. Our studies found that BGM could enhance learners' learning experience and performance (Hu et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2019), often through emotion modulation (Que et al., 2023). It was also found that learning with BGM could induce better engagement (Liu et al., 2023), but could also distract learners’ attention and impose heavier cognitive load (Que et al., 2023). Nevertheless, these effects also depended on several factors. First, fine-grained acoustic features, such as loudness, tempo, and instrumentation, were found to be correlated with learning performance (Li & Hu, 2023; Liu et al., 2023). Second, learners’ individual traits, including working memory capacity (Que et al., 2023) and personality (Hu et al., 2023), moderated their music-induced emotions and learning experience. Third, learner-preferred BGM was beneficial for maintaining positive emotions, without compromising learning performance (Que et al., 2020). Fourth, in both lab-based tasks (Que et al., 2020) and authentic learning contexts (Li & Hu, 2023), the benefits of BGM became more prominent on mentally or temporally less demanding tasks (Li et al., 2021). Our results also showed the interplay of these factors, such as that between the learners’ individual traits, acoustic features (e.g., Que et al., 2020) and types of learning tasks (Hu et al., 2019). Complementing self-report, this project has realized the methodological advancement of capturing learners’ music-induced emotions during learning through measuring their physiological signals (Que et al., 2023) and eye movements (Hu et al., 2019) using wearable devices (Ba & Hu, 2023), and the former can be predicted by the latter (Hu et al., 2023). This project has also demonstrated interdisciplinary and multimodal research methods on music and learning, collecting wide-ranging data sources: self-reports, music and its properties, system logs, learning performances, and physiological signals (Ba & Hu, 2023; Li et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Que et al., 2020). For practical contributions, our findings have produced design implications for personalized recommendations in music services (Que et al., 2020), including those potentially incorporating emotion-related physiological input (Hu et al., 2018; Liu & Hu, 2020).

17607018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17607018.value: Multiple directions have been attempted to further develop the research. First, additional modalities of data can be taken into consideration, such as neurological signals of learners. With the reactivation of the Neuroscience for Education (NfE) lab facilities in the Faculty, we have piloted a new experiment collecting electroencephalography (EEG) data from learners and analyzing their relationships with BGM and learning performances. Another modality we have started analyzing is the facial expression of learners, where the fine-grained units of facial movements can be calculated for recognizing learners’ emotion. Second, more types of learning tasks can be studied beyond reading comprehension. We have tried examining a novel task of viewing virtual reality scenes where BGM is often used to enhance viewers’ experience. Third, given the rise of generative AI, we can further explore the effect of AI-generated BGM on learning. Lastly, computer or mobile applications can be developed based on findings of this project, for learners to optimize their learning with music in daily life. For example, BGM recommenders can incorporate learners’ physiological signals and music listening histories to find BGM conducive to their learning scenarios.

17607018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17607018.value: Listening to background music (BGM) while learning is common among learners, yet its effects remain inconclusive, partly due to the limitations of behavioral measures dominating existing studies. This project innovatively involved physiological measures in this topic. Collected by cutting-edge wearable devices, physiological measures such as electrodermal activity and heart rate can reflect people’s learning-related affective status including concentration and frustration which can be modulated by BGM. Through conducting user experiments in laboratories and everyday settings, this project collected multiple modalities of learners’ data during reading and self-learning. Statistical analysis and predictive modeling showed the effect of BGM was influenced by the cognitive load of learning tasks, music types, and learners’ personal traits. Specifically, BGM did not affect reading comprehension performances as any increased cognitive load could be compensated by learners’ more positive emotion. BGM had stronger effects when the tasks were easier or less urgent, or when learners had a lower working memory capacity or multitasking ability. This project’s findings enrich theories of BGM on learning with evidence on both behavioral and physiological levels, and from both laboratory and naturalistic settings. They also yield practical implications for optimizing learning with BGM.

17607418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17607418.value: My research seeks to produce a comprehensive account of how the doctrine of mistake operates within different substantive areas of private law and whether the different rules and remedies available to relieve a mistaken transfer can be rationalised to develop a more coherent framework for the law of mistake. It examines all the private law contexts in which a mistake may arise. The research is doctrinal and comparative in approach, and will contribute significantly to our understanding of the policy goals of different areas of law, of the interaction between law and equity, and of the possibility of postulating a rational and coherent law of mistake. 此研究旨在全面闡述錯誤原則於不同私法領域中的運用，以及理順受錯誤影響的財產轉移之不同規則和濟助的可能性。錯誤在私法背景下如何產生亦會被探討。此研究將以原則性和比較性角度顯著地增進我們對不同法律領域的政策目標、普通法與衡平法的相互影響及擬定一個合理和連貫的錯誤原則的可能性的認知。

17607418.label: Realisation of objectives
17607418.value: Objective 1: I carried out research on the doctrine of mistake in Contract Law in major Common Law jurisdictions (including Hong Kong, England and Singapore). Several recent high-profile mistake cases were also examined. A book chapter will be published by an international publisher in due course following an international conference on the subject. Objective 2: I carried out research to study the equitable and statutory doctrine of mistake and its role in relieving trustees’ mistakes in tax planning in major offshore jurisdictions including Jersey and Cayman Islands. Specifically, I reviewed how offshore jurisdictions have received the doctrine of equitable mistake in the post-Pitt v Holt era, including the requirements for pleading mistake, the relevance of the doctrine of unconscionability. An inventory of materials has been collected. Objective 3: I applied the research findings from Objectives 1 and 2 to examine the interaction between the operation of mistakes in different areas of private law, focusing on how the rules of mistake operate in different settings. I analysed the role, function and operation of mistake in different private law areas. Specifically, in the context of trusts and succession, I considered the English and offshore cases where mistakes have occurred in aggressive tax avoidance schemes and their impact on freedom of testation in trusts. Further, given that the doctrine of mistakes in equity is able to absolve trustees from the consequences of even gross negligence (which is considered to be not inconsistent with the trustee’s core obligations), I also examined the irreducible core of obligations owed by the trustees to the beneficiaries which is fundamental to the concept of a trust. Objective 4: I applied the research findings to determine the impact of the above developments on the prospects for the development of a rational and coherent mistake framework. Whilst I have considered the possibility of a unified approach to the doctrines of mistake for the equitable jurisdiction for voluntary dispositions and unjust enrichment on the basis of the policy of protection of autonomy by relieving transferors of the consequences of vitiated consent, I note the difficulties of a unified approach for contract and unjust enrichment because of the different levels of risk-taking involved in contractual bargains vis a vis gifts which suggests that contractual bargains should not be easily set aside compared to gifts. I was unable to fully utilise the research funding, largely because of the inability to spend the funding on conference expenses. My research project coincided with extended periods of disruptions and travel bans caused by the territory-wide social unrest in 2019 and the covid-19 pandemic since 2020. As a result, many all my scheduled conference trips were cancelled. The research findings were presented in international conferences (mostly online), and have been / will be published in 1 journal article and 2 book chapters. The book chapters were invited participation in book projects based on high-level academic conferences participated by eminent academics in the field and published with prestigious academic press in Law. Publication of the book chapters, which involved coordination by the editors with contributors from other jurisdictions, was delayed because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

17607418.label: Major findings and research outcome
17607418.value: I have made the following theoretical findings about this area of law as follows :- (1) Hong Kong courts have gone even further than their English counterparts in entrenching a restrictive doctrine of mistake in contract law to ensure commercial certainty and protection of freedom of contract. (2) Since Pitt v Holt; Futter v Futter, both the English and offshore courts have viewed aggressive trust planning and tax avoidance schemes with great circumspection. The court’s attitude on mistakes in tax planning will impose limits on freedom of testation in trusts and succession law. (3) Given that the doctrine of mistakes in equity is able to absolve trustees from the consequences of even gross negligence (which is considered to be not inconsistent with the trustee’s core obligations), the irreducible core of obligations owed by the trustees to the beneficiaries which is fundamental to the concept of a trust should be redefined. Specifically, insofar as professional trustees are concerned, the duty to act honestly and in good faith should entail a duty to perform the trust honestly on an objective standard and in good faith which, in particular, requires him to not act gross negligently. This would have an impact on whether trustees should be relieved for gross negligence mistakes in tax planning. (4) The prospects for the development of a rational and coherent mistake framework should be re-assessed. In view of the different policy goals of the different areas of private law, it would be difficult to have a unified doctrine of mistake. Rather, a sliding but coherent scale of difficulty in setting aside transactions on the ground of mistakes could be considered. I attended several international conferences to disseminate the research findings. I was able to publish 3 journal article/book chapters as stated in the objectives.

17607418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17607418.value: My research project examined the major private law contexts in which a mistake may arise. It showed that there were different policy goals in different areas of law. For example, the need to ensure commercial certainty and protection of freedom of contract; the need to impose limits on freedom of testation to avoid abuse of the doctrine in correcting mistakes in tax planning; the need to delineate the irreducible core duties of the trustees to ensure trustees are not absolved from all instances of mistakes. These research findings led to the conclusion that, given the variety of policy goals underlying the doctrine of mistake in different areas of private law, a unified doctrine of mistake may be difficult, but rather a coherent sliding scale of difficulty in setting aside transactions on the ground of mistake may be considered. My research led to the publication of conference papers, book chapters and journal article which has enriched the intellectual debate both locally and internationally.

17608018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17608018.value: Beethoven is popularly known in the history of music as 'The Man who Freed Music'. This idea conflates musical autonomy with human autonomy, and aligns Beethoven's heroic image with the Enlightenment narrative of secular humanism. Although often unacknowledged, this framework forms the basis for the interpretation of the composer's life and works, particularly from the later nineteenth-century onwards. However, there is no historical basis of this narrative of secularisation; the sweeping tale of Enlightenment freedom jars with the local details of Beethoven's life in Bonn and Vienna which were conditioned by Catholic thought and practices under the reforms of Joseph II. Indeed, the idea of a Enlightenment despot, such as Joseph II, who held both sovereign power and religious authority stands at variance with the image of the heroic Beethoven who is largely is based on the French model of the Enlightenment with its anti-clerical and anti-monarchist revolution. Current research on the Enlightenment has also pointed out the anomaly of positioning the French narrative as the dominant definition; there were different 'Enlightenments' most of which were 'religious Enlightenments'. In this context, Beethoven has clearly been mis-placed or dis-placed from his own 'Enlightenment'. Beethoven's religious position requires re-evaluation. But the stakes are high due to the investment in the secular myth; the religious question cuts to the very core of some of its most cherished values - freedom, humanity, progress and autonomy. The project does not seek to replace existing values (since this is part of Beethoven's reception history) but to complicate it in order to prevent simple dichotomies between religious and radical thought, or sacred and secular meaning. Such dichotomies, currently prevalent in Beethoven scholarship, flatten out the issues and fail to represent the nuanced intellectual climate at the time. To date there is no serious attempt to understand Beethoven's religious position in the Austrian Enlightenment; and hermeneutic readings of his works are based on false dichotomies that cannot square the secular Beethoven with his religious music. The projects aims to: (i) evaluate the 'secular narrative' in current research and its use of archival sources to bolster the narrative (ii) understand Beethoven's music in a more complex context that holds in tension the sweep of intellectual history and the details of local history (iii) provide a more nuanced understanding of the religious context in Bonn and Vienna (iv) provide new hermeneutic readings for understanding Beethoven's works in the light of objectives 1, 2 and 3. 貝多芬在音樂史上被稱為“解放音樂的人”。這種觀念將音樂自律性與人類自主性融合在一起，並將貝多芬的英雄形象與世俗人文主義的啟蒙敘事聯繫起來。雖然經常不被意識到，但這個框架構成了對作曲家生活和作品解釋的基礎，特別是從十九世紀後期開始。然而，這種世俗化的敘述沒有歷史基礎。傳說中啟蒙自由的故事與貝多芬在波恩和維也納當地受到約瑟夫二世改革下的天主教思想和實踐製約的生活細節並不一致。事實上，擁有主權和宗教權威的像約瑟夫二世這樣的啓蒙專制者的觀念與英雄貝多芬的形像绝不相符，後者主要是基於反教士和反君主制革命的法國模式的啟蒙運動。 目前關於啟蒙運動的研究也指出了將法國敘事定位為主導定義的問題。當時有不同的“啟蒙運動”，其中大多數是“宗教啟蒙運動”。在這種情況下，貝多芬明顯被錯誤地置於他自己的“啟蒙運動”之外。貝多芬的宗教立場需要重新評估。但由於世俗傳說的影響令這一重估關係重大。宗教問題切入了價值觀的核心——自由、人性、進步和自律。 該項研究並不尋求取代現有的價值觀（因為這是貝多芬接受歷史的一部分），而是使其複雜化，以防止宗教和激進思想之間的簡單二分，或神聖和世俗的庸俗對立。目前貝多芬研究中普遍存在的這種二分法，使問題變得過於簡單，並且無法傳遞當時微妙的思想氛圍。

17608018.label: Major findings and research outcome
17608018.value: Four broad themes (i.e. research outcomes) recur throughout the chapters listed above. Almost all of the essays address at least two of these themes. These commonalities ensure a strong sense of coherence for the book as a whole. I use 'we' rather than 'I' below because the work was done in discussion over many Zoom meetings with the authors to hone the outcomes. 1. Bonn and the Enlightenment Bonn, in the Beethoven narrative, is the site and seed of Beethoven’s Enlightenment credentials. So we have made an important ‘intervention’ that should change the usual narrative. Of particular interest here is the inclusion of the religious element: Bonn experienced a religious Enlightenment. 2. Understanding the Enlightenment through Material Objects and Media Giving proper respect to objects is one way of revitalizing object-based historical research. How do these objects and their distribution, especially in the devotional practices of the Catholic Enlightenment, produce knowledge, disciplines and behaviors? The objects Beethoven collected and used can give insight into knowledge as a form of acquisition, as a type of discipline, as a religious practice. We position Beethoven (the subject) within a network of Enlightenment objects that form an often tacit epistemological structure to illumine the religious aspect of his life. 3. The Enlightenment and Enlightenments There is a tension between The Enlightenment as a single simple narrative that drives much of our scholarship in Beethoven studies (and musicology in general) and the fractured and distributed idea of Enlightenments as local, different and pluriform. Both are real, but in different ways. In teh book, we unmask this Enlightenment narrative to illuminate its detrimental effect on Beethoven studies, while at the same time acknowledging that it is part of the history of Beethoven reception. In doing so, we hope to complicate the religious component in this history. The Protestant/Catholic dynamic in Vienna reflects the same tension found in the single-Enlightenment/pluriform-Enlightenments conflict. 4. Deconstructed Enlightenments The Enlightenment is not a light in the darkness: it flickers. Concepts such as freedom, autonomy, independence, universal humanity, cosmopolitanism, tolerance, reason usually elicits their opposite to function – censorship, nationalism, exclusion, authoritarian rule, violence, enthusiasm (genius, sublime). These opposites are integral to the Enlightenment in in its various forms (as famously theorized in Adorno and Horkheimer’s Dialectic of the Enlightenment). In the book, we propose that the Enlightenment necessarily generates its own contradictions, paradoxes and negations, leading to complex consequences. This means that we can’t just reverse a narrative or switch Beethoven form one side to the other: all sides are implicated in a complex, impure, process.

17608018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17608018.value: Beethoven's heroic narrate does not just pertain to Beethoven himself: the composer stood as the representative of a larger discourse in Western music history. Re-evaluating Beethoven and the Enlightenment in a religious context challenges how we do music history and the stories we tell about its development in general. Below are some larger questions for research as a result of the present project. 1. What is the relation between cosmopolitanism and nationalism, or between universal concepts and exclusion? How is Beethoven woven into these relations both in his own time or subsequent reception? 2. Is Protestantism a vital supplement of the Catholic Enlightenment? How did the Protestant supplement take over Beethoven reception (and music historiography), ultimately suppressing the Catholic? 3. Is censorship inherently a mode of freedom? After all, Kantian freedom is a duty, a law; and autonomy is a self-binding discipline. Perhaps the ‘Enlightened despot’ is not a contradictory term but the very condition of the Enlightenment. 4. Does Beethoven, the Enlightened Catholic, because of his commitments to artistic beliefs in freedom and progress, contribute to the secularization of his own sacred works? After all, leading thinkers of this period generated both a right and left version of themselves: Hegel’s legacy does not only remain on the religious and political right but also results in Marx and Feuerbach. The same can be said of Kant. What about Beethoven?

17608018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17608018.value: Beethoven is the dominant figure in modern Western music history. He is portrayed as the 'Man who Freed Music' (Schauffler). In other words, he is the hero who emancipates music and sets the scene for its progress from the nineteenth-century onwards. This narrative is driven by a secular reading of the Enlightenment. However, a secular reading does not align with Beethoven's life or works; and great pains have been taken by scholars to suppress or explain away the religious dimension of Beethoven. In this project, instead of using a generalised secular Enlightenment as a framework, we place Beethoven in the intellectual and cultural sphere in which he lived - in the religious Enlightenment of Bonn and Vienna. By doing so, we are able to provide a clearer context for Beethoven's sacred works as part of the Enlightenment. In this historical approach, the dichotomy between the sacred and secular as conservative and progressive forces that undergirds much of Beethoven's scholarship no longer holds true, resulting in a more nuanced understanding of the composer and his music.

17608318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17608318.value: Collaboratively observing dialogic videos—an approach that combines dialogic videos with collaborative problem solving—is known to be effective for improving student learning outcomes. However, ensuring that young learners benefit from the videos is challenging. Students often lose focus when the content overwhelms them and many lack the skills to interact with others while observing. To address these issues, we propose the Analytics-Supported Collaborative Observation of Videos (ASCOV) approach, in which paired students observe videos of classroom lessons they have participated in and perform problem-solving tasks together. Students observe classroom videos through a video-observation platform that offers visual and analytic representations of lessons while automatically synchronizing the videos and transcripts. This analytic feature facilitates students’ viewing, reviewing, and reflection by reducing the cognitive load for non-learning-related activities. Drawing on theories of sociocultural learning and situated learning, which emphasize the importance of learning through scaffolding and interaction in a socially meaningful context, the approach features a Scaffolding Guide for Video-observation (SGV) in the platform, designed to promote student interaction while observing. Using a mixed-methods, quasi-experimental design, the project will evaluate the ASCOV approach and test its effectiveness with young learners. Eight middle schools will be sampled randomly in Hong Kong. In each school, two eighth-grade mathematics teachers, each of whom teaches two classes, will participate in the study with their students (for a total of 16 teachers, 32 classes, and approximately 960 students). One class of each teacher will be randomly assigned to the treatment and the other to the control condition. Students in both conditions will conduct problem-solving tasks in pairs during tutorial sessions of approximately 40 minutes held at one- or two-week intervals during the year; the treatment students will engage in analytics-supported collaborative video observation, while the control students will perform the same tasks through normal instruction. The project’s main activities will include (1) preparation and piloting, (2) a year-long student learning intervention to compare the treatment and control conditions, and (3) post- and delayed post-tests to measure the effect of the ASCOV approach on students’ engagement and achievement in mathematics. The proposed learning approach holds considerable promise. It could potentially transform classroom videos into reusable resources, encourage students to interact and collaborate with peers in and outside the classroom, enhance student performance in mathematics and other STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects, improve school efficacy, and lower education costs. 本項研究聚焦協同觀摩對話類視頻—一種被認為能夠有效地提高學生學業成果的方法。然而，這種方法在如何確保學生從中獲益方面依舊充滿挑戰。學生在面對大量視頻資源的觀摩中容易失去焦點及缺乏與他人溝通。為了解決這一問題，本研究基於社會文化學習及情景學習理論， 讓學生成對協同觀摩課堂視頻，並以可視化和學習分析支持來減輕他們的認知負荷並完成與學習相關的任務。 本項目採用混合研究的方式對此方法進行檢驗，研究其對於學習者的學習成效。項目將在每一所樣本學校抽取兩名數學老師和他們的學生，其中每個老師一個班級學生作為實驗組，另一個班級的學生作為等待組參與研究。在實驗進行的兩個學期中，實驗組的學生平均每一兩周將進行一次分析支持下的視頻協同觀摩學習活動，而等待組的學生將以相同頻率進行日常的教學活動。 項目的主要活動包括：1）准備及先導研究階段；2）為期一年的實驗比較兩組學生學業成就差別； 3）后測及延遲后測來測量此視頻協同觀摩對學生數學參與和成就的影響。本項研究利用視頻資源鼓勵學生互動及協同學習，它對於促進學生STEM等學科的學習、提高學校效能以及降低教育成本有著積極的意義。

17608318.label: Realisation of objectives
17608318.value: We have successfully fulfilled all the three research objectives of the project. To realize them, we conducted the following research activities: 1. To fulfill the first objective, we investigated the use of learning analytics for improving students’ collaborative discussions in the classroom and developed an analytics-supported collaborative observation of videos (ASCOV) approach and a video-observation platform. First, we identified a research gap in existing literature regarding young learners’ lack of dialogic skills for collaborative problem solving. We then conducted research synthesis on: a) the affordances of learning analytics for supporting students’ learning and discussions; b) a repository of productive talk moves that are useful for students’ group discussions. This work has been published in Educational Research Review and is under review in the Journal of Behavioral Education (^student author). Hu, L.^, & Chen, G. (2021). A systematic review of visual representations for analyzing collaborative discourse. Educational Research Review, 34, 100403. Hu, L^. & Chen, G. (under review, major revision). A systematic review and meta-analysis of productive peer talk moves. Journal of Behavioral Education. Second, we adapted the productive talk moves and developed them into analytics and visualizations in the video-observation platform as a guide for students to code, review, and reflect on peer discussions. Third, we discussed the ASCOV approach with two leading experts in the field and piloted the platform and the talk move analytics and visualizations with 24 teachers from a variety of schools. Based on the participants’ feedback, we refined the platform and added a participatory component in the video-observation platform to facilitate students’ awareness and engagement in using productive talk moves and their sense of equity in group discussions. Part of the work appears in the following publications. Chen, G., Chan, C. K. K., Chan, K. K. H., Clarke, S. N., & Resnick, L. B. (2020). Efficacy of video-based teacher professional development for increasing classroom discourse and student learning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 29(4-5), 642-680. Chen, G., & Chan, C. K. K. (2022). Visualization-and analytics-supported video-based professional development for promoting mathematics classroom discourse. Learning, Culture and Social Interaction, 33, 100609. Hu, L.^, Wu, J.^, & Chen, G. (2022). iTalk–iSee: A participatory visual learning analytical tool for productive peer talk. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. 2. To fulfill the second objective, we conducted empirical studies to investigate the effects of using the ASCOV approach on students’ engagement and achievement in learning mathematics. We first collected empirical data to understand students’ discourse patterns and strategies in collaborative problem solving. With the data from 168 participating students, we defined different patterns of student discourse at the turn level which are: 1) turn receivers (receiving the floor assigned by the last speaker), 2) turn-usurpers (usurping the floor when it was offered to another person), 3) turn-claimers (claiming the floor when it was opened to the whole group), and 4) turn-balancers (no strong turn-taking tendency). The turn-usurper pattern was found to be significantly correlated with their participation rates and academic performance. The findings highlighted the importance of ensuring students’ equitable access to the conversational floor in promoting equity and respect in collaborative problem solving. Hu, L.^, & Chen, G. (2021). Trajectories of idea emergence in dialogic collaborative problem solving: Toward a complex dynamic systems perspective. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 735534. Hu, L.^, & Chen, G. (2022). Exploring turn-taking patterns during dialogic collaborative problem solving. Instructional Science, 50(1), 63-88. We then conducted two empirical studies about the effectiveness of the ASCOV approach using a quasi-experimental design. In the first study, we investigated the effects of the new analytics and visualization framework of productive peer talk moves on students’ collaborative problem solving in mathematics. We found that the treatment students, who used the visualization and collaboration tool in groups to observe and reflect on their peer discussions had significant improvement in using productive peer talk moves from the pre- to post-test, relative to the comparison group. The treatment students also engaged in significantly more productive talk related to regulating group discussions and organizing problem-solving activities. In addition, they had more equitable dialogues with peers than the comparison group. Hu, L.^, Wu, J., & Chen, G. (2022). iTalk–iSee: A participatory visual learning analytical tool for productive peer talk. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. In the second study amid the COVID-19 pandemic, normal teaching was interrupted and face-to-face teaching in schools was forced to switch to emergency remote or online teaching from time to time. The change was challenging for this project involving extensive teaching and learning activities, but it was also an opportunity for the project to understand the resilience of such an ASCOV approach for its use in the online mode of teaching and learning in schools. So, we examined the effects of using the ASCOV approach with students to observe their online lesson videos while solving problems with their classmates in the online video-observation platform. Although the video sources for observation have changed to online lessons instead of face-to-face classroom lessons and tutorials, the principles of using the ASCOV approach for multiple representations, interactive and participatory visualizations, and view of discourse evidence in context still applied. In the experiment with two classes of students, we found that the ASCOV class that had analytics to support students’ collaborative observation of lesson videos reported higher motivation for discussing mathematics problems than the comparison class. In addition, the ASCOV class showed significant improvement in mathematics achievement from the pre- to post-test, relative to the comparison class. We concluded that the ASCOV approach is useful for enhancing students’ engagement in learning mathematics and their mathematics achievement. The findings have been presented in the in the International Society of the Learning Sciences Annual Meeting (ISLS 2022) and are under review in the British Journal of Educational Technology. Wang, P.^, Chen, G., Tong, Y.^, & Yang, C.^ (2022). Post-flipped classrooms: Designing a video-based visualization learning approach for supporting emergency remote teaching. Paper presented in the International Society of the Learning Sciences Annual Meeting (ISLS 2022). Hiroshima, Japan: International Society of the Learning Sciences. Wang, P.^, Tong, Y.^, Yang, C.^, & Chen, G. (under review). Supporting emergency remote teaching: A post-flipped video-based learning approach. British Journal of Educational Technology. 3. For the third objective, to understand how and why the ASCOV approach may influence student engagement and achievement, we conducted individual and group interviews with the participating teachers and the students. Based on the studies we conducted in the project, we find that the ASCOV approach is likely to drive students’ active learning by increasing students’ motivation and engagement in collaboration while reducing their non-learning related cognitive load. In addition, the data-based evidence afforded by the analytics- and visualization-supported approach may help young learners increase their awareness for more productive peer dialogues and more equitable social interactions in collaborative mathematics problem solving. The newly added participatory mode in the analytics in particular is likely to afford more such opportunities. More detailed explanations of the effectiveness are reported in Chen and Chan (2022), Hu, Wu, and Chen (2022), Wang, Chen, Tong, and Yang (2022), and Wang, Tong, Yang, and Chen (under review).

17608318.label: Major findings and research outcome
17608318.value: The project has at least four major findings. 1) The project showed that analytics and visualizations can be designed and developed to support students’ observation of classroom lessons and group interactions. The systematic review and meta-analysis identified four dimensions of visualization representations for analyzing collaborative discourse (i.e., goals, data sources, visualization designs, analytical techniques) and pointed out the inadequacy of merely mirroring collaborative discourse for visual representations. The findings contribute to the design of analytics-supported collaborative observation approaches (published in the Educational Research Review in 2021; SSCI, IF = 10.207). 2) This project studied students’ collaborative problem-solving process as complex dynamic systems and established a new analytical framework for understanding collaborative turn-taking patterns. Applying the framework to empirical classroom data, we find the respective ratio of the four participatory profiles (i.e., turn-receivers, usurpers, claimers, and balancers) and their significant correlations with students’ academic performance. The research findings provide suggestions for helping young learners improve their collaborative problem-solving skills and create a more equitable social and learning process (published in Frontiers in Psychology in 2021 [SSCI, IF = 4.232] and Instructional Science in 2022 [SSCI, IF = 2.255]). 3) The project identified a repository of productive peer talk moves after conducting a systematic review and meta-analysis, and then designed an analytics-supported collaborative observation of videos (ASCOV) tool to help students who work in groups to visualize discourse process, review, and reflect on group talk as well as enhance collaborative problem-solving engagement and learning outcomes. The tool has been found to be empirically effective while students apply the three-steps of code, visualize, and reflect on classroom discourse. The findings were published in the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (SSCI, IF = 5.611) in 2022 and are under review (with major revision) by Journal Behavioral Education (SSCI, IF = 2.469). 4) The project finds that the ASCOV approach is helpful for supporting emergency remote teaching (ERT) during the COVID-19 pandemic. While online teaching has been challenging in providing students interactive opportunities and social presence, the ASCOV approach and tool compensates for such constrains. The re-watching of classroom videos supported by analytics and visualizations of classroom videos can increase students’ learning engagement and achievement as a post-flipped classroom pedagogy. The findings were presented in the Annual Meeting of the International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS 2022, a prestigious international conference) and are under review by the British Journal of Educational Technology (SSCI, IF = 5.268).

17608318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17608318.value: Previous studies find that videos of classroom lessons and tutorials are useful for student learning. While students observe videos and solve problems together, they benefit from monitoring and coaching one another?s speech. However, studies also find that it is not always the case, especially for young learners?they may lack communication skills during collaborative problem solving. To address this problem and propose technological solutions using learning analytics and visualizations, we conducted rigorous reviews, developed an analytics-supported approach and web tools, and evaluated the effectiveness on improving student problem solving engagement and mathematics achievement. We found that a participatory model in the design of the analytics approach is important, which does not just mirror the dialogic process of lessons or tutoring. Relative to the comparison groups, students who participated in the analytics-supported dialogic collaborative problem-solving showed significant improvement in learning productive peer talk and had more equitable participation in collaboration. Meanwhile, we also found that during the COVID-19 pandemic when schools adopted online teaching, the analytics-supported collaborative observation of and discussion on classroom videos showed significant effects on improving students? mathematics achievement. This analytics-supported video-based learning approach has great potential to support students? learning during emergency remote teaching as well.

17608918.label: Realisation of objectives
17608918.value: This project aimed to conduct a three-arm randomised controlled trial to examine the efficacy of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) and adjunctive bright light therapy (BLT) in reducing insomnia severity in adolescents with insomnia and eveningness. Eligible participants were randomised into one of the following groups: CBT-I with adjuvant BLT (CBTI+BLT), CBT-I without adjuvant BLT (CBTI-BLT), and waitlist control (WL). Assessments were conducted at baseline / pre-treatment (Week 0), during the treatment (Week 2 and Week 4) and post-treatment (one-week after the last therapy session). The two active treatment groups were additionally followed up one month and six months after the intervention to examine the maintenance effects following the respective interventions (CBT-I with vs. without BLT). The project was completed with all objectives fully achieved. We have successfully recruited the targeted number of participants sufficiently powered to test the study hypotheses. We screened 207 potential participants, and 159 eligible participants were recruited and randomised in a simple 1:1:1 approach into one of the treatment arms: 54 were randomised to CBTI+BLT, 53 were randomised to CBTI-BLT, and 52 were randomised to a waitlist control. Most recruited participants were late adolescents (aged 20.1 ± 2.2 years, 55.3% female) and in tertiary education (n = 140, 88.1%). Across all groups, 68/159 (42.8%) met the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for insomnia disorder, whereas 91/159 (57.2%) met the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder. Mood disorders were the most common psychiatric comorbidities amongst the recruited participants, with 60 participants (37.7%) having either major depressive disorder or dysthymia. All three groups were comparable in demographic and clinical characteristics at baseline, demonstrating successful randomisation. The CBT-I programme consisted of six weekly sessions (90-minute each) conducted in a group format with an average of five participants per group. The group sessions were structured with the programme content addressing the behavioural, cognitive, and physiological perpetuating factors of insomnia. Participants in both intervention groups were instructed to wear a portable light therapy device (Re-Timer, Re-time, Inc, Adelaide, SA, Australia, https://www.re-timer.com) for 30 minutes daily immediately after awakening. Participants in the CBTI+BLT group received active BLT using the original Re-Timer, a pair of portable light glasses, whereas participants in the CBTI-BLT group received the placebo BLT using a modified version of Re-Timer. The modified device had the LEDs covered by red cellophane filters and red colour cardboard paper (250 g/m2), which turned the visual light spectrum towards red colour and blocked most of the light emitted from the LEDs (< 10 lux). This level of the light emitted from the modified Re-Timer was considered insufficient to have a phase-shifting effect on the circadian rhythm. Seven out of the 54 participants (13.0%) in the CBTI+BLT group, one out of the 53 participants (1.9%) in the CBTI-BLT group, and 10 out of the 52 participants (19.2%) in the WL group dropped out during the intervention/waiting period due to personal reasons (e.g., a lack of time to commit to the group sessions). There were no differences in demographic and clinical characteristics between treatment completers and non-completers. Forty-seven (100.0%) from CBTI+BLT, 50 (96.2%) from CBTI-BLT, and 41 (97.6%) participants from WL completed the post-treatment assessment. The CBTI+BLT and CBTI-BLT groups each had three participants lost to follow-up at 1-month follow-up.

17608918.label: Major findings and research outcome
17608918.value: A three-group comparison (CBTI+BLT, CBTI-BLT, and WL) showed a significant treatment*time interaction effect on insomnia severity (F(2, 135.17) = 6.75, p = .002). Specifically, both CBT-I+BLT and CBTI-BLT showed a significant improvement in insomnia severity as measured by the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) compared to WL, where both groups showed a large and comparable treatment effect (CBTI+BLT: Cohen’s d = -0.81; CBTI-BLT: d = -0.80) at post-treatment. There was a significant difference in the percentage of participants who had clinically significant changes in insomnia symptoms (ΔISI ≥ 6) across the three groups at post-treatment, with CBTI-BLT having a slightly higher percentage, followed by CBTI+BLT and WL (CBTI+BLT: 60.9%, CBTI-BLT: 62.2%, WL: 26.8%; p < .001). Similarly, there was also a significant difference in the percentage of participants who achieved a remission of insomnia (ISI ≤ 8) across the three groups at post-treatment, with CBTI+BLT having a slightly higher percentage than CBTI-BLT, followed by WL (CBTI+BLT: 68.1%, CBTI-BLT: 65.8%, WL: 43.9%; p = .045). The treatment effects, percentage of clinically significant changes, and percentage of insomnia remission were not significantly different between CBTI+BLT and CBTI-BLT groups at all time points. Lastly, Cox proportional hazard analysis showed that the CBTI+BLT group did not significantly differ from the CBTI-BLT group in the probability of remission of insomnia (ISI ≤ 8; HR = 1.01, 95% CI [0.77, 1.34], p = .922. Regarding other outcome measures, there was a significant treatment*time interaction effect across the three groups on clinician-rated mood measures (i.e., Children’s Depression Rating Scale [CDRS]; F(2, 129.62) = 7.17, p = .001). Specifically, both intervention groups significantly had a greater improvement in CDRS scores at post-treatment compared to WL, where CBTI-BLT had a larger effect on improving depressive symptoms (d = -0.86) than the CBTI+BLT group (d = -0.76). At post-treatment, only the CBTI+BLT group showed significant treatment effects on self-report mood measures as assessed by the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS; p = 0.02, d = -0.48) and on chronotype as measured by the Morningness Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ; p = 0.01, d = 0.59). Both intervention groups showed significant improvements in self-reported sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and fatigue at post-treatment (all p < 0.05). There were no differences in the treatment effects between CBTI+BLT and CBTI-BLT on any measures at post-treatment and long-term follow-ups except that the CBTI+BLT group had a significantly higher level of fatigue than CBTI-BLT at 6-month follow-up.

17608918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17608918.value: To the best of our knowledge, this project was the first study to directly compare the effects of adjunctive bright light therapy with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia in youths with insomnia and eveningness. Our results showed that CBT-I effectively improves insomnia severity, subjective sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and daytime functioning in youth with insomnia and eveningness. CBT-I with adjunctive bright light therapy additionally advanced the circadian rhythm and improved self-reported mood measures in the short term. Overall, the project supported that CBT-I with adjunctive BLT might be feasible for managing insomnia and eveningness in youths. Future research could examine the potential moderating effects of circadian rhythm on treatment outcomes of CBT-I, as well as optimising treatment modality to increase accessibility and scalability of the interventions in this vulnerable group.

17608918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17608918.value: Youth is a vulnerable period often associated with circadian changes (e.g., increased evening tendency) and an increased prevalence of sleep problems. Both insomnia and eveningness are linked to a wide range of adverse health-related and functioning outcomes (e.g., an increased risk for psychopathology) in youth. The intricate linkage between insomnia and eveningness and their associated consequences underscore the need for concurrently addressing eveningness and insomnia in managing youth insomnia. The current study was a randomised controlled trial to test the efficacy of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) with adjunctive bright light therapy – an intervention modality specifically targeting circadian rhythm – on youth’s sleep and mental health outcomes. The findings of this study supported that the delivery of CBT-I therapy is a safe and effective approach to managing insomnia and eveningness in youths, with the addition of adjunctive bright light therapy showing extra benefits of advancing circadian rhythm in youths. Overall, this study provided evidence and insight into the interplay between insomnia and eveningness, which helped to inform clinical practice and provided a foundation for developing clinical guidelines for managing adolescent insomnia.

17609218.label: Project Objectives
17609218.value: To complete a systematic anthropological study of Daoism among the Lanten Yao as a living tradition, combining ethnological and textual data, by documenting the full ritual repertoire of the Lanten Yao of Luang Namtha (Laos), especially ordination rituals, death rituals and healing rituals; creating a database correlating social context, ethnographic description, emic interpretations, oral history, textual usage and content, and audiovisual recording. To bring the case of the Lanten Yao to bear on broader debates on the historical role of Daoism in the articulation of local society and the state in the Chinese world. 17609218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17609218.value: This project will investigate the role of Daoism in the interaction between local society and the state, in the case of borderland ethnic minorities. The research will focus on the Lanten Yao ethnic minority, which straddles the borders between Laos, China and Vietnam, and for whom Daoist ritual and cosmology are at the core of collective organization and culture. An international team of scholars specializing in the three countries, combining expertise in anthropology, history and Daoist studies, and mastery of the relevant languages and dialects (Lanten, Chinese, Lao and Vietnamese), will collect ethnographic, textual and oral history data to construct a systematic description of the ritual traditions of the Lanten Yao minority, and compare their evolution and socio-political role in an ethnic community that straddles the borders of three socialist regimes. The objectives of the project are: (1) to conduct a comprehensive study, combining anthropological and textual data, of Daoism among the Lanten Yao as a living tradition, and open significant ground in the newly emerging field of studies of the interactions between Daoism and ethnic minority religions; (2) by examining local ritual traditions among non-Han people in Laos and Vietnam, to open a new field in the study of transnational Daoism; (3) by conducting a cross-border comparison between the Peoples’ Republic of China, the Peoples’ Democratic Republic of Laos and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, it will propose a new approach for the comparative study of religion, ethnicity and the state in Asian socialist regimes; (4) by bringing together specialists in the anthropology of South-East Asia and in the historical, textual and ethnographic study of Daoism and Chinese popular religion, it will break down disciplinary and methodological barriers that have been an obstacle in the study of the interface between Chinese civilization and local societies in continental Southeast Asia, and advance a new paradigm for collaborative research on inter-Asian connections. 本計劃將以邊陲少數民族為例，調查道教在地方社會與國家互動之間的角色。是項計劃將集中研究聚居於寮國、中國、越南邊界的藍靛瑤族群社會中道教的儀式與世界觀正在集體組織與文化中的角色。本研究團隊的學者專研老撾、中國、越南三地，各人精通相關的語文與方言（藍靛瑤語、中文、老撾語、越南語），並可結合人類學、歷史學、道教研究等學科方法，蒐集田野資料、文本資料、口述歷史資料，建立資料庫，藉此有系統地梳理藍靛瑤族群的儀式傳統。上述的藍靛瑤民聚居於三個社會主義政權的邊陲地方，此研究將比較各處族群的演變情況，從而理解其社會政治角色。本計劃的研究目標有三：（1）結合人類學考察資料與文本資料，進行全面的調查，研究道教行於藍靛瑤民之活傳統，並開闢學術領域，考察道教與少數民族的互動關係；（2）研究寮國與越南的非漢人地方儀式傳統，開闢跨國道教的研究領域；（3）實行橫跨中華人民共和國、寮國人民民主共和國、越南社會主義共和國的比較研究，從而提出宗教比較、民族比較、亞洲社會主義政權比較的新研究方法；（4）結合東南亞人類學家、道教研究學者與中國民間宗教學者，綜合歷史資料、文本資料、田野考察資料，消除阻礙學者研究東南亞大陸中國文化與地方社會互動的學科分歧與方法論分歧，並推動亞洲各地合作研究的新學術範式。

17609218.label: Realisation of objectives
17609218.value: Main challenge: This proposal was initially heavily focused on field research in Laos, Vietnam and China. However, pandemic-related travel restrictions remained in place for the entire second and third year of the project. We always kept the hope that things would improve within a few months, but this was not to be. Fortunately, we were able to adjust our work and, thanks to the wealth of the data generated in the first year and previously, as well as by hiring local helpers who were able to conduct part of the research from a distance, we were able to keep very busy, and the project was highly fruitful. Essentially, we were able to complete the work on Laos and to go beyond the original objectives for our research on Laos. But we were only able to conduct preliminary research in Vietnam and China, during the first year. Thus, we were unable to complete the comparative dimension of the project. We went on an exploratory trip to Vietnam in Jan. 2019, following cross-border kinship and trade ties, and established relationships with two Lanten villages in Vietnam for future data collection. We also made contacts and met with Chinese Lanten Yao scholars and local cultural heritage activists, who are willing to facilitate our entry to the field in Lanten villages near the Vietnam border in Yunnan and Guangxi provinces. Unfortunately, the constant extension of pandemic-related travel restrictions during the entire period from Feb 2020 until the end of the grant made it impossible to conduct additional field research. The Laos component of the project, as mentioned in objective 1, involved completing the systematic anthropological study of Daoism among the Lanten Yao. This part was already well advanced before this grant began. Multiple field trips (N=7) during the first year were sufficient to collect most of the remaining ethnographic data, and local helpers were able to carry out some remaining follow up during the subsequent years. Beyond the ethnographic data collection, what the team focused on during years two and three was to process the massive digital database of Lanten manuscripts. Digital scanning of ritual manuscripts in villages was completed during year one; 1352 new manuscripts were scanned, adding to 768 texts already digitised prior to this grant, bringing the total digitized textual collection to 2120 manuscripts (88,008 pages). The discovery and digitization of these additional manuscripts was an unexpected additional outcome of the research during this period. We can now safely say that we have collected virtually the entire textual corpus of the Lanten Yao of Laos. During years two and three, the basic catalogue of the 2120 manuscripts was almost completed (and has now been completed as of writing this report). Out of the corpus, a reference collection of 79 texts was identified after devising a methodology to evaluate and select the manuscripts. This reference collection represents the living ritual tradition as observed in ethnography. We are currently transcribing the manuscripts of this reference collection and linking them to the ethnographic and video data on their usage. Other than Joseba Estevez who worked on his PhD dissertation focusing on the ethnographic study, three RPg students, with the assistance of a research assistant, worked on the cataloguing and transcriptions, and each selected a group of manuscripts to work on as the focus of their thesis: Guo Huiwen on the "Pacifying the Dragon" rituals, Martin Tse on the "Breaking the Hell" rituals, and Sun Jiayue on the "Woman Huang" folktale in the Lanten oral stories, written manuscripts, and ritual performances. (Martin Tse completed his study on the “Breaking the Hell” but ended up doing his M. Phil on a different topic, but he was admitted to the PhD programme with a Presidential Fellowship and will work on the manuscripts of the ordination rituals). We also used mapping software to draw up a detailed multilayered map of routes, villages and migration history of the Lanten Yao over the borderlands of China, Vietnam and Laos. This mapping work will be the foundation of two articles on the ethnohistory of the Lanten Yao, one of which is currently under preparation. Knowledge Exchange The other major achievement of the grant, going beyond our initial objectives, was in the field of knowledge exchange and promoting cultural heritage preservation in the local Lanten communities. The foundation of this work was laid in the years prior to this grant as well as during the field trips of year one; while the efforts started to bear fruit in years two and three, with the help of local helpers and by keeping in touch with our local collaborators as well as relevant governmental and embassy officials. The foundation for these heritage preservation efforts was laid through the Lanten Stories Project, funded by the EU and Australian Aid, which had involved collecting the oral stories of the Lanten Yao, publishing them as storybooks, and distributing them to the villages through a mobile library. Following the completion of that grant, the field trips of this GRF grant and online follow-up allowed us to continue the momentum in the direction of local empowerment and capacity building. This can be seen through the creation of a “Lanten Council” comprised of seven Lanten elders representing their community and supported by the Provincial Dept. of Information, Culture, and Tourism. This council was created to unify, coordinate, and endorse efforts to preserve and promote the Lanten cultural heritage. Given the small population of Lanten in Laos (indeed a rather minor and disadvantaged community in the region), the support of the local Lao government constitutes a major contribution of our project in this matter. Since the start of our project, the Lanten have become one of the key cultural attractions in the Province of Luang Namtha – the Tourism Dept. now promotes visits to Nam Dee Village. This (re)valorization of the Lanten society and culture by the Lao State has been proven to be instrumental in preventing the implementation of policies aimed at ‘modernizing’ and/or ‘Laotising’ the Lanten communities. The visibility provided by our project is functioning as cultural shield while the cultural value of the local minorities is being interiorized by the local officers. This council is now the foundation in Laos for what we hope to build into the “Lanten Yao Digital Culture Network”. Dissemination of preliminary results and collecting feedback from experts from key academic networks: The other major advance of this project has been in the field of academic exchanges. The field of Yao studies is highly specialized and technical, involving different branches of knowledge ranging from the anthropology of Southeast Asia to Daoist Studies, Sinology and manuscript studies. During the period of the grant, we were able to establish collaborations with some of the leading research groups and centres in these fields, making our projet known and collecting valuable feedback: Centre for the Study of Manuscript Cultures, Hamburg; the Centre for the Study of Chinese Religions at Southwest Jiaotong University, China; the Institute of Anthropology of Zhejiang University; and the Institute for the Study of Yao Culture, Kanagawa University, Japan.

17609218.label: Major findings and research outcome
17609218.value: The team has generated findings in many areas, which will be the subject of numerous publications in the years to come. In the areas pertaining specifically to the stated objectives of this research, the findings are as follows (listed according to the numbering of the project objectives -- objectives 1 and 2 were empirical and are addressed in section 5.3, while objectives 3, 4 and 5 were theoretical and addressed below): 3(a) Political subjectivity: we have conceptualised the notion of “imperial magic” to describe the Lanten appropriation of the Chinese imperial imaginary in their rituals, both reinforcing and inverting Chinese political relations; 3(b) The formation of ethnic identity: the concept of “infrastructural sedimentation” shows how, as the Lanten have migrated through empires, kingdoms, polities and states over the centuries, their ethnic identity is inseparable from the “sedimented” layers of physical, cultural and religious infrastructures with which they have had to engage and co-construct. 3(c) The growth of cross-border transnational circulations: The recent increases of circulations through new transportation infrastructures and initiatives such as the BRI are reviving and intensifying historical routes that had been cut off during the cold war. This “remote” region has historically been crisscrossed by trade routes. 4. To bring the case of the Lanten Yao to bear on broader debates on the historical role of Daoism in the articulation of local society and the state in the Chinese world: the notion of “imperial magic” mentioned above holds a key for understanding the role of Daoism in both ethnic minorities on the imperial borderlands as well as in local societies in Han regions. 5. To compare the case of Lanten Daoism with discussions on the role of universal religions (especially Theravada Buddhism, Islam and Christianity) in the articulation of local society and the state in Southeast Asia: we gave developed the notion of “territorial animism” to conceptualise the management and control of a territory through establishing relations of domination or cooperation with local spirits. This concept can help to understand how religions such as Daoism and Buddhism attempt to subjugate without eliminating the “animist substratum” of Southeast Asian societies, and how these practices of religious subjugation are deployed by polities seeking to control territory.

17609218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17609218.value: This grant has opened up many avenues for future development of research. We have collected enough material to continue publishing until I retire. The textual work we began in years two and three of this grant is being continued through a new GRF grant on "Rituals and Manuscripts of the Lanten Yao", from 2021-2024. The outcome of this grant, buidling on the current one, will be a three-volume set of studies on the Lanten seasonal rituals, Daoist ordination rituals, and manuscript studies. When conditions allow, we will collaborate with colleagues from China and Vietnam to finally conduct our comparative research in those countries. The location of the Lanten Yao of Laos near the route of the new high speed railway between China and Laos, and other BRI projects has opened up lines of inquiry on the impact of these transformations on Lanten culture and religion. Our case was thus included in a CRF grant I coordinate on "Infrastructures of Faith: Religious Mobilities on the Belt and Road", and in a new RGC Fellowship grant I direct on "Chinese Modernity and Soft Power on the Belt and Road". These grants include many case studies in different BRI countries conducted by team members and collaborators. We also plan to develop the Knowledge Exchange component of the research, both for the promotion of cultural heritage among the Lanten Yao, and for the dissemination of their cultural heritage to international audiences.

17609218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17609218.value: This project investigated the role of Daoism in the interaction between local society and the state, in the case of the Lanten Yao ethnic minority of Northern Laos, for whom Daoist ritual and cosmology are at the core of collective organization and culture. We conducted a comprehensive study, combining anthropological and textual data, of Daoism among the Lanten Yao as a living tradition. We digitalised over 2000 manuscripts used by the ritual specialists of the communities, and undertook studies of how the Lanten use Daoist ritual and cosmology to manage the interface between the visible and invisible worlds. Through this research, we discovered how their religion allows the Lanten to construct a unique identity by means of which they negotiate their relationships with political authorities and other groups, both historically and in the present.
