17612418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612418.value: Background: Dementia is a disabling chronic condition affecting over 47 million people worldwide. Chinese population will be one of the main driver in the increasing trend in dementia prevalence. Accumulating evidence suggests effectiveness of certain non-drug interventions in maintaining cognition and quality of life in people with mild-to-moderate dementia, such as cognitive stimulation therapy (CST). These interventions are designed and tested in western populations with issues of cultural adaptation when applied in Chinese. Culturally appropriate and effective interventions for Chinese people with mild-to-moderate dementia are lacking. The Six Arts stem from ancient Confucian philosophy, which promotes behaviours that can impact on multiple mind-body functional domains. These domains correspond to social, physical, and cognitive activities with theoretical basis and empirical evidence of benefits in cognition, functioning, and quality of life. Using the Six Arts as a cultural framework, a group-based multimodal intervention has been developed in Hong Kong for Chinese people with mild-to-moderate dementia. Aims: To investigate the effectiveness of the Six Arts intervention as compared with cognitive stimulation therapy and usual care provided at specialized dementia care facilities in improving quality of life and maintaining cognition in Chinese people with mild-to-moderate dementia; and to explore family caregiver acceptance and understanding of the Six Arts intervention and CST. Methods: We will recruit 210 people with mild-to-moderate dementia in a randomized single-blind controlled trial consisting of three groups: (1) Six Arts intervention; (2) CST; and (3) usual care. Neuropsychological and clinical assessments will be conducted at randomization (T0/baseline) and upon completion of the 24-session, twice-weekly intervention (T1/3 months), by an assessor unaware of group membership. Focus groups will be conducted after completion of the intervention in 60 family caregivers who have observed at least one session of the Six Arts intervention or CST. We hypothesize that (1) The group who have received Six Arts intervention will show superior quality of life (Primary Outcome 1); (2) both Six Arts and CST groups will show superior cognitive improvement compared with usual care (Primary Outcome 2); (3) the Six Arts group will show greater improvements in behavioural and psychological symptoms and functioning compared with the groups receiving CST or usual care (Secondary Outcomes). This study will provide evidence on the effectiveness of two intervention protocols with potentials for large-scale implementation in the growing Chinese population with dementia. 背景: 認知障礙症是一種可致殘的慢性疾病, ​​影響全球超過4千700萬人。華人將是認知障礙症症患病率上升趨勢的主因之一。越來越多證據顯示, 一些非藥物介入法, 例如認知刺激治療 (CST), 能有效維持輕度至中度認知障礙症患者的認知功能和生活質素。這些介入法是在西方人中設計和測試的; 應用於華人時, 有文化合適性的考慮。現時仍缺乏適合華人文化、對輕度至中度認知障礙有效的介入法。六藝源於古代儒家哲學, 是一套鼓吹多元身心功能行為的思想。這些身心功能範疇對應於社交、身體及認知活動, 有理論基礎和證據顯示對認知、活動功能和生活質素有益。本港有一套以六藝作文化框架、為輕度至中度認知障礙症華人患者而設的多元介入法。 目的: 在專門提供認知障礙症照顧的機構中, 研究六藝、CST、與常規照顧相比, 對改善輕度至中度認知障礙症患者生活質素及維持認知功能的療效, 並探索家庭照顧者對六藝和CST的接受程度和理解。 方法: 我們將招募210名輕度至中度認知障礙症患者, 接受一項三組隨機單盲對照試驗: (1) 六藝; (2) CST; (3) 常規照顧。神經心理學和臨床評估將在隨機分組時 (T0 /基線) 及完成每星期兩節、共24節的介入後 (T1 / 3個月) 由評估員進行。評估員並不會獲知患者的分組結果。完成介入後, 將邀請60名家庭照顧者參與焦點小組研究; 家庭照顧者須曾至少觀察過一節六藝或CST。 我們假設 (1) 接受六藝的患者生活質素會較佳 (主要結果1); (2) 與常規照顧相比, 六藝與CST組的認知功能較高 (主要結果2); (3) 與接受CST或常規照顧的患者相比, 六藝組的行為和心理症狀和功能會有更大改善 (次要結果)。本研究將為兩種介入法的療效提供證據; 這些介入法具有在不斷增長的認知障礙症華人患者中大規模實行的可能。

17612518.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612518.value: This proposal builds upon my 2014 ECS award that I will complete on schedule. I propose to complete two publications in high impact journals and, finally, a single-authored book for publication with a university press to examine the puzzle of China’s varied response to intervention at the UN Security Council. While China has gradually eased into accepting intervention, China in principle rejects the possibility of foreign-imposed regime change via the UN Security Council. Amongst other reasons, this is because foreign-imposed regime change – the “alteration of a country’s fundamental political institutions” (Owen 2010, 1) – challenges China’s most fundamental core interest: longevity and security of the Chinese Communist Party as the Chinese state. Cases where intervention occurs against a public discourse calling for foreign-imposed regime change, and where UN Security Council measures could pave the way for foreign-imposed regime change are therefore the most vexing for China to address. The project answers the research question: what explains China’s varied response to intervention at the UN Security Council? In examining the Darfur, Sudan (2004 – 2008), Libya (2011 – 2012), and Syria (2011 – 2016) cases, I deal with the universe of such difficult cases for China in the period of its rise. These cases show variation on China’s position on intervention: supporting intervention in Darfur and Libya, while issuing six vetoes to halt action in Syria. I argue that material factors shaping China’s strategic choices regarding intervention are necessary, but insufficient to explain China’s acceptance or resistance to intervention. Status – a shared consensus on a state’s standing in the international system – has independent and significant effects for China’s position on intervention. These three case studies establish a tough test for status in presenting three least-likely cases for status explanations. I show China is most concerned to maximize status following a status trigger and when its peer groups effectively influence China. In so doing, the book project illuminates China’s status dilemma as China secures status recognition from its great power and Global South peer groups. I draw upon three unique data sources: my Chinese-language dataset regarding foreign-imposed regime change; over two hundred interviews of foreign policy elites and UN officials, and participant observation at United Nations Headquarters. The book, tentatively entitled Reconciling Status, will advance literatures on status; foreign-imposed regime change and intervention, and Chinese foreign policy. The two journal publications will draw from chapter materials from the book project. 我計劃在具影響力的學術期刊上發表兩篇論文，然後於大學出版社出版一本個人撰寫的書本。它們會研究中國對聯合國安理會的干預行動所作出的不同反應。雖然中國逐漸接受干預行動，但原則上，中國反對透過安理會以外部勢力推動政權更迭（下略稱：政權更迭）。因此，如何應付某些輔以公眾論述要求政權更迭的干預行動，及面對為政權更迭舖路的安理會措施，是中國面臨的一大難題。本項目會解答一個研究問題：為何中國對安理會的干預行動會有不同的反應？ 我疏理了達爾富爾，蘇丹（2004年至2008年）、利比亞（2011年至2012年）、敘利亞（2011年至2015年）–––– 這些讓中國在其國勢上昇時難以處理的個案。它們顯示了中國對干預行動的立場的變化。我認為，物質因素所塑造的戰略抉擇是中國會否接受干預行動的必要條件，但未能完全解釋其因果關係。而地位是指國際體系對一個國家的等級所產生的共識。地位單獨地、而且重要地影響着中國對干預行動的立場。因為這三個案例貌似最不能夠以地位作解釋，所以是之案例探究着實地考驗着地位的論述效果。我指出，中國會在（一）地位觸發後（二）同輩群體有效地影響中國時，最熱衷於提昇地位。暫名《調和不同的地位》，本書將推動有關地位、政權更迭及干預行動、中國外交政策的學術研究。另外兩份期刊文章將探討本書項目中其餘的研究難題。

17612518.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612518.value: What explains China's response to intervention at the UN Security Council? China and Intervention at the UN Security Council argues that status is an overlooked determinant in understanding its decisions, even in the apex cases that are shadowed by a public discourse calling for foreign-imposed regime change in Sudan, Libya, and Syria. It posits that China reconciles its status dilemma as it weighs decisions to intervene: seeking recognition from both its intervention peer groups of great powers and developing states. Understanding the impact and scope conditions of status answers why China has taken certain positions regarding intervention and how these positions were justified. Foreign policy behavior that complies with status, and related social factors like self-image and identity, means that China can select policy options bearing material costs. China and Intervention at the UN Security Council offers a rich study of Chinese foreign policy, going beyond works available in breadth and in depth. It draws on an extensive collection of data, including over two hundred interviews with UN officials and Chinese foreign policy elites, participant observation at UN Headquarters, and a dataset of Chinese-language analysis regarding foreign-imposed regime change and intervention. The book concludes with new perspectives on the malleability of China's core interests, insights about the application of status for cooperation and the implications of the status dilemma for rising powers.

17612518.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612518.value: When I completed this GRF project, I compiled a list of unanswered questions that I could address in new research. I used these new queries to write my application for my second GRF project (award no.17608020), examining how China shapes a global information order, regarding the norms and institutions that manage the cross-border flows of data. Working on the question of international order, norms, and human protection issues is an extension of my line of academic inquiry, but new research questions altogether for me to consider. ‘Cyber norms’ are the preferred tool to govern cross-border flows of information, given the rapidity of technological change. Concurrently, China’s technological advantages, growing material power, and ambitions to be a ‘cyber superpower’ all underscore the point that no major social or political issue can be multilaterally mediated without at least tacit PRC cooperation. This project addresses how China applies ‘cyber-sovereignty’ norms when information technologies (networked systems, drones, blockchain, internet etc.) are used in UN human protection operations – empirical material that is yet to be systematically interrogated in a theoretically-informed manner.

17612518.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612518.value: China is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, the highest arena for addressing matters of international peace and security. China has steadily become more permissive regarding intervention, though concerned about a segment of cases that occur with a public discourse calling for foreign-imposed regime change, which seeks to extend the boundary for acceptable intervention to include legal and military tools to target governments with egregious domestic human rights records. However, in such cases, China has responded inconsistently: acquiescing or supporting intervention in Sudan and Libya, but refusing intervention in Syria. To explain this variation, I argue that status – a shared consensus of a state’s standing in the international system – has independent and significant effects for China’s position on regime change. By better understanding the impact and scope conditions of status we can answer fundamental questions of why China took certain positions regarding intervention and how these positions were justified.

To generate a dataset on eminent domain in Chinese courts that the academic community including scholars of property rights, courts and China studies can utilize.
To publish two articles and the first book on eminent domain in China that combines both comprehensive statistical analysis and qualitative research.

17612618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612618.value: I will investigate how courts in China adjudicate eminent domain (i.e., land and housing expropriation) cases. With a combination of quantitative and qualitative research, I will explore what are the key factors contributing to the decisions of courts at all levels, and whether there are any different approaches taken by them respectively. My hypothesis is that judicial behaviours are subject to three constraints: power, expertise and information—the higher the court, the more power and expertise it has, but less information with the increased distance from local governments which exercise the eminent domain power. The overall role and general approach of the judiciary, in light of the balance/tension between economic development and individual property right protection, will be statistically tested and qualitatively observed in answering the practical question, i.e. to what extent can Chinese courts, in adjudicating eminent domain cases, protect individual property rights and how can the courts play a better role? Theoretically, an individual property owner can challenge a government’s eminent domain decision under the current legal regime. However, property right of individuals might still be under risk if the protections provided by the judicial branch are weak. This seems to be the case as the assumption of weak courts has been widely taken in studies concerning the role of the judiciary in Chinese law and development. I will examine how Chinese courts review local governments’ eminent domain decisions and whether the problem of weak courts has indeed incurred. I employ the data on eminent domain cases published in the China Judicial Decisions Website (中国裁判文书网), which was fully launched on January 1, 2014. I plan to investigate cases at all levels of the courts, including the Supreme People's Court (SPC), the High People's Courts, the Intermediate People's Courts at the city or prefecture level, and the Basic People's Courts at the county or urban district level. By coding and analyzing these judicial decisions, I plan to generate the pattern of adjudication of Chinese courts and find the similarity and differences therewith. Apart from quantitative studies, my team and I will also conduct qualitatively interviews with judges of different levels of courts with the aim of facilitating and verifying our observation. The final research output would include two articles published in first-tier international law journals and a book published by a first-tier university press. 一般認為中國的法院是弱勢法院，在產權保護方面起到的作用很少。本項研究將會檢驗這一在學術研究中普遍存在的判斷，并更好地理解中國法院在產權保護中的作用和局限，以及背後的制度因素。本研究項目將通過定量和定性研究分析中華人民共和國各級法院如何裁判行政征收和拆遷案件。司法權力的運用會受到多方因素的影響，本文將通過縱向比較各級法院和橫向比較各地法院來探討司法權力是否在能經濟發展與產權保護之間起到協調和平衡的作用。不同法院之間是否存在差異？是什麼原因導致了這種差異？本文數據來源主要是中國裁判文書網和對從事行政審判的法官的訪談。

17612718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612718.value: How and why does a peaceful protestor choose to participate in a violent riot? This project seeks to understand the radicalization of collective action among young adults. The social identity model of collective action posits that identifying with a political cause (e.g., gender equality) is a crucial factor in mobilizing one to engage in collective action (e.g., a demonstration). Researchers have recently begun to examine the differences between the processes underlying peaceful, normative collective actions (e.g., petitions, protests) and those underlying violent, nonnormative collective actions (e.g., arson, violent clashes), finding important cognitive and affective distinctions between them. What is unclear, however, is how peaceful and prosocial tactics transform into violent and destructive ones. We suggest that the transition is contingent on identification with a radical, politicized group and that such identification is related to two factors: perceived threat and mistrust in political institutions. When there is a perceived threat, be it about tangible resources or way of life, and when there is mistrust in the institutions that should protect one from such threats, the person would be more likely to identify with a radical political movement. Identification with such a movement leads to participation in nonnormative collective action to interfere with that state of affair. We propose that participation in such action further intensifies identification with the radical political movement or group. Our pilot studies provide support for these associations. Further empirical evidence is required to ascertain the causal and temporal relationships between them, especially how changes in one lead to changes in the other. We propose a mixed-methods study of young adults in Hong Kong. Across 16 months, we will track our participants’ identification with the more radical political movements in Hong Kong and their participation in and willingness to participate in normative and nonnormative collective action. With an experimental design, we will test the impact of the perception of local political institutions on identification and action. With multiple waves of qualitative and quantitative data, we will examine the relationship between the changes in the constructs in question. Our qualitative results will also help identify themes in the participant’s understanding of their action and their decision-making process. The results of our study will help elucidate some of the causes of identification with a radical political movement, and the dynamic relationship between identification with such movement and participation in normative and nonnormative collective action. 和平集會為何會為演變為暴力騷亂？此研究項目旨在了解年輕人的社會運動如何變得激進。 心理學的「社會身份認同論」假設一個人對某政治身份（例如，性別平權者）的認同是動員參與社會運動（例如示威）的關鍵誘因。學者近年研究和平、規範的社會運動（如請願，抗議）和暴力、非規範的社會運動（如縱火，暴力衝突）之間的差異。他們發現倆者之間在認知和情感方面確有明顯的區別。然而，由前者到後者的演變過程有待闡明。 社會身份認同論認為這種轉變取決於一個人對激進的、政治化的群體的認同。我們推論這種認同與兩個因素有關：（1）感到外來的威脅和（2）對制度的不信任。當一個人在資源方面或生活方式受到威脅，而同時不信任制度的保護，該人就更有可能認同激進的社會運動，以改變現況。而參與此類行動會進一步加強對激進社會運動以及激進團體的認同。我們初步的研究結果支持這些推論。下一步，我們需要收取縱向證據來確定它們之間的因果關係。 此研究項目利用質量混合方法研究香港的年輕人。 我們會訪問參與社運的年輕人對激進政治運動的認同，以及他們參與規範性和非規範性社會運動的意願。我們將進行實驗測試不信任政治制度帶來的影響。 通過多輪縱向問卷數據，我們可以進一步理解以上各因素之間的關係。 我們的研究結果有助確定年輕社運人士怎樣理解其行動及怎樣作出決策。 我們的研究結果將有助於闡明年輕人認同激進社會運動的原因，以及這種身份認同與參與規範性和非規範性社會運動之間的關係。

17612718.label: Realisation of objectives
17612718.value: We have completed all four objectives. Some additional methodology and findings were added due to the unexpected 2019 social unrest. In total, six manuscripts were produced. Some of the results were also presented at three conferences. 5.1: We have completed a series of qualitative studies. The results of these studies are included in two manuscripts that are currently under review: "Bystanders, Protesters, Journalists: A qualitative examination of different stakeholders’ motivation to participate in collective action in Hong Kong" and "Political mistrust, perceived threat, and intentions to engage in normative and violent collective action: A mixed-methods study". 5.2: We have completed the experiment. The results are included in the manuscript that is under review "Political mistrust, perceived threat, and intentions to engage in normative and violent collective action: A mixed-methods study". 5.3: We completed a 3-wave longitudinal study. The results are included in the under review manuscript "The bidirectional relationship between localist attitudes and both violent and non-violent collective action: A three-wave longitudinal study". 5.4: We completed a longitudinal study and examined the potential mediation. We reported the findings in a manuscript, which is under review, "The Influence of Perceived Threat and Political Mistrust on Politicized Identity and Normative and Violent Nonnormative Collective Action". In addition to the above four under-review manuscripts, owing to the rapid changes in collective action in Hong Kong after the study began in 2018, we have reported additional findings that stemmed from this project. They are reported in: Lam, C., Chan, C. S.*, & Hamamura, T. (2021). Time-dependent association between mass protests and psychological distress on social media: A text mining study during the 2019 anti-government social unrest in Hong Kong. Journal of Affective Disorders, 291, 177-187. Chan, C. S.*, Wong, C. Y. F., & Fan, A. Y. C. (2021). Firing the monk when the ceremony is over: A study on the split between student protesters and their leaders after the 2014 Umbrella Movement. Asian Journal of Social Psychology, 24, 565-572. In sum, this GRF project has produced two peer-reviewed publications, four under-review manuscripts and three conference papers.

17612718.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612718.value: In total, six manuscripts were completed. Among them, two are published and four are currently under review. In sum, we found: -perceived threat to Hong Kong values alongside mistrust of political institutions spurred collective action engagement and support for defensive violent non-normative collection action. (Gulliver, Chan, Tam, Lau, Hong, & Louis, under review) -localist attitudes predicted non-violent and violent behavior and non-violent intentions, while non-violent intentions predicted localist attitudes. (Gulliver, Chan, Wong, & Louis, under review) -individuals with higher localist attitudes are more likely to have higher intentions to engage in non-violent collective action. (Gulliver, Chan, Wong, & Louis, under review) -Different actors have different concerns: Among bystanders, barriers to participation include their lack of issue consensus, low efficacy perceptions, and negative view of violent action. Among journalists: collective identity precluded overt protest participation, however, their emotional responses to injustice or violent actions generated tensions between their role obligations and desire to intervene. Among activists: collective identification, anger, and injustice motivate participation in collective action. (Gulliver, Chan, Chan, Tam, & Louis, under review) -Social media content reveals discussions of psychological distress stemming from, or exacerbated by, social unrest. There are potential mutual influences between mass protests and online reactions, as well as the func­tional differences between online forums and SNS. Street protests and their associated psychological distress can be readily detected on popular online forums. (Lam, Chan, & Hamamura, 2021) -lower perceived integrity-based and competence-based trustworthiness predict the decision to disaffiliate with movement leaders. Voters’ group identification with Umbrella Movement protesters predicted disaffiliation with the movement leaders because they were viewed as lacking integrity but not competence. (Chan, Wong, & Fan, 2021) -Significant indirect effects of social threat and political mistrust on both normative and violent nonnormative collective action intentions through politicized identity. Politicized identity and a broader Hong Kong identity were both directly associated with normative action intentions. However, only politicized identity was associated with violent nonnormative action intentions. (Chan, Gulliver, Awale, Tam, & Louis, under review)

17612718.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612718.value: The pro-democracy collective action landscape has changed drastically since the beginning of this project in 2018. We have several ongoing follow-up studies but participant recruitment has shown to be challenging, especially after the enactment of the National Security Law in 2020. We have adjusted our strategy to focus more on social media and online forum data (e.g., Lam, Chan, & Hamamura, 2021). We are also designing experiments that bypass the sensitivity of the topic of interest while allowing us to make relevant inferences. We will continue to pursue this line of work to help understand how and why social movements become radicalized.

17612718.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612718.value: Across multiple studies we examined the interplay of social threat, political mistrust, and identity on nonviolent and violent collective action intentions and behaviour in Hong Kong. We found that individuals with higher perceptions of mistrust and threat were more likely to support and engage in collective action. We examined whether localist attitudes—which seek to preserve Hong Kong values, identity, and culture—influenced collective action intentions. We found that individuals with higher localist attitudes were more likely to have higher intentions to engage in non-violent collective action. We also compared collective action across bystanders, protesters, and journalists. Interview data supported the role of identity, anger, and injustice in motivating protesters, whereas lack of issue consensus, low efficacy perceptions, and negative views of violent action were barriers to bystander participation. Journalists’ collective identity precluded overt protest participation; however, their emotional responses to injustice or violent actions generated tensions between their role obligations and desire to intervene. In our study of the interplay between online and street protests, we found that the two are linked and that street protests can impact the mental health of netizens. Finally, we examined the factors that lead to mistrust in movement leaders; Integrity matter more than competence.

17612818.label: Project Objectives
17612818.value: Compile a directory of women filmmakers engaging with China’s economic and political rise in the twenty-first century which includes biographical information, filmographies, and a bibliography of scholarly articles, books, reviews, publicity materials, news commentaries. Gather supplemental information from sociology, anthropology, ethnography, law, education, Asian area studies, as well as women’s studies to provide a context for understanding these female filmmakers’ approach to China’s changing social and cultural landscape. Construct the appropriate theoretical scaffolding, drawing on interdisciplinary feminist scholarship involving cosmopolitanism, intersectionality, postcolonial and queer critique in order to analyse the ways in which female filmmakers tell stories about women’s lives in relation to the rise of China globally in fiction and nonfiction films. Uncover the dynamics behind transnational co-productions, film festival circulation, and the various ways in which networks of production, distribution, and exhibition impact women filmmakers and shape the material seen on screen as well as its potential use as “soft power” for nationalist ends. Provide detailed case studies of specific motion pictures by established and emerging women filmmakers in order to examine how they create cultural meaning in their depiction of women in relation to changing perceptions of contemporary China. Consider female filmmakers’ critiques of China’s rise as they document and dramatize issues of concern to women such as reproductive rights, gender violence, lesbian visibility, femininity and consumerism, body image, labor migration, trafficking, domesticity, access to the media, and women’s suffrage. Disseminate this research in scholarly publications as well as through seminars, lectures, workshops, websites, social media, and in other venues accessible to the professional community, women’s organizations, cultural leaders and policymakers as well as the general public.

17612818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612818.value: The aim of this project is to map and analyse the ways in which women filmmakers from around the world depict gender and sexuality in China in the first two decades of the twenty-first century. While much has been written on cinema in post-Mao and post-Deng China, few scholars have looked systematically and critically at the ways in which women filmmakers have depicted the impact of these enormous economic, technological, social, political, and cultural changes on gender and sexuality in mainland China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and throughout the Chinese diaspora. This project gathers information on female filmmakers from around the world who have made fiction features, documentaries, experimental, hybrid and digital motion pictures depicting gender and sexuality in relation to China’s rise. The research plan places special emphasis on films portraying Chinese women’s lives in relation to issues of particular importance to feminist scholarship, including, for example, reproduction, romance, family relations, gender roles, generational differences, body image, sex work, labor migration, career options, minority women, media access, suffrage and political rights. As feminist research on global screen culture demonstrates, many female filmmakers see the world differently, while the constraints of the industry often limit them to “women’s films” in which they are encouraged to address female viewers in melodramas, romantic comedies, and other genres hospitable to female protagonists. Women residing in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Macau, Singapore, and throughout the Chinese diaspora view women from the People’s Republic of China in distinct ways, while mainland Chinese female filmmakers’ depiction of women outside the PRC conveys a different inflection. Women living outside of the Chinese cultural sphere take up the camera to look at China, and their films also play a part in this investigation. Research begins with the compilation of a filmography of motion pictures by women filmmakers depicting China in the twenty-first century. Systemic scanning of film festival offerings, distribution records, and other sources continues throughout the project. An expanded bibliography of film reviews, commentaries, festival catalogue copy, filmmakers’ biographies, directors’ statements, and scholarly articles on key female filmmakers and their films provides supplementary support for the analysis of the films. After careful analysis of selected films using feminist methodologies to pinpoint the ideological underpinning of the depiction of gender and sexuality in the cinema, research concludes with publication of findings on general trends as well as specific cases of women’s engagement with China’s rise on screen. 本研究旨在描繪(map)和分析自二十一世紀以降，世界各地的女性導演如何呈現「性與性別」(gender and sexuality)議題在中國的發展。儘管學界已有不少關於「後毛」(post-Mao)和「後鄧」(post-Deng)時期電影發展的研究，但該時期女性導演如何通過電影媒介表現中國在經濟，技術，社會，政治和文化上的巨大變遷，及其對「性與性別」議題產生的深遠影響，則常常被忽略，鮮有學者對此進行系統化和批判性的研究。本研究收集和整理一系列女性導演製作的電影，範圍涵蓋劇情片，紀錄片，實驗電影，混合和數位影像。把性別議題放置於二十一世紀的歷史脈絡下，這些文本從不同角度探究「中國崛起」對中國大陸，香港，台灣和其他華語地區的性別政治議題產生的影響。是次研究計劃重點審視電影如何觸及一連串女性主義研究關注的重要議題，包括生育議題，浪漫，家庭關係，性別角色，世代差異，身體影像(body image)，性工作議題，勞工移民，職業選擇，邊緣女性，媒體存取 (media access)，選舉和政治權利。電影行業內對女性電影工作者作品的主流印象往往局限為“女性電影”(women’s films)，即某種只能以女性觀眾為主要對象，形式上僅限於悲喜劇(melodramas)，浪漫喜劇(romantic comedies)，或其他以女性角色為主導的類型電影。然而，不少女性主義電影研究已指出，女性電影工作者不只是某種特定類型電影的生產者，其電影更能以不同的視點閱讀並介入世界。香港，台灣，澳門，新加坡，和其他華語地區的女性影人，其作品以獨特的視野觀察中國大陸的女性。同樣地，中國大陸女性電影工作者對海外華人女性的描寫也表達出一些不同的變形(inflection)。另外，不少居住在中華文化圈(Chinese cultural sphere)以外的女性導演也把鏡頭對準了發展中的中國，本研究也會對這些作品進行討論。

17612818.label: Realisation of objectives
17612818.value: I am delighted to report that I have achieved all seven of my objectives for this project. Even though the COVID-19 pandemic forced me to rethink aspects of my project, I can happily say that I have been able to maintain my research focus with only slight modifications that included participating in conferences, lectures, and other public events online rather than in-person. Women Filmmakers and Transnational China in the Twenty-First Century, a directory (Objective 1) of women filmmakers engaging with China’s economic and political rise in the twenty-first century, can be accessed at https://chinesewomenfilmmakers.wordpress.com/ The site disseminates information on 261 women filmmakers (including 33 crossovers with the Hong Kong Women Filmmakers partner website: https://hkwomenfilmmakers.wordpress.com/) working within Chinese-language and diasporic cinemas from around the world from 2000 to 2022. This unique resource features biographical information, filmographies, and bibliographies of scholarly articles, books, reviews, publicity materials, news commentaries, and other materials related to key female film artists. In compiling information on women filmmakers, special emphasis has been placed on directors making films portraying Chinese women’s lives in relation to reproduction, romance, family relations, gender roles, generational differences, body image, sex work, labor migration, career options, minority representation, media access, suffrage and political rights. My monograph, “Women Filmmakers and the Visual Politics of Transnational China in the #MeToo Era”, under contract at Amsterdam University Press, has been completed and delivered to the press. This book includes an extensive bibliography (Objective 2) that draws on publications in sociology, anthropology, ethnography, law, education, Asian area studies, as well as women’s studies to provide a context for understanding female filmmakers’ approach to China’s changing social and cultural landscape. For its theoretical scaffolding (Objective 3), it builds on intersectional feminist, transnational queer, postcolonial, and other contemporary critical approaches to global culture in order to understand the impact the #MeToo Movement has had on the gendered and racialized notion of the “gaze” in contemporary Chinese cinema. The intersectional understanding of the visual politics of the gaze that emerged through my research paved the way for a methodology that allowed me to analyze women’s filmmaking practice in transnational China in a very productive way. Women filmmakers demonstrate oppositional, feminist, queer, and other activist ways of seeing beyond white, male, heterosexual, cisgender eyes, and the #MeToo moment calls out for further theoretical vigilance and a critical return to the intersectional politics of looking in transnational film productions. For Laura Mulvey, the gaze combines the perspectives of the filmmaker, fictional character, and spectator. Noting the absence of African American women behind as well as in front of the camera, bell hooks focuses on the spectator’s oppositional gaze at the intersection of race and gender in film. In a speech on the female gaze at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2016, Jill Soloway called for an intersectional approach to the visualization of gender in motion pictures. In the wake of #MeToo, Nina Menkes and Rebecca Harrison, among others, have argued for a reconsideration of the cinematic gaze through the eyes of women filmmakers. Switching back the gaze to transnational Chinese women filmmakers as well as their female subjects and viewers can help to uncover how they exercise their agency to push back against male authority within a global visual culture that defines ethnic Chinese women in particular ways. In “China on Screen”, Chris Berry and Mary Ann Farquhar ask the question, “How Should a Chinese Woman Look?” They tackle this question by analyzing key performances by Xie Fang, Gong Li, Ruan Lingyu, and Maggie Cheung in order to interrogate the ways in which nationalism, modernity, and gender intertwine from the Republican era through the establishment of the People’s Republic and, finally, the years leading up to the Handover of Hong Kong in 1997. This book focuses on that question as it resonates through the twenty-first century. In particular, #MeToo in transnational China opens up the question to interrogation in new ways. In fact, many films by women filmmakers display visual tactics for subverting certain aspects of male visual power. As #MeToo opens the door wider, the feminist potential of these women’s films may have a greater chance of being realized, distributed, exhibited, programmed, reviewed, and even actually seen by viewers eager for relief from the constricting blindness of the male gaze. This book highlights how women filmmakers bring particular perspectives on Chinese women to global screens by expanding on the visual politics of the gaze in contemporary cinema. It contributes to theoretical thinking about Chinese women and screen culture by putting developments in feminist theory on the male gaze into closer conversation with evolving critical and analytical methods used to understand China’s rise and its impact on women. In addition to sections of my monograph devoted to women’s film networks, my journal articles, “The Networked Storyteller and Her Digital Tale: Film Festivals and Ann Hui’s ‘My Way’” (Global Storytelling: Journal of Digital and Moving Images 1:2 [2022] https://doi.org/10.3998/gs.1702) and “Where in the World are Chinese Women Filmmakers? Transnational China and World Cinema in the Twenty-First Century” (Studies in World Cinema [published online ahead of print 2021] https://doi.org/10.1163/26659891-01020002), as well as a book chapter, “Women as Cross-Cultural Intermediaries within the Chinese Diaspora: The Search for Esther Eng in S. Louisa Wei’s Golden Gate Girls (2013),” (in Eyal Ben-Aria and Heung Wah Wong, eds. “Cultural Intermediaries in East Asian Film Industries” [London: Routledge, 2022], pp. 128-146), specifically address transnational co-productions, film festival circulation, and the various ways in which networks of production, distribution, and exhibition shape women’s filmmaking across and beyond the Chinese-speaking world (Objective 4). These publications provide detailed case studies (Objective 5) of documentary, fiction, and experimental works that include “Golden Gate Girls” (2013), “Anna & Anna” (2007), “The Truth about Beauty” (2014) “My Way” (2012), “Unfinished” (2013), “Angels Wear White” (2017), “Hooligan Sparrow” (2016), “Female Directors” (2012), “Girls Always Happy” (2018), “Small Talk” (2017), “A Dog Barking at the Moon” (2019), “Lotus” (2012), “Outcry and Whisper” (2020), “A Tiny Hand-Held Camera” (2014), “Denise Ho: Becoming the Song” (2020), “Fear(less) and Dear” (2020), “Our Youth in Taiwan” (2018), “To Singapore, with Love” (2013), “Many Undulating Things” (2019), “Miasma, Plants, Export Paintings” (2017), and “The Farewell” (2019). My analyses of these films showcase female filmmakers’ critiques of China’s rise (Objective 6) as they document and dramatize issues of concern to women such as #MeToo and gender violence, lesbian visibility, femininity and consumerism, labor migration, trafficking, reproductive rights, domesticity, activism and access to the media, and the ways in which discourses surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic resonate with the depiction of Asian women’s bodies in the global visual archive. In addition to the website and publications mentioned above, I have disseminated my findings widely (Objective 7) at online conferences organized by the University of Nottingham-Ningbo, Sichuan University, Istanbul Bilgi University, and Newcastle University, among others. I have delivered guest lectures online hosted by Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University, The Center for Global Asia (CGA) at NYU Shanghai, Chinese University of Hong Kong, and the University of Hong Kong. I have spoken on the radio, at online film festivals, and delivered guest lectures in online courses as well.

17612818.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612818.value: My major findings reflect the dramatic changes that have taken place in the first two decades of the twenty-first century on Chinese screens. Women filmmakers address a world on screen through the Internet, at a growing variety of film festivals beyond the A-list (from Udine to Vancouver), and through increasingly transnational networks with production and post-production often separated by continents. In other words, they operate as women in a very different cinematic environment than filmmakers experienced in the 1970s, 80s, 90s, and even the early years of the twenty-first century. Female filmmakers bring a particular agenda of issues of concern to Chinese women to world screens. These women know the world through the process of making their films transnationally or within cosmopolitan production contexts in cities such as Hong Kong, Taipei, Shanghai, or New York. Scattered around the world, many embrace migrant, nomadic, diasporic, exilic identities, which become a critical component of how they envision the world and their place in it as well. Focusing on their oeuvres not only expands cinema’s world view, it also substantially transforms it by highlighting female perspectives on issues of global concern. The #MeToo movement highlights the fact that the digital has reshaped transnational Chinese cinema culture for women in ways that go far beyond the expansion of global markets through streaming. Online activism expands awareness of women’s issues from the prevalence of sexual harassment to feminist calls for economic transformation and inclusive democratic governance. Access to technology and social media penetration of daily life allow women to voice their concerns more widely, network more effectively, and push for progressive change. Still, the digital harbors opportunities for backlash, harassment, commercialization, and marginalization as well. Moving into the third decade of the new millennium, women filmmakers inside and outside China’s borders face these challenges as they tilt the globe of world cinema to accommodate different ways of seeing. The impact of #MeToo continues its ripple effects across the industry that includes the Chinese-speaking world. As COVID-19 lingers and streaming options expand, production opportunities open for diverse women, and a wider range of stories come to the screen. Other emerging Chinese American talents include writers and producers such as Celeste Ng, Adele Lim, Constance Wu, and Ali Wong, as well as Oliver Siu Kuen Chan and Norris Wong in Hong Kong, Feng-I Fiona Roan in Taiwan, and Jia Ling in the PRC.

17612818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612818.value: I plan to continue to work with the filmmakers I highlight in my study in order to chart the development of their careers in the future. Since I have relocated to Pratt Institute in Brooklyn, New York, I have become increasingly aware of the tremendous reserves of creative energy within the Chinese diaspora. I have been in touch, for example, with one of the filmmakers in my study, Yang Mingming, about her own interest in studying a production company in New York City, A24, as a model for independent film production and distribution in the PRC. Hopefully, there will be additional opportunities for international research collaborations based on my initial project. I envision the next phase of my research to involve charting the impact of COVID-19, the Sino-American Trade War, the “new” Cold War, and #MeToo on the representation of women onscreen as well as behind the camera. I continue to deliver talks on my GRF-funded research in venues such as the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C. (December 4, 2022), and I am confident I will speak extensively about this research when my book appears in print.

17612818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612818.value: Women filmmakers depict gender and sexuality on Chinese screens in the twenty-first century by refining the concept of the “male gaze” to include intersectional, oppositional, alienated, queer, and other critical “gazes.” This project demonstrates how women shape Chinese visual politics through the depiction of the look, leer, glare, glance, and gaze on screen. This study draws on a range of motion pictures by women depicting the impact of economic, technological, social, political, and cultural changes on women’s lives in mainland China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and throughout the Chinese diaspora. Special emphasis falls on films dealing with female perspectives on reproduction, romance, family relations, gender roles, generational differences, body image, sex work, labor migration, career options, minority women, media access, feminist activism and political rights. The impact of the #MeToo movement and COVID-19 on women involved in Chinese screen culture highlights the urgency of this critical investigation into the gendered nature of the visual politics of transnational China.

17612918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612918.value: Half of Shenzhen’s population lives in “Villages in the City” (ViC), dense urban blocks that are outside of the city’s formal planning and building regulations. Such illegal buildings and their total floor areas are estimated to be 50% of Shenzhen’s total formally planned and constructed buildings. The prevalent governmental and general public attitudes view the ViC as problem areas tarnishing Shenzhen’s image as a modern city. The Shenzhen municipal government launched a Redevelopment Masterplan in 2005 with the goal to demolish the city’s ViC and redevelop them with formalized real estate properties. The redevelopment policy and the resultant decade of “demolish-and-rebuild” campaigns have been challenged by scholars in recent years for their negative social impacts, a position this proposed research intends to further reinforce. In November 2016, after a decade of aggressive campaigns to demolish the city’s ViCs, the Shenzhen government released a new urban planning policy that no longer viewed “demolish-and-rebuild” as the predominant treatment of the city’s ViCs. The policy stated that while most of the ViCs in the city’s outer districts should be demolished and rebuilt, for the majority of the ViCs inside the city’s urban center (the original SEZ), the primary action should be one of “integrated regeneration” that upgrades the ViCs' basic infrastructure but “does not change the buildings' built structure or programs.” The majority of existing literature on ViC redevelopment focuses on the “demolish-and-rebuild” precedents without detailing the existing conditions of specific ViCs, as they are generally viewed as expendable. The new policy of “integrated regeneration” that aims to improve the existing spatial and infrastructural qualities necessitates a new direction in ViC research that examines local specificities and needs of each individual ViC. Moreover, despite the ambitious planning, the number of large-scale ViC redevelopments and the volume of demolitions and redevelopments are far below the planned intentions. Through the theoretical framework of urban informality as a vital process of urban development, this research focuses on the under-examined phenomenon of incremental self-renovations and infrastructure upgrades by individual ViCs that often are not associated with governmental policies or formal planning. Through detailed documentation and analysis of the redevelopment process of four ViCs as representative case studies throughout the various developmental stages of Shenzhen, this research examines the complex spatial and institutional transformations with the goal to generate knowledge that could inform future research, design, planning, and policies on urban regeneration. 在深圳，将近一半的人口居住在“城中村”里，这是一种游离在城市正规规划和建筑法规之外的高密度城市街区。 据估计，这些不受法律承认的建筑群的总建筑面积约占深圳市正式规划下所建造的建筑总量的50%。政府和大众普遍认为这些城中村对深圳这样的一个新生现代城市形象会产生极大的负面影响。早在2005年深圳市政府就已经启动了城市更新的总体规划，其目标是拆除大部分的城中村并代之以正规的房地产物业。诸多城市更新政策的出台以及十年间所启动的“拆除-重建”运动因其所产生的负面社会影响而受到许多学者的质疑和挑战。本研究提案亦对深圳市政府所启动的这些城中村更新项目持审慎的立场。 2016年11月，在经历了十年激进的城中村拆除运动之后，深圳市政府发布了一项新的城市规划政策，提出不再以“拆除-重建”作为城中村更新的主要途径。该政策指出位于深圳关外的大部分城中村因其建筑质量低下而应予以拆除重建，而对于大部分位于关内（原经济特区范围）城中村原则上应以综合整治为主，在提升基础设施的同时能够对原有建筑结构和村落肌理进行保留。 当前大多数有关城中村更新的文献主要讨论的是已经实施完成的“拆除-重建”的案例，但是却极少关注特定类型的城中村里所具有的独特的物质和社会条件。新发布的“综合整治”政策致力于提升城中村的空间品质及基础设施建设，而这需要学术研究对于每个城中村的特性及其特定的改造需求给予更多的关注和探索。 以城市非正规性作为研究城市发展过程的重要理论框架，本研究探讨那些未被充分关注到的由单个城中村所自发展开的增量式更新活动及基础设施改善行为。通过对四个能够反映深圳不同发展阶段的城中村进行详尽的文献资料考察及其更新过程的调查分析，本研究探讨这些城中村在城市发展过程中其复杂的空间及制度变革，旨在为当前及以后的城市更新在学术研究、城市设计、城市规划以及政策的制定方面提供可资借鉴的知识和启示。

17612918.label: Realisation of objectives
17612918.value: The research objectives of this study were mainly realized, overcoming many challenges posed by COVID-19, especially in limiting physical site visits. There was a change of the grant project’s Principal Investigator in May 2021 due the PI- Dr. Juan Du’s change of employment from The University of Hong Kong to the University of Toronto in July 2021. PI of the grant was changed in May 2021 from Dr. Du to Mr. Donn Holohan, and Dr. Du remained as Co-I of the grant. The grant's original completion date was 2021-09-29, and due to Covid-19's impact on prohibiting cross-border travels from Hong Kong to the research sites in Shenzhen, a 1-year extension was applied for and approved for the grant project." While physical access to the research site remained closed by the grant’s end date of September 2022, with digital mapping technologies and online workshops, most of the challenges were able to be mitigated. Here, we elaborate on each objective regarding the process and outcomes: Objective 1: To identify and elaborate on the capacities of Shenzhen’s ViCs to self-provide upgrades to basic infrastructure and community provisions, outside of the formal public service provisions of the city. • Analysis of case study ViCs, such as Shuiwei Village and Futian Village, showcased their ability to initiate and execute redevelopment projects independently. • The analysis of redevelopment plans revealed shifts in lead applicants, indicating varying degrees of village, government, and developer involvement. • The ViCs demonstrated significant capacities for self-provision of basic infrastructure and community upgrades. The research confirmed that ViCs possess substantial self-provisioning capabilities. By examining representative case studies, we observed that ViCs could initiate and manage their own infrastructure and community improvement projects. Shuiwei Village, for instance, demonstrated the capacity for village-led redevelopment. This contrasts with previous policies that relied heavily on government or developer-led approaches. The evolving roles of different stakeholders, as identified in the research, highlighted the complex interplay between formal and informal institutions within ViCs' redevelopment processes. Objective 2: To document the previously under-examined Shenzhen’s ViC incremental renovations and infrastructural upgrades that span the city’s developmental history from 1979 till the present. • Spatial analysis and documentation of incremental renovations revealed the evolution of ViCs' physical environments. • Interviews with stakeholders provided insights into the motivations and outcomes of these renovations. • The study captured the transformation of outdoor spaces and village buildings over time. The research succeeded in documenting the incremental renovations that have occurred in ViCs over time. Through combined spatial and data collection methods, including site surveys, building surveys, mapping, and photographic documentation, the research unveiled the dynamic changes in ViCs' physical landscapes. While due to the impacts of Covid-19, we were not able to interview as many key stakeholders, we utilized local news publications as well as online and social media information to enrich this documentation by providing narratives and motivations behind these renovations. This multifaceted approach allowed for a temporal and spatial comparison of ViCs' development stages, showcasing the evolution from informal settlements to more structured communities. Objective 3: To analyze the institutional and spatial qualities of the incremental renovations of representational ViCs through key indicators. • Institutional analysis identified the roles of formal and informal institutions in ViCs' redevelopment. • Interviews with stakeholders illuminated interactions between various actors and their impact on redevelopment outcomes. • The concept of "planned informality" emerged, emphasizing the intertwined nature of formal planning and informal development in ViCs. The research delved into the institutional and spatial qualities of ViCs' incremental renovations. By distinguishing between formal and informal institutions, the study revealed the intricate web of actors involved in ViCs' redevelopment. Participation through several local government and community organize workshops allowed for exchanges of information and perspectives with local villagers, planners, and community groups and provided valuable insights into how these institutions shaped decision-making and outcomes. Notably, the concept of "planned informality" emerged as a central theme, emphasizing that ViCs' development was a result of, and influence on, formal planning and government policies. This recognition challenges the conventional dichotomy of formal and informal and underscores the need for a more nuanced understanding of ViCs' developmental history. Objective 4: To advance knowledge on guiding principles for future planning and design of ViC development based from the villages’ self-initiatives and upgrades. • Systematic policy review identified shifts from a "negative" to a "positive" discourse towards ViCs. • Existing policies primarily focused on infrastructure development, sanitation, and beautification, overlooking informal rules and resident participation. • The research emphasized the necessity of integrating informal practices and resident involvement into future policies. The research findings allow for formulation of guiding principles for future ViC development by critically analyzing implemented urban policies and developments led by governments or government partnerships with developers. The synthesis and analysis of collected information, including case studies, mappings, and policy reviews, serves as the foundation for formulating design guidelines and policies for future ViC redevelopments. By bridging the gap between formal planning and informal development mechanisms, the research offered a holistic and inclusive approach to ViC development. It underscored the importance of recognizing ViCs as valuable contributors to urban development and advocated for policies that empower these communities to shape their own futures. In conclusion, this research not only realized its objectives but also provided a nuanced understanding of ViCs in Shenzhen. It revealed their self-provisioning capabilities, documented their developmental history, analyzed the role of institutions, and proposed guiding principles for their sustainable development. These major findings underscore the multifaceted nature of ViCs and the need for flexible, community-driven policies. These findings also highlight deficiencies in current policies, emphasizing the importance of addressing root causes and engaging residents. Moving forward, urban development must embrace the diversity of ViCs and leverage their autonomous capacities, guided by tailored principles that prioritize inclusivity, local identity, and sustainability. These final findings lead to guidelines to integrate key theories of community development to ensure a holistic and inclusive approach to ViC development: Community-Based Development: Local communities are not passive recipients of external interventions but active agents in shaping their own futures. In line with this theory, our research underscores the importance of engaging ViC residents in the decision-making processes that impact their neighborhoods. It advocates for policies that are rooted in the unique contexts and aspirations of each ViC, thereby fostering a sense of ownership and empowerment among community members. Recognition of Informal Practices: Significance of informal practices, economies, and social networks within communities. In ViCs, informal practices often play a crucial role in shaping daily life and communal resources. Our research highlights the need to integrate these informal dynamics into policy-making and urban planning. By recognizing and building upon these informal strengths, we can create policies that resonate with the lived experiences of ViC residents and align with the socio-cultural fabric of these communities. Empowerment and Capacity Building: Empowerment lies at the core of community development theories. Empowering communities involves not only granting them a voice in decision-making but also building their capacity to participate effectively. Our proposed guiding principles prioritize the empowerment of ViCs by providing them with the tools, knowledge, and agency needed to actively contribute to their redevelopment.

17612918.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612918.value: Major Findings: Dynamic ViC Transformation Along with Development of Planned City: ViCs have experienced significant changes in building quality, urban spaces, and infrastructure in parallel with the city's formal planning and urban development. ViCs have played a crucial role in contributing to urban growth and affordable housing, aligning with the government's goals. Institutional Oversight as Main Contributor to ViC’s Lack of Provisions: Many issues within ViCs stem from institutional limitations in the formal urban planning system. This includes the absence of basic infrastructure services, which results in subpar living conditions in some ViCs. Conversely, self-upgrades by other ViCs have exceeded both ViC and non-ViC neighborhood standards. Mixed Development and Management Models: ViCs are classified into four types based on their redevelopment models: village-led, government-led, developer-led, and government-developer-partnership-led. While type exhibits unique characteristics, challenges, and responses to government policies, the Village-led developments exhibits attributes that are not commonly found in government or developer-led cases. Shift in Attitudes, Models, and Policies: Over time, public and government attitudes towards ViCs have transitioned from negative to reluctant acceptance and, currently, positive dependence. This shift has led to policies favoring integrated regeneration over total demolition, indicating the growing recognition of ViCs' value. Current Policy and Development Limitations: While Shenzhen's policies aim to modernize and homogenize ViCs, they often overlook the root causes of environmental issues. Neglect of informal rules and community involvement hinders policy effectiveness. Recommendations include policy adjustments that consider local contexts and specific issues. Transcending the Formal/Informal Binary: The research seeks to transcend the traditional binary perspective on urban informality. It highlights the intertwined relationships between formal and informal elements in ViCs, emphasizing the need for a nuanced, socio-spatial framework for analysis. Research Outcome: Academic Presentations: The research findings have been presented at several international conferences and workshops, including the National University of Singapore, the University of OSLO, and School of Environment and Architecture in India. Academic Publications: Research outcomes have been published in a few peer-reviewed articles. Including chapter in Routledge published book "The Emerging Public Realm of the Greater Bay Area: Approaches to Public Space in a Chinese Megaregion,” and journal article in Land Use Policy “Towards sustainable urban transition: A critical review of strategies and policies of urban village renewal in Shenzhen, China”.

17612918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612918.value: Current development is an article under review for submission to the academic journal - Cities. The paper integrates findings from the "Integrated Regeneration" approach with theories of community development, ensuring a holistic and inclusive approach to ViC development. Its aim is to provide insights into how the ongoing government-led renovations of the ViCs (Tongzhu) could benefit from lessons learned from successful self-renovations and improvements carried out by ViCs. These self-initiated improvements have not only enhanced quality but also minimized rent increases and residents' negative responses, addressing two critical issues that have stalled both developer-led redevelopments (such as Vanke's Wancun, 2017-2022) and the current government-led ViC regeneration (2022-2023). The paper utilizes community-based development principles to emphasize the importance of involving ViC residents in decision-making, customizing policies to each ViC's unique context, and promoting community ownership and empowerment. The paper will advise future policies on ViC renovations or redevelopments to consider empowering ViCs with the tools, knowledge, and agency needed to actively contribute to their redevelopment, thereby enhancing their resilience and sustainability.

17612918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612918.value: This research on Shenzhen's "Villages in the City" (ViCs) offers insights with far-reaching implications. It reveals that ViCs possess a remarkable ability to independently enhance essential infrastructure and services, showcasing their adaptability and self-sufficiency. This autonomy has implications for urban development worldwide, emphasizing the potential of grassroots initiatives in addressing urban challenges. The research fills a historical documentation gap, shedding light on ViCs' incremental renovations over decades. This historical perspective provides valuable lessons for revitalizing informal settlements and urban areas in other cities globally, promoting sustainable development practices. The institutional and spatial analysis within ViCs yields a nuanced understanding of their development, crucial for crafting tailored policies that respect their uniqueness. Furthermore, the study formulates guiding principles that prioritize community engagement and local identity preservation. The research underscores the evolution of attitudes and policies towards ViCs, emphasizing the need for adaptable governance and root-cause-focused policies. It advances the theoretical framework for comprehending urban informality, with global relevance, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions. It carries implications for inclusive and sustainable urban renewal practices on a global scale. This research's significance lies in its potential to shape urban development, inspire inclusive policies, and enhance our grasp of informal settlements, benefiting cities worldwide as they grapple with urbanization challenges.

17613218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17613218.value: Family caregiving plays a significant role in enabling older adults to stay as long as possible in their familiar community. This concept, known as Aging-In-Place, is preferred by older adults worldwide and is advocated by government policies. According to the latest statistics, adult children account for the largest proportion of family caregivers in Hong Kong, and the demand for family caregivers is expected to escalate in coming years. Dementia family caregivers are continuously challenged by care demands that are often highly variable and unpredictable, putting them at risk for adverse effects on both physical and mental well-being. Concurrently, adult children often have their own developmental needs including career development, family responsibility, and social networking. The Meaning Making model suggests that people are instinctively searching for meaning, in particular after encountering a life challenge and/or stressful condition. Research has shown that taking care of parents with dementia in Hong Kong is associated with “making meaning” on affirming self and enriching life. The proposed study furthers this knowledge by testing hypotheses based on a generation model towards meaning making in dementia caregiving. The Baby Boomer Generation and Generation X have differences in their shared global meaning, which may have implications on their situational meaning making processes and ultimate adjustment. As members of the Baby Boomer Generation age and their children, members of Generation X, are becoming their caregivers, we propose a longitudinal survey of 760 adult child dementia caregivers. It aims to 1) investigate differences of meaning making in dementia caregiving between the Baby Boomer Generation and Generation X and 2) test the hypothesized relationship between meaning making in dementia caregiving, meaning made, and well-being indicators between and within the two generations. The longitudinal survey will inform the ongoing discussion amongst researchers, policymakers, and service providers on the need to crystallize different needs amongst generations and to generate dementia-related policies and services that are sensitive to the characteristics and needs of specific generations.

17613218.label: Realisation of objectives
17613218.value: All three objectives have been achieved successfully. The methodology and process of achieving were illustrated below. Objective 1: Investigate the differences between dementia caregivers of two specific generations – the Baby boomer Generation and Generation X – in meaning making, including the meaning making process and meaning made. 100% achieved. Research design: Self-administered survey with a standardized questionnaire was used. Later one in order to minimize the impacts of COVID in recruiting participants, sequential sampling was adopted. Hence, the sampling process has been continued till the end of the project period. Measures: Key measures include generation, meaning making, meaning made, and psychological characteristics that were illustrated below. Reliabilities of all measures were satisfactory in the research sample. Sampling method: The sample of the present study was defined using the below inclusion and exclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria: (1) Hong Kong residents; (2) birth year between 1946 to 1980; (3) providing care to at least one parent (aged 65 or above, with dementia) on ADL or IADL not less than 8 hours in three months prior to the survey; (4) able to read Chinese; and (5) voluntary participation. Exclusion criterion: (1) being challenged by stressful life events in his/her own life during the survey time, e.g., diagnosis of life-threatening disease, unemployed, the current loss of close family members or friends. Participants were recruited through community services, care associations, and social networks of the research team who are providing services to people with dementia and/or networking with stakeholders of people with dementia. Sample: A total of 873 participants were recruited as of April 8, 2022. Excluding those who provided incomplete surveys, did not fulfil inclusion and exclusion criteria, and those who have not responded or decided to drop out from the study, there was 791 valid sample. The mean age of the participants was about 56 years, the majority of whom (78.27%) were female caregivers. Around half of the participants (52.75%) reported an education level of high school or less. More than half of them (53.66%) reported being married. Most of the care recipients (85%) were community-dwelling, and more than half of them (55%) lived with their caregivers. Specifically, around 56% of the BG caregivers reported living with the care recipients, compared to 53% of the GX caregivers. Meaning making process: The average score of the subscale Losses/Powerlessness (LP) for all participants (N = 764), BG (n = 412) and GX (n = 352) were 58.79 (SD = 10.89), 57.99 (SD = 10.57), 59.72 (SD = 11.19), respectively. The average score of the subscale Provisional Meaning (PM) for all participants, BG, and GX were 69.67 (SD = 9.61), 70.57 (SD = 9.06), and 68.63 (SD = 10.14), respectively. The average summed score of FMTC for all participants, BG, and GX were 124.88 (SD = 15.51), 126.57 (SD = 14.35), 122.91 (SD = 16.57), respectively. Meaning made: The average score of Positive Aspects of Caregiving (PAC) for all participants, BG and GX were 37.56 (SD = 6.99), 38.67 (SD = 6.53), and 36.36 (SD = 7.28), respectively. On the item level, the most agreed (combining “Agree” and “Strongly Agree”) items were “Enable me to learn new skills” (58.12%), “Feel needed” (57.46%), and “More positive towards life” (48.69%). Data analysis strategy: After data cleaning and reliability testing, an independent t-test was applied to test generation differences between BG and GX in the meaning making process and the meaning made (detailed findings refer to Section 6); Conclusion: The self-administered questionnaire design, together with data analysis strategies adopted ensured a successful achievement of objective 1. Objective 2: Test the relationships between the meaning making process, meaning made, and adjustment among Baby Boomer Generation and Generation X caregivers. 100% achieved. Research design: Self-administered longitudinal survey with a 12-month interval with a standardized questionnaire was used. Measures at follow up stage: Meaning making, meaning made, generation, and psychosocial characteristics were measured same as the baseline survey.. Adjustment was measured by Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) with satisfactory reliabilty. Five levels of depression were also recoded using a cutoff score to indicate the level of depressive symptoms. Sampling method: After 12 months of the baseline survey, participants will be contacted by phone calls with an online questionnaire followed upon consent. If the phone call was unanswered more than three times, the participant would be regarded as dropping out of the study. At this moment, we are still conducting follow up survey according to the baseline survey completion date. In terms of the active working sample (N = 764) at baseline, 445 participants have already finished the follow-up survey questionnaire, 60 reported decease of the care recipients, 179 not yet responded and/or dropped out. The follow-up rate was about sixty-six per cent. Sample: Among those 445 participants who finished both the baseline and follow-up questionnaires, an active panel sample of 385 was cleaned and checked to develop as an active panel sample. Meaning making: At the follow-up phase, the mean score of for all participants on Losses/Powerlessness (LP), Provisional Meaning (PM), and FMTC total were 60.59 (SD = 10.42), 69.34 (SD = 9.70), and 122.74 (SD = 15.45), respectively. Meaning made: At the follow-up phase, the average score of Positive Aspects of Caregiving (PAC) for all participants, BG and GX were 36.51 (SD = 6.75), 37.24 (SD = 6.66), and 35.57 (SD = 6.76), respectively. Adjustment: The mean score of PHQ-9 for all participants baseline and follow up were 4.38 (SD = 5.06) and 5.21 (SD = 5.64), respectively. At follow up, 26.75% reported having no depressive symptoms, 30.13% reported having mild depression, 24.68% reported having moderate depression, 9.87% reported having moderately severe depression, and 8.57% reported having severe depression. Analytic strategies: After data cleaning and reliability testing, regression, SEM, and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were applied. Conclusion: The longitudinal design with a 12-month interval developed a unique panel data among adult children caregivers. The fsQCA methodology applied revealed solutions contributing to the complexity of relationships between meaning making and adjustment in one year (details in Section 6). Objective 3: Inform policy and service developments to support family caregiving in the context of a rapidly aging population and social development. 100% achieved. Dissemination activities: For the public, a caregiver website has been developed to synthesize knowledge generated from this project (https://www.caregiving.hku.hk/meaning-making). For the stakeholders, a plenary speech was delivered at the annual congress of Hong Kong Gerontology Association 2020 with over 800 participants (https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1MO3o2iLv1G3ZIERyh8oe4IEY8YHCBz1H). Carer-centered responsive intervention strategies have been translated into capacity building training curricula for both the professional workforces (delivered twice in 2021 and 2022 with over sixty beneficiaries) and students in professional training (delivered twice in 2021 and 2022 for over seventy students). Policy and service development implications: 1) Meaning making process and meaning made are important considerations in developing interventions for adult children caregivers; 2) generation sensitive strategies were recommended to differentiate service development for BG and GX caregivers; 3) policies and services targeting working caregivers (i.e., Generation X) should take life course perspective so that caregivers would be empowered to comprehend their life choices on working and caregiving; 4) workplace accommodative measures should be promoted and further examined; and 5) for caregiver support workforce, capacity building on generation responsive interventions should be emphasized to create a supportive ecology.

17613218.label: Major findings and research outcome
17613218.value: Hypothesis 1: Significant differences between BG and GX – in meaning making, including the meaning making process and meaning made were identified. Generation X caregivers were significantly more likely to feel the sense of loss/powerlessness than Baby Boomers caregivers (MGX= 59.72; SDGX= 11.19; MBG= 57.99; SDBG = 10.57; t = 2.19; p < .05). Generation X had a significantly weaker tendency to search meaning in caregiving process compared to Baby Boomers (MGX = 68.63; SDGX = 10.14; MBG = 70.57; SDBG = 9.06; t = -2.79; p < .01). Generation X experienced a significantly weaker sense of meaning made compared to the Baby Boomer Generation (MGX = 36.26; SDGX = 7.28; MBG = 38.67; SDBG = 6.53; t = -4.82; p < .001). Hypothesis 2: Relationships between meaning making, generation, and adjustment were found to be very complex. Using the moderated meditation model consisting of two moderators (generation and role adaptation) and one mediator (provisional meaning), it was found that the conditional indirect effects were significant for participants who reported greater provisional meanings and who have adapted to their role as a caregiver (B = 0.16, p = 0.002). Applying the fsQCA method, causes leading to categories of depressive symptomatology after a 12-month interval were explained by four solutions attributed to complex interactions between contributing variables. For example, Solution 1: For GX caregivers, the presence of a high sense of powerlessness, high caregiver burden, high depressive symptoms, and taking care of a care recipient with high NPI severity and high NPI disturbance, lead to high depressive symptomatology, regardless of provisional meaning and adaptation time. Solution 2: For BG caregivers, the presence of high sense of powerlessness, low provisional meaning, high caregiver burden, hight depressive symptoms, low resilience, short adaptation time, taking care of a care recipient with high NPI severity, lead to high depressive symptomatology, regardless of NPI disturbance. Solution 3: For BG caregivers, the presence of high sense of powerlessness, high provisional meaning, high caregiver burden, hight depressive symptoms, long adaptation time, taking care of a care recipient with high NPI severity and high NPI disturbance, lead to high depressive symptomatology, regardless of resilience. Solution 4: For BG caregivers, the presence of high sense of powerlessness, low provisional meaning, high caregiver burden, hight depressive symptoms, low resilience, high adaptation time, taking care of a care recipient with low NPI severity and disturbance, lead to high depressive symptomatology.

Findings from this project will inform meaning-based self-help intervention to empower caregivers. Knowledge exchange: My presentation at GSA 2020 based on this project attracted peer scholars’ attention to dementia care. In 2021, I was invited to be an international advisor for the Living Alone with Cognitive Impairment (LACI) project led by Dr. Elena Portacolone, Institute for Health & Aging, University of California San Francisco (https://livingalone.ucsf.edu/). It is expected that I will conduct a presentation on the meaning making of dementia caregivers through the LACI platform in late 2022. We are planning to apply to Germany/Hong Kong Joint Research Scheme 2022/2023. Moreover, I have been in an active research partnership under the Global Ageing Research Partnership (GARP). 17613218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17613218.value: Adult children account for the largest proportion of family caregivers in Hong Kong, who play a significant role in enabling older adults to stay as long as possible in their familiar community. This concept, known as Aging-In-Place, is preferred by older adults worldwide and is advocated by government policies. Dementia family caregivers are continuously challenged by care demands that are often highly variable and unpredictable, putting them at risk for adverse effects on both physical and mental well-being. Meaning Making model suggests that people are instinctively searching for meaning, in particular after encountering a life challenge and/or stressful condition. Based on a longitudinal study among around 800 adult children caregivers to people with dementia, we found 1) the Baby Boomer caregivers experienced higher levels of meaning made and meaning searching as compared to Generation X caregivers; 2) Generation X caregivers experienced higher levels of sense of powerlessness as compared to Baby Boomer Generation caregivers; and 3) adult children caregivers adjustment over a 12 month of the period was affected by only their generation status, meaning making, but also a complex combination with care recipients’ behavioral problems, burden, resilience, and caregiving adaptation. A generation responsive policy and service implications were recommended.
