18300618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18300618.value: Results indicated that ingested microplastic by cultured-fishes is highly variable and is affected not only by ambient pollution level of their living environment, but also by fish feed and fishing operations. This points to the need of a systematic assessment of contributing factors identified by this study.

18300618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18300618.value: This project aimed to assess the presence of microplastic (MP) in commercial fish in the Pearl River Estuary (PRE). Microplastic refers to tiny plastic debris with diameter of less than 5 mm. Wild and cultured fish were sampled at the PRE, and MP were extracted from the digestive tract of the fish samples. MP were observed in 42% and 100% of the wild and cultured fish samples respectively. In addition, MP abundance in cultured fishes were found to decrease further away from the PRE, which indicates an influence from river discharge. Results of the project indicated a prevalence of plastic contamination in local fishes intended for human consumption and the quantity found were relatively high compared to international averages. Although the risk to human health of this pollutant is yet to be determined, results of the study pointed to an urgent need to reduce plastic pollution in the marine environment locally, regionally and globally.

18301418.label: Realisation of objectives
18301418.value: In line with the objectives, we synthesized several series of transition-metal catalysts of different chelating ligands. Structures for some complexes were determined by X-ray diffraction. Their activities for reductive coupling of CO2 with nucleophilic substrates were evaluated electro- and photochemically. Electronic structures and photophysical properties of some compounds were studied by DFT computation. A series of 3d transition-metal complexes bearing multidentate ligands with 2,2'-bipyridine and 1,10-phenanthroline moieties were synthesized. 3d metal (Co and Ni) complexes [M(L1)]2+, M(L2), M(L3) and M(L6) bearing different ligands (L1 = 2,2’:6’,2”:6”,2”’-quaterpyridine; L2 = 6,6'-bis(benzimidazolyl)-2,2'-bipyridine; L3 = 6,6'-bis(tetrazolyl)-2,2'-bipyridine; L6 = 2,2'-bipyridine-6,6'-dicarboxylate) were prepared by metathesis of M(ClO4)2 with the ligands in solution. Besides, cobalt complexes [Co(L9)]2+ bearing tripodal iminopyridine (L9 = cis,cis-1,3,5-tris(pyridine-2-carboxaldimino)-cyclohexane and its substituted derivatives), as well as Co(L10)X2 (X = Cl or Br) and Co(L11)Br2 bearing diimine-dioximes were prepared by literature methods. Heteroleptic complexes (Ag, Cu, Ru and Pb) bearing the anionic L2 – L8 were also prepared. Dinuclear Ru(II) complexes [Ru2(L2)(PPh3)2(CNR)4]2+ and [Ru2(Me2L2)(PPh3)2(CNR)4]2+ were obtained from RuCl2(PPh3)3 with 6,6'-bis(benzimidazolyl)-2,2'-bipyridine (L2) and its N-methyl derivative (Me2L2) respectively. Besides, Pb complexes [Pd(L3)(OH2)2] (L3 = 6,6'-bis(tetrazolyl)-2,2'-bipyridine) and [Pb(L4)(OH2)X]n (L4 = 2,2'-bipyridine-6-tetrazolate; X = Br-, Cl- and NO3-) were prepared under hydrothermal conditions. Complexes M(L5)(P^P) (M = Cu and Ag; L5 = 5-(2-pyridyl)tetrazolate and its derivatives; P^P = diphosphines) were made from [CuI(MeCN)4]ClO4 and AgNO3 with the ligands. Moreover, multinuclear Pb complexes [Pb(L6)(OH2)]n (L6 = 2,2'-bipyridine-6,6'-dicarboxylate), [Pb(L7)]n (L7 = 1,10-phenanthroline-2,9-dicarboxylate) and [Pb(L8)(OH2)2Cl]2 (L8 = 2,2'-bipyridine-6-carboxylate) were obtained under hydrothermal conditions. In collaboration with Université Paris Cité, reactivity of these metal complexes was evaluated electrochemically. Cyclic voltammogram (CV) was performed in CO2-saturated solutions in the presence of different nucleophilic substrates: amines (R2NH), thiols (RSH) and carboanionic agents (CAA) and weak acid (water). By comparison to CVs in control conditions (without CO2, substrates or catalysts), catalytic potential (Ecat) and related oxidation states were identified. Initially, [M(L1)]2+ (M = Co and Ni) were found to catalyze CO2 reduction in acetonitrile (MeCN), as revealed by the catalytic wave in their CVs with onset potentials (Ecat) = –1.65 V and –1.75 V vs SCE respectively. Reaction with secondary amines (R2NH) was then studied using [Ni(L1)]2+ (0.5 mM) in CO2-saturated MeCN. Addition of morpholine (5 mM) to the solution shifted Ecat to –1.5 V and enhanced the catalytic current (icat). With increasing [morpholine] (5 – 250 mM), icat increased further and Ecat shifted anodically by ca. 200 mV. The changes suggested multielectron reaction of CO2 with morpholine. ESI-MS revealed a carbomate adduct [(L1)Ni–O(CO)NR¬2)]+ (m/z = 498) was formed in the CV solution. With increasing [H2O] (250 – 2000 mM), further enhancement of icat was observed. Similar changes to CO2 catalytic wave were observed with [Co(L1)]2+ in the presence of morpholine (Ecat = –1.35 V vs SCE) and morpholine/water (Ecat = –1.15 V). The CO2-amine reaction was investigated using [Ni(L1)]2+ and [Co(L1)]2+ (0.5 mM) respectively by controlled-potential electrolysis (CPE) under CO2 (1 atm) in MeCN containing 0.5 M morpholine and 2M H2O. Formyl morpholine was detected (GC-MS) in CPE at varied applied potentials (–1.55 to – 1.75 V). A maximum yield of formyl morpholine (171 µmol, turnover number (TON vs catalyst) = 43) was observed at –1.6 V, together with H2 (TON = 350) and formate (4.2 µmol). When thiomopholine and benzylamine were added instead, corresponding formyl amines (60.5 µmol, TON = 15 and 31.7 µmol, TON = 8 respectively) were obtained. With n-butylamine, N,N'-dibutyl urea was obtained instead (131.6 µmol, TON = 33). When electrocatalysis was performed at –1.4 V vs SCE using [Co(L1)]2+ and morpholine, formyl morpholine was also yielded (48.4 µmol, TON = 12). The CO2 catalysis of [Ni(L1)]2+ was also studied by CV with different amines and other nucleophilic substrates. Though similar changes in catalytic wave were observed with thiomorpholine and benzylamine, while insoluble products were formed with some amines, as well as with various RSHs and CAAs, rendering further studies impossible. The catalytic activities of 3d metal (Co and Ni) complexes M(L2) – M(L4), could not be evaluated similarly, due to their poor solubility in common organic solvents (MeCN, DMF and DMA) for electrochemical studies. Though cobalt complexes [Co(L9)]2+, Co(L10)X2 and Co(L11)Br2 exhibited similar catalytic wave under CO2 in CVs, they decomposed gradually in the presence of amines and water, probably due to hydrolysis of imine bonds. Photocatalysis (> 420 nm) was performed using [Ni(L1)]2+ and [Co(L1)]2+ (2 µm) respectively in CO2-saturated MeCN containing 0.5 M morpholine and 2 mM tributyl-triazaangulenium (TATA+) as photosensitizer (PS). Formylated amines were detected at similar TONs (ca. 50) together with CO (TONs = ca. 89 and 210 respectively). However, the same products were also obtained in similar quantity in control experiments without catalyst and the yields increased upon purging the reaction solutions with air, suggesting the products originated from photooxidation of the amines by O2. As CO was yielded in the reactions, photocatalysis was performed in aqueous MeCN (5 – 20% H2O, v/v) under similar conditions by replacing morpholine with triethanolamine (TEAO) or triethylamine (TEA) and 0.1 M 1,3-dimethyl-2-phenyl-2,3-dihydro-1Hbenzo[d]imidazole (BIH). With 20% H2O, CO was formed selectively (ca. 93%) at high TONs of ca. 19000 (95 µmol, TEOA) and 6330 (31.6 µmol, TEA) Under the same conditions, CO was produced (11.5 µmol, TON = ca. 2300) using [Ni(L1)]2+. Formylation of secondary amines occurred similarly via competitive photo-oxidation in CO2-saturated MeCN with [Ru2(L2)(PPh3)2(CNR)4]2+ and [Ru2(Me2L2)(PPh3)2(CNR)4]2+ respectively as photocatalyst. Interestingly, the Ru complexes were found to be emissive (543 – 558 nm) in MeCN and acted as self-sensitized photocatalyst for CO2 reduction. Upon CO2 saturation, CVs of the complexes in MeCN exhibited catalytic wave (Ecat = –1.59 to –1.85 V). Photocatalysis (> 420 nm) was performed (without external PS) in CO2-saturated aqueous MeCN (5% H2O, v/v) containing 0.1 mM Ru catalyst and 0.1 M 1,3-dimethyl-2-phenyl-2,3-dihydro-1Hbenzo[d]imidazole (BIH). CO was formed selectively after 20 hrs at TONs of 261 (yield = 65.1 µM, 98%) and 53 (yield = 13.2 µM, 93%) respectively. In collaboration with City University and Yangtze University, photophysical properties of heteroleptic metal complexes (Ag, Cu and Pb) bearing the anionic ligands (L3 – L8) were studied by spectrophotometric methods and DFT computations. [Pd(L3)(OH2)2] (L3 = 6,6’-bis(tetrazolyl)-2,2’-bipyridine), [Pb(L4)(OH2)X]n (X = Br-, Cl- and NO3-) and [Pb(L5)2]n were found to exhibit solid-state photoluminescence (504 – 645 nm) of varied parentages as revealed by photophysical and DFT studies. Particularly, emission of [Pb(L4)(OH2)Cl]n (PLQY = 16.5%) is sensitive to vapor of volatile organics and temperature. Photoluminescence of M(L5)(P^P) (L5 = 5-(2-pyridyl)tetrazolate and its derivatives; M = Cu and Ag; P^P = diphosphines) was studied. Though they exhibited only weak emission (539 – 600 nm) in solution, high PLQY (39 – 85%) were observed for the solid-state emission (528 – 567 nm) of Cu(L5)(P^P). Their electronic structures and photophysics were also studied by DFT calculation. Meanwhile, [Co(L9)]2+ was showed to catalyze reduction of H2O to H2 (TON = 1430 – 2810) in aqueous MeCN (5% H2O, v/v) containing 0.2 M TEA, 0.1 M acetic acid and TATA+. Co(L10)X2 and Co(L11)Br2 were found to catalyze the regeneration of a NADH analogue, 1-benzyl-1,4-dihydronicotinamide (BNAH), from its conjugated cation (BNA+) with an optimized yield of 10 µmol (TON = 19.9) with TEOA/TATA+ in MeCN.

18301418.label: Major findings and research outcome
18301418.value: A series of transition-metal catalysts for the reduction and reductive functionalization of CO2 was developed. Co and Ni catalysts [M(L1)] (M = Co and Ni; L1 - L1 = 2,2’:6’,2”:6”,2”’-quaterpyridine) for CO2-amine reductive coupling were studied electrochemically. Previously, such processes were reported using H2 (at high pressure) or metal hydrides respectively as the reductant. With [Ni(L1)]2+ and [Co(L1)]2+ as catalyst, formylated amines (TON = 8 – 43) and N,N’-dialkyl urea (TON = 33) were conveniently obtained from corresponding amines in electrocatalysis (E = –1.6 V and –1. 4 V vs SCE) performed under 1 atm CO2. The catalysts enable CO2 to be reductively coupled with different amines under mild conditions at low potentials. The two complexes also efficiently catalyse photoreduction of CO2 to CO (TONs = ca. 19000 and 2300 respectively), using tributyl-triazaangulenium (TATA+) as an organic photosensitizer (PS) and TEOA/BIH. Our systems have demonstrated exceptionally high efficiency for selective CO2-to-CO reduction and advanced conventional three-component CO2 photocatalysis by avoiding the use of precious-metal light harvester. Besides, a series of emissive dinuclear complexes [Ru2(L2)(PPh3)2(CNR)4]2+ and [Ru2(Me2L2)(PPh3)2(CNR)4]2+ (L2 = 6,6'-bis(benzimidazolyl)-2,2'-bipyridine and Me2L2 = its dimethyl derivative; CNR = phenyl isocyanides) were developed as self-sensitized photocatalysts for reduction of CO2 to CO (TON = 261 and 53). The catalysts, though composed of Ru, allow the photocatalysis to be carried out in a more atom-efficient manner without using an external PS. As a consequence of the three-year pandemic and the substantial amount of works performed, the dissemination and publication of results have been partly delayed. An article on photocatalytic CO2 reduction with [Co(L1)]2+ was already published (ACS Catalysis 2023). Recently, a conference paper on CO2-amine reductive coupling by [Ni(L1)2+] was also published (Dalton 2023, UK), while related research article is being prepared and will soon be submitted for publication. The article on CO2 reduction with the dinuclear Ru catalysts is also in preparation and will be published in due course. Meanwhile, related photocatalytic studies (H2O reduction and organohydride regeneration) were also performed with the other cobalt catalysts (Co(L9)]2+, Co(L10)X2 and Co(L11)Br2) developed in the project and were published (Eur. J. Inorg. Chem 2022 (cover feature) and Chem. Commun. 2020). Moreover, photophysical studies of related heterleptic (Cu, Ag and Pb) complexes (Polyhedron 2023, RSC Adv. 2022 and Inorg. Chem. 2022) and two review articles (Chem. Soc. Rev. 2020 and Energy Fuels 2021) on related topics of photocatalysis were also published.

18301418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18301418.value: It is observed the nature of products from CO2-amine reductive coupling are highly dependent on the structure of amines added. ESI-MS suggested the reaction may occur initially via a carbomato adduct, i.e. M–O(CO)–NR2, which then undergoes 2-electron reduction to give formyl amine (H(CO)NR2). Probably due to the facile dissociation of H(CO)NR2 from the metal centre [M(L1)]2+ (M = Ni and Co; L1 = 2,2’:6’,2”:6”,2”’-quaterpyridine), which bears two vacant sites in trans- positions, only a negligible amount of six-electron reduced product, i.e. methyl amines (CH3NR2), was detected in the reactions. To suppress the dissociation of substrates from metal centre, catalysts with two cis- vacant coordination sites is suggested. Such catalysts may allow the carbomate (R2N–(CO)–O-) to coordinate via both N and O, facilitating thus multielectron (> 2 electrons) reduction of the substrate and formation of more reduced products. Meanwhile, the insoluble adducts formed by the catalysts with some substrates and CO2 very often prevent the homogenous catalysis from occurring efficiently and limit its application. Therefore, it is suggested the solubility of catalysts be enhanced by introducing alkyl- or alkoxy- moieties onto the ligands, which may allow a more diverse classes of substrates to be used.

18301418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18301418.value: A series of inexpensive transition-metal catalysts have been prepared and their reactivity for reductive coupling of CO2 with different substrates were evaluated electrochemically. Particularly, nickel and cobalt quaterpyridine catalysts mediate CO2-amine reductive coupling, producing N-formyl amine and N,N’-dialkyl urea as the major products under mild conditions (1 atm CO2 and accessible reaction potentials). These catalysts also mediate photoreduction of CO2 to CO selectively with impressive metrics with an organic light harvester, circumventing the need of using precious-metal compounds in conventional photocatalytic conditions. On the other hand, dinuclear ruthenium (Ru) catalysts bearing di(benzimidazolyl)-bipyridine ligands were also prepared. The Ru complexes not only exhibit greenish-yellow photoluminescence, but also act as function-integrated photocatalysts for selective reduction of CO2 to CO, which do not require the use of an external light harvester and improve the atom efficiency for related reactions. Other cobalt catalysts developed in this project were found to mediate the reduction of water to hydrogen and the regeneration of organohydride donor. Meanwhile, heavier transition-metal (copper, silver and lead) complexes of related chelating ligands were found to exhibit interesting photoluminescence properties with potential applications in sensing and electroluminescence device.

18600218.label: Project Objectives
18600218.value: To construct assessment tasks to measure Chinese learners’ perceptions and productions of English word stress; To develop new teaching kits for phonological rule-based training and acoustic perceptual-based training; To conduct an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of the new training programs to improve Chinese learners’ perception and production of English word stress; To reveal participants’ views on the effectiveness and feasibility of the new training programs.
rows: To construct assessment tasks to measure Chinese learners’ perceptions and productions of English word stress;
To develop new teaching kits for phonological rule-based training and acoustic perceptual-based training;
To conduct an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of the new training programs to improve Chinese learners’ perception and production of English word stress;
To reveal participants’ views on the effectiveness and feasibility of the new training programs.

18600218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18600218.value: English is stress-timed while Chinese is syllable-timed, which makes English word stress placement difficult for Chinese learners of English. A shift of the stress from the left syllable to the right syllable seriously hampers intelligibility (e.g. PERmit vs perMIT) and inappropriate word stress affects comprehension more adversely than segmental errors. While many theorists and practitioners have observed that first language (L1) learners can easily acquire the stress as a by-product of the acquisition of a new word, it is commonly found that second language (L2) learners with a tone-language background (e.g. Chinese) encounter much more difficulty in English stress acquisition than L1 learners. The inconsistent research findings in English word stress lead to the on-going debate of “word stress deafness.” Specifically, the debate involves two theoretically and practically important questions: Is learning stress on a word-by-word basis an efficient way for L2 learners to acquire an understanding of word stress rules? If not, is there a better way? This project aims to answer these two questions with new empirical evidence. Specifically, the project will develop assessment tasks to identify Chinese learners’ difficulties in English word stress placement in perception and production, design training programs to examine whether word stress can be acquired systematically, and conduct a teaching experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of the training programs in facilitating the learning of word stress. This project is innovative in four aspects: (a) this project integrates linguistics and education, (b) the assessment tasks cover both production and perception; (c) each training program targets a distinct approach, namely, phonological rule-based and acoustic-perceptual-based approaches; (d) unlike observational or correlational studies that are commonly adopted in the social sciences, the teaching experiment is well controlled in that random assignment, innovative teaching materials, effective assessment, and recall protocols are implemented. This project will generate substantial impact in both theory and practice. Theoretically, factors that weigh most heavily on learners’ acquisition of word stress will be identified, new empirical evidence to the debate on the learnability and teachability of word stress will be collected, and a new research paradigm of word stress learning will be created. Practically, diagnostic profiles of learners’ pronunciation can be established, optimal training program of English word stress will be obtained, the assessment tasks and teaching kits can be further adapted to different levels of learners (primary, secondary, college, and adults) and learners with different language backgrounds (e.g., Thai, Vietnamese, Japanese and Korean).

18600218.label: Realisation of objectives
18600218.value: Objective 1 – to construct assessment tasks to measure Chinese learners’ perceptions and productions of English word stress Objective 1 has been fully achieved. The assessment tasks were constructed by two steps – test word selection, and task generation for the pre-, post- and delayed post-tests. In the first step, the test materials used in the three tests were the 62*3 relatively less common words mainly chosen from the Graduate Examination Records (GRE) vocabulary (word frequency determined by the British National Corpus online). The purpose of such selection was to ensure that the participants read the word by their linguistic knowledge but not their prior knowledge of the words. Among the 62 words in each set of word list, 12 had specific syllabic structures (half of them fitted the regular stress pattern and the other half did not), 26 had specific phonological similarity patterns (prefix, neutral suffix, non-neutral suffix, compound structure etc.), and 24 involved specific stress-vowel reduction patterns (primary stressed-unreduced, secondary stressed-unreduced, unstressed-unreduced, and unstressed-reduced). In the second step, a production task and a perception task were generated for the three tests to measure participants’ proficiency to correctly assign lexical stress to uncommon English words. In the production task, the participants were instructed to read aloud each listed word in the sentence frame ‘I said _ this time’ continuously. The perception task involved the words as in the production task were shuffled in different orders and recorded by a native English speaker to examine whether the participants’ perception of English stress placement was consistent with their production. The participants listened to the recording and indicated the syllable with primary stress. The recall protocols were integrated in the post-test to assess the participants’ meta-phonological awareness (e.g., noticing their own problems with L2 word stress, self-repair, and categorization of problems) and to examine the effectiveness of the training programs. After completing the production and perception tasks, the participants were asked to play back the recordings of their readings in the production task and perform analytic listening by following a set of instructions, which were immediate retrospective protocols. They self-corrected the mistakes noticed following the immediate retrospective protocols and attempted to express their thoughts and reflections. After that, the participants followed the introspective protocols and performed self-reflection on their own English word stress acquisition and training experience at the phonological level with the help of guided questions. Objective 2 – to develop new teaching kits for phonological rule-based training and acoustic perceptual-based training Objective 2 has been fully achieved. The teaching kits are available for public access on a webpage in the English pronunciation teaching and learning website (https://corpus.eduhk.hk/english_pronunciation/index.php/word-stress-teaching-kit/). There are four integral elements for the teaching kits – an overview of English word stress knowledge, materials used for the training in this project, tips for teaching English word stress obtained from the results of this project, and useful websites related to English word stress teaching. The overview of English word stress knowledge is presented in the form of an Edpuzzle video, which includes visual and audio presentations of basic information of English word stress in terms of phonetics and phonology, together with quick quizzes to help teachers and learners grasp the gist of the topic. PowerPoints and worksheets of eight sessions of the phonological rule-based and the acoustic perceptual-based training respectively are available for public access. Contents of the two training approaches used in the project are summarized below. In Session 1, both groups of participants learnt symbols and pronunciation of English consonants and vowels, English vowel chart and basic articulatory knowledge, and how to divide English words into syllables. For the rule-based instruction group, in Session 2, they were guided to apply the normal stress rule in reading an unfamiliar word. From Sessions 3 to 8, the participants follow the procedure of observing word stress placements in words with particular syllable structure, phonologically similar words, and words with vowel reduction, and then generalize word stress rules. For the acoustic-based instruction, in Session 2, the participants learnt how to locate, download, and listen to sample recordings of native English speakers’ pronunciation of words and how to observe word stress by duration, intensity, and pitch using Praat. From Sessions 3 to 8, the participants followed the same procedure to analyze word stress in their reading and compare with native speakers: 1) Divide English words into syllables 2) Visually observe and measure pitch height, intensity, and duration of each syllable of their own reading and decide which syllable receives primary word stress 3) Visually observe and measure the same cues of native speakers’ reading of the same word 4) Visually observe the acoustic cues and compare the values of their own reading and the native speakers’ reading 5) Adjust their reading based on the comparison. The teaching tips summarized the suggestions obtained from the project, such as useful rules for English word stress assignment, the most frequently mistaken word stress patterns, and flowcharts for deciding word stress assignment, conducting an acoustic comparison of word stress, and performing the metaphonological awareness task. The useful websites compiled a list of online resources which contain content focusing on the teaching and learning of English word stress, and also quizzes and exercises. Objective 3 – to conduct an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of the new training programs to improve Chinese learners’ perception and production of English word stress Objective 3 has been fully achieved. This project developed a new research paradigm from both phonological and phonetic approaches to exploring the possibilities of word stress learning. The experiment was designed to investigate the differences in English stress acquisition before and after phonological rule-based and acoustic perceptual-based instructions. There are five stages of the whole experiment – a pre-test, eight face-to-face rule-based or acoustic-based instruction sessions, an immediate post-test with recall protocols, and a delayed post-test. In the pre-, post- and delayed post-tests, the participants performed both production and perception tasks as described in Objective 1. Two groups of participants (30 in each group) received an eight-session phonological rule-based instruction or acoustic perceptual-based instruction (as summarized in Objective 2) and one control group (30 participants) had regular English classes. Retrospective and introspective protocols were completed by the participants after the immediate post-test to investigate participants’ self-reflections and comments on the training program they have attended. All five stages of the experiments were fully executed. Objective 4 – to reveal participants’ views on the effectiveness and feasibility of the new training programs Objective 4 has been fully achieved. The participants’ views on the effectiveness and feasibility of the new training programs were revealed by applying recall protocols which elicited the participants’ meta-phonological awareness and opinions towards the training programs. The recall protocols generated qualitative data as they involved the participants’ self-reflections and comments. For each participant, qualitative data about the extent to which they felt the training program was helpful for their English word stress improvement, whether they would apply the training approaches in their own learning and teaching, and what strategies they would use in deciding word stress placement were obtained.

18600218.label: Major findings and research outcome
18600218.value: The relationship between English word stress production and perception and how the stress patterns (listed in manuscript 1 under review) affected the relationship for Chinese ESL learners were examined. Several observations were made – a) accuracy of word stress perception was generally higher than production; b) accuracy of production was higher than perception for 11 stress patterns; c) production of English word stress was better than perception for the stress patterns with high production-perception symmetry; and d) deciding the existence of vowel reduction in unstressed syllables was more challenging when the target vowel is /ɒ/ than /æ/. After receiving instruction, the participants’ mean accuracy rate of English word stress placement from both experiment groups had been improved. The ANOVA results revealed that the changes were significant from the pre-test to the delayed post-test for both production and perception tasks (rule-based: production - F(2,87) = 10.642, p < .001**, perception - F(2,87) = 9.749, p < .001**; acoustic-based: production - F(2,87) = 6.985, p = .002*, perception - F(2,87) = 12.748, p < .001**). For the participants from the control group, no significant changes on their performances in both production and perception tasks can be decoded. Furthermore, the rule-based instruction approach was more effective for the improvement of word stress placement accuracy for the production tasks. The acoustic-based instruction approach was more effective for the improvement of word stress identification accuracy for the perception tasks. Over 70% of the participants in the rule-based instruction group expressed that English word stress rules were explicit yet complex and could not be applied to every word. It is more suitable for adult learners. Over 80% of the participants in the acoustic-based instruction group indicated that the training was beneficial, useful, and effective for their English word stress learning. They could understand the gaps between their own production with the native speaker’s speech with help of the visualization and quantification of acoustic cues though it might be rather time-consuming (qualitative data provided in Manuscript 3). The use of recall protocols elicited the participants’ metaphonological awareness regarding the acquisition of English word stress. In the retrospective protocols, both low- and high-level learners reported the greatest number of medium level awareness, and high-level learners also showed more high-level awareness. In the introspective protocols, the participants opined that cognitive and memory strategies were commonly used in their English word stress learning (please refer to Manuscript 2 for more details).

18600218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18600218.value: The project can be further developed from three aspects – large scale examination, knowledge transfer in adult education institutions and APP production. The well-designed assessment tasks and training materials had been evaluated by 90 participants in the current study. To consolidate the effectiveness of the tasks and materials, they could be further examined in authentic English classrooms in a larger scale. As the results indicate clear improvements of English word stress accuracy for adult learners, knowledge transfer activities such as workshops and seminars could be conducted in tertiary-level institutions. Teachers and learners may be invited to attend the activities and be informed of the new English word stress teaching and learning approaches (i.e. rule-based and acoustic-based). To further implement the pedagogical output of this project, especially for the acoustic-based training which used Praat to visualize and measure acoustic cues of English word stress, an APP may be developed to reduce the difficulty in understanding the acoustic cues. It is expected that the tool can measure the acoustic cues such as formant values, intensity, duration, and pitch height, and translate the meaning of the acoustic cues into layman’s language so that learners without knowledge about acoustic phonetics can understand the information easily.

18600218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18600218.value: It is widely recognized that English word stress is challenging for both teachers and learners, since it is highly unpredictable and difficult to be generalized. Traditionally, English word stress is acquired on a word-by-word basis, which is inefficient. To address this issue, the research project aimed to a) identify Chinese learners’ difficulties in English word stress production and perception; b) design and examine two innovative English word stress training approaches (i.e., rule-based and acoustic-based); and c) provide teaching implications and learning suggestions for the public based on the results. The project has its significance and values in four aspects. First, the project provided empirical evidence to reveal the impact of various factors that was claimed to affect English word stress placement in both production and perception. Second, the project developed two English word stress training approaches phonologically and phonetically to explore the new possibilities of word stress acquisition other than word-by-word memorizing. Third, results of the project had been developed into teaching kits with ready-made teaching materials which can be easily adopted or adapted by language teachers. Finally, impact of this project is realized by gaining visibility in public websites, workshops, seminars, and prestigious international conferences.

18600318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18600318.value: An understanding of both magnitude and arithmetic operations is essential to mathematics learning. However, the current research on mathematics learning mostly focuses on magnitude. The operation aspects have received much less attention. One way to look at people’s understanding of the operation aspects of mathematics is to investigate their understanding of arithmetic principles (APs), which are the rules and regularities that apply to arithmetic operations. The commutativity principle, which states that the order of operands is irrelevant in addition (e.g., 2+3=3+2), is an example of AP. Although some studies have been conducted to investigate children’s understanding of APs, most of these used single-faceted, cross-sectional assessments of a subset of AP, which does not provide a complete picture of children’s understanding of APs. We also have limited knowledge about the cognitive correlates of children’s AP understanding. Furthermore, although the link between children’s AP understanding and their mathematics achievement seems to be obvious, direct evidence of the relation is lacking. To fill these research gaps, a three-year longitudinal study is proposed. Three-hundred fourth graders will be assessed five times over three years in order to examine the development of their understanding of a comprehensive set of APs with a multifaceted assessment. The potential cognitive correlates of children’s AP understanding (e.g., IQ, working memory, inhibition, numerical magnitude understanding) will be assessed so that their unique contribution to children’s AP understanding can be identified. The mathematics achievement of these children will also be examined so that the relation between their AP understanding and mathematics achievement can be verified. A significant AP-math relation is expected. The proposed study is significant in three ways. First, it will be the first comprehensive longitudinal investigation of children’s AP understanding. The findings will substantially increase our knowledge about the underlying constructs and the developmental pathways of children’s AP understanding. Second, the investigation of the AP-math relation will inform us about the important factors of learning mathematics and has a great potential to shift researchers’ and teachers’ attention from the magnitude aspects of mathematics to the operation aspects of it. This enables educators to improve the mathematics curriculum by devoting more effort on the operation aspects. Third, the identification of cognitive correlates of children’s AP understanding will provide insights to the development of AP interventions. Given the significance of mathematical skills in predicting one’s well-being, efforts in improving children’s mathematics learning will pay off in the long run. 在學習數學的過程當中，對數量以及四則運算的理解同樣重要。然而，現今對數學學習的研究徧重於對數量的理解，對四則運算的理解的研究相對較少。要研究人們對四則運算的理解，可從他們對運算法則的理解著手。運算法則是指四則運算背後的一些規律，例如在加數中，加數和被加數的位置並不影響其結果 ( 2 + 3 永遠等於 3 + 2 )。這個法則稱為互換法則，是運算法則的其中一種。現時運算法則的研究集中於運用單面向以及以橫斷研究去了解兒童對運算法則的理解。然而，因為對運算法則的理解是多面性的，現時的研究並不能全面地反映兒童對這些運算法則的理解。除此之外，我們並不清楚有甚麼認知能力與兒童對運算法則的理解有關，而運算法則的理解與數學能力的關係亦欠缺直接的證據支持。 由於以上原因，本研究希望藉著一個為期三年的追蹤研究，更全面地了解兒童對運算法則的理解。本研究小組會邀請約三百名小四的學童參與是次研究。參與的兒童會在三年內接受五次多面向的運算法則評估，以檢視他們在這段時間中對運算法則理解的進展。除此之外，研究小組亦會評估參加者各項認知能力 (如智力、工作記憶，反應抑制能力，對數量的理解等等) 以及其數學成績，以找出與運算法則理解相關的認知能力，以及確認運算法則理解與數學能力之關係。 是項研究是首個以多面向的評估去了解兒童對運算法則的理解之研究，結果將讓我們更深入地了解運算法則理解背後的本質以及其發展路程。除此之外，如運算法則理解與數學能力之關係得以被確認，將鼓勵更多的研究去探索這方面的能力。長遠來說，這會令我們對數學學習的認知變得更全面。最後，透過找出一些與運算法則理解有關的認知能力，我們期望能夠啟發出一些更有效的訓練方法，以增加兒童對運算法則的理解。希望通過提升兒童對運算法則的理解，學童的數學成績得以被提升。

18600318.label: Realisation of objectives
18600318.value: Overall project description The current study has investigated children’s understanding of arithmetic principles (APs) and its relation with mathematics achievement through a longitudinal design. Six APs were targeted (commutativity, associativity, two complement principles, relation to operands, and direction of effect), and each AP was assessed using three different measures, namely evaluation of examples, explicit recognition, and application of procedures. Participants of this study (n = 235 in at the final time point) completed five assessments of their AP understanding as well as their mathematics achievement. The data obtained from this longitudinal study has been analyzed to answer the following research questions: Factor structure (Research question 1) First of all, the question concerning the factor structure of children’s AP knowledge is addressed. With six targeted constructs, each being assessed using three different methods, a multi-trait-multi-method factor analysis was conducted to examine the factor structure of the children’s AP understanding. This method allows me to extract the pure variance of the constructs by removing the method variance. Unfortunately, this model is too complicated, and the factor analysis failed to converge. The model was simplified by only including three of the six APs that are more similar to each other (i.e., commutativity and the two complement principles). Although the model converged, further analyses suggested that the understanding of these three APs is better summarized by a single AP factor. I therefore conclude that the understanding of commutativity and the two complement principles belong to the same theoretical construct (see Publication 2 for details). Cognitive correlates (Research question 2) Based on the single AP factor obtained from the multi-trait-multi-method factor analyses done, I further included various cognitive factors (e.g., nonverbal intelligence, verbal and visuospatial working memory, processing speed, inhibition, and numerical magnitude) to examine whether these cognitive factors are significantly related to the AP factor using structural equation modeling. The results suggested that all the aforementioned factors (except for processing speed) significantly predicted the AP factor, and the relation between visuospatial working memory and the AP factor was mediated by children’s numerical magnitude knowledge (see Publication 2 for details). The findings have informed us about the important factors that are relevant to children’s AP understanding and thus shed light on potential ways to improve children’s AP knowledge. Development of AP understanding (Research question 1) Given the complexity of the factor structure of children’s AP knowledge, the examination of the developmental changes in AP understanding focused mainly on complement, the AP that is most relevant to children’s mathematics achievement. The findings suggest that the greatest growth in complement understanding appears to fall within the start of fifth grade (see Publication 3 for details). It should, however, be noted that the pandemic kicked in at Time 2, and the slower development of complement understanding at later time points may be due to the school suspension because of the pandemic. Future studies are needed to confirm whether the development of complement understanding does slow down from fifth grade onwards. The relation between AP understanding and mathematics achievement (Research question 3) The relation between AP understanding and mathematics achievement is perhaps the most important research question to be addressed, as it has implications on whether educators should focus more attention on the construct of AP understanding. Various analyses have been conducted to address this issue. In the first analysis, my student and I have examined the potential bi-directional relation between children’s complement understanding and their computation skills using a random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). The results suggest that while children’s complement understanding predicts their future computation skills, the reverse pathway was not significant, thus suggesting a one-way pathway from complement understanding to computation skills (see Publication 3). In another analysis, my team showed that children’s understanding of the relation to operands principle predicted the growth in their arithmetic/algebraic problem solving across two years (see Publication 4). These relations, however, do not appear to be mediated by children’s ability to construct the correct number sentences, as initially predicted in the proposal. These findings, together with two other publications which showed that AP understanding mediated the relation between spatial skills and mathematics achievement (Publication 5), as well as that AP understanding predicted the trait factor of mathematical development (Publication 6), have illustrated the roles of AP understanding on children’s mathematics learning, and thus urge educators to devote more attention to this domain. Based on the aforementioned analyses, all the project objectives have been fully achieved. It should, however, be noted that the current project has yielded a large amount of data about children’s AP and mathematical development, and thus the dataset might be further utilized to address the remaining issues on this topic.

18600318.label: Major findings and research outcome
18600318.value: The current project has generated at least nine manuscripts, with six of them being directly relevant to children’s AP understanding (five have been accepted/published). These findings not only illustrated the factor structure of children’s AP understanding and its cognitive correlates, but also demonstrated the significant role that AP understanding plays in children’s mathematical development. Published manuscripts on children’s AP understanding: 1. Wong, T.T.-Y., Leung, C.O.-Y.#, & Kwan, K.-T.# (2021). Multifaceted assessment of children’s inversion understanding. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 207, 105121. Utilizing the pilot data of the current project, this study showed the importance of using multifaceted assessment to assess children’s AP understanding. 2. Wong, T.T.-Y. (2023). Cognitive predictors of children’s arithmetic principle understanding. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 227, 105579. This study examined both the factor structure of children’s AP understanding as well as its cognitive correlates. A one-factor model was suggested to best explain children’s AP understanding, and this factor was predicted by nonverbal intelligence, verbal and visuospatial working memory, inhibition, and numerical magnitude knowledge. 3. Yip, E.S.-K.#, Wong, T.T.-Y., & #Kwan, K. T. (2022). The relation between complement understanding and computational skills: A random intercept cross-lagged panel model. Developmental Psychology. This study examined the potential bi-directional relation between complement understanding and computation skills using random intercept cross-lagged panel model. The findings suggest a one-way relation from complement understanding to computation skills. 4. Wong, T.T.-Y., & Kwan K.T.# (In press). The sums are larger than their natural number addends: Relation to operands understanding predicts growth in arithmetic/algebraic problem-solving. Developmental Psychology. This study showed children’s understanding of the relation to operands principle significantly predicted the growth in arithmetic/algebraic problem solving. 5. Leung, C. O.-Y.#, & Wong, T. T.-Y. (Accepted). How are Spatial Ability and Math Related? The Mediating Roles of Numerical Magnitude Knowledge, Understanding of Arithmetic Operations, and Word-Problem Representation. Journal of Educational Psychology. This study showed that children’s understanding of AP significantly mediated the relation between spatial skills and mathematics achievement. The sixth study generated from this dataset, which utilized the state-trait model which differentiated the trait factor of mathematical competence (the stable variance) from its state factor (the time-to-time variation) and showed that children’s AP understanding was one of the factors that predict the trait factor of mathematical competence, is currently under review in Contemporary Educational Psychology. Three more manuscripts have been written up based on the dataset generated from this project (see Publications 7 to 9).

18600318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18600318.value: Given the established relation between children’s arithmetic principle understanding and their mathematics achievement, it is important for researchers and educators to put more emphasis on this construct. A logical next-step would be to develop interventions that facilitate children’s understanding of various important APs. Based on the findings from this project, I have already developed a learning package that may facilitate children’s acquisition of these APs. The learning package consists of conceptually-sequenced arithmetic problems that enable children to discover the regularities behind arithmetic problems more easily (e.g., the conceptually related problems are put together, and children are asked to line up the identical numbers in different problems). An evaluation study, which has got the in-principle acceptance from Journal of Educational Psychology, is now on-going. If this learning package has been proven effective, my research team will make it available to primary schools in Hong Kong.

18600318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18600318.value: Children’s understanding of arithmetic principles (e.g., if 3 + 7 = 10, then 10 – 7 = 3) has been a largely neglected area in mathematics learning literature. The current longitudinal study utilized a comprehensive assessment of children’s understanding of six arithmetic principles. The findings illustrated that (1) children’s understanding of some of these arithmetic principles can be summarized as a single construct; (2) this construct is related to various cognitive factors, such as intelligence, working memory, inhibition skills and numerical magnitude knowledge; and (3) children’s understanding of arithmetic principles significantly predicted their future mathematics achievement even when the effects of other cognitive factors have been considered. Arithmetic principle understanding is thus an important aspect of mathematics that educators should focus more attention on. The findings about the cognitive correlates of children’s arithmetic principle understanding also enable educators to develop effective arithmetic principle interventions.

18601118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18601118.value: Computer programming has been around in schools and universities for half a century. It can be characterized as a complex process of planning, creating, testing and debugging a sequence of instructions executed by a computer to achieve a specific goal. From a pedagogical point of view, it has been shown that computer programming can help develop students’ creativity, problem solving and higher-order thinking skills. The potential benefits brought by computer programming have been increasingly recognized as vital to the competitiveness and success of graduates in the globalized knowledge economy, stimulating a renewed interest in equipping university students from different disciplinary backgrounds with fundamental programming skills. Despite this, learning computer programming has long been regarded as a major challenge for novices and high failure rates of introductory programming courses are prevalent in higher education. Attempts have been made to determine the cause of this poor performance in novice programmers, with a focus on students’ internal characteristics such as age, gender and learning styles. But little is known about students’ use of learning strategies during the programming process and which strategies are more effective for gaining programming knowledge and skills, especially in the context of teacher education. To fill this gap in the literature, this project will draw on the concept of self-regulated learning (SRL) to engage students of teacher education in goal setting, progress monitoring and strategic management through electronic portfolio (e-Portfolio). Students’ use of SRL strategies to attain specific learning goals will be identified from a multitude of data sources, including their written reflective entries on an e-Portfolio platform, their eye-tracking and think-aloud data recorded in a computer lab, as well as their verbal feedback collected from semi-structured interviews. More importantly, the project will investigate differences in the use of SRL strategies between high- and low-performing students and explore the relationship between students’ use of SRL strategies and their programming performance. The findings of this project are expected to not only contribute to an improved understanding of the significance of SRL strategies in developing students’ programming ability, but also provide a promising basis for future research and development of appropriate pedagogical strategies and adaptive learning tools for computer programming education. 近半個世紀以來，電腦編程一直有滲入到學校和大學的課程當中。它被視為一種規劃、創建、測試及調試一系列電腦指令以達致某特定目標的複雜過程。從教與學的角度來看，有研究顯示電腦編程能幫助培養學生的創造力、解難能力及高階思維能力。電腦編程所帶來的潛在好處逐漸被視為對全球化知識型經濟中畢業生的競爭力和成功至關重要，人們亦因此重新關注為不同學科背景的大學生提供基本的編程技能培訓。儘管如此，學習電腦編程多年來一直為初學者帶來很大的挑戰，在大學開辦的電腦編程入門課程合格率一向偏低。有些研究嘗試透過分析初學者的內在特徵（例如：年齡、性別和學習方式）找出其編程表現欠理想的原因，但是在教師教育的背景下，對於學生在編程過程中運用了什麼學習策略，以及哪些學習策略比較有效地讓學生獲取編程的知識和技能，我們所知甚少。 為了填補文獻中的這個缺口，本研究項目將利用自我調適學習（SRL）的概念，並透過使用電子學習歷程檔案（e-Portfolio），讓學生參與學習目標的設定、學習進度的監測和學習策略的管理。此項目亦會透過分析不同的數據源（包括：電子學習歷程檔案平台上的反思報告、在電腦實驗室中記錄的眼動追踪和放聲思考數據、半結構性訪談所收集的口頭反饋），以識別出學生運用了哪些SRL策略以實現其設定的學習目標。更重要的是，此項目將調查高績效學生和低績效學生之間使用SRL策略的差異，並探討學生使用SRL策略與其編程表現之間的關係。本研究項目的結果不僅有助於更深入地了解SRL策略在培養學生編程能力方面的重要性，亦為今後進一步研究及開發電腦編程相關的教學策略和自適應學習工具提供了基礎。

18601118.label: Realisation of objectives
18601118.value: The project has satisfactorily fulfilled the four stated objectives, as explained below: Objective 1. To develop facilities and processes in the e-Portfolio environment that assist with student learning of computer programming The first objective was successfully achieved by drawing on the literature on the principles of self-regulated learning and e-Portfolio for independent learning to develop an e-Portfolio environment on a course management system called Moodle. At the beginning of the programming course, all participants were given a 30-minute technical workshop on creating an e-Portfolio to plan, monitor and reflect on their learning experiences and strategies for a specific programming topic such as programming basics (e.g. variables, console input, operators and expressions), flow control, objects and classes, and file input and output. They were trained to go through four phases when developing their e-Portfolio: goal setting, artifact collection, artifact selection, and reflective writing. In the goal setting phase, participants were asked to identify specific learning goals in computer programming. In the artifact collection phase, participants were required to collect a set of learning products that demonstrate their programming ability. In the artifact selection phase, participants needed to choose learning products that clearly indicate their programming progress and achievement towards the intended goals. Lastly, in the reflective writing phase, participants were expected to reflect on their strategies adopted to achieve the goals and consider how to make improvements. A total of 758 e-Portfolio entries were collected from 174 participants during the project period. Each entry contains a self-determined learning goal in computer programming, some digital evidence (e.g. program code, outputs and screenshots) of progress and achievement towards the goal, as well as a reflection (in around 200 words) on the use of strategies during the programming process and the future improvements. According to the semi-structured interviews, about 90% of interviewees (N=98) agreed that e-Portfolio development is helpful to promoting their learning autonomy in computer programming and enhancing their awareness of using appropriate efforts and strategies to study computer programming. Objective 2. To identify students’ use of SRL strategies specific to computer programming from a multitude of data sources The second objective was successfully achieved by collecting, processing and analysing student data from questionnaire survey, reflective writing and eye-tracking experiment. First, the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) was used to evaluate students’ use of SRL strategies. The MSLQ is an 81-item, self-report instrument made up of two sections, comprising motivational orientations and use of learning strategies. The motivation section contains 31 items assessing students’ goals and value beliefs, their beliefs about their skills to succeed, as well as their test anxiety in a course. The learning strategies section includes 50 items concerning students’ use of cognitive, metacognitive control and resources management strategies, which was administered to all participants to identify their use of SRL strategies. Second, students’ use of SRL strategies was also evaluated from their reflective writing on e-Portfolio using the open coding scheme. A coding framework was initially based on the previous work of a general SRL strategy model. During the open coding process, a set of SRL strategies specific to computer programming and their examples were built from the reflective writing of the participants. A total of 10 main categories and 26 sub-categories of SRL strategies in relation to computer programming were identified. Furthermore, participants were invited to join an eye-tracking experiment to identify their use of SRL strategies specific to computer programming. They were asked to read a computer program code displayed on screen and determine its output. The screen consists of five panes, including program code, question and answer, teaching notes, notepad, and hints (see the figure given at https://gp.ied.edu.hk/coding/help/). Students’ eye-tracking data, such as gaze positions and eye movement patterns, were recorded for analysis. Moreover, students were asked to watch the playback of their eye movements and verbalize their thoughts on how they work out the answer. Both the eye-tracking data and retrospective think-aloud data were analysed to determine the SRL strategies used by the participants. Objective 3. To examine differences in the use of SRL strategies between high- and low- performing students The third objective was successfully achieved by identifying the differences in the use of SRL strategies between high and low achieving students enrolled on an introductory programming course. The MSLQ was administered to all participants to evaluate their use of SRL strategies at the beginning of the course. Two types of individual assessment were used in the course to measure student achievement in computer programming. The first was continuous assessment (CA, constituting 70% of the course grade) where students were asked to complete practical hands-on class exercises throughout the course. The second was end of course assessment (EA, constituting 30% of the course grade) where students were required to take a final written examination at the end of the course. Both CA and EA were designed and marked by an experienced teacher in computer programming. Participants were divided into two different groups based on a median split of the assessment scores. Those with a score higher than the median were assigned to a high achieving group (HG), while the remaining were assigned to a low achieving group (LG). Correlational analysis was used to show the strength and direction of the relationship between students’ SRL strategy use and their computer programming achievement. Independent samples t-test was also employed to examine if there was statistically significant difference in each subscale of SRL strategies between the two groups. Objective 4. To seek out students’ views on the strengths and weaknesses of using e-Portfolio to support their learning of computer programming The fourth objective was successfully achieved by conducting semi-structured interviews on an individual basis to collect qualitative data from a sample of participants. Ninety-eight participants joined the interview sessions and each interview session lasted for 10-15 minutes. All interview sessions were audio-recorded and subsequently transcribed verbatim. The purpose of the interviews was to elicit the views of participants on the strengths and weaknesses of using e-Portfolio to support their learning of computer programming. A set of interview questions were designed, including: (1) Can you describe your experience in using e-Portfolio to report and reflect on your choice and use of learning strategies for computer programming – the good and the bad? (2) What are the benefits and drawbacks of using e-Portfolio in the introductory programming course? (3) Besides e-Portfolio, what do you find helpful in improving your computer programming skills? (4) Do you have any suggestions for improvement of the e-Portfolio activities? According to the interview results, a clear majority (90%) of interviewees found it useful in using e-Portfolio to record and reflect on what they have learned from the programming course and the areas where they still need improvement. This could subsequently stimulate their thoughts and ideas concerning how to reduce the gap between their desired and actual programming performance in future. In contrast, a few interviewees (10%) did not see the value of e-Portfolio and expressed the view that they could not learn the knowledge and skills of computer programming directly from e-Portfolio. They would prefer doing more hands-on exercises to strengthen their understanding of computer programming.

18601118.label: Major findings and research outcome
18601118.value: The research has successfully yielded the following findings and outcome: (I) Development process of e-Portfolio in support of the study of computer programming An iterative development process of e-Portfolio was designed to engage students in four phases of SRL, including goal setting, artifact collection, artifact selection and reflective writing. Student can follow the process to develop their e-Portfolio for computer programming. This part is published in Cheng (2021). (II) Coding framework for students’ use of SRL strategies specific to computer programming A coding framework for SRL strategy use in computer programming was developed. The framework covers 10 main categories of SRL strategies specific to computer programming. The categories include C1: rehearsal, C2: elaboration, C3: organisation, C4: critical thinking, C5: planning, monitoring and regulating, C6: time management, C7: study environment management, C8: effort regulation, C9: peer learning, and C10: help seeking. The main categories can be further divided into 26 sub-categories. Details of the framework are illustrated at https://gp.ied.edu.hk/coding/help. Part of the results is published in Cheng, Poon, Lau and Zhou (2019b). (III) Differences in the use of SRL strategies between high- and low-performing students It is found that there are significant differences in the use of higher-order cognitive strategies (elaboration, organization, critical thinking) but not rudimentary cognitive strategies (rehearsal or rote memorisation) between high- and low-achieving groups. It is also found that students’ use of metacognitive control strategies (planning, monitoring and regulating) and resource management strategies (time and study environment management, help seeking) tended to be significantly correlated with their performance in the end of course assessment. Detailed analysis and discussion are published (Cheng, Poon, Lau, & Zhou, 2019b; Cheng 2021). (IV) Strengths and weaknesses of using e-Portfolio to support their learning of computer programming In this project, most students agreed that e-Portfolio development could bring benefits to them. The benefits include an improved awareness of their learning goals and progresses, an enhanced effort to reduce the gap between their desired and actual programming performance, and an increased autonomy in programming study. Nevertheless, some students were dissatisfied with e-Portfolio development because they could not directly acquire programming skills nor receive teacher support from e-Portfolio. These issues are worthy of consideration because the provision of practical activities and sufficient support in programming from instructors are identified as key factors leading to learner satisfaction in programming courses (Chen, Cheng, Xie, Chen, & Zou, 2021).

18601118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18601118.value: The main objective of this project was to identify the use of self-regulated learning (SRL) strategies by students to demonstrate that SRL can benefit students in computer programming, but it may not be sufficient to enhance our understanding of the fine-grained behaviour of students during their programming process. In addition, little is still known about what kind of online support can be provided to guide student behaviour towards SRL in computer programming, especially during the pandemic and other unexpected crisis situations. Going forward, further research could be conducted to explore the feasibility of using advanced technologies to engage and support students in practising, monitoring and reflecting on their computer programming skills in the online learning environment. More specifically, the fine-grained programming behaviour of students could be captured by keylogger. Their programming output could be compared with the standard program code using code analysis to identify possible errors. Based on the data collected, timely and individualised feedback would be generated on the programming behaviour and output of students using machine learning techniques to promote and facilitate online learning in computer programming.

18601118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18601118.value: The research project has two major implications for researchers and practitioners of computer programming education. First, the project contributes to developing an e-Portfolio environment to facilitate student learning of computer programming. It lends further support to the view that e-Portfolio development can play a beneficial role in encouraging students to plan, monitor and reflect on their use of strategies for computer programming achievement. The findings of this project indicate the significance of SRL strategies in developing the computer programming ability of students. Second, the project offers evidence to highlight that most participants value the usefulness of e-Portfolio in raising awareness of their learning goals and achievements, promoting their learning autonomy in computer programming, as well as reducing the gap between their desired and actual computer programming performance. The findings can help teachers gain insights into which SRL strategies are more likely to be effective for students to acquire computer programming skills, and therefore enhance their pedagogies and practices to focus more on those SRL strategies in computer programming education.

18601318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18601318.value: 在全納教育環境中建立學校 - 家庭 - 社區伙伴關係：探索有特殊教育需求的學生所取得成就的預測因素 近幾十年來，在香港包容性環境下，有特殊教育需求的學生數量迅速增加。在包容的情景下，有不同特殊教育需求的學生同處一個教室。在整個過程中，最大的挑戰之一是學校、家庭和社會的合作關係更好地支持在包容背景下的學生。在西方社會中，有關學校、家庭和社會合作關係的研究中，三者重疊模型的影響已經被研究過，並得出了三方合作會對學生成績有積極影響的結論。然而，有關教師-家長-社區在合作關係對學生表現影響中的中介效應和特殊教育需求對這種影響的調節效應的研究卻嚴重缺乏。基於學校-家庭-社會的模型，本研究旨在通過檢驗教師效能感，父母自我效能感，父母和社會成員對包容教育的態度，這三者在合作關係對學生表現（學業表現和社會行為）影響中的中介效應，以及學生特殊需求對合作關係對學生表現影響的調節效應來填補這一空缺。 本研究將會採取定量與定性相結合的方法進行研究。我們將會檢驗學校-家庭-社會合作關係對教師效能感，父母自我效能感，父母及社會成員對包容教育態度的影響，學生的學業自我概念，學生在情緒和行為方面的優劣勢，以及這些變量之間的關係。共有600名學生（300名有特殊教育需求，300名無特殊教育需求）和他們的家長、主流學校的主要的教師、與學校合作的社區成員將會被招募使用便利抽樣。考慮到預期聯系中學校之間差異和學校內部的相似性，數據將用多層次廣義分析結構方程模型。焦點小組訪談將與參與者和學校的社區合作者進行三角測量定量調查，深入了解他們關於合作關係的參與如何影響他們與學生之間的互動以及如何提高學生學習與發展的看法。 所提出研究的結果將對包容性實踐中學習者多樣化的進一步發展產生重大影響。研究結果具有一定的實用價值，會幫助學校管理層，家長和社區成員更好地理解學校-家庭-社區的合作關係，並因此為有特殊教育需求的學生在社會和學業的發展上提供更好地支持，同時也會促進教師/家長教育計劃和社區活動的發展，培育積極的學校-家庭-社區合作關係。

18601318.label: Realisation of objectives
18601318.value: Despite the fact that the past 2.5 years have been extremely challenging for the research to be conducted, particularly in terms of data collection, the research team still managed to: • generate 4 manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals; • present findings from the project in 4 international conferences; • deliver a series of 6 knowledge transfer workshops with a total of ~2,650 attendees, including in-service teachers, parents, front-ine workers in Non-Government Organizations, government officials, and researchers; • produce a user handbook for parents who have children with ASD; • support 3 doctoral students whose dissertations are related to the present GRF. Before describing each of the above points in detail, the research team would like to express our appreciation to the participants. We understand amid the pandemic, some of them have been infected with the virus, a number of them were close contacts of someone who had COVID-19, a few families even experienced financial difficulties. We not only thank them for participating in the research, but also wish them well and healthy. Research Manuscripts (i) Construction of “Family-School-Community” Collaborative Support Model for Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder: the main purpose of the present study was on model development; we constructed a “family-school-community” collaborative support model for students with ASD; the model includes 20 concepts, 7 subcategories, and 3 core elements through three-level coding of interview data based on grounded theory. (ii) Teachers' Participation in School-Family-Community Partnerships for the Support of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder: it was also an aim of the study to identify factors associated with the level of participation of teachers in the FSCP to support students with ASD; using a structured questionnaire covering six domains including (i) parenting and family skills; (ii) communicating; (iii) volunteering; (iv) learning at home; (v) decision making; and (vi) collaboration with community, we found that age groups, qualifications, class size, city level, and training hours were factors related to the level of engagement by teachers in FSCP. (iii) Inclusive Education for People with Autism Spectrum Disorder: Knowledge Graph and Visualized Literature Analysis: as explained in the Mid-Term Progress Report, data collection would be carried out in mainland China; the research team would like results of our research to be able to make a bigger impact on the educational system in China, particularly the support of students with ASD. During the time when data collection could not be carried out (e.g., lockdowns and severe travel restrictions), the research team conducted an analysis of 726 published articles, including 241 written in Chinese and 485 in English, using the VOSviewer software; and use the results to encourage researchers and the education profession in China to have multi- and inter-disciplinary research involving education, medicine, pedagogy, sociology, arts and technology, as well as emphasized the importance of the support system created as a result of the 3-way collaboration among families, schools and the local community. (iv) Facing the School and Community under Inclusive Education--Mode of Adjustment for Parents of Autistic Children: this has been included in the Mid-Term Progress Report; we therefore will not repeat the description in the Final Report. Conference Presentations For details of the conference presentations, please refer to Section 9 of the Final Report. Knowledge Transfer Workshops The Project team collaborated with government agencies and universities in mainland China and overseas to deliver the workshop series in inclusive education. More than 2,600 shareholders participated, with coverage by the local media. (i) Collaboration with Nanchang Bureau of Education: participants were mainly school teachers and parents who have children with ASD; the keynote was on skills for teaching students with ASD in the inclusive setting; coverage was provided by the local official media “Jiang Xi Ke Jiao Xin Wen Wang”. (ii) Collaboration with Chengdu University and the Chengdu Bureau of Education: participants were mainly school teachers and research students; the keynote was on strategies working with the community in supporting children with ASD; coverage was provided by “Si Chuan Jiao Yu Xin Wen Wang”. (iii) Collaboration with Shanghai City Symphony Orchestra and Shanghai Teenagers Activity Center: participants were mainly parents who have children with ASD; the keynote was on strategies for helping the development of children with ASD at home; coverage was provided by the co-organizers in Shanghai. (iv) Collaboration with Almaty Management University (AMU), Kazakhstan: the workshop was held in Batumi, Georgia; participants were mainly university lecturers teaching special and inclusive education; the keynote was on the role of universities on training in-service teachers who have students with special needs in their classrooms; promotional activities were carried out by AMU. (v) Collaboration with Nanshan Bureau of Education: the workshop was held in Foshan; participants were mainly school teachers; the keynote was on Family-School-Community partnership in supporting students with ASD; promotional activities were carried out by the local organizer. (vi) Collaboration with Shenzhen Bureau of Education: this 4-day workshop was conducted via Zoom and attracted more than 850 participants who were mainly teachers; topics covered in the workshop included all topics described in the 5 workshops above. Parent Handbook The Project team developed and produced a user handbook for parents: Enhancing Parents Efficacy and Positive for Support Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder. The handbook aims to share the knowledge gained from the research and further the provision of inclusive education to help facilitate the establishment of family-school-community partnerships for supporting students with special education needs. The main contents of the handbook include: (i) tips and comments by professionals on the upbringing of children with SENs in the inclusive educational setting through an easy way of expression; (ii) real-life experience shared by researchers, in-service teachers, and front-line community workers on supporting children with ASD; (iii) stories by parents: successful cases and difficulties overcome when caring for children with ASD. Doctoral Training Three doctoral students were involved in the projects. They were able to develop their research from the present study but each with a different concentration: (i) One student was more interested in the “parents” group; the aim of her research is to study home-management models for supporting students with ASD in the Family-School-Community Partnership. (ii) One student was more interested in the “teachers” group; she is researching on curriculum and adaptive teaching for students with special educational needs. (iii) One student is applying the Overlapping Spheres Theory to study the Family-School-Community Partnership. Problems and Under-Achievements The main challenges encountered were due to the social unrest in Hong Kong as well as the coronavirus pandemic. One of the variables proposed to be investigated was learning outcome and student performance. During the lockdown periods, classes had to be conducted online (in fact, some were cancelled), the assessment methods had to be changed to online assessment accordingly. Many teachers and parents believed, some with a strong view, that evaluating performance may not be unbiased under these circumstances. The research team therefore have decided not to collect data on learning outcome. We do not consider this as an under-achievement, but this would be an important area to be further investigated. For the same reason, it was also difficult to get data from community members, and hence analysis has not been carried out. This could be considered an under-achievement but we hope the Review Panel could understand that data collection has caused us a lot of problems during the last ~3 years. We did not have any solutions for that, but will seek other sources of funding to continue this part of the research.

18601318.label: Major findings and research outcome
18601318.value: Major findings of the study can be categorized into 4 areas, each of which has been written into a manuscript. For these 4 manuscripts, one has been published, one has been submitted, and the final version of the remaining two will be ready for submission very soon. Three of the 4 manuscript are written in English; but we have intentionally written one of them in Chinese. This is because we would like to attract the attention of more education professionals, including government officials, in China. The four key areas are: (i) Model Construction: to construct a “Family-School-Community” Collaborative model for supporting students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); (ii) Teachers in the School-Family-Community Partnerships (FSCP): to examine teachers' participation in the support of students with ASD and to identify factors associated with their level of involvement. (iii) On the Research and Enhancement of Supports to Students with ASD in Mainland China: we used Knowledge Graph and Visualized Literature Analysis to analyze 726 published articles, including 241 written in Chinese and 485 in English; the results could shed light on ASD research in China, namely to have multi- and inter-disciplinary research involving education, medicine, pedagogy, sociology, arts and technology, as well as to emphasize the importance of the support system created as a result of the 3-way collaboration among families, schools and the local community. (iv) Parents when Facing the School and Community under Inclusive Education: using action research, we tested and found the usefulness of an adjustment model to help parents to reduce their stress level and enhance parent-child interaction. Details of the four manuscripts, including full copies of each manuscript, are included in this Final Report. Please refer to Part C of the Report.

18601318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18601318.value: Learning outcome is an important dependent variable when assessing the supports provided to students with ASD. Partly due to the pandemic, an increasing number of classes are being conducted online. Similarly, online assessments have also become more widely used. On the other hand, in the Family-School-Community Partnership, involvement of the community could potentially be enhanced using online mode. Furthermore, in our study, we have identified several factors associated with the level of involvement of teachers in the FSCP; these could be used to formulate strategies for helping teachers to be more pro-active in the FSCP, and such strategies could be tested for effectiveness. All the above are potential topics for further investigations. Three doctoral students have been trained as part of the current funded project. They will be encouraged to continue the research along the above line of thought. The team will work with them to prepare proposals to seek for external funding when they finish their degrees (and continue to be an assistant professor or a post-doctoral fellow).

18601318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18601318.value: The main purpose of this research was to examine the ?Family-School-Community Partnership (FSCP) in supporting students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). By interviewing parents, teachers, and frontline community workers, we constructed a ?family-school-community? collaborative support model for students with ASD. This model provides a detailed description of the mechanism by which different groups cooperate with other members to support students with ASD. On the other hand, using a questionnaire, we found that age groups, qualifications, class size, city level, and training hours were factors related to the level of engagement by teachers in FSCP. The results can be used to formulate strategies for helping teachers to be more active and collaborate better with other parties in the FSCP to support the development of students with ASD. We also conducted an analysis of 241 published articles written in Chinese and 485 in English; and found that researchers and the education profession in China could consider having more multi- and inter-disciplinary research involving education, medicine, pedagogy, sociology, arts and technology, as well as emphasizing more the importance of the support system created as a result of the 3-way collaboration among families, schools and the local community.
