18602918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18602918.value: There is a gap between the traditional art education model and the needs of contemporary society. The main content of Discipline-based Art Education (DBAE), developed by art educators in the 1980s-90s, has been adopted by the Hong Kong Education Bureau since 1996. The aim of DBAE is to educate students to become an elite in high/fine arts. However, the assumptions in DBAE about art education fail to justify the use of a modernist paradigm for teaching and learning art in the postmodern era. Art educators criticize DBAE’s monotype mode of teaching for producing students who do not have the ability to think critically. Since DBAE celebrates only modern art and culture, it fails to fulfill the needs produced by the rapid changes that take place in contemporary society and in the students’ social lives. It cannot cultivate the higher order thinking or visual literacy skills that students require to appreciate and interpret artworks, and to create meaning about society and themselves. As a new model for art education, art educators claim that Visual Culture Art Education (VCAE) facilitates students’ critical thinking skills and creativity related to their daily, postmodern lives. It critically reflects the complexity of the relationships between students’ social lives, everyday life experiences and the visual images they encounter. The aim of VCAE is to nourish critical, reflective and creative thinking skills to prepare the new generation with the level of visual literacy they need for the 21st century. In the long run, VCAE can provide an educational method that nourishes students’ critical and interpretive abilities to suit the needs of Hong Kong culture. However, we do not know how effective VCAE is and teachers do not know how to use VCAE to teach. A VCAE model is necessary for knowledge transfer, but one has not yet been established. By developing such a model the proposed study will bridge the gap between theory and practice. It will also help to bridge the gaps between students’ learning, their everyday socio-cultural life and the real world. This study will adopt a design-based research methodology, combining quantitative and qualitative approaches, to examine the effectiveness of VCAE and to identify its teaching and learning approaches. Data collection and evaluation methods include pre-test, post-test and delayed post-test evaluations of students’ portfolios, observations, interviews with teachers and students and document analysis. Senior high schools, teachers and their students will be involved in the study. 傳統藝術教育模式與當代社會需求之間存在著差距。由藝術教育工作者在20世紀80至90年代開發的以學科為本的藝術教育 (DBAE) 的主要內容，自1996年以來一直由香港教育局採用。DBAE 的目的是教育學生成為高級/精緻藝術的精英；然而，DBAE對於藝術教育的假設，未能支撐在後現代時代使用現代主義範式來教授和學習藝術的合理性。藝術教育家批評DBAE的單一教學模式，僅在培養沒有批判性思考能力的學生。由於DBAE只頌揚現代藝術和文化，它未能滿足當代社會和學生社交生活中發生的快速變化所產生的需求，它也不能培養學生欣賞和詮釋藝術作品所需要的更高思維或視覺素養能力，並創造出對社會和自身的意義。作為一種新的藝術教育模式，藝術教育家聲稱視覺文化藝術教育 (VCAE) 能促進學生的批判思考能力和與他們日常的後現代生活相關的創造力。它批判地反映了學生的社會生活、日常生活經歷和他們所遇到的視覺形象之間的關係的複雜性。VCAE的目的是培養批判性、反思性和創造性思考技能，使新一代具備21世紀所需要的視覺素養水平。長遠來說，VCAE可以提供一種教育方法，助長學生的批判和詮釋能力，以適應香港文化的需要。然而，我們不知道VCAE的效果如何，教師也不知道如何使用VCAE進行教學。VCAE的模式對於知識轉移是必要的，但尚未建立。通過建立這樣的一個模式，該研究將填補理論與實踐之間的間隙。這也將有助於拉近學生的學習、他們的日常社會文化生活和現實世界之間的距離。本研究將採用以設計為本的研究取向，結合定量和定性的方法，研究VCAE的有效性，並確定其教學和學習方法。資料收集和評估方法包括學生的前測、後測和延後測試、課堂觀察、師生訪談和文件分析，高中學校、教師和學生將參與這項研究。

18602918.label: Realisation of objectives
18602918.value: All the four objectives have been achieved, although the Covid-10 pandemic and social incidents occurred and became severe during 1999-2020. During 1999-2020, the Hong Kong Government announced the social distancing policy. In light of the worsening situation of the COVID-19 epidemic, the Education Bureau (EDB) also announced that all kindergartens, as well as primary and secondary schools, suspended face-to-face classes and school activities. Therefore, all face-to-face classes were almost suspended for one semester, affecting the learning and teaching of visual arts. However, all the incidents mentioned previously and policies slightly affect the research plan. They only affected the arrangement and organization of the research activities of Phase I of the project. In fact, based on the research plan, the focus of Phase I was mainly on preparation, organizing and conducting seminars/workshops for teachers and independent assessors and the unit/lesson plans design. Because of the incidents and policy, all the teachers who participated in the study needed to revise and adjust their VCAE unit and lesson plans in order to fulfil the requirements of the research study. Under such circumstances, the research team closely worked with the teachers and tried their best to assist the teachers in implementing their VCAE teaching. Fortunately and eventually, the field-test and the evaluation of the outcomes and impact of VCAE have been smoothly completed on schedule. Meanwhile, the findings of the study have identified various meaningful learning and teaching approaches to VCAE, including 1) impact on increasing the awareness of students’ identity, 2) impact on knowledge transfer using interdisciplinary learning strategies, and 3) impact of everyday technology on visual culture learning. The study also suggests a revised VCAE pedagogical model at the senior high school level. These approaches will undoubtedly contribute to the subject knowledge and enrich our understanding of VCAE. Finally, the research results are disseminated primarily through publications in peer-reviewed journals and presentations. Since the social distancing policy in Hong Kong, it is impossible to conduct a face-to-face knowledge transfer seminar/workshop to share the study's findings with art teachers, art educators and relevant stakeholders. The sharing seminar/workshop was thus changed to be conducted via Zoom on 23/11/2021. All the Experimental Group (EG) teachers were invited to present in the seminar/workshop. Besides, local art educators, art teachers and pre-service teachers, and EDB officials were also invited to participate in the seminar/workshop (N = 32). On the other hand, in the sharing meeting, the research team described, analyzed and interpreted the findings and challenges of the study. They recommend some possible ways to implement VCAE. All the participants shared their learning and teaching activities, difficulties and challenges, and views on improving the VCAE curriculum. Upon request, the research team will send the video clip of the sharing meeting to art teachers in Hong Kong.

18602918.label: Major findings and research outcome
18602918.value: 1. Major findings and research outcomes no. 1, 2 & 4 In the field-test, a comparison of the control group (CG) and the experimental group (EG) test score shows a significant overall difference in the improvement of the EG in the four domains (i.e. Creativity, Critical Thinking Skills, Visual Presentation/Analysis and Self-reflection in Learning. Specifically, the EG’s test score improvement in Creativity rated the highest (7.71 per cent), with that in Critical Thinking Skills rating second (7.66 per cent), followed by Visual Presentation/Analysis (3.13 per cent) and finally Self-reflection in Learning (1.32 per cent). In sum, both the senior secondary school students’ creativity and critical thinking skills increased significantly after the study’s intervention. It can thus be concluded that VCAE can effectively facilitate students’ creativity and critical thinking skills at the senior secondary school level. The results indicate that VCAE has a positive effect on students’ learning. 2. Major findings and research outcomes no. 2, 3 & 4 In the case studies, three main themes have been identified. They are 1) Impact on increasing the awareness of students’ identity, 2) Impact on knowledge transfer using interdisciplinary learning strategies and 3) Impact of everyday technology on visual culture learning. In sum, both students and teachers determine the value of identity in VCAE. They realize that the visual culture curriculum content can produce an authentic, interdisciplinary learning and teaching environment in which they may become critical thinkers. Second, the study suggests that visual culture learning involves an interdisciplinary knowledge transfer process. During the inquiry process of VCAE, students cognitively and autonomously employ interdisciplinary learning strategies, intentionally comparing and contrasting their art knowledge and knowledge from other disciplines to respond to contemporary issues. Third, the study indicates that everyday technology is not only an effective means by which students may study but also an interdisciplinary, intellectual platform on which they may communicate with both identity and socio-cultural issues to construct knowledge about contemporary society.

18602918.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18602918.value: Several pedagogical implications can be drawn from the study. 1. Future research could focus on investigating the three main elements of VCAE (i.e. identity and change, interdisciplinary strategies and the technology in everyday life) and how they suit the context of the contemporary world. 2. Teachers should consider including various learning activities in the art curriculum to help develop students’ identities and evaluate how they change through visual culture learning. The "change" can be one of the important research topics and should be examined and studied through action research. 3. Although the teachers in the study confessed that it could be difficult and challenging to facilitate students’ critical thinking with the traditional curriculum, teachers could encourage students to make changes by introducing interdisciplinary learning approaches in the existing art curriculum.

18602918.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18602918.value: In Hong Kong, the Curriculum Development Council regards creativity and critical thinking skills as learning focuses for visual arts students. However, the Education Bureau has promoted Discipline-based Art Education (DBAE), developed by art educators in the 1980s and ’90s, to teachers since 1996. As DBAE disconnects students’ everyday life experiences from the contemporary socio-cultural context, it cannot cultivate the higher-order thinking or visual literacy skills necessary for students to appreciate artworks and create meaning in society and themselves. As a current model for art education, art educators invent a new model called "Visual Culture Art Education" (VCAE). They claim that this model can facilitate students’ critical thinking skills and creativity related to their daily lives. VCAE aims to nourish critical, reflective and creative thinking skills to equip rising generations with the level of visual literacy required in the 21st century. However, we do not know how effective VCAE is in cultivating Hong Kong senior secondary school students’ creativity and critical thinking skills or what its outcomes are. It was the first VCAE study in Hong Kong. It would thus offer international scholars alternative directions for future research and give local teachers guidelines regarding how to teach visual culture.

18603018.label: Project Objectives
18603018.value: To examine the relationships between effective teaching and childhood development: a) Whether children can learn more from teachers who show more positive teacher-student interactions; b) Whether child-led, play-based teaching and teacher-led, academically-focused teaching approach have different impacts; c) Whether a dominant type of teaching approach results in different learning outcomes; To examine a) whether the above relationships change or strengthen over time (following up across three school years) and b) whether there are individual differences; To understand how school factors and broader contexts affect effective teaching in Finland and Hong Kong; To advance the existing practices through extensive data disseminations and professional development workshops; To understand how family factors affect child learning in Hong Kong.

To examine a) whether the above relationships change or strengthen over time (following up across three school years) and b) whether there are individual differences;

18603018.label: Realisation of objectives
18603018.value: To achieve the first objective, we observed 1147 20-min sessions (approx. 382 hours) in three years of the teacher-children interactions of 189 teachers and 322 children of twenty-eight kindergartens using a prevalent early childhood classroom observation instrument, the Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS) (Pianta, La Paro & Hamre, 2008). Despite COVID-19 and attritions, we could still retain data from 315 children from 22 kindergartens. We considered this achievement to reflect our effort to provide annual reports to kindergartens and parents (evidence of accomplishment of Objective Four). Only one kindergarten officially withdrew, while the other kindergartens failed to arrange a time for observation or assessment. This issue was grave in the final year because the outburst of COVID shortened the length of school days, and we had to collect data till mid-August. As far as we know, we did the first study that concurrently observed teacher-children interaction and children’s class involvement using a tool developed by our Finnish Co-I. Collecting concurrent data on children’s class involvement provided more valuable and reliable data on a crucial mediating variable to connect teaching quality and children’s learning performance as the outcome variable. Another critical mediator in our theoretical model was children’s self-regulation because it was hypothesised to play a more significant role when children are engaged in child-led, play-based activities. Our results indicated that we initially overestimated the impact of teaching quality on learning and underestimated the significance of children’s self-regulation and class involvement. Regarding the second objective, we found that conducting a longitudinal study and assessing children’s self-regulation made a difference. Individual differences in both self-regulation and learning performances were huge, starting from K1. The early high onset of self-regulation meant early and subsequent achievements in Personal, social and self-care (PSS) and Pre-academic learning (PAL), two domains of the Hong Kong Early Childhood Development Scale (HKECDS) (Rao et al., 2013). What surprised us most was that nearly one-fourth of our K1 participants passed the dimensional change card sort (DCCS) (Zelazo, 2006) we used to assess children’s self-regulation. Predicting that children would get full marks in K2 forced us to make the sorting test more challenging by adding one more dimension. We have no data on children in different regions or countries regarding their ability to do sorting tests. However, we can conclude that local children who excel in self-regulation are likely to academically outperform those children who are weaker in this aspect, particularly when children are in K3 and the role of self-regulation becomes prominent. Since we could not travel during COVID for three years, we could not explore and compare how school factors and broader contexts affect effective teaching in Finland. Still, we addressed the third objective in Hong Kong through interviews with principals and teachers of three exceptionally effective kindergartens in the first two years. To enrich the findings, the PI is conducting interviews with these kindergartens again and comparing their professional development with that of the awardees of the Chief Executive Awards. Our Finnish Co-I would compare the Hong Kong findings with the Finnish ones in our publications. More importantly, since our Finnish Co-I developed the social-development scale and the child involvement scale, which we collected data annually and concurrently respectively, and collected Finnish data, he would help compare the data and discuss the variations from school factors and broader contexts. We considered that we did exceptionally well in disseminating the findings. Though we could not conduct professional workshops regularly, we organised three half-day seminars. First, a professional development online seminar was conducted on Aug 22, 2021, for Preschool education, “Nursery Engineering” famous teacher training for Shenzhen Guangming District Summer Training Activities [學前教育‘苗圃工程’名師培訓深圳光明區暑期研訓活動]. Second, a webinar was held on Jan 29, 2022, for 50+ local kindergarten principals and teachers on ‘Effective Teaching and Its Impact on Early Childhood Development (EffECT) Interim Results Release and Professional Sharing Session [有效教學及其對兒童早期發展的影響(EffECT)中期結果發佈及專業分享交流會]. Finally, we held the Effective Teaching and Its Impact on Early Childhood Development (EffECT) Project Sharing and Ending Ceremony [有效教學及其對兒童早期發展的影響(EffECT)項目終結結果發佈及同業分享交流會] on May 27, 2023. To address the fifth objective, we based on the demographic information collected from the kindergartens on their evaluations of children’s familial support and social-economic status. Our initial results indicated that children from better socioeconomic family backgrounds showed stronger preparations at kindergarten entry, and they tended to outperform their peers in other kindergartens in self-regulation and self-care.

18603018.label: Major findings and research outcome
18603018.value: 1) The validation of multidimensional properties of teaching effectiveness is addressed in Ouput_6, as Pianta and colleagues (2008) assumed for the CLASS, the classroom observation instrument we used in the project. Unlike other studies, we evaluated teacher-children interactions with an additional indicator level. We evaluated the corresponding teaching behaviours on a 7-point Likert scale for each indicator in the CLASS Manual. The results showed the relative significance of indicators and dimensions and their relationships. 2) Output_7 shows the relationships between effective teaching and childhood development. Child-led, play-based teaching might not be significant for K2 children because the self-regulation of most children is still not well-developed. However, the impact of teacher-led, academically-focused teaching approaches on children’s learning is not necessarily as strong as assumed. Year 3 results suggested that once the self-regulation of children is developed, child-led, play-based pedagogy may become more critical. 3) In Output_8, we explore the relative significance of teaching practices of effective early childhood education from a longitudinal perspective. While teachers’ emotional support affects both classroom management and instructional support, the impact of classroom management on instructional support fluctuates over three years, from negative in K1 to positive in K2 and K3. Interestingly, the role of Emotional Support in Instructional Support becomes weaker, which means effective teaching requires extra effort in Instructional Support. 4) Output_9 addresses effective early childhood education teaching practices in Hong Kong in four effective kindergartens case studies. Eight characteristics were identified successfully: congruency in practice, a close collaboration of the teaching team, a highly effective teaching team, parent-school collaboration, uniqueness of curriculum and teaching aids, teacher leadership in learning, and good relationship between teachers and children. Most characteristics were consistent with the ten characteristics we identified and recorded in our field notes during lesson observations. 5) Output_10 addresses the relationship between social and educational inequalities. In general, children enrolled in morning sessions performed better, but children in the afternoon sessions were among the weakest. Interestingly, there was a significant interaction effect between SSB and the programme identified in both personal, social, self-care and pre-academic learning but not in self-regulation scores. 6) Output_11 reported how we revised the DCCS sorting test when we found many local children unexpectedly accomplished high scores and how the self-regulation of Hong Kong children improved over three years from a newly revised assessment. Our results suggested that many local children were good at sorting, probably because they might have many similar practices in their daily lives.

18603018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18603018.value: We attempted to expand our knowledge transfer through two grant applications: Item 1 and Item 4 in Section 11 below. Both grant proposals addressed the teaching effectiveness of co-teaching extensively found in kindergartens. Item 4 proposed to enhance effectiveness through a highly structured curriculum with VR content in a dynamic blended learning environment enabled with avatars created by a business partner. Item 1 addressed co-teaching through a professional development program between Shenzhen teachers and teachers working in kindergartens in Guangxi. These kindergartens were expected to join as sister schools where teachers were willing to share practices in a professional learning community. Both projects would fit well to expand research to new research areas and enhance the social impact treasured by practitioners.

18603018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18603018.value: This study adopted an educational effectiveness framework to explore the relationship between teacher-children interaction using an improved version of the Classroom Observation Scoring System (CLASS) with indicator-level data and children’s class involvement. Children’s self-regulation is hypothesised as the mediator in a child-initiated, play-based pedagogy similar to a Finnish approach that encourages children’s self-exploration and autonomy. Such a pedagogy contrasts with a teacher-directed, academic-focused pedagogy expected to be prevalent in Hong Kong. The K2 results successfully validated CLASS in the Hong Kong context. Still, the impact of teaching quality on children’s self-regulation, class involvement, and subsequent achievements in self-care and pre-academic learning was unexpectedly marginal. However, three-year data consistently confirmed emotional support influences both classroom management and instructional support in structural equation models. Moreover, the role of self-regulation appeared to grow significantly from K2 to K3, lending support to the Finnish approach for its enormous benefits to children’s learning. Interviews with principals and teachers of effective schools highlighted their successes in tight team collaboration, uniquely blended learning, and expansive home-school collaboration. The research team has contributed new evidence on the significant role of self-regulation in early childhood learning, providing justifications for the value of increasing self-exploration and learner autonomy of K3 children.

18603618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18603618.value: 在技術發展和文化交流加速的資訊時代，思辨能力已經成為全球中小學和高等教育的重要培養目標。在香港，思辨能力也已成為中小學英語語言課程的發展重點(CDC, 2002; 2004)。教師需要教導學生分析、比較資訊，同時檢視和反思不同的理念和價值觀來解決現實生活中的複雜問題。然而，由於各種環境因素的制約（如缺少制度支援、以考試為導向的教育體制等），語言教師在思辨能力教學中通常會遇到很多挑戰。這在英語作為外語的地區，如香港，尤其明顯（Mok，2009）。因此，在職前英語教師教育中堅定和明確地聚焦思辨能力就顯得尤其重要。職前教師教育尤其應該培養師範生的思辨能力，並提升其在課堂教學中教授思辨能力的專業素養。 雖然目前關於如何在語言課堂中促進思辨能力發展的研究越來越多，卻很少有人關注師範生在職前教師教育課程中如何學習教授思辨能力。考慮到思辨能力對語言教師和語言學習者的重要性，本研究將調查師範生如何在香港的一個職前英語教師教育項目中學習教授思辨能力。本研究將採用民族志個案研究設計，以教師教育的生態觀為理論框架，來探索師範生如何學習教授思辨能力。本研究將重點關注思辨能力在教師教育項目中的覆蓋度、一致性和適用性，同時還將從語言教師教育者、項目領導或協調者的角度出發，來探索思辨能力如何融入已有的的教師教育課程。民族志範式的研究設計不僅能加深我們對思辨能力的本質及其在語言教學和教師教育中作用的瞭解，還能增加我們對教師在多場域下專業學習的動態性與複雜性的認識。此外，本研究結果還可以幫助香港（以及其他的“英語作為外語”的地區）的語言教師教育者和課程設計者更加明確如何培養優秀的英語教師以滿足學生對語言學習和思辨能力發展的多重需要。

18603618.label: Realisation of objectives
18603618.value: The four research objectives have been fully achieved in the project. The following sections present the research process and explain how the process helped meet the research objectives. The research process The research team recruited four language teacher educators and 37 pre-service language teachers at language teacher education programmes in a Hong Kong university. The teacher educators consisted of 3 females and 1 male. While one participant was the programme leader, the others were course instructors. They were invited to join the study given their rich experience of language teacher education (ranging from 8 to 15 years) and their active engagement (e.g., teaching pedagogy courses and providing supervision) in the programme. Also, of the 37 students, 32 were from the Bachelor of Education programme, and 5 were from the MATESOL programme. 20 of them had Cantonese as their first language and 17 Mandarin Chinese. They were invited to join the study on a voluntary basis to explore their past and ongoing learning experience regarding CT and its teaching as future language teachers. The data were collected from various sources, including semi-structured interviews, field observations, and relevant artefacts. Over an academic year, the four teacher educators were observed in one of their teacher education courses, which respectively focused on Teaching English grammar, Integrating IT in language classrooms, Teaching English listening and speaking, and Teaching English reading and writing. This set of data enhanced our understanding of how they integrated CT into language teacher education and how this might equip student teachers with the necessary knowledge and skills to teach CT in the future. Upon the completion of the courses, the teacher educators were interviewed to understand their pedagogical beliefs and values about CT with reference to their classroom teaching as well as the underlying personal and contextual factors. Among the 37 student participants, upon their approval, eight were observed in their courses focusing on language teaching pedagogy to explore how they developed CT and learned to teach CT in the teacher education programme. All the student participants were interviewed one to three times to investigate their individual backgrounds and past learning experiences in relation to CT. They were specifically invited to share whether and how the different components of the teacher education programme, including general and pedagogy courses, teaching practicum, immersion experience, formal research experience (i.e., final year project experience), extracurricular research experience (i.e., participation as student assistant in faculty members’ research projects), and online learning experience (especially during the COVID-19 pandemic), shaped their understanding of CT and its teaching in language classrooms. The interviews, each lasting from 1.5 to 2 hours, were conducted in English and audio-recorded for transcription and analysis. Furthermore, relevant documents developed by the participants were all collected to enrich our dataset. For instance, the teacher educators shared their teaching materials and handouts in relation to CT and its related pedagogical practice. The student teachers also submitted their course assignments, personal reflections, and teaching portfolios (developed during their teaching practicum). Also, the final year research project reports written by the year-five participants were also collected. All the documents served to shed light on the participants’ perceptions and practice regarding CT teaching. Following a qualitative research approach, data collection and analysis were iterative and recursive throughout the research process. Informed by theoretical insights generated from the literature on CT, the interview data was first analyzed inductively to yield codes and categories about the participants’ perceptions and practices about CT and its instruction in language classrooms. After that, the observation data was repeatedly reviewed and analyzed to compare with, verify, and supplement the interview findings. To ensure the validity of the findings, the PI and the research assistant analyzed the data respectively and engaged in rounds of discussion and data (re-)interpretation to refine the final results. Meeting the research objectives To meet the first research objective regarding how CT is perceived by student teachers, teacher educators and curriculum designers in language teacher education, the research team interviewed four teacher educators (one of whom is the programme leader who is responsible for curriculum design) and 37 student teachers in the Bachelor of Education (English) programme andMATESOL programme. In the interviews, the participants were probed to share their understanding of CT and its role in language teaching and teacher education. They were also invited to comment on their perceptions about whether and the extent to which CT was integrated into the programme curriculum and courses. The second research objective concerning the programme components, coherence and applicability was met by interviewing the student teachers about their practice and experience of learning CT and learning to teach CT as they participated in different teacher learning activities in the programme. The teacher learning activities included coursework, teaching practicum, final-year research project, extracurricular research work, and overseas immersion. Specifically, in the interviews, the student teachers were asked to comment on how they connect and apply their learning of CT in university classrooms to the other learning activities. In addition to interviews with the student teachers, the teacher educators were also interviewed and their pedagogy courses were observed. The interviews with the teacher educators and lesson observations served to enrich understanding of student teachers’ learning to teach CT through university coursework. The third objective regarding the influencing factors, was achieved through interviews with the teacher educators and student teachers, lesson observations of the teacher educators’ pedagogy courses, as well as the relevant artefacts collected from the student teachers and the teacher educators. In the interviews with the student teachers, questions that focused on their concerns and decision making in teaching CT were asked. They were probed to share their thoughts from different angles, including their personal preference as a learner and a teacher, their students’ preference and interest, the school context, and the university learning experience. The interviews with the teacher educators targeted their concerns and decision-making regarding whether and how to include CT into their language teacher education practice. They were also prompted to comment on their perceptions of their student teachers’ practice and experience of CT teaching in their situated university and school context. The interview data was then compared and verified against the lesson observation data and the relevant artefacts collected (e.g., course syllabus, teaching and learning materials). The final objective, to generate practical implications on how to effectively integrate CT with current language teaching and teacher education practice, was met as the PI and the research team interviewed the teacher educators and the student teachers as well as examined the lesson observation data and relevant artefacts (e.g., course syllabus, teaching and learning materials). In the interviews, the student teachers were prompted to share the learning opportunities and challenges regarding CT instruction they encountered in the programme, while the teacher educators were invited to talk about how they tried to integrate CT into language teacher education, including their motivations, effort, and challenges. More importantly, both groups of participants were asked to provide suggestions on how to overcome the potential difficulties and effectively integrate CT into their learning and practice to benefit themselves and their students. With reference to the interview accounts, the lesson observation data and relevant artefacts were examined to supplement understanding of how to infuse CT into current language teacher education programmes to develop CT-oriented language teachers.

18603618.label: Major findings and research outcome
18603618.value: Built upon previous studies on CT (Abrami et al., 2015; Facione, 1990), this project has provided insights into the role of CT and its instruction in language teaching and pre-service language teacher education. The findings revealed that CT is indispensable for teachers’ daily teaching practice and can be developed as they participate in a variety of professional learning activities, including coursework, research, immersion, and teaching practicum. So far, the research findings have been reported in four published SSCI journal articles. Adopting a practitioner research approach, Yuan, Yang, and Stapleton (2020) focused on pre-service English teachers’ development of CT through joining research projects and learning to analyze and interpret research data. The findings shed light on the transferability of the students’ CT from their research experience to their professional learning as future teachers. Yuan, Yang, and Mak (2021) zoomed in on the relationship between students’ cognition (including CT skills) and motivation through their extracurricular research engagement, contributing to our current knowledge about the power of informal learning in shaping student teachers’ professional learning. Yuan, Yang and Lee (2021) investigated how overseas field experience provided opportunities for pre-service English teachers to develop CT and to embrace a CT-oriented pedagogy. Furthermore, Yang, Mak, and Yuan (2022) explored how the online feedback experience of the pre-service English language teachers facilitated their development of CT and the findings throw light on how these teachers can be supported to enhance their CT and reflective ability. In addition, one paper (i.e., Mak et al., under review), which focused on how pre-service English teachers cultivated their professional competence including critical thinking skills and dispositions through conducting classroom-based research during teaching practicum, is currently under review in an international journal in the field of teacher education. Based on the current findings, the PI will continue probing in-depth into the data with an aim to generating more research outputs in order to benefit the wider academic community, particularly those who are interested in pre-service language teacher education and the CT pedagogy.

18603618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18603618.value: The findings of the project speak to the importance of CT in language teaching and teacher education. Three future research directions are suggested: 1. Pre-service English teachers’ learning of CT takes place in different activities, including coursework, research, immersion, and teaching practicum. The findings also reveal that systematic integration of different activities, such as the integration of research project and teaching practicum, can lead to CT development for pre-service teachers. Future research can continue to explore how these different activities are integrated and implemented not only in individual teacher education classrooms but also at the programme and school level to shed light on how pre-service teachers are supported to develop as critical thinkers in language teaching. 2. Future research can include teacher educators and student teachers from different linguistic and sociocultural backgrounds. An inclusion of diverse participants allows comparison of perspectives, practices, and experiences, which would enrich the current understanding of CT in language teacher education. 3. Future research can also closely observe pre-service teachers in their daily learning and practice, in addition to interviewing them and collecting their learning documents, to reach a deeper understanding of how they learn and develop as CT-oriented future teachers in their daily work.

18603618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18603618.value: This study carried theoretical, pedagogical and practical significance. Theoretically, by examining how CT was perceived and practised by pre-service teachers, teacher educators, and curriculum designers in language teacher education programmes in a university in Hong Kong, the study shed light on the context-bound and culture-sensitive nature of CT and its integration with language teacher education. Specifically, adopting a longitudinal and ethnographic design, the study generated theoretical insights into the complex, dynamic, and situated nature of the learning of pre-service teachers, which were mediated by various personal, institutional and socio-cultural factors. In respect to practical significance, the study enhanced our understanding of how the pre-service teachers integrated CT into language teacher education. Such an understanding could inform teacher educators on how to bridge the gap between theory and practice, as well as how to support pre-service teachers to infuse CT in their teaching contexts. The findings also enhanced the pre-service language teachers’ understanding of CT and its role for language teaching. From a pedagogical perspective, the study gained insights into the effective pedagogical practice that facilitated pre-service student teachers’ CT development.

18603818.label: Realisation of objectives
18603818.value: The project has been completed on schedule with three research outputs - two peer-reviewed articles (one is published, one in preparation) and one conference paper. More than 100 children with ASD have been recruited for study related to the current related to the study. All the objectives have been successfully achieved and details are as follows: Objective 1: To determine if learning to ride a bicycle and/or engaging in stationary cycling lead to improvements in executive function and self-regulation in children with ASD The interventional studies generated from the projects showed that cognitive deficits were common in children with autism, and that learning component of motor skill would be an effective intervention to lessening such deficits in the population. In the first study, the research team has recruited 62 children with autism and they were randomly assigned to three groups: learning to ride a bicycle (2 weeks; 10 sessions), stationary cycling (2 weeks; 10 sessions) and control groups. Executive functions (EFs) including planning, working memory, flexibility and inhibition were assessed. Results showed that there were significant improvements in all cognitive functions in the learning to ride a bicycle group, but not in the other two groups. The findings of this study highlight the value of learning component in exercise program that plays an important role in improving cognition in children with autism. And this is an important finding that leads to a better design of the exercise programs for children with autism. The first study has been published last year in MSSE. In the second study, the research team has further investigated the effectiveness of exercise intervention groups on enhancing the self -regulation (SR) and to examine whether the mediating roles of social, emotional and physical needs of participants in exercise-EFs and exercise-SR relationship. These needs were expressed by perceived social support, enjoyment, stress, physical self-efficacy and perceived physical fitness of an individual. Results showed that both exercise intervention groups could enhance SR, and that the perceived social support, physical self-efficacy and physical fitness mediated exercise-EF relation. The manuscript is 90% ready for submission and the target journal is MSSE. Objective 2: To find out if the changes in executive function and self-regulation are sustained over a 12-week period In both first and second studies, we have investigated the sustainability of the benefits of the exercise interventions on EF and SR. The EFs and SR benefits were shown not sustainable over the 12-week period. It is suggested that regular exercise participation is important to maintain such benefits in children with ASD. Objective 3: To determine if self-regulation mediates the relation between physical activity and executive function In the second study, it is shown that SR and EF are highly associated. However, no mediation relationship was shown. One possible explanation may lie on the relatively small sample size of the second study, which consisted of 64 participants (23 in the learning to ride a bicycle group, 19 in the stationary cycling group and 22 in the active control group). In sum, the study is regarded as pioneer in linking exercise, all core components of EF (i.e. cognitive planning, flexibility, working memory and inhibition control). These two papers have provided direction and advice for implementing future research to examine how different exercise parameters (e.g., various intensity, frequency, duration and time for exercise) impacts on EF and SR and what pathways that underlie the exercise-cognition and exercise-self-regulation relations, particularly in those children with ASD.

18603818.label: Major findings and research outcome
18603818.value: There are three major findings yielded from the project: First, cognitively engaging exercise (i.e. learning to ride a bicycle group) is shown more beneficial to EF than non-cognitively engaging exercise (i.e. stationary cycling group) in children with ASD. Second, both types of exercise interventions in the present study showed beneficial to enhance self-regulation. Finally, cognitive and self-regulatory benefits of exercise interventions cannot be sustained 6 weeks after the exercise intervention, which suggested that exercise should be on regular basis in order to induce such benefits in children with ASD. Additionally, this research project also discovered that perceived social support, physical self-efficacy and physical fitness were mediators in exercise-EF and exercise-SR relationships. These additional findings open many research opportunities to explore the underlying mechanism of how exercise impacts on cognitions and behavioral in children with ASD.

18603818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18603818.value: There were several limitations of the current research projects that require further investigations First, there is a lack of measurement on cognitive engagement and motivation level of participants. Without such criteria, we may not be able to determine if cognitive engagement and motivation were the key factors leading to improvements of EFs in the learning group. Second, the sample size of the current research project was relatively small for mediation analysis, which may explain why the emotional needs of participants (e.g., stress, enjoyment) stress level were not mediating the exercise-EF and exercise-SR relationships, further study should consider recruiting more participants. Meanwhile, further research should be continued with the focus on tracing the underlying mechanism of how physical exercise impacts executive functions and self-regulation. Apart from the aforementioned psychological factors, other factors including neurotrophic and hormonal biomarkers (e.g., BDNF, cortisol, melatonin) that may plausibly drive the EF and SR improvements should also be examined. In that way, the underlying mechanism could be unveiled, which in turns lead to optimization of exercise intervention to treat the EF and SR deficits in children with ASD and other populations with lower cognitive and behavioral functions.

18603818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18603818.value: Cognitive and self-regulation problems are commonly found in children with ASD and disturbed their daily lives. The present study was to investigate whether physical exercise could benefit cognitive and self-regulation for children with ASD. Moreover, we also investigated how physical activity impacts on cognition and self-regulation through satisfying the social, emotional and physical needs of the children participants. In this study, we have conducted a three-group randomized controlled trial that compares a cognitively engaging exercise – learning to ride a bicycle group, non-cognitively engaging exercise – stationary cycling group and a control group. We monitored the changes of their cognitive functions as depicted by four core components, namely cognitive planning, flexibility, working memory and inhibition control as well as their self-regulation level. We also incorporated mediation assessments by assessing their perceived social support, stress, enjoyment, physical self-efficacy and physical fitness in the mid of the interventions. The findings of this proposed study provided evidence on the importance of using cognitively engaging exercise intervention in improving cognitive functions and enhancing self-regulation in children with ASD.

18604618.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18604618.value: A large proportion of mobile assisted language learning (MALL) takes place outside the classroom and university students frequently report that they are easily distracted by various external factors when using mobile devices for learning purposes. Effective learning of second language (L2) vocabulary hinges on the learners’ ability to self-regulate their learning. However, little research interest has been shown in how students self-regulate when they are left on their own to explore MALL. Personalisation also features in a number of mobile vocabulary learning applications in the form of intelligent design, but these do not necessarily improve learners’ ability to learn vocabulary following a personalised path determined by the learners themselves. Also, many learners do not possess sufficient pedagogical knowledge of how L2 vocabulary should be learned. This proposed research will address these issues by adding two key components, vocabulary pedagogy and enhanced personalisation, to an existing self-regulation model (Zimmerman, 2011). Based on this revised model, a self-regulated and personalised (SRP) vocabulary learning approach is developed and its effectiveness measured where the mobile technologies mediate, the vocabulary pedagogy informs and the personalisation shapes students’ L2 vocabulary learning. This research aims to help students develop a heightened capacity for self-regulation while using mobile technologies and appropriate pedagogical knowledge to learn L2 vocabulary more efficiently and effectively in the long term. This research will adopt a mixed-method design. An experimental design will be adopted to find out to what extent students can learn L2 vocabulary using the SRP approach in a mobile technology-mediated environment via a self-directed intervention for a period of one semester. It will also examine whether the self-directed SRP approach can help students learn L2 vocabulary receptively and productively better than those who adopt their usual learning approach. Personalised vocabulary tests at both receptive and productive levels will be developed for each participant to measure their learning outcome. In addition, a multi-case study will be conducted to provide qualitative evidence to verify whether the self-directed SRP approach can lead to a heightened capacity for self-regulation. The qualitative evidence collected can also be used to triangulate and validate the quantitative findings. 大部分移動技術輔助語言學習(MALL)在課外進行，並且大學生時常宣稱使用移動設備學習時，他們很容易被各種外界因素幹擾。有效的第二語言單詞學習取決於學習者的自律學習能力。然而，鮮少有研究表明學生自己在探索移動輔助語言學習過程中如何自我調節。個性化也在衆多智能設計的單詞學習移動應用上起重要作用，但是這幷不會必然導致學習者在自我學習道路上根據自身情况學習單詞能力的提升。此外，許多學習者也沒有充分掌握二語單詞學習的有效途徑。 此項研究將會通過在已有的自律學習模型(Zimmerman，2011)上增加兩個核心要素，單詞教學和個性化提升，來解决這些問題。在修改的模型上，創立一種自律個性化(SRP)單詞學習方式。它的有效性體現在移動技術在哪方面融合二語單詞學習，單詞教學在哪方面引導二語單詞學習，以及個性化學習在哪方面構建二語單詞學習。本研究旨在幫助學生在使用移動技術和恰當教學知識進行二語單詞學習時，提升自律能力，從而從長遠發展上更加高效地學習二語單詞。 此項研究將采取綜合方法的形式進行研究。將使用一個實驗設計來探究學生可以使用自律個性化方式，在依託移動技術的環境中，在進行為期一學期的自我安排二語單詞學習後測量達到哪種程度。該實驗也會研究使用自我主導的自律個性化學習方式會的學生是否比那些使用常規學習方法的學生在輸入和輸出二語單詞上會取得更大的學習進步。此外，將實施一個多案例研究來提供定性證據，核實是否自我主導的自律個性化方式可以帶來自我管理能力的提升。

18604618.label: Realisation of objectives
18604618.value: 1. Ways to achieve the objectives We integrated the SRP approach in a voluntary IELTS preparation to train Hong Kong university students to become self-regulated and personalized learners of vocabulary to help them prepare for taking the IELTS. To recruit suitable participants for this research, an invitation to the IELTS preparation scheme was distributed to year one and year two undergraduate students. Four briefing sessions were held for students who were interested in learning more about the SRP vocabulary scheme to acquire knowledge and strategies in self-regulating and pesonalising their vocabulary learning assisted with mobile technology. First, during the registration process, students were invited to complete a pre-self-regulation survey designed by researchers to measure their initial self-regulation capacity. The survey includes originally 54 items with 44 items retained after factor analysis. All sub-scales have the reliability of larger than 0.90. Followed with the pre-survey, participants were then invited to take Vocabulary Levels Test (Nation, 2001) to assess their initial vocabulary. The training started with a face-to-face briefing session where students learned about the SRP approach (EG: Experimental group) or the SR only approach (CG: Control group) introduced in the online learning platform via Schoology. Then, to fully understand the SRP approach, the EG participants underwent a two-week online self-training. For the EG students, they are required to learn four components: (1) self-regulated learning, (2) vocabulary pedagogy, (3) personalized learning, and (4) resources for IELTS vocabulary. For the CG students, only (1) and (4) are included. The online learning activities are conducted in both individual and group learning modes with various forms of activities. For example, based on the three-phase for self-regulation proposed by Zimmerman (2011), we tailor-made some e-learning materials for students to learn how to self-regulate their language learning. Students were also guided with instructions for how to do the tasks for each activity, and a discussion form was provided to allow the students to post their personalized stories and comment on others’ stories. In addition, a IELTS vocabulary learning resources package for students to equip them with essential learning resources were provided. After the self-training, participants developed a study plan by completing the critical tasks of the SRP approach (i.e., self-regulated learning, vocabulary pedagogy, and personalized learning) involved in developing their academic L2 vocabulary to help them prepare for their IELTS test. They were asked to set an achievable goal based on their vocabulary baseline, language ability, time span, etc., and develop an individualized strategic plan to achieve their goal. Participants began their vocabulary learning program and uploaded their weekly recorded vocabulary items to the online platform using a researcher-designed vocabulary learning record (VLR) sheet, which was easily accessible via mobile devices (i.e., VLR tasks). The minimum requirement for each participant was to select and record at least 30 self-chosen words weekly. The EG and CG students used different VLR sheet. For EG, they were required to use the sheet to record 6 categories of lexical information (1. Item; 2. Meaning; 3. Source; 4. Word information; 5. p ersonalized strategy; 6. Word use). While for the CG, they only recorded 3 categories of the lexical information (1. item; 2. meaning; 3. word information). In addition, we introduced gamification to motivate our participants to engage in their self-guided learner training. The final stage is the personalized vocabulary test, including a receptive and productive test. We selected 40 items randomly from the 100 items uploaded by each student. 20 was used to develop the receptive and the other 20 for the productive test. We followed three procedures in selecting the vocabulary items. First, we created a profile of the student’s initial vocabulary size information and followed three procedures in selecting the vocabulary items: (1) initial vocabulary level test results, (2) the analysis of the frequency level of students’ selected vocabulary, and (3) word length. In summary, we used different instruments for data collection: (1) a self-designed Self-Regulating Survey for Language Learning (SRSLL) to measure whether the students had enhanced their self-regulation capacity after experiencing the SRP approach; (2) personalised vocabulary tests to measure their vocabulary learning outcomes both receptively and productively; and (3) semi-structured interview to provide qualitative evidence to verify whether the self-directed SRP approach can lead to a heightened capacity for self-regulation and improve their personalized vocabulary learning. Other supplementary measurements included learning evidence submitted by the students and their VLR sheets. 2. To what extent the project objectives have been achieved For Objective 1, a personalized 50-word vocabulary test in which 25 items are used to assess receptive vocabulary knowledge and the remaining 25 items are used to assess productive knowledge was conducted for the participants by analyzing the frequency level of their selected vocabulary using the Nation’s Range program. The test results suggest that the SRP method is superior in improving students' productive vocabulary learning but not clearly in receptive vocabulary learning. In short, although the findings did not demonstrate the effectiveness of the SRP method for receptive vocabulary learning, Objective 1 was achieved. For Objective 2, a post Vocabulary Level Test was conducted for measuring to what extend the SRP approach can help participants increase their vocabulary size. Surprisingly, the results indicate that the SRP method helped participants increase their vocabulary size by about 8%. From this result, it is examined that the SPR method can increase learners' vocabulary size to a certain extent and help strengthen to empower their performance in vocabulary learning. For Objective 3, each participant were invited to complete the post-self-regulating survey and scheme evaluation form at the end of the 4-week intervention. A key conclusion was found based on the survey and scheme evaluation: SRP approach enhanced students’ intrinsic motivation and future planning. In other words, SRP approach can help students develop a heightened capacity for self-regulation, which indicated that Objective 3 was achieved.

18604618.label: Major findings and research outcome
18604618.value: For answering Objective 1, the productive vocabulary test scores of the experiment group(M=13.33) compared to the productive vocabulary test scores of the control group (M= 9.53) indicated a significant improvement (t=-1.81; p<0.05). In other words, the SRP approach is superior to the SR-only approach in enhancing students’ productive vocabulary learning. However, the SRP condition did not show superiority over the Self-regulated condition in terms of receptive vocabulary learning. This situation may be explained by the test nature of the receptive test, which only requires meaningful recognition of the vocabulary items and can be easily achieved by both conditions. For answering Objective 2, there was a considerable increase in the vocabulary size of the participants. They generally increased their vocabulary by 8% before and after participating in this program (a 4-week vocabulary learning). For answering Objective 3, although the metacognitive planning of participants in the experimental group and the control group were improved after the post-test, the participants in the experimental group obtained additional gain in improving their intrinsic motivation. A plausible explanation for this finding is due to enhanced personalization under the SRP condition. What is more, the results demonstrated that the SRP approach could also help students with future planning. The interview data revealed some specific roles of personalization in enhancing students' self-regulation. First, personalization enhanced students' learning interests and helped them engage in vocabulary learning. Second, students found personalized sharing to be constructive in facilitating self-regulated vocabulary learning. This is because personalized sharing can help learners reflect on themselves and improve their learning methods by reflecting on and addressing their weakness. In this sense, the SRP approach can help students develop a heightened capacity for self-regulation compared with SR-only approach to some extent.

18604618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18604618.value: Our study has demonstrated some evidence of students’ improved capacity for self-regulation scaffolded by self-regulated and personalized (SRP) approach; the SPR approach also helped students learn more L2 academic vocabulary productively. During our study, we noticed that personalized learning appears to be a socially constructed concept in MALL contexts and empower learners in various self-regulation phrases. It is recommended that both individual and group learning tasks be included in designing PL elements for MALL implementations. In this sense, we believe that it is necessary to go one step further to validate the effectiveness of personalized learning by including collaborative learning opportunities for English vocabulary learning. In addition, learners’ word selection fitness will also be taken into account to promote connections between learner’s vocabulary choice and personalized learning. In this sense, our future line of research action will focus on two aspects: Can students self-select newly learnt words appropriate to their level? How do students benefit from their personalized vocabulary learning by collaborating with other learners?

18604618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18604618.value: First, this study will be the first MALL research that integrates explicitly three key factors: self-regulation, personalization, and vocabulary pedagogy. In particular, this research will develop an increased capacity for self-regulation in students to use mobile technologies, deploy appropriate pedagogical knowledge and use personalized strategies to learn L2 vocabulary more efficiently and effectively in the long run. Second, holding students accountable for their learning behavior can motivate them to participate more in the training process and have a longer-lasting impact on students. Third, this self-directed learning, targeting vocabulary acquisition and developing self-regulation skills, can inspire language teachers to innovate classroom language pedagogy by gathering valuable information on how students use mobile technology to facilitate learning inside and outside the classroom. Fourth, on the practical side, this research can help university students expand their academic vocabulary and improve their self-regulation skills, which will better prepare them for high-stakes language exams and improve their language proficiency to increase their capitals for future career prospects.

18604918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18604918.value: This project investigates literary fields of Taiwan and Hong Kong in the 1960s, and the dissemination and reception of literature via literary publications across Taiwan and Hong Kong during the 1960s to 70s, with the Hong Kong versions of Chun wenxue (Pure literature) and Wen Xing Cong Kan as examples. Wang Jingxi (1932-2008) was chief editor of these publications. Wang studied in Taiwan after completing secondary education in Hong Kong. He returned to Hong Kong and founded the Zheng Wen publishing house and published Hong Kong version of Chun wenxue , and introduced Wen Xing Cong Kan series from Taiwan via his Wen Yi Bookstore which opened in 1968. After Wen Xing was banned in Taiwan, publication of Wen Xing Cong Kan continued in the name of Wen Yi Bookstore. It was owing to Hong Kong version of Chun wenxue that Hong Kong readers could came into contact with works by writers such as Yin Hai-guang(1919-1969), Li Ao(1935-), Bo Yang (1920-2008), Pai Hsien-yung (1937-), Yu Guangzhong (1928-), etc. This is why Wang was also known as the "bridge between cultural scenes in Taiwan and Hong Kong." On the other hand, his poor management led to accusation of not paying royalties to the authors and infringements of copyrights. What Wang created from the mid1960s to 70s was a complicated case regarding cultural publishing. This project aims to investigate the significance of Wang Jingxi in the dissemination of literature across Hong Kong and Taiwan, and in the fields of literature. 本計劃擬以王敬羲主編之港版《純文學》及港版「文星叢刊」為例子，研究六十年代臺、港文學場域，以及六七十年代臺、港兩地文學出版所涉的文學傳播與接受課題。王敬羲（1932-2008）早年在香港完成中學課程後到台灣升學，回港後透過他開設的正文出版社，出版《純文學》（香港版），又透過一九六八年開設的文藝書屋引進「文星叢刊」，以至當「文星叢刊」在台灣被查禁後，以文藝書屋名義在香港延續出版，許多香港讀者透過港版《純文學》接觸台灣文學，透過文藝書屋讀到殷海光、李敖、柏楊、白先勇、余光中等作家著作，因此，王敬羲被視為六、七十年代「港台文化橋樑」。但另一方面，他未能妥善處理版權和版稅事務，屢屢被指責不予作者版稅、損害知識產權，王敬羲在六十年代中至七十年代所造成的，是複雜的文化出版事件，本計劃擬全面探討王敬羲在臺、港兩地的文學出版流佈，以及文學場域上的意義。

18605118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18605118.value: This project responds to the need for research into the teaching of English to young learners (TEYL), defined as children between the ages of 5-12. Despite the significant increase in popularity of TEYL globally, including mainland China, our knowledge of how TEYL is implemented, the attitudes of teachers, and the challenges they face is scant. This project, therefore, addresses this gap in our understanding of English language teaching and learning by exploring the experiences of one group of primary school English teachers in mainland China. A particular contribution of this project is to examine the experiences and perceptions of teachers of English to young learners using the theoretical lens of teacher identity, which in the past decade has emerged as a powerful analytic framework for understanding teachers and teaching. The results of this project will be of interest to policy makers, teacher educators, school authorities, researchers, and teachers of young learners themselves, both in mainland China and analogous educational settings worldwide. For policy makers, the findings generated by this study will offer insights into how future policies and programs can be tailored to best meet the needs of young English language learners and their teachers in mainland China and beyond. For teacher educators, the results of this study will provide insights into how they can best support the professional identity construction of preservice and inservice teachers. School authorities will benefit from this project as recommendations will be made for school-based professional development programs that support the ongoing identity construction goals of inservice teachers of English to young learners. This project, by documenting the experiences of teachers in mainland China, will also offer new opportunities for researchers as it will represent one of the first steps in establishing a database for comparative research as future studies continue to explore the identity construction experiences of English language teachers of young learners within different educational contexts. Finally, school-based teachers will benefit from this project as the results will contribute to the international sharing of ideas and experiences, which has been identified as crucial in supporting frontline educators responsible for implementing English language programs for young learners around the globe. 近年，全球關注兒童英語教學 (TEYL，Teaching of English to young learners) ，愈來愈多專家學者從事相關的研究，然而，我們對TEYL 教學法如何實踐、教育工作者的心態和他們所面對的挑戰等仍認識不深。為了填補這個缺口，本研究項目會探討一班來自中國的英語教師的教學經驗，從而加深對英語教與學的了解。在過去的十年間，用理論角度去分析身份認同成為了理解教師和教學一個強大的分析框架，本研究也會從這個角度出發，去探討兒童英語教師的身份認同，從而了解他們的教學經驗和理念。本研究所得的成果相信會為中國以至全球相似的教育環境中的政策制定者、教師教育工作者、學校管理層、教研人員和兒童英語教師本身帶來切身利益。對教育決策者而言，本研究的所獲得的結果可作為他們的指南針，引領他們如何制定可適切地配合兒童語言發展和教師期望的教育政策和課程。對教師教育工作者而言，本研究所得可作為他們的教學參考，在培訓職前教師和支援在職教師時協助兩者建立專業身份。學校管理層亦可參考本研究對校本專業發展的建議，去調整對在職教師的支援。由於這個研究記錄了中國教師的教學經驗，這可作為教研人員建立數據庫的第一步，日後可探討不同地區的兒童英語教師身份建構及進行深入的比較性研究。是次研究結果可望在國際交流層面上與前線教育工作者分享所研所得，支援在校老師實踐英語課程，此舉可令在校教師受惠。

18606718.label: Project Objectives

18606718.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18606718.value: Whether law is a profession for public service or a self-serving monopoly has been the subject of perennial academic contestations. This project seeks to shed some light on the debate by investigating the professional identity of Hong Kong solicitors through event analysis and in-depth interviews. By exploring the lived experiences of a cross-section of solicitors who practice law in a variety of settings, this project will create new knowledge in two ways. First, it transcends a dominant research paradigm that focuses on prominent members of the profession or elite lawyers in international law firms by shifting focus to ordinary legal practitioners. Second, it goes beyond a widely held assumption that Hong Kong solicitors are profit-driven and inward-looking through an investigation of their professional identity and its relationships with the process of professional socialization. In doing so, this project will help highlight the diversities and complexities within the legal profession and enrich the international literature on lawyers and professionalism with a case study from Hong Kong. This project is set against the backdrop of Hong Kong’s transformation from a British colony to China’s Special Administrative Region, and hence uses the year of 1997 as a watershed. Sovereignty change in 1997 ushered in a new political era including the merger of two different legal systems, common law and socialist law, which subtly (yet fundamentally) changed the legal framework within which Hong Kong lawyers practice – most of them solicitors. To investigate whether and how solicitors’ professional identity and their perceptions to the profession and society have changed along Hong Kong’s trajectory, this project will employ the methods of event analysis and in-depth interviews. A critical analysis of major legal and political milestones since 1997 sets the context for the semi-structured interviews with a cross-section of solicitors. A sample of at least 60 solicitors will be drawn equally from those who entered the profession before and after 1997, which will cover solicitors who belong to different levels of seniority, social and education backgrounds, areas of expertise, and practice settings. This in-depth study of a cross-section of solicitors will produce valuable insights about how they perceive the current state of the legal profession, the public roles of lawyers, their views about Hong Kong’s future, as well as how their views might have changed through time, experience, and socio-political changes. 法律是一個為公眾服務，還是一個自利的壟斷行業，在學術上一直存在爭議。本研究旨在透過事件分析和深入訪談，探討香港事務律師的專業身份認同。透過探索事務律師的生活經驗，本研究在兩方面建設了新觀點。首先，本研究重點探討普通法律從業者，而不僅是行業內或國際律師事務所的精英律師。其次，本研究將深入探究香港事務律師的身份認同、和社會普遍對事務律師都是自顧自利的假設。本研究因此能夠突出法律行業的多樣性和複雜性、及利用香港作為個案研究，豐富有關國際法律專業的文獻。本文針對香港由英國殖民地轉變為中華人民共和國特別行政區的背景進行研究，以1997年為分水嶺。1997年的主權移交引發了一個新的政治時代，普通法和社會主義法在“一國兩制” 之下，改變了香港的法律框架。本研究會利用事件分析和深入訪談，探討事務律師的專業身份認同及他們對行業和社會的看法如何隨著香港的發展而改變。本研究會平均抽取至少60個，從1997年前後進入行業的事務律師的樣本，當中包括屬於不同資歷，社會和教育背景、專業領域和在不同規模律師事務所工作的律師。這項深入研究，將會對香港事務律師如何看法律行業的現狀、律師的公眾角色、香港的未來、以及他們的看法如何隨著時間和社會政治的變革而改變，提供珍貴的見解。

18607118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18607118.value: 進展性評估一直被認為是促進學生學習最有效的策略之一(Black & Wiliam, 1998a; Hattie, 2009)。雖然香港早於上世紀九十年代已經在政策層面推行進展性評估，但至今不少香港學校和教師仍更看重評估的選拔功能(Berry, 2011)。這一現象表明有幾方面的工作急需進行：1）我們需要了解教師實施進展性評估的意願，以及影響其意願的因素。有少量研究涉及過這一議題，但都只是聚焦於某一方面因素，沒有嘗試將不同因素包含在內，提供全面的理解。2）我們需要了解教師的進展性評估實踐，而且要結合學生對這些評估實踐的反應進行記錄。現有的相關研究大部分是簡單描述，而且沒有將教師實踐與學生反應結合起來。這種方式不利於全面及深入地理解進展性評估的通用原則。3）進展性評估是一種基於情境的活動，因些其在特定情境下，如香港，所表現出來的特點和細節需要進行深入研究。 本研究將會探究教師實施進展性評估的意願和實踐，以及其相應的影響因素。個人因素——例如Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) (Ajzen, 1991)所包含的態度、主觀常模、和自我效能——以及情境因素都將會被考慮在內，這有助於提供關於進展性評估的全面理解。學生的反應，例如他們的態度以及對評估策略有效性的認知，亦將是重要的關注點。基於此，本研究不僅僅是記錄某些個案，而是將進展性評估置於適當理論框架之下，進行全面的審視。 本研究將采用混合式研究方法。約800位教師將會參加一系列問卷調查。所使用問卷改編自一項先導研究(Yan & Cheng, 2015)。約54位教師將參與問卷前的焦點訪談。另一組約27位教師將參與觀察研究。每位教師會被觀察兩次連堂課，並接受個人訪談。而這27位教師所教授的約750位學生，將會參與問卷調查，部分學生會接受訪談。 本研究將從理論和實踐兩方面推動進展性評估的研究。基於來自教師和學生的量化和質化數據，研究發現將提供關於進展性評估的全面理解。將情境因素加入TPB理論的框架，亦有助於這一心理理論的發展。本研究所發展的工具將有助於將來進一步的研究。研究發現可以直接應用於改善教學實踐、教師專業發展、以及政策制訂。此外，本研究亦為旨在促進教師進展性評估的干預研究打下基礎。

18607118.label: Realisation of objectives
18607118.value: Research objective 1: To explore and assess predictors of teachers’ intentions and practices regarding formative assessment This objective has been 100% achieved. The predictors of teachers’ intentions and practices regarding formative assessment have been identified through literature review, interviews (focus group and think-aloud task) and survey studies. As a preparation for the whole study, a systematic review of relevant studies has been carried out. Consequently, a review article entitled “A systematic review on factors influencing teachers’ intentions and implementations regarding formative assessment” was published in Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice (Yan et al., 2021). Following the literature review, focus group interviews with 27 teachers (The reduction of the sample size for the pre-survey interview from 54 to 27 has been officially approved by RGC) and think-aloud interviews with 10 teachers were conducted. The interviews have obtained an in-depth understanding of the potential predictors of teachers’ intentions and practices regarding formative assessment. Furthermore, the insights generated from the literature review and interviews have helped fine-tune the theoretical framework used in this study and develop the Teacher’s Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ). The TCPFAQ has been administered to a sample of 612 teachers from 16 Hong Kong schools (8 primary and 8 secondary) (The reduction of the sample size for the teacher survey from 800 to 600 has been officially approved by RGC) to assess teachers’ formative assessment intentions and practices as well as the predictors, including instrumental attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy, examination culture, teaching environment, school support, and student attribute. Research objective 2: To examine the extent to which the Theory of Planned Behaviour, together with contextual factors, can explain teachers’ formative assessment intentions and practices in the Hong Kong context This objective has been 100% achieved. An extended Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) covering contextual factors has been applied to explain Hong Kong teachers’ formative assessment intentions and practices. The TCPFAQ questionnaire has been administered to a sample of 612 teachers from 16 Hong Kong schools (8 primary and 8 secondary) to explore the relationship between teachers’ formative assessment intentions and practices and its predictors. Based on around one half of the sample (N=296) who completed all subscales at two waves of the survey, a journal article entitled “Predicting teachers’ formative assessment practices: Teacher personal and contextual factors” was published in Teaching and Teacher Education (Yan et al., 2022). The results showed that some TPB factors (e.g., self-efficacy) influenced teachers’ formative assessment practices but, at the same time, many non-TPB personal (e.g., teacher rank and years of teaching experience) and contextual factors (e.g., school support, total number of teachers in a school, and teaching grade) also significantly impacted teachers’ formative assessment practices. Research objective 3: To profile the characteristics of teachers’ formative assessment practices in Hong Kong classrooms This objective has been 100% achieved. The characteristics of teachers’ formative assessment practices in Hong Kong classrooms have been investigated through individual interviews, class observations, and survey studies. COVID-19 has significantly influenced the implementation of the interviews and class observations. We proposed to observe 54 lessons in the three core subjects (Chinese, English, and Math) in a face-to-face mode, i.e., 27 teachers each teaching two double-lessons. However, school closure made the face-to-face observation impossible and, therefore, some of the observations were conducted in an online mode. We have successfully observed a total of 39 teachers (15 Chinese, 12 English, 12 Math; 9 face-to-face mode, 30 online mode), which was a different sample from that mentioned in Research Objective 1, and their students. Among them, 17 teachers were observed for two double-lessons and 22 for one double-lesson, resulting in a total of 56 double-lessons being observed. A total of 28 teachers and 70 students (2-4 students per class from 22 classes) were interviewed after the lessons. A journal paper based on the teacher interview and class observation results is under preparation. The results revealed that Hong Kong teachers carried out a wide range of formative assessment practices, which could be grouped into two major categories, i.e., teacher-directed formative assessments (e.g., sharing learning goals and providing feedback) and student-directed formative assessments (e.g., student self-assessment and peer-assessment). Based on the interview and observation results, the Teacher Formative Assessment Practice Scale (TFAPS) was developed and validated with two samples of primary and secondary school teachers: one from Hong Kong (N = 449) and the other from Italy (N = 309) (The Italy sample was an addition to the research proposal). The validation study “Assessing teachers’ strategies in formative assessment: The Teacher Formative Assessment Practice Scale” was published in Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment (Yan & Pastore, 2022). The survey results showed that Hong Kong teachers implemented teacher-directed formative assessments more frequently than student-directed formative assessments. Research objective 4: To examine students’ attitudes towards formative assessment strategies and their perceptions of its usefulness in terms of learning This objective has been 100% achieved. Students’ attitudes toward formative assessment strategies and their perceptions of its usefulness in terms of learning have been investigated through focus group interviews and survey studies. As mentioned in Research Objective 3, a total of 70 students were interviewed on their attitudes and perception regarding formative assessment. Furthermore, all students from 22 observed classes (N=495) completed a short survey on the same topic. A journal paper based on the student interview and survey is under preparation. The results suggested that students had a generally positive attitude towards formative assessment, but their attitudes varied across different formative assessment strategies. Students’ opinions were consistent with teachers’ in that teacher-directed formative assessment (e.g., sharing learning goals and providing feedback) was perceived as more useful in supporting their learning than student-directed formative assessment (e.g., student self-assessment and peer-assessment). Other outcomes In addition to the proposed activities, we have extended our research agenda around the project’s overall theme. For example, based on the literature review for the whole project, we published the article “Assessment for learning in the Hong Kong assessment reform: A case of policy borrowing” in Studies in Educational Evaluation (Yan & Brown, 2021). This article depicts the development of the formative assessment policy in the Hong Kong context and evaluates the effectiveness of the policy. We also proposed a three-dimension framework for teachers’ formative assessment literacy covering conceptual, practical, and social-emotional aspects. Based on this framework, we developed and validated a Teacher Formative Assessment Literacy Scale based on the data from a group of Hong Kong teachers. The Teacher Formative Assessment Literacy Scale and the Teacher Formative Assessment Practice Scale formed a valuable package to assess teachers’ conceptions, skills, and practices regarding formative assessment. The manuscript “Are teachers literate in formative assessment? The development and validation of the Teacher Formative Assessment Literacy Scale” is currently under the 2nd round of review (Yan & Pastore, under review). As a further step in this line of research, we have conducted a small-scale study to evaluate a professional development programme in developing teachers’ formative assessment literacy. The findings of this project were embedded into the programme and the newly developed instruments were used to collect pre- and post-training data. A journal article “The role of professional development programs in developing primary teachers’ formative assessment literacy” is currently under review (Li, Yan, et al., under review).
