18607118.label: Major findings and research outcome
18607118.value: The major findings generated from this project have made theoretical contributions to the literature, and have the potential to inform policies and practices related to educational assessment. • Key finding 1 (predictors of teachers’ formative assessment practices): Yan et al.’s (2021) systematic review identifies personal and contextual factors influencing teachers’ formative assessment intentions and practices. In addition, Yan et al. (2022) empirically test a comprehensive model of predicting teachers’ formative assessment practices with a Hong Kong sample. The results showed that personal (teacher rank, teaching experience, and self-efficacy) and contextual factors (school support, total number of teachers in a school, and teaching grade) significantly impact teachers’ formative assessment practices. Significance: Despite teachers’ crucial roles in formative assessment, our understanding of factors that might facilitate or hinder teachers’ practices is limited. Past studies identified isolated factors but did not show a comprehensive model of it. The above-mentioned review and empirical study provided a structural understanding of predictors of formative assessment practices. The findings may benefit researchers, school leaders, and policy-makers when they aspire to facilitate formative assessment. • Key finding 2 (profiling and measurement of formative assessment practices): The results revealed that teachers conducted two types of formative assessment, i.e., teacher-directed formative assessments (e.g., sharing learning goals and providing feedback) and student-directed formative assessments (e.g., student self-assessment and peer-assessment). Accordingly, Yan & Pastore (2022) developed the Teacher Formative Assessment Practice Scale (TFAPS), which contains 10 items assessing these two types of formative assessment. In addition, Yan & Pastore (under review) developed the Teacher Formative Assessment Literacy Scale (TFALS), which assesses the conceptual, practical, and social-emotional aspects of formative assessment literacy. Significance: There is a lack of theory-driven instruments that specifically assess teachers’ formative assessment practices and literacy. The two newly developed instruments not only facilitate the profiling of teachers’ formative assessment practices, but also lay the groundwork for future investigations in this field and teacher professional development that aim to enhance teachers’ formative assessment practices. • Key finding 3 (students’ perceptions of formative assessment): The data collected through interviews and surveys revealed that students had a generally positive attitude towards formative assessment, but their attitudes varied across different strategies. Students regarded teacher-directed formative assessment as more useful than student-directed formative assessment. Significance: Students’ voices have been largely ignored in formative assessment literature. Investigating the usefulness of formative assessment strategies from the student’s perspective is crucial. The findings can be fed directly into improving teaching practice, teacher education and policy-making.

18607118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18607118.value: This study contributes to a structural understanding of the elements that need to be considered when designing support measures or teacher professional development programmes aiming to promote formative assessment. There are three directions to develop this line of research further. First, the findings of this project highlight the complexity in predicting formative assessment practices. Future studies can provide a more nuanced analysis of predictors of formative assessment practices by including additional explanatory variables and specifying the nexus between personal and contextual factors in influencing formative assessment practices. Second, it will be meaningful to develop teacher professional development programmes based on the findings of this project and evaluate the effectiveness of the developed programmes. A small-scale study is currently being undertaken to evaluate a professional development programme, offered by EdUHK, in developing teachers’ formative assessment literacy. Third, as the engagement of both teachers and students in assessment processes is crucial to maximising the positive impact of assessment on student learning, it is important to develop synergies between teacher-directed and student-directed formative assessment in research and practice. A QEF project involving four seed schools is currently undergoing to develop and implement effective classroom assessment strategies that synergise teacher-directed and student-directed formative assessment.

18607118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18607118.value: The research outcomes of this project have addressed three important issues: 1) exploring the predictors of teachers’ formative assessment practices; 2) profiling teachers’ formative assessment practices and developing valid instruments for assessing teachers’ formative assessment practices and literacy; and 3) examining students’ attitudes towards formative assessment strategies and their perceptions of its usefulness in supporting learning. This project has contributed to a structural understanding of formative assessment practices and their predictors. The comprehensive model of formative assessment covering both personal and contextual factors, together with the developed instruments, laid a solid foundation for future research on formative assessment. The findings of the characteristics of teachers’ formative assessment practices and students’ perceptions of formative assessment strategies can benefit researchers, school leaders, and policy-makers when they aspire to facilitate the implementation of formative assessment and maximise the positive impact of formative assessment.

18607418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18607418.value: Creativity commonly refers to the ability to generate novel yet feasible ideas, solutions or insights. It is considered as one of the most complicated and important human quality. Creativity is often obvious in children but is more and more difficult to find when they are older. Adolescence is a crucial phase of human development and a window to enhance creativity. The focus of the proposed study is on adolescents. Most children today are exposed to video games on a daily basis. There is a growing interest in leveraging games to enhance students’ learning, motivation and creativity. A new imaginative game, called Doris, was recently reported and claimed to raise interest in the expression of creativity, build self-confidence, and enhance creative ways of thinking. The Doris tool is an award-winning board game with 24 physical pieces. A video game to implement Doris was initially proposed. The web-based version of the educational game was subsequently implemented. The implementation can free the players from the physical constraints of the board game and can play at anywhere with a basic computer connected to Internet. This new interactive environment allows the players to focus more on creative expression and innovative ways of thinking. The first objective of this proposed study is to examine the effects of the web-based video game implementing the Doris tool on enhancing creativity among Hong Kong adolescents. Recent studies suggest that praise can have a mixed effect on students. Specifically, praising a student’s inherent ability such as intelligence may teach them a fixed mindset or the belief that intelligence is not changeable. On the other hand, praising a student’s effort may encourage the growth mindset, which means that intelligence can be improved through practice and hard work. Students with a fixed and growth mindset respond to difficulties in learning differently. The second objective of the proposed study is to examine the effects of the growth mindset incentive in the game on creativity performance with the traditional reward format. To our knowledge, fostering a growth mindset incentive to enhance creativity in an educational game has not been researched before. The research can contribute to an innovative way of promoting growth mindset in creativity to adolescents through an educational game.

18607418.label: Realisation of objectives
18607418.value: The creativity game, DORIS, has been developed with multi-users' database support in the initial 6 months as planned. We also obtained the Figural and Verbal Forms of Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) (Chinese Version) from Psychological Publishing in addition to the Test for Creative Thinking Drawing Production (TCT-DP) published in the research community for the research instruments. A research assistant was hired and trained to conduct the experiment. Due to the social unrest in 2019 and the subsequent long period of the COVID-19 pandemic, the PI could not enter schools and organize the experiment to be carried out among the secondary schools’ adolescents. In other words, we did not have a window of opportunity to organize and conduct the testing instruments in schools. The situation is rather unfortunate. After a prolong and delayed period of not able to conduct the experiment in schools, the PI decided to switch the targeted participants from secondary schools to our university students. Experiment was conducted to the students taking General Education courses taught by the PI in this university and therefore covered a whole spectrum of undergraduate students. The effects of the growth mindset incentive in the DORIS game on creativity performance were studied with three student groups of no intervention, the game with a fixed mindset incentive, and the game with a growth mindset incentive. The instruments mentioned above were used for the pre-test and pro-test. Four tasks of interventions were administrated in stages for the duration of a semester. Using the imaginative game, the first task was to make any figures in the simplest way. The second task was to make as many figures the students feel positive and related to joy and happiness. The third task was to create an animal, a famous landmark, and a transport vehicle. The fourth task was to make three figures that are related to known problems in the immediate environment among the students’ family, friends, neighborhood, in the city, or the planet. Students were required to login into the system for each task. Growth mindset messages were given to the participants in the group of the game with a growth mindset incentive. Fixed mindset messages were given to the other participants.

18607418.label: Major findings and research outcome
18607418.value: Creativity is considered as one of the most complicated and important human quality. It has a significant and widespread impact on many domains ranging from daily life problem solving to science and the arts. Creativity commonly refers to the ability to generate ideas, solutions, or insights that are novel yet feasible. Many researchers believed that creativity can be enhanced using the appropriate creative environment. In this research, we demonstrate nurturing creativity with the use of a web-based educational game. We developed a web-based educational game called Doris to act as agents of innovation and engage the players in the expression of creativity, build self-confidence and enhance their creative ways of thinking. The web-based implementation allows the players to play the game at anytime and anywhere. With multi-users’ database support, we can keep track of the players’ profile, artefact creations, puzzle pieces’ movement and rotation, and dialogic responses. The database support is very importance. It stores the profile of each player and creates the required storage space for interaction. It permits the players to store their artefact creations and allows the facilitator to respond and comment on their creations. It records each puzzle’s position and allows the system to log the piece’s movement over time. The abstraction and re-creation are possible. We can study the player’s thinking on the artefact creation. From the experiment conducted among higher education students, the findings indicated that creativity could be improved with the web-based educational game. Nurturing creativity with the creative environment is possible. The details of these findings are reported in the prepared paper and another paper under preparation as shown in Part C of this report.

18607418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18607418.value: Given the database support of the developed game, we are able to track the pieces' movement, orientation and interaction of the players, we can analyze their creative thinking through their moves computationally and abstraction to their artefact creations. This is the potential for further development.

18607418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18607418.value: The new game-based environment called DORIS to enhance creativity was developed. A database system to track and support user interaction to DORIS was implemented. The game allows the players to focus more on creative expression and innovative ways of promoting growth mindset in creativity. Fostering a growth mindset incentive to enhance creativity in an educational game has not been researched before. This research pioneered the world's first game-based development in the important fields of mindset and creativity. Furthermore, the approach of the growth mindset incentive structure is not only beneficial to video games, but also can apply to other activities in education. This research has a significant impact to the embodiment of growth mindset in educational activities including educational games.

18608018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18608018.value: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are typically less physically active and with lower exercise tolerance due to their limitation in social interaction and communication. They are therefore more prone to chronic diseases in adulthood, which may be avoidable by early intervention. Although exercise training is proven to improve not only physical health but also various behavioural outcomes in school-aged children with ASD, little has been done to study exercise training programmes that caters for their special needs and limitations. Parents play an important role in children’s participation of physical activities. However, parents of children with ASD often find it difficult to encourage their children to take part in physical activities due to lower parenting efficacy. It has been reported that Chinese mothers of children with ASD has high parenting stress, which is associated with negative perception of a child’s disability and low parental confidence. Parent training programs have been reported to have positive effects on children with disabilities and their parents. However, the effectiveness of parent training in an exercise training programme to promote physical activity in children with ASD, specially in the Chinese setting, is not known. Guided by Eccles’s (1998) expectancy-value theory, we propose testing the impact of parental involvement in an exercise training programme specially designed for children with ASD. Children in the experiment group (with parent training) and control group will receive an exercise training program for eight weeks. In the experiment group, parents of the children will be additionally equipped with knowledge of Sport Sciences, Developmental Pediatrics and Developmental Psychology, and will act as an observer and motivator to their child’s physical activity participation during the 8-week training period. They will also serve as the provider of physical activity opportunities to their child during the one-year follow up period, during which parents’ support group and reinforcement sessions will be arranged. Children’s outcomes and parents’ outcomes will be compared between the experiment and control group. The proposed work will provide unique data on the impact of parent involvement in an exercise training programme on physical and psychological well-being in children with ASD, as well as parenting stress and efficacy, with important implications on the health promotion in children of ASD and their families.

18608018.label: Realisation of objectives
18608018.value: To achieve the objectives of this study, we have completed eight exercise intervention programs with or without the involvement of parents in five primary schools, with each exercise program including 16 sessions conducted twice a week, lasting for eight weeks. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, our study's progress was impacted for approximately a year. However, we were fortunate enough to have finished the exercise training intervention in some schools, and the participants underwent a one-year follow-up period. After the condition of the COVID-19 pandemic has been turning better, we took advantage of the summer holidays and conducted two more exercise intervention programs for data collection. Our initial proposal aimed to include 30 children in the experimental group and another 30 in the control group. We used the school-based randomization procedure to ensure that training strategies do not affect children within the same school during the training period. This involved forming groups of six to eight children from the same school who underwent the same training at their school for a semester. We recruited sixty children (32 from the experimental and 28 from the control group). Two children from the control group withdrew from the study due to their involvement in other school programs that conflicted with our training schedule. Therefore, data from 58 children were included in the analysis. Objectives 1: By comparing children’s study outcomes in the study group (training with parental involvement; PI group) and the control group (training without parental involvement; NPI group) at baseline, after the 8-week exercise intervention, and at one-year follow-up, the effectiveness and sustainability of the training program for both groups were assessed. Objective 1 is 100% achieved. Objectives 2: By comparing children’s physical activity level, physical fitness and psychological function in the PI group and the NPI group before and after the exercise intervention, we evaluated the changes in the study outcomes for both groups. Objective 2 is 100% achieved. Objective 3: By comparing parental stress level, and parent-child relationship in the PI group and the NPI group at baseline, after the 8-week exercise intervention, and at one-year follow-up, we learn the changes and differences for both groups. Regarding the couple’s relationship satisfaction, some teachers in the participating schools expressed concern that this topic may be a sensitive issue for certain families. As it is not the main focus of our study, we only gathered information on the parents’ marital status at the beginning of this study. We found that 17% of parents in this study had undergone divorce. We estimate that Objective 3 is 98% achieved. Objective 4: We measured parents’ physical activity levels using a validated physical activity questionnaire, and children’s physical activity levels objectively using the Actigraph activity monitor. It was found that there was no significant difference in the physical activity levels of children when comparing parents with different activity levels. Objective 4 is 100% achieved. Objective 5: We measured parents’ support for children’s physical activity using a validated questionnaire, and children’s physical activity levels by a validated activity log during the one-year follow-up period. It was found that parents’ support for children’s physical activity was significantly associated with children’s physical activity level. Object 5 is 100% achieved. During the COVID-19 pandemic when the condition didn’t allow our team to conduct exercise programs at schools, we took the time and the available manpower supported by this grant to conduct a side project “To examine the understanding of the concept peak oxygen uptake among children and adolescents at different ages from a developmental perspective”. A questionnaire survey was conducted on 549 children and adolescents. The result of this side project was published in the Frontiers in Pediatrics: Wong SWL, Yu CCW, Li AM. The Understanding of Peak Oxygen Uptake in Children Aged 8-16. Front Pediatr. 2021 Jan 14;8:599571. doi: 10.3389/fped.2020.599571. PMID: 33520890; PMCID: PMC7841111. A full paper on this study has been written and is undergoing submission to the peer-review journal process.

18608018.label: Major findings and research outcome
18608018.value: There was a significant between-group difference in the changes in the hand grip strength for the non-dominant hand from baseline [p(time*group)= 0.022]. Post-hoc analysis showed that the difference may mainly attribute to the increase in the PI group after the 8-week intervention (p<0.05). There was a significant within-group improvement in the PI group regarding increased peak expiratory flow after the 8-week intervention (p<0.05). There was no significant between-group difference in the changes in daily physical activity from baseline. Data showed that children in both groups spent only 6% of the time in moderate-vigorous physical activities during the monitoring period before and after the 8-week intervention. There was a significant between-group difference in the changes in the hit standard error by block from baseline [p(time*group) = 0.007]. Hit standard error by block is one of the Conners’ Continuous Performance Test II parameters to measure children’s selective attention - the ability to consistently focus on some continuous stimuli. Post-hoc analysis showed that the difference may be attributed to the improvement in the PI group and deterioration in the NPI group during the one-year follow-up period. In addition, there were significant within-group improvements in attention, visual search, and sequencing skills assessed by the Comprehensive Trail Marking Test; and theory of mind in children of the PI group after the 8-week exercise intervention (p<0.05). There was a significant between-group difference in the changes from baseline in parents’ belief that exercise is beneficial for their child's life enhancement [p(time*group) = 0.043]. Post-hoc analysis showed that the difference may be attributed to the higher score at one-year follow-up compared to the baseline level in the PI group (p<0.05). Noteworthy, parents in the PI group also showed a significant increase in their beliefs that exercise is beneficial for their child's psychological outlook, and health and disease prevention after the 8-week intervention (p<0.05). There was no significant between-group difference in the changes in parental stress and parent-child relationships from baseline. Parents in the PI group scored significantly greater improvement in their child’s physical endurance (p=0.025) and attention to finish a task (p=0.043) using a 7-point Likert Clinical Global Impression for improvement scale. There were significantly more parents in the PI group (15 out of 30, 50%) than the NPI group (5 out of 26, 19%) rated “much improved” to “very much improved” in children’s attention to finish a task after participating in the exercise intervention (p=0.017).

18608018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18608018.value: We adopted Eccles’s (1998) expectancy-value model to construct the conceptual framework of the present study. In this model, parents who expect their children would be successful in sports or physical activities and value success in this area will be more likely to influence their children to pursue this behavior. Our team has developed parent workshops on technical skills when coaching children with ASD during exercise practices. Additionally, our workshops provide information on the health benefits of exercise. We also invited parents to visit their child’s exercise training classes regularly, to witness their progress. These approaches were shown to be effective that parents in the training with parental involvement (PI) group have a stronger belief in the benefits of exercise for their children’s health and development, and children in this group demonstrated improvements in handgrip strength and attention after the 8-week exercise intervention compared to their peers in the training group without parental involvement. Our study did not show any significant increase in daily physical activity level of children in the PI group. This suggests that practical guidelines for daily physical activity scheduling for families, achievable targets for parents, and a better monitoring system may be worth exploring in further studies.

18608018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18608018.value: This is the first randomized-controlled trial studying the effects of parental involvement in exercise training for children with autism spectrum disorder. Our study results showed that even for a relatively short period of exercise training, children in the training with parental involvement (PI) group had significant improvement in their handgrip strength, and selective attention - the ability to consistently focus on some continuous stimuli compared to the children in the training without parental involvement (NPI) group. Handgrip strength is an indicator of overall muscle strength, and is closely associated with a person’s cardiovascular health. If parents can encourage children to exercise regularly over a prolonged period, children’s physical and psychological functions are expected to be further improved. After one year of follow-up, it was found that parents in the PI group had a stronger belief in the benefits of exercise for their children's life enhancement compared to parents in the NPI group. This suggests that the parent workshops and exercise class visits provided in our study effectively sustain parents' belief in the benefits of exercise for their children. Parents actively involved in children’s exercise practice can help to promote children’s physical and psychological functions.

18610218.label: Co - Investigator(s)
18610218.value: Prof Chiu, Ming Ming Prof Heyman, Gail Dr Zhou, Qing

18610218.label: Project Objectives
18610218.value: To examine the prevalence of parental differential treatment in Hong Kong. To determine the extent (i) to which PDT is perceived as being fairer by children when parents have a higher level of empathy; (ii) to which children’s perception of PDT is moderated by child personality and child empathy; (iii) to which children who perceive PDT as less unfair have better psychosocial health; and (iv) to which a child’s perception of the fairness of PDT mediates the link between PDT and psychosocial health (see Figure 1). 18610218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18610218.value: Some adolescents believe that their parents treat them differently (parental differential treatment, PDT). PDT is prevalent worldwide, occurring in up to 65% of the families. Despite the fact that extensive research on PDT has been conducted in the West, there has been a dearth of research in Hong Kong. Although it is well known that PDT can have a profound effect on the mental health of affected individuals, very little is known about the prevalence rate of PDT in Hong Kong, particularly among adolescents, whose mental health is in decline. In addition, a major limitation of the current literature is that existing studies have focused on socio-demographic variables, such as gender, age, and birth order to explain PDT. The problem with this approach is that those characteristics are largely immutable and can therefore do little to inform efforts to improve the situation of adolescents experiencing PDT. The proposed study overcomes these limitations by investigating factors of PDT such as empathy that can be targeted for intervention in future studies. The overall aim of this study is to examine the impact of PDT on adolescent psychosocial well-being and test adolescents’ perception of fairness as a mediation mechanism. We will further explore whether the mediated pathway via adolescent perception of fairness may be moderated by parental empathy, adolescent empathy and adolescent personality. Effects on adolescents’ psychosocial adjustment will be investigated as assessed by measures of self-esteem, depression, anxiety, and trust in relationships with parents. This study will utilize structural equation modelling in a 2-year longitudinal design. Data will be collected from 760 Chinese adolescents studying in Secondary One to Secondary Three in Hong Kong and from their parents. The proposed research is a pioneering attempt which will both inform efforts to promote adolescent psychosocial well-being in Hong Kong and to address important theoretical debates about relations between PDT, child perception of fairness and psychosocial well-being and the role played by empathy in the relationship between those three variables. This study also uses a novel approach as it investigates the problem by taking into account perspectives from different levels of analysis, including individual (i.e., adolescents’ psychological health), familial (parenting), economical and societal levels. The work is also innovative as it focuses on modifiable factors and behaviors, and informs future intervention. 父母差別待遇的影響：子女和父母因素對子女心理社交健康的縱向研究 一些青少年認為他們的父母對待他們與家中的兄弟姊妹有差異(父母差別待遇)。有研究指出父母差別待遇的現象在世界各地普遍存在，甚至在高達百分之六十五的西方家庭中出現。儘管西方學者對父母差別待遇進行了大量的研究，但香港在這方面的研究卻極少。眾所周知，父母差別待遇對受影響個體的心理健康產生深遠影響。但是，我們對父母差別待遇的現象在香港家庭中的出現率所知有限。現在，香港青少年的心理健康每況愈下，父母差別待遇對青少年心理健康的影響，我們所知不多。另外，現存文獻中有一個主要的局限，就是大部分的研究都側重於用社會人口統計學的變量，如性別，年齡和出生順序等來解釋父母差別待遇的現象。這些不可改變的變量不能幫助我們解決問題，因此無法為經歷父母差別待遇的青少年提供幫助。因此，本研究希望通過對如同理心等變量的研究，可克服現存文獻中的局限性及為未來制定介入措施提供重要信息。 本研究旨在探討父母差別待遇對青少年心理社交健康的影響，並探索青少年對公平的看法會否在父母差別待遇中產生調節作用。此外，我們會探討青少年對公平的看法會否因父母和青少年的同理心以及青少年的性格而有差別。我們會透過量度青少年的自尊感、抑鬱、焦慮程度和對父母的信任度來評估父母差別待遇對青少年社交心理的影響。本研究將利用結構方程模型對收集到的資料進行分析，研究設計以兩年的縱向研究為基礎。研究資料將來源於760名在香港就讀中學一年級至中學三年級的青少年及其父母。 本研究是一項開創性的嘗試，既可為促進香港青少年社會心理健康提供重要的信息，也可以解決有關父母差別待遇的現象，並就青少年對公平看法和心理社交健康的關係以及同理心在當中所起的作用提供重要的理論依據。本研究採用的研究方法是透過考慮個體（即青少年的心理健康），家庭（家庭教育），經濟和社會等不同層次的觀點來探索問題的本質。這項研究亦具有創新性，因為它側重於可以改變的因素和行為，研究結果可為未來制定預防策略提供線索。

18610218.label: Realisation of objectives
18610218.value: (i) Pilot study Prior to the data collection for the main study, we invited a randomly selected secondary school in Yau Tsim Mong district to join our pilot study. The results of the pilot study showed that the measurements demonstrated good psychometric properties and provided us with an opportunity to refine the logistics of data collection. (ii) Main study To achieve the objectives 1-3 as stated in the preceding section 5.1, we recruited one secondary school from each 18 districts, totaling 18 schools. See details of the data collection in Ng et al. (2020). Student participants completed a survey regarding their perceptions of parental differential treatment (PDT), their personality, perception of fairness, level of empathy, socio-demographic variables and psychosocial well-being (self-esteem, anxiety, depression and trust in relationships). Their parents also completed surveys regarding their parenting, level of empathy and demographics. We successfully recruited 1,010 boys, 739 girls, and 1,749 student-parent dyads at Time One which exceeded the target stated in the proposal (N = 760 dyads). With this sample size, we estimated the prevalence of PDT (objective 1), conducted mediation/moderation analyses (objective 2) and determined whether adolescents’ experience of PDT at Time One predicted psychosocial health at Time Two (objective 3). Therefore, the objectives were fully achieved and the results of all three objectives are presented in section 6.1.

18610218.label: Major findings and research outcome
18610218.value: Most Chinese adolescents viewed their parents as treating their siblings and themselves equally regarding differential affection (mother: 80.9%; father: 77.3%) or control (mother: 69.4%; father: 68.1%) rather than: (a) favoring them over their siblings regarding affection (mother: 10.2%; father: 12.1%) or control (mother: 17.0%; father: 17.7%), (b) favoring their sibling over them regarding affection (mother: 8.4%; father: 9.9%) or control (mother: 12.1%; father: 12.9%), (c) strongly favoring them (all 0.5%) or (d) strongly favoring their sibling (all 0.1%). Collectivist values in Hong Kong focus on the family as a unit rather than as individuals, which might explain the less frequent PDT in Hong Kong than in the individualistic West whose parents more often prioritize the concerns of one child over another. See demographic antecedents of PDT in Ng et al. (submitted to Current Psychology) in section 8. Our multilevel analysis showed that PDT was linked to psychosocial well-being including life satisfaction, self-esteem, depression, anxiety, and stress at Time 2. Children who perceived 10% greater maternal differential control showed 2% less life satisfaction. Moreover, children who perceived their mother's PDT as 10% fairer or 10% greater paternal affection showed 2% more life satisfaction. Children who perceived 10% greater differential maternal control showed 0.9% less self-esteem. Furthermore, children who perceived their mother's PDT as 10% fairer or 10% greater father affection showed 1% more self-esteem. Child’s perception of the fairness of PDT mediated 27% of the link between PDT, maternal control and self-esteem (z = -3.045, p = .002). Children who perceived 10% greater maternal differential control showed 0.7% more depression. Also, children who perceived their mother's PDT as 10% fairer or 10% greater father affection showed 1% less depression. Children who perceived 10% greater differential maternal control or 10% greater prevalence of father’s PDT showed 0.6% more anxiety (respectively, 0.6% and 0.2%). However, children who perceived their mother's PDT as 10% fairer or 10% greater differential paternal affection showed less anxiety (respectively, 0.5% and -0.7%). Children who perceived 10% greater prevalence of mother PDT showed 0.3% more stress. Child’s perception of the fairness of PDT mediated differential maternal control's and differential paternal affection's links with life satisfaction (respectively, 36% and 33%), depression (57%; 27%), and anxiety (33%; 22%). Child’s perception of the fairness of PDT also mediated 10% of the link between perceived father PDT prevalence and anxiety. Other links among key variables were insignificant.

18610218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18610218.value: There are at least two areas for future research. The first area focuses on exploring the demographic antecedents, particularly the socioeconomic status, of PDT. As our current results revealed that Chinese fathers with higher SES showed more PDT, our findings differ from those in Western societies where parents of lower SES showed more negative parenting practices, including PDT. Further examining fathers and children recruited from high SES families can improve understanding of this phenomenon. Given the lack of research on PDT including Chinese fathers, using a mixed methods approach can yield more insights about this parenting practice. The second area focuses on developing interventions to improve the psychological well-being of disfavored children. Since our study focused on modifiable rather than unchangeable factors such as gender and birth order predicting PDT in previous studies, our study results revealed that child perceived fairness played an important role, in particular, in mediating the relationship between perceived differential maternal control and depression. It would therefore be useful to include perceived fairness as one of the key elements in the interventions and evaluate its effectiveness to determine whether it can improve the psychological well-being of disfavored children and their relationships with parents and siblings.

18610218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18610218.value: This study examined the impact of parental differential treatment (PDT) on adolescent psychosocial well-being. Survey responses by 1,749 adolescents (mean age = 12.9 years) and their parents in Hong Kong indicated less PDT in Hong Kong than in Western societies. Child's perception of fairness mediated the relationship between PDT, life satisfaction, self-esteem, anxiety and depression. Child personality, child empathy, or parent empathy did not moderate PDT's link with any outcome. The adolescent participants who perceived more PDT at baseline showed less life satisfaction, lower self-esteem, more stress, more anxiety, and more depression at follow-up. Our study is among the first to examine PDT in the Chinese context which has advanced our understanding of PDT in a non-Western society and allows us to make comparisons with the results from the West. As China has recently implemented a three-child policy, this study examines a changing Chinese society and stimulates future research in China and other Asian countries.

18610818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18610818.value: China, as one of the fastest growing countries in the past few decades, is anticipated to accelerate its consumption of global natural resources, and sharks are one of the most significant examples of how the country’s economic growth could threaten wild animals worldwide. The increased consumption of Shark Fin Soup, which is regarded as a symbol of wealth and vitality of the family in Chinese society, has led to over-exploitation of sharks, rendering Hong Kong and later China to become the largest shark fin importers globally. We believe education in China, especially in the early stages of schooling when pro-environmental attitudes are being formed, is a more sustainable solution to shark conservation in the long run. Based on the dual process theory in learning, the proposed study aims at addressing which factors, perception towards sharks and the conceptual understanding of the ecological role of shark, will govern primary school students’ attitudinal and behavioural intentions to conserve sharks in three Chinese communities. The proposed 15-month study will sample over 500 students from 12 primary schools in Hong Kong and other cites in Taiwan and mainland China, adopting the theoretical framework of wildlife value orientation (WVO) as the principal model in explaining behavioural intention for shark conservation. A questionnaire survey, the items of which were sourced or modified from Tsoi et al. (2016), Manfredo et al. (2009) and Thompson & Mintzes (2002), will be conducted to reveal five psychometric constructs, namely the conceptual understanding and perception towards sharks, WVO and attitude towards wildlife and behavioural intention for pro-shark behaviour. Structural equation modelling will be used to illustrate the causal relationship between the constructs, especially the role of conceptual and perceptual learning process in affecting behavioural intentions. Semi-structured interviews with different stakeholders, including parents and teachers, will be conducted to further study the factors affecting students’ attitude and behavioural intention towards shark conservation. This study is the first quantitative study to apply the WVO model on Chinese society. It has the potential to expand to other parts of mainland China and serve as an important reference for future studies on other threatened species associated with Chinese consumption habits. The findings of the proposed study will also provide theoretical foundations for the future development of education modules regarding shark conservation in China. 中國作為過去幾十年增長最快的國家之一，預計將加速其對全球自然資源的利用。鯊魚是國家經濟增長如何威脅全球野生動物的最重要例子之一。魚翅的消費被視為中國社會內家庭財富和地位的象徵，國內消費量的增加導致對鯊魚的過度開發，使香港和其後的中國成為全球最大的魚翅進口地區。長遠來看，利用中國的教育，尤其在形成親環境態度的早期學校教育階段，是一種更可持續的鯊魚保育解決方案。基於學習的雙歷程理論，本研究旨在解決哪些因素，包括對鯊魚的感知以及對鯊魚生態作用的概念性理解，將決定在三個華人社區內的小學生保育鯊魚的態度和行為意圖。本研究為期15個月，將對來自香港、台灣及中國大陸其他城市的12所小學及500多名學生進行抽樣調查，採用野生動物價值取向（WVO）理論框架作為解釋鯊魚保護行為意向的主要模式。問卷調查項目分別來自Tsoi等人。 （2016），Manfredo等。 （2009年）和Thompson ＆ Mintzes（2002年）。本研究將研究學生的五種心理建構，分別是對鯊魚的概念理解和感知，野生動物價值取向和對野生動物的態度，以及親鯊魚的行為意圖。結構方程模式分折將用於說明五種心理建構之間的因果關係，尤其是概念和感知學習過程在影響行為意圖中的作用。研究亦會對包括家長和教師在內的不同持份者進行半結構化訪談，以進一步了解影響學生對鯊魚保護態度和行為意向的因素。本研究是第一個將WVO模型應用於中國社會的定量研究。此研究方法有可能擴展到中國大陸的其他地區，並作為未來研究與中國消費習慣相關的其他受威脅物種的重要參考。此研究之結果也將為未來中國鯊魚保育教學單元的發展，提供理論基礎。

18610818.label: Realisation of objectives
18610818.value: Basically, all the three objectives have been completed. Due to the unforeseen impact of COVID-19, the sampling in mainland China and Hong Kong were restricted, rendering a relatively few samples from the areas. The cross-regional mixed method research was conducted throughout the planned sampling sties in Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Xiamen and Taiwan. The responses from 781 school pupils from grades 4 to 6 (403 males, 366 females, and twelve unreported genders) aged between 9 and 13 years old (M=11.5, SD=.749) were collected. Regarding the qualitative study, we have interviews with 16 parents and 19 students from southern parts of China (Shenzhen and Xiamen), Hong Kong, and Taiwan. The objectives were achieved as stated below: Objective 1 -To investigate Hong Kong, Taiwan and Mainland China primary students' perceptions of sharks and their conceptual understanding of the ecological role of sharks in marine ecosystems. The perceptual mean score among the Chinese communities was 5.04 (SD=1.11), showing a slight positive perception of sharks. Almost two-thirds of Chinese pupils expressed optimistic perceptions about the human-shark relationship, meaning that humans are not often attacked by sharks (65.9%) with the item mean score (5.07, SD= 1.65). Another reverse coded statement revealed that 27.9 % of respondents agree that swimming without sharks in the sea would be safe (M= 5.30, SD= 1.71). This statement reflects that the majority of pupils do not think sharks are "man-eaters". There was no statistically significant difference (t (767) = 7.525, p = .648) between male (M=5.06, SD= 1.19) and female (M=5.03, SD= 1.04) pupils, but there was among geographical regions. Hong Kong students (M=4.65, SD= 1.13) had a lower perceptual score than Taiwan students (M=5.10, SD= 1.09) based on the results from the post hoc test (t (2,778) = 6.25, p = .002). The conceptual mean score in the Chinese communities was 5.74 (SD= 1.07). A total of 87.2% of pupils disagreed that "Human is the main diet of sharks" (M=5.98, SD= 1.37), but almost 50% of respondents totally opposed this reversed statement. Similarly, 87.2% of respondents rejected that "The decline of the shark population would enhance the biodiversity of the marine ecosystem" (M=6.07, SD= 1.30), and 54.4% of respondents totally disagree with this negative statement. These results suggested that students in Chinese communities have correct concepts regarding the ecological roles of sharks, but the understanding on how human activity affects the sharks' population are relatively limited. There was no statistically significant difference (t (767) = 2.34, p = .069) between male (M=5.81, SD= 1.12) and female (M=5.67, SD= 1.01) students in conceptual understanding about sharks. but students in Taiwan (M=5.78, SD= 1.07) had significantly higher conceptual scores than students from Hong Kong (M=5.47, SD= 1.13), as shown in the post hoc test (t (2,778) = 3.30, p = .037). Objective 2- To investigate the basic wildlife belief, the wildlife value orientation and behavioral Intention for shark conservation in the Chinese communities using wildlife value orientation model. In terms of the domination belief for wildlife, the mean score was 2.85 (SD= 0.96). A minority of children realized that human needs outweighed wildlife and fish protection (18.1%) (M=2.83, SD= 1.86). Similar numbers of respondents reflected the acceptance of the scenarios that humans killed wildlife when people think wildlife caused a threat to their property (18.7%)(M=2.90, SD= 1.76) and humans used wildlife and fish in research even though that the research may hurt or kill them (16.4%)(M=2.82, SD= 1.74). In contrast, more students echoed the acceptance of killing the wildlife when wildlife posed a threat to their lives (30.7%)(M=3.35, SD= 1.95). Male students (M=3.01, SD=.1.02 ) had a stronger domination wildlife belief than female pupils (M=2.68, SD=.86 ) (t (4.87) = 7.33, p = .000). Pupils from Hong Kong (M=3.20, SD=.99 ) were with a more dominant view to the wildlife (t (2,778) = 6.71, p = .001) than students from both Taiwan (M=2.82, SD= .95 ) and mainland China (M=2.75, SD=.91). In contrary, Chinese pupils got a higher mean score in mutualism wildlife belief (M= 5.27, SD= 1.02) than the domination belief. Most of the students considered all living things are as one big family (85.2%) (M=6.04, SD= 1.39), among 54.5% of those students strongly agreed with this statement. Most students also thought of having similar rights between humans and animals (78.5%) (M=5.74, SD= 1.49). 68 % of Chinese pupils mentioned the relationship with wildlife was like a family and to protect them (M=5.27, SD= 1.63); similar results showed that students cared about animals as more than other people (66.8%) and received the companionship feeling from animals (73.7%) (M=5.49, SD= 1.55). No gender statistical significance difference was found (t (767) = 16.56, p = .30), but there was for regions (t (2,778) = 3.48, p =.031 ). Students from Hong Kong (M=5.01, SD=.96 ) got lower mutualism score than those from Taiwan (M=5.30, SD=1.03) and Mainland China (M=5.36, SD=.96 ). Objective 3 - To test which factors, perceptions, conceptual understandings about sharks and other demographic factors, will affect the value orientation, attitudes, and behavioral intentions of Chinese primary students to conserve sharks. Using Maximum likelihood method of SEM analysis, three models have been set up with the respect to Objective 3. In the first model, we have accessed how perceptions and conceptual understanding about sharks affects value orientations. The chi-square value was yielded 1158.74 (df= 226, p<0.01). With regard to the model result, conceptual understanding (Estimate = -.76, p<0.01) and perception (Estimate = -.37, p<0.01) contribute to domination belief. The conceptual understanding (Estimate = .58, p<0.01) was more influential than perception (Estimate = .23, p<0.01) to mutualism belief. The pathway from those latent constructs , meaning that the understanding contributes and perception of sharks influence both beliefs. The second model displayed how perception and conceptual understanding impact different wildlife attitudes from Kellert's typology. The chi-square value 1160.18 (df= 226, p<0.01) was resulted. The model illustrates that perception attributes to moralistic attitude with the estimate .40 (p<0.01), scientific attitude with the estimate .45 (p<0.01), utilitarian and negativistic attitude with the estimate -.70 (p<0.01) and naturalistic attitude with the estimate .25 (p<0.01). On the other hand, conceptual understanding contributes to moralistic attitude with the estimate 1.99 (p>0.05), scientific attitude with the estimate 9.46 (p>0.05), utilitarian and negativistic attitude with the estimate -1.41 (p>0.05) and naturalistic attitude with the estimate 9.10 (p>0.05). Although the conceptual understanding of sharks affects much than perception, the pathway of conceptual understanding is not statistically significant. The third model analyzed how perception, conceptual understanding of sharks and gender contribute to behavioural intention for shark conservation. After adding in the demographic parameter (gender), the Chi square value was 756.30 (df= 75, p<0.01). This model indicated that perception (Estimate = .34, p<0.01) , conceptual understanding (Estimate = .32, p>0.05) and gender (Estimate = .024, p>0.05) influence the behavioural intention. Only the pathway from perception to behavioural intention is statistically significant.

18610818.label: Major findings and research outcome
18610818.value: Two papers were under preparation for submitting to top-tier journals. The first one is a general account on psychological constructs studied among students in Chinese communities. The perceptual mean score among the Chinese communities was demonstrated a slight positive perception of sharks. The conceptual mean score of the Chinese primary students was 5.74 (SD= 1.07). Students in Chinese communities have correct concepts regarding the ecological roles of sharks, but the understanding on how human activity affects the sharks' population are relatively limited. For both perception and conception, there was no statistically significant difference between genders. Students in Taiwan demonstrated significantly higher conceptual scores than students from Hong Kong, but Hong Kong students had a lower perceptual score than Taiwan students. In terms of the domination belief for wildlife, pupils from Hong Kong were with a more dominant view to the wildlife than those from both Taiwan and the southern parts of China. No gender statistical significance difference was found in the mutualism belief but there was the statistical significance among regions. Students from Hong Kong got lower mutualism score than the counterparts in Taiwan and Mainland China. The second paper is on the relative contribution between conceptual understanding and perception towards shark on the shark-conserving behavioural intention. Based on the structural equation modeling analysis, three models have been set up. In the first model, we have accessed how perceptions and conceptual understanding about sharks affects value orientations. Conceptual understanding and perception contributed to domination belief, with the conceptual understanding was more influential to the mutualism belief. The second model investigated how perception and conceptual understanding impact different wildlife attitudes from Kellert's typology. The model illustrates that perception attributes to the utilitarian and negativistic attitude with the most estimate -0.70 (p<0.01). The conceptual understanding contributes to the scientific attitude with the estimate 9.46 (p>0.05) and naturalistic attitude with the estimate 9.10 (p>0.05). Although the conceptual understanding of sharks affects much than perception, the pathway of conceptual understanding is not statistically significant. The third model analyzed how perception, conceptual understanding of sharks and gender contribute to behavioural intention for shark conservation, showing that perception (Estimate = 0.34, p<0.01) , conceptual understanding (Estimate = 0.32, p>0.05) and gender (Estimate = 0.024, p>0.05) influence the behavioural intention. Only the pathway from perception to behavioural intention is statistically significant.

18610818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18610818.value: The study has illustrated the relative contribution of the conceptual understanding and perception about sharks on the behavioural intention of the primary students, and elucidated the wildlife value orientation of the students in Chinese communities. The research team is now designing and testing an effective intervention (educational modules) in primary schools in Hong Kong to be adopted in the subject General Studies to enrich the knowledge of shark and nurture students' altitude, through the incorporation of conceptual and perceptual components reviewed by the current studies. The successful development of the educational modules would benefit the educational communities through improving the wildlife education and ocean literacy education in the formal education in Hong Kong and other Chinese communities.

18610818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18610818.value: The proposed study aims at addressing which factors, perception towards sharks and the conceptual understanding of the ecological role of shark, will govern primary school students’ attitude and behavioural intentions to conserve sharks in the Chinese communities. Adopting the theoretical framework of wildlife value orientation (WVO), the study sampled quantitively 781 pupils from grades 4 to 6 and qualitatively from 16 parents and 19 students from mainland China (Shenzhen and Xiamen), Hong Kong, and Taiwan. Structural equation modelling was used to illustrate the causal relationship between the constructs, especially the role of conceptual and perceptual learning process in affecting behavioural intentions. The results indicated an overall slightly positive perception and conception about sharks. Students have correct concepts regarding the ecological roles of sharks, but the understanding on how human activity affects the sharks' population are relatively limited. There is a geographical difference between mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong, in which students from Hong Kong possessed lower conceptual and perceptual scores. Compared to mainland China and Taiwan, Hong Kong students adopted a more domination belief toward wildlife. Perception was found exerting a higher influence on the shark conserving behavioural intention among the students studied, compared to the conceptual counterparts.

18611218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18611218.value: This project examines the role of writing readiness skills in the early development of Chinese character writing. Despite a pedagogical shift towards digital literacy for very young children, handwriting with paper and pencil have significantly more impact on the brain development of young children than typing or writing on tablet computers. For alphabetic languages, handwriting skills - seen as part of embodied cognition - also predict later academic performance, including reading and mathematics achievement (Cameron et al., 2016). Chinese, as an orthographically complex language, makes comparatively high cognitive demands on writing acquisition. This creates a tremendous challenge for second language (L2) Chinese learners in particular. Our research over the past 5 years has demonstrated how L2 children recruit different sets of skills from their peers of L1 at primary school in terms of Chinese early literacy acquisition. Worryingly, they also perform consistently more weakly than their peers on almost all Chinese literacy related skills, even though they receive the same kind and amount of language and literacy instructions as those peers at school. (Zhou, 2012; Zhou, McBride, & Chung, in preparation). This difference persists even through middle school and results in disadvantages in terms of university choices and job opportunities. In Hong Kong, children - including L2 Chinese speaking children (e.g. ethnic minority children) - typically learn to read and write at 3 years of age in kindergartens. Children at this age show accelerating growth in visual and visual-motor skills, which are significant correlates for Chinese early reading acquisition. Yet little is known about how these skills develop differently for the two populations and how they are related to Chinese character writing. The proposed study aims 1) to identify the developmental progress of writing readiness skills such as basic visual and visual-motor skills in relation to Chinese early writing skills. 2) to compare the developmental trajectories of these skills in L1 and L2 Chinese-speaking children. 3) to determine the impact of writing readiness skills on subsequent Chinese character writing for the two populations. 4) to identify intervention strategies for Chinese early writing acquisition. The project will generate recommendations for parents, teachers and policy makers concerning pedagogical design to develop L1 and L2 Chinese-speaking children’s early writing at kindergarten level in Hong Kong. This project will identify solutions in helping L2 children acquire Chinese literacy in the early years that would help save a significant amount of resources in their subsequent school years. 該專案考察在漢字書寫發展中準備技能的作用。寫作是一種人類活動，在幼兒用蠟筆畫畫時就開始。儘管目前早期幼兒教學正朝數碼素養轉向，但用紙和筆進行書寫對幼兒的大腦發育的影響要大於在平板電腦上打字或書寫。手寫技巧被視為體現認知的一部分，也可以預測後期包括閱讀和數學成就（Cameron，et al.2016）。 相比之下，漢語作為一種正字法複雜的語言文字，對書寫/寫作習得有很高的認知需求。這對第二語言（L2）中國學習者來說尤其是一項巨大的挑戰。我們在過去5年的研究結果證明了L2初小兒童和L1的同齡人相比在早期中文識字習得中運用不同的技能。令人擔憂的是，儘管他們在學校獲得與同齡人相同的語言和讀寫能力指導，他們在幾乎所有中文相關技能方面的表現始終弱於L1同齡人（Zhou，2012; Zhou＆McBride，2017）。這種差異在中學仍然存在，導致對選擇他們大學和就業機會產生不利。香港兒童（包括少數族裔L2兒童）通常在幼稚園3歲時開始學習閱讀和寫字。這個年齡段的兒童在視覺和視覺小肌肉協調技能方面的加速增長，這些技能與中文早期識字習息息相關。然而，這些技能是如何發展的，以及它們如何與中文讀寫的其他方面相關，特別針對這兩組人群的中文漢字書寫技能的研究鮮為人知。 這項擬議的研究旨在1）確定於讀寫萌發相關的寫作準備技能的發展規律，諸如基本視覺，視覺運動技能等。 2）比較L1和L2香港兒童在這些技能上的發展軌跡。 3）確定寫作準備技能對這兩組兒童隨後的漢字書寫寫和寫作技能的影響。 4）確定中國早期寫作習得的干預策略。該專案將為家長，教師和政策制定者提供有關香港L1和L2中文兒童早期書寫、寫作學習政策和幼稚園教學設計的建議。該專案將幫助確定L2兒童在早期中文讀寫習得的解決方案，這將有助於在隨後的學年中節省大量資源。

18611218.label: Realisation of objectives
18611218.value: 1) The study aims to determine if there is a significant difference in the development of writing readiness skills between L1 and L2 Chinese-speaking children throughout their kindergarten years, from 3 to 5 years old. Our hypothesis is that the two groups will have similar basic visual and visual-motor skills at the beginning of kindergarten. However, as they learn more Chinese characters over the years, the L2 group will exhibit weaker print-specific copying skills. Additionally, the two groups differ significantly in general language and metalinguistic skills, which may affect their overall writing readiness. As expected, the results of this study align with previous research (Zhou & McBride, 2015; Zhou et al., 2018). L2 Chinese-speaking kindergarten children exhibit weaker Chinese language-related reading and metalinguistic skills compared to their L1 peers. This disparity becomes apparent at the beginning of kindergarten in Hong Kong and persists throughout the year. The initial weakness of L2 children in oral language appears to be a key factor in their slower development of Chinese writing readiness skills. Interestingly, both groups show consistent development in their basic visual and visual-motor skills across the three time points. However, L2 Chinese-speaking children's print-related visual skills gradually lag behind their L1 peers over time, despite showing no significant differences initially. This suggests a need for targeted interventions to support L2 children's print-specific copying skills. 2) In recent years, there has been a growing interest in understanding the developmental patterns of basic visual and visual-motor skills in relation to Chinese early writing skills. Some researchers have hypothesized that basic visual and visual motor skills are the foundation for acquiring early Chinese character writing skills. However, the growth patterns of early writing skills may differ significantly between different groups of children. In this study, the two groups under investigation were L1 and L2 children learning to read and write Chinese characters. The results showed that the two groups shared similarities in terms of growth patterns on visual and visual-motor skills. However, by time 3, the L2 group's visual orthographic skills in Chinese and copying skills lagged significantly behind the L1 group. Interestingly, the structural equation modeling analysis revealed that children's orthographic knowledge in Chinese, rather than basic visual skills or visual-motor skills, was the only visual-related skill that served as a significant predictor of their Chinese character reading and writing skills. This finding contradicts some previous findings on the importance of visual skills in learning to read and write Chinese characters. Moreover, the study found that phonological skills and working memory skills were significant predictors in both groups of children's Chinese character reading and writing. This suggests that these skills may play an important role in the acquisition of Chinese early writing skills, in addition to basic visual and visual-motor skills. Overall, the study sheds light on the developmental patterns of basic visual and visual-motor skills in relation to Chinese early writing skills. It highlights the importance of orthographic knowledge in Chinese as a significant predictor of children's Chinese character reading and writing skills. The findings have implications for educators and parents who seek to support children's learning of Chinese characters. 3) The question of what role writing readiness skills play in the subsequent Chinese character writing abilities of L1 and L2 children is a complex one. However, our hypothesis is that writing readiness skills contribute significantly to the overall Chinese character writing skills of both L1 and L2 children. Our findings have confirmed this hypothesis. Interestingly, while strong writing readiness skills significantly contribute to early writing skills in L1 children, the same may not be true for L2 children if they are weak in general Chinese language and metalinguistic skills. This is an important consideration when it comes to supporting L2 children's development of Chinese character writing skills. Our research has shown that L2 speaking children perform similarly to L1 children in basic visual skills, including speed of visual processing. However, their subsequent Chinese character reading and writing skills are signaled by their initial and continuous general oral language skills. These skills include metalinguistic skills such as phonological awareness skills. Therefore, it is crucial to support L2 children's development of these oral language skills in order to aid their development of Chinese character writing skills. In conclusion, our research has highlighted the significant role of writing readiness skills in both L1 and L2 children's development of Chinese character writing skills. It has also emphasized the importance of considering general Chinese language and metalinguistic skills, particularly for L2 children, in supporting this development. The COVID-19 pandemic presented major challenges to our research objectives, particularly during the second phase of data collection in 2020. This is because the outbreak caused a four-month shutdown of kindergartens in 2020, our data collection required face-to-face interaction with very young children, an interaction that could not be replaced with computer-based apps. This meant that for Time 2, we were only able to collect data from 41 children (L1: 27/L2: 14). This has significantly affected the data collection and would influence the power of Time 2 data analysis. However, as soon as kindergartens resumed half-time, we immediately took action to collect data for Phase 3. We were able to acquire data from 281 children (L1: 174/L2: 107). As a research team, we worked tirelessly to overcome the grave difficulties posed by the pandemic, and our efforts paid off. We obtained valuable data that helped us identify crucial patterns and indicators for both L1 and L2 Chinese-speaking children's Chinese language learning during their kindergarten years in Hong Kong. The irreversible loss of time 2 data collection cause a large number of missing data, statistically our research team has been working out solutions to filling the data gap making use of the T1 and T3 data for data collection and model identifications. Our research has shown that writing readiness skills play a significant role in the subsequent Chinese character writing abilities of L1 and L2 children. We hypothesize that writing readiness skills contribute significantly to the overall Chinese character writing skills of both L1 and L2 children. Our findings have confirmed this hypothesis. Interestingly, while strong writing readiness skills significantly contribute to early writing skills in L1 children, the same may not be true for L2 children if they are weak in general Chinese language and metalinguistic skills. This is an important consideration when it comes to supporting L2 children's development of Chinese character writing skills. Our research has also shown that L2 speaking children perform similarly to L1 children in basic visual skills, including speed of visual processing. However, their subsequent Chinese character reading and writing skills are signaled by their initial and continuous general oral language skills. These skills include metalinguistic skills such as phonological awareness skills. Therefore, it is crucial to support L2 children's development of these oral language skills in order to aid their development of Chinese character writing skills. In conclusion, our research has highlighted the significant role of writing readiness skills in both L1 and L2 children's development of Chinese character writing skills. It has also emphasized the importance of considering general Chinese language and metalinguistic skills, particularly for L2 children, in supporting this development. Despite the challenges posed by the pandemic, we were able to gather valuable data that can help inform future research and policy decisions in this area.

18611218.label: Major findings and research outcome
18611218.value: This study investigates the development of writing readiness skills among L1(i.e. First language) and L2 (i.e. Second language) Chinese-speaking children during their kindergarten years (ages 3 to 5). The researchers hypothesized that both groups would have similar basic visual and visual-motor skills at the beginning of kindergarten. However, as they learn more Chinese characters over time, the L2 group is expected to exhibit weaker print-specific copying skills. The study finds that the L2 Chinese-speaking kindergarten children showed weaker Chinese language-related reading and metalinguistic skills compared to their L1 Chinese Speaking peers. This ultimately affects their development of Chinese writing readiness skills. Nonetheless, both L1 and L2 children exhibit consistent development in their basic visual and visual-motor skills across the three time points. However, L2 Chinese-speaking children's print-related visual skills gradually lag behind their L1 peers over time, despite showing no significant differences initially. Therefore, the study suggests that targeted interventions are needed to support L2 children's print-specific copying skills. Interestingly, the study highlights the importance of orthographic knowledge in Chinese as a significant predictor of children's Chinese character reading and writing skills. This finding contradicts some previous findings on the importance of visual skills in learning to read and write Chinese characters. Moreover, phonological skills and working memory skills were significant predictors of Chinese character reading and writing skills in both L1 and L2 groups of children. Overall, this study sheds light on the developmental patterns of basic visual and visual-motor skills in relation to Chinese early writing skills. It emphasizes the importance of supporting L2 children's development of oral language skills, including metalinguistic skills such as phonological awareness, to aid their development of Chinese character writing skills. The findings have implications for educators and parents seeking to support children's learning of Chinese characters. We are currently revising two manuscripts for publication. The first paper is titled "Receptive and Expressive Chinese Character Recognition in 3-Year-Old L1 and L2 Chinese-Speaking Kindergarteners." This paper has been accepted and will be orally presented at the Society of Scientific Studies of Reading Conference in Port Douglas, Australia in July 2023. The second paper is titled "Chinese Kindergarteners' Name Writing and Early Literacy Skills." Other publications resulting from this GRF include Zhou, Y. & McBride, C. (2023) "Invented Spelling in English and Pinyin in Multilingual L1 and L2 Cantonese Chinese-Speaking Children in Hong Kong." Frontier in Psychology, 13, 1039461.

18611218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18611218.value: There are at least three major lines of research that we could pursue based on this GRF project. The first line involves intervention studies that target children's oral language skills, Chinese orthographic skills, and print-specific visual and visual-motor skills. The key to this intervention strategy lies in the experimental design, which can help us to identify how innovative pedagogy aimed at addressing children's general language skills and specific Chinese code-related skills can enhance their overall language acquisition as a result of Chinese character acquisition. These intervention studies can help us to pinpoint the appropriate pedagogical and curriculum designs for both L1 and L2 Chinese-speaking children. The second line of research involves longitudinal intervention studies that examine the impact of a home literacy program on language and literacy skills in both L1 and L2 Chinese-speaking children, especially those at risk of developing inadequate literacy skills. This program will engage children in age-appropriate video and audio literacy activities at home. The third line of research focuses on language teacher education, specifically, how to empower teachers to design curricula and pedagogies that are child-centered and tailored to the learning needs of Chinese-speaking students.

18611218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18611218.value: In this study, researchers analyzed the development of writing skills in kindergarten children who spoke either L1 or L2 Chinese. The study discovered that as the L2 group learned more Chinese characters, their print-specific visual skills were weaker compared to their L1 peers. Additionally, the study showed that the L2 children's general Chinese language and metalinguistic skills were weaker than their L1 peers initially. This weakened language ability affected the L2 children's development of writing readiness skills. Despite the differences between the L1 and L2 groups, both sets of children developed their basic visual and visual-motor skills consistently across the three time points. However, the rate of developing all Chinese language-related skills slowed down drastically for L2-speaking children. As a result, targeted support is necessary to help L2 children improve their Chinese character reading and writing skills. This support should focus on improving the L2 children's general language skills, print-specific visual skills, and orthographic skills. This includes providing opportunities for the L2 children to speak and use Chinese language in Chinese literacy activities. By applying the implications of this study, parents and teachers who want to support children's learning of Chinese can better promote their language development.
