21302018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21302018.value: Wave vortex states have long been of interest to physicists because of their broad relevance to a variety of fields including fluid dynamics, condensed matter, photonics, and acoustics. Light and sound can have such states characterized by a spatial phase singularity and labeled with a topological charge. These states can be applied to trap microscopic particles/molecules, and their intrinsic orbital angular momentum can be multiplexed for communications. Although generating light/sound vortex states has been demonstrated by using artificial structures, manipulating these states remains a challenge, and the mechanisms of vortex-structure interactions are still not well understood. To fill this gap, we will carry out theoretical and experimental studies of artificial periodic structures that can manipulate light/sound vortex states in three dimensions. In particular, we aim to achieve charge-selective transport of vortex states. We will first design and fabricate acoustic metamaterials with this functionality. A theoretical framework will be developed to understand the vortex–structure interactions which account for the transport properties of vortex states. We will then study the effects of loss on vortex transport and explore the associated non-Hermitian phenomena. Finally, we will extend the study to photonic systems to elucidate the difference between light vortex states and sound vortex states. The results of the proposed project could uncover the relationship between the microscopic vortex-structure interactions and the macroscopic bulk material properties. It will not only deepen our understanding about the geometric phase effects in classical systems but also provide insights into how topology connects different branches of physics, and hence nourish the fields of photonics and acoustics with new perspectives and concepts. In addition, the proposed project could generate new degrees of freedom for encoding information for communication, and give rise to novel functionalities for developing wave-based technologies. 波渦旋態長期以來一直受到物理學家的關註，它與諸多領域都有廣泛的相關性，比如流體動力學、凝聚態、光學和聲學。光波和聲波中也存在渦旋態，其特征在於拓撲電荷標記的空間相位奇點。這種態可用於束縛微觀粒子或分子，其固有的軌道角動量可以多路復用以進行通訊。盡管通過人造結構生成渦旋態已被證明可行，但操縱這些態仍然是一個挑戰，並且渦旋—結構的相互作用機制並未得到很好的理解。 我們將通過理論和實驗研究填補這一空白，設計人造周期結構以實現三維空間裏聲渦旋態的操縱。具體來講，我們的目標是實現渦旋態的基於拓撲電荷的選擇性傳輸。我們將首先設計和制造具有此功能的聲學超材料，並提出相應的理論框架來理解渦旋-結構的相互作用以及其對渦旋態傳輸特性的影響。而後，我們將研究損耗對渦旋態傳輸的影響，並探索相關的非厄米現象。 該項目的結果可以揭示微觀渦旋-結構相互作用與宏觀材料特性之間的關系，不僅有助於我們理解經典系統中的幾何相位效應，而且對拓撲如何銜接不同物理分支提供新的見解，從而為光學和聲學帶來新的視角和觀念。此外，該項目可以產生新的自由度用於信息編碼，並提供新穎的功能用於開發基於波的新技術。

21302018.label: Realisation of objectives
21302018.value: Objective 1 (100% achieved) The first objective of this ECS project is “to design acoustic metamaterials that can selectively generate and transport sound vortex states in three dimensions in order to elucidate how the vortex–structure interactions modify the flow of sound waves.” We first designed acoustic chiral resonators that can support chiral dipole resonance, i.e., localized sound vortex carrying orbital angular momentum. We then assemble the resonators into a one-dimensional (1D) lattice. By conducting full wave finite-element simulations, we confirmed that the 1D lattice can give rise to circularly polarized transverse sound. This transverse sound is characterized by a velocity field perpendicular to the propagation direction of the sound. We then generalize the design to a three-dimensional (3D) metamaterial. We calculated the band structures of the metamaterial and investigated its eigenmode properties at the Gamma point of the momentum space. We found that the metamaterial is isotropic and homogenous near the Gamma point and thus can be described by an effective medium theory. The transverse sound inside the metamaterial can carry both spin and orbital angular momentum and give rise to acoustic spin-orbit interactions. We demonstrated two novel phenomena enabled by this metamaterial. In one configuration, we show that the metamaterial can induce negative refraction of the transverse sound due to the spin-orbit interaction in momentum space. In the second configuration, we demonstrated that the metamaterial can generate sound vortex beams when the transverse sound is scattered by a dipole particle locating inside the metamaterial, which is attributed to geometric phase effect induced by the spin-orbit interaction in real space. In addition, selective generation of sound vortices can be achieved by controlling the handedness of the circularly polarized transverse sound. The above results are summarized in the publication [Nature Communications 12, 6125 (2021)]. In addition to 3D metamaterial, we also investigated metasurfaces for manipulating the transport of sound vortex states. The metasufaces can be considered a special type of metamaterials that comprise only one layer of artificial structures. We considered a metasurface with a prescribed phase gradient and apply rigorous plane-wave decomposition method to calculate the transverse Fedorov-Imbert linear shift of sound vortex beams upon reflection and refraction at the metasurface. We found that the sound vortices carrying opposite topological charge (i.e., opposite orbital angular momentum) are shifted to opposite directions after reflection/refraction. The shift is proportional to the topological charge and represents the orbital Hall effect of sound. We developed a generalized momentum conservation relation to uncover the mechanism of the phenomena. A very interesting result of this work is that the metasurface can generate Fedorov-Imbert transverse shift of sound vortex even for normal incidence and total reflection. The work provides a solid theory for understanding the interactions between sound vortex states and artificial structures. The results are summarized in the publication [Physical Review B 104, 174301 (2021)]. Objective 2 (100% achieved) The second objective is “to experimentally realize the acoustic metamaterials and characterize their vortex-manipulating functionalities”. The PI collaborated with Dr. Guancong Ma (Hong Kong Baptist University) to conduct the experiments and has fully achieved this objective. There are two types of sound vortex states in our metamaterial system: the localized sound vortex in individual resonators and the propagating sound vortex beam generated by dipole scattering. In the experiment we mainly focused on characterizing the properties of the transverse sound derived from the localized sound vortices. We first applied 3D printing technique to fabricate the resonators and connecting tubes. We then assembled the resonators into the 1D chiral and achiral lattices. We measured the band structures of the lattices to verify the transverse nature of the sound wave. The experimental results agree well with the numerical results. We then applied 3D printing to fabricate the 3D metamaterial. To demonstrate the negative refraction phenomenon, we excited the transverse sound using an array of speakers and measured the amplitude and phase of the transmitted pressure field behind the metamaterial. The experimental results are in agreement with the full wave numerical results. The above results of experimental realization and characterization are also summarized in the journal publication [Nature Communications 12, 6125 (2021)]. Objective 3 (100% achieved) The third objective is “To elucidate the effects of loss on vortex transport and the associated non-Hermitian phenomena.” To achieve this objective, we designed an 1D lattice of acoustic chiral resonators and introduced loss into the resonators. We conducted numerical simulations of the structure and calculated the reflection and transmission of acoustic vortices with opposite orbital angular momentum (i.e., topological charge). It is found that the effect of loss on vortex transport strongly depends on the symmetry of the unit cell resonators. When the resonators are of C4 rotational symmetry, the sound vortices with opposite topological charges exhibit similar reflection, transmission, and absorption. However, if we break the C4 symmetry by adding inhomogeneous loss to the resonators, reducing the symmetry to C2, the sound vortices with opposite topological charge exhibit significant differences in transport properties and give rise to large differential absorption. This phenomenon corresponds to the acoustic version of helical dichroism, which is a very important optical phenomena with rich applications. To uncover the underlying physical mechanism, we then computed the complex band structures of the 1D lattice and analyze the damping of its eigenmodes. We found that the significantly different transport properties of sound vortices with opposite topological charge in the C2 system are attributed to two mechanisms: the orbital angular momentum partial band gaps and the emergence of non-Hermitian exceptional points near the Brillouin-zone center and boundaries. The former enables selective transmission of one-type of the sound vortices. The latter induces large difference in the imaginary parts of the eigenfrequencies of opposite sound vortex states. The two mechanisms together lead to significantly enhanced helical dichroism of acoustic vortices in the C2 system. We applied an effective Hamiltonian to develop an analytical model to explain the phenomena; the analytical results well agree with the full wave numerical results. The above results are summarized in the publication [Physical Review B 105, 024111 (2022)] .

21302018.label: Major findings and research outcome
21302018.value: This ECS project generated 8 journal publications, including two papers in Nature Communications, two papers in Physical Review B, three papers in Optics Express, and one paper in Scientific Report. The major findings directly related to the objectives are summarized as follows: 1. While textbooks tell us that airborne sound is a longitudinal wave, we discover that airborne sound can be a transverse wave under certain conditions [Nature Communications 12, 6125 (2021)]. This is achieved with a metamaterial formed of acoustic resonators (with air filling inside). The resonances of sound vortex states inside the resonators give rise to a circularly polarized transverse sound on the macroscopic scale with the velocity field vector perpendicular to the sound propagation direction. We demonstrate that the metamaterial can induce negative refraction of the transverse sound and generate acoustic vortex beam via dipole scattering. 2. We investigated the transmission and reflection of sound vortices at a metasurface with prescribed phase gradient [Physical Review B 104, 174301 (2021)]. We find that the metasurface can induce a transverse Fedorov-Imbert shift of the sound vortices, which is proportional to the topological charge of the vortices; sound vortices carrying opposite topological charges are shifted to opposite directions (a phenomenon termed acoustic orbital Hall effect). The phenomenon derives from momentum conservation and modulation of the reflection/transmission coefficient at the metasurface. 3. We demonstrate that sound vortex can give rise to helical dichroism [Physical Review B 105, 024111 (2022)], a phenomenon that is well studied for optical vortices but has never been demonstrated in acoustics. By designing a 1D metamaterial lattice, we reveal that the acoustic helical dichroism is closely related to the rotational symmetry of the structures. The structure with C2 rotational symmetry can induce a much larger absorption difference of sound vortices with opposite topological charge, compared to the structure with C4 rotational symmetry. We reveal that the enhancement is attributed to the orbital angular momentum partial gaps and the non-Hermitian exceptional points. In addition, we have achieved more output than planned by extending the study from acoustics to optics. These additional achievements are summarized here. 1. Our research about sound vortices inspires us to extend the study of acoustic spin-orbit interactions to photonics. We find that photonic spin-orbit interactions can give rise to arbitrary order non-Hermitian exceptional points in a coupled resonator system [Nature Communications 10, 832 (2019)]. 2. We designed a logarithmic spiral metasurface to manipulate the energy vortex flow (i.e., orbital angular momentum) of microwave. The metasurface has a thickness of 5 mm and can absorb >95% of incident microwave energy in the frequency range of 6GHz-37 GHz [Scientific Reports 9, 14078 (2019)]. 3. We demonstrate that optical vortex states combined with time-reversal symmetry breaking can give rise to robust exceptional point of arbitrary order and enhanced optical isolation [Optics Express 27, 28114 (2019) and Optics Express 29, 29720 (2021)].

21302018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21302018.value: Since the transverse sound deriving from local acoustic vortex resonances carries full vector properties like light, there are numerous interesting physics we can explore further. For example, the transverse sound has well defined linear or circular polarizations, we may design acoustic polarizers to achieve selective transport of the sound with a particular polarization state. Since the transverse sound carries well-defined spin, it is possible to demonstrate the acoustic spin-Hall effect by employing a metamaterial-air interface to induce reflection/refraction of the transverse sound. Another possible direction of development is to investigate the acoustic circular dichroism, i.e., differential absorption of the transverse sounds with opposite circular polarizations, by using the 3D metamaterial we designed in the current project.

21302018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21302018.value: This ECS project investigated artificial structures (e.g., metamaterials and metasurfaces) for manipulating sound vortex states and revealed the mechanisms of vortex-structure interactions. We designed a metamaterial that can transform normal longitudinal sound to intriguing transverse sound carrying both spin and orbital angular momentum. The transverse sound derives from the local resonance of sound vortex states in the acoustic resonators forming the metamaterial. It carries full vector properties similar to light and thus provides more degrees of freedom for manipulating sound transport. Using a metasurface with prescribed phase gradient, we demonstrate that the reflection/refraction of sound vortex states at the metasurface can give rise to a transverse shift proportional to the topological charge of the vortex. In addition, we demonstrate that a chiral metamaterial lattice can induce differential absorption of sound vortex states carrying opposite topological charge. This project not only discovered a new type of airborne sound wave (i.e., transverse sound) beyond our conventional understanding but also offers novel mechanisms for manipulating sound/light for applications in communications, imaging, and sensing.

21303218.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21303218.value: In recent years emergent two-dimensional (2D) materials such as graphene, h-BN, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), black phosphorous have been hot topics in basic research. However further processing such as patterning, functionalization and integration are often needed for further applications. In this project we will explore efficient approaches to chemically functionalize the 2D van der Waals (vdW) layered materials such as TMDs in parallel with controllable patterning. The unique mono-atomic thickness with full surface and various defects such as vacancies, dopants, dislocations and grain boundaries provide bunches of functionalization routes in the TMDs. As one step further, we will combine the patterning strategies like growth control, strain engineering, self-assembly together with the chemical functionalization processes, in the aim of design and fabrication of artificial 2D TMD blocks for specific applications such as integrated electronics, photonic crystals, solar cells, sensors, displays, etc. The main target or deliverable of current project is to accomplish the controllable and tunable patterning in the functionalization processes in 2D materials, understanding the underlying physical/chemical processes, and apply to the products for optoelectronic applications.

21303218.label: Realisation of objectives
21303218.value: All the objectives have been completely achieved. We outline our main achievements in this project associated with each of the three objectives above: 1. To functionalize graphene, TMDs without damage and byproducts on their surface with desired patterns. Realisation (100%): We have synthesized large area graphene and 2D TMDs, and functionalize these 2D materials using chemical or physical ways. In specific, we have grown 2D MoS2 following the kinetic catalytic approach developed in our group (JACS, 142, 13130, 2020). We have studied the functionalization effects on graphene, and 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. The UV exposure method are applied and oxygen, transition metals, etc are successfully doped, with controllable n or p type carriers, particularly cause reversible doping in 2D ReS2 (Adv Funct Mater, 2021, 31, 2009166). 2, To understand basic science in mechanical, thermodynamics and chemical stability of 2D graphene and TMDs. Realisation (100%): We have successfully found out the reason behind the chemical degradation of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides, which is related to the oxidation effect and can be accelerated by the external substrates or protection layers. The chemical stability and aging of 2D materials have been particularly studied via the AFM and spectroscopies, which both point to the common origin-the atomic defects which can activate the chemical reactions. Meanwhile, the mechanical properties of 2D materials have been studied with AFM and in situ TEM-STM approaches, the excellent intrinsic strengths have been confirmed and explained by the atomic origins-such as the fracture behavior and edge structures (Nat Commun 11, 3982, 2020; Sci Adv 6, eabc2282, 2020; Physical Review Letters 125, 246102, 2020). 3, To facilitate further investigations and applications of 2D-layered TMDs, graphene using this technique, such as the periodic 2D blocks embedded in nonconductive grids composed of oxides, metallic photonic crystals in 2D for solar cell or lighting, sensors or displays. Realisation (100%): We have successfully applied the functionalized graphene and 2D transition metal dichalcogenides in the solar cell applications, giving a promising performances, and further investigation is going to on use the patterned 2D materials for more optoelectronic devices, especially with metallic structures. Particularly, we have developed new method for periodic building blocks for graphene using "sandwich" structure (Nano Lett, 20, 8420, 2020). The field effect transistor, photonic crystals for light trapping or lighting enhancement, or other applications have been fabricated and tested.

21303218.label: Major findings and research outcome
21303218.value: In this project, we made three major achievements: 1, We obtained high quality, clean, and transferrable 2D samples by atmosphere pressure chemical vapor deposition, such as graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides. The relevant output is JACS, 142, 13130, 2020 (PI as corresponding author). Meanwhile, we developed new annealing method to obtain large area flat 2D sample without wrinkles and elucidate the mechanism of wrinkle elimination, the relevant output is ACS Nano, 14, 2137, 2020 (PI as corresponding author). The high quality 2D sample is the prerequisite for studying their properties and applications. The PI of this project built the lab and start to prepare the samples with the support of this ECS project, and it turns out the first step, sample fabrication is very successful and ensure the success of the entire project. 2, We studied the basic properties such as electrical and mechanical properties through AFM and TEM, as well as in situ TEM. The representative publications are Nature Communications 11, 3982, 2020 (PI as corresponding author), Sci Adv 6, eabc2282, 2020(PI as corresponding author); Physical Review Letters 125, 246102, 2020(PI as corresponding author). The major findings in the specific electrical contact with 2D materials, the fracture behavior in anisotropic 2D TMDs, etc., will form solid basis for future applications of 2D materials. The basic structural properties in anisotropic 2D materials are also elucidated thoroughly with origin clearly understood (Adv Sci, 7, 2001742, 2020 (PI as corresponding author) and Communications Materials 2, 87, 2021 (PI as corresponding author)). 3, We have demonstrated the applications that utilize the advantage of 2D materials: thin and facile functionalization. We apply UV on the 2D TMD samples and achieve reversible functionalization which can tune the carrier density and mobility by order of magnitude (Adv Funct Mater, 2021, 31, 2009166 (PI as corresponding author)). we have developed new method for periodic building blocks for graphene using "sandwich" structure (Nano Lett, 20, 8420, 2020(PI as corresponding author)). The field effect transistor, photonic crystals for light trapping or lighting enhancement, or other applications have been fabricated and tested, they indeed show promising properties for next generation electronic and optoelectronic devices. Overall, this is the start of PI's research career, and with the support ECS, many new materials, new properties and new applications in 2D materials emerge in PI's lab.

21303218.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21303218.value: For further development of 2D materials research following this project, we think several major open questions remain: 1, Large area (wafer scale) growth of 2D TMD materials. So far the CVD growth only achieve relatively small sample growth, we have study in-depth the growth mechanism of several materials and hope that we will improve the size and quality of CVD grown 2D TMDs further. 2, The in situ study of atomic scale properties in 2D TMD materials. The state of the art AFM and TEM and STM will be employed to study the atomic scale properties. We have devleoped new approaches for different modes in AFM (located in COSDAF CityU) and TEM. We hope the deepened understanding will help us to better design the atomic structures of 2D devices. 3, We have to improve the stability of 2D materials and devices. The atomic structure intrinsically degrade the stability however the devices in 2D require much higher stability than all the current devices. Therefore, we may develop new stabilization technique for 2D TMDs such as using suitable packing layer.

21303218.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21303218.value: We have achieved a series of important breakthroughs related to 2D TMD materials, these important findings will guide the future research and development of 2D TMDs. Specifically: 1, We obtained high quality, clean, and transferrable 2D TMDs by atmosphere pressure chemical vapor deposition. Meanwhile, we developed new annealing method to obtain large area flat 2D sample without wrinkles and elucidate the mechanism of wrinkle elimination. 2, We studied electrical and mechanical properties through AFM and TEM, as well as in situ TEM. The major findings in the specific electrical contact with 2D materials, the fracture behavior in anisotropic 2D TMDs, etc., will form solid basis for future applications of 2D materials. The basic structural properties in anisotropic 2D materials are also elucidated thoroughly with origin clearly understood. 3, We have demonstrated the applications that utilize the advantage of 2D materials: thin and facile functionalization. We apply UV on the 2D TMD samples and achieve reversible functionalization which can tune the carrier density and mobility by order of magnitude. We have developed new method for periodic building blocks for graphene using "sandwich" structure. The field effect transistor, photonic crystals for light trapping or lighting enhancement, or other applications have been fabricated and tested.

21502018.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21502018.value: A large body of literature on social networks suggests that social connections between individuals are an important determinant of economic performance (Granovetter 1985, 2005; Burchardi and Hassan 2013). Recent studies in finance and accounting argue that top-management networks (e.g., boardroom networks, social ties between senior executives and analysts/auditors) play an important role in decision-making processes, yet little is known about the potential implications of connections between rank-and-file employees. Moreover, the extant literature focuses on one aspect (e.g. sharing boardrooms or educational background) among the many different channels through which individuals can connect with one another. In this proposed study, we aim to tackle these limitations by exploiting a unique dataset on interfirm employee networks through a business card management application in Korea. Using this proprietary dataset, we will construct interfirm employee network metrics that cover various employee levels and investigate their relation to firm-level economic outcomes. Specifically, we will first construct measures that capture the quantity and quality of connections between employees, including the total number of connections, the centrality of connections, and connections to economically linked firms. Then we will examine how those connections affect firm performance, including operating performance, productivity, and innovations. We predict that firms with better-connected employees outperform others. In addition, we expect our main results to be stronger for connections between economically related firms and with high-ranking employees, and for firms with a high-quality internal information environment. Finally, to draw a causal inference, we will exploit Korea’s so-called Kim Young-Ran Act, officially the Anti-Corruption and Bribery Prohibition Act, as an exogenous shock to the connections. To our knowledge, our study is one of the first to empirically estimate the effects of rank-and-file employee networks on firm growth. The prior literature remains silent on low-ranking employee connections, largely because the relevant data are unavailable. Our study overcomes this challenge by using a unique dataset on interfirm employee networks. This study will also extends the literature on social networks by providing evidence from more direct and credible connection measures. Prior research on social ties generally assumes that individuals have connections if they have common experiences, such as attending the same educational institution, working at the same company, or serving in the military. In contrast, our measures of connections are based on the exchange of business cards, which happens primarily through face-to-face meetings in which information transfers take place.

21502018.label: Realisation of objectives
21502018.value: 1. In this paper, we examine the link between the social capital embedded in employee networks and firm performance. We show that the social capital embedded in employees’ networks contributes to firm value and provide evidence on the mechanisms. To this end, we construct a novel firm-level measure of employee social capital using professional connections that a firm’s employees, across all job levels, have built with business contacts outside the firm. We identify the types of employee connections that are valuable to firms and discover the economic benefits that firms obtain from these connections, thus contributing to a more granular understanding of social capital in corporations. We begin by constructing firm-level measures of employee social capital (ESC) by appropriately averaging the employee-level degree measures (In-degree, Out-degree, Total degree) within a firm. Drawn from a comprehensive sample of Korean public firms in the OSIRIS Industrials database from 2014 to 2018, our initial analysis examines the average Total degree of a firm’s employees without regard to the direction of connections; baseline regressions show that firms with more employee social capital have significantly higher profitability and sales growth in the following year. We then investigate whether the direction of connections matters in the relation between employee social capital and firm performance. We re-estimate the model when firm-level employee social capital takes the value of ESC in-degree (“who knows you”) and ESC out-degree (“who you know”). Results show that the positive association with future performance arises mainly from ESC in-degree, which captures the extent to which a firm’s employees are remembered or valued by their external contacts. In sharp contrast, the coefficient estimates on ESC out-degree are largely insignificant. While the social capital literature argues that networks endow employees with access to resources, our findings suggest that the extent to which employees can mobilize these benefits for their employers depends on whether their business contacts value them. In this sense, having a broad network of business contacts who know you appears more valuable to your employer than having a broad network of contacts whom you know. Establishing a causal link between employee social capital and firm performance, we exploit the 2016 enactment of the Kim Young-ran Act (the Act) as a plausibly exogenous negative shock to professional networking in Korea. We use a difference-in-differences framework surrounding the enactment of the Act and set the treatment intensity as the fraction of a firm’s preexisting employee social capital derived from its employees’ connections with the media and the public sector. We find that firms with ESC more exposed to the Act experience a significant decline in performance after the Act relative to those less exposed. For instance, a one standard deviation increase in treatment intensity yields an increase in Tobin’s q by 17.5% relative to the sample mean before the Act, but only by 4.4% after. 2.To shed light on the mechanisms through which employee social capital contributes to firm value, we consider the benefits that firms can derive from their employees’ connections with the sectors affected by the Act—the media and the public sector. Motivated by the literature on media coverage and firm value, we predict that employees’ media connections foster reciprocity and information sharing with journalists, which in turn promotes news coverage of the firm, and news stories with a positive tone. Indeed, we find that firms with more employee media connections have substantially more news articles and a greater fraction of positive coverage. Moreover, the positive effects diminish after the enactment of the Act, reinforcing our causal inference. We then turn to the benefits of employee connections with the public sector. Drawing on evidence that public officers allocate more procurement contracts to firms with a connected CEO (Schoenherr, 2019), we expect that employees with public sector connections may also help their firms secure procurement contracts. Our evidence is consistent with this prediction. For example, a one standard deviation increase in the fraction of employee social capital accumulated from public sector connections leads to a 6.8% increase in the number of newly signed contracts before the Act and to only a 3.4% increase after. 3. Several aspects of our data are novel and noteworthy, allowing us to construct more direct and credible connection measures. First, our final sample consists of 2.4 million employees, with 12.4 million professional connections between them. The data’s broad coverage of employees across ranks, including managers and rank-and-file employees, allows us to quantify employee social capital at the firm level. Second, because in Asian culture business cards are typically exchanged in face-to-face meetings (it is not the norm to pass on cards on behalf of others), our data depict real-world professional connections more reliably than those from online networking platforms, such as LinkedIn where people can connect even though they have never met. Third, while card exchanges are mutual between the two parties, uploading cards to the app is not necessarily mutual because users are more likely to upload the cards of contacts that they value and thus want to remember (apropos the name of the app). Using language from the network literature, we refer to the network as directed: each connection is directed from the employee who uploads the card to the employee whose card is uploaded. This directed feature allows us to determine whether one of the two connected parties is a more valued contact. We calculate several connection measures at the individual employee level—In-degree (the number of others who have uploaded the employee as a contact), Out-degree (the number of business contacts uploaded by the employee), and Total degree (the sum of In-degree and Out-degree). In other words, In-degree counts the people who remember or value the employee by uploading the employee’s card on the app, which we refer to as “who knows you”; Out-degree counts the contacts the employee remembers or values by uploading their cards, which we refer to as “who you know.” As we discuss below, the directed nature of our network data enables us to move beyond “who knows who” and analyze the extent to which social capital—as distinguished by “who knows you” versus “who you know”—matters for the firm.

We identify the types of employee connections that are valuable to firms and discover the economic benefits that firms obtain from these connections, thus contributing to a more granular understanding of social capital in corporations. The research outcome of this project is a research paper entitled "It’s Not Who You Know—It’s Who Knows You: Employee Social Capital and Firm Performance." It has been presented in the well recognized international conferences including 2020 Northern Finance Association Conference, 2021 Midwest Finance Association Conference, 2021 Society of Labor Economists meeting, 2021 Future of Financial Information Conference, 2021 Financial Intermediation Research Society Conference, 2021 China International Conference in Finance, 2022 Napa/Sonoma Finance Conference, and American Finance Association 2023 Annual Meeting (scheduled).

21502018.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21502018.value: There are a few glaring advantages of our business network data drawn from a professional networking app (Remember) over other data used in the literature (e.g., LinkedIn, Facebook, or Twitter). First, our network is directed: each connection is a link that points from the employee who registered the business card to the employee whose card was registered. This directed feature separately accounts for business contacts that remember the employee and those that the employee remembers. Second, the data’s extensive coverage of individual employees (both top management and rank and file) enables us to overcome a significant limitation of the literature that mostly focused on small managerial networks. Finally, since business cards are typically exchanged during face-to-face meetings, our data represent actual professional relationships more reliably. With that said, there are many exciting and promising future projects I can work on with this unique big data. Using the same network data, I also investigate whether employees of a firm effectively serve as information intermediaries by transmitting value-relevant information from inside the firm to the capital markets through their professional networks. In this project, entitled “The Role of Employees as Information Intermediaries: Evidence from Their Professional Connections” with DuckKi Cho (Peking University HSBC Business School) and Stephen A. Hillegeist (Arizona State University), we find that firms with highly connected employees have more efficient prices.

21502018.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21502018.value: The role of physical capital, human capital, and intellectual capital in corporations is well studied. Yet, another type of capital, perhaps equally important, has received much less attention: a firm’s social capital, consisting of the relationships that a firm and its employees have built with economically related agents outside the firm. Social capital is a broad concept that can be understood as the norms of reciprocity and trustworthiness within social networks. A large literature shows that the social capital of individuals—such as the size of their Rolodex—provides access to resources and enables them to reap benefits from interactions with others. At the firm level, individual social capital is important since employees, including both management and rank and file, interact directly with business partners, clients, and other stakeholders. Yet, due to the latent nature of social networks, how the social capital embodied in employees’ connections contributes to firm value and performance remains an open question. In this paper, we examine the link between the social capital embedded in employee networks and firm performance. We show that the social capital embedded in employees’ networks contributes to firm value and provide evidence on the mechanisms. To this end, we construct a novel firm-level measure of employee social capital using professional connections that a firm’s employees, across all job levels, have built with business contacts outside the firm. We identify the types of employee connections that are valuable to firms and discover the economic benefits that firms obtain from these connections, thus contributing to a more granular understanding of social capital in corporations.

21504818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21504818.value: We propose a nonparametric local series estimation method for unknown policy functions in an exchange economy (Epstein and Zin, 1989), which will allow the true dynamics of time-varying state variables to determine asset prices. Unlike current numerical solution methods, this new method does not require the imposition of tight auxiliary parametric assumptions on the conditional distributions or matching moments of state variables and thus avoids spurious model conclusions due to misspecification errors. Blanchard (2016) advocates for efforts to make general equilibrium models less insular to the real economy by allowing empirical data to determine the true dynamics of the structural model. However, the asset pricing literature still does not have a clear understanding of how to connect policy functions, such as price-dividend and wealth-consumption ratio functions, with empirical data which exhibit time-varying features. This proposal will allow for true evolutions of both stationary and nonstationary state variables, such as consumption and dividend growth rates and income innovations instead of assuming some time- and event-invariant pseudo data generating processes for computational convenience. This will allow researchers to carry DSGE models from the laboratory to the real world. The method proposed provides a particularly powerful and reliable way to reveal the role time-varying state variables, such as income risks, play in determining the time-series properties of the risk-free rate, return on wealth and market returns. We also intend to examine to what extent the declining predictability ability of dividend-price ratios on excess returns after 2002 can be explained by the time-varying features of price-dividend ratios and state dynamics. This proposal is also among the first to combine local and global estimation methods, which have been employed as substitutes in most cases. For the first time in the literature, we will establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of unknown policy functions, which offers another salient contribution to econometric studies. In addition, this method will become a pivotal approach for obtaining a consistent estimation of unknown policy functions in the presence of time-varying state variables with unknown dynamics. Our proposal can be extended in many directions and applied in many contexts. First, the methodology can be applied to DSGE models of the production economy that has latent state variables. In addition, this method can be further extended from the time series framework to a panel data structure to analyze heterogeneous agent models with both stationary and nonstationary state variables.

21504818.label: Realisation of objectives
21504818.value: With the support of the ECS grant, I have extensively engaged in conducting research in line with my planned objectives. My research mainly lies at the intersection between econometric methodologies and empirical finance, with a primary focus on developing and integrating econometric estimation and machine learning methods to solve practical financial problems, cope with financial data, both low- and high-frequency, and provide rigorous empirical evidence to inform policy decisions. By leveraging advanced econometric techniques and analyzing large datasets, I have aimed to make meaningful contributions to the field and advance our understanding of financial markets and policy impacts. On the methodological side, I have two primary research lines that are central to my grant objectives. The first is to develop new machine learning methods and integrate them with econometric methodologies to conduct factor analysis, capture asset co-movements, and perform risk management with high-dimensional and high-frequency data. My second critical and major research interest is to develop novel time-varying and cross-sectional heterogeneous econometric estimation methods. My aim in this area is to overcome the misspecification errors that often arise in traditional econometric models and establish their theoretical advantages in the GMM framework. I specialize in practical issues such as many moment conditions, high cross-sectional dimension, many instrumental variables, unknown policy function estimation, cross-sectional individual grouping, and variable selections, among others. Firstly, dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models have been widely adopted as a main vehicle in finance and macroeconomics to investigate the connection between agent preferences, asset prices, and economic fundamentals. Enormous efforts have been made on the development of asset pricing models under DSGE, and there is a pressing interest in evaluating different models' explanatory powers on market anomalies. Solving dynamic optimization problems involves finding solutions to single or multiple unknown functions of state variables that satisfy the conditional moment restrictions characterized by Euler equations. However, because nonlinear rational expectation models often do not allow for analytic solutions, solving unknown functions from the moment restrictions of this class is a widely acknowledged challenge. Significant efforts have been made to solve general equilibrium models, mainly using numerical approximation techniques by assuming a specific functional form for unknown functions and a pre-assumed probability distribution function of state variables. However, there is no guarantee that the distributional and functional form assumptions made for computational convenience can capture the true dynamics of the underlying processes. Hence, to obtain reliable model implications, it is crucial to capture the true dynamics of state variables and avoid misspecifications in unknown functions. On the other hand, Euler equations are framed under conditional moment restrictions, in which empirical practitioners often face a large set of candidate state variables from the information set. Existing numerical and estimation-based methods adopt a preselected and small common set of state variables for all unknown functions, which may risk omitted variable biases and misspecification errors. However, when estimating unknown policy functions by incorporating a large-dimensional set of state variables, we may encounter the curse-of-dimensionality issue, especially when the sample size is relatively small in practice, given its quarterly or monthly sampling frequency. Therefore, in addition to achieving functional estimation consistency, it is also urgent to ensure state variable selection consistency and correctly detect heterogeneous influences that different state variables exhibit on different unknown functions. With the help of the ECS grant, I have produced two related papers that are published in top peer-reviewed journals, namely the Journal of Econometrics and Cities. Meanwhile, I have another research paper that is under the second round revised and resubmitted to the Journal of Business and Economic Studies. Full papers are available to download from the Research Output Section. Except for the applicability in dynamic stochastic general equilibrium modeling, I have actively investigated high-frequency modeling and received satisfactory achievements in this field under my ECS grant. High-frequency intraday observations for assets are increasingly available, providing an exciting new source of rich information for studying vital statistics at finer intervals that are lacking in low-frequency data. High-dimensional covariance estimation is essential, among other uses, for constructing vast optimal portfolios, understanding leverage effects, pricing financial instruments, managing tail risks, and estimating risk premia of risk factors. However, this comes at the cost of microstructure noises and asynchronous trading, thus contaminating the observed price series. When estimating integrated covariance matrices based on high-frequency data, econometricians must carry out particular efforts to mitigate the influences from microstructure noises and ensure finite-sample positive definite property without impairing the convergence rate. However, these difficulties become more challenging when analyzing high-dimensional and high-frequency observations. Meanwhile, to capture assets' co-movements, factor models employ the key idea of dimension reduction and have become an effective way of extracting latent factors and modeling high-dimensional asset returns, together with principal component analysis (PCA) techniques. Factor models assume that common factors possess strong signals relative to idiosyncratic errors. However, empirical studies have difficulty recovering covariance structures and extracting latent factors due to the existence of weak factors. Weak factors result in a reduced spectral gap between the systematic-risk induced and idiosyncratic risk-driven components in the covariance matrix. Existing PCA-based methods often fail to detect weak factors and thus may lead to inconsistent factor detection and covariance matrix estimation. Failing to detect weak factors may lead to omitted variable biases and affect reliable estimation and testing of risk premia. The analysis of weak factors in high-frequency econometrics is still at an early stage. I propose a novel regularized covariance estimator under a general factor framework to capture the covariance structure and latent factors among high-dimensional returns with high sampling frequencies. Our method balances estimation unbiasedness and positive-semi definiteness, preserving the underlying true covariance matrix structure without impairing the convergence rate. Importantly, my research explores the heterogeneous roles played by different factor strengths in the estimation accuracy of the integrated covariance matrix. We establish an appealing equivalence between our regularized covariance estimator and a weighted group-LASSO least-squares estimator, which assigns heterogeneous penalties on different factors according to their signal strengths. This enables us to recover the latent factor structure, both strong and weak, and detect different strength patterns without prior knowledge of factor types. Following this line of research, I have produced two research papers, that are published in top Finance and Economic journals, namely the Management Science and International Economic Review. The full papers are available to download in the Research Output Section. In general, the project objectives have been fulfilled in a satisfactory and fruitful manner in the way of research publications.

21504818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21504818.value: I believe fruitful and impactful research papers, both methodological and empirical, can be produced in the research directions outlined in my ECS grant. For example, in a recent working paper of mine, I am developing novel regularized machine learning estimation methods in the many-moment GMM framework to allow for nonparametric and consistent estimation of time-varying and individual heterogeneous coefficient values. I also plan to propose a set of new forecast combination methods that can deal with many individual forecasts, whose relative importance can change over time. I will keep my efforts on exploring the usefulness of machine learning in factor analysis with time variation. I will investigate how to detect weak factors of various types, which can not only include the class that exhibits weak but universal influences on the entire cross-section but also the class that is strong on a particular class of assets. These future research topics are particularly important in the high-dimensional panel data econometric literature. Moreover, such a direction has long-run and critical impacts on empirical asset pricing studies. My future research papers will carefully answer these critical questions.

21505318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21505318.value: This study investigates how the geographic location of a firm affects the probability of the firm being selected as an acquisition target by a potential acquirer. Among various implications of geographic location, we focus on knowledge spillovers in clusters. The agglomeration literature has long argued and corroborated that firms located in a cluster—defined as a geographically proximate group of interconnected and complementary companies and associated institutions in a particular industry—can access to and benefit from knowledge spillovers localized within the cluster. Therefore, a potential acquirer, though located outside a cluster, can have an indirect path to the pool of knowledge spillovers available in the cluster if it acquires an in-cluster firm, which makes the in-cluster firm more likely to be chosen as an acquisition target. Our interest in the resources to which a target can provide an access as an indirect conduit is novel to the existing literature on acquisition target selection because it has tended to focus only on the resources targets internally possess. We also distinguish rival-specific knowledge spillovers (i.e., from rivals) and non-rival-specific knowledge spillovers (i.e., from non-rivals including other companies that are not direct competitors but are in the same industry as well as research institutions and universities). The reason behind this distinction is that a potential acquirer might perceive distinct benefits from knowledge spillovers depending on the sources, and some acquirer-, target-, and market-factors can differently shape the relationships between the two distinct knowledge spillovers and target choice. Regarding acquirer characteristics, we argue that the direct effect of rival-specific (non-rival-specific) knowledge spillovers is dampened (intensified) when the acquirer is a market leader because non-rivals’ knowledge can contribute more to differentiation than rivals’ knowledge. Regarding target characteristics, we claim that the direct effect of non-rival-specific knowledge spillover is dampened when the target is young and small because it might not be well embedded yet in the social and economic networks in the cluster and thus cannot absorb non-rival-specific knowledge spillovers properly. Lastly, in terms of the acquirer’s market characteristics, we maintain that the direct effect of rival-specific knowledge spillovers is intensified as the product markets of the acquirer become more concentrated, grow slowly, and experience higher environmental uncertainty because in such market conditions the acquirer has a higher incentive to closely watch other rival firms. We plan to test these hypotheses using the U.S. domestic acquisitions in the biopharmaceutical industry which is featured by geographic agglomeration. N/A

21506318.value: We plan to provide an interpretable and scalable computational algorithm for asset pricing, which decomposes the data-generating process of a characteristics-based factor model within a deep neural network architecture. We will also develop the statistical package for the algorithm in the TensorFlow architecture and make it available to the research community. We plan to design an estimator for the predictive variance of the neural network factor model. We have three candidates for comparison: one is the Fama-Macbeth-type estimator, one is a bootstrap estimator, and the last is a stochastic gradient descent estimator. The predictive variance estimate is used to assesses the asset-pricing test with a GRS-type (Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken, 1989) regularized criterion. The PI already has the zoo of firm characteristics for the U.S. market from his previous work. But we plan to replicate these firm characteristics in the international markets, especially in Hong Kong and China. We also plan to make the own constructed characteristics available to the community and to invite researchers for a Kaggle-type online competition. Empirically, we plan to construct the most useful predictors from the dynamic space of firm characteristics. We also expect to design a Diebold-Mariano test to assess the incremental contribution of those commonly used firm characteristics in the literature.

21506318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21506318.value: Both academic and industry researchers keep finding tradable anomalies that produce excess returns. The increasing dimension of risk factors raises concerns among academics about data mining, data snooping, and the issue of multiple measurements. The financial statistics literature mainly focuses on factor testing for the risk premium. In this project, we take a predictive perspective and construct a multi-layer neural network to perform a sequential dimension process starting from the space of firm characteristics, and let the neural network to build its best tradable factors. We want to show the characteristics-based factor model, which begins since Fama and French (1993), is a shallow learner to a deep learning architecture. The asset pricing test tests the hypothesis that pricing errors, model implied expected returns minus realized returns, are jointly statistically and economically insignificant. However, after decades of factor fishing, there still exist significant pricing errors to challenge the asset pricing test in the sense of Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken (1989). We want to propose a data-driven optimization problem that minimizes the mispricings of the stock cross-section relative to a synthetic asset pricing model. To build a multi-layer neural network, we expect to explore a latent factor structure to perform a sequential dimension process from the space of firm characteristics to the best predictors, which is a regularization path to visualize a neural network factor model. We plan to provide an interpretable and scalable computational algorithm (TensorFlow) of asset pricing with two goals. One is to eliminate the model mispricings, namely, alphas, by detecting and exploiting those economically invisible nonlinearities and interactions in the data. The other is to illustrate a sequential dimension reduction process within a neural network, to which statistical factor models are shallow learners. 是否存在一個因子模型可以解釋所有資產定價的異常呢？為了回答這個問題，我們提供了一個因子自動搜索的算法，可以通深度學習的框架來自動生成可交易的對衝因子。為了最小化定價偏差，這個方法對多元的公司基本面數據通過深度激勵的函數來尋找股票排序的預測指標。股票排序在金融實踐中是很常見的，在我們的框架下，按照預測指標排序就是神經網絡的一個非線性激勵函數。我們的算法可以通過時間序列模型在現有的因子模型下，例如法馬-佛倫奇因子模型，增加額外的深度因子。除此之外，我們還設計了一套科學的因子生成，驗證到預測的機制來檢驗我們的深度因子，希望得到更好的預測效果。

21506318.value: (1) The first objective, 5.1, is perfectly realized. Given the feedback from the seminar and conference participants, and the journal referees, our deep learning procedure is a real innovation that adopts cutting-edge deep learning optimization to combine with the conventional security sorting in empirical asset pricing. This paper is the first to recognize the characteristics-sorted factor model as a deep neural network and provides a systematic approach for the implementation. We want to emphasize that our paper is not directly related to the literature on predicting asset returns using machine learning. The current prediction literature studies the predictive performance between firm characteristics and security returns, and skips the intermediate channel involved with risk factors. 21506318.label: Major findings and research outcome
21506318.value: (1) The first research outcome is the paper "Deep Learning in Characteristics-Sorted Factor Models", which is under minor revision in the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis. This paper is directly derived from this project and has been revised substantially, given helpful comments from seminar and conference participants, journal referees, and editors. This is the SSRN link to the working paper , and below is the paper abstract. Many view deep learning as a "black box" used only for forecasting. However, this paper provides an alternative application by constructing a structural deep neural network to generate latent factors in asset pricing. The conventional approach of sorting firm characteristics to generate long-short factor portfolio weights is underappreciated nonlinear modeling. First, we describe the complete mechanism for fitting cross-sectional returns by firm characteristics through risk factors. Second, unlike statistical models, our model has an economic-guided objective function that minimizes pricing errors. Empirically, we find asset pricing and investment improvements using individual stocks and test portfolios for in-sample and out-of-sample analysis. (2) The second research outcome is the paper "Real-Time Macro Information and Bond Return Predictability: A Weighted Group Deep Learning Approach", which is under review by the Journal of Banking and Finance. This paper is not directly related to the proposed project but contributes to the same research area of empirical asset pricing via deep learning. This is the SSRN link to the working paper , and below is the paper abstract. Relying on a weighted group neural network model, this paper reexamines whether treasury bond returns are predictable when real-time, instead of fully-revised, macro information is used. Two types of real-time macro information are taken into account: macro vintage data and news-based topic attention. For non-overlapping bond returns, the evidence for predictability is weak. When forecasting overlapping bond returns, using only traditional macro variables, the neural network improves over standard machine learning tools for forecasting short-maturity bonds, but this predictability can hardly be translated to economic gains in the presence of realistic leverage constraints. In contrast, when adding textual factors to forecast overlapping returns, using the neural network becomes crucial and improves forecasting performance for all maturities. Adding news to the forecasters also increases economic gains when large leverage is allowed.

21506318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21506318.value: One further development of the research is a third research outcome. We have a recent working paper, "Deep Tangency Portfolios", under a dual submission to the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis. This paper is an immediate extension and further application of the proposed project. This is the SSRN link to the working paper , and below is the paper abstract. We propose a parametric approach for directly estimating the tangency portfolio weights by combining fundamental finance theory and deep learning techniques. The deep tangency portfolio is a combination of the market factor and a deep long-short factor constructed using a large number of characteristics. We apply our approach to the corporate bond market. Albeit acting as a market-hedged portfolio, the deep factor achieves a sizable risk premium with an out-of-sample annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.08. The deep tangency portfolio outperforms those constructed from commonly used observable or latent factors with an out-of-sample annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.90.

21506318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21506318.value: Chicago Booth Review has a practitioner version covering our research "How Machine Learning Can Improve Money Management" . Below is the executive summary of our first research paper. According to Merton's ICAPM, a combination of common risk factors captures the cross section of expected returns. If one regresses the return time series of an asset on common factors, the intercept is supposed to be zero. Unlike the regular objective function in statistics and machine learning, the model fitness in asset pricing is not about the proportion of explained variation but the magnitude of intercepts, or alphas. This non-arbitrage restriction on alphas implies that adding factors might lead to statistical overfitting (increase regression R2) but does not necessarily improve asset pricing fitness (decrease regression intercept). This paper proposes a structural deep neural network that performs dimension reduction on thousands of individual stocks to a few latent factors by approximating the conventional security sorting. Our approach sorts trained characteristics, creates long-short factors, and estimates factor models to minimize realized pricing errors. Standard deep/machine learning aims to optimize statistical fitness. However, the asset pricing model fitness reduces unexplained pricing errors in the intercept. Therefore, our deep learning optimization focuses on this economic-guided objective function under the non-arbitrage condition.

21506418.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21506418.value: In the standard neoclassical investment theory, decision makers are assumed to have perfect knowledge of the parameters characterizing firms' operation. From the perspectives of firm managers, however, many of underlying parameters are unknown at the beginning, and instead, they are what the managers need to learn over time by observing related variables. Among such parameter uncertainties, this project focuses on the uncertainty regarding the systematic risk of a firm's productivity, that is the covariance between the productivity and the pricing kernel. This project proposes a dynamic model where the agent learns about the systematic risk from the up-to-date history of productivity and accordingly makes capital investment decisions. A key element is that the systematic risk is industry-specific, so firms learn about it by observing not only their own productivity shocks but also shocks to peers in the same industry. This collective learning takes place because firms that belong to the same industry tend to have similar systematic risks. Once calibrated, the model will predict certain quantitative relationships among learning-related variables, capital investment, and stock returns, which can be tested empirically. The preliminary result shows that a firm's capital investment increases with a learning-related variable, the cumulative number of firm-year observations in the industry to which the firm belongs. This evidence supports the presence of the collective-learning mechanism.

21506418.label: Realisation of objectives
21506418.value: All of the project objectives have been achieved. First, as intended, I have built the theoretical model where firms learn about their own risk exposures and make investment decisions accordingly. Also, I have successfully solved this theoretical model via a numerical method, and in turn, generated the model-based predictions on how parameter learning should influence firm variables. Second, I have conducted all empirical tests that I initially planned to see whether learning matters to corporate decisions and valuations practices. In particular, I have tested how empirical firm variables, including capital investment, valuation ratio, realized stock returns, and the cost of capital, respond to the parameter beliefs. Lastly, I have completed the draft and presented this paper at several international conferences since December 2019. The draft was once submitted to a top-tier finance journal and subsequently rejected. Since then, however, the draft has been improved substantially, and I am about to submit it to a journal.

21506418.label: Major findings and research outcome
21506418.value: I build and structurally estimate an investment-based asset pricing model where firms' systematic risk is unknown. Facing the parameter uncertainty, agents form and update beliefs about the parameter, which in turn affect corporate decisions and valuations. In particular, the model predicts that as the mean belief of risk exposure is revised upward, firms suppress capital investment, the market-to-book ratios fall, and simultaneously, the costs of capital rise. I find that all of these model predictions hold in the empirical data, both qualitatively and quantitatively. That is, the empirical responses of firm variables to the risk exposure beliefs are reasonably close to those in the simulated firm panel that I generate from the estimated model. These findings suggest that learning about systematic risk is an important consideration in corporate policies and valuation practices. Furthermore, I find that firms' peers, which belong to the same industry, provide an essential source of learning in this context. Prior studies have suggested that industry peers tend to have similar, if not identical, levels of systematic risk. Then, peers' observations are as informative of a firm's risk profile as its own observations. Motivated by this intuition, I view the parameter beliefs as being formed from the collective observations, and empirical tests confirm that firms indeed respond to these particular beliefs. In contrast, alternative beliefs, which are based on the observations of each firm's own or randomly assigned other firms, do not predict firm variables as in the baseline results. This research paper has been presented at multiple conferences, and it has now developed to be suitable for journal submission. In fact, through dual submission to a top-tier conference, the editor just invited this paper to submit to the Review of Financial Studies, and I will soon submit it accordingly.

21506418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
21506418.value: A possible extension of the study is to incorporate firms’ endogenous entry or exit. The decision to enter or exit, which would change the dataset used for learning, is likely to correlate with the aggregate state of the economy. This correlation, in turn, could amplify or mitigate the risk associated with uncertainty over the parameter. Incorporating this consideration has the potential to explain richer dynamics of firms' investment and operation decisions.

21506418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
21506418.value: Companies typically grow business through a series of investments -- for instance, opening a new store or expanding a production line. Along the way, they face critical decisions of whether to go ahead with a certain investment opportunity. Common sense tells that companies should invest only when benefits from investment outweigh costs. As the costs and benefits tend to occur at different points in time, this valuation almost always requires discount rates. In turn, the discount rates depend largely on firms' exposure to systematic risk. Specifically, firms whose outputs tend to correlate strongly with the overall market are perceived riskier. As a result, investors require higher returns on these firms' securities. Despite its importance, this systematic risk parameter is hard to pin down. Manifesting this, academia has not agreed on how to best identify this parameter or even whether this parameter is constant or dynamic. In recognition of this challenge, this paper considers ambiguity and subsequent learning about this crucial firm characteristic. That is, decision-makers begin with diffuse beliefs about risk exposure and update the beliefs over time. The belief updates are based on observations likely to reveal the underlying parameter. As rational decisions should reflect firm characteristics, the perceived value of this key parameter and its changes are expected to affect a wide range of firm variables. The paper confirms this intuition and shows that this parameter learning explains time variations in corporate policies and firm valuations.

21606918.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
21606918.value: Justice in legal settings largely hinges on the quality of evidence. This is especially true for a young forensic field like forensic voice comparison. The task of forensic voice comparison typically involves the comparison of a known voice of the suspect with an unknown voice of the offender. In cases which involve speech recordings (e.g. hoax calls, ransom demands, threatening voice message, conversation with an accomplice), the comparison of voices can help the trier of fact (e.g. judge/jury) or investigating authorities (e.g. police) decide whether the two voices were produced by the same speaker or different individuals. Therefore, research findings in forensic voice comparison may have direct impact on the quality of speech analysis as evidence and hence in achieving justice. A major goal of forensic voice comparison research is to identify features in speech which are useful for distinguishing voices. Voice quality (e.g. breathy/creaky/hoarse/nasalised voice) analysis has been reported to be useful for characterising speakers and widely conducted in forensic casework, but voice quality as forensic evidence is mostly assessed subjectively by experts and reported in terms of categorical auditory labels. Across different fields of forensic comparison sciences, there has been increasing pressure from regulating bodies (e.g. US National Research Council and UK Law Commission) for forensic experts to shift from relying on subjective judgments to the quantitative assessment of the strength of the evidence using the likelihood ratio framework (i.e. the ratio probability of observing the evidence given the prosecution hypothesis to the probability of evidence given the defence hypothesis). Therefore, there is pressing need to explore more on the quantitative aspects of speech features, and the acoustic measures of voice quality are cases in point. The proposed project involves likelihood-ratio analyses of the evidential value of both long-term and short-term variation in voice quality acoustics. Non-contemporaneous spontaneous speech data of 169 Australian English speakers from a forensic database will be analysed. The findings will be directly translatable to forensic voice comparison casework. Specifically, forensic experts will benefit from knowing the population statistics on voice quality acoustics, and to what extent voice quality acoustics can be incorporated into the existing ‘toolbox’ for forensic casework. In the long run, members of the public and society in general may also indirectly benefit from the anticipated improvement in the quality of forensic voice analysis in terms of a decrease in the miscarriages of justice. 司法公義很大程度上取決於法證證據的質素，這點對新興鑑證領域如聲線比對鑑證來說尤爲重要。聲線比對鑑證一般涉及犯人與疑犯的聲線比對。在涉及說話錄音的案件中（例如惡作劇電話、勒索贖金、威脅留言、與共犯之對話等），聲線比對鑑證能評估犯人與疑犯的聲線是否一致，從而協助法官、陪審團或 警察調查案件或作出裁決 。因此，聲線比對鑑證的研究成果有可能直接影響錄音證據的質素以至司法公義。 聲線比對鑑證研究的其中一個主要目標爲找出有助辨認聲線的語音特質。過往研究指出聲線特質分析（例如呼吸聲/氣聲、喉頭音、沙啞聲線或鼻音）能有效描繪聲線的特質而被廣泛應用於聲線比對鑑證，但現時聲線特質分析大多依賴語音鑑證專家以其聽覺作主觀評估。在不同的鑑證比對領域中，鑑證科學監管機構（例如美國國家科學研究委員會及英國法律委員會）不斷促請驅使鑑證專家從依賴主觀判斷轉向於「概似比」(Likelihood ratio) 的框架下量化法庭證據的價值（即比較於檢控假設下檢測出該證據之概率和辯護假設下檢測出該證據之概率 ）。所以，我們實有迫切需要探索語音特質的量性層面，而聲線特質的聲學測量便爲箇中例子。 本研究項目旨在於「概似比」(Likelihood ratio) 的框架下量化評估聲線特質聲學中長期特質的證據價值。本項目將於一個澳洲英語的語音鑑證資料庫，抽取169名人士之非同期語音數據作分析。研究成果將可直接應用於往後的聲線比對鑑證。鑑證專家將受惠於聲線特質聲學的人口統計數據，及得知聲線特質聲學能否用於聲線比對鑑證中。長遠而言，公衆及社會人士亦會間接受惠於因聲線比對鑑證質素之提升而減少的司法不公。

21606918.label: Realisation of objectives
21606918.value: All objectives are achieved with concrete research findings. Objective #1: central to forensic voice comparison research and casework is the information on how different speech parameters vary within a population, especially under forensically-relevant conditions. During the project period, 300 speech samples from 75 males Australian English speakers were processed and 10 voice quality acoustic parameters were analyzed. The distributions and descriptive statistics of these parameters are reported in publication #1. Such information will help forensic speech scientists to determine the typicality of voice quality features in forensic casework, and arrive at conclusions that are supported by empirical data rather than relying on subjective assessment. Objective #2: The evidential value of long-term acoustic measures of voice quality was assessed under the Bayesian likelihood ratio framework based on four sets of recordings from 75 male Australian English speakers in New South Wales. Two commonly used metrics in the empirical validation of forensic evidence were reported: log-likelihood-ratio cost and equal error rate. Contrary to the claim among forensic experts that the voice quality of our speech offers useful information for distinguishing speakers in forensic contexts, it was found that laryngeal voice quality acoustic parameters generally offered little speaker-discriminatory value, especially when speech style mismatch and non-contemporaneous recordings (which are common in forensic contexts) were involved. Other key findings related to this objective can be found in the “major findings and research outcome” section below. It is hoped that the findings of this project will help forensic practitioners make informed decisions in their analysis given the circumstances of the case at hand.
