28606418.label: Major findings and research outcome
28606418.value: The research outcomes of the project include: (1) one research paper entitled 'Craftspeople's new identity: The impact of digital fabrication technologies on craft practices' published in International Journal of Technology and Design Education (see section C-8); (2) one paper presentation entitled 'A case study of craftspeople's experiences with learning digital fabrication technologies' in the conference EdMedia + Innovate Learning (See section C-9); (3) curation of an art exhibition entitled 'Post-Digital Materiality' at 1a space in Hong Kong (See section C-11 &12). The project's findings revealed that craft practitioners in Hong Kong had had little exposure to digital craft practices enabled by digital fabrication technologies(DFT). It is mainly because of few training opportunities in tertiary institutions where most young practitioners in Hong Kong are trained. Through the short-term educational workshop with 18 craft practitioners in Hong Kong, it was found that both professional and amateur craftspeople have a positive outlook on the status and sustainability of craft in the creative industries. After the workshop, the participants identified the potential advantage for the craft practitioners to adopt DFT as the craft knowledge and skills that can be creatively combined with DFT. In order to maximize the potential benefit for craftspeople using DFT, a tailored DFT training education for craft practitioners will be required as well as sufficient exposure to case studies in the application of DFT in craft, art and design fields. To further promote the DFT integration into artistic practices, the PI curated an exhibition entitled ' Post-Digital Materiality.' It showcased local and international artists' works questioning the materiality of physical and digital objects and exploring the conceptual and physical dimensions of DFT. The show attracted diverse audiences in Hong Kong and overseas (through online events). The audio-visual data and documents produced during the exhibition were used as educational resources in the PI's classes.

28606418.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28606418.value: Since this qualitative case study was cross-sectional, a long-term impact was not measurable. Learning digital fabrication technologies and applying them to craft practices require intensive training and a long period. Hence, a longitudinal study can be designed with a bigger sample size to quantitatively measure the long-term impact of digital fabrication technologies on craft practices in socio-cultural and economic aspects. Since there is no existing nationwide data on craftspeople, including contemporary practitioners (e.g., designer-makers) in Hong Kong, a demographic survey will be necessary. Additionally, a study developing a new craft curriculum for secondary and tertiary institutions that could integrate traditional hand-making and digital-making processes would be needed to sustain and develop craft practices in Hong Kong.

28606418.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28606418.value: This research was one of the first studies investigating the current status of contemporary craft in Hong Kong with a focus on digital craft. Through qualitative data collection and analysis of the educational workshop with 18 craftspeople in Hong Kong, it was found that the participants are aware of the availability of digital fabrication technologies (DFT) beyond its industrial uses and the need to adopt the technologies. The craftspeople envision that DFT would benefit them by enhancing productivity and creativity. They also perceive that their craft knowledge and skills would be an advantage to thrive in the creative industries. However, most craft practitioners lack opportunities to learn hands-on and apply it to their practices. They found that DFT is not advanced enough to replace manual skills and tacit knowledge, and it would require intensive training for craftspeople to apply to their practice. The project's findings revealed that the development of a new DFT training curriculum tailored for craft practices would be necessary to maximize the DFT's positive impact on craft practices.

28606818.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28606818.value: Reading is a complex cognitive process involving visual decoding and lexical access. Most of the current theories and computational models on eye movements in reading are based on findings from alphabetic languages. In recent years, however, much effort has been devoted to logographic scripts, given the fundamental differences in orthography, phonology, morphology, and semantics between these scripts. In this context, there are a large number of studies on lexical processing during horizontal reading of Simplified Chinese (SC) sentences based on Mandarin readers. However, there are varieties in both written and spoken Chinese, as well as in reading direction. For example, Traditional Chinese (TC) is widely used outside of Mainland China, mostly in Hong Kong and Taiwan. Also, besides Mandarin as the official spoken language in Mainland China and Taiwan, Cantonese (a.k.a, Yue subdivision of Chinese) is one of the most popular spoken varieties of Chinese, with over 80 million speakers, including people in Hong Kong and Chinese immigrants overseas. Given its importance, however, only a small amount of studies have looked into TC reading by native Cantonese speakers. Despite similarities, there are substantial differences between the two written Chinese scripts and the two spoken Chinese varieties. This proposed project is a pioneering attempt aimed at investigating this issue from cross-cultural and developmental perspectives. With the assistance of eye tracking technique, four studies (five experiments in total) are proposed to explore two aspects of reading, including perceptual processing and phonological processing. In Studies 1 and 2 (i.e., Experiments 1 & 2) we will test the influence of reading direction (i.e., horizontal vs. vertical), reading development (i.e., participants of different ages), and script type (i.e., SC vs. TC) on the size of the perceptual span during reading. In Studies 3 and 4 (i.e., Experiments 3, 4 & 5), we will explore cross-language phonological activation among Cantonese-Mandarin bilingual adults and children using homophone target words. From a theoretical perspective, the findings of these experiments allow us to estimate visual processing and reading ability during development, and provide a better understanding of oculomotor activities in vertical and horizontal directions. In addition, the current project will also add to our knowledge of cross-language activation during sentence reading, and how this effect is modulated by reading proficiency. On the practical side, the results will provide an important reference for education policy makers and language education teachers in Hong Kong. 閱讀是一個很複雜的認知過程。閱讀涉及到視覺加工和詞彙解碼。現有關於閱讀過程中眼動模式的理論和計算模型主要是基於拼音文字的研究證據而建立的。由於中文和拼音文字在正字法、語音、語素和語義上存在很大差別，近年也有大量研究探討中文閱讀過程中的眼動模式。這些研究主要探討了使用簡體中文的普通話讀者在橫向閱讀時的眼動特徵。然而，不論是書寫還是口語，中文都有不同的變體，並且書寫方向也有不同。例如，在書寫方面，有繁體中文和簡體中文。在口語方面，除了普通話，在香港和海外地區約有八千萬人說粵語。雖然有如此多華人使用繁體中文和說粵語，目前只有少量研究探討母語為粵語的繁體中文讀者在閱讀中的眼動特徵和詞彙加工。雖然不同的中文書寫和口語變體之間有很多相似之處，然而它們之間也有很大的差異。本研究計劃將從跨語言和成長的角度探討這些差異對閱讀的影響。本研究將會探討閱讀方向（橫向vs縱向）、年齡（兒童vs成人）和文字（繁體中文vs簡體中文）對閱讀時眼動模式的影響。另外，本研究還將會探討廣東話-普通話雙語者閱讀時的語音加工特點，以及兒童普通話流利程度對漢字語音加工的影響。從理論的角度，本研究計劃將會讓我們更好地了解閱讀過程中的視覺和語音加工，以及閱讀中眼動模式的發展。從實際應用的角度，本研究的結果可為教育政策制定者和教育工作者提供普通話教學的指引。

28606818.label: Realisation of objectives
28606818.value: This project aimed to understand information processing of different written and spoken variants of Chinese during sentence reading. Specifically, we focused on the eye movement characteristics during reading in simplified and traditional Chinese sentence reading. We also investigated cross-language activation of Cantonese-Mandarin bilinguals. Several studies were conducted to examine these research questions. All Objectives had been achieved. For Objective 1 in this project, we looked at the perceptual span and eye movement characteristics in different written Chinese systems. The perceptual span is important because it is the foundation of different theories related to eye movement control during reading. We observed development of the perceptual span and other eye movement indicators from children to adults. We found that the perceptual span was larger for simplified Chinese than traditional Chinese. The comparison of traditional and simplified Chinese, using almost identical experimental materials in both scripts, allowed us to illustrate how low-level information (i.e., visual complexity) affects attentional allocation during reading without other confounding factors. For Objectives 2 and 3, we focused on cross-language phonological activation among Cantonese-Mandarin bilingual readers and whether activation of phonological codes would be affected by language proficiency. Studying Cantonese-Mandarin bilinguals offers us a chance to investigate bilingual phonological processing without confounding with script familiarity. Because the two spoken languages (Cantonese and Mandarin) we used corresponded to the same written script (Chinese). We developed two sets of critical materials and created experimental sentences for both children and adults. Different conditions of the materials were strictly matched in a number of linguistic properties, such as frequency and number of strokes, predictability, and plausibility. We tested bilingual readers’ phonological processing of Cantonese and Mandarin during silent sentence reading. We found that they activated the phonological representations of characters in both L1 and L2 even when they were reading sentences silently. The findings suggest that phonological processing is a crucial process in word recognition. However, the degree to which the phonological codes of one language is activated depends on the language that is being used. When their L1 was activated, mainly L1 phonological representations would be used by the readers. However, when L2 was activated, both L1 and L2 phonological codes would be processed. Phonological processing of L1 and L2 was also modulated by their language proficiency. Readers with higher L2 proficiency had a stronger activation of L2 then those with lower L2 proficiency.

28606818.label: Major findings and research outcome
28606818.value: This project aims to understand eye movement characteristics during reading of traditional and simplified Chinese. The eye-tracking methodology was adopted. We measured reading speed and a number of eye movement indices among children at different ages and adults. Overall, we found that children’s eye movements were still developing (Yan & Pan, revision under review), and that children had a smaller perceptual span than adults (Yan, Li, Su, Cao, & Pan, 2020). In addition, individual reading ability also affected the size of the perceptual span and eye movement characteristics during sentence reading. We found that children with higher reading fluency exhibited a larger and more adult-like perceptual span than non-fluent readers (Yan, Li, Su, Cao, & Pan, 2020). But different individual skills were related to children’s eye movement characteristics at different developmental stages (Yan & Pan, revision under review). To investigate how orthographic visual complexity affects eye movements during reading, we compared the perceptual span in traditional Chinese with that in simplified Chinese. The materials used for traditional Chinese were almost identical to those used in simplified Chinese, except that some words were replaced due to the vocabulary differences in the two scripts. Our findings showed that traditional Chinese readers had a smaller perceptual span than simplified Chinese readers. Given the similarity of experimental materials used in the two scripts, this finding indicated that the higher visual complexity in traditional Chinese led to higher processing load, reducing the size of the perceptual span, as compared to simplified Chinese (Pan & Yan, Accepted in 2023). The present project also aims to study cross-language phonological processing during sentence reading. We tested Cantonese-Mandarin bilingual readers when they were reading sentences silently. In each experimental sentence, a target word was replaced by either a homophone in both languages, a homophone in either one language, or an unrelated character. Results showed that native Cantonese activated phonological representations of both Cantonese as L1 and Mandarin as L2 even when they were reading silently. However, readers had different levels of phonological activations in the two languages, depending on the proficiency of a language and the language that was pre-activated (Yan, Luo, & Pan, 2023).

28606818.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28606818.value: The current project for the first time showed that the perceptual span is smaller in traditional Chinese than simplified Chinese. On the one hand, this shows us that orthographic visual complexity affects information processing. On the other hand, traditional Chinese characters preserve more semantic information than simplified Chinese characters. How this trade-off affects semantic processing in traditional Chinese is not clear, as little research has been conducted to study eye movement characteristics among traditional Chinese readers. Future studies could further compare the time course of semantic processing in simplified and traditional Chinese. In addition, the current project also found that when pre-activated in the L2 mode, the bilingual readers had stronger homophone recovery effects than in the L1 mode. This shows that Cantonese-Mandarin bilinguals might rely more on phonological processing in their L2 than L1. It would be worthwhile to investigate the time course of semantic and phonological processing in L1 and L2 reading.

28606818.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28606818.value: There are different variants in the written and spoken Chinese. In terms of written Chinese, traditional and simplified Chinese are used in different Chinese societies. As for spoken Chinese, Mandarin and Cantonese are two widely used variants. The present project investigated eye movement characteristics during reading of traditional and simplified Chinese and cross-language phonological processing among Cantonese-Mandarin bilinguals. The findings from the project show that because of higher visual complexity in traditional Chinese characters as compared to simplified Chinese characters, traditional Chinese readers were less efficient in information processing during reading. In addition, we also demonstrated that when Cantonese-Mandarin bilinguals were primed with Cantonese, which was their first language, only Cantonese sound information of the characters was used. However, when they were primed with Mandarin (their second language), readers made use of the sounds of characters in both Cantonese and Mandarin. These findings suggest that readers rely more on sound information when they use their second language than their first language.

28608318.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28608318.value: Hong Kong citizens have contradictory views about citizenship; the pro-Beijing view emphasizes strengthening nationalism and patriotic education, whereas the pro-democratic view advocates democracy, autonomy, and freedom. Consequently, Hong Kong has become a polarized society with highly divided positions. Better understanding is needed to build mutual trust through civic education. Civic education helps students learn how to navigate the complexities of living among and with differences. Teachers play an essential role in helping students understand different perspectives. Given substantial school autonomy in Hong Kong, different school leadership practices can yield different school environments for teachers, different degrees of teacher empowerment, and different civic teaching approaches. Principals can influence their school environment in civic learning and allocate resources to support civic education. Considerable attention has been given to the concept of ‘leading for learning’ (Goker, 2006) but there has been little attention given to civic learning in schools and how it might be facilitated by principals (Xu and Law, 2015). Given the volatile and uncertain external environment that students as future citizens face, civic learning must now be considered a priority. Kennedy, Li and Chan (2015) and Kennedy and Li (2017) have shown that school level factors (particularly principals’ roles) can influence students’ civic learning, although the results are somewhat mixed, clearly this requires further investigation. This study extends this line of research by examining how principals create school civic teaching environments and how these influence teachers in their roles as civic educators. A mixed methods research design will be used and surveys and interviews employed to assess how principal leadership affects teacher autonomy and self-efficacy. Structural equation modeling will identify factors that influence civic teaching and descriptive data analyses will provide overall views and patterns of school leadership for civic teaching. Multilevel structural equation modeling will be used to assess the proposed model: A Two-level Conceptual Model of the Effects of School Leadership on Civic Teaching. Thematic analysis will identify the variables that influence school leadership for civic teaching. Content analysis will reveal principals’ and teachers’ perspectives of how school leadership affects teacher autonomy and self-efficacy. This study expands the theories of school leadership and civic education by determining the factors that affect civic teaching, and informs policy-makers and educators by identifying the kinds of civic education that would help students to understand different perspectives and build a mutually respectful society. 在香港，不同黨派對公民身份有不一致的看法; 親中派強調加強民族和愛國主義教育，而民主派主張民主、自治和自由。因此香港已經成為一個不同陣營高度分化的社會。在撕裂的社會裡， 通過公民教育，學生能夠學習到如何在生活中求同存異，從而達到彼此理解和建立互信。那麼教師在其中的角色便尤為重要。 香港學校擁有頗高的自治權；不同學校的校長可以為教師提供不一樣的教學環境 ，給予教師不同程度的授權，導致在公民教育中出現不同的教學方法。在公民教育中， 校長可以影響其學校的教學環境，並在資源分配上有決定權以支援公民教育。當前，“營造學習”的概念受到了相當多的關注，但很少將研究重點放在校長如何營造公民教學的氣氛以及校長如何促進公民教育上。 鑑於未來種種不明朗和不確定的外部因素，學生作為未來公民，他們的公民教育必須被視為優先事項。學生才能夠學習到如何在生活中求同存異，從而達到彼此理解和建立互信 。學術研究指出學校（特別是校長）在影響學生的公民學習中扮演重要的角色。對此，不同的研究有不同的結果，而顯然這需要進一步調查。本項目通過研究校長如何營造學校公民教學的氣氛，以及這些校長如何影響教師作為公民教育工作者的角色，以進一步延伸研究脈絡。 本研究將使用混合研究設計方法，透過問卷調查和訪談來評估校長如何影響教師的自主和自我效能。結構方程模型將用來確定影響公民教學的因素，描述性數據分析將為公民教學提供校長及教師的整體觀點和模式。多層級結構方程模型將用於評估本研究所提出的模型：學校領導對公民教學影響的兩級概念模型。主題分析將用來確定校長影響公民教學的變量。內容分析將揭示校長和教師對校長如何影響教師的自主和自我效能感的看法。 這項研究透過結合量性與質性分析，更深入地了解影響公民教學的各項因素，將會擴展學校領導和公民教育的理論；藉此希望告知政策制定者和教育工作者如何培養學生理解不同的觀點和建立一個相互尊重的社會的公民教學類型。

28608318.label: Realisation of objectives
28608318.value: This research aimed at better understanding how principals create safe environments for civic teaching and how these influence teachers in their roles as civic educators. The ultimate goal is to identify the kinds of citizenship education that help nurture students to understand different perspectives and build a mutually respectful society. The above objectives have been achieved, and the details articulated below. First, three main themes emerged from our data analyses: (A) school leaders who advocated laissez-faire approach to civic education emphasized knowledge, social concerns, common norms, and conventional participation of “good citizens”, (B) school leaders who mediated students' diverse needs and balanced school staff's different expectations emphasized critical activity, in addition to sharing knowledge, social concerns, common norms, and conventional participation (C) School leaders with school's clear civic mission, we found two types of schools with clear civic missions: pro-China and pro-democracy. Principals and teachers with a pro-China school mission theme emphasized school activities to help students to become “good citizens,” with a national China identity, critical thinking skills, and positive values. Schools with clear pro-democracy civic missions prepared their students to become critical “good citizens.” Second, the results of this study highlighted that the dynamic interplay between the micro, meso and macro levels have affected school leadership for civic learning. “The complicated relationship between schools and the larger political context creates ethical challenges for teachers and administrators” (Hess and McAvoy, 2015, p. 3). At the micro level, principals negotiated with the school sponsoring body and different school stakeholders in providing academic freedom and professional autonomy for teachers. At the meso level, principals navigated between the education policy and the current socio-political context in providing academic freedom for teachers. At the macro level, the Education Bureau played a critical role in shouldering frontline educators’ burdens and alleviating fears. Principals of non-religious schools were influenced by society conditions. In religious schools, the purpose of citizenship education was aligned with the mission of the school sponsoring body. In pro-China schools, principals were often influenced by education policies and the school sponsoring body and the goals were to cultivate students to become patriotic citizens. In pro-democratic schools, principals were influenced by democratic values. Third, the challenges of the complex and dynamic socio-political contexts in Hong Kong influenced principals’ and teachers’ relationships and interactions. Autonomy is not simply granted by the principals, it is influenced by society and school conditions, and key stakeholders. When school leadership lacked a clear vision of citizenship education as in Pattern A, most teachers were compliant and avoided discussing controversial topics with their students. These teachers had less autonomy and consequently less self-efficacy. When school leadership mediated the diverse needs of students and balanced different expectations of school stakeholders as in Pattern B, there were both compliant and critical teachers and teacher autonomy and self-efficacy were affected by the complicated socio-political context. When school leadership had a clear school civic mission as in Pattern C, the results differed across schools. These findings confirmed some common knowledge: teacher self-efficacy is always regulated by institutional and socio-political forces. Fourth, Learning how to live together in polarized and pluralistic societies, front-line educators (such principals and teachers) play a critical role in citizenship education. “Leadership in any endeavor is a moral task but even more so for educational leaders, for their behaviors are commentaries on how things should be done” (Pellicer, 2007, p. 9). This quote suggests that how principals run their schools would have effects on other institutions, now and in the future because school cultures not only reflect the civic culture of the society, but can also be a shaper of that civic culture.

28608318.label: Major findings and research outcome
28608318.value: This study was based on the concept of leadership for civic learning and had three major findings. First, the results indicated that the complex historic -cultural (i.e the merging of Hong Kong’s colonial history with its Chinese heritage) and socio-political (i.e the combined influences of the social and political on school leadership) contexts of Hong Kong influenced school leadership in civic learning. Three main patterns of leadership for civic teaching have been highlighted: (1) leading without a clear vision of citizenship education, (2) leading through mediating the diverse needs of students and balancing different expectations of school stakeholders, and (3) leading with a clear school civic mission. While non-religious schools often showed Pattern 1, religious schools often showed Pattern 2, and pro-China schools and pro-democratic schools often showed Pattern 3. Second, these school staff in the laissez-faire theme reported acting as facilitators that emphasized knowledge, social concerns, and norms of “good citizens” to their students. Staff in the mediate diversity theme reported helping students integrate different perspectives. Staff in the school mission theme reported supporting student engagement in citizen responsibilities and political processes; while pro-China schools emphasized a national China identity, pro-democracy schools emphasized an international view. Staff from all of these schools reported that media negatively influenced students’ values and perspectives. To reduce students' confirmation bias, seek evidences to support the pre-existing views, teachers in all schools taught critical thinking skills and media literacy. The data showed that understanding how schools can nurture student-citizens amid teachers’ concerns around negative media influence, can help inform instruction and policies in schools regardless of their affiliation. Third, principals were more positive than teachers in regard to their schools and citizenship education, and attempted to provide teachers with the autonomy to facilitate civic teaching while teachers showed less confidence than principals in the possibility of nurturing students’ patriotism. As research outcome, the findings of this study were incorporated in EdUHK courses (such Teacher and Teaching in Context) to help pre-service teachers to develop their self-efficacy and enhance their teaching. The results of this study also were shared with more than 200 teachers and principals in a Forum on Leading Teams in a Time of High Teacher Mobility which held March 12 2022. The purposes of the sharing at the Forum were to (a) strengthen positive and supportive principal-teacher relationships and to enhance teacher well-being, help (b) principals enhance their roles as leaders of civic teaching and (c) teachers to develop their self-efficacy and enhance their teaching.

28608318.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28608318.value: Extending my ECS study, I have submitted two research projects. First, colleagues and I (served as a co-principal investigator) applied Young Collaborative Research Grand and proposed an interdisciplinary project to study how individuals’ global competence, especially in perspective-taking and adaptive thinking, interact with identities, physiological responses, and media information literacy. This new knowledge can be applied to help educate youth with skills and attitudes that enable them to adeptly navigate the increasingly polarized online world towards using this diversity as a strength.Without global competence, especially skills for coping effectively with different perspectives (OECD, 2020), social diversity can lead to intolerance, exclusion, and social disengagement (Buchtel et al., 2020; Lee, 2021a; Wong & Chiu, 2022). Such tendencies are exaggerated in online social networks (OSNs). To help youths develop global competence to embrace diversity, we will study how individual and sociocultural factors serve as facilitators and barriers to youths’ global competence, providing research insights for targeted action to help youths embrace and learn from diversity. Second, my submitted GRF (Nov 2021) proposes and tests a new 3-level theoretical model of school leadership, teachers, and student learning in Hong Kong and Chinese Taipei. The model will test the relations among school leadership, teacher autonomy, self-efficacy, and trust.

28608318.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28608318.value: This study have four types of contributions: theory, policy, practice and international. At the theoretical level, this study contributes by adding an additional layer (such as the Education Bureau and the School Sponsoring Body) into the framework of school leadership for civic learning. It is because creating “an atmosphere of trust within school faculty and community” (Cosner, 2009, p. 250) is the responsibility of all school stakeholders, At the policy level, education polices including capacity-building measures and allocation of resources from the governments to schools are needed to help teachers and principals to cope with challenges and improve practices. At the practical level, civic education teachers in Hong Kong face many students with negative views of China, powerful social media influences that corroborate these views, and sharply contested ideas, so they need professional development support to acquire appropriate skills to help their students navigate them. At the international level, many countries have polarized societies and teachers face tremendous social pressures which affected their self-efficacy in civic education. The findings of this study could help educators in other places determine whether some of the choices of Hong Kong principals and their consequences are applicable to their circumstances.

28609118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28609118.value: Learning to read is a complex task and reading a non-native language is particularly challenging. As more people become multilingual, the incidence of reading failure also rises. In Hong Kong, efforts are being made to help non-Chinese speaking students recognize Chinese characters, while methods are being developed to assist multilingual dyslexic students with their learning. These methods rely on empirical evidence of how people read diverse languages and how reading differs between individuals. Increasingly, researchers have used neuroscience techniques to directly observe how the human brain processes language. However, there are comparatively few neuroimaging studies involving multilingual individuals, particularly those who speak and read Asian languages. The proposed study thus aims to characterize how people with multilingual skills represent words in different writing systems and how this is influenced by individual differences in proficiency and age of acquisition. In addition, language interactions in multilingual reading will be investigated using cognates, which are words with similar orthographic or phonological forms referring to the same concept in different languages, e.g., “table” is visually identical in French and English and similar in pronunciation. Cognates are easier to recognize and learn compared to non-overlapping translation pairs such as “dog” and “chien”, and they have long been used to establish overlapping processes in bilingual word processing (e.g., Lemhöfer & Dijkstra, 2004). Most previous studies examined cognate pairs that shared visual and phonological forms written in the Roman alphabet. By investigating cognates with both alphabetic and non-alphabetic languages, the proposed study will tease apart visual and phonological overlaps in word forms. Chinese/Japanese Kanji same-script cognates and English/Japanese Katakana cross-script cognates will be presented to Chinese-English-Japanese trilinguals and two control groups of Chinese-English and Japanese-English bilinguals in Hong Kong. Participants will engage in lexical decision and delayed word-naming with simultaneous eye-tracking and ERP recordings. Results will clarify and contrast the roles of orthography and phonology in three languages and four scripts. Task-related differences will reveal whether multilingual word processing is context-dependent and moderated by top-down control. From a theoretical perspective, the prevailing model for bilingual word processing in alphabetic languages, the Bilingual Interactive Activation plus (BIA+) Model (Dijkstra & Van Heuven, 2002), will be tested in non-alphabetic scripts. The proposed study uses a novel design to delve into the neural underpinnings of multilingual reading, and will generate a large-scale dataset that can benefit local research and education practices as well as impact future psycholinguistic studies. 學習閱讀是一項複雜的任務，閱讀非母語尤其具有挑戰性。隨著懂得多種語言的人增多，發生閱讀問題的機率亦跟著上升。香港近年一直致力幫助非華語學生識別漢字，同時開發不同方法來協助閱讀障礙學生在各個語言上的學習。這些方法必須建基於人們閱讀不同語言時個體差異的科學證據。研究人員能使用腦神經科學技術直接觀察人類處理語言時大腦的情況，然而，涉及使用亞洲語言及多語言個體的研究仍然相對較少。因此，是項研究旨在表徵具有多種語言技能的人如何在不同的書寫系統中處理單詞，以及這些過程如何受到熟練程度和習得年齡的個體差異的影響。此外，是項研究將使用同源詞來研究多語言閱讀中的語言交互。同源詞是在不同語言中具有相似字形或字音並有相同概念的詞，例如，“table” 在法語和英語中的字形、字音及字義上均相似。與 “dog” 和 “chien” 的非重疊翻譯相比，同源詞更容易識別和學習，因爲它們長期以來被用於在雙語詞處理中建立了重疊的過程（Lemhöfer＆Dijkstra，2004）。以往的研究大多使用以羅馬字母書寫、字形和語音上都相似的同源對。是項研究將通過用字母和非字母語言的同源詞梳理單詞中視覺和語音的重疊。漢英日三語的使用者、漢英雙語和日英雙語的對照組將閲讀漢語/日語的同源詞和英語/日語片假名跨語言同源詞。參與者將進行詞彙決策和延遲單詞命名，並同時進行眼動追踪和ERP 記錄。結果將闡明和對比三種語言和四種文字中視像和語音上的作用。與任務相關的差異將揭示多語言文字處理是否依賴於自上而下的控制。從理論的角度，此實驗將在非字母文字中測試雙語互動激活模型（BIA +，Dijkstra和Van Heuven，2002）。研究以新的設計來深入研究多語言閱讀的神經基礎，並將生成一個大規模的數據集，相信可使本地的研究和教育實踐受益並影響未來的心理語言學研究。

28609118.label: Realisation of objectives
28609118.value: The current project aimed to examine how cross-language interactions occur and influence single word processing in multilingual readers. Data were successfully collected from over 100 multilingual participants: 42 trilingual Chinese-English-Japanese participants from Hong Kong, 30 Chinese-English participants from Hong Kong, and 30 Japanese-English participants from Japan. The resulting dataset is rich and allows for different levels of analyses. However, the recruitment of participants was affected due to social unrests in Hong Kong and the global outbreak of Covid-19, and the planned eye-tracking/ERP data collection in Hong Kong and Japan was not feasible even with project extension for 6 months [institutional approval in June of 2020]. To meet the challenges, the project team opted to collect data online. Nineteen of the trilingual participants and all 30 Japanese bilingual participants completed the experiment via an online platform. However, since eye-tracking and ERP data could not be collected remotely, not all analyses in the original proposal could be done. Additional analyses were performed to explore the complex relationships between variables in the collected data. Regarding the neural representations of languages in multilingual readers (Objective 1), as we only had complete ERP dataset in the Chinese-English bilingual group, we tested if the orthographic uniqueness point (OUP) effect in English words was found in ERP responses of non-native Chinese-English readers (Yum, 2020). OUP refers to the letter position in which a printed word is distinguishable from other words in a lexicon. For instance, “sandwich” has an OUP of 5 because at the 5th letter “w”, one would be able to uniquely identify the word in English. Processing advantage of early OUP words compared to late OUP words had been taken to indicate that letters are processed serially from the left, but recent studies have reported processing advantage for late OUP words. Analyses were done to examine whether non-native readers use similar online processing strategies, and if task demands may influence this effect. Results showed that consistent with some reports in native English readers, non-native readers responded to late OUP words (666ms) significantly faster than early OUP words (702ms) in the lexical decision task (t = 2.13, p = .039), with no significant difference in behavioral accuracy in either task. In the ERP data, at the P1 component, a main effect of task was seen where delayed naming elicited more positive amplitudes than lexical decision (t = 2.42, p = .023). Task interacted with OUP, and post hoc tests with Bonferroni corrections indicated that only words with late OUP showed the task effect (t = 3.18, p = .016), but not words with early OUP. In the N170 time window, a significant main effect of OUP showed that late OUP words had increased negativity relative to early OUP words (t = 2.25, p = .025). An interaction with task showed that the N170 OUP effect was driven by the delayed naming task (t = 3.21, p = .008), but not present in lexical decision. The results for faster response time and enhanced N170 component in late OUP words relative to early OUP words offered support to the view that rather than proceeding strictly from left to right, the end of the word might be scanned in to provide facilitation for single word reading in non-native readers. The overall time course of the ERP effects was comparable to that of native English readers in previous studies. Additionally, the top-down task influence in these early ERP components suggested that this mechanism in orthographic processing is not purely automatic and may be preferentially engaged to fit task demands. Cognates in same-script language pairs tend to have both orthographic and phonological similarities, while these overlaps may be separable in non-alphabetic languages and different-script language pairs. In this project, we teased apart the cognate effects using non-alphabetic but same-script Chinese/Kanji cognates and different-script English/Katakana cognates (Objective 2). In the lexical decision task, linear mixed-effects models of real word RTs showed a main effect of cognate status in the trilingual group (p = .015) and a main effect of script (p < .001; Chinese < Kanji = English < Katakana), but no interaction of cognate and script. Among Chinese-English and Japanese-English control participants, no cognate or interaction effect was apparent. Same-script and different-script cognates showed similar degrees of facilitation, suggesting that both orthographic and phonological information contributes to the cognate facilitation effects, supporting the predictions of the BIA+ model. Consistent with previous reports, shared lexical forms facilitated the processing of less familiar languages (Kanji and Katakana in trilinguals), but not dominant languages (i.e., Chinese and English in trilinguals; Katakana in Japanese-English participants). In the naming task, analyses confirmed significant cognate effects in all scripts on naming accuracy (cognates > non-cognates) in the trilingual group (p < .001) but not the control groups. This suggested that cognate effects in phonological production were robust with minimal orthographic overlap (English/Katakana), among cognate pairs with one-to-many phonological mappings (Chinese/Kanji), and across language dominance. An interesting cross-language relationship also emerged where success in reading irregular English words correlated with Katakana but not Kanji naming accuracy, regardless of cognate status. This implied that reading of English and Katakana may share common phonological processing skills independent of shared lexical representations. A separate set of analyses examined how task influences cognate processing in Japanese for trilingual readers, using Kanji and Katakana cognates and non-cognates (Objective 3). It was predicted that cognate effects would be stronger for Kanji in lexical decision and Katakana in naming based on the characteristics of the scripts and the tasks, i.e., Kanji is morphologically-based while Katakana is phonologically-based. Kanji is orthographically nearly identical with Chinese characters and thus is visual familiar. Accuracy data in a subset of trilingual participants were analyzed using generalized mixed model with cognate status, script, task, and their interactions as predictors. Results showed higher accuracy for cognates than non-cognates (p < .001), higher accuracy for lexical decision than naming (p < .001), a Cognate x Task interaction (p < .001), and a Script x Task interaction (p = .008). Posthoc analyses indicated that cognate facilitation was significant in lexical decision (p < .001) but not naming, and Katakana was processed more accurately than Kanji in lexical decision (p = .013) but not in naming. Script did not moderate the cognate by task interaction, suggesting that both orthographic and phonological activations contribute to the cognate facilitation in lexical decision. Interestingly, although Katakana is a transparent syllabic script while Kanji is opaque in orthography-phonology mapping, the naming accuracy pattern did not differ either by script or cognate status, which suggested reliance on lexical over sublexical phonological pathway. The lack of significant cognate effect in naming in this analysis was at odds with the results when the naming task performance was analyzed alone. We suggest that the different patterns of results highlight the importance of considering different comparison conditions, including task, language, and native control group.

28609118.label: Major findings and research outcome
28609118.value: This study used a within-subject design in trilingual participants and two control groups to examine language interaction effects in multilingual readers. Cognate effects were contrasted in different scripts, in both the dominant and non-dominant languages, using two tasks. First, results indicated that word representations in different languages of multilingual readers are intricately linked on different levels. Cognate effects were found to be robust across same-script and cross-script language pairs with different writing systems (Yum & Fan, 2020; Yum & Okahisa, under preparation). The cognate facilitation effects were stronger for the less-dominant languages, but still present in the dominant languages, supporting theoretical accounts of language-general co-activation of word forms (Liang, Yum, & Okahisa, 2022). Both same-script and different-script cognates showed processing facilitation, suggesting that orthographic and phonological information contribute to the cognate effects in multilingual readers (Yum & Lee, 2020; Yum & Okahisa, under preparation). Readers were sensitive to reading contexts and the response patterns are moderated by both the bottom-up characteristics of the languages and the top-down processing determined by the task (Yum & Fan, 2021). Analyses of the non-native orthographic representation of English words showed that the overall time course of the ERP effects was comparable to that of native English readers in previous studies. Additionally, the top-down task influence in these early ERP components suggested that this mechanism in orthographic processing is not purely automatic and may be preferentially engaged to fit task demands (Yum, 2020; Yum, under preparation). These main findings were presented at international conferences (e.g., Meetings for the Society for the Neurobiology of Language, the Psychonomic Society, and the Association for Reading and Writing in Asia) and are being written up as articles to be submitted to appropriate journals.

28609118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28609118.value: The project team is working on writing up the results and we expect to publish the findings in 3 or more journal articles, on the same-script and cross-script cognate effects and the neural representations of Chinese and English words. Based on the current findings and dataset, we may further investigate the individual differences that influence cross-language effects, such as the perceived orthographic, phonological, and semantic similarity between cognates. It would also be worthwhile to examine the within-language and cross-language neighborhoods of the items, as these could exert indirect effects and may have contributed to the observed task differences. Since the eye-tracking and ERP data collection could not be completed for some participants due to the pandemic, we will seek further funding support to continue the data collection. The complete dataset could offer opportunities to compare and triangulate measures of word processing based on behavioral performance, eye movements, and electrophysiological activations.

28609118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28609118.value: Multilingual reading is complex and could be challenging for the readers. The neurocognitive underpinnings of how the languages are accessed and used are under active research. This study was a comprehensive investigation into cross-language lexical interactions in multilingual readers of Chinese, English, and Japanese. By contrasting the characteristics between the scripts and tasks, results shed light on how linguistic information co-activate and affect each other under different reading contexts. Similarities on both the orthographic and phonological levels across languages led to facilitated processing, and the facilitation was stronger for the less-dominant languages. Results also showed that although cognate effects were robust, task demands could moderate the amount of facilitation. Task performance was not strictly determined by the nature of the script and may be affected by the familiarity of the script. Results of the study extended the current understanding of cognate processing to languages in three different writing systems and four related but distinct scripts. Studying non-alphabetic languages such as Chinese and Japanese with greater language distance from English gave strong support for claims of language universality and allowed cross-validation of language models developed based on alphabetic languages.

28611118.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28611118.value: 在過去十年，學者開始研究「自我悲憫 」或「自我關懷感 」(Self-compassion)這一概念，並研究其對心理健康及學習動機的影響。然而，許多研究證明：在困境中，人能否以慈愛的心態去面對，是與正向情緒、生活滿意度、較低的抑鬱感和焦慮病徵有關。後來，亦有研究發現了自我悲憫與良好的動機（例如：以學習為目標、內在動機和自我改進動機）有關聯。雖然自我悲憫的重要性已經得到充分的理據支持，但是對於自我悲憫的先行條件、自我悲憫是否能提升及如何提升，我們所知甚少。另外，究竟「自我悲憫」中的三個元素（即：自我慈愛 “Self-kindness”，靜觀 “Mindfulness”，和 人的共性 “Common Humanity”）是如何互相關聯及達致如上述所提及的良好果效呢？這一點也逐漸引起更多的關注。至於自我悲憫對於華裔青少年的影響，這一推論亦未有很多的支持。 首席研究員假設子女的自我悲憫是建基於兩個前提之上，即是：（1） 父母自身的自我悲憫的程度；及（2）父母如何將此概念傳達到其子女。相比之下，面對子女的過錯和缺失，具有較高自我悲憫的父母會較包容和接納，而具有低自我悲憫的父母則會較多負面的指責和批評及冷待其子女。從這些潛移默化的言教和身教行為中，也可能預示出其子女的自我悲憫。 此研究另一個目標是探討「自我悲憫」中的三個元素的相互關係。靜觀（“Mindfulness”）是指一種集中於此時此刻、不加批判的意識，它可以令人以豁達、開放的態度去看待自身的不幸和苦難。人的共性（“Common Humanity”）則是指人類所遭受相同的經歷和體驗，例如各種痛苦和挫敗是人皆有之的。當人能感悟到苦與錯是全人類難以避免之事時，就有助增強他對別人和自己的同理心和同情心。首席研究員假設靜觀和人的共性是（達致）自我仁慈（“Self-kindness”）的先行條件。 最後，此研究嘗試加深對自我悲憫的正面影響的了解，將其推展到與其他幸福感的量度指標的關係（例如：活力感 vitality、自我實現感 self-actualization、自主決定感 autonomous functioning）。 此項目是一項為期兩年的追蹤研究，研究對象為本港中學生及其父母，旨在探討中學生的自我悲憫的先行條件及其效果。此追蹤研究分五次進行並貫穿兩個學年，以探究（1）自我悲憫的跨代傳導性；（2）自我悲憫與享樂幸福感（hedonic well-being）、心理幸福感（eudaimonic well-being）的關聯性；（3）自我關懷感與其學習動機的關聯性。此研究包含了理論層面和實踐層面的重大意義，對應了現時有關自我悲憫先行條件的知識和見解的缺口。另外，此研究亦可以確認令自我悲憫增強的要素，以求最終提升香港中學生的心理健康及加強其良好的學習動機。

28611118.label: Realisation of objectives
28611118.value: Objective 1: To examine the intergenerational transmission of self-compassion from parent to children, and the possible processes of the transmission. This was achieved by collecting data from parent and children. We collected survey data from adolescents and their parents from 8 local schools and in the community, asking them to report on their self-compassion level. In addition, we also asked the child respondents on how their parents interact with them such as the use of conditional regard (praising the child more when they are behaving, and distancing from them when they are not), listening to them when they are talking and etc. Through this data set, I was able to identify the level of concordance between parent self-compassion and child self-compassion and identified high quality listening and negative conditional regard as transmission mechanism. This part of the data was presented in the 26th International Congress of the International Association for Cross-cultural Psychology conference and was written up as a manuscript that’s under review in the journal Mindfulness. Objective 2: To examine whether and how mindfulness and common humanity can increase one’s self-kindness and its subsequent outcomes, such as psychological well-being and achievement motivation, in a longitudinal study. This was achieved by collecting multiple-wave data from a large sample. We are able to model that common humanity and mindfulness can predict self-kindness and self-kindness can then predict less depression, anxiety, stress, and higher well-being and school engagement. By having longitudinal data, instead of cross-sectional data, this provides more confidence in the directionality of the variables. I have presented part of this data in the 22nd World Psychiatric Association World Congress of Psychiatry. In addition, I am preparing a manuscript for publication in international journal for these results. Objective 3: To replicate and extend the beneficial findings of self-compassion with adolescents in a collectivistic culture. This was achieved by collecting data from a sample (n = 754) comprised of S.1 – 3 students from age 12-16 covering schools of all three ability Bandings (Band 1, 2, and 3) in Hong Kong. Because previous findings have been mainly focused on college students sample and in western societies, this project created a very valuable dataset that could test previous findings to adolescents in Hong Kong – answering the question about the generalizability of the existing results. In the current project, I was able to replicate the findings that self-compassion was associated with lower ill-being and better well-being, and more adaptive achievement motivation and extend these findings to different well-being indicators and different forms of school engagement. For this part, I have written up brief reports for participating schools to let them understand the benefits of self-compassion in order to encourage a more compassionate culture in these schools for the emotional and academic goods of the students.

28611118.label: Major findings and research outcome
28611118.value: There are four major research findings in this project. First, my research revealed that there is a certain degree of concordance between parent self-compassion and child self-compassion. In other words, when parents could be kind to themselves in face of difficulties or sufferings, there is a higher likelihood that their child could also apply kindness to themselves when they are facing their own difficulties or sufferings. Before this project, the developmental origin or perspective of self-compassion was not examined in the self-compassion literature. Second, this research showed two possible parental socialization patterns 1) high quality listening, and 2) negative conditional regard, that could account for the concordance between parent self-compassion and child self-compassion. Put it in another way, when parents are more self-compassionate, they are more likely to extend their compassion to their child through listening to them warmly and attentively and reducing the use of love withdrawal when their child is struggling or failing. This in turn would lead their child to be more self-compassionate. Third, for the three self-compassion components (self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness) it was unclear how they relate to each other. Do they have an independent addictive effect? Or do some components support the others? The current results showed that common humanity and mindfulness uniquely predict self-kindness and self-kindness further predicts common self-compassion outcomes. When adolescents are more mindful and understand that sufferings are part of human experiences, they can treat themselves more kindly. When adolescents are kind to themselves, they experience less depression, anxiety and stress and more well-being, and engagement in school. Fourth, self-compassion is beneficial to Hong Kong parents and adolescents. This finding is valid before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The current project started in 2019 and continued during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our data showed that self-compassion would predict well-being and motivational outcomes before the start of COVID-19 and such connection continue to exist in COVID-19 times. This shows that self-compassion would could buffer the impact of COVID-19 and help individuals to maintain well and motivated in difficult times. The benefits of self-compassion is shown to be important to parents and adolescent in Eastern culture, which traditionally promotes self-criticism and aversion focus.

28611118.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28611118.value: This research opens up a lot of new avenues for self-compassion and parenting research. Specifically, the findings of project informed the literature on the promotion of self-compassion in adolescents through parenting method such as the use of high-quality listening and reduce the use of conditional regard (or apply unconditional acceptance). In future research, I will try to replicate the findings using longitudinal study with more timepoints and experimental method. I will continue to understand if there are other ways self-compassion could be transmitted or cultivated. I would also design intervention that targets to promote high-quality listening and unconditional acceptance to oneself and children. In addition, besides the parenting domain, I tend to extend the findings to other close relationships, e.g., couples or friends. Can high-quality listening and conditional regard affect partners and friends’ self-compassion level? The current research also informed a burgeoning research area – high-quality listening (Weinstein, Hill & Law, 2023). The PI has now started an area of research on how listening could cultivate a more compassionate culture. The PI would apply funding with his international collaborators to understand the connection between these factors cross-culturally.

28611118.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28611118.value: Self-compassion involves directing care and kindness to oneself in times of suffering. Many researchers in Western societies have found that self-compassion is associated with a myriad of positive outcomes. For example, it is related to lower anxiety and depression, and better well-being. However, is self-compassion relevant to adolescents in Hong Kong? If it is relevant, what are some developmental factors that could impact child’s self-compassion? Our results showed that self-compassion is associated with high well-being and lower depression, anxiety and stress for both parents and adolescents. For adolescents, self-compassion is also correlated with more school engagement. Regarding the developmental origin, our results showed that when parents are more self-compassionate, their child is more likely to be self-compassionate themselves. This could be attributed to the use of two parenting techniques. Self-compassionate parents are more likely to listen attentively and warmly when their child speaks, and also refrain from the use of conditional regard such as withdrawing love when their child is struggling or not up to standard. This study identified key parenting practices that could have important implications to adolescents’ self-compassion, well-being and school motivation.

28611618.label: Realisation of objectives
28611618.value: Four objectives listed in the proposal have been addressed. The following results provide detailed information. Phase I Survey study (Part A) Participants were 328 secondary 4 to 6 students from seven mainstream schools integrated students with special educational needs (SEN). For comparison purposes, those typically-developed students are named as non-SEN students in coding and analyzing. After dealing with missing values, statistical analyses were conducted with 317 students (143 SEN students and 174 non-SEN students). 1. Comparisons between SEN and non-SEN students’ academic and career-related self-concepts and school engagement: The results show satisfactory reliabilities of all three scales used for this project (ranging from .82 to .91). We found no statistically significant differences between SEN and non-SEN students in terms of the three key variables examined in this project, although non-SEN students scored higher in career-related self-concept and mid-way school engagement than those of SEN students. The results show significantly positive correlations between school engagement and academic and career-related self-concepts. The correlational pattern of SEN students is consistent with that of non-SEN students. Interestingly, correlation coefficients among these variables in SEN students are stronger than those of non-SEN students. Specifically, among SEN students, we found a stronger link between academic self-concept and career-related self-concept and stronger links between both domains of self-concept (academic and career) with SEN students' school engagement. See regression results in point 2 for a clearer picture of their predictive effects on school engagement. 2. The predictive effects of academic and career self-concepts on students’ school engagement The results show that both academic and career-related self-concepts are significant predictors of all students' school engagement (path model 1). This predictive pattern is consistent in both groups (SEN and non-SEN) of students (path models 2 and 3). Compared with the academic self-concept of non-SEN students, SEN students' academic self-concept appears to be a stronger predictor of school engagement. In addition, 30% variance of school engagement of SEN students could be explained by academic and career-related self-concepts, which doubles the result found in non-SEN students and consistently support the positive role of both self-concepts in engaging SEN students’ learning in inclusive classrooms. Phase II Survey study (Part B) Positive changes in academic self-concept and career self-concept as desirable outcomes of inclusive education: After one school year, we conducted post-test to assess whether (S4 to S5) students' academic self-concept could be enhanced by schooling and whether students' career self-concept could be positively changed by career guidance and life planning education. The results showed both academic and career self-concepts were enhanced. By examining the two groups (SEN and non-SEN students, we found among non-SEN students, there was a statistically significant change in post-academic self-concept and post-career self-concept after a school year. Comparatively, SEN students' post-academic self-concept slightly increased compared to pre-academic self-concept. Consistently, SEN students' career self-concept was positively enhanced after a school year by school-based career guidance and career planning education as part of desirable education outcomes aside from academic achievement. Overall, the results of both groups of students support positive outcomes of school teaching and career guidance, and life planning education. Positive correlations of academic self-concept, career self-concept, school engagement, and achievement: Academic self-concept and career self-concept, no matter as predictors (collected at the beginning of a school year) of school engagement (mid-way) or as outcomes (collected after one school year) of inclusive education integrated with career planning support to students, positively and significantly correlated with school engagement and academic achievements except for the correlation between pre-career self-concept and post-academic achievement was not statistically significant, although positive. The pattern is consistent across both SEN and non-SEN students. Testing the predictive pattern between pre-and post-academic and career self-concepts and the mediating effect of school engagement between their relationships: Given that we have pre-and post-data of academic self-concept and career self-concept, we conducted two cross-lagged panel analyses. The first cross-lagged panel model showed 1) pre-academic self-concept predicted post-academic self-concept positively and significantly and 2) pre-career self-concept predicted post-career self-concept positively and significantly. For the cross-paths (from pre-academic self-concept to post-career self-concept; and from pre-career self-concept to post-academic self-concept), although cross-paths are positive, they are not statistically significant. The second cross-lagged panel model showed pre-academic self-concept and school engagement (mid-way) were statistically significant predictors of post-academic self-concept; the same pattern was found for pre-academic self-concept and school engagement in predicting post-career self-concept. Pre-academic self-concept and school engagement (mid-way) were positive and significant predictors of post-academic achievement. The predictive effect of pre-career self-concept on post-academic achievement was not statically significant after controlling for pre-academic self-concept and school engagement. Although pre-academic self-concept and pre-career self-concept were positive predictors of school engagement, school engagement showed no significant mediating effects between the pre- self-concepts and post- self-concepts and academic achievement. The predictive patterns are consistent in two groups of students. Given the fourth objective of this project was to test gender and age effects, we controlled the two demographic variables. We found no significant gender and age effects on post self-concepts (academic and career) and academic achievement. In supplementary interviews with 12 SEN students (ranging from S4-S6) to learn more about school-based support for their career planning, we found: Most students shared the availability of school-based guidance and training, and they felt all resources they have received were informative to help them explore their goal of pursuing higher education and future careers. However, students also shared they have not yet received personalized career guidance and life planning support they felt more/most beneficial for them by taking account of their SEN types. Compared with their peers without SEN, they felt some school-based guidance activities were less meaningful and practical for helping them know their strengths in preparing for post-school transition. Although SEN students could list at least one personal strength, they have in planning higher education and exploring future careers. Most of the SEN students told a variety of difficulties they faced in exploring their goals of studying higher education and exploration of future careers. Only two of them shared they have coping strategies to seek social support from family members. This supplementary information supplements our quantitative finding that SEN students' career self-concept was enhanced over one school year, however, non-SEN students' career self-concept gained a more positive change (please note there was no group difference in their pre-test career self-efficacy). All these results indicate the current practice of career guidance and life planning education may favor non-SEN students more than SEN students. School stakeholders need to review school-based practices, modify them and effectively provide more tailor-made career guidance and life planning education to address the needs of students with different types of SEN. One size does not fit all! Note: In terms of challenges and difficulties we met in conducting this project, the research progress ‘suffered’ from the worldwide and lasting negative impacts of COVID-19 (2019-present). But, the research team tried to cope with these difficulties. Although sample size declined inevitably to some extent due to uncontrollable impacts, we did not change the core design and nature of this study (Phase I, II, and supplementary interview maintained). The originally-proposed objectives have been achieved despite various difficulties amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Acknowledgment: We sincerely thank the support from all parties (EdUHK, RGC, local schools, students, and SEN students' parents who accompanied their children during our zoom-based interviews).

28611618.label: Major findings and research outcome
28611618.value: Although, as crucial as it affects school achievement, academic self-concept might not be the only variable influencing SEN students’ post-school transition. Students’ formation of career-related competencies and interests (career-related self-concept) may also play a salient role in students’ successful post-school transition. In this study, we took the initiative to explore the relationship between SEN students’ academic and career self-concepts, school engagement, and academic achievement in inclusive education integrated with career planning. This project consisted of two main quantitative phases to collect data. In Phase I, three hundred and twenty-eight students participated with about half-half distribution of SEN and non-SEN student. In Phase I, we conducted a pre-test of SEN students’ academic self-concept and career self-concept, and students’ school engagement (mid-way) was also assessed. Over one school year, in Phase II we collected again students’ academic self-concept, career self-concept, and academic achievement to check for any significant positive change in SEN students’ academic self-concept as an outcome of inclusive education and significant change in career self-concept as an outcome of career guidance and life planning education integrated into inclusive classrooms. We then conducted ANOVA and regression analyses to generate findings for answering our original research objectives. In responding to research objectives, no differences in means of these key variables were found between SEN and non-SEN students. All key variables, academic self-concept, career self-concept, school engagement, and academic achievement were positively and significantly correlated with each other. Based on the self-system processes model of motivation, we analyzed the predictive pattern of academic self-concept and career self-concept as two predictors of school engagement and academic achievement. The results showed that both self-concepts are significant predictors of SEN students' school engagement, with career self-concept having a more substantial effect than academic self-concept. For non-SEN students, academic self-concept appears to be a stronger predictor of school engagement than career self-concept. As for academic achievement, the academic self-concept of SEN students was the stronger positive predictor of it as compared to career self-concept. This pattern is consistent in non-SEN students. No significant gender and age effects were found as previously hypothesized. The results have implications for more focused programs for enhancing the career self-concept of SEN students aside from helping them maintain a positive academic self-concept. Research outputs: two peer-reviewed publications achieved; two peer-reviewed international conferences achieved; two webpages are available to stakeholders as recourses to support ASD students’ career development in the workplace; two peer-reviewed journal articles are under preparation (one was an invited paper to a special issue on Career development in the educational system in Frontiers of Psychology: Developmental Psychology; the other will be submitted to Career Development International). 28611618.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28611618.value: Based on key findings of the study, it is necessary to consider both career self-concept and academic self-concept as two important antecedents of SEN students’ school engagement and learning outcomes including the post-school transition to higher education and employment. Previous research and practice have largely isolated the two constructs and studied them in two research lines (self-concept in education and career self-beliefs in career counseling fields). The significantly positive link between academic self-concept and career self-concept also call for strengthening and enhancing professional communications between regular school teachers and school career guidance coordinator to promote SEN students’ self-concepts of the two domains. The reciprocal relationship between academic self-concept and academic achievement has been widely tested and supported, however, the reciprocal relationship between career self-concept, academic achievement, and school engagement has not yet been explored. More research can be conducted with not only SEN students but also pre-and in-service teachers who will/are supporting SEN students so as to help SEN students develop positive academic self-concept, school engagement, and career self-concept for enabling smooth post-school transition. Given the more salient role of career self-concept of SEN students in school engagement than academic self-concept, also given the strong links between school engagement and academic achievement, this study suggested a strong need for school stakeholders to promote SEN students’ positive career self-concept, with more enhancement activities of career education tailor-made to cater the needs of SEN students.

28611618.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28611618.value: With the increasing number of students with special educational needs (SEN) worldwide, schools face various difficulties and challenges in catering to the needs of SEN students' academic success. Given their undesirable learning outcomes, SEN students are prone to have a low academic self-concept, reducing further learning engagement and academic achievement in a vicious cycle. Aside from academic self-concept and academic achievement, we also assessed SEN students’ career self-concept and its change after one school year with schools’ implementation of career guidance and life planning education officially launched in 2014/2015 with financial support by Hong Kong Education Bureau. The results showed SEN students’ academic self-concept and career self-concept are positively associated with their school engagement and academic achievement. Over one school year, SEN students’ career self-concept was positively and apparently changed compared to their academic self-concept. Comparatively, SEN students’ academic self-concept appeared relatively stable. Its positive change was slight. The results generally support a positive effect of school-based career guidance and life planning education on SEN students. Given the stronger link between career self-concept and school engagement among SEN students than academic self-concept found in this study, this finding may call for more focused enhancement activities to promote SEN students' career self-concept aside from existing practices.
